HB1.one_line: Appropriates funds for the 69th Legislature and initial 70th‑Legislature costs, effective immediately.
HB1.summary: The bill appropriates money from the state general fund for the 69th Legislature and the start of the 70th, with amounts for the Senate, House, and Legislative Services Division, and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Appropriates $5,806,249 for the Senate and $9,616,828 for the House for FY 2025‑2027
Appropriates $2,379,018 for the Legislative Services Division for FY 2025‑2027
Appropriates $475,009 for the Senate, $839,512 for the House, and $16,500 for the Legislative Services Division for FY 2027 to cover initial 70th‑Legislature costs
The act becomes effective on the day it is passed and approved

HB2.one_line: Appropriates funds for all state agencies, sets spending rules, and ties many allocations to other bills.
HB2.summary: HB 2 is the 2025 General Appropriations Act that appropriates money for every state agency for the 2027 biennium, sets rules for how those appropriations may be spent, and contains a large number of contingent funding adjustments tied to other bills. The act does not create any new programs or crimes; it merely allocates existing funds and establishes accounting procedures.
changes: Appropriations for all state agencies are set for FY 2026 and FY 2027, with most line items marked as biennial, restricted, or one‑time‑only as specified in the text.
The Office of Budget and Program Planning must create separate appropriation accounts for any item designated “Biennial,” “Restricted,” or “One Time Only” and for each line item in the act.

For the Legislative Audit Division’s Federal Single Audit, the Office of Budget and Program Planning may move the appropriation between agencies based on actual audit hours worked, but the “Restricted” and “Biennial” designations must remain.
Personal‑services funding for the 2029 biennium must be shown separately in each agency’s budget request; the Montana University System is exempt from this requirement.

The act contains a series of conditional appropriations that will be increased or decreased depending on whether other bills (e.g., HB 100, HB 111, SB 237, etc.) are passed and approved; many of these adjustments are one‑time‑only or biennial and are tied to specific program line items.
The effective date of the act is July 1, 2025, and the act is severable if any provision is found unconstitutional.
The act does not create any new state program, office, fund, account, license, or criminal offense.
The act is complex, involving many agencies, contingent adjustments, and detailed accounting rules.
affected: State agencies and their programs; employees whose personal‑services funding is affected; the Office of Budget and Program Planning; the Legislative Audit Division; the Montana University System; and any agencies whose appropriations are contingent on other bills.
numbers: $28,353,448 total appropriation for Legislative Branch FY 2027
$1,000,000 for Montana State Hospital bed program
$500,000 for Montana State Hospital personal‑services funding
$1,000,000 for School for the Deaf and Blind

HB3.one_line: HB 3 appropriates funds for multiple agencies for FY 2025 and continues one into the next biennium.
HB3.summary: HB 3 appropriates funds for several state agencies for FY ending June 30, 2025, and continues one appropriation into the next biennium. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Appropriates $1,700,000 to the Department of Revenue, Property Assessment Division, and the Health Facilities Division of the Department of Public Health and Human Services.
Allocates $22,200,000 to the Department of Justice, Montana Highway Patrol, and $27,200,000 to the Department of Justice, Legal Services Division.
Provides $4,067,348 to the Office of State Public Defender, Conflict Division, and $4,167,744 to the Department of Corrections, Public Safety Division.
Funds $12,500,000 to the Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation & Programs Division.
Allocates $11,550,000 and $21,801,470 to the Department of Corrections, Public Safety Division (duplicate line likely a typo).
Appropriates $380,000 to the Office of Public Instruction, State Level Activities, and $26,655 to State Level Activities Distribution to Public Schools.
Provides $3,870,205 to the State Auditor's Office, Insurance Division.
Allocates $950,000 to the Wildlife Division, $500,000 to the Administration Division, and $617,000 to the Department of Fish, Wildlife, & Parks.
Continues the appropriation for the Department of Revenue into the biennium beginning July 1, 2025.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB4.one_line: HB 4 appropriates 2025 funds, extends many into 2026/27, and directs ARPA interest to natural‑resource and capital‑development accounts.
HB4.summary: HB 4 appropriates a wide array of state and federal funds for 2025, extends many of those appropriations into 2026 and 2027, and directs specific interest‑earning transfers from American Rescue Plan Act funds to natural‑resource and capital‑development accounts. The bill has an immediate effective date and includes a schedule for quarterly deposits of interest earnings until the end of 2026.
changes: Appropriates $290,750 for Montana community justice workers and $30,560 for the Montana Justice Institute for FY 2025; allocates $3,537,516 to the Department of Justice’s Johnson‑and‑Johnson settlement; and provides $13,905 for Montana Highway Patrol dispatch services, among many other line‑item appropriations across dozens of agencies.

Extends all remaining FY 2025 federal budget‑amendment authority for a long list of programs (e.g., adult treatment courts, ARPA funds, ARPA emergency assistance, Help America Vote Act grants, etc.) into FY 2026 and FY 2027.

Authorizes the state treasurer to transfer $1,749,052, $2,250,000, and $224,500 from the interest on American Rescue Plan Act funds to designated natural‑resource special revenue accounts, with the remainder going to the capital‑development long‑range building program account.

Mandates that, on a quarterly basis, all interest earnings on those ARPA funds be deposited into the capital‑development account until December 30, 2026, after which the funds must be expended or returned to the federal government.
Sets the act’s effective date as the day of passage and approval, with no additional implementation dates specified.
affected: Federal grant recipients (e.g., ARPA, HAVA, ARPA emergency assistance)
State agencies receiving extended appropriations (e.g., judiciary, education, transportation, health, natural resources)
State treasurer and related fiscal offices

HB5.one_line: HB 5 funds major repairs, capital projects, and a new behavioral‑health facility while raising thresholds and requiring reporting.
HB5.summary: HB 5 appropriates and transfers money for major repairs and capital development of state buildings, amends long‑range building program rules, raises major‑repair thresholds, and sets reporting and coordination requirements. It also authorizes specific projects for the 2025‑2027 biennium and creates a new behavioral‑health facility plan.
changes: Appropriates $1.3 billion for major‑repair projects and $55 million for capital‑development projects in the 2025‑2027 biennium, plus additional earmarked funds for specific agencies and facilities.
Transfers $150 million from the general fund to the capital‑development long‑range building program account and $2 million to a state‑special revenue account for petroleum‑tank remediation.
Increases the major‑repair threshold from $150,000 to $300,000 and requires that at least 80 % of major‑repair funds be spent on safety, envelope, structural, or essential‑systems work.

Amends sections of the Montana Code to modify definitions of “capital development,” “major repair,” and “new facility,” and to require a statewide facility inventory and condition assessment by September 1 of the year before a regular session.

Creates a new behavioral‑health facility plan, authorizing $26.5 million to be transferred to the board of investments for that purpose, and requires reporting to the health‑services interim budget committee and the long‑range planning budget committee.

Authorizes the combination of the UM Forestry Conservation & Science Lab project with the Clapp Building replacement into a single facility of no more than the existing Clapp Building’s square footage.
affected: State agencies (e.g., Department of Administration, Public Health, Corrections, Fish & Wildlife, Transportation, Military Affairs)

HB6.one_line: HB 6 funds and prioritizes renewable‑resource grants for Montana’s water and irrigation projects.
HB6.summary: HB 6 authorizes and funds a renewable‑resource grant and loan program for the 2025‑2026 biennium, allocating specific amounts to emergency, planning, irrigation, and wastewater projects. It sets priority lists, conditions for award, and coordination rules to avoid duplicate funding.
changes: Appropriates $5.25 million for named projects and $3.4745 million for irrigation projects, plus smaller earmarked amounts for emergency, planning, irrigation, and pollution‑reduction grants.
Creates a priority list of 42 wastewater and 27 irrigation projects with $125,000 each, plus a few smaller amounts.
Establishes conditions that recipients must have approved scope, budget, matching funds, project‑management plan, and audit compliance before disbursement.
Prohibits a recipient from receiving funds from both the Reclamation/Development Grants Program and the Renewable Resource Grant and Loan Program for the same project in a single biennium.
Amends §85‑1‑612 to give the Department rule‑making authority over application fees, criteria, loan servicing, and ranking criteria.
Requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to all federally recognized tribal governments.
Provides severability and coordination provisions for other funding sources.
Effective July 1 2025.

HB8.one_line: HB 8 expands DNRC loan authority, funds via coal‑severance bonds, and sets supermajority approval requirements.
HB8.summary: HB 8 authorizes the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) to make loans up to $121 million for listed renewable‑resource projects, finances those loans with coal‑severance‑tax bonds, and sets conditions for disbursement and repayment. The bill requires supermajority votes to create state debt and to approve the bond program, and it mandates notification to federally recognized tribes. No new program beyond the existing grant‑and‑loan framework is created, but the bill expands borrowing authority and specifies bond issuance limits.
changes: Authorizes DNRC to issue loans to specified political subdivisions and local governments for renewable‑resource projects listed in Sections 1 and 2, with maximum amounts per project listed in the bill.
Authorizes the Board of Examiners to issue coal‑severance‑tax bonds up to $121,198,444 in the 2025–2026 biennium, with $12,119,844 reserved for a bond reserve.
Requires that loan disbursement be conditioned on scope‑of‑work approval, documented matching funds, completion of grant‑program recommendations, and execution of a loan agreement.
Allows the DNRC to purchase, discount, and sell loans, bonds, warrants, and notes to itself under the program, and establishes appropriations for each loan at award.
Mandates that the legislature vote two‑thirds to create state debt (Section 7(1)) and three‑fourths to approve the bond program (Section 7(2)).
Orders the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Political subdivisions and local governments listed in the bill

HB10.one_line: Appropriates $38.7 M for state IT projects, transfers to LRITP, and sets CIO‑approved security and procurement rules.
HB10.summary: HB 10 appropriates $38.7 million for a range of state IT capital projects and transfers that money from the General Fund to the Long‑Range Information Technology Program (LRITP) for use through June 30 2027. It also sets requirements for CIO‑approved security plans and procurement approvals before funds are released.
changes: Appropriates $38,702,846 for IT capital projects across multiple agencies (e.g., DOA, Corrections, Higher Education, Natural Resources, Public Health, Revenue, Transportation).
Transfers the appropriated amount from the General Fund to the LRITP on an as‑needed basis through June 30 2027.

Requires all business application systems to have a Chief Information Officer‑approved plan covering design, implementation, and security, including authentication, data protection, and data removal policies.
Mandates that the CIO and budget director approve plans and procurement documents before funds may be released for any project.
Lists specific projects and their combined costs for each agency, ensuring funds are earmarked for those projects.
Provides severability language and sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.
affected: State agencies listed in the appropriation schedule (DOA, Corrections, Higher Education, Historical Society, Judicial, Natural Resources & Conservation, State Public Defender, Public Health & Human Services, Revenue, Transportation).
Chief Information Officer and budget director of the Department of Administration.
State treasurer (responsible for the fund transfer).

HB11.one_line: HB 11 appropriates coal‑endowment funds for water, bridge, emergency and planning grants with strict conditions.
HB11.summary: HB 11 appropriates money from the Montana Coal Endowment accounts to fund specific infrastructure projects, emergency and planning grants, and regional water‑system projects, with detailed conditions and priority lists for recipients.
changes: Appropriates $20,287,391 for water and wastewater projects listed in §1(2) and $3,544,750 for bridge projects in §1(5) for the 2025–2026 biennium.
Appropriates $150,000 for emergency infrastructure grants and $1,500,000 for infrastructure‑planning grants in §5 and §6.
Appropriates $10 million from the regional water‑system special revenue account for the four regional water authorities in §7.
Sets strict disbursement conditions (matching funds, project plans, audit compliance, etc.) in §3 and §9.
Allows the Department of Commerce to reduce grant amounts if actual expenses fall short or exceed projections, and to withdraw grants if conditions are not met by specified dates.
Requires grant recipients to execute agreements and comply with design and accounting standards.
Notifies federally recognized tribes of the act.
Effective July 1 2025.
affected: Local governments (towns, cities, counties, water and sewer districts)

HB12.one_line: HB 12 appropriates $6.23 million for historic‑preservation grants, sets strict conditions, and amends a 2023 appropriation.
HB12.summary: HB 12 appropriates $6.23 million from the historic‑preservation grant account for the 2025–2026 biennium, authorizes specific grants to a list of projects, and sets conditions for disbursement and completion. The bill also amends a 2023 appropriation and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments.
changes: Appropriates $6,229,375 (plus $5,918,092) to the Department of Commerce for the 2025–2026 biennium.
Authorizes grants to 73 named projects in a specified priority order, with set dollar amounts for each.
Imposes conditions on grant recipients: matching‑fund commitment, approved project‑management plan, compliance with auditing/reporting, and execution of a grant agreement.

Requires recipients to enter a binding contract with a qualified contractor by Sept 30 of the even‑numbered year before the next legislature; allows a single 2‑year extension for fire damage or contractor‑search failures.
Mandates that grant funds be disbursed on a reimbursement basis and may be reduced if actual expenses fall below projections.
Amends Section 4(1) of Chapter 710, Laws of 2023 to change two specific appropriations.
Requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Sets the effective date as July 1, 2025.
affected: Grant recipients (municipalities, nonprofits, tribal governments, etc.)

HB13.one_line: HB 13 revises state employee pay, per‑diem, and benefit rules, sets new legislator rates, and appropriates funds.
HB13.summary: HB 13 revises state employee pay, per‑diem rules, and group‑benefit contributions, sets new legislator hourly rates, and appropriates funds to implement the changes. It also adjusts highway patrol salary surveys and expands per‑diem and mileage rules for legislators.
changes: Amends 2‑18‑303 to raise base salaries by $1.50 or 4% (whichever is greater) for all state employees beginning July 1 2025 and July 1 2026, and provides one‑time lump‑sum payments of $1,040, $780, or $520 depending on hours worked.

Revises 2‑18‑501 to modify meal, lodging, and transportation reimbursement limits, authorize actual‑cost reimbursements for certain circumstances, and add special provisions for firefighters and non‑commercial lodging.

Amends 2‑18‑703 to increase employer contributions for group benefits to $1,054–$1,107/month for most state employees and legislators, with limits tied to excise‑tax thresholds, and sets different contribution amounts for university employees.

Rewrites 5‑2‑301 to set legislator hourly rates for future biennia (80 % of state average in 2027, 100 % in 2029+), add a $5/day bonus for Senate President and House Speaker, and clarify per‑diem, mileage, and salary options during sessions.
Provides appropriations for FY 2026 and FY 2027 to implement the pay, per‑diem, and benefit changes, and a $1 000 000 contingency fund for vacancies or retirements.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1 2025.
affected: State employees (all levels), legislators, highway patrol officers, university staff, firefighters, and other government employees subject to per‑diem rules
numbers: $5/day bonus for Senate President & House Speaker

HB15.one_line: HB 15 raises Montana school‑funding formulas for inflation, effective July 2025.
HB15.summary: HB 15 updates Montana’s school‑funding formulas to reflect inflation, increasing the base amounts and per‑student entitlements for all school‑district categories. The changes take effect July 1, 2025 and apply to fiscal years beginning thereafter.
changes: Adjusts the base entitlement dollar amounts for high‑school, elementary, and K‑12 districts for FY 2024‑2026 and beyond, raising them to account for inflation.
Re‑sets the per‑student entitlement rates (per‑ANB) for each district type, with higher rates for larger districts and additional increments for districts exceeding specified enrollment thresholds.

Increases the amounts for special‑education, quality‑educator, at‑risk‑student, Indian‑education, American‑Indian‑achievement‑gap, and data‑for‑achievement payments, using new per‑student multipliers that rise each fiscal year.
Re‑establishes the calculation of the maximum general‑fund budget and the special‑education allowable‑cost ratio, allowing a 200% maximum ratio.
Defines the new “BASE budget” and “BASE budget levy” amounts and the associated guaranteed tax‑base aid limits.
Sets the effective date (July 1, 2025) and applicability date (FY 2025 onward).
affected: School districts (high‑school, elementary, K‑12), teachers, students (especially at‑risk, Indian, and special‑education populations), and district fiscal planners

HB16.one_line: HB 16 tightens infrastructure loans, limits wage‑raising, and restricts tax‑credit use.
HB16.summary: HB 16 revises Montana’s infrastructure loan program, tightening eligibility and limiting tax‑credit claims. It removes the ability to use the program to raise wages for existing workers, bars infrastructure‑use fees from being deducted or credited, and sets new loan limits and conditions.
changes: Amends §17‑6‑309 to prohibit loans that only raise wages or incomes of existing employees or employers, and limits loans to projects that create or expand jobs for at least 15 Montana residents or raise salaries for existing workers.
Adds a new subsection to §17‑6‑309 allowing a working‑capital loan to a coal‑fired unit only if it prevents job loss and stabilizes the community.

Rewrites §17‑6‑311 to cap total loan amounts ($80 M for §17‑6‑309(2), $70 M for §17‑6‑317, $50 M annually for §17‑6‑309(3)) and imposes debt‑to‑fund limits (10 % of the permanent coal tax trust fund, 6 % debt with 30 % commercial lender share).

Revises §17‑6‑316 to require that loans be used for infrastructure that enables business location, to be made to local or tribal governments, and to allow a tax credit only for fees paid on that infrastructure, capped at the loan amount and carry‑forwardable 7 years.
Prohibits claiming the infrastructure‑use fee as a tax deduction or credit if it was already deducted.
Adds a notification requirement to federally recognized tribal governments.
Sets the act’s applicability to loans made on or after its effective date and credits claimed after Dec 31 2025.
affected: Local governments, Indian tribal governments, businesses seeking infrastructure loans, coal‑fired generating unit owners, taxpayers claiming infrastructure‑use fee credits

HB17.one_line: HB 17 revises forest‑land valuation rules and redefines the advisory committee’s composition and terms.
HB17.summary: HB 17 amends the statutory framework for forest‑land valuation and reorganizes the Forest Lands Taxation Advisory Committee, setting new appointment rules and term lengths. It also clarifies the calculation of productivity value, capitalization rate, and effective tax rate for forest‑land taxes.
changes: Rewrites §15‑44‑103 to detail the formula for forest‑land productivity value, net income, and capitalization rate, including a minimum 8 % cap on the rate.

Redefines the Forest Lands Taxation Advisory Committee to have nine members: four appointed by legislative leaders and five by the governor, with specified industrial/non‑industrial landowner and county commissioner representation.
Sets appointment deadlines: committee must be formed by July 1 two years before each reappraisal cycle, with terms expiring June 30 of the first year of the cycle.
Imposes term lengths: 4‑year terms for most members, with initial 2‑year terms for legislative appointees; governor‑appointed members receive staggered 1‑, 2‑, 3‑, and 4‑year terms.

Mandates committee duties: review valuation data, recommend adjustments, verify income approximations, suggest valuation techniques, meet at least annually, and report biennially to the revenue interim committee.
Provides that the act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Forest landowners (private and industrial), state forestry department, legislative leaders, governor, county commissioners, and the general public through tax assessments.
numbers: 10‑year base period for net income calculation

HB18.one_line: HB 18 channels school‑equalization and related tax revenue into a dedicated state account and sets detailed distribution rules.
HB18.summary: HB 18 directs that revenue from school‑equalization levies and related taxes be deposited into the state’s School Equalization and Property Tax Reduction Account. It amends several statutes to specify how the money is apportioned, when it is remitted, and what records must be kept.
changes: Amends 15‑39‑110 to allocate bentonite‑tax proceeds to the state special revenue fund, state general fund, and two counties, and to the School Equalization and Property Tax Reduction Account for new‑production taxes.
Amends 17‑3‑222 to split money received under 17‑3‑221: 50 % to county treasurers and 50 % to the School Equalization and Property Tax Reduction Account for elementary BASE funding.

Amends 20‑9‑331 and 20‑9‑333 to require that revenue from county basic taxes for elementary and high‑school equalization be deposited into the same account and that surplus funds be remitted to the state.
Amends 20‑9‑332 to mandate that all fines and penalties (except those paid to a justice’s court) be deposited into the elementary county equalization fund, with required reporting.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
Requires the department to remit county shares of bentonite‑tax proceeds by October 1 and April 1 each year and to provide county treasurers with gross‑yield data for debt‑limit calculations.

HB19.one_line: HB 19 requires a public hearing before extending a tax‑increment district beyond 15 years.
HB19.summary: HB 19 amends Montana’s tax‑increment‑financing law to require a public hearing before a local government pledges tax increments to pay bonds that would extend a district’s financing beyond 15 years.
changes: Amends §7‑15‑4289 to add a public‑hearing requirement for pledging tax increments to bond payments that extend a district’s financing beyond 15 years.
The hearing must be held by the legislative body that approved the original tax‑increment provision.
Notice of the hearing must be given to the county and school district where the district is located.
The amendment applies to any such pledge made on or after the act’s effective date.
No new program, fund, or offense is created.
The act does not alter existing bond‑issuance procedures beyond the hearing requirement.
affected: Local governments that use tax‑increment financing
County and school district governments in the affected districts
Residents of districts whose financing is extended

HB20.one_line: HB 20 changes voter‑approved levies from mills to dollars and expands calculation rules to all levies except school districts.
HB20.summary: HB 20 requires that any levy approved by voters be expressed in dollar amounts rather than mills, and it expands the calculation rules of 15‑10‑420 to apply to non‑school‑district levies. The bill amends the levy‑calculation statutes, clarifies how newly taxable property is treated, and repeals a prior election‑requirement provision.
changes: Replaces mill‑based voter‑approved levies with dollar‑based levies.
Extends the 15‑10‑420 calculation formula to all levies except school‑district levies and newly created regional resource authorities.
Amends 15‑10‑420 to define newly taxable property, inflation adjustments, and carry‑forward authority.
Rewrites 15‑10‑425 to require a resolution or charter amendment that specifies dollar amounts, mill equivalents, purpose, and duration for any levy exceeding statutory limits.
Repeals section 7‑6‑4431, which previously required an election to exceed or impose less than the maximum mill levy.
Adds provisions for rounding, statewide calculation limits, and special exceptions for certain levies (judgment, emergency, airport, etc.).
affected: County, consolidated government, incorporated city or town, school district, and other taxing entities that impose levies
Taxpayers whose property taxes may increase
numbers: one‑half of the average rate of inflation for the prior 3 years
tenth of a mill rounding rule

HB22.one_line: HB 22 updates school‑district levy‑notice rules and home‑value examples for impact statements.
HB22.summary: HB 22 amends the notice‑and‑resolution requirements for school districts that plan to raise non‑voted levies, aligning the home‑value examples used in impact statements with other statutes. It updates the dates, adds a $300,000 and $600,000 home example, and clarifies publication requirements.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑116 to change the deadline for adopting a resolution to June 1 (2017) and March 31 (2018 onward).
Adds a $300,000 and $600,000 home value to the list of examples in the impact statement.
Requires the resolution to include the estimated mill change, revenue change, and impacts on homes at $100,000, $200,000, $300,000, and $600,000.
Mandates publication of the resolution in a newspaper that reaches the largest number of district residents and posting it on the district’s website.
Clarifies that the resolution must also include the resolution under §20‑9‑502(3)(a)(i) if adopted.
Terminates the previous version of §20‑9‑116 on June 30 2027 and makes the new language effective July 1 2027.

HB26.one_line: Repeals all Mercury‑Added Thermostat Collection Act provisions, ending state regulation of these thermostats.
HB26.summary: HB 26 immediately repeals Montana’s Mercury‑Added Thermostat Collection Act, removing all prohibitions, collection requirements, reporting, and rule‑making authority related to mercury‑containing thermostats. The repeal takes effect upon passage and approval, ending the state’s regulatory framework for these devices.
changes: All sections 75‑10‑1501 through 75‑10‑1509 of the Montana Code Annotated are repealed.
The prohibition on sale and installation of mercury‑added thermostats is removed.
Manufacturer collection and recycling program requirements are eliminated.
Initial education and outreach obligations are eliminated.
Annual reporting requirements are eliminated.
Wholesaler collection site mandates are eliminated.
Rule‑making authority over the program is removed.
affected: Wholesalers and retailers of such thermostats
Consumers who own or install mercury‑added thermostats
Municipalities and local governments that previously managed collection sites
numbers: Effective date: upon passage and approval

HB24.one_line: HB 24 tightens kindergarten hour rules, expands ANB counting, and updates trustee reporting duties.
HB24.summary: HB 24 revises Montana’s kindergarten and enrollment‑counting rules, tightening hour requirements, clarifying how kindergarten programs are counted for funding, and expanding the list of programs that can affect a district’s average‑number‑belonging (ANB). The bill also updates the duties of county superintendents and trustees’ information‑disclosure duties.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑301 to set 360‑hour (half‑time) and 720‑hour (full‑time) kindergarten minimums and ties missing hours to a two‑hour‑rate deduction of BASE aid for non‑proficient students.
Rewrites §20‑3‑205 to broaden the county superintendent’s administrative responsibilities, including budgeting, audits, and reporting.

Rewrites §20‑3‑326 to require trustees to provide annual, comprehensive information on a wide array of educational and extracurricular opportunities, including special‑education, remote instruction, and career‑technical programs.

Rewrites §20‑7‑117 to clarify kindergarten program eligibility, financing, and the ability to enroll a child half‑time in a full‑time program, and to allow free preschool programs that cannot be funded by equalization aid.

Rewrites §20‑9‑311 to detail the ANB calculation, including new rules for counting kindergarten, preschool, and special‑education students, and to set limits on enrollment counts for certain programs.

Rewrites §20‑9‑313 to specify when ANB may be increased—new or reopened schools, closing schools, kindergarten openings, and early‑graduation students—and to exclude half‑time kindergarten expansions from this rule.
Adds an effective date of July 1 2025 and an applicability date of July 1 2025 for fiscal years.
No new state program or crime is created; the bill amends existing statutes.

HB29.one_line: HB 29 mandates an eight‑year review of exempt property and public mapping of exemptions.
HB29.summary: HB 29 requires the Department of Revenue to periodically review all property exempt from taxation, report biennially on the review, and maintain publicly accessible maps of exempt parcels.
changes: 1. Establishes an eight‑year review cycle for all exempt properties that require an application.
2. Mandates biennial reporting to the Revenue Interim Committee on number of properties reviewed, types of exemptions, approvals/denials, and estimated market and taxable values.
3. Requires the Department to keep a public database/map of exempt parcels organized by county and exemption type, including owner, address, legal description, area, and building size.
4. Gives the Department authority to adopt rules to implement the review process and public‑information requirements.
5. Codifies these provisions as part of Title 15, Chapter 6, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
affected: Property owners with tax‑exempt real property
Taxpayers (indirectly through potential changes in taxable base)

HB28.one_line: HB 28 sets 90‑day approval, 5‑year charters, and new funding rules for Montana public charter schools.
HB28.summary: HB 28 clarifies the timelines and procedures for approving, opening, and funding new public charter schools, and it requires the Board of Public Education to keep state officials informed. The bill amends several charter‑school statutes, establishes a 90‑business‑day approval window, sets a 5‑year initial charter term, and details how operating‑year funding is calculated and clawed back if enrollment falls short.
changes: Board must publish annual charter‑school reports and inform the Office of Public Instruction and county superintendents of charter status
Charter proposals must be solicited by the Board by October 1 each year and approved or denied within 90 business days
Approved charters receive a 5‑year contract that can be extended only for one year beyond the first year
Funding for charter schools is calculated on a per‑pupil basis; first‑year schools are not eligible for the per‑ANB entitlement and are subject to clawback if enrollment is lower than planned
Local‑board charter schools are treated as separate budget units; charter‑school districts receive a specific mix of base, ANB, and special‑education funds
The bill sets detailed performance metrics and renewal procedures for charter schools
Retroactive applicability to schools approved to begin operation on or after July 1 2025
Effective immediately upon passage
affected: Students and families in charter schools

HB32.one_line: HB 32 lets government entities record children at public events without parental consent, but protects most other parental rights.
HB32.summary: HB 32 expands when a government entity can record a child without parental consent, allowing recordings during public events and certain official activities. It also tightens parental rights over records and recordings, requiring consent for most other situations.
changes: Allows government entities to record children without consent during public events, court proceedings, law‑enforcement investigations, forensic interviews, security/surveillance, and photo‑ID cards.  Requires parental consent for all other audio/video recordings of children.  Adds a list of fundamental parental rights that remain protected, including control over education, health, and biometric data.  Provides parents the right to sue for violations and recover attorney fees.  Clarifies definitions of “child,” “education record,” and “government entity.”

HB31.one_line: HB 31 tightens bond rules, creates a lien, and funds a decommissioning account for wind/solar plants.
HB31.summary: HB 31 clarifies bonding rules for wind and solar plants, creates a decommissioning lien, and sets up a dedicated decommissioning account. It tightens deadlines for bond submission, adds penalties for non‑compliance, and allows the department to foreclose on assets if a plant is not properly decommissioned.
changes: Amends §75‑26‑304 to require owners to submit a decommissioning plan, lease abstracts, and a bond within specified timeframes based on operation start date.
Adds a decommissioning lien (§2) that the department can file on a facility’s assets if no bond is posted or if the facility is abandoned.
Creates a wind‑and‑solar decommissioning account (§3) to hold penalties, proceeds from lien foreclosures, and interest, and authorizes the department to use those funds for decommissioning.
Provides penalties up to $1,500 plus $1,500 per day for failure to submit a bond, and allows appeal to the board.
Allows the department to modify decommissioning plans, set bond amounts, and foreclose on liens if the owner fails to rectify deficiencies within 90 days.
affected: Owners/operators of wind and solar generation facilities
numbers: 25 MW wind / 2 MW solar size exemptions

HB37.one_line: HB 37 requires local governments to disclose prior‑year and projected tax data in preliminary budgets.
HB37.summary: HB 37 amends the Montana Code to require local governments to include detailed prior‑year and current‑year tax and expenditure data in their preliminary budgets, and to disclose projected property‑tax increases for specific property values.
changes: Amends §7‑6‑4020, MCA, adding new subsections (4)‑(6) that require listing of prior‑year, current‑year, and proposed‑year revenue and expenditures for each fund;
Requires a projection of fund and cash balances, including beginning balance, revenue, expenditures, reserves, and ending balance;
Mandates a detailed list of proposed capital expenditures and major projects;
Adds a requirement that any fund levying an ad‑valorem property tax must show the estimated tax revenue;
If a property‑tax increase is planned, the budget must state the dollar amount of the increase for homes valued at $100,000, $300,000, and $600,000;
Requires the budget to include the prior‑year property‑tax revenue on $100,000 of residential value and the estimated revenue for the current year.
affected: Local governments that levy ad‑valorem property taxes

HB38.one_line: HB 38 raises disability‑parking fines, adds a cure period, and criminalizes fraud in obtaining credentials.
HB38.summary: HB 38 revises Montana’s disability‑parking statutes, raising fines for violations, allowing a brief cure period with a valid permit, and creating a misdemeanor for fraudulently obtaining or aiding in the acquisition of disability parking credentials. It also clarifies enforcement authority and penalties for false information.
changes: Increases the base fine for a first violation to $150–$250 and for a second or subsequent violation to $250–$500.
Adds a 3‑business‑day cure period during which a valid, previously issued disability permit can excuse a violation.
Makes the registered owner personally liable if the vehicle was not with the operator at the time of the violation.

Creates a new misdemeanor offense for providing false information or assisting an unqualified person in obtaining a disability license plate, wheelchair plate, or placard, punishable by a fine of at least $300 or up to 10 hours of community service.
Expands law‑enforcement authority to enter any public parking space or right‑of‑way to enforce the new provisions.

HB39.one_line: Allows political parties to fund judicial candidates, amending election and fundraising rules.
HB39.summary: HB 39 would let political parties contribute to judicial candidates, specifically justices of the peace, by amending election and fundraising rules and repealing the existing prohibition. It also updates the joint‑fundraising‑committee provisions to allow party participation.
changes: Amends §3‑10‑201 to allow parties to contribute to justices of the peace; the prohibition in §13‑35‑231 is removed.
Amends §3‑10‑206 to keep vacancy‑filling rules unchanged but now applies to party‑contributed candidates.
Amends §13‑37‑211 to permit a joint fundraising committee to include a political party committee as a participant, while preserving limits on contributions and expenditures.
Repeals §13‑35‑231, the statute that bars political‑party contributions to judicial officers.
No new program or office is created; only the legal restriction is lifted and fundraising rules are broadened.

HB40.one_line: HB 40 creates a plan‑review revenue account and amends water‑system fee rules.
HB40.summary: HB 40 creates a dedicated plan‑review special revenue account, amends fee rules and fund accounting, and expands the Department’s authority to review, approve, and enforce public water‑supply and sewage‑system plans.
changes: Establishes a plan‑review special revenue account within the state special revenue fund and requires that fees collected under 75‑6‑108(3) be credited to it
Amends 75‑6‑104 to broaden the Department’s duties—including rule‑making, monitoring, enforcement, and the review of technical, managerial, and financial capacity of proposed systems

Rewrites 75‑6‑108 to set fee limits ($2.25 per connection for 1991‑93, $2 thereafter, minimum $100, $50 for transient non‑community systems), allows municipalities to raise rates without a public hearing, and requires fees on plan submissions to be deposited in the new account
Rewrites 75‑6‑115 to clarify that the public‑drinking‑water special revenue fund is used only for department costs and that its receipts come from the fees in 75‑6‑108(4)
Adds codification instructions and sets the effective date July 1 2025
affected: Proponents of new or altered water‑supply or sewage systems
Taxpayers who fund the special revenue accounts

HB41.one_line: HB 41 revises Schedule V, adding gabapentin and clarifying drug limits.
HB41.summary: HB 41 revises Montana’s Schedule V of controlled substances, adding gabapentin and clarifying limits for several narcotics, stimulants, depressants, anticonvulsants, and antimigraine drugs. The bill amends the statutory list and does not create new programs or penalties.
changes: Amends Section 50‑32‑232 to redefine Schedule V and list specific drugs and dosage limits;
Adds gabapentin to the list of depressants in Schedule V;
Specifies maximum quantities for codeine, dihydrocodeine, ethylmorphine, diphenoxylate, opium, and difenoxin;
Defines stimulants containing pyrovalerone;
Lists lacosamide, pregabalin, and gabapentin as depressants;
Adds ezogabine, brivaracetam, cenobamate, ganaxalone as anticonvulsants;
Adds lasmiditan as an antimigraine substance.
affected: Pharmacists, prescribers, patients, law‑enforcement agencies, and drug manufacturers in Montana

25 µg atropine sulfate per dosage unit

HB43.one_line: HB 43 clarifies parking, bicycle, school‑bus, and abandoned‑vehicle rules without creating new programs.
HB43.summary: HB 43 amends several Montana traffic‑law sections to clarify definitions, expand bicycle and school‑bus rules, and streamline enforcement of abandoned‑vehicle removal. The bill does not create new programs or criminal offenses beyond the existing framework.
changes: Rewrites §49‑4‑302 to clarify when a disabled‑parking permit permits stopping in an accessible space and allows local governments to waive time limits under specific conditions.
Amends §61‑6‑301 to explicitly allow insurance policies to exclude named family members while still requiring liability coverage for all other occupants.
Redefines “ways of this state open to the public” and related terms in §61‑8‑101 and §61‑8‑102, adding a definition of “paved shoulder” and clarifying bicycle and pedestrian terminology.
Revises §61‑8‑351 to set precise stopping distances and light‑activation distances for school buses, add extended stop‑arm requirements, and establish misdemeanor penalties for violations.
Updates §61‑8‑387 to detail how drivers should yield to moving emergency vehicles and the penalties for non‑compliance.
Rewrites §61‑8‑605 to clarify bicycle operation on roadways and paved shoulders, including lane‑use rules and safe‑margin requirements.
Amends §61‑12‑401 to specify which law‑enforcement agencies may take abandoned vehicles into custody, the removal‑charge limits, and private‑landowner removal rights.
Consolidates all definitions for traffic regulation into a single section for consistency.

HB42.one_line: HB 42 revises highway statutes for clarity, updates abandonment rules, and adds new right‑of‑way use and rail‑bed acquisition provisions.
HB42.summary: HB 42 revises a broad range of Montana highway and transportation statutes to clarify definitions, streamline procedures, and update funding and abandonment rules. It does not create new programs but reorganizes existing authority and adds new guidance for right‑of‑way use, rail‑bed acquisition, and municipal sidewalk encroachments.
changes: Rewrites definitions of abandonment, county road, bridge, and other key terms to align with the state’s bill‑drafting manual.

Replaces the old abandonment statute (60‑4‑208) with a new, detailed abandonment framework (60‑4‑213‑218) that requires public notice, hearings, and limits abandonment to cases where sale or exchange is not cost‑effective.
Adds a right‑of‑way use‑agreement process (60‑4‑601) that allows utilities and other projects to obtain long‑term access to interstate highways for a fee or in‑kind contribution.
Revises procurement rules (60‑2‑112) to expand competitive bidding thresholds and clarify when non‑competitive contracts may be used.
Updates funding apportionment formulas for secondary (60‑3‑206) and urban (60‑3‑211) highway systems to reflect land area, rural population, and road mileage.
Reorganizes and clarifies the sale and exchange of unnecessary highway property (60‑4‑202‑203, 60‑4‑201).
Revises the rail‑bed identification and acquisition process (60‑11‑111) to enable state acquisition of abandoned lines for local use.
Rewrites municipal sidewalk encroachment rules (60‑6‑106) to give incorporated cities authority to permit impermanent encroachments without state permits.
Replaces sections 60‑4‑208 and 60‑11‑112 with the new abandonment and rail‑bed provisions.
Adds new definitions and clarifications in several sections (e.g., 60‑1‑103, 60‑2‑134, 60‑5‑102).
affected: State and federal agencies involved in highway funding
numbers: $90,000 minimum sale value for abandoned interest
$100 application fee for right‑of‑way use agreements
$3,000 per mile for 30‑year right‑of‑way use agreement
$100 per mile per year for annual payment option
$90 days for final payment after acceptance
$30‑year maximum term for right‑of‑way use agreements
$90 days to approve right‑of‑way use agreement after federal approval
$90 days to approve right‑of‑way use agreement after federal approval

HB44.one_line: HB 44 adds a harsher penalty for tampering that hinders homicide death‑determination.
HB44.summary: HB 44 strengthens penalties for tampering with physical evidence, adding a harsher sentence for cases tied to homicide investigations that affect a coroner’s or medical examiner’s ability to determine cause or manner of death.
changes: Amends §45‑7‑207, MCA, to add a new subsection (2)(b) that imposes up to 40 years imprisonment or a $100,000 fine for tampering that interferes with a coroner or medical examiner’s determination of cause or manner of death in a homicide case.
Keeps the existing general penalty of up to 10 years imprisonment or a $50,000 fine for other tampering offenses.
Clarifies that the harsher penalty applies only when the tampering occurs in connection with a homicide or homicide investigation.
Does not create a new program, fund, or office.
Does not change any other statutes beyond §45‑7‑207.
affected: Individuals who tamper with or fabricate physical evidence in criminal investigations.
Persons who tamper with evidence in homicide investigations that affect death‑determination processes.
Courts and prosecutors handling homicide cases.

HB45.one_line: Bill eliminates PSC rate regulation, universal fund, and exempts IP services.
HB45.summary: The bill removes Montana’s public‑service‑commission rate regulation, eliminates the universal service fund and performance‑assurance account, exempts all internet‑protocol‑enabled services from regulation, and repeals a large block of telecom‑regulation statutes while amending several definitions.
changes: Repeals PSC rate‑regulation provisions (69‑3‑808‑910) and all universal‑service‑fund rules (69‑3‑842‑845).
Eliminates the Montana State Universal Fund and the Performance Assurance State Special Revenue Account.
Exempts all internet‑protocol‑enabled services from state regulation and prohibits the PSC from regulating their rates or terms.
Keeps the requirement that any provider file a notice with the PSC (69‑3‑805) but removes many other regulatory and reporting obligations.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage and approval.
affected: The Public Service Commission and its staff.
State agencies that fund or administer the universal service fund and performance‑assurance account.

HB46.one_line: Exempts public defenders from standard change‑of‑attorney rules in Montana law.
HB46.summary: HB 46 removes the standard change‑of‑attorney requirements for public defenders, allowing the state public defender office to reassign or replace a public defender without the client‑or‑attorney consent or court order that normally applies to other attorneys.
changes: Amends §37‑61‑403, MCA, to exclude public defenders from the section’s change‑of‑attorney rules.
Specifies that assignments or reassignments of a public defender by the Office of the State Public Defender are not subject to client or attorney consent or court order.
Leaves all other attorneys subject to the existing change‑of‑attorney procedures.
No new programs, funds, or offenses are created.
No fiscal provisions are included.
affected: Public defenders appointed under the Montana Public Defender Act
Clients represented by those public defenders
The Office of the State Public Defender
Courts handling cases with public defenders

HB48.one_line: HB 48 exempts wastewater ponds from the Dam Safety Act, adding a new category to § 85‑15‑107.
HB48.summary: HB 48 removes certain wastewater ponds—dams used for public sewage or disposal systems—from the Montana Dam Safety Act. It amends the statutory exemption list to add this new category while keeping all other existing exemptions unchanged.
changes: Amends § 85‑15‑107 to add a new exemption for dams used for public sewage systems or public sewage disposal systems regulated by the Department of Environmental Quality.
The amendment does not alter any other Dam Safety Act provisions or create new requirements for these facilities.
The bill does not establish new programs, funds, or penalties.
No fiscal impact is specified in the text.
The change applies only to the specified category of dams and does not affect other dam types.
affected: Municipalities or entities that own or operate wastewater ponds

HB47.one_line: Rewrites Montana’s building‑energy program, cuts bond authority, adds new accounts, and sets a 3 % interest cap.
HB47.summary: HB 47 revises Montana’s State Building Energy Conservation Act, removing the Department of Environmental Quality’s (DEQ) power to issue bonds, allowing it to set an annual interest rate (max 3 %), and reorganizing how energy‑saving projects are funded, tracked, and repaid. The bill creates new accounts for program costs, savings, and debt service, and requires agencies to transfer savings back to the state to pay for future projects.
changes: 1. DEQ can no longer issue energy‑conservation program bonds (repeals §§ 90‑4‑611 & 90‑4‑612).
2. DEQ may set an annual interest rate for projects, capped at 3 % (Section 90‑4‑605(6)).
3. New energy‑conservation program account and repayment account are created in the state special revenue fund (Sections 90‑4‑613 & 90‑4‑615).

4. Energy‑cost savings estimates must be reported to the governor each even‑numbered year and used to transfer funds from participating agencies to the repayment account (Sections 90‑4‑614 & 90‑4‑616).
5. A capital projects account is established to hold excess repayment funds and pay for future projects (Section 90‑4‑617).
6. A debt‑service account is created to hold bond principal and interest payments and can be transferred to the major repair long‑range building program (Section 90‑4‑625).
affected: State agencies owning or operating buildings
numbers: $2 million threshold for excess repayment funds

HB49.one_line: HB 49 tightens synthetic‑cannabinoid rules, expands licensing, and adds enforcement tools.
HB49.summary: HB 49 updates Montana’s marijuana laws to tighten rules on synthetic cannabinoids, expand licensing authority, and add enforcement tools. It amends definitions, limits potency, requires child‑safe packaging, and gives the department broad rule‑making power.
changes: Amends the Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act to prohibit manufacturing, storing, or selling synthetic cannabinoid products and to limit THC potency to 0.3% for most products and 0.5 mg per serving for hemp‑derived items.

Adds new definitions for synthetic cannabinoids, synthetic marijuana cannabinoid products, and related terms, and expands the list of prohibited activities (e.g., visible cultivation, sale to minors).
Authorizes the Department of Revenue to adopt rules on licensing, testing, packaging, labeling, advertising, and renewable‑energy incentives, and sets fee limits tied to administrative costs.

Provides a new enforcement framework (Section 16‑12‑305) allowing local governments and state agencies to issue cease‑and‑desist orders, impose daily penalties, and pursue civil or criminal remedies for violations of synthetic‑cannabinoid prohibitions.

Expands the definition of unlawful transactions with children (Section 45‑5‑623) to include sales of synthetic marijuana cannabinoid products to minors, with fines up to $1,000 and up to six months’ jail for a second offense.
Sets the act’s effective date to the day of passage, with no sunset clause.
affected: Licensed marijuana cultivators, manufacturers, dispensaries, and transporters
Consumers and cardholders of medical marijuana
numbers: $500 fine or 6‑month jail for first unlawful transaction with child
$1,000 fine or 6‑month jail for second unlawful transaction with child

HB53.one_line: HB 53 lets state agencies use troop labor for projects, with bidding rules and special historic‑preservation exceptions.
HB53.summary: HB 53 amends Montana’s public‑contract law to allow state agencies to use troop labor for construction and preservation projects, with specific bidding and inflation‑adjustment rules. It also creates exceptions for inmate work and certain historic‑preservation projects at Bannack, and for military‑affiliated maintenance.
changes: Amends §18‑2‑301 to require a 3‑week public notice and sealed bids for contracts ≥$150,000, with inflation adjustments every five years starting July 1 2028.
Allows agencies to contract for work after two failed bid attempts if cost‑effective.
Exempts inmate labor at correctional institutions from the bidding requirement.

Exempts the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks from bidding for historic‑building projects at Bannack when cost‑effective or necessary to prevent loss, permitting MOUs, volunteer work, training programs, or combinations thereof.
Exempts the Department of Military Affairs from bidding when performing upgrades or maintenance for military training purposes.
Sets the inflation‑adjustment formula based on CPI June values, rounding to the nearest $1,000 and adopting by rule.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Local, state, or federal entities or nonprofits involved in historic preservation at Bannack

HB54.one_line: HB 54 eliminates the commissioner’s countersignature on unemployment fund warrants, effective immediately.
HB54.summary: HB 54 removes the need for the Department of Labor and Industry commissioner to countersign warrants issued from the unemployment trust fund. It amends the unemployment administration account language and repeals the old signature requirement. The change takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends § 39‑51‑406 to clarify the composition and use of the unemployment insurance administration account.
Repeals § 39‑51‑405, which required the commissioner’s countersignature on warrants from the unemployment trust fund.
No new programs, funds, or penalties are created.
The amendment does not alter funding levels or administrative procedures beyond the signature requirement.
The act is effective immediately upon approval.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry (commissioner and staff)

HB55.one_line: HB 55 tightens utility planning, adds independent evaluators, and creates a special revenue account.
HB55.summary: HB 55 revises Montana’s public‑utility resource‑planning rules, tightening fee limits, expanding public‑comment requirements, and creating an independent evaluator to oversee competitive solicitation processes. It also establishes a special revenue account, sets new timelines for plan review, and authorizes a $200,000 appropriation for the Public Service Commission. The bill is effective July 1, 2025.
changes: Limits most commission‑set fees to $500 and requires certain fees to be deposited in a special revenue fund.
Mandates public utilities to file an integrated least‑cost plan every three years, with detailed content requirements and a 60‑day public comment period.
Requires utilities to hold at least two public meetings before submitting a plan and two after submission, with additional review by the Department of Environmental Quality and Consumer Counsel.

Creates a requirement that competitive solicitation processes for new resources use an independent evaluator selected from a commission‑maintained list, with defined duties and fee recovery provisions.
Adds new timelines for the commission to review and approve resource‑approval applications (45‑day adequacy review, 180‑day approval for PPAs, 270‑day approval for leases or new plants).
Establishes a special revenue account and appropriates $200,000 for the biennium beginning July 1, 2025 to support the act’s implementation.

HB56.one_line: Montana will levy a 5.75 % fee on ambulance providers, use the revenue to supplement Medicaid payments, and enforce collection through audits and penalties.
HB56.summary: Montana will impose a 5.75 % assessment fee on ambulance providers’ net operating revenue, collect it through the Department of Revenue, and deposit the proceeds into a special Medicaid‑reimbursement account.  The funds will first reimburse the state for collection costs, then be used to supplement Medicaid payments for emergency ambulance services, with penalties, interest, and audit provisions for non‑payment or misreporting.
changes: Creates a 5.75 % assessment fee on ambulance providers’ net operating revenue.
Mandates annual reporting of net operating revenue and payment of the fee by March 31 of each year.
Establishes a special Medicaid‑reimbursement account to hold the fee proceeds and related penalties/interest.
Requires the account to reimburse the General Fund for collection costs, fund Department of Revenue personnel, and provide supplemental Medicaid payments up to the average commercial rate.
Gives the Department of Revenue authority to audit providers, impose penalties and interest, and issue warrants for distraint.
Provides for protest, hearing, and credit for overpayment, with specified interest rules.
affected: Ambulance providers (ground, non‑air, non‑public, non‑federal, non‑tribal)
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB58.one_line: HB 58 reallocates environmental‑quality funds, adds a CR Kendall transfer, and extends Libby cleanup support.
HB58.summary: HB 58 revises how Montana’s environmental‑quality fund is funded and spent, adds a biennial transfer for the CR Kendall mine, and extends the state’s contribution to the Libby asbestos Superfund site. The bill also amends the orphan‑share account rules and sets a 2038 termination date.
changes: Amends §75‑10‑704 to require 50 % of the fund’s annual deposits to go to Libby and 50 % to metal‑mine reclamation, with a $500,000 biennial transfer for CR Kendall maintenance and water treatment until 2038.
Adds a 50 % split of the fund’s deposits between Libby and abandoned‑mine projects, except for exploration after March 9 1971.
Revises §75‑10‑743 to clarify how the orphan‑share account reimburses remedial‑action costs, limits early reimbursement, and sets limits on data‑collection spending.
Extends the state’s contribution to Libby’s cleanup, operation, and maintenance beyond the current deadline.
Sets the act’s effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2038.
Provides that the act does not affect pre‑existing rights, penalties, or proceedings.
Adds reporting requirements to the environmental quality council on orphan‑share expenditures.
affected: Liable parties under the natural‑resource‑damage program
Private donors to specific remediation projects
Residents near Libby and CR Kendall sites
numbers: $1.2 million annual transfer to water‑treatment trust

HB59.one_line: HB 59 tightens water‑well contractor licensing, bonds, and discipline rules.
HB59.summary: HB 59 revises Montana’s water‑well contractor laws to tighten licensing, expand bond requirements, clarify who may contract on a licensed contractor’s behalf, and update complaint‑and‑disciplinary procedures.
changes: Licensed contractors must be the individual who contracts on behalf of a firm, corporation, or partnership (Section 1).
A person may work on a well on land they own or lease for farming, ranching, or residence only if a permit is obtained and minimum construction standards are met (Section 2).
Licensure now requires a surety bond of $4,000–$25,000, or $10,000–$25,000 for firms with more than two licensed contractors (Section 3).
The board’s complaint and investigation process is clarified: licensees must be given a chance to respond before disciplinary action (Section 4).
Disciplinary actions now include repair/reconstruction, training, probation, suspension (≤1 yr), and revocation with a 3‑yr re‑application ban (Section 4).
affected: Firms, corporations, and partnerships that contract for well work
Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

HB61.one_line: HB 61 revises inter‑entity loan rules, allowing temporary loans and limited negative balances with new reporting requirements.
HB61.summary: HB 61 revises how Montana agencies can borrow from one another, allowing temporary, interest‑free loans and permitting certain federal special revenue funds to run slightly negative balances while awaiting reimbursement. It adds reporting requirements and limits on negative balances, and clarifies loan terms for university funds.
changes: Amends §17‑2‑107 to permit temporary, interest‑free inter‑entity loans when a fund’s cash is insufficient, provided repayment is expected within one calendar year and the loan is recorded.

Allows the commissioner of higher education to authorize interest‑bearing loans from other university funds for specific sub‑funds, with a single one‑year extension possible under written justification.
Permits federal special revenue funds to carry a negative cash balance at fiscal‑year end if they will be reimbursed for federal expenditures, subject to monthly billing recertification.
Establishes a dedicated accounting entity within each fund/sub‑fund to record loans, and limits negative balances to no more than seven working days unless otherwise authorized.

Requires written reports to the Legislative Fiscal Analyst by September 1 for any accounting entity that receives a second loan or has a negative balance for two consecutive fiscal‑year ends, including solvency analysis and repayment plans.
Adds interest requirements for loans from unrestricted sub‑funds to certain university sub‑funds, tying the rate to the board of investments’ short‑term return.
Specifies that loans cannot be made to entities owed third‑party funds unless timely billing is certified and recertified monthly; failure to recertify cancels the loan.
affected: University of Montana system and its funds
numbers: 7 working days limit on negative balances
interest rate tied to short‑term investment pool

HB60.one_line: Amends Montana securities and insurance laws, updates definitions, and expands consumer‑protection rules.
HB60.summary: HB 60 amends a wide range of Montana securities and insurance statutes, revises definitions, clarifies school‑health‑trust rules, removes a securities‑issuer fee, and updates numerous regulatory and consumer‑protection provisions. The bill also extends the expiration of a pharmacy‑benefit‑manager prohibition and amends several other statutes.
changes: Amends the definition of state employee and related personnel terms in §2‑18‑101, adding new categories such as short‑term worker, student intern, and telework provisions.

Rewrites §20‑3‑369 to establish a $40 million one‑time distribution from the state school health trust operating reserve account to the first qualified self‑funded district health‑insurance trust, with a June 30 2026 qualification deadline.
Revises §27‑1‑306 to make actual replacement value the default damages measure for motor‑vehicle repairs, unless parties agree to use book value.
Expands §30‑10‑104 to exempt a broad set of securities (e.g., federal, Canadian, bank, railroad, etc.) from the state securities‑registration requirements.

Rewrites §30‑10‑201 to tighten registration and notice filing requirements for broker‑dealers, salespersons, investment advisers, and federal‑covered advisers, including new notice‑filing deadlines and fee structures.
Rewrites §30‑10‑307 to impose civil liability limits for securities fraud and to set a 2‑year statute of limitations for filing actions within one year of discovery.

Rewrites §30‑10‑1005 to restrict temporary eligibility for restitution assistance to victims who have not yet paid full restitution and to terminate assistance if the restitution award is overturned on appeal.
Extends the termination date of the prohibition against pharmacy‑benefit managers or health carriers that require federally certified health entities to identify 340B drugs to a later effective date.
affected: Montana state employees, insurance producers, surplus‑lines insurers, securities issuers, broker‑dealers, salespersons, investment advisers, federal‑covered advisers, insurance policyholders, and victims of securities fraud.

HB63.one_line: Extends bond validation to pre‑March 16, 2023 bonds, effective immediately.
HB63.summary: HB 63 extends the Bond Validating Act to cover bonds issued and proceedings taken before March 16, 2023, and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §17‑5‑205, MCA, to broaden the Act’s application to bonds issued and proceedings taken prior to March 16, 2023.
No other substantive changes are made to the Act or related statutes.
The amendment takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Bond issuers and parties involved in bond proceedings before March 16, 2023.

HB62.one_line: HB 62 revises Montana retirement laws, tightening reporting, benefit rules, and definitions.
HB62.summary: HB 62 amends many public‑employee retirement statutes to clarify eligibility, benefit conversion, reporting, and survivor rules, and to align definitions with federal law. It adds new rules for disability retirement, payroll‑reporting penalties, and optional membership for certain employees.
changes: Allows legislators to retire from non‑legislative employment and continue participation in their retirement system, with a one‑time irrevocable election to decline further participation.

Extends the post‑termination deadline for disability‑retirement applications to 12 months and requires that disability benefits not convert to normal retirement benefits when the retiree reaches normal retirement age.
Imposes a 9 % annual interest penalty (or $10/day) on employers who fail to pay or report contributions on time, and requires retroactive contributions for payroll‑reporting errors.
Prorates service‑credit purchases if a member stops making installment payments and allows payroll‑deduction authorization for additional contributions.
Removes the ability for members to renounce benefits and clarifies that disability benefits cannot begin before application completion.
Revises excess‑earnings limits for calculating highest and final average compensation, and updates minimum‑distribution and inherited‑account rules to meet federal requirements.
Defines “allowance” and revises the definition of compensation to exclude bonuses and certain reimbursements.
Exempts retired members who are subpoenaed in legal proceedings related to prior employment from working‑retiree provisions.
Adjusts bonus exclusions for several specific retirement systems (judges, highway patrol, game wardens, police, firefighters).

Aligns working‑retiree limits in the sheriff’s retirement system with other systems and clarifies that termination of service is required before retirement in the game‑warden and peace‑officer systems.
Revises survivorship benefits for inactive firefighters with less than 20 years of service.
affected: public employees in Montana’s retirement systems

HB64.one_line: Eliminates the advisory council and redefines the representative’s duties in Montana’s Clean Air Act.
HB64.summary: HB 64 eliminates the Small Business Compliance Assistance Advisory Council and revises the duties of the Small Business Stationary Source Representative. The representative remains, but its responsibilities are redefined and the council’s authority is removed. The bill does not create new programs or impose new costs.
changes: Repeals the Small Business Compliance Assistance Advisory Council and its duties (MCA §§ 2‑15‑2110 and 75‑2‑106).

Amends MCA § 75‑2‑109 to redefine the Small Business Stationary Source Representative’s duties, keeping the position but limiting its supervisory status and adding specific tasks such as monitoring compliance assistance, reviewing regulations, facilitating participation, preparing reports, drafting guidelines, encouraging voluntary compliance, helping locate financing, consulting with stakeholders, and performing other necessary duties.
Requires the representative to consult with the now‑eliminated council at regular intervals, effectively removing that advisory function.
Maintains the confidentiality restriction that the representative may not provide source information to the department unless it reveals an imminent danger.

HB66.one_line: Adopts federal military laws and UCMJ for the Montana National Guard effective Oct 1 2023.
HB66.summary: HB 66 adopts the federal military laws, regulations, and the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) that were in effect on October 1, 2023, for the Montana National Guard, replacing the state’s existing provisions. The act applies to all Guard members and events occurring on or after that date. It does not create new programs or funds.
changes: Amends Section 10‑1‑104, MCA, to state that federal regulations in effect on Oct 1 2023 apply to the Montana National Guard where not inconsistent with state law.
Adds the UCMJ, as in effect on Oct 1 2023, for Guard members on active duty under Title 32 when not serving in a federal capacity under Title 10.
Specifies the applicability date: Oct 1 2023 (events and proceedings beginning on or after that date).
No new state program, office, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Montana National Guard members (active duty and reserve)
Guard units and state military authorities
Legal and administrative personnel handling Guard matters

HB68.one_line: County commissioners may now file mandamus suits and recover legal costs; fines up to $1,000 for non‑compliance.
HB68.summary: County commissioners are now empowered to file mandamus suits against local government entities and to recover legal costs. The bill also clarifies enforcement penalties for non‑compliance with such writs.
changes: Adds subsection (f) to §7‑4‑2110 giving commissioners the power to initiate civil proceedings for a writ of mandamus against a local government entity or its governing body.
Adds subsection (g) to §7‑4‑2110 allowing commissioners to hire outside counsel and recover attorney fees and costs as determined by a court.
Rewrites §27‑26‑206 to specify that a fine of up to $1,000 may be imposed for refusal to obey a mandamus writ, and that persistent refusal can lead to imprisonment and other enforcement orders.
Adds a provision that an elected or appointed official found in contempt for not complying with a mandamus writ may be subject to recall under Title 2, Chapter 16, Part 6.
Clarifies the definition of “local government entity” in §7‑4‑2110 to exclude counties, consolidated city‑counties, incorporated cities or towns, and school districts.
Leaves all other statutory language unchanged.
affected: Local government entities (excluding counties, consolidated city‑counties, incorporated cities or towns, and school districts)
Elected and appointed officials subject to mandamus writs

HB67.one_line: HB 67 revises the Teachers’ Retirement System’s rules on membership, reporting, and distributions, effective July 1 2025.
HB67.summary: HB 67 revises the Teachers’ Retirement System to clarify definitions, employer reporting, membership rules, and distribution dates, and to align the system with federal law. It adds detailed reporting requirements for employers, expands credit for substitute‑teacher service, and tightens rules for dormant and disabled members. The bill takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Amends definitions in §19‑20‑101 to clarify terms such as earned compensation, employer, and member status.
Rewrites §19‑20‑208 to require employers to report monthly payroll data, contributions, and to notify the system of all eligible employees, including independent contractors and volunteers.
Expands §19‑20‑302 to list additional positions that must be active members, sets a 210‑hour threshold for substitute teachers and aides, and clarifies election procedures for membership.
Revises §19‑20‑303 to detail the transition to dormant status for inactive members, including deadlines for withdrawal or re‑activation and the handling of account balances.
Adds §19‑20‑417 to allow creditable service for substitute teachers and aides who defer membership for the first 210 hours, and permits purchase of the first 30 days of service.
Amends §19‑20‑703 to set new required minimum distribution dates based on age and termination, and to specify when retirement allowances may begin.
Rewrites §19‑20‑905 to clarify the cancellation of allowances for disabled retirees who exceed earnings limits and the restoration of active membership.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1 2025.
affected: Teachers, principals, administrators, and other education staff
Substitute teachers, part‑time aides, and paraprofessionals
Employers of public school employees (school districts, universities, etc.)
Disabled retirees of the Teachers’ Retirement System
Members who become inactive or dormant

HB70.one_line: HB 70 mandates a $50,000 study of Montana’s wildfire suppression and reports findings by Sept 2026.
HB70.summary: HB 70 directs the Environmental Quality Council to conduct a comprehensive study of Montana’s wildland‑fire suppression operations, policies, and costs, and requires a report to the Legislature by September 15, 2026. The bill appropriates $50,000 for the study and includes provisions that void the act if the appropriation is missing or vetoed.
changes: Authorizes the Environmental Quality Council to conduct a study of state and federal wildfire suppression operations, equipment, personnel, and policy impacts on private land and tribal land.
The study must examine efficient use of resources, impact on private land, and forest‑management and grazing policies that may affect wildfire frequency and suppression effectiveness.
The Council must submit findings, recommendations, and proposed legislation to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
Appropriates $50,000 from the general fund to the Legislative Services Division for the biennium beginning July 1, 2025, to pay for the study.
The act is void if it is transmitted to the governor without an appropriation, or if the appropriation is vetoed.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and terminates December 31, 2026.
affected: State and federal wildfire suppression agencies

HB69.one_line: HB 69 creates a new hard‑rock permitting account and adds fees, bonds, and reporting for miners.
HB69.summary: HB 69 establishes a new hard‑rock mining permitting program account, adds several new fees and reporting requirements for small miners, exploration license holders, and operating permit holders, and amends existing hard‑rock mining statutes to clarify fee schedules, bond requirements, and enforcement procedures.
changes: Creates a hard‑rock mining permitting program account in the state special revenue fund and directs the department to use those funds for permitting and enforcement.
Imposes a $100 annual administrative fee and a $100 late fee on small miners who meet written exemption conditions.
Adds a $25 renewal fee for exploration licenses and a $5,000 application fee (or $500 for rock‑product operations) for operating permits, plus optional additional fees for contractor expenses.
Sets bond and reclamation requirements for placer/dredge mining, cyanide use, and impoundments, including performance bonds up to $10,000 and limits on reclamation bonds.
Revises fee schedules for exploration licenses, operating permits, and annual permit fees based on disturbed acreage and bond status.
Adds reporting and notification requirements for large‑scale developers, including annual activity reports and fee adjustments.
Provides rule‑making authority for the department to adopt criteria for major vs. minor permit amendments and to set fee amounts.
Amends several MCA sections (82‑4‑305, 82‑4‑331, 82‑4‑332, 82‑4‑335, 82‑4‑339, 82‑4‑342, 82‑4‑343) to reflect the new fees, bonds, and enforcement provisions.

HB72.one_line: HB 72 eliminates the 15‑day cap on double pay for enlisted militia on state duty.
HB72.summary: HB 72 removes the 15‑day cap on pay for enlisted militia members on state active duty, doubling their pay for the entire period and aligning it with federal rates. The bill amends the state’s militia compensation statute and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §10‑1‑502, MCA to eliminate the 15‑day limit on double‑rate pay for enlisted militia members on state active duty.
Enlisted members ordered to active duty now receive twice the federal pay for the full duration of their state service, not just the first 15 days.
The amendment clarifies that after the 15‑day period, pay reverts to the standard federal rate, but the new language removes that restriction entirely.
No new program, office, or criminal offense is created; it merely revises existing compensation rules.
The effective date is the day the act is passed and approved.
The bill does not alter officer pay, aviation officer pay, or National Guard pay provisions.
It does not change funding sources or authorize new expenditures beyond the existing militia budget.
affected: Enlisted militia members on state active duty

HB74.one_line: HB 74 tightens fish‑pond licensing, raises fees, adds record‑keeping, and repeals paddlefish‑caviar sales.
HB74.summary: HB 74 revises Montana’s private fish‑pond rules, tightening licensing, record‑keeping, and fees while adding new penalties for violations. It also repeals the paddlefish‑caviar sale provision and updates several game‑fish possession and sale statutes.
changes: Licenses for private fish ponds now require a $500 surety bond for sales and a $2,500 bond for selling eggs or fry; licenses are valid for 10 years (or 1 year for temporary licenses).
Application and renewal fees are increased to $600 for new licenses and $250 for renewals; a $250 fee applies for license transfers.
Licensees must submit annual reports and maintain detailed sales records; the department may impose conditions to prevent fish escape or disease spread.
The department is granted rule‑making authority to set health standards, inspection frequency, and other compliance measures for private ponds.
