The law repeals section 87‑4‑601, eliminating the paddlefish‑caviar sale provision, and modifies sections 87‑6‑202, 87‑6‑206, and 87‑6‑707 to tighten penalties for unlawful possession, sale, and transport of game fish and related products.
Temporary licenses are available for ponds that do not meet full private‑pond criteria but pose no unacceptable risk; they expire after one year and require annual renewal if fish or eggs are sold.
affected: Individuals who sell or transport game fish or related products
The Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks

HB75.one_line: HB 75 tightens training deadlines and clarifies basic‑course rules for Montana public‑safety officers.
HB75.summary: HB 75 revises Montana’s public‑safety officer standards, tightening training timelines, clarifying when basic courses are required, and allowing limited extensions. It also adds a 10‑day notice requirement for military duty and clarifies that reserve officers are exempt from the new basic‑course rule.
changes: Amends §44‑4‑404 to require appointing authorities to enforce a one‑year deadline for completing minimum training standards and to terminate officers who fail to meet them.

Requires that, if no basic‑equivalency course exists in a discipline, an officer must complete the basic course required in §7‑32‑303(6) within one year of hire, unless the officer has a break in service of 3–5 years.
Exempts reserve officers (defined in §7‑32‑201) from the new basic‑course requirement.
Allows an appointing authority to request a council‑approved extension of up to 180 days for an officer to meet training standards, with specified justification and council‑review factors.

Adds a 10‑day notice requirement to the council when an officer is called to state or federal military duty within the first year, suspending the one‑year training deadline, and a 10‑day notice when the officer returns, at which point the deadline resumes.
affected: Public safety officer standards and training council

HB76.one_line: HB 76 expands behavioral‑health licensing, adds peer‑support certification, and exempts clergy from licensing.
HB76.summary: HB 76 revises Montana’s behavioral‑health licensing laws, adds certification rules for peer‑support specialists, and exempts clergy from licensing requirements. It expands definitions, clarifies supervision and exam rules, and creates a new certification pathway for peer‑support and family‑peer‑support specialists.
changes: Amends §37‑39‑101 to broaden the scope of regulated behavioral‑health practices and emphasize public interest.
Rewrites §37‑39‑102 with new definitions (e.g., “peer support,” “family peer support,” “approved program”) and clarifies licensing criteria.
Adds §37‑39‑303 exemptions that allow clergy, other licensed professionals, volunteers, and students to perform duties without holding a board license, provided they do not use a licensed title.
Revises §37‑39‑307 to create a “candidate” status for applicants who finish education but not supervised experience, limits candidate years, and requires a training‑and‑supervision plan.

Rewrites §37‑39‑312 to establish a new licensing/certification requirement for peer‑support specialists, including diagnosis, treatment, recovery, and completion of an approved program; also sets requirements for family‑peer‑support specialists.
Introduces a new licensing exemption for religious officials performing clergy duties.
Creates a list of approved peer‑support and family‑peer‑support programs and allows faith‑based, cultural, and educational content.
affected: Behavioral‑health professionals (social workers, counselors, marriage‑family therapists, addiction counselors), peer‑support specialists, family‑peer‑support specialists, clergy, other licensed professionals, volunteers, students, and employers of these workers

HB77.one_line: HB 77 revises child‑abuse law, removes temporary investigative authority, and updates petition and hearing procedures.
HB77.summary: HB 77 revises Montana’s child‑abuse and neglect laws, removes the temporary investigative authority, and amends several sections governing petitions, hearings, and court costs. The bill clarifies procedures for filing petitions, service requirements, burden of proof, and the role of the Department of Public Health and Human Services.
changes: Replaces Section 3‑5‑901 with a new state‑funded district‑court expense program, detailing which costs are covered and when counties must reimburse the court administrator
Amends Section 41‑3‑422 to expand the types of relief that may be requested in an abuse/neglect petition and clarifies the filing and service requirements for petitions
Rewrites Section 41‑3‑427 to require a detailed affidavit, specify evidence standards (probable cause or clear‑convincing evidence), and limit the duration of emergency protective orders to 90 days

Rewrites Section 41‑3‑432 to set a 20‑day deadline for a show‑cause hearing, outline the burden of proof for temporary investigative authority, and detail the court’s written findings and procedural safeguards
Repeals Section 41‑3‑433, eliminating the statutory authority for temporary investigative authority
Adds a notification requirement to federally recognized tribal governments
All changes take effect July 1 2025
affected: County attorneys, attorneys general, Department of Public Health and Human Services staff, parents and guardians of children, foster parents, tribal governments

HB78.one_line: HB 78 mandates pet‑insurance disclosures, limits waiting periods, and requires producer training in Montana.
HB78.summary: HB 78 establishes a comprehensive legal framework for pet insurance in Montana, requiring detailed disclosures, limits on pre‑existing condition exclusions and waiting periods, and training for producers. It also sets rules for wellness programs and gives the commissioner rule‑making authority. The bill does not create a new state program or fund.
changes: Pet insurers must disclose pre‑existing condition exclusions, hereditary disorders, congenital anomalies, chronic conditions, waiting periods, deductibles, coinsurance, and limits before sale.
Insurers may impose up to 30‑day waiting periods for illnesses or orthopedic conditions (not for accidents) and must allow waivers via a veterinary exam.
Insurers must provide a 15‑day free‑look period for consumers to examine and return policies before claims are filed.

All pet insurance producers must complete 2 hours of state‑approved training on pre‑existing conditions, waiting periods, wellness programs, and underwriting before selling, and repeat the training every 24 months.
Wellness programs cannot be marketed as insurance, cannot be required for insurance purchase, and must be clearly separated and identified in advertising and documentation.
The commissioner may adopt rules to implement the act and enforce penalties under existing Title 33 provisions.

HB79.one_line: HB 79 exempts small‑scale slash‑hazard activities from fire‑hazard agreements, requiring written approval for sales.
HB79.summary: HB 79 allows small‑scale forest‑product activities (e.g., fire‑wood harvest) to be exempt from the usual fire‑hazard‑reduction agreement requirements.  It creates a written exemption process for activities that generate only a minimum slash hazard and keeps the existing bond and certification rules for larger operations.
changes: Exempts activities that produce a minimum slash hazard from the fire‑hazard‑reduction agreement and bond requirements unless forest products are sold, in which case a written exemption is required.
Defines “small‑scale activity” as sales of ≤2 log‑truck loads or <10,000 board‑feet (log scale).
Adds a new definition of “minimum slash hazard” and clarifies when an exemption applies.
Maintains the existing bond limits ($6 per 1,000 board‑feet) and release provisions for larger agreements.
Requires that any written exemption be issued by the Department and provided to the purchaser at delivery.
Limits written exemptions to one per parcel per year for sales.
Leaves the rest of Sections 76‑13‑401 and 76‑13‑408 unchanged except for the new exemption language.
affected: Private forest landowners and contractors engaged in small‑scale timber or fire‑wood harvesting
Purchasers of forest products from such activities

HB80.one_line: Allows cash‑basis competitive bidding for state agricultural leases with new deposit, renewal, and penalty rules.
HB80.summary: HB 80 allows state‑land agricultural leases to be awarded on a cash‑basis competitive bid instead of the traditional crop‑share basis.  The bill amends deposit rules, lease‑renewal options, and payment deadlines, and it creates a new cash‑lease option for agricultural land.
changes: 1. Requires a 100 % deposit of the annual rental bid for grazing land or $20 per acre for crop‑share agricultural bids; the deposit is applied to the first‑year rental and returned if unused.

2. Allows agricultural leases issued by competitive bidding to be awarded as cash leases (dollars per acre) if the bid exceeds one‑third crop share; the lease may later be renewed on a crop‑share basis.
3. Permits cash lease renewals for improved irrigation land at a minimum of $15 per acre.

4. Sets new payment deadlines and penalties: cash or crop‑share rentals must be paid by November 15 (or March 1 for grazing) with a $25 penalty for late payment and lease cancellation if unpaid by December 31 (or April 1).
5. Adds a 30‑day reinstatement option for canceled leases with a penalty not less than $500 and not more than three times the annual rental.
6. Directs forfeited deposits and penalties to the state’s interest and income trust account.
affected: state Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
numbers: $15 per acre minimum cash lease renewal

HB81.one_line: HB 81 expands veteran services duties and moves the administrator’s supervision to the Adjutant General.
HB81.summary: HB 81 amends the Veterans’ Affairs Division’s duties and shifts the supervisor of its administrator from the Board of Veterans’ Affairs to the Adjutant General. It expands the board’s responsibilities for veteran services, advocacy, information, grant‑seeking, and reporting, and requires the Adjutant General to hire an administrator to carry out those duties.
changes: Amends Section 10‑2‑102 to broaden the Board’s duties in veteran services, advocacy, information programs, grant seeking, and reporting.
Adds a requirement that the Board’s administrator be hired by the Adjutant General rather than the Board itself.
Specifies that Board employees must be state residents, preferably former military personnel, and that disabled veterans receive employment preference.
Requires the administrator to implement the expanded duties and report biennially to the governor, Department of Military Affairs, and other stakeholders.

HB82.one_line: HB 82 creates a new grooming offense, expands child‑porn laws, and tightens penalties for child sexual crimes.
HB82.summary: HB 82 creates a new crime of grooming a child for a sexual offense, expands existing child‑sexual‑offense statutes to cover computer‑generated child pornography and law‑enforcement officers who are believed to be children, and tightens penalties for many child‑sexual‑offense crimes. The bill takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Adds a new offense: grooming of a child for a sexual offense, with penalties up to 100 years and mandatory treatment for certain offenders
Rewrites sexual‑abuse of children to include possession of computer‑generated child pornography and to impose life or up to 100‑year sentences for victims 12 or younger
Amends indecent exposure, prostitution, child‑sex trafficking, obscenity, and other statutes to include victims who are minors or believed to be minors, and to increase fines and prison terms
Replaces the definition of sexual conduct and adds detailed definitions for grooming, electronic communication, and computer‑generated child pornography
Revises the sexual‑offender registration and risk‑level system (46‑23‑502, 46‑23‑509) to require psychosexual evaluations and to allow petitions to change risk levels
Adds new penalties for obscenity involving minors, including fines up to $1,000 and jail up to 6 months

HB83.one_line: Creates a special revenue account for the Missing Indigenous Persons Task Force, allowing deposits and a $1 appropriation.
HB83.summary: HB 83 creates a special revenue account for the Missing Indigenous Persons Task Force, allows any lawful funds to be deposited, and authorizes a $1 appropriation for the Department of Justice. The account is subject to audit and must be used only for costs approved by the task force. The act takes effect July 1 2025 and expires June 30 2033.
changes: Establishes a dedicated account in the state special revenue fund for the Missing Indigenous Persons Task Force.
Permits deposits from gifts, grants, donations, securities, and other assets, public or private.
Requires that all funds be used only for allowable costs as determined by the Department of Justice and approved by the task force.
Mandates that interest, income, and any unspent money remain in the account.
Provides a $1 appropriation to the Department of Justice for the biennium beginning July 1 2025.
Orders the Secretary of State to notify each federally recognized tribal government of the act.
Codifies the account provisions as part of Title 44, Chapter 2, Part 4.
Sets effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2033.
affected: Federally recognized tribal governments in Montana

HB84.one_line: HB 84 establishes a prescribed‑fire‑manager program, limits liability, and requires permits for prescribed fires.
HB84.summary: HB 84 creates a state‑approved prescribed‑fire‑manager certification program, limits liability for certified managers and landowners who follow the rules, and establishes a special revenue account and permit requirements for prescribed fires. The bill amends existing fire‑law sections to reflect these changes and requires a study of a claims fund. The act takes effect upon passage, with some provisions contingent on funding approval.
changes: Establishes a prescribed‑fire‑manager certification program with training, standards, fees, and reciprocity rules.
Provides that certified managers and landowners are not liable for wildfire damage unless negligence or fault is proven.
Creates a special revenue account within the state special revenue fund to hold money for program administration and claim payments.
Requires a written permit from the recognized agency before any prescribed fire may be ignited or set, except for small recreational fires under specific conditions.
Amends civil penalty and liability sections (50‑63‑102, 50‑63‑103) to exclude certified managers under the new liability standard.
Amends permit and compliance sections (76‑13‑121, 76‑13‑122) to codify the new permit requirements and enforcement.
Mandates the department to study the feasibility of a prescribed‑fire claims fund and its coverage of property damage.
Sets an effective‑date contingency: Sections 5 and 11 become effective only after legislative appropriation of funds to the special revenue account.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Property owners potentially affected by prescribed fires
HB84.effective: Effective on passage; Sections 5 and 11 contingent on appropriation

HB85.one_line: HB 85 restores former employer contributions for key public‑employee retirement systems, sets judges’ rate to 0 % and provides appropriations.
HB85.summary: HB 85 restores the former employer contribution rates for the judges’, highway patrol officers’, sheriffs’, and game wardens’/peace officers’ retirement systems, sets a 0 % employer contribution for judges, and provides appropriations and retroactive application. The bill amends several statutory sections to implement the new rates, defines actuarial and funding terms, and specifies effective dates.
changes: Restores the former employer contribution rates for the judges’, highway patrol officers’, sheriffs’, and game wardens’/peace officers’ retirement systems.
Sets the employer contribution rate for the judges’ retirement system to 0 %.
Provides appropriations of $4,010,436 and $713,013 from the general fund for the highway patrol employer contribution.
Specifies that the changes are effective July 1 2025 and retroactively apply to employer contribution rates from July 1 2023.

HB87.one_line: DFWP land now taxed like private owners; counties reimbursed for those taxes.
HB87.summary: HB 87 requires the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (DFWP) to assess its land holdings for property tax just like any private owner, and it sets up a payment system to reimburse counties for those taxes. The bill amends tax‑exemption language and preserves existing exclusions while making the changes effective immediately and retroactive to the 2025 tax year.
changes: All DFWP‑owned land is now subject to property‑tax assessment by the Department of Revenue, treated as a private citizen would be assessed
County treasurers may request a tax‑warrant payment equal to the amount that would have been payable if the land were taxable; the DFWP director approves or disapproves the request

Payments to counties are limited: no payment for land purchased before May 10 2009 that totals less than 100 acres, or for land bought before that date for game/bird farms, fish hatcheries, or Title 23 lands
The bill amends §15‑6‑201 to preserve existing property‑exemption categories and clarifies definitions for tribal, church, and nonprofit exemptions
Section 87‑1‑603 is amended to specify the procedure for drawing warrants, the director’s authority, and the statutory appropriation for county payments
The act is effective upon passage and applies retroactively to property‑tax years beginning after December 31 2024
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

HB86.one_line: HB 86 creates a new distributor license and overhauls beer‑and‑wine wholesaling rules.
HB86.summary: HB 86 establishes a new “Beer and Table Wine Distribution Act” that creates a distributor’s license, sets licensing fees, and codifies rules for beer and table‑wine wholesaling, including service obligations, financial‑interest prohibitions, and record‑keeping.  It also revises many existing statutes, repeals older provisions, and adds new requirements for agreements between breweries, wineries, and distributors.
changes: Creates a new distributor’s license for beer, table wine, or sacramental wine with a $400 initial fee and a 6‑month expiration; license must be displayed at the licensed premises and any sub‑warehouse.
Imposes a $400 annual license fee for each beer or table‑wine distributor, and $200 for each winery; sets a range of other license fees based on location and type of license.
Mandates that distributors cannot have a financial interest in a retailer, cannot advance money for licenses or taxes, and cannot extend credit beyond 7 days to a retailer.

Requires written agreements of distributorship that set territory, brand selection, pricing authority, and a 60‑day written notice of termination; provides procedures for good‑cause disputes and arbitration.

Adds service‑obligation rules: a distributor must call on and offer its beer to at least 75 % of retailers in its territory every 3 weeks (or all available brands if the beer is not generally available).
Rewrites rules for shipping, storage, and delivery of beer and table wine, including new dock‑sales restrictions, alternative delivery arrangements, and record‑keeping requirements.
Repeals a large block of older sections (16‑3‑217 through 16‑4‑113) and replaces them with the new provisions above.
Creates new definitions (e.g., “agreement of distributorship,” “good cause”) and clarifies existing ones (e.g., “beer,” “table wine”).
Adds new reporting requirements for distributors and wine retailers (quarterly returns, inventory records).
Establishes penalties for violations (up to $1,500 civil penalty, license suspension or revocation, and potential criminal penalties for unlawful sales).
affected: Beer and table‑wine distributors, breweries, beer importers, wineries, wine importers, retailers, agency liquor stores, and the Montana Department of Revenue.

HB88.one_line: Allows automatic return of unclaimed property ≤$1,000 to verified owners.
HB88.summary: HB 88 amends Montana’s unclaimed‑property law to let the Department of Revenue automatically return property worth $1,000 or less to the apparent owner without a claim form, provided the owner’s identity is verified. The change applies immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §70‑9‑815 to allow the administrator to waive the claim‑file requirement for property ≤$1,000.
Specifies that the administrator may pay or deliver such property directly to the apparent owner if the owner’s identity and address are validated.
Requires the administrator to keep records of proof of ownership, identity, and that the property was returned.
Maintains the existing 90‑day claim review period and 30‑day delivery period for claims that are filed.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Property owners (individuals or entities) who are the apparent owners of unclaimed property worth $1,000 or less.
The Department of Revenue and its administrators who will process and document the automatic returns.

HB89.one_line: HB 89 sets a two‑year deadline for disaster‑tax relief claims and amends proration rules.
HB89.summary: HB 89 establishes a two‑year filing deadline for taxpayers to claim property‑tax relief after a natural disaster and amends the calculation method for prorated tax reductions.
changes: Amends §15‑16‑611 to set a 2‑year filing window for disaster‑related tax relief claims.
Revises the proration formula for calculating tax due on destroyed property and replaced personal property.
Adds a notification requirement for replacement personal property within 30 days to avoid penalties.
Defines “natural disaster” broadly, but excludes arson convictions from relief.
Keeps the immediate effective date upon passage.
Does not create new programs or funds.
Does not impose new taxes or fees.
affected: Property owners whose real or personal property is destroyed by a natural disaster
County treasurers who adjust tax bills

HB90.one_line: Mandates biennial reappraisal of non‑centrally assessed real property in Montana’s class 3, 4, 10.
HB90.summary: HB 90 requires all non‑centrally assessed real property in Montana’s class 3, 4, and 10 to be reappraised every two years, with the reappraisal cycle beginning January 1 2024 and retroactive to tax years after December 31 2024. The Department of Revenue will administer the program, conduct inspections, and provide taxpayers with inflation and tax‑rate information.
changes: All non‑centrally assessed real property in class 3, 4, and 10 must be revalued every two years (instead of annually for other property).
The reappraisal cycle is set to complete on December 31 of every second year, with effective values starting January 1 of the following year.
The Department of Revenue must adopt rules and a reappraisal plan, conduct inspections, permit reviews, sales‑data verification, and may use new technologies.
In each reappraisal notice, taxpayers receive CPI‑adjusted population data, personal‑income growth rates, and estimated annualized tax‑rate changes for the past decade.
The Department must publish this information in a general‑circulation newspaper in each county every even‑numbered year by the second Monday in October.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and applies retroactively to property‑tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
affected: Property owners in Montana’s class 3, 4, and 10 real‑property categories
numbers: second Monday in October publication deadline

HB91.one_line: Taxpayers may elect to receive Department of Revenue communications electronically, subject to department rules.
HB91.summary: Taxpayers may opt to receive all Department of Revenue communications electronically. The department must create rules to administer the option, and the law takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Allows taxpayers to elect electronic receipt of correspondence, letters, notices, and other communications from the Department of Revenue.
The department must adopt rules to administer the election and delivery of electronic communications.
The election is voluntary and only applies when the taxpayer chooses it on a department‑provided form.
The law is codified as part of Title 15, Chapter 1, Part 2 of the Montana Statutes.
The act becomes effective on the date it is passed and approved.

HB92.one_line: HB 92 revises alcohol‑law sections to clarify department powers, restrict sales, require fingerprints, and regulate license security interests.
HB92.summary: HB 92 amends several Montana alcohol‑law sections to clarify department duties, restrict wholesale sales to the public, tighten retailer purchase limits, require fingerprints for license applicants, and establish rules for security interests in licenses. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §16‑1‑302 to expand the Department of Revenue’s powers over liquor sales, licensing, and employee management;
Rewrites §16‑3‑233 to prohibit wholesalers from selling beer to the public except as allowed in §16‑3‑316;
Revises §16‑3‑301 to set stricter limits on retailer purchases, prohibit certain transfers, and require placards for under‑21 sales;
Amends §16‑4‑414 to mandate fingerprints and background checks for license applicants, location managers, and certain corporate officers;
Rewrites §16‑4‑801 to define and regulate security interests in alcoholic‑beverage licenses, including transfer procedures, lender rights, and notification requirements;
Provides an immediate effective date for all changes.

HB95.one_line: Allows closed‑season trapping of beavers/muskrats that damage structures, with permits and penalties.
HB95.summary: HB 95 amends Montana’s trapping law to allow hunting or trapping of beavers and muskrats during the closed season when they damage certain structures, and expands the list of protected structures to include rural and urban developments. It also sets penalties for violations and specifies an effective date of September 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §87‑6‑602 to permit trapping or hunting of beavers or muskrats during the closed season if they cause severe injury or are a menace to irrigation works, stock water ponds, or rural/urban developed structures, provided a permit is obtained from the director (except June 1‑Aug 31 when no permit is needed).
Requires a permit for all other circumstances, except the June‑Aug exemption.
Adds rural and urban developed structures to the list of protected structures.
Sets penalties: fines $100‑$1,000, up to 6 months in county jail, loss of hunting/fishing/trapping license for 24 months, confiscation of unlawful pelts, and possible restitution orders.
affected: Irrigation project or district employees and landowners
Owners or employees of entities with rural or urban developed structures
Anyone who hunts or traps beavers or muskrats during the closed season without a permit (outside June‑Aug)

HB96.one_line: HB 96 creates a trapping apprentice certificate and expands apprentice hunting rules with mentor requirements.
HB96.summary: HB 96 creates a trapping apprentice certificate, expands the existing apprentice hunting certificate to include trapping, sets mentor requirements, and adjusts which licenses and tags apprentices may obtain. It also amends rules on hunter safety courses and supplemental game‑damage licenses.
changes: Creates a new apprentice trapping certificate that allows holders to use Class C or Class C‑2 trapping licenses for up to two years before completing a formal trapper education course.
Revises the apprentice hunting certificate to permit use of hunting and trapping licenses, but limits certain high‑value or restricted licenses (e.g., black bear, mountain lion, elk under 15).

Establishes mentor eligibility criteria: at least 21 years old, must hold a current hunting or trapping license, must have completed the appropriate safety course, and must supervise the apprentice at all times.
Adds a $5 fee for the apprentice certificate, deposited into a state special revenue fund for hunter education.
Amends Section 87‑2‑520 to clarify issuance of supplemental game‑damage licenses, including that apprentices may receive such licenses in unlimited‑quota districts.
Modifies Section 87‑2‑105 to expand hunter safety course requirements and to allow apprentices to obtain certain licenses without a full safety course if they hold an apprentice certificate.
affected: Trappers and hunters 10 + years old who have not yet completed safety courses
Mentors (hunters or trappers) who supervise apprentices
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (for fee collection and rulemaking)
License holders who may be restricted from certain high‑value licenses while apprentices
numbers: 2 license years before completing safety course
January 1 1985 birth cutoff for safety course requirement

HB97.one_line: MDOT must study, rule, and permit truck platooning with new fees and licensing requirements.
HB97.summary: The bill requires the Montana Department of Transportation (MDOT) to study whether truck platooning can be safely practiced in the state, then, if feasible, to develop rules and standards. It amends the state’s special‑permit fee schedule and adds a new category of special permit for platooned trucks, with associated fees and licensing requirements for lead‑vehicle operators.
changes: MDOT must conduct a feasibility study on platooning, considering terrain, weather, and communication networks.
If the study finds platooning safe, MDOT must draft and adopt rules and standards, after consulting stakeholders.
The bill creates a new special‑permit category for platooned truck operations, with a $200 term fee or $20 per trip fee.
It amends Section 61‑10‑124 to include platooning permits and clarifies fee amounts for various special permits.
Lead‑vehicle conductors and anyone who could take control of a platooned vehicle must hold a commercial driver’s license.
The bill does not set an effective date; it is to be codified as part of Title 61.
affected: Stakeholders in transportation and law enforcement
numbers: $20 per trip fee for platoon permit
$10 per trip fee for other special permits
$75 per term fee for other special permits
$125 term fee for certain over‑length permits
$20 per trip fee for truck‑trailer‑trailer permits

HB98.one_line: HB 98 revises hunting‑license rules, adds validation, and expands penalties for unlawful possession.
HB98.summary: HB 98 amends Montana’s hunting and fishing license laws to clarify who may physically control a license, to require license holders to validate their licenses, and to impose penalties for unlawful possession and use of licenses, including special rules for spouses, minors, and commercial operators.
changes: Amends §87‑6‑304 to clarify limits on multiple licenses, replacement‑license use, and validation requirements for the license holder; adds fines and imprisonment provisions for violations.

Amends §87‑6‑305 to define unlawful possession of a valid, unused license or permit, with an exception for a spouse or minor and for electronically issued licenses; expands penalties for commercial activities involving multiple licenses.
Adds a new validation requirement that the license holder must validate the license before use.
Provides that violations can result in forfeiture of current hunting, fishing, or trapping licenses and loss of recreational privilege for a court‑set period.
Specifies that felony violations for commercial operators carry up to $50,000 fine, 5‑year state‑prison term, and up to life revocation of hunting privilege.
Makes the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Spouses and minors who may physically control a spouse’s or minor’s license
Commercial operators (taxidermists, meat processors, outfitters, guides)
numbers: 3‑year to life revocation for commercial operators

HB100.one_line: Standardizes state‑agency public‑records rules, caps fees, sets deadlines, and creates a court remedy.
HB100.summary: HB 100 standardizes Montana’s public‑records rules for state agencies, setting uniform response times, fee limits, and a 2‑year public‑access record retention. It also gives citizens a court remedy when a non‑local state agency misses a deadline.
changes:
Imposes a 5‑day acknowledgment and 90‑day (or 6‑month) response deadline for executive‑branch agencies; local governments are exempt from the 90‑day rule but must still respond promptly.  
Sets fee caps: first hour free, thereafter $25 per hour, with a $5 filing fee for non‑specific requests; limits total fees to actual costs.  
Requires agencies to publish a public‑information request process, statistics, and all requests/responses on a state website for 2 years, except for requests for personal data or already‑public information.  
Allows a person to file a district‑court complaint if a non‑local agency fails to meet the response deadline or denies a request without written explanation.  
Adds a termination date: the act ends June 30 2026, with sections 2 and 3 effective July 1 2026 and the rest effective October 1 2025.
affected: State agencies (executive branch and local governments)

HB102.one_line: HB 102 reorganizes the public defender system, adds a conflict division, and expands reporting and training duties.
HB102.summary: HB 102 revises the Montana Public Defender Act to clarify duties, create a separate conflict‑defender division, and streamline reporting and training. It removes a child‑abuse‑specific standard, expands the central services division’s role, and updates titles and reporting requirements for all divisions.
changes: Creates a conflict‑defender division and a conflict defender division administrator who may not handle cases but hires and supervises conflict public defenders.
Rewrites duties of the director, conflict, appellate, and central services division administrators to include strategic planning, caseload management, training, complaint handling, and reporting.
Removes the director’s obligation to establish child‑abuse‑and‑neglect standards and instead requires child‑case standards to be set by the director under a new subsection.
Expands the central services division’s responsibilities to manage eligibility, contracting, training, and budgeting, and makes all contracting exempt from the Montana Procurement Act.
Adds detailed reporting requirements for the biennial report and annual fiscal‑year report, including caseload, staffing, training, and expenditure data.
Replaces titles such as “regional public defender” with “regional public defender” and “managing public defender” for consistency.
Repeals sections 47‑1‑120 (training program coordinator) and 47‑1‑121 (contracted services) and codifies the new provisions.
Adjusts the structure of regional offices, deputy regional public defenders, and appellate defender division to align with the new administrative hierarchy.
affected: State public defender staff (directors, administrators, attorneys, non‑attorney staff)
Contracted public defenders and service providers
Courts and defendants who receive public defender services
State budget and finance offices (new reporting)
numbers: minimum client caseloads set by director
no county/city obligation for regional office expenses

HB104.one_line: HB 104 expands agent powers to investigate human trafficking, prostitution, and internet crimes against children.
HB104.summary: HB 104 expands the investigative powers of state agents, giving them concurrent jurisdiction over human trafficking, prostitution, and internet crimes against children, and clarifies the definition of those offenses.
changes: Amends §44‑2‑115 to define an agent as a peace officer who can assist law‑enforcement agencies and investigate a broader list of crimes.
Adds concurrent jurisdiction for agents to investigate human trafficking, prostitution, and internet crimes against children.
Provides a statutory definition of “internet crimes against children” covering several sexual‑offense categories.
Keeps existing agent duties such as investigating gambling, audit‑disclosed violations, and state‑workers’ compensation referrals.
Allows agents to assist in law‑enforcement training when requested.
affected: State agents appointed by the attorney general
City, county, state, and federal law‑enforcement agencies
Victims and perpetrators of human trafficking, prostitution, and internet crimes against children

HB105.one_line: HB 105 sets a $300 game‑bird‑farm fee, extends licenses to five years, and tightens record‑keeping.
HB105.summary: HB 105 revises Montana’s game‑bird‑farm statutes, simplifying licensing, setting a $300 fee, extending the license term to five years, and tightening record‑keeping. The bill removes some notification requirements and changes application timelines, but it does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Sets a $300 game‑bird‑farm license fee and annual renewal fee, deposited into the state special revenue fund.
Extends the license term to five years (expires February 28 of the fifth year).

Requires applicants to submit a written application on a department‑provided form with specific information (name, address, species, land description, fence type, bird source, and resident agent for non‑residents).
The department must decide on an application within 30–60 days, approving it if fencing is incomplete but requiring completion before operation.
Licensees must keep detailed records of birds purchased, transferred, or sold, and file an annual report by January 31; records must be kept for at least five years.
Licensees must notify the department of any proposed changes in species, size, or location of the enclosure before implementation.
The bill amends sections 87‑4‑902, 87‑4‑904, 87‑4‑905, 87‑4‑906, and 87‑4‑912 to reflect these changes.
affected: Game‑bird‑farm owners and operators (both residents and non‑residents).
The Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (DFWPA).
Warden and director staff responsible for inspections and record reviews.

HB106.one_line: HB 106 tightens preserve rules, raises fees, and streamlines reporting while removing some harvest limits.
HB106.summary: HB 106 revises Montana’s shooting‑preserve laws to tighten land‑use rules, raise license fees, and streamline reporting, while eliminating certain harvest limits and the game‑recovery restriction. The bill requires preserves to be on private property, imposes higher fees, and mandates record‑keeping and tagging for all harvested game. It also removes the 100‑bird release requirement and the 87‑4‑523 game‑recovery limits, but keeps enforcement penalties for violations.
changes: Preserves must be entirely on private property and no larger than 2,560 contiguous acres.
License fee increased to $100 for the first 320 acres plus $40 for each additional 160‑acre block (or fraction).
The 100‑bird minimum release requirement in §87‑4‑522(2) is removed.
The game‑recovery restriction in §87‑4‑523 is repealed.
Operators must post exterior boundary signs every 250 ft or less and at least two signs total.
All harvested game must be tagged with a self‑sealing tag and a harvest form; the department supplies tags and forms at nominal cost.
Violations of hunting or tagging rules can result in fines of $50‑$1,000, up to 6 months imprisonment, and possible forfeiture of hunting privileges.
affected: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

HB108.one_line: Eliminates the need for a supplemental manual for unlisted agricultural equipment in property valuations.
HB108.summary: HB 108 amends Montana’s property‑valuation rules so that the Department of Revenue no longer must create a supplemental manual for agricultural implements and machinery that are missing from official guides. The changes clarify how market value is determined for these items and other property classes.
changes: Replaces §15‑8‑111 with a new definition of market value and specifies depreciation handling.
States that agricultural implements and machinery are valued at the average wholesale value in national guides; if no guide exists, a supplemental manual is no longer required.
Adds detailed appraisal procedures for class‑four residential and commercial properties, including condominium units.
Clarifies that assessed value equals appraised value and that taxable value is market value times the class tax rate.
Specifies that land and improvements are separately assessed under certain ownership or location conditions.
Defines “compelling reason” for using the cost approach in residential valuation.
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

HB107.one_line: HB 107 revises licensing, records, and fees for taxidermists, fur dealers, fur farms, exotic‑wildlife owners, and wildlife facilities, effective March 1 2026.
HB107.summary: HB 107 revises licensing and record‑keeping for taxidermists, fur dealers, fur farms, exotic‑wildlife owners, and wildlife menageries, sanctuaries, and zoos. It sets new license‑expiration dates, establishes fees, and requires detailed written records that must be kept for specified periods. The act also authorizes the Department to adopt rules for exotic‑wildlife permits and sets fee schedules for those permits.
changes: Taxidermists must obtain a license, pay a $50 annual fee, and keep written records of all wildlife articles for the longer of the time the articles are in possession or five years; licenses expire Feb 28 each year.
Fur dealers must keep a detailed transaction book for at least one year after license expiration and for as long as furs remain in possession; the book must be open to inspection.

Wildlife menageries, sanctuaries, and zoos must obtain permits, pay $10 (≤5 animals) or $25 (>5 animals) annually, and keep a five‑year record; permits expire Dec 31 and are valid through Feb 28 of the following year.

Fur farms must pay an $85 annual license fee, keep records for five years, and renew by paying the fee and submitting required reports; expired licenses after one year are treated as new applications.
Exotic‑wildlife owners must obtain a department permit (fee $125 for possession/renewal, $500 for sale/breeding/exchange) and keep records; permits expire Feb 28 of the fifth year.
The Department and Commission are granted authority to adopt rules for exotic‑wildlife importation, possession, sale, and control, including lists of controlled and prohibited species.
affected: Owners of wildlife menageries, sanctuaries, and zoos

HB109.one_line: Amends non‑exclusive‑practice clauses for behavioral‑health professionals and corrects code citations.
HB109.summary: HB 109 amends Montana’s professional‑licensing law to correct typographical errors and clarify the scope of non‑exclusive‑practice clauses for several behavioral‑health professions. It also directs a renumbering of a code section. No new programs or funds are created.
changes: Amends §28‑2‑724, MCA, to clarify that employment or partnership contracts cannot restrict a health‑care provider’s right to practice, treat, or solicit patients after termination, for the listed professions (psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, professional counselors, addiction counselors, marriage‑and‑family therapists, and behavioral‑health peer‑support specialists).
Specifies that the prohibition applies to contracts with the listed professions and does not apply to contracts related to the sale or purchase of a practice.
Directs the code commissioner to renumber §37‑23‑104 into Title 37, Chapter 39 (a clerical code change).
affected: Licensed psychiatrists, addiction‑medicine physicians, psychologists, social workers, professional counselors, addiction counselors, marriage‑and‑family therapists, behavioral‑health peer‑support specialists, employers of these professionals, and their patients

HB110.one_line: HB 110 eliminates single‑copy sales, mandates electronic documents, and updates fee procedures for legislative materials.
HB110.summary: HB 110 removes the Legislative Services Division’s obligation to sell single copies of bills, resolutions, and amendments and eliminates a subscription service for status sheets. It requires the division to provide electronic versions of all legislative documents and modifies fee‑collection procedures for complete sets of proceedings.
changes: Eliminates the sale of single copies of bills, resolutions, and amendments
Eliminates the subscription service for daily status sheets
Mandates that the Legislative Services Division supply electronic versions of every bill, resolution, and amendment
Amends §5‑11‑212, MCA to clarify fees for complete sets of proceedings and mailing
Requires the executive director to account for all funds collected and remit them to the state treasurer
Keeps the ability to sell complete sets of proceedings and status sheets, but now only in electronic form unless mailed
No new program or office is created
No criminal offense is added
affected: Legislators and staff who purchase documents
Members of the public who buy single copies

HB111.one_line: Montana adopts the Uniform Electronic Legal Material Act, requiring authentication, preservation, and public access to official electronic legal materials.
HB111.summary: Montana adopts the Uniform Electronic Legal Material Act, requiring official publishers to authenticate, preserve, and make publicly accessible electronic legal materials and to follow national standards. The act also clarifies how the Montana Code Annotated is treated as the official law and limits its interaction with federal e‑signature law.
changes: Official publishers must designate electronic records as official and authenticate them so users can verify they are unaltered.
Authenticated records are presumed accurate, and contesting the authenticity requires a preponderance of evidence.
Publishers must preserve and secure official electronic records, ensuring integrity, backup, disaster recovery, and continued usability.
Publishers must make official electronic legal materials reasonably available to the public on a permanent basis.
Publishers must follow national standards for authentication, preservation, security, and public access, and consider user needs and compatibility with other states.
The Montana Code Annotated is treated as a continuation of the Revised Codes, not a new enactment, and its editorial material is not part of the law.
affected: Official publishers of Montana legal materials (code commissioner, legislative services division)
Members of the public accessing Montana legal materials
Courts and attorneys relying on electronic legal materials
Montana legislative process regarding the Code Annotated

HB114.one_line: HB 114 expands consumer‑protection rules for insurance and financial‑planning activities, adding disclosure, record‑keeping, and anti‑deceptive advertising requirements.
HB114.summary: HB 114 tightens consumer‑protection rules for insurance and financial‑planning activities, adding disclosure and fee‑agreement requirements for producers, expanding definitions of lead generators, and tightening claim‑settlement and advertising standards. It also imposes new record‑keeping and disclosure duties on insurers and lenders.
changes: Insurance producers must disclose they are also producers and that they will receive a commission when offering financial‑planning services, and they may not charge extra fees without a signed written agreement.
Producers may not present themselves as financial planners unless they hold a recognized certification or designation.

Lead‑generating devices that compile or qualify lists of potential health‑insurance customers are defined and regulated; producers may not use such devices to solicit or sell health insurance without a license.
Unfair claim‑settlement practices are expanded; insurers may not misrepresent coverage, delay investigations, or offer settlements below a reasonable amount.
False or deceptive advertising of insurance policies is prohibited; insurers cannot misrepresent benefits, dividends, or financial condition.
Lenders and depository institutions are barred from conditioning credit on purchasing insurance from a particular insurer or producer, and must disclose that borrowers can choose insurers.
Insurers and health‑insurance lead generators must keep detailed complaint records for five years and provide them to the commissioner upon request.

HB115.one_line: HB 115 expands the Montana Code Commissioner’s publication duties and reporting requirements.
HB115.summary: HB 115 amends Montana’s code‑commissioner duties, clarifies definitions, and expands the materials the commissioner must publish with the Montana Code Annotated. It also requires the commissioner to report on recommended legislative changes and to maintain an ongoing recodification program.
changes: Amends §1‑11‑101 to define "Code," "Publication," and "Recodify" and to list specific recodification tasks;
Amends §1‑11‑204 to require the commissioner to submit a pre‑session report recommending elimination of archaic, redundant, duplicated, or unclear laws;

Mandates the commissioner to prepare and publish a wide range of materials with the Code—including statutory histories, court‑decision annotations, editorial notes, the Declaration of Independence, U.S. Constitution, Montana Constitution, federal‑state relations ordinances, court procedure rules, and various indexes;
Requires the commissioner to annotate, arrange, and recodify new laws each session, assign catchlines and section numbers, and publish an annual “Official Report of the Montana Code Commissioner”;
Allows the commissioner to recodify the Code title‑by‑title as needed;
Authorizes periodic consultation with judges and the state bar on recodification procedures.

HB118.one_line: Amends Montana’s compact participation, sets assessment formula, creates commission, and establishes enrollment and funding rules.
HB118.summary: The bill amends Montana’s participation in the Interstate Compact on Educational Opportunity for Military Children, clarifying how the state’s annual assessment is calculated and updating statutory references. It establishes a state‑level commission and liaison, sets procedures for student enrollment, placement, and graduation, and creates an Interstate Commission with rule‑making and enforcement powers.
changes: Amends Section 20‑1‑230, MCA to incorporate the compact’s provisions into state law
Clarifies that Montana’s annual assessment equals a per‑student amount multiplied by the number of military‑family children in the state
Revises U.S. Code citations and other statutory references to match current law
Creates a state‑level “Interstate Commission on Educational Opportunity for Military Children” and a military‑family education liaison
Establishes procedures for rapid transfer of records, enrollment, placement, and graduation for military children
Provides for waivers of course requirements, immunization deadlines, and extracurricular participation
Sets rules for dispute resolution, default, and termination of state participation
Defines funding limits: assessment may not exceed $2 per student times the latest headcount
Requires annual audit of the Interstate Commission’s finances
Mandates immediate effective date upon passage
affected: Military families with school‑aged children in Montana

HB121.one_line: HB 121 mandates sex‑specific use of multi‑occupancy restrooms, changing rooms, and sleeping quarters in public and correctional facilities.
HB121.summary: HB 121 requires all multi‑occupancy restrooms, changing rooms and sleeping quarters in certain public and correctional facilities to be designated for either males or females and limits use to people of that sex, with specific exceptions for maintenance, medical and emergency services.  It creates a private cause of action for violations and applies immediately upon passage.
changes: Covered entities must label each multi‑occupancy restroom, changing room or sleeping quarter as exclusively for males or females.
Only individuals of the designated sex may use those spaces, except for custodial, medical, law‑enforcement, or emergency personnel.
Facilities must take reasonable steps to provide privacy from the opposite sex in these spaces.
The act allows covered entities to adopt ADA‑compliant policies, single‑occupancy facilities, or change a designation from one sex to the other.
Individuals who encounter the opposite sex in a designated space may sue for declaratory and injunctive relief, nominal damages, and attorney fees.
Claims must be filed within two years of the alleged violation.
affected: Correctional centers, juvenile detention facilities, local domestic‑violence programs, public buildings, and public schools.
Employees and residents of those facilities.
Students in public schools who share sleeping quarters.
numbers: exclusive use for males or females

HB120.one_line: Amends definitions to broaden clean‑energy criteria in multifamily property‑assessed financing.
HB120.summary: HB 120 amends the definitions in the Commercial Property‑Assessed Capital Enhancements Act to clarify what counts as an energy‑conservation measure, an energy‑conservation project, a renewable‑energy system, and related terms for multifamily financing. The bill does not create new programs or impose new costs.
changes: Amends Section 90‑4‑1302 to add detailed definitions for "Energy conservation measure," "Energy conservation project," "Renewable energy," and "Renewable energy system."
Clarifies that a "Multifamily housing facility" is a property with at least five residential units each having a full bathroom and kitchen.
Defines "Authority," "Program," "District," "Governing body," "Local government," "Person," "Real property," and "Record owner."
affected: Local governments (counties, cities, towns, consolidated city‑counties)
Record owners of commercial, industrial, or agricultural property
Persons, firms, partnerships, corporations, trusts involved in such properties

HB122.one_line: Adds natural‑gas pipelines to Montana’s right‑of‑way utility statutes.
HB122.summary: HB 122 amends Montana’s right‑of‑way statute to explicitly include natural‑gas pipelines, allowing utilities to install and operate lines on public roads, streets, and highways while ensuring they do not endanger or inconvenience the public. The amendment clarifies that the authority granted does not limit city or town council powers.
changes: Adds natural‑gas pipelines to the list of utilities authorized to use public right‑of‑way for installation and operation.
Specifies that such lines must be constructed so as not to endanger or inconvenience the public.
Affirms that the amendment does not restrict city or town council powers.
Retains the existing framework for telegraph, telephone, electric light, and electric power lines.
Maintains the requirement for necessary fixtures (posts, piers, abutments) for all lines and pipelines.
affected: Public bodies owning or operating such utilities

HB123.one_line: HB 123 revises self‑pour rules, permits electronic dispensing, and clarifies payment definitions for beer and wine.
HB123.summary: HB 123 amends Montana’s beer‑and‑wine self‑service rules to allow controlled self‑pouring, permits electronic dispensing devices, and clarifies that such payments are not gift certificates. It also revises premises requirements and adds application fees for certain storage and delivery arrangements.
changes: Redefines “self‑service” to exclude customer self‑pouring of beer and wine when the retailer, its employees, or a concessionaire has provided the alcohol and when the service is monitored or limited by an approved electronic device.
Allows licensed retailers to use electronic or technology‑based devices to dispense predetermined volumes of beer or wine, provided the device is monitored by the licensee or its employees.
Adds new provisions for non‑contiguous storage areas and for delivery/pre‑stocking of alcoholic beverages in hotel or short‑term lodging units, with a $100 application fee.
Permits on‑premises retailers adjacent to breweries or wineries to operate without permanent floor‑to‑ceiling walls, provided adequate physical separation and safeguards are in place.
Amends Section 30‑14‑102 to clarify that payments made through electronic devices for beer and wine do not constitute gift certificates, and expands the definition of “gift certificate.”
Requires licensees to demonstrate adequate safeguards (locks, gates, key‑card access, etc.) to prevent public access to alcohol after hours in various settings.
Provides that alterations to approved floorplans that do not increase square footage may be made without prior department approval, while increases require approval.
Sets a $100 fee for applications to approve non‑contiguous storage areas and for hotel delivery/pre‑stocking arrangements.
affected: Concessionaires and employees of licensed retailers
Brewery and winery operators adjacent to on‑premises retailers
Consumers purchasing beer and wine via electronic devices

HB125.one_line: Broadens election‑judge eligibility to all qualified county voters while preserving conflict‑of‑interest limits.
HB125.summary: HB 125 amends Montana’s school‑district election law to broaden who can serve as election judges. It allows any qualified registered voter in the county where the election is held to act as a judge, while keeping the existing restrictions on candidates and relatives.
changes: Amends §20‑20‑109 to permit election judges to be any qualified registered elector in the county, not just those in the school district;
Keeps the prohibition that judges cannot be a candidate, a direct relative of a candidate, or the spouse of a candidate or a relative of a candidate;
Requires all school‑district election judges to meet the training and certification standards set in §13‑4‑203;
Specifies that the act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval;
Does not create any new program, office, fund, or criminal offense.
affected: Qualified registered voters in counties holding school‑district elections
Candidates and their relatives in school‑district elections

HB126.one_line: HB 126 expands electronic comment, sponsor contact, and justification requirements for Montana rule‑making.
HB126.summary: HB 126 modernizes Montana’s rule‑making process by requiring agencies to accept and publish public comments electronically, giving legislators and the public more notice and opportunities to comment, and tightening the record‑keeping and justification required for adopting rules.
changes: Agencies must accept public comment via email and disclose their email address in rule‑making notices and other public channels.
Agencies must send a copy of each proposal notice to the appropriate administrative rule review committee and to the Secretary of State for publication.

Agencies must provide a concise statement of reasons for and against each rule, including any differences between the proposal and the final rule, and must publish the primary sponsor’s unredacted comments if the sponsor’s comments are not incorporated.
The notice of proposed rulemaking must include an estimate of the total monetary impact and the number of people affected when a fee or benefit is proposed.
Agencies must give at least 30 days’ written notice of a proposed rule and at least 20 days’ notice of a hearing, with additional notice if a hearing is held.
The bill imposes a 6‑month window for publishing the adoption notice and restricts rule adoption between Oct 1 and Dec 31 unless an exemption applies.
The bill requires agencies to keep a list of interested persons and to inform them of the list in the proposal notice.
The bill requires agencies to cite the specific statutory authority and section of the Montana Code that the rule implements.

The bill requires agencies to contact the primary sponsor of the legislation that the rule implements at least 10 days before publishing the proposal notice and to publish the sponsor’s comments if not adopted.
affected: Members of the public who comment on rulemaking

HB127.one_line: HB 127 revises the fire‑suppression account, adds transfer rules, and mandates annual reporting.
HB127.summary: HB 127 amends the fire‑suppression account to eliminate specific date references, expands the list of allowable uses, adds new transfer rules tied to general‑fund balances, and requires annual reporting by the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation.
changes: Amends § 76‑13‑150 to remove dated appropriations and broaden permissible uses of the account (e.g., fuel reduction, forest restoration, equipment grants, road maintenance, fire preparedness).

Adds transfer provisions that move money from the general fund to the fire‑suppression account when the general‑fund ending balance exceeds 8.3 % of general‑revenue appropriations, and limits the account balance to 6 % of those appropriations in even‑year fiscal years.

Allows the account to spend up to 1 % of general‑revenue appropriations (and up to 5 % of that for collaborative groups) when the account balance exceeds 3 % of those appropriations in odd‑year fiscal years.
Provides a statutory appropriation of up to 0.5 % of general‑revenue appropriations each year for fire‑preparedness items.
Requires the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation to report, by November 1 each fiscal year, expenditures made under each subsection of § 76‑13‑150(4).
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Local governments involved in federal forest litigation

HB128.one_line: HB 128 protects volunteer emergency‑service employees from wrongful termination after probation.
HB128.summary: HB 128 bars employers from firing employees who serve as volunteer emergency‑service providers after probation, unless the employee’s absence would jeopardize public safety.  Employees must notify employers and cannot claim regular pay for volunteer‑service absences.  Violations give employees a civil remedy for reinstatement and damages.
changes: 1. Requires written notification of volunteer service within 30 days of becoming a volunteer, joining a unit, or being hired. 2. Prohibits termination of a volunteer‑service employee after probation unless the employee’s absence would imperil public safety or essential functions. 3. Allows employers to require prior authorization for emergency absences that could endanger safety. 4. Empowers employers to request a written statement from the volunteer organization confirming the emergency response. 5. Prohibits employees from receiving regular pay for time spent on volunteer duties; pay may be deducted if claimed. 6. Provides a civil action under § 39‑2‑904 for wrongful termination, with possible reinstatement, back wages, fringe benefits, seniority rights, and attorney‑fee recovery. 7. Defines “volunteer emergency services provider” as a volunteer firefighter, enrolled volunteer fire‑department member, or volunteer EMT not paid full‑time by the entity where services are rendered.
who_is_affected':['public and private employers','employees who serve as volunteer firefighters or EMTs','volunteer emergency‑service organizations'],
affected: employees who serve as volunteer firefighters or EMTs

HB129.one_line: Provides a $3,000 deduction for qualified volunteer firefighters and emergency‑care providers, adjusted for inflation.
HB129.summary: HB 129 creates a Montana income‑tax deduction for qualified volunteer firefighters and emergency‑care providers, limits the deduction to full‑service volunteers, and increases the deduction each year by an inflation factor. The deduction is available for tax years beginning after December 31 2025 and takes effect January 1 2026.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2120 to add a new subtraction (3)(o) of $3,000 for each qualified volunteer firefighter or emergency‑care provider.
The subtraction is increased annually by the inflation factor, effective for tax years beginning after 2026.
The deduction is limited to volunteers who are active, non‑paid members for the entire calendar year and have completed the required training hours.
The deduction is available only for five consecutive years after a person becomes a Montana resident (or remains a resident after receiving military pension).
The act specifies that the deduction is not available if claimed before becoming a non‑resident.
The deduction is applied only to income tax years beginning after December 31 2025 and is effective January 1 2026.
The department of revenue is directed to update the subtraction amount in 15‑30‑2120(3)(o) and apply the inflation adjustment for years beginning after December 31 2026.
The act terminates the subtraction for volunteers on June 30 2025 and other related provisions on December 31 2033.
affected: Montana residents who qualify for the deduction

HB130.one_line: HB 130 lets Montana bill federal agencies for suppression costs within five miles of state or county fire‑protection activities.
HB130.summary: HB 130 revises Montana’s wildfire policy to emphasize public and firefighter safety, rapid suppression, and interagency cooperation. It allows the state to bill federal agencies for suppression costs within five miles of state or county fire‑protection activities and clarifies responsibilities for private owners and land managers.
changes: Amends § 76‑13‑115 to add language on safety, rapid attack, and interagency coordination.
Adds a provision that the Department may bill the responsible federal protection agency for costs incurred in suppression when appropriate.
Clarifies that all private property owners and federal/state public land agencies must manage resources and mitigate fire hazards.
Reinforces the duty of the Department to engage in suppression regardless of policy.
Specifies that catastrophic wildland fire from inadequate federal land management threatens Montana’s constitutional right to a clean environment.
Provides immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: State Department of Natural Resources (fire suppression duties)
Federal and state public land management agencies

HB135.one_line: HB 135 limits appraisal‑related claims to 5 or 8 years, depending on the applicable statute of repose.
HB135.summary: HB 135 establishes a five‑year statute of repose for most claims against real‑estate appraisers, firms, and appraisal‑management companies, with an eight‑year period for claims that fall under the existing 27‑2‑202(1) limitation. The bill codifies these limits in Title 27 and defines key terms.
changes: Creates a 5‑year statute of repose for damages or relief arising from an appraisal or appraisal review, unless the claim is governed by the 8‑year period in 27‑2‑202(1).
Provides an 8‑year limitation for claims that fall under the existing 27‑2‑202(1) period.
Clarifies that the new limits do not extend the general period prescribed by Montana law.
Defines “appraisal,” “appraisal review,” “real‑estate appraisal firm,” “appraisal management company,” and “real‑estate appraiser” for the purposes of the statute.
Codifies the new limits as part of Title 27, Chapter 2, Part 2.
affected: Litigants seeking damages for appraisal‑related claims

HB136.one_line: Allows insurers to give written discounts for homeowner fire‑, wind‑ or hail‑preventative measures.
HB136.summary: The bill lets insurers give homeowners a written discount or credit for installing fire‑, wind‑ or hail‑preventative measures, without treating it as a mid‑term rate hike. It also updates rate‑filing rules and clarifies that such discounts are not prohibited rebates. No new program or fund is created.
changes: Allows insurers to offer a written benefit or premium reduction to homeowners who take specified fire‑, wind‑ or hail‑preventative actions.
The discount must be disclosed in writing and is not considered a mid‑term premium increase.
Amends §33‑15‑1108 to permit insurers to provide these reductions while still limiting mid‑term rate changes.
Amends §33‑16‑203 to require that rates filed may include a premium reduction for the new preventative‑measure benefit.
Amends §33‑18‑210 to exempt these benefits from the general prohibition on rebates, making them legal under the statute.
numbers: Rates filed must include reductions for 55‑year‑olds and Montana National Guard members

HB137.one_line: Standardizes salesperson and adviser fees, eliminating in‑state/out‑of‑state differences, and applies retroactively to 2019.
HB137.summary: HB 137 eliminates the fee difference between in‑state and out‑of‑state salespersons and investment adviser representatives, standardizing registration and renewal fees for all. It also sets a retroactive effective date for fees paid since May 9 2019.
changes: Standardizes the fee for registering a salesperson or investment adviser representative to $100 for both in‑state and out‑of‑state, eliminating the former $50 in‑state rate.
Keeps the $400 fee for broker‑dealer or investment adviser registration and renewals unchanged.
Applies the new fee schedule retroactively to fees paid on or after May 9 2019.
Maintains existing fee structures for securities registration, notice filings, and other related fees.
Specifies that fees collected from March 7 2013 through June 30 2027 are deposited in a special revenue account, with a shift to the general fund after July 1 2027.
Allows a salesperson who paid a fee before the act’s effective date to avoid paying again for the same registration, renewal, or transfer.
Provides that overpayments above $10 may be refunded.
Sets the act’s effective date as passage and approval.
affected: Salespersons and investment adviser representatives (both in‑state and out‑of‑state)
Issuers of securities and investment companies
Commissioners and state departments handling securities registration
numbers: $100 fee for all salespersons and investment adviser reps
$400 fee for broker‑dealer/investment adviser registration and renewals
$50 fee for name changes of investment‑company series
March 7 2013 – June 30 2027 special revenue account period

HB140.one_line: HB 140 provides income‑based property‑tax relief for injured first responders and their surviving spouses.
HB140.summary: HB 140 creates a property‑tax‑reduction program for first responders who are injured in the line of duty and for spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty.  It sets income‑based tax‑rate multipliers, establishes eligibility rules, and gives the Department of Revenue authority to administer and verify the program.
changes: Creates a new property‑tax‑reduction program for qualified first responders and surviving spouses; sets income‑based multiplier tables for single, married, and head‑of‑household applicants; requires primary‑residence ownership and a letter from the employer for deceased responders; mandates annual income verification and adjustment of income limits using the PCE inflation factor; expands rule‑making authority for the Department of Revenue under Sections 15‑6‑301, 15‑6‑302, and 15‑6‑312; applies to property‑tax years beginning January 1, 2026.
The program remains in effect as long as income limits are met and the property is the primary residence.
The Department of Revenue must file applications by April 15, conduct annual verifications, and may award the greatest benefit available.
The bill amends existing tax‑assistance statutes to incorporate the new program and its rules.
affected: Qualified first responders injured in the line of duty
Spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty
County treasurers and the Department of Revenue

HB141.one_line: Allows nonprofits and schools to accept credit cards for raffles while keeping prize limits and ticket‑sale restrictions.
HB141.summary: The bill amends Montana’s gambling statutes to permit nonprofit organizations, colleges, universities, and school districts to accept credit‑card payments for raffle tickets. It also clarifies definitions of credit gambling and internet gambling so that these entities can use credit cards for raffles while maintaining existing limits on prize values and ticket sales.
changes: Amends §23‑5‑112 to update definitions related to credit gambling and internet gambling for nonprofit raffles.
Revises §23‑5‑157 to allow credit‑card payments for raffle tickets (but not for other gambling activities) and clarifies that credit gambling remains prohibited elsewhere.

Amends §23‑5‑413 to exempt nonprofit, college, university, and school‑district raffles from the $5,000 prize limit and from the prohibition on credit‑card ticket sales, while preserving restrictions on internet sales and use of proceeds.
Specifies that nonprofit raffles may sell tickets outside Montana if not prohibited in the purchaser’s jurisdiction.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to June 1 2025.
affected: Nonprofit organizations, colleges, universities, school districts, raffle organizers, ticket purchasers, and the Department of Justice

HB142.one_line: HB 142 expands interim committee duties and allows up to five partisan bill drafts per committee.
HB142.summary: HB 142 amends the statutory duties of interim committees, clarifies what counts as a partisan vote, and allows each committee to request up to five bill drafts on a partisan basis (unlimited on a bipartisan basis). The changes also expand the committees’ review scope and require the Legislative Services Division to keep records. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §5‑5‑215 to broaden interim committees’ review duties and add new review items (e.g., advisory councils, statewide initiatives).
Clarifies the definition of “partisan basis” and “bipartisan basis” for requesting bill drafts.
Increases the maximum number of bill drafts that a committee may request on a partisan basis from one to five.
Adds a requirement that the Legislative Services Division keep accurate records of each committee’s activities.
affected: State agencies subject to committee review

HB143.one_line: HB 143 lets physician assistants serve as treating physicians and impairment evaluators in Montana workers’ compensation cases.
HB143.summary: HB 143 expands the Montana Workers’ Compensation definition of a treating physician to include physician assistants (PAs) even when other qualified providers are nearby. The change amends the statutory definition and the impairment‑evaluation rules, but imposes no new costs or programs.
changes: Revises §39‑71‑116 to add PAs as treating physicians when no other qualified provider is present in the area;
Amends §39‑71‑711 to allow PAs to serve as impairment evaluators under the same conditions as other providers;
Maintains existing requirements for admitting privileges, licensing, and scope of practice for all listed providers;
No new funding or administrative bodies are created;
Effective immediately upon passage and approval;
No change to impairment‑rating methodology or dispute resolution procedures.
affected: Insurers and the state workers’ compensation fund
Physician assistants and other medical providers involved in workers’ compensation cases

HB144.one_line: HB 144 expands the Building Codes Council to 13 members, adding a fire‑chiefs’ association representative.
HB144.summary: HB 144 expands Montana’s Building Codes Council from 12 to 13 members and specifies the new member’s qualifications. It also clarifies appointment terms and compensation provisions.
changes: Increases council size to 13 members (previously 12).
Adds a representative of the Montana State Fire Chiefs’ Association as the new member.
Specifies that all members are appointed by the governor and serve 3‑year terms.
Reaffirms that council members are compensated per 2‑15‑122 and are administratively allocated to the Department of Public Health and Human Services.
Maintains that the council works with the Department, industry representatives, and the public to harmonize building codes.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
affected: Building industry professionals (architects, engineers, contractors, electricians, plumbers, elevator mechanics)
Public health and human services director

HB145.one_line: Rises non‑resident base hunting license fee to $15, allocating $10 to hunting‑access programs.
HB145.summary: HB 145 raises the non‑resident base hunting license fee to $15, designating $10 of that as a hunting‑access fee that must be used to fund programs authorized in §87‑1‑265. The resident fee remains $10 with a $2 access fee.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑116 to set the resident base license fee at $10, of which $2 is a hunting‑access fee.
Sets the non‑resident base license fee at $15, of which $10 is a hunting‑access fee.
Requires the department to use the access‑fee portion to fund programs authorized in §87‑1‑265.
Does not alter eligibility requirements for other licenses.
Does not create new programs or offices.
Does not impose new penalties.
No change to the overall license‑year requirement for base licenses.
affected: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks

HB146.one_line: Adds crane and swan fees, directs proceeds to wetlands, effective March 1, 2026.
HB146.summary: HB 146 adds $10 resident and $50 non‑resident application fees for sandhill crane and swan licenses, sets $10 resident and $75 non‑resident license fees for each species, and requires all proceeds to go into a special‑revenue account for wetlands. The act takes effect March 1, 2026.
changes: Adds sandhill crane and swan to the list of species that carry special application fees ($10 resident, $50 non‑resident).
Sets a $10 resident and $75 non‑resident license fee for sandhill crane and swan, in addition to the existing migratory game‑bird fee.
Mandates that all money collected from these licenses be deposited in the state special revenue fund and may only be spent on wetland protection, conservation, and development.
Maintains the existing $5.50 (resident) and $150 (non‑resident) fees for migratory game‑bird licenses, with a $10 resident and $75 non‑resident fee for sandhill crane and swan licenses.
Requires a sandhill crane or swan license holder to also purchase a migratory game‑bird license.
Effective date is March 1, 2026.
affected: Montana residents and non‑residents who wish to hunt sandhill cranes or swans
Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks

HB147.one_line: HB 147 defines enforcement action, sets a 15‑year abandonment period, and requires consistent enforcement over two years.
HB147.summary: HB 147 amends Montana’s covenant‑enforcement law to define an "enforcement action" and set a 15‑year inactivity period before a covenant can be considered abandoned. It also clarifies when covenants remain enforceable and requires consistent enforcement over a two‑year period.
changes: Amends §70‑17‑210 to add a definition of "enforcement action" and a 15‑year inactivity rule for abandonment.
Allows a parcel owner to claim abandonment if no enforcement action has been taken for 15 years, provided evidence is offered under §27‑2‑202.
Specifies that covenants remain enforceable if needed to comply with laws, easements, infrastructure, court orders, utilities, or nuisance abatement.
Requires that enforcement be consistent across all properties for at least two years to qualify as an enforcement action.
