Adds a clause that an association that has not met for 15 years cannot enforce covenants against a similarly used parcel, except where the covenants are still necessary as listed.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Homeowners and parcel owners in developments governed by covenants
Homeowners’ associations and other parties with covenant interests
County clerks and recorders handling abandonment notices

HB150.one_line: HB 150 revises alcohol and gambling laws, tightening ownership rules and lender authority.
HB150.summary: HB 150 amends Montana’s alcohol and gambling statutes to clarify ownership rules, expand regulated‑lender authority, and tighten licensing requirements. It adds definitions, revises security‑interest provisions for licenses, and updates transfer‑of‑ownership rules for gambling operations.
changes: Rewrites 16‑4‑801 to define and regulate security interests in alcoholic‑beverage licenses, including notice, transfer, and non‑use procedures.
Amends 23‑5‑118 to clarify ownership‑interest transfers in licensed gambling operations and to allow regulated lenders to obtain security interests without creating undisclosed ownership.
Adds new definitions (e.g., “caffeinated or stimulant‑enhanced malt beverage,” “guest ranch,” “growler”) that affect licensing and sales.
Revises 23‑5‑176 to tighten eligibility for gambling licenses, adding criminal‑record and financing‑source criteria.
Replaces 16‑1‑106 with expanded definitions for alcohol, beer, wine, and related terms.
Adjusts procedures for regulated lenders under 31‑1‑111, including notification fees and department review of security‑interest documents.
Modifies transfer‑of‑ownership notification requirements for gambling and alcohol licenses.
Updates rules for “security interest” and “ownership interest” reporting to the Department.
Revises definitions of “public gambling,” “illegal gambling device,” and related gaming terms to clarify enforcement.
affected: Department of Revenue and Department of Justice
Business owners with ownership interests in alcohol or gambling licenses
Consumers of caffeinated or stimulant‑enhanced malt beverages

HB151.one_line: HB 151 expands loan repayment, quality‑educator payments, residency, and transport for Deaf/Blind students.
HB151.summary: HB 151 amends Montana’s education statutes to broaden eligibility for loan repayment and quality‑educator payments, expands the teacher‑residency program, and authorizes the Montana School for the Deaf and Blind to provide bus transportation for residential students. It also revises incentive rules for districts meeting pay benchmarks and clarifies applicability dates.
changes: Re‑defines “quality educator” to include sign‑language interpreters and expands eligible entities for loan repayment and quality‑educator payments;
Adds a teacher‑residency program with defined roles, compensation, and a loan‑conversion clause for non‑completion;
Allows the Montana School for the Deaf and Blind to provide school‑bus transportation for residential students and sets reimbursement limits;
Revises incentive formulas (20‑9‑324) for districts meeting competitive base‑pay goals and the quality‑educator payment formula (20‑9‑327);
Provides effective dates: most changes July 1 2025, overall act effective upon passage, with applicability to FY 2026 for sign‑language interpreters;
Includes coordination provisions with House Bill 252 to avoid duplicate amendments.
affected: Montana School for the Deaf and Blind
Students at the Deaf and Blind school
numbers: 70% of teacher average pay for first‑class districts
HB151.effective: July 1 2025 (most provisions); overall act effective upon passage

HB153.one_line: HB 153 revises the school‑funding commission’s structure, adds a working group, and funds staff for 2025‑2026.
HB153.summary: HB 153 revises the statutory framework for Montana’s school‑funding interim commission, redefining its membership, appointment deadlines, and adding an innovation‑working group for the 2025‑2026 interim. It also allocates $10,000 for commission staff and requires a report and implementation plan by January 30 2026.
changes: Amends §5‑20‑301 to specify the commission’s composition: 6 House members, 6 Senate members, 4 public members, and key state officials.
Sets a May 1 deadline for all commission appointments each year the commission is to form.
Mandates the commission select a legislative presiding officer and vice‑presiding officer at its first meeting.
Creates an Innovation and Excellence in Education Working Group to benchmark against high‑performing systems and publish recommendations by Jan 30 2026.
Provides a $10,000 appropriation from the general fund for commission staffing in May‑June 2025.
Requires the commission to issue a report to the legislature and to include draft legislation for funding‑formula changes.
Adds staff‑assignment language tying the commission to the Legislative Services Division.
Specifies compensation rules for non‑legislative commission members.
affected: State officials (Board of Public Education, Superintendent, etc.)
Public members appointed to the commission
Students and parents of Montana public schools

HB156.one_line: County levies replace district levies for school BASE budgets, lowering tuition and reallocating non‑levy revenue.
HB156.summary: HB 156 replaces each school district’s guaranteed‑tax‑base‑aid‑supported BASE levy with a countywide levy that supports all district BASE budgets, lowers tuition payments accordingly, and revises how non‑levy revenue is applied. The bill also changes the duties of trustees, clerks, county superintendents and treasurers, amends many funding‑related statutes, and repeals the 2015‑issued guaranteed‑tax‑base‑aid exemption for certain properties.
changes: Countywide levies replace district levies for BASE budgets, shifting the source of guaranteed‑tax‑base aid from districts to counties.
Tuition payments are reduced to reflect the new countywide levy amounts.
Non‑levy revenue (e.g., property‑tax‑protest funds, oil and gas taxes) is reallocated to district general funds and other specified accounts.
District guaranteed‑tax‑base aid is replaced by county guaranteed‑tax‑base aid for the countywide levy.
Duties of trustees, district clerks, county superintendents, and county treasurers are updated to administer the new levy system and related revenue streams.
Section 15‑1‑409 (guaranteed‑tax‑base‑aid exemption for certain properties) is repealed.
affected: Property owners (through changes to tax‑increment remittance)
numbers: $70,000 maximum tuition per student for out‑of‑state placement
$1 million minimum district budget for oil‑and‑gas tax rules

HB157.one_line: HB 157 mandates two training programs—shorter for off‑premises staff—effective Jan 1, 2026.
HB157.summary: HB 157 amends Montana’s responsible‑server training law to require two distinct training programs—one for on‑premises servers and a shorter one for off‑premises staff—while preserving the existing curriculum requirements. The act takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: Amends §16‑4‑1006, MCA to add a new subsection (2) that requires the department to certify two classes of training programs based on employment setting.
Specifies that the off‑premises program must be completed in at most half the time of the on‑premises program.
Retains the existing curriculum elements (effects of alcohol, penalties, ID checks, documentation, skills for difficult situations, final test, certificate).
Adds a clause that the department may not provide a responsible‑server program outside the two certified classes.
Sets the effective date for the amendments to January 1, 2026.
affected: Server and sales staff at licensed on‑premises establishments
Employees of licensees that only sell alcohol for off‑premises consumption
The Department of Revenue (or the agency responsible for certification)
numbers: half the time for off‑premises program

HB159.one_line: HB 159 expands rural improvement district rules to include maintenance districts and eases petition requirements.
HB159.summary: HB 159 amends Montana’s rural improvement district statutes to broaden the types of districts that can be created, streamline the petition process, and clarify notice and protest procedures. It allows districts to be formed for maintaining existing public improvements, removes the petition requirement when all property owners waive protest rights, and tightens the rules for city‑county cooperation and assessment methods.
changes: Creates a new category of rural improvement district that may be established solely for maintaining existing public improvements;
Permits a petition to create such a district even when the district’s purpose is maintenance, not new construction;
Eliminates the need for a petition if every property owner in the proposed district waives their right to protest;
Adds a requirement that a petition for a maintenance‑only district must contain consent from more than 85 % of the area (or 50 % if all roads are public improvements);
Specifies that districts may include properties inside city limits only if a joint city‑county resolution is adopted and city protest thresholds are met;
Revises the notice, protest, and resolution‑of‑intention procedures to reflect the new district types and assessment methods.
affected: Property owners in rural areas, especially those in subdivisions;
County commissioners and city councils involved in district creation;
Residents and taxpayers who may be assessed for maintenance costs;
Engineers and contractors hired for district improvements.

HB158.one_line: Allows certain retired teachers to be rehired full‑time for up to five years while keeping retirement benefits.
HB158.summary: HB 158 revises Montana’s Teachers’ Retirement System to allow certain retired teachers, specialists, and administrators to be rehired full‑time for up to five years without losing retirement benefits, provided they meet service‑credit and certification requirements. The bill also extends the life‑time limit on reemployment to five years, changes the termination dates of related statutes, and sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §19‑20‑732 to permit reemployment of retired members for a maximum of five years (up from three) while preserving retirement payments; requires 27+ years of creditable service, a valid certificate, and annual employer certification that the position cannot be filled by a non‑retired teacher.
Adds a requirement that employers contribute monthly to the retirement system equal to the sum of specified contribution rates.
Exempts reemployed retirees from the earnings and employment limits in §19‑20‑731.
Mandates that reemployed retirees be subject to collective‑bargaining agreements if the position is covered.
Allows the retirement board to adopt rules implementing the section.
Amends §4 of Chapter 307 (2019) and §4 of Chapter 135 (2023) to change their termination dates to June 30, 2029.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025 and the termination date of §1 to June 30, 2029.
affected: Retired teachers, specialists, and administrators; school districts employing them; the Montana Retirement Board; the Montana Office of Public Instruction; education interim committees; state administration and veterans’ affairs interim committee.

HB161.one_line: Creates a vending‑machine revenue account for the Department of Public Health and Human Services.
HB161.summary: HB 161 creates a special revenue account for vending‑machine income on federal and state property, directs the Department of Public Health and Human Services to collect and deposit a set percentage, and amends the statutory‑appropriation rules to allow this new account to be funded.
changes: Establishes a vending‑machine account in the State Special Revenue Fund credited to the Department of Public Health and Human Services;
Mandates the department to collect a percentage of vending‑machine income on federal and state property (excluding blind‑vendor‑operated machines) and deposit it in that account;
The collected funds are statutorily appropriated under §17‑7‑502 and may be used only for purposes consistent with federal law;
Amends §17‑7‑502 to clarify the definition and requirements for statutory appropriations;
Codifies the new account as part of Title 18, Chapter 5, Part 4;
Effective July 1, 2025.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Vending‑machine operators on federal and state property

HB162.one_line: HB 162 expands resort‑tax infrastructure to include housing and sets new tax limits.
HB162.summary: HB 162 expands the definition of “infrastructure” in the resort‑tax law to include workforce and community housing projects, and it allows the resort tax revenue to be used for those projects. The bill also revises the resort‑tax rate limits and clarifies which businesses are subject to the tax.
changes: Amends 7‑6‑1501 to add workforce and community housing projects to the definition of infrastructure.
Sets a maximum resort‑tax rate of 3% and allows an optional additional 1% levy for infrastructure, limited to communities established before Jan 1 2025.
Specifies that the resort tax applies to retail sales by lodging, food service, alcohol‑serving, and recreational facilities, and requires tax collection on luxury goods.
Provides that if Senate Bill 172 amends 7‑6‑1503, its amendment is void and 7‑6‑1503 is replaced by the language in HB 162.
Voids certain amendments to 7‑6‑1504, 7‑6‑1541, and 7‑6‑1542 that would otherwise be made by Senate Bill 172.
Makes the act effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Businesses in resort areas (lodging, food service, alcohol, recreation)
numbers: Population limits: <2,500 for resort area, <5,500 for resort community

HB164.one_line: HB 164 revises Montana’s unclaimed‑property rules, adds payroll‑card definition, and requires email reporting.
HB164.summary: HB 164 revises Montana’s unclaimed‑property rules, expands the list of property presumed abandoned, adds a definition for payroll cards, and requires holders to report abandoned property by email or mail. The bill also tightens notice requirements and clarifies reporting deadlines.
changes: Amends the definition of “payroll card” and other terms in §70‑9‑802.

Extends the statutory presumption of abandonment to many new property types and shortens the time periods (e.g., traveler’s checks to 15 years, money orders to 7 years, payroll‑card deposits to 5 years).
Replaces the former “report by mail” requirement with a new rule that holders may send the required report by electronic mail if the owner has consented to e‑mail delivery.
Adds detailed reporting requirements for holders, including personal‑information fields and a 120‑day notice to owners before filing the report.
Sets specific filing deadlines: reports must be filed by November 1 each year (May 1 for life‑insurance reports).
Allows the administrator to grant extensions for good cause and permits interim payments to stop further interest accrual.
Requires holders to file an affidavit confirming compliance with the notice requirement.
affected: Holder of unclaimed property (banks, credit unions, insurance companies, etc.)
Apparent owners of the property (individuals, businesses, trusts)
Owners who have consented to receive electronic notices
numbers: May 1 filing deadline for life‑insurance reports

HB166.one_line: Repeals expiration dates for two special revenue accounts, keeping them active forever.
HB166.summary: The bill deletes the expiration dates for the Montana Historical Society and the Montana Original Governor’s Mansion special revenue accounts, keeping those funds in place indefinitely. It simply repeals a 2015 law and takes effect immediately.
changes: Repeals Section 6, Chapter 423, Laws of 2015, which set termination dates for the two special revenue accounts.
The repeal takes effect upon passage and approval, with no further procedural steps.

HB165.one_line: HB 165 allows vehicle title transfers with affidavits, removes notarization, and gives the Motor Vehicle Division rule‑making authority.
HB165.summary: HB 165 lets people transfer vehicle titles with an affidavit instead of a notarized document, removes the requirement that the affidavit be notarized, and gives the Motor Vehicle Division rule‑making authority over title‑affidavit and bond requirements. The bill also updates related title and registration procedures.
changes: 1. Amends §61‑3‑208 to allow a title to be issued when an applicant submits an affidavit (signed and sworn before an authorized officer) and meets one of several conditions, including bond or value proof for certain vehicles.
2. Removes the notarization requirement for the affidavit; the affidavit may be sworn before any authorized officer, not necessarily a notary.
3. Adds bond requirements for vehicles over $1,000 in value or older than 30 years, with specific bond amounts and conditions to indemnify prior owners or lienholders.
4. Provides that the department may issue a title within 3 years or upon surrender of the title if the vehicle no longer needs a title in Montana.

5. Updates §61‑3‑216, §61‑3‑218, §61‑3‑220, §61‑3‑303, and §61‑14‑101 to reflect the new affidavit rules, clarify electronic record transfers, and grant the department rule‑making authority over title‑affidavit and bond procedures.
6. Grants the department authority to adopt rules for various registration and licensing matters, including fleet definitions, temporary registration permits, and fee collection.

HB167.one_line: HB 167 removes the requirement to post absentee voter lists at polling places.
HB167.summary: HB 167 eliminates the requirement that election judges post a list of absentee voters at polling places, while preserving the record‑keeping and reporting duties for absentee ballots. The changes affect election officials and voters who use absentee ballots. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑13‑233 to remove the posting requirement for absentee voter lists at polling places.
Revises §13‑13‑234 to reflect the removal of the posting duty, keeping other duties (noting absentee status and reserving numbers for late voters).
Preserves the requirement that election administrators keep records of absentee ballots issued and delivered, and provide a certificate to election judges.
Maintains the requirement that election judges note absentee status on the pollbook and reserve numbers for late voters.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.

HB168.one_line: HB 168 lets preschool children with disabilities be counted for state funding through ANB changes.
HB168.summary: HB 168 allows preschool‑aged children with disabilities who are in a district’s special‑education program to be counted in the district’s Average Number Belonging (ANB) calculations, thereby making them eligible for state funding. The bill amends the admissions rule to treat such children as pupils and expands the ANB definition to include them.
changes: Amends §20‑5‑101 to permit trustees to admit children under 5 who are in a special‑education program, treating them as pupils for funding purposes.
Modifies §20‑9‑311 to allow preschool children with disabilities to be counted in ANB calculations based on their instructional hours.
Clarifies that preschool children with disabilities are considered “exceptional circumstances” for admission and ANB inclusion.
Sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date and applies to fiscal years beginning on or after that date.
Leaves all other ANB rules unchanged; the bill does not create new programs or funds.
No new criminal offenses are created.

HB171.one_line: Bill eliminates the alfalfa seed committee, transfers duties to Agriculture, and creates a new bee‑registration system.
HB171.summary: HB 171 eliminates the Montana Alfalfa Seed Committee, transfers its duties to the Department of Agriculture, and rewrites related statutes. It creates a new registration system for alfalfa‑leaf‑cutting bees, sets fee rules, and establishes a special revenue account. The bill also repeals the existing Alfalfa Seed Industry Act and related provisions.
changes: A. The Montana Alfalfa Seed Committee is abolished and its responsibilities are transferred to the Department of Agriculture.
B. The Department is given authority to set rules, fees, and maintain a laboratory for bee‑related services.
C. A new registration requirement is imposed on anyone who possesses alfalfa‑leaf‑cutting bees, with fees determined by rule.
D. A special “leaf‑cutting bee” account is created in the state special revenue fund to hold fees, assessment revenue, and donations.
E. The existing alfalfa seed assessment and payment statutes (80‑11‑307, 80‑11‑308) are repealed.
F. The bill requires the Department to hold a biennial public meeting on the continuation of the alfalfa seed assessment.
G. Unspent funds in the former alfalfa seed account must be transferred to the general fund by June 30 2026.
affected: Montana taxpayers (through fee and assessment changes)

HB173.one_line: Revisions to Youth Court definitions take effect immediately, with no new programs or fiscal changes.
HB173.summary: The bill amends the Montana Youth Court Act’s definition section, revising several terms but leaving the victim definition unchanged. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends the text of Section 41‑5‑103, MCA, redefining many terms used in the Youth Court Act (e.g., “adult,” “agency,” “assessment officer,” “commit,” “conditional release,” etc.).
The only change to the victim definition is the removal of any reference to corporations or other entities; the definition remains limited to natural persons and their adult relatives.
No new programs, offices, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The bill does not alter any procedural rules, funding, or reporting requirements.
The effective date is the day the bill is signed into law.
The bill does not contain any fiscal provisions or budgetary allocations.
affected: Youth adjudicated under the Youth Court Act
Parents, guardians, and legal custodians of those youth
Youth court judges, probation officers, and assessment officers
State agencies that administer youth court programs

HB175.one_line: DFW&P must publish annual reports on elk, deer, and antelope hunting‑district data.
HB175.summary: HB 175 requires the Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (DFW&P) to publish an annual public report on hunting‑district data for elk, deer, and antelope, and it amends the department’s governing statute to clarify its duties.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑201, MCA, to clarify DFW&P’s powers and duties.
Mandates an annual public report on hunting‑district data for elk, deer, and antelope, including resident/non‑resident hunter counts, days hunted, and species hunted.
Requires an annual report on non‑resident license sales and the programs through which those licenses were issued.
Adds a requirement to publish an annual game‑count estimate for each species in each hunting district and administrative region.
Adds a requirement to report annual sage grouse population data to the oversight team and environmental quality council.
Leaves other statutory provisions (e.g., firearm regulation, land‑access programs) unchanged.
affected: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

HB178.one_line: Limits AI use by Montana government, bans manipulation, requires disclosure and human review.
HB178.summary: HB 178 limits how Montana state and local governments can use AI, bans certain manipulative or discriminatory uses, requires disclosure when AI‑generated content is released, and mandates human review for decisions that affect people’s rights.
changes: Prohibits AI use for cognitive behavioral manipulation, discriminatory classification, malicious purposes, or general public‑space surveillance (except for locating missing persons or facial surveillance under existing law).
Requires any AI‑produced material that is not human‑reviewed to carry a disclosure that it was generated by AI; also requires disclosure when an AI interface is used with the public.
Exempts peace officers from the disclosure requirement when revealing the AI use could jeopardize an investigation or trial.
Mandates that any AI recommendation or decision that could impact a person’s rights must be reviewed and can be rejected or modified by a qualified human officer.
Defines key terms such as “AI system,” “cognitive behavioral manipulation,” and “human in an appropriate responsible position.”
Codifies the provisions as part of Title 2 of the Montana Code.
Includes severability language to preserve valid portions if parts are invalid.
affected: Citizens receiving AI‑generated content or decisions

HB179.one_line: HB 179 clarifies inactive voter reactivation rules and prohibits petition signing as a trigger.
HB179.summary: HB 179 amends Montana’s voter‑registration law to clarify that a voter on the inactive list cannot be reactivated simply by signing a petition for a statewide ballot issue. The bill requires a voter to either vote in person, submit an absentee‑ballot application, notify the county of a new residence, or complete a reactivation form before being moved to the active list. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑2‑222, MCA to add subsection (2)(b) prohibiting reactivation by petition signing
Specifies that reactivation requires voting in person, absentee‑ballot application, written residence notice, or a county‑provided reactivation form
Clarifies that after any of those actions, the county election administrator must place the voter on the active list
Defines a reactivated voter as a legally registered elector for that election
Effective immediately upon passage
No new programs or funds created

HB181.one_line: Allows state patrol officers to arrest or serve warrants on the Capitol complex.
HB181.summary: The bill expands the definition of “police officer” to include state patrol officers so they may arrest people or serve warrants on the Capitol complex. It amends the criminal‑law section that lists where patrol officers can make arrests to add the Capitol as a covered location. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Adds the Capitol complex to the list of places where patrol officers may arrest or serve warrants.
affected: Individuals arrested or served warrants on the Capitol complex

HB180.one_line: HB 180 restricts health board mixing‑zone approvals that encroach on neighbors and updates related definitions.
HB180.summary: HB 180 limits local health boards from permitting mixing zones that extend onto neighboring property, exempts certain older drainfield zones, and updates definitions in the sanitation‑in‑subdivisions statutes.
changes: Prohibits local boards of health from adopting regulations that allow a mixing zone to encroach on adjacent property for parcels created after March 30 2011, except where specifically allowed by 76‑4‑104(7)(i).
Exempts drainfield mixing zones that existed or were approved before March 30 2011 (and those approved before October 1 2025 under Title 50, ch. 2, part 1) from the new restrictions.
Amends the definition of “mixing zone” in 76‑4‑102 to clarify what constitutes a proposed drainfield or well‑isolation zone and to update related terminology.

Adds language to 50‑2‑116 that requires local boards to adopt regulations that are no less stringent than state standards for sewage control and that prohibit subsurface wastewater treatment systems whose mixing zones would encroach on adjacent property.
Requires that if a board regulates well drilling, it must prohibit drilling when the well isolation zone would encroach on adjacent private property without the owner’s authorization.

Maintains existing powers of local boards of health to adopt fees, regulations, and directives, but clarifies that such actions cannot compel private businesses to deny customers or impose fines, revocations, or criminal charges for non‑compliance with the new mixing‑zone restrictions.
The bill does not create a new state program or criminal offense.
affected: Private businesses that may be affected by new mixing‑zone rules

HB182.one_line: Creates a $5 million grant program for nonprofit senior‑citizen centers with matching‑fund and reporting requirements.
HB182.summary: HB 182 creates a state grant program that funds capital construction, maintenance, repair, and equipment for nonprofit senior‑citizen centers. It authorizes up to $5 million in grants, sets eligibility and matching‑fund requirements, and establishes an administrative account. The program runs from July 1 2025 to June 30 2031.
changes: Creates a senior‑citizen‑center infrastructure account in the state special revenue fund and authorizes the Department of Commerce to administer it.
Provides up to $5 million in grants for property acquisition, construction, remodeling, repairs, and equipment for nonprofit senior‑citizen centers.
Sets eligibility: nonprofit corporations or governmental entities over 60 years old, in good standing, with required matching funds and project plans.
Imposes conditions: matching funds 1:1 for grants ≥$25,000, grant agreements, project‑management plans, design‑standard compliance, and quarterly progress reports.
Limits funding: no more than $350,000 per county, no more than two funded applications per county, and no single grant >$250,000.
Includes administrative cost allowance of up to 3 % of appropriated funds and a 3 % cap on administrative costs in the account.
affected: Senior citizens served by the centers

HB183.one_line: Montana adopts the PA Licensure Compact, creates a commission, and mandates criminal background checks for PA licensure.
HB183.summary: HB 183 adopts the national Physician Assistant (PA) Licensure Compact, creates a compact commission, and requires criminal‑background checks for PA licensure. It establishes a data system, rule‑making authority, and procedures for granting and revoking compact privileges.
changes: Adopts the PA Licensure Compact and creates a PA Licensure Compact Commission with rule‑making authority; establishes a statewide data system for PA licensure, adverse actions, and investigative information; requires all PA license applicants to submit fingerprints for state and federal criminal‑background checks; mandates that each participating state maintain a mechanism for complaints, adverse actions, and reporting; allows compact privileges to be granted to PAs with qualifying licenses, subject to criminal history, controlled‑substance license status, and jurisprudence requirements; provides for adverse action, subpoenas, and dispute resolution among participating states; allows states to withdraw or be terminated from the compact; and amends Montana’s §37‑20‑402 to require criminal‑background checks for PA licensure.
numbers: $0 (no fee specified for compact privilege in Montana)
4 years (time to invalidate a rule if rejected by majority of states)
90 days (maximum for emergency rule to be retroactively applied)
HB183.effective: not stated (effective when seventh state enacts the compact)

HB186.one_line: Adds a sixth member to the parole board, sets staggered terms, and requires Senate confirmation.
HB186.summary: HB 186 expands Montana’s Board of Pardons and Parole from five to six members, sets staggered six‑year terms, and establishes a transition process for the new seat. The bill also clarifies qualifications, compensation, and voting requirements for board decisions.
changes: Board size increased to six members (from five).
Members must have a college degree in criminology, corrections, or related social science; or 5 years of corrections/criminal‑justice experience; or a law degree.
Board must consider expertise in American Indian culture, serious mental illness recovery, and victim awareness.
Members serve staggered six‑year terms; vacancies filled by the governor for the remainder of the term.
Governor designates the presiding officer; can change the presiding officer at any time.
Board may hire its own personnel; it is a quasi‑judicial body but with specific compensation rules.
A majority vote of the board is required to adopt policies, procedures, or rules; a majority of a hearing panel is required for parole and clemency decisions.

Transition provision: within 60 days of the effective date the governor appoints the sixth member for a term ending Jan 1 2029; thereafter the governor appoints a full six‑year term (subject to Senate confirmation).
Effective date: July 1 2025.

HB184.one_line: HB 184 expands insurance coverage, interpreter rights, and state services for deaf and hard‑of‑hearing residents.
HB184.summary: HB 184 amends a wide range of Montana statutes to strengthen protections, benefits, and services for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. The bill updates insurance requirements, expands coverage for hearing‑related care, clarifies interpreter rights in legal settings, and enhances the state’s newborn hearing‑screening program and school‑for‑the‑deaf‑and‑blind services.
changes: Amends insurance statutes (e.g., 2‑18‑704) to require group plans to keep retirees, survivors, and children covered until Medicare eligibility or equivalent coverage is obtained, and to allow continued membership for legislators and judges under specific conditions.
Adds coverage mandates for hearing‑related services in group and individual plans, including diagnosis, treatment, hearing devices, telehealth, and well‑child care for children with hearing loss.
Rewrites interpreter provisions (49‑4‑502, 49‑4‑602) to define qualified, intermediary, and principal parties, and to require qualified interpreters in legal proceedings for deaf persons.

Revises the Montana School for the Deaf and Blind statutes (20‑8‑102, 20‑8‑104, 20‑8‑107, 20‑8‑116) to authorize fee‑based consulting, tracking, admission of non‑residents, and employment placement services.
Updates newborn hearing‑screening program (53‑19‑402) to mandate screening before discharge or within one month, establish reporting and follow‑up protocols, and allow private contributions.
Amends definitions and policy language in 13‑1‑101, 33‑22‑128, and 37‑16‑102 to clarify disability, hearing‑loss coverage, and licensing of hearing‑aid dispensers.
affected: Montana School for the Deaf and Blind

HB190.one_line: Designates American rodeo as Montana’s official state sport, effective immediately.
HB190.summary: The bill designates American rodeo as Montana’s official state sport and makes the designation effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Establishes American rodeo as the official state sport of Montana.
Codifies the designation as part of Title 1, Chapter 1, Part 5 of the Montana Statutes.
The act takes effect upon passage and approval; no additional actions or programs are required.
No funding, penalties, or new agencies are created.
The bill contains no other provisions beyond the designation and codification.
The act does not alter existing laws or create new obligations.
The act does not require any reporting or oversight beyond the codification instruction.
affected: Montana residents and participants in rodeo events
State officials responsible for codifying statutes
Anyone interested in the official state sport designation

HB189.one_line: Revises Montana’s petroleum tank cleanup fund rules, tightening eligibility and adding a balance threshold.
HB189.summary: HB 189 revises the Montana Petroleum Tank Release Cleanup Fund’s reimbursement rules, tightening eligibility, adjusting payment percentages, and adding a fund‑balance threshold. It also expands the board’s rule‑making authority and sets a July 1, 2025 effective date.
changes: Amends §75‑11‑307 to clarify eligible costs, exclusions, and reimbursement limits for releases discovered after 1989 (or 1984 for heating‑oil tanks).

Revises §75‑11‑308 to specify eligibility requirements, including compliance with state/federal rules, accidental release, and exclusion of certain tank types (refinery, rail, federal, convicted owners, mobile tanks).
Adds a fund‑balance provision (§6) that bars reimbursements when the monthly balance falls below $1.5 million, except for emergency responses.
Extends the board’s rule‑making authority to adopt implementation rules for the amended sections.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.
affected: The Montana Department of Environmental Quality and the Petroleum Tank Release Cleanup Fund board
Property owners with underground storage tanks
Stakeholders in refinery, terminal, and production facility tanks
numbers: $500,000 max for heating‑oil or small residential tanks

HB191.one_line: HB 191 revises child‑welfare endangerment law, adds new conduct, and sets penalties.
HB191.summary: HB 191 amends Montana’s child‑welfare‑endangering statute to add new conduct, clarify existing exceptions, and set penalties, including a misdemeanor for partner or family member assault in the presence of a child.
changes: Amends §45‑5‑622 to define the offense of endangering the welfare of children and list specific conduct that is and is not a violation, including independent activities and drug‑related offenses.
Adds a new subsection (4) making it a separate misdemeanor when a person commits a partner or family‑member assault (under §45‑5‑202, ‑206, ‑213, or ‑215) in the presence of a child.
Creates a felony subsection (3) for methamphetamine production or exposure to a child.

Specifies penalties: up to $500 fine or 6‑month county jail for a first offense, up to $1,000 fine or 6‑month jail for a second offense; felony for meth‑related conduct (up to 5 years state prison, $10,000 fine, or 10 years if serious injury); misdemeanor for partner/family assault in presence of child (fine $100‑$1,000, jail 72 hrs‑1 year).
Revises evidentiary rules to allow evidence of cruelty, neglect, and past injury.
Provides that a court may order forfeiture of fines or bonds to benefit the endangered child.
affected: Parents, guardians, and other supervisors of children under 18
Adults who supply or encourage drugs to minors
Individuals who assault a partner or family member in front of a child
Law‑enforcement and courts handling child‑welfare cases
Courts that may order forfeiture of fines or bonds

HB192.one_line: HB 192 hikes recording fees and earmarks more revenue for state preservation and geospatial funds.
HB192.summary: HB 192 raises the fees that county clerks and recorders charge for recording documents and requires a larger share of those fees to be deposited into state‑funded accounts.  The bill also gives the Department of Revenue authority to adjust the fees and related deposits for inflation every two years starting July 1 2027.
changes: Increases the base fee for mechanical recording to $7 for the first page (or fraction) and $10 for each additional page.
Sets a new standard recording fee of $8 per page, with a $20 first‑page rate and $10 for each additional page, subject to biennial inflation adjustment.

Mandates that a larger portion of each fee be deposited into the records‑preservation fund, the county land information account, and the Montana geospatial information account, with specific dollar amounts and inflation‑adjusted rules.
Adds rule‑making authority for the Department of Revenue to set the inflation factor and the amounts to be deposited each month.
Specifies that the new fee schedule and deposit rules take effect on October 1 2025 and apply to documents recorded on or after that date.
affected: Property owners and other parties who file documents for recording
County land information and geospatial information accounts

HB193.one_line: HB 193 requires a signed request for voter‑registration cancellation, effective immediately.
HB193.summary: HB 193 amends Montana’s voter‑registration law to require a signed written request from the elector for cancellation, while preserving other existing cancellation grounds. The change takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Adds a new requirement that the elector must submit a signed written request for cancellation.
Leaves all other existing cancellation reasons (death, unsound mind, felony incarceration, court order, duplicate registration, inactivity, failure to vote, or loss of qualification) unchanged.
Does not alter any administrative procedures beyond the added signature requirement.
The amendment is limited to Section 13‑2‑402 of the Montana Code Annotated.
The act has no new programs, funds, or penalties.
The change is purely procedural and does not affect voter eligibility or election administration beyond the signature requirement.
affected: Electors who wish to cancel their registration
County clerks and the Secretary of State’s office
Courts and the Department of Public Health and Human Services (for death reports)

HB194.one_line: Revises jury notice, summons, service limits, and discharge motions for Montana courts.
HB194.summary: HB 194 revises how jurors are notified, summoned, and can be challenged, tightening procedures for jury selection and discharge. It also sets a new 90‑day service limit for regular jurors and allows a one‑day or one‑trial service option.
changes: Amends §3‑15‑405 to require mailed notice and affidavit, with sheriff serving personally if no response;
Revises §3‑15‑411 to set a 1‑year term for regular jurors, a 90‑day limit for those drawn after a new jury list, and allows continued service beyond 1 year if a case continues;
Rewrites §3‑15‑501 to clarify when a court must order a jury, allow “one‑day or one‑trial” service, and detail summons procedures and sheriff’s role;
Amends §46‑16‑112 to require a motion to discharge a jury panel to be filed at least 5 days before trial start, with written affidavit and good‑cause exception;
Adds severability, immediate effective date, and applicability to jury pools noticed on or after May 1 2026.
affected: Parties in civil and criminal cases

HB196.one_line: HB 196 adds digital‑ID checks to alcohol‑service training and expands fraud definitions.
HB196.summary: HB 196 amends Montana’s alcohol‑service training and age‑restriction laws to add requirements for checking government‑certified digital ID cards and to treat such cards as fraudulent if altered. It also expands the definition of fraudulent identification and clarifies civil liability for sellers who provide alcohol to minors.
changes: Adds a new training requirement for server and sales programs to cover procedures for checking government‑certified digital ID cards.
Expands the definition of fraudulent identification to include falsifying or altering any identification card, including tribal and digital IDs.
Clarifies that a person who provides alcohol to a minor in an intoxicating quantity is guilty of a misdemeanor and may face civil liability.
Adds a new subsection that makes it unlawful to fraudulently misrepresent age or alter any ID card.
Maintains existing age‑restriction provisions but adds the digital‑ID clause to the training and liability language.
affected: Individuals who use or alter digital ID cards
numbers: Misdemeanor for providing alcohol to minors

HB195.one_line: HB 195 sets a $250,000 noneconomic damage cap in Montana malpractice cases and schedules annual increases.
HB195.summary: HB 195 raises Montana’s cap on noneconomic damages in medical‑malpractice cases and sets a schedule for annual increases, applying to both new and pending claims. The cap is now $250,000 per claimant, with the statutory limit rising from $300,000 in 2025 to $500,000 in 2029 and then increasing 2 % each year thereafter.
changes: Amends §25‑9‑411 to set a $250,000 cap on past‑and‑future noneconomic damages per claimant in a single‑incident malpractice claim.
Establishes a statutory schedule: $300,000 effective 2025, $350,000 (Jan 1 2026), $400,000 (Jan 1 2027), $450,000 (Jan 1 2028), $500,000 (Jan 1 2029), then 2 % yearly increases thereafter.

Defines the applicable limit as the one in effect on the date the claimant first files a claim with the Montana Medical Legal Panel or, if not panel‑subject, the date the suit is first filed in court.
Requires that any award exceeding the $250,000 cap be reduced first to the cap and then to the statutory limit, with reductions applied in a specified order (27‑1‑702, 27‑1‑703, setoffs/credits).
Prohibits discounting future noneconomic damages to present value and bars disclosure of the $250,000 cap to the jury.
Includes definitions of claimant, health‑care provider, malpractice claim, noneconomic loss, and patient.
affected: Courts and the Montana Medical Legal Panel

HB197.one_line: HB 197 lets insurers end temporary total‑disability benefits when a worker returns to full duty, with notice and physician checks.
HB197.summary: HB 197 amends Montana’s workers’‑comp rules to allow insurers to end temporary total‑disability benefits when a claimant is released to full duty before reaching maximum medical improvement, with a 14‑day notice requirement. It adds physician‑determination criteria for converting benefits and clarifies termination timing for those released to work.
changes: Amends §39‑71‑609 to permit termination of temporary total‑disability benefits when a claimant is released to full duty before maximum medical improvement.
Requires insurers to provide 14‑day written notice before terminating or converting benefits, except when the claimant has returned to work.
Adds physician‑determination requirements: medical stability, physical restrictions, and job‑fit analysis must be documented before converting to permanent partial benefits.
Allows termination of benefits as of the date the worker is released to work or after 14 days’ notice, whichever is earlier.
Clarifies that termination can occur even if the claimant is not yet at maximum healing.
Sets the effective date to July 1 2025.

HB198.one_line: Expands anti‑kick‑back prohibition to more behavioral‑health and nursing professionals.
HB198.summary: HB 198 amends Montana’s anti‑kick‑back law to broaden the list of health‑care professionals whose contracts cannot restrict post‑employment practice. The changes apply immediately to new or renewed contracts and do not create new programs or penalties. The bill simply expands the scope of the existing prohibition.
changes: Amends §28‑2‑724 to add several behavioral‑health and nursing professions to the list of providers covered by the anti‑restriction provision.
Specifies that the prohibition applies to employment, partnership, or other professional relationships that create or establish contractual terms.
Clarifies that the restriction covers practice, patient relationships, and solicitation of patients after termination of the relationship.
Excludes contracts related to the sale or purchase of a practice from the prohibition.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and applies to contracts made or renewed on or after that date.
affected: Health‑care providers listed in the amended section
Contracting parties in employment or partnership agreements
Patients of the providers (indirectly through the prohibition on solicitation)

HB201.one_line: Paid signature gatherers must identify themselves and wear a badge with name, state, and status.
HB201.summary: The bill requires anyone paid to gather signatures for petitions to verbally identify themselves, state of legal residence, and wear a badge with that information. It applies immediately upon passage and is incorporated into Montana’s election‑signature‑gathering statutes. No new programs or fees are created.
changes: Paid signature gatherers must verbally disclose their first name, state of legal residence, and status as a paid gatherer to anyone approached for a petition signature.
They must also wear a badge displaying that same information, including their full first name and last initial.
The disclosure requirement is codified as part of Title 13, Chapter 27 of the Montana Code.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.

HB202.one_line: HB 202 tightens aircraft‑hunting rules, bans UAVs, raises penalties, and sets a 2027 effective date.
HB202.summary: HB 202 amends Montana’s unlawful‑aircraft‑for‑hunting law to ban hunting from aircraft, extend the waiting period after locating game, prohibit unmanned aircraft use, and raise fines and penalties. The bill also sets specific effective and termination dates for the amendments.
changes: Amends §87‑6‑208 to prohibit hunting from aircraft, including after locating game within 24 h and after using an aircraft to spot game within 48 h; bans use of unmanned aerial vehicles for hunting; extends the waiting period after locating game to 24 h; adds new penalties and fines for violations; allows forfeiture of hunting, fishing, and trapping licenses for up to 36 months; requires confiscation of unlawfully possessed fur‑bear pelts; provides coordination with Senate Bill 106 and sets effective dates (January 1 2027 for the amended section) and a termination date (December 31 2026 for the original amendment).
affected: Hunters, pilots, UAV operators, license holders, wildlife enforcement officers

HB203.one_line: HB 203 designates February 9 as Montana Mining Day, a ceremonial observance with no new programs or costs.
HB203.summary: HB 203 designates February 9 as Montana Mining Day to honor the state’s mining heritage. The bill simply establishes the date; it does not create programs or impose new duties.
changes: Establishes a state‑designated day—Montana Mining Day—on February 9 each year.
Codifies the day as part of Title 1, Chapter 1, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
No additional regulations, funding, or administrative actions are attached.
The bill contains no fiscal provisions or enforcement mechanisms.
The act is purely ceremonial and commemorative.
It does not create a new agency, office, or criminal offense.
affected: businesses and organizations that may host events on the designated day

HB206.one_line: HB 206 clarifies who may request an electrician’s license and authorizes citations for non‑display.
HB206.summary: HB 206 amends Montana’s electrician‑licensing law to clarify who may request a license and how a failure to display it can be enforced. The bill expands the list of authorized requesters and gives department employees the power to issue citations for non‑display.
changes: Amends §37‑68‑315 to add private/public employment‑agency employees, labor‑union employees, building‑code inspectors, department employees, and professionals on the job site as persons who may request an electrician’s license.
Clarifies that an electrician on the same job site also has the right to request a license from another electrician.
Adds that a department employee may issue a citation and collect a fine under §37‑68‑316 for failure to display a license.
Maintains the existing fine structure and reporting mechanism to the board or department.
affected: Electricians and other licensed electrical workers
Employees of employment agencies, labor unions, building‑code inspectors, department staff
Other professionals on job sites who may request licenses

HB207.one_line: HB 207 tightens filing rules, bars primary losers from general‑election write‑ins, and raises petition signature thresholds.
HB207.summary: HB 207 tightens Montana’s candidate‑filing rules. It requires local and state candidates to file before the primary, bars primary losers from running as write‑ins in the general election, and raises the signature thresholds for third‑party and independent petitions. The bill also revises deadlines, withdrawal rules, and election‑cancellation procedures for local offices and special‑purpose districts.
changes: Candidates for local and state offices must file nominations before the primary election deadline.
Unsuccessful primary candidates cannot seek nomination by write‑in or petition for the same office in the general election.
Signature requirements for independent and third‑party petitions are increased to 4%–5% of the last election’s vote.
Write‑in candidacy declarations must be filed by 5 p.m. on the 65th–90th day before the election.

Election administrators may cancel elections if the number of candidates equals or is less than the number of positions; the governing body may then declare a sole candidate elected or appoint a replacement.
Withdrawal of a candidate is prohibited after the filing deadline.
Petition signatures must be verified and certified before filing, and the filing fee is refunded if certification fails.
numbers: 145–105 days before election for primary filing
1 week before filing deadline for petitions

HB208.one_line: HB 208 lets cities prohibit unauthorized camping and storage on municipal property.
HB208.summary: HB 208 expands municipal powers so that cities can regulate unauthorized camping and storage of personal property on municipal real‑property. It amends the general‑powers statute to add a new power (25) that allows municipalities to prohibit or regulate such activities.
changes: Adds power (25) to §7‑1‑4124, giving municipalities the authority to prohibit or otherwise regulate (a) temporary or permanent storage of personal property on municipal real property and (b) sleeping or camping on or inhabiting municipal real property.
The amendment does not create new penalties, fines, or enforcement mechanisms beyond those already authorized for civil infractions under §7‑1‑4150.
The change is purely statutory; it does not establish a new program, fund, or criminal offense.
Municipalities may enact ordinances or resolutions to enforce the new power.
The amendment does not alter any existing enforcement or civil‑infraction procedures.
No new funding or budgetary provisions are included.
affected: Residents and visitors who might camp or store property on municipal land

HB211.one_line: HB 211 creates a third‑party alcohol delivery license and sets strict rules for retailers and drivers.
HB211.summary: HB 211 authorizes off‑premises beer and wine retailers to use third‑party delivery services and creates a new third‑party delivery license. It sets detailed licensing, training, record‑keeping, and delivery‑time rules for both retailers and delivery operators.
changes: Creates a new third‑party delivery license for alcohol with a $1,000 initial fee and annual renewal fee; requires applicants to meet all off‑premises retail license requirements and submit an application and fee.
Allows an off‑premises retail licensee to contract with a third‑party delivery licensee to deliver beer or table wine to end consumers only; the retailer retains control over inventory and pricing.

Imposes strict delivery rules: deliveries must occur only during the retailer’s open hours, be completed within one hour after sales close, and be returned if undeliverable; drivers must be 21+, have valid ID, no recent DUI or felony, and complete responsible‑server or delivery training.

Mandates age verification at delivery via scanning software or approved alternative; prohibits delivery to intoxicated persons and to certain locations (other licensed retailers, college campuses, addresses without a street name/number).

Requires both retailers and delivery licensees to maintain 3‑year records of each delivery and make them available to the Department; imposes $50, $200, and $350 penalties for non‑compliance with training requirements.
Adds new training program certification requirements for delivery drivers and updates the Department’s rule‑making authority for responsible server and delivery training.
Amends existing alcohol‑licensing statutes (16‑4‑115, 16‑4‑501, 16‑4‑1001‑1008) to incorporate the new delivery provisions and fee schedule.
Sets the effective date of the act to January 1, 2026.
affected: Third‑party delivery companies and their drivers
Department of Revenue and its enforcement staff

HB214.one_line: Allows Montana to prosecute and surrender detained immigrants for state crimes.
HB214.summary: The bill allows Montana to prosecute state crimes committed by people who are in federal immigration detention, and lets the state hand them over to federal authorities while a state case is pending. It also requires prosecutors to inform the attorney‑general before deciding not to prosecute such individuals.
changes: Permits state criminal prosecution of a person who is or may be in federal immigration detention for a state crime.
Allows the state to surrender the person to the federal government on demand while a state case is pending.
Requires a prosecutor to notify the attorney‑general before declining to prosecute a person described in subsection (1).
Codifies the provisions as part of Title 46, chapter 1, part 1 of the Montana Code.
affected: Persons in federal immigration detention who commit state crimes

HB215.one_line: Mandates gender and racial balance in state appointments with monthly reporting.
HB215.summary: HB 215 amends Montana law to require state appointing authorities to pursue gender and racial balance in appointments and to report progress to the legislature. It establishes monthly publication of appointments and vacancies by the Secretary of State and a gubernatorial report. The bill does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑108 to mandate that all appointing authorities of state boards, commissions, committees, and councils take positive action to attain gender balance and proportional representation of minorities.
Requires the Secretary of State to publish a monthly list of recent appointments and upcoming vacancies in the Montana Administrative Register.
Mandates the governor to report to the legislature, as provided in §5‑11‑210, on progress toward these diversity goals.
The bill removes any prior reporting requirements that were not specified in the text.
No new offices, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The text does not specify an effective date; it presumably takes effect when enacted.
No monetary amounts or budgetary allocations are mentioned.
The bill does not alter any existing appointment procedures beyond the added diversity and reporting requirements.
affected: State appointing authorities (board, commission, committee, council members).

HB218.one_line: HB 218 expands optometrists’ scope to include limited anterior‑segment surgery and laser procedures, effective July 1, 2025.
HB218.summary: HB 218 expands optometrists’ scope of practice to include limited in‑office surgical and laser procedures on the anterior eye and adnexa, subject to board certification. It amends the optometry definition and licensing rules and takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §37‑10‑101 to allow optometrists to perform non‑penetrating anterior‑segment surgery and laser procedures, excluding intraocular, intravitreal, and refractive surgery; requires board certification for laser work.
Amends §37‑10‑302 to establish board rules for certifying optometrists to perform laser surgical procedures, including didactic and clinical training requirements.
Adds a requirement that applicants for a license be of good moral character and have graduated from an accredited optometry school.
Specifies that the board issues a license indicating certification to perform laser surgery.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
numbers: anterior segment of the eye and adnexa
association of regulatory boards of optometry

HB217.one_line: HB 217 transfers the state building energy‑conservation program to DOA while preserving federal funds and revising reporting rules.
HB217.summary: HB 217 moves the state building energy‑conservation program from the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) to the Architecture & Engineering Division of the Department of Administration (DOA). It keeps DEQ in control of certain federal funds and amends several statutes to reflect the new agency structure and reporting requirements. The bill also sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
changes: Transfers program authority and day‑to‑day operations to DOA’s Architecture & Engineering Division.
Allows DEQ to retain and manage specific federal American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) funds for the program.

Amends MCA sections 90‑4‑602, 90‑4‑605, 90‑4‑607, 90‑4‑615, 90‑4‑616, and 90‑4‑617 to redefine the “Department” and “Division” terms, update reporting and repayment procedures, and establish an energy‑conservation repayment account.
Requires the new division to identify candidate buildings, conduct energy analyses, prepare annual reports, and submit them to the governor by September 1 of each even‑numbered year.
Mandates that energy‑cost savings be transferred to the repayment account until the full cost of a project (including a 3 % interest charge) is paid.
Sets a cap of $2 million on unencumbered funds in the repayment account, after which excess is moved to the capital projects account.
affected: State agencies owning or operating state buildings
Department of Administration – Architecture & Engineering Division
State agencies participating in the energy‑conservation program

HB219.one_line: Allows wolf‑harvest reimbursements and clarifies contest prize limits.
HB219.summary: HB 219 allows licensed hunters and trappers to receive reimbursements for costs incurred when legally harvesting wolves and amends the unlawful‑contest provision of §87‑6‑214 to clarify prize limits and add a new subsection on wolf‑harvest reimbursements.
changes: Adds subsection (1)(d) to §87‑6‑214 permitting reimbursements to licensed wolf‑hunters/trappers for lawful harvests.
Clarifies that prizes may be awarded for a single game bird or fur‑bearing animal based on size, quality, or rarity.
Limits monetary prizes for contests based on size/weight of a game animal to $50, except for nationally recognized Boone & Crockett trophies.
Maintains existing penalties for violations of the unlawful‑contest provision (fine $50‑$1,000, up to 6 months in county jail, possible forfeiture of hunting/fishing/trapping license).
Does not create a new program or criminal offense; it merely amends existing law.
affected: Law enforcement and courts handling violations of §87‑6‑214

HB225.one_line: HB 225 tightens home‑inspection licensing, insurance, reporting, and fees, aligning the program with other state licensing offices.
HB225.summary: HB 225 updates Montana’s home‑inspection rules, tightening licensing, insurance, reporting, and fee structures while aligning the program with other state licensing offices. It adds new standards, raises the minimum E&O insurance, and creates a fee‑based registration system that funds an industry‑consumer education program.
changes: Requires a home‑inspection license and 40‑hour approved training, national association membership, and $100,000–$125,000 E&O insurance for all licensed inspectors.
Mandates a written inspection report that lists inspected systems, major visible defects, and recommendations, unless the client waives the obligation.
Imposes fee limits ($70 for contractors, a rule‑set amount for inspectors) and deposits fees into a special revenue account for administration and enforcement.
Creates a joint industry‑consumer information program funded with 15 % of the registration fees.
Rewrites sections on complaints, investigations, and licensing definitions to bring the home‑inspection program in line with other Department of Labor and Industry licensing programs.
Repeals two older sections (39‑9‑212 and 39‑9‑213) that dealt with penalties and prohibitions for home inspectors.
Sets penalties up to $5,000 for violations of registration and business‑practice rules.
Establishes a public, bimonthly‑updated list of registered contractors and inspectors available for a reasonable fee or online.
Effective January 1, 2026, unless House Bill 239 modifies or repeals any of the amended sections.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB226.one_line: Employers must verify work eligibility or face escalating fines and possible license suspension.
HB226.summary: Employers must verify every new employee’s legal work status before hiring and face escalating penalties for non‑compliance. The Department of Labor and Industry will enforce the law, collect fines into a special revenue fund, and may suspend licenses after repeated violations.
changes: Mandates employers to use E‑Verify or complete Form I‑9 for all hires before work starts.
Creates a state special revenue fund to hold penalties collected from non‑compliant employers.

Sets civil penalties: up to $500 per employee for a first violation, $1,000 per employee for a second, and up to $2,500 per employee plus a 30‑day‑to‑6‑month license suspension for third or subsequent violations.
Authorizes the Department of Labor and Industry to investigate, audit, and compel records or testimony from employers.
Allows the department to issue subpoenas and, if necessary, seek court orders to enforce compliance.
Requires that fines be deposited in the lawful employment enforcement fund and used only for enforcement and education activities.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB227.one_line: Creates a fund to pay licensing board legal fees over $15,000 for low‑revenue boards.
HB227.summary: HB 227 creates a special‑revenue account for occupational‑licensing boards to cover legal fees when disciplinary costs exceed $15,000. The fund is limited to boards with ≤$200,000 revenue, can be used only for fees above that threshold, and is governed by rules the Department of Labor and Industry may issue.
changes: Establishes a contingent litigation fund in the state special revenue fund for licensing boards and programs.
Allows the Department of Labor and Industry to pay legal fees and costs only when those costs exceed $15,000 and when the board’s three‑year average revenue is $200,000 or less.
Authorizes the department to rule on fund distribution, priority, and fee setting (maximum $25 per licensee per year).
Prevents the fund from covering penalties or sanctions imposed on boards or programs.
Requires that any unspent balance remain in the account and that interest and income stay in the fund.
The fund is funded by statutory appropriation under Section 17‑7‑502 and is effective July 1, 2025, terminating June 30, 2031.
Any remaining money at termination is disbursed pro‑rata to covered boards or programs.
affected: Occupational licensing boards and programs with ≤$200,000 revenue

HB228.one_line: HB 228 tightens bi‑annual cost reporting for large‑expenditure bills and extends the requirement beyond its prior end date.
HB228.summary: HB 228 revises Montana’s bi‑annual reporting of actual costs for bills that projected large expenditures, tightening the reporting schedule and details while extending the reporting requirement beyond its prior termination date. The bill amends the statutory reporting rule, repeals a 2021 law, and takes effect June 30 2025.
changes: Amends §5‑4‑208, MCA to require bi‑annual (February 1 and October 1) reports of actual costs for bills that projected >$1 million or >$500 k from the general fund in any of the four fiscal years noted in the bill’s fiscal note.

Specifies the content of each report: bill name, actual expenditures for the first or last two quarters of the preceding fiscal year, a description of how funds were expended, and a comparison to the projected costs in the fiscal note.
Limits reporting to bills that have been in effect for at least one fiscal year and that had a fiscal note prepared.
Mandates that reports be submitted electronically and also to the legislature per §5‑11‑210.
Repeals Section 6 of Chapter 350, Laws of 2021, which previously set a termination date for the reporting requirement.
Sets the effective date of the act to June 30 2025.
affected: State budget and program planning office
Legislators and staff preparing fiscal notes

HB233.one_line: HOAs can petition to take title of open‑space areas in a final plat after a public hearing.
HB233.summary: HB 233 lets a homeowners’ association (HOA) petition a county or city to take ownership of open‑space areas that were set aside in a final subdivision plat, provided the HOA is governed by the covenants and the subdivider intended the HOA to own the land.  The bill requires a public hearing and records the transfer, and it amends several subdivision‑related statutes to clarify definitions and filing procedures.
changes: HOAs may file a petition to transfer title of open‑space, parks, or similar common‑use areas in a final plat to the HOA if the HOA is organized per the covenants, the covenants require maintenance/insurance, the governing body finds the subdivider intended HOA ownership, and the property is not owned by a person.
A public hearing must be held; the governing body issues written findings and, if approved, records the transfer with the clerk and recorder.
The bill amends definitions in MCA §§ 76‑3‑103, 76‑8‑101, 76‑25‑103, and 76‑25‑411 to include the new transfer provision and clarify related terminology.
The act applies retroactively to final plats recorded on or after Oct. 1, 1973, and takes effect immediately upon passage.

HB231.one_line: HB 231 cuts residential rates, adds rebates, and freezes local mill limits.
HB231.summary: HB 231 revises Montana’s class‑four property‑tax rates, creates new homestead and rental‑property reduced‑rate programs, establishes a $400 rebate for 2024 principal‑residence owners, and adjusts local‑government mill‑levy limits. The bill also updates related statutes, provides a new property‑tax‑assistance account, and sets appropriation amounts.
changes: Replaces the existing class‑four residential rate (1.35%–1.9%) with a graduated rate for homestead and long‑term‑rental owners: 0.76% for values ≤ median, 0.90% for > median to <2× median, 1.10% for 2–4× median, and 1.90% for ≥4× median; a 1.10% rate for rental multifamily units qualifying for the rental‑rate program; and a 1.40× multiplier for single‑family homes valued >$1.5 million.

Creates a homestead reduced‑rate program that applies to a principal residence if the owner owns and lives there for ≥7 months in the tax year, with an electronic or mailed application deadline of March 1 for the first year and automatic renewal unless ownership or occupancy changes.
Creates a rental‑property reduced‑rate program for long‑term rentals (≥28 days rented for ≥9 months or vacant ≤5 months) with annual reapplication; the first application deadline is March 1, 2026.

Provides a $400 (or less if total taxes paid were smaller) rebate for 2024 principal‑residence owners who paid Montana property taxes that year; the rebate is claimed by filing a form between August 15 and October 1, 2025.

Adjusts local‑government fixed‑mill‑levy limits: charter‑based limits are frozen at the 2025 level for 2026 and thereafter, and voted‑mill levies may be converted to dollar‑based levies equal to 2025 revenue.
Adds a $90 million transfer to a new property‑tax‑assistance account and appropriates $500 k (FY 2025) and $3.5 m (FY 2026) for implementation.
Revises sections 15‑6‑134, 15‑7‑102, 15‑15‑101‑103, 15‑16‑101, 15‑17‑125, and 15‑30‑2120 to reflect the new rates, programs, and administrative procedures.

Sets effective dates: most provisions take effect January 1, 2026, with the rebate and some administrative rules effective upon passage; the bill applies retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.
Terminates the new rates and rebate on December 31, 2025 (rebate) or June 30, 2026 (most other provisions).
affected: Property owners of class‑four residential and commercial properties (including single‑family homes, manufactured homes, trailers, and commercial buildings), long‑term rental owners, local governments with fixed‑mill‑levy charters, and taxpayers who paid 2024 property taxes.
HB231.effective: January 1, 2026 (most provisions); retroactive to tax years after December 31, 2024

HB234.one_line: HB 234 extends 2023 lead‑in‑school funding to 2027 for original projects.
HB234.summary: HB 234 extends the use of 2023 lead‑in‑school funding through 2027, re‑appropriating the money for the original projects. The bill amends the 2023 law to allow the funds to be used for the biennium ending June 30 2027 and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends Section 5, Chapter 763, Laws of 2023 by adding subsection (11) that re‑appropriates the 2023 lead‑in‑school appropriations for the biennium ending June 30 2027.
The re‑appropriation allows the same money to be used for the original projects rather than being spent in 2023.
The act has no new programs, offices, or criminal offenses.
The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
No additional funding is added; it merely extends the use of existing appropriations.
affected: State agencies responsible for lead‑in‑school capital improvement projects

HB235.one_line: Owners can cancel or suspend registration; drivers of such vehicles are liable for all resulting fines and damages.
HB235.summary: HB 235 lets vehicle owners voluntarily cancel or suspend their registration, prohibits driving such vehicles, and makes the driver liable for any resulting fines or damages. It also expands the Department of Motor Vehicles’ rule‑making authority and amends a section of the motor‑vehicle code.
changes: Owners may cancel or suspend registration under rules the DMV will later set; all owners on a vehicle must consent.
A vehicle with a canceled or suspended registration may not be driven on public roads.
The driver of a vehicle with a canceled or suspended registration is personally liable for all tolls, fines, and damages arising from its use, and the owner may implead the driver in civil suits.
The bill amends §61‑14‑101 to give the DMV broad rule‑making authority over many aspects of registration, fleet plates, and temporary permits.
The amendment codifies the new voluntary cancellation/suspension provisions into Title 61, Chapter 3, Part 3, and the liability provisions into Title 61, Chapter 6.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
The DMV will adopt rules for voluntary cancellation/suspension, fleet definitions, plate issuance, and many other administrative matters.
affected: Vehicle owners who wish to cancel or suspend registration
Drivers of vehicles with canceled or suspended registrations
Motor‑vehicle insurers and dealers (indirectly through rule‑making)

HB238.one_line: HB 238 expands evaluation and suspension authority for professional licensees to protect public safety.
HB238.summary: HB 238 expands the authority of licensing boards and the Department of Labor & Industry to require mental or physical evaluations of licensees or applicants who pose a risk to public safety, and it amends existing statutes to clarify investigation procedures and suspension authority.
changes: 1. Boards (e.g., Alternative Health Care, Behavioral Health, Veterinary Medicine, medical licensing boards) may order an evaluation if they reasonably believe a licensee/applicant poses a significant risk to public health and safety.
2. The Department of Labor & Industry may likewise order an evaluation under the same reasonable‑belief standard.
3. Boards and the Department may suspend a license or halt an application if the individual refuses to submit to the evaluation.

4. The bill amends § 37‑3‑323 (medicine), § 37‑6‑311 (podiatry), and § 37‑12‑322 (chiropractic) to add language that the investigation may include a physical or mental examination ordered by the board, and to clarify suspension conditions for mentally incompetent or substance‑addicted licensees.
5. The amendments codify the new evaluation and suspension procedures as integral parts of the respective chapters of the Montana Code Annotated.
affected: Other professional licensees under the specified boards

HB239.one_line: HB 239 creates a new licensing program for Montana construction contractors and home inspectors, replacing registration with licensing and adding enforcement and wage‑setting rules.
HB239.summary: HB 239 replaces Montana’s construction‑contractor registration system with a new licensing program administered by the Department of Labor and Industry.  The bill requires all contractors and home inspectors to obtain a license, sets application and fee rules, creates penalties for unprofessional conduct, and establishes a statewide prevailing‑wage survey for construction work.
changes: All construction contractors and home inspectors must register and obtain a license from the Department of Labor and Industry; registration is replaced by licensing.
Applicants must submit SSN, workers’‑comp compliance, EIN, and detailed ownership/management information; fees are set by rule and deposited in a special revenue account.
The Department may adopt rules for unprofessional conduct; violations can result in up to $5,000 penalties and suspension or debarment from public‑works contracts.
The bill amends wage‑setting statutes (18‑2‑413, 18‑2‑414) to require annual surveys and statewide prevailing‑wage rates for heavy and highway construction.
It creates a consumer‑education program funded by 15 % of registration fees and requires the Department to publish and update contractor and inspector lists.
The bill repeals the old registration sections (39‑9‑201, 39‑9‑204) and codifies the new licensing provisions as a new chapter of Title 37.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB241.one_line: Montana adopts a national compact that expands psychologists’ ability to practice across state lines and creates a new regulatory commission.
HB241.summary: Montana would join a national compact that lets psychologists licensed in one member state provide tele‑psychology and short‑term in‑person services in other member states. The bill creates a new inter‑state commission, sets up a shared database, and establishes rules for licensing, adverse actions, and enforcement.
changes: Creates the Psychology Interjurisdictional Compact Commission and gives it rule‑making and enforcement authority

Allows psychologists licensed in a compact state to practice tele‑psychology in any other compact state without first obtaining a local license, provided they meet the compact’s credential and background‑check requirements
Permits psychologists to provide temporary in‑person, face‑to‑face services for up to 30 days in a distant state, again subject to the compact’s rules
Requires each state to report adverse actions, significant investigatory information, and other licensure data to a coordinated database
Imposes that a psychologist’s home‑state license be active, current, and free of adverse action for the psychologist to be authorized to practice in another state
Sets out a process for adverse actions and revocation of the compact’s “e.passport” or inter‑jurisdictional practice certificate if a psychologist is disciplined
Provides for default, termination, and dispute‑resolution mechanisms for states that fail to comply with the compact
Amends Montana’s psychology licensing statute (Section 37‑17‑202) to require fingerprint‑based background checks for all applicants and renewals
affected: Licensed psychologists in Montana and other compact states
Montana and other compact states’ regulatory authorities
Clients receiving tele‑psychology or temporary in‑person services
The new Psychology Interjurisdictional Compact Commission
numbers: 10 years after activation of the compact

HB242.one_line: HB 242 raises fines for invasive‑species violations and removes the warning‑without‑penalty option.
