HB242.summary: HB 242 raises fines for illegally transporting aquatic invasive species and eliminates the ability to issue a warning without penalty. The bill amends the penalty schedule in Section 80‑7‑1014, MCA, and requires civil penalties to be deposited in the general fund.
changes: Replaces the existing fine ranges for negligent violations with $500–$700 for first offenses and $750–$1,400 for subsequent offenses.
Replaces the existing fine ranges for purposeful violations with a maximum fine of $975–$1,950 and adds forfeiture of fishing licenses, vessel decals, and possible vessel surrender and restitution.
Creates a felony offense for knowingly or intentionally introducing an invasive species, punishable by up to 2 years’ prison, a fine up to $10,000–$25,000, or both.
Adds a civil penalty of up to $2,500 for other violations not covered in the first three subsections.
Removes the provision that allows a warning without penalty to be issued for violations of the invasive‑species rules.
Mandates that all civil penalties collected under the amended section be deposited into the state general fund.

HB244.one_line: HB 244 expands hunting/fishing benefits for deployed Montana residents and veterans, with free licenses and reset eligibility.
HB244.summary: HB 244 expands hunting and fishing benefits for Montana residents who serve in deployed military operations, adding free and discounted licenses and resetting eligibility after each qualifying deployment. It also guarantees replacement licenses for those who lose a drawing‑issued permit while deployed. The bill amends existing statutes to codify these benefits.
changes: Adds free resident conservation, Class A fishing, or Class AAA combination sports licenses for qualifying deployed Montana residents, excluding Class A‑6 black‑bear tags.
Allows a 5‑year entitlement period that resets after each qualifying 2‑month deployment outside the state, with no limit on resets.
Provides a 50 % discount on special antelope licenses for veterans or disabled service members with combat‑connected injuries.
Guarantees replacement of a lost drawing‑issued license or permit without additional fee when the member returns from deployment.
Requires quarterly reimbursement from the general fund to the general license account for costs of free licenses.
Specifies documentation (DD‑214, proof of contingency operation) required for eligibility.
affected: Montana residents in the National Guard, Army Reserve, or federal reserve who serve ≥2 months outside the state in a contingency operation.
Veterans or disabled service members with combat‑connected injuries.
License holders who lose a drawing‑issued permit while deployed.

HB245.one_line: HB 245 revises HELP Act workforce rules, adds reporting, and shortens the program’s end date.
HB245.summary: HB 245 amends Montana’s HELP Act workforce‑development rules, removes a training‑contract requirement, and shortens the program’s termination date. It adds new reporting and fraud‑prevention measures while repealing several earlier HELP Act provisions.
changes: Amends §39‑12‑103 to allow participants to take an employment assessment and receive workforce‑development services, including training and supportive services such as clothing, transportation, and equipment.
Requires the department to contract with private entities for workforce services and to report quarterly on enrollment, credentials earned, exits, employment outcomes, outreach, and expenditures.
Adds a fraud‑prevention clause that enhances technology to verify identity and employment status for unemployment benefits.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and approval, with the amended §39‑12‑103 taking effect on Oct 1 2025.
Terminates the HELP Act’s original termination date (June 30 2025) for the specified sections.
No new program, office, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Individuals receiving health‑care assistance under Title 53, ch. 6, part 13
Private nonprofit or for‑profit entities providing workforce services
The Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB246.one_line: Standardizes equivalency determinations for Montana professional licenses, revises reciprocity rules, and repeals duplicate statutes.
HB246.summary: HB 246 standardizes how Montana boards and the Department of Labor & Industry determine whether out‑of‑state education, exams, and experience are substantially equivalent to state standards. It amends several licensing statutes, clarifies the definition of substantial equivalency, and repeals older reciprocity and verification provisions. The bill does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Adds a statutory definition of “substantial equivalency” and clarifies who (board or department) must make the determination.
Rewrites 37‑1‑304 to require that an out‑of‑state applicant’s license standards be substantially equivalent to Montana’s before endorsement, and allows suspension if verification is falsely claimed.
Amends 37‑26‑201, 37‑33‑405, 37‑50‑203, and 37‑73‑204 to give boards authority to adopt rules for equivalency, reciprocity, continuing education, and examination fees.
Repeals sections 37‑39‑203 (out‑of‑state reciprocity) and 37‑65‑310 (license verification) to eliminate duplicate or conflicting language.
Allows the Department to issue a license to a valid out‑of‑state license holder without examination if the other state’s standards are substantially equal.
numbers: 12 hours of continuing education every 2 years

HB248.one_line: HB 248 expands voter‑registration cancellation grounds and takes effect immediately.
HB248.summary: HB 248 amends Montana’s voter‑registration cancellation rules, expanding the circumstances under which an election administrator may cancel a voter’s registration and making the changes effective immediately.
changes: Replaces Section 13‑2‑402 with a new list of cancellation reasons, including written requests, death certificates, court‑determined unsound mind, felony incarceration, court‑issued cancellation orders, notices of registration elsewhere, inactivity after two missed federal elections, and failure to meet any voter qualification.
Adds a new cancellation reason (8) for failing to meet any qualification listed in 13‑1‑111.
Makes the amended section effective upon passage and approval, with no delay.
affected: Registered voters whose registration could be cancelled under the new or expanded reasons.
Election administrators who must enforce the new cancellation criteria.

HB250.one_line: HB 250 revises out‑of‑district attendance rules, adding new denial grounds, tuition caps, and reporting requirements.
HB250.summary: HB 250 revises Montana’s out‑of‑district attendance rules, clarifying tuition, transportation, and reporting duties, and adding new denial grounds for trustees. It also updates remote‑instruction limits and non‑operating‑district funding. The bill takes effect July 1, 2025 for fiscal years beginning thereafter.
changes: Amends §§ 20‑5‑320, 20‑5‑322, 20‑5‑323, 20‑5‑324, 20‑7‑118, 20‑7‑421, and 20‑9‑505 to clarify application, approval, and reporting procedures for out‑of‑district attendance agreements.

Adds a new denial authority: trustees may refuse an application if it would jeopardize the district’s accreditation or if the student has been suspended, expelled, or truant in the past three years (except for special‑education students).

Revises tuition formulas to cap the amount the district of residence pays at 35.3 % of the tuition per‑ANB amount, with special‑education and out‑of‑state placement rules, and limits out‑of‑state tuition to $2,500 per student.
Clarifies transportation responsibilities: parents pay unless the student is a special‑education child with transportation in the IEP, or the district of attendance provides it by policy.
Requires districts to report out‑of‑district attendance data to the superintendent by June 30 and to the Education Interim Committee annually, including enrollment and tuition details.

Expands remote‑instruction eligibility to out‑of‑district students who cannot receive equivalent courses in their home district, and removes the requirement that remote instruction be sought from the nearest district offering it.
Creates a non‑operating fund for districts that do not operate a school, detailing how balances are transferred and used for tuition, transportation, and other limited functions.
Sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date and limits applicability to school fiscal years beginning on or after that date.
affected: Parents/guardians of students seeking out‑of‑district attendance

HB251.one_line: HB 251 tightens charter‑school rules, limits costs, and expands funding options while prioritizing personalized learning.
HB251.summary: HB 251 revises Montana’s public charter‑school laws to tighten the proposal process, limit costs, and prioritize personalized, proficiency‑based learning. It adds new definitions, requires fiscal analysis, and expands funding options for charter districts while clarifying special‑education obligations.
changes: Amends the charter‑school definition and related statutes (20‑6‑803, 20‑6‑805, 20‑6‑811, 20‑6‑812) to clarify roles, boundaries, and funding formulas.
Mandates the Office of Public Instruction to provide a fiscal analysis of projected state and local costs before charter proposals are reviewed.
Sets a 90‑day approval window and requires the Board of Public Education to limit the estimated annual additional state cost to the amount authorized by the legislature.
Prioritizes proposals that emphasize personalized and proficiency‑based learning and requires evidence of community support.
Prohibits the Board from waiving statutory requirements in charter contracts and requires transparency of approval decisions.
Allows public charter school districts to receive other public funding and donations under the Innovative Education Tax Credit program.
Establishes that a child’s resident school district must financially support a charter district that serves that child with a disability.
Defines a public charter school district as a non‑taxing, governing entity that receives state aid at specified percentages of basic entitlement and other payments.
Requires charter schools to adopt competitive bidding for purchases over $80,000 and to report financial activities annually.
affected: Public charter school applicants and governing boards
numbers: 80% of basic entitlement for charter districts

HB253.one_line: Department must publish twice‑weekly hospitalization and death data during a declared public‑health emergency.
HB253.summary: HB 253 requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to publish twice‑weekly updates on hospitalizations and deaths related to a governor‑declared public‑health emergency, including age, gender, length of stay, date of death, and underlying conditions, unless privacy concerns prevent disclosure.
changes: Department must post minimum twice‑weekly health‑information summaries on its website during a declared public‑health emergency.
Summaries must include total hospitalized and deceased counts identified by the governor.
For each category, the department must provide age‑cohort totals, gender totals, hospitalization duration, death dates, underlying conditions, and other causally related personal characteristics.
The department may modify or withhold data if privacy could be compromised.
The provision is codified into Title 50, Chapter 16, Part 6 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services
Montana residents hospitalized or deceased during a public‑health emergency

HB252.one_line: HB 252 expands funding incentives, adds housing‑cost authority, and restores full advanced‑opportunity aid.
HB252.summary: HB 252 revises Montana’s school‑funding formula, adds new incentive programs for teacher pay, resource sharing, and advanced opportunities, and expands eligibility for state aid. It also creates a housing‑cost budget authority, a data‑dashboard requirement, and restores full funding for the Advanced Opportunities Program.
changes: Amends the state funding formula to add incentives for teacher base pay, resource sharing, and advanced‑opportunity programs, and expands eligibility to more educational entities.
Creates a new housing‑cost budget authority that allows districts with high housing costs to use additional funds to offset those costs.
Adds a new K‑12 “Future Ready” funding component tied to post‑secondary preparation and career‑technical education.
Reinstates full funding for the Advanced Opportunities Program and includes district clerks and emergency‑authorized staff in the quality‑educator payment component.
Requires the Legislative Fiscal Analyst to develop a publicly available school‑funding data dashboard.
Provides a $100,000 biennial appropriation for advanced‑opportunity aid.
Effective on passage and applies to school years beginning July 1 2025.
affected: Students in advanced‑opportunity and Indian language immersion programs
numbers: $17,175 per 80 ANB over 800 for high schools
$5,724 per 45 ANB over 450 for middle schools

HB254.one_line: HB 254 eliminates fingerprint background checks for Montana PEO license applicants.
HB254.summary: HB 254 removes the fingerprint‑based criminal background check requirement for professional employer organization (PEO) license applicants and makes related procedural changes to the licensing process.
changes: Eliminates the requirement that applicants and controlling persons submit fingerprints for background checks by the Montana Department of Justice and the FBI.
Keeps the existing fee structure for initial licenses ($750 unrestricted, $500 restricted).
Maintains other licensing standards (age, partnership/LLC/corporate disclosures, net‑worth, security deposits, etc.).
Allows the department to issue restricted or provisional licenses under the same conditions as before.
Preserves the prohibition on license transfer.
Does not create a new program or criminal offense.
affected: Professional employer organizations and groups applying for licensure in Montana
numbers: 100 leased employees limit for restricted license

HB257.one_line: HB 257 expands critical‑infrastructure definitions to include broadband and revises trespassing and damage penalties.
HB257.summary: HB 257 expands Montana’s list of critical‑infrastructure facilities to include broadband and wired communications, and revises penalties for trespassing and damaging those facilities.
changes: Adds cable‑TV, broadband, and wired‑communications infrastructure to the statutory definition of a critical‑infrastructure facility.
Rewrites the definition of a critical infrastructure facility to list many new categories, including telecommunications and broadband assets.
Amends criminal‑penalty provisions so that trespassing on a fenced or sign‑marked critical‑infrastructure site with intent to damage is a felony (up to $4,500 fine or 18 months imprisonment).
Adds misdemeanor and felony penalties for damaging or tampering with equipment, with a $1,500 damage threshold for misdemeanors and up to $150,000 fine or 30 years imprisonment for larger damages.
Provides that an organization conspiring with offenders may be fined up to ten times the offender’s fine.
No new program, fund, or office is created.
No fiscal impact is specified in the bill text.
affected: Organizations that may be involved in conspiracies

HB259.one_line: HB 259 expands wolf‑management tools, permits landowner takes, and adds reporting and quota rules.
HB259.summary: HB 259 amends Montana’s gray‑wolf management rules to give the Fish and Wildlife Commission broader, region‑specific hunting and trapping options, allows use of thermal/infrared scopes, and creates a land‑owner‑take quota with reporting requirements. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑901 to let the Commission set multiple hunting licenses, allow unlimited harvests in some regions, and use bait and night‑vision/thermal scopes for wolf hunting/trapping.
Allows landowners or their agents to take wolves on private property without a Class E‑1/E‑2 license if the wolf poses a threat, subject to a yearly quota and mandatory reporting.
Provides a special kill permit for public‑land permittees who have livestock depredation, again without needing a Class E license.
Requires the Department to report annually to the Environmental Quality Council on implementation of the new rules.
All changes take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
numbers: unlimited number of wolves per license

HB260.one_line: HB 260 raises national‑board teacher stipends, sets state/district shares, and mandates annual inflation adjustments.
HB260.summary: HB 260 raises the maximum stipend for teachers with national‑board certification and sets a formula for state and district contributions, with an inflation‑adjustment mechanism. The law takes effect July 1, 2025 and applies to school years beginning thereafter.
changes: Increases the stipend cap for national‑board certified teachers from $1,500 to $2,500 for those in high‑poverty or impacted schools.
Defines the state’s share of the stipend (up to 75 % for the $1,500 level, 85 % for the $2,500 level) and the district’s matching contribution.
Requires the superintendent of public instruction to distribute payments by March 1 each year.
Provides a process for supplemental appropriations if state funds are insufficient.
Adds an annual inflationary adjustment tied to the quality‑educator payment amount in 20‑9‑306.

Specifies eligibility criteria (full‑time teacher, librarian, or other full‑time employee, certified under Montana law, employed by a public school district, education cooperative, school for the deaf and blind, or correctional facility).
affected: School districts, cooperatives, schools for the deaf and blind, correctional facilities

HB261.one_line: HB 261 expands the Department’s rule‑making and fee‑setting powers for all boards and sets new procedures for contested cases.
HB261.summary: HB 261 expands the Department of Labor and Industry’s authority to create rules for all boards, sets timelines for routine license issuance, and gives the department powers to monitor board finances and enforce fee adjustments. It also establishes procedures for contested administrative cases and requires public notice of hearings.
changes: Amends §37‑1‑101 to give the department broad administrative, legal, and clerical duties for all boards, including routine license issuance within 45 days and fee setting.
Adds a 10‑day notice requirement for deficiencies in routine license applications and a timeline‑setting requirement for non‑routine licenses.
Gives the department authority to monitor board cash balances, adjust fees, and recover costs through one‑time charges if a board is not cost‑effective.
Creates uniform rules for all boards to establish procedures for contested cases and to comply with public‑notice requirements.
Allows the department to suspend board duties (except renewals) and recommend legislative action if a board cannot operate cost‑effectively.
Provides for the department to investigate complaints of illegal or unethical conduct by board members or licensees.
Includes provisions for the department to adopt rules setting administrative fees, expiration, renewal, and termination dates for licenses.
Requires the department to keep official records of boards in Helena and to provide meeting facilities as requested.
affected: Boards of the Department of Labor and Industry
numbers: two times the board's annual appropriation level

HB264.one_line: HB 264 restricts release of hunted animal location data, with limited study and permitting exceptions.
HB264.summary: HB 264 limits the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (DFWP) from releasing wildlife‑location data or telemetry frequencies for hunted or trapped animals, except under specific study or permitting circumstances, and amends the public‑information statute to reinforce those limits.
changes: 1. DFWP may not release hunted/trapped animal location data or telemetry frequencies except as set out in subsections (2)‑(5).
2. Data used in a study with a completion report may be released one year after the report is finished.
3. Data not tied to a study may be released one year after the department acquires it.
4. Data may be released for environmental permitting activities.
5. Data may be shared with project partners or other government agencies via data‑sharing agreements, subject to the same timing restrictions.

6. Section 2‑6‑1003 of the Montana Code is amended to clarify that the DFWP and parties sharing data under a data‑sharing agreement may not release such data for hunted/trapped animals, except as provided in Section 1.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
project partners and other government agencies

HB266.one_line: Revises Montana’s K‑12 base‑aid inflation adjustments, caps increases, and adds reporting.
HB266.summary: HB 266 revises how Montana’s K‑12 base aid is adjusted for inflation, setting a specific calculation method, reporting requirements, and a cap on annual increases. The bill also creates a mechanism for committees to recommend higher adjustments and makes Senate Bill 258 void if both pass. The changes take effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑326 to prescribe a two‑year inflation‑factor calculation based on the U.S. CPI for July 1 of relevant years.
Limits the calculated inflation factor to a maximum of 3 % per year, but allows the superintendent, governor, or legislature to recommend or adopt larger adjustments.

Requires the superintendent to submit a detailed report on base‑aid increases and CPI changes to the interim budget and education committees by September 1 and to the finance committee by December 31, starting FY 2026 and every even‑numbered year thereafter.
Establishes that if Senate Bill 258 and HB 266 both pass, SB 258 is void, thereby giving HB 266 priority.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1, 2025.
affected: Education interim budget and education committees

HB267.one_line: Bill creates new DUI homicide crime, tightens penalties, and expands license‑suspension rules.
HB267.summary: The bill creates a new felony—aggravated vehicular homicide while under the influence—adds it to the DUI statutes, and amends several DUI‑related sections to tighten penalties, expand license‑suspension rules, and clarify sentencing options. It also revises definitions in the biometric‑data section of the law.
changes: Creates the crime of aggravated vehicular homicide while under the influence, punishable by 3‑30 years imprisonment, $10‑$50 k fine, or both.
Amends DUI penalty statutes (61‑8‑1007, 61‑8‑1008) to increase fines, extend imprisonment, and add mandatory license revocation for certain offenses.
Revises implied‑consent rules (61‑8‑1016) to broaden the scope of tests, clarify refusal consequences, and establish procedures for license seizure and temporary permits.
Amends Section 44‑15‑103 to update biometric‑data definitions and clarify law‑enforcement authority.
Revises Section 46‑18‑201 to modify sentencing deferment and suspension limits for felony offenders.
Adds new sentencing guidelines for DUI‑related felonies, including mandatory treatment and probation conditions.

HB268.one_line: Revises registration rules, adds petition process, and requires county attorneys to notify the Attorney General.
HB268.summary: HB 268 revises Montana’s sexual‑and‑violent‑offender registration rules, adding new relief‑to‑register procedures and requiring county attorneys to notify the Attorney General when a petition is filed.
changes: Amends §46‑23‑506 to set life‑time registration for sexual offenders, 10‑year registration for most violent offenders, and automatic relief after 10 years unless a new conviction occurs.

Creates a formal petition process for relief from registration, requiring service to the county attorney and, for violent offenders, mailing a copy to the last‑offense victim; for sexual offenders, mailing to both the victim and the Attorney General.
Allows courts to grant relief if the offender has been law‑abiding and continued registration is unnecessary for public protection.
Provides a 25‑year registration period for level 3 sexual offenders who were adjudicated delinquent as juveniles and have a clean record for 25 years.
Defines a “clean record” as no felony or sexual offense, no revocation of supervised release, and completion of a treatment program.
Permits closing of relief hearings to the public, with limited victim presence and support‑person rules.
Excludes certain offenders (e.g., those convicted of 45‑5‑503 or 45‑5‑507 with a victim under 12, second offenses, or designated sexually violent predators) from the 10‑ or 25‑year petition windows.
Adds a requirement that county attorneys mail a copy of any petition to the Attorney General’s office.

HB269.one_line: HB 269 creates a new state organic certification program and eliminates the advisory council.
HB269.summary: HB 269 eliminates the Organic Commodity Advisory Council and rewrites the state organic certification program, giving the department authority to develop, approve, and administer a Montana‑specific organic certification system. The bill creates a new state‑level program that may be more restrictive than federal rules and establishes a separate account for program revenues.
changes: Eliminates the Organic Commodity Advisory Council and its duties.

Amends §80‑11‑601 to require a petition by ≥50 % of certified organic producers, processors, and handlers to develop a state organic certification plan, which the governor submits to the USDA for approval.
If approved, two‑thirds of petitioners may petition the department to implement the program; the department then implements it.
Adds a new §80‑11‑602 creating a special revenue fund account for gifts, grants, assessments, penalties, and other monies collected under the program, separate from other department accounts.
Provides the department with rule‑making authority to adopt administrative rules consistent with federal and trade laws.
Allows producers to be certified under both the state program and other certifying organizations; the state program does not prohibit other certifiers.
Requires the department to seek regular input from the Montana Organic Association and other stakeholders.
Establishes procedures for assessment collection, enforcement, penalties, and investment of account funds.
affected: Certified organic producers, processors, and handlers in Montana

HB270.one_line: HB 270 tightens MEPA reviews, limits greenhouse‑gas analysis, and restricts court remedies.
HB270.summary: HB 270 revises Montana’s Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) to tighten the environmental‑review process, limit greenhouse‑gas analysis, and restrict judicial remedies for agency decisions. The bill amends sections 75‑1‑102, 75‑1‑201, and 75‑1‑208, sets an immediate effective date, and applies to all pending or new cases after that date.
changes: Amends MEPA’s intent and procedural sections to clarify that environmental reviews are for informing the legislature and the public, not for granting regulatory authority to agencies;

Replaces the existing alternative‑analysis requirements with a new framework that requires agencies to consider unquantified environmental values, private‑property impacts, and a detailed statement of impacts, alternatives, and fiscal analysis;
Limits environmental reviews from evaluating greenhouse‑gas emissions unless the review is required by a federal agency or Congress amends the Clean Air Act to treat CO₂ as a regulated pollutant;
Adds a 60‑day challenge window for final agency actions and restricts judicial review to the agency’s certified record, with no new evidence unless it is certified as new, material, and significant;
Prevents courts from vacating, voiding, or delaying leases, permits, or licenses on the basis of greenhouse‑gas analysis unless a federal requirement applies;
Requires agencies to provide written findings on the likelihood that a permit would violate statutory or regulatory requirements before withholding action;
Establishes that the Department of Public Service Regulation is exempt from the new requirements;
Sets specific time limits for scoping (60 days), review (90 days), and detailed statement (180 days) and allows one 50 % extension.
Provides that project sponsors may appear before the Environmental Quality Council or Water Policy Committee with 30‑day notice to discuss reviews;
Defines that the bill applies to all pending or newly filed cases after its effective date.
affected: Judges and courts handling environmental‑review challenges
Environmental Quality Council and Water Policy Committee
numbers: 1 year loss‑wage/ revenue cap for injunctions

HB276.one_line: HB 276 streamlines service of process and contact‑info updates for professional licensees.
HB276.summary: HB 276 standardizes how professional boards serve notices and require licensees to update contact info, adds optional electronic service, and removes duplicate rules. It amends several Montana Code sections to streamline service of process and update record‑keeping requirements.
changes: Licensees and applicants must provide current address and any change within 30 days, and if consenting to electronic service must provide a current e‑mail address and update it within 30 days.
Boards may serve notices by certified mail, electronic means (with consent), or personal service; electronic service is now expressly authorized.
The bill amends 37‑1‑309 and 37‑1‑403 to clarify notice content, hearing request deadlines, and service methods.
It requires dentists and dental hygienists to notify the board of name, address, or status changes within 10 days and prohibits local governments from imposing license fees on them.
Hearing‑aid dispensers must maintain a permanent business location, designate a non‑trainee in‑charge, keep records, and report address changes within 30 days.
Veterinary dispensing technicians must register annually, display their license, wear a name badge, and report address or employment changes within 15 days.
Section 37‑3‑310 (notice of change of address or name for applicants/licensees) is repealed.
The new Section 1 is codified as part of Title 37, Chapter 1, Part 1.
affected: Professional licensees (dentists, dental hygienists, hearing‑aid dispensers, veterinary dispensing technicians)
Professional licensing boards and the Department of Licensing
Local governments (in relation to fee prohibition)

HB278.one_line: Allows officers to check immigration status during lawful stops and report it to federal agencies.
HB278.summary: HB 278 amends Montana’s stop‑and‑frisk law to allow a peace officer to check a stopped person’s immigration status and to report that status to a federal agency if the person is not lawfully present. The bill does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Amends §46‑5‑401 to add subsection (3)(4) permitting a peace officer to determine a stopped person’s immigration status when reasonably practicable, except when it would hinder an investigation.
Requires the officer to report the person’s immigration status to a federal immigration agency if the person is not lawfully present.
Adds a notice requirement that an off‑uniform officer must identify themselves as a peace officer before questioning the person.

HB280.one_line: Repeals the Interagency Coordinating Council for State Prevention Programs and its reporting duties.
HB280.summary: HB 280 repeals Montana Code § 2‑15‑225, which established the Interagency Coordinating Council for State Prevention Programs, and eliminates the reporting requirements associated with that council. The bill simply removes the statutory authority and obligations for the council; no new programs or funds are created.
changes: Repeals § 2‑15‑225, MCA, the statutory basis for the Interagency Coordinating Council for State Prevention Programs.
Eliminates any reporting requirements that were tied to that council.
No other provisions are added or modified.
affected: State agencies that were members of the Interagency Coordinating Council
Any officials who previously reported to or through the council

HB279.one_line: Redefines appointment districts for four state boards, effective after the act’s date.
HB279.summary: HB 279 amends the list of counties that make up the districts used to appoint members to Montana’s Board of Public Education, Board of Regents, Coal Board, and Hard‑Rock Mining Impact Board. The changes only affect how vacancies are filled after the act’s effective date.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑156, MCA to redefine District 1 and District 2 counties for appointments to the four boards mentioned.
The new district boundaries are listed in full for each district.
The act applies only to vacancies occurring after its effective date and does not affect current officeholders.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The bill does not contain any fiscal provisions or funding changes.
affected: Candidates and appointees for the four boards
County residents who now fall into a different district for appointment purposes
numbers: District 1 counties: Lincoln, Flathead, Glacier, Sanders, Lake, Mineral, Missoula, Ravalli, Powell, Granite, Deer Lodge, Silver Bow, Jefferson, Broadwater, Beaverhead, Madison, Gallatin, Park, Sweet Grass, Stillwater, Carbon

District 2 counties: Glacier, Toole, Liberty, Hill, Blaine, Phillips, Valley, Daniels, Sheridan, Roosevelt, Richland, McCone, Garfield, Petroleum, Fergus, Judith Basin, Cascade, Chouteau, Teton, Pondera, Lewis and Clark, Jefferson, Broadwater, Meagher, Park, Sweet Grass, Wheatland, Golden Valley, Stillwater, Carbon, Musselshell, Treasure, Rosebud, Custer, Prairie, Dawson, Wibaux, Fallon, Carter, Powder River, Big Horn, Yellowstone

HB281.one_line: Creates a statutory appropriation and dedicated account for reinsurance program assessments, effective immediately, terminating 2031.
HB281.summary: HB 281 creates a statutory appropriation for the Montana Reinsurance Association’s member assessments, establishes a dedicated reinsurance program account in the state special revenue fund, and sets rules for depositing and using those funds. The act is effective immediately and expires June 30, 2031.
changes: Amends §17‑7‑502 to authorize statutory appropriations for reinsurance program assessments and related bond payments.
Amends §33‑22‑1321 to create a reinsurance program account in the state special revenue fund and a federal counterpart, specifying deposit sources and permitted uses.
Adds a coordination clause that voids any commissioner appropriations for reinsurance assessments if this act is passed.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and its termination date to June 30, 2031.
affected: State agencies issuing bonds for the program
State and federal special revenue funds

HB283.one_line: Allows annual lottery/auction of one male mountain‑sheep and one male Shiras‑moose tag, with proceeds for species management.
HB283.summary: HB 283 allows the Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Commission to sell one male mountain‑sheep and one male Shiras‑moose tag each year via a lottery or auction, with up to 10 % of proceeds retained by the conducting organization for expenses. All remaining money must be used for species management and reported to the budget office. The law takes effect March 1, 2026.
changes: Creates a single annual lottery/auction for a male mountain‑sheep tag and a separate one for a male Shiras‑moose tag
Allows a wildlife conservation organization to conduct the lottery/auction and keep up to 10 % of proceeds for reasonable expenses
Mandates that all remaining proceeds be used by the Department for the substantial benefit of the respective species
Requires the Department to report the use or investment of the proceeds to the Office of Budget and Program Planning
Specifies an effective date of March 1, 2026
affected: Wildlife conservation organizations involved in moose or mountain‑sheep conservation
Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks
Montana taxpayers (through reporting and use of funds)

HB284.one_line: Creates a temporary committee to investigate university civil‑rights violations and censorship, funded $23,000.
HB284.summary: HB 284 creates a temporary Montana University Investigation Committee to probe civil‑rights violations and censorship at public universities, reports findings to state and federal officials, and is funded with $23,000. The committee must finish its work by September 15, 2026 and is dissolved December 31, 2026.
changes: Establishes a six‑member committee (three from the House, three from the Senate) to investigate civil‑rights violations and censorship at Montana public universities.

Mandates the committee to gather testimony from students, produce findings and recommendations, and submit reports to the U.S. President, DOJ, Department of Education, Congress, Montana state officials, and the Montana congressional delegation.
Provides a $23,000 appropriation from the general fund for committee member compensation and expenses.
Limits the committee to no more than three meetings and requires completion of its work by September 15, 2026.
Includes a contingent‑voidness clause: the act is void if an appropriation is not included before the governor receives it or if the appropriation is vetoed.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1, 2025, and its termination date as December 31, 2026.
affected: Montana public university students and staff

HB285.one_line: HB 285 revises MEPA to clarify procedural limits, venue, and review timelines while removing older policy sections.
HB285.summary: HB 285 revises the Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) to clarify that it is purely procedural, limits judicial review of licensing decisions, sets venue requirements, and updates several MEPA sections while repealing older policy provisions. It does not create new programs or criminal offenses.
changes: Reaffirms MEPA is procedural and does not grant new regulatory authority to agencies.
Requires plaintiffs to prove unconstitutionality of the underlying statute before challenging a licensing or permitting decision under Titles 75 or 82.
Sets district‑court venue to the county where the proposed activity will occur.
Updates environmental‑analysis requirements, time limits, and procedural safeguards for public scoping and agency reviews.
Provides that challenges to environmental reviews must be filed within 60 days of the final agency action and may only be brought in district or federal court.
Establishes that the Environmental Quality Council and other boards have advisory roles in reviewing significance determinations.
Adds new procedural language regarding greenhouse‑gas assessments and limits their inclusion unless mandated by federal law or a separate Senate bill.
affected: State agencies issuing permits or licenses under Titles 75 or 82
Project sponsors and developers seeking permits
Environmental Quality Council and related advisory boards
Public and local governments involved in environmental reviews

HB291.one_line: Limits state and local air‑quality rules to not exceed federal standards, with strict public‑participation requirements.
HB291.summary: HB 291 limits the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) and local air‑pollution control programs from setting air‑quality standards that are stricter than federal Clean Air Act limits, except in a few narrowly defined circumstances. It amends several Montana statutes to codify the limits, establish procedures for public hearings and written findings, and clarify when local programs may adopt stricter rules.
changes: Amends §75‑2‑203 to prohibit DEQ from setting emission limits more stringent than federal standards, except for pre‑existing rules or non‑attainment areas; allows more stringent rules only if a public hearing, comment period, and written finding are completed.

Revises §75‑2‑207 to require a public hearing, comment period, and written finding before DEQ may adopt a rule that is more stringent than comparable federal regulations; provides a petition process for affected parties.

Amends §75‑2‑301 to set procedures for local air‑pollution control programs, including public notice, hearing, and written findings when adopting rules that are more stringent than state or federal standards; limits local authority over large or complex sources; allows DEQ to take over control if local programs are inadequate.
Adds a petition process for local rules adopted between 1996 and 2001 that are more stringent than state or federal standards.
Specifies that the act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Businesses and facilities subject to emission limits

HB292.one_line: HB 292 creates a uniform act that lets parties quickly dismiss civil actions that violate free‑speech or assembly rights.
HB292.summary: HB 292 creates a Uniform Public Expression Protection Act that allows private parties to seek expedited dismissal of civil actions that infringe on free‑speech or assembly rights. The act sets up a special motion, automatic stays, and fee awards, and applies immediately to new cases filed after passage.
changes: Establishes a new statutory framework (the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act) for protecting free‑speech and assembly claims in civil litigation.
Provides a special motion for expedited relief that can dismiss an entire action or part of it with prejudice if the claim applies.
Imposes automatic stays on all related proceedings, discovery, and hearings while the motion is pending, with limited exceptions.
Sets a 60‑day deadline for filing the motion and for the court to hear it, and a 60‑day deadline for the court to rule.
Allows the court to award reasonable attorney fees, costs, and litigation expenses to the prevailing party, and to award them to the respondent if the motion was frivolous or intended to delay.
Specifies that the act applies to civil actions filed on or after its effective date and does not affect claims asserted before that date.
affected: Private individuals, businesses, nonprofits, and other entities filing civil actions that involve free‑speech or assembly claims.
Responding parties in such actions, including governmental units and their employees acting in official capacity.
Courts handling civil litigation involving the protected rights.
numbers: 60 days (appeal deadline for actions involving the U.S. or Montana)

HB293.one_line: Revises election‑administrator rules, requiring appointed officials to report to county governing bodies.
HB293.summary: The bill amends Montana’s election‑administrator statute so that a county clerk is the default administrator, but a county governing body may appoint another official. The appointed administrator must report directly to that governing body and may appoint deputies for each political subdivision. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: County clerk remains default election administrator unless county governing body designates another official or appoints one.
An appointed election administrator must report directly to the county governing body.
The administrator is charged with all voter‑registration and election‑conduct duties and must keep all related records.
The administrator may appoint a deputy election administrator for each political subdivision that holds elections.
The amendment replaces the existing language in §13‑1‑301, MCA.
The act becomes effective on passage and approval.

HB296.one_line: HB 296 expands board disciplinary powers, tightens practice rules, and repeals old injunction provisions.
HB296.summary: HB 296 revises several Montana licensing statutes, clarifying board disciplinary powers, tightening rules on optometry, physical therapy, naturopathy, and real‑estate appraisal, and repeals old injunction‑penalty provisions. It expands the scope of injunctions and adds new misdemeanor penalties for unlicensed practice.
changes: Boards may adopt rules for revocation, suspension, probation, reprimand, or other disciplinary actions and must conduct contested‑case hearings under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Boards can seek injunctive relief in district court to stop unlicensed practice and may prosecute such cases with legal counsel.
Optometry rules now prohibit practice, sale, or use of fraudulent licenses and allow boards to seek injunctions for violations.
Physical‑therapy statutes forbid unlicensed use of PT titles and unlicensed assistants from aiding PTs, making such conduct a misdemeanor.
Naturopathy statutes restrict use of “doctor” and related titles to licensed practitioners and allow injunctions for misuse.
Real‑estate‑appraiser rules limit the use of the title “licensed real estate appraiser” to individuals, require license display, and set misdemeanor penalties for false claims.
Sections 37‑1‑411 and 37‑1‑412 (old injunction‑penalty provisions) are repealed.

HB299.one_line: Expands easement purposes and eases survey requirements for state‑land easements.
HB299.summary: HB 299 expands the list of public‑use purposes that the State Land Board may grant easements for and streamlines the application process by relaxing survey requirements for certain types of easements. The bill also clarifies when easements terminate and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Adds new public‑use categories—schoolhouse sites, public parks, trails, community buildings, cemeteries, and conservation purposes—to the easement grant list in §77‑2‑101(1).

Allows easements for right‑of‑way across state lands for highways, streets, canals, ditches, aqueducts, reservoirs, railroads, private roads, telephone lines, water conveyances, and other public uses in §77‑2‑101(2).
Permits easements for private buildings or sewage systems that encroach on state lands, and for private access roads, county roads, and utilities built before Oct. 1, 1997, in §77‑2‑101(2)(d).

Reduces survey requirements for easements used for electrical transmission, pipelines, telephone, telegraph, radio, and regional water authorities, and allows the department to waive survey requirements for certain pre‑1997 rights‑of‑way in §77‑2‑102(6).
Specifies that easements terminate when the purpose ceases and the holder is notified, in §77‑2‑105.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

HB300.one_line: HB 300 prohibits male athletes in female sports and denies students access to sex‑designated facilities.
HB300.summary: HB 300 amends Montana’s anti‑discrimination law to make it unlawful for schools to let a male student compete in female‑only sports or to deny a student access to a restroom, locker room, shower or sleeping area that is not designated for the student’s sex.  It also clarifies what is and isn’t considered discriminatory in admissions and allows certain exceptions for maintenance, medical, emergency, or safety reasons.
changes: Amends §49‑2‑307 to add a new subsection (3) prohibiting male participation in female‑only athletic programs.
Adds subsection (4) making it unlawful to deny a student access to a restroom, locker room, shower area, or sleeping quarter that is not designated for the student’s sex while in use.
Provides specific exceptions in (4)(a) for custodial, medical, emergency, or safety purposes.
Allows institutions to adopt policies for persons with disabilities, young children, or elderly persons under (4)(b)(i‑iii).
Clarifies that calling or referring to a student by legal name or sex is not discriminatory in (2).
Maintains existing prohibitions on discrimination by race, creed, religion, sex, marital status, color, age, physical or mental disability, or national origin.
Includes a severability clause in Section 2.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.

HB307.one_line: Revises hunting‑license donation rules for disabled veterans, tightening eligibility and use restrictions.
HB307.summary: HB 307 amends Montana’s hunting‑license donation rules so that only certain veterans can receive donated licenses and limits the donation to nonprofit rehab groups. It tightens eligibility, removes refunds, and clarifies use restrictions.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑815 to require donated licenses be reissued only to disabled veterans or armed‑force members who are Purple‑Heart recipients, medically retired with ≥70 % disability, or on active duty; no residency or fee required.
Prohibits the donor from designating the recipient veteran or the specific nonprofit; the license must be surrendered before the season starts.
Disallows sale, trade, auction, or monetary value of donated licenses; they may only be used by eligible veterans.
Adds that a veteran cannot have received a donated license in the past calendar year.
Allows the Department to adopt implementing rules.
Clarifies that restrictions in §87‑2‑702(3) and (4) do not apply to licenses issued under this section.
affected: License holders who wish to donate
numbers: no prior donation in past calendar year

HB311.one_line: Landlords must refund application fees if no lease is signed, but may keep costs for services actually performed.
HB311.summary: Landlords must refund application fees if a tenant never signs a lease, but can keep costs for services actually performed.  Wrongful withholding can be sued for damages.  The bill applies to multi‑unit properties beginning on its effective date.
changes: Landlords of four‑plus unit properties must refund the full application fee if the applicant never signs a lease or an equivalent agreement.
Landlords may deduct only the costs of services actually performed, as itemized in written notice given at the time of fee collection.
If a landlord wrongfully withholds or deducts a fee, the applicant may sue for the full amount plus attorney fees.
The bill defines “application fee” and “cost” and clarifies that time and effort are not deductible costs.
The provisions are codified into Title 37, Chapter 56, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
The act applies to application fees collected on or after its effective date.
affected: Landlords and property managers of four or more dwelling units

HB308.one_line: Extends the termination dates for statutes governing county distribution of metal‑mine license‑tax revenues.
HB308.summary: HB 308 amends the termination dates of existing statutes that govern the distribution of metal‑mine license‑tax revenues to counties.  The bill does not create new programs or change the tax itself, but it extends the period during which the current distribution framework remains in effect.
changes: Amends Section 5 of Chapter 442, Laws 2009, to change its termination date to June 30 2019 (with additional numeric references that appear to be typographical errors).
Amends Section 5 of Chapter 387, Laws 2015, to set its termination date to June 30 2027, with a secondary clause referencing June 30 2027 again.
Amends Section 1 of Chapter 213, Laws 2017, to include a termination clause that references June 30 2019, 2027, 2037, and 2035.

HB317.one_line: Repeals the requirement for a memorandum of understanding between the Board of Regents and Idaho College of Osteopathic Medicine.
HB317.summary: HB 317 repeals Montana’s statutory requirement that the Board of Regents maintain a memorandum of understanding with the Idaho College of Osteopathic Medicine, eliminating section 20‑25‑811 of the Montana Code. The repeal takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Repeals section 20‑25‑811, which required a memorandum of understanding between the Board of Regents and the Idaho College of Osteopathic Medicine.

HB312.one_line: HB 312 raises speed limits on four‑lane national highways and expands record‑keeping exemptions for speed violations.
HB312.summary: HB 312 raises daytime and nighttime speed limits on four‑lane national highways, adds a 10‑mph pass‑over rule, and expands the record‑keeping exemptions for speed‑limit violations. It also revises the fine schedule for exceeding limits.
changes: Increases the daytime limit on expanded national highways from 70 to 75 mph and the nighttime limit from 65 to 70 mph.
Adds a 10‑mph pass‑over exception for overtaking on two‑lane roads and in designated passing zones.
Rewrites the fine schedule for exceeding limits, setting specific fines for 1–10, 11–20, 21–30, and 31+ mph over the limit.
Expands the record‑keeping exemption so that most speed‑limit violations (≤10 mph daytime, ≤5 mph nighttime) are not recorded or used to raise insurance premiums.
Specifies that violations of 90 mph or more may be recorded and affect insurance.
Clarifies that the exemption does not apply to violations in special speed zones or by commercial drivers.
Allows the Transportation Commission or local authorities to alter limits as authorized in existing statutes.

HB321.one_line: HB 321 expands hygienist practice settings and creates a limited‑access permit for public‑health programs.
HB321.summary: HB 321 expands the settings in which dental hygienists may practice and clarifies the supervision requirements, adding a new limited‑access permit for public‑health and school‑based programs.
changes: Amends §37‑4‑405 to allow hygienists to work under general supervision in dentist offices, public‑health facilities, and school‑based programs;
Defines "direct supervision" (dentist on premises) and "general supervision" (dentist’s intent/knowledge, need not be present);
Creates a "public health supervision" category permitting limited preventive services without a dentist’s presence;
Establishes a limited‑access permit that the Board may issue to hygienists working in qualifying public‑health or school programs;
Specifies services allowed and prohibited under public‑health supervision (e.g., no local anesthesia, no temporary restorations);
Mandates referral to a dentist for any treatment outside the hygienist’s scope and requires adherence to board‑adopted guidelines.

HB318.one_line: HB 318 requires local health boards to provide an appeal process for sewage‑permit rules and limits how they can regulate private businesses during emergencies.
HB318.summary: HB 318 amends the state’s public‑health law to require local health boards to set up an appeal process for certain sewage‑disposal permit requirements, and it expands the boards’ powers and limits how they can regulate private businesses during emergencies.
changes: Amends §50‑2‑116 to add a requirement that local health boards adopt regulations for sewage control that include an appeal mechanism for variance and permit‑stringency decisions.
Mandates that those regulations must mirror state standards, provide appeals to the Department of Environmental Quality, and prohibit subsurface wastewater systems that encroach on adjacent property.

Expands the scope of local health boards’ authority to adopt fees, rules, and cooperation agreements with tribes and to enforce public‑health measures without imposing punitive actions on private businesses during emergencies.
Adds a coordination clause that voids overlapping amendments from other bills (HB 180, HB 658) and clarifies the definition of “private business.”
Limits emergency directives to the duration of the declared emergency and prohibits interference with religious facilities.

Prevents health‑board orders from denying customers access to private businesses or imposing fines, license revocations, or criminal charges for non‑compliance with health orders, except for isolated cases involving communicable disease.
Defines “private business” broadly as any non‑government entity, including nonprofits, for‑profits, corporations, sole proprietorships, or LLCs.
affected: Property owners and applicants for sewage‑disposal permits
Private businesses subject to health regulations
Tribal governments and Indian health services
Individuals with communicable diseases under isolation orders

HB324.one_line: HB 324 broadens voluntary‑payment protections for all liability claims, effective Oct 1, 2025.
HB324.summary: HB 324 expands Montana’s voluntary‑payment protections so that any liability claim—whether for personal injury, death, or property damage—may be paid without the payer admitting fault or waiving future claims. The law also clarifies that bad‑faith insurance actions do not apply to such payments and sets an effective date of October 1, 2025.
changes: Adds a new legislative policy statement (Sec. 26‑1‑701) affirming that voluntary payments are not admissions of liability.
Rewrites Sec. 26‑1‑703 to broaden the non‑admission rule to all liability claims, except specified insurance‑related actions and attorney‑fee disputes.
Rewrites Sec. 26‑1‑706 to treat prior voluntary payments as credits against any judgment, preventing recovery of amounts already paid.
Specifies that the amendments apply to claims accrued on or after October 1, 2025.
Clarifies that bad‑faith insurance actions do not apply to voluntary payments under the new rules.
affected: Claimants and defendants in personal‑injury, death, and property‑damage cases

HB323.one_line: Allows counties to pay reserve deputy sheriffs and adjusts county officer salaries.
HB323.summary: The bill amends the state’s county‑official salary statute to allow counties to pay reserve deputy sheriffs and to add specific salary adjustments for several county officers. It also expands the county compensation board’s authority and sets new rules for salary increases for deputy county attorneys.
changes: Adds a new subsection (i) to §7‑4‑2503 allowing reserve deputy sheriffs to be compensated as determined by the county commissioners
Provides a $2,000 annual add‑on for the county sheriff and allows additional discretionary salary, with longevity payments of 1% per year of service
Adds a $400 annual add‑on for elected county superintendents of schools, with a possible $2,000 bonus for those with certain advanced degrees
Allows the clerk‑and‑recorder, treasurer, clerk of district court, and justice of the peace to receive up to $2,000 additional salary
Revises the county compensation board composition and its annual hearing and recommendation process
Sets detailed longevity‑based salary increases for deputy county attorneys (e.g., $1,000 after 4 years, $1,500 after 5 years, $500 annually thereafter up to year 11)
Requires that the county attorney’s salary increase at least match any uniform base salary increase unless it would exceed a district court judge’s salary

HB328.one_line: Allows 75‑plus residents to harvest antlerless elk on private land with a general elk license.
HB328.summary: HB 328 lets Montana residents 75 + use a general elk license to harvest antlerless elk on private land in districts where youth under 15 can do so. It also revises the 62‑plus license list to include a half‑price conservation license and other tags.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑801 to add a new 75‑plus provision allowing a general elk license for antlerless elk on private land in districts where youth under 15 may harvest antlerless elk.
Keeps the existing 62‑plus list of discounted licenses (conservation, fishing, upland game, deer A, elk A, AAA combination).
Does not create new taxes, fees, or programs.
Does not alter any other hunting regulations.
No new enforcement or administrative offices are created.
affected: Hunters on private land in eligible districts
Youth under 15 who already harvest antlerless elk

HB325.one_line: HB 325 limits covenant enforcement after 15 years of inactivity while preserving essential covenants.
HB325.summary: HB 325 amends Montana’s covenant‑enforcement statute to clarify who may sue, how abandonment is proved, and limits enforcement after 15 years of inactivity. It also preserves enforcement for covenants that serve public or legal purposes.
changes: Amends §70‑17‑210 to list the parties that may initiate enforcement actions (agreement parties, owners, or governing bodies).
Adds a defense that a covenant is abandoned if no enforcement action has been taken for the period specified in §27‑2‑202 and if a court order or governing‑body approval records abandonment.

Prohibits an association or governing body that has not met for 15 years from enforcing a covenant against a parcel owner whose use is substantially similar to other parcels, except for covenants that serve legal, infrastructural, or nuisance‑abatement purposes.
affected: Owners of interest in covenanted property

HB330.one_line: Allows annual auction/lottery of antelope and swan licenses, with proceeds earmarked for species conservation.
HB330.summary: HB 330 would allow the Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Commission to auction or lottery a single license each year for antelope and for swans, with the proceeds earmarked for the conservation of those species.  The bill also lets a qualified wildlife‑conservation organization run the auction or lottery and keep up to 10 % of the proceeds for expenses.
changes: Creates a yearly auction or lottery license for antelope (one per year, any sex).
Creates a yearly auction or lottery license for swans (one per year).
Empowers the Commission to set rules for use of the license and conduct of the auction/lottery.
Allows a wildlife‑conservation organization focused on antelope or migratory game birds to conduct the auction/lottery and retain up to 10 % of proceeds for reasonable expenses.
Mandates that all remaining proceeds be used by the Department for the substantial benefit of the respective species, in addition to other management funds.
Codifies Sections 1‑2 into Title 87, Chapter 2, Part 8 of the Montana Code.
affected: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks
numbers: up to 10 % of proceeds retained by authorized organization
proceeds used for substantial benefit of species

HB329.one_line: Tax breaks for Montana ammunition‑component makers and their lenders, effective 2025, ending 2035.
HB329.summary: HB 329 creates tax incentives for Montana businesses that manufacture ammunition components and for lenders who finance those businesses, while amending several tax statutes to exclude related income from state tax calculations. The bill is temporary, effective immediately, retroactive to 2025, and expires 2035.
changes: Manufacturers of ammunition components receive exemptions from state property taxes, business‑equipment tax, individual and corporate income taxes, and other business taxes, except local property tax and payroll‑related taxes.
Exemptions apply only to the portion of the business devoted to ammunition‑component manufacturing and to property within 500 yards of a manufacturing or storage structure.
Lenders who provide bona‑fide loans to such manufacturers may claim exemptions from individual and corporate income taxes on the loan income, subject to the same restrictions.
Section 4 amends the property‑exemption list to add ammunition‑component manufacturing equipment as an exempt property category.

Section 5 amends the rules for determining Montana taxable income, adding and subtracting specific items related to ammunition‑component manufacturing and financing, and adjusting other income‑tax provisions.
Section 6 amends the definition of gross income for corporations to exclude income from ammunition‑component manufacturing and related loans.
The act is codified in Title 30, Chapter 20 (manufacturing) and Title 15, Chapter 24 (property tax).
The law applies retroactively to tax years beginning 1 Jan 2025, is effective upon passage, and terminates 31 Dec 2035.
affected: Lenders and investors financing those manufacturers
Montana businesses with related property within 500 yards of a manufacturing site

HB332.one_line: HB 332 expands district‑court jurisdiction for youth, revises transfer and consent‑adjustment rules, and updates supervisory transfer procedures.
HB332.summary: HB 332 expands the range of youth offenses that can be tried in district court, adds detailed procedures for transfer hearings and consent‑adjustment remedies, and clarifies how cases may be moved between juvenile and adult courts. It also revises the consent‑decree process and the revocation of stay rules.
changes: Adds 20+ new offenses that a 12‑ or 16‑year‑old can be charged with in district court, including violent, drug‑related, and trafficking crimes
Allows a youth or counsel to waive the mandatory transfer hearing; the court may still deny the waiver if it finds a transfer is warranted
Provides a detailed process for revoking a consent adjustment or consent decree when a youth fails to meet its terms
Revises the transfer of supervisory responsibility to adult probation services for youths aged 18‑25
Expands the circumstances under which a stay of execution can be revoked and the case moved to district court
Clarifies that a youth under 16 cannot be confined in a state prison and sets conditions for adult‑facility detention
Adds requirements for written notice, hearings, and rights for youths in transfer and revocation proceedings
affected: youths charged with the newly listed offenses
youths and their counsel in transfer hearings
youths under consent adjustments or decrees
numbers: 18‑25 years age window for supervisory transfer

HB333.one_line: Mandates police departments or sheriff contracts, sets fee rules, and replaces unfunded‑mandate laws.
HB333.summary: HB 333 requires every city or town to have a police department or contract with a county sheriff, sets fee‑setting procedures, and replaces earlier unfunded‑mandate laws.
changes: Amends §7‑32‑4101 to mandate a police department in every city/town unless a contract with a county sheriff is in place
Allows third‑class cities or towns to contract with a state‑recognized local law‑enforcement agency
If no department or contract exists, the county sheriff must provide services and the municipality must pay
Establishes a dispute‑resolution process: local government center mediation, then binding arbitration if no agreement after 30 days
Limits arbitration‑issued agreements to no more than two years
Requires equal cost sharing of local government center fees between county and municipality
Supersedes existing unfunded‑mandate statutes (§1‑2‑112‑116)
Includes a severability clause
Defines “sheriff” as an elected or appointed county sheriff or designee
affected: Local government center at Montana State University

HB335.one_line: HB 335 mandates biennial reports from licensing boards and governor appointment deadlines.
HB335.summary: HB 335 amends Montana’s professional licensing law to require the governor to appoint qualified board members within a set period, and it adds detailed biennial reporting requirements for each board.
changes: Amends §37‑1‑106, MCA to mandate a biennial report from each licensing board, detailing activities, finances, complaints, disciplinary actions, and member tenure;
Requires the department to submit these reports to the Economic Affairs Interim Committee and the Office of Budget and Program Planning;
Imposes a new reporting schedule but does not create new boards or offices;
The bill does not alter appointment procedures beyond the governor’s requirement to act within a specified timeframe (not detailed in the text).
affected: Montana Department of Labor and Industry
Office of Budget and Program Planning

HB336.one_line: Montana expands licensure to apprentices in many trades and health‑care fields.
HB336.summary: Montana will allow a number of licensed professions to grant licenses to applicants who finish a nationally‑recognized apprenticeship, subject to the same exam and fee requirements as those who complete a traditional educational program. Boards or programs must adopt rules to implement the change. The bill does not create a new program or fund, but expands the pathways to licensure for many trades and health‑care occupations.
changes: Boards or programs may award a license to anyone who completes an apprenticeship in the listed occupations.
Applicants must still pass the required exam and pay the same fees as traditional candidates.
The bill lists 21 license categories (e.g., barbering, nursing, plumbing, radiology, etc.) that may use apprenticeship pathways.
Each board or program must adopt rules to carry out the new licensing authority.
The provisions are codified as part of Title 37, chapter 1, part 1.
affected: Licensed professionals and apprenticeship candidates in the listed occupations
Boards and licensing programs in those professions

HB337.one_line: HB 337 lowers Montana income‑tax brackets, raises lower‑rate income, cuts top rate, and expands earned‑income credit for 2026‑27.
HB337.summary: HB 337 lowers Montana’s income‑tax brackets, raises the amount of income taxed at the lower rate, cuts the top rate, and expands the earned‑income tax credit. The changes apply to 2026‑27 tax years and expire at the end of 2026 for the bracket adjustments.
changes: Replaces current 15‑30‑2103 brackets with new, higher thresholds and lower top rate (5.9% to 5.4%) for 2026‑27; increases the amount of income taxed at 4.7% before the higher rate applies.
Adjusts net‑long‑term‑capital‑gain brackets similarly, with new thresholds and rates (3.0%/4.1%).
Applies a modified inflation factor to adjust brackets each year starting 2028.
Expands the state earned‑income tax credit to 10‑20% of the federal credit, with a refund provision.
The bracket changes (Section 1) are effective Jan 1 2026 and terminate Dec 31 2026; the capital‑gain changes (Section 2) are effective Jan 1 2027.
The earned‑income credit changes (Section 3) are effective Jan 1 2026.
Effective date of the act overall is Oct 1 2025.
The bill does not create a new program or crime.
affected: Montana residents filing individual income tax returns (married, head of household, single, estates, trusts).

HB338.one_line: HB 338 expands early‑literacy interventions to include numeracy, adds evaluation flexibility, and revises reporting and enrollment‑count rules.
HB338.summary: HB 338 expands early‑literacy targeted interventions to include numeracy, gives districts more flexibility to evaluate children for eligibility, and revises reporting and enrollment‑count rules. The bill amends several education statutes, adds new reporting requirements, and clarifies how early‑literacy programs affect average‑number‑belonging (ANB) calculations.
changes: 1. Adds numeracy to the definition of early‑literacy targeted interventions and allows districts to use numeracy‑based evaluation methods. 2. Grants school trustees greater flexibility to evaluate children for eligibility, including using research‑based, cost‑effective methods and allowing parents to request evaluations. 3. Requires districts to report annually on the efficacy of interventions, including anonymized student progress data and statewide assessment results. 4. Revises ANB calculations to count classroom‑based, home‑based, and jump‑start programs as full‑time, half‑time, or quarter‑time enrollment, and adds specific rules for jump‑start programs and other special programs. 5. Adds new reporting obligations to the legislature on early‑literacy program outcomes, enrollment counts, and funding. 6. Updates related statutes (20‑3‑326, 20‑5‑101, 20‑7‑1801‑4, 20‑9‑311) to reflect the expanded scope and reporting requirements.

who_is_affected':['school districts','trustees','students and families','Montana Office of Public Instruction','Montana Board of Public Education','Montana Legislature','Montana Department of Education','Montana Department of Revenue','Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services','Montana Department of Labor and Industry','Montana Department of Transportation','Montana Department of Environmental Quality','other state agencies required to report'],

HB342.one_line: HB 342 limits how a specific risk can raise a medical provider’s duty of care.
HB342.summary: HB 342 limits how a specific risk can affect a medical provider’s duty of care, stating that foreseeability of a risk does not raise the standard beyond what is reasonable. The law takes effect immediately and applies to malpractice suits filed after that date.
changes: 1. Clarifies that in medical‑malpractice cases, the foreseeability of a specific risk does not increase a provider’s duty beyond the reasonable standard of care.
2. Codifies this rule as part of Title 27, Chapter 1, Part 7 of the Montana Code.
3. Establishes that the act is effective upon passage and applies to malpractice actions filed on or after that effective date.

HB341.one_line: HB 341 adds an opt‑out $1 donation to vehicle registrations to fund TBI education and support.
HB341.summary: HB 341 creates a new automatic $1 donation for every motor‑vehicle registration that can be opted out of, directs the money to a special revenue account for traumatic brain injury (TBI) education and support, and amends several motor‑vehicle registration statutes to incorporate the donation and related notice requirements. The bill also appropriates $600,000 for the biennium to fund the TBI account.
changes: Adds an automatic $1 donation to the TBI account for every vehicle registration, unless the registrant opts out.
Requires county treasurers or authorized agents to post a notice explaining the donation and opt‑out option.
Specifies that donation proceeds be deposited into the special revenue account 2‑15‑2218 for TBI prevention, education, and support.
Amends 61‑3‑303 to allow the donation and opt‑out process and to clarify fee payment and notice posting.
Amends 61‑14‑101 to give the Department of Public Health and Human Services rule‑making authority over registration procedures that involve the new donation.
Adds a $600,000 appropriation for the biennium to fund the TBI account.
Leaves the cancer screening account (33‑22‑2104) unchanged except for noting that it receives donations for cancer screening.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Individuals and families affected by traumatic brain injury

HB343.one_line: Mandates religious‑instruction released‑time programs and optional academic credit in Montana schools.
HB343.summary: HB 343 requires every Montana school district to offer a religious‑instruction released‑time program that lets students be released at least one hour per week for religious instruction.  Districts may also award academic credit for such courses, but only on secular criteria and without using public funds or school property for the instruction.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑308, MCA, to mandate that school‑district trustees provide a released‑time program for religious instruction, with a minimum of one hour per week per student upon written parental request.
Requires that the program cannot use public school property or public money for religious instruction.
Allows districts to award academic credit for completed released‑time courses, provided the credit is evaluated on secular criteria and is neutral to religious content or denomination.
Specifies that released time counts toward the school day and week for attendance and funding calculations, and cannot adversely affect enrollment or attendance records.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1, 2025.

HB345.one_line: Clarifies MDT and commission roles in allocating federal transit and highway funds.
HB345.summary: HB 345 amends Montana’s transportation funding law to clarify that the Montana Department of Transportation (MDT) may allocate federal transit and freight funds, while the Montana Transportation Commission retains authority over highway‑related federal aid. The amendment also allows the commission to transfer funds between programs and delegate its duties to the department.
changes: Rewrites Section 60‑2‑129 to state that the commission may allocate federal‑aid highway funds for projects not on the defined highway system, without regard to the financial district.

Specifies that within its jurisdiction the commission (and the department) shall allocate all federal transit administration funds, freight assistance funds, and any legislative‑appropriated funds for rail or transit intermodal projects.
Adds a provision that the commission may authorize transfers of federal funds between qualified programs, including highway and transit programs.
Allows the commission to delegate its functions and responsibilities under this section to the department.
affected: Federal‑aid highway and transit program recipients

HB344.one_line: HB 344 adds a drug‑based DUI offense, tightens penalties, and expands rehabilitation and license‑suspension rules for all drivers.
HB344.summary: HB 344 expands Montana’s DUI laws to cover non‑alcohol drugs, creates a new DUI‑type offense, and tightens penalties, rehabilitation requirements, and license‑suspension rules for both commercial and non‑commercial drivers.
changes: Adds a new DUI‑type offense for drivers who have prohibited non‑alcohol, non‑marijuana substances in their blood or other bodily fluid, with specific thresholds listed in §61‑8‑1002(f).
Amends evidence rules in §23‑2‑535 so that any measured alcohol or drug level is admissible and refusal to test is admissible as evidence.
Rewrites §61‑2‑302 to allow suspended or revoked drivers to enroll in a driver‑rehabilitation program, with the possibility of a restricted probationary license and fee schedule.

Revises §61‑5‑212 to increase fines and imprisonment for driving during a suspension or revocation, especially when the suspension was due to a prior DUI or refusal to test, and adds automatic license‑suspension extensions for repeat offenses.
Rewrites §61‑5‑231 to let DUI courts issue probationary licenses to participants and to revoke them if conditions are violated.

Revises §61‑8‑805 to impose a 1‑year (or 3‑year for hazardous‑materials transport) suspension for a first 0.04+ BAC in a commercial vehicle, and a life suspension for a second or subsequent violation.
Rewrites §61‑8‑1001 to define “aggravated driving under the influence” and other key terms, including thresholds for THC and prohibited substances.
Rewrites §61‑8‑1002 to define the offense, add drug‑threshold provisions, and clarify evidence inferences for alcohol levels.

Rewrites §61‑8‑1007, §61‑8‑1008, §61‑8‑1009, and §61‑8‑1011 to set harsher penalties, mandatory treatment, and license‑suspension rules for first through fourth+ offenses, and to clarify how prior convictions are counted.
Adds detailed requirements for chemical‑dependency assessment, education, and treatment, including cost responsibilities and monitoring.
Clarifies how convictions are counted for sentencing and how license suspensions are enforced.
No new program or office is created; the bill merely expands existing statutes and adds a new offense type.

HB348.one_line: HB 348 revises special‑session polling rules, raising thresholds and adding draft legislation requirements.
HB348.summary: HB 348 amends Montana’s special‑session polling rules, raising the threshold to 10/30 legislators, requiring draft legislation in the request, and tightening the polling procedure and timing. The changes make it harder to call a special session and give legislators more information before voting.
changes: Raises the number of legislators needed to request a special‑session poll from 10/30 to 10/30 (unchanged but clarified)
Requires the request to include draft legislation to be proposed during the session, drafted by the Legislative Services Division
Adds the proposed convening date and time to the request
Expands the Secretary of State’s polling procedure to include the draft legislation and a stamped return envelope
Sets a 30‑day return deadline for normal polls and a 7‑day deadline for emergency/disaster‑related polls
Allows electronic delivery for emergency/disaster polls instead of certified mail
