Makes the act effective immediately upon passage

HB346.one_line: Exempts Commerce grant/loan programs from MEPA review, effective July 1, 2025.
HB346.summary: HB 346 removes the requirement that the Department of Commerce and several related agencies conduct Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) reviews for a wide range of grant and loan programs, from micro‑business development to historic preservation, workforce training, agritourism, and housing. The bill also directs the Secretary of State to notify all federally recognized tribes and codifies the exemptions into existing statutes, taking effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Exempts the Department of Commerce from MEPA review when authorizing, administering, or creating loan programs for micro‑business development, the wood‑products industry, and housing (including reverse annuity mortgages and veterans’ home loans).

Exempts the Department of Commerce from MEPA review for grant programs related to historic preservation, workforce training, agritourism, heritage and cultural tourism, business investment in historic downtowns, Montana‑based films, regional development corporations, and economic‑development projects.
Exempts the State‑Tribal Economic Development Commission and the Heritage Preservation and Cultural Tourism Commissions from MEPA review for grants or loans in the same areas.
Requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.

Codifies each exemption into the appropriate title of the Montana Code (e.g., Title 17, Chapter 6, Part 4 for micro‑business loans; Title 22, Chapter 3, Part 13 for historic‑preservation grants, etc.).
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
affected: Heritage Preservation and Cultural Tourism Commissions
Board of Housing (reverse annuity mortgage program)
Federally recognized tribal governments in Montana

HB350.one_line: Montana bans enforcement of WHO, UN, and WEF mandates on all political subdivisions.
HB350.summary: HB 350 bars Montana and its local governments from enforcing or funding any mandates issued by the World Health Organization, the United Nations, or the World Economic Forum. The law takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Prohibits enforcement of any requirement or mandate issued by the WHO, UN, or WEF by the state and all political subdivisions.
Prohibits allocation of public funds or resources for enforcing such mandates.
Adds a codification instruction to insert the prohibition into Title 2, Chapter 1 of the Montana Code.
Includes a severability clause ensuring any valid portions remain effective if part of the act is struck down.
Sets the effective date to the day the act is passed and approved.
affected: County, city, municipal, school district, special improvement or taxing district, and any other political subdivision or public corporation

HB349.one_line: Allows eligible retired teachers to rejoin the state school system for up to five years without losing benefits.
HB349.summary: HB 349 lets teachers who have been retired for at least two months and have 27+ years of service re‑join the state school system on a full‑time basis for up to five years without losing their retirement benefits, provided the superintendent can prove the position cannot be filled by a non‑retired teacher.  The bill sets reporting and contribution rules and ends on June 30 2031.
changes: Allows eligible retirees to be rehired by the superintendent for up to five years without loss of retirement benefits.
Requires the superintendent to certify that the position cannot be filled by a non‑retired teacher and to submit the retiree’s name, SSN, and contract to the Teachers’ Retirement System board.
The board must verify eligibility, notify parties, and report biennially to the Education Interim Committee and the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee.
Employers must contribute monthly to the retirement system equal to the sum of the standard contribution rates for retirees.
Re‑employed retirees are exempt from the earnings and employment limits that normally apply to active members.
The board may adopt rules to implement the section.
The provision is codified as part of Title 19, Chapter 20, Part 7 and expires June 30 2031.
affected: Retired teachers with 27+ years of service
State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee

HB352.one_line: HB 352 revises child‑support guidelines, creates a review committee, and requires a software contract.
HB352.summary: HB 352 amends Montana’s child‑support guideline law to create a periodic review process, establishes a committee with public members, and requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to contract a private software vendor. The bill also mandates notification of tribal governments.
changes: Amends §40‑5‑209 to require the department to adopt uniform guidelines and to review them at least every four years;
Creates a Guidelines Review Committee within the department that meets quarterly and recommends policy changes;
Mandates the committee include one non‑employee child‑support expert and one person with lived experience;
Allows committee members to be reimbursed under existing statutes;
Requires the department to notify the Supreme Court, district courts, and state bar before adopting guidelines;
Orders the secretary of state to send a copy of the act to each federally recognized Montana tribal government.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
Parents and children subject to child‑support orders

HB351.one_line: Clarifies fuel tax point of taxation, updates licensing, rates, and penalties for Montana distributors.
HB351.summary: HB 351 clarifies that Montana’s gasoline and special‑fuel taxes are due to the first licensed distributor who owns the fuel when it is withdrawn from a terminal or imported into the state. It amends definitions, licensing requirements, tax incidence, and penalties for dyed fuel, and sets a July 1, 2026 effective date.
changes: Defines the point of taxation as the first licensed distributor who owns the fuel at withdrawal or importation
Revises definitions of agricultural use, aviation fuel, biodiesel, distributor, etc.
Requires all gasoline and special‑fuel distributors to obtain a license and security (bond or deposit) before operating
Sets tax rates (33¢/gal gasoline, 29.75¢/gal special fuel, 5¢/gal aviation fuel) and specifies how revenue is allocated to state, highway, and local accounts
Imposes penalties for use of untaxed dyed special fuel, including civil fines up to $5,000 and potential criminal penalties
Limits tax exemption for dyed fuel to certain livestock‑feeding vehicles over 12,000 lb with a permanent feed box
Allows export of fuel without tax if the distributor is unlicensed and the fuel is shipped outside Montana
Provides a 1‑year rounding rule for distributor tax calculations
affected: Motor‑vehicle operators using dyed special fuel
State and local governments receiving tax revenues
numbers: $1,000 first‑offense civil penalty for dyed fuel

HB355.one_line: Clarifies that canal/ditch easement rights survive pipeline conversion and prohibits encroachment.
HB355.summary: HB 355 amends Montana’s easement law to make clear that owners of canal or ditch easements keep those rights even if the waterway is turned into a pipeline, provided the pipeline is clearly marked. It also preserves the prohibition against encroaching on such easements and allows written consent to override the restriction.
changes: Amends §70‑17‑112 to state that a canal or ditch easement holder retains a secondary easement to enter, inspect, repair, maintain, or operate the waterway after it is converted to a pipeline that is conspicuously marked.
Adds a prohibition against encroaching on or impairing easements for canals, ditches, or pipelines converted from them, unless written consent is obtained.

Clarifies that the prohibition applies to easements obtained by prescription or conveyance, but does not create new easements where none existed before April 14, 1981, and does not affect pre‑1981 contracts.
Provides that a prevailing party in a legal action enforcing the section may recover costs and reasonable attorney fees.
affected: Property owners adjacent to converted pipelines

HB354.one_line: Revokes hunting, fishing, and trapping privileges for up to 24 months after trespass convictions during those activities.
HB354.summary: HB 354 amends Montana’s criminal trespass law to add a mandatory revocation of hunting, fishing, and trapping privileges for anyone convicted of trespassing while engaged in those activities or collecting antlers, antler sheds, or horns. The revocation can last up to 24 months and applies to convictions or bond forfeitures. The bill does not create new offenses or programs, only expands the consequences of existing trespass convictions.
changes: Adds a new subsection (3) to §45‑6‑203 that requires revocation of hunting, fishing, and trapping privileges for up to 24 months when a trespass conviction or bond forfeiture occurs on state wildlife property or while the person is hunting, fishing, trapping, or collecting antlers, antler sheds, or horns.
Sets the maximum fine for criminal trespass at $500 and the maximum jail term at 6 months.
Specifies that the privilege revocation applies to convictions or bond/bail forfeitures, not just convictions.
Leaves the existing exemptions in §45‑6‑203 (e.g., 15‑7‑139, 70‑16‑111, 76‑13‑116, and subsection (4)) unchanged.
Provides an applicability date, but the exact date is not specified in the bill text.
Includes a clause (4) that clarifies that a lack of vaccination proof or mask requirement does not constitute criminal trespass in certain public places.
affected: Individuals convicted of criminal trespass while hunting, fishing, trapping, or collecting antlers/antler sheds/horns
Property owners or administrators of state wildlife lands
Law‑enforcement officers issuing convictions or bond forfeitures

HB356.one_line: HB 356 expands livestock loss programs to include black bears, adding reimbursement rules and grant priorities.
HB356.summary: HB 356 expands Montana’s livestock loss programs to cover black bears, adding new reimbursement rules, grant priorities, and a board‑run claim process. The bill amends several statutes to create the framework for cost‑share grants and reimbursements, sets eligibility and payment criteria, and establishes reporting and audit requirements.
changes: Creates a livestock loss board that administers programs for wolves, mountain lions, black bears, and grizzly bears; the board is appointed by the governor and includes five members.
Adds black bear predation to the list of predators covered for cost‑share grants and reimbursement payments.
Defines eligibility, claim, and reimbursement procedures, including confirmation and probable loss definitions, fair‑market‑value limits, and a multiplier option by region.
Establishes grant priorities that favor wolf and grizzly bear prevention over mountain lion or black bear prevention.
Requires the board to submit monthly and annual reports, conduct audits, and maintain confidential claim records.
Allows the board to sell or auction carcasses from large predators and deposit proceeds into a special revenue account.
Amends the special revenue account statute to direct all state and federal funds for these programs into the designated livestock loss account.
Adds a notification requirement to federally recognized tribes and sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
affected: Tribal governments with predator management plans
State and federal agencies handling predator carcasses
Program participants receiving grants or reimbursements

HB357.one_line: HB 357 funds middle‑grade CTE and directs the Superintendent to set distribution rules.
HB357.summary: HB 357 authorizes $240,000 for middle‑grade career and technical education (CTE) and requires the Superintendent of Public Instruction to develop rules for distributing the funds. The money is intended to supplement federal Perkins funding and is not limited by school size.
changes: Authorizes a $240,000 appropriation for fiscal year 2027 to support middle‑grade CTE.
Mandates the Superintendent of Public Instruction to annually distribute the money to accredited junior‑high, middle‑school, or 7th‑8th‑grade programs.
Requires the Superintendent to prescribe distribution methods, application forms, budget procedures, and accounting rules for the funds.
Allows the Superintendent to add other requirements consistent with Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 3.
The appropriation is intended to become part of the ongoing base for future sessions.
affected: Elementary and K‑12 school districts with accredited middle‑grade programs

HB271.one_line: HB 271 narrows executive‑privilege exemptions, sets a 60‑day limit, and awards costs to prevailing parties in records litigation.
HB271.summary: HB 271 limits the governor’s executive‑privilege exemption to very narrow, privacy‑based cases, requires court review, sets a 60‑day expiration, and awards costs to prevailing parties in records litigation.
changes: 1. Gov. may assert an executive exemption only when personal privacy clearly outweighs public interest, and only for policy, politics, or legislative matters is the exemption denied.
2. Exemptions must be narrowly tailored, may only redact the specific information, and are subject to court review for over‑breadth.
3. Exemptions expire when the underlying issue is resolved or after 60 days, whichever comes first, and are waived if the information is voluntarily disclosed to a third party.
4. Section 2‑6‑1002 is amended to define “confidential information” and clarify who is a constitutional officer and what constitutes a constitutional‑officer record.
5. Section 2‑6‑1009 is amended to award costs and reasonable attorney fees to a prevailing party in a public‑records lawsuit.
6. Section 90‑1‑105 is amended to expand the Commerce Department’s economic‑development functions (no new program created).
affected: Montana governors and other constitutional officers

HB340.one_line: Establishes a state‑wide mentor program for new teachers with $1 million annual funding and stipend payments.
HB340.summary: HB 340 creates a statewide Montana B.E.S.T. teacher‑training program to mentor early‑career teachers for one year, funded with $1 million per biennium and $2,500/teacher stipends. The program runs from July 1 2025 to June 30 2031 and requires annual reporting to the Education Interim Committee.
changes: Creates the Montana B.E.S.T. teacher‑training program administered by the Office of Public Instruction.
Mandates a one‑year mentor‑early‑career teacher pairing with criteria for mentor selection and training.
Provides $2,500 stipends for mentor teachers and $600 stipends for early‑career teachers (minimum $300 from the district).
Allocates $1 million from the state general fund each biennium for the program and caps administrative costs at 15 % of state funding.
Requires annual reporting on program status and impact to the Education Interim Committee.
Defines “early‑career teacher” as a teacher in the first three years of their career.
Sets the program’s effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2031.
affected: Office of the Commissioner of Higher Education

HB21.one_line: Creates a state tax credit for low‑income housing projects with limits and recapture rules.
HB21.summary: The bill creates a Montana workforce housing tax credit that can be claimed against state income, insurance premium, and property taxes for qualified low‑income projects. It sets limits on annual credit allocation, establishes a 6‑year claim period, and requires board‑issued eligibility statements and recapture rules tied to federal low‑income credits.
changes: Creates a new state tax credit for qualified low‑income housing projects beginning 2026.
Limits total annual allocation to $1.5 million plus carry‑over and revoked credits.
Allows the credit to be claimed for up to 6 years after a project is placed in service.
Requires the Board of Housing to issue eligibility statements and administer the credit per a qualified allocation plan.
Imposes recapture of the credit if the related federal low‑income housing credit is recaptured or disallowed.
Prevents developers from receiving remuneration from the credit beyond a developer fee.
Prohibits credit reservations after Dec. 31 2031.
Adds the credit to the biennial review list of the Revenue Interim Committee.
Codifies the credit into specific Montana tax code chapters.
Sets the effective date as Jan. 1 2026 for tax years.
affected: Taxpayers owning interests in qualified low‑income housing projects

HB25.one_line: Exempt entities leasing property for non‑exempt use must report annually or face taxation.
HB25.summary: HB 25 requires exempt entities that lease property for non‑exempt use to file an annual report with the Department of Revenue. If they fail to report, the property is taxed under existing rules. The bill amends the exemption list to clarify reporting requirements and to codify the new reporting rule.
changes: Exempt entities leasing property for non‑exempt use must submit an annual report describing the property and a copy of the lease agreement.
Failure to report triggers the tax provisions of 15‑8‑601, making the property taxable.
The bill amends §15‑6‑201 to incorporate the new reporting requirement and to clarify that exempt property leased for non‑exempt use is subject to taxation.
The amendment codifies the reporting rule as part of Title 15, Chapter 6, Part 2.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The bill does not alter any tax rates or create new revenue streams.
The amendment does not change the definition of exempt property beyond the reporting requirement.
affected: Exempt entities that lease property for non‑exempt use
Taxpayers whose property is leased by exempt entities

HB30.one_line: Shifts burden of proof to challengers in constitutional challenges to Montana statutes.
HB30.summary: The bill amends Montana law to require the Supreme Court to uphold a legislative act unless the challenger proves it unconstitutional beyond a reasonable doubt. It effectively shifts the burden of proof onto the plaintiff in constitutional challenges to statutes. The change applies to all civil actions in Montana courts.
changes: Amends §3‑2‑701, MCA, to add a new standard of review for constitutional challenges to legislative acts.
The Supreme Court must uphold a legislative act unless the challenger demonstrates unconstitutionality beyond a reasonable doubt.
The amendment clarifies that the Court’s rules may not abridge, enlarge, or modify substantive rights or be inconsistent with the state constitution.
No new program, fund, or office is created.
The amendment does not alter any procedural rules beyond the burden‑of‑proof requirement.
The change applies to all civil actions in Montana courts.

HB27.one_line: HB 27 redefines agricultural land classifications, adds application and review processes, and updates tax rates and appraisal rules.
HB27.summary: HB 27 revises Montana’s agricultural‑land classification rules, creating a new application process for sustenance‑use, idle‑land, and forest‑land categories while tightening income and use requirements. It also amends tax‑rate schedules, appraisal rules, and several related statutes, with a delayed effective date of Jan 1 2027.
changes: Land must now apply annually (by March 1) for sustenance‑use classification, proving non‑commercial use, 60 % food cultivation, 100 hrs of active work, and a residential dwelling on the parcel.
The $500 annual‑gross‑income cap from surplus production is imposed for sustenance‑use land.
Idle land (20‑160 acres) is re‑classified as non‑qualified agricultural idle land and taxed at the average grazing‑land value.
New forest‑land classifications (non‑productive forest land) are added with specific valuation and tax‑rate formulas.

The bill amends several tax‑rate sections (15‑6‑133, 15‑6‑134, 15‑6‑143, 15‑7‑202, 15‑7‑206, 15‑7‑307, 15‑8‑111, 15‑10‑420, 15‑18‑219, 15‑30‑2660, 15‑44‑102) to reflect the new classifications and rates.
A new application and review process is established for agricultural land, requiring proof of income, use, and active cultivation.
The act removes the automatic “non‑qualified agricultural” classification and replaces it with a formal review and re‑application schedule.
The effective date is Jan 1 2027, applying to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2026.
affected: Landowners of agricultural, sustenance‑use, idle, and forest land
Municipal and county governments setting mill levies
Entities participating in the Montana Health and Economic Livelihood Partnership Act

HB33.one_line: Allows agencies to dismiss petition portions outside their jurisdiction and requires written, informative decisions.
HB33.summary: The bill amends Montana’s rule‑making law to let agencies dismiss portions of petitions that address matters outside the agency’s jurisdiction, and requires written decisions that explain the dismissal and point petitioners to the proper agency. The change applies immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §2‑4‑315 to allow an agency to summarily dismiss any portion of a petition that raises an issue beyond the agency’s regulatory jurisdiction or rule‑making authority.
Requires the agency to provide a written decision within 60 days of petition receipt, including reasons for denial or initiation of rule‑making.
The written decision for a summary dismissal must also give contact information for any agency or body that may have jurisdiction over the issue.
Allows, but does not require, the agency to hold a hearing or oral presentation to develop a record and give the petitioner an opportunity to present views.
The agency must prescribe the form and procedure for petitions by rule.
affected: Other agencies that may have jurisdiction over the dismissed issues

HB35.one_line: Reallocates the judicial standards commission to the Department of Justice while preserving its independence.
HB35.summary: The bill moves the judicial standards commission from its previous placement to the Department of Justice for administrative purposes while preserving its independence. It also redefines the commission’s membership and term structure. The change takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Amends §3‑1‑1101 to create a five‑member commission: 2 district‑court judges, 1 attorney, 2 non‑lawyer citizens.
Members are appointed by the speaker, attorney general, and governor, all confirmed by the senate.
Commission members serve staggered four‑year terms.
The commission is allocated to the Department of Justice for administrative purposes only, but may hire its own staff.
Commission functions remain independent of the Department of Justice.

HB34.one_line: Creates a permanent disaster resiliency fund and transfers $100 million into it.
HB34.summary: HB 34 establishes a permanent Montana local disaster resiliency fund, removes its termination date, and directs the state treasurer to transfer $100 million from the general fund into the fund. The bill also amends the statutory appropriation amount and clarifies eligible uses of the money.
changes: Amends §17‑7‑133, MCA, to make the local disaster resiliency fund permanent and sets an annual appropriation of up to $15 million beginning FY 2023; the appropriation is void in any year with a projected general‑fund deficit.
Replaces the termination provision in §24, Ch. 722, L. 2023, eliminating the June 30 2025 and June 30 2027 termination dates.
Adds a new §3 directing the treasurer to transfer $50 million from the general fund to the resiliency fund by June 30 2025 and another $50 million during the biennium ending June 30 2027.
Specifies that the act takes effect immediately upon passage.
Clarifies eligible uses of the fund: mitigation projects, non‑federal cost share for mitigation program management, and matching funds for hazardous‑material equipment and training.
Amends §17‑7‑133 to state that the appropriation is void in any year with a projected general‑fund deficit.

HB36.one_line: Prohibits judges from chairing the Judicial Standards Commission, preserving its composition and terms.
HB36.summary: The bill amends the Judicial Standards Commission to prohibit any district court judge from serving as its presiding officer. It clarifies the commission’s composition and term lengths while maintaining the existing appointment process. No new programs or funds are created.
changes: Amends §3‑1‑1101, MCA to add a prohibition that a district court judge cannot be the presiding officer of the Judicial Standards Commission.
Leaves the commission’s five‑member structure unchanged: 2 judges, 1 attorney, 2 citizens.
Preserves the staggered four‑year term schedule for all members.
Maintains the existing appointment and senate confirmation procedures for each member type.
Does not alter any other statutory provisions or create new offices or funds.
numbers: 10 years of legal practice required for attorney

HB50.one_line: Expands Good Samaritan immunity for parents and pregnant women with substance‑use disorders.
HB50.summary: HB 50 amends Montana’s Good Samaritan law to expand immunity for parents and pregnant women with substance‑use disorders, and limits how a parent’s drug test can trigger child‑abuse proceedings.
changes: Adds new immunity for parents who seek medical help for an overdose or who themselves need help after an overdose, preventing arrest, charge, or prosecution based on that assistance.
Extends Good Samaritan immunity to pregnant women seeking treatment or prenatal care, and to women seeking postpartum care up to 12 months after delivery.
Prevents a parent’s positive drug test from being the sole basis for child‑abuse investigations, protective‑care placement, or termination of parental rights.
Allows a parent’s first‑aid act during an overdose to be a mitigating factor in unrelated criminal prosecutions.
Prohibits revoking pre‑trial release or parole for incidents covered by the new immunity.
affected: Pregnant and postpartum women with substance‑use disorders

HB52.one_line: HB 52 limits agency deference, tightens emergency rules, and expands legislative control over Montana’s administrative rules.
HB52.summary: HB 52 revises Montana’s Administrative Procedure Act to limit judicial deference to agency interpretations, tighten emergency‑rulemaking, expand legislative oversight of rules, and require public posting of settlements and stipulations. It also clarifies evidence rules and the standard of review in contested‑case proceedings.
changes: Rewrites §2‑4‑101 to state that judges must interpret law without deference to agency interpretations.
Rewrites §2‑4‑102 to define key terms and exempt certain boards and agencies from contested‑case review.
Rewrites §2‑4‑303 to impose stricter notice and justification requirements for emergency rules and prohibit emergency rules for budget cuts.
Rewrites §2‑4‑412 to give the legislature the power to repeal or direct changes to rules and require agencies to adopt new rules consistent with legislative objections.
Rewrites §2‑4‑506 to allow declaratory judgments that invalidate rules found arbitrary or contrary to statutory intent.
Rewrites §2‑4‑603 to make informal settlements public record, deposit settlement proceeds in designated accounts, and allow parties to waive formal proceedings.
Rewrites §2‑4‑612 to clarify evidence and cross‑examination procedures in agency hearings.
Rewrites §2‑4‑704 to set a de‑novo standard of review, prohibit judicial substitution of agency fact‑finding, and require courts to interpret statutes and agency rules without agency deference.

HB51.one_line: Raises university employers’ supplemental contribution to the TRS to 14.21%.
HB51.summary: The bill raises the supplemental employer contribution rate for Montana university system employers to 14.21% of total compensation, effective July 1 2025, to fully amortize the system’s past‑service liability by July 1 2033. It replaces the previous 4.04% and 4.72% rates and requires periodic review of the rate. The change applies only to university‑system employees who participate in the Teachers’ Retirement System.
changes: Amends §19‑20‑621 to set the supplemental contribution rate at 14.21% of total compensation for all university‑system employees in the TRS.
Replaces the former 4.04% rate (July 1 2001‑June 30 2007) and 4.72% rate (July 1 2007‑present) with the new rate.
Mandates that the board periodically review the rate and recommend adjustments to keep the liability amortized by July 1 2033.
Specifies the effective date of the change as July 1 2025.
affected: Teachers and other employees in the TRS

HB57.one_line: Adds California and Gambel’s quail to the definition of upland game birds, effective March 1 2026.
HB57.summary: HB 57 amends Montana’s definition of “upland game birds” to add California quail and Gambel’s quail. The change has no new programs or fees and takes effect March 1, 2026.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑101 to list California quail and Gambel’s quail among upland game birds.
No other statutory provisions are altered.
The amendment does not create new regulations, fees, or enforcement mechanisms.
The act becomes effective March 1, 2026.
The change applies statewide to all hunting, fishing, and wildlife‑management activities.
The bill is purely definitional and does not affect existing hunting seasons or permits.
affected: Hunters and anglers who target upland game birds

HB65.one_line: Audit the Montana State Bar’s finances; judicial branch pays; confidential files exempt.
HB65.summary: HB 65 requires the Legislative Audit Division to conduct a one‑time financial performance audit of the Montana State Bar, with the judicial branch paying for the audit. The audit must cover funding sources, expenditures, and budgets over the past decade, but cannot examine confidential attorney‑related files.
changes: Mandates a single financial performance audit of the Montana State Bar by the Legislative Audit Division.
Specifies that the audit must cover funding sources, spending over the past 10 years, and budget analysis.
Excludes examination of confidential or sensitive attorney‑related files (e.g., trust accounts, disciplinary files, continuing‑education files).
Requires the judicial branch to pay the entire cost of the audit.

Sets a completion deadline of December 15, 2026, after which the audit is to be presented to the Legislative Audit Committee, the Law and Justice Interim Committee, the Budget Subcommittee, and posted on the Legislative Audit Division website.
Amends MCA §5‑13‑102 to define “committee” as the Legislative Audit Committee and “state agency” in a broad sense.
affected: Members of the Legislative Audit Committee

HB73.one_line: Repeals the state’s permission for livestock owners to kill eagles, hawks, and owls.
HB73.summary: The bill removes Montana’s authorization that allowed livestock or poultry owners to kill eagles, hawks, or owls. It repeals Section 87‑5‑209 of the Montana Code and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Repeals Section 87‑5‑209 of the Montana Code, which previously permitted livestock or poultry owners to destroy eagles, predatory hawks, and owls.
The repeal takes effect immediately upon the bill’s passage and approval.

HB71.one_line: Allows a second lion license and ends Tendoy sheep reporting requirements.
HB71.summary: HB 71 revises Montana’s special‑license rules for mountain lions and sheep, allowing a hunter to hold more than one lion license in a year and eliminating the department’s reporting obligations for Tendoy Mountain sheep. The bill also amends the existing special‑license statute to clarify restrictions on multiple licenses for other big‑game species.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑702 to permit a hunter who has killed a mountain lion to receive a second lion special license in the same license year.
Rewrites §87‑2‑702 to clarify that a person who has taken a game animal other than deer, elk, antelope, or mountain lion cannot receive a second special license for that species in the same year.

Adds a provision that a hunter who takes a legal ram mountain sheep under an unlimited or population‑management license is barred from receiving another special license for that species for seven years.
Eliminates the requirement that the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks report on Tendoy Mountain sheep harvests, tissue‑sampling efforts, and data sharing to the Environmental Quality Council.
Leaves unchanged the existing limits on grizzly bear, moose, mountain goat, and limited mountain‑sheep licenses.
The bill does not create a new program, office, or criminal offense.
affected: Hunters seeking special licenses for mountain lions, mountain sheep, moose, mountain goats, and other big‑game species
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (reporting duties)

HB93.one_line: Montana creates a civil‑claim process and special fund to compensate wrongfully convicted felons.
HB93.summary: Montana will now allow people who were wrongfully convicted of felonies to file civil claims for compensation, expungement, and related benefits. The bill sets out the filing process, damages schedule, and a special fund to pay awards, while requiring counties or consolidated governments to share the cost.
changes: Creates a civil‑claim procedure for wrongful‑conviction exonerates, including filing, evidence, and court‑determined damages;
Establishes a special revenue account (the Exoneree Compensation Fund) to pay awards and allows counties or consolidated governments to contribute 50‑75% of the award;
Provides a schedule of damages ($65‑$80k per year of imprisonment plus additional amounts for parole, probation, or registration);
Mandates expungement of convictions and arrest records upon a court’s certificate of innocence;
Includes a transition‑assistance grant of $5,000 and rental‑voucher provision for claimants while their case is pending;
Imposes a waiver of other claims against the state and its subdivisions, with an offset provision if other damages are later awarded.
affected: Wrongfully convicted felons who have been exonerated
County and consolidated governments where the conviction occurred
Montana Department of Justice and Department of Administration
Montana courts and attorneys handling wrongful‑conviction claims

HB94.one_line: Allows securities‑and‑insurance investigations to use tax‑record data while preserving confidentiality for most purposes.
HB94.summary: HB 94 amends Montana’s tax‑record confidentiality law to allow the Commissioner of Securities and Insurance, along with other state agencies, to access taxpayer information for investigations of fraud and abuse. The bill also clarifies when records can be disclosed, sets penalties for violations, and establishes procedures for sharing data with federal and state partners.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2618 to permit the Commissioner of Securities and Insurance to obtain and use taxpayer return information for securities‑and‑insurance investigations, subject to a judicial order or other legal authority.

Adds a new subsection that authorizes the Department of Revenue to provide taxpayer return data and payroll‑withholding information to the Department of Labor and Industry, the State Fund, the Office of the State Auditor, and the Commissioner of Securities and Insurance for fraud‑prevention purposes.

Specifies that the Department may share abstracted or specific income‑tax information with federal and other state tax authorities only if those authorities have comparable privileges under their own statutes.
Clarifies that the confidentiality of tax records remains intact for most purposes, except for the newly listed exceptions and for the purposes of the agencies listed in the bill.
Sets a fine of up to $500 for violations of the confidentiality provisions and requires dismissal and a one‑year bar from public office for state officers who violate the law.
Requires that tax reports and returns be preserved for at least three years, or until the Department orders destruction.
affected: Taxpayers whose income‑tax returns are filed in Montana
State agencies: Department of Revenue, Department of Labor and Industry, State Fund, Office of the State Auditor, Commissioner of Securities and Insurance
Federal and other state tax authorities who request access

HB103.one_line: Creates a state rail inspection program funded by 8 % of railroad‑car‑property taxes.
HB103.summary: The bill creates a state‑run rail inspection program, establishes a dedicated revenue account funded by 8 % of certain railroad taxes, and requires the commission to report annually to the Energy and Telecommunications Interim Committee.
changes: Amends 15‑23‑215 to divert 8 % of railroad‑car‑property taxes into a new Montana Rail Inspection Account.
Amends 17‑7‑502 to define statutory appropriations and list the new account as a statutory appropriation.
Amends 69‑14‑111 to give the commission authority to supervise railroads, adopt regulations, bring civil actions, and develop a rail inspection program staffed with specific inspectors.
Creates Section 4, establishing the special‑revenue account, its funding source, appropriation to the Department of Public Service Regulation, and an annual reporting requirement to the committee.
Adds a codification instruction tying Section 4 to Title 69, Chapter 14.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.
affected: Railroad companies with car‑property in Montana
Montana Department of Public Service Regulation
Montana taxpayers (indirectly through the tax diversion)
numbers: September 1 of each even‑numbered year reporting deadline

HB101.one_line: Reclassifies gray wolves as furbearers, creates new tagging offenses, and aligns wolf licensing with furbearer rules.
HB101.summary: HB 101 reclassifies gray wolves as furbearers, creates new wolf‑tagging offenses, and aligns wolf‑licensing with existing furbearer rules. It also amends many furbearer‑related statutes, adds penalties for hunting‑related violations, and repeals the former wolf‑license classes.
changes: Defines gray wolves as furbearers and makes wolf licenses furbearer licenses.
Creates a new furbearer‑tagging offense for gray wolves, requiring electronic validation or cutting the tag before carcass removal.
Establishes Class E‑1 (resident) and Class E‑2 (non‑resident) wolf‑licenses with fees of $12 and $50, respectively, and allows certain discounts for holders of other licenses.
Adds penalties (fines up to $1,000, up to 6‑month county detention, license forfeiture, and restitution) for violations of the new tagging offense and for various hunting‑related violations.
Repeals the former wolf‑license classes (Class E‑1 and Class E‑2).
affected: Trappers and hunters who use motion‑tracking devices or hunt in cities, highways, or private property without permission
numbers: $10 discount for Class A‑6 bear tag holders
$50 discount for Class B‑10/11 non‑resident big‑game license holders
$1 fee for Class C‑1 landowner trapper license
$250 fee for Class C‑2 non‑resident trapper license

HB113.one_line: Revises residency rules, adds affidavit penalties, extends contract terms to 10 years, and expands land‑acquisition study authority.
HB113.summary: HB 113 revises Montana’s resident‑preference rules for public contracts, adds affidavit requirements and penalties for false claims, extends contract term limits to 10 years for most supplies and services, and amends the Department of Administration’s study authority for state‑park land acquisitions.
changes: Amends §18‑1‑106 to give the Department of Labor and Industry the authority to determine contractor residency and to issue prima‑facie attestations; allows redetermination if a contractor later qualifies as a resident.
Revises §18‑1‑113 to require bidders claiming a resident preference to submit an affidavit or declaration; false statements result in a five‑year disqualification from future goods contracts.

Modifies §18‑4‑313 to set a maximum contract term of 10 years for most supplies and services (previously 7 years); allows extensions only if the total term does not exceed 10 years and funds are available; specifies exceptions for IT, liquor‑store, corrections, employee‑benefit, park‑concession, and innovative‑financing contracts.

Amends §23‑1‑102 to require the Department of Administration to conduct a study of scenic, historic, archaeological, scientific, and recreational resources and to acquire or lease land for state‑park purposes, subject to legislative appropriation and board approval for large acquisitions.
affected: Public contractors bidding on Montana contracts

HB116.one_line: Allows remote appearances for public‑defender counsel at non‑substantive hearings, with court‑ordered in‑person appearance if good cause exists.
HB116.summary: The bill allows public‑defender attorneys to appear remotely at non‑substantive court hearings, requiring a camera and two‑way audio‑video. A court may order in‑person appearance if good cause exists, with notice at least five business days prior. The bill defines key terms and will be codified into existing court procedure statutes.
changes: Permits remote appearance for public‑defender counsel at non‑substantive hearings (e.g., arraignments, bond hearings, status conferences).
Requires the attorney to use a camera and two‑way audio‑video so all parties can see and hear each other.

Gives a court authority to order the attorney to appear in person if good cause exists, such as lack of technology or other reasons, with a written order at least five business days before the hearing.
Defines “remote appearance” and “non‑substantive hearing” for the purposes of the rule.
Codifies the rule into Title 3, Chapter 1, Part 3 of the Montana Statutes.
numbers: non‑substantive hearing categories (arraignments, bond, status, scheduling, omnibus, calendar calls)

HB131.one_line: HB 131 revises unemployment benefit duration tables effective July 1, 2025.
HB131.summary: HB 131 changes how long people can receive unemployment benefits by redefining the table that links a claimant’s earnings ratio to the number of full weeks of benefits. The new schedule increases benefit weeks for higher‑ratio earners and applies to all claims filed after July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends § 39‑51‑2204 to replace the existing benefit‑duration table with a new table that assigns 8–24 full weeks of benefits based on the claimant’s ratio of total base‑period earnings to the highest quarter of earnings.
Extends benefit weeks for claimants whose ratio is 2.75 or higher, giving them 22 weeks instead of the previous 20.
Applies the new schedule only to claims filed on or after July 1, 2025.
Leaves the special 24‑week rule for mass‑layoff claimants unchanged.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No fiscal impact figures are provided in the bill text.
affected: Unemployed workers filing claims after July 1, 2025

HB119.one_line: Creates a cattle committee, imposes a $1 per head assessment, and requires a 2027 referendum to enact the program.
HB119.summary: The bill creates a Montana Cattle Committee that will manage a $1‑per‑head cattle assessment, fund industry‑wide research and marketing, and hold referendums on the assessment. The committee is appointed by the governor from nominees supplied by cattle‑industry groups, serves staggered three‑year terms, and may not receive a salary but may be reimbursed for travel. The assessment revenue is deposited in a special revenue account, and the committee can use those funds for industry programs, administrative costs, and legal actions. The bill also amends several statutes to allow the committee to collect the assessment, to impose penalties, and to exempt the committee’s officers from certain state employee regulations. The act is contingent on a referendum passed by June 30 2027; if the referendum fails, the entire act is void.
changes: Establishes a seven‑member Montana Cattle Committee with staggered three‑year terms and a governor’s appointment process from industry nominees.
Creates a $1 per head cattle assessment on all Montana cattle sold, with collection and revenue deposited in a special cattle revenue account.
Authorizes the committee to use assessment revenue for research, marketing, education, staff, equipment, and legal actions, and allows it to adopt rules and contracts.
Provides for a referendum on the assessment by June 30 2027; the act is void if the referendum is not approved.
Amends statutes to allow the committee’s officers to be exempt from certain state employee regulations and to set penalties for non‑payment of the assessment.
numbers: 5% penalty plus 1% per month for non‑payment
HB119.effective: effective on passage and approval; sections 12‑16 effective after referendum approval

HB134.one_line: Allows the Department to offer rewards and permits in its crimestoppers program.
HB134.summary: The bill amends Montana’s fish‑wildlife‑parks crimestoppers statute to let the Department create a statewide program that can offer cash rewards, reward permits, and other incentives to the public for information on related crimes. It also allows the department to accept gifts and promote the program through media. No new funding or criminal offense is created. The changes are administrative in scope.
changes: Amends §87‑5‑605 to add the department’s authority to offer financial rewards, reward permits, or other incentives to the public.
Adds language that the department may accept gifts, grants, or donations for the program and spend them in compliance with donor conditions.
Expands the department’s duties to promote the program through media and adopt necessary rules.
Retains existing powers to advise local programs and encourage public reporting of crimes.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

HB132.one_line: Exempts certain reported interest income from Montana income tax, limited by filing status and effective 2026.
HB132.summary: HB 132 exempts a portion of interest income from Montana’s individual income tax, but only if the interest is reported on a federal Form 1099 and the taxpayer’s filing status limits the deduction. The bill amends the state’s tax code to add a new subtraction for qualifying interest, sets limits based on filing status, and specifies a delayed effective date of January 1, 2026. The changes apply only to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
changes: Adds a new subtraction for interest income that is reported on a federal Form 1099 and is not already exempt under Montana law.
Limits the amount of the subtraction to a percentage of the taxpayer’s filing status (the text specifies limits but does not list the exact percentages).
Amends Section 15‑30‑2120 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new subtraction and related adjustments to federal taxable income.
Specifies that the new deduction is effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, with the law taking effect on January 1, 2026.
Provides that the interest deduction is only available if the taxpayer reports the interest on a federal Form 1099 under § 6049.
Includes a sunset clause: the interest‑income subtraction terminates on June 30, 2025 (per the text), but the overall act remains in force beyond that date for other provisions.
affected: Montana residents who receive interest income reported on a federal Form 1099.
Taxpayers whose filing status determines the allowable deduction amount.
Tax preparers and state tax agencies who must apply the new subtraction.
numbers: Applicability: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025
Interest deduction termination: June 30, 2025 (for the interest‑income subtraction)
Maximum deduction limits tied to filing status (exact percentages not specified in the bill text)
Sunset dates for specific subtractions: December 31, 2033 for military‑pension related subtractions

HB138.one_line: Clarifies superintendent duties and mandates immediate implementation of the changes.
HB138.summary: The bill amends the state’s education law to clarify that the superintendent must execute all board‑issued directives and lists the superintendent’s duties in detail. It adds a new section that makes the changes effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends Section 20‑3‑106, MCA, to state that the superintendent must faithfully execute board directives and to list specific supervisory duties.

Expands the superintendent’s duties to include resolving cost‑proration disputes, issuing teacher certifications, negotiating tuition agreements, approving school openings, managing budgets, supervising finances, handling federal funds, accreditation, textbook licensing, career education, special education, traffic and food‑service programs, building plans, assessment data, and tax‑aid distribution.
Adds a new Section 2 that sets the effective date to the day the act is passed and approved.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No monetary amounts or new funding mechanisms are specified.

HB139.one_line: Limits the commission’s ability to close mule‑deer buck hunting during the November general rifle season.
HB139.summary: The bill protects mule‑deer buck hunting during the November general rifle season by limiting how often and where the commission may close that season. It preserves the long‑standing tradition of rut‑season buck harvest while allowing local management in specific districts.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑304 to add a new subsection (10) that restricts the commission’s ability to close mule‑deer buck hunting during the general rifle season.
The new rule bars closing buck hunting in more than 20 % of districts in a season, in any district for more than two years within six years, or before November 6 in any district.
The restriction does not apply to closures that were already in place before December 1 2024.
The bill does not create new programs, funds, or offenses; it only limits existing closure authority.
It preserves the current practice of allowing buck harvest during the rut while giving the commission some flexibility for district‑level management.
The bill is a statutory amendment, not a resolution or study request.
affected: Mule‑deer hunters, particularly those who hunt bucks during the November general rifle season
Hunting districts that might previously have closed buck hunting
The Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Commission

HB148.one_line: HB 148 removes the state tax exemption on Social Security benefits, effective 2026.
HB148.summary: HB 148 removes Montana’s income‑tax exemption on Social Security benefits, making those benefits taxable under the state income tax. The bill amends the definition of Montana taxable income and the calculation of adjustments, and it sets a delayed effective date of January 1 2026 for income‑tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2101 to redefine Montana taxable income so that Social Security benefits are no longer exempt from state income tax
Amends §15‑30‑2120 to adjust the list of additions and subtractions used to compute Montana taxable income, removing the exemption for Social Security benefits
Sets the act to take effect on January 1 2026 for tax years beginning after December 31 2025
Provides no new programs, funds, or penalties; it only changes tax treatment
All other tax provisions, definitions, and exemptions remain unchanged
The bill does not alter federal law or create new state‑level enforcement mechanisms
affected: Montana residents receiving Social Security benefits
Montana taxpayers who file state income tax returns for years beginning after 2025

HB152.one_line: Revises county attorney retention ballots to include a yes/no question and remove nonpartisan labels.
HB152.summary: The bill changes how county attorney retention elections are presented on the ballot. It requires the incumbent’s name to appear with a yes/no question and removes any nonpartisan label or write‑in option when the incumbent is the sole candidate.
changes: Requires the incumbent county attorney’s name to be listed on the general election ballot with the question, "Shall [name], the county attorney of [county], be retained in office for another term?"
Prohibits the election administrator from including a nonpartisan designation or write‑in space for the office when the incumbent is the only candidate
Mandates that voters be given a clear yes/no option to indicate retention
Codifies this requirement as part of Title 7, Chapter 4, Part 27 of the Montana Code

HB149.one_line: Separates alternative‑nicotine and vapor products from tobacco law, adds licensing, age restrictions, and penalties.
HB149.summary: HB 149 separates alternative‑nicotine and vapor products from tobacco regulation, creates a new licensing scheme, sets age‑restriction rules, and imposes civil penalties for non‑compliance.
changes: Defines “alternative nicotine product” and “vapor product” and excludes tobacco, cigarettes, and FDA‑regulated drugs.
Requires a $20 retail license from the Department of Revenue for selling either product, with annual renewal and a $100 civil penalty for failure to obtain or renew.
Prohibits sale to anyone under 18 and requires sales venues to be age‑restricted; sellers must display a state‑provided sign and verify age with photo ID.
Limits vending‑machine sales to alcohol venues under direct line‑of‑sight supervision; restaurants may only sell if they have a bar and meet the same supervision requirement.
Imposes escalating civil penalties (verbal notice, written notice, $500 fine, 3‑month or 1‑year license suspension) for repeated violations of age restrictions or vending‑machine rules.
Authorizes the Department of Public Health and Human Services to conduct inspections, notify violators, and refer license suspensions to the Department of Revenue.
Provides that minors assisting enforcement are not liable for possession or attempted purchase of these products.
Allows local governments to adopt ordinances on these products that are no more stringent than state law.
Amends a wide range of existing Montana Code sections (16‑11‑122, 16‑11‑302‑311, 30‑16‑301, 45‑5‑623, 45‑5‑637, 50‑50‑207) to incorporate the new definitions, licensing, and penalties.
Repeals section 16‑11‑313, which previously prohibited local ordinances on alternative nicotine and vapor products.
Codifies the new provisions as a new chapter in Title 16.
affected: Retailers of alternative‑nicotine and vapor products
Department of Revenue and Public Health and Human Services

HB154.one_line: Creates a housing‑fairness tax credit for Montana owners and renters of qualified residences.
HB154.summary: HB 154 creates a new housing‑fairness income tax credit that lets Montana taxpayers claim a credit against property taxes paid or a rent‑equivalent amount for qualified residences. The credit is available to residents who meet income, residency, and ownership/rental requirements and is limited to one claim per household. The bill also amends related property‑tax‑assistance statutes and sets an effective date of Jan. 1 2026.
changes: Creates a new housing‑fairness property‑tax credit for owners and renters of qualified residences; credit equals 75 % of property tax or rent‑equivalent tax minus a progressive threshold based on household income; credit is limited to one claim per household; credit cannot be claimed with the residential property tax credit for the elderly or other assistance programs; credit is disallowed for subsidized or non‑taxable properties; credit may be adjusted if rent is excessive; credit may be refunded if it exceeds tax liability; credit claims must be filed with the tax return or by April 15 for non‑filers; false claims are punishable as unsworn falsification; the bill amends several sections of the Montana Code (15‑6‑240, 15‑6‑302, 15‑7‑102, 15‑16‑101, 15‑17‑125, 15‑30‑2303, 15‑30‑2341) to incorporate the new credit and clarify interactions with existing programs; the credit becomes available for tax years beginning Jan. 1 2026 for property taxes billed after Dec. 31 2025.
affected: Montana taxpayers who own or rent qualified residences

HB160.one_line: Repeals the state ban on local auxiliary‑container regulation and clarifies initiative limits.
HB160.summary: HB 160 repeals Montana’s statewide prohibition that bars local governments from regulating auxiliary containers, and it amends the initiative‑and‑referendum statute to explicitly exclude such regulation from local initiative powers.
changes: Repeals Section 7‑1‑121, which prohibited local governments from regulating auxiliary containers;
Amends Section 7‑1‑111 to remove the prohibition on local‑government regulation of auxiliary containers;
Amends Section 7‑5‑131 to state that local initiative powers do not extend to regulating auxiliary containers;
Leaves all other provisions of Sections 7‑1‑111 and 7‑5‑131 unchanged;
No new programs, offices, or criminal offenses are created.
No fiscal impact is specified in the bill text.
affected: Local governments (cities, counties, school districts, etc.)
Residents and businesses that may be subject to local auxiliary‑container ordinances

HB155.one_line: Rewrites Montana’s property‑tax rates, adds a homestead exemption, and creates a new appeal process.
HB155.summary: The bill revises Montana’s property‑tax framework, lowering rates for agricultural, forest, and residential/commercial property, adding a homestead exemption, and creating a new appeal process for that exemption. It also amends the tax‑rate schedule for class‑four residential and commercial property and adjusts forest‑land rates for class‑ten property.
changes: Amends 15‑6‑133 to reduce class‑three (agricultural) tax rates to 2.16%/2.05% of productive capacity value.

Rewrites 15‑6‑134 to lower class‑four residential rates (e.g., 1.11% of market value for most single‑family homes, with graduated rates above $1.5 million) and sets a 1.75% rate for commercial/industrial property with a $200,000–$400,000 exemption.

Adds a new homestead exemption for principal residences, automatically applying to owners who received a 2023/2024 property‑tax rebate and allowing new applications by July 1 2025 (2025 tax year) and March 1 2026 (2026 tax year).
Creates a formal appeal and review process for homestead‑exemption denials, including informal review, county and state tax‑appeal boards, and court review.
Amends 15‑6‑143 to adjust class‑ten forest‑land tax rates (0.29% in 2023, 0.27% in 2024, 0.37% thereafter).
Provides rule‑making authority for the Department of Revenue to implement the changes.
Specifies retroactive applicability to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2024.

HB169.one_line: HB 169 clarifies permissible political activities for Montana judges and judicial candidates.
HB169.summary: HB 169 revises Montana’s judicial conduct rules to clarify what political activities judges and judicial candidates may engage in. It lists specific actions that are permitted or prohibited, and codifies the changes into the state’s judicial‑conduct statutes.
changes: Judges and judicial candidates may act as leaders or hold office in a political organization if allowed by law to campaign with a party designation.
They may give speeches on behalf of a political organization or any partisan/independent non‑judicial officeholder or candidate.
They may seek, accept, or use endorsements from a political organization or partisan/independent officeholder or candidate.
They may attend or purchase tickets for dinners or other events sponsored by a partisan or independent candidate for non‑judicial office.
They may publicly endorse or oppose a partisan or independent candidate for any non‑judicial public office.
They may solicit funds for, pay an assessment to, or make a contribution to a political organization or to a partisan/independent officeholder or candidate.
They may publicly self‑identify as a candidate of a political organization.

HB163.one_line: Montana offers a $5,000 tax credit to unpaid health‑care preceptors for each year they supervise eligible students.
HB163.summary: Montana would give a non‑refundable $5,000 tax credit to any licensed health‑care professional who voluntarily precepts a student in an eligible training program and receives no compensation. The credit is limited to the taxpayer’s liability and cannot be carried forward.
changes: Creates a $5,000 per‑year tax credit for unpaid health‑care preceptors.
Limits the credit to $1,000 per eligible clinical rotation (minimum 100 hrs).
Precludes the credit if the preceptor receives any form of compensation.
Requires the Department of Revenue to adopt rules, forms, and record‑keeping procedures for the credit.
Amends §15‑30‑2303 to include the new credit in the biennial review schedule.
Codifies the credit as part of Title 15, Chapter 30, Part 23.
Effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
affected: Unpaid licensed health‑care professionals who precept students in eligible programs
Taxpayers who could claim the credit

HB172.one_line: Bill expands reporting duties for transportation agencies and formalizes legislative project recommendations.
HB172.summary: HB 172 adds duties to the Transportation Interim Committee, the Transportation Commission, and the Department of Transportation so that the committee prepares joint resolutions recommending projects for prioritization, the commission reports biennially on those projects, and the department assists the commission. The bill amends existing statutes to formalize these reporting and consultation requirements.
changes: Amends §5‑5‑233 to require the Transportation Interim Committee to prepare a joint resolution each session recommending construction and reconstruction projects for prioritization by the Transportation Commission.
Adds a provision allowing the committee to prepare additional legislation to help prioritize projects previously recommended but not yet prioritized.

Amends §60‑2‑110 to require the Transportation Commission to report biennially to the Transportation Interim Committee on the status of projects recommended by the legislature, with a May deadline for even‑numbered years.
Requires the commission to include technical, financial, and other factors in its report when a recommended project is not prioritized.
Mandates the Department of Transportation to assist the commission by providing information, documents, and recommendations for projects recommended by the legislature.
Specifies consultation with county and local governments when setting priorities for secondary and urban highway systems.
affected: Motor vehicle division of the Department of Justice

HB174.one_line: Adds drug‑assault crime, penalties up to $500 fine or six months jail.
HB174.summary: The bill amends Montana’s assault statute to make it a crime to give certain drugs—such as rohypnol, flunitrazolam, GHB, alcohol, any vaccine, or diphenhydramine—to another person without that person’s consent.  The offense carries a maximum fine of $500, up to six months in county jail, or both.  The amendment excludes medical providers, patients, parents with valid prescriptions, and opioid‑overdose reversal drugs from liability.
changes: Adds a new assault element: knowingly providing specified drugs without consent.
Defines the drugs covered (rohypnol, flunitrazolam, GHB, alcohol, any vaccine, diphenhydramine).
Exempts medical providers, patients, parents/guardians with prescriptions, and opioid‑reversal drugs from the new assault provision.
Sets penalties: fine up to $500, up to six months in county jail, or both.
affected: Individuals who provide the listed drugs without consent
Medical providers and patients exempted from liability

HB176.one_line: Allows unlimited wolf hunting when the population is 450‑550 wolves, with special rules for Yellowstone and private‑land takings.
HB176.summary: The bill amends Montana’s wolf‑management law to allow an unlimited statewide hunting quota when the gray‑wolf population reaches 450–550 wolves, with special rules for areas near Yellowstone and for hunting on private land after daylight. It also expands the types of licenses and hunting practices that can be used and requires consistent population‑estimation methods.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑901 to set a 450‑wolf threshold for sustainable population and allows unlimited hunting when the population is 450–550 wolves.

Authorizes the Fish and Wildlife Commission to issue multiple wolf‑hunting licenses, permit unlimited harvest by a single license holder, allow baiting (with a 30‑ft rule), and permit night hunting with artificial light or night‑vision scopes.
Provides an exception for the area adjacent to Yellowstone National Park, where the unlimited quota does not apply.
Allows landowners or their agents to take wolves on their property without a Class E‑1 or E‑2 license if the wolf poses a threat, with reporting and carcass‑preservation requirements.
Requires the Commission to adopt consistent integrated patch‑occupancy modeling for population estimates and to report annually to the Environmental Quality Council.
Establishes a quota for annual wolf takings under the landowner exception and allows a moratorium if needed.
affected: Landowners with wolves on their property

HB177.one_line: HB 177 expands tobacco licensing, age rules, and penalties, and removes the ban on local ordinances that prohibit alternative‑nicotine and vapor products.
HB177.summary: HB 177 revises Montana’s tobacco laws to treat alternative‑nicotine and vapor products as tobacco, expands licensing and enforcement, and removes the state ban on local ordinances that prohibit those products.  It adds new definitions, licensing fees, age‑verification rules, vending‑machine restrictions, civil penalties, and a tobacco‑education fee, while repealing the prior prohibition on local bans.
changes: Defines alternative‑nicotine and vapor products as tobacco and requires a retail sales license for them; the license fee is deposited in the general fund.
Mandates conspicuous age‑restriction signs and prohibits sales to anyone under 18, with ID‑verification requirements.
Limits vending‑machine sales to alcohol‑serving venues under direct supervision, and prohibits vending in restaurants without a bar.

Imposes a $100 civil penalty for non‑compliance and establishes a tiered penalty system (warnings, fines, license suspension) for repeated violations, including a $500 tobacco‑education fee for owners.
Requires local governments to adopt ordinances on these products only if they are no more stringent than state law and repeals the state statute that banned such local ordinances.
Repeals Section 16‑11‑313, which previously prohibited local bans on alternative‑nicotine and vapor products.
affected: Retail tobacco, alternative‑nicotine, and vapor product sellers
Department of Revenue and Department of Public Health & Human Services

HB185.one_line: HB 185 extends continuous eligibility for children under six in the Healthy Montana Kids Plan.
HB185.summary: HB 185 would let children under six stay continuously enrolled in the Healthy Montana Kids Plan for up to 3 years 1 month from their first enrollment or re‑enrollment, even if family circumstances change. The department must seek waivers, report to the legislature, and implement the rule within six months of approval.
changes: Creates a 3 years 1 month continuous eligibility period for children <6 in the Healthy Montana Kids Plan.
Allows continuous enrollment even if the child would otherwise become ineligible due to family changes.
Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to apply for CMS waivers and state‑plan amendments by July 1, 2025.
Mandates audits to ensure compliance with the new continuous‑eligibility rule.
Requires the department to report waiver decisions to the legislature and the code commissioner within 30 days.
If approved, the continuous‑eligibility rule must be implemented within six months of the CMS decision.
affected: Children under 6 enrolled in the Healthy Montana Kids Plan
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB187.one_line: Revises tabulation rules, removes continuous‑machine requirement, sets new reporting schedule.
HB187.summary: The bill amends Montana’s election‑tabulation rules to eliminate the requirement that vote‑counting machines run continuously the day before an election. It sets new timing and reporting deadlines for public observation and result release, and allows the Secretary of State to adopt rules for election‑night reporting. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Rewrites §13‑15‑101 to remove the continuous‑tabulation mandate and replace it with a schedule that allows tabulation to stop at 5 p.m. or when all ballots are counted, whichever comes first.
Specifies that results may not be released to the public until after polls close and all voters have finished voting in the county.
Requires that on election day tabulation begin immediately and continue without adjournment until all legally countable ballots are processed, except for unresolved, provisional, or overseas ballots.

Mandates that the election administrator provide initial results no earlier than 8 p.m. and update them at least every three hours until completion, with statewide results first sent to the Secretary of State’s election‑night system.
Adds provisions for securing documents and restricting access outside regular business hours.
Authorizes the Secretary of State to adopt rules for notifications and prioritization of results reporting, but prohibits more frequent reporting than the bill already requires.

HB188.one_line: Revises interim‑committee appointments to mirror chamber partisan makeup and updates the Environmental Quality Council.
HB188.summary: HB 188 revises how interim committee members are appointed, requiring the Speaker to consult the minority leader and ensuring each committee’s partisan makeup mirrors the chamber’s composition. It also updates the Environmental Quality Council’s membership rules and makes the changes retroactive to the act’s effective date.
changes: Replaces Senate interim‑committee appointments with the committee on committees; House appointments must be made by the Speaker with minority‑leader advice.
Mandates that each interim committee have four House and four Senate members, three from the majority party and one from the minority, with no minority majority allowed.
Allows the Legislative Council to add one or two extra members from either party if workload demands, but those additions must still reflect the chamber’s partisan balance.
Amends 5‑5‑234 to permit a non‑majority party member to be appointed when more than one majority or minority member is required, and clarifies vacancy‑replacement procedures.

Rewrites 5‑16‑101 to set the Environmental Quality Council at 17 members: 12 legislators (6 House, 6 Senate) with a 4/2 majority/minority split per house, 4 public members (2 appointed by the Speaker with minority consent, 2 by the Senate President with minority consent).
Adds a new section making the act effective on passage and retroactive to all interim‑committee appointments made on or before that date.
affected: State legislators (House and Senate members), Speaker of the House, Senate President, minority leaders, Legislative Council, Environmental Quality Council members, public appointees

HB199.one_line: Amends the Board of Medical Examiners to include a physician assistant and reduce doctor seats.
HB199.summary: The bill amends the composition of the Montana Board of Medical Examiners, reducing doctors and adding physician assistants. It changes the statutory language to specify the new member mix.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑1731 to set the board at 12 members.

Replaces five doctor seats with four physicians (one emergency‑medicine), one osteopathic physician, one podiatrist, one nutritionist, one physician assistant, one emergency‑care provider, and two public members.
Removes the requirement for a fifth doctor and eliminates a separate physician‑assistant seat, consolidating it into the new single PA seat.
Maintains the county‑distribution rule that no two doctors may be from the same county.
Leaves the board’s allocation to the department unchanged.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.

HB200.one_line: Increases Montana film‑tax‑credit cap to $12.35 million for 2025‑2026 tax years.
HB200.summary: HB 200 raises Montana’s film‑tax‑credit cap for the 2025‑2026 tax years from $10 million to $12.35 million, making the higher limit effective immediately and applying to income‑tax years beginning after Dec 31 2024.
changes: Section 1 amends §15‑31‑1010 to raise the total annual claim limit for film‑tax credits from $10 million to $12.35 million.
The new limit applies to credits under §§15‑31‑1007 and 15‑31‑1009.
Claims are still processed on a first‑come, first‑served basis and cannot be carried forward beyond the statutory carry‑forward periods.
If the limit is reached, the Department of Revenue may waive penalties and interest under §15‑1‑216.
The act becomes effective upon passage and applies to income‑tax years beginning after Dec 31 2024.
The Department of Commerce and Revenue are required to post available credit amounts on their websites.
The bill does not create a new program or offense.
affected: Film producers and other taxpayers seeking Montana film‑tax credits

HB204.one_line: Mandates visible gambling‑addiction info on all Montana video gambling machines from Oct 1 2025.
HB204.summary: HB 204 requires every video gambling machine in Montana to display clear, visible information about gambling‑addiction resources. It amends the state’s gambling statutes to add this requirement, limits the number of machines a licensed operator may offer, and sets an applicability date of Oct 1 2025.
changes: Amends §23‑5‑110 to add a new policy goal: provide information about gambling addiction on machines.
Amends §23‑5‑603 to require that each video gambling machine display addiction‑help information on its front, fully legible and visible while in use.
Adds a rule that non‑compliant machines may not be used by the public until they meet the display requirement.
Limits operators to only the number of approved machines for which permits have been granted; allows temporary replacement of a broken machine with another approved machine at no fee.
Specifies that machines must be located in areas where alcohol is sold or consumed and under the operator’s control to prevent access by persons under 18.
Sets the effective date of the new requirements to October 1 2025.
Leaves other statutory language (e.g., licensing privilege, revenue sources) unchanged.
affected: Video gambling machine operators and owners
Licensed operators of venues that sell alcohol
Gamblers who use video gambling machines
numbers: no fee for temporary replacement machine
no fee for manufacturer use of machine

HB205.one_line: Revises death‑penalty procedure, fixes execution method, witness limits, and administrative timelines.
HB205.summary: HB 205 revises Montana’s death‑penalty rules, specifying the method of execution, witness limits, and administrative procedures. It requires a lethal‑injection protocol and sets strict timelines for execution dates and warrants.
changes: Amends §46‑19‑103 to set execution dates 30‑60 days after sentencing (or 20‑90 days if a stay is lifted).
Requires the death penalty to be carried out by continuous IV injection of a barbiturate plus a paralytic agent.
Limits witnesses to 12, with specific categories (media, victim’s family, defendant’s family, corrections).
Mandates that the executioner be a warden‑selected, trained person whose identity remains anonymous.
Requires a death warrant signed by the judge and clerk, delivered to the Department of Corrections within 5 days.
Requires the warden to provide a suitable execution room and return the warrant within 20 days after execution.

HB209.one_line: New tax credit for private‑school and homeschool expenses, limited to 44.7 % of the state per‑student maximum.
HB209.summary: HB 209 creates a state income‑tax credit for families that pay tuition, textbooks, extracurriculars, and other qualifying expenses at nonpublic schools, including private schools and homeschool. The credit is limited to 44.7 % of the state’s per‑student maximum and cannot be carried forward or back. The bill also adds the credit to a list of credits the legislature must review every eight years.
changes: Establishes a new tax credit for nonpublic‑school education expenses, limited to the lesser of actual expenses or 44.7 % of the per‑student maximum set in 20‑9‑306.

Defines qualifying expenses (tuition, textbooks, extracurriculars, and a list of additional items) and a qualifying student (dependent who attended a nonpublic school full‑time for at least one semester).
Limits the credit to one taxpayer per qualifying student per year and bars carry‑forward or carry‑back.
Allows a non‑custodial parent to claim the credit under specific court‑ordered conditions.
Authorizes the Department of Revenue to adopt rules, forms, and records to implement the credit and requires the superintendent to set rules for certain additional expenses.
Adds the new credit to the biennial review list in §15‑30‑2303, MCA, and requires the Revenue Interim Committee to evaluate it every eight years.
Specifies the credit applies to income‑tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Taxpayers who pay tuition or related expenses at private schools or homeschool
Non‑custodial parents in divorce or separation
State Department of Revenue and Superintendent of Public Instruction

HB212.one_line: Limits non‑economic damages for agricultural vehicles and sets a duty of care for operators.
HB212.summary: HB 212 limits the amount of non‑economic damages that owners, lessees, or operators of agricultural vehicles can be sued for on highways, while preserving full liability for economic losses. It also imposes a duty of care on operators toward people and livestock and amends several motor‑vehicle statutes to clarify definitions and registration procedures.
changes: Limits non‑economic tort damages to $750,000 per claim and $1.5 million per occurrence for agricultural vehicles on highways.
Insurers cannot cover excess damages unless they agree in writing to waive the statutory limits.
Defines “agricultural vehicle” as a farm tractor, implement of husbandry, self‑propelled farm equipment, tractor‑to‑wed unit, or hay‑hauling vehicle.
Imposes a duty of care on operators, with speeding, erratic driving, or unsafe passing as prima facie evidence of breach.
Amends sections 61‑1‑101, 61‑3‑317, 61‑5‑112, and 61‑8‑102 to update definitions, registration grace periods, reciprocal agreements for farm‑vehicle operators, and uniformity of interpretation.
Codifies the new liability limits and duty‑of‑care provisions as part of Title 27, Chapter 1, Part 7.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.
Includes severability and applicability provisions for claims filed after the effective date.
affected: Owners, lessees, and operators of agricultural vehicles on highways
Farmers and ranchers using tractors, implements, or hay‑hauling vehicles
Legal professionals handling agricultural vehicle tort cases

HB213.one_line: HB 213 lowers class‑four property tax rates and applies a 1.4× multiplier for high‑value or commercial properties.
