HB213.summary: HB 213 revises the tax rate for class‑four residential and commercial property, lowering the base rate to 1.35% and applying a 1.4× multiplier for values above $1.5 million or for commercial use. The changes are retroactive to tax years beginning after December 31 2024 and take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §15‑6‑134 to redefine class‑four property and its taxable percentage.
affected: Property owners of class‑four residential and commercial real estate in Montana
numbers: retroactive to tax years after Dec 31 2024

HB216.one_line: Allows private landowners in Flathead Reservation to obtain deer/elk licenses, revenue goes to tribal council.
HB216.summary: HB 216 amends the state game‑law to allow the Fish and Wildlife Commission to issue deer and elk hunting licenses to private landowners whose fee land lies within the Flathead Indian Reservation, and requires revenue from those licenses to be transferred to the reservation council.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑304, MCA, to add rule‑making authority for issuing licenses to private landowners within the Flathead Indian Reservation.
Creates a new licensing program limited to deer and elk hunting on land owned by the license holder inside the reservation boundaries.
Mandates that revenue from these licenses be transferred to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes council under §87‑1‑228.
Adds a notification requirement that the Secretary of State send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Does not alter any other game‑law provisions or create new criminal offenses.
affected: Private landowners within the Flathead Indian Reservation
Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes council

HB220.one_line: Montana adds a $1,200 refundable child tax credit for children 5 yrs or younger, phased out above $50k AGI.
HB220.summary: Montana will create a refundable child tax credit of $1,200 for each child aged five or younger, subject to income limits and a phased‑out reduction. The credit is available to residents who qualify under the federal IRC and can be claimed on a Montana return. The bill also amends the state tax‑credit review schedule to include the new credit and codifies it in the state tax code.
changes: Establishes a $1,200 refundable child tax credit for qualifying children 5 yrs or younger.
Limits the credit to taxpayers with federal AGI ≤ $56,000; the credit is reduced by $90 for every $1,000 of AGI above $50,000.
Adds the credit to the list of tax credits subject to biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
Codifies the credit as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
Sets the credit’s applicability to income‑tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Montana residents who qualify for the federal child tax credit
Taxpayers with children aged five or younger

HB221.one_line: Shifts all municipal elections to even years, with transition elections for current officeholders.
HB221.summary: HB 221 moves all municipal elections to even‑numbered years, with a transition plan for current officeholders and adjustments to primary‑election timing.
changes: Amends §13‑1‑104 to require municipal elections only in even‑numbered years, with a one‑year term election in 2025 for officers whose terms end January 2026 and special one‑year elections in the preceding even‑year for terms ending January 2028 or 2030.

Rewrites §13‑1‑107 to set primary‑election dates: first Tuesday after the first Monday in June before an even‑year general election, and the Tuesday after the second Monday in September before an odd‑year general election.
Adds a cost‑payment clause that municipalities must pay the cost of their own municipal elections.
Includes a saving clause protecting pre‑existing rights, penalties, and proceedings.
Sets the act’s effective date as passage and applicability to all municipal elections scheduled on or after that date.
numbers: first Tuesday after the first Monday in November
first Tuesday after the first Monday in June
Tuesday after the second Monday in September

HB222.one_line: Year‑round wolf hunting until 600 wolves, with seasonal closures for denning and a new muzzle‑loader deer/elk season.
HB222.summary: HB 222 would allow year‑round wolf hunting in Montana, with the season automatically closed when the state wolf population falls to 600 or fewer.  The bill amends the game‑season rules to give the commission broad authority to open, close, or modify seasons for any species, including wolves, and adds a special muzzle‑loader deer/elk season.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑304, MCA, to give the commission authority to set, open, close, or modify hunting seasons for all game species, including wolves;
Creates a year‑round wolf‑hunting season with an unlimited quota that ends only when the wolf population is 600 or fewer;
Allows the commission to close the wolf season in May and June for denning and whelping;
Adds a special muzzle‑loader heritage hunting season for deer/elk that begins the second Saturday after the regular season and lasts nine days;
Preserves existing provisions for special seasons, closed seasons, and district‑based hunting rules;
Includes a severability clause that keeps valid portions of the act in effect if other parts are struck down.
affected: Montana residents and property owners in wolf‑management units.

HB223.one_line: Commercial tow trucks must be covered for towing, recovery, and cleanup costs under liability insurance.
HB223.summary: HB 223 requires commercial tow‑truck operators to be covered for reasonable towing, recovery, and debris‑cleanup costs under motor‑vehicle liability policies, with specified limits. The bill amends §61‑6‑103 to add these coverage requirements and sets an applicability date of October 1 2025.
changes: Amends §61‑6‑103 to add coverage for reasonable towing, recovery, and debris‑cleanup services by commercial tow‑truck operators
Specifies limits: $25,000 per person for bodily injury, $50,000 for multiple persons, and $20,000 for property damage
Requires policies to list insured, coverage, premium, period, and limits, and to state that coverage applies to towing services
Establishes that the policy must be issued or renewed on or after October 1 2025
Maintains existing policy provisions (e.g., no cancellation after injury, settlement rights, etc.)
Does not create a new program or fund

HB224.one_line: Judges and judicial candidates cannot accept or benefit from party endorsements or contributions.
HB224.summary: The bill makes it unlawful for a judge or judicial candidate to seek, accept, or benefit from a political‑party endorsement or contribution. It simply adds this prohibition to Montana’s criminal code. No new programs or funds are created. The law applies to judges and judicial candidates only. The bill is a straightforward amendment to existing criminal statutes. The text contains no monetary amounts or dates beyond the legislative session. The bill is a modest, targeted change. The effective date is not specified, so it would take effect upon enactment. The bill does not create a new crime beyond the prohibition itself. Complexity: 2. One‑line summary: Judges cannot accept or benefit from party endorsements or contributions.
changes: Adds a prohibition that judges or judicial candidates may not knowingly seek, accept, use, advertise, promote, or benefit from a political‑party endorsement or contribution.
Codifies this prohibition as part of Title 13, Chapter 35, Part 2 of the Montana Code.

HB229.one_line: Rewrites Montana’s environmental review law, removes greenhouse‑gas ban, tightens court review and time limits.
HB229.summary: HB 229 revises Montana’s Environmental Policy Act to remove the prohibition on evaluating greenhouse‑gas emissions, expands the scope and detail of environmental reviews, and tightens the judicial review process for agency actions. The bill also clarifies time limits, public participation, and the role of the Environmental Quality Council.
changes: Amends 75‑1‑102 to state that the Act’s purpose is to ensure environmental attributes are considered and the public is informed of impacts; the prohibition on evaluating greenhouse‑gas emissions is removed.

Rewrites 75‑1‑201 to require agencies to use a systematic, interdisciplinary approach, to consider alternatives, to provide detailed statements on impacts, regulatory effects on private property, and fiscal impacts, and to allow joint reviews with federal agencies.
Adds a new subsection (2)(b) that permits greenhouse‑gas analysis only if a federal agency requires it or Congress amends the Clean Air Act.

Revises 75‑1‑208 to set specific time limits (60‑day scoping, 90‑day review, 180‑day detailed statement), allows one 50 % extension, and clarifies that agencies may not withhold permits after the deadline unless a written finding of likely violation exists.

Introduces detailed procedures for judicial review of agency decisions, including limits on challenges, requirement of a 60‑day notice, certification of records, and prohibition of attorney‑fee awards.

Creates a process for project sponsors to appear before the Environmental Quality Council and the Water Policy Committee, and for boards to review agency decisions on time‑extension and design‑detail requests.
affected: state agencies that prepare environmental reviews

HB230.one_line: Rewrites Medicaid law to eliminate work requirements, expand eligibility, modernize services, and create new advisory and workforce programs.
HB230.summary: HB 230 (“Generally revise Medicaid laws”) removes work‑and‑premium requirements, expands continuous eligibility, modernizes application and renewal processes, creates a client advisory board, and amends several Medicaid statutes, including the Montana HELP Act. The bill also establishes local public‑assistance offices and revises fraud‑prevention rules.
changes: Eliminates Medicaid work requirements and premiums for eligible adults
Authorizes 12‑month continuous eligibility for parents, caretakers, and expansion‑eligible adults
Mandates online, phone, and mobile‑app application/renewal and electronic document submission
Requires the department to provide text‑messaging, email, and a hotline with callback and 90‑day reconsideration for procedural terminations
Creates a 7‑member client advisory board with quarterly meetings and staff support
Amends sections of the Montana HELP Act to allow workforce‑development services, third‑party administrators, and special revenue accounts
Reopens ten public‑assistance offices by June 30 2026 and establishes criteria for local office placement
Rewrites fraud‑prevention and truth‑in‑submission requirements for Medicaid claims and applications
Repeals several tax‑fee and community‑engagement statutes and related HELP Act provisions
Appropriates $3 million per biennium for implementing the new local‑office requirement
affected: Montana Medicaid beneficiaries (parents, caretakers, expansion‑eligible adults), Medicaid applicants, providers, public‑assistance office staff, and the state Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB232.one_line: Associations >10 parcels must report budgets, limit fee hikes, and get owner approval for increases.
HB232.summary: Homeowners’ associations with more than ten parcels must produce an annual budget and financial report and can only raise fees or dues by a limited amount, with written approval from a majority or two‑thirds of owners, depending on the increase. The bill also amends corporate‑governance definitions and allows remote meetings. Associations with ten or fewer parcels are exempt.
changes: Requires associations >10 parcels to submit an annual budget report by fiscal‑year end and a financial report within 30 days after fiscal‑year end, mailed or emailed to all owners.
Mandates that any fee/dues/charge increase be approved in writing by a majority of owners for increases ≤15% (or $100, whichever is greater) and by two‑thirds for larger or more frequent increases.
Prohibits fee increases that exceed 15% or $100 in a single year unless approved as above; allows remote meetings unless bylaws say otherwise.
Amends sections 35‑2‑114 and 35‑2‑525 to clarify voting and remote‑meeting definitions.
Exempts associations of ten or fewer parcels from all reporting and fee‑increase requirements.
Defines “homeowners’ association” and related terms for the purposes of the amendments.
No new state program or criminal offense is created.
No specific fiscal impact is quantified in the text.
affected: Owners of parcels in exempt associations

HB236.one_line: Allows mental‑health exams in detention centers and clarifies cost responsibilities.
HB236.summary: The bill allows mental‑health examinations of defendants in detention centers, expands the Department of Public Health’s rule‑making authority, and amends the existing fitness‑to‑proceed statute to clarify who may conduct examinations, where they may take place, and how costs are paid.
changes: Permits a fitness‑to‑proceed examination to be conducted at a detention center, not just at a state hospital.

Delegates the Department of Public Health and Human Services to adopt rules specifying examiner qualifications, remote‑exam protocols, follow‑up criteria, and timing of the qualification determination.

Amends §46‑14‑202 to clarify that the court may order a defendant’s commitment for up to 60 days (or longer if needed) for examination and that the examiner may be a psychiatrist, psychologist, or advanced‑practice RN.

Specifies cost‑paying responsibilities: court pays if requested by court or prosecution; defendant pays if requested by defendant or counsel; joint requests split costs; costs for Department‑staff exams are exempt from court or public‑defender billing.
Adds definitions for “other associated expenses” (transport, housing, medical/dental care).
Codifies the new section as part of Title 46, Chapter 14, Part 2.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: $0 (costs paid by court or defendant, not state)

HB237.one_line: Prohibits sentencing to Galen, allowing review if mental condition changes.
HB237.summary: The bill bars courts from sentencing defendants to the state forensic mental‑health facility at Galen, directing them instead to other approved facilities. It also allows the director or defendant to petition for review if the defendant’s mental condition changes. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §46‑14‑312 to exclude the state forensic mental‑health facility at Galen from the list of permissible placement sites for sentenced defendants with mental disease or disorder.
Requires courts to consider professional recommendations before placing a defendant in an appropriate correctional, mental‑health, residential, or developmental‑disabilities facility.
Allows the director or the defendant to petition the sentencing court for review of the sentence if the defendant’s mental condition changes, with specific criteria for review.
Preserves all rights, penalties, and proceedings that existed before the act’s effective date.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Defendants with mental disease or disorder
Director of the Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB243.one_line: Provides a refundable tax credit for volunteer emergency first responders, capped at $1,500 per year.
HB243.summary: Montana would give a refundable income‑tax credit to volunteer emergency first‑responders, up to $1,500 per year, based on hours worked. The credit is available for the 2026 tax year and later, and the bill also adds the credit to a list of credits that the revenue interim committee must review biennially.
changes: Creates a new refundable tax credit for volunteer emergency first responders, capped at $1,500 or $15 per hour of volunteer service, whichever is less.
Defines eligibility: active, uncompensated service as a volunteer firefighter, EMS provider, air‑search‑and‑rescue volunteer, or other specified volunteer responder roles.
Requires taxpayers claiming the credit to report hours of service on forms provided by the state.
Adds the new credit to the list of credits subject to biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
Specifies that the credit is codified as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date of the credit to income‑tax years beginning January 1, 2026.
affected: Taxpayers who provide volunteer emergency services
Montana Department of Revenue (for reporting and review purposes)
numbers: December 31, 2028 termination dates for some review items
December 31, 2031 termination date for some review items

HB247.one_line: HB 247 eliminates duel‑related damages by amending and repealing relevant code sections.
HB247.summary: HB 247 removes the statutory provision that allows a person who is injured or killed in a duel to recover damages. It amends the damages clause to exclude any reference to dueling and deletes the specific duel‑damage section from the Montana Code.
changes: Amends Section 27‑1‑301 to state that damages are prescribed by other sections and are exclusive of exemplary damages and interest, unless expressly mentioned.
Repeals Section 27‑1‑223, which previously provided damages for injuries or death inflicted in a duel.
affected: Individuals injured or killed in a duel
Legal claimants seeking damages for duel‑related injuries or death

HB255.one_line: Revises pupil‑record privacy law, mandates strict contracts, allows approved model contracts, voids non‑compliant ones.
HB255.summary: HB 255 revises Montana’s online data‑privacy law for K‑12 pupil records, requiring school districts to use detailed, privacy‑compliant contracts with third‑party providers and allowing the use of model contracts from approved consortia.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1326 to set strict contract requirements for any third‑party service that stores, manages, or accesses pupil records;

Mandates that contracts include: ownership statement, pupil‑control options, purpose‑limitation clauses, review/correction procedures, security responsibilities, breach‑notification protocols, data‑retention guarantees, FERPA compliance, and prohibition on targeted advertising;
Allows districts to satisfy contract obligations by adopting a model contract approved by a private or public consortium that meets or exceeds these standards;
Provides that non‑compliant contracts are void after notice and cure, and that all records must be returned if voided;
Exempts contracts in effect before May 7 2019 from these new requirements until they expire or are renewed.
affected: Third‑party service providers for pupil records
Parents, legal guardians, and eligible pupils

HB256.one_line: Creates water‑development and storage revenue accounts, mandates earnings splits, and funds transfers.
HB256.summary: HB 256 creates a Montana Water Development State Special Revenue Account and a Water Storage State Special Revenue Account, directs investment earnings to be split 90/10 between them, and mandates two $50 million transfers from the general fund. It also amends the natural‑resources and water‑storage accounts to receive new revenue sources and limits appropriations to water‑storage projects.
changes: Creates a Montana Water Development State Special Revenue Account (MWDS‑SRF) under 17‑2‑102.

Mandates that 90 % of the account’s investment earnings be transferred to the Water Storage State Special Revenue Account (WS‑SRF) and 10 % to the Natural Resources Projects State Special Revenue Account (NR‑SRF).
Amends §15‑38‑302 to define the NR‑SRF, specify its funding sources, and allow appropriations for grants, loans, and projects under §§85‑1‑602 and 90‑2‑1102.

Amends §85‑1‑631 to define the WS‑SRF, list its funding sources, and restrict its use to construction, operation, rehabilitation, expansion, maintenance, and modification of state‑owned water‑storage projects.
Requires the state treasurer to transfer $50 million from the general fund to the MWDS‑SRF by August 1 2025 and another $50 million by August 1 2026.
Adds codification instructions and makes the act effective immediately upon passage.

HB258.one_line: Extends wolf hunting season, sets quotas, bag limits, and aligns with bear season.
HB258.summary: The bill amends Montana’s game‑law section to set specific wolf harvest quotas and bag limits, extend the wolf hunting season so it ends with the spring bear season, and add a short muzzleloader heritage season.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑304 to give the Fish & Wildlife Commission authority to set wolf hunting seasons, quotas, and bag limits.
Specifies a quota of two wolves and a bag limit of one wolf within 15 mi of Yellowstone and Glacier National Parks.
Allows the commission to open a wolf trapping season from the first Monday after Thanksgiving to March 15, with possible unit‑specific adjustments.
Requires the wolf hunting season to end concurrently with the spring bear season, with unit‑specific adjustments allowed.
Adds a 9‑day muzzleloader heritage season after the regular season for deer and elk hunting with specified rifles.
Provides that illegally harvested wolves count against the quotas.
Does not create new programs, funds, or offenses.
No fiscal impact is stated in the text.
numbers: Trapping season: first Monday after Thanksgiving to March 15

HB262.one_line: Mandates evidence‑based early‑literacy instruction and bans non‑research‑based methods.
HB262.summary: The bill mandates that all early‑literacy instruction in Montana public schools be evidence‑based, following a scope‑and‑sequence that includes phonics, phonemic awareness, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. It bars instruction that relies on meaning‑from‑context or the three‑cue system unless it meets the stated minimums. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Defines state policy that reading instruction must be evidence‑based and include a specified set of literacy components.
Prohibits the use of meaning‑from‑context, structure‑syntax, visual‑cue, picture, or memory‑based strategies (e.g., the three‑cue system) unless they meet the minimum requirements of subsection (3).
Requires a scope and sequence for early‑literacy instruction that is direct, systematic, explicit, and responsive.
Codifies the policy as part of Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
Sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
requires school districts to adopt the policy through their local curriculum development process.
affected: students in kindergarten through third grade

HB263.one_line: HB 263 mandates annual electricity‑use reporting for Montana data centers and large digital‑asset‑mining sites.
HB263.summary: HB 263 requires data centers and large‑scale digital‑asset‑mining operations to report their annual and projected electricity use to the Montana Public Service Commission. It also clarifies definitions and prohibits discriminatory rates for these activities.
changes: Amends §69‑3‑332 to add a reporting requirement for data centers and digital‑asset‑mining businesses (excluding home mining).
Defines key terms: data center, digital asset mining, digital asset mining business, discriminatory rates, home digital asset mining.
Mandates annual reports by March 1 of each year with actual and projected megawatt‑hour consumption.
Prohibits the commission from establishing rate classifications that would create unduly discriminatory rates for digital‑asset‑mining activities.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to March 1, 2026.
affected: Digital‑asset‑mining businesses consuming >1 MW average annual power

HB265.one_line: Allows automatic over‑BASE levy increases tied to inflation, with voter approval for excess amounts.
HB265.summary: HB 265 revises Montana’s school‑funding law to let school boards increase an over‑BASE levy automatically when inflation raises the allowable budget, while still requiring voter approval for amounts that exceed the prior five‑year cap. The changes make the general‑fund formula self‑executing and set a clear inflation‑adjustment mechanism. The act takes effect immediately and applies to fiscal years beginning July 1 2025.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑308 to allow school boards to raise the over‑BASE levy without a vote if they reduce other non‑voted levies by at least the same amount, and requires future reductions if other levies rise.
Adds a new subsection (2)(b) that permits automatic over‑BASE levy increases tied to the legislature’s inflation adjustment for basic and per‑ANB entitlements.
Rewrites §20‑9‑353 to clarify the election requirements for over‑BASE levies that exceed the permissible inflation‑adjusted amount, including the need for a vote before August 1 of the fiscal year.
Specifies that any over‑BASE levy authorized by election must be levied by county commissioners on all taxable property.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and its applicability to school fiscal years beginning July 1 2025.
affected: Montana Department of Revenue (for levy calculations)
numbers: inflationary adjustment for basic and per‑ANB entitlements

HB272.one_line: Bill makes legislative drafting files public while clarifying privilege limits.
HB272.summary: HB 272 declares that all legislative bill‑drafting files are public records and clarifies how the Speech‑or‑Debate privilege applies to those files. It allows public access to draft bills, research, and communications with bill drafters, while protecting a legislator’s private writings and personal‑staff communications from disclosure unless the legislator voluntarily shares them.
changes: Designates legislative bill‑drafting files as public records under Title 2, Chapter 6, Part 10 of the Montana Code.
Defines the contents of a bill‑drafting file (draft versions, research, legal analysis, emails, etc.).

Clarifies that the Speech‑or‑Debate privilege protects a legislator from prosecution for legitimate legislative acts but does not shield the contents of a bill‑drafting file from public‑records disclosure.
Establishes that a legislator waives privilege if they voluntarily provide writings or communications to another person.
Excludes communications between a legislator and chamber staff or legislative‑branch staff from privilege and allows those communications to be disclosed.
Provides definitions for “chamber staff,” “legislative‑branch staff,” and “personal staff.”
Includes severability, codification, and an effective‑date clause.
affected: Members of the public requesting records
numbers: Effective date: on passage and approval

HB273.one_line: HB 273 protects patients from aggressive medical‑debt collection and sets a 120‑day waiting period.
HB273.summary: HB 273 limits how medical debt can be collected in Montana. It bans wage garnishment, bank‑account liens, and other aggressive tactics, requires a 120‑day waiting period before a debt can be sent to collections, and protects up to $3,000 in a patient’s bank accounts. The bill also amends the state’s exemption law to include medical‑debt interests.
changes: Bans wage garnishment and bank‑account liens for medical debt; prohibits threatening arrest, foreclosing, or reporting to credit bureaus for medical debt collection.
Requires a 120‑day waiting period after the first bill before a debt can be sent to a third‑party collector or sued.
Mandates a 30‑day notice to the patient before any extraordinary collection action, stating the action and deadline.
Prohibits any collection action during a state or public‑health emergency.
Prevents collection actions while an insurance appeal is pending or within 180 days of an appeal.
Exempts up to $3,000 in aggregate value from execution in bank accounts, savings, stocks, bonds, or other securities.
Amends the state’s personal‑property exemption statute to add the $3,000 medical‑debt exemption.

HB274.one_line: Establishes Medicaid‑covered medical respite care for homeless people, with reporting and CMS waiver requirements.
HB274.summary: HB 274 establishes a Medicaid‑covered medical respite care program for homeless people who are medically eligible. It authorizes the Department of Public Health and Human Services to reimburse providers, sets reporting requirements, and requires a waiver or state‑plan amendment by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).
changes: Creates a new Medicaid‑covered medical respite care program for homeless individuals;
Authorizes the department to reimburse eligible providers for short‑term housing plus supportive medical services;
Defines medical respite care services (treatment plans, medication management, immunizations, screening, discharge planning, care coordination, social services assistance, transportation, meals);
Mandates annual reporting to the legislature on participants, costs, and cost savings;
Directs the department to apply for a CMS waiver or state‑plan amendment no later than Jan 1 2026;
Makes the program effective only after CMS approval, with certification required within 10 days of approval;
Codifies the program as part of Title 53, Chapter 6, Part 1.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
HB274.effective: Contingent on CMS approval; otherwise effective upon passage

HB275.one_line: Creates a new driving privilege card and amends licensing rules, fees, and administration.
HB275.summary: HB 275 creates a new “driving privilege card” that can be issued to people who are ineligible for a regular driver’s license, sets the application, eligibility, and revocation rules, and authorizes fees and rule‑making. The bill also amends many existing licensing statutes to recognize the new card, expand who may drive, and clarify fee distribution.
changes: Establishes a new driving privilege card for those ineligible for a driver’s license, with defined eligibility, expiration, and revocation provisions
Requires applicants to provide proof of identity, Montana residence, and lawful U.S. presence, and to pass vision, knowledge, and (if required) road or skills tests
Mandates that cardholders possess minimum liability insurance and that the card contain photo, signature, expiration, endorsements, and optional medical declarations
Authorizes the department to adopt rules on proof of identity, expiration dates, and other administrative matters, including a digital license program
Amends sections 61‑5‑104, 105, 110, 116, 121, 201, 203, 204, 503, and 14‑201 to recognize the new card, expand eligibility for non‑residents, and clarify fee disposition
Provides detailed fee‑distribution formulas for license, commercial license, motorcycle endorsement, and replacement fees, directing portions to county or state funds and specific accounts
Sets the act’s effective date to January 1 2026
affected: County treasurers and other authorized agents
Individuals with disabilities or medical conditions
numbers: $2.5% of driver’s license fee to county general fund
$20.7% of driver’s license fee to state traffic education account
$63.46% of motorcycle endorsement fee to state motorcycle safety account
$3.75% of replacement license fee to county general fund
$3.34% of motorcycle endorsement fee to county general fund
$8.75% of replacement license fee to state traffic education account
$33.2% of motorcycle endorsement fee to state general fund

HB277.one_line: Mandates a two‑year minimum lease term for mobile‑home lot rentals, with limited early‑termination damages.
HB277.summary: HB 277 requires mobile‑home lot leases to be at least two years long, unless the tenant waives the minimum term. It amends the lease‑agreement statute to set a default 2‑year term and modifies holdover remedies to reflect the longer lease.
changes: Amends §70‑33‑201 to make a 2‑year minimum lease term the default for mobile‑home lot rentals.
Allows a tenant to request a shorter term only if they sign a documented, informed waiver.
Adds a clause that if either party terminates the lease early, the non‑terminating party may recover up to one month’s rent in damages.
Rewrites §70‑33‑429 to clarify holdover remedies for leases longer than month‑to‑month, including limits on recoverable damages.
Adjusts the language around notice and filing deadlines for possession actions.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.

HB286.one_line: Bill mandates citizenship verification for all Montana voters and allows removal of non‑citizens.
HB286.summary: HB 286 requires the Secretary of State to record and verify the U.S. citizenship status of all registered voters, establishes procedures for new applicants to prove citizenship, and allows removal of voters who cannot demonstrate citizenship. It amends several voter‑registration statutes and gives the Secretary rule‑making authority to implement these changes.
changes: Amends §§13‑2‑108, 13‑2‑109, 13‑2‑110, 13‑2‑402, and 61‑14‑301 to add citizenship‑verification requirements.
Mandates that the Secretary of State adopt rules to record citizenship status for all registered electors and to determine citizenship for new applicants.
Requires new voter‑registration applicants to provide proof of U.S. citizenship (e.g., driver’s license, ID card, SSN, or other approved documents).
Allows election administrators to register applicants as provisionally registered if citizenship proof is incomplete or unverified.
Provides that an elector who fails to demonstrate citizenship can have their registration cancelled under §13‑2‑402.
Gives the Secretary of State rule‑making authority to establish procedures for notifying electors of their registration status and for distinguishing legal vs. provisional registrants.
Includes a severability clause and sets effective dates: the act takes effect Oct 1 2025, with §§2‑4 effective once the Secretary certifies federal law permits state citizenship verification.
affected: Secretary of State and state election officials

HB287.one_line: HB 287 toughens dangerous‑drug penalties, adds firearm and fentanyl provisions, and expands fine‑eligible crimes.
HB287.summary: HB 287 revises Montana’s dangerous‑drug statutes, adding harsher penalties for distribution and possession‑with‑intent, especially when a firearm is used or fentanyl is involved, and expands the list of crimes that may carry a fine. It also clarifies when fines can be imposed and how they are calculated.
changes: Amends §45‑9‑101 to impose up to 25‑year prison terms, $50,000 fines, and mandatory 2‑to‑10‑year sentences when a firearm is used during a dangerous‑drug offense; adds special 40‑year maximum for fentanyl‑related distribution and life sentences for repeat offenses involving minors; exempts licensed practitioners.

Amends §45‑9‑103 to impose up to 20‑year prison terms or $50,000 fines for possession‑with‑intent, with a 2‑to‑40‑year range for fentanyl and mandatory 2‑year non‑parole period; exempts licensed practitioners.

Amends §46‑18‑231 to broaden the list of felony and misdemeanor offenses that may carry a fine, set a $50,000 ceiling on felony fines, and establish a 3% interest rule for unpaid fines after six months.
The bill does not create a new program or office; it only revises existing statutes.
affected: Persons convicted of dangerous‑drug distribution or possession‑with‑intent, especially those involving firearms or fentanyl; licensed medical or other practitioners who are exempt from the new penalties.
Judges who impose sentences and fines under the revised statutes.

HB289.one_line: Adds felony endangerment for exposing children to fentanyl, heroin, or cocaine and expands penalties.
HB289.summary: The bill amends Montana’s child‑endangerment law to make it a crime for a parent, guardian, or any adult to expose a child to the production or use of fentanyl, heroin, or cocaine. It also expands the definition of endangerment to include any adult who produces or possesses these drugs in a place where a child might be present, and it adds harsher penalties for such conduct. The bill does not create a new program or office, but it does create a new felony offense under the existing child‑endangerment statute.
changes: Adds a new subsection (3) that makes it a felony for any adult who produces, manufactures, or possesses methamphetamine, fentanyl, heroin, or cocaine in a location where a child could be present, or who allows a child to be exposed to those drugs or their paraphernalia.
Expands the definition of endangerment to include the act of exposing a child to the production or manufacture of fentanyl, heroin, or cocaine (subsection (3)(c)).

Raises the maximum penalty for a first offense under subsection (3) to a felony of up to 5 years in state prison and a fine up to $10,000; for a second offense up to 10 years and a fine up to $25,000 if the child suffers serious injury.
Keeps existing penalties for other child‑endangerment conduct (up to 6 months in county jail and $500 fine for a first offense; up to 6 months and $1,000 fine for a second offense).
Adds a list of evidence admissible in determining a violation of duty of care (e.g., neglect, abuse, lack of medical care).

Allows parents or guardians to request a person who has no legal right to contact a child to stop contacting the child, and provides a mechanism for petitioning for an order of protection under Title 40, Chapter 15.
affected: Parents, guardians, and other adults supervising children
Adults who produce, manufacture, or possess methamphetamine, fentanyl, heroin, or cocaine in child‑present locations
Children who might be exposed to those drugs
Law enforcement and courts handling child‑endangerment cases

HB288.one_line: HB 288 allows fathers to be ordered to pay child support retroactive to conception and tightens enforcement and paternity testing procedures.
HB288.summary: HB 288 expands Montana’s child‑support system so that a father’s financial obligation begins at conception and can be enforced during pregnancy. It amends the child‑support statutes to allow orders before birth, requires paternity testing unless the mother objects, and tightens enforcement and record‑keeping procedures.
changes: 1.  Fathers may be ordered to pay child support retroactive to the month of conception, even before the child is born.
2.  A mother may object to paternity genetic testing while pregnant; if she does, the court may not order support until after birth and may award retroactive support once paternity is established.

3.  The bill amends §§ 40‑4‑204, 40‑5‑225, 40‑5‑226, 40‑5‑232, 40‑5‑233, 40‑6‑107, 40‑6‑112, and 40‑6‑116 to incorporate the new conception‑based support rule and to require paternity testing procedures.
4.  Courts must include detailed medical‑support orders and enforceability provisions (income withholding, penalties, etc.) in every child‑support judgment or order.
5.  The department is empowered to serve notices of parental responsibility before birth, to subpoena for genetic testing, and to enforce paternity determinations through administrative hearings.
6.  The bill establishes strict confidentiality and reporting requirements for personal and insurance information used in support orders.

who_is_affected":"fathers, mothers, children, courts, child‑support enforcement agencies, health‑insurance carriers, and employers of parents","policy_area":"Family Law / Child Support","secondary_area":"Paternity / Genetic Testing","fiscal_impact":"Not specified; no new funding or fees are created; the bill mainly changes enforcement procedures and timing of support orders.","key_numbers":["July 1 2025","conception month","20‑day deadline for denial of paternity","$500 maximum contempt penalty per count"],"effective_date":"July 1, 2025","creates_new_program_or_crime":false,"complexity":4,

HB295.one_line: Allows judicial candidates to disclose party affiliation on nomination papers and ballots.
HB295.summary: HB 295 allows judicial candidates to disclose their political party affiliation on nomination paperwork and the ballot, and permits them to announce endorsements. It amends several Montana Code sections to add party labels to judicial candidates while preserving existing nonpartisan rules.
changes: 1. Adds a new section permitting a judicial candidate to indicate party affiliation on the declaration for nomination.
2. Adds a new section allowing a judicial candidate to announce party affiliation or endorsements publicly.
3. Amends §13‑10‑209 to require a candidate’s party name to appear on the ballot if the candidate indicates affiliation on the declaration.
4. Amends §13‑10‑602 to clarify that a candidate may use the name of the party by which they are nominated.
5. Amends §13‑12‑203 to require the party designation (≤3 words) to appear next to a judicial candidate’s name on the ballot, or “Undisclosed” if none is indicated.
6. Amends §13‑14‑112 to allow a judicial candidate to indicate party affiliation on the declaration and to list “Undisclosed” if not indicated.
7. Amends §13‑14‑115 to require that judicial candidates on nonpartisan primary ballots be listed with their party affiliation as provided in the amended sections.

HB290.one_line: Ban PFAS‑containing cosmetics, juvenile, menstrual products and regulate firefighting foam and gear.
HB290.summary: HB 290 prohibits the sale of cosmetics, juvenile and menstrual products that contain intentionally added PFAS, and regulates the use of PFAS‑containing firefighting foam and gear. It requires manufacturers to certify compliance, gives distributors immunity if they rely on such certificates, and imposes reporting, containment, and recall requirements for firefighting foam and gear.
changes: 1. From Jan 1 2028, no person may manufacture, sell, or offer for sale in Montana cosmetics, juvenile products, or menstrual products that contain intentionally added PFAS. 2. Manufacturers must provide a signed certificate of compliance to sellers; distributors may rely in good faith on that certificate. 3. The prohibition does not apply to used products. 4. From Jan 1 2028, class B firefighting foam containing intentionally added PFAS may not be discharged or used for training; manufacturers may not sell or distribute such foam unless the purchaser files a notice with the state fire marshal. 5. Purchasers who file a notice must provide evidence of no commercial alternative, report usage, and demonstrate containment and transition plans. 6. Users must report use and any environmental release within five business days and must contain all releases, implement containment measures, and document actions. 7. Manufacturers must notify sellers at least one year before the effective date and may be required to recall prohibited foam by Mar 1 2028. 8. Firefighting personal‑protective equipment containing PFAS must carry written notice to purchasers at sale, which must be kept for three years. 9. First‑time violations carry a civil penalty up to $5,000; repeat violations up to $10,000.
affected: Manufacturers of cosmetics, juvenile, and menstrual products
Retailers and distributors of those products
Manufacturers and distributors of class B firefighting foam
Terminals and other users of firefighting foam
Manufacturers and sellers of firefighting personal‑protective equipment
State fire marshal and environmental quality department

HB297.one_line: Montana mandates paid sick leave for employers with 10+ employees, sets use rules, record‑keeping, and anti‑retaliation protections, and gives the Labor Department enforcement authority.
HB297.summary: Montana will require employers with 10 or more employees to provide paid sick leave, with accrual of at least one hour per 40 hours worked and a maximum carry‑forward of 80 hours.  The bill sets use‑rules, record‑keeping, confidentiality, and anti‑retaliation protections, and gives the Department of Labor authority to enforce the law.
changes: Employers with 10+ employees must offer paid sick leave, accruing 1 hour per 40 hours worked, capped at 80 hours per year.
Employees may use leave for illness, preventive care, or caring for a family member, including victims of domestic violence or sexual assault.
Leave must be taken in 1‑hour increments; employers may require documentation for four or more consecutive days.
Employers must provide written notice of leave rights and anti‑retaliation protections, and keep 2‑year records of hours worked and leave used.
The Department of Labor can issue rules, investigate complaints, and enforce the law as a wage‑claim action.
Collective‑bargaining agreements that already provide equal or better leave are exempt.
The law does not preempt other higher‑standard leave laws.
The law applies to conduct occurring on or after its effective date (not specified).
affected: Department of Labor and its staff

HB298.one_line: Revises local election rules for marijuana businesses to require 5,000‑resident municipalities to vote separately and clarifies approval and prohibition procedures.
HB298.summary: The bill revises Montana’s local election rules for marijuana businesses, limiting municipal votes to towns with 5,000+ residents and clarifying when county and city approvals are required. It also sets immediate effect and retroactive applicability for elections held after passage.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑301 to require municipal approval only in municipalities with 5,000+ residents for most marijuana‑business categories.
Specifies that a county election can be held if the county’s qualified electors petition, and that a municipality’s vote is separate if it has 5,000+ residents.
Provides that a county may allow a category if a majority of county voters approve, and a municipality may allow or prohibit a category based on its own majority vote.
Allows former medical‑marijuana licensees to operate without new local approval if they do not seek adult‑use dispensary licensure.
Prevents local governments from banning the transport of marijuana on public roads.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and applies retroactively to elections held on or after that date.
affected: Qualified electors in counties and municipalities
numbers: 90 days after local election for overturning approvals
retroactive to elections held on or after effective date

HB301.one_line: Revises when real‑property injury claims accrue and limits the period to file them.
HB301.summary: HB 301 revises Montana’s statutes of limitations for real‑property injury claims. It defines when a claim accrues, when the limitation period starts, and when it ends, and bars claims that are not filed within the period.
changes: Amends §27‑2‑102 to clarify that a claim accrues when all elements exist, the right to sue is complete, and jurisdiction is available; the action is deemed commenced when the complaint is filed.
Specifies that for real‑property injury claims the claim arises when the injurious conduct is complete and the owner knows or should know of the injury.
Establishes that the limitation period begins at accrual, regardless of the plaintiff’s knowledge, except where facts are concealed or the defendant actively hides the injury.
Provides an exception for claims involving the limitations in §27‑2‑205.
Barred claims that are not brought within the limitation period against the current and all subsequent owners of the property.
affected: Courts and other agencies with jurisdiction over such claims

HB302.one_line: Revises punitive‑damages procedure, requiring briefing, affidavits, evidence, and a 50/50 state split of awards.
HB302.summary: The bill amends Montana’s punitive‑damages law to require a pre‑amendment briefing, affidavits, and, if requested, an evidentiary hearing before a judge may grant a motion to amend a pleading to add a punitive‑damages claim. It also sets strict evidentiary standards, limits the use of a defendant’s financial condition in liability determinations, and mandates that any punitive‑damages award be split equally between the prevailing party and the state, with the state’s share deposited in the general fund.
changes: Requires a motion to amend a pleading to add a punitive‑damages claim to be briefed with affidavits and documentation before the court may grant it.
Allows a party to request an evidentiary hearing where live testimony is presented and the court must make findings on the existence of a triable issue.
Sets a clear‑and‑convincing‑evidence standard for all elements of a punitive‑damages claim.
Prohibits use of a defendant’s financial condition in determining liability, but allows it in a separate proceeding to set the amount of damages.
Mandates that punitive‑damages awards be split 50/50 between the prevailing party and the state, with the state’s share deposited in the general fund.
Specifies that the state may not intervene in the proceeding except to enforce the judgment and limits attorney‑fee deductions from the state’s share to 20%.
affected: Juries and judges hearing punitive‑damages cases
The State of Montana (as recipient of half the award)
numbers: 20% cap on attorney‑fee deductions from state’s share
no use of financial condition in liability determination

HB303.one_line: Revises fault‑apportionment rules, allowing non‑party causation arguments and clarifying contribution and settlement defenses.
HB303.summary: HB 303 revises Montana’s fault‑apportionment rules, allowing a defendant to argue that a non‑party caused all injuries without seeking apportionment and clarifying how joint, severable, and contributory liability is calculated.
changes: Amends §27‑1‑703 to define joint‑and‑severable liability, contribution, and the 50% threshold for severance.
Adds a 50% or less negligence clause that limits a party’s liability to its share and requires proportional contribution from others if a party cannot pay.
Permits a defendant to claim that a settled or released party caused the injury and seek apportionment, but requires proof of that party’s negligence and the standard of care.
Allows a defendant to assert a settlement or release as a defense and requires affirmative pleading of that defense.
Mandates notification by certified mail to settled or released parties when a defendant alleges their fault.
Clarifies that a party’s release or settlement does not automatically bar apportionment but reduces the claimant’s claim by the released party’s share.
Provides that a non‑party may be argued as the sole cause of injury even if not a party to the action.
Leaves the overall liability framework unchanged but adds procedural safeguards and clarifications.
No new program, fund, or crime is created.
No monetary amounts are specified.
affected: Plaintiffs in negligence or warranty cases
Defendants (including those who are settled or released parties)
HB303.effective: Effective on occurrence of contingency (as in existing law)

HB304.one_line: HB 304 gives tenants 48 hours to fix cleaning issues and bars landlords from inspection fees.
HB304.summary: HB 304 revises Montana’s security‑deposit rules to give tenants clearer notice about cleaning deficiencies, a 48‑hour window to remedy them, and bans landlord inspection fees. It also tightens the types of deductions landlords may take.
changes: Adds a 48‑hour period after written notice for tenants to complete required cleaning unless the tenancy has already ended or a court claim is pending.
Requires landlords to provide an itemized list of unfinished cleaning and cost estimates before deducting cleaning charges.
Prohibits landlords from charging a fee to inspect cleaning performed by the tenant during the 48‑hour remediation period.
Clarifies that cleaning charges may only be deducted for tenant‑caused negligence, not for routine maintenance.
Limits deductions to damage, unpaid rent, late charges, utilities, lease penalties, and actual cleaning expenses, including reasonable labor costs.
States that no other amounts may be withheld from the security deposit.
Defines notice delivery methods and timelines (certified mail counts after 3 days).

HB305.one_line: HB 305 creates a mobile‑home park dispute‑resolution program with registration, fees, and enforcement powers.
HB305.summary: HB 305 creates a state‑run dispute‑resolution program for mobile‑home parks, requiring registration, educational outreach, and a fee‑based account that funds investigations, penalties, and administrative hearings.  Landlords must post notices, register annually, and pay a $24 per‑home assessment; tenants may file complaints and seek remedies without first exhausting state action.
changes: Establishes a Montana Mobile Home Park Dispute Resolution Program administered by the Department of Commerce;
Requires landlords to post a notice and register each park annually, paying $24 per mobile home;
Creates a dedicated program account funded by registration fees, fines, and penalties;
Provides a complaint process with investigations, negotiations, written determinations, and administrative hearings;
Imposes fines up to $250 per day for uncorrected violations and up to $5,000 for retaliation;
Mandates written notice of intent to sell a park, giving tenants a right of first refusal within 70 days.

HB306.one_line: Tax credit for landlords renting below 110 % of fair‑market rent, carry‑forwardable for 3 years.
HB306.summary: The bill creates a state income‑tax credit for landlords who rent a dwelling for less than 110 % of the county’s fair‑market rent.  The credit is $200 for every $100 the rent falls below that threshold, can be carried forward three years, and is subject to review by the revenue interim committee.
changes: Creates a $200 credit for each $100 rent below 110 % of fair‑market rent; applies to individuals and corporations; credit may be carried forward up to three years; requires a lease of at least one year and meeting HUD housing‑quality standards; disallows the credit if rent is already limited by another program; requires documentation of rent and utilities; credit is reviewed biennially by the revenue interim committee; codified under Title 15 chapters 30 and 31; effective for tax years beginning after Dec. 31 2025.
affected: Landlords (individuals and corporations) who rent below market rate

HB309.one_line: Clarifies the two‑year term and vacancy rules for precinct committee representatives.
HB309.summary: The bill amends the law to specify that a precinct committee representative’s two‑year term starts on the certification of the election that elected them and ends on the certification of the next election. It also clarifies how vacancies are filled and when a term expires.
changes: Amends §13‑38‑202 to state the term of a precinct committee representative is exactly two years from the certification of the election that elected them.
Specifies that the term begins on the county’s certification of the election and ends on the county’s certification of the next election.
Clarifies that if a representative is appointed, the term ends at the certification of the next election.
Defines vacancies as occurring only upon death, resignation, loss of residency or voter registration, and not by removal otherwise.
States that remaining members of the county central committee may select a precinct resident to fill a vacancy.

HB310.one_line: HB 310 creates a two‑year state‑matching grant program for homeless shelter expansion with a $250,000 county cap and a 1,000‑point scoring system.
HB310.summary: HB 310 creates a state‑matching grant program to expand homeless shelter capacity, funding up to $2 million over two years and limiting each county to $250,000 in matching funds.  Grants are awarded by a 1,000‑point scoring system that prioritizes geographic diversity, capacity, affordability, community need, and impact.
changes: Establishes a $2 million appropriation for state matching grants to local governments and 501(c)(3) nonprofits that plan to expand shelter capacity for specified vulnerable groups.
Provides a one‑to‑one matching ratio of state funds to applicant‑provided funds, with a cap of $250,000 per county.
Requires applicants to submit a detailed collaboration plan and evidence of matching funds.
Imposes a 1,000‑point weighted scoring system (up to 250 points for geographic diversity, 100 for capacity, 150 for affordability, 250 for community need, 250 for potential impact).
Mandates the Department of Public Health and Human Services Commerce to adopt rules for application, award criteria, and reporting.
Requires the department to report to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Economic Affairs Interim Committee by August 30 2026.
Reverts any unencumbered funds to the general fund by June 30 2027.
Sets effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2027.
affected: Youth transitioning out of foster care

HB313.one_line: Montana creates a $5 million grant program for public swimming pools, requiring matching funds and administrative oversight.
HB313.summary: Montana will create a $5 million grant program for nonprofit organizations and local governments to build, repair, or operate public swimming pools, requiring matching funds and administrative oversight. The program runs from July 1 2025 to June 30 2029 and is funded from a special revenue account.
changes: Establishes a public swimming pool infrastructure account in the state special revenue fund and authorizes the Department of Commerce to administer it.
Provides up to $5 million in grants for construction, remodeling, equipment, and up to one year of operational costs for public pools.
Requires grant recipients to provide matching funds or in‑kind contributions at a 1:5 ratio for grants $25,000 or more, and to submit a project management plan and reporting.
Limits state funding per county to $1 million and per project to $500,000, with no more than two funded projects per county.
Mandates a $5 million transfer from the General Fund Capital Developments Long‑Range Building Program Account to the new account by July 15 2025.
Sets the program’s effective date (July 1 2025) and termination date (June 30 2029).
affected: County, city, town, township, school district, tribal government, and other local public entities

HB314.one_line: Montana creates an Energy Authority funded by a $700,000 annual tax allocation to coordinate state energy development.
HB314.summary: Montana will create a new Energy Authority to coordinate and promote the development of the state’s energy resources, funded by a portion of the wholesale energy transaction tax. The Authority will be staffed by 14 appointed members, have a set of powers and reporting duties, and will receive up to $700,000 annually from the tax to cover administrative costs. The Authority will operate from July 1 2025 to December 31 2031.
changes: Establishes the Montana Energy Authority, a new state agency with a 14‑member board and executive director.
Authorizes the Authority to plan, coordinate, and analyze energy generation and transmission projects, hire staff, contract services, and receive gifts or grants.
Creates a special revenue account in the state special revenue fund and appropriates up to $700,000 annually from the wholesale energy transaction tax to fund the Authority’s administrative costs.
Mandates annual reporting to the Energy and Telecommunications Interim Committee and requires cooperation from all state agencies in permitting and data sharing.
Sets the Authority’s term of existence from July 1 2025 to December 31 2031 and provides for its dissolution thereafter.
affected: State agencies involved in energy permitting and data provision
Montana taxpayers through the wholesale energy transaction tax
Members of the new Authority and its staff
numbers: up to $700,000 annually from the tax

HB315.one_line: HB 315 tightens food‑income ratios, expands quota limits, and adds flexible hours and new fees for restaurant beer‑and‑wine licenses.
HB315.summary: HB 315 revises Montana’s restaurant beer‑and‑wine licensing rules, tightening food‑income ratios, expanding quota‑area limits, and allowing more flexible operating hours while adding new fee schedules and reporting requirements.
changes: Requires restaurants to show at least 65‑70 % of gross income from food for the first year and annually thereafter, with audit authority.
Expands quota‑area licensing limits for restaurants (up to 200 % in resort communities) and allows one‑time adjustments and transfers of licenses between overlapping quota areas.
Permits beer and wine to be sold for off‑premises consumption (curbside, pickup, delivery) between 11 a.m. and 11 p.m., with price limits tied to food and inclusion on the bill.

Sets initial licensing fees ($5,000–$20,000) based on seating capacity and an annual fee of $400, with adjustments for capacity changes and a cap that 25 % of large‑capacity licenses may be issued per quota area.
Allows restaurants to set their own operating hours within the 11 p.m.–11 a.m. window, provided they notify the Department and obtain approval; city ordinances may impose tighter limits.
Adds new reporting and enforcement provisions, including a prohibition on selling beer/wine without food purchase and limits on gaming activities on licensed premises.

HB316.one_line: Amend constitution to include unborn as persons, require two‑thirds vote and voter approval.
HB316.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Constitution to define “person” as including all humans from fertilization onward, bars legal claims for harm to unborn babies, and requires a two‑thirds legislative vote and a public referendum. The amendment would take effect only after voters approve it in the 2026 election.
changes: Amends Article II §17 to state that “person” includes all humans from fertilization/conception regardless of age or condition.
Adds a prohibition that no cause of action may arise from harm to an unborn baby caused unintentionally by its mother.
Requires the legislature to enact implementing laws.
Adds a severability clause for the amendment.
Mandates a two‑thirds roll‑call vote in the legislature to pass the amendment.
Specifies the amendment will be on the November 2026 ballot and become effective only if voters approve it.

HB319.one_line: Prohibits employers from mandating attendance at training that promotes a controversial social vision.
HB319.summary: HB 319 prohibits employers from requiring employees to attend training that promotes a “controversial social vision.” It amends the election‑registration and anti‑discrimination statutes to define the term and to make such a requirement unlawful. The bill does not create a new program or fund.
changes: Amends §13‑1‑116 to add a definition of “controversial social vision” and to clarify that it is not a protected class in election‑registration contexts.
Amends §49‑2‑101 to define “controversial social vision” and related terms (e.g., employee, employer, labor organization).

Amends §49‑2‑303 to add a new unlawful practice: an employer may not refuse, bar, or discriminate against an employee for refusing to attend any training outside the scope of employment that promotes a controversial social vision.
The amendment makes refusal to attend such training a form of discrimination under the state’s anti‑discrimination law.
The bill does not alter any funding, create new offices, or impose new penalties beyond the existing statutory framework.
The bill does not apply to Indian reservations for certain employment practices.

HB320.one_line: Creates a private‑school tax‑credit program with council oversight, donor credits, and enrollment exemptions.
HB320.summary: The bill creates Montana’s Academic Prosperity Program for Scholars (MAPPS), a voluntary, privately‑funded education‑tax‑credit program that lets parents pay for qualified private‑school or post‑secondary expenses and receive a state tax credit.  It establishes a council, a program manager, and detailed procedures for applications, funding, reporting, and audits.
changes: Creates MAPPS council and program manager to administer a private‑school tax‑credit program
Allows parents to receive an education tax credit for qualified expenses and donors to receive a credit for contributions to MAPPS
Sets an annual educational assistance maximum based on state aid per student
Defines eligibility, application, lottery, and prioritization rules for participating students
Requires public‑school districts to provide records for MAPPS students and allows MAPPS students to be exempt from compulsory enrollment
Imposes reporting, audit, and oversight requirements on the program manager and council
Amends tax‑credit statutes to include MAPPS credits and establishes limits and carry‑forward rules
Adds procedural rules for appeals, audits, and confidentiality of taxpayer information
numbers: $4 million aggregate tax‑credit limit (2026 and subsequent years)
Annual educational assistance maximum (state‑aid per student)

HB322.one_line: Reduces Montana Supreme Court associate justices from six to four, eliminating two seats.
HB322.summary: The bill cuts the Montana Supreme Court’s number of associate justices from six to four by eliminating seats 5 1 and 6 2. Those positions will not be filled after the 2028 election, and the change takes effect on the first Monday of January 2029. All other court functions and duties remain unchanged.
changes: Amends §3‑2‑101, MCA, to state the court has a chief justice plus four associate justices.
Eliminates associate justice seats 5 1 and 6 2, whose terms expire in 2029‑2031.
No elections will be held for the eliminated seats in the November 2028 election.
The amendment does not alter any existing rights, penalties, or pending proceedings.
The act becomes effective upon passage and approval, specifically the first Monday of January 2029.

HB326.one_line: HB 326 taxes non‑coal electricity at 10%, redirects revenue, and amends coal tax rates.
HB326.summary: HB 326 creates a 10% tax on the sale price of electricity produced from non‑coal sources, exempts coal‑generated power, and redirects revenue to a trust and special revenue accounts for state projects and a coal endowment. It also amends the coal severance tax schedule to lower rates and establishes a Montana Energy Authority if created.
changes: Imposes a 10% tax on the sale price of electricity from non‑coal generators; coal‑generated electricity is exempt.

Divides tax revenue 50% to a state energy resources trust account and 50% to a Montana coal endowment special revenue account (or 40% to an energy‑authority operations account and 10% to a resource trust account if an energy authority is created).
Amends the coal severance tax rates, lowering them for certain mining methods and providing a 50,000‑ton exemption.
Creates the Montana Energy Authority operations and resource trust accounts and gives the department rule‑making authority over the new tax.
Requires quarterly reporting, filing, and enforcement procedures for the new tax.
Provides for penalties, interest, and refund limits consistent with existing Montana tax law.
Sets effective dates: the tax becomes effective Jan 1 2026, with contingent dates tied to the creation of a state energy authority.
Includes a contingent termination date tied to the same contingency.
affected: Electrical energy producers (non‑coal), coal producers (exempt from new tax), Montana taxpayers receiving revenue from the trust and special accounts
State Department of Revenue, Department of Commerce, State Treasurer
numbers: $250 million threshold for trust principal release
contingent dates tied to energy authority creation
HB326.effective: January 1, 2026 (with contingent dates for sections 14‑16 and 20 tied to creation of a state energy authority)

HB327.one_line: Legislature may refund excess revenue to residents, pending 2026 voter approval.
HB327.summary: The bill allows the Montana Legislature to create a program that refunds excess state revenue to resident income‑taxpayers and requires the proposal to be approved by voters in a 2026 referendum. The bill itself contains no specific refund rules, only a framework for the Legislature to set them. The act takes effect only if the electorate votes “Yes.”
changes: Authorizes the Legislature to enact a refund program for excess revenue to resident taxpayers.
Allows the Legislature to set the trigger amount, refund calculation, eligibility, and distribution method.
Requires the proposal to be placed on the November 2026 ballot as a referendum.
The act becomes effective only upon voter approval.

HB331.one_line: HB 331 restricts marijuana advertising and gives the Department rule‑making authority.
HB331.summary: HB 331 limits how Montana marijuana businesses can advertise. It bans outdoor signage that uses colloquial terms or images of marijuana, prohibits social‑media, TV, radio, print, and targeted internet ads, and bars billboards, mascots, and youth‑appealing imagery. The bill also requires age and residency verification on websites and gives the Department rule‑making authority to set further advertising rules.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑102 to define advertising and set new advertising limits for licensed marijuana businesses.
Bans outdoor signage that uses colloquial terms, images of marijuana or related paraphernalia, and requires compliance with local sign ordinances.
Prohibits marijuana businesses from using social‑media accounts, TV/radio/print ads, targeted internet ads, billboards, mascots, youth‑appealing imagery, rewards programs, or event sponsorships.
Requires marijuana‑business websites to verify that visitors are 21+ and Montana residents before allowing access.
Gives the Department rule‑making authority to adopt additional advertising rules and to set fees, but limits fees to cover administrative costs.
Repeals the existing §16‑12‑211 (previous advertising limits).

HB334.one_line: HB 334 expands and caps governor’s disaster spending, adds a DMA fund, and transfers unspent money to fire suppression.
HB334.summary: HB 334 increases the statutory appropriation available to the governor for disaster and emergency spending, expands the use of that money to more agencies, and sets a new transfer rule for unspent funds. The bill also limits the amount the governor can spend in a biennium and creates a small federal‑grant‑matching provision for presidential‑declared disasters.
changes: Amends §10‑3‑312 to raise the governor’s maximum biennial discretionary appropriation from $20 million to $22 million (with a $16 million baseline for certain uses).
Adds a $3 million annual allocation for the Department of Military Affairs’ Disaster and Emergency Services Division that can be used without a formal disaster declaration.
Limits the governor’s spending on presidential‑declared disasters to $500,000 per biennium for federal grant matching.
Requires that any unexpended portion of the $22 million appropriation be transferred to the fire‑suppression account at the end of each biennium.
Preserves the existing rule that the governor may spend up to the statutory amount minus any amounts appropriated under §10‑3‑310.
Sets the effective date of the changes to July 1 2025.
affected: State agencies designated by the governor

HB339.one_line: Adjusts 6th‑grade funding to match 7th‑8th grades and mandates CTE spending in accredited middle‑school programs.
HB339.summary: The bill amends Montana’s school‑funding formulas so that 6th‑grade students in accredited middle‑school or junior‑high programs receive the same per‑student funding as 7th‑ and 8th‑grade students. It also requires those districts to spend a minimum amount of that extra money on career‑and‑technical‑education (CTE) opportunities for grades 6‑8. The changes take effect immediately and apply to fiscal years beginning July 1 2025 (2026 school year).
changes: Amends §20‑9‑306 to set 6th‑grade funding at the midpoint between elementary and high‑school ANB rates for districts with accredited middle‑school or junior‑high programs.
Amends §20‑9‑311 to clarify ANB calculations for such districts.
Adds §3 requiring accredited middle‑school or junior‑high districts to spend at least $100 × ANB on CTE programs for grades 6‑8.
Provides an immediate effective date and specifies applicability to fiscal years beginning July 1 2025 (2026 school year).
affected: Montana school districts with accredited middle‑school or junior‑high programs
district CTE program planners and administrators
numbers: midpoint between elementary and high‑school ANB rates

HB347.one_line: HB 347 gives the Commission rule‑making power on hunter orange and repeals the hunter orange mandate.
HB347.summary: HB 347 revises Montana’s wildlife laws to give the Fish and Wildlife Commission new rule‑making authority over hunter orange and related hunting practices, while removing the existing statutory requirement that hunters wear hunter orange while big‑game hunting.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑301 to grant the Commission authority to adopt rules on hunter orange and other hunting equipment and licensing matters.
Amends §87‑6‑404 to allow dogs to be used in hunting while wearing hunter orange and to clarify dog‑related hunting rules.
Repeals §87‑6‑414, eliminating the statutory mandate that hunters wear hunter orange during big‑game hunting.

Adds provisions that a hunter using a dog to track a wounded animal must wear hunter orange and maintain a 50‑foot lead, but exempts dog handlers from separate licensing when accompanied by a licensed hunter.
Clarifies penalties for violations of the amended dog‑hunting rules, including fines, imprisonment, and loss of hunting privileges.

HB353.one_line: Establishes shed‑collecting licenses and clarifies rules for collecting naturally shed antlers in Montana.
HB353.summary: The bill creates a new system for collecting naturally shed antlers and horns (shed collecting) in Montana. It establishes resident and non‑resident licenses, a waiting period for non‑residents, and clarifies that landowners and their families may collect on their own land without a license. The bill also amends several game‑law sections to define “shed,” adjust penalties for unlawful possession, and codify the new license provisions.
changes: Creates Class F‑1 resident shed‑collecting license for $10 and Class F‑2 non‑resident license for $50.
Allows landowners, their families, and employees to collect shed antlers on their own land without a license.
Defines “shed” as a naturally shed antler or horn with a skull or skull portion attached that died from natural causes.
Amends sections 87‑1‑201, 87‑1‑304, 87‑2‑101, 87‑2‑106, 87‑2‑201, 87‑2‑202, 87‑6‑202, and 87‑6‑206 to incorporate the new license framework and clarify penalties for unlawful possession and sale.
Adds a 12‑day advance access period for residents to collect shed before non‑residents on the same land.
Codifies Sections 1 and 2 as part of Title 87, Chapter 2, Part 5.
No new program or crime is created beyond the shed‑collecting license system.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks

HB23.one_line: Move the second enrollment count date one week earlier for school‑funding calculations.
HB23.summary: HB 23 changes the date used to count students for Montana’s school‑funding formula, moving the second enrollment count one week earlier. The bill amends the calculation rules in §20‑9‑311 and sets July 1 2025 as the effective and applicability date.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑311 to use a new enrollment‑count date that is one week earlier than the current second count date.
Specifies that the new count date applies to all school fiscal years beginning on or after July 1 2025.
Leaves the rest of the ANB calculation methodology unchanged.
Requires districts to report enrollment counts using the new date for funding purposes.
Sets July 1 2025 as the effective date of the amendment.
Limits applicability to fiscal years that start after the effective date.
numbers: First Monday in February (original second count)

HB124.one_line: Bicycles must ride against traffic unless escorted by a flag vehicle, repealing two existing statutes.
HB124.summary: The bill requires all bicycles to be ridden against the flow of traffic unless a flag‑vehicle escort is present, and it repeals two existing bicycle‑traffic statutes. It does not create a new program or fund. The bill’s impact is limited to bicycle riders and traffic enforcement. The effective date is not specified. The bill is straightforward and does not impose new costs.
changes: Bicycles must be ridden opposite the flow of traffic unless accompanied by a flag‑vehicle escort.
Bicycles ridden with a flag‑vehicle escort must ride with the flow of traffic.
Section 61‑8‑602 (traffic laws for bicycles/mopeds) is repealed.
Section 61‑8‑605 (riding on roadways) is repealed.
Section 1 is codified as part of Title 61, chapter 8, part 6.
The bill does not create new programs, offices, or criminal offenses.

HB133.one_line: Hunters must report each game animal hunted before buying a new license for the next year.
HB133.summary: Hunters who buy a game‑animal license must report each animal they hunt, and they must do so before buying a new license for the next year. The department can set rules and penalties for this reporting requirement. The law takes effect March 1, 2026.
changes: Requires hunters to report each game animal they hunt to the Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks (DFW),
Mandates that the report be filed before the hunter can purchase a new license for the following license year
Empowers the DFW to create rules, deadlines, and penalties to enforce the reporting requirement
Codifies the reporting requirement as part of Title 87, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Code
Sets a delayed effective date of March 1, 2026
affected: DFW staff responsible for rulemaking and enforcement

HB170.one_line: HB 170 mandates legislative review of all federal‑grant applications and requires biennial reporting.
HB170.summary: HB 170 requires every state agency to submit federal‑grant applications to the legislature for review before sending them to the federal government, and mandates an annual report on all such applications. The bill creates a formal legislative‑review process and reporting requirements but does not create a new program or crime.
changes: All federal‑financial‑assistance applications must be reviewed by the legislature before submission.
affected: State agencies that apply for federal funds

HB240.one_line: Revises river laws, mandates map updates, and tightens hunting/shooting rules on Montana’s rivers.
HB240.summary: HB 240 revises Montana’s navigable‑river laws, mandates that all digital maps match the state library’s map, and tightens hunting and shooting rules on rivers and islands. It also expands the state library’s GIS duties and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: All digital‑map distributors must update to the state library’s map by Aug 1 2025 and 30 days after each annual update; maps must label former river beds as private land requiring permission.
Section 23‑2‑302 is amended to prohibit big‑game hunting, overnight camping, permanent or seasonal structures, and shooting from watercraft on navigable rivers, except as allowed by commission rules.

Section 90‑1‑404 expands the state library’s GIS responsibilities: it must coordinate with stakeholders, update the Global Information System map within 30 days of receiving data, prepare a 3‑year reviewable geospatial plan, and manage a grant‑funding account for GIS projects.
The state library must provide the most recent river mapping data to the library by June 1 2025 and each January 1 of subsequent years.
Commission rules (87‑1‑303) are required to adopt procedures for public requests, restrictions, and identification of streams not suitable for recreation.
The act does not create new criminal offenses but imposes new regulatory limits on recreational use of class I and II waters.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
