affected: Recreational users of rivers and islands

HB282.one_line: Expands tuition waivers for Indian students, veterans, and others, notifying tribes and effective July 1 2025.
HB282.summary: The bill amends Montana’s tuition‑waiver law to expand eligibility for non‑resident and resident tuition waivers, especially for American Indian students and other special groups, and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments. It takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Amends §20‑25‑421 to broaden tuition‑waiver categories, adding a new subsection for students with one‑quarter Indian blood or tribal descendants who are bona‑fide Montana residents for one year.
Adds waivers for non‑resident students under WICHE reciprocal agreements, for residents 62 + years, and for various military and first‑responder survivors.
Creates a new notification requirement: the Secretary of State must send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Sets the effective date of the amended law to July 1 2025.
affected: American Indian students and tribal descendants
Military veterans, families of fallen soldiers, POW survivors, and first‑responder families
Montana university system and its regents

HB294.one_line: Transfers the adult basic education fund to Labor and Industry and changes reporting rules.
HB294.summary: The bill moves the adult basic education (ABE) fund from the Office of Public Instruction to the Department of Labor and Industry, changes how funds are directed and reported, and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments. It takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Transfers the ABE fund to the Department of Labor and Industry (DLI).
The superintendent of public instruction now directs fund distribution through DLI.
Applicants for ABE funds must apply to the superintendent via DLI.
Financial administration, accounting, and reporting of ABE funds must follow DLI policies.
The Secretary of State must send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
The act becomes effective July 1, 2025.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB7.one_line: HB 7 appropriates $13.91 M for reclamation, development, and water‑storage grants, prioritizes projects, and sets strict conditions.
HB7.summary: HB 7 creates a biennial grant program for reclamation and development projects, appropriating up to $1.5 M for planning, $5.3 M for pilot water‑storage projects, and $7.11 M for political subdivisions. Grants are awarded in a priority list, subject to conditions on scope, matching funds, and reporting. The act takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Appropriates $1.5 M for planning reclamation & development projects (July 1 2025‑June 30 2027)
Appropriates $5.3 M for pilot water‑storage planning & projects (July 1 2025‑June 30 2027)
Appropriates $7.11 M for grants to political subdivisions & local governments (July 1 2025‑June 30 2027)
Establishes a priority list of 17 projects with specified award amounts
Requires recipients to submit approved scope, matching funds, management plan, audit compliance, and a grant agreement
Prohibits a recipient from receiving funds from both this program and the renewable‑resource grant program for the same project in the same biennium
Provides a mechanism for using unspent funds to award lower‑priority projects or other eligible projects
Notifies federally recognized tribes and coordinates with other acts that provide additional funding
Sets July 1 2025 as the effective date
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

HB9.one_line: HB 9 appropriates $953,500 for 73 cultural grants, requires coal‑tax credit, and reverts unused funds to the trust.
HB9.summary: HB 9 creates a $953,500 grant program for cultural and aesthetic projects in Montana, lists specific recipients and amounts, and requires recipients to credit the coal‑tax‑funded trust. Grants must be paid by July 1 2025 and any unused funds revert to the trust in 2027. The bill also sets a $30,000 allocation for the Montana Historical Society and outlines pro‑rata cuts if the trust is short‑funded.
changes: Appropriates $953,500 from the Cultural and Aesthetic Projects Trust Fund for the Montana Arts Council to award grants for the biennium ending June 30 2027.
Specifies 73 individual grant recipients and the exact award amounts for each.
Mandates that each grant contract require the grantee to display a statement acknowledging coal‑tax support on its website and materials.
Provides a $30,000 allocation to the Montana Historical Society for Capitol complex artwork care.
Requires any unspent grant money to revert to the trust account on July 1 2027.
If the trust account is insufficient, projects receiving more than $2,000 will be reduced on a pro‑rata basis.
affected: Montana Cultural and Aesthetic Projects Trust Fund
grant recipients’ websites and promotional materials

HB99.one_line: Revises Montana motor‑vehicle statutes for clarity, consolidates definitions, and updates fees and penalties.
HB99.summary: HB 99 revises Montana’s motor‑vehicle statutes to streamline definitions, eliminate duplicate citations, and update registration, fee, and penalty provisions. The bill consolidates overlapping language, clarifies the scope of many vehicle‑type definitions, and revises the fee schedule for registration, dealer plates, and temporary permits. It also repeals a few outdated penalty sections.
changes: Rewrites the definitions section of §61‑1‑101 and related chapters to consolidate overlapping terms (e.g., motorboat, personal watercraft, sailboat, vessel).
Replaces numerous specific citations (e.g., to §61‑1‑101) with broader references and removes duplicate penalty provisions.
Updates registration‑fee schedules in §61‑3‑321, including new fee amounts for light vehicles, trailers, and special‑use vehicles.
Adds new fee and penalty amounts for temporary registration permits in §61‑3‑224 (e.g., $19.50, $24.50, $24).
Repeals §§61‑9‑513, 61‑9‑514, and 61‑9‑519, eliminating old penalty provisions for lighting, firefighter vehicle use, and tire restrictions.
Revises dealer‑plate and dealer‑reassignment rules in §§61‑4‑102, 61‑4‑104, 61‑4‑110, 61‑4‑111, 61‑4‑121, and 61‑4‑123 to clarify issuance, use, and reporting requirements.
numbers: $250 penalty for unlawful use of a boat
$1,000 fine for unlawful use of a boat
$2,000 fine for unlawful use of a boat to kill large game
$500 fine for unlawful use of a boat to kill medium game
$100 fine for unlawful use of a boat to kill small game

HB117.one_line: HB 117 funds and directs a state criminal‑justice data warehouse and requires reporting and data‑sharing agreements.
HB117.summary: HB 117 directs the Board of Crime Control to set priorities for a criminal‑justice data warehouse for 2025‑26, outlines new data‑collection projects, and authorizes $1.48 million in appropriations to support software, staff, and grants. The bill amends the law to clarify the warehouse’s purpose, ownership, and data‑sharing procedures, and requires regular reporting to the Oversight Council and legislative committees.
changes:
Establishes a 2025‑26 project plan for the criminal‑justice data warehouse, including software acquisition, data‑linking, and vendor inventory.  
Creates a $480,000 appropriation for software and a $504,243 appropriation for a project‑manager and analyst position.  
Provides a one‑time $500,000 grant to the judiciary for data contributions.  
Amends §44‑7‑126 to define the warehouse’s purpose, data ownership, and confidentiality safeguards.  
Mandates the Board to report to the Oversight Council, the Law & Justice Interim Committee, and other committees by September 15, 2026.  
Requires the Board to adopt memoranda of understanding with contributing entities and with the Department of Administration.
affected: Tribal and federal entities that may contribute data

HB210.one_line: HB 210 tightens unemployment‑insurance integrity, revises employer rates, and expands limited motor‑vehicle record disclosure.
HB210.summary: HB 210 revises Montana’s unemployment‑insurance rules to tighten program integrity, overhaul employer tax rates, and expand limited motor‑vehicle‑record disclosure. It also creates a new lower‑rate tax schedule for employers, allows penalty and interest carry‑forward, and amends several statutory sections.
changes: Amends the integrity‑data‑hub provisions (S. 39‑51‑702 & 706) to require weekly cross‑matching of unemployment rolls with new‑hire, prison, and motor‑vehicle databases and authorizes MOUs with other agencies.

Revises the employer contribution‑rate tables (S. 39‑51‑1218) to introduce a new lower‑rate schedule for eligible employers and higher rates for deficit employers, with detailed percentage tables for each rate class.

Adds penalties for false statements (S. 39‑51‑3201 & 3202) that impose disqualification, repayment, and a 50‑% or up to 100‑% penalty, and directs 70‑% of penalty proceeds to a special account for tax‑and‑benefit enforcement.

Permits limited disclosure of motor‑vehicle records (S. 61‑11‑508) to the claimant, law‑enforcement agencies, or parties with express consent, and restricts SSN release to specific federal or state purposes.
Repeals S. 39‑51‑703 and sets effective dates: most provisions take effect Oct 1 2025, while the penalty and interest carry‑forward sections become effective upon passage.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB249.one_line: HB 249 lets sellers use digital ID scans for age checks, with strict data‑handling rules.
HB249.summary: HB 249 updates Montana’s age‑verification rules to allow the use of digital driver‑license scans for alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana sales, and it amends licensing procedures for marijuana businesses.
changes: 1. Requires sellers of age‑restricted items to use only the age‑determining data from a scanned physical or digital ID, prohibits transferring that data, and mandates deletion within 180 days (amending §16‑3‑313).
2. Adds a requirement that, if a seller is unsure of a customer’s age, the seller must request a physical or digital ID that includes a photo (amending §16‑11‑305).
3. Extends the same data‑handling rules to tobacco and marijuana sellers when they scan IDs (amending §16‑11‑305).
4. Amends §16‑12‑104 to clarify licensing procedures, timelines, and data‑handling rules for marijuana licensees, including the use of digital IDs for age verification.
5. Provides that marijuana licensees may not use a scanned ID to identify customers beyond age determination, and that such data must be deleted within 180 days (amending §16‑12‑104).
affected: Retailers selling alcohol, tobacco, or marijuana

HB358.one_line: HB 358 raises volunteer firefighter pensions and adds service‑based increases up to 30 years.
HB358.summary: HB 358 raises the base monthly pension for volunteer firefighters from $175 to $200, adds a $7.50 per‑year bump for service beyond 20 years (up to 30), and allows an additional $7.50 per year after 30 years if the trust fund is sound and unfunded liabilities can be amortized in 20 years or less.
changes: 1. Full monthly pension increased to $200 for all eligible members.
2. Adds $7.50 per month for each year of active service earned after 20 years, capped at 30 years of service.

3. Provides a further $7.50 per month for each year of credited service earned after 30 years, but only if the pension trust fund is actuarially sound and unfunded liabilities can be amortized within 20 years; otherwise the benefit reverts to the 30‑year level.
4. The 30‑year‑plus benefit applies only to members who retire after July 1 2011.
5. Effective date of the changes is July 1 2025.
affected: Volunteer firefighters who are members of the Volunteer Firefighters’ Compensation Act pension plan
numbers: $7.50 monthly increase per year beyond 20 years
$7.50 monthly increase per year beyond 30 years

HB359.one_line: HB 359 shortens retirement break‑in‑service, allows limited mentoring, and sets a 2029 termination date.
HB359.summary: HB 359 revises Montana’s teachers’ retirement rules to shorten the required break‑in‑service period for retired teachers, allows them to mentor new teachers for up to 45 days, and sets a 2029 termination date for the changes.
changes: Shortens the break‑in‑service requirement from 150 days to 120 days for retirees who left after 2024
Allows retired teachers to work as substitute classroom teachers or mentors for no more than 45 days during the break‑in‑service period
Maintains that a retired teacher may continue in a position previously reported to the retirement system
Provides penalties (reinstatement to active status, repayment of benefits, and employer contributions) if a retiree works in a prohibited position
Terminates the amended provisions on June 30 2029
Effective July 1 2025
Amends Section 6 of Chapter 135 (2023) to set termination dates
Amends Section 19‑20‑734, MCA, to reflect the new break‑in‑service rules
affected: Retired teachers in Montana’s teachers’ retirement system

HB365.one_line: HB 365 bars using legislative actions as evidence of bad faith in cost/fee awards.
HB365.summary: HB 365 removes legislative conduct from consideration in bad‑faith analyses for awarding costs or attorney fees in civil actions against state entities. It amends §25‑10‑711, MCA, to prohibit using legislative actions as evidence of bad faith and makes the change retroactive to all laws passed in the 69th session.
changes: Amends §25‑10‑711, MCA, to state that legislative branch conduct in passing legislation cannot be considered in a bad‑faith analysis for costs or fees.
Adds a new subsection (2) declaring legislative conduct inadmissible for bad‑faith analysis or cost/fee awards.
Specifies that costs may be granted under subsection (1) notwithstanding any contrary provision.
Codifies the new subsection as part of Title 26, Chapter 1, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and applies retroactively to all legislation passed or approved on or after the start of the 69th legislative session.
affected: State government entities, political subdivisions, and agencies that are defendants in civil actions
Courts that award costs and attorney fees
Plaintiffs and defendants in civil actions against state entities

HB367.one_line: HB 367 amends workers’ comp to remove transportation status from coverage and tighten drug‑use limits.
HB367.summary: HB 367 clarifies when workers’ compensation covers injuries that happen while an employee is traveling for work, and it tightens the rules around alcohol, drugs, and medical‑marijuana use. The bill amends the Montana Workers’ Compensation Act to make transportation status irrelevant to coverage, adds stricter liability tests, and sets an effective date of October 1, 2025.
changes: Rewrites §39‑71‑407 to state that an employee’s coverage is not affected by whether the employer provides transportation or reimburses travel costs.
Adds a new subsection that limits coverage when an employee’s injury is caused by alcohol or non‑prescribed drugs, with a presumption if the employee refuses a post‑accident drug test.
Creates a new limitation that employees who use medically‑prescribed marijuana for a debilitating condition are not eligible for benefits if that use is the major contributing cause of the injury.
Specifies that insurers must prove an injury by objective medical findings and that the injury is more probable than not; it also defines presumptive occupational disease coverage.
Establishes rules for liability when multiple insurers are involved, requiring the most recently filed insurer to pay until another insurer is proven responsible.
Sets the effective date of the amendments as October 1, 2025, applying only to claims occurring on or after that date.
affected: Insurers under plan No. 1 or No. 2
Employees who use alcohol, drugs, or medically‑prescribed marijuana

HB368.one_line: HB 368 creates a Colstrip water‑infrastructure account and reallocates coal severance‑tax revenue.
HB368.summary: HB 368 establishes a dedicated water‑infrastructure mitigation account for the town of Colstrip and requires coal‑fired power plants to fund it. It also revises how coal severance‑tax revenue is allocated, adding a $2 million credit to the new account and detailing other distribution percentages.
changes: Creates a Colstrip water‑infrastructure mitigation account within the state special revenue fund and mandates $2 million from coal severance taxes be deposited there each fiscal year.
Revises Section 15‑35‑108 to specify new percentages for coal severance‑tax allocations to various state funds and programs.
Adds a $250,000 annual credit to the coal and uranium mine permitting and reclamation program account.
Outlines a $2 million credit to the Colstrip account after other allocations.
Requires the department to review the Colstrip account every 10 years and report to the Economic Affairs Interim Committee.
Clarifies financial assurance requirements for coal‑fired units to provide perpetual water access to an attendant city or town.
Amends definitions and other sections (75‑8‑103, 75‑10‑721) related to water access (details omitted).
affected: Various state agencies receiving severance‑tax allocations
numbers: 50% of coal severance taxes to trust fund
12% to major repair long‑range building program

HB372.one_line: HB 372 raises hunting license fees, caps non‑resident combo licenses, and adds resident‑sponsor rules for certain licenses.
HB372.summary: HB 372 revises the fees for several upland‑game and big‑game hunting licenses and updates how the revenue is used for the upland game‑bird enhancement program. The bill also changes the sale schedule and limits for non‑resident combination licenses and adds a resident‑sponsor requirement for some licenses.
changes: Replaces current fee amounts for Class A‑1, B‑1, B‑2, AAA, and B‑10 licenses with new dollar values (e.g., Class A‑1 $2 → $4.50, Class B‑1 $23 → $40).
Adjusts the fee for Class B‑11 (non‑resident deer combination) from $577 → $760 and sets a cap of 4,600 licenses per year.
Imposes a 28.5 % deposit of the Class B‑10 and B‑11 fees into the account established in §87‑1‑290.
Limits Class B‑10 sales to 17,000 per year and requires annual CPI‑U‑based price adjustments for B‑10 and B‑11 licenses.
Introduces a resident‑sponsor program for Class B‑10 and B‑11 licenses, reserving 2,000 B‑11 licenses for applicants with a sponsor who owns ≥640 contiguous acres, and requires sponsor certification.
Changes the sale date of Class B‑10 and B‑11 licenses to April 1 and adds drawing procedures for unreserved licenses.
affected: Non‑resident hunters purchasing Class B‑1, B‑2, B‑10, B‑11, and B‑7 licenses
Resident hunters buying Class A‑1 and AAA licenses
Landowners who may sponsor non‑resident hunters
Fish, Wildlife, and Parks Office staff handling license sales
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks budget and revenue accounting

HB380.one_line: Aligns Montana elector meeting date with federal law, effective immediately.
HB380.summary: The bill changes the date on which Montana’s presidential electors meet so that it matches the federal requirement. It amends the state law to set the meeting for the first Monday or Tuesday after the second Wednesday in December, and it takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends Section 13‑25‑307, MCA, to change the meeting date for electors to the first Monday or Tuesday after the second Wednesday in December.
Specifies that the meeting will occur in Helena at 2 p.m. on that date.
Leaves all other procedures for ballot handling and acceptance unchanged.
Provides that the act is effective on passage and approval.
No new program, office, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Montana voters (indirectly, through the electoral process)
numbers: first Monday or Tuesday after the second Wednesday in December

HB381.one_line: High‑school students can earn elective credit for 250‑hour care‑facility work, capped at two credits.
HB381.summary: High‑school students in 11th or 12th grade can earn up to two elective credits by working 250 hours at approved care facilities. Schools must vet applications, verify hours, and set work‑type conditions. The program applies to both public and non‑public schools.
changes: Allows 11th‑ and 12th‑grade students to earn elective high‑school credit for paid or voluntary work in congregate‑care, child‑care, or school‑age programs.
Students must submit a written application detailing employer, supervisor, job description, and hours worked.
Schools set deadlines, verify hours, and may impose work‑type requirements before approving credit.
Credit is capped at two elective credits (500 hours total).
Schools may not award credit unless the application is approved and all requirements are met.
Definitions clarify the types of facilities that qualify.
The act is codified in Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 3.
Effective July 1, 2025.

HB384.one_line: Allows assistants who worked before July 15 2025 to qualify for licensure retroactively.
HB384.summary: HB 384 changes the eligibility rules for speech‑language pathology and audiology assistants, allowing those who have worked as unlicensed assistants before July 15 2025 to qualify for licensure retroactively. The act amends the statutory qualifications and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: Amends §37‑15‑303 to add a new subsection for assistant licensure.
Requires assistants to have either completed the academic requirements or to have worked as an unlicensed assistant before July 15 2025.
Mandates the board to rule on evidence and equivalency conditions for prior experience.
Makes assistant licensure retroactive to the date the equivalency requirements were satisfied.
Sets the act’s effective date to the day it is passed and approved.
affected: Board of Speech‑Language Pathology and Audiology

HB387.one_line: HB 387 revises highway filing requirements and limits compensation for new structures after filing.
HB387.summary: HB 387 amends the required filing documents for new or reconstructed highways, clarifying what must appear in a right‑of‑way plan and limiting compensation for buildings erected after filing. The changes take effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Adds detailed description requirements to Section 60‑2‑209, including centerline, width, boundary lines, owner name, parcel number, and project number for each right‑of‑way parcel.
Specifies that no compensation may be paid for buildings or improvements erected after the plan is filed (Section 60‑4‑108(1)).
Imposes a one‑year deadline after filing for condemnation or acquisition actions to be commenced, otherwise the plan becomes ineffective (Section 60‑4‑108(2)).
Excludes crops or similar improvements from the new compensation rules; those remain governed by Section 70‑30‑302 (Section 60‑4‑108(3)).
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1, 2025.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
No significant fiscal impact is specified in the bill text.
affected: Property owners along new or reconstructed highways
Builders of new structures on right‑of‑way land

HB388.one_line: Prohibits state or local regulation of pregnancy centers that do not provide abortion or contraception services.
HB388.summary: HB 388 bars state or local governments from regulating pregnancy centers on the basis that they do not provide or promote abortion or contraception. It creates civil remedies for violations and allows legislators to intervene in constitutional challenges.
changes: Prohibits any law, rule, or policy that would require a pregnancy center to offer, perform, or refer abortions, abortion‑inducing drugs, or contraception, or to counsel in favor of those services.
Prohibits any law that would prevent a pregnancy center from providing pregnancy‑related services because it does not offer or promote abortion or contraception.
Prevents interference with a center’s hiring or staffing decisions based on staff’s alignment with the center’s pro‑life mission.
Provides civil damages of at least $50,000 (or actual damages if higher) plus attorney fees, with treble damages for malice.
Allows the legislature to appoint sponsoring members to intervene in lawsuits challenging the act’s constitutionality.
Mandates codification of the act as a new part of Title 50, chapter 4 of the Montana Code.
Includes severability and immediate effect upon passage.
affected: Employees and staff of pregnancy centers
Individuals who may be sued for violating the act

HB391.one_line: HB 391 lets licensees pay concessionaires a percentage of sales and sets limits, fees, and approval rules.
HB391.summary: HB 391 amends Montana’s alcohol‑concession rules to allow licensees to pay concessionaires a percentage of gross or net sales, employee overhead, or a fixed fee. It sets limits on the number of agreements, requires department approval for changes, and imposes application and renewal fees.
changes: Limits each license to three concurrent concession agreements.
Requires the licensed premises to be contiguous and gives the licensee ultimate control over sales, discipline, reconciliation, and termination of the agreement.
Permits compensation of the concessionaire by (i) a percentage of gross or net sales, (ii) a percentage of employee overhead, or (iii) a negotiated fixed dollar amount.

Allows the licensee to change the compensation structure without department denial, provided the new arrangement is submitted; other modifications (e.g., ownership changes) must be approved within 30 business days.
Creates a standardized concession agreement form and requires a $500 application fee for new agreements and a $100 annual renewal fee.
Defines “contiguous premises” to include interior continuous areas, multiple floors, and shared common areas such as hallways and elevators.

HB392.one_line: HB 392 mandates trust contributions, deletion rights, and damages for minors in monetized family videos.
HB392.summary: HB 392 creates a trust‑based system that requires family‑content creators who earn money from videos featuring their children to set aside a percentage of those earnings for the child. It also gives minors a right to have such videos removed once they turn 18 and a private right of action for damages. The bill imposes record‑keeping and reporting duties on creators and defines the thresholds that trigger the trust contributions.
changes: Establishes a trust contribution for any content creator who earns ≥$0.10 per view or meets the view‑threshold of the platform, and whose videos feature a minor in ≥30% of the content for ≥30 days.
Sets the contribution rate at 10 % of gross earnings if the minor appears 30‑49 % of the time, 25 % if 50‑74 %, and 50 % if ≥75 %.
Allows a minor who turns 18 to request permanent deletion of any video segment that includes their likeness, name, or photograph from any platform that paid the parent for that content.
Provides a private right of action for the minor, including injunctive relief, damages of at least $1,500 or actual damages, and recovery of profits attributable to the violation.
Requires content creators to keep annual records of the child’s age, video counts, minutes featured, compensation, and trust deposits, and to provide these records to the child upon request.
Mandates that contracts with platforms include notification of the child’s future rights under the act.
affected: Family‑content creators (parents or guardians) who produce monetized videos featuring their children
Minor children who appear in such videos
Online platforms and networks that host or monetize the videos
Lawyers and courts handling private right‑of‑action claims

HB393.one_line: Mandates audio/video recording of most town and county meetings, with online posting within set deadlines.
HB393.summary: HB 393 requires most Montana town and county boards to record public meetings in audio (and video for many boards) and post the recordings online within a set time—1–5 business days for larger boards, 14 for smaller ones. The bill amends the state’s recording statute, adds new posting deadlines, and allows certain boards to use audio only.
changes: Amends §2‑3‑214 to add new boards that must record meetings in audio/video.
Sets posting deadlines: 1 business day for boards (a)–(e), 5 business days for boards (f)–(i) and 14 business days for boards in subsection (7).
Allows boards that lack a website to use a social‑media page for links.
Clarifies that recordings are not the official record unless designated, and may be destroyed after one year if not official.
Provides that a board need not reschedule if a recording fails, but must post a notice explaining the failure.
Exempts certain small boards from video recording, allowing audio only.
Defines that school‑district expenditures for compliance qualify as a facility project under §20‑9‑525.
affected: First‑ and second‑class city governing boards
First‑ and second‑class school district boards
Boards of investments, public education, higher education

HB394.one_line: HB 394 tightens notice, hearing, and assessment rules for Montana local governments.
HB394.summary: HB 394 revises Montana’s local‑government notice, hearing, and assessment rules, tightening publication deadlines, clarifying assessment procedures, and adding new requirements for public hearings on growth, annexation, zoning, and subdivision matters.
changes: Municipal notice publication deadlines are shortened and clarified, with specific requirements for newspaper and website posting, and a new 6‑day separation rule for second notices.
The timing of budget hearings, maintenance‑assessment resolutions, and subdivision‑approval hearings is re‑sized, adding new deadlines and notice periods.
New public‑hearing requirements are added for growth‑policy proposals, annexations, interim zoning ordinances, and certain subdivision applications.
The bill expands the scope of property‑assessment rules for maintenance districts, requiring a 75% levy and annual estimation of costs.
It adds a new property‑tax exemption for affordable‑housing units that meet federal and state criteria.
The bill amends several sections to align notice and hearing timelines with existing statutory schedules.
It requires municipalities to publish interim‑zoning ordinances only after a public hearing and limits their duration to one year.
It adds detailed application requirements for “four‑or‑more‑building” developments on a single tract.
affected: Municipalities, county commissions, town councils, property owners, residents, utility customers, developers, and affordable‑housing operators

HB397.one_line: HB 397 expands Montana’s privacy law to cover mental‑health apps and websites.
HB397.summary: HB 397 extends Montana’s existing health‑privacy laws to cover mobile apps and websites that provide mental‑health or substance‑use services, requiring them to follow the same confidentiality rules as traditional providers and giving patients remedies if those rules are broken.
changes: 1. Defines a "mental health digital service" as a mobile app or internet website that collects, uses, or accesses mental‑health or substance‑use information, markets itself as a mental‑health service, and uses that information to provide diagnosis, treatment, or therapy.
2. Requires such services to be subject to the disclosure and confidentiality provisions of Title 50, Chapter 16, Part 5 when handling health‑care information.
3. Makes violations of those provisions enforceable under the same penalties and remedies as other health‑care privacy violations (Sections 50‑16‑552 and 50‑16‑553).
4. Codifies the new definition and requirements as an integral part of Title 50, Chapter 16, Part 5.
5. No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created; the bill merely expands existing statutes.
affected: Mental‑health digital service providers (apps and websites)

HB396.one_line: Revises bail law to require judge appearance, risk tools, and detailed bail‑amount criteria.
HB396.summary: HB 396 revises Montana’s bail statutes to require a judge’s appearance before bail, expand the use of risk‑assessment tools, and set detailed criteria for bail amounts. It clarifies how interstate compacts apply and emphasizes factors such as community ties, financial ability, and danger to the public. The bill does not create new programs or criminal offenses.
changes: Mandates that a person cannot be granted bail without first appearing before the judge who issued the warrant, or another judge if unavailable.
Allows courts to use validated pre‑trial risk‑assessment tools when deciding release or detention.
Expands the list of factors courts must consider, including the nature of the offense, defendant’s history, community ties, financial resources, and potential danger.
Sets a comprehensive set of criteria for determining bail amount, requiring it to be reasonable, sufficient, non‑oppressive, and commensurate with the offense and defendant’s circumstances.
Requires that bail be sufficient to ensure appearance, compliance with conditions, and protection of persons from bodily injury.
affected: Law enforcement agencies handling interstate transfers

HB399.one_line: HB 399 removes prior‑authorization for many generics, inhalers, and insulin, requiring insurers to list alternatives on denial.
HB399.summary: HB 399 removes prior‑authorization requirements for a wide range of generic and inhaled drugs, including asthma/COPD inhalers and insulin, and requires insurers to list therapeutic alternatives when denying coverage. It also limits prior‑authorization for certain specialty drugs and mandates physician review for adverse decisions.
changes: Prohibits prior authorization for any generic prescription drug not listed in specific subsections after 6 months of continuous use
Exempts all inhaled prescription drugs used for asthma, COPD, or chronic lung disease from prior authorization
Exempts all insulin products for diabetes from prior authorization
Exempts long‑acting injectable antipsychotics from prior authorization
Exempts formulary oral or inhaled non‑biologic generics that are not specialty tier or controlled substances from prior authorization
Requires a physician with relevant specialty to make any adverse determination
Mandates insurers to provide a written notice with a list of reasonable therapeutic alternatives when denying a drug
Amends MCA §33‑32‑221 to incorporate these exclusions and requirements
affected: Patients using generic, inhaled, or insulin drugs

HB398.one_line: HB 398 extends chronic‑condition authorizations to 12 months and tightens who may make adverse determinations.
HB398.summary: HB 398 revises Montana’s utilization‑review rules to strengthen continuity of care when people change plans, tighten who may make adverse determinations, and extend the validity of chronic‑condition authorizations. It also updates definitions and codifies the changes into the state’s insurance statutes.
changes: Health‑plan changes trigger automatic honoring of prior certifications for the first 3 months, with the new plan’s utilization‑review organization allowed to conduct its own review during that period.

Only physicians (or a licensed professional in the same specialty, or a physician in any case) may make or review adverse determinations; they must hold a current, non‑restricted license and have relevant clinical experience or refer to a qualified physician.
All grievance reviews must be conducted by a physician with a non‑restricted license and a specialty related to the condition in question.
Adverse determinations must be overseen by a medical director of the utilization‑review organization, who must be a licensed physician.
The definition of “adverse determination” is expanded to include denials, reductions, terminations, and eligibility‑based refusals.
Prior‑authorization (certification) for chronic‑condition services is now valid for 12 months (vs. 6 months for other services).
The act amends §33‑32‑102 to clarify definitions of adverse determination, certification, chronic condition, etc.
The act amends §33‑32‑107 to set the new 12‑month validity for chronic‑condition authorizations and to specify the 3‑6‑month minimum for other services.
affected: Physicians and other licensed health‑care professionals

HB400.one_line: HB 400 bars disciplining students or employees for refusing to use pronouns or names that match another person’s legal sex.
HB400.summary: HB 400, the Free to Speak Act, bars public schools and the state from disciplining or otherwise penalizing a student or employee who refuses to identify pronouns or use a name or pronoun that matches another person’s legal sex. It creates a private civil remedy for violations.
changes: Prohibits disciplinary or adverse employment actions for refusing to identify pronouns or use a name/pronoun inconsistent with another person’s legal sex.
Extends the prohibition to all public schools, charter schools, and public institutions of higher education.
Allows victims to sue for injunctive relief, damages, attorney fees, and costs within two years of the violation.
Codifies the provisions as part of Title 49, chapter 1, part 1.
Includes severability language and immediate effect upon passage.
affected: Employees of public schools, charter schools, and public higher‑education institutions

HB401.one_line: HB 401 bans cell‑cultured meat sales in Montana, imposes misdemeanors, and authorizes enforcement rules.
HB401.summary: HB 401 bars the manufacture, sale, holding, or distribution of cell‑cultured edible products in Montana and sets penalties for violators. It also amends food‑labeling and meat‑definition statutes to clarify that such products are not considered meat or misbranded if labeled correctly.
changes: Prohibits manufacturing, selling, holding, offering for sale, or distributing cell‑cultured edible products in Montana.
Empowers the Department of Public Health and Human Services to adopt rules to enforce the ban.
Defines “cell‑cultured edible product” and “retail food establishment” per existing statutes.
Makes violating the ban a misdemeanor and allows disciplinary action against retail food establishments that violate it.
Allows suspension of business licenses for owners or employees found guilty of a violation.
Adds an immediate stop‑sale order for products found in violation.
Amends the definitions in 50‑31‑103, 50‑31‑203, 50‑31‑501, and 81‑9‑217 to reflect the new prohibition and labeling requirements.
Requires that cell‑cultured products be labeled as derived from muscle, fat, connective tissue, blood, or other meat components if sold.
Clarifies that such products are not considered meat or misbranded if labeled per the new definition.
affected: Retail food establishments (restaurants, grocery stores, etc.)
Owners and employees of affected businesses
Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB403.one_line: Legislators must have unrestricted, immediate access to the Montana State Hospital, respecting patient privacy.
HB403.summary: HB 403 requires every Montana legislator to have unrestricted, immediate access to the Montana State Hospital at all times, subject only to routine security checks, and obliges legislators to respect patient privacy and welfare while there. The bill also directs that this provision be codified into the existing state hospital statutes.
changes: Mandates unlimited, immediate access for all state legislators to the Montana State Hospital at any time.
Access is subject only to the facility’s routine security and safety procedures.
Legislators must prioritize patient health, dignity, privacy, and welfare while on site.
The new access requirement is to be codified as part of Title 53, Chapter 21, Part 6 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Patients at the Montana State Hospital

HB409.one_line: HB 409 mandates courts use only federal criteria for preliminary injunctions, banning sliding‑scale tests.
HB409.summary: HB 409 amends Montana’s preliminary‑injunction statute to require courts to apply only the four federal Supreme Court criteria and expressly forbid the use of sliding‑scale or “serious questions” tests. The law takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §27‑19‑201, MCA to restate the four federal criteria for preliminary injunctions and temporary restraining orders.
Adds a prohibition that courts may not use sliding‑scale, serious‑questions, flexible‑interplay, or other circuit‑based tests when evaluating such applications.
Clarifies that the applicant bears the burden of demonstrating the need for an injunction.
Specifies that the statute applies to cases between private persons and excludes actions involving a person sued in an official capacity.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: Courts and litigants seeking preliminary injunctions or temporary restraining orders in Montana.
Legal practitioners advising clients on injunction applications.

HB406.one_line: HB 406 tightens school‑district election filing and certification deadlines to align with local elections.
HB406.summary: HB 406 revises Montana’s school‑district election deadlines, tightening filing windows for write‑in and trustee candidates and aligning certain school‑election dates with local government elections held on the same day. It also updates the timing for calling, certifying, and conducting school elections.
changes: Extends the write‑in declaration deadline to 5 p.m. on the 10th day before the earliest ballot‑availability date, and allows a late filing only if the original candidate dies or is feloniously charged.

Sets a 40‑day minimum and 85‑day maximum filing window for trustee candidates, and requires write‑in trustee declarations no later than 5 p.m. on the 65th day before the ballot‑certification deadline.

Mandates that school elections be called by resolution at least 70 days (or 145 days for regular elections) in advance, with the resolution transmitted to the county election administrator within 3 days.
Requires the clerk to certify ballots no less than 30 days (or 37/40 days) before the election, and to print absentee ballots at least 20 days prior.
Aligns the deadlines for school elections with local‑government elections held on the same day, ensuring consistency across election types.
affected: Voters in school and local elections

HB411.one_line: Exempts agricultural and forest land from open‑space tax levies, effective 2026.
HB411.summary: HB 411 removes agricultural land, its improvements, and forest land from the property‑tax base that funds open‑space levies and bonds. The exemption applies to all open‑space levies and bonds, effective for property‑tax years beginning January 1, 2026, and does not alter the overall structure of the open‑space program. The bill merely amends the tax‑exemption language in the Montana Code.
changes: Amends Section 76‑6‑109 to state that property taxes used to pay open‑space levies and bonds may not be levied on agricultural land, forest land, agricultural improvements, non‑commercial forest improvements, or agricultural implements and equipment.
affected: Owners of agricultural implements and equipment

HB413.one_line: Revises Montana residency rules for voting, excluding temporary military and work stays.
HB413.summary: HB 413 amends Montana’s residency rules for voting and candidacy, clarifying that temporary stays—such as military duty, work, training, or education—do not create or change a voter’s residence. It preserves a person’s existing residence unless they intend to permanently relocate elsewhere, and it removes the ability to gain residency by being stationed on a military reservation or transient camp. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑1‑112 to specify that a person’s residence is where they habitually live and intend to return to when absent.
Prohibits gaining or losing residency while involuntarily confined, imprisoned, or stationed on a military reservation or transient U.S. camp.
Clarifies that a reserve component member stationed outside Montana retains resident status if no intent to change residency.
States that temporary travel to another state or district does not lose residence unless the person votes there.
Precludes gaining residency in Montana by temporary relocation for work, training, or education without intent to make it permanent.
Defines that a person’s family residence is presumed to be their residence, but a different primary residence with intent to remain counts as the true residence.
Requires a change of residence to be effected by removal of the old residence and intent to remain elsewhere.
affected: Temporary workers, trainees, and students in Montana

HB414.one_line: HB 414 revises Montana’s licensing laws, standardizes provisional licenses, and creates screening panels for non‑routine applications.
HB414.summary: HB 414 updates Montana’s professional‑licensing rules, standardizes provisional‑license procedures, creates screening panels for non‑routine applications, and amends many existing statutes. It also repeals several temporary‑license provisions.
changes: Creates a new screening panel that reviews all non‑routine licensing applications and can grant, deny, or restrict licenses within 45 days
Standardizes provisional‑license rules for all boards, including time limits, conditions, and automatic inactivation if conditions are unmet
Rewrites and consolidates numerous licensing statutes (e.g., 37‑1‑131, 37‑1‑307, 37‑14‑305, 37‑27‑201, etc.) to clarify terminology and remove redundancies
Replaces temporary‑practice‑permit provisions (37‑1‑305, 37‑73‑208, 37‑73‑216) with new rules for provisional and temporary licenses
Adds detailed requirements for temporary practice permits in nursing, midwifery, and other professions, including supervision and expiration dates
Introduces new fee and penalty provisions for trust‑account compliance (e.g., §37‑51‑324, §37‑56‑106)
Sets specific eligibility, examination, and supervision rules for a wide range of professions (e.g., psychologists, genetic counselors, electricians, plumbers, elevator mechanics, etc.)
Provides for temporary registration of out‑of‑state appraisers and private‑security licensees with fingerprinting and background‑check requirements
affected: Licensed professionals seeking provisional or temporary licenses
Department of Labor and Industry staff
numbers: 21 days for out‑of‑state practitioners to practice without licensure

HB415.one_line: Limits bail for defendants with out‑of‑state warrants and clarifies judge authority.
HB415.summary: HB 415 limits a judge’s ability to grant bail to defendants who are on a warrant from another jurisdiction, requires bail to be continued when a defendant is bound over, allows appellate judges to admit defendants to bail, and confirms that a defendant’s appearance can be in person or via two‑way audio‑video.
changes: A judge may admit a defendant to bail only if the defendant is not on a warrant from another jurisdiction.
If a defendant is bound over to a court or judge that has jurisdiction over the offense, bail must be continued, though that court may adjust the amount.
On appeal, a judge who heard the trial or who can issue a writ of habeas corpus may admit the defendant to bail.
A defendant’s appearance before a judge may be either physical or via two‑way audio‑video communication.
affected: Defendants on warrants from other jurisdictions

HB416.one_line: HOAs must get owners’ permission before entering a property, with owners able to require presence of owner or agent.
HB416.summary: HB 416 requires homeowners’ associations (HOAs) to obtain owners’ permission before an HOA agent can enter a property, and owners may insist the owner or an agent be present. It preserves existing public‑access rights and excludes condominiums, easements, and common‑element access already covered by covenants.
changes: 1. HOA agents must seek owners’ consent before entering any unit.
2. HOA must propose a convenient date/time and specify the area to be accessed.
3. Owners may require the owner or an agent to be present during entry.
4. Public‑access areas (sidewalks, front pathways, front doors) remain exempt from this requirement.
5. The rule does not apply to condominiums with unit‑access rules, or to recorded easements benefiting the HOA.
6. The act is codified under Title 70, Chapter 16, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.

HB419.one_line: Mandates cost reporting from selected Medicaid providers to assess rate adequacy and funds the effort.
HB419.summary: HB 419 requires Montana’s Medicaid program to collect standardized cost reports from certain service providers and use the data to assess rate adequacy. The bill creates a reporting framework, authorizes rulemaking, and funds the effort with $1.2 million in state and federal money.
changes: Establishes a standardized cost‑reporting format for adult mental health, children’s mental health, substance‑use disorder, developmental disabilities, and senior/long‑term‑care services funded through Medicaid or related sources.
Mandates that identified Medicaid service providers submit actual revenue and expenditure data for their most recent fiscal year and cooperate with audits.
Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to compile a report on rate adequacy at least every four years, drawing on cost reports, claims, and national data.
Authorizes the department to adopt rules governing what costs to report, the report format, and filing deadlines.
Amends Section 53‑6‑402 to clarify the department’s authority to administer home‑and‑community‑based services waivers and related financial participation requirements.
Repeals Section 53‑6‑406, which previously required a legislative report on fiscal accountability for home‑and‑community‑based services.
Appropriates $600,000 from the general fund and $600,000 in federal special revenue for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to develop the cost‑reporting system.
affected: Medicaid service providers in the five specified service categories
Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: data collection every 4 years but not more than once every 2 years

HB421.one_line: HB 421 raises DNRC fire‑protection assessment fees for forest land owners.
HB421.summary: HB 421 raises the per‑owner and per‑acre fire‑protection assessment fees that the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) collects from owners of forest land in wildland fire protection districts. The new rates take effect July 1 2025.
changes: Increases the base fee for each landowner in a protection district from $50 to $58.70.
Raises the additional fee for acreage over 20 acres from 30 cents to 49 cents per acre per year.
Leaves the overall assessment, payment, and collection procedures unchanged.
Maintains the prohibition on other charges except for proved negligence or violations of 50‑63‑103.
Applies only to land classified as forest land within a wildland fire protection district or under contract with a recognized agency.
Effective July 1 2025.
affected: Landowners of forest land in wildland fire protection districts

HB423.one_line: HB 423 updates voter‑registration rules to improve address verification and inactive‑list procedures.
HB423.summary: HB 423 amends Montana’s voter‑registration rules to require the Secretary of State to adopt procedures that annually compare the voter list with national address‑change files, mail confirmation notices, and, if necessary, move non‑responding voters to the inactive list. The act also mandates that these procedures be finished at least 90 days before a primary or general election and gives the Secretary of State authority to adopt additional rules for provisional registrants.
changes: Amends §13‑2‑220 to require at least one of several address‑verification procedures each year, including comparison with national change‑of‑address files and mailing confirmation notices to all registered voters;
Adds a requirement that any notices returned undeliverable or unanswered be followed within 30 days by a forwardable confirmation notice;

Mandates that voters who fail to respond within 30 days after the final notice be moved to the inactive list and that the election administrator work with the Secretary of State and the motor‑vehicle division to verify the address;
Specifies that the address‑verification procedure must be completed at least 90 days before a primary or general election;
Provides that the Secretary of State may adopt rules to maintain applicants, including removing provisionally registered electors;
Leaves reactivation and cancellation of registration to existing §§13‑2‑222 and 13‑2‑402.

HB424.one_line: HB 424 changes data‑center tax rules, limits power sales, and updates tax‑increment and property‑tax provisions.
HB424.summary: HB 424 revises how data‑center property is taxed, extends the construction window, changes ownership rules, and sets limits on power sales. It also amends tax‑increment and property‑tax provisions and applies retroactively to 2025 tax years.
changes: Reclassifies qualified data‑center property as class 17 and sets a 0.9 % tax rate on it.
Extends the construction period for qualifying data centers to 48 months after Jan 1 2019 (or 2 years for larger projects).
Adds ownership requirements: a single‑entity owner (parent or wholly‑owned subsidiary) must hold 100 % ownership of contiguous parcels.
Limits the price at which a data‑center generator can sell power to a public utility or cooperative to the cost of production.
Amends tax‑increment rules so that school equalization mills must be paid on class 17 property in districts that use tax‑increment financing.
Adjusts definitions and exclusions in sections 7‑15‑4286, 15‑6‑156, and 15‑6‑162 to reflect the new class 17 rules.
Provides an immediate effective date and retroactive applicability to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2024.
affected: Local school districts in tax‑increment districts
numbers: 300,000 sq ft or 25,000 sq ft thresholds
Retroactive to tax years after Dec 31 2024

HB426.one_line: HB 426 tightens ownership rules for Montana appraisal‑management firms and adds background‑check requirements.
HB426.summary: HB 426 amends Montana’s appraisal‑management registration rules to tighten ownership restrictions and add background‑check requirements, clarifying what constitutes a substantive cause for revoking an appraiser’s license.
changes: Amends §37‑54‑503 to prohibit ownership of an appraisal‑management company by anyone whose appraiser license has been refused, denied, canceled, revoked for substantive cause, or surrendered in lieu of revocation in any state, unless the license was later reinstated or granted.
Adds a similar prohibition for ownership by an entity whose owner meets the same disqualifying criteria.
Requires each owner of an appraisal‑management company to be of good moral character as determined by the board and to submit to a background examination.

Mandates that each applicant certify that no direct or indirect owner has ever had an appraiser or appraisal‑management license refused, denied, canceled, revoked, or surrendered in lieu of revocation in any state.
affected: Applicants for registration of appraisal‑management companies
The Montana Board of Appraisal Registration

HB427.one_line: HB 427 forces building agencies to disclose code sections used to delay permits and imposes daily penalties for non‑compliance.
HB427.summary: HB 427 requires the Department of Labor and Industry or a local building department to disclose the exact building‑code sections that are being used to delay or halt a permit or construction project. If the agency fails to provide the requested text within seven days, it must pay $50 per day until it does, and the aggrieved party may sue for damages.
changes: 1. Mandates that the department or local building department provide the specific building‑code text or citation that is being relied upon to delay a permit or stop construction within seven calendar business days.
2. If the agency fails to comply within that period, it waives the application of those code sections to the project and must pay $50 for each day of non‑compliance.
3. Grants the applicant or contractor the right to file a civil action in district court for compensatory damages and court costs/attorney fees.
4. Allows the agency to require zoning, subdivision, or other approvals before deeming a building application complete.
5. Codifies the new requirement into Title 50, Chapter 60, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.

HB428.one_line: HB 428 expands employer definition, creates an admin fund, adds insurer reporting and a new medical‑status form.
HB428.summary: HB 428 revises Montana’s workers’ compensation rules, expanding who is considered an employer, tightening insurer reporting, and adding a new medical‑status form. It also creates a workers’‑compensation administration fund that will collect fees and assessments to pay for program administration and reimburse certain premiums.
changes: Redefines “employer” to include a wide range of public entities, private corporations, and certain religious and nonprofit entities for workers’‑compensation purposes.
Creates a workers’‑compensation administration fund and authorizes the department to collect fees, penalties, and assessments from insurers and employers to cover administrative costs.
Imposes a 4 % assessment on plan No. 1 employers and a 4 % premium‑surcharge on plan No. 2 and plan No. 3 insurers, with payment deadlines and penalties for non‑payment.
Mandates insurers to file quarterly summary reports of benefits, medical expenditures, and miscellaneous expenses, and imposes a $250–$1,000 penalty for late filing.
Introduces a new medical‑status form that insurers must provide to health‑care providers and complete after each office visit, detailing diagnosis, treatment plan, and work‑restriction information.
affected: Employers (plan No. 1, 2, 3), insurers, workers, health‑care providers

HB430.one_line: Repeals Montana law authorizing county‑owned public weighing scales and related regulations.
HB430.summary: The bill removes the statutory framework that allows counties to establish, own, and operate public weighing scales, along with related rules on design, appointment, bonding, record‑keeping, fees, and misconduct. It effectively eliminates the legal authority for county‑owned scales in Montana.
changes: Repeals §7‑21‑3101: Establishment of public scales
Repeals §7‑21‑3102: Ownership of public scales
Repeals §7‑21‑3103: Capacity and design of public scales
Repeals §7‑21‑3104: Appointment of public weigher
Repeals §7‑21‑3105: Bond of public weigher
Repeals §7‑21‑3106: Record of weighing
Repeals §7‑21‑3107: Fee for weighing
Repeals §7‑21‑3108: Misconduct by public weigher
affected: Businesses and individuals who use county‑owned scales

HB431.one_line: HB 431 lets the House Speaker appoint a Judicial Standards Commissioner via a House‑appointed nomination panel.
HB431.summary: HB 431 amends the legislative nomination panel rules for the Judicial Standards Commission, allowing the Speaker of the House to appoint a replacement when a vacancy is expected. The changes establish a panel of House members that recommends candidates to the Speaker, who then selects a commissioner. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §3‑1‑1115 to create a legislative nomination panel of three House members, including at least one from the minority party; the Speaker appoints the panel at the start of each regular session.
The panel must forward no fewer than three qualified district‑court judges to the Speaker when a vacancy is anticipated on the Judicial Standards Commission.
The Speaker selects a commissioner from the panel’s list of candidates.
Panel members serve until the first regular session after appointment, unless reappointed.
The panel may meet between sessions to fill vacancies.
The act is effective immediately upon passage.
affected: House of Representatives members (as panel members)
Speaker of the House (as appointing authority)

HB112.one_line: HB 112 amends many statutes, adds a tax rebate, and clarifies administrative reporting.
HB112.summary: HB 112 amends a wide range of Montana statutes to correct references, update reporting requirements, and clarify existing provisions. It largely focuses on administrative, reporting, and procedural matters, with no new programs or criminal offenses created.
changes: Directs the Code Commissioner to correct erroneous references to 5‑11‑210 in new legislation and to add or remove the corresponding reports in 5‑11‑222
Adds a one‑time income‑tax rebate for 2021 taxpayers (up to $2,500) and clarifies eligibility
Revises the small‑business computer‑equipment deduction to limit it to 30% of net income and to 5‑year‑old equipment
Creates a catering endorsement for beer/wine licensees, with a $200 fee and specific conditions
Defines a new “spousal privilege” for electronic communications
Revises the Montana Medicaid program to clarify covered services and reporting requirements
Amends the meat‑establishment licensing fee structure and penalties
Amends the equine‑slaughter injunction rule to allow damages for delay
Adds new definitions for garbage, garbage feeder, and person in the garbage‑feeding statute
affected: state agencies, the Secretary of State, the Department of Administration, the Department of Revenue, small‑business corporations, beer and wine licensees, spouses, Medicaid beneficiaries, meat‑establishment operators, equine‑slaughter facilities, and the general public

HB432.one_line: HB 432 streamlines certain water‑right changes while tightening notice and review procedures.
HB432.summary: HB 432 amends Montana water‑right law to allow certain changes in appropriation—such as redundant wells, replacement wells, replacement points of diversion, and municipal use changes—without prior department approval, provided specific conditions are met and a notice is filed. It also expands the department’s authority to review, approve, or deny such changes and clarifies the role of water judges and temporary change procedures.
changes: Allows redundant water‑supply wells in public water systems to be constructed without department approval if they use the same aquifer and are required by a state or federal agency, with a 60‑day notice required.

Permits replacement wells to be built without prior approval if the new well draws from the same aquifer, replaces an existing well, and meets flow‑rate limits; a notice must be filed within 60 days of completion.

Enables replacement points of diversion without approval when the existing diversion is inoperable, capacity is unchanged, and the new point is on the same surface source; a notice must be filed within 60 days.

Allows municipalities and county water districts to change the place of use for unperfected permits or water reservations without approval, provided flow/volume limits are not exceeded and the new location is within approved municipal or county boundaries; a notice must be filed within 180 days of annexation or addition.
Provides stock‑tank changes (add, move, remove) without approval if flow and animal‑unit limits are respected and a 60‑day notice is filed.
Adds detailed notice, review, objection, and public‑notice procedures for all these changes, including timelines (60‑day notice, 90‑day review, 45‑day objection period).
Expands the department’s ability to issue temporary change authorizations and to renew, modify, or revoke them, and clarifies the role of water judges in certifying disputes.
Amends sections 3‑7‑224, 85‑2‑309, 85‑2‑402, and 85‑2‑407 to reflect the new authority and procedural requirements.
affected: Appropriators of groundwater and surface‑water rights
Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Water judges and the Montana Supreme Court
Water‑right holders who may object to changes

HB434.one_line: Clarifies that interactive teller machines are not branch banks when off‑premises and updates related definitions.
HB434.summary: HB 434 amends Montana banking definitions to clarify that an interactive teller machine (ITM) is not a branch bank when it meets certain criteria. The bill updates the definitions in §§32‑1‑109 and 32‑6‑103, MCA, and adds a new definition of ITM.
changes: Amends §32‑1‑109 to define an ITM as an automated, unstaffed facility that allows customers to interact with remote bank personnel and perform core banking transactions without staff assistance.
Revises §32‑6‑103 to include ITMs in the definition of satellite terminals and clarifies that ITMs are not considered branch banks when located off‑premises.
Adds a new definition of “Interactive teller machine” and expands the definition of “Satellite terminal” to encompass ITMs.
Revises related terms such as “Branch,” “Satellite terminal,” and “Electronic terminal” to reflect the new ITM definition.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No fiscal impact is specified in the text.
affected: Banks and savings associations operating ITMs

HB435.one_line: HB 435 standardizes professional‑licensing discipline rules, reporting, and sanctions across Montana.
HB435.summary: HB 435 revises Montana’s professional‑licensing discipline rules, standardizing misconduct definitions, sanctions, and reinstatement procedures while adding reporting and immunity provisions. It reorganizes several sections of the Montana Code and repeals duplicate or outdated language. The bill does not create a new program or criminal offense.
changes: Defines a new, uniform list of unprofessional conduct for all licensed professions.
Sets a maximum probationary license period of three years and limits sanctions to those necessary to protect the public.
Requires license applicants and licensees to report actions against them within 30 days and to report other licensees’ misconduct in good faith.
Adds liability immunity for anyone who reports misconduct in good faith.
Creates a new reporting system for mental or physical impairment that can trigger board‑initiated evaluations.
Rewrites and consolidates sanctions, reinstatement, and administrative suspension procedures across multiple boards.
affected: Health‑care facilities and staff who report misconduct

HB438.one_line: Consolidates six health‑care licensing boards into one new board effective 2026.
HB438.summary: HB 438 consolidates several professional licensing boards—athletic trainers, occupational therapists, physical therapists, speech‑language pathologists, and audiologists—into a single Board of Physical, Rehabilitative, and Developmental Health Care Professionals.  The new board will set licensure criteria, adopt fees, and issue licenses for all six professions, while repealing the separate boards and their statutes.  The act takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: Creates a single Board with 12 members (2 athletic trainers, 2 occupational therapists, 4 physical therapists, 2 speech‑language pathologists, 1 audiologist, 1 public member).
Transfers rule‑making, licensing, and fee‑setting authority for the six professions to the new board.
Repeals the separate boards and associated statutes (sections 2‑15‑1739, 2‑15‑1748, 2‑15‑1749, 2‑15‑1771, and related Title 37 sections).
Amends definitions in Title 37 chapters 11, 15, 24, and 36 to reflect the new board’s authority.
Provides a delayed effective date of January 1, 2026, preserving pre‑existing rights and penalties.
Directs the code commissioner to rename references to the former boards in future legislation.
affected: Licensed athletic trainers, occupational therapists, physical therapists, speech‑language pathologists, audiologists, and their applicants; the Department of Labor and Industry; the Montana Code Commissioner's office; and the public who receives services from these professionals.

HB441.one_line: HB 441 aligns provisional permits with final decrees and sets a petition process for owners to challenge them.
HB441.summary: HB 441 revises Montana’s water‑rights law to make provisional permits subject to final decrees, establishes a notice‑and‑petition process for owners to challenge those permits, and clarifies how certificates of water right and changes in appropriation rights are verified after a final decree.
changes: Amends §85‑2‑313 to declare all permits issued before a final decree provisional and subject to reduction, modification, or revocation after a show‑cause hearing; owners of existing rights must be notified within 60 days of a final decree and may file petitions within 180 days.

Provides a detailed petition procedure: petitions must be filed on a prescribed form, served on all provisional‑permit owners, and the department must respond to defects within 60 days; the petitioner must prove by preponderance that the provisional permit would have been denied or modified if the final decree had been available.
Sets a 120‑day period for the department to deny or propose action on a petition, and requires a show‑cause hearing if the department proposes a change; a denial is final.

Revises §85‑2‑315 to require that the department review a certified statement of completion before issuing a certificate of water right, and to allow the department to require a show‑cause hearing if the completion is not in substantial accordance with the permit or final decree.

Revises §85‑2‑402 to clarify the definition of a change in appropriation right, the criteria for approval, and the procedures for notice, hearings, and verification of completion, including specific rules for replacement wells, redundant supply wells, and replacement points of diversion.
Adds a notification requirement to federally recognized tribal governments.
No new program or criminal offense is created; the bill merely amends existing statutes.
affected: Owners of existing water rights in basins with final decrees
Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) staff
Applicants for changes in appropriation rights

HB442.one_line: HB 442 removes certain reporting duties for medical and chiropractic panels and insurers, adding a one‑month suspension for non‑compliance.
HB442.summary: HB 442 amends Montana’s medical‑legal and chiropractic‑legal reporting rules, removing the requirement that panels send decision outcomes to licensing boards and eliminating insurers’ reporting duties. It also revises reporting language for certain professional boards and creates a one‑month suspension for willful non‑reporting.
changes: Amends §27‑6‑605 to require only that a decision be written to parties, attorneys, and retained in panel files; the copy to the provider’s licensing board is no longer required.
Amends §27‑12‑605 to remove the copy‑to‑licensing‑board requirement, keeping only party/attorney notification and panel file retention.
Amends §37‑3‑404 to clarify that good‑faith information providers to the Board of Medical Examiners are immune from civil suits.
Amends §37‑3‑405 to allow a licensing agency to suspend a license or privilege for up to one month for willful failure to comply with reporting requirements.
Repeals §37‑3‑402, eliminating the insurer‑to‑board reporting requirement for alleged professional negligence.

HB443.one_line: HB 443 removes state licensing for transient retail merchants, allowing counties to regulate if desired.
HB443.summary: HB 443 removes the state’s licensing requirements for transient retail merchants and gives counties the authority to regulate or license them if they choose. The bill eliminates the fee, application, bond, and display requirements that previously governed these merchants.
changes: Repeals state statutes 7‑21‑2404 through 7‑21‑2411 that required a license, fee, bond, and application process for transient retail merchants.
Leaves open the possibility for counties to create their own regulations or licensing schemes under Section 1.
No new fees, bonds, or display mandates are imposed at the state level.
The repeal does not create a new criminal offense or state program.
County commissioners retain jurisdiction to regulate or license if they adopt local rules.
The bill does not alter any other state or local statutes.

HB444.one_line: Revises security‑deposit rules, permitting e‑mail notices and electronic refunds, with 30‑day list deadlines.
HB444.summary: HB 444 revises Montana’s security‑deposit rules, allowing landlords to send notices and refunds by e‑mail or electronic transfer, and clarifies when and how deductions may be made. It also sets 30‑day deadlines for lists and refunds and specifies mailing to a tenant’s last‑known address if no new address is given.
changes: Landlords may now send security‑deposit notices and refunds by e‑mail or electronic fund transfer.
Deductions for cleaning, damage, unpaid rent, utilities, penalties, and labor are limited to amounts expressly authorized in the amended §70‑25‑201.
Tenants must receive a written list of deductions within 30 days of tenancy termination, accompanied by any refund if the deposit exceeds the charges.
If no damages or unpaid amounts exist, the landlord must return the full deposit within 10 days by electronic transfer or mail.
Tenants who fail to provide a new address are still entitled to recover the deposit; landlords may mail to the last‑known address but remain liable for the amount owed.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.

HB446.one_line: HB 446 redefines indecent exposure, updates penalties, and expands related definitions.
HB446.summary: HB 446 redefines indecent exposure to include intent to violate dignity and adds a specific exception. It amends the penalty schedule, clarifies definitions, and sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date.
changes: Rewrites 45‑5‑504 to define indecent exposure as intentional exposure of intimate parts to the opposite sex or opposite‑sex‑assigned-at-birth individuals with intent to violate dignity or to arouse sexual desire.
Adds a new subsection (3) that allows a minor who is a parent/guardian or a developmentally disabled person to be exempt from prosecution under this section.
Adjusts penalty tiers: first conviction fine up to $500 or 6‑month jail; second up to $1,000 or 1‑year jail; third or more up to $10,000 or 10‑year state prison.
Adds a separate penalty for indecent exposure to a minor: fine up to $50,000 or 4‑year minimum state prison, with possible longer terms.

Amends 46‑23‑502 to expand definitions of “Department,” “Foreign offenses,” “Mental abnormality,” “Municipality,” “Personality disorder,” “Predatory sexual offense,” “Registration agency,” “Residence,” “Sexual offender evaluator,” “Sexual offense,” “Sexual or violent offender,” “Sexually violent predator,” “Transient,” and “Violent offense” with detailed language.
affected: Individuals who expose intimate parts in public to the opposite sex or opposite‑sex‑assigned-at-birth persons
Offenders convicted of indecent exposure or indecent exposure to a minor
Persons subject to the new definitions of sexual and violent offenses

HB447.one_line: Creates a compact for interstate respiratory therapy practice, mandates background checks, and establishes a commission to administer it.
HB447.summary: The bill creates a statewide Respiratory Care Interstate Compact that lets licensed respiratory therapists practice in other member states, requires criminal‑background checks for all applicants, and establishes a commission to administer the compact.  Montana must meet the same rules as other states and may charge fees for the privilege.  The compact becomes effective when the seventh state enacts it.  The bill also codifies the background‑check requirement into state law.
changes: Establishes a Respiratory Care Interstate Compact and a governing commission
Requires all license applicants to submit fingerprints for state and federal criminal‑history checks
Mandates that each member state submit data on licenses, adverse actions, and investigations to a shared data system
Allows member states to charge fees for granting and renewing compact privileges
Provides for rulemaking authority, dispute resolution, and enforcement mechanisms by the commission
Sets a contingent effective date tied to the enactment by the seventh member state
Codifies the background‑check requirement into Title 37, Chapter 28 of Montana law
affected: Montana Department of Labor and Industry
Montana residents who are active military members or spouses
HB447.effective: when the compact is enacted by the seventh member state

HB448.one_line: Designates a highway segment as a memorial and directs signage and map updates.
HB448.summary: The bill designates a stretch of highway in Great Falls as the Jim Loud Thunder Gopher Memorial Highway, requires the Department of Transportation to sign it and add it to state maps, and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Establishes a memorial highway on the northwest bypass and Vaughn Road from 14th St NW to 27th St NW.
Directs the Montana Department of Transportation to design and install signs marking the memorial highway.
Mandates that state maps be updated to include the memorial highway when the department publishes new maps.
Codifies the provision as part of Title 60, Chapter 1, Part 2 of the Montana Statutes.
The act becomes effective on the day it is passed and approved.
affected: Local residents and motorists on the specified roadway

HB449.one_line: Repeals the statutory basis for Montana’s adult basic education fund.
HB449.summary: The bill simply repeals Montana Code § 20‑7‑712, which created and distributed the adult basic education fund.  No new programs, funds, or regulations are added—state agencies will no longer be required to maintain that fund.  The repeal takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Repeals § 20‑7‑712, eliminating the statutory basis for the adult basic education fund and its distribution.  No new provisions, programs, or regulations are introduced.  Existing funding mechanisms for adult basic education are no longer mandated by state law.  The repeal does not alter any existing contracts or obligations already in place.  The act contains no fiscal allocations or new expenditures.  The only action is the removal of the statutory reference.
affected: State agencies that previously administered the adult basic education fund
Montana taxpayers indirectly affected by the removal of the fund

HB454.one_line: Revises PT‑assistant visit frequency to once per 6‑8 visits or every 2 weeks, whichever first.
HB454.summary: HB 454 changes how often a licensed physical therapist must visit a client when supervising a physical‑therapy assistant. The new rule allows a visit once every six or eight assistant visits, or once every two weeks, whichever comes first, and keeps other limits on concurrent supervision unchanged.
changes: Amends § 37‑11‑105 to require a licensed PT to make an onsite or telehealth visit at least once for every six or eight visits performed by a PT assistant, or once every two weeks, whichever occurs first.
Keeps the existing cap of two full‑time assistants per PT and the limits on supervising aides unchanged.
Does not alter any other supervisory or staffing provisions in the statute.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
No new program, fund, or offense is created.

HB450.one_line: Revises bird‑dog training laws, adds fees, reporting, and commission rule‑making authority.
HB450.summary: HB 450 revises Montana’s bird‑dog training laws, adding a fee schedule, requiring applicants to state how many dogs will be trained, and giving the Fish and Wildlife Commission rule‑making authority to limit licenses and dogs per license.
