changes: Amends §87‑3‑602 to set a $5 fee for resident and $10 for non‑resident Class D‑5 licenses, and allows free licenses for youths 12‑18 years old.
Requires applicants to report the number of dogs to be trained; that number must appear on the issued license.
Adds a provision that a Class D‑5 license is not required for training with captive game birds that are tagged or marked, provided the birds come from an approved source.
Adds a reporting requirement for taking an untagged or unmarked bird outside the season or without a license.
Amends §87‑3‑604 to grant the Fish and Wildlife Commission authority to adopt rules limiting the number of Class D‑5 licenses issued to non‑residents and limiting the number of dogs per license.
affected: Residents and non‑residents who wish to train bird‑hunting dogs
Youth 12‑18 years old who wish to train bird‑hunting dogs
numbers: 12‑18 year olds may receive free license

HB455.one_line: HB 455 shortens COPP notification deadlines for municipal elections, effective immediately.
HB455.summary: HB 455 shortens the Commissioner of Political Practices’ (COPP) notification deadline for municipal candidates, setting specific dates for primary and general elections and making the change effective immediately.
changes: Amends §13‑37‑126 to specify COPP notification deadlines for municipal elections.
Sets a 5‑day post‑filing deadline for municipal primary notifications.
Sets a September 30 (or preceding Friday) deadline for municipal general notifications, with a secondary September 24 (or preceding Friday) deadline for certain general elections.
Applies to all municipal primary and general elections held on or after April 20, 2025.
The act takes effect upon passage and approval.

HB458.one_line: Limits noneconomic malpractice damages to $250,000 per patient and adds physician assistants to the provider definition.
HB458.summary: HB 458 revises Montana’s medical‑malpractice law to cap noneconomic damages at $250,000 per patient, expands the definition of “health‑care provider” to include physician assistants, and makes the cap apply to both new and pending claims. The bill also requires annual cost‑of‑living adjustments to the cap and sets the changes in effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §25‑9‑411 to set a $250,000 limit on noneconomic damages per patient in malpractice cases.
Adds physician assistants to the statutory definition of “health‑care provider.”
Applies the new cap to both future and existing malpractice claims.
Requires the cap to be increased annually (cost‑of‑living adjustment).
Specifies the order of reductions for awards exceeding the limit and prohibits disclosure of the limit to a jury.
Effective immediately upon passage.

HB463.one_line: Allows Montana LLCs to convert to corporations or LLPs with written approval and filing requirements.
HB463.summary: HB 463 lets a Montana limited‑liability company (LLC) convert into a domestic corporation or a limited‑liability partnership (LLP). The bill sets out the approval, documentation, filing, and effective‑date requirements for such conversions and clarifies how assets, liabilities, and member interests carry over. It also amends the statutory definition of “conversion” and related terms.
changes: Allows an LLC to convert to a domestic corporation or an LLP.
Requires the conversion plan to be approved by all members or the required majority in the operating agreement.
The plan must be in writing and include terms of conversion, names, jurisdiction, and governing documents of the new entity.
The LLC must file articles of conversion with the Secretary of State, including a statement of approval and the new entity’s articles or registration application.
The conversion becomes effective upon filing or a later date not more than 90 days after filing.
Assets, contracts, debts, and member interests transfer automatically to the new entity without winding up the LLC.
The bill amends the definition of “conversion” and related terms in § 35‑8‑1205.
No new program or fund is created.
No criminal offense is created.
affected: Members and interest holders of those LLCs
Potential new domestic corporations or LLPs formed from LLCs

HB464.one_line: HB 464 clarifies that a change of interest on death does not defeat real‑property insurance and extends coverage to beneficiaries for up to 45 days.
HB464.summary: HB 464 amends Montana insurance law to clarify that a named insured’s property‑interest change on death—whether by will, succession, or a transfer‑on‑death deed—does not defeat existing real‑property insurance. It also expands the rules for how insurance coverage is carried over to beneficiaries after the insured’s death.
changes: Amends §33‑15‑206 to state that a change of interest on death (by will, succession, or transfer‑on‑death deed) does not avoid existing insurance and that the insurance passes to the new interest holder.
Adds language to §33‑15‑206 that a transfer of interest among joint owners does not terminate insurance even if the policy was intended to cease upon alienation.

Rewrites §72‑6‑412 to detail how a transfer‑on‑death deed transfers property interests, the survivorship rules, and how real‑property insurance coverage is automatically extended to the beneficiary for up to 45 days or until the policy expires or a replacement policy is placed.
Clarifies that the beneficiary’s temporary coverage ends at the earlier of 45 days after death, policy expiration, or placement of a replacement policy.
Maintains that the beneficiary’s coverage does not affect other insureds listed on the policy.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.
No new program or office is created.
No new criminal offense is created.
affected: Named insureds on property insurance policies
Policyholders who are household members or other insureds

HB466.one_line: HB 466 defines categorical exclusions and exempts certain state actions from MEPA review.
HB466.summary: HB 466 codifies the term “categorical exclusion” in the Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) and exempts certain state actions—construction on state land and historic‑preservation grants—from MEPA review. It also requires agencies to track and report use of exclusions and amends the definition section of 75‑1‑220, MCA.
changes: Defines “categorical exclusion” and authorizes state agencies to designate actions as such, exempting them from MEPA environmental assessment or impact statement requirements unless extraordinary circumstances exist.
Creates a rebuttable presumption that no environmental analysis is needed for actions designated as categorical exclusions.
Mandates that state agencies track and report the number and use of categorical exclusions to the Environmental Quality Council.
Exempts the Department of Administration from MEPA review for construction, renovation, or repair of buildings or infrastructure on state land and for projects in the long‑range building program.
Exempts the Department of Commerce from MEPA review when authorizing, administering, or creating historic‑preservation grant programs.
Amends 75‑1‑220, MCA, to include the new definition of “categorical exclusion” and other related terms.
affected: State agencies (e.g., Department of Administration, Department of Commerce, other agencies defined in 2‑4‑102)
Construction and renovation projects on state land
Public and private entities proposing state‑sponsored projects
numbers: Title 22, chapter 3, part 13 (Department of Commerce exemption)

HB467.one_line: Adds oral‑fluid testing and tightens license suspension for commercial drivers.
HB467.summary:
HB 467 expands the state’s implied‑consent DUI rules to include oral‑fluid testing, tightens license‑suspension procedures for commercial drivers, and clarifies definitions and penalties for aggravated DUI.

what_changes:[
- Adds oral‑fluid as an accepted test for alcohol and drugs in the implied‑consent framework.
- Requires peace officers to obtain a preliminary breath screening before any blood, breath, or oral‑fluid test.
- Extends automatic license suspension for commercial drivers who refuse any test, with a 1‑year suspension for a first refusal and lifetime suspension for a second or subsequent refusal.
- Creates a temporary 5‑day non‑commercial driving permit issued by the officer when a license is seized.
- Defines “aggravated driving under the influence” to include a 0.16 BAC, ignition‑interlock orders, prior suspensions, or refusal to provide a breath sample.
- Lowers the BAC threshold for commercial drivers to 0.04 and for drivers under 21 to 0.02.
- Grants municipalities the authority to enact ordinances implementing this section.
- Clarifies that refusal of a preliminary screening does not satisfy the consent requirement.
- Provides that a refusal to submit to any test can trigger a search warrant for blood or oral‑fluid.
- Requires the department to suspend the driver’s license for the period specified in 61‑8‑1032.
- Mandates that non‑resident license holders’ refusals be reported to their home state licensing authority.
- Adds that a prior conviction for a major DUI offense counts as a refusal for purposes of lifetime suspension.

HB468.one_line: HB 468 removes validation decals, updates numbering, right‑of‑way, accident reporting, safety rules, and eliminates the Boating Advisory Council.
HB468.summary: HB 468 removes the requirement for a validation decal on Montana watercraft, updates numbering and registration rules, revises right‑of‑way and restricted‑area rules, changes accident‑reporting requirements, tightens personal‑watercraft safety rules, and eliminates the Boating Advisory Council while reallocating its funding.
changes: Eliminates the validation‑decal requirement and related numbering rules, allowing motorboats, sailboats, and personal watercraft to operate without a decal once a certificate of number is issued;
Revises right‑of‑way rules to give sailboats priority over motorboats and clarifies passing rules for all vessels;
Adds new restricted‑area provisions (e.g., 20‑ft buffer around swimming areas, 75‑ft buffer around fishing/hunting waterfowl, 200‑ft diver safety zones) and updates speed limits in those zones;

Rewrites accident‑reporting requirements so that any collision, accident, or casualty involving a death, disappearance, injury, or $2,000+ property damage must be reported immediately to the sheriff or game warden and a standardized form must be filed;
Strengthens personal‑watercraft safety by requiring a Coast Guard‑approved PFD, lanyard‑type engine cutoff, and speed limits near docks, swimmers, and restricted waters;
Abolishes the Boating Advisory Council and reassigns its funding to the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks for boating‑facility improvements and matching federal funds;
Repeals Section 23‑2‑536 (the council’s creation, appointment, and duties).
affected: Boat owners, operators, and passengers of motorboats, sailboats, and personal watercraft; fishing and hunting waterfowl participants; local law‑enforcement and game‑warden personnel; the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks; the former Boating Advisory Council members.
numbers: 3‑year renewal period for validation decals (now eliminated)

HB471.one_line: HB 471 mandates parental consent and advance notice for identity instruction and expands curriculum transparency in Montana public schools.
HB471.summary: HB 471 requires Montana public schools to obtain written parental permission before a child can receive identity instruction, mandates advance notice and annual summaries of human‑sexuality and identity curricula, and requires schools to make materials publicly available. It also bars abortion‑service providers from supplying related instruction and obliges trustees to report violations to the Board of Public Education.
changes: Parents must give written consent for a child to attend any identity‑instruction class; absence without consent is excused.

Schools must give parents at least 48 hours (5 school days) notice before any human‑sexuality or identity instruction event or assembly, and no later than 14 school days before first use of materials.

Each school district must annually notify parents of the content of any human‑sexuality or identity instruction course, provide a summary of the curriculum, and give parents the right to withdraw their child.
Curriculum materials for human‑sexuality and identity instruction must be made available for public inspection before use, with an electronic link to summaries.
Schools may not allow any person or entity that provides abortion services to offer or sponsor any course or instruction related to human sexuality or sexually transmitted diseases.
Trustees of a district must investigate and report any violations of this section to the Board of Public Education.
Definitions of “human sexuality instruction” and “identity instruction” are expanded to include a broader range of topics.

HB473.one_line: HB 473 authorizes automatic adoption of CMS Medicare fee schedules and expands rule‑making authority for the department.
HB473.summary: HB 473 lets the Department of Public Health and Human Services automatically adopt and update Medicare fee schedules issued by CMS, while expanding the department’s rule‑making authority and tightening notice requirements for all agency rules.
changes: Allows the department to adopt CMS‑issued Medicare fee schedules by rule and to incorporate any CMS updates automatically during the year.
Amends rule‑making statutes (2‑4‑302, 2‑4‑305, 2‑4‑306, 2‑4‑307) to give the department broader authority and stricter notice, hearing, and publication requirements for all rules.
Specifies that fee schedule updates are exempt from the usual reference‑to‑model‑code provisions of 2‑4‑307.
Adds a new subsection to 53‑6‑113 authorizing the department to adopt Medicare fee schedules and to automatically incorporate CMS changes.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Health care providers reimbursed under Medicare
Other state agencies subject to rule‑making changes
Public and professional stakeholders who must be notified of rule changes.

HB475.one_line: Limits restraints on pregnant inmates during labor to extraordinary cases, banning leg‑restraints.
HB475.summary: HB 475 limits the use of restraints on pregnant inmates during labor and delivery, allowing them only in extraordinary circumstances and banning leg‑ or waist‑restraints entirely.  It also requires restraints to be removed when the risk is mitigated or a medical professional requests it.
changes: Prohibits use of any restraints on a pregnant inmate during labor and delivery, except in specified extraordinary circumstances.
Defines extraordinary circumstances as a flight risk or a clear threat to self or others, subject to individualized determination by the detention center.
Bans leg‑ or waist‑restraints (e.g., leg shackles, belly belts) at all stages of labor and delivery.
Mandates that any restraint used must be the least restrictive option and be removed when the risk is mitigated or upon a medical professional’s request.
Codifies the rule as part of Title 7, Chapter 32, Part 22 of the Montana Code.
affected: Pregnant inmates in state detention facilities
Medical staff treating inmates during labor and delivery

HB474.one_line: HB 474 moves the hospital Medicaid payment deadline to May 5, effective immediately.
HB474.summary: HB 474 shortens the deadline for the Department of Public Health and Human Services to disburse annual supplemental Medicaid payments to hospitals from May 15 to May 5 each year. The bill amends the state special‑revenue‑fund account rules to enforce this earlier date and specifies that the change takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §53‑6‑149, MCA, to require the department to provide funding for increases in hospital Medicaid payments no later than May 5 each year (instead of May 15).

Reaffirms that all money collected under §15‑66‑102, except the portion deposited into the Montana HELP Act account, must be deposited into the hospital Medicaid reimbursement account in the state special revenue fund.
Specifies that the account’s funds may be used for the increased payments and for related administrative costs.
The amendment terminates the earlier May 15 deadline on June 30, 2025, if a contingency occurs under §48, Ch. 415, L. 2019.
The act becomes effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
State special revenue fund account holders

HB480.one_line: HB 480 expands jury‑trial rights in constitutional challenges to state laws and ballot measures.
HB480.summary: HB 480 expands the right to a jury trial in civil actions that challenge the constitutionality of a law or ballot measure, allowing any party to demand a jury on disputed factual issues. The bill amends §27‑8‑302 to make that right explicit and codifies the change in Title 3, Chapter 15. It takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to new cases filed after the effective date.
changes: Adds a new subsection to §27‑8‑302 granting any party in a constitutional challenge a jury trial on disputed factual matters.
Codifies the jury‑trial right as part of Title 3, Chapter 15, ensuring it applies to all civil actions under the chapter.
Specifies that the act is effective immediately upon approval and applies only to proceedings where a jury‑trial demand is made on or after that date.
Clarifies that the right applies when the case involves a challenge to a legislative act or ballot issue defined in §13‑1‑101.
Leaves existing procedures for other civil actions unchanged.
Does not create new funds or offices.
affected: Plaintiffs and defendants in civil actions challenging state laws or ballot measures
numbers: applicability: on or after effective date

HB476.one_line: HB 476 creates a $160,000 grant program for newborn safety devices, ending June 30, 2027.
HB476.summary: HB 476 creates a $160,000 grant program that gives up to $20,000 to fire departments, hospitals, and law‑enforcement agencies for installing and maintaining newborn safety devices. The program runs from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2027, with the department setting rules and reporting to a committee.
changes: Establishes a competitive grant program for newborn safety devices.
Limits each grant award to $20,000.
Allocates $160,000 from the general fund for the program for the 2025‑2026 biennium.
Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to adopt rules for application, evaluation, and reporting.
Mandates annual reporting to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee by September 30, 2027.
Unspent funds by June 30, 2027 must revert to the general fund.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Children, families, health, and human services interim committee

HB486.one_line: HB 486 raises deputy sheriff pay to 97 % of the sheriff’s salary across all counties.
HB486.summary: HB 486 amends the state law that sets deputy sheriff pay, raising the percentage of the sheriff’s salary used to calculate deputy pay and adding a new schedule based on county population.
changes:
Amends §7‑4‑2508 to set deputy sheriff compensation as a percentage of the sheriff’s salary, with a fixed 97 % rate for all population brackets; previously the range was 72‑95 %.
Replaces the prior range with a single 97 % figure for all counties.
Adds a new definition that “compensation” means base pay only.
Keeps the 98 % rate for undersheriff compensation unchanged.
Allows the sheriff to adjust within the new 97 % range based on rank structure.
Clarifies that “salary of that sheriff” includes all statutory salary components.

HB483.one_line: HB 483 keeps equalization mills fixed, tightens reappraisal reporting, and boosts transportation aid to offset tax changes.
HB483.summary: HB 483 revises Montana’s school‑funding and property‑tax rules to keep the 95‑mill state equalization and fixed vocational‑tech mill rates, while tightening reappraisal reporting, adjusting guaranteed‑tax‑base multipliers, and raising transportation mileage rates to offset reappraisal‑driven tax increases. The bill also changes how county and state equalization levies are calculated and how school‑transportation reimbursements are shared.
changes: Replaces the 95‑mill state equalization and fixed vocational‑tech mill rates with fixed amounts that are no longer subject to Section 15‑10‑420 adjustments.

Mandates the Office of Public Instruction and the Department of Revenue to annually report on how reappraisal affects school funding and property taxes, and to adjust guaranteed‑tax‑base multipliers so that statewide property taxes do not rise.
Increases transportation mileage reimbursement rates (up to 200%) to provide additional state aid to districts and to offset any tax‑revenue shortfall caused by reappraisal.
Alters the calculation of county and state equalization levies (Sections 20‑9‑331, 20‑9‑333, 20‑9‑360) and the share of on‑schedule transportation reimbursements (Section 20‑9‑336).
Adds new reporting requirements for the Department of Revenue and the Office of Public Instruction on reappraisal impacts and guaranteed‑tax‑base adjustments.
affected: Local governments that levy equalization taxes

HB487.one_line: Amends DOT law to mandate five core divisions within the department.
HB487.summary: The bill amends the state’s transportation law to specify that the Department of Transportation must contain five particular divisions: highways, aeronautics, administration, rail and transit, and motor carrier services. It does not create new programs or funds, nor does it impose new costs. The change simply codifies the required structure of the department.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑2501, MCA, to state that the Department of Transportation must have the following divisions: highways; aeronautics; administration; rail and transit; and motor carrier services.
Clarifies that the department may have additional divisions beyond those listed, but the five listed divisions are mandatory.
No new offices, funds, or criminal offenses are created by the amendment.
affected: Montana Department of Transportation employees and management
State agencies that interact with the DOT

HB490.one_line: HB 490 requires wildfire‑mitigation plans for utilities and limits their liability if they follow those plans.
HB490.summary: HB 490 requires electric facilities providers to develop, submit, and update wildfire‑mitigation plans and gives them liability protection if they substantially follow those plans. It also sets a statutory standard of care for wildfire‑related claims and limits punitive damages.
changes: Mandates that all electric facilities providers prepare a written wildfire‑mitigation plan by Dec. 31 2025 and resubmit every three years.
Creates a formal approval process: the provider’s approval authority reviews the plan, holds a public comment period (≤45 days), and must approve or identify deficiencies within 60 days.
Requires biennial reports (by June 1 each year) summarizing mitigation efforts and compliance.

Provides liability protections: a provider that substantially follows an approved plan is presumed to have acted reasonably, and cannot be held strictly liable for wildfire damage under common‑law theories.

Limits recovery: only real and personal property damage, economic damages, and noneconomic damages tied to bodily injury or death are recoverable; punitive damages require clear‑and‑convincing evidence of gross negligence or intent.
Sets a 3‑year statute of limitations for wildfire‑related civil actions and a 6‑month service‑of‑process window.
affected: Electric facilities providers (regulated utilities, electric cooperatives, municipal utilities, joint‑owned facilities, and federally regulated transmitting utilities)
Utility approval authorities (commission, board of trustees, city councils)
Utility customers and property owners potentially affected by wildfire damage

HB492.one_line: Limits municipal parking mandates and requires developer compensation for extra parking.
HB492.summary: HB 492 limits how many parking spaces municipalities can require in zoning, allows developers to provide more than the minimum, and requires municipalities to compensate developers who must build extra parking. The law amends several Montana Code sections and takes effect October 1, 2026.
changes: 1. Rewrites §7‑14‑4501 to clarify that cities may acquire, construct, maintain, and charge for parking facilities. 2. Amends §76‑2‑304 to set maximum parking requirements: no more than one off‑street parking space per residential unit (or an equivalent shared space) and no more than one parking space for units under 1,200 sq ft. 3. Prohibits zoning regulations that require more than one parking space per residential unit, any minimum parking for existing buildings changing use, child‑care facilities, deed‑restricted affordable housing, or assisted‑living facilities. 4. Amends §76‑25‑303 to reinforce the parking limits and to prohibit other restrictive zoning provisions (e.g., for manufactured housing, amateur‑radio antennas, agricultural use, and certain care facilities). 5. Requires municipalities to compensate developers who are forced to provide additional parking beyond the minimum. 6. Sets the effective date for the amendments to October 1, 2026.

HB493.one_line: New felony for stolen gun possession, up to 10‑year prison, expands gang‑activity definition.
HB493.summary: HB 493 creates a new felony for possessing a stolen firearm or ammunition, imposes up to 10‑year prison, and expands the state’s definition of a criminal‑street‑gang pattern to include that offense. It also revises youth‑court filing rules and codifies the new crime into the Montana Code.
changes: Establishes a new crime: possession of a stolen firearm or ammunition;
Convicts are punishable by up to 10 years in state prison;
Adds “possession of a stolen firearm” to the list of offenses that constitute a pattern of criminal street‑gang activity;
Amends §41‑5‑206 to modify youth‑court filing procedures for certain serious offenses;
Codifies the new offense into Title 45, Chapter 8, Part 3 of the Montana Code;
No new program, fund, or office is created.
affected: Individuals who possess stolen firearms or ammunition
Law‑enforcement agencies and courts handling gun‑related offenses
Youth courts and district courts under the amended filing rules
Offenders who could be charged with gang‑activity offenses
numbers: Section 45‑8‑405 list of 22 offenses (including the new one)

HB491.one_line: HB 491 expands alcohol service rules for retirement communities, golf courses, hotels, and guest ranches.
HB491.summary: HB 491 revises Montana’s continuing‑care retirement community (CCRC) alcohol rules, allowing multiple on‑campus service locations, delivery to residents’ units, and new licensing requirements. It also updates golf‑course, hotel, and guest‑ranch alcohol provisions and tightens training and record‑keeping for staff.
changes:
Amends §16‑3‑302 to permit licensed retailers to sell beer on golf courses, hotels, and guest ranches under specified conditions and fees.  
Adds §16‑4‑315 provisions that create a limited, non‑transferable all‑beverages license for a single CCRC campus, with a $500 application fee and $100 per additional service location.  
Allows CCRC licensees to operate multiple on‑campus alcohol service buildings, patios, decks, and swimming‑pool areas, provided they meet suitability requirements and include food service.  
Permits delivery of alcohol to residents’ individual living units on campus, subject to resident verification and a minimum 18‑year‑old, trained deliverer.  
Revises §16‑4‑1005 to require all employees who sell, serve, or deliver alcohol to complete responsible‑server training within 60 days of hire and every 3 years thereafter, and to keep employment records of training.  
Clarifies definitions of “campus,” “dining area,” and “graduated level of care” for CCRC licensing.  
Sets the effective date for the changes to July 1, 2025.
affected: Golf‑course, hotel, and guest‑ranch alcohol licensees
Employees who sell, serve, or deliver alcohol
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB495.one_line: HB 495 repeals the Federal Mandates Act and related reporting provisions, renumbering two sections.
HB495.summary: HB 495 repeals Montana’s Federal Mandates Act and related reporting provisions, and directs the code commissioner to renumber two sections into new locations. The bill does not create new programs or funds. It merely removes existing statutory requirements for reporting on federal mandates.
changes: Repeals sections 2‑1‑401, 2‑1‑403, 2‑1‑404, 2‑1‑405, 2‑1‑406, 2‑1‑407, 2‑1‑408, and 21‑409 of the Montana Code Annotated.
Directs the code commissioner to renumber section 2‑1‑409 into a new section in Title 5, Chapter 11, Part 1.
Directs the code commissioner to renumber section 2‑1‑402 into a new section in Title 5, Chapter 11, Part 1.
affected: Montana state agencies that previously complied with the Federal Mandates Act

HB496.one_line: Gov. may accept retrocession of federal lands used for parks or military purposes.
HB496.summary: HB 496 authorizes the Montana governor to accept retrocession of jurisdiction over federal lands used for national parks or military purposes, and specifies the filing process for such acceptance.
changes: Adds a provision that the governor may accept retrocession of jurisdiction over federal lands used for national park or military purposes.
Amends 2‑1‑215 to give the state consent to retrocession for those lands.
Amends 2‑1‑216 to set out the notification, acceptance, and filing steps required for retrocession to take effect.
Specifies that retrocession becomes effective upon filing the acceptance with the secretary of state.
affected: Residents and users of federal lands in Montana

HB497.one_line: Amends electrician licensing to accept apprenticeships or equivalent programs and clarifies experience definitions.
HB497.summary: HB 497 amends Montana’s journeyman and residential electrician licensing rules to allow applicants to qualify through an approved apprenticeship or a substantially equivalent program, and it adds detailed definitions of practical experience and electrical maintenance.
changes: Replaces Section 37‑68‑305, MCA, with new qualification criteria for journeyman and residential electrician licenses
Allows an applicant to qualify by completing an approved apprenticeship program or a substantially equivalent program in the electrical trade

Adds a requirement that applicants provide written evidence of at least 8,000 hours of legally obtained practical experience, with a minimum of 8,000 practical hours if the applicant’s hours come from an apprenticeship that was not completed
Defines “electrical maintenance” and “legally obtained practical experience” for the purposes of licensing
Specifies that the journeyman examination will consist of 60 questions and the residential examination 50 questions, covering the National Electrical Code and board rules
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created
No fiscal impact is specified in the text
affected: Applicants for journeyman or residential electrician licenses

HB499.one_line: Extends Grow Your Own Grants, adds colleges, raises scholarships, and removes loan conversion.
HB499.summary: HB 499 extends Montana’s Grow Your Own Grant program through June 30 2029, adds postsecondary institutions as eligible grantees, expands scholarship limits, and removes a conversion‑to‑loan requirement. It also appropriates $500,000 for the biennium and requires annual reporting to the education interim committee.
changes: Extends the program’s termination date to June 30 2029
Adds postsecondary institutions (tribal, community, 2‑year, and university units) as eligible grant recipients
Allows grants to be awarded for up to two years to develop or expand Grow Your Own programs
Provides a last‑dollar scholarship of up to $5,000 per year (max $10,000 total) for qualifying students
Removes the requirement that the commissioner convert a grant to a loan under certain circumstances
Requires a matching component and sustainability plan for one‑time startup grants
Mandates annual reporting to the education interim committee on participation and outcomes
Appropriates $500,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025
affected: Students in Grow Your Own programs

HB502.one_line: Creates a single board to license lab scientists, radiologic technologists, and respiratory therapists, replacing three former boards.
HB502.summary: HB 502 creates a single Board of Facility Allied Health Care Professionals that will oversee licensure for clinical laboratory scientists, radiologic technologists, and respiratory therapists. The board will set licensing criteria, fees, and rules, and will replace the three former specialty boards. The act takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: Establishes a new seven‑member board (2 lab scientists, 2 radiologic technologists, 2 respiratory therapists, 1 public member) to replace the separate boards for each profession.
Transfers licensure authority for the three professions to this new board and gives the board rule‑making and fee‑setting power.
Repeals the existing statutes that created and governed the former specialty boards and related procedural provisions.
Replaces references to the old boards with the new board in the Montana Code.
Provides that the board may adopt rules to implement Title 37 chapters 14, 28, 34 and related sections.
Sets the effective date of the new board and its authority for January 1, 2026.
affected: Clinical laboratory scientists, radiologic technologists, respiratory therapists, their employers, patients, and the Montana Department of Labor and Industry

HB503.one_line: HB 503 reclassifies and penalties for fleeing a peace officer, adding aggravated and injury‑related felonies.
HB503.summary: HB 503 revises Montana’s fleeing‑from‑a‑peace‑officer law, clarifying penalties and creating a new felony category for aggravated fleeing. It sets maximum prison terms and fines for misdemeanor, felony, and aggravated‑fleeing offenses and amends the statutory language to match the rest of Title 61, Chapter 8.
changes: Reclassifies the basic fleeing offense as a misdemeanor with up to 1 year imprisonment or $2,000 fine.
Creates a felony for aggravated fleeing, defined by prior conviction, reckless driving, property damage >$5,000, or leaving the state, with up to 5 years imprisonment or $5,000 fine.
Adds a separate felony for fleeing that causes serious bodily injury or death, with up to 10 years imprisonment or $10,000 fine.
Amends §61‑8‑316 to specify the conduct that constitutes fleeing and the signals a peace officer may give.
Reorganizes the provisions to conform to the pattern used in other Title 61, Chapter 8 offenses.
Codifies the new penalties as part of Title 61, Chapter 8, Part 7.
affected: Drivers who flee or elude a peace officer
Montana Department of Justice for enforcement

HB504.one_line: HB 504 expands livestock loss coverage to include domestic bison and sets new claim procedures.
HB504.summary: HB 504 expands Montana’s Livestock Loss Mitigation Program to cover domestic bison, adding new eligibility rules, claim and appeal procedures, and confidentiality safeguards. The act amends the program’s statutes, authorizes the board to set reimbursement rates, and requires per‑capita fee payment before claims are paid. The law takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Adds domestic bison to the list of livestock eligible for reimbursement under the program.
affected: Montana livestock producers (cattle, swine, horses, mules, sheep, goats, llamas, livestock guard dogs, and domestic bison)
Tribal members and tribal entities participating in authorized agreements
Department of Revenue (certification of per‑capita fee payment)
U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services (final determination of confirmed or probable loss)

HB505.one_line: Expands the housing loan fund, retains interest, eliminates density priority, and transfers $50 million.
HB505.summary: HB 505 expands the Montana Housing Infrastructure Revolving Loan Fund (MHIRLF) by allowing it to retain all interest and income, use those funds to back bonds, and transfer $50 million from the general fund. It removes the prior density‑and‑population eligibility priority and sets new terms for loans and bond purchases.
changes: Amends §17‑6‑801 to require all interest and income earned on the MHIRLF account to be retained in the account and limits principal appropriation to a two‑thirds legislative vote.
Eliminates the density and population eligibility priority in §17‑6‑804, allowing any eligible project to receive funding regardless of unit density or county population.

Expands §17‑6‑805 to let the Board of Investments make loans and purchase up to 50 % of bonds for infrastructure, set loan terms (up to 20 years), waive or require impact fees, and require long‑term affordability provisions.
Mandates the state treasurer to transfer $50 million from the general fund to the MHIRLF account by June 30 2025.
Provides retroactive application to interest and income earned on the account since June 14 2023.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Eligible government units and residential developers

HB509.one_line: Expands loan forgiveness to all new teachers, prioritizes impacted schools, and adds prorating.
HB509.summary: HB 509 expands the Quality Educator Loan Assistance Program to include all newly hired teachers in Montana public schools, prioritizes those in impacted schools, and adds a prorating process when funds are insufficient. It amends the statutory language governing eligibility, award amounts, and documentation, and sets July 1, 2025 as the effective and applicability date.
changes: Adds newly hired quality educators to the program’s eligibility pool.
Gives priority to newly hired teachers at impacted schools for loan repayment assistance.
Introduces a prorating mechanism when appropriated funds cannot cover all eligible teachers.
Adjusts the statutory text of sections 20‑4‑503, 20‑4‑504, and 20‑4‑505 to reflect the new eligibility and priority rules.
Maintains the existing maximum lifetime assistance of 3 years state‑funded plus 1 year district‑funded.
Sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date and the cutoff for new applications.
affected: State budget appropriations for loan assistance

HB511.one_line: HB 511 funds local firefighting training facilities with matching grants and strict caps.
HB511.summary: HB 511 establishes a $5 million grant program to fund capital construction, maintenance, repair, and equipment purchases for local firefighting training facilities. Grants require a 1 % cash or in‑kind match for projects $25,000 or more, and are limited to $250,000 per project and $500,000 per county. The program runs from June 30 2025 to June 30 2031.
changes: Creates a dedicated firefighting training facility infrastructure account in the state special revenue fund.
Authorizes the Department of Military Affairs to award up to $5 million in grants for property acquisition, construction, remodeling, repairs, and equipment for local firefighting authorities.
Requires a 1 % cash or donated‑services match on grants $25,000 or greater.
Limits each grant to $250,000 and caps total funding per county at $500,000, with no more than two funded applications per county.
Mandates grant recipients to submit a project management plan, reporting requirements, and comply with applicable design or industry standards.
Transfers $5 million from the General Fund capital‑development account to the new account and appropriates those funds for the 2025‑2029 biennium.
Sets the act to take effect June 30 2025 and terminate June 30 2031.

HB513.one_line: Montana law gives residents property rights in their likeness and imposes civil damages for unauthorized commercial use.
HB513.summary: The bill establishes that Montana residents and those domiciled in the state at death own property rights in their name, voice, and visual likeness. It sets out civil remedies and damages for unauthorized commercial use, defines key terms, and lists First‑Amendment defenses. The law becomes effective Jan. 1, 2026.
changes: Recognizes property rights in name, voice, and visual likeness for Montana residents and those domiciled at death, including heirs and executors for up to 20 years after death.
Creates civil liability: $50,000 per violation (or greater actual damages) for unauthorized digital voice or visual depictions used commercially; $5,000 per violation for other unauthorized uses.
Allows punitive damages and reasonable attorney fees.
Defines “digital voice replica depiction” and “digital visual depiction” and other related terms.
Specifies that claims must be filed within four years of discovery and lists First‑Amendment exemptions (news, commentary, satire, etc.).
Excludes broadband internet access providers from the scope of the law.
affected: Montana residents and those domiciled in Montana at death
Heirs, executors, and transferees of such individuals
Companies or individuals who create or distribute unauthorized digital voice or visual depictions for commercial use

HB514.one_line: HB 514 criminalizes threatening to disclose real or digitally fabricated sexual images, adding penalties and definitions.
HB514.summary: HB 514 expands Montana’s privacy‑in‑communications law to make it a misdemeanor to threaten or disclose real or digitally fabricated sexual images, and a felony for repeated offenses. It adds new penalties, defines “digitally fabricated,” and clarifies exceptions for public officials and law‑enforcement activities.
changes: Amends §45‑8‑213 to include possession and threat to disclose real or digitally fabricated sexual images as a violation.
Adds new definitions for “digitally fabricated” and “interactive computer service.”
Sets fines up to $500 (first offense) and up to $25,000 (repeat offenses) and jail terms up to 5 years for certain violations.
Provides a tiered penalty schedule: misdemeanor for first offense, second‑offense misdemeanor or felony, third‑offense felony with harsher penalties.
Specifies that the law does not impose liability on interactive computer services for user‑generated content.
Includes exemptions for public officials, public meetings, health‑care emergency calls, and lawful disclosures in the public interest or law‑enforcement contexts.
affected: Individuals who threaten, disclose, or possess real or digitally fabricated sexual images of identifiable persons
Law‑enforcement and public‑officials who record or disclose communications under certain circumstances
Interactive computer service providers (though not liable for user content)

HB515.one_line: HB 515 consolidates school‑facility funding, boosts aid, and replaces an old natural‑resource payment.
HB515.summary: HB 515 revises Montana’s school‑facility and technology funding system, consolidates two special‑revenue accounts, and adjusts formulas to give districts more aid without raising property taxes. It also replaces an old natural‑resource‑development payment with a new one and makes several administrative changes to how funds are transferred and reported.
changes: Consolidates the coal severance‑tax trust funds, creating a single school‑facilities fund and a single school‑major‑maintenance‑aid account.
Increases the base amount and multiplier in the state school major maintenance aid formula, allowing more money for major maintenance projects.

Replaces the former natural‑resource‑development K‑12 school facilities payment with a new payment that grows with oil and natural‑gas production taxes and can support maintenance aid and debt‑service assistance.
Repeals the statutory appropriation for school technology purposes (section 20‑9‑534) and re‑allocates that money to the new school‑facility‑and‑technology account.

Adds new transfer provisions that move excess coal severance‑tax bond‑fund money to the school‑facilities fund, the coal‑board fund, and the big‑sky economic‑development fund, and requires certification of fund balances.
Adjusts the building‑reserve and technology‑acquisition fund rules, including limits on levies and depreciation schedules.
Creates a guarantee account to stabilize the permanent fund and to provide the first source of equalization aid.
Sets effective dates: the act takes effect on passage, with most sections effective July 1 2025.
numbers: $275 million transfer to school facilities fund
$1 million annual appropriation for technology grants
$10 million base for new natural‑resource‑development payment (2020‑2023)
10 mill levy limit for building‑reserve funds
65% and 10% transfer percentages from coal severance‑tax bond fund

HB516.one_line: HB 516 transfers the workers’ compensation judge to the judicial branch, creates a court fund, and preserves the judge’s rights and retirement options.
HB516.summary: HB 516 moves the workers’ compensation judge from the Department of Labor and Industry to the judicial branch, places the court under Supreme Court supervision, creates a dedicated court fund, and sets up a transition and retirement‑election process for the judge. The bill also amends related statutory sections and codifies the changes in Title 3.
changes: Transfers the office of workers’ compensation judge from the executive branch to the judicial branch and places the court under the Montana Supreme Court’s supervision.

Creates a workers’ compensation court fund in the state special revenue fund and requires the Department of Labor and Industry to transfer $500,000 annually (or the amount appropriated) into that fund by July 15 each fiscal year.

Amends the appointment, qualifications, salary, and retirement provisions for the judge to mirror those of district court judges and allows the judge to elect to remain in the public employees’ retirement system by October 1, 2025.
Rewrites sections 19‑5‑301 and 39‑71‑201 to clarify retirement eligibility for the judge and to detail the administration and funding of the workers’ compensation system.

Provides a detailed transition plan that preserves the judge’s and staff’s rights, property, rules, and ongoing proceedings, and directs the Supreme Court to succeed the Department’s assets and contracts.
Instructs the code commissioner to renumber and codify the new provisions as a chapter in Title 3.
affected: Employees of the office of workers’ compensation judge

HB520.one_line: Clarifies that family‑transfer parcel rules don’t apply to lender conveyances and amends subdivision review procedures.
HB520.summary: HB 520 amends Montana’s subdivision law to clarify that family‑transfer parcel restrictions do not apply when the land is conveyed to a lender, and it revises § 76‑3‑207 to streamline certain family‑transfer divisions and set limits on fees and penalties.
changes: Rewrites § 76‑3‑207 to exempt family‑transfer divisions from certain subdivision reviews when the land is sold or gifted to a lender or immediate family member
Sets a maximum $400 fee for local governing bodies to examine such divisions
Requires county treasurer certification that all taxes on the land are paid before a division
Allows a 2‑year restriction on resale of a family‑transfer parcel, except for mortgage or foreclosure conveyances
Provides a $5,000 civil penalty for evading subdivision rules via family‑transfer divisions
Permits local governing bodies to grant variances for hardship situations
affected: Local governing bodies handling subdivision applications
County treasurers and the Department of Revenue

HB521.one_line: Convicted offenders injured during a crime cannot sue for those injuries if the victim’s force was not unjustified.
HB521.summary: HB 521 removes the right of a convicted person to sue for injuries or damages sustained while committing a crime, provided the victim’s force was not unjustified. The law applies only to those who are convicted and injured during the commission of the offense.
changes: 1. A convicted person who is injured or suffers damages during the commission of a crime cannot file a civil lawsuit to recover those injuries or damages. 2. The prohibition applies only when the victim’s force was not unjustified (i.e., no force or justifiable force per Title 45, ch. 3, part 1). 3. The provision is codified as part of Title 27, ch. 1, part 5, and is subject to the same rules that govern that title.
affected: Convicted offenders injured during the commission of a crime
Victims who used no force or justifiable force

HB523.one_line: HB 523 creates a petition process for abandoned cemetery lots, requires public notice, and allows purchase if unclaimed.
HB523.summary: HB 523 establishes a process for determining when a lot in a public cemetery is abandoned, allows a petitioner to request a finding of abandonment, requires public notice, and lets the petitioner purchase the lot if no owner claims it.
changes: Defines abandonment as 75 years of no interment and no contact with owner/ heirs.
Creates a petition procedure that must include owner search, lot description, and purchase request.
Mandates weekly newspaper notices for three weeks with specific information about the lot and owner.
Requires an affidavit of publication from petitioner or administrator.
If no claim is made, the lot is legally abandoned and the administrator sets a purchase price for the petitioner.
Allows the administrator to validate or reject any claim that is made.
Exempts veteran‑burial lots, lots with known remains, and private cemeteries from the rule.
Codifies the rule into Title 7, Chapter 35 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Owners, heirs, or assignees of cemetery lots
Municipalities and local government units that own cemeteries
Private cemetery operators (who may adopt the rule)

HB527.one_line: HB 527 tightens mail‑election plan posting and review requirements.
HB527.summary: HB 527 amends Montana election law to tighten the written‑plan process for mail elections, requiring plans to be posted on county election websites and adding stricter notice and amendment rules. It also updates school‑election calling procedures to ensure plans are forwarded to county officials. The bill does not create new programs or funds.
changes: Adds a requirement that a mail‑election plan be posted on the county election office’s website (or otherwise publicly noticed) at least 60 days before the election.
Specifies that the plan must include a timetable, a plan for voter‑interface devices, and sample instructions covering postage, deposit locations, and other statutory instructions.
Allows the election administrator to amend the plan up to 35 days before election day, but any amendment must be notified to the Secretary of State in writing.
Imposes a 5‑day review period for the Secretary of State to approve, disapprove, or recommend changes to the plan or its amendments.
If a plan is not posted 60 days before the election, the election automatically defaults to a polling‑place election.

Updates the school‑election calling process so that the resolution calling the election must be transmitted to the county election administrator within 3 days, and the school clerk must forward the approved mail‑plan to the county administrator.

HB530.one_line: HB 530 streamlines domestication for Montana’s LLCs, partnerships, benefit and nonprofit corporations.
HB530.summary: HB 530 modernizes Montana’s domestic‑entity rules by allowing limited‑liability companies, partnerships, benefit corporations, and nonprofit corporations to domesticate—i.e., move from one jurisdiction to another—under a single, streamlined process. The bill sets out the required plan, approvals, and filing steps, and clarifies how interests, liabilities, and records transfer during domestication.
changes: Allows a domestic entity to become a foreign entity (or a foreign entity to become a Montana entity) of the same type if the foreign jurisdiction’s law authorizes domestication.
Requires a written plan of domestication that lists the entity’s name, type, jurisdiction, conversion terms, and proposed public and private organic rules.
Mandates approval of the plan by the entity’s governing body or all voting interest holders, and by the foreign jurisdiction’s law for foreign‑to‑Montana domestications.
Provides procedures for amending or abandoning a domestication plan before it becomes effective, including filing a statement of abandonment with the Secretary of State.
Defines the effective date of the domestication (filing date or a later date up to 90 days), and specifies that the domesticated entity is the same legal entity without interruption.
Clarifies how interests, liabilities, and records transfer, and that the domesticated entity’s public organic record becomes effective upon filing.
affected: Limited‑liability companies, professional LLCs, LLC partnerships, professional LLC partnerships, benefit corporations, nonprofit corporations, and their interest holders in Montana and other jurisdictions
numbers: effective date may be up to 90 days after filing
domestication may involve any type of entity listed in the bill
HB530.effective: not stated (effective upon filing or a later date specified in the statement of domestication)

HB531.one_line: Legislature alone may rule its own procedures; courts barred from review unless constitutional conflict.
HB531.summary: HB 531 declares that only the Montana Legislature may create, enforce, interpret, suspend, repeal, or waive its own procedural rules, and bars courts from reviewing those rules unless they conflict with the state or U.S. constitutions. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Affirms the legislature’s sole constitutional authority over its procedural rules.
Prohibits judicial review or interpretation of those rules except when a rule conflicts with the Montana or U.S. Constitution.
Defines “judicial officer” for this purpose.
Codifies the new authority as part of Title 5, Chapter 5 of the Montana Code.
Effective immediately upon enactment.

HB533.one_line: Insurers must disclose wildfire‑risk scores and related details to insureds within 30 days.
HB533.summary: HB 533 requires insurers that use a wildfire‑risk score in underwriting residential property to disclose the score, its range, creator, creation date, and key adverse factors to the insured or applicant within 30 days of request, enhancing transparency.
changes: Insurers must provide the current wildfire‑risk score of a residential property upon request.
They must disclose the possible score range used by the model.
They must identify the person or entity that created the score.
They must state the date the score was created.
They must explain the key factors that lowered the score.
The insurer must respond in writing no later than 30 days after the request.

HB532.one_line: HB 532 makes abuse, neglect, exploitation, and false reporting of vulnerable adults felony offenses and revises identity‑theft penalties.
HB532.summary: HB 532 creates new felony and misdemeanor offenses for abuse, sexual abuse, neglect, personal degradation, exploitation and false reporting of vulnerable adults, and revises theft‑of‑identity penalties. It also amends many criminal‑procedure and definition statutes and repeals older provisions.
changes: Creates felony for purposeful or knowing abuse, sexual abuse, or neglect of a vulnerable adult (up to 10 years, $10,000 fine).
Creates misdemeanor for negligent abuse (first conviction up to 1 year, $1,000 fine; second conviction becomes felony).
Creates misdemeanor for personal degradation in a private place (first conviction up to 6 months, $500 fine; second conviction becomes felony).
Creates felony for exploitation of an incapacitated person or vulnerable adult (up to 10 years, $10,000 fine).
Creates offense of failure to report or false reporting of abuse/neglect (penalties under 46‑18‑212).
Revises theft‑of‑identity penalties with graduated fines and prison terms based on economic benefit and victim type.
Amends procedural statutes (46‑16‑222, 46‑18‑104, 46‑18‑111, 46‑23‑502, 46‑23‑509, 52‑3‑803) to reflect new definitions and sentencing requirements.
Repeals older statutes 45‑6‑333 (exploitation) and 52‑3‑825 (penalties).
affected: Vulnerable adults (60+ or 18+ with impairment), incapacitated persons, caregivers, employees of care facilities, attorneys, law‑enforcement officers, and anyone who reports or fails to report abuse.

HB534.one_line: Allows county water/sewer districts to exceed system capacity with approved plans and new rules.
HB534.summary: HB 534 lets an eligible county water or sewer district connect to a water or wastewater system even if the connection would exceed the system’s rated capacity, provided a department‑approved development plan authorizes it. The bill amends several water‑utility statutes to give the Department of Environmental Quality rule‑making authority and to clarify definitions and reporting requirements.
changes: Allows county water/sewer districts to add connections beyond rated capacity if a Department‑approved development plan permits it.
Requires the Department to adopt rules governing such connections, including safety, capacity, and environmental impact criteria.
Mandates annual compliance reports from districts with approved plans.
Provides the Department and the Board of Environmental Review with enforcement, investigation, and approval powers over these connections.
Amends definitions in water‑utility statutes to clarify terms such as “eligible county water and/or sewer district,” “development plan,” and “rated capacity.”
Adds provisions for revoking or modifying approved development plans if conditions change or violations occur.

HB535.one_line: Revises Montana’s extradition law to align with federal standards and strengthen habeas‑corpus rights.
HB535.summary: HB 535 updates Montana’s extradition law to align procedures with the federal model, clarifies definitions, tightens warrant and transport processes, and strengthens habeas‑corpus rights for extradited persons.
changes: Replaces the federal Extradition Act timeline for transferring a person after a governor’s warrant with the federal 18 U.S.C. § 3182, effective 12/17/2024; tolls the timeline if a hold exists under § 46‑30‑202.
Adds new definitions (e.g., “executive authority,” “governor’s warrant of arrest and rendition,” “waiver of extradition”) and updates all statutes to use them.
Revises the governor’s authority to issue, recall, or reissue a warrant of arrest and rendition and the procedures for its execution and delivery.
Expands the conditions that must be satisfied before a person can be released on bail after extradition, and requires a judge to inform the person of habeas‑corpus rights before delivery.
Creates a new, detailed process for a waiver of extradition, including judicial oversight and mandatory forwarding of the waiver to the governor’s office.
Adds penalties for officers who willfully disobey habeas‑corpus requirements (misdemeanor, up to $1,000 fine or 6 months imprisonment).
Revises the transport‑cost approval and reimbursement procedures, requiring audit and state‑treasury payment for agents who return fugitives.
Clarifies that no compensation may be paid to public officers for assisting in the return of a fugitive, except as provided in § 46‑30‑411.
Revises the application and requisition process for returning a person to Montana, including required affidavits, indictments, and other documentation.
Adjusts bail and commitment rules for persons awaiting extradition, limiting bail for death‑ or life‑sentence offenses and allowing up to 60‑day extensions.
affected: Montana attorneys general and prosecuting officers
Montana public employees involved in transport

HB538.one_line: Revises Montana’s 9‑1‑1 laws, expanding the advisory council, setting new fees, and tightening grant rules.
HB538.summary: The bill updates Montana’s 9‑1‑1 laws, expanding the advisory council, clarifying fee collection, and tightening grant and funding rules. It adds new council members, sets new fee amounts, and requires the department to adopt detailed rules for allocation, distribution, and grant awards.
changes: Adds 18 members to the 9‑1‑1 advisory council, including representatives from law‑enforcement, public safety, telecommunications, and tribal and local governments
Sets a 75‑cent monthly fee per access line for 9‑1‑1 services and a 25‑cent fee for grant‑related services; establishes a $1 fee per transaction for prepaid wireless 9‑1‑1 services
Mandates the department to adopt rules for fee distribution, grant eligibility, award criteria, and post‑disbursement monitoring
Requires the department to develop a statewide 9‑1‑1 plan that promotes use of existing commercial infrastructure and next‑generation technologies
Allows the department to withhold funding if local or tribal governments fail to comply with information requests
Revises the allocation of the 9‑1‑1 systems account to use 2017 fiscal‑year shares and later census data
Rewrites grant award priorities, giving preference to private telecom providers working with local/tribal governments
affected: Local and tribal governments that host public safety answering points
numbers: July 1 2018 start of new fee regime

HB543.one_line: Repeals sunset on reporting violence against health‑care employees.
HB543.summary: HB 543 repeals the sunset provision that required reporting and disclosure of violence against health‑care employees. The act simply removes that requirement, ending the obligation to file reports. No new programs or penalties are created.
changes: Repeals Section 4, Chapter 516, Laws of 2023, which imposed a reporting deadline for violence against health‑care employees.

HB539.one_line: Mandates daily tally of veto‑override votes and tightens procedural timelines.
HB539.summary: HB 539 amends Montana’s veto‑override procedure, tightening timelines and adding a daily public tally of legislators’ votes. It requires the Secretary of State to conduct and publish the tally, and sets specific deadlines for mailing ballots and counting votes.
changes: Amends §5‑4‑306 to require the Secretary of State to conduct a daily tally of veto‑override votes and publish it on the state website.
Specifies that the Secretary must mail ballots, instructions, and a return envelope to each legislator within 5 working days of receiving a veto message.
Sets a 30‑day period for legislators to return their votes, with the option to mail or fax ballots.
Requires the Secretary to tally all votes within 1 working day after the return deadline and declare the result if two‑thirds of each house vote to override.
Establishes a 15‑day window for the Secretary to conduct the daily tally after ballots are sent.
Maintains that the bill becomes law if two‑thirds or more of each house vote to override.
Leaves the legislature’s ability to reconvene for reconsideration unchanged.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.

HB544.one_line: HB 544 bars retroactive denials, expands biologic coverage for minors, and amends group‑plan rules for retirees and dependents.
HB544.summary: HB 544 revises Montana’s health‑utilization‑review rules, bars most retroactive denials, expands biologic‑therapy coverage for minors, and amends group‑plan provisions for retirees, spouses, and dependents. It also adds detailed coverage requirements for state employee and university plans and sets a January 1, 2026 effective date.
changes: Prohibits insurers from rescinding prior‑approval for a covered service after it has been provided, except for fraud, non‑payment, benefit exhaustion, or mis‑match cases.

Allows treating providers to prescribe biologic therapies to patients under 18 if the drug is FDA‑approved for adults, medically necessary, and supported by peer‑reviewed literature for the patient’s life phase.
Amends 2‑18‑704 to require group plans to allow retirees, surviving spouses, and children to stay covered until Medicare eligibility or until they have equivalent coverage elsewhere.

Adds specific coverage mandates for state employee and Montana university group plans (e.g., inborn errors of metabolism, Down syndrome therapies, fertility preservation, mental‑health, telehealth, well‑child care, and diabetes self‑management).
Requires state plans to provide hospital inpatient coverage for breast‑cancer surgery and to cover diabetic supplies and education per defined minimums.
Imposes COBRA continuation rules for law‑enforcement officers who die or suffer catastrophic injury in the line of duty, including a 4‑month paid period.
affected: Health insurers, health‑plan administrators, treating providers, patients under 18, retirees, surviving spouses and children of deceased members, state employees and university staff, law‑enforcement officers and families

HB549.one_line: Allows distilleries to sell and resell warehouse receipts for aging liquor without transferring ownership.
HB549.summary: HB 549 lets Montana distilleries sell and resell warehouse receipts for aging liquor, allowing third‑party marketing and brokerage of those receipts without giving the buyer ownership of the distillery. It also revises licensing criteria in 16‑4‑401 and sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date.
changes: 1. Distilleries may issue and sell warehouse receipts for liquor stored on their bonded premises; the sale does not transfer ownership of the distillery or its license.
2. Warehouse receipts may be resold by holders to any person, and intermediaries may market, manage, or broker such sales.
3. Receipt holders cannot accept delivery of liquor unless they are legally permitted to receive it.

4. The sale or purchase of receipts does not require any application or report to the Department, provided the liquor remains physically on the distillery’s premises until transferred in bond or otherwise disposed of.
5. Section 16‑4‑401 is amended to clarify licensing eligibility, ownership limits, and financial‑source requirements for various applicant types.
6. The act becomes effective July 1, 2025.

HB553.one_line: HB 553 clarifies training definitions and requires faculty to give students 15 business days to make up missed coursework.
HB553.summary: HB 553 amends Montana’s Military Higher Education Act to clarify definitions of active, inactive, and annual training, and requires faculty to offer make‑up work for coursework missed during such training. Eligible reserve and National Guard students must give 5‑business‑day notice, and faculty must provide at least 15 business days to complete missed work, unless a shorter period is justified.
changes: Defines "inactive duty training" and "annual training" as federally funded duty under Title 10 or 32 U.S.C. (Section 20‑1‑603).
Clarifies that active duty does not include regular weekend or annual training or duty ordered by the service member (Section 20‑1‑603).
Requires eligible students to give at least 5 business‑day notice to faculty before missing coursework due to inactive or annual training (Section 20‑1‑604).
Mandates that faculty, when consistent with accreditation, give the student at least 15 business days to make up missed assignments, exams, midterms, or finals (Section 20‑1‑604).
Allows a shorter make‑up period only if the institution certifies it is necessary for federal aid or graduation requirements, but the period may not be less than 5 business days (Section 20‑1‑604).
Preserves existing rights for eligible students regarding admission, readmission, and grading during active duty (Section 20‑1‑604).
affected: Eligible reserve component members and Montana National Guard members
numbers: 5 business days minimum for shorter make‑up

HB545.one_line: HB 545 creates a temporary MIP task force, grant program, and special fund to improve missing‑person investigations.
HB545.summary: HB 545 establishes a temporary Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons (MIP) Task Force Advisory Council, creates a looping‑in‑native‑communities grant program, and requires detailed reporting to the legislature and state‑tribal relations committee. It also sets up a special revenue‑fund account for MIP‑related funds and authorizes a $1 appropriation for the first biennium.
changes: Creates a temporary MIP Task Force Advisory Council staffed by the Attorney General and appointed members from tribes, law enforcement, and education.
Defines the council’s duties: identify jurisdictional barriers, recommend solutions, improve interagency communication, and administer the looping‑in‑native‑communities grant program.
Establishes a competitive grant program for tribal entities to build a central network for reporting missing Indigenous persons, with specified technical and data‑management criteria.

Mandates the council to submit an annual written report (by July 1) to the state‑tribal relations committee, including database statistics, recovery numbers, and analysis of missing‑person characteristics.
Creates a special revenue‑fund account for MIP funds, allows deposits from gifts, grants, and securities, and requires use of funds only for approved MIP activities.
Provides a $1 appropriation from the account to the Department of Justice for the 2025‑2026 biennium.
Requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally recognized Montana tribes of the act.
Includes coordination provisions with House Bill 83 to audit the account and set up the appropriation.
