HB561.one_line: Repeals all state licensing requirements for itinerant vendors.
HB561.summary: HB 561 removes the state’s requirement that itinerant vendors obtain a county license, along with all related fees, application procedures, and enforcement provisions. The bill simply repeals the cited Montana Code sections; it does not create new rules or programs.
changes: Repeals sections 7‑21‑2301 through 7‑21‑2310 of the Montana Code Annotated that govern itinerant vendor licensing.
affected: Itinerant vendors operating in Montana counties.

HB562.one_line: HB 562 amends reporting, data‑sharing, and administrative rules across several state agencies, with no new programs or crimes.
HB562.summary: HB 562 amends a dozen Montana statutes to clarify reporting requirements, expand data‑sharing for unemployment and water resources, and create new administrative procedures, while repealing four reporting statutes. The bill does not create new programs or criminal offenses.
changes: Amends 15‑70‑433 to require biodiesel distributors and retailers to file quarterly statements and receive refunds for Montana‑produced biodiesel; the department must report biennially to the transportation interim committee.

Amends 15‑70‑450 to allow the department and Indian tribes to negotiate cooperative agreements to avoid dual motor‑fuel taxation and requires reporting of negotiations to the transportation interim committee.
Amends 17‑1‑102 to establish a uniform accounting system for all state agencies, with multi‑level expenditure reporting and mandatory encumbrance reporting to the budget office and legislature.
Amends 37‑1‑107 to require the department to convene joint meetings of related professional boards every two years and report attendance to the economic affairs interim committee.

Amends 39‑51‑706 to mandate weekly checks of unemployment rolls against the corrections list and national new‑hire directory, with authority to enter MOUs and report to the economic affairs interim committee.
Amends 53‑6‑116 to allow the department of public health and human services to develop and contract for Medicaid managed‑care and capitated systems, subject to legislative finance committee review.
Amends 60‑3‑304 and 60‑3‑309 to clarify funding and maintenance responsibilities for shared‑use paths, including allocation formulas and district‑level use requirements.

Amends 61‑10‑154 to authorize the department of transportation to adopt motor‑carrier safety standards, designate peace officers, and enforce those standards, reporting enforcement to the transportation interim committee.

Amends 85‑1‑203 to require the department to develop a comprehensive, basin‑wide state water plan with public hearings, advisory councils, and periodic updates, and to report the plan to the legislature.
Amends 85‑1‑501 to require the department to study the feasibility of small‑scale hydroelectric projects on its water projects and report findings to relevant interim committees.
Amends 87‑2‑702 to impose restrictions on special licenses for bear, mountain lion, and other game, and to require biennial reporting to the environmental quality council.

Amends 90‑1‑182 to allow the department of commerce to conduct socioeconomic impact reviews of federal land‑management proposals on behalf of local governments and report to the local government interim committee.
Repeals sections 5‑12‑208, 75‑1‑314, 77‑1‑820, and 77‑2‑366, eliminating their reporting requirements.
affected: State agencies and university system units
Local governments reviewing federal land proposals
numbers: 20% of optional registration fees to transportation

HB563.one_line: Protects complaint filing and cooperation; voids restrictive contracts; defines retaliation as unprofessional conduct.
HB563.summary: HB 563 protects individuals who file or cooperate in licensing‑complaint investigations by voiding any contract that bars such activity and defines retaliation as unprofessional conduct. The law takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Contracts that prohibit or discourage filing a complaint under §37‑1‑308 or §37‑1‑402 are voided.
Contracts that bar an individual from participating in or cooperating with an investigation of such a complaint are voided.
Licensees who are parties to a violating contract are deemed to have engaged in unprofessional conduct.
Licensees who retaliate against a person filing a complaint under §37‑1‑308 or §37‑1‑402 are deemed to have engaged in unprofessional conduct.
General waivers of claims cannot be interpreted to apply to complaints under §37‑1‑308 or §37‑1‑402.
The provisions are codified as part of Title 37, Chapter 1, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
The act does not alter rights, duties, penalties, or proceedings that already existed before its effective date.
affected: Individuals filing or cooperating in licensing‑complaint investigations

HB566.one_line: Reassigns veterans’ long‑term‑care study to the Veterans’ Affairs Division and adds stakeholder input and reporting.
HB566.summary: HB 566 re‑designates the Montana Veterans’ Affairs Division as the lead agency for the decennial long‑term‑care needs study of veterans, adds stakeholder participation, requires a study plan and budget, and updates reporting requirements.
changes: Shifts primary responsibility for the decennial veterans’ long‑term‑care needs study from the Department of Public Health and Human Services to the Montana Veterans’ Affairs Division.

Mandates the Veterans’ Affairs Division to develop a study plan and budget estimate before the census data are available and submit them to the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee.
Requires the division to include a personal survey of veterans (online, paper, focus groups) and to evaluate existing veterans’ home services and cemetery needs.
Creates an advisory committee of stakeholders (veterans’ outreach orgs, legislators, caregivers, local groups) to assist with the survey.
Adds reporting obligations: at least one interim update to the committee during the study and a detailed final report with recommendations.
Amends sections 10‑2‑901, 10‑2‑902, and 10‑2‑903 of the Montana Code to reflect these changes.
No new funding or criminal offense is created.
No fiscal appropriation is specified in the bill.
affected: Legislators and local groups involved in veteran services
State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee

HB567.one_line: HB 567 expands school‑district collaboration and rewards county‑wide sharing with a 50 % educator‑payment boost.
HB567.summary: HB 567 expands how Montana school districts can collaborate, allowing broader agreements—including with private entities—and rewards county‑wide cooperation with a 50 % boost to the total quality educator payment. It amends the law to clarify fund transfers, dissolution terms, and eligibility for the incentive.
changes: Amends §20‑3‑363 to broaden multidistrict agreements, add private‑entity participation, and set a 3‑year maximum term.
Rewrites §20‑3‑363 (1)(b) to permit culturally rooted instruction and Indian immersion programs.
Adds §20‑3‑363 (5) that gives districts a 50 % increase in the total quality educator payment if they meet a county‑wide resource‑sharing goal beginning FY 2027.
Revises §20‑9‑306 to define the total quality educator payment and to link the incentive to the new §20‑3‑363 (5).
Clarifies interlocal cooperative fund transfer limits and prohibits use of retirement or debt‑service funds.
Allows districts to enter additional multidistrict agreements beyond the county‑wide one and to form multicounty regional agreements.
Defines “multidistrict cooperative” to include public and private entities that meet the section’s requirements.
affected: Private entities that may join agreements
numbers: 50 % increase in total quality educator payment

HB554.one_line: Amends wolf delisting rules to allow special kill permits and game/furbearer status after protection is deemed unnecessary.
HB554.summary: HB 554 amends the state’s wolf‑delisting procedure so that, once the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service removes the gray wolf from the endangered list, the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (DFWP) can delist the wolf and manage it as a species in need of management.  The bill allows the DFWP, with the Department of Livestock, to issue special kill permits for livestock protection and to regulate wolves as game or furbearers only after a formal determination that protection is no longer needed.
changes: Amends §87‑5‑131 to authorize the DFWP to delist the gray wolf when the U.S. federal list is removed and to manage it as a species in need of management until a commission determination is made
Provides that the DFWP and the Department of Livestock may control wolves for livestock protection under a jointly approved wolf‑management plan
Requires any approved wolf‑management plan to allow issuance of special kill permits (shoot‑on‑sight authorizations) to landowners or public‑land permittees who have experienced livestock depredation
Allows the commission to declare the wolf a game animal or furbearer only after the wolf no longer needs protection as a species in need of management
Does not create a new state program or criminal offense; it merely changes the regulatory framework for wolf management
Does not alter funding or budget allocations
Does not affect other wildlife species or general wildlife policy
The bill does not specify an effective date; it takes effect upon enactment
affected: Landowners and ranchers who may receive special kill permits
DFWP and Department of Livestock staff involved in wolf management
Commission members who will make the game/furbearer determination

HB571.one_line: Prohibits using ADS‑B data to calculate fees for Montana aircraft.
HB571.summary: HB 571 bars any entity from using ADS‑B data to calculate or collect fees from aircraft owners or operators in Montana. It defines the aircraft and ADS‑B terms and codifies the prohibition within the state’s aeronautics statutes.
changes: Prohibits use of ADS‑B In or Out data for fee calculation or collection within Montana.
Applies only to aircraft with gross weight ≤ 9,000 lb operating under 14 CFR Part 91.
Does not alter any other aeronautics rules.
Codifies the prohibition as part of Title 67, Chapter 1, Part 1.
No new programs, funds, or offenses are created.
affected: Private companies, government divisions, and corporations that might use ADS‑B data for fee purposes

HB568.one_line: Mandates a state study on non‑resident hunting impacts, to be completed by Dec 2026.
HB568.summary: HB 568 requires the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks to study how non‑resident hunters affect deer, elk, upland game, and waterfowl hunting in Montana, then publish a report with findings and recommendations by December 1, 2026. The act is effective immediately and expires December 31, 2026.
changes: Creates a state‑wide study of non‑resident hunting impacts on deer, elk, upland game birds, and waterfowl.
Mandates use of data such as hunter days, harvest reports, land use, population trends, and licensing.
Requires the department to publish a public report that includes assessment, methodology, and identified issues for legislative and agency consideration.
Sets a completion deadline of December 1, 2026, with the act terminating December 31, 2026.
The study’s scope covers each Fish and Wildlife Commission administrative region.
No new licensing rules or programs are established; the bill only directs a study.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Montana landowners and public land managers
numbers: 40‑year review period referenced in the preamble

HB572.one_line: HB 572 expands prison‑industry training, raises construction limits, and revises inmate wages and restitution rules.
HB572.summary: HB 572 expands and modernizes Montana’s prison‑industries program, adding educational coursework, raising the cap on inmate‑built construction projects, and allowing the state to offer vocational training that meets private‑sector demand. It also creates a pre‑apprenticeship program, relaxes contract‑network requirements, and revises wage, restitution, and benefits rules for inmates.
changes: Adds educational programming to the prison‑industries curriculum and allows the department to contract with public and private educational entities
Increases the maximum aggregate value of construction projects inmates may build from $200,000 to $600,000 and limits those projects to prison grounds
Creates a pre‑apprenticeship training program in partnership with labor unions and building‑trade representatives
Permits the Montana Correctional Enterprises (MCE) program to provide vocational programs that support private‑market demand and to sell products through dealer networks
Eliminates the requirement that all products and services be supplied through contracts and dealer networks

Revises wage and benefit provisions: inmates in federally certified programs must be paid at least federal minimum wage, 15% of wages may be collected for restitution or victim‑compensation, and room‑and‑board charges are deposited into an enterprise fund
Revises Sections 53‑30‑131 and 53‑30‑132 to reflect the new educational and vocational scope, wage rules, and restitution collection
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and terminates the pre‑apprenticeship mandate on December 30, 2026
affected: Private‑sector employers interested in MCE products
State and local government agencies purchasing MCE goods

HB573.one_line: Revises, shortens, and adds a new grant program for transformational learning in Montana schools.
HB573.summary: HB 573 revises Montana’s transformational‑learning statutes, shortens the existing grant program’s end date, and creates a new Phase II grant program for the most innovative districts. It sets detailed application, reporting, and funding rules for both the original and Phase II programs and requires the superintendent to award and manage the new grants.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1601 to clarify definitions of proficiency‑based and transformational learning and to affirm their constitutionality.
Rewrites §20‑7‑1602 to establish a 4‑year transitional funding and flexibility package for qualifying districts, including a 50 % aid payment and limits on total aid (≤25 % of total payments).

Creates a new Phase II grant program (Section 3) administered by the superintendent, allowing up to five districts to receive grants (90 % of appropriated funds) to expand district‑wide transformational learning.
Sets application, reporting, and reporting‑to‑committee requirements for Phase II grantees and requires a joint report by September 1 , 2028.
Terminates the existing grant program on June 30 , 2026 and the Phase II program on December 31 , 2028.
Provides coordination language with House Bill 2 to use its appropriation for the Phase II program.
Effective July 1 , 2025.
affected: School districts applying for or receiving transformational‑learning aid or Phase II grants
District teachers and staff participating in transformational learning
Local tax levies and flexibility funds
numbers: 10 % of appropriated funds for technical assistance

HB574.one_line: Montana creates a state‑certified behavioral‑health clinic program with reimbursement, reporting, and incentive rules.
HB574.summary: Montana will create a state‑run program to certify community behavioral‑health clinics, set reimbursement rules, monitor quality, and offer incentives for high performance. The Department of Public Health and Human Services will oversee certification, billing, reporting, and evaluation, with an immediate effective date.
changes: Establishes a certification program for community behavioral‑health clinics by Oct. 1, 2026, subject to funding.
Sets detailed criteria for reimbursing clinics under the Healthy Montana Kids Plan and Medicaid, including a prospective payment system and bi‑annual rate rebasing.
Mandates monitoring and evaluation of clinic services, quality measures, fraud prevention, and cost‑savings analysis, with quarterly reports to state committees.
Requires clinics to provide specific services (case management, peer/family support, outreach, urgent care, diagnostic evaluation) and to coordinate with other providers.
Imposes billing practices: private insurance billed first, Medicaid last, sliding fee scale, and no refusal of care for those unable to pay.
Creates an incentive program for clinics that achieve exceptional quality outcomes, with rules to be adopted by the department.
Codifies the provisions into Title 53, Chapter 21, Part 10 of the Montana Statutes.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
State committees (Children, Families, Health & Human Services; Health & Human Services Budget)

HB575.one_line: HB 575 broadens public‑defender assignments and allows representation in parent‑termination cases.
HB575.summary: HB 575 amends Montana’s public‑defender statute to broaden the types of cases in which a court may order a public defender, allows a public defender to represent a parent in a child‑termination proceeding, and lets a public defender serve on a treatment‑court team. The bill also clarifies who may act as a special advocate or guardian ad litem.
changes: Expands the list of proceedings that trigger a court‑ordered public‑defender assignment, adding parent‑termination and various involuntary‑commitment cases
Authorizes a public defender to represent a parent in a proceeding to involuntarily terminate that parent’s rights
Permits a public defender to serve as a member of a treatment‑court team
Restricts public defenders from acting as court‑appointed special advocates or guardians ad litem in youth‑court and abuse‑and‑neglect cases, except when a private attorney is separately contracted
Provides that a private attorney contracted under 47‑1‑121 may serve as a special advocate or guardian ad litem if no conflict exists
Amends §47‑1‑104 to incorporate the above changes and sets an effective date of July 1 2025
affected: Courts handling the newly listed cases
Private attorneys contracted to the public‑defender system

HB576.one_line: HB 576 reallocates tobacco‑settlement and special‑revenue funds to expand Medicaid and children’s health services.
HB576.summary: HB 576 revises Montana’s Medicaid and health‑support funding rules, allowing a portion of tobacco‑settlement proceeds and state special‑revenue funds to be used for children’s health insurance, Medicaid waivers, and services for the aged, blind, or disabled. It amends the statutes that govern how those funds are deposited, allocated, and matched to federal programs. The bill does not create a new program but changes the use of existing revenue streams.
changes: Redefines the purpose of the tobacco‑settlement account to include funding for children’s health insurance and services for the aged, blind, or disabled.
Specifies that 32 % of yearly tobacco‑settlement proceeds go to a state special‑revenue account for tobacco‑prevention programs, and 17 % for matching federal funds for Medicaid and related services.
Adds a requirement that unappropriated funds in the special‑revenue account be transferred to the trust fund after two years.

Amends the special‑revenue account statute to allow its money to be used only for expanding Medicaid enrollment, matching federal funds for children’s health insurance, Medicaid waivers, and services for infants and toddlers with disabilities.
Provides that the department may reduce eligibility requirements if the account lacks sufficient funds.
Allows private‑nature programs to be funded through contracts under the tobacco‑settlement account.
affected: Providers of home‑visiting and early‑childhood services
State Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: 2 years before transfer to trust fund

HB578.one_line: HB 578 removes offender financial consideration from restitution, lets victims submit loss data to probation, and amends related criminal statutes.
HB578.summary: HB 578 revises Montana’s restitution rules so that a court no longer considers an offender’s financial resources when ordering restitution, allows victims to submit loss information to a probation officer without a court order, and updates several criminal‑law sections to align with these changes. The bill also clarifies when courts may grant petitions to modify restitution and amends related sentencing and criminal‑mischief provisions.
changes: Removes consideration of an offender’s financial resources and future ability to pay from the restitution calculation in sentencing.
Permits victims to provide evidence of pecuniary loss or property loss to a probation officer outside a court order.
Allows courts to grant petitions to revise restitution after the sentence is imposed, subject to procedural limits.
Amends sections 45‑5‑206, 45‑5‑503, 45‑5‑507, 45‑5‑627, 45‑6‑101, 46‑18‑101, 46‑18‑242, and 46‑18‑246 to reflect the new restitution framework and related sentencing policies.
Adds procedural requirements for restitution hearings and victim notice under 46‑18‑246.

Adjusts sentencing guidelines for partner/family‑member assault, sexual intercourse without consent, incest, ritual abuse of a minor, and criminal mischief to incorporate restitution and counseling requirements.
numbers: $1,000 maximum fine for partner/family assault first offense
$10,000 maximum fine for certain sexual offenses
$50,000 maximum fine for certain sexual offenses
$50,000 maximum fine for certain sexual offenses

HB580.one_line: Clarifies abandonment rules, protects rights used for conservation or drought plans, and adds reporting requirements.
HB580.summary: HB 580 amends Montana’s water‑right abandonment rules to clarify when a right is considered abandoned, especially during droughts, and gives the Department of Natural Resources rule‑making authority. It preserves rights that are reduced or unused under conservation or drought plans and limits the presumption of abandonment for non‑use of 10 years when water is available.
changes: Amends §85‑2‑404 to specify that abandonment occurs only when an appropriator intentionally ceases use or fails to meet terms; otherwise the right does not expire.
Adds a 10‑year non‑use presumption of abandonment when water is available, but excludes non‑use caused by conservation agreements or set‑asides.
Exempts reductions or cessations during droughts that comply with a drought plan and occur in a county in D1 or worse drought, requiring a report to the Department by Dec 30 of that year.
Clarifies that leases or temporary changes of appropriation rights do not constitute abandonment.
States that the new rules do not apply to existing rights until they are finally determined under part 2 of the chapter.

HB582.one_line: HB 582 expands sentencing options, clarifies credit for pre‑sentencing time, and tightens revocation rules.
HB582.summary: HB 582 revises Montana’s criminal‑sentencing rules, expanding how courts can defer or suspend sentences, clarifying credit for time served, and tightening revocation procedures. It also limits credit for time spent in custody that is not directly tied to the offense for which a person is convicted.
changes: Amends §46‑18‑201 to broaden deferment and suspension options, add limits on supervision periods for sexual, homicide, violent, drug‑related, and other felony offenders, and allow credit for pre‑sentencing incarceration tied to the same conduct.

Rewrites §46‑18‑203 to set detailed procedures for revocation hearings, including notice, rights to counsel, and conditions under which a suspended or deferred sentence may be continued, modified, or revoked.

Revises §46‑18‑403 to clarify when and how incarcerated persons receive credit for days spent in custody before conviction, tying credit to the same conduct and preventing double credit for multiple sentences.
Adds new sentencing options such as community corrections placement, chemical‑treatment commitments, and various restrictions (e.g., home arrest, community service).
Requires courts to consider restitution, license suspension, and registration requirements for sexual/violent offenders.
Sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date and applies only to offenders sentenced on or after that date.
affected: District courts, sentencing judges, probation/parole officers, correctional facilities, offenders sentenced to felony or misdemeanor convictions, and victims of violent or drug‑related crimes.

HB584.one_line: HB 584 lets the Board set anesthesia rules, issue permits, and charge fees for dental sedation.
HB584.summary: HB 584 authorizes the Montana Board of Dentistry to set standards, issue permits, and conduct inspections for dentists who administer anesthesia. It also allows temporary permits and establishes fee authority, while adding detailed definitions of sedation levels.
changes: 1. Grants the Board of Dentistry authority to adopt rules on qualifications, education, and equipment for deep sedation, general anesthesia, moderate sedation, and minimal sedation.
2. Requires an initial inspection of each facility providing these services, with reinspections no more than every five years.
3. Gives the Board discretion to charge application, renewal, initial inspection, and reinspection fees.
4. Allows the Board to issue temporary permits (up to 120 days or until inspection) and extend them upon approval.
5. Adds comprehensive definitions of anesthesia terms and expands the definition of “practicing dentistry” to include anesthetic administration.
numbers: fees to be set by Board

HB585.one_line: Sets a $39.56 Medicaid conversion factor for PT, SLP, OT and allows yearly CPI‑based adjustments.
HB585.summary: HB 585 sets the Medicaid reimbursement conversion factor for physical therapists, speech‑language pathologists, and occupational therapists at $39.56 for FY 2026 and allows the Department to adjust it each year to match the medical‑care CPI. It also updates definitions in the state code and codifies the rule in Title 53.
changes: Establishes a fixed conversion factor of $39.56 for FY 2026 for the specified providers.
Authorizes the Department of Public Health and Human Services to raise the conversion factor each subsequent fiscal year to reflect the consumer price index for medical care.
Amends Section 53‑6‑124, MCA, to define terms such as “conversion factor,” “policy adjuster,” and “relative value unit.”
Codifies the new conversion factor rule as part of Title 53, Chapter 6, Part 1.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB586.one_line: HB 586 tightens child‑seat‑belt rules and expands vehicle exemptions in Montana.
HB586.summary: HB 586 updates Montana’s child‑seat‑belt rules, tightening age and weight limits for child safety restraint systems and adding new vehicle exemptions. It clarifies definitions, expands the list of vehicles that are exempt, and allows medical exemptions for children who cannot be placed in a restraint.
changes: Revises §61‑9‑419 to define "properly restrained," "booster seat," and related terms.

Rewrites §61‑9‑420 to set specific age/weight thresholds: under‑6 yrs < 60 lb, 2‑4 yrs rear‑ or forward‑facing harness, 4‑8 yrs forward‑facing harness or booster, 9 yrs or taller/weighted out of booster use adult belt.
Adds a rule that the department may exempt a child with a physical/medical condition from the restraint requirement.

Rewrites §61‑9‑421 to list vehicle types exempt from the new age/weight rules (motorbus, motorhome, school bus, taxi, farm tractor, bicycle, moped, quadricycle, motorcycle, motor‑driven cycle, ambulance, other emergency vehicle, vehicles with two seats and two occupants ≥4 yrs, and emergencies threatening life).
Requires all child safety restraint systems to be installed, adjusted, and used per manufacturer instructions and federal standards.
Establishes that the department will set standards and rules to enforce these provisions.
affected: Children under 9 years old in passenger vehicles
Vehicle operators of the exempted vehicle types

HB587.one_line: HB 587 tightens mine‑reclamation permitting and data requirements, adding a retroactive window and contingent voidness clause.
HB587.summary: HB 587 amends Montana’s mine‑reclamation statutes to tighten permitting, expand required hydrologic and geologic data, clarify definitions, and give the Department of Environmental Quality rule‑making authority. The bill also creates a retroactive application window and a contingent‑voidness clause tied to federal disapproval. The changes are largely procedural and definitional, with no new program or criminal offense created.
changes: Amends Section 82‑4‑203 to add detailed definitions for terms such as “adjacent area,” “material damage,” and “hydrologic balance.”

Rewrites Section 82‑4‑222 to require permit applicants to submit extensive plans, maps, cross‑sections, hydrologic impact determinations, and monitoring plans, plus insurance certificates and detailed reclamation plans.
affected: Mine operators, surface owners, and the Department of Environmental Quality.

HB588.one_line: HB 588 regulates motorized scooters as bicycles, setting safety, registration, and racing rules.
HB588.summary: HB 588 defines motorized scooters and applies most bicycle‑law rules to them, including licensing, safety equipment, and roadway use. It also amends registration, racing, and head‑gear requirements for motorized scooters and related vehicles.
changes: Defines “motorized scooter” as a vehicle without a seat that may be propelled by muscle or an independent power source up to 30 mph, excluding electrically assisted bicycles.
Applies bicycle traffic laws to motorized scooters, making them subject to the same rights and duties as drivers of other vehicles, except where specifically exempted.
Requires motorized scooters to carry front white lamps, rear red lamps or reflectors, and a brake that stops within 25 ft from 10 mph, and mandates helmet‑mounted lights if no front lamp is used.
Prohibits riding motorized scooters on sidewalks or crosswalks unless on a designated bicycle lane or highway shoulder, and limits moped or scooter use on sidewalks to human propulsion only.

Allows state or local authorities to approve highway racing events for bicycles, mopeds, or motorized scooters under safety conditions, and permits race participants to be exempt from ordinary traffic laws if control is adequate.
Requires riders and passengers under 18 on motorcycles, mopeds, motorized scooters, or quadricycles to wear protective headgear unless the vehicle is an enclosed autocycle.
Amends the grace‑period registration rule (Section 61‑3‑317) to allow temporary registration permits for newly purchased vehicles, including motorized scooters, during the 40‑day period.
Clarifies that violations of the new motorized‑scooter rules are misdemeanors (Section 61‑8‑601).

HB589.one_line: HB 589 creates a new training council, expands approved academies, and sets a 1‑year deadline for peace‑officer basic training or equivalency.
HB589.summary: HB 589 revises Montana’s peace‑officer education and certification rules, creating a new Public Safety Officer Standards and Training Council that can approve basic training courses and set equivalency requirements. It expands the list of qualifying academies, clarifies background‑check and health‑screening standards, and establishes a 1‑year window for new officers to complete basic training or equivalency courses, with provisions for extensions and probationary certification.
changes: Creates the Montana Public Safety Officer Standards and Training Council, a quasi‑judicial board that can hire staff and adopt rules for officer training and certification

Expands the list of approved training providers to include the Montana Law Enforcement Academy and any accredited college or university law‑enforcement academy whose curriculum is approved by the council
Sets a 1‑year deadline for new or returning officers to complete the council‑approved basic course or an equivalency course, with up to 180‑day extensions for good cause
Defines detailed background‑check, mental‑health, physical‑health, oral‑exam, and driver‑license requirements for appointment
Requires a 1‑year probationary period before a council may issue a peace‑officer basic certificate
Imposes misdemeanor penalties for officers who act while their certification is suspended or revoked
Provides that the council may adopt rules under the Montana Administrative Procedure Act to implement these standards
Effective immediately upon passage
affected: County sheriffs, city mayors, and other appointing authorities
Montana Law Enforcement Academy and other accredited academies
Montana Public Safety Officer Standards and Training Council
numbers: 6‑month jail term for violating certification rules

HB590.one_line: Health carriers must build CMS‑standard APIs and share rapid test results with patients, with commissioner‑approved extensions.
HB590.summary: HB 590 requires Montana health carriers to build and keep specific electronic interfaces that let patients, providers, and payers exchange health data. It also mandates rapid release of certain test results to patients and allows the commissioner to grant extensions.
changes: Health carriers must establish patient‑access, provider‑directory, provider‑access, payer‑to‑payer, and prior‑authorization APIs in line with federal CMS standards.
APIs must be available to the carrier’s insureds and contracted providers by the earliest CMS‑mandated dates for each type.
Carriers may request a written extension if compliance would be unduly burdensome or cause economic harm; the commissioner must approve in writing and publish the decision.
Providers cannot engage in information blocking when ordering lab tests, except as specified in §2.
Certain pathology, radiology, genetic, HIV, and hepatitis test results must be disclosed to patients within 72 hours of finalization or upon provider request.
The act codifies its provisions into Montana’s Title 33 (health carriers) and Title 50 (privacy).

HB591.one_line: Montana will observe a mandatory Celebrate Freedom Week with instruction and recitation of founding documents.
HB591.summary: Montana will officially observe a “Celebrate Freedom Week” during the last full week of September in public schools, requiring at least three hours of instruction on the Declaration of Independence, the U.S. Constitution, and the Montana Constitution, and mandating that students in grades 3‑12 recite a specified passage. School districts must adopt policies to carry out these commemorative activities, with options for parental, conscientious‑objection, or foreign‑representative exemptions. The law takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Adds “Freedom Week” to the list of commemorative days in §20‑1‑306, MCA
Requires all districts to conduct appropriate exercises during Freedom Week
Mandates a minimum of 3 hours of instruction on founding documents during Freedom Week
Requires students in grades 3‑12 to recite a specified passage from the Declaration of Independence
Allows exemptions for parental requests, conscientious objections, or children of certain foreign representatives
Requires district trustees to adopt a policy to ensure effective conduct of the exercises

HB592.one_line: HB 592 expands sponsor contact, electronic comment, and small‑business impact rules in Montana’s rulemaking process.
HB592.summary: HB 592 amends Montana’s Administrative Procedure Act to give agencies more notice and input from the primary sponsor of legislation that a rule implements, expands electronic comment procedures, requires a formal interested‑persons list, and tightens committee objection and small‑business impact rules. The bill does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Agencies must email the primary sponsor of any legislation they are implementing before drafting a rule, provide dates and a timeline for comment, and explain why sponsor comments are not adopted; the sponsor is treated as an interested person.
Rulemaking notices and comments may now be submitted and received electronically; agencies must publish the electronic address and may not charge a fee for electronic documents.
Each agency must maintain an interested‑persons list, notify persons of the list within 3 days of notice publication, and allow hard‑copy requests.
Small‑business impact analyses are required for rules that significantly affect small businesses, with required identification of affected classes and alternative methods to mitigate impacts.

The administrative rule review committee’s objections (informal or formal) must be documented and can delay adoption until the end of the legislative session or until the committee resolves the objection.
The bill amends several MCA sections (2‑3‑301, 2‑4‑110, 2‑4‑111, 2‑4‑302, 2‑4‑305, 2‑4‑306, 2‑4‑406, 37‑1‑122) to implement these new requirements.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to rule proposals published on or after its effective date.
The bill does not create a new state program, office, fund, or criminal offense.
affected: State agencies, legislative sponsors, interested persons, small businesses, the administrative rule review committee

HB595.one_line: HB 595 creates a correctional education program and sets instructor qualifications.
HB595.summary: HB 595 establishes a correctional education program that offers high‑school equivalency and adult basic‑education courses to inmates and sets minimum qualifications for instructors.
changes: Creates a Montana Correctional Education Program within the Department of Corrections
Requires the program to provide high‑school equivalency and adult basic‑education courses
Sets instructor eligibility: 18+, good moral character, and proof of at least one of: associate degree, bachelor’s degree, out‑of‑state teaching certificate, or prior teaching/military training
Allows the Department to adopt policies determining inmate eligibility for the program
Codifies the provisions into Title 53, Chapter 30, Part 1 of the Montana Code
Effective July 1, 2025
affected: Potential instructors of correctional education programs
Montana Department of Public Instruction (via policy adoption)

HB599.one_line: HB 599 expands parental rights over school data collection and requires notification for health screenings.
HB599.summary: HB 599 expands parental control over school data collection, requiring opt‑in/opt‑out options and parent notification for health surveys and screenings. It amends the state’s parental‑rights statute to clarify consent and notification duties for schools and other government entities.
changes: Amends §40‑6‑701 to codify parents’ rights to direct a child’s education, health, and privacy decisions;
Requires schools to obtain parent consent before biometric, blood/DNA, audio/video recordings unless specific exceptions apply;
Creates opt‑out and opt‑in provisions for non‑PII and PII‑based evaluations, surveys, and data collection;
Mandates parent notification of any physical or mental‑health screening or survey and of any resulting concerns;
Prohibits government employees from encouraging a child to withhold information from parents or withholding relevant health information;
Allows parents to seek relief and attorney fees in administrative or judicial actions when rights are violated.
affected: School districts and other government entities that collect student data

HB600.one_line: Schools may keep and use stock albuterol for emergencies, with liability limits and reporting requirements.
HB600.summary: The bill amends Montana’s emergency‑medication law to allow schools to keep a supply of stock albuterol and to let students self‑administer asthma or allergy medication with parental and medical approval. It sets liability limits for schools, requires training and reporting, and establishes protocols for use and documentation.
changes: Amends §20‑5‑420 to define key terms (anaphylaxis, asthma, authorized personnel, medication, etc.) and to allow students with asthma or severe allergies to possess or self‑administer prescribed medication with written parental and medical authorization.
Authorizes public and nonpublic schools to maintain a stock supply of albuterol (including disposable spacers) for emergency use, requiring a prescription, a protocol, and secure storage.
Requires schools to train authorized personnel annually in asthma education and to develop a protocol for administering stock albuterol, including when to call 9‑1‑1.
Imposes liability limits on schools and their employees, except for gross negligence or intentional misconduct, and requires parents to sign indemnification statements.
Mandates schools to inform parents about stock albuterol availability and to provide the protocol on request.
Requires schools to document each use of stock albuterol and to report to the Department of Public Health and Human Services within 3 days, plus an annual summary report.
Exempts youth correctional facilities from the provisions.
Effective July 1 2025.
