affected: Students with asthma or severe allergies
School nurses and other authorized staff

HB601.one_line: Mandates a Medicaid community assister portal with core and optional services by May 2026.
HB601.summary: HB 601 requires the Montana Department of Health and Human Services to create an online portal by May 1, 2026 that lets community assisters help Medicaid applicants and enrollees with applications, document submission, and status tracking. The portal will also let applicants designate assisters and allow assisters to view and update information on the applicants’ behalf.
changes: Creates a mandatory online portal for Medicaid community assisters by May 1, 2026.
Requires the portal to provide core functions: review application status, view notices, report eligibility changes, view required actions, and update contact info.
Allows optional functions: submit applications or upload verification documents on the applicant’s behalf.
Mandates that applicants can designate one or more community assisters through the portal.
Defines “community assister” as any person or organization that helps individuals apply for Montana Medicaid.
Codifies the portal provisions as part of Title 53, Chapter 6, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
No funding or cost details are provided in the bill.
affected: Montana Department of Health and Human Services

HB602.one_line: Mandates board notice and public comment for non‑renewal of non‑tenure teachers for financial reasons.
HB602.summary: School districts must notify the board and the public by June 1 when a non‑tenure teacher is proposed for non‑renewal due to financial reasons, and the board must add the proposal to the next public meeting agenda and allow public comment. The bill also clarifies that such non‑renewals are “without cause” and amends the teacher‑notification rules in §20‑4‑206.
changes: Requires written notice to the board by June 1 when a district administrator proposes to non‑renew a non‑tenure teacher for financial reasons.
Mandates that the proposed non‑renewal be placed on the agenda of the next public school‑board meeting and that the public be given an opportunity to comment.
Defines a non‑renewal for financial reasons as a non‑renewal without cause under §20‑4‑206.
Amends §20‑4‑206 to specify June 1 notice, 20‑day acceptance, and that the board may non‑renew with or without cause after notice.
Leaves collective‑bargaining agreements in place; the new rules do not override negotiated terms.
Effective July 1 2025.

HB603.one_line: HB 603 removes the attorney‑membership requirement from Montana’s quasi‑judicial boards.
HB603.summary: HB 603 removes the statutory requirement that at least one member of any Montana quasi‑judicial board be a licensed attorney. The bill amends the statutes that create several boards—state compensation insurance, hard‑rock mining impact, pardons and parole, transportation, livestock loss, fish and wildlife, and state parks and recreation—to allow a non‑lawyer member while preserving all other qualifications and procedures.
changes: 1. Deletes the attorney‑membership requirement from §2‑15‑124 and all boards that cite it.

2. Amends the statutes for the state compensation insurance fund, hard‑rock mining impact board, pardons and parole board, transportation commission, livestock loss board, fish and wildlife commission, and state parks and recreation board to explicitly state that a non‑lawyer may serve.
3. Maintains all other appointment, confirmation, compensation, and quorum rules for those boards.
4. Provides that the changes apply only to vacancies occurring after the effective date and do not affect current members.
5. Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.

HB610.one_line: Eliminates prior‑auth for FDA‑approved antipsychotics under Medicaid for adults 18+.
HB610.summary: HB 610 removes the requirement that the Department of Public Health and Human Services obtain prior authorization for Medicaid‑covered antipsychotic drugs for adults 18 and older. The change is limited to drugs approved by the FDA for their indicated uses and takes effect 30 days after passage.
changes: Discontinues prior‑authorization requirements for all FDA‑approved antipsychotic drugs under Medicaid for adults 18+.
Does not alter coverage rules for drugs that are not eligible under 42 U.S.C. 1396r‑8.
The change applies only to claims submitted on or after the effective date.
No new programs, funds, or offenses are created.
The Department may still deny coverage for drugs not meeting federal eligibility criteria.
The act does not affect other Medicaid services or non‑antipsychotic drugs.
affected: Pharmacy benefit managers and providers of antipsychotic drugs
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB606.one_line: HB 606 modernizes reorganization rules, expands superintendent duties, and adds building‑reserve levy authority for school districts.
HB606.summary: HB 606 revises Montana’s school‑district reorganization laws to streamline the creation of unified K‑12 districts, clarify county superintendent duties, and update terminology, while adding new procedures for building‑reserve levies and transition costs.
changes: Replaces the word “consolidation” with “reorganization” throughout the education statutes.
Creates a formal pathway for elementary, high‑school, and K‑12 districts to reorganize into a single unified K‑12 district, including required petitions, elections, and county‑superintendent orders.
Expands county superintendent responsibilities to modify district boundaries, maintain records, and oversee reorganization elections and interim boards.

Adds new building‑reserve levy provisions (Section 20‑9‑502) that allow districts to create sub‑funds for construction, major maintenance, and transition costs, with limits on levy duration and amount.
Establishes detailed rules for tenure and hiring preferences during reorganization (Section 20‑6‑410).
Specifies cash and debt disposition procedures when districts dissolve or reorganize (Sections 20‑6‑413 and 20‑6‑414).
Introduces new ANB (average number belonging) calculation rules for budgeting and entitlement purposes (Section 20‑9‑311).
Sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
affected: Teachers, principals, and other certified employees
numbers: 5% of max general‑fund budget or $250 per ANB (transition‑cost levy limit)
20‑month boundary‑change window (January 1 to fourth Monday of August)

HB611.one_line: Revises auditor salary review and clarifies dual role, effective 2028.
HB611.summary: HB 611 revises the salary‑setting process for the state auditor (who is also the ex‑officio commissioner of insurance and securities) and sets an effective date of January 1, 2028. The bill amends the statutory list of officials whose salaries are reviewed and clarifies the auditor’s dual role. No new program or crime is created.
changes: Amends §2‑16‑405, MCA to include the state auditor as the ex‑officio commissioner of insurance and securities in the list of officials whose salaries are reviewed.

Replaces the previous list of officials with a new list that includes the auditor/commissioner and removes the superintendent of public instruction and public‑service commission presiding officer from the list.
Specifies that the salary survey will compare Montana officials with counterparts in North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Idaho.
Sets the effective date of the amendment to January 1, 2028, applying only to the state auditor.
Leaves the salary‑survey procedure (average‑salary rule) unchanged.
Does not alter any salary amounts directly; it only changes the officials covered and the effective date.
affected: State auditor (ex‑officio commissioner of insurance and securities)
numbers: North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, Idaho

HB612.one_line: Revises revocation rules so new sentences run consecutively unless originally concurrent.
HB612.summary: The bill amends Montana’s criminal‑procedure statutes to require that any new sentence imposed after a revocation of a suspended or deferred sentence run consecutively with any other existing sentence, unless the original sentence had run concurrently. It also clarifies how sentences are merged and documented when a revocation occurs.
changes: Amends §46‑18‑203 to state that a revocation hearing must be held and that the new sentence must run consecutively to any other sentence unless the original sentence ran concurrently.
Adds language to §46‑18‑401 that, when a sentence is revoked, the new sentence must run consecutively to any other previously existing sentence unless the revoked sentence ran concurrently.
Specifies that courts must immediately furnish authenticated copies of any merged sentences to other courts and penal institutions.
Clarifies that separate sentences for multiple offenses must run consecutively unless the court orders otherwise.
Reiterates that a revoked sentence cannot be merged into a new sentence.
affected: Offenders with suspended or deferred sentences

HB614.one_line: Allows counties to terminate zoning districts via referendum or resolution when adopting land‑use planning or merging districts.
HB614.summary: HB 614 lets a county terminate a zoning district if it joins the Montana Land‑Use Planning Act or if the district is absorbed into a larger one. It amends the petition, referendum, and resolution procedures for ending a district.
changes: Amends §76‑2‑118 and §76‑2‑229 to allow a county to terminate a zoning district via referendum or resolution
Requires 20 % of property‑owner signatures to petition for a referendum
Validates signatures within 60 days and limits a new petition to 3 years after an unsuccessful vote
Allows the county commission to pass a resolution to terminate a district when the county adopts the Land‑Use Planning Act or creates a larger district that includes the area
Specifies that the referendum election follows Title 13, chapters 1 part 4 or 5 (depending on the section)
Maintains notice and public‑hearing requirements for the resolution process
Does not create a new program or criminal offense
No fiscal provisions are included
No effective‑date clause is stated
numbers: Title 13, chapter 1, part 4 or 5 for elections

HB616.one_line: HB 616 lets mine operators use data modeling to release performance bonds and adds extensive reclamation and procedural requirements.
HB616.summary: HB 616 amends Montana’s mining bond rules to allow operators to use predictive data modeling when applying to release performance bonds, sets detailed procedural steps for bond release, and creates a contingency that voids the act if the U.S. Interior Secretary disapproves.  The bill also expands reclamation requirements and gives the department rule‑making authority.
changes: Amends §82‑4‑232 to permit use of predictive modeling in bond‑release applications and to require detailed documentation of reclamation results.
Establishes a multi‑step administrative process: application, completeness check, public notice, objection period, hearing, inspection, and acceptability determination.
Defines specific bond‑release schedules (e.g., 60 % release after plugging/backfilling, further release after revegetation), with conditions for retaining portions of the bond.
Adds new reclamation criteria for topsoil handling, slope stability, and wildlife habitat enhancement, and allows operators to propose higher‑value post‑mining land uses.
Creates a contingent‑voidness clause that voids the act if the U.S. Interior Secretary disapproves it under 30 CFR 732.
Provides the department with rule‑making authority over the new requirements.
affected: Mining operators and their bond holders

HB620.one_line: Extends anti‑restrictive‑contract law to all Montana physicians, effective Jan. 1 2026.
HB620.summary: HB 620 expands Montana’s anti‑restrictive‑contract law to cover all licensed physicians, not just psychiatrists and addiction‑medicine doctors. It keeps the same prohibitions on post‑employment restrictions and adds a few exceptions for practice sales and loan‑repayment arrangements. The bill takes effect Jan. 1 2026 and applies to contracts made or renewed from that date.
changes: Amends §28‑2‑724 to include all licensed physicians in the definition of “health‑care provider” subject to the prohibition.
Adds a new subsection (3) that exempts contracts related to the sale/purchase of a practice and certain loan‑repayment provisions from the prohibition.
Keeps the existing exceptions for practice‑sale and loan‑repayment provisions that were already in the statute.
Sets the effective date of the amendment to Jan. 1 2026 and limits applicability to contracts made or renewed on or after that date.
Does not create any new program, office, or criminal offense.
No monetary amounts or funding changes are included.
affected: Physicians of all specialties licensed in Montana

HB621.one_line: HB 621 authorizes peer‑support programs for first responders with strict confidentiality and reporting limits.
HB621.summary: HB 621 lets police, sheriff’s offices, fire departments, and EMS agencies set up peer‑support programs for their staff, but the programs must follow a written policy that spells out qualifications, confidentiality rules, and reporting limits.  Peer supporters cannot testify about sessions, except in a few mandated exceptions.
changes: Allows local first‑responder entities to establish peer‑support programs under state law.
Requires each program to adopt a written policy covering qualifications, session definitions, confidentiality, HIPAA compliance, and protection from supervisory pressure.
Prohibits recording of peer‑support sessions in any form.
Limits peer‑supporters from testifying about session content, except when the employee threatens crime, self‑harm, or others, or when a licensing board or mandatory reporting law requires disclosure.
Provides that employees may use multiple peer‑supporters and may not be forced to use a supervisor as a supporter.
Adds coordination language with Senate Bill 518 to broaden the definition of “appropriate licensing board” and “reporting requirements.”

HB623.one_line: Legislature approves temporary spent‑fuel storage sites, requiring DEQ review and federal coordination.
HB623.summary: HB 623 authorizes Montana legislature to approve the siting of temporary spent‑nuclear‑fuel storage sites on existing nuclear plant sites, requires state‑level review and recommendation, and amends the state’s regulatory process for federal filings.
changes: Authorizes siting of temporary spent‑nuclear‑fuel storage facilities on the site of a Montana nuclear power plant that produces the fuel.

Requires the Montana Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) to issue a state recommendation to the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) or Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) after receiving a federal application.
Mandates that applicants file a notice and copy of the federal application with DEQ and pay a fee not exceeding half the amount that could be assessed under 75‑20‑215.
Imposes a penalty for failure to file the required notice in a timely manner, subjecting the applicant to 75‑20‑408.
Notifies all federally recognized Montana tribes of the act’s passage.
Codifies the new authority as part of Title 75, Chapter 20 of the Montana Code.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Nuclear power plant operators in Montana
Applicants for NRC/FERC permits for spent‑fuel storage

HB624.one_line: HB 624 expands hobby‑apiary limits, tightens ownership, and restricts registration transfer.
HB624.summary: HB 624 amends Montana’s hobby‑apiary law to allow more hives and sites per applicant, limits ownership to five 10‑hive units, and clarifies registration rules.
changes: Amends § 80‑6‑114 to permit up to five 10‑hive units per hobbyist and up to two site registrations per family;
Requires all hives to be on the registered hobbyist site;
Mandates that the applicant personally owns and manages the bees and hives;
Prohibits leasing, assigning, or transferring a hobbyist apiary site registration;
Restricts any third‑party from exercising rights granted by the registration certificate;
Limits each applicant to one registration and a family unit to two registrations.

HB625.one_line: HB 625 cuts county entitlement shares for child‑abuse reporting failures and requires attorney‑general reporting.
HB625.summary: HB 625 would cut a county’s entitlement share if it fails to meet child‑abuse reporting duties and requires the attorney general to notify the Department of Revenue. It amends the entitlement‑share statute and the county‑attorney reporting rules to create a new penalty mechanism.
changes: County entitlement share payments can be reduced by 2 % if the county is found non‑compliant with child‑abuse reporting requirements.
The attorney general must notify the Department of Revenue when a county fails to comply with the reporting duties in 41‑3‑210.
County attorneys must file detailed annual reports to the attorney general on child‑abuse and exploitation cases, including case identifiers, dates, charges, and outcomes.
County attorneys must retain all related records for 25 years and provide certifications to reporters of abuse or exploitation.
The Department of Revenue may withhold or reduce entitlement payments for counties that miss reporting deadlines or fail to remit state‑collected funds.
The bill amends the entitlement‑share calculation in 15‑1‑121 to allow such reductions and clarifies the reporting and penalty procedures.

HB626.one_line: HB 626 tightens DUI penalties, expands prior‑offense definitions, and links sentencing to treatment completion.
HB626.summary: HB 626 revises Montana’s DUI statutes to tighten penalties, broaden what counts as a prior offense, and expand treatment‑based sentence options. It adds new definitions, expands the list of offenses that trigger harsher sentences, and allows more suspended sentences tied to treatment completion.
changes: Defines a prior offense to include pending or subsequent DUI charges that result in a conviction before sentencing of the current offense
Replaces references to “violation” with “offense” in several statutory sections
Adds new sentencing tiers for first‑through‑third offenses, including higher fines and longer minimum prison terms when a passenger under 16 is present
Allows courts to suspend up to one year of an imprisonment sentence if the defendant completes a chemical‑dependency treatment program
Requires mandatory participation in DUI courts, 24/7 sobriety monitoring, or drug‑court programs during any suspended sentence
Expands the definition of aggravated DUI and sets specific penalties for those cases
Amends §61‑8‑1011 to clarify what counts as a conviction and how prior convictions are used in sentencing
Provides for home‑arrest or community‑based pre‑release facilities for eligible inmates
Mandates license suspension periods of 90, 180, or 365 days depending on the number of convictions
Precludes deferral of sentence under the revised sections

HB627.one_line: HB 627 revises procurement reporting thresholds to $200,000 and sets quarterly reporting deadlines.
HB627.summary: HB 627 updates Montana’s procurement reporting rules, requiring the Department of Administration to send quarterly reports to the Legislative Finance Committee and to collect similar data from all governmental bodies. The bill sets new thresholds for reporting, specifies reporting dates, and limits the new requirements to a one‑year period.
changes: Replaces the $250,000 reporting threshold with $200,000 for all procurement solicitations, contracts, and modifications.
Mandates the Department of Administration to submit written reports on March 1, June 1, September 1, and December 1 each year.
Requires every governmental body to submit the same procurement data to the department by February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15 each year.
Codifies the new reporting rules as part of Title 18, Chapter 4, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
Makes the provisions effective July 1 2025 (Section 1) and July 1 2026 (Section 2).
Terminates the new reporting requirements for Section 1 on June 30 2026.
affected: All Montana governmental bodies that issue procurement solicitations, contracts, or modifications

HB628.one_line: HB 628 expands early‑literacy interventions, adds on‑target enrollment limits, and sets new reporting and funding rules.
HB628.summary: HB 628 revises Montana’s early‑literacy intervention program to broaden its focus to include scholastic literacy, allows districts to enroll a limited number of on‑target students, and sets new reporting and funding rules. The bill amends the statutory language, clarifies definitions, and establishes an immediate effective date with an applicability date of May 1, 2025.
changes: Expands the definition of early‑scholastic‑literacy intervention to include classroom‑based, home‑based, and jump‑start programs and adds a new definition of “scholastic literacy.”
Requires school districts to use a board‑selected, research‑based evaluation methodology to identify eligible children and to re‑evaluate them annually.
Allows districts to opt in to enrolling on‑target children in classroom or jump‑start programs, limited to one on‑target child for every three‑to‑five eligible children.
Mandates that on‑target children be counted in ANB enrollment calculations for classroom and jump‑start programs.
Provides that home‑based program costs not exceed $1,000 per child and that the superintendent pay for these costs from appropriated funds.
Imposes annual reporting requirements on trustees and the superintendent, including anonymized student progress data and statewide outcome analyses.

HB629.one_line: HB 629 mandates public water/sewer systems to accept subdivision connections under specified conditions.
HB629.summary: HB 629 requires county and municipal water and sewer systems to accept a proposed subdivision’s connection request when the subdivision is within 501‑1,000 feet of the system and the system meets capacity, regulatory, and water‑right criteria. It amends ARM 17.36.123 and codifies the new rules in Title 7.
changes: Amends ARM 17.36.123 to mandate that new subdivision water and sewer facilities be supplied by a public system if the subdivision requests connection, is within 501‑1,000 ft of the system, and the system meets specified criteria.

Creates a rule that county water/sewer districts must supply services to a subdivision under the same conditions, with additional administrative requirements for capacity, authorization, compliance, and water rights.
Creates a similar rule for municipal water/sewer systems, with identical administrative requirements.
Codifies the county rule into Title 7, chapter 13, part 22 and the municipal rule into Title 7, chapter 13, part 43.
Sets the act in effect immediately upon passage and approval.

HB631.one_line: Amends student‑privacy definitions to clarify K‑12 online use and protected data.
HB631.summary: HB 631 amends Montana’s student‑privacy statute to clarify definitions around K‑12 online applications and protected information, removing wording that could hinder postsecondary opportunities. The changes do not create new programs or impose new obligations beyond the statutory language.
changes: Amends Section 20‑7‑1324, MCA, redefining terms such as "deidentified information," "K‑12 online application," "K‑12 school purposes," "operator," "protected information," "pupil records," "pupil‑generated content," and "third party."
Clarifies that "K‑12 school purposes" exclude postsecondary credit courses and work‑based learning courses.
Specifies that "protected information" includes a broad list of personally identifiable data and other sensitive categories.
Defines "pupil records" to exclude deidentified information used for educational improvement or marketing.
Adds that "pupil‑generated content" excludes standardized assessment responses.

HB632.one_line: HB 632 sets new daily pay rates for three state board members and updates board rules.
HB632.summary: HB 632 revises the daily compensation for members of three state boards—Mental Disabilities Board of Visitors, Burial Preservation Board, and Montana Facility Finance Authority—setting new pay rates and confirming reimbursement rules. It also updates board composition rules and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Changes the daily pay for Mental Disabilities Board members to $100 per day.

HB633.one_line: HB 633 tightens Montana’s mine‑permit rules, adds new environmental safeguards, and gives the department rule‑making power.
HB633.summary: HB 633 amends Montana’s mine‑permit rules to tighten reclamation, environmental‑impact, and hearing procedures, and gives the department new rule‑making authority. The bill also adds a contingent‑voidness clause that voids any provision disapproved by the U.S. Interior Secretary.
changes: Amends §82‑4‑206 to expand the list of decisions that trigger a contested‑case hearing and clarifies the 30‑day request window
Rewrites §82‑4‑231 to require a detailed reclamation plan, set stricter public‑notice and objection periods, and impose tighter environmental‑impact‑statement timelines
Adds new requirements for operators to control toxic materials, water quality, subsidence, and wildlife impacts during and after mining
Provides the department with authority to issue new rules under the amended sections
Includes a contingent‑voidness provision that voids any part of the act if the U.S. Interior Secretary disapproves it under 30 CFR 732
Keeps pre‑effective‑date rights, penalties, and proceedings unchanged
affected: Landowners and local communities near mining sites

HB636.one_line: HB 636 tightens marijuana packaging, THC limits, and licensing fees, effective July 2026.
HB636.summary: HB 636 revises Montana’s marijuana statutes to tighten packaging, labeling, and THC limits, especially for edibles, and updates dispensary licensing fees and requirements. The bill takes effect July 1 2026.
changes: Limits edible THC per package to 100 mg and per serving to 10 mg; allows a 10 % deviation for edibles.
Requires all marijuana products to be sold in child‑resistant, resealable packaging with a white label that lists business name, product name, THC/CBD content, ingredients, and health warnings.

Adds a $5,000 initial dispensary license fee (plus $5,000 for each additional location) and allows adult‑use dispensaries to operate at a shared location with a medical dispensary if owned by the same person.
Prohibits sale of hemp flower, hemp plants, synthetic cannabinoids, or alcohol from a licensed dispensary.
Mandates pre‑approval of packaging and labeling by the department before sale, including certification of child‑resistance and a fee.
Sets maximum THC concentrations for various product types (e.g., 35 % THC in flower, 6 % in topicals, 800 mg per package for most products).
Requires dispensaries to comply with local government approval if the county voted against Initiative 190, and prohibits sales that would exceed personal possession limits.

HB638.one_line: HB 638 bars state/local agencies from requiring or favoring diversity statements, except when federal law requires it.
HB638.summary: HB 638 bars state and local agencies from demanding or giving preference for diversity statements, except when federal law requires it. It defines a diversity statement and clarifies that agencies may still enforce anti‑discrimination laws.
changes: Prohibits agencies from requiring, requesting, soliciting, or compelling a diversity statement.
Prohibits agencies from granting preferential treatment to anyone who submits a diversity statement.
Allows agencies to accept a diversity statement only when federal law mandates it, and limits use of the information to what is required by that law.
Does not restrict agencies from creating policies needed to comply with state or federal anti‑discrimination statutes.
Defines “diversity statement” and “state or local government agency.”
Codifies the provisions as a new chapter in Title 49 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Local agencies (county, city, school district, etc.)
Individuals applying for state or local positions or contracts

HB641.one_line: Repeals Lewis & Clark Bicentennial plates, account, and related statutes, effective Dec 31, 2025.
HB641.summary: HB 641 repeals the Lewis & Clark Bicentennial license‑plate program, eliminates the related state account, amends a statutory‑appropriation statute, and removes two code sections that authorized the plates and their proceeds. The act takes effect December 31, 2025.
changes: Repeals Section 2‑15‑151 (license‑plate authorization and sponsor proceeds) and Section 90‑1‑115 (related provisions).
Removes the Department of Commerce’s Lewis & Clark Bicentennial account from the state ledger.
Amends Section 17‑7‑502, MCA, to list a new set of laws that contain statutory appropriations.
Establishes December 31, 2025 as the effective date of all changes.

HB642.one_line: HB 642 makes prohibited camping a public nuisance and sets a $500 daily fine.
HB642.summary: HB 642 amends Montana’s public‑nuisance statute to declare that camping where a city ordinance or state statute prohibits it is a public nuisance. It also clarifies other nuisance definitions, limits nuisance claims against long‑operating farms or businesses, excludes shooting‑range noise during permitted hours, and sets a $500 fine per day for violations.
changes: Amends §45‑8‑111(a)(1) to add camping in violation of an ordinance or statute as a public nuisance.
Reaffirms that any premises used for unlawful conduct and any condition that endangers public safety or obstructs public use are nuisances.
Adds a new subsection (4) exempting long‑operating agricultural or commercial operations from nuisance status if they have been in operation for a resident or commercial establishment’s duration.
Excludes noises from shooting ranges during established operating hours from being considered nuisances (subsection 5).
Sets a maximum fine of $500 per day for each day a person maintains a public nuisance (subsection 6).
affected: Individuals or entities camping where prohibited by city or state law
Farmers and commercial operators with long‑standing operations

HB648.one_line: DFW&P must notify local and tribal authorities before relocating large predators, per HB 648.
HB648.summary: HB 648 requires the Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks (DFW&P) to notify local and tribal authorities before relocating a large predator and amends the state’s predator‑management policy to clarify priorities and consultation procedures.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑217, MCA to add a new subsection (5) that mandates DFW&P to provide verbal and written notice to county commissioners, sheriff’s offices, and tribal governments before relocating a large predator.

Specifies four notification triggers: (i) finalization of an annual relocation plan, (ii) finalization of a change to such a plan, (iii) within 24 hrs of capture if the predator will be relocated outside its capture county, and (iv) within 24 hrs of relocation if the site had prior approval for bear relocation.
Defines “consultation,” “large game species,” and “large predators” (bears, mountain lions, wolves).
Adds Section 2 directing the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Does not create new funding, programs, or criminal offenses.
No fiscal impact is specified.

HB643.one_line: Revises detention center cost payments, adds surcharge, authorizes $6 M reimbursement, expires 2027.
HB643.summary: HB 643 revises how Montana agencies pay for holding people in detention centers, adds a 10 % surcharge on actual costs, and authorizes a one‑time $6 million appropriation to reimburse counties for certain health‑related detentions. The act ends on June 30 , 2027.
changes: Amends §7‑32‑2242, MCA to require the arresting agency to pay the actual cost of holding a person in a detention center, plus a 10 % surcharge in specified circumstances.
Redefines “actual costs” to be the greater of (i) the daily per‑inmate provider rate for a correctional facility less 10 % or (ii) $82, and similarly for private facilities with >500 inmates.
Adds a provision that if a fugitive from an out‑of‑state jurisdiction is held pending extradition, the out‑of‑state jurisdiction must pay all costs, including medical expenses.

Creates a one‑time appropriation of $6 million from the state special revenue account to the Department of Public Health and Human Services for the biennium beginning July 1 , 2025, to reimburse counties for holding individuals awaiting evaluation or placement under various public health statutes.
Sets the reimbursement rate at 135 % of the daily per‑inmate provider rate of a private correctional facility with >500 inmates that contracts with the Department of Corrections.
Establishes a termination date of June 30 , 2027, after which the provisions expire.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Individuals held in detention for health‑related reasons

HB650.one_line: Broadband projects may now be financed with municipal bonds under Montana law, effective 2028.
HB650.summary: HB 650 authorizes Montana municipalities and counties to issue bonds for broadband projects and expands the statutory definition of “project” to include broadband service in unserved or underserved areas. The law takes effect on January 1, 2028.
changes: Adds broadband service to the list of projects that may be financed with municipal or county bonds under Section 90‑5‑101, MCA
Amends the definition of “Project” to include broadband service exclusively to unserved/underserved areas or satellite‑only locations
No new funding sources or limits are imposed; the bill merely expands eligibility for existing bonding authority
The effective date is delayed to January 1, 2028, giving local governments time to prepare
The amendment does not create a new program, office, or criminal offense
The bill does not alter any fiscal allocations or appropriations
The amendment does not change the definition of other terms in the statute
affected: Residents in unserved or underserved areas

HB651.one_line: Allows approved temporary door locks in public buildings during emergencies, exempting them from fire‑exit obstruction rules.
HB651.summary: HB 651 permits temporary door‑locking devices in public buildings during shelter‑in‑place or emergency lockdowns, creating a limited fire‑code exception. It defines the devices, amends the unlawful‑obstruction fire‑exit statute, and takes effect immediately.
changes:
Allows temporary door locks on fire exits, hallways, corridors, or entranceways during shelter‑in‑place or emergency lockdowns.  
Requires such locks to be approved by the local fire department, law enforcement, or code official.  
Defines a "temporary door locking device" with specific construction, installation, and removal requirements.  
Amends §50‑61‑106 to exempt these devices from the unlawful‑obstruction rule.  
Codifies the exception as part of Title 50, Chapter 61, Part 1.  
Effective immediately upon passage.

HB655.one_line: Prohibits state discrimination against faith‑based adoption/foster‑care providers and provides remedies within two years.
HB655.summary: HB 655 prohibits Montana state agencies from discriminating against adoption or foster‑care providers whose services are guided by sincerely held religious beliefs. It defines the protected actions, sets a two‑year statute of limitations, and allows victims to seek injunctive relief, damages, and attorney fees.
changes: 1. Establishes a new prohibition on state‑government discriminatory actions against faith‑based or religiously motivated adoption/foster‑care providers.
2. Defines “discriminatory action” broadly to include tax, grant, contract, benefit, license, or employment‑related discrimination.
3. Grants a 2‑year statute of limitations for bringing claims or defenses under the act.
4. Provides remedies: declaratory or injunctive relief, compensatory damages, reasonable attorney fees and costs, and other appropriate relief.
5. Requires that any state benefit or service be available to protected persons regardless of religious status.
6. Includes a construction clause that the act must be interpreted to give the broadest protection of free exercise of religion consistent with state and federal law.
affected: Faith‑based adoption and foster‑care agencies and individuals
State agencies that grant custody or administer state benefits to such providers

HB656.one_line: Expands ESA funding to include community service, human rights, education, and reentry programs and moves the office under Labor and Industry.
HB656.summary: HB 656 expands the Employment Security Account (ESA) to fund the Office of Community Service, the Commission for Human Rights, education and reentry programs, and moves the Office of Community Service under the Department of Labor and Industry.
changes: Adds new ESA spending categories: Office of Community Service, Commission for Human Rights, education programs, and reentry programs
Transfers the Office of Community Service from the Office of the Governor to the Department of Labor and Industry
Amends §39‑51‑409 to list the new ESA expenditures and allows transfers to the unemployment insurance fund with budget‑director approval
Rewrites §90‑14‑103 to establish the Office of Community Service, define its purpose, appoint its director, and outline its duties and funding sources
Maintains existing ESA uses for unemployment insurance, administration, apprenticeship, research, wage‑law enforcement, and bond interest
Provides that ESA funds may be moved between federal and state special revenue accounts for employment‑service programs
Requires the director to seek federal grants and other funding and to report accountability
No new criminal offenses or state‑wide programs beyond the Office of Community Service are created
affected: Montana Department of Labor and Industry

HB665.one_line: Shield volunteer officers of small nonprofits from personal tax liability under specific conditions.
HB665.summary: The bill amends Montana tax law to shield volunteer officers of small nonprofits from personal liability for unpaid withholding taxes and filing failures, but only if they are unpaid, uncompensated, and the nonprofit has been compliant for at least 12 months. It keeps the standard liability rules for other employers and defines “small nonprofit” as one with ≤10 paid employees.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2503 to add an exemption for volunteer officers of small nonprofits (subsection 7).
Limits that exemption to officers who receive no compensation, have no outstanding unpaid taxes for >12 months, and are not engaged in fraud or misconduct.
Defines a “small nonprofit corporation” as a nonprofit with 10 or fewer paid employees during the calendar year.
Retains the existing liability provisions for other officers, partners, LLC members, and managers.
Preserves the rule that individual liability is not affected by corporate bankruptcy.
Leaves the rest of §15‑30‑2503 unchanged.
affected: Small nonprofit corporations with ≤10 paid employees

HB664.one_line: HB 664 eliminates numeric nutrient standards, dissolves the Nutrient Work Group, and authorizes DEQ to update water‑quality rules.
HB664.summary: HB 664 removes Montana’s numeric nutrient standards, deletes the Nutrient Work Group, and gives the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) authority to update rules. The bill repeals several administrative rules and sections of the Montana Code that codified those standards.
changes: DEQ must amend ARM 17.30.507, 17.30.516, 17.30.602, 17.30.619, 17.30.622‑629, 17.30.702, and 17.30.715 to delete references to DEQ‑12A and numeric nutrient standards
DEQ repeals DEQ‑12A (the base numeric nutrient standards) and all guidance that relies on it
The bill amends MCA §75‑5‑103 to replace the definition of “nutrient work group” and other definitions with a new, expanded definition of “associated supporting infrastructure”
The Nutrient Work Group is eliminated
MCA §75‑5‑321 and ARM 17.30.660 and 17.30.1388 are repealed
The bill directs DEQ to codify the new rules as part of Title 75, Chapter 5, Part 3
The act takes effect immediately upon passage
affected: public and private stakeholders involved in water quality

HB667.one_line: Protects Montana employees’ rights to run for public office and maintain benefits during mandatory leaves.
HB667.summary: HB 667 protects Montana employees who run for or hold public office from employer retaliation or restrictions, and preserves their benefits during mandatory leaves. The act takes effect immediately and applies retroactively to January 1, 2025.
changes: Employers may not prohibit or discriminate against employees seeking election or appointment to city, county, or state office.
During a mandatory leave of absence for public office, employers may not require employees to use leave or benefits without consent, nor force them to work.
If an employee’s personal use of a company phone, computer, or number is allowed, the employer may not forbid that use during the leave.
Health‑care benefits must continue unchanged for employees on leave.
The provisions are codified into Title 39, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
The act is effective upon passage and applies retroactively to all actions on or after January 1, 2025.
affected: Montana employees seeking or holding public office

HB668.one_line: Prohibits certain military‑ and veterans‑related alcohol licenses from offering gambling under Montana law.
HB668.summary: HB 668 amends Montana’s alcohol‑licensing law to bar enlistment‑person, non‑commissioned‑officer, or officer‑club licenses located on military reservations, veterans’ posts, or recognized national fraternity lodges from offering gambling. The amendment replaces the existing 23‑5‑119 language with new eligibility rules that effectively prohibit those licensees from providing gambling services under Title 23, Chapter 5, Parts 3, 5, or 6.
changes: Amends § 23‑5‑119, MCA, to prohibit gambling by licenses held by enlisted persons, non‑commissioned officers, or officer clubs on military reservations, veterans’ posts, or national fraternity lodges.
Replaces the previous eligibility criteria for offering gambling with new rules that exclude the specified licensees.
The amendment does not create a new program or office; it only changes existing licensing requirements.
The effective date is the day the act is passed and approved, with no additional transition period.
The bill does not alter tax or funding provisions, only the scope of who may offer gambling.
The text does not contain any new criminal offenses or penalties.
affected: Enlisted personnel, non‑commissioned officers, and officer clubs on military reservations
Alcohol‑licensing authorities and applicants for gambling licenses

HB669.one_line: HB 669 clarifies tuition rates and reporting for inpatient treatment of children with serious emotional disturbances.
HB669.summary: HB 669 amends Montana’s education statutes to clarify how daily tuition rates are set for children receiving inpatient treatment for serious emotional disturbances, expands the superintendent’s rule‑making authority, and requires reporting on program costs and outcomes.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑419 to give the superintendent authority to adopt rules for tuition calculation, fund distribution, and responsibilities of treatment facilities and schools
Amends §20‑7‑435 to specify that the superintendent may contract with qualifying facilities, set a daily rate based on documented costs, and require regular academic reporting
Defines that a child’s school district pays 40 % of the tuition‑per‑ANB amount (as defined in §20‑5‑323) divided by 180, and that the district may fund this from its tuition or general fund

Provides that if a facility fails to provide education, the superintendent may either use state‑employed specialists or negotiate with the facility’s school district, with reimbursement at the same daily rate
Mandates that funds received under this section be deposited in the district’s miscellaneous programs fund and are exempt from the 20‑9‑308 budget limits
Requires the superintendent to report to the education interim budget and education interim committees by September 30 of even‑numbered years, detailing daily rates and program evaluations
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025
affected: Children receiving inpatient treatment for serious emotional disturbances
Qualifying children’s psychiatric hospitals, residential treatment facilities, therapeutic group homes
Public school districts that receive or reimburse funds for these children
The Montana Department of Public Instruction
Montana state budget and education committees

HB671.one_line: Amends ABLE Act definitions to match federal IRS language, effective immediately and retroactive to 2025.
HB671.summary: HB 671 amends the Montana Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act’s definition section so that the state’s definitions match those in the federal Internal Revenue Code.  The changes take effect immediately and apply retroactively to income‑tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.
changes: Amends Section 53‑25‑103 to replace the state’s definitions of key terms (e.g., “Annual contribution limit,” “Disability certifications,” “Eligible individual,” etc.) with the corresponding federal definitions from the Internal Revenue Code.
Adds a definition for “Internal Revenue Code” that mirrors the state’s definition of the federal code.
Provides that the amended definitions are effective upon passage and retroactively apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.
No new programs, offices, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The bill does not alter any substantive program requirements or funding.
The amendment only updates terminology to ensure consistency with federal law.
affected: Financial institutions that administer ABLE accounts
The Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB672.one_line: DOT gains rule‑making power, sets cost shares, and limits liability for utility relocations on highways.
HB672.summary: HB 672 amends Montana’s utility‑relocation statutes to give the Department of Transportation (DOT) new rule‑making authority, set timelines, and allow cost reductions if utilities fail to relocate on time. It also limits DOT liability for removals and specifies when DOT will pay for public water‑and‑sewer relocations.
changes: DOT may adopt rules governing right‑of‑way occupancy, relocation, and permits for utilities and non‑utilities on state highways and commission‑designated highways.

DOT must pay 75 % of relocation, dismantling, and removal costs for most utilities, but will pay 100 % for publicly owned water/sewer facilities with ≤500 connectors and 85 % for those with 501–999 connectors, under specified conditions.
DOT may reduce its cost share to 0 % if a utility does not relocate within a reasonable time after a preliminary notice; the reduction can only begin 90 days after notice.
DOT may remove a facility that fails to relocate or was not installed per a permit, after giving reasonable written notice.

DOT’s liability for removal is limited: it and its contractors cannot be sued for loss of service or for removal performed in compliance with the new rules, except for willful misconduct, gross negligence, or violations of 69‑4‑523.
The changes apply only to design‑bid‑build highway projects.
affected: Telecommunications, broadband, and cable TV companies
Non‑utility facility owners on highway right‑of‑way

HB679.one_line: HB 679 revises state‑vehicle commute rules, allowing limited exceptions for certain criminal‑investigation staff.
HB679.summary: HB 679 amends Montana’s state‑vehicle use rules to allow certain Division of Criminal Investigation employees to commute in state‑owned cars, while tightening mileage limits for other employees. The bill also adds a 30‑mile exception for emergency‑response staff and requires documentation and governor notification for all exceptions.
changes: Section 2‑17‑425 is amended to permit state‑owned vehicle commutes of less than 30 miles for employees who must be on‑call for emergencies and have responded frequently in the past six months; the exception must be documented and sent to the governor.
The exception is specifically extended to Division of Criminal Investigation employees in the fire marshal or narcotics/major‑crime agent roles who are subject to unscheduled call‑outs.
Commutes over 30 miles are prohibited unless the department director authorizes them under existing rules, with the same documentation and governor notification requirements.
The definition of “state agency” is clarified to include all executive, judicial, and legislative entities, including the university system.
The bill does not apply to the psychiatrist at the state prison, to employees whose vehicle is effectively their worksite, or to 24‑hour use authorized by law for elected or appointed officials.
affected: Division of Criminal Investigation employees (fire marshal, narcotics/major‑crime agents)
Other state agency employees who use state vehicles for commuting
Department directors and agency heads who must document and file exceptions

HB680.one_line: Amends commission contract rules, extends terms, adds property sale procedures, and requires reporting.
HB680.summary: HB 680 amends the Montana Heritage Preservation and Development Commission’s contract rules, extending permissible contract terms, relaxing procurement and wage requirements, and adding new procedures for property sales and trust‑fund creation. The bill also requires the commission to report financial activities to the governor and legislature and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: Amends §22‑3‑1003 to allow contracts up to 20 years (99 years for certain commercial leases) and to be negotiated directly without state procurement laws.
Requires contracts to pay prevailing wages and, for building projects over $300,000, mandates legislative consent unless urgent damage or cost‑increase concerns arise.
Adds profit‑reinvestment and general‑fund deposit rules for contract profits.
Permits the commission to solicit federal funds and use volunteers with workers’‑comp coverage but no wages.
Creates a subcommittee of equal members from the Montana Historical Society and the commission to review property sales and requires majority support for sale recommendations.
Establishes rules for acquisition/sale of real and personal property, including public notice, hearings, and a list of policy considerations.
Mandates that sale proceeds be placed in a designated account unless a trust fund is created for historic properties.
Requires the commission to report financial activities to the governor and legislature each biennium.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.

HB681.one_line: HB 681 tightens subdivision review timelines, expands water‑right requirements, and updates groundwater permitting rules.
HB681.summary: HB 681 revises Montana’s subdivision and water‑right rules, tightening review timelines, expanding water‑availability requirements, and clarifying how water rights are defined and certified. The bill adds new deadlines, penalties, and procedural steps for both local governments and applicants, and it updates the water‑right permitting process for groundwater that is exempt from standard permitting.
changes: Local subdivision regulations (76‑3‑501) now require that any subdivision plan address water availability and may not be approved solely on the basis of educational or wildland‑urban interface concerns.

The subdivision application review process (76‑3‑604) is shortened: the agency must respond within 5 working days for required elements and within 15 working days for sufficiency of information; the governing body must decide within 60 working days (80 if 50+ lots) unless an extension is granted.
A $50‑per‑lot‑per‑month penalty is imposed on governing bodies that miss the 60‑day decision deadline, capped at the total review fee collected.

Water and sanitation information (76‑3‑622) is expanded to require detailed maps, water‑source adequacy, soil‑profile data, and preliminary groundwater‑quality impact analyses for all new subdivisions, with specific thresholds for lot size and water‑right documentation.

Section 76‑4‑104 now authorizes the Department to adopt rules that set standards for water‑right certification, including the requirement that a certificate of water right be issued only after a correct and complete notice of intent to appropriate groundwater is filed and approved.

Section 85‑2‑306 is amended to clarify the notice‑of‑intent and completion requirements for groundwater appropriations that are exempt from permitting, including timelines for filing, defect resolution, and the conditions under which a certificate of water right may be issued.
The bill provides a delayed effective date: the act takes effect January 1 , 2026, and applies to subdivisions reviewed on or after that date.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Local health departments and boards of health
numbers: 10 acre‑feet per year limits for some groundwater uses

HB682.one_line: HB 682 expands insurance and Medicaid coverage for detransition treatment and sets a statute of limitations for related tort claims.
HB682.summary: HB 682 revises Montana law to set a statute of limitations for tort claims involving gender‑transition treatment of minors, requires insurance plans to cover detransition treatment when they cover transition treatment, and expands Medicaid and Healthy Montana Kids coverage to include detransition services. It also amends several statutory provisions related to insurance, health‑maintenance organizations, and Medicaid. The bill takes effect October 1, 2026.
changes: Establishes a 25‑year statute of limitations for tort claims arising from gender‑transition treatment received as a minor, with a 4‑year discovery rule and a hard cap at age 30.
Mandates that any private or public insurance policy that covers gender‑transition treatment must also cover detransition treatment under equivalent cost‑sharing terms.
Requires that if a plan stops covering transition treatment it must still cover detransition treatment for those who were enrolled when coverage existed.
Adds the same reciprocal coverage requirement to Montana Medicaid and Healthy Montana Kids programs.
Amends sections 2‑18‑704, 27‑2‑204, 27‑2‑205, 33‑31‑111, 33‑35‑306, 53‑4‑1005, and 53‑6‑101 to incorporate the new coverage and limitations provisions.
Sets the act’s effective date to October 1, 2026, with certain provisions retroactive to the passage date.
Includes coordination language with Senate Bill 218 if both bills pass.
Provides severability language.

HB683.one_line: HB 683 bars undisclosed conflicts in county and municipal construction contracts and amends procurement statutes.
HB683.summary: HB 683 tightens conflict‑of‑interest rules for county and municipal construction contracts, requiring bidders to disclose any ties to designers or engineers and treating undisclosed conflicts as non‑responsive. It also amends several procurement statutes to reinforce bidding procedures and codify the new conflict rules.
changes: 1. Counties and cities may not award construction contracts to contractors with ownership or financial interests in any person or entity that participated in the project’s design or engineering, unless the contractor discloses the conflict at bid time.
2. Failure to disclose a conflict makes the bid non‑responsive; the governing body must announce all disclosed conflicts at bid opening and hold a public meeting for comment before award.

3. The bill defines “financial interest” as ownership of 24 % or more of a legal or equitable interest, or an active role such as director or advisor, with several exclusions (mutual funds, charitable orgs, etc.).
4. Sections 7‑3‑1323, 7‑5‑2301, 7‑5‑4301, and 7‑14‑2404 of the Montana Code are amended to incorporate the new conflict‑of‑interest prohibition and to reinforce competitive bidding requirements.
5. The new conflict rules are codified as integral parts of Title 7, chapters 5, parts 23 and 43.
6. The bill does not create a new program or fund; it merely revises existing statutes.
affected: Contractors bidding on public construction projects
Designers and engineers involved in public projects

HB684.one_line: Eliminates the 60‑day data‑review deadline, setting a 180‑day period for DEQ water‑quality assessments.
HB684.summary: The bill amends the water‑quality assessment statute to eliminate the 60‑day deadline for the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) to review data submitted for listing or delisting water bodies, replacing it with a 180‑day review period and clarifying public‑notice, comment, and appeal procedures.
changes: Amends §75‑5‑702 to replace the 60‑day data‑review deadline with a 180‑day deadline for DEQ to review submitted data.
Requires DEQ to provide public notice and a 60‑day comment period before publishing a final list or taking action on a request.
Allows a person to request addition, removal, or reprioritization of a water body by providing supporting data; DEQ must review the data within 180 days.
Maintains existing procedures for public access to documentation and for charging reasonable fees for requested information.
Preserves the 5‑year interval for revising the list and priority rankings and the 14‑member statewide TMDL advisory group.
Keeps all other statutory provisions (e.g., TMDL development timelines, appeal rights) unchanged.
affected: Local conservation districts and watershed advisory groups
Members of the public who comment on draft lists

HB685.summary: HB 685 creates a new “feasibility allowance” that lets the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) permit limited degradation of high‑quality waters for energy projects when no other options exist and the benefits outweigh the costs. It amends definitions, nondegradation rules, and fee structures, and sets new procedures for outstanding‑resource‑water petitions.
changes: Creates a new feasibility‑allowance authorization process under 75‑5‑303 for high‑quality waters; requires preponderance of evidence that no other options exist, that the project yields net economic/social benefits, and that all feasible protection practices are implemented.
Amends 75‑5‑301 to add rules for mixing zones, nondegradation implementation, and criteria for nonsignificant changes, including specific nitrate limits for groundwater and septic systems.

Rewrites 75‑5‑316 to clarify that outstanding‑resource waters cannot receive feasibility‑allowance authorizations and establishes a petition‑and‑rulemaking process for classifying waters as outstanding resources.

Revisions to 75‑5‑516 set fee limits ($5,000 per discharge point, $3,000 per million gallons/day) and fee‑reduction incentives for compliant facilities, and require DEQ to recover costs for permit review, monitoring, and rulemaking.
Amends 75‑5‑605 to clarify prohibited activities and exemptions, especially regarding disposal systems and routine irrigation maintenance.
Adds rule‑making authority for DEQ to update ARM 17.30.707 and 17.30.708 to reference feasibility allowances.
Provides immediate effective date upon passage.

HB686.one_line: Shifts physician‑assistant licensing to Labor and Industry, reduces board oversight, and updates licensing rules.
HB686.summary: HB 686 moves physician‑assistant licensing from the Board of Medical Examiners to the Department of Labor and Industry, changes board composition to include fewer physician‑assistant members, and updates licensing rules and definitions.
changes: Replaces the Board of Medical Examiners’ role in physician‑assistant licensing with the Department of Labor and Industry’s licensing program.
Reduces physician‑assistant representation on the Board of Medical Examiners from five to one member.

Amends the board’s composition to include a single physician‑assistant, a podiatrist, a nutritionist, a doctor of osteopathy, a doctor of medicine (including an emergency medicine physician), an emergency‑care provider, and two public members.
Updates the collaborative‑agreement requirement for physician assistants with fewer than 8,000 post‑graduate clinical hours.
Revises fee, application, renewal, and disciplinary procedures for physician assistants.
Revises definitions of key terms such as “board,” “physician assistant,” and “license.”
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff
Patients receiving care from physician assistants

HB687.one_line: Adjusts the age limits for Medicaid community‑engagement requirements.
HB687.summary: The bill changes the age range for expanded Medicaid participants who must do community‑engagement work, setting the lower limit at 19 and the upper limit at 55‑62 years. It also keeps the 80‑hour‑per‑month requirement and the same list of exemptions and administrative rules.
changes: Amends §53‑6‑1308 to set the age range for community‑engagement requirements to 19‑55/62 years.
Maintains the 80‑hour‑per‑month community‑engagement requirement for participants in that age range.
Preserves the existing list of exemptions (medical frailty, disability, pregnancy, etc.) and the income‑based exemption.
Keeps the department’s authority to determine compliance or exemption using administrative data.
Leaves the termination date of the temporary provision (June 30 2025) unchanged.
affected: Department of Health and Human Services staff administering Medicaid

HB690.one_line: HB 690 revises child‑abuse definitions, expands confidentiality, and allows congressional members to challenge privilege designations.
HB690.summary: HB 690 revises Montana’s child‑abuse statutes, clarifies that gender‑congruent care is not abuse, expands confidentiality rules for congressional and legislative members, and amends record‑keeping provisions. The bill does not create a new program or fund.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑102 to add a definition that gender‑congruent care is not abuse or neglect; expands the definition of “abused or neglected” to exclude such care.
Adds a new subsection to §41‑3‑102 that allows a member of Congress or the Montana Legislature to challenge the department’s designation of a record as attorney‑client privileged.

Rewrites §41‑3‑205 to broaden the list of entities that may receive confidential child‑abuse records and to clarify the circumstances under which records may be disclosed to Congress or the legislature.
Replaces the prior definition of “abandonment” with a more detailed, multi‑part definition and clarifies that voluntary surrender for lack of public‑funded services is not abandonment.
Adds a new definition of “adequate health care” and limits the use of religious belief as a defense for failing to provide such care.

Expands the list of persons who may receive records under §41‑3‑205, including federal agencies, Indian tribal organizations, health professionals, and members of the U.S. Congress or Montana Legislature.
Introduces a new exception that allows a member to disclose records that are designated as attorney‑client privileged if the member believes the designation is improper.
Clarifies that a member may file a challenge in district court to a privilege designation, with filings sealed.
Adds procedures for the department to provide records to the attorney general, county attorneys, peace officers, and the child‑and‑family ombudsman.
Provides that records may be disclosed to the news media only if the disclosure is limited to factual confirmation and does not violate privacy rights.
affected: Members of Congress and Montana Legislature
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB692.one_line: Mandates annual, measurable plans for all state departments, posted online.
HB692.summary: The bill amends the SMART Act to require every state department to submit an annual plan by September 1, 2023, and thereafter every two years, detailing its functions, program‑level initiatives, and measurable performance measures. The plans must be posted online and provide ongoing, quantitative data for policymakers and the public.
changes: Amends § 2‑12‑104, MCA, to set a September 1, 2023 deadline for the first annual plan and a September 1 every two years thereafter.
Adds a requirement that each plan include a description of the department’s functions, program‑level initiatives, and specific, measurable performance measures.
Mandates that performance measures be tracked continuously, be quantitative when possible, and provide useful information to policymakers and the public.
Requires each department to publish its annual plan on its website.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.

HB693.one_line: HB 693 clarifies multi‑judge district court organization and gives the Supreme Court ordering power.
HB693.summary: HB 693 amends Montana Code §3‑5‑403 to clarify how judges in multi‑judge districts organize departments, assign judges, and create specialized dockets. It also gives the Supreme Court authority to order apportionment if district judges fail to comply.
changes: Amends §3‑5‑403 to allow more than one court session per judge in multi‑judge districts
Requires judges to divide the court into numbered departments and assign each judge to one department
Gives judges in districts with more than five judges the power to create specialized dockets within departments
Provides that if judges cannot apportion business or assign departments, the Supreme Court may issue an order to do so
The Supreme Court order must be entered in the minute book of each county in the district and remains effective until changed or repealed
Failure or refusal to obey a Supreme Court order constitutes contempt of the Supreme Court
affected: Interested persons who apply to the Supreme Court
District courts and their minute books

HB694.one_line: HB 694 revises child‑abuse policy, adds a relative registry, and prefers domestic placements.
HB694.summary: HB 694 revises Montana’s child‑abuse policy and placement rules, adding a voluntary registry for relatives, clarifying that out‑of‑country placements are disfavored, and tightening the department’s review of criminal convictions before removal.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑101 to require the department to investigate criminal convictions of anyone living in the home before approving a placement
Creates a voluntary registry for close relatives to be notified when a child is removed
Allows the department to charge a fee to registrants to cover registry costs
Rewrites §41‑3‑450 to give placement preference to extended family, community, and culturally similar homes, and to disfavor placements outside the United States
Adds a definition of “fictive kin” for placement purposes
Maintains that Indian child welfare cases are exempt from the out‑of‑country disfavor rule
affected: Children in foster or adoptive care
Parents and legal guardians of children in care
Close relatives of children in care
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB696.one_line: Legislature approves uranium conversion/enrichment sites after state recommendation and NRC license, with fee limits.
HB696.summary: The bill authorizes the Montana Legislature to approve the siting of uranium conversion and enrichment plants that process uranium mined in Montana or transported from out‑of‑state. It amends the state’s environmental‑review process to require a state recommendation for any federal application and sets fee limits for applicants. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Legislature may approve siting of uranium conversion/enrichment facilities that process Montana‑mined or transported uranium, provided the facility has a state recommendation and an NRC license.
Amends §75‑20‑204 to require the Department of Environmental Quality to file a state recommendation with the federal Energy Regulatory Commission or NRC for any such facility.
Applicants must file notice and a copy of their federal application with the department and pay a fee not exceeding half the amount that could be assessed under §75‑20‑215.
The fee must be used to develop the state recommendation and participate in federal proceedings.
Failure to file timely notice triggers §75‑20‑408 penalties.
The bill codifies its provisions as part of Title 75, Chapter 20.
Effective immediately upon passage.

HB699.one_line: HB 699 tightens tailings review panels, expands fees, and sets new review schedules for Montana mines.
HB699.summary: HB 699 updates Montana’s metal‑mine tailings regulations, tightening the independent review panel’s composition, duties, and reporting requirements. It also expands fee rules, clarifies definitions, and sets new periodic review schedules for tailings storage facilities.
changes: Redefines key terms such as “independent review engineer panel member,” “tailings storage facility,” and “small miner.”
Requires operators to select at least three licensed engineer panel members; the panel must be majority licensed and cannot include employees of the operator, design consultant, or constructor.
Mandates a written panel report that is conclusive; if the report recommends changes, the engineer of record must revise the design and obtain panel concurrence before submitting to the department.

Adds a periodic review requirement: panels must meet at least annually during construction and at least once every five years thereafter, with detailed inspection, record review, and corrective‑action reporting.
Expands operating‑permit fee structure: a $500 basic fee plus an additional fee not to exceed actual contractor/employee expenses, with a $5,000 cap and itemized estimate if higher.
Specifies that a draft permit may not be issued until the applicant has paid the required bond, submitted certifications, and complied with impact‑plan and other statutory conditions.
affected: Local governments and communities near tailings sites

HB703.one_line: Exempts building‑code agencies from MEPA GHG analysis for appliances, vehicles, and engines.
HB703.summary: HB 703 removes the requirement for certain state and local building‑code agencies to analyze greenhouse‑gas (GHG) emissions from appliances, vehicles, and engines under the Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA). It also bars analysis of GHGs from out‑of‑state sources that are not subject to state enforcement.
changes: Exempts the Department of Buildings and local building departments from MEPA analysis of GHGs for appliances or engines used in building‑code adoption or enforcement.

Exempts the Department from analyzing GHGs from new motor vehicles, new motor‑vehicle engines, new nonroad engines, or new nonroad vehicles that are not subject to state enforcement under the Clean Air Act.
Exempts the Department from analyzing GHGs that occur outside Montana’s borders.
Codifies these exemptions into Title 50, Chapter 60, Part 1 (for building‑code agencies) and Title 75, Chapter 2, Part 1 (for the Department).
Provides no new regulatory authority beyond the stated exemptions.
affected: Other state agencies that might otherwise conduct MEPA GHG analyses

HB707.one_line: HB 707 mandates family‑attachment consideration for out‑of‑state inmate placements and revises overcrowding protocols.
HB707.summary: HB 707 requires the Department of Corrections to consider an inmate’s family ties when sending them to out‑of‑state facilities and revises the rules for overcrowded institutions, allowing temporary transfers and reimbursement arrangements. The bill does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Adds a requirement that the department consider an inmate’s attachment to family and ability to maintain those ties when placing them in or transferring to an out‑of‑state correctional institution.

Amends § 53‑30‑106 to allow the director to declare emergency capacity exceeded for 30 consecutive days, stop admissions, and require the population to fall to 95 % or less before new admissions resume.

Provides that inmates who cannot be admitted due to overcrowding may be held in a detention center in the jurisdiction where they are currently located, or in another jurisdiction if that one is at capacity.
Mandates that the department reimburse the holding jurisdiction for reasonable costs of detention beyond the normal delivery period, at a mutually agreed rate.

Permits the department to contract with federal, state, county, public or private entities for confinement of selected inmates when no suitable state institution is available, within budgetary limits and in compliance with the family‑attachment requirement.
affected: Inmates held in detention centers due to overcrowding
Department of Corrections staff making placement decisions
Local sheriffs and district courts receiving notifications
Detention jurisdictions receiving inmates and reimbursement

HB708.one_line: Expands CDL waiver eligibility to all reserve component members with specific documentation requirements.
HB708.summary: HB 708 expands the definition of “current or former military service member” to include all reserve component members, allowing them to request waivers of the skills and knowledge tests required for a commercial driver’s license (CDL). The bill amends §61‑5‑123, MCA, to set specific eligibility criteria and documentation requirements for these waivers.
changes: Amends §61‑5‑123, MCA, to broaden the definition of a military service member to include anyone serving full‑time in a reserve component or who has been honorably discharged from one;
Provides that the Department of Transportation may waive the skills test, knowledge test, or both for current or former military service members who meet the new criteria;
Specifies detailed certification and evidence requirements for each type of waiver (skills test, knowledge test, or both for passenger, tank, or hazardous‑materials endorsements);

Requires applicants to demonstrate recent military employment involving operation of a commercial‑motor‑vehicle type, lack of recent civilian license issues, and no recent serious traffic convictions or accidents;
Adds a new subsection (5) covering waivers for passenger, tank, or hazardous‑materials endorsements with its own set of eligibility conditions.
affected: Current and former military personnel seeking CDLs

HB710.one_line: HB 710 authorizes judge‑issued subpoenas, creates a Judicial Standards Commission, and expands Supreme Court rule‑making authority.
HB710.summary: HB 710 lets a Supreme Court justice or district court judge issue subpoenas for internet‑crime investigations, creates a new Judicial Standards Commission, and clarifies its composition and powers. It also codifies a rule‑making authority for the Supreme Court and sets the act’s effective date to passage.
changes: Supreme Court justices and district court judges may issue subpoenas requested by an Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force officer for investigations involving sexual exploitation of a minor.
The subpoena can compel production of specific digital‑account records (e.g., account holder name, billing address, email, IP address, etc.).
A Judicial Standards Commission is created with five members: two district court judges, one attorney, and two non‑lawyer citizens; members serve staggered four‑year terms.
The Commission is assigned to the Department of Justice for administrative purposes and a judge on the Commission may not serve as its presiding officer.

The Supreme Court is granted the power to promulgate rules governing pleading, practice, and procedure in civil actions, provided those rules do not alter substantive rights or conflict with the state constitution.
The act is codified as part of Title 46, Chapter 4, and becomes effective upon passage and approval.
affected: Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force officers
Members of the Judicial Standards Commission

HB711.one_line: Limits Supreme Court from appointing a redistricting chair with recent major‑party contributions.
HB711.summary: HB 711 amends the state’s redistricting law to bar the Supreme Court from appointing a commission chair who has made a major‑party campaign contribution in the past decade. The change limits the Court’s selection power to those without such recent contributions.
changes: Amends §5‑1‑102, MCA, adding a restriction on the Supreme Court’s selection of the commission’s presiding officer.
The Court may no longer appoint a chair who has contributed to a major‑party candidate for state or federal office within the last 10 years.
The selection process remains: four commissioners pick the fifth member; if they fail, the Court selects, subject to the new restriction.
No new program or office is created.
No monetary penalties or fees are imposed.

HB713.one_line: HB 713 tightens municipal zoning procedures and removes a protest method, with no new programs or costs.
HB713.summary: HB 713 amends Montana’s municipal zoning law to clarify how regulations, restrictions, and boundaries may be changed, requiring a public hearing and 15‑day notice for most actions. It also eliminates a former protest‑by‑petition method for zoning changes and updates annexation procedures. The bill does not create new programs or impose costs, but it tightens the procedural steps municipalities must follow when altering zoning rules.
changes: Amends § 76‑2‑303 to require a public hearing and 15‑day notice before most zoning changes take effect.
Specifies that boundary‑only changes can be adopted by resolution and become effective immediately.
Allows a joint hearing for annexations that also addresses zoning of the annexed area.
Repeals § 76‑2‑305, eliminating the protest‑by‑petition method for zoning alterations.
affected: Municipal councils and other local legislative bodies
Citizens and interested parties in municipalities

HB712.one_line: Mandates restitution for children of victims in vehicular‑homicide‑while‑under‑the‑influence cases, with new sentencing and interest rules.
HB712.summary: HB 712 requires people convicted of vehicular homicide while under the influence to pay monthly restitution for each minor child whose parent or guardian was the victim. The bill amends the definition of that offense and expands sentencing rules for restitution, including interest and community‑service credits.
changes: 1. Adds a restitution requirement for each minor child when the victim of vehicular homicide while under the influence dies.
2. Defines the offense of vehicular homicide while under the influence and sets maximum prison term (30 years) and fine ($50,000).
3. Requires monthly payments until the child turns 18 or graduates high school, whichever is later.
4. Gives courts discretion to set payment amounts based on child’s needs, surviving parent’s resources, and defendant’s resources.
5. Provides that if the defendant is incarcerated and cannot pay, payments may begin after release and continue until arrears are cleared.
6. Allows civil judgments against the defendant to offset or eliminate restitution payments.
7. Amends sentencing statutes (46‑18‑201) to clarify deferment and suspension limits for violent and vehicular‑homicide offenders.
8. Amends restitution interest rules (46‑18‑241) to set 3 % interest after 6 months of non‑payment and to require a 10 % supervisory cost for felony offenders.
affected: Defendants convicted of vehicular homicide while under the influence
Department of Public Health and Human Services
