numbers: payments until child turns 18 or graduates high school

HB716.one_line: HB 716 clarifies property‑ownership qualifications for county water‑and‑sewer board directors, effective immediately.
HB716.summary: HB 716 amends the qualifications for county water‑and‑sewer board directors, clarifying that property ownership may be in a corporation, partnership, LLC, or trust in which the individual is an officer, partner, member, or trustee. The bill also maintains the existing residency and voting‑registration requirements and allows non‑voting ex‑officio members to reside outside the district. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §7‑13‑2233, MCA to specify that an individual may qualify as a property owner if the property is held in a corporation, partnership, LLC, or trust where the individual is an officer, partner, member, or trustee.
Retains the requirement that directors be registered voters, 18 or older, U.S. citizens, and residents of the district or owners of district property who are Montana residents.
Allows non‑voting ex‑officio members to reside outside the district and removes the property‑ownership requirement for them.
Requires a municipal appointee to have knowledge of the municipal water system.
The act is effective immediately upon passage.
affected: County water and sewer board directors
Individuals who own property in corporations, partnerships, LLCs, or trusts within a district
numbers: resident of district or owner of real property in district

HB714.one_line: HB 714 expands local review of exempt land divisions, adds fees, affidavits, and higher penalties for evasion.
HB714.summary: HB 714 amends Montana’s subdivision‑exemption rules to require local governing bodies to review certain land divisions, impose fees, and use an attorney‑general‑prepared affidavit. It adds notice and public‑hearing requirements, limits transfers to immediate family, and raises civil penalties for evasion.
changes: Local governing bodies must review and approve divisions or aggregations that fall outside the existing exemption list, or that increase lots in a platted subdivision beyond six or create more than five lots.
The governing body may charge up to $400 for the examination and must decide within 20 working days.
Applicants must submit an affidavit (in a form supplied by the Attorney General) stating that the division is not intended to evade subdivision regulations.
Divisions for immediate‑family transfers are limited to parcels of at least 5 acres unless the zoning district allows smaller lots, and transfers to minors must follow Title 72, §26.
A 2‑year restriction is imposed on immediate‑family or spouse recipients of a division, unless the governing body sets a shorter period.
If a governing body proves that a division was used to evade the law, it may impose a civil penalty of $5,000‑$10,000 or 10 % of the sales price (whichever is greater).
The act requires that all real‑property taxes and special assessments be paid before a division, and allows prorating of centrally assessed taxes.
affected: Landowners seeking to divide or aggregate land
Appraisers and attorneys handling subdivision matters

HB718.one_line: Creates a new reentry office to coordinate services for people leaving incarceration.
HB718.summary: HB 718 creates an Office of Reentry Services within the Department of Labor and Industry to coordinate job‑training, placement, housing, transportation, and behavioral‑health support for people leaving incarceration. The office will work with state agencies, businesses, and community groups and must report its activities and costs to the legislature each biennium.
changes: Establishes a new Office of Reentry Services in the Department of Labor and Industry.

Defines the office’s purpose and duties, including expanding job‑training, placement, education, entrepreneurship, housing, transportation, food security, and behavioral‑health services for people exiting incarceration.

Mandates collaboration with the Departments of Commerce, Corrections, Justice, Public Health & Human Services, Higher Education, and Public Instruction, as well as private companies and stakeholder organizations.

Requires the office to consult with the Montana State Workforce Innovation Board and engage stakeholders from business, mental‑health, substance‑use treatment, criminal‑justice advocacy, and affordable‑housing sectors.

Obligates the department to submit a biennial report (by July 1 before each legislative session) to the Legislative Finance Committee and the Law & Justice Interim Committee, detailing services, costs, and number of individuals served.
Codifies the new office as part of Title 39, Chapter 11 of the Montana Code.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: People exiting or preparing to exit incarceration

HB717.one_line: HB 717 expands transfer rules, adds eminent‑domain power, and strengthens reclamation enforcement for Montana mining operators.
HB717.summary: HB 717 revises how a mining operator can transfer its permit and property to a successor, adds new eminent‑domain authority for the Department of Natural Resources, and expands the Department’s ability to enforce reclamation and bond forfeiture. The bill amends §§ 82‑4‑340 and 82‑4‑341 of the Montana Code, adding new procedural steps, fees, and bond calculations, and allows the Department to take possession of land and minerals when a former operator is prohibited from mining. The changes are effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends § 82‑4‑340 to allow the Department to release a former operator and transfer the permit to a successor operator when both comply with the part and the successor assumes reclamation duties, with a $2,000 fee and bond requirements.

Adds a new subsection that authorizes the Department to initiate eminent‑domain proceedings to acquire surface, mineral, or other property interests within a permit boundary when the Department finds it in the public interest and the former operator is prohibited from mining.

Specifies that the Department may take immediate possession of condemned property and that the court will determine compensation based on bond forfeiture, reclamation costs, tax liens, and mineral value.

Expands § 82‑4‑341 to clarify the Department’s authority to inspect, require reclamation, and forfeit bonds, and to take reclamation work itself if necessary, with detailed procedures for bond forfeiture and recovery.

Adds new language allowing the Department to suspend permits for up to five years, use bond proceeds for reclamation or emergency work, and transfer suspended permits to a successor operator under eminent‑domain rules.
Provides that the Department may extend suspensions, revoke permits, and recover insufficient bond amounts, and that the Department may modify permits and reclamation plans as needed.

HB720.one_line: HB 720 revises board composition rules for Montana’s massage therapy board.
HB720.summary: HB 720 amends the statutory qualifications for the Montana Board of Massage Therapy, specifying the composition of the board and the eligibility of its members. It does not create new programs or funds. The changes are limited to the board’s membership rules.
changes: The board must have five members: one health‑care provider (not a school owner), three massage therapists (none school owners and not all from the same national association), and one public member.
The amendment replaces the previous board composition language in §2‑15‑1782, MCA.
No new offices, funds, or licensing requirements are created.

HB719.one_line: Mandates voter DOB on registration and absentee ballots, requiring verification before counting.
HB719.summary: The bill amends Montana’s election statutes to require voters to list their date of birth on registration and on absentee ballot signature envelopes, and it adds procedures for election officials to verify that date before counting absentee ballots.
changes: Adds a mandatory date‑of‑birth field to voter registration applications (Section 13‑2‑110).
Requires absentee voters to write their date of birth on the signature envelope (Section 13‑13‑201).
Mandates election administrators to compare the date of birth on the envelope with the registration record before accepting the ballot (Section 13‑13‑241).
Adds notice procedures for voters whose ballots are provisional or rejected because of a missing or mismatched date of birth (Section 13‑13‑245).

Updates related absentee‑ballot handling, early‑tabulation, and mail‑ballot rules to incorporate the new date‑of‑birth requirement (Sections 13‑13‑232, 13‑15‑201, 13‑19‑106, 13‑19‑301, 13‑19‑304, 13‑19‑312).

Leaves other election‑administration provisions (e.g., electronic ballots for disabled persons, performance testing of voting systems) unchanged but ensures they also reference the new DOB requirement where applicable.
affected: Election administrators and county election officials
numbers: 10% of each type of voting system

HB723.one_line: Mandates annual reporting of infants born alive after abortion, with fines for non‑compliance.
HB723.summary: HB 723 requires every medical facility that delivers an infant alive after an abortion or attempted abortion to file an annual report with the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS). The DPHHS will publish an aggregated, anonymized report by June 30 each year.
changes: 1. Mandates annual reporting by medical facilities on infants born alive after abortion or attempted abortion, due February 28 each year.
2. Requires reports to include gestational age category, medical actions taken, outcome, and medical conditions of the infant.
3. DPHHS must adopt a standardized reporting form and distribute it to all facilities.
4. DPHHS must publish an anonymized aggregate report by June 30 each year, including year‑to‑year totals.
5. DPHHS may impose civil fines up to $500 for each 30‑day delay in filing and can seek injunctive relief for prolonged non‑compliance.
affected: Medical facilities that deliver infants alive after abortion or attempted abortion
Department of Public Health and Human Services
Patients and families (indirectly, through aggregated data)

HB721.one_line: Revises Montana apprenticeship law to clarify duties, standards, and voluntary employer participation.
HB721.summary: HB 721 revises Montana’s apprenticeship law to clarify the Department of Labor’s duties, set standards for apprenticeship agreements, and confirm that employer participation is voluntary. It also limits credit for prior training to 50% and requires a minimum of 2,000 apprenticeship hours and 144 instruction hours per year.
changes: Amends §39‑6‑101 to expand the Department’s duties: promotion, registration, record‑keeping, certification, termination, assistance for non‑apprenticeable occupations, wage standards, rule‑making, and federal‑regulation compliance.

Revises §39‑6‑103 to make state and local vocational‑education boards responsible for related instruction, coordination with job experience, and teacher/coordinator selection in partnership with the state apprenticeship agency.

Revises §39‑6‑106 to set detailed contents of apprenticeship agreements, including minimum hours, age, wage scale, probation, dispute resolution, employer transfer, apprentice‑to‑journeyman ratio, and limits credit for prior training to 50%.
Revises §39‑6‑107 to state that all employer participation is voluntary and that the chapter’s provisions apply only after a firm elects to comply.
Adds a requirement that the Department report biannually to the Governor, Legislature, and public about its apprenticeship activities.
affected: Employers who wish to run apprenticeship programs
Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB725.one_line: HB 725 bars a precinct‑committee member from serving multiple parties in the same two‑year term.
HB725.summary: HB 725 limits precinct‑committee representatives to one party per two‑year term, amending the election‑appointment rules to enforce this restriction.
changes: Amends §13‑38‑201 to prohibit an individual from serving as a precinct‑committee representative for more than one political party during the same two‑year term.
Requires each party to appoint or elect one representative of each sex for every precinct at each primary election.
Preserves existing procedures for appointments, elections, acclamations, write‑ins, and tie‑breakers under the amended section.
Leaves all other rights, duties, penalties, and ongoing proceedings unaffected by a saving clause.
Does not create a new program, office, or criminal offense.
affected: Registered voters who are potential committee members
Political parties and their governing bodies
numbers: one person of each sex per precinct

HB726.one_line: Revises bail bond licensing: new training, education, and fee‑disclosure rules.
HB726.summary: HB 726 revises Montana’s surety bail bond licensing rules, tightening qualifications, adding a 16‑hour basic training course, requiring biennial continuing education, and mandating fee disclosure. It also allows temporary licenses for supervised applicants and exempts existing agents from initial training.
changes: Adds new minimum age and citizenship requirements for license applicants
Requires a 16‑hour basic training course (or equivalent law‑enforcement training) before a license can be issued
Mandates biennial continuing education of 1 hour on legal updates and 4 hours of industry credits
Allows a 12‑month temporary license for supervised applicants, but prohibits renewal
Exempts currently licensed agents from initial training but requires them to complete the continuing‑education program
Requires disclosure of all fees and interest at contract execution
Amends sections 33‑17‑1601 and 33‑17‑1602 of the Montana Code
affected: Defendants and their families (through fee disclosure)
numbers: 5‑year active business requirement for supervising agent

HB732.one_line: HB 732 mandates prompt settlement of critical‑access hospital cost reports and appropriates funds to cover the process.
HB732.summary: HB 732 establishes a new prompt‑settlement process for critical‑access hospital cost reports, requiring the Department of Public Health and Human Services to make an interim payment within 240 days and a final payment within 90 days after audit. It also appropriates funds to cover the additional administrative costs.
changes: Department must perform a tentative retroactive adjustment and interim settlement within 240 days of receipt of a cost report, or 30 days after Medicare’s interim settlement, whichever comes first.
If a final audit finds an overpayment, the provider has 60 days to repay or set up a repayment schedule; if an underpayment is found, the Department must pay within 90 days of notification.
The Department must settle all cost reports filed before the act’s effective date within 240 days of that date.
The act appropriates $33,900 from state and federal funds for FY 2025, $33,900 for FY 2026, and $15,000 for the biennium as ongoing base.
The provisions are codified as part of Title 53, Chapter 6.
The act is effective upon passage and applies retroactively to cost reports filed before the effective date.
affected: Critical‑access hospitals participating in Montana Medicaid
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB735.one_line: HB 735 expands fingerprint requirements for Montana alcohol‑licensing applicants and managers, with a five‑year reuse rule.
HB735.summary: HB 735 amends Montana’s alcohol‑licensing code to add new definitions, expand the list of licenses that require applicant and location‑manager fingerprints, and allows a single background check for multiple licenses within five years. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §16‑1‑106 to add a comprehensive set of definitions for alcohol‑related terms.

Rewrites §16‑4‑414 to require fingerprints and background checks for applicants and location managers of a broad array of alcohol‑licensing categories, including wineries, breweries, beer‑and‑wine licenses, all‑beverages licenses, and several special licenses.
Adds an exception that a publicly traded corporation’s officers and its location managers must also submit fingerprints.
Allows a single background check to cover multiple license applications for up to five years, provided no new criminal charges arise.
Clarifies that a change in business entity structure that does not create new ownership interest does not trigger a new fingerprint requirement.
affected: Location managers of licensed alcohol‑retail or production entities
Publicly traded corporations applying for alcohol licenses
The Department of Revenue and Department of Justice (background‑check processing)

HB739.one_line: Motor‑vehicle drivers must slow for agricultural vehicles and agricultural vehicles must move aside when safe.
HB739.summary: HB 739 requires motor‑vehicle drivers to slow to the speed of an on‑road agricultural vehicle or to half the posted speed limit when approaching from the opposite direction, and it obliges agricultural vehicles to move to a safe turnout or shoulder when a line of cars is behind them.
changes: Motor‑vehicle operators must reduce speed to match an agricultural vehicle traveling in the same direction, or to half the posted speed limit when traveling opposite.
Drivers may pass an agricultural vehicle only when it is safe and passing is allowed.
Agricultural vehicles behind a line of cars must move off the roadway to a safe turnout or shoulder if available.
The bill defines “agricultural vehicle” to include tractors, implements, self‑propelled units, tractor‑to‑wed combinations, and hay‑hauling vehicles.
The provisions are codified as part of Title 61, Chapter 8, Part 3 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Operators of agricultural vehicles on highways

HB736.one_line: HB 736 creates a nutrient‑offset trading system for Montana water permits.
HB736.summary: HB 736 lets point‑source dischargers earn nutrient‑offset credits by reducing nutrient loads from other sources, and allows the Department to issue or modify permits based on those offsets. The bill creates a framework for measuring, approving, and trading such offsets.
changes: 1. Grants dischargers the ability to obtain nutrient‑pollutant loading offsets or trading credits to meet permit limits under §75‑5‑401 and §75‑5‑703.
2. Requires the Department to issue or modify permits when offset actions reduce nutrient loading in the same 12‑digit hydrologic unit code (HUC) subbasin or an adjacent HUC.
3. Authorizes offsets for increases in discharges if a net decrease in loading is achieved elsewhere in the subbasin or adjacent subbasin.
4. Sets minimum credit ratios: 100 % for point‑source reductions, 80 % for up‑gradient non‑point reductions, and 50 % for down‑gradient non‑point reductions.
5. Gives the Department authority to establish statewide acceptable methodologies for non‑point source offsets (e.g., riparian fencing, vegetation, wetlands, septic removal).
6. Requires the Department to amend DEQ‑13 and ARM 17.30.1701 to implement the new rules.
7. Codifies the provisions as part of Title 75, Chapter 5, Part 4, and makes the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Point‑source dischargers of nutrients to state surface waters
Non‑point source projects that can provide offset credits
The Montana Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ)
Permittees seeking to modify or obtain permits based on offsets

HB742.one_line: Revises nuisance law to require three nearby complaints before county inspections.
HB742.summary: HB 742 amends Montana’s nuisance statutes to require that at least three nearby property owners file a complaint before a county officer may inspect a site, while still allowing health‑violation actions without complaints. It also clarifies definitions of public nuisance and updates enforcement language for county ordinances.
changes: Adds a three‑property‑owner complaint threshold for county inspections under §7‑5‑2111.

HB740.one_line: HB 740 tightens pharmacy fee rules, price updates, and PBM contracting to protect pharmacies and patients.
HB740.summary: HB 740 updates Montana pharmacy law to limit how pharmacies and pharmacy‑benefit managers (PBMs) can charge fees, recoup funds, and set drug prices. It adds new definitions, tightens recoupment rules, requires frequent price updates, and protects pharmacy rights to disclose costs and participate in litigation.
changes: PBMs and third‑party payers may not charge dispensing, claim‑submission, enrollment, credentialing, or other claim‑related fees unless the fee is disclosed on remittance advice before the claim is adjudicated
PBMs may not use “effective‑rate” contracting; all reimbursement must be based on a fixed price or reference price
Plan sponsors and PBMs must update maximum‑allowable‑cost (MAC) lists or reference prices at least every 10 calendar days and provide pharmacies with searchable, up‑to‑date lists
Independent pharmacies must receive at least the national average drug acquisition cost plus a $15 (inflation‑adjusted) professional dispensing fee; PBMs cannot reimburse below the contract price
PBMs may not impose performance‑based fees that reduce the cost of goods sold; they may only charge on the professional dispensing fee if a pharmacy fails a performance‑measurement test

Pharmacies have a private right of action for violations; PBMs must provide key contract and payment information to pharmacies and cannot prohibit pharmacists from disclosing reimbursement details or participating in class‑action suits
The act applies to conduct from Oct 1 2025 and expires June 30 2029
affected: Pharmacy benefit managers and third‑party payers

HB743.one_line: HB 743 mandates reporting of elder exploitation cases to county attorneys, the Attorney General, and the Law & Justice Interim Committee.
HB743.summary: HB 743 creates mandatory reporting and record‑keeping procedures for alleged exploitation of incapacitated persons or vulnerable adults.  County attorneys must receive materials from the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) and file annual reports to the Attorney General, who then reports to the Law & Justice Interim Committee.  The bill amends the content of exploitation reports and includes coordination provisions with a potential House Bill 532.
changes: DPHHS must forward all credible exploitation materials to the county attorney where the victim resides, and the county attorney must keep those records throughout the investigation or prosecution.
Each county attorney must submit a detailed annual report to the Attorney General by July 1, including case identifiers, dates, charges, convictions, and outcomes for each referral.
The Attorney General must create a standardized reporting form and compile aggregated data for each county, reporting to the Law & Justice Interim Committee by September 1.
DPHHS must report the number of referrals to county attorneys each even‑numbered year by September 15, and advise the Attorney General when it believes prosecution is warranted.
Section 52‑3‑812 is amended to specify the required content of exploitation reports (names, addresses, nature of abuse, etc.).
Coordination clauses provide that if House Bill 532 is enacted and repeals the current exploitation offense, the reporting requirements in HB 743 would be replaced by alternate language.
No new criminal offense or state program is created; the bill only changes reporting procedures.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB744.one_line: Allows school‑district aides to work without a license under 20 % supervision, pending board rules.
HB744.summary: HB 744 authorizes speech‑language pathology aides and audiology aides to work in school districts without a state license, setting supervision and activity limits. It gives the board rule‑making authority to define qualifications and permits a limited license for supervised experience. The act takes effect on passage but is contingent on rule adoption, ending 30 days after final rules are adopted.
changes: Amends §37‑15‑301 to allow speech‑language pathology aides and audiology aides employed by school districts to work without a state license.
Requires such aides to work under a speech‑language pathologist or audiologist for at least 20 % of their time and prohibits independent judgment tasks.
Gives the board authority to establish qualifications and permitted activities for these aides by rule, but rules cannot be more restrictive than the statutory limits.
Provides for a limited license for qualified individuals engaged in supervised professional experience.
Makes the act effective upon passage but contingent on the board adopting rules within 30 days; the act terminates 30 days after rule adoption if not adopted.
Requires the Department of Labor and Industry to certify to the code commissioner within 14 days after the contingency occurs.
affected: Board of Speech‑Language Pathologists and Audiologists
HB744.effective: upon passage, contingent on rule adoption

HB745.one_line: Mandates background checks for all staff and volunteers with student contact and adds a check to teacher licensure.
HB745.summary: HB 745 requires every Montana school district to adopt a student‑protection policy that mandates fingerprint‑based background checks for anyone who may have unsupervised contact with students, and it adds a criminal‑history check to the teacher‑licensure process. Districts that fail to comply must submit a correction plan to the Superintendent of Public Instruction. The act also amends several existing school‑law sections and takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: 1. Amends §20‑3‑323 to require districts to adopt a student‑protection policy that requires a fingerprint‑based national criminal‑history background check before any individual—regardless of employment status—may have unsupervised contact with students, at school, a school‑sponsored activity, or in transit to such an activity.

2. Adds a requirement that the individual provide the Montana Department of Justice with information sufficient to obtain the background check, and that a designated trustee, superintendent, or other official review the results.
3. Requires districts that do not comply with the new policy to submit a correction plan to the Superintendent of Public Instruction.
4. Amends §20‑3‑324 to clarify that the board’s duties include adopting and enforcing the student‑protection policy and submitting a correction plan if non‑compliance occurs.
5. Amends §20‑4‑104 to add a fingerprint‑based national criminal‑history background check as a qualification for teacher certification.
6. Provides an effective date of July 1, 2025.
affected: Individuals seeking employment or volunteer positions with unsupervised student contact
numbers: 15 cents per page for minutes copy

HB752.one_line: HB 752 bars Montana content providers from distributing child sexual abuse material and creates civil remedies for victims.
HB752.summary: HB 752 bars Montana‑based content providers from making child sexual abuse material (CSAM) reasonably accessible in the state, gives victims and private parties a civil remedy, and authorizes the Department of Justice to enforce the law. The bill sets statutory damages, a detailed apportionment scheme, and a 10‑year statute of limitations for private claims.
changes: 1. Prohibits any content provider that publishes or distributes a substantial amount of sexually explicit visual content from also distributing CSAM that is reasonably accessible in Montana.
2. Bars any content provider that earns ≥ $500,000 and ≥ 50 % of its income from sexually explicit content from distributing CSAM in Montana.
3. Requires a 48‑96‑hour removal defense for content providers that delete CSAM after it becomes accessible.
4. Creates a private right of action for victims (or their guardians) and for any private person who can identify a victim, with a 10‑year statute of limitations.
5. Grants the Montana Department of Justice the authority to file civil actions and to serve victims with copies of complaints.

6. Establishes statutory damages ($100 k, $1 M, or $5 M depending on negligence, recklessness, or intentionality) and a detailed apportionment of punitive and statutory damages among victims, the plaintiff, and the Department of Justice.
affected: Content providers that publish or distribute sexually explicit visual content
Victims of child sexual abuse material
Private persons who can identify a victim

HB756.one_line: HB 756 updates grant criteria for Montana historic‑preservation projects, adding public‑access and matching‑fund rules.
HB756.summary: HB 756 revises the Montana Museums Act to update the criteria the Department of Commerce uses when recommending historic‑preservation grants. It adds detailed competitive factors—such as building protection, economic impact, public access, and organizational track record—and requires for‑profit applicants to match grant dollars.
changes: Amends Section 22‑3‑1306, MCA, to set new grant‑recommendation criteria for historic preservation projects.
Specifies that funded projects must keep a significant portion open to public use; projects with only private benefit are ineligible.

Introduces a list of competitive criteria (building envelope protection, economic stimulus, project purpose, timing, historic value, organizational record, ongoing economic benefit, local contribution, public benefit).
Adds a matching‑fund requirement: for‑profit entities must match $1 for every $1 of grant money.
Mandates the Department of Commerce to adopt implementation rules compatible with other state grant programs.
Requires government applicants to comply with specific constitutional and statutory provisions; non‑government applicants are exempt.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Eligible entities applying for historic preservation grants (historical societies, museums, historic sites), especially for‑profit organizations.
Department of Commerce (responsible for rulemaking and recommendations).

HB757.one_line: HB 757 revises grant ranking criteria, adds a small‑budget waiver, and amends the advisory committee’s duties.
HB757.summary: HB 757 revises how the Cultural and Aesthetic Projects Advisory Committee ranks grant applications, adds a waiver for small‑budget applicants to avoid a federal SAMs number, and amends the committee’s statutory duties. The bill does not create a new program or fund.
changes: The committee now ranks applicants first by prior grant award history (none, one, two, or three awards in the past three cycles) and second by annual operating budget (<$99,999; $100,000‑$249,999; $250,000‑$499,999; ≥$500,000).
Between funding cycles the committee, with the budget director, will adjust the budget‑size thresholds for inflation.

Applicants whose total program budget does not exceed $100,000 and who do not use federal funds may request a waiver of the federal SAMs number requirement; the committee may not unreasonably deny the waiver.

Section 22‑2‑302 is amended to clarify that the advisory committee reviews all proposals before they reach the legislature, makes advisory recommendations, and must present those recommendations to the Appropriations Committee by the 15th day of any regular session.
Sections 1 and 2 are codified as part of Title 22, Chapter 2, Part 3, and the existing statutory framework applies to them.

HB759.one_line: HB 759 restricts LLC and partnership contributions to candidates, requiring member‑level reporting and prohibiting separate individual contributions.
HB759.summary: HB 759 limits campaign‑finance contributions from limited‑liability companies (LLCs) and partnerships. Only LLCs or partnerships taxed as sole‑proprietorships or partnerships may give money to a candidate, and the contribution must be reported under the name of the member or partner who actually gave the money. The member or partner cannot also give a separate individual contribution that would exceed individual limits.
changes: Only LLCs or partnerships taxed as sole‑proprietorships or partnerships may contribute to a candidate; C‑ or S‑corporation‑taxed entities are barred.
Contributions from such entities must be reported under the name of the member or partner who made the contribution, not the entity name.
The member or partner who reports the contribution cannot also make a separate individual contribution that would violate individual contribution limits.
The bill codifies these rules as a new part of Title 13, Chapter 37.
affected: LLCs and partnerships that wish to contribute
Members or partners of those entities

HB760.one_line: HB 760 gives Montana solar buyers a 3‑day cancellation right and bans deceptive sales practices.
HB760.summary: HB 760 creates a 3‑day cancellation right for Montana solar buyers and requires sales agents to disclose this right in capital letters. It also bars deceptive statements about costs and terms in solar sales.
changes: Solar buyers may cancel a solar installation contract within 3 business days of signing, with written notice by e‑mail or certified mail.
If a buyer rescinds, the solar company or sales agent cannot enforce any contract terms or seek payment for labor and materials.
Solar sales agents must provide a written, capital‑letter explanation of the buyer’s right to cancel at the time of solicitation.
Agents are prohibited from making deceptive statements about costs, financing, or contract terms.

HB762.one_line: DFW&P must publish a biennial river‑use report funded by state park revenues, with a $2.6 million appropriation and sunset in 2028.
HB762.summary: HB 762 requires the Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks (DFW&P) to publish a biennial river‑use report and authorizes the use of state park account funds for that report. The bill also amends fee‑collection and reporting provisions and appropriates $2.6 million for the 2025‑2026 biennium, with a sunset date of October 2 2028.
changes: Amends §23‑1‑105 to allow use of motor‑vehicle registration‑fee revenue for the river‑use report and to clarify fee‑collection rules.
Amends §87‑1‑201(15) to require a biennial public report on watercraft use on specified river stretches, detailing private and commercial vessels and total counts.
Adds a $2.6 million appropriation from the state park account for the 2025‑2026 biennium to fund the report.
Specifies that unspent funds by October 3 2028 revert to the state park account.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and termination to October 2 2028.
Requires the report be filed no later than October 1 of even‑numbered years.
affected: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks
river‑use stakeholders (commercial and private watercraft operators)

HB763.one_line: HB 763 expands rule‑making for block‑management, simplifies adjacent‑land agreements, and caps landowner payments.
HB763.summary: HB 763 amends Montana’s block‑management program to give the Fish & Wildlife Commission broader rule‑making authority, allows simplified agreements that only grant access to adjacent public lands, and sets limits on payments to landowners.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑265 to clarify that the department may develop alternative programs to the block‑management program
Provides the Fish & Wildlife Commission the power to adopt rules for simplified agreements that only give access to adjacent public lands
Sets a maximum annual payment of $50,000 (or $25,000 for agreements that only provide access to public land) to participating landowners
Requires cooperative agreements to detail conditions for use, services, ranch rules, and other management information
Mandates consultation with affected landowners, public‑land leaseholders, and other agencies when agreements may affect game management or habitat
Allows the commission to exempt certain agreements from tracking days of public hunting or to pay flat‑fee rates
Specifies that liability restrictions under §70‑16‑302(1) apply to participants
Provides for direct payments for weed control, fire protection, and insurance costs, and for assistance with roads, gates, and parking facilities
affected: Private landowners participating in hunting‑access programs
County weed‑control boards and fire districts

HB764.one_line: HB 764 expands transit district creation, adds removal rules, and clarifies municipal bus‑service limits.
HB764.summary: HB 764 revises Montana’s public‑transit statutes to streamline the creation, expansion, and removal of urban transportation districts and to clarify municipal bus‑service authority, including an 8‑mile limit that can be exceeded with external funding. The bill adds petition procedures, public‑hearing requirements, and debt‑limit rules for city‑run bus lines. It also allows property owners to be removed from districts if no service has been provided for five years, without incurring existing indebtedness.
changes: County commissioners may file a petition and initiate the creation or enlargement of an urban transportation district by resolution, requiring a map and a public hearing.
Petitions to create or enlarge districts must be signed by at least 20 % of registered electors in the proposed area; insufficient signatures void the petition.
A public hearing is mandated, followed by a vote of qualified electors on the district creation or expansion.

Property owners can petition to be added to a district, and districts may remove added areas if no direct service has been provided for five years and 51 % of voters in the area sign a removal petition.
Municipal bus service may extend beyond 8 miles from a city or town’s limits only if funded by an external source or inter‑local agreement.
Cities and towns may borrow money or issue bonds for bus service only after a majority vote of taxpayers, and the total indebtedness cannot exceed the state debt limit.
Municipalities may levy an annual tax on taxable property to fund bus service, subject to a voter‑approved levy if it exceeds the standard limit.
Municipalities may solicit bids from independent carriers for bus service contracts and operate the system under the authority granted in the amended sections.
affected: Registered voters in proposed district areas
Property owners within or adjacent to transportation districts

HB767.one_line: HB 767 adds goats to predator control, authorizes fees, and lets owners petition for program changes.
HB767.summary: HB 767 expands Montana’s predator‑control framework to cover goats, allowing counties to levy a per‑capita license fee, create a dedicated fund, and let goat owners petition for program changes.
changes: County commissioners may establish a goat‑specific predator‑control program and set a per‑capita license fee for goats 1 year 9 months or older.
Fees are collected by the county treasurer, become a lien on the owner’s property, and are deposited in a new predatory‑animal‑control fund separate from existing livestock funds.
Proceeds from the sale of skins and furs of captured predators are also deposited in that fund.

Goat owners who own at least 51 % of the county’s goats can petition the board to start or terminate the program and to change the fee; petitions must be filed by the first Monday in December and cannot be withdrawn after the hearing hour.
The bill amends Sections 81‑7‑303 and 81‑7‑603 to apply the same per‑capita fee structure to sheep and cattle, aligning age thresholds.
The new provisions are codified as a new part of Title 81, Chapter 7.

HB768.one_line: HB 768 limits liability for equine sponsors, mandates risk disclosure in waivers, and permits legal challenge.
HB768.summary: HB 768 amends Montana’s equine‑activity liability law to clarify when sponsors and professionals are not liable, requires waivers to list inherent risks and a jury‑trial waiver statement, and allows waivers to be challenged on other legal grounds.
changes: Adds a new subsection (2) requiring participants to act safely and be aware of risks.

Expands subsection (3) to list specific conditions that defeat liability protection, including equipment failure, failure to assess participant ability, latent dangerous conditions, willful disregard, intentional injury, and products‑liability claims.
Introduces subsection (4) mandating that any waiver must state known inherent risks and include a bolded jury‑trial waiver statement.
Allows waivers that meet the new requirements to still be challenged on any legal grounds.
Clarifies that compliant waivers are not subject to 28‑2‑702.

HB769.one_line: Revises night‑shift meal‑allowance timing and limits claims, adds midday allowance for board members.
HB769.summary: HB 769 revises Montana’s meal‑allowance rules for employees working night shifts, redefining the time windows for each allowance and limiting how many can be claimed in a single travel period. It also adds a midday‑meal entitlement for state board members attending meetings and requires the Department of Administration to issue implementation policies.
changes: Redefines the time periods that qualify for morning, midday, evening, midnight, and early‑morning meal allowances for night‑shift workers.
Limits eligible employees to one allowance if travel occurs within the assigned shift, or up to two allowances if travel starts before or ends after the shift but does not exceed 24 hours.
Introduces a new midday‑meal allowance for appointed members of state boards, commissions, or councils (and legislative subcommittees) when attending meetings, except during a legislative session.
Prescribes that the Department of Administration shall issue policies to administer the new provisions.
Amends Section 2‑18‑502, MCA, to incorporate the above changes.
No new program or criminal offense is created.
affected: State board, commission, council, and legislative committee members attending meetings

HB770.one_line: Candidates must file reports even with no money; failure removes them from the ballot.
HB770.summary: HB 770 amends Montana’s campaign‑finance reporting rules so that candidates and committees must file reports even when no money is exchanged, sets specific filing dates, and makes failure to file a disqualifying offense that removes a candidate from the ballot. The bill also clarifies reporting thresholds for local‑issue activities and expands the definition of when a report is required for special elections.
changes: Candidates must file quarterly, monthly, and special‑election reports even if they receive no contributions or make no expenditures.

Reporting deadlines are tightened: quarterly reports by the 5th of the month after each quarter; monthly reports by the 20th of most months; and rapid reports within two business days for large contributions or expenditures near an election.
Local‑issue committees and candidates only file reports if total contributions or expenditures exceed $500.
Failure to file any required report results in the candidate’s name being removed from the official ballot.
The bill amends §13‑37‑226 to incorporate these new filing requirements and clarifies definitions of participation.
affected: Candidates for state, local, and municipal offices
Political committees and joint fundraising committees
numbers: Monthly due 20th day of March, April, May, June, August, September, October, November
Rapid reports within 2 business days for $500+ contributions or expenditures

HB775.one_line: Repeals sunset date for water‑rights judicial review, extending Water Court authority.
HB775.summary: HB 775 removes the sunset provision that would have ended judicial review of water rights, keeping Water Court authority in place. It also authorizes Water Court review of certain Department of Natural Resources decisions and clarifies the Court’s duties. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Repeals Section 6, Chapter 126, Laws of 2017, which contained a sunset date for water‑rights judicial review.
Keeps Water Court authority active for reviewing water‑rights matters.
Authorizes Water Court to review certain decisions of the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation.
Clarifies the duties of the Water Court.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The act is effective on passage and approval.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

HB778.one_line: Separates home‑school and non‑public school requirements for enrollment exemption and record‑keeping.
HB778.summary: HB 778 separates the rules that apply to home schools from those that apply to non‑public schools, revising the state’s compulsory‑enrollment‑exemption requirements for each type. The bill amends §20‑5‑109, MCA, to clarify record‑keeping, instructional‑hour, health‑safety, and curriculum requirements for both home schools and non‑public schools and requires home schools to notify the county superintendent each fiscal year. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Rewrites §20‑5‑109 to split requirements for non‑public schools and home schools into distinct subsections.

Specifies that non‑public schools must maintain attendance and immunization records, provide minimum instructional hours, occupy a building meeting local health‑safety rules, and offer a curriculum covering public‑school subjects.

Specifies that home schools must notify the county superintendent each fiscal year, keep attendance records, provide minimum instructional hours, and offer a curriculum covering public‑school subjects.
Both school types must keep attendance records available to the county superintendent on request.
The bill does not create new programs or funds; it merely clarifies existing statutory language.
Effective immediately upon passage.

HB785.one_line: HB 785 establishes a new filing process for treating manufactured homes as real‑property improvements.
HB785.summary: HB 785 revises Montana’s rules for treating manufactured homes as real‑property improvements. It creates a new “statement of intent” filing process and an alternate path for homes built before 2005 that lack factory tags. The bill requires removal of running gear, permanent foundation, and county‑recorded intent, and it authorizes the county treasurer to process the transfer and fee.
changes: Amends §15‑1‑116, MCA, to add a new filing procedure for declaring a manufactured home an improvement to real property.
Requires owners to record a statement of intent that includes serial number, property description, security interests, lienholder approval, and signature.
The county treasurer must accept the surrendered certificate of origin or title, pay a fee, and forward records to the Department of Justice.
The Department of Justice must issue a completion statement to the owner.
Adds a special provision for pre‑2005 homes lacking factory tags, allowing them to be treated as improvements if the home has been taxed as real property for at least one year.
The new process applies to lending institutions and the Department of Revenue in the same way as other residences.

HB786.one_line: Amends council leadership language, clarifying presiding officer as chief executive officer.
HB786.summary: HB 786 amends the Montana Arts Council statute to clarify that the presiding officer is the council’s chief executive officer and that the governor appoints a presiding and vice‑presiding officer for the council’s term. The amendment also specifies that vacancies are filled for the remainder of the term and that council members receive compensation and travel expenses as set out in the state’s travel statute. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §22‑2‑103 to state that the presiding officer is the chief executive officer of the Montana Arts Council.
Specifies that the governor appoints a presiding officer and a vice‑presiding officer from council members for the duration of their term.
Requires vacancies in the council to be filled for the balance of the unexpired term in the same manner as the original appointment.
Reaffirms that council members are compensated and receive travel expenses per §2‑15‑124.
The amendment takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: State employees who travel for council business

HB791.one_line: Rewrites nuisance law, limits liability, and restricts damages for public and private nuisances.
HB791.summary: HB 791 rewrites Montana’s nuisance statutes, tightening definitions, limiting liability, and restricting remedies for both public and private nuisances. It bars many traditional causes of action, limits damages, and gives the state broad authority to abate nuisances while protecting private property owners from class actions. The bill takes effect for claims arising after Oct. 1 2025.
changes: Redefines public nuisance to exclude lawful, licensed, or statutory activities and shooting‑range noise; adds a list of non‑nuisance conditions.
Creates a private nuisance definition that excludes statutory or licensed activities and shooting‑range noise.
Preempts common‑law nuisance and all other state statutes that conflict with the new definitions.
Limits liability for public nuisances to the proximate cause and prohibits strict‑liability claims; successive owners are liable only if they neglect to abate.
Allows government entities to sue only for injunctions and cost‑based abatement, not for damages; prohibits damages in public‑nuisance actions.
Permits private persons to sue only for compensatory damages for a “special injury” proven by clear and convincing evidence; class actions are barred.
Adds emergency abatement provisions for private nuisances, allowing injured parties to remove or destroy the nuisance with notice if necessary.
Repeals numerous old nuisance sections (27‑30‑102‑105, 201‑203, 301‑302) and codifies the new provisions into Title 27, Chapter 30.
Applies only to causes of action that accrue on or after Oct. 1 2025; pre‑existing claims remain governed by prior law.
affected: Businesses operating under statutes or licenses
Owners of agricultural or farming operations
numbers: no class actions for private nuisance
no damages for future nuisance abatement

HB792.one_line: HB 792 tightens Montana cannabis labeling, adds warning posters, and expands regulatory rule‑making authority.
HB792.summary: HB 792 amends Montana’s cannabis laws to tighten labeling, packaging, and advertising rules, requires warning posters at sales points, and gives the Department of Revenue rule‑making authority. The act takes effect July 1, 2026.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑112 to grant the Department of Revenue broad rule‑making authority over licensing, security, testing, labeling, advertising, and fee structures for marijuana businesses.

Rewrites §16‑12‑215 to mandate specific warning labels on all marijuana exit packaging and to require every point‑of‑sale location to display a consumer‑education poster that includes the same warnings, a universal symbol, and contact information for addiction resources.
Adds new requirements for child‑resistant packaging, limits on THC potency, and testing/retesting standards, including procedures for sample collection and destruction of non‑compliant products.
Specifies that warning posters must be at least 8½ × 11 inches, include a universal symbol, the mandated warnings, and a quick‑reference code to addiction resources.
Provides that the Department may consult or contract with other public agencies and may not adopt rules that are unduly burdensome.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2026.
affected: Marijuana licensees, manufacturers, retailers, and distributors in Montana
Consumers of marijuana and marijuana products
Public agencies involved in enforcement and regulation
numbers: one‑sixteenth of an inch font size for the letter "o"
THC and other cannabinoid content in milligrams per serving

HB793.one_line: HB 793 redefines POST Council membership, adding new roles and limiting size to 13.
HB793.summary: HB 793 revises the composition of the Public Safety Officer Standards and Training (POST) Council, adding several new member categories and limiting the council to 13 voting members. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Council size capped at 13 voting members
Adds a state‑government law‑enforcement representative
Adds a chief of police (recommended by the Montana Association of Chiefs of Police)
Adds a sheriff (recommended by the Montana Sheriffs and Peace Officers Association)
Adds a representative from the Department of Corrections
Adds a local law‑enforcement officer in a non‑administrative role (recommended by the Montana Police Protective Association)
Adds a detention center administrator or officer
Adds a Montana‑certified tribal law‑enforcement representative
Adds a county attorney (recommended by the Montana County Attorneys Association)
Adds two members from the Board of Crime Control
Adds a public‑safety communications officer (recommended by the Montana chapter of the Association of Public‑Safety Communications Officials)
Adds a misdemeanor probation officer (certified by POST and recommended by an association of misdemeanor probation officers)
Adds two Montana citizens with law‑enforcement experience
All appointments are made by the governor in accordance with 2‑15‑124

HB794.one_line: Revises pharmacy law, expands board authority, and removes utilization‑plan requirement for mail‑order pharmacies.
HB794.summary: HB 794 updates Montana pharmacy law, modernizes definitions, expands the board’s rule‑making power, and removes the utilization‑plan requirement for in‑state and out‑of‑state mail‑order pharmacies. It also creates a new clinical‑pharmacist‑practitioner endorsement, clarifies pharmacy‑wholesale licensing, and revises several related statutes.
affected: Pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, out‑of‑state mail‑order pharmacies, patients, insurance carriers, and the Board of Pharmacy

HB796.one_line: Expands licensing board subpoena authority for health‑care records while preserving privacy safeguards.
HB796.summary: HB 796 expands the circumstances under which a professional licensing board or program may obtain health‑care records by administrative subpoena, adding that such boards may request records for investigative and disciplinary purposes. The bill amends existing Montana statutes to include this new exception while preserving all other privacy safeguards.
changes: Adds subsection (l) to §50‑16‑535 and §50‑16‑811 allowing health‑care information to be requested by an administrative subpoena issued for investigative or disciplinary proceedings before a professional or occupational licensing board or license program.

Retains all prior privacy exceptions (patient authorization, waiver, party status, will relevance, deceased patient, commitment proceeding, law‑enforcement use, compelling state interest, federal subpoena, coroner investigation).
Clarifies that the new exception does not override any prohibition already in law.
Maintains the two‑part structure of the statutes: (1) conditions for disclosure, (2) statement that no disclosure is authorized where otherwise prohibited.
affected: Professional licensing boards and license programs
Health‑care providers who may be compelled to disclose records
Patients whose records could be subpoenaed for disciplinary purposes

HB801.one_line: Limits negligent‑marketing suits against Montana firearms makers and sellers, tightening PLCAA exceptions.
HB801.summary: HB 801 limits lawsuits against Montana firearms manufacturers and sellers for negligent marketing, tightens the PLCAA predicate exception, and creates a private right of action for harmed parties.
changes: Defines "negligent marketing" and sets four strict conditions for a claim to be valid.
Restricts the PLCAA predicate exception to statutes that explicitly regulate firearms and provide clear, concrete requirements.
Prohibits use of general consumer‑protection or nuisance laws as predicate exceptions.
Authorizes the attorney general to enforce the act and imposes dismissal and attorney‑fee penalties for wrongful claims.
Allows a manufacturer or seller harmed by a wrongful claim to sue for damages and injunctive relief and recover reasonable attorney fees.
Codifies the act into Title 45, Chapter 8, Part 3 of the Montana Code.
Includes severability provisions.

HB804.one_line: HB 804 raises lobbying payment threshold to $3,000 and adds inflation adjustment and reporting rules.
HB804.summary: HB 804 raises the lobbying payment threshold to $3,000, adds an inflation‑adjustment rule, and requires principals to file electronic reports when payments exceed that threshold.
changes: Increases the payment threshold for lobbying from $2,150 to $3,000 for the 2025 calendar year.

Mandates the commissioner to adjust the threshold after each even‑year general election using a consumer‑price‑index‑based inflation factor, rounded to the nearest $50 and effective January 1 of the following odd year.
Requires principals who make lobbying payments above the threshold to file electronic reports with the commissioner.
Sets specific filing deadlines: February 15 of a legislative session year, the 15th of the month following a month in which $5,000 or more was spent, and within 30 days after a session adjourns.
Defines detailed reporting categories (printing, advertising, travel, salaries, entertainment, etc.) and itemization requirements for payments above $25, $100, or $250 thresholds.
Specifies that reports must be retained by the commissioner for four years.

HB806.one_line: HB 806 creates a new licensing system for dietitians and nutritionists, adds a board member, and requires background checks.
HB806.summary: HB 806 establishes a new licensing framework for dietitians and nutritionists, adds a nutrition‑related member to the Board of Medical Examiners, and requires criminal background checks for all license applicants. It also creates provisional licenses, clarifies exemptions, and sets detailed education, supervised‑practice, and examination requirements.
changes: Adds a nutritionist/dietitian member to the Board of Medical Examiners and specifies board composition;
Rewrites the licensing chapter (37‑25‑101‑305) to define dietetics and nutrition practice, licensing requirements, and criminal‑background‑check procedures;
Creates provisional and limited permits for individuals to practice under supervision for up to one year;
Establishes detailed education, supervised‑practice, and examination criteria for dietitian and nutritionist licensure;
Defines exemptions from licensure for certain professionals and activities;
Repeals previous sections 37‑25‑301 and 37‑25‑302 and codifies new provisions in Title 37, Chapter 25, Part 3;
Requires applicants to submit fingerprints for state and federal background checks and to pay related fees;
Mandates that the board adopt rules setting professional, practice, and ethical standards for licensed dietitians and nutritionists.
affected: Applicants for dietitian or nutritionist licensure
Health‑care providers who may offer medical nutrition therapy
Students, interns, and paraprofessionals in dietetics programs
Montana Department of Justice (for fingerprint data)
numbers: 200 hours each in assessment, intervention, monitoring

HB807.one_line: Prohibits mandating EUA‑approved or trial vaccines while preserving other exemptions.
HB807.summary: HB 807 bars the state from mandating any vaccine that is only authorized under an emergency use authorization (EUA) or is still in safety trials. It amends the existing anti‑discrimination statute to add this prohibition while preserving other vaccine‑related exemptions.
changes: Amends §49‑2‑312, MCA, to prohibit requiring any vaccine that is EUA‑approved or in safety trials.
Adds a new subsection (4) stating individuals may not be compelled to receive such vaccines.
Preserves existing exemptions for school and day‑care vaccine mandates and for health‑care facilities that ask for voluntary status and provide reasonable accommodations.
Defines "immunity passport" and "vaccination status" for clarity.
Does not create a new program, fund, or criminal offense.

HB808.one_line: Establishes a state brownfields program, fund, and rules, replacing the old petroleum‑brownfields law.
HB808.summary: The bill creates a state‑funded brownfields program that authorizes the Department of Environmental Quality to award federal brownfields grants, defines eligibility and viability rules, and establishes a dedicated account for petroleum‑related cleanup. It repeals the old petroleum‑brownfields law, transfers $200,000 each to the new fund for FY 2026‑2027, and gives the department rule‑making authority.
changes: Creates the Montana Brownfields Revitalization Act and a dedicated state fund for brownfields cleanup.
Defines “brownfield site,” “brownfields redevelopment,” and eligibility criteria for federal brownfields funding.
Establishes viability rules that presume petroleum‑contaminated sites are viable unless proven otherwise, and limits the use of petroleum‑tank‑release funds for brownfields projects.
Authorizes the Department to issue rules on applications, eligibility, award limits, and compliance for the new fund.
Transfers $200,000 from the general fund to the brownfields redevelopment fund for FY 2026 and FY 2027.
Repeals the previous Montana Petroleum Brownfields Revitalization Act (sections 75‑11‑401‑409).
affected: Eligible entities (cities, counties, tribal governments, nonprofits, economic development orgs)

HB809.one_line: Local governments barred from enacting or enforcing extreme‑risk protection orders and from receiving related funds.
HB809.summary: The bill bars Montana local governments from creating, enforcing, or funding extreme‑risk protection orders (red‑flag laws) and amends state law to prohibit local entities from exercising any power that would affect the right to keep or bear arms. Violations trigger a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per offense.
changes: 1. Local governments may not enact, adopt, or implement any ordinance, rule, or policy that would enforce an extreme‑risk protection order against a resident.
2. Local governments may not accept grants or other funding to aid in the adoption, implementation, or enforcement of such orders.
3. Local governments that violate the prohibition face a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per instance of enforcement or attempted enforcement.
4. The bill amends Section 7‑1‑111, MCA, adding a new prohibition (paragraph 31) that bars any local power related to an extreme‑risk protection order.
5. The amendment also clarifies that the prohibition applies to any local power that would affect the right to keep or bear arms.
6. The act contains a severability clause and codification instructions for the new provisions.
affected: Residents subject to extreme‑risk protection orders

HB810.one_line: Limits payment‑type fees and standardizes rent rules for Montana landlords and tenants.
HB810.summary: HB 810 revises Montana’s landlord‑tenant statutes to clarify definitions, limit payment‑type fees, and standardize rent‑payment rules for both residential and mobile‑home rentals. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends definitions in sections 70‑24‑103, 70‑33‑103 to clarify terms such as “abandon,” “rent,” and “rent‑payment type.”

Rewrites sections 70‑24‑201 and 70‑33‑201 to set uniform rent‑payment procedures: rent may be paid by cash, check, electronic transfer, or other agreed‑upon methods, with payment due at the landlord’s address or via electronic funds transfer.
Prohibits landlords from charging any fee based on the tenant’s payment type, except a fee to recover an electronic bank charge incurred by the landlord.
Specifies that rent is payable at the beginning of each month (or at the start of a month‑or‑shorter term) and is uniformly apportionable day‑to‑day.
Provides that a party terminating without cause may recover up to one month’s rent in damages, but not more than that amount.
Maintains that landlords may collect rent from defaulting tenants up to the date a new tenancy begins or the lease term expires.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
who_is_affected

HB817.one_line: HB 817 creates a free, one‑season special hunting permit for ill youths under 18 and revises safety‑course rules.
HB817.summary: HB 817 amends Montana’s hunting‑license rules to allow a free, one‑season special permit for elk, deer or antelope for youths under 18 with a life‑threatening illness, and sets new eligibility, safety‑course waivers, and annual caps. It also revises the general safety‑course requirements for all hunters and clarifies minor‑age licensing rules. The bill creates a new state‑administered special‑permit program and modifies existing licensing statutes.
changes: Creates a free, one‑season special permit license for elk, deer or antelope for youths under 18 diagnosed with a life‑threatening illness and recommended by a Montana charity or nonprofit.
affected: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks
General hunting license holders (new safety‑course rules)
numbers: 5 elk, 5 deer, 5 antelope permits per year (subsection 5)
one‑half price for minors 12‑17 on certain licenses
$17 and $7 deposits for nonresident upland game bird license

HB818.one_line: HB 818 bars foreign nationals from funding statewide ballot measures and creates civil enforcement authority.
HB818.summary: HB 818 bars foreign nationals from contributing to or spending money on statewide ballot measures, gives the commissioner or county attorneys enforcement power, and creates a civil cause of action for violations.
changes: Prohibits foreign nationals (and their intermediaries) from making any contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure related to statewide ballot issues.
Requires political committees that support or oppose a ballot issue to obtain a donor affirmation that the donor is not a foreign national and to keep records of that affirmation.

Empowers the Commissioner of Political Practices or an appropriate county attorney to investigate and bring civil actions for violations, with damages up to three times the unlawful amount or $500, whichever is greater.
Defines “foreign national” broadly to include foreign governments, political parties, foreign‑based entities, and non‑immigrant individuals who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents.
Adds a limitation that civil actions must be filed within two years of the alleged violation and that only one judgment may be obtained per set of facts.
Amends campaign‑treasurer certification requirements to include ballot‑issue committees and to require donor affirmations for foreign‑national checks.
Provides that violations may also be grounds for contesting an election or removal from office, but are not subject to misdemeanor penalties.
affected: Political committees and candidates involved in statewide ballot measures
County attorneys and the Commissioner of Political Practices

HB819.one_line: Limits government property flag displays to official and non‑political symbols, banning political viewpoints.
HB819.summary: HB 819 limits which flags and banners may be displayed on Montana government property, allowing only officially recognized flags and a set of specified exceptions. It prohibits political or ideological symbols while permitting flags honoring law‑enforcement, military, schools, tribes, and historical U.S. flags. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: 1. Establishes a list of permissible flags/banners (U.S., Montana, county, school, foreign, tribal, military, historical, POW/MIA, mascot, law‑enforcement).
2. Bars any flag or banner that expresses a political viewpoint, including party, race, sexual orientation, gender, or ideology, from being displayed on government property.
3. Exempts flags that recognize official government entities, law‑enforcement agencies, military branches, or public‑service organizations from the political‑viewpoint prohibition.
4. Clarifies that the restrictions apply only to government‑controlled displays, not to private speech or personal clothing of employees.
5. Codifies the provisions as part of Title 1, chapter 1, part 6 of the Montana Code.
6. Provides severability and immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: Government property owners (state, county, municipal, school districts, universities, special districts)
Government employees who display flags or banners
Individuals or groups wishing to display political symbols on government property
numbers: historical U.S. flags (e.g., Betsy Ross, Gadsden)

HB823.one_line: HB 823 revises the state plan committee, adds labor appointees, and aligns the plan with the Perkins Act.
HB823.summary: HB 823 amends the state plan committee’s composition and meeting schedule, adds labor‑industry appointees, and requires coordination with the Perkins state plan. It also changes references in law from a 5‑year to a 4‑year career‑and‑technical‑education plan.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑330 to add two labor‑industry appointees to the state plan committee (one executive director/board chair of the State Workforce Innovation Board and one labor‑community representative).

Requires the committee to meet at least four times a year with the Board of Regents and at least three times a year with the Commissioner of Labor and Industry, teachers, students, labor organizations, businesses, and vocational‑education agencies.
Mandates that the committee discuss the state plan, identify issues with the Perkins Act, assess needs of students and employers, and make necessary changes.
If a new or revised 4‑year state plan is submitted, it must coordinate with or be included in the federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act combined state plan.
Directs the Code Commissioner to replace all references to a “5‑year state plan” in Title 5, Title 20, and all laws enacted by the 69th Legislature with “4‑year state plan.”
affected: Teachers, students, labor organizations, businesses, vocational‑education agencies
numbers: at least four times a year
at least three times a year

HB825.one_line: HB 825 creates a patient‑designated trusted decisionmaker and sets a hierarchy for surrogate selection.
HB825.summary: HB 825 lets patients name a trusted decisionmaker (TD) who can act when the patient lacks capacity, sets a clear order for who may act, and expands patient‑rights language in the hospital bill of rights.
changes: Allows a patient to designate a TD at any time after hospital admission and before the provider determines lack of capacity; the designation must be witnessed and documented in the record
Requires the attending provider to notify family and record the TD’s identity and contact info
Gives the TD priority over other proxies unless the provider cannot contact the TD
Establishes a nine‑step hierarchy for selecting a decisionmaker when capacity is lost, placing the TD third after a legally appointed guardian and an agent under a durable power of attorney
Amends the patient‑bill‑of‑rights section to explicitly include TDs as authorized surrogates and expands the list of patient rights
Amends definitions to add “trusted decisionmaker” and clarify related terms
Amends the notification rules so that the TD designation overrides the usual lay‑proxy notification process
affected: Patients who may lack decisional capacity
Family members and other interested persons

HB831.one_line: Raises and adjusts Montana’s elderly property‑tax credit, expanding eligibility and increasing the cap.
HB831.summary: The bill expands the Montana elderly homeowner and renter property‑tax credit by raising the maximum credit, adjusting income thresholds and phase‑out levels for inflation, and clarifying definitions of household income. It also repeals a 2021 law that limited the credit and applies the changes retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
changes: 1. Increases the maximum credit amount to $1,400 (from $1,150).
2. Raises the income threshold for the credit phase‑out and adjusts the phase‑out schedule for inflation, applying new percentages to gross household income between $35,000 and $50,000.
3. Replaces the 2021 law that capped the credit at $1,000 with the new higher cap and updated income limits.
4. Adjusts the definition of household income by subtracting $14,100 (instead of $12,600) from gross household income.
5. Provides an inflationary adjustment to the maximum credit and phase‑out income each year, effective the following tax year.
6. Makes the changes effective immediately upon passage and retroactive to tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
affected: Elderly homeowners and renters in Montana
numbers: Retroactive to tax years after Dec 31 2024

HB832.one_line: Montana funds a two‑year PTSD training grant program for non‑medication therapies.
HB832.summary: Montana will create a $600,000 grant program to train health‑care providers in non‑medication PTSD therapies. The Department of Labor and Industry will award a two‑year project to a competitively selected entity that must train mental‑health professionals and report quarterly results. The program begins July 1, 2025, and the appropriation is one‑time only.
changes: Establishes a new provider‑training grant program for PTSD non‑medication therapies
Allocates $600,000 from the state general fund for the program
Requires the Department of Labor and Industry to award the grant to a competitively selected entity
Mandates community and stakeholder engagement before training begins
Requires quarterly reporting on number of professionals trained and cost per professional
Requires an annual report to the Economic Affairs Interim Committee by July 1
Effective July 1, 2025
Appropriation is a one‑time, biennial allocation for 2025‑2026

HB834.one_line: Creates a two‑year commission to design data‑driven government performance tools.
HB834.summary: HB 834 creates a temporary Government Evidence, Data, and Impact Commission that will meet quarterly to develop a system for collecting and analyzing state‑wide data, recommend efficiencies, and report on program performance. The commission is funded for two years and will be staffed by state officials and a public member.
changes: Establishes a new commission with 10 voting members and 5 ex‑officio non‑voting members.
Mandates the commission to develop a data‑collection and impact‑analysis system and to recommend program efficiencies to the legislature and executive.
Requires the commission to meet quarterly (starting June 1 2025) and to reserve time for public comment.
Provides a $75,000 appropriation from the general fund for the biennium ending June 30 2025 and the following biennium.
Sets the commission’s term from passage to December 31 2026, after which the act terminates.
Outlines staff support from the Department of Administration, Office of Budget and Program Planning, Legislative Fiscal Division, and Legislative Services Division.
affected: State legislators, executive‑branch agency directors, the Department of Administration, the Office of Budget and Program Planning, the Legislative Fiscal Division, the Legislative Services Division, and the public.
State agencies subject to impact analysis.

HB833.one_line: HB 833 creates a corrections fund, appropriates $250 million for new facilities, and sets reporting and contingency rules.
HB833.summary: HB 833 creates a dedicated “Future of Corrections Fund” and appropriates $4 million for assessment and planning, while authorizing a $246 million transfer to build or renovate correctional facilities. It sets reporting requirements and allows lease‑to‑own agreements, but requires a two‑thirds vote if a lease‑to‑own option is used.
changes: Establishes a new account in the state special revenue fund called the Future of Corrections Fund, administered by the Department of Corrections.
Appropriates $4 million from the general fund for assessment, transitional costs, planning, technology, and system studies.
Mandates a $246 million transfer from the general fund to the capital developments long‑range building program account by June 30 2027 for construction/renovation of state correctional facilities.
Authorizes $246 million for capital projects and $3.5 million for operations/maintenance of new facilities, with conditions on reversion if not used.
Allows build‑to‑lease or lease‑to‑own agreements for new facilities and agreements with private facilities under existing statutes.
Requires quarterly reporting to three legislative committees until construction is complete.
Includes a contingency: if the budget director finds the projects not in the state’s best interests, funds can be transferred back to the Future of Corrections Fund.
Specifies that passage without a two‑thirds vote triggers a revised Section 1 that removes lease‑to‑own authority, and mandates a two‑thirds vote if lease‑to‑own is authorized.
affected: Judicial Branch, Law Enforcement, and Justice Interim Budget Committee

HB845.one_line: HB 845 expands and inflates the state deduction for education‑savings contributions, retroactive to 2025.
HB845.summary: HB 845 increases the Montana state income‑tax deduction for contributions to family education savings accounts (FESA) and related 529‑type plans, adds inflation adjustments, and amends related tax‑code sections. The changes apply retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2024 and take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Raises the maximum deduction for FESA contributions to $3,000 per person (or $9,000 for married couples filing jointly) and allows a half‑spouse election for joint filers.
Introduces an inflation factor that increases the deduction each year, calculated from the consumer‑price index for June of the prior year.

Amends §15‑30‑2120 to add the new deduction and to adjust other federal‑to‑state income adjustments, including a $5,500 subtraction for taxpayers age 65 and inflation‑adjusted military‑pension subtractions.
Amends §15‑62‑207 to clarify that the deduction applies to the total contributions in a tax year and limits it to $3,000 per taxpayer.
Provides coordination language that voids overlapping changes from Senate Bill 53 if both bills amend the same subsection.
Sets the effective date to the day the bill is passed and the retroactive applicability to tax years beginning after 12/31/2024.
Includes a provision that the $5,500 age‑65 subtraction is multiplied by the inflation factor each year and rounded to the nearest $10.
Defines the scope of military‑pension subtractions and limits their use to five consecutive years for qualifying residents.
affected: Montana residents who contribute to FESA or other 529‑type education savings accounts
Military retirees receiving pensions or retirement income
Businesses and pass‑through entities claiming related deductions
numbers: inflation factor based on CPI June of prior year
retroactive to tax years beginning after 12/31/2024

HB846.one_line: HB 846 establishes a petition‑based reconciliation payment system and new rules for territory transfers and isolated‑pupil advisory councils.
HB846.summary: HB 846 revises how school districts tax property and share revenue when isolated pupils attend neighboring districts. It creates a petition process for reconciliation payments, sets rules for territory transfers, and requires a 3‑year split of taxable value after a transfer. The bill also establishes advisory councils for isolated‑pupil districts and amends existing transfer‑territory law.
