changes: School districts may petition the county superintendent for a reconciliation payment when they enroll isolated pupils from a contiguous district with a taxable value ≥$100 million and a per‑ANB value >1.5× that of the attending district.
Petitioners must pay a $100 processing fee and file by June 1; the superintendent reviews and decides within 30 days.
If approved, the resident district imposes a levy calculated to generate the payment, which is deposited in its tuition fund and paid to the attending district (half by Dec 31, half by Jun 15).

When territory is transferred between districts, the taxable value of the transferred property is split 50/50 for three fiscal years, and each district levies its share of operational mills on the full value of the transferred area.
If a district that received a reconciliation payment also receives territory, it must levy enough to reimburse the former district for the amount of the prior payment over three years.
Districts with ≥5 % isolated‑pupil enrollment must create an advisory council composed mainly of parents/guardians to discuss isolated‑pupil issues.
Section 20‑6‑105 is amended to clarify petition, hearing, and appeal procedures for territory transfers, including a 4‑year waiting period for new petitions.
affected: School districts that enroll isolated pupils
Taxpayers in districts receiving or transferring territory
School trustees and advisory council members
numbers: 60‑minute travel time definition for isolated pupils
5 % isolated‑pupil enrollment threshold for advisory council
4‑year waiting period for new transfer petitions

HB849.one_line: Special motorcycle plates raise $30 per plate to fund safety nonprofit grants.
HB849.summary: Montana will offer special motorcycle plates that honor local nonprofit safety groups. Owners pay a $30 fee ($5 admin, $5 plate, $20 donation) and the money is split between the county general fund and a state special revenue account that funds grants to those nonprofits. The bill also amends the statutory‑appropriation statute to allow the funds to be used without a biennial appropriation.
changes: Creates a new special motorcycle license plate program for Montana residents who own a motorcycle or quadricycle.
Imposes a $30 fee on each plate: $5 administrative, $5 plate, $20 donation.
Collects the $5 administrative fee into the county general fund and the $25 (plate + donation) into a state special revenue fund.
Transfers $5 of the plate fee to the state general fund and $20 to the special revenue account for grant funding.
Authorizes the Department of Transportation to use the special revenue account to award grants to Montana‑based nonprofits that promote motorcycle safety.
Amends Section 17‑7‑502 to allow the statutory appropriation of these funds without a biennial legislative appropriation.
Effective January 1 2026.
The Department of Justice designs the plate and the Department of Transportation administers the grant program.
affected: Montana nonprofit organizations focused on motorcycle safety

HB850.one_line: HB 850 creates a licensing program for community health workers with education, fee, and reimbursement rules.
HB850.summary: HB 850 creates a licensing system for community health workers, setting education, experience, and fee requirements, and gives the Department of Labor and Industry authority to regulate and reimburse them. It amends existing licensing and Medicaid statutes to incorporate the new program.
changes: Establishes a new license for community health workers under Title 37.
Defines required qualifications: 18+ years old, completion of a recognized training program, and supervised experience.
Creates fee structure and reimbursement authority for services performed by licensed workers.
Allows the Department of Labor and Industry to adopt rules, review curricula, and grant endorsements for additional education.
Provides exemptions for certain professionals, volunteers, and employees of businesses from licensing requirements.
Amends sections 37‑1‑401 and 53‑6‑101 to incorporate the new licensing provisions and Medicaid service descriptions.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB855.one_line: Creates a wildlife‑crossing fund funded by a specialty license plate and a $100 transfer.
HB855.summary: HB 855 creates a special revenue account and a specialty license plate to fund wildlife‑vehicle‑collision projects, authorizes the Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks to match federal money, and amends the statutory‑appropriation rule. The bill also transfers $100 from the general fund to the new account and requires notification to tribal governments.
changes: Establishes a $20 specialty license plate whose proceeds go to a new state special revenue account for wildlife crossings;
Creates a dedicated special revenue account within the state special revenue fund for design, construction, maintenance, and study of wildlife crossings;
Authorizes the account to match federal funds, conduct studies, plan, staff, and otherwise support crossing projects;
Provides a $100 transfer from the general fund to the account by June 30 2025;
Amends 17‑7‑502 to clarify statutory‑appropriation language;
Requires the Secretary of State to notify federally recognized tribes of the act.

HB853.one_line: Revises Montana licensing fees, raises costs, adds seasonal categories, and updates definitions.
HB853.summary: HB 853 revises Montana’s licensing fee schedule for a wide range of licensed establishments—retail and wholesale food, public accommodations, campgrounds, and public swimming pools and spas—by increasing fees, adding seasonal and year‑round categories, and updating definitions. The bill also clarifies fee allocation and late‑fee rules.
changes: 1. Raises license fees for small, medium, and large retail food establishments and mobile food establishments, and for wholesale food establishments. 2. Sets new fee levels for public accommodation (hotel‑type) licenses based on room counts. 3. Increases campground and trailer‑court license fees and adds a seasonal/year‑round distinction for public swimming pools and spas. 4. Adds a $115–$225 fee for other licensed establishments (e.g., non‑hotel lodging). 5. Introduces or updates definitions for terms such as “cottage food operation,” “mobile food establishment,” and “seasonal” vs. “year‑round.” 6. Requires a $25 late fee for any license renewal not submitted before expiration. 7. Specifies how collected fees are split among local inspection funds, the state general fund, and special revenue accounts.

HB861.one_line: Funds a statewide K‑12 digital toolkit for 2025‑2029.
HB861.summary: HB 861 appropriates funds to give all Montana K‑12 schools access to a statewide digital toolkit of standards‑aligned, multimodal instructional materials, including career‑tech resources and industry partner content. The program runs from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2029, with $1.1 million for the Office of Public Instruction and $750,000 for the Department of Labor and Industry each year for 2026‑27. The appropriations are intended to become part of the ongoing budget base for future sessions.
changes: Appropriates $1.1 million annually (2026‑27) to the Office of Public Instruction for the digital toolkit.
Appropriates $750,000 annually (2026‑27) to the Department of Labor and Industry for the same purpose.
Establishes the toolkit program as effective July 1, 2025.
Sets termination of the program for June 30, 2029.
Designates the appropriations as part of the ongoing base for the next legislative session.

HB860.one_line: Creates a state‑funded loan program to place veterinarians in rural Montana, with forgiveness tied to service.
HB860.summary: HB 860 creates a state‑funded loan program to encourage veterinary students to practice in rural, underserved Montana communities.  Students receive up to $100 k in loans, must commit to four years of full‑time practice in an underserved area, and receive loan forgiveness after each year of service.  The program is funded for ten years and includes reporting and tax‑adjustment provisions.
changes: Establishes a veterinary training loan program for students who commit to practice in underserved Montana areas.
Provides up to $100,000 in loans (max $25,000 per year for 4‑year programs, $33,333 per year for 3‑year programs).

Requires a program agreement that obligates completion of a veterinary degree, licensure, and four years of full‑time practice in an underserved area within 180 days of graduation or post‑degree training.

Imposes loan forgiveness of 25 % of the total loan for each full year of qualifying practice; if the participant fails to meet obligations, the remaining loan plus interest (≤8 %) must be repaid within 10 years.
Creates an advisory committee of seven members (state‑appointed and public) to advise the commissioner of higher education.
Mandates biennial reports to the legislature on program selection, progress, and impact on veterinary services.
Amends Montana tax code to exclude forgiven loan amounts from taxable income.
Appropriates $425,000 for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 and designates the funds as part of the ongoing base for future sessions.
Specifies effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2035.
affected: State higher‑education commissioner and advisory committee

HB864.one_line: HB 864 expands school tech funding, creates a college FTE adjustment account, and raises tribal college payments.
HB864.summary: HB 864 implements House Bill 2 provisions, expands the school facility and technology account, creates a community‑college FTE adjustment account, increases payments to tribal colleges for resident non‑beneficiary students, and authorizes interim studies and reporting. It also contains coordination instructions with other pending bills and sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends the school facility and technology account to prioritize technology, other technology, major maintenance aid, and debt service assistance, and requires specific revenue deposits from timber and land income.
Creates a community‑college FTE adjustment account that will transfer over‑ or under‑payments based on actual weighted FTE each year.
Revises the community‑college appropriation formula (Section 20‑15‑310) to include new definitions and calculation methods for adjusted base, inflationary factor, and FTE weighting.
Increases the payment to tribal colleges for resident non‑beneficiary students to a maximum of $4,183 per full‑time equivalent and sets conditions for accreditation, contracts, and fee waivers.

Authorizes the Education Interim Budget Committee to study inter‑library resource sharing and the Office of Public Instruction’s structure, and requires quarterly reporting from several state agencies.
Provides coordination instructions that modify or void overlapping amendments in other pending bills (e.g., HB 252, HB 515, HB 251).
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1, 2025 and terminates the study and reporting provisions on December 31, 2026.
affected: State agencies (Office of Public Instruction, Commissioner of Higher Education, Montana Historical Society, Montana Digital Academy, School for the Deaf and Blind)
numbers: $1 million annual grant for school technology
$4,183 maximum per FTE for tribal college payments
$18 million board‑feet average sale value for timber revenue
$3,280 minimum annual amount per FTE for tribal college payments

HB863.one_line: HB 863 revises finance laws, adds studies, and authorizes new appropriations.
HB863.summary: HB 863 amends several finance statutes, creates new reporting and study requirements, and authorizes a handful of appropriations. It changes how the Board of Investments is organized, how estimated taxes are paid, how a lodging‑tax proceeds are distributed, and how the state’s budget base is defined. It also allows temporary use of the accommodations tax for two historic sites, provides for a special‑session trigger on federal actions, and sets a June 30, 2025 effective date.
changes: Reconstitutes the Board of Investments as a nine‑member quasi‑judicial board, adds a chief investment officer and executive director, and requires bi‑annual budget reports to specific committees.

Rewrites the estimated‑tax payment schedule, adds an annualized‑income installment option, and gives the Department of Revenue authority to waive interest on under‑paid estimated taxes for 2024 tax year.

Revises the lodging‑tax (15‑65‑111) distribution formula, allocating percentages to the historical society, university system, fish & wildlife, invasive‑species account, and the Department of Commerce, and sets a temporary 4 % deduction for in‑state lodging.
Amends the definition of “base budget” and related budget‑stabilization provisions in the 17‑7‑102 chapter, limiting base‑budget increases to the previous legislature’s level.
Creates a $350,000 appropriation for a 2025‑26 study of executive‑agency structure and a $10.6 M‑$7.6 M‑$5 M‑$2.6 M appropriation for a market‑wage study of executive‑branch employees.
Authorizes a $280,000 contingent appropriation for the Legislative Services Division if a special session is called in 2027 to address federal actions or a recession.
Provides a $250,000 appropriation for the Department of Commerce to implement Senate Bill 320 and a one‑time $7.35 M appropriation for forensic‑fitness evaluations.
Allows temporary use of the accommodations tax for Reeder’s Alley and Virginia City and mandates the audit division move to new space by June 30, 2025.
affected: State agencies subject to the lodging‑tax distribution
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB866.one_line: Allows “emotional disability” in place of “emotional disturbance” for special‑education eligibility, with a $100 funding notice.
HB866.summary: HB 866 lets Montana use the phrase “emotional disability” in place of “emotional disturbance” when referring to special‑education eligibility, and funds a brief public‑instruction notice. The change is purely terminological and includes a $100 appropriation for communication. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Replaces the term “emotional disturbance” with “emotional disability” in all Montana Code and administrative rules that relate to special‑education services.
Authorizes a $100 appropriation from the general fund for the Office of Public Instruction to publish the change in its special‑education materials.
Codifies the new term as part of Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 4 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date of the change to July 1, 2025.
affected: Students eligible for special education under the emotional‑disability category.
Montana public‑instruction officials and school districts.
Parents and guardians of those students.

HB867.one_line: HB 867 creates a medical‑assistance program for chiropractors and veterinarians, funds it via renewal fees, and amends board statutes to support it.
HB867.summary: HB 867 creates a state‑wide medical‑assistance program for chiropractors and veterinarians, requires licensees with substance‑use or mental‑health impairments to enroll, and ties program funding to renewal fees. It amends board‑governance, confidentiality, audit, and organizational statutes to support the new program.
changes: Establishes a medical‑assistance program for licensees of the Boards of Chiropractic and Veterinary Medicine; requires impaired licensees to enroll as a condition of licensure or reinstatement.
Mandates that the program be funded by adjusting the renewal fee to cover its costs.
Amends §37‑1‑131 to give boards authority to discipline licensees in the program and to set standards for program expansion.
Amends §37‑2‑202 to make program proceedings and records confidential, except in disciplinary actions.
Amends §37‑2‑316 to require bi‑annual audits of the program, with external audits every five years and internal audits midway, and allocates audit costs to boards.
Amends §37‑12‑201 to add the program’s establishment, enrollment, and funding provisions to the board’s organizational duties.
affected: Licensees of the Boards of Chiropractic and Veterinary Medicine

HB872.one_line: Revises appraisal licensing, clarifies definitions, and allows non‑licensed market‑value opinions.
HB872.summary: HB 872 amends Montana’s real‑estate appraisal statutes to clarify definitions, expand who may provide market‑value opinions, and set new licensing rules. It creates an $1,000 appropriation for implementation and takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends § 37‑54‑102 to define key appraisal terms and expand the definition of an appraisal management company and related services.

Rewrites § 37‑54‑201 to restrict the use of the title “licensed real‑estate appraiser” to individuals, prohibit misrepresentation, and allow non‑licensed persons to give market‑value opinions for non‑federal transactions.
Adds a new subsection allowing licensed appraisers to provide evaluations with a required disclaimer and no need to display the license on the evaluation.
Provides a $1,000 appropriation to the Department of Labor and Industry for FY 2025 to implement the changes.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
affected: Non‑licensed individuals who provide market‑value opinions
Appraisal management companies and their panels
Department of Labor and Industry staff

HB869.one_line: Montana requires school cardiac plans, coach training, AEDs, and a reimbursement grant.
HB869.summary: The bill requires Montana school districts to create cardiac‑emergency plans, train coaches and staff in CPR and AED use, and allow removal of athletes showing warning signs. It also authorizes AED purchases, provides a reimbursement grant program, and amends school‑budget statutes to allow AEDs as a safety expense. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Mandates each school district or nonpublic school with an athletic program to develop a cardiac‑emergency response plan beginning the 2026‑2027 school year.
Requires coaches to obtain CPR, first‑aid, and AED certification and hold an informational meeting with students, parents, and assistant coaches each season.

Allows coaches, trainers, or officials to remove a student from participation if the student shows symptoms or warning signs of sudden cardiac arrest, and requires medical clearance before the student may return.
Authorizes the purchase of automatic external defibrillators (AEDs) as a school‑safety expense and requires the superintendent to provide an information sheet on cardiac‑arrest signs.
Creates a $240,000 biennial appropriation for the Office of Public Instruction to administer a grant program that reimburses schools 100 % of AED costs up to $700 per device.
Amends §§ 20‑9‑236 and 20‑9‑502 to allow AEDs to be counted as a school‑safety improvement and to create a sub‑fund for safety‑related expenditures.
affected: School districts, nonpublic schools, coaches, athletic trainers, officials, and youth athletes in Montana

HB876.one_line: Creates a special account to fund sawmill revitalization loans, transfers $12 million, and expires June 30, 2027.
HB876.summary: HB 876 creates a special revenue account to fund loans for reviving closed sawmills, transfers $6 million into it, authorizes the Board of Investments to lend at up to 4 % interest, and sets a 2025‑2027 funding window. The act ends on June 30, 2027.
changes: Establishes a sawmill revitalization special revenue account within the state special revenue fund.
Transfers $6 million from the Big Sky Economic Development Fund and $6 million from the Capital Developments Long‑Range Building Program Account into the new account by June 30, 2025.
Authorizes the Board of Investments to administer the account and make loans at no more than 4 % interest to qualified parties reviving closed sawmills.
Prioritizes loan applicants based on the length of time a sawmill has been closed (within 12 months or 12‑36 months before Jan 1, 2025).
Appropriates $6 million from the account for the biennium ending June 30, 2027 to fund these loans.
Unspent funds at the end of the biennium revert to the Capital Developments Long‑Range Building Program Account.
The act is codified as part of Title 90, Chapter 1 and is effective immediately upon passage, terminating June 30, 2027.

HB882.one_line: HB 882 expands where licensed alcohol can be sold and tightens enforcement of non‑agency liquor sales.
HB882.summary: HB 882 revises Montana’s alcohol‑sales rules, expanding where licensed retailers can sell on‑premises, adding fees for extra structures, and tightening limits on non‑agency liquor. The bill also updates resort‑area licensing and clarifies penalties for unlawful liquor sales.
changes: Allows all‑beverages and resort‑area licensees to operate up to two additional licensed alcohol‑service structures on the same property for hotels, ski hills, golf courses, and swimming pools, subject to a $100 application fee per structure.
Permits golf‑course licensees to sell beer and wine in the clubhouse, one building per nine holes, and portable satellite devices, with consumption allowed anywhere on the course.
Enables guest‑ranch licensees to serve alcohol outdoors and in up to three permanent buildings, requiring floor‑plan submission and a $100 fee per additional building.
Expands the definition of suitable premises for on‑premises consumption, allowing non‑contiguous storage areas and certain hotel‑guest‑unit deliveries, with a $100 application fee.
Revises resort‑area retail all‑beverages licensing to cap licenses by accommodation units or by acreage/valuation, and adds a $100 fee for alternate storage facilities and curb‑side pickup.

Clarifies that only liquor purchased from an agency liquor store or transferred per 16‑4‑404(7) may be sold on premises; violations trigger fines of $500‑$1,500, imprisonment of 3 months‑1 year, and possible license revocation.
Effective June 1 2025.
affected: All‑beverages licensees, resort‑area licensees, golf‑course licensees, hotel and ski‑hill owners, guest‑ranch operators, and any retailer seeking additional structures or storage areas.
numbers: $100 fee per additional structure or storage area

HB888.one_line: Prohibits boards from tying vaccination to release from isolation or quarantine orders.
HB888.summary: HB 888 amends Montana’s local board of health authority to prohibit requiring vaccination or medication for release from isolation or quarantine orders, clarifies other powers, and provides a $300 notification appropriation.
changes: Amends §50‑2‑116 to add a prohibition that a local board of health may not require a person to receive any vaccination, medication, supplement, or other drug treatment as a condition of release from an isolation or quarantine order.

Reaffirms and expands the board’s existing powers to adopt regulations, issue orders, and enforce public‑health measures while limiting punitive actions against private businesses for non‑compliance with those orders.
Provides a $300 appropriation for the Department of Public Health and Human Services to notify local boards of health of the statutory changes.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1, 2025.
Defines “private business” for the purposes of the prohibition.
No new program, office, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Individuals subject to isolation or quarantine orders
Private businesses that may be subject to public‑health orders

HB891.one_line: Allows the Inspector General to subpoena records for waste, fraud, or abuse investigations, with $5,000 funding.
HB891.summary: HB 891 authorizes the Department of Public Health and Human Services’ Inspector General to issue subpoenas for records related to waste, fraud, or abuse investigations and allocates $5,000 for implementation. The act becomes effective July 1, 2025.
changes: Creates subpoena authority for the Inspector General to compel production of financial, documentary, or electronic records in investigations of waste, fraud, or abuse within health‑care services and public‑assistance programs.
Requires subpoenas to be signed by both the department director and the Inspector General.
Appropriates $5,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1, 2025, to implement the new subpoena authority.
Codifies the subpoena authority as part of Title 53, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
entities subject to subpoenas (e.g., hospitals, contractors, public‑assistance program participants)

HB897.one_line: Creates a $50 non‑resident shed‑hunt license, sets penalties, and amends hunting rules.
HB897.summary: HB 897 creates a $50 Class F license for non‑residents to shed hunt on wildlife‑management areas, adds a waiting period, sets penalties for violations, and amends several MCA hunting‑related sections to clarify definitions and rule‑making authority.
changes: Establishes a $50 Class F non‑resident shed‑hunt license and a 7‑day waiting period before a non‑resident may hunt after a resident.
Defines “shed hunt” and “shed hunting” in the statutes.

Adds a tiered penalty schedule: first offense – warning; second offense – misdemeanor, fine up to twice the license fee, possible forfeiture; third offense – misdemeanor, fine up to $500, forfeiture and possible hunting ban.
Amends §87‑1‑304 to give the commission authority to fix seasons, bag limits, and special seasons, and to open or close areas for hunting, fishing, or trapping.
Amends §87‑2‑101 to expand definitions of bait, fur‑bearing animals, game animals, game fish, and to include a detailed definition of “shed hunt.”
Amends §87‑2‑201 to require a conservation license for all hunting, fishing, non‑resident shed‑hunt, and trapping licenses, and mandates reporting of license sales.
Amends §87‑2‑202 to set conservation‑license fees ($8 for residents, $10 for non‑residents), outline application requirements, and provide for a voluntary search‑and‑rescue donation.
affected: Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Montana residents who hunt on WMA’s

HB898.one_line: Revises LLC operating agreement rules, clarifies dissolution ambiguity, and funds a website update.
HB898.summary: HB 898 amends Montana’s LLC statutes to clarify how operating agreements are interpreted, especially when ambiguous about dissolution, and updates rules on management, voting, and series. It also authorizes a small appropriation for the Secretary of State to update the website and applies retroactively to existing agreements.
changes: Amends §35‑8‑109 to specify that operating agreements need not be in writing except for certain record‑keeping, distribution, or admission provisions, and that they cannot unreasonably restrict information rights, eliminate duties of loyalty or care, or otherwise violate core duties.

Amends §35‑8‑307 to clarify management and voting rights in member‑managed and manager‑managed LLCs, including the default equal rights of members or managers, majority‑vote requirements, and the special consent needed for major actions such as amending the operating agreement, admitting new members, or dissolving the company.
Adds a new subsection that, when an operating agreement is ambiguous about whether to maintain or dissolve the LLC, the agreement must be construed in favor of maintaining the company.
Provides a $100 appropriation to the Secretary of State for website updates reflecting the statutory changes.
Sets the act to take effect on passage and approval, with the appropriation effective July 1 2025, and makes the act retroactive to operating agreements in existence before its effective date.
Specifies that the new dissolution‑clarification provision is part of Title 35, Chapter 8, Part 9 of the Montana Code.
affected: LLC members, managers, and operating agreement drafters in Montana
HB898.effective: on passage and approval; appropriation July 1 2025

HB901.one_line: Montana creates a $10,000 cap grant program for fire‑department safety equipment funded by donations and a $10 fee.
HB901.summary: Montana will create a new grant program that lets fire departments, companies, or districts buy safety equipment. Grants are funded by charitable donations and a $10 application fee, capped at $10,000 per department per year, with priority given to smaller, rural, and regionally diverse units.
changes: Establishes a special revenue account for fire‑department health and safety grants.
Allows fire departments, companies, or districts to apply for grants up to $10,000 each year.
Requires a $10 non‑refundable application fee that is deposited into the grant account.
Limits each applicant to one grant per year and one grant per department per year.
Prioritizes grants to smaller budgets, rural locations, various state regions, and units that can demonstrate broad safety needs.
Permits the Disaster and Emergency Services Division to administer the program, retain up to 1% for admin costs, and adopt implementing rules.
Amends statutory appropriation language (17‑7‑502) to include the new grant account as a statutory appropriation.
Codifies the grant provisions as part of Title 7, Chapter 33.
Effective July 1, 2025.
affected: Fire departments, fire companies, and fire districts in Montana

HB899.one_line: Task force to plan a state shooting complex; $55k appropriation; account for future funding; expires 2027.
HB899.summary: The bill creates a task force to study and recommend a location and design for a state‑run shooting complex, establishes a special revenue account for the project, appropriates $55,000 for the first biennium, and sets reporting and termination dates. The task force must report by June 30 2027, and the act expires then. The bill does not create a new shooting facility yet, only the planning framework.
changes: Creates a Montana State Shooting Complex Facilities and Improvements Development and Oversight Task Force with 12 members from government, industry, and public groups.

Task force must develop a location framework, review existing facilities, draft preliminary specs, prepare a RFP, and recommend a site and administrative structure to the governor and relevant committees.
Establishes a Montana State Shooting Complex Facilities and Improvements Account in the state special revenue fund, allowing deposits of gifts, grants, donations, securities, and other assets.
Funds from the account may only be used for siting, construction, and related improvements of the shooting complex.
Appropriates $55,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 for task‑force activities; unspent funds revert to the general fund.
Sets effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2027 for the task force.
affected: State government officials (Governor, Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks, Department of Commerce, etc.)
Task force members (government, industry, public representatives)
Local governments and private entities that may submit proposals for the complex
State taxpayers (through appropriation and potential future project costs)
numbers: $100 per day compensation for task force members

HB913.one_line: HB 913 expands judges, mandates corrections reporting, studies legal services, sets detention costs, and funds an Indigenous task force.
HB913.summary: HB 913 amends court‑judge numbers, requires corrections‑department reporting on inmate communications, mandates studies on legal‑service consolidation and wages, sets a daily detention‑center cost, revises child‑welfare counsel rules, transfers $40,000 to an Indigenous‑persons task force, and outlines funding and coordination provisions.
changes: Amends 3‑5‑102 to specify new judge counts for each judicial district
Requires the Department of Corrections to report quarterly on inmate electronic communications and filtering effectiveness
Directs the General Government Interim Budget Committee to study legal‑service consolidation and wage disparities, with reports due Sept 15 2025 and a proposal by June 30 2026
Amends 7‑32‑2242 to set a daily cost of $82 (or $85.30) for detention‑center confinement and clarifies payment responsibilities
Revises 41‑3‑425 to expand automatic appointment of state public defender counsel in child‑welfare cases
Transfers $40,000 from the general fund to the Missing Indigenous Persons Task Force account by July 15 2025
Provides funding thresholds ($25,000 to Dept. of Administration, $20,000 to Legislative Fiscal Division) for the studies; if unmet, the study provisions are void
Includes coordination clauses that void overlapping amendments from HB 643
Sets effective date July 1 2025 and terminates the reporting and study provisions on Sept 30 2026

HB908.one_line: HB 908 expands job‑growth tax credit to include construction apprentices and removes its sunset.
HB908.summary: HB 908 expands Montana’s job‑growth tax credit to cover registered apprentices in construction, removes the credit’s sunset date, and updates related statutes. Employers may claim the credit in the year the apprentice is approved, and the credit is limited to 50 % of the employer’s estimated taxes on qualifying wages.
changes: Adds registered apprentices to the definition of “qualifying new employee” for the job‑growth tax credit.
Allows employers to claim the credit in the tax year the apprentice is approved by the Department of Labor and Industry.
Extends the credit’s validity beyond the previous sunset date (December 31 2028).
Revises Sections 15‑30‑2357, 15‑30‑2361, 15‑31‑175, and 39‑11‑404 to reflect the new apprentice eligibility and reporting requirements.
Repeals Section 24 of Chapter 550 (2021) and Section 4 of Chapter 391 (2023) which previously limited the credit.”

HB918.one_line: Mandates quarterly Olmstead compliance reports, effective July 2025, ending September 2026.
HB918.summary: The bill requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to report quarterly on its progress developing a plan to comply with the Olmstead decision, and sets an effective date of July 1 2025 and a termination date of September 15 2026.
changes: Mandates quarterly reports to the Health and Human Services Budget Committee on the department’s Olmstead plan progress.
Specifies the act becomes effective July 1 2025.
Specifies the act terminates September 15 2026.
No new programs or funds are created; it only requires reporting.
The act does not alter any existing statutes or regulations beyond the reporting requirement.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Health and Human Services Budget Committee

HB917.one_line: HB 917 updates campaign‑finance definitions, eases incidental‑committee filing, and appropriates $1,000 for reporting.
HB917.summary: HB 917 amends Montana’s campaign‑finance statutes to clarify definitions, expand disclosure for incidental committees, and provide a small appropriation for the commissioner. It does not create a new program or criminal offense.
changes: Amends 13‑1‑101 to add detailed definitions of election‑related terms (e.g., “active elector,” “ballot issue committee,” “incidental committee”).

Rewrites 13‑37‑232 to exempt incidental committees that receive or spend less than $250 from forming a political committee and filing requirements, while tightening disclosure of contributions and expenditures for those that do report.
Adds a $1,000 appropriation for the commissioner of political practices to update and administer campaign‑finance reporting for FY ending June 30 2026.
Clarifies that a non‑resident may sign an incidental‑committee report if the committee is located outside Montana.
No new criminal offenses or state programs are created.

HB920.one_line: HB 920 grants temporary property‑tax exemptions for approved senior‑care development projects.
HB920.summary: HB 920 creates a temporary property‑tax exemption for senior‑care and senior‑housing development projects that receive local‑government approval.  The exemption lasts up to five years, can be renewed, and ends when the property is sold or leased to a non‑tax‑exempt operator.  The bill also amends tax‑assessment rules and requires annual reporting to local governments.
changes: Allows tax‑exempt senior‑care sponsors to petition local governments for a property‑tax exemption for development projects.

HB923.one_line: HB 923 amends nondegradation rules, adds a new exclusion, and appropriates $500 for the change.
HB923.summary: HB 923 amends the state’s nondegradation rule to add a new categorical exclusion for certain wastewater discharges and allows a county commission to exclude an area from a nondegradation authorization if it meets specific drinking‑well and water‑trench criteria. It also authorizes a $500 appropriation for the rule change and sets effective dates.
changes: Amends ARM 17.30.716 by adding subsection (8) permitting review of wastewater discharges without a background nitrogen sample when groundwater cannot be sampled.

Creates a new categorical exclusion for nondegradation authorizations if a county commission demonstrates that the area has no drinking‑well permits and that the absorption trench is at least 1,000 ft from downstream high‑quality surface waters.
Provides a $500 appropriation from the general fund for the Department of Environmental Quality to amend its rules.
Sets the rule amendment to take effect on January 1, 2026 and the appropriation to take effect July 1, 2025.
Limits the changes to nondegradation applications received on or after May 1, 2025.

HB931.one_line: Allows workforce‑housing development on state trust land under commercial leases.
HB931.summary: HB 931 clarifies that a commercial lease of state trust land may include single‑family or multifamily residential development for attainable workforce housing, and it amends definitions in §77‑1‑902. The bill does not create new programs or impose new costs; it simply expands the permissible uses of commercial leases. The changes apply to state‑trust‑land lessees and the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation.
changes: Expands the definition of “commercial purpose” in §77‑1‑902 to include single‑family or multifamily residential development for attainable workforce housing under a master lease.
Allows a nonprofit corporation to execute such a master lease for workforce‑housing development.
Revises related definitions (attainable workforce housing, cancellation, commercial lease, land value, limited valuation, termination) to reflect the new use.
No new statutes, fees, or funding mechanisms are introduced.
affected: Nonprofit corporations leasing state trust land
Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

HB932.one_line: HB 932 creates new conservation accounts, reallocates marijuana revenue, and revises wildlife habitat rules.
HB932.summary: HB 932 creates new conservation‑focused state special revenue accounts, reallocates marijuana tax proceeds, and revises the wildlife habitat improvement program, including council membership and project ranking rules. It also appropriates funds and sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
changes: Establishes a Habitat Legacy Account and three new special revenue accounts for wildlife stewardship, habitat improvement projects, and wildlife crossings.

Mandates annual transfers from the Habitat Legacy Account: normally 75% to the stewardship account, 20% to the improvement account, and 5% to the crossings account, with a higher‑transfer schedule if the stewardship account exceeds $50 million.

Reallocates excess marijuana tax revenue: up to $6 million to a HEART account, 20% to wildlife habitat, 4% each to state park, trails, and nongame wildlife accounts, 3% or $200 k to veterans, $300 k to DOJ for drug‑detection canines, $150 k to crime‑control training, and the rest to the general fund.
Amends the Kelly Flynn Montana Wildlife Habitat Improvement Act to rename it, redefine terms, and revise council composition and project‑ranking criteria.
Adds a rule‑making authority for the department to adopt a scoring system for ranking projects.
Provides appropriations of $7.5 M, $2 M, and $0.5 M for the three new accounts for the 2025‑2026 biennium.
Sets effective date July 1, 2025, and terminates the stewardship account’s 4% water‑project limit on June 30, 2033.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
numbers: 4% each to park, trails, nongame accounts

HB935.one_line: Study and suspend high‑volume groundwater permits in the Fox Hills‑Hell Creek aquifer until 2027.
HB935.summary: HB 935 directs the Department of Natural Resources to suspend or close new groundwater permits in the Fox Hills‑Hell Creek aquifer for high‑volume requests and orders a feasibility study of the aquifer’s availability. The study must be reported to a water‑policy committee, which will advise the legislature on whether to suspend or close new appropriations. The act is effective immediately and expires June 30, 2027.
changes: 1. The Department may suspend or close permit applications for groundwater withdrawals of 3,000 gallons per minute or more from the Fox Hills‑Hell Creek aquifer within specified administrative boundaries.

2. The Bureau of Mines and Geology must conduct a feasibility study of groundwater availability in those boundaries, including data compilation, limited field sampling, a preliminary water budget, and a preliminary pumping‑impact model.
3. The Bureau must report study progress and results to the Water Policy Interim Committee.
4. The committee will review the study and recommend to the legislature whether the Department should suspend or close new groundwater appropriations from the aquifer.
5. The act is codified as part of Title 85, Chapter 2, Part 3, and is effective upon passage, terminating on June 30, 2027.
affected: Groundwater users in the Fox Hills‑Hell Creek aquifer

HB936.one_line: HB 936 authorizes fund uses, mandates reporting, and creates a committee to study HB 872’s sustainability.
HB936.summary: HB 936 authorizes specific uses of the Behavioral Health System for Future Generations Fund, mandates reporting on hospital hiring and treatment outcomes, creates a committee to study long‑term sustainability of HB 872, and amends fund‑account rules. The bill also ties a 2025 appropriation to the passage of HB 574 and sets a July 1, 2025 effective date with termination June 30, 2027.
changes: Amends the Behavioral Health System for Future Generations Fund to allow one‑time use of funds for student‑loan repayment programs and additional licensed beds at the Montana State Hospital.

Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to submit monthly hiring‑data reports for the Montana State Hospital and quarterly outcome/cost reports for comprehensive school and community treatment services.
Creates a House‑appointed committee to study and propose sustainable funding mechanisms for the long‑term objectives of HB 872.

Amends the hospital Medicaid reimbursement account rules (53‑6‑149) to clarify use of hospital utilization fees for quality and efficiency incentives and payments to independent critical‑access hospitals.
Makes the 2025 appropriation for certified community behavioral health centers contingent on passage of HB 574.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1, 2025 and termination date to June 30, 2027.
affected: Montana State Hospital staff and applicants
Behavioral health and developmental disability service providers
Montana residents receiving behavioral health services
House and Senate staff involved in HB 872
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB924.one_line: HB 924 creates a trust, new revenue accounts, and a property‑tax relief program with detailed transfer rules.
HB924.summary: HB 924 creates a Montana Growth and Opportunity Trust, establishes several new state‑special‑revenue accounts, and sets rules for transferring volatile revenues, distributing interest, and reinvesting portions of the trust for pensions and housing. It also creates a state property‑tax‑relief account, a water‑development account, a better‑local‑bridge account, and an early‑childhood account with a board and grant program. The bill revises property‑tax‑assessment procedures, establishes a primary‑residence certification process with penalties for fraud, and amends many finance statutes. The act is effective upon passage.
changes: Creates the Montana Growth and Opportunity Trust and defines its funding, distribution, and reinvestment formulas; requires a 2/3 vote for any bill appropriating trust funds.

Establishes new state‑special‑revenue accounts: state property‑tax‑relief, Montana water‑development, better‑local‑bridge, and Montana early‑childhood, each with specific funding and distribution limits.

Mandates annual transfers of volatile revenues (capital‑gains, partnership, and interest‑earnings) to the trust, with detailed calculation formulas and limits tied to general‑fund deficits and operating reserve levels.
Provides for annual distribution of interest earnings from the trust to the four special‑revenue accounts (20% each, capped at $10‑$15 million) and to a pension fund; any excess remains in the trust.
Creates a pension fund within the trust, limits transfers to teachers’ and public‑employees’ retirement systems, and sets a 25% cap on transfers when actuarial rates are below target.
Revises property‑tax‑assessment rules (15‑7‑102) to include detailed notice, appeal, and certification procedures for primary residences, and adds penalties for false applications (45‑7‑202).
Provides a detailed schedule of transfers from the general fund to the trust and other accounts for FY 2024‑2027, including amounts and dates.
Adds reporting, rule‑making, and coordination provisions, and repeals the 2023 Montana local‑bridge trust (17‑7‑134).
affected: State Treasury and Department of Revenue
numbers: $10 million transfer to water‑development account FY 2024

HB939.one_line: HB 939 sets 1,500‑ft setbacks and de‑icing rules for large wind turbines, effective 2026.
HB939.summary: HB 939 sets new setback rules for large wind turbines and requires a de‑icing standard for turbines in high‑ice‑risk areas. The law takes effect on Jan. 1, 2026 and amends the wind‑energy agreement statute to codify these provisions.
changes: Imposes a 1,500‑ft setback from an occupied residence for turbines 500 ft or taller unless the property owner approves a shorter distance.

Mandates that turbines 500 ft or taller, built in ice‑class 4+ zones and within 1,500 ft of a residence, use commercially reasonable efforts to mitigate icing during de‑icing, limiting rotor‑blade speed to 10 % of maximum unless the property owner approves a higher speed.
Adds the setback and de‑icing requirements to Title 75, Chapter 26, making them part of the state’s wind‑energy agreement framework.
Keeps the existing requirements of §70‑17‑406 (e.g., notarization, compensation, liability, tax‑exemption) but incorporates the new standards into that statute.
Effective date is Jan. 1, 2026.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.

HB940.one_line: HB 940 bans overnight camping on state highways, imposes fines, and allocates $15,000 for enforcement.
HB940.summary: HB 940 bans overnight camping and the storage of personal property on state highway right‑of‑way, except for emergencies, authorized crews, or designated rest areas. Violators may be given 72 hours to vacate and face a civil fine up to $50; unattended property may be removed after 120 hours. The law authorizes the Department of Transportation to adopt rules and provides a $15,000 appropriation for enforcement.
changes: Prohibits overnight camping and storage of personal property on all state highway right‑of‑way except in specified exceptions.
Empowers the Department of Transportation and law‑enforcement to issue written notices and enforce the prohibition.
Sets a civil fine of up to $50 for non‑compliance with a notice and allows disposal of remaining property after 120 hours.
Authorizes the Department to adopt rules for implementation, including recovery of fines and cleanup costs.
Appropriates $15,000 from the highway restricted account for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to implement the act.
Codifies the provisions as a new part of Title 60, Chapter 6 of the Montana Code.
HB940.effective: effective on passage and approval; appropriation effective July 1 2025

HB943.one_line: Creates a 17‑member Rare Disease Advisory Council with $16,000 funding and reporting duties.
HB943.summary: The bill creates a 17‑member Rare Disease Advisory Council under the Department of Public Health and Human Services, appoints its members, sets meeting and reporting requirements, and appropriates $16,000 for its first biennium. The council will advise the governor, legislature, and public on rare‑disease needs and policy.
changes: Establishes a state‑wide Rare Disease Advisory Council with 17 members representing diverse stakeholders.
Governs appointment, term lengths, and election of a presiding officer.
Mandates the council to hold regular meetings, publish resources, and submit annual reports to the governor and legislature.
Allows the council to seek external funding (gifts, donations, grants).
Appropriates $16,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to cover council costs.
Codifies the council’s duties and membership in Title 50, Chapter 12 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Rare‑disease patients and caregivers in Montana

HB949.one_line: DPHHS must set fees for behavioral‑health commitments and report on them biennially.
HB949.summary: The bill requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) to create a fee schedule and rules for paying costs when people are committed to community or inpatient behavioral‑health facilities, and mandates biennial reporting on such commitments. It also amends the law to clarify treatment conditions and adds a one‑time $5,000 appropriation for implementation.
changes: DPHHS must establish a fee schedule and administrative rules for costs associated with commitments to community facilities or behavioral‑health inpatient facilities.

DPHHS must report annually (by September 1 of each even‑numbered year) to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee the number of individuals committed or detained and aggregate facility data.
Sections 53‑21‑149 and 53‑21‑193 of the Montana Code are amended to incorporate the new fee‑schedule requirement and clarify treatment conditions and transfer procedures.
The bill authorizes a one‑time appropriation of $5,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to cover implementation costs.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Individuals committed or detained for behavioral health reasons

HB953.one_line: Allows Medicaid to cover direct‑primary‑care contracts and bars mandatory case‑management for those enrollees.
HB953.summary: HB 953 lets Montana Medicaid cover direct‑primary‑care contracts, bars the department from forcing enrollees into case‑management if they have such a contract, and defines the contract. It also amends Medicaid statutes and appropriates $5,000 for implementation.
changes: Allows Medicaid to reimburse direct‑primary‑care contracts; defines those contracts; prohibits the department from requiring case‑management for enrollees with a direct‑primary‑care contract; amends Medicaid statutes (53‑6‑101, 53‑6‑116, 53‑6‑124) to reflect these provisions; appropriates $5,000 for the biennium beginning July 1 2025; effective July 1 2025.
affected: Medicaid enrollees, Medicaid providers, the Department of Public Health and Human Services, managed‑care plans

HB954.one_line: Extends Lake County’s jurisdiction withdrawal deadline to June 30, 2031.
HB954.summary: HB 954 extends the deadline for Lake County to withdraw from enforcing state criminal jurisdiction within the Flathead Indian Reservation to June 30, 2031. The act amends a 2021 law and takes effect immediately upon passage. No new programs or funds are created.
changes: Amends Section 5, Chapter 556 of the 2021 laws to change the termination date to June 30, 2031
Extends the period during which Lake County may withdraw from state criminal jurisdiction within the Flathead Indian Reservation
The amendment takes effect immediately upon passage and approval
No additional provisions or requirements are added
The bill does not alter any other aspects of the 2021 law
No new state program, office, or criminal offense is created

SB1.one_line: Redefines blighted areas, requires a resolution, and limits condemnation to true blight.
SB1.summary: The bill amends Montana’s urban‑renewal statutes to broaden the definition of a blighted area and clarify the conditions under which municipalities may use tax‑increment financing and eminent domain to redevelop such areas. It requires a formal resolution finding that at least three listed blight factors exist before any urban‑renewal action can be taken and expands the list of public uses that justify condemnation for blight removal. The changes take effect immediately and apply to any new municipal resolution adopted after the effective date.
changes: Amends §7‑15‑4202 to restate the policy that blighted areas are a serious menace and that their elimination is a state concern.
Redefines “blighted area” in §7‑15‑4206 to include any area with at least three of a detailed list of physical, sanitary, and economic conditions.

Adds a requirement in §7‑15‑4210 that a local governing body must adopt a resolution finding a blighted area exists and that rehabilitation or redevelopment is necessary before any urban‑renewal power can be exercised.
Expands §7‑15‑4259 to clarify condemnation procedures, prohibit pass‑through use of eminent domain for private gain, and limit compensation increases tied to project‑induced value changes.
Amends §70‑30‑102 to list urban‑renewal projects as a public use only when the property is a blighted area and prohibits condemnation for the purpose of increasing tax revenue.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and specifies that it applies only to municipal resolutions adopted after that date.
affected: Property owners in areas that may be designated as blighted
numbers: Resolution requirement: at least three blight factors

SB3.one_line: Mandates advisory committees for all TIF districts and fixes urban renewal board terms.
SB3.summary: The bill amends Montana’s urban renewal statutes to require that any district using tax‑increment financing (TIF) create an advisory committee. The committee must include representatives from all overlapping municipalities, counties, and school districts, and the bill also revises the composition and appointment terms of urban renewal agency commissioners.
changes: Amends §7‑15‑4234 to set fixed term lengths (1, 2, 3, and two 4‑year terms) for the five‑member urban renewal agency board and requires filing of appointment certificates with the municipal clerk.
Rewrites §7‑15‑4282 to mandate that a municipality or county adopting a TIF provision must first notify and consult with overlapping county and school districts in a public meeting.

Adds a requirement that the local governing body appoint an advisory committee for any TIF plan, with at least one representative from each incorporated city/town, county, or school district that overlaps the district.
Allows an urban renewal area administered by an agency under §7‑15‑4232(2) to waive the advisory‑committee requirement.

Provides a transition rule that if the agency already has five commissioners at the effective date, the mayor must appoint a county representative followed by a school‑district representative to fill vacancies.
Clarifies that commissioners may not receive compensation but may be reimbursed for expenses.
affected: Counties and school districts overlapping TIF districts

SB5.one_line: Revises county tax‑appeal board compensation and meeting procedures.
SB5.summary: SB 5 revises how county tax‑appeal board members are paid, sets new daily rates, clarifies travel and incidental expenses, and adds procedural details for board meetings and notices. The bill takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑15‑101 to establish daily compensation of $45–$60 for ≤4 hrs and $90–$120 for >4 hrs per meeting.
Requires travel and incidental expenses to be paid from the Montana tax‑appeal board appropriation, not the county.
Mandates an annual organizational meeting before the first hearing and designates a presiding officer.
Limits appeal hearings to three members even if the board has more than three members, with the presiding officer selecting the panel.
Adds notice requirements for scheduled protests, to be published by May 15 each year.
Clarifies that challenges to department rules apply only to the taxpayer who brings them, not to all similar taxpayers.

SB9.one_line: Allows bi‑weekly state agency deposits of $200+ cash or $750+ collections, with optional approved schedules.
SB9.summary: SB 9 lets state agencies deposit cash and collections in bi‑weekly intervals—$200 in coin/currency or $750 in total collections—rather than weekly, with optional modified schedules approved by the Department of Administration and the Board of Investments.
changes: Amends §17‑6‑105 to allow deposits of coin/currency over $200 or total collections over $750 every 14 days instead of weekly.
Requires agencies to deposit into the state treasurer’s name or an approved depository when thresholds are exceeded.
Allows agencies to propose modified deposit schedules; approval must come from the Department of Administration and the Board of Investments.
If approved, agencies may implement the new schedule; if disapproved, they must continue the 14‑day rule.
The Department must report approved modified schedules to the Legislative Fiscal Analyst and Legislative Auditor by the 15th of the month before a regular session.
Defines “agency” to include contractors collecting at least $50,000 annually on behalf of the state.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Contractors collecting ≥$50,000 annually on behalf of the state

SB10.one_line: SB 10 extends inspection and recommendation deadlines for emergency projects during a state of emergency.
SB10.summary: SB 10 extends the time allowed for onsite inspections and written recommendations on emergency projects when the governor declares a state of emergency, and it amends the reporting and review process in the Natural Streambed and Land Preservation Act. The changes add 10‑day extensions to the existing deadlines and clarify the steps for supervisors, team members, and applicants. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Extends the onsite inspection deadline from 20 to 30 days when a state of emergency is declared (subsection 4(b)).
Extends the written recommendation deadline for team members from 30 to 40 days when a state of emergency is declared (subsection 5(b)).
Adds a 60‑day deadline for supervisors to review and decide on the emergency project (subsection 6).
Requires applicants who are denied or modified to file a notice within 90 days to seek mitigation and long‑term solutions (subsection 7).
Provides for arbitration or court appeal options for parties disagreeing with supervisors’ decisions (subsection 8).
Maintains penalties for failure to provide emergency notice, submit required notices, or implement mitigation (subsection 9).

SB11.one_line: SB 11 overhauls local initiative rules, tightening petition procedures and penalties for false signatures.
SB11.summary: SB 11 revises Montana’s local‑government initiative and referendum rules, adding new procedures for petitions, signatures, and ballot language while tightening penalties for false signatures. It also amends several related statutes, including those on justice courts, resort taxes, and marijuana regulation.
changes: Replaces the existing petition‑and‑signature framework with a new 13‑section chapter that sets out definitions, petition requirements, signature thresholds (15% of qualified electors), and a 90‑day certification window.
Introduces a serial numbering system for petitions and requires a concise (≤135‑word) statement of purpose and a standardized yes/no ballot statement.
Adds a $500 fine and up to 6 months jail for knowingly forging signatures or signing multiple times, and a misdemeanor penalty for physically preventing signature gathering.
Allows governing bodies to take action on a petition within 60 days to avoid a ballot vote; if not, the issue is placed on the next local election ballot.
Revises related statutes on justice courts, resort taxes, marijuana business approvals, and local‑option excise taxes, tightening local control and clarifying election procedures.
Repeals sections 7‑5‑132, 7‑5‑133, 7‑5‑134, and 7‑5‑135, removing the old petition‑processing rules.
Codifies the new provisions as a separate chapter of Title 13 and applies only to ballot issues filed on or after the act’s effective date.
affected: Local governments (cities, towns, counties, consolidated city‑counties)
Electors registered in those local governments

SB12.one_line: Eliminates county printing board, transfers duties to Dept. of Administration, sets price rules.
SB12.summary: The bill dissolves the Board of County Printing and moves its responsibilities to the Department of Administration. It gives the department rule‑making authority over maximum prices for county legal advertising and printing standards, while preserving the board’s former duties for printed county forms.
changes: A new Department of Administration office is created to replace the Board of County Printing.

SB17.one_line: SB 17 extends hearing deadlines for emergency child‑removal cases and updates related statutes.
SB17.summary: SB 17 extends the time allowed for emergency‑protective‑services hearings and pre‑hearing conferences from five days to five working days, and changes the show‑cause‑hearing deadline from 20 to 21 days. It amends the statutes that govern child‑removal notifications, pre‑hearing conferences, and show‑cause orders, and requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government.
changes: Changes the notification deadline for emergency‑protective‑services hearings from 5 days to 5 working days
Extends the pre‑hearing‑conference deadline from 5 days to 5 working days
Changes the show‑cause‑hearing deadline from 20 days to 21 days
Amends sections 41‑3‑301, 41‑3‑307, and 41‑3‑432 of the Montana Code to reflect the new deadlines and procedural details
Adds a requirement that the Secretary of State send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government
Effective July 1, 2025
affected: Parents, guardians, and other custodians of children
Courts handling child‑abuse and neglect petitions

SB18.one_line: Rewrites Montana’s child‑abuse definition to include drug exposure and trafficking while clarifying exclusions.
SB18.summary: SB 18 amends the Montana child‑abuse statute to broaden the definition of abuse and neglect, adding drug‑distribution, trafficking, and certain risk factors while clarifying exclusions such as religious‑belief‑based care decisions. The bill also revises related definitions and clarifies the scope of protective services.
changes: Redefines “child abuse or neglect” to include actual or potential physical/psychological harm, abandonment, exposure to dangerous‑drug distribution, and child sex or human trafficking.
Adds a new definition of “dangerous drugs” and clarifies that substance use by a parent, obesity, or economic status alone do not constitute abuse.

Excludes self‑defense, defense of others, and prevention of self‑harm that does not cause harm, as well as lack of supervision due solely to parental inability to control behavior, from the definition of abuse.
Clarifies that religious‑belief‑based refusal of medical care does not automatically constitute abuse, but the state may still intervene if there is imminent substantial risk.

Updates related definitions (e.g., “abandonment,” “person responsible for a child’s welfare,” “adequate health care”) and adds new terms such as “child protection specialist” and “qualified expert witness.”
Requires that “child protection specialist” investigations and “safety and risk assessments” be conducted under the revised definitions.
Makes no new program or funding; it only amends statutory language.

SB19.one_line: SB 19 raises theft‑related penalties and expands the common‑scheme definition.
SB19.summary: SB 19 raises penalties for a range of theft‑related offenses, expands the definition of a common scheme, and amends sentencing provisions for theft, bad checks, deceptive practices, forgery, and identity theft. The bill also updates the definition of “common scheme” and clarifies how convictions are counted.
changes: Revises the definition of a common scheme to include losses of $1,500 or more and repeated offenses against the same victim or property.
Raises penalty thresholds for theft, bad checks, deceptive practices, forgery, and identity theft, setting higher fines and longer prison terms for larger or repeated offenses.
Amends sections 45‑6‑301, 45‑6‑309, 45‑6‑316, 45‑6‑317, 45‑6‑325, 45‑6‑332, and 45‑6‑345 to reflect the new thresholds and sentencing ranges.
Adds provisions that a conviction for a similar offense in another state counts toward Montana’s conviction tally for sentencing purposes.
Specifies that a second or third conviction for the same offense carries progressively harsher penalties.
Provides that restitution can include victim costs such as attorney fees and credit‑repair expenses.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
affected: Individuals charged with theft, bad checks, deceptive practices, forgery, or identity theft; courts and prosecutors; victims of those offenses

SB22.one_line: Extends hearing deadlines and clarifies protest limits for motor‑carrier applications.
SB22.summary: The bill amends Montana’s motor‑carrier rules to extend the time the Public Service Commission has to schedule a hearing on a carrier’s application, clarifies protest limits, and allows denial of certain public‑convenience applications without a hearing if prior investigations found no need. The changes take effect July 1 , 2025.
changes: 1. Extends the Commission’s deadline for setting a hearing to 60‑90 days after a protest or hearing request, instead of the previous shorter period.
2. Limits protests for Class E carriers to issues about meeting 69‑12‑323(5) requirements only.
3. Identifies interested parties (county, town, city boards, and any concerned persons or corporations) who may testify in proceedings.

4. Allows denial of a Class D or 69‑12‑311(1)(b) application for public convenience and necessity without a public hearing if prior investigations found no need, unless the applicant shows material changes in conditions.
5. Provides that a hearing must be held if the applicant demonstrates materially changed conditions affecting transportation facilities.
affected: Class A, D, and E motor carriers
County, town, and city governing boards
Interested parties and the general public

SB23.one_line: Allows the commission to set accident‑reporting thresholds for Montana railroads.
SB23.summary: The bill amends Montana’s railroad accident‑reporting law to let the Public Service Commission set thresholds for when a railroad must file a report, while preserving the requirement to report any accident that meets those thresholds. The change gives the commission rule‑making authority over the reporting criteria.
changes: Amends Section 69‑14‑252, MCA to specify that a railroad must report an accident to the commission when it meets a threshold set by the commission.
Adds a clause that the commission may adopt rules to establish those reporting thresholds and implement the section.
Retains the requirement that the report include time, place, names of persons killed or injured, and value of property destroyed.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage and approval.
affected: Railroad companies operating lines in Montana
Montana residents affected by railroad accidents

SB26.one_line: Montana lets public officials claim IRS mileage rates for private vehicle use, with special rules for state officers.
SB26.summary: The bill amends Montana’s mileage‑reimbursement law so that legislators, jurors, witnesses, county agents, and other public‑service users of private vehicles can claim the IRS standard mileage rate for the first 1,000 miles each month, with a 3‑cent reduction thereafter. State officers who use private cars instead of government vehicles receive only 48.15 % of the IRS rate unless a vehicle is unavailable, in which case the full rate applies for the first 1,000 miles and the 3‑cent reduction thereafter.
changes: Amends §2‑18‑503 to allow legislators, jurors, witnesses, county agents, and other eligible persons to claim the IRS mileage allotment for the first 1,000 miles per month, with a 3‑cent per‑mile reduction thereafter
State officers who choose a private vehicle when a government vehicle is available are reimbursed at 48.15 % of the IRS rate
If a government vehicle is unavailable or a specific exemption is attached, state officers receive the full IRS rate for the first 1,000 miles and the 3‑cent reduction thereafter
Legislators, jurors, witnesses, county agents, and other eligible persons may claim the IRS rate for private aircraft travel at twice the motor‑vehicle rate
The Department of Administration must prescribe policies for implementation; the Montana Administrative Procedure Act does not apply to those policies
The act takes effect immediately upon passage
affected: Other public‑service personnel using private vehicles

SB27.one_line: SB 27 expands licensing, limits new premises, and tightens inspection and THC rules.
SB27.summary: SB 27 removes the 2021 moratorium on new marijuana license applicants, but limits new premises to those linked to existing licensed sites until 2027. It also sets a 2025‑2027 moratorium on opening additional licensed premises and tightens licensing rules, fees, and inspection requirements.
changes: Reinstates the ability of the Department of Revenue to accept applications from non‑former medical licensees starting July 1 2025, but only for premises already licensed or for new premises after July 1 2027
Creates a moratorium on issuing licenses for new premises until July 1 2027, allowing only expansion of existing licensed sites
Amends the licensing fee schedule for cultivators, adding tiered canopy limits and associated fees up to $37,000
Rewrites the dispensary fee schedule to $5,000 per location, with cumulative increases for additional sites
Revises inspection limits to a maximum of two unannounced inspections per year unless a citation has been issued
Adds detailed THC‑content limits for products sold at dispensaries
Expands the definition of a licensee’s “controlling beneficial owner” and requires written notification for ownership changes
Clarifies that licensees may not operate at a shared location with a medical dispensary unless owned by the same person
Reinforces that licensees must keep records open for inspection by state and local law enforcement
affected: Existing licensed cultivators, manufacturers, dispensaries, and transporters
Local governments in counties that voted against Initiative 190

SB29.one_line: SB 29 allows electronic bid bonds for state construction projects and amends bid‑security rules.
SB29.summary: SB 29 permits state agencies to accept electronic bid bonds for construction projects and amends the bid‑security rules to allow electronic signatures and verification. It also clarifies that agencies may waive bid‑security requirements for projects under $150,000.
changes: Amends §18‑2‑302 to allow electronic bid bonds signed electronically or otherwise verified by the bidder and the surety
Specifies that electronic bid bonds may be accepted by state or other governmental entities
Maintains the 10 % bid‑security requirement for all bids, except for projects under $150,000 where the agency may waive it
Clarifies that the state cannot require a particular surety company or insurance producer for a bid bond
Preserves the list of acceptable forms of bid security (cash, checks, money orders, certificates, letters of credit, etc.)
Requires the bid security to be signed by an authorized individual or entity on whose behalf it is submitted
Leaves other procedural requirements (e.g., compliance with specifications) unchanged
affected: State agencies and other governmental entities that award construction contracts
Bidder firms and surety companies that provide bid bonds

SB30.one_line: SB 30 bars the rule of necessity when a less‑conflicted judge can serve and expands recusal triggers.
SB30.summary: SB 30 amends Montana’s judicial conflict‑of‑interest rules to prohibit the use of the rule of necessity when a less‑conflicted judge is available, and expands the definition of recusal triggers.
changes: Amends §3‑1‑611, MCA, adding a new subsection (4) that bars a judge from invoking the rule of necessity when another judge with a lesser conflict could serve.

Expands the definition of a conflict to include contributions that exceed $10,000 for a supreme‑court candidate or $5,000 for other judicial candidates, and clarifies that the total must be from a lawyer, lawyer’s firm, or party to the proceeding.
Requires the moving party to provide sufficient facts that the conflict criteria have been met before the judge recuses.
Clarifies that the rule of necessity cannot be used to avoid recusal when a suitable substitute judge is available.
Adds definitions for “contribution” and “judicial officer” in the subsection (5).
affected: Political committees and entities that make independent expenditures

SB33.one_line: State buildings’ plan review and permitting shift to Labor and Industry, local governments keep non‑state authority.
SB33.summary: SB 33 transfers the authority to review plans, issue permits, and enforce building codes for state‑owned or operated public buildings from local governments to the Department of Labor and Industry. It amends the state building‑code statute to give the department jurisdiction over all state‑agency buildings, while preserving local jurisdiction for non‑state buildings.
changes: Amends § 50‑60‑106 to state that all state‑agency buildings fall under the Department of Labor and Industry’s plan‑review, permitting, and inspection authority.
The department must provide local governments with building plans and a comment period before issuing decisions.
Local governments retain full authority over non‑state buildings, including plan review, permitting, and enforcement.
The department may collect and reserve excess building‑fee revenue for enforcement and education programs.
Local governments may still adopt voluntary energy‑conservation standards for new construction, but only if contractors elect to receive incentives.
The department may conduct inspections of buildings outside its jurisdiction only upon written request and cannot enforce its own powers during such inspections.
The department must notify local jurisdictions of actions taken and send copies of final plans.
affected: State agencies owning or operating public buildings
County, city, and town building officials
Building contractors and owners of state‑agency buildings
numbers: 0.5% of building fees for education program
10 working days for permit issuance after checklist submission

SB34.one_line: Revises K‑12 district law to clarify budgeting, tuition, and transition procedures, effective July 1, 2025.
SB34.summary: SB 34 updates Montana’s K‑12 district law to remove outdated tuition language, clarify how budgets and funding are calculated for new K‑12 districts, and streamline the transition process when an elementary district attaches to a high‑school district. The bill amends §§ 20‑6‑702 and 20‑6‑703 of the MCA and takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends § 20‑6‑702 to require separate calculations for elementary and high‑school programs in a K‑12 district, including ANB, basic county tax, guaranteed tax‑base aid, levy‑authority limits, and retirement obligations.

Rewrites § 20‑6‑703 to detail the administrative steps (property conveyance, record transfer, fund balance transfer, tax payment, and budget combination) that occur when an elementary district attaches to a high‑school district on July 1.
Removes obsolete tuition‑calculation language from § 20‑6‑702 and clarifies that tuition for elementary and high‑school pupils is determined separately under existing statutes.
Sets a single effective date of July 1, 2025 for the entire act.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No fiscal allocations or appropriations are specified.
affected: K‑12 school districts (both elementary and high‑school districts)

SB35.one_line: Clarifies enrollment counting and reporting for early‑literacy jumpstart programs in non‑resident districts.
SB35.summary: SB 35 clarifies how children who attend a district‑run early‑literacy jumpstart program in a non‑resident district are counted for funding and reporting. It amends enrollment rules, sets a $1,000 cap for home‑based programs, and requires annual reporting on program efficacy.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1804 to require jumpstart participants to be counted as quarter‑time enrollment for ANB calculations and removes the need for out‑of‑district attendance agreements or tuition for such students.
Adds a $1,000 per‑year cost cap for home‑based early‑literacy programs and limits participation on a first‑come, first‑served basis if funds are insufficient.
Mandates that trustees report annually on program efficacy, including anonymized student progress data, to the superintendent by July 15.
Requires the superintendent to report ANB‑related data to the education interim committees by September 1 each year.

Amends §20‑9‑311 to allow a jumpstart participant to be counted as up to 1 ¼ enrollment for ANB purposes and to add one‑quarter enrollment for the district’s jumpstart program to the October and February counts.
Provides that the act is effective July 1 2025 and applies retroactively to jumpstart programs conducted after the 2025 school‑year calendar end.
numbers: retroactive to programs after 2025 school‑year end

SB25.one_line: SB 25 bans deepfakes in election ads unless a clear AI‑disclosure is provided, with civil and criminal penalties.
SB25.summary: SB 25 prohibits the use of deepfakes in election communications unless a clear disclosure is provided.  It creates civil and criminal penalties for violations and allows candidates to seek injunctive relief.
changes: Defines AI‑generated content, deepfakes, and related terms
Bans the distribution of deepfakes in election communications within 60 days of voting unless a disclosure is included
Sets specific disclosure requirements for printed, video, internet, and audio media
Provides a list of exceptions for news broadcasts, paid ads, satire, and platform‑disseminated content
Creates civil remedies (injunctions, damages, attorney fees) and criminal penalties (fines, jail) for violations
Allows complaints to be filed with the Commissioner of Political Practices and outlines a multi‑tier enforcement process
affected: Candidates, political parties, election committees, broadcasters, advertisers, distribution platforms, and any entity producing or disseminating election communications

SB37.one_line: Clarifies how and when districts receive significant enrollment‑increase payments.
