SB37.summary: SB 37 amends the state’s school‑funding law to clarify that significant enrollment‑increase payments are calculated separately for each budget unit of a school district. It sets specific eligibility criteria, calculation methods, notification deadlines, and the process for district trustees to accept or decline the payment.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑166 to require enrollment‑increase calculations at the budget‑unit level.
Defines eligibility: October enrollment count must be ≥110 % of the district’s budget‑limit ANB from the prior fiscal year.
Specifies calculation: payment equals 80 % of the district’s total per‑ANB entitlement minus 80 % of the entitlement based on the adjusted enrollment (actual enrollment – absorption factor).
Sets deadlines: superintendent must calculate by Dec 1, notify by Dec 15, trustees decide by March 1.
Allows trustees to accept full or partial payment and adopt a budget amendment; the payment is disbursed from the BASE aid appropriation.
Requires districts to deposit the payment into the general fund and use it for enrollment‑increase costs.
Establishes effective date July 1 2025 and applicability to fiscal years beginning on or after that date.

SB36.one_line: Amends school‑funding law to delete expired contingency language for coal‑unit closures.
SB36.summary: The bill amends the Montana school‑funding statute to delete expired contingency provisions that tied a coal‑fired power‑plant closure to a special block grant for school districts. It keeps the existing grant framework but removes the time‑limited repayment schedule that applied to units closing before July 1 2022. The change simply updates the language, not the grant itself.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑638 to remove the contingency repayment schedule that applied to coal‑fired units closing before July 1 2022.
Leaves the block‑grant eligibility criteria (≥200 MW, in service before 1980, closing by 2022) unchanged.
Retains the 70%/30% annual distribution rule for the grant.
Keeps the requirement that any repayment be limited to the amount actually allocated to a district.
Does not create new funds, offices, or criminal offenses.
affected: School districts receiving the coal‑fired unit closure mitigation block grant
Owners of coal‑fired generating units slated for retirement before July 1 2022
State general fund (as the repayment recipient)

SB38.one_line: Prevents attorney‑fee awards to government in failed veto‑override polls.
SB38.summary: SB 38 amends Montana law to bar courts from awarding attorney‑fee costs to a state or local government when a legislative veto‑override poll fails to override the veto, even if the government’s defense was frivolous or in bad faith. The change applies to all such actions beginning on the act’s effective date.
changes: Amends §25‑10‑711, MCA, to add a new subsection (2) that excludes a government entity from being considered a prevailing party when a legislative veto‑override poll does not result in an override.
The amendment clarifies that costs and attorney fees may not be awarded to a government entity in these circumstances, regardless of any finding of frivolous or bad‑faith conduct.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to all actions involving a legislative veto‑override poll that commence on or after that date.
affected: Plaintiffs and defendants in civil actions involving legislative veto‑override polls
numbers: applicability: actions commencing on or after effective date

SB39.one_line: SB 39 tightens state attorney fee awards with detailed requirements and reasonableness standards.
SB39.summary: SB 39 tightens the rules for awarding attorney fees against the state, requiring detailed, itemized requests and setting rebuttable limits on certain fee‑related practices. It amends the state’s frivolous‑action cost‑award statute to make reasonableness a condition and applies only to cases pending after the effective date.
changes: Adds a detailed requirements checklist for fee‑award requests in state‑challenging civil suits (date, task description, timekeeping, expenses, etc.)

Creates a rebuttable presumption that certain fee claims—multiple attorneys at depositions/trials, certain research costs, and rates above the statewide average for attorneys with <10 years practice—are unreasonable
Mandates courts to compare requested rates with the state’s own attorney rate and explain any higher rate
Allows courts to consider additional factors beyond the new checklist when determining reasonableness
Exempts fee claims under $10,000 from the new requirements
Amends §25‑10‑711 to make reasonableness a condition for awarding costs in frivolous or bad‑faith state actions
Codifies the new requirements as part of Title 25, Chapter 10
Sets the applicability date for pending civil lawsuits
affected: Private attorneys litigating against the state
Plaintiffs and defendants in civil suits involving the state

SB40.one_line: SB 40 opens Supreme Court meetings, records closed deliberations, and releases them after finality.
SB40.summary: SB 40 expands Montana’s public‑records law to make all Supreme Court meetings open, requires recording and written minutes of any closed deliberations, and makes those records available after a case is final. The bill also updates definitions of confidential information and public records to cover judicial deliberations. It takes effect October 1, 2025.
changes: All Supreme Court meetings must be open to the public, except when privacy or litigation strategy requires closure under limited circumstances.
affected: Montana Supreme Court, its justices, clerks, and staff; public agencies and their meetings; the public at large.

SB41.one_line: Mandates random selection of replacement district judges with geographic proximity requirements.
SB41.summary: The bill requires that when a district court judge is substituted, disqualified, or recused, a new judge must be chosen by a random‑selection process that still keeps the new judge geographically close to the original district. The court administrator must set up the procedure by October 1, 2025, and share it with judges by October 15, 2025. The law takes effect on passage, with the random‑selection rule becoming operative on October 1, 2025.
changes: Mandates random selection for replacement judges in district courts when the incumbent is substituted, disqualified, or recused.
Defines random selection as a chance‑based choice that also requires geographic proximity to the original judge’s district.
Compels the Office of the Court Administrator to develop and publish a procedure by October 1, 2025, and distribute it to all district judges by October 15, 2025.
Codifies the requirement as part of Title 3, Chapter 1, Part 8 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date of the random‑selection rule to October 1, 2025, while the rest of the act takes effect upon passage.

SB45.one_line: Montana creates a judicial evaluation commission that surveys, reports, and publishes judges’ performance to inform voters.
SB45.summary: Montana will create a 11‑member Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission that will conduct mid‑term and pre‑election surveys and reports for district court judges and Supreme Court justices.  The commission will publish results in voter pamphlets and on its website, and the reports become public when a judge files a candidacy declaration.
changes: Establishes an independent Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission with 11 members appointed by the Senate, House, Governor, and Chief Justice.

Commission must conduct mid‑term (3rd year) and pre‑election (5th year for district judges, 7th year for Supreme Court justices) performance evaluations using surveys, courtroom observations, and disciplinary records.
Creates a third‑party contracted survey covering attorneys, jurors, and court staff, with confidentiality safeguards.
Mandates the commission to publish evaluation summaries in voter information pamphlets and on its website, and to provide reports to judges, the Supreme Court, and court administrators.
Amends election statutes to require the Secretary of State to include judicial evaluation summaries in absentee ballot pamphlets for judges running in elections.
Provides a one‑time appropriation of $1 million ($500,000 FY 2025 and $500,000 FY 2026) to fund the commission’s operations.
numbers: mid‑term evaluation in 3rd year, pre‑election in 5th/7th year

SB46.one_line: SB 46 raises underground‑tank registration fees and updates regulatory authority, effective immediately.
SB46.summary: SB 46 amends the state’s underground‑storage‑tank rules to set new annual registration fees and clarifies the department’s authority to adopt related regulations. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §75‑11‑505 to establish a fee schedule: up to $108 000 for tanks over 1,100 gal and up to $36 000 for tanks 1,100 gal or less, per tank, to cover program costs; fees may be prorated for non‑12‑month periods.
Adds a clause that the department may adopt rules on petroleum‑mixing‑zone inclusion in corrective‑action plans and may reference other groundwater‑mixing rules.
Clarifies that the department may delegate inspection and implementation authority to local agents, but only to complement, not duplicate, existing authority.
Provides that the act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Owners and operators of underground petroleum or hazardous‑substance storage tanks

SB48.one_line: SB 48 lets citizens publicly share judge complaints and expands the commission’s public‑statement powers.
SB48.summary: SB 48 lets a citizen publicly share a complaint about a judge at any time and amends the complaint process so that the Judicial Standards Commission may issue public statements when the matter becomes public. The bill does not create a new program or fund.
changes: Adds a right for a complainant to make their complaint public at any time (Section 1(a)).
Requires the commission to give written notice to the judge when a complaint is filed and when a verified affidavit is submitted (Section 1(b)).
Allows the commission to issue public statements in cases where the subject matter becomes public (Section 2).
Preserves the commission’s authority to order hearings, recommend disciplinary actions, and involve special masters as before.

SB51.one_line: Amends provider registration rules, adds filing requirements, and gives commission rule‑making power.
SB51.summary: The bill amends Montana’s telecommunications‑provider registration statute to require a detailed notice and ongoing reports from providers before they begin service in the state. It also gives the Public Service Commission rule‑making authority to clarify or waive requirements.
changes: Amends §69‑3‑805 to add a comprehensive list of items that a provider must file with the commission before beginning service, including contact info, service description, tariffs, facilities, ownership, and prior penalties.
Requires providers to file a report of any judgment, penalty, or sanction in other jurisdictions that could affect their ability to serve Montana.
Allows the commission to waive any of the listed filing requirements.
Empowers the commission to adopt rules to implement the new registration requirements.
The effective date is the day the act is signed, with no delay.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.

SB54.one_line: Large‑value state taxes must be paid electronically, with new rules to be adopted.
SB54.summary: SB 54 requires that any Montana tax of $500,000 or more be paid by electronic funds transfer (EFT) and gives the Department of Revenue authority to create rules for EFT payments. The law applies to taxes paid by EFT after December 31, 2025.
changes: All taxes due the state that are $500,000 or more must be paid by EFT.

SB53.one_line: Revises Montana income‑tax rules, adds credits, adjusts deductions, and removes a probate certificate requirement.
SB53.summary: SB 53 amends Montana’s income‑tax rules to incorporate changes from earlier simplification bills, updates filing‑status references, extends filing deadlines that fall on federal holidays, and clarifies qualified withdrawals from education‑savings accounts. It also removes a certificate requirement for probate estate‑tax filings, revises several tax‑credit and deduction statutes, and applies the changes retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2023.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2120 to adjust how federal taxable income is modified for Montana purposes, adding and subtracting specific items such as certain interest, S‑corp income, and medical‑care‑savings‑account withdrawals.

Revises §15‑30‑2339 to change the filing‑date rules for the elderly residential‑property‑tax credit, allowing claims on the same day as the tax return or April 15 (or the next business day if that date is a federal holiday).

Revises §15‑30‑2342 to allow a credit for historic‑building rehabilitation that can be used only by a single business entity and not split between spouses unless the property is used by a small business corporation or partnership.
Revises §15‑30‑2538 to require a 6 % withholding on mineral‑royalty payments, except where otherwise provided.
Rewrites §15‑62‑103 to update definitions for the family‑education‑savings program, including new terms for contributors, beneficiaries, and withdrawals.
Rewrites §15‑62‑207 and §53‑25‑117 to clarify the $3,000 deduction limit for contributions to education‑savings accounts and specify who may claim it.
Repeals §72‑3‑1006 (the “certificate” requirement for probate estate‑tax filings).
Provides that the act is effective immediately upon passage and applies retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2023.
affected: Montana taxpayers who file income tax returns
Owners of historic buildings seeking rehabilitation credits
numbers: April 15 filing deadline (or next business day if holiday)

SB55.one_line: Bill codifies Montana’s intent to support coordinated streamflow data collection and sharing.
SB55.summary: The bill declares the Legislature’s intent to support the collection and sharing of Montana streamflow data and instructs that this intent be codified into the state water statutes. It does not create new programs or impose new duties, but formally records the Legislature’s policy stance. The intent is to promote coordination among state, tribal, federal agencies and water users for better water‑management decisions.
changes: Codifies the Legislature’s intent regarding streamflow information as part of Title 85, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
Recognizes that streamflow data are gathered by multiple state, tribal, and federal entities and are essential to water‑use administration.
Declares that supporting and encouraging coordination in the collection and distribution of streamflow information is in the public interest.
No new programs, offices, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No specific actions or requirements are imposed on agencies or individuals beyond the intent statement.

SB57.one_line: SB 57 expands canvassing boards’ audit and recount authority in Montana elections.
SB57.summary: SB 57 amends Montana election law to give county canvassing boards more power to audit vote totals, investigate discrepancies, and order recounts. The changes require boards to compare votes cast with electors and voters, document errors, and act within two days. Recount thresholds for candidates and ballot questions are also clarified.
changes: Amends §13‑15‑403 to require county canvassing boards to publicly audit returns, compare votes cast to electors and voters, record write‑ins, and investigate any discrepancy or error that would affect election results, with a two‑day deadline for investigation.
Adds authority for the board to petition the election administrator to conduct a recount or ballot inspection as part of its investigation.

Rewrites §13‑16‑201 to set specific margin thresholds (≤¼ % of total votes or ≤10 votes, whichever is greater) for candidates and ballot questions that trigger a recount petition, and specifies the petitioning process and required signatures.
Clarifies that recounts must be conducted in all precincts of affected counties when a petition is filed.
Provides that the act takes effect immediately upon passage.
No new program or fund is created; the bill merely expands existing canvassing procedures.
affected: Candidates and voters in contested races or ballot questions

SB56.one_line: SB 56 raises supplemental employer contributions for public‑employee retirement systems and adds new rates for patrol, sheriff, and game‑warden programs.
SB56.summary: SB 56 increases and extends supplemental employer contribution rates for Montana’s public‑employee retirement systems and adds new rates for the Highway Patrol, Sheriff, and Game Warden/Peace Officer systems.  The bill amends the statutory contribution formulas, sets new actuarial‑based rates, and provides for additional temporary contributions that expire when actuarial valuations show the unfunded liabilities can be amortized within 25 years.
changes: Amends 19‑3‑316 to raise the base supplemental employer contribution for public employees to 6.9% and adds a 1.27%‑to‑3.27% additional rate that rises annually until 2035, then 2.27%‑3.27% thereafter.

Amends 19‑6‑404 to set a 38.33% state contribution for Highway Patrol officers for 2023‑24, add a $500,000 annual transfer to the Highway Patrol pension trust fund, and replace the 2024–2025 contribution with an actuarially‑determined rate that includes legacy, contemporary, and normal‑cost components.

Amends 19‑7‑404 to set a 13.115% employer contribution for sheriffs for 2023‑24, then switch to an actuarially‑determined rate with legacy, contemporary, and normal‑cost components, and allows counties to levy a mill tax to meet the obligation.

Amends 19‑8‑504 to set a 10.56% employer contribution for game wardens/peace officers for 2023‑24, then switch to an actuarially‑determined rate with legacy, contemporary, and normal‑cost components, and allows a 0.1%‑to‑1% additional temporary contribution that ends when actuarial valuations permit.

Provides that each supplemental contribution (the additional 1.27%‑to‑3.27% for public employees, the 0.1%‑to‑1% for sheriffs, game wardens, and patrol officers) is reviewed annually by the Public Employees’ Retirement Board and can be terminated when an actuarial valuation shows the unfunded liabilities can be amortized within 25 years.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1 , 2025.

SB59.one_line: Designates a Libby bridge as a memorial and directs signage and plaque installation.
SB59.summary: The bill designates the Kootenai River bridge on Highway 37 in Libby as the Staff Sergeant Arthur J. Rambo Memorial Bridge and directs the Montana Department of Transportation to install signage and a plaque. No new funding or programs are created.
changes: Designates the existing bridge on Highway 37 over the Kootenai River as a memorial bridge.
Mandates the Department of Transportation to design and install signs at each end of the bridge bearing the memorial name.
Mandates the Department of Transportation to design and install a memorial plaque near the bridge.
Codifies the designation as part of Title 60, Chapter 1, Part 2 of the Montana Code.

SB58.one_line: Revises absentee ballot‑counting rules to require investigation and reporting of ballot‑count discrepancies.
SB58.summary: The bill amends Montana’s absentee ballot‑counting rules to require the election administrator to investigate any mismatch between the number of ballots counted and the pollbook record, and to report that investigation to the county canvassers. It also clarifies procedures for handling unmarked, folded, or otherwise questionable ballots.
changes: Amends §13‑15‑201 to add a requirement that if the counting board cannot reconcile the total ballots with the pollbook record, it must submit a written report to the election administrator.

If the discrepancy is not satisfactorily explained, the election administrator must conduct an investigation (including recounting and record review) and report the findings to the board of county canvassers.
The bill clarifies that unmarked ballots are void unless all judges agree they were mis‑marked by officials, in which case the ballot must be marked “unmarked by error” and initialed by all judges.

It adds language that folded or stuck‑together ballots must be set aside until the count is complete and, if a majority of judges believes they were marked by one elector, they must be rejected per §13‑15‑108.

It reiterates that only valid absentee ballots may be counted and specifies the conditions under which a marked absentee ballot is considered valid, including signature verification and receipt time limits.
The bill does not create a new program or fund; it only revises existing procedures and reporting requirements.

SB61.one_line: Adds a policy statement on streamflow measurement to Montana law.
SB61.summary: The bill adds a policy statement to Montana law that explains why measuring streamflow is important for water appropriation and management.
changes: Codifies a policy statement (Section 1) into Title 85, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
The statement reiterates constitutional and legal principles about water ownership, appropriation, and the need for accurate, real‑time streamflow data.
No new programs, funds, or regulations are created.
The bill contains no fiscal provisions or enforcement mechanisms.
The statement is intended to guide future water‑management decisions but does not alter existing law.
The bill is a non‑binding policy directive rather than a regulatory act.
affected: Public and private stakeholders who rely on streamflow data

SB60.one_line: Revises captive insurer taxes with new rates, minimums, and limits effective 2026.
SB60.summary: SB 60 revises Montana’s tax rules for captive and special‑purpose insurers, setting new premium‑tax rates, a minimum tax, and limits on aggregate taxes. It also clarifies how protected‑cell and series captives are treated and establishes a common‑ownership grouping rule. The law takes effect for tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
changes: Amends §33‑28‑201 to impose a 0.4 % tax on the first $20 million of direct premiums and 0.3 % thereafter, and a 0.225 % tax on the first $20 million of assumed reinsurance premiums, 0.150 % on the next $20 million, and 0.050 % thereafter.
Introduces a $5,000 minimum annual tax for captives whose calculated tax falls below that amount, with prorated amounts for first‑year authorization or surrender.
Limits aggregate taxes for non‑protected‑cell captives to $100,000 per year.
Treats each protected‑cell and each series of a special‑purpose captive separately for tax purposes, but applies the minimum tax only once per captive.
Requires captives under common ownership and control to be taxed as a single entity.
Excludes branch business of branch captives from the new tax, and requires annual calculation even for multiyear policies.
Sets the effective date for the changes to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Insurers under common ownership and control

SB64.one_line: Clarifies interim legislative compensation, mileage, lodging, and meal rules, and expands council appointment authority.
SB64.summary: SB 64 clarifies how legislators are paid and reimbursed when the legislature is not in session, amending meal‑allowance rules and adding detailed mileage, lodging, and salary provisions for remote and in‑person work. It also expands the legislative council’s appointment authority and compensation rules for members serving on interstate, international, and Pacific Northwest economic‑region bodies.
changes: Amends §2‑18‑502 to redefine meal‑allowance eligibility and limits, adding a midday allowance for board/committee members regardless of distance.
Rewrites §5‑2‑302 to specify salary, mileage, lodging, and meal allowances for legislators working remotely or in person during interim business, with tiered rates based on round‑trip distance.

Revises §5‑11‑305 to clarify the legislative council’s appointment process for interstate, international, and intergovernmental entities, including party‑balance requirements and compensation authority.
Rewrites §5‑11‑708 to set compensation and expense rules for legislators appointed to the Pacific Northwest economic region.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: State board, commission, and council appointees
Employees of the Department of Administration

SB65.one_line: Revises name‑change rules, adds DOC victim‑contact and sealed‑record provisions.
SB65.summary: SB 65 amends Montana’s change‑of‑name rules to streamline notice requirements, allow sealed‑record petitions for safety reasons, and give the Department of Corrections (DOC) a role in petitions filed by inmates or those under DOC supervision. It also requires DOC to contact victims and share records when a petition is granted.
changes: Rewrites §27‑31‑201 to set hearing dates and notice rules for name‑change petitions.
Eliminates mandatory newspaper publication for minor name changes when both parents/guardians consent.
Allows sealed‑record petitions when safety is at risk and the petitioner is not evading debt or a criminal record.
Requires DOC to be served on petitions filed by persons committed to or supervised by DOC, and DOC must be given a reasonable opportunity to appear and respond.
DOC must make reasonable efforts to contact victims (as defined in §46‑18‑243) to obtain information relevant to the petition.
If granted, DOC and the Department of Justice may maintain and disseminate the petitioner’s records to satisfy offender‑registration, testing, victim‑notification, or other statutory duties.
No new program or criminal offense is created.
The bill does not alter funding or create new offices.
affected: Inmates or persons under DOC supervision
DOC and Department of Justice staff

SB67.one_line: Authorizes ADS vehicles on highways and gives DOT/DOJ rule‑making power to regulate them.
SB67.summary: SB 67 authorizes the use of vehicles equipped with automated driving systems (ADS) on Montana public highways, defines ADS levels, and gives the Department of Transportation and the Department of Justice rule‑making authority to regulate their use, especially in dangerous conditions.
changes: Allows level 1‑3 ADS vehicles to operate on state highways without restriction; level 4‑5 vehicles may operate only if the Department of Transportation adopts rules limiting use in dangerous conditions or exempting proven safe systems.
Creates a statutory framework that defines ADS levels, operational design domain, and fallback‑ready user requirements.
Empowers the Department of Transportation to adopt rules limiting commercial ADS vehicles during dangerous road conditions and to exempt vehicles proven safe.
Empowers the Department of Justice to adopt rules for ADS vehicles and requires both departments to consult stakeholders before rule‑making.
Preserves local governments’ authority to regulate traffic on streets within their jurisdiction, provided they do not discriminate against ADS vehicles.
Codifies the act as part of Title 61 (motor vehicles) so existing motor‑vehicle laws apply to ADS vehicles.
affected: Vehicle owners and operators of ADS vehicles

SB69.one_line: Revisions require county attorneys to report child‑sexual‑abuse cases annually and expand record‑keeping and department reporting duties.
SB69.summary: The bill expands and formalizes the reporting duties of county attorneys on child‑sexual‑abuse cases, requiring annual reports to the attorney general and the law‑and‑justice interim committee, and mandates the department to provide detailed referral data. It also updates procedures for recording and notifying reporters of abuse reports.
changes: County attorneys must collect all investigative materials for reports involving alleged perpetrators 12 + years old and certify receipt to the original reporter or department.
County attorneys must retain all related records for 25 years.
County attorneys must file an annual report (by Jan 1 and June 1) to the attorney general, detailing case identifiers, dates, charges, convictions, sentences, certifications, and unresolved cases.
Attorney general must create a standardized reporting form and keep the information confidential as criminal‑justice data.
Attorney general must submit an annual aggregated report to the law‑and‑justice interim committee, including counts of cases, charges, convictions, and actions taken.
The department must report annually (by July 15) the number of referrals to county attorneys and advise the attorney general if a prosecution should be pursued.
affected: Department of Children, Youth, and Families

SB70.one_line: SB 70 lets probation officers remove conditions without a hearing if no one objects, and strengthens victim notification.
SB70.summary: SB 70 revises Montana’s probation‑revocation rules, letting a probation officer remove a supervision condition without a hearing if no one objects, and tightening victim notification requirements. It also updates the procedure for modifying or adding conditions and clarifies when a judge may grant or deny a petition.
changes: Amends §46‑18‑203 to allow a probation‑and‑parole officer to submit written notice of intent to remove a supervision condition; if no objection within 14 days the condition is removed, otherwise a hearing is held.
Requires the county attorney and the victim to be notified in writing when a condition affecting restitution, interest, or contact with the victim is removed or reinstated.
Expands the definition of a compliance violation to include stalking, harassment, or threatening behavior toward a victim or their family.
Adds detailed procedures for conditional discharge, including risk‑based time thresholds and victim input.
Clarifies that a judge may modify or add conditions at any time, and that the probation officer must report reasons for such changes.

SB71.one_line: Extends termination date for natural‑resource revenue revisions to June 30 2029.
SB71.summary: The bill extends the termination date for revisions to the Natural Resources Operations State Special Revenue Account and its transfer to the General Fund to June 30 2029, and sets the act’s effective date as July 1 2025. It merely amends existing statutes, not creating new programs or funds.
changes: Amends §3, Ch. 137, Laws of 2021 to set termination date to June 30 2029.
affected: Montana state government, specifically the Department of Environmental Quality and the state treasury

SB73.one_line: Revises child‑protective‑care laws to tighten notification and pre‑hearing requirements.
SB73.summary: SB 73 revises Montana’s child‑protective‑care statutes to tighten notification and pre‑hearing requirements. It mandates that anyone who removes a child must inform parents and a pre‑hearing facilitator within 24 hours, and requires a pre‑hearing conference before any emergency protective‑services hearing. The bill also expands parents’ rights and clarifies procedures for domestic‑violence‑related removals.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑301 to require the person or agency placing a child to notify parents/guardians immediately and to provide a written notification within 24 hours to the pre‑hearing facilitator and the state public defender.
Adds a requirement that a pre‑hearing conference be held within 5 days of removal and before any emergency protective‑services hearing.
Expands parents’ rights to receive the affidavit, attend hearings, have a support person, and request kinship placement.
Specifies procedures for domestic‑violence‑related removals, including efforts to protect the child and referral to domestic‑violence programs.
Prohibits placement of a child in jail if removed for protection or care.
Clarifies that an affidavit must be filed within 2 working days and a petition filed within 5 working days unless a prevention plan exists.
Requires the department to locate and contact extended family members for placement and case planning.
affected: Parents, guardians, and other custodians of children removed from homes
Child‑protective‑services specialists, peace officers, county attorneys
Extended family members of removed children

SB72.one_line: Establishes a presumptive Medicaid eligibility process for home‑based services for disabled and elderly Montanans.
SB72.summary: The bill creates a presumptive Medicaid eligibility process for home‑and‑community‑based services for people with physical disabilities or who are elderly.  It sets up a screening and certification system, limits the period of presumptive coverage, and requires a formal waiver application to the federal program before the program can begin.  The bill also mandates notification to tribal governments and gives the department authority to extend or modify the presumptive period.
changes: Establishes presumptive eligibility for certain home and community‑based services for persons with physical disabilities or who are elderly, pending a screening process and departmental authorization.
Defines the services covered (personal care, meal delivery, emergency response, medical equipment, assistive technology, and transition services).
Creates a screening process that may be performed by the department or certified entities, requiring an application, self‑attestation of income/resource, and a functional assessment.
Limits presumptive eligibility to a single 12‑month period per person and requires a formal Medicaid application within 10–30 days after presumptive determination.
Allows the department to grant time extensions or exceptions to the 12‑month limit to avoid preventable health declines or institutionalization.
Requires the department to submit a Section 1115 waiver or state‑plan amendment to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services before the presumptive eligibility program can take effect.
Mandates the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
affected: Persons with physical disabilities or elderly persons seeking home and community‑based services
Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS)
Certified screening entities (area agencies on aging, tribal entities, hospitals, etc.)
Montana Medicaid program and its applicants
SB72.effective: Contingent: effective upon passage and approval, but Section 1 becomes effective only after the department certifies that the federal waiver has been approved, within 7 days of that event.

SB75.one_line: Allows unlimited, retroactive revisions of statutory sunset dates with a latest‑date conflict rule.
SB75.summary: SB 75 allows the legislature to change the sunset (termination) dates of statutes by amending the original law, with no limit on how many times the date can be altered.  Conflicting changes in the same session are resolved by the latest‑dated revision, and the act takes effect immediately and applies retroactively to all laws passed since the start of the 69th session.
changes: Permits unlimited revisions of a statute’s termination date by amending the original session law
Resolves conflicting revisions in the same session by keeping only the latest‑dated revision
Requires that a revision be enacted before the later of the original or revised termination dates
Allows the amendment of a termination date to coexist with prior amendments in the same enactment
Codifies the procedure as part of Title 1, Chapter 2, Part 2 of the Montana Statutes
Makes the act effective upon passage and retroactively applicable to all laws passed after the 69th session began
affected: Government agencies affected by sunset provisions
numbers: retroactive to all laws passed after session start

SB74.one_line: SB 74 revises marijuana licensing, ownership, fees, and product limits, adding a reporting hotline.
SB74.summary: SB 74 updates Montana’s marijuana statutes, tightening ownership rules, clarifying licensing fees and product limits, and adding a reporting hotline. It amends definitions, licensing procedures, and fee schedules for cultivators, manufacturers, and dispensaries, and sets new THC limits for products.
changes: Revises the definition of “retail price” for tax purposes and clarifies ownership terms such as “controlling beneficial owner,” “employee,” and “financial interest.”
Eliminates probationary licenses for testing laboratories and removes the option for laboratories to operate on a probationary basis.
Creates a state‑run hotline for reporting suspected violations of marijuana laws and requires the department to investigate or refer complaints to law enforcement.

Adjusts licensing fees: cultivator and manufacturer fees now depend on monthly concentrate production ($5k–$20k), and dispensary fees start at $5k per location with $5k added for each additional location.
Sets THC limits for marijuana and marijuana products sold at dispensaries (e.g., 1 oz flower ≤35% THC, capsules ≤100 mg THC, edibles ≤100 mg THC with 10 mg per serving).
Adds a 10% variance allowance on the THC limits and allows higher‑potency products for registered medical cardholders.
affected: Montana residents with medical cardholder status

SB76.one_line: Revises water‑right permitting to speed preliminary determinations and strengthen public‑comment procedures.
SB76.summary: SB 76 amends Montana’s water‑right permitting process to streamline preliminary determinations, clarify public‑comment timelines, and set a firm 60‑day deadline for the department to issue a draft determination. The bill also tightens notice requirements and gives applicants a 15‑business‑day window to request extensions for additional evidence.
changes: Amends §85‑2‑307 to require the department to publish a notice of receipt on its website and to update it when the application is correct and complete.
Sets a 60‑day deadline (120 days if no technical analyses are prepared) for the department to issue a written draft preliminary determination, with optional conditions.

Gives applicants 15 business days to request an extension of up to 180 days to submit additional information, and requires the department to issue an updated draft within 60 days of the extension deadline or receipt of all evidence.
Mandates a public‑comment notice that must be published in a local newspaper and posted on the department’s website, with a 30‑day comment period and specific standing requirements for commenters.
Requires the department to consider public comments within 30 days, respond, and issue a final preliminary determination, holding a hearing if the determination is to deny the application.
Adds detailed service‑by‑mail and proof‑of‑service requirements for notice of the opportunity to comment.
affected: Applicants for water‑right permits or changes in appropriation rights
Property owners whose water rights may be affected
General public with standing to comment

SB77.one_line: Conservation districts must follow state procurement rules for state‑funded contracts, with new bidding and contract‑value thresholds.
SB77.summary: SB 77 requires Montana conservation districts to follow the state’s public‑procurement rules when using state‑funded grants and loans. It amends several procurement statutes to clarify bidding, advertising, and contract‑value thresholds for district contracts.
changes: Conservation districts must comply with state procurement laws for all state‑funded expenditures (Section 1).
Contracts for architectural, engineering, and land‑surveying services must meet Title 18, Chapter 8, Part 2 procurement requirements (Section 2).
Section 76‑15‑1005 is amended to allow districts to award contracts to the lowest responsible bidder, postpone, reject, or re‑advertise bids under specified conditions (Section 3).
Section 76‑15‑1006 is amended to set advertising requirements for bids and proposals, including publication timing and criteria disclosure (Section 4).
Section 76‑15‑1011 is amended to provide emergency procurement exemptions, direct‑negotiation limits, and a tiered purchase‑technique procedure based on contract value (Section 5).
Section 76‑15‑1012 is amended to set contract term limits (max 7 years), extension rules, and payment/continuation requirements tied to fund availability (Section 6).
Section 76‑15‑1004 (service contracts) is repealed (Section 7).
Sections 1 and 2 are codified as part of Title 76, Chapter 15, Part 10 (Section 8).

SB78.one_line: SB 78 removes mandatory carcass stamping and updates hide‑inspection and bill‑of‑sale rules.
SB78.summary: SB 78 removes the requirement that every dressed carcass of a slaughtered animal be stamped, updates the bill‑of‑sale process, and amends the record‑keeping rules for hide and meat inspection. The changes apply immediately upon passage.
changes: Eliminates the mandatory ink stamp on each dressed carcass of slaughtered cattle or horses
Requires licensed slaughter establishments to keep the entire hide (tail and ears) until inspected, but allows inspection to be waived if a preslaughter inspection has already occurred
Revises the bill‑of‑sale procedure: the inspector must receive the original bill of sale, attach it to the inspection certificate, and provide a receipt describing any remaining livestock on the sale
Maintains that a person who kills livestock in good faith for personal use is exempt from inspection or stamping
Keeps the inspector’s record‑keeping and certificate‑issuance requirements unchanged
Effective immediately upon passage
affected: State and deputy state stock inspectors
Owners of slaughtered cattle or horses
Individuals who kill livestock for personal use

SB79.one_line: Repeals feedlot dead‑animal inspection requirement and its penalty, effective immediately.
SB79.summary: The bill removes Montana’s statutory requirement that feedlot operators inspect dead animals and eliminates the penalty for failing to do so. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Repeals §81‑3‑215, which required inspection of dead animals in feedlots.
Repeals §81‑3‑232, which imposed a penalty for non‑inspection of dead animals in feedlots.
The act becomes effective on the day it is signed, with no additional conditions or implementation steps.
affected: Feedlot operators and owners in Montana
State regulatory agencies that previously enforced the inspection requirement

SB80.one_line: Allows digital livestock‑transport documents and expands transport permits.
SB80.summary: The bill amends Montana’s livestock‑transport laws to allow a digital copy of inspection certificates, permits, and other required documents to be shown to law‑enforcement officers. It also expands the types of transportation permits that may be issued and clarifies when a change of ownership requires inspection.
changes: Amends §81‑3‑211 to permit a digital copy of required livestock‑transport documentation to be exhibited to law‑enforcement officers.
Adds new categories of transportation permits (travel, permanent, grazing, rodeo) and specifies their requirements and validity periods.
Clarifies that a permanent transportation permit is void upon a change of ownership and must accompany the animal at all times.
Extends §81‑3‑204 to include livestock transported or sold under the new permits.
Requires sellers to obtain inspections and pay fees before removal or change of ownership.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.
affected: State stock inspectors and deputy inspectors
numbers: per‑horse or per‑bull permit fee (amount not specified)
state treasury special revenue fund (for permit fees)

SB82.one_line: Establishes a blindness‑adjustment program for under‑55 consumers with severe visual impairment.
SB82.summary: The bill creates an adjustment to Montana’s blindness program, allowing the Department of Public Health and Human Services to provide independent‑living services to people under 55 with severe visual impairment. It sets eligibility criteria, outlines a list of services, gives consumers a right to a fair hearing, and authorizes the department to adopt implementing rules. The program becomes effective July 1, 2025.
changes: Establishes a new blindness‑adjustment program within the Department of Public Health and Human Services
Defines eligibility for independent‑living services for persons under 55 with severe visual impairment
Lists seven categories of services (outreach, training, assistive tech, Braille instruction, peer counseling, guide/reader services, and other appropriate services)
Allows the department to pay for services when funds are available, considering consumer resources and other needs
Provides a right to a fair hearing for consumers aggrieved by department actions
Empowers the department to adopt rules to implement the program
Codifies the provisions as part of Title 53, Chapter 7
Effective July 1, 2025
affected: Consumers with severe visual impairment under age 55
Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
Service providers contracted by the department

SB83.one_line: Expands Fish & Wildlife Commission rule‑making for public use of private land under access agreements.
SB83.summary: The bill amends the Montana Code to give the Fish and Wildlife Commission authority to adopt rules that govern how the public can use private land when an active public‑access agreement exists.  It expands the commission’s rule‑making powers to include many aspects of hunting, fishing, and land use on such private property, while preserving limits on firearms regulation.  The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑301 to add a new subsection (d) giving the commission the power to adopt rules for public use of private property managed by the department under active access agreements.
Expands the commission’s rule‑making authority to cover archery equipment, special licenses, nonresident big‑game combinations, mountain‑lion hunting limits, and hound‑license quotas.
Clarifies that the commission may not regulate firearms, accessories, or ammunition except for certain safety‑related restrictions.
Reiterates that the commission does not oversee state‑park or recreational‑area activities under Title 23.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: Hunters and anglers using such private land
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

SB86.one_line: Revisions tighten AED program rules, enforcement, and liability protections while removing the department’s rule‑making power.
SB86.summary: SB 86 revises Montana’s automatic external defibrillator (AED) laws, tightening program requirements, clarifying enforcement, and limiting liability for AED users. It removes the Department of Public Health and Human Services’ rule‑making authority and repeals a previous rule‑making section.
changes: Amends the definition of AED and related terms in §50‑6‑501.
Rewrites §50‑6‑502 to require a written AED program plan, public notice, training, maintenance, and coordination with EMS before use.
Adds enforcement procedures in §50‑6‑504, allowing the department to issue cease‑order notices and permitting hearings within 30 days.

Expands liability protections in §50‑6‑505, shielding AED users, CPR providers, medical oversight staff, and training providers from civil liability unless gross negligence or willful misconduct occurs.
Repeals §50‑6‑503, eliminating the department’s rule‑making authority for AED programs.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No monetary allocations are specified.
No specific effective date is stated; the act takes effect upon passage.
affected: Public agencies, private corporations, and other entities that operate AEDs
Emergency medical services and public safety answering points
County attorneys and district courts for enforcement actions

SB87.one_line: Eliminates election‑day holiday for legislative staff and adds a yearly floating holiday for them.
SB87.summary: SB 87 removes the State General Election Day from the list of statutory holidays for legislative employees and establishes a single annual floating holiday for each full‑time or part‑time employee in the legislative branch. It also revises the definition of “holiday” and updates related statutory language.
changes: Eliminates State General Election Day as a holiday for legislative employees.
Creates one paid floating holiday per calendar year for each full‑time or part‑time legislative employee; unused days expire at year‑end and are not paid out.
Revises the statutory definition of “holiday” to clarify which days are covered for legislative employees and other agencies.
Adds a new definition of “floating holiday” and updates related sections 2‑18‑601 and 2‑18‑603 of the Montana Code Annotated.
Leaves short‑term workers and student interns ineligible for holiday or floating‑holiday pay.
Maintains existing prorated holiday pay rules for part‑time employees and specifies that unused floating holidays do not accrue or pay out on termination.
affected: Short‑term workers in the legislative branch
Student interns in the legislative branch
numbers: 1 floating holiday per employee per year
Unpaid unused floating holiday days expire at year‑end

SB88.one_line: Revises C‑N letter publication, timelines, and notice requirements, notifying tribes.
SB88.summary: SB 88 amends Montana’s certificate‑of‑need (C‑N) law to clarify the publication and review process for letters of intent, sets specific timelines for notice, application completeness, and decision‑making, and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments.
changes: Amends § 50‑5‑302 to specify that the department may adopt rules for the form, scheduling, hearing formats, comparative review, and bed‑type approvals for C‑N letters of intent

Replaces the existing publication requirement with a rule that the department must publish each letter of intent received in the prior month on the 10th of each month in a local newspaper and on its website
Adds a 30‑day notice to each letter‑of‑intent submitter of the deadline for a full application, and sets a 30‑day minimum between notice and application deadline
Imposes a 20‑working‑day initial review of applications for completeness, with a written request for missing information and a 15‑day response window, followed by a 15‑working‑day final review
Limits the overall review period to 90 calendar days (or 90 days for comparative reviews) unless all parties consent to a longer period
Allows a public hearing during the review period if requested or deemed appropriate
Mandates that the department issue a decision within five working days after the review period ends, and provides a writ of mandamus remedy for unreasonable delays
Section 2 requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government in Montana
Section 3 sets the effective date as July 1 2025
affected: Affected persons (e.g., patients, staff, community members)
Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: 30 days before acquisition of 50% or more of a long‑term care facility
10th day of each month for publication
20 working days for initial completeness review
15 working days for final completeness review

SB91.one_line: SB 91 mandates an eagle citizenship marker on Montana driver’s licenses and IDs from Jan 1 2026 onward.
SB91.summary: SB 91 requires Montana driver’s licenses and ID cards issued on or after Jan 1 2026 to display a U.S. citizenship marker (an eagle image). It amends the licensing statutes to add the marker, sets the effective date, and preserves existing procedures for renewal, replacement, and veteran designation.
changes: Adds an eagle image to licenses/IDs for U.S. citizens beginning Jan 1 2026
Amends 61‑5‑111 and 61‑12‑501 to require the citizenship marker and to verify lawful presence for non‑citizens
Keeps all current renewal, replacement, and veteran‑designation rules unchanged
Sets the effective date of the new requirement to Jan 1 2026
Allows the department to use existing resources for design and implementation
Maintains a single non‑voided license or ID per person
affected: Non‑citizen residents applying for ID cards

SB93.one_line: Expands and extends Montana’s tax exemption for military pensions and related benefits, removing limits and sunset provisions.
SB93.summary: SB 93 expands Montana’s tax‑exempt status for military pensions, retirements, and survivor benefits, removes the five‑year claim limit and sunset provision, and amends the state’s income‑tax code to allow more residents to benefit. The bill also revises related deductions and repeals a 2023 law that limited the exemption.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2120 to broaden the exemption for military‑related income and eliminate the 5‑year claim limit and statutory sunset.
Expands eligibility to residents who became Montana residents on or after June 30 2023 or who were residents before and remained residents after receiving military benefits.
Allows up to 50 % of military pension/retirement income or 50 % of survivor benefits to be excluded, subject to Montana‑source wage limits.
Adds new deductions for contributions to Montana family‑education savings accounts and other qualified education or savings programs (up to $3,000 per spouse).
Repeals §4, Chapter 650, Laws of 2023, which previously restricted the exemption.
Sets the act’s effective date to Jan 1 2026 and applicability to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025.
affected: Montana residents who receive military pensions, retirements, or survivor benefits
Military retirees who became residents after June 30 2023
Taxpayers contributing to Montana family‑education savings accounts

SB95.one_line: Allocates $800,000 for veteran and service‑member suicide prevention grants, effective July 2025, ending June 2027.
SB95.summary: The bill allocates $800,000 for suicide‑prevention grants to the Department of Public Health and Human Services, directing the money toward screening, education, care coordination, and lethal‑means safety for veterans, service members and their families. It requires annual reporting and ends in June 2027.
changes: Allocates $500,000 plus $300,000 from the state special revenue account to the Department of Public Health and Human Services for a biennium beginning July 1 2025
Funds are earmarked for grants under 53‑21‑1101 and 53‑21‑1111 to support suicide‑prevention activities

Mandates use of funds for (a) strategy development with federal partners, (b) risk screening and education, (c) connectedness and care‑transition initiatives, and (d) lethal‑means safety campaigns and training
Requires the department to report results in its annual performance report under 2‑12‑105
Notifies all federally recognized tribal governments of the act
Effective July 1 2025 and terminates June 30 2027
affected: Providers and peers involved in intake
Federal and state agencies participating in grants

SB97.one_line: Revises venue for constitutional challenges to laws enacted in the current biennium to sponsor‑district counties.
SB97.summary: SB 97 changes Montana’s venue rules so that lawsuits challenging a law passed in the current biennium must be heard in a county that lies in the legislative district of the bill’s primary sponsor. It amends the state’s civil‑trial venue statutes to give courts the authority to move such cases to those counties.
changes: 1. Establishes that a challenge to a statute or session law enacted or amended within the current legislative biennium is properly tried in any county wholly or partially within the legislative district of the bill’s primary sponsor.
2. Amends §25‑2‑118 to give courts the power to change venue to the sponsor‑district county when a party pleads a law is unconstitutional.
3. Amends §25‑2‑125 and §25‑2‑126 to preserve the new venue rule for actions against public officers and the state, while maintaining existing venue provisions for other civil actions.
4. Updates §25‑2‑201 to list the new venue rule as a ground for a judge to order a change of venue.
5. Codifies the new rule as part of Title 25, Chapter 2, Part 1, and preserves pre‑existing rights and penalties.
6. Provides definitions for “challenge” and “legislative biennium.”
affected: Plaintiffs seeking venue in sponsor‑district counties
numbers: first Monday of January odd‑numbered year
any county within sponsor’s legislative district

SB101.one_line: SB 101 criminalizes squatting and fraudulent property sales, expands removal powers, and adds indemnification for law‑enforcement.
SB101.summary: SB 101 makes unlawful squatting a misdemeanor, creates a new felony for fraudulent sale or lease of property, and amends the removal‑trespasser statute to clarify law‑enforcement authority and indemnification. It also codifies the new provisions in Title 45, Chapter 6, Part 2.
changes: Defines unlawful squatting as knowingly entering a property without consent and residing there; makes it a misdemeanor with restitution equal to fair‑market rent and possible criminal mischief if damage occurs.
Creates a new offense of fraudulent sale or lease of property, punishable by a fine of at least $1,000, a minimum six‑month county jail term, or both.
Allows law‑enforcement officers to remove an unlawful occupant immediately and indemnifies them under 2‑9‑305 for good‑faith actions.

Amends §70‑24‑113 to clarify that an unauthorized person or trespasser may be removed immediately, defines valid authorization, and requires property owners to indemnify law‑enforcement if they provide false information.
Codifies Sections 1 and 2 as part of Title 45, Chapter 6, Part 2, making the new offenses part of the state criminal code.
Adds a civil cause of action for wrongful removal and a fee‑for‑service provision for law‑enforcement (not detailed in the text).
affected: Individuals who squat or falsely advertise property
Potential offenders of fraudulent sale or lease

SB103.one_line: Raise foreclosure sale fee to $25, deposit extra $20 in county district court fund.
SB103.summary: SB 103 raises the fee for issuing an execution or order of sale on a foreclosure of a lien from $5 to $25 and requires that the extra $20 be deposited in the county district court fund. It also amends the fee schedule in §25‑1‑201, MCA, adding new allocation rules for several other court fees.
changes: Increases the execution/order‑of‑sale fee from $5 to $25.
Deposits the $20 increase into the county district court fund (or county general fund if no district court fund exists).
Amends §25‑1‑201, MCA, to include new fee‑allocation provisions for various filing and service fees.
Adds specific deposit requirements for divorce, legal‑separation, and marriage‑related fees into designated trust and assistance accounts.
Provides that certain fees (e.g., for contested parenting‑plan amendments) may be waived if the non‑moving party signs an agreement not to contest.
Clarifies that unallocated fees go to the state general fund.
affected: Plaintiffs and defendants filing the affected actions

SB104.one_line: Expands bond‑financing authority for nonprofits and public‑benefit projects, raising the cap to $1.5 billion with inflation adjustments.
SB104.summary: The bill expands the Montana Facility Finance Authority’s borrowing power and broadens the types of projects that may be financed, especially for 501(c)(3) nonprofits and other public‑benefit facilities. It raises the authority’s bond‑issuance cap to $1.5 billion, adds a 3 % biennial inflation adjustment, and amends definitions and procedures for qualifying projects and public‑interest hearings.
changes: Increases the authority’s maximum bond issuance to $1.5 billion (from $500 million) and adds a 3 % biennial inflation adjustment starting July 1 2027.

Expands the definition of “project” and “eligible facility” to include 501(c)(3) nonprofit entities, family‑services providers, higher‑education facilities, electric‑energy generation facilities, and other public‑benefit projects.
Requires a public hearing and local government notification before financing projects that qualify under the new definitions.
Mandates that any contract for a public project costing >$25,000 include a prevailing‑wage provision unless covered by a collective bargaining agreement.
Adds lease‑or‑agreement requirements to ensure bond repayment, reserves, and cost coverage before issuance.
Amends procedural sections (90‑7‑225 and 90‑7‑229) to clarify timing and notice requirements for public‑interest hearings.
affected: municipalities and counties where projects are located

SB105.one_line: Expands electioneering ban to all voting periods and requires tribal notification.
SB105.summary: SB 105 expands Montana’s election‑electioneering ban to cover the entire period from when absentee ballots become available until all voting is finished, and it requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally recognized tribal governments.
changes: Amends §13‑35‑211 to prohibit electioneering at polling places and within 100 feet of any entrance from the time absentee ballots are available until all voting is complete.
Adds a prohibition on candidates, family members, or campaign workers from distributing alcohol, tobacco, food, drink, or any value to voters during that same period.
Bans the sale, display, or wearing of campaign‑related badges, buttons, or insignia at or near polls during the voting window.
Prevents any person from soliciting a voter’s intent before or after ballot completion.
Requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1 , 2025.

SB106.one_line: Amends hunting‑aircraft rules, expands penalties for unlawful use, and allows permits for property protection.
SB106.summary: The bill amends Montana’s hunting‑aircraft statutes to allow permits for using aircraft to herd or protect property, while tightening restrictions on using aircraft for hunting. It also expands penalties for unlawful aircraft use during hunting, including higher fines and longer license suspensions for certain game.
changes: Amends §87‑3‑126 to permit use of manned or unmanned aircraft for herding, driving, or hazing wildlife that damages private property or crops, subject to a department‑issued permit and rules; permits only during legal hunting seasons and must comply with federal law.

Rewrites §87‑6‑208 to clarify that, except as permitted by §87‑3‑126, a person may not kill, take, or shoot game from an aircraft; may not use an aircraft to spot or locate game within 24 hours; may not concentrate, pursue, rally, or stir up game; may not land on private property without permission; and may not communicate a game location from an aircraft within 24 hours.

Adds a new penalty schedule: general violations fine $300‑$1,000 or up to 6 months in county jail; special higher penalties for killing or taking large game ($500‑$2,000 fine, 6‑month jail, 30‑month license suspension) and for taking fur‑bearing animals ($100‑$1,000 fine, 6‑month jail, 24‑month license suspension, confiscation of unlawful pelts).
Defines “aircraft” as in §87‑6‑101.
Provides exemptions for emergency, search‑and‑rescue, predator control, and agricultural support.
No new program or office is created; the bill only amends existing statutes.

SB107.one_line: Adds trafficking prevention to school goals and directs statewide education efforts.
SB107.summary: SB 107 adds child‑sex‑trafficking and human‑trafficking prevention to the list of instructional goals for public elementary and secondary schools and directs the Office of Public Instruction to develop resources and coordinate prevention efforts. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑102 to include instruction on avoiding participation in child sex trafficking and human trafficking as a legislative goal for schools
Amends §20‑7‑1316 to require the Office of Public Instruction to undertake activities to educate Montanans about and prevent child sex trafficking and human trafficking

Specifies that activities may include reviewing best practices, providing educational resources, coordinating with law enforcement and health agencies, and supporting districts in developing policies and curricula
Establishes July 1, 2025 as the effective date
No new funding or criminal penalties are created
affected: Teachers, child‑care providers, and community members
Law enforcement, public health, and human services agencies

SB109.one_line: Physical therapists can now serve as treating physicians in Montana workers’‑compensation cases.
SB109.summary: SB 109 expands the definition of a treating physician in Montana’s workers’‑compensation law to include licensed physical therapists. The change allows physical therapists to coordinate medical care for injured workers, just as physicians, chiropractors, and other listed providers already can.
changes: Amends Section 39‑71‑116, MCA, adding subsection (h) that lists a licensed physical therapist as a treating physician.
Physical therapists may now be the primary coordinator of medical services for workers’‑compensation claims.
No other substantive changes to the workers’‑compensation statute are made.
The amendment does not create a new program or fund.
The change applies to all workers’‑compensation claims in Montana.
The amendment takes effect on the date the act becomes law (effective date not specified in the text).
affected: Employers covered by the workers’‑compensation system
Insurers and the state workers’‑compensation fund

SB110.one_line: Montana mandates annual inspections, insurance, and safety signage for all amusement rides, with penalties for non‑compliance.
SB110.summary: Montana will require all amusement rides to be inspected annually by a qualified inspector, issue certificates, and maintain liability insurance. Operators must keep first‑aid stations, post safety signs, and follow ASTM standards, while passengers must obey posted rules and report injuries. Serious injuries trigger an inspector‑led investigation and the ride may be shut down until safe.
changes: All amusement rides must receive a qualified‑inspector certificate at least once every 12 months; rides cannot operate without a certificate.
A qualified inspector may not issue a certificate if the ride is unsafe; unsafe conditions must be corrected before certification.
Rides that have undergone major modifications must be inspected before passengers are admitted.
Operators must maintain liability insurance of at least $500,000 per person or $1 million for multiple persons per occurrence.
Operators must post comprehensive safety and operational signs, maintain a first‑aid station, and conduct daily pre‑opening inspections per ASTM standards.
Passengers must follow posted rules, cannot operate ride controls, and must report injuries within six months; serious injuries trigger an inspector investigation that can shut the ride down.

SB111.one_line: Limits green lights to DOT snow‑removal and incident‑command vehicles, tightening highway lighting rules.
SB111.summary: SB 111 amends Montana’s motor‑vehicle lighting code to restrict green lights on public highways, allowing them only on snow‑removal equipment operated by the Department of Transportation or other government entities and on on‑scene incident‑command vehicles. The bill also clarifies red‑light restrictions and other lighting rules.
changes: Amends §61‑9‑226 to prohibit green lights on vehicles unless the vehicle is snow‑removal equipment or an on‑scene incident‑command vehicle;
Red‑light restriction clarified to allow red lights only when expressly authorized;
Flashing or rotating lights are prohibited except on authorized vehicles or for indicating turns/traffic hazards;
Disallows decorative license‑plate or undercarriage lighting that mimics police colors;
Defines “school bus” per §20‑10‑101 for the purposes of the section.
affected: Snow‑removal equipment operators (DOT or other government entities)
All other motor‑vehicle operators on public highways

SB113.one_line: Clarifies towing lien exemptions and expands non‑possessory lien rules.
SB113.summary: SB 113 amends Montana’s towing‑and‑storage lien law to clarify which personal property is exempt, adding specific categories of food, consumer goods, prescription items, documents, and records. It also expands the definition of a non‑possessory special lien and sets notice requirements for competing liens.
changes: Amends §71‑3‑1201, MCA, to list new exempt categories: non‑resale food items, perishable goods, prescription items, original driver’s licenses and other identifying documents, cash‑related items, original personal/legal/business records, child safety items, and wallets/purses containing the listed items.

SB115.one_line: Shortens notice window to 10 days before elections, requiring broadcast or publication of absentee‑ballot and voting‑system info.
SB115.summary: SB 115 shortens the window for public notices about absentee ballot counting and voting‑system information to a 10‑day period before an election, while keeping the 2‑day minimum. It requires the election administrator to broadcast or publish the notices and lets the administrator choose the most effective method. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Limits the notice period for absentee‑ballot‑counting and voting‑system information to no more than 10 days and no less than 2 days before an election.
Mandates that the election administrator broadcast on radio/TV or publish in a county newspaper a notice about the absentee‑ballot‑counting method, location, and time.
If counting begins before polls close, the notice must state that observers must take an oath and are subject to the oath‑penalty law.

Requires the election administrator to broadcast or publish a diagram of the voting system, a sample ballot layout (newspaper only), locations of systems on public exhibition, and voting instructions.
Gives the election administrator discretion to choose the notification method that reaches the largest number of electors.
The act becomes effective immediately upon passage.

SB116.one_line: Revises Montana Heritage Commission membership, qualifications, staff, and administrative processes, effective July 1, 2025.
SB116.summary: The bill amends the Montana Heritage Preservation and Development Commission to change its membership size, qualifications, appointment process, and staff structure, and sets a July 1, 2025 effective date.
changes: Commission size is set at 149 members, down from 14 to 9 for those appointed by the governor, with a phased transition as existing terms expire
Nine members are appointed by the governor, two by the Senate President, and two by the House Speaker; if they fail to appoint within six months, the governor fills the vacancy
Three specific directors (historical society, fish‑wildlife‑parks, commerce) automatically serve as members
Appointees must meet specific expertise criteria (tourism facilities, community planning, historic preservation, business, tourism advisory council, Montana historian, public at large)
Governor‑appointed members serve three‑year terms; Senate/House‑appointed or governor‑filled vacancies serve two‑year terms
The commission may employ an executive director, curator, and other staff; salaries and duties are set by the commission
The Department of Commerce provides staff and services under the state pay plan and assesses the commission for reasonable costs
Transition clause requires reduction of governor‑appointed members to nine only when current terms end and they are not reappointed
Effective date is July 1, 2025
affected: Montana Heritage Preservation and Development Commission members
Montana Historical Society, Fish‑Wildlife‑Parks, Commerce departments
Commission staff and Department of Commerce personnel

SB117.one_line: Creates a reserve account for large taxpayers and tightens mill‑levy limits for local governments.
SB117.summary: SB 117 creates a new “large taxpayer reserve account” for cities, counties and consolidated city‑counties, changes how mill levies are calculated, and sets new limits on how much a governmental entity may impose. The bill applies to property‑tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
changes: Local governments may open a large‑taxpayer reserve account and deposit 10 % of revenue from newly taxable property (excluding class 4) each year.

Deposits may be used to pay technology‑assessment costs, to cover capital‑bond payments when a large taxpayer ceases or drops 25 % in taxable value, to reduce levies for up to 10 years, to attract industry, provide employment incentives, or fund related infrastructure.
Funds in the account must remain untouched until the large taxpayer permanently ceases or drops 25 % in taxable value, except for the 10 % reduction in levies (subsection 5(b)).
The bill amends §15‑10‑420 to raise the inflation‑adjustment factor from 0 % to ½ of the average rate of inflation over the prior three years, but caps the total mill authority at 4 %.
It adds specific percentages of newly taxable value that can be counted toward the mill‑authority calculation (100 % for certain abatements, 50 % if a reserve account is used, 40 % otherwise).

The maximum number of mills a governmental entity may impose is recalculated each year based on current taxable value minus 75 % of the prior year’s newly taxable value from class 4 and other specified classes.
The bill allows carry‑forward of unused mill authority to future years.
The bill clarifies that newly taxable property includes annexations, construction, transfers, subdivisions, and TI‑district changes, but excludes incremental value increases within TI‑districts.
It provides that certain levies (e.g., school districts, regional resource authorities, airports) are exempt from the new mill‑authority limits.
The department may adopt rules to implement the changes.
The act applies to property‑tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
affected: Local governments’ finance and budgeting staff
Property owners in newly taxable classes
numbers: ½ of average inflation rate over 3 years
25 % decrease in taxable value triggers account use

SB121.one_line: SB 121 expands local‑government land‑use authority, public‑participation, and subdivision‑review procedures with a 2027 sunset.
SB121.summary: SB 121 revises Montana’s Land Use Planning Act to clarify local‑government authority, expand public‑notice and comment requirements, allow cities to keep extraterritorial zoning, and modify subdivision‑review exclusions. It also creates a new public‑hearing process for planning‑commission appeals and sets a termination date for most provisions.
changes: Clarifies that a local government may approve or deny development applications and sets detailed notice‑and‑comment procedures for land‑use decisions.
Expands public‑participation requirements for adopting land‑use plans, zoning, and subdivision regulations, including written and electronic notice and a 15‑day comment period.

Allows cities to retain extraterritorial zoning authority up to 3 miles (first‑class), 2 miles (second‑class), or 1 mile (third‑class) beyond their limits, unless the county adopts matching regulations.
Amends the list of land‑division exclusions from subdivision review and requires a notice of certification of adequate storm‑water drainage and municipal facilities for certain cities.
Creates a public hearing before the planning commission when an appeal is filed, and allows the commission to hear appeals de novo.
Sets an immediate effective date (upon passage) and a termination date of June 30 2027 for Sections 11–13 (subdivision‑review procedures).

Revises definitions and procedural language in Sections 2‑3‑102, 2‑3‑104, 7‑2‑4734, 76‑2‑310, 76‑4‑125, 76‑4‑127, 76‑25‑103, 76‑25‑104, 76‑25‑106, 76‑25‑301, 76‑25‑305, 76‑25‑408, 76‑25‑410, and 76‑25‑503 to reflect the new authority and processes.
affected: Public residents and property owners in affected jurisdictions

SB124.one_line: Amends Montana’s electronic license law to clarify that showing a license to police is not consent to search.
SB124.summary: The bill amends Montana’s electronic driver‑license privacy law to clarify that showing an electronic license to a police officer does not equal consent to search the device. It also directs the code commissioner to renumber and re‑codify the provision.
changes: Amends §61‑5‑310, MCA, to state that displaying an electronic driver’s license on a device or handing that device to a peace officer does not constitute consent to a search or seizure of the device.
Instructs the code commissioner to renumber §61‑5‑310 and update all internal references in the Montana Code Annotated to reflect the new section number.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The amendment applies to all electronic driver‑license holders and peace officers in Montana.
The bill does not alter any enforcement procedures or impose new penalties.

SB132.one_line: Creates new misdemeanor offenses for minors who possess or try to buy alcohol, marijuana, or other intoxicants with a tiered penalty schedule.
SB132.summary: The bill creates new, separate criminal offenses for minors who possess or try to buy alcohol, marijuana, or other intoxicants, and sets a detailed sentencing scheme that includes fines, community service, mandatory substance‑abuse courses, license confiscation, and, for repeat offenders, chemical‑dependency assessments and possible jail time. It also amends existing alcohol‑and‑marijuana statutes to clarify penalties and procedural requirements.
changes: Creates distinct misdemeanor offenses for minors who possess or attempt to purchase alcohol, marijuana, or other intoxicants; establishes a tiered penalty schedule (first, second, third+ offenses) with fines, community service, mandatory courses, and driver‑license confiscation; requires chemical‑dependency assessment and treatment for repeat offenders; adds license‑confiscation and suspension provisions; amends existing statutes (16‑3‑301, 16‑3‑323, 16‑6‑314, 16‑12‑106, 45‑5‑624) to reflect new definitions and penalties; provides procedural safeguards for minors seeking medical treatment; and codifies the changes under Title 45, Chapter 5, Part 6.

who_is_affected':['Minors under 21 (especially under 18)','Adult offenders of the same offenses','Drivers with licenses','Courts and judges','Licensed addiction counselors','Health‑care facilities and law‑enforcement personnel','Retailers and licensees of alcohol and marijuana','Community‑based substance‑abuse programs','Department of Public Health and Human Services','Department of Corrections','Department of State Police','County jails'],
affected: Adult offenders of the same offenses
Retailers and licensees of alcohol and marijuana
Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB133.one_line: Rewrites impact‑fee rules to cap increases, remove admin fee, and tighten documentation.
SB133.summary: SB 133 revises Montana’s impact‑fee rules, eliminating the 5 % administration fee, capping fee increases to inflation, and tightening documentation and calculation requirements. It requires local governments to prepare detailed service‑area reports and limits fees to the proportionate share of capital costs, excluding operations, maintenance, and existing deficiencies.
changes: Eliminates the 5 % administration fee that could be added to impact fees.
Limits any increase in impact‑fee amounts to the Producer Price Index inflation rate.
