Mandates that impact‑fee ordinances include a service‑area report with detailed methodology, cost estimates, and a five‑year budget schedule.
Requires that impact fees be based on actual or reasonably estimated capital‑improvement costs, not on operations or maintenance costs.
Prohibits including costs for correcting existing deficiencies or for user‑fee, tax, or other funding sources in the fee calculation.
Requires public availability of the service‑area report upon request.
Sets a requirement that the impact‑fee ordinance include a schedule for periodic updates of the documentation.
Adds a definition that a “capital improvement” must have a useful life of at least 10 years.
Adds a definition that a “connection charge” is limited to the cost of connecting a property to a public utility system.
Clarifies that an impact fee may not exceed the proportionate share of the costs incurred by the governmental entity for the development.
affected: Local governments (counties, cities, towns, consolidated governments)
Developers and property owners subject to impact fees
Residents and taxpayers who may see fees reflected in property taxes or utility bills
numbers: Inflation cap based on Producer Price Index (1982‑84 base of 100)
Service‑area report must cover at least a 5‑year period
Proportionate share cannot exceed costs incurred by the governmental entity
Capital improvements defined as 10‑year useful life

SB137.one_line: Montana will automatically excuse 75‑plus prospective jurors upon request.
SB137.summary: The bill amends Montana’s jury‑service law to automatically excuse anyone 75 or older from jury duty if they request it. It adds this age‑based exemption to the existing hardship‑based excusal provisions.
changes: Amends §3‑15‑313, MCA, adding a new subsection that requires the court or jury commissioner to excuse any prospective juror who is 75 years or older upon request.

SB134.one_line: SB 134 gives donors legal recourse for breach of endowment restrictions and requires charities to notify donors of any inability to comply.
SB134.summary: SB 134 creates the Safeguarding Endowment Gifts Act, giving donors legal recourse if a charitable organization violates donor‑imposed restrictions on an endowment. The act allows donors or their legal representatives to file civil complaints within three years of discovery and requires charities to notify donors of any inability to meet the agreement’s terms.
changes:
Establishes a new statutory framework (the Safeguarding Endowment Gifts Act) for endowment agreements.  
Defines key terms such as “charitable organization,” “donor,” “donor‑imposed restriction,” and “endowment agreement.”  
Prevents a charitable organization from violating a donor‑imposed restriction without potential penalty.  
Allows a donor or legal representative to file a complaint in a general‑jurisdiction court within three years of discovery, 90 days after written notice.  
Requires charities to notify donors 90 days in advance if they cannot fulfill a term and to offer an alternative solution.  
Permits a charitable organization to seek a judicial declaration of the rights and duties in an endowment agreement.  
Gives courts the power to order remedies consistent with the charitable purpose but not to return funds to the donor.
affected: Courts of general jurisdiction in Montana

SB143.one_line: Extends Montana’s civil limitation periods for contracts and real‑property improvement damages.
SB143.summary: SB 143 extends Montana’s statute‑of‑limitations periods for many civil actions.  Contracts and other obligations in writing now have an 8‑year limit, while non‑written contracts are 5 years and other non‑contractual obligations are 3 years.  For damages tied to real‑property improvements or land surveying, the limit is 10 years from completion, with a one‑year window for injuries that occur in the 10th year after completion.
changes: Changes Section 27‑2‑202 to set new limitation periods: 8 years for written contracts, 5 years for non‑written contracts, 3 years for other obligations.

Rewrites Section 27‑2‑208 to set a 10‑year limitation for damages from work on real‑property improvements or land surveying, with a 1‑year window for injuries occurring in the 10th year after completion.
Adds a definition of “completion” and clarifies that the new limits do not affect owners, tenants, or occupants who are in control of the property when the right of action arises.
Specifies that the new rules apply only to actions filed on or after October 1 2025.
affected: Individuals or entities filing civil actions based on contracts, covenants, or other obligations
Owners, tenants, or occupants of real‑property improvements or surveyed land
Contractors, surveyors, and other professionals involved in real‑property improvements

SB144.one_line: Renames the mental‑health advisory council to behavioral health advisory council.
SB144.summary: SB 144 changes the name of the Mental Health Oversight Advisory Council to the Behavioral Health Advisory Council and amends the statutory language that defines the council’s composition and duties. The amendment does not create new programs, funds, or fees, nor does it alter eligibility criteria beyond the existing framework. The bill simply updates terminology and clarifies the council’s role in the public mental‑health system.
changes: Renames the Mental Health Oversight Advisory Council to the Behavioral Health Advisory Council.
Amends Section 53‑21‑702, MCA, to reflect the new council name and to specify that the council is not subject to 2‑15‑122.
Reiterates that the council’s membership must include one‑half consumers and the other half advocates, providers, legislators, and department representatives.
Adds language that the council may be administered to satisfy federal advisory‑council requirements for federal funding.
Maintains geographic representation requirements for council appointments.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services staff

SB147.one_line: Repeals 2023 Section 55, notifies tribes, effective immediately.
SB147.summary: SB 147 repeals a 2023 law, notifies federally recognized Montana tribes, and takes effect immediately. The bill does not add new provisions beyond these actions.
changes: Repeals Section 55, Chapter 716, Laws of 2023.
affected: State agencies involved in child welfare

SB148.one_line: Landowners may give free hunting licenses to family, employees, or disabled persons under Montana’s block‑management program.
SB148.summary: The bill lets landowners who enroll in Montana’s block‑management program give free hunting or fishing licenses to immediate family, employees, or people with developmental or physical disabilities. It also expands landowner preference rules for elk, deer, and antelope licenses and permits, and allows designated persons to receive those licenses under the same eligibility requirements.
changes: 1. Landowners in the block‑management program may designate an immediate family member, employee, or person with a developmental or physical disability to receive a conservation license and a Class AAA (resident) or Class B‑10 (non‑resident) combination license at no charge.
2. The department may limit the total number of such licenses issued to landowners.

3. Landowners who offer free public elk hunting may issue an either‑sex or antlerless elk license, permit, or combination to a designee who is an immediate family member, employee, or person with a developmental or physical disability.

4. Landowners who own qualifying acreage (640 acres or more of elk habitat, or 160 acres of production land with recent elk damage) may designate a family member, employee, or person with a developmental or physical disability to apply for Class A‑9, B‑12, or special elk permits, with 15 % of those licenses set aside for landowners.

5. Non‑resident landowners owning at least 2,500 contiguous acres may designate a family member, employee, or person with a developmental or physical disability to receive a Class B‑10 non‑resident big‑game combination license, with up to five licenses per qualifying landowner.

5. Landowners owning 160 acres or more of primarily agricultural land may designate a family member, employee, or person with a developmental or physical disability to receive a deer or antelope license or permit, with 15 % of the limited licenses set aside for landowners.
affected: Immediate family members of those landowners
Persons with developmental or physical disabilities
Public hunters accessing landowners’ property for free elk hunting

SB149.one_line: Revises Montana’s ESA documentation rules to require detailed practitioner statements and animal health proof.
SB149.summary: The bill amends Montana’s housing statutes to tighten the documentation required for tenants seeking to keep emotional‑support animals (ESAs).  Landlords must now obtain a health‑care practitioner’s written statement that includes the practitioner’s license details, proof of the tenant’s disability, and evidence that the animal meets state vaccination and licensing rules.  The changes do not create a new program or crime.
changes: Amends sections 70‑24‑114 and 70‑33‑110 to require a health‑care practitioner’s written statement that includes the practitioner’s effective date, license number, and type of license.
Adds a requirement that the ESA meet state and local licensure and vaccination requirements and that proof of this be provided to the landlord.
Mandates that if a tenant wants more than one ESA, documentation must be provided for each animal.
Specifies that a landlord may deny an ESA if it poses a direct threat to safety or property that cannot be mitigated by other accommodations.
States that a tenant is liable for damage caused by the ESA and that the practitioner may face disciplinary action for violating the new rules.
Clarifies that the ESA registration card alone is not sufficient proof of a disability‑related need.
Reaffirms that the new rules do not override federal Fair Housing Act or ADA rights.
Defines “emotional support animal” and “health‑care practitioner” in the context of the statute.
affected: Tenants with disabilities who want to keep ESAs
Mental‑health professionals who provide ESA documentation

SB154.one_line: Revises Montana’s anatomical‑gift law to ban sale of body parts or whole bodies and sets felony penalties.
SB154.summary: The bill updates Montana’s anatomical‑gift law to clarify definitions, prohibit the sale or purchase of any human body part or whole body for any purpose, and set penalties for violations. It amends the Uniform Anatomical Gift Act provisions and takes effect immediately.
changes: Amends Section 72‑17‑102 to revise definitions of key terms such as “adult,” “agent,” “anatomical gift,” and others.

Amends Section 72‑17‑302 to prohibit knowingly buying or selling a body part for transplantation, therapy, research, education, or search‑and‑rescue training when removal is intended after death, and to prohibit buying or selling a whole body for any of those purposes.
Defines “valuable consideration” to exclude reasonable payment for removal, processing, disposal, preservation, quality control, storage, transportation, or implantation of a part or whole body.
Establishes a felony penalty for violations, with a fine up to $50,000, imprisonment up to 5 years, or both.
Sets the act’s effective date to the day it is passed and approved.
affected: Individuals who might sell or purchase body parts or whole bodies
Organizations involved in organ or tissue procurement
Legal professionals dealing with anatomical‑gift records
Law enforcement and courts handling related offenses

SB161.one_line: Exempts aquaculture products from most food‑regulation requirements while allowing accurate sale practices.
SB161.summary: The bill amends Montana’s commodity‑sale and cottage‑food statutes to add aquaculture products to the list of items exempt from most food‑regulation requirements.  It clarifies that aquaculture products may be sold directly to consumers without the licensing, labeling, or inspection normally required for homemade food, while still allowing the department to set rules for accurate measurement and sale practices.
changes: Amends §30‑12‑301 to exempt aquaculture products from general commodity‑sale rules; allows liquid or weight sales only if accurate.

Amends §50‑49‑203 to exempt producers of aquaculture products from licensure, permitting, labeling, testing, and inspection, provided sales are direct to consumers within Montana and for home or community use.
Amends §50‑50‑102 to define “raw agricultural commodity” to include aquaculture products, expanding the scope of cottage‑food and homemade‑food definitions.
Amends §80‑3‑302 to define aquaculture, aquaculture products, and related terms, and to give the director of agriculture authority to regulate production and sale.
Provides that the department may adopt rules to ensure accurate measurement of aquaculture products sold.
Effective immediately upon passage (no later‑than date specified).
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB162.one_line: Revises council membership, expands judge eligibility, and directs re‑codification of the statute.
SB162.summary: SB 162 revises the Montana Criminal Justice Oversight Council’s membership rules, expands eligible local court judges, and directs the Code Commissioner to re‑codify the statute. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends Section 53‑1‑216 to add a municipal court judge and a justice of the peace to the council’s two‑judge slot, and expands the governor’s appointment list to include a federally recognized Indian tribe member, a board of pardons and parole member, a crime‑victim representative, a civil‑rights advocate, and two community‑corrections providers (one treatment facility, one prerelease center).

Replaces the former “district court judge” and “municipal court judge” language with a single clause that allows either a municipal court judge who presides over a city or municipal court or a justice of the peace.
Adds a requirement that the governor and attorney general consider appointing members who also serve on the Board of Crime Control.
Specifies that the council’s presiding officer must be a legislator and that the council shall report to the governor and legislature and may request new legislation.
Provides procedures for filling vacancies, reimbursement rules for travel and salaries, and updates to the Law and Justice Interim Committee and Legislative Finance Committee.
Instructs the Code Commissioner to renumber Section 53‑1‑216 and update all internal references to reflect the new section number.
affected: Montana Criminal Justice Oversight Council members
State agencies listed in the council’s membership
Legislators serving as council presiding officers

SB163.one_line: Expands privacy protections to neurotechnology data and tightens government access to genetic and neurotechnology information.
SB163.summary: The bill expands Montana’s Genetic Information Privacy Act to cover neurotechnology data, adds new privacy‑notice and consent requirements, limits government access to genetic and neurotechnology data, and imposes stricter rules on data sharing and storage. It also updates exceptions and clarifies when a warrant is required for database searches.
changes: Adds the term “neurotechnology data” to the Act and defines it as data captured by devices that record, interpret, or alter nervous‑system activity.

Requires entities that collect or use genetic or neurotechnology data to provide a high‑level privacy policy and a prominent notice, and to obtain express consent for each use, disclosure, or transfer of the data.
Creates a consumer right to access, delete, revoke consent for, and request destruction of their genetic or neurotechnology data, with limited waivers for clinical research.
Prohibits disclosure of such data to health‑insurance, life‑insurance, long‑term‑care insurers, or employers without express consent.

Mandates that any government agency collecting or using genetic or neurotechnology data must do so under a specific state law, a search warrant, or an investigative subpoena, and that database searches (including familial or partial matches) require a warrant or subpoena unless the consumer has waived privacy rights.
Adds restrictions that data of Montana residents may not be stored in countries under U.S. sanctions and may only be transferred outside the U.S. with the resident’s consent.
affected: Consumers of genetic and neurotechnology testing services
Companies and laboratories that collect, process, or store genetic or neurotechnology data
Government agencies and law‑enforcement entities that seek to access such data
Insurance companies and employers that might request data
Researchers conducting clinical or scientific studies with genetic or neurotechnology data
numbers: June 1 2025 – effective date for government data use provisions
14‑day minimum for obtaining written consent in clinical research
2‑year maximum retention for certain laboratory samples
size 12‑point font requirement for consent forms
warrant or subpoena required for database searches

SB165.one_line: Adds a $5 rental fee for snowmobiles, revises pass fees, and allocates revenue for trail maintenance.
SB165.summary: SB 165 adds a $5 trail‑enhancement fee for each snowmobile or motorized‑equipment rental, requires rental vendors to remit the fee to the department, and specifies how the money is split between vendors, enforcement, and trail grooming. It also revises the winter trail‑pass fee schedule and clarifies use of the pass and penalties for non‑compliance.
changes: Adds a $5 trail‑enhancement rental fee that renters must pay to the vendor and that vendor must remit to the department each month.

Specifies that the fee is deposited in the state special revenue fund and that 2 % is used for trail‑grooming operations while the rest is distributed to entities that groom and maintain trails in rental areas.
Revises the winter trail‑pass fee schedule: $20 for registered equipment or resident operators (valid up to 2 years) and $35 for unregistered or non‑resident operators (valid up to 1 year).
Requires trail passes to be affixed in a conspicuous place and makes them non‑transferable, except when a snowmobile is sold with an affixed pass.
Imposes a misdemeanor penalty (fine $40–$100) for failure to affix a pass or for making false statements when obtaining a pass.
Defines “motorized equipment” and “snowmobile” for the purposes of the act.
affected: Renters of snowmobiles and motorized equipment
Trail‑grooming entities that receive fee distributions
Department of Natural Resources (or equivalent) that administers the program

SB166.one_line: Amends CPA education and audit rules, effective Jan 1 2026.
SB166.summary: The bill amends Montana’s CPA licensing law to require a bachelor’s degree with at least 150 semester‑hour credits and specific accounting and business coursework, and it gives the board authority to set continuing‑education requirements. It also allows the board to audit all licensees in a year if a prior audit finds more than 15 % non‑compliance. The changes take effect on January 1, 2026.
changes: Replaces the education requirement in §37‑50‑305 to mandate 150 semester‑hour baccalaureate degrees and board‑specified accounting/business credits for initial licensure.
Adds a continuing‑education requirement that licensees must meet as set by board and department rules.
Provides that if an audit finds >15 % of licensees non‑compliant, the board may audit up to 100 % of licensees in the following audit year.
Defines “initial licensure” as a first‑time application for CPA licensure in any jurisdiction.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to January 1, 2026.
No new program, office, fund, or criminal offense is created.
No monetary amounts are specified in the text.
affected: Prospective and current certified public accountants in Montana

SB167.one_line: Transfers $10 million to the Noxious Weed Trust Fund and amends its administration rules.
SB167.summary: The bill transfers $10 million from the general fund to the Noxious Weed Management Trust Fund, amends the trust‑fund statute to clarify its composition and income rules, and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §80‑7‑811 to establish a $10 million trust corpus and specify that one‑quarter of the trust’s interest and income must remain in the fund.
Allows deposits to the trust’s principal from federal contributions, private donations, and state contributions.
Mandates the state treasurer to transfer $10 million from the general fund to the trust by June 30 2025.
Sets the act’s effective date to the day it is passed and approved.
affected: Department of Natural Resources (trust fund administrator)
Federal agencies and private donors who may contribute to the trust
numbers: one‑quarter of interest and income retained

SB168.one_line: Limits enforcement to 3 years and exempts minor lakeshore work from permitting.
SB168.summary: SB 168 shortens the time a local body or the state can sue a property owner or contractor for violating lakeshore regulations to three years after construction or permit issuance, except for illegal structures that cause significant harm. It also exempts minor maintenance or remodeling of existing lakeshore structures from future permitting, while still allowing the state or local government to compel removal or alteration if needed.
changes: Establishes a 3‑year statute of limitations for enforcement actions against owners or contractors for violations of lakeshore regulations, based on completion of construction or permit issuance, whichever is later.

Excludes the statute of limitations for structures built illegally that cause documented material harm to lakeshore stability, water quality, aquatic life, navigation, recreation, or create a public nuisance.

Exempts minor ongoing maintenance, remodeling, or modifications to existing lakeshore structures from lakeshore protection review unless the work involves significant excavation, dredging, in‑fill, or interference with navigation or recreation.
Defines “minor” as changes costing less than $10,000 over a 5‑year period, excluding free personal services provided by the owner.
Allows local governing bodies or the state to compensate a property owner to remove or alter a structure if deemed in the best interests of lakeshore protection and aquatic life.
Codifies the new provisions as part of Title 75, Chapter 7, Part 2 of the Montana Statutes.
Makes the act effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Contractors performing work on lakeshore structures
Local governing bodies and the state
Residents and users of lakeshore recreation areas

SB170.one_line: Eliminates termination date for community health aide program, amending Medicaid coverage provisions.
SB170.summary: The bill removes the termination date for Montana’s community health aide program and updates the Medicaid coverage language. It also repeals two earlier provisions and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends Section 5 of Chapter 412, 2019 to revise Medicaid coverage language for certified community health aides.
Repeals Section 7 of Chapter 412, 2019 and Section 1 of Chapter 298, 2023.
Mandates the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
The act becomes effective upon passage and approval.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB174.one_line: Reclassifies recreational vehicles and mobile homes as buildings, adding subdivision‑review and water‑right requirements.
SB174.summary: SB 174 expands the definition of a “building” to include recreational camping vehicles and mobile homes so that such sites must be reviewed under subdivision‑planning rules. The bill amends several subdivision‑and‑building statutes, adds new requirements for water rights, easements, and park‑dedication calculations, and creates new exemption and regulation provisions for multi‑unit lease‑or‑rent developments.
changes: Reclassifies recreational camping vehicles and mobile homes as buildings for lease or rent, subjecting them to subdivision‑review requirements.
Amends subdivision statutes (76‑3‑103, 76‑3‑504, 76‑3‑621) to include new definitions, water‑right, and easement rules, and to adjust park‑dedication formulas.
Adds new exemption rules (76‑8‑103) and regulatory requirements (76‑8‑107) for buildings on a single tract, including limits on the number of buildings and water‑sewer compliance.
Requires pre‑application meetings, environmental assessments, and public‑utility reviews for subdivisions that include vehicle or mobile‑home spaces.
Establishes a coordination clause that voids overlapping amendments from other bills.
Specifies that the changes apply to sites created on or after the effective date.

SB172.one_line: SB 172 expands resort‑tax options, earmarks extra revenue for housing, and tightens bond limits.
SB172.summary: SB 172 revises Montana’s resort‑tax rules, allowing an extra 1 % levy that must be earmarked for infrastructure or workforce housing. It updates definitions, election procedures, and board powers, and adds limits on bond issuance and debt service for resort‑area districts.
changes: Amends the resort‑tax rate cap to allow an additional 1 % levy that must be used for infrastructure or workforce‑housing projects.
Rewrites the definition of a resort area and resort community, tightening population limits and economic‑activity criteria.
Revises the election process for resort‑tax questions, requiring notice, a 35‑day minimum lead time, and limiting the number of elections per fiscal year.
Expands the powers of resort‑area‑district boards to issue bonds backed by resort‑tax revenue, but imposes a $500,000 single‑project limit and a 25 % debt‑service‑to‑revenue cap.
Adds a 70 % debt‑service limit on cumulative annual payments when the district relies on the additional 1 % levy for infrastructure.
Requires that any bond or additional levy be approved by qualified electors and that the board submit a petition identifying specific uses of the extra tax revenue.
affected: Resort communities, resort areas, and resort‑area districts; their residents (qualified electors); local businesses subject to the resort tax; resort‑area‑district boards; county commissioners; and the state treasury (through bond limits).
numbers: 35‑day minimum lead time before tax takes effect

SB175.one_line: Revises zoning‑adoption rules to require public hearings and notice before county commissioners act.
SB175.summary: SB 175 revises Montana’s zoning‑adoption rules to require a public hearing and notice before county commissioners can adopt or amend zoning regulations. It sets specific notice periods, publication requirements, and a comment window for property owners.
changes: Adds a mandatory public hearing for any proposed zoning‑district boundary or regulation change.
Requires notice of the hearing to be posted at least 45 days (or 15 days for amendments) in five public places and published weekly for two weeks in a county newspaper.
Mandates that proposed regulations be on file at the county clerk’s office for public inspection.
Provides a 30‑day written‑comment period for property owners listed on the last assessment roll after a resolution of intent is published.
Allows commissioners to adopt the resolution within 30 days after the comment period expires.
Extends the notice and comment requirements to amendments of existing regulations, with a 15‑day pre‑hearing posting and two‑week newspaper publication.
Clarifies that the board may adopt an amendment only after the public hearing.
affected: Property owners within proposed zoning districts

SB177.one_line: Allows the community‑choice school commission to accept private gifts and seek public funds, with new membership rules and reporting requirements.
SB177.summary: The bill amends Montana’s community‑choice school commission statute to allow the commission to seek public money and to accept and spend private gifts. It also sets out the commission’s membership, appointment terms, and reporting duties.
changes: Amends §20‑11‑106, MCA to authorize the commission to receive and expend gifts from private entities and to seek public funding
Defines a seven‑member commission with staggered terms and specifies appointing authorities (governor, superintendent, senate and house leaders)
Requires the commission to adopt bylaws and officers within 180 days of July 1 and to hold open meetings
Mandates annual reporting of academic and financial performance of authorized choice schools to the state board of public education
Allows the commission to hire staff and to use board‑provided centralized services if deemed efficient
Provides reimbursement procedures for commission members and removal procedures for vacancies
Sets an immediate effective date upon passage and approval
affected: Choice schools authorized by the commission
numbers: 3‑year terms for superintendent and minority leaders
2‑year terms for senate president and house speaker

SB178.one_line: Creates a temporary water‑right leasing program with strict limits and objection procedures.
SB178.summary: SB 178 creates a new, temporary water‑right‑leasing program that lets appropriators lease up to five years of their consumptive use, subject to strict limits and a 30‑day objection period.  The bill amends definitions of “beneficial use” and “abandonment” and requires the Department of Natural Resources to report annual leasing activity.
changes: Allows an appropriator to temporarily lease an appropriation right for up to five years, but not more than 20 40‑day periods per year and not exceeding 2 acre‑feet per acre irrigated for irrigation rights
Sets a hard cap of 2,000 acre‑feet per year of leased water, tied to the original right’s consumptive volume
Requires a 30‑day written notice to proximate appropriators and a 30‑day objection window; a valid objection suspends the lease until a hearing
Mandates that the leased water be measured at diversion, reported annually, and that a lease agreement be filed with the Department
Amends 85‑2‑102 to expand the definition of “beneficial use” to include temporary leases and certain aquifer projects
Rewrites 85‑2‑404 to clarify that temporary leases or changes do not constitute abandonment of a right
Adds a reporting requirement to the Water Policy Interim Committee and a rule‑making authority extension
Excludes the Flathead Indian Reservation from the new leasing rules
affected: Proximate appropriators who may be affected by a lease

SB181.one_line: SB 181 strengthens Indian education by mandating tribal consultation, curriculum, and strict financial accountability.
SB181.summary: SB 181 amends Montana’s Indian Education for All laws to require every school district to provide American Indian studies, mandate tribal consultation, and impose strict financial reporting and accountability for state‑funded Indian education dollars. The bill also revises definitions, accreditation standards, and reporting requirements for the Office of Public Instruction.
changes: All certified teachers and students must receive instruction in American Indian studies, with districts required to use licensed Indian language and culture specialists.

School districts must submit annual, detailed financial reports showing how Indian Education for All funds were spent on curriculum, materials, and teacher training, and must not divert those funds for other purposes.
Failure to file or to spend funds appropriately triggers reductions in a district’s BASE and maximum budget limits and aid until compliance is restored.

The Board of Public Education must incorporate Montana Indian heritage into content and performance standards and include tribal representatives on negotiated rulemaking committees for accreditation standards.
The Office of Public Instruction must create an online portal for feedback, respond to it, and report annually to the Education Interim Committee and the State‑Tribal Relations Committee.
The Secretary of State must notify each federally recognized Montana tribal government of the act.
affected: Montana Indian tribes and tribal education departments
numbers: 1‑month advance review period for accreditation standards
BASE budget component for Indian Education for All funds
Full amount of Indian Education for All payment deducted if reporting fails
Reduction of BASE and maximum budget limits for non‑compliant districts
Publication of non‑compliant districts on the Office of Public Instruction website

SB183.one_line: Guide licenses now require an outfitter endorsement and renewal signatures.
SB183.summary: SB 183 requires that all applicants for a guide license and renewals be endorsed by a licensed outfitter. The amendment adds an outfitter endorsement requirement to the existing guide‑licensing statute and makes the rule effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends § 37‑47‑303 to add a mandatory outfitter endorsement for new guide license applicants.
Requires that a renewal application be signed by an outfitter employing the guide; otherwise the renewal is denied.
The only other change is the immediate effective‑date provision.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Licensed outfitters who must provide endorsements

SB182.one_line: Revises the Indian Language Preservation Program to broaden partners, clarify reporting, and protect tribal IP.
SB182.summary: SB 182 amends the Montana Indian Language Preservation Program to give tribes more flexibility in choosing partners, clarify reporting and funding rules, and require use of tribal‑produced materials housed at the Montana Historical Society. The bill also mandates notification to tribes and sets July 1 2025 as the effective date.
changes: Amends Section 20‑9‑537, MCA to expand partner types (public, community‑choice, nonpublic schools, tribal schools, postsecondary institutions, early‑learning providers).
Requires program guidelines to define tribal roles, language‑fluency metrics, performance standards, fund distribution, and accounting.
Mandates tribal governments submit detailed applications including partner commitments, designated program administrators, specialist roles, curriculum plans, and budgets.
Imposes annual reporting to the Office of Public Instruction; failure to report can suspend funding.
Office of Public Instruction must report to the legislature and relevant committees, including program guidelines, activity summaries, and language‑promotion metrics.
Affirms tribal ownership of cultural and intellectual property from program efforts; allows negotiated use by partners.
Allows tribes to use program funds as matching funds for federal or private sources.
affected: Tribal education, culture, or language departments
Partnering school districts (public, community‑choice, nonpublic, tribal, postsecondary, early‑learning)

SB184.one_line: Only contested precinct‑committee races need to appear on the primary ballot.
SB184.summary: SB 184 amends the law so that only contested precinct‑committee races appear on the primary ballot. If a party has only one candidate for a male or female committee seat, the election can be cancelled or the candidate elected by acclamation. The change clarifies when write‑in votes are counted and how ties are resolved.
changes: Amends §13‑38‑201 to allow a party to cancel a primary election for a precinct‑committee seat if the number of candidates is less than or equal to the number of positions.
If cancelled, the sole candidate (or a write‑in who filed a declaration of intent) is elected by acclamation and receives a certificate of election.
Write‑in votes for a precinct‑committee seat are counted only if the write‑in candidate filed a declaration of intent by the prescribed deadline.
In the event of a tie, the county central committee decides the winner.
The amendment does not create new programs, offices, or criminal offenses.
The bill does not alter funding or impose new costs.

SB188.one_line: Creates shared‑solar framework with on‑bill credits and utility interconnection rules.
SB188.summary: The bill creates a framework for shared‑solar projects that lets multiple customers receive on‑bill credits for electricity generated by a community solar plant. It requires utilities to interconnect such plants, sets size limits (50 kW–5 MW), and gives the Public Service Commission rule‑making authority. The act is effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Utilities must interconnect shared‑solar facilities that meet size and location criteria and provide on‑bill credits to subscribing customers.
Owners of shared‑solar facilities must cover all administrative and safety costs and supply the utility with customer lists and credit allocations.
The Public Service Commission may adopt rules on credit rates, participation, transferability, portability, consumer protection, and nondiscrimination within one year.
The bill establishes that subscribing customers cannot be customer‑generators and must have a utility account in the same service territory.
On‑bill credits are calculated net of utility supply; excess credits are carried forward and minimum fees apply if credits exceed usage.
Subscribing customers may transfer credits to new accounts or to a new eligible customer, and may assign their share to a nonprofit or low‑income program.
The act codifies these provisions into Title 69, chapter 3 and preserves pre‑existing rights and penalties.
The bill is effective on passage and approval.

SB190.one_line: Water‑right holders may waive the adverse‑effects analysis for permits or changes by filing written consent.
SB190.summary: SB 190 lets water‑right holders consent to waive the usual adverse‑effects analysis that the Department must perform when a permit or change application is filed. The bill amends several water‑right statutes to allow a written consent to skip the analysis, while preserving other procedural and environmental safeguards.
changes: 1. Adds a new subsection (9) to §85‑2‑311 that allows the Department to forgo an adverse‑effects analysis if the water‑right holder files a written consent to approval for a permit application.
2. Adds a similar written‑consent exemption to §85‑2‑402 for change‑in‑appropriation‑right applications.
3. Adds a written‑consent exemption to §85‑2‑408 for temporary change authorizations to maintain or enhance instream flow.

4. Keeps all existing criteria for permitting and changing rights (physical availability, beneficial use, no adverse effect on prior rights, etc.) but removes the requirement to conduct an adverse‑effects analysis when a consent is filed.

5. Preserves the requirement that a written consent must be filed in connection with the specific application and that the Department may still issue a permit or change if the other statutory criteria are met.
6. Does not create new programs, funds, or criminal offenses.
7. Maintains all other procedural rules (notice, hearings, evidence standards, etc.) unchanged.
8. Does not alter the Department’s authority to adopt rules implementing the new consent provisions.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
other water‑right holders who may be affected by a change

SB193.one_line: Chief Justice appoints and can replace up to seven attorneys‑examining board members.
SB193.summary: The bill changes the appointment process for Montana’s Attorneys’ Examining Board so that the Supreme Court Chief Justice, not the governor, selects its members. It limits the board to seven people and gives the Chief Justice authority to add, remove, or replace members at any time.
changes: Amends §37‑61‑102, MCA to state that the Supreme Court Chief Justice appoints board members.
Limits the board to no more than seven members.
Gives the Chief Justice power to release, dismiss, or remove any member and to appoint replacements.
Defines a majority of the board as a quorum for conducting examinations.
States the board’s duties are governed by rules the Chief Justice may prescribe.
affected: Members of the Attorneys’ Examining Board
Applicants for admission to the Montana bar

SB191.one_line: Creates licensing rules for Montana residential treatment centers and updates education and facility definitions.
SB191.summary: The bill creates a licensing framework for residential treatment centers (RTCs) and gives the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) authority to set detailed rules.  It also amends education and facility‑definition statutes so that children in RTCs can receive appropriate schooling and that RTCs are treated as a distinct type of health‑care facility.
changes: DPHHS must license all RTCs and adopt rules covering staff ratios, qualifications, training, services, insurance, background checks, policies, abuse reporting, provisional licensure, and other safety measures.
Licensure can be provisional for up to one year while a facility seeks full accreditation from a CMS‑approved accrediting body.

The bill amends education statutes to define “appropriate educational opportunity” for children in RTCs and clarifies the roles of children’s psychiatric hospitals, RTCs, therapeutic group homes, and public schools.
It amends the definition of “residential treatment center” in 50‑5‑101 to include the specific services, age limits, and accreditation requirements set out in the bill.
The bill requires that RTCs align their licensing and other requirements with those in 52‑2‑805 and 52‑2‑810 (state health‑care licensing standards).
The bill codifies Section 1 as part of Title 50, Chapter 5, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
No new funding or program is created; the bill only establishes licensing and regulatory rules.
No criminal offense is created.
No new state office is created beyond the existing DPHHS authority.
affected: Staff, volunteers, and contractors working in RTCs
Children and youth receiving care in RTCs
Parents and guardians of those children
numbers: <21 years (age limit for residential treatment facilities)

SB198.one_line: Revises private‑security law, removes licenses, adds fingerprint checks for armed guards.
SB198.summary: SB 198 revises Montana’s private‑security statutes, redefining key terms, removing the license requirement for firms and guards, and adding fingerprint‑based background checks for armed endorsements. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Rewrites §37‑60‑101 to clarify definitions of electronic security firm, private security guard, and security alarm installer
Eliminates the state license requirement for private‑security firms and private‑security guards
Adds a requirement that armed endorsements be supported by a fingerprint‑based background check
Maintains existing definitions for armed, armed carrier service, and other related terms
Does not create new criminal offenses or state programs
No changes to funding or administrative structures are specified

SB194.one_line: Eliminates the Board of Public Assistance, transferring all appeal authority to the Department of Public Assistance.
SB194.summary: The bill eliminates Montana’s Board of Public Assistance and moves all appeal authority to the Department of Public Assistance. It amends the appeal statute so that the department, not a board, conducts hearings and reviews decisions, and it repeals the board’s allocation authority.
changes: Replaces the Board of Public Assistance with the Department of Public Assistance for all appeals and hearings related to food stamps, cash assistance, non‑financial assistance, and Medicaid.
Amends §53‑2‑606 to give the department the right to review decisions, issue notices, and hold fair hearings, removing the board’s role.
Repeals §2‑15‑2203, which authorized the board’s allocation and quasi‑judicial functions.
Allows the board to remain operational only until all appeals filed before the effective date are resolved; any vacancies are filled per the repealed section.
Applies to appeals filed on or after the effective date; earlier appeals and ongoing proceedings are unaffected.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval, with the repeal of §2‑15‑2203 taking effect October 1 2025.
affected: Applicants and recipients of public assistance programs (food stamps, cash assistance, non‑financial assistance, Medicaid).
Department of Public Assistance staff and local office personnel.
Individuals currently appealing decisions before the board.
SB194.effective: as stated (effective on passage and approval; repeal effective October 1 2025)

SB201.one_line: Creates contractor certification, sets cleanup standards, and requires owner notice for contaminated properties.
SB201.summary: The bill creates a state‑level certification program for contractors who clean up methamphetamine and fentanyl residues, sets specific decontamination standards, and requires owners to notify future occupants of contaminated properties. It also establishes reporting lists for law‑enforcement‑reported sites and limits owners’ liability once a property meets the new standards.
changes: Establishes a certification requirement for contractors and their employees who assess or remediate properties contaminated with methamphetamine or fentanyl.
Sets a decontamination standard of ≤1.5 µg of methamphetamine per 100 cm² of surface material and authorizes the department to adopt standards for fentanyl and precursors.
Mandates that property owners notify future occupants or purchasers of known contamination unless remediation meets the new standard.
Creates a public list of contaminated properties reported by law enforcement and requires removal from the list once remediation is verified.
Provides penalties (license revocation, fines up to $2,000, and mandatory training) for un‑certified individuals who advertise remediation services.
Allows the department to train, test, and certify contractors, maintain a certified‑contractor list, and set reasonable fees for certification.
affected: Future occupants and purchasers of contaminated properties

SB200.one_line: SB 200 expands cooperative rights, tightens filing rules, and clarifies Secretary of State duties.
SB200.summary: SB 200 revises Montana’s cooperative statutes, expands duties of the Secretary of State, and grants out‑of‑state cooperatives the same rights, exemptions, and privileges as in‑state ones. It also adds new definitions and filing requirements for cooperative associations.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑401 to broaden the Secretary of State’s duties, including electronic filing, fee tracking, and registration of cooperative names and marks.
Adds a prohibition on accepting filings that use the term “cooperative” for entities that are not cooperatives, with fines of $50‑$1,000 for violations.
Rewrites §35‑17‑103 to define key terms (e.g., “association,” “out‑of‑state”) and clarify that cooperatives are nonprofit entities.
Rewrites §35‑17‑104 to allow any five or more persons producing agricultural products to form a nonprofit cooperative, with or without capital stock.
Rewrites §35‑17‑202 to set detailed article‑of‑incorporation requirements for cooperatives, including membership, capital, and stock provisions.
Creates a new chapter in Title 35 that grants out‑of‑state cooperatives the same rights, exemptions, and privileges as in‑state cooperatives.
Requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally recognized Montana tribes of the act.
affected: Secretary of State and county clerks
Non‑cooperative entities that might use the term “cooperative” in filings
Fishermen, farmers, and other agricultural producers who may form cooperatives

SB208.one_line: Amends dependent‑child definition and compensation rules in Montana’s law‑enforcement and firefighter retirement systems.
SB208.summary: SB 208 amends the definition of a “dependent child” in the retirement systems for highway patrol, police, and firefighters so that the child must be unmarried, under 18, or under 24 and a full‑time student. It also updates related compensation and calculation language in the affected statutes.
changes: Revises the definition of “dependent child” to require the child be unmarried and either under 18 or under 24 while attending an accredited secondary or postsecondary institution full‑time.
Modifies compensation definitions in Sections 19‑6‑101, 19‑9‑104, and 19‑13‑104 to clarify what counts toward average compensation and how lump‑sum payments are treated.
Adjusts the calculation of highest average compensation and final average compensation to apply excess‑earnings limits.
Reaffirms definitions of “surviving spouse” and “survivor.”
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No fiscal appropriation language is included.
affected: Retired highway patrol officers, police officers, and firefighters; their surviving spouses and dependent children

SB206.one_line: Rewrites child‑abuse law, creates new investigator roles, and tightens removal and permanency rules.
SB206.summary: SB 206 revises Montana’s child‑abuse and neglect laws, creates new roles for child‑protection investigators and reunification specialists, sets certification standards, expands reporting and confidentiality rules, and tightens removal and permanency procedures. The bill takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Creates the positions of child protection investigator and child reunification specialist, defines their authority and prohibits the same person from performing both roles in a single case unless staff are lacking
Establishes certification requirements for those positions, including a training course, competency exam, background check, and annual 20‑hour continuing education
Amends numerous child‑abuse statutes (41‑3‑102, 108, 127‑130, 201‑205, 216, 301, 307, 427, 445) to expand definitions, reporting duties, and procedural safeguards
Adds new reporting obligations for a broad list of professionals (healthcare, educators, clergy, law‑enforcement, etc.) and details how reports are to be handled
Revises emergency protective‑services removal procedures, including notification timelines, affidavit requirements, and kinship‑placement options
Rewrites permanency‑hearing rules to set timelines, required reports, and factors the court must consider when ordering removal or placement
Expands confidentiality exceptions for case records, specifying who may receive information and under what conditions
Introduces new requirements for child‑protection teams and family‑engagement meetings, including independent facilitation and content of discussions
affected: state Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
parents and guardians of children in removal proceedings
courts and judges handling child‑abuse cases
tribal authorities in Indian child cases
numbers: 6‑month report to court after permanency hearing

SB211.one_line: Allows epinephrine nasal spray in schools, updates student self‑administration rules, and revises stock‑keeping and liability provisions.
SB211.summary: The bill expands Montana’s school epinephrine policy to allow nasal spray as an approved emergency medication, updates the rules for student self‑administration, and revises school stock‑keeping requirements. It adds documentation, liability protections, and training standards while making the law effective immediately.
changes: Adds epinephrine nasal spray to the list of medications that may be prescribed and self‑administered by students with asthma, severe allergies, or anaphylaxis.
affected: Students with asthma, severe allergies, or anaphylaxis

SB212.one_line: Bill creates a constitutional right to compute and requires AI‑controlled critical infrastructure to adopt risk‑management policies.
SB212.summary: The bill declares a “right to compute” as a constitutional property and free‑expression right, limits state restrictions on lawful use of computing tools, and requires any AI‑controlled critical‑infrastructure system to adopt a risk‑management policy. It also clarifies that federal law and IP rights remain unaffected.
changes: Establishes a constitutional right to own and use computational resources for lawful purposes.
Mandates that any critical infrastructure facility controlled in whole or part by a critical AI system must develop a risk‑management policy after deployment, following recognized AI standards.
Defines key terms such as “critical AI,” “critical infrastructure facility,” and “computational resources.”
Preserves existing federal and state intellectual‑property rights and explicitly states the act does not preempt federal law.
Provides severability and codification instructions for the new provisions.
Sets the act into effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Montana residents and businesses that own or use computational resources
Operators of critical infrastructure facilities that use AI systems
State and local governments that regulate or oversee such facilities
Federal agencies that may interact with Montana’s AI‑controlled infrastructure

SB213.one_line: SB 213 permits single‑stair exits for certain multi‑unit homes if they meet strict safety and sprinkler requirements.
SB213.summary: SB 213 amends Montana’s building‑code rule‑making authority to allow certain residential buildings, including group R‑2 dwellings up to six stories, to use a single stairwell if they meet specific safety requirements. It also clarifies rules for medical gas piping, religious‑worship overnight use, and limits on sprinkler and energy‑equipment mandates.
changes: Amends §50‑60‑203 to give the Department of Environmental Quality (or equivalent) authority to adopt, amend, or repeal building‑code rules by reference to national codes and to set stricter standards.

Allows a single stairwell as the sole exit for group R‑2 residential buildings that are no more than six stories, have no more than four units per floor, are automatically sprinkler‑protected, and provide a window or other emergency exit per unit.
Specifies that a single‑family dwelling or a residential building with two or fewer units may not be required to have a fire‑sprinkler system under the state code.
Adds rules permitting medical‑gas piping installations and inspections, and requires inspectors to verify endorsements for medical‑gas work.

Provides that places of worship may accommodate overnight visitors for up to 75 days per year (or unlimited if a state emergency is declared) without charging, but must have either an automatic sprinkler system or a hard‑wired fire‑alarm system and an exit to a public way.
Maintains that the state code may not prohibit or limit the use of approved refrigerants or energy sources such as solar panels, electric vehicles, or natural gas.
Clarifies that the use of a place of worship for temporary overnight accommodations does not constitute a change in occupancy, purpose, or use.
affected: Residential building owners and developers of group R‑2 dwellings

SB214.one_line: SB 214 favors existing non‑conforming uses and removes historic‑preservation‑board review of zoning permits.
SB214.summary: SB 214 revises Montana’s zoning statutes to give priority to existing non‑conforming uses and to remove the historic‑preservation‑board review exception. It clarifies that any ambiguity in zoning language must be interpreted in favor of the use in question and expands the definition of tiny dwelling units. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §§ 76‑2‑105, 76‑2‑113, 76‑2‑208, 76‑2‑210, 76‑2‑302, 76‑2‑308, and 76‑25‑301 to state that any ambiguity about whether a non‑conforming use is allowed must be resolved in favor of that use
Replaces the historic‑preservation‑board review exception so that historic preservation boards no longer review zoning‑permit or variance applications
Adds a rebuttable presumption that manufactured‑home placement will not adversely affect conventional‑housing values
Defines “tiny dwelling unit” and allows tiny houses governed by Appendix Q of the 2023 International Building Code
Requires local governments to adopt zoning maps that identify hazardous or limited‑development areas and to allow continued use of land or buildings that were legal when a regulation was adopted
Specifies that any ambiguity about a use’s violation must be interpreted in favor of the use
Mandates that local governments may not require a fee or dedication of property for housing at specified income levels or sale prices
Provides that local governments may appoint enforcing officers to enforce zoning provisions
affected: Municipalities and counties adopting or enforcing zoning regulations
Residents in areas subject to zoning maps and hazard designations

SB217.one_line: Probationers and parolees earn a day credit per 40‑hour workweek, subject to documentation and revocation rules.
SB217.summary: Probationers and parolees may receive a one‑day credit for every 40‑hour workweek if they stay compliant and pay restitution.  They must submit proof of employment within five business days after 30 days of work, and the credit is revoked for violations, new felony or certain misdemeanor charges, or if they are under lifetime supervision or a youth court proceeding.
changes: Creates a work‑time credit system for eligible probationers and parolees
Requires documentation of employment within 5 business days after 30 days of work
Allows probation/parole officers to verify employment and deny credit
Revoke credit if the individual violates conditions, is charged with a new felony, or a misdemeanor that could lead to >6‑month incarceration
Excludes individuals under lifetime supervision, sexual/violent offender registration, or youth court proceedings from the credit
Defines eligible employment and supporting documentation
Codifies the provision into Title 46, Chapter 23, Part 10
numbers: 30 days of eligible employment before submission
6 months incarceration threshold for misdemeanor revocation

SB218.one_line: SB 218 gives minors a 25‑year right of action for injuries from gender‑dysphoria treatments and amends malpractice limits.
SB218.summary: SB 218 creates a private right of action for minors who suffer injuries from gender‑dysphoria treatments, sets a 25‑year statute of limitations, amends the medical‑malpractice statute, and repeals a prior private‑action provision. The bill allows civil claims for a wide range of surgical, hormonal, and puberty‑blocking procedures performed on minors when the treatment deviates from the standard of care.
changes: 1. Establishes strict liability for health‑care professionals who provide listed gender‑dysphoria treatments to minors, allowing civil suits for physical, psychological, emotional, or physiological harms within 25 years of the last treatment.
2. Sets a 25‑year statute of limitations, with tolling provisions for minors under disability, minors under 23, or when fraud or intimidation occurs.
3. Permits compensatory, punitive, declaratory, injunctive, and attorney‑fee relief in such suits.
4. Amends MCA §27‑2‑205 to extend the malpractice limitations period to 5 years and to toll the period when the injury or causal link is undisclosed.
5. Repeals MCA §50‑4‑1005, which previously provided a private cause of action for subsequent harm.
6. Codifies the new private‑action provision as a new part of Title 50, Chapter 4, and specifies an effective date of July 1 2025.
affected: Parents or guardians of affected minors
Legal practitioners handling related civil claims

SB221.one_line: Mandates GHG assessments for fossil‑fuel projects and revises MEPA review rules and fee procedures.
SB221.summary: SB 221 requires Montana agencies to assess greenhouse‑gas (GHG) emissions for every state action that is a fossil‑fuel activity, and it amends MEPA to clarify when and how those assessments must be done. The bill also revises definitions, procedural rules, and fee‑setting provisions related to environmental reviews, but it does not create a new program or criminal offense.
changes: All state agencies must conduct a GHG assessment for any proposed action that is a fossil‑fuel activity, unless the action is exempt from MEPA review or a categorical exclusion applies.
Section 75‑1‑201 is amended to allow agencies to include a GHG assessment in their environmental review, with guidance to be issued by the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ).
The bill amends fee‑setting rules (75‑1‑202) so that agencies may charge a fee to cover the cost of compiling an environmental impact statement, but the fee may only be used for that purpose.
Definitions are expanded (e.g., “fossil‑fuel activity,” “greenhouse‑gas emissions,” “project sponsor”) and clarified in 75‑1‑220.
Procedural changes clarify that agencies cannot withhold permits based on MEPA review alone, and set limits on judicial review of environmental reviews.
affected: Montana state agencies that issue permits, leases, or licenses for fossil‑fuel projects.
Project sponsors of fossil‑fuel activities (e.g., oil, gas, coal, power plants).
DEQ and other state agencies that will develop guidance and collect fees.

SB223.one_line: Retains all interest on the $12 million workforce‑housing appropriation.
SB223.summary: SB 223 amends the 2023 workforce‑housing appropriation to require that all interest and income earned on the $12 million be kept in the fund, and it applies retroactively to earnings from June 14 2023 onward.
changes: Amends Section 15, Chapter 774, Laws of 2023 to add a new clause (4) that all interest and income earned on the $12 million must be retained in the fund.
Specifies that the amendment is effective immediately upon passage.
Provides retroactive applicability to interest and income earned on or after June 14 2023.
affected: State‑owned facilities that house inmates or behavioral‑health patients
Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB224.one_line: Establishes Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a Montana legal holiday and requires notification of state and local entities.
SB224.summary: The bill designates Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a legal state holiday in Montana, adding it to the list of official holidays and requiring state, local, tribal, and court entities to recognize the change. It also mandates that the Secretary of State notify relevant parties of the new holiday.
changes: Adds Indigenous Peoples’ Day (second Monday in October) to Montana’s list of legal holidays in Section 1‑1‑216, MCA.
Amends the holiday list to include Columbus Day on the same day as Indigenous Peoples’ Day.
Requires the Secretary of State to notify the Montana Supreme Court, local governments, and federally recognized tribal governments of the change.
No new funding or programs are created; the bill only alters holiday status and requires notifications.
The bill does not alter any other statutes or create new offices.
The bill does not impose penalties or new regulations beyond holiday observance.

SB226.one_line: SB 226 imposes earlier filing deadlines for petition affidavits based on signature‑collection dates.
SB226.summary: SB 226 tightens the timing for submitting petition affidavits and signature sheets to county election officials, requiring earlier delivery based on how long before the filing deadline the signatures were collected.
changes: Adds a new subsection (2)(a) to §13‑27‑302 that sets specific filing deadlines for affidavits tied to signature sheets collected at various intervals before the petition filing deadline (287, 196, 126, and 98 days).
Requires the affidavit and attached signature sheet to be submitted to the county election administrator by those deadlines.
The election administrator must date‑stamp, log, and provide a receipt once the affidavit is received.
If the affidavit and signature sheet are not submitted within the required timeframe, the administrator must reject the filing and cannot process it further.

SB227.one_line: SB 227 standardizes board seals and clarifies licensing board duties, eliminating redundant statutes.
SB227.summary: SB 227 removes individual board seals, standardizes how licensing boards authenticate documents, and clarifies board duties. It amends several statutory sections to require a common seal, sets rules for issuing licenses, and repeals older, redundant provisions.
changes: Eliminates individual board seals; all boards must use a common seal for licenses and official documents.

Rewrites sections 37‑3‑301, 37‑10‑202, 37‑13‑201, 37‑13‑304, 37‑15‑202, 37‑18‑305, 37‑24‑202, 37‑50‑201, 37‑51‑201, 37‑66‑303, and 37‑68‑201 to require a common seal, specify licensing procedures, and clarify board powers.
Adds requirements that licenses be signed by the board president and secretary‑treasurer and that the seal be judicially noticed.
Repeals sections 37‑3‑201, 37‑4‑201, 37‑8‑201, 37‑17‑201, 37‑28‑103, 37‑31‑201, and 37‑67‑201, removing older, redundant organizational rules.
affected: Professional licensing boards (e.g., medicine, optometry, acupuncture, veterinary, landscape architecture, electrical contractors)

SB228.one_line: Revises EV charging laws, adds a 3‑cent/kWh tax, mandates meters, and redirects revenue to highways.
SB228.summary: The bill amends Montana’s electric‑vehicle charging laws to clarify definitions, impose a 3‑cent per‑kWh tax on public charging stations, require dedicated meters, mandate rate disclosure, and set registration and tax‑remittance rules. It eliminates a planned 30 % reduction in electric‑vehicle registration fees and directs tax revenue to the highway restricted account.
changes: Defines “charging station,” “charging station operator,” “charging station owner,” and “public legacy charging station.”
Imposes a 3‑cent per‑kWh tax on electricity delivered at public charging stations (new and legacy) and requires the tax to be added to the utility’s rate.

Mandates that all new public charging stations (effective July 1 2023) and all existing stations (effective July 1 2025) have a dedicated electric meter; legacy stations must be upgraded by July 1 2028.
Requires public charging station operators to disclose the per‑kWh rate on site.
Requires operators to register with the Department of Transportation within 30 days of opening and to provide owner and technical information.

Establishes that the utility collects the tax, remits 2.75 ¢ per kWh to the Department of Transportation, retains 0.25 ¢ for collection costs, and deposits the revenue into the highway restricted account.
Eliminates the previously scheduled 30 % reduction in electric‑vehicle registration fees effective July 1 2028.
Effective date of the act is July 1 2025.
numbers: July 1 2028 (legacy meter requirement & fee reduction removal)

SB232.one_line: Expands procurement exemptions and adds a direct‑purchase rule for Montana‑produced food.
SB232.summary: SB 232 amends Montana’s procurement law to broaden the list of contracts that can bypass the standard RFP process, adding many new exemptions and a special rule for buying Montana‑produced food.
changes: Expands Section 18‑4‑132 to exempt additional contract types (e.g., certain construction, lottery, insurance, professional‑service, and university energy contracts) from the RFP requirement.
Adds a new provision (4) allowing direct purchase of Montana‑produced food when quality, quantity, and price meet specified criteria.
Creates a rule‑making authority for the department to administer the new food‑procurement exception.
Keeps existing exemptions (e.g., grants, student‑fee equipment, low‑value lottery contracts) unchanged but clarifies their scope.
affected: State agencies and political subdivisions that procure goods and services
University of Montana and Montana State University
Private contractors hired for specialized professional services

SB235.one_line: SB 235 requires 640‑acre ownership for land‑owner elk license preference, eliminating contract‑to‑purchase qualification.
SB235.summary: SB 235 tightens land‑owner preference for elk licenses, requiring actual ownership of 640 acres of contiguous land (or 160 acres of production agricultural land) and eliminating the prior “contract to purchase” qualification. It also clarifies who may receive or designate a license and preserves a 15 % quota for land‑owners.
changes: Replaces the former “contract to purchase” requirement with a strict ownership requirement of 640 acres of contiguous land (or 160 acres of production agricultural land) for land‑owner preference elk licenses.
Adds a definition of “employee” as a paid worker with state or federal taxes withheld.
Maintains the 15 % quota of Class A‑9/B‑12 and special elk permits that must be set aside for qualifying land‑owners.
Allows a qualifying land‑owner, corporation, or employee to designate an immediate family member or employee to apply for the license or permit.
Keeps the drawing procedures for excess applications and the department’s authority to set rules.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Land‑owners who own 640 acres or more of contiguous land
Land‑owners who own 160 acres or more of production agricultural land
Immediate family members of qualifying land‑owners

SB233.one_line: Montana adopts a multistate massage‑therapy licensing compact with background checks and shared disciplinary data.
SB233.summary: Montana adopts the Interstate Massage Compact, creating a multistate licensing program for massage therapists and establishing a commission to administer it. The bill requires background checks, sets eligibility criteria, and allows states to share disciplinary information. It also provides mechanisms for dispute resolution, default, and withdrawal.
changes: Creates the Interstate Massage Compact Commission and gives it rule‑making and enforcement authority.
Establishes a multistate license that authorizes a therapist to practice in all member states, subject to the home state’s jurisdiction.
Mandates full fingerprint‑based criminal background checks for all multistate license applicants and renewals, with fees paid by the applicant.
Requires member states to report adverse actions, investigative information, and disciplinary actions to a shared data system.
Allows a state to take adverse action against a multistate license based on its own or another state’s findings, and requires deactivation of all authorizations while an adverse action is pending.
Provides for default, termination, and withdrawal procedures for member states, including notice and 180‑day grace periods for license recognition.
Includes dispute‑resolution rules, mediation, and binding arbitration for conflicts among states.
Sets a contingent effective date: the compact becomes effective when the seventh member state enacts it.
Provides for codification of the compact into Montana law and specifies that the compact does not preempt other state laws unless inconsistent.
affected: Active military members and spouses who are massage therapists
Montana Department of Labor and Industry
SB233.effective: Contingent on enactment by the seventh member state

SB236.one_line: SB 236 creates a 1 % longevity payment for county detention officers and related staff.
SB236.summary: SB 236 would give county detention officers a yearly “longevity payment” equal to 1 % of the minimum base annual salary for each year of service, paid in monthly installments. It also amends two Montana Code sections to clarify that this payment applies to detention officers just as it does to deputy sheriffs and undersheriffs, and it supersedes certain unfunded mandate provisions.
changes: Amends §7‑4‑2507 to state that, when there is a conflict, the provisions of §§7‑4‑2508‑2510 govern for undersheriffs, deputy sheriffs, and detention officers employed by a county sheriff’s office.

Amends §7‑4‑2510 to create a longevity payment for deputy sheriffs, undersheriffs, and detention officers: 1 % of the minimum base annual salary per year of service, paid in equal monthly installments, beginning on the first anniversary of employment and adjusted annually.
Supersedes the requirements of §1‑2‑112 through §1‑2‑116 (unfunded mandate laws).

SB237.one_line: Mandates the Revenue Interim Committee to recommend property‑tax‑rate changes based on reappraisal reports.
SB237.summary: SB 237 requires the Revenue Interim Committee to recommend whether to adjust property‑tax rates based on a taxable‑value‑neutrality report and amends the committee’s duties and the reappraisal schedule for certain property classes.
changes: Amends §5‑5‑227 to add a duty for the Revenue Interim Committee to recommend property‑tax‑rate revisions based on the report in §15‑7‑111.
Amends §15‑7‑111 to require the Department of Revenue to revalue all class 3, 4, and 10 property every two years and all other property annually.
The reappraisal cycle now mandates a report to the committee in the second year of each cycle, with a recommendation to the legislature.
The committee must prepare revenue estimates by Dec 1 each regular session and may prepare estimates for special sessions.
The committee’s estimate becomes the legislature’s current estimate until amended or adopted by both houses.
The committee may request assistance from various state agencies for its duties.
The Department must publish annual property‑tax‑change information in county newspapers each even‑numbered year.

SB238.one_line: Allows optional donations on archery licenses to fund disabled hunters’ equipment.
SB238.summary: The bill creates a program that lets hunters donate extra money when buying certain archery‑hunting licenses. Those donations go into a special state account and are used to buy or donate modified archery gear for hunters with disabilities. The bill also amends fish‑and‑game revenue rules and license‑agent fee rules to accommodate the new program.
changes: Allows hunters to add $1 or more to the price of qualifying archery‑hunting licenses as a voluntary donation.
Creates a “Supporting Bowhunters with Disabilities” account in the state special revenue fund to receive those donations, interest, and other gifts.
Provides the Department of Fish and Game with rule‑making authority to set up donation forms, payment procedures, and guidelines for distributing equipment.
Authorizes the Department to pay a 501(c)(3) nonprofit to purchase modified archery equipment for licensed hunters with disabilities.
Amends §87‑1‑601 to include the new donation program as an exception to the general rule that all license revenue goes to the state special revenue fund.
Amends §87‑2‑903 to clarify that donations collected under the new program are not subject to the license‑agent commission and convenience‑fee rules.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1 2025.
affected: Hunters who purchase qualifying archery licenses
Non‑profit organizations that provide modified archery equipment
License agents handling archery‑hunting license sales
The Montana Department of Fish and Game
numbers: 50 cents commission per license agent transaction
Interest rate per 15‑1‑216 for late payment

SB241.one_line: Allows license transfers even if seller owes taxes, but still enforces lien payments and strict penalties for non‑agency liquor sales.
SB241.summary: SB 241 removes the Department of Revenue’s power to deny a license transfer solely because the seller owes taxes, penalties, or interest, while still allowing the department to collect on existing liens. It amends the alcohol‑license code to clarify transfer procedures and penalties for selling non‑agency liquor.
changes: 1. Section 16‑4‑404 is amended so the department may not deny a license transfer only because the seller has outstanding taxes, penalties, or interest. 2. Proceeds from a license sale may be applied to any existing liens or warrants the department has against the seller. 3. The definition of a license transfer is expanded to include bona‑fide sales, probate transfers, and certain inventory transfers under specified conditions. 4. Section 16‑6‑303 is amended to clarify that only liquor purchased from an agency store or transferred under the new 16‑4‑404(7)(8) rules may be sold; violations carry fines of $500‑$1,500, imprisonment of 3 months‑1 year, or both, and may trigger immediate revocation. 5. The act becomes effective immediately upon passage and applies to all license transfers filed before or after that date.

SB242.one_line: Mandates uniform ballot rules and “official ballot” stamping for all paper ballots.
SB242.summary: SB 242 amends Montana’s election statutes to establish statewide uniform rules for ballot form and to clarify how paper ballots are marked and distributed. The bill requires the Secretary of State to adopt detailed guidelines for every ballot type and mandates that election judges stamp each ballot with “official ballot” before it reaches an elector.
changes: Amends §13‑12‑202 to require the Secretary of State to adopt uniform ballot‑form rules covering corrections, write‑ins, stubs, labeling, unvoted ballots, vote counts, and ballot order.
Adds a new subsection that all candidate names on a ballot must use the same font, size, and style.
Mandates that when stubs are detached, ballots cannot be distinguished from one another for the same office or issue.
Requires ballots to list only certified candidates, except for presidential/vice‑presidential names as set by law.
Amends §13‑13‑116 to require election judges to stamp each paper ballot with “official ballot” before delivery and to ensure each elector receives one ballot of each eligible type.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.

SB243.one_line: Amends zoning to allow taller, multi‑unit buildings in larger cities and relaxes several local zoning restrictions.
SB243.summary: SB 243 amends Montana’s zoning code to allow taller, multi‑unit buildings in cities with at least 5,000 residents and to relax parking and height restrictions for certain commercial‑zone parcels. It also removes a number of previously‑allowed restrictions on local zoning authority, including limits on manufactured housing, housing‑price fees, and certain special‑use exemptions.
changes: Adds a requirement that cities with 5,000+ residents must permit duplex housing on lots where single‑family homes are allowed, and may not impose stricter regulations on duplexes than on single‑family homes.

Allows cities that meet the population threshold to permit multiple‑unit dwellings and mixed‑use developments on commercial‑zone lots that have municipal water and sewer service, and removes the requirement for more than one off‑street parking space per unit or a height limit under 60 ft for downtown commercial, heavy commercial, or industrial zones.

Amends §76‑25‑303 to prohibit local governments from treating manufactured housing, foster homes, community residential facilities, day‑care homes, or certain agricultural activities differently from other residential uses, and removes the ability to impose special fees or property‑dedication requirements tied to income or sale price.

Reinstates the ability for local governments to impose zoning standards on the special‑use categories listed in §76‑25‑303(1)(f) and (1)(g) if those standards do not conflict with the new prohibitions.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to October 1, 2026.
affected: Developers of multi‑unit and mixed‑use projects
Foster homes, community residential facilities, day‑care homes

SB244.one_line: Montana insurers must cover optional behavioral‑health screenings at no cost to the insured, effective 2026.
