SB244.summary: SB 244 requires most Montana health‑insurance plans to cover optional behavioral‑health screenings and assessments at no cost to the insured, and it amends several state statutes to clarify coverage in state employee and self‑funded plans.
changes: 1. Mandates coverage for optional behavioral‑health screenings and assessments that use a standardized, evidence‑based instrument, with no out‑of‑pocket cost, in all disability policies, health‑maintenance organizations, and self‑funded multiple‑employer welfare arrangements.
2. Requires that the insured be informed the screening is optional and may opt out; the screening must be requested by the insured or subscriber.
3. Amends §2‑18‑704, §33‑31‑111, and §33‑35‑306 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new coverage requirement into state employee group benefit plans and self‑funded arrangements.
4. Provides a delayed effective date: the act becomes effective January 1, 2026, and applies to policies issued or renewed on or after that date.
5. Adds language clarifying that the coverage applies even to high‑deductible plans that qualify for health‑savings accounts, except for preventive services that are exempt from the deductible.
6. Includes a provision that if the insured has a high‑deductible plan, the coverage applies only after the deductible is met, except for preventive services.
who_is_affected:
affected: Montana health‑insurance policyholders (disability, HMO, self‑funded plans)
state employees and retirees covered by state group benefit plans

SB245.one_line: Mandates free human‑trafficking training for school bus drivers and updates related statutes.
SB245.summary: SB 245 requires school bus drivers to complete a free, transportation‑industry‑specific human‑trafficking recognition course and directs the Office of Public Instruction to provide the training materials at no cost. It also amends the child‑sex‑trafficking prevention statute to encourage education and coordination with law enforcement and to support school districts in developing related policies and curricula.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1316, MCA, to add a requirement that the Office of Public Instruction provide cost‑free, industry‑specific training materials for bus drivers on human‑trafficking recognition and reporting.
Mandates that all school bus drivers complete this training as part of their annual training requirements.
Directs the Office of Public Instruction to make the training materials available to driver candidates and current drivers at no cost.
Requires the Office to recommend in‑service training requirements for bus drivers to the Board of Public Education.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1, 2025.

SB247.one_line: Reclassifies shooting ranges as class‑four property and sets a 0.7 % tax rate.
SB247.summary: The bill reclassifies shooting ranges as class‑four property for tax purposes, sets a new tax rate for them, and defines what constitutes a shooting range. It also adjusts the tax rate for commercial property and clarifies how mixed‑use properties are valued.
changes: Reclassifies all non‑exempt shooting ranges as class‑four property under §15‑6‑134.
Sets the tax rate for shooting ranges at 50 % of the commercial rate (i.e., 0.7 % of market value).

Defines a shooting range as up to 150 acres of buildings, improvements, and appurtenant land necessary for safe firearm discharge, excluding residences, 1‑acre residential parcels, and non‑integral improvements.
Adjusts the commercial property tax rate to 1.4 × the residential rate (1.35 % of market value).
Leaves the residential portion of mixed‑use properties taxed at 1.35 % of market value, with a higher rate for values over $1.5 million.
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
affected: Property owners with mixed residential/commercial use
numbers: 1.4× multiplier for commercial and excess residential values

SB246.one_line: Requires food vendors on large state contracts to report Montana‑produced purchases and categories.
SB246.summary: The bill amends Montana’s procurement law to require that any government contract for food products worth $100,000 or more must include a reporting clause. Vendors must annually report how much food they sold to the state, how much was Montana‑produced, and, where possible, the dollar value by food category. The bill also clarifies when Montana‑produced food may be bought by direct purchase and excludes a handful of contract types, including alcoholic beverage purchases by the Department of Revenue, from the new reporting requirement.
changes: Amends §18‑4‑132 to clarify that food products produced in Montana may be procured by direct purchase under specific conditions.
Adds a new §2 that requires contracts for food products ≥$100,000 to contain a provision obligating the vendor to submit an annual report to the governmental body.

Defines the required report items: total dollar value of food purchased, total dollar value of Montana‑produced food, and, where available, dollar values by category (meat, produce, alcoholic/non‑alcoholic beverages, dairy, pulse crops, grain).
Exempts alcoholic beverage purchases made by the Department of Revenue under Title 16 from the reporting requirement.
Specifies that the new reporting requirement applies to contracts entered or renewed after June 30 2025 and is effective July 1 2025.
Codifies §2 as part of Title 18, Chapter 4, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
affected: State and local governmental bodies that purchase food products
Vendors supplying food to those bodies
Department of Revenue for alcoholic beverage contracts
State agencies that must adopt rules to implement the new requirement

SB249.one_line: Revises child‑abuse adjudication to require caregiver testimony and tighter hearing timelines.
SB249.summary: SB 249 amends Montana’s child‑abuse adjudication rules to require courts to hear evidence from caregivers, set tighter timelines for hearings, and expand the court’s authority to order protective measures. The bill also clarifies privilege exceptions and adds a requirement for expert testimony in Indian‑child cases.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑437 to mandate an adjudicatory hearing within 90 days of a show‑cause hearing, with limited exceptions;
Requires the court to hear evidence from anyone caring for the child, including caregivers and persons who have provided care to the child;
Expands the court’s power to issue temporary dispositional orders and to order visitation, support, evaluations, and removal of alleged abusers;
Adds a requirement that, in Indian‑child cases, a qualified expert testify about the risk of serious harm if the child remains in parental custody;
Clarifies that attorney‑client and mediation privileges apply, but other child‑examination privileges do not;
Provides that if a child is not found abused or neglected, the petition is dismissed and any prior orders are vacated.
affected: Parents and guardians of children in abuse/neglect proceedings
Caregivers and other adults who provide care to children

SB248.one_line: Expands access to child‑abuse records to include drug‑testing data for legislators and certain officials under strict confidentiality.
SB248.summary: SB 248 expands who may view child‑abuse case files to include drug‑testing results and gives legislators a limited, confidential window to review those records. It amends the confidentiality rules in §41‑3‑205 to add drug‑testing data to the list of records that can be disclosed to certain state officials and to legislators under strict conditions.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑205 to allow disclosure of drug‑testing results held by the Department of Public Safety in child‑abuse investigations.
Adds a new subsection that permits a member of Congress or the Montana Legislature to request and view a child’s case records, including drug‑testing data, for up to six months after the request.
Requires that such requests be written, signed, and accompanied by an orientation of the records; the records must remain in the Department’s possession and may not be copied.

Specifies that the Department must promptly disclose drug‑testing results to county attorneys, peace officers, or the child‑family ombudsman when a child is exposed to Schedule I or II drugs or drug paraphernalia.
Maintains existing confidentiality safeguards, including penalties for unauthorized dissemination and limits on news‑media disclosure.
Provides that copies of records given to parents or their attorneys are free of charge.
Leaves other confidentiality provisions (criminal court records, medical records, etc.) unchanged.
affected: County attorneys, peace officers, child‑family ombudsman
Parents and legal guardians of children in abuse investigations

SB251.one_line: SB 251 protects confidentiality of ombudsman investigations, with limited court‑disclosure exceptions.
SB251.summary: SB 251 makes all investigations conducted by the Child and Family Ombudsman confidential, with limited court‑disclosure exceptions. It codifies the confidentiality rules into the existing statutory framework.
changes: Treats all ombudsman‑investigated matters as confidential.
Allows court‑in‑camera inspection of records when relevant to a case.
Permits court‑ordered disclosure only if deemed necessary for fair resolution.
Keeps the identity of persons who contact or file requests confidential, except where state law 41‑3‑1214 allows.
Codifies these confidentiality provisions into Title 41, Chapter 3, Part 12 of the Montana Statutes.

SB252.one_line: SB 252 removes zoning discrimination against manufactured and factory‑built homes, treating them like other residential units.
SB252.summary: SB 252 removes special zoning restrictions on manufactured and factory‑built homes, treating them the same as other residential units and allowing them as a commercial use on state‑trust land. It also updates definitions and limits local governments from imposing income‑based fees or property‑dedication requirements for these homes.
changes: Local zoning ordinances may not treat manufactured or factory‑built homes differently from other residential units.
A rebuttable presumption is added that placing such homes will not lower conventional property values.
Manufactured homes are expressly permitted as a commercial purpose on state‑trust land leases.
Definitions of “manufactured housing,” “factory‑built housing,” and “tiny dwelling unit” are clarified and added to the statutes.
Local governments may not require fees or property dedication for income‑based housing or impose other discriminatory standards on these homes.

SB253.one_line: Mandates certification, reporting, and transparency for Montana student‑scholarship organizations.
SB253.summary: SB 253 requires Montana student‑scholarship organizations to obtain certification from the Department of Revenue, sets strict reporting and accountability rules, and guarantees parents the right to choose any qualified education provider. The bill also creates a public website listing certified organizations and their scholarship policies.
changes: Requires certification before accepting tax‑credit‑eligible donations and limits certification to two tax years; certifying agency must decide within 60 days.
Mandates a 90% scholarship‑to‑revenue ratio and prohibits limiting scholarships to a single provider.
Imposes annual fiscal reviews by an independent CPA and detailed reporting of contributions, scholarships, and provider usage.
Creates a public Department of Revenue website listing certified organizations, scholarship policies, and provider data.
Provides a $206,000 appropriation for implementation and specifies effective dates (July 1 2025 for the act, Oct 1 2025 for the new sections).
affected: Parents and guardians of eligible students

SB256.one_line: Expands record access for abuse cases while tightening confidentiality and discovery rules.
SB256.summary: SB 256 expands who may receive child‑abuse investigation records, clarifies when records can be disclosed, and amends discovery rules in custody cases. It keeps the core confidentiality protections but adds many new authorized recipients and tighter procedures for disclosure.
changes: Adds a long list of new entities (e.g., licensed youth‑care facilities, health professionals, foster parents, tribal agencies, federal agencies, congressional members, etc.) that may request and receive child‑abuse records under specified conditions.
Rewrites 41‑3‑205 to broaden disclosure exceptions, including to parents, attorneys, and certain investigative agencies, while preserving protection of reporters’ identities.
Amends 41‑3‑431 to require the department to provide parents with a wide range of investigative documents and to allow courts to order additional discovery when parents cannot obtain it otherwise.
Specifies prompt disclosure timelines (e.g., 5 business days for sexual‑abuse reports) and conditions for releasing records to law‑enforcement and court officials.
Allows news media limited disclosure of factual information that does not violate privacy rights.
Clarifies that records may be shared between state courts and with other states to expedite interstate child placement.
Requires that any authorized recipient keep records confidential and may not disclose them beyond the listed parties.
Provides that copies of records given to parents or their attorneys must be free of charge.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Members of Congress and Montana legislature
Parents and guardians of children in custody proceedings

SB257.one_line: SB 257 raises non‑resident Smith River bonus‑point fees and re‑allocates corridor‑enhancement funds for protection projects.
SB257.summary: SB 257 revises the Smith River corridor enhancement account, changes how user‑fee revenue is allocated, and raises the non‑resident bonus‑point fee to $125. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §23‑2‑409 to specify that $50 of each commercial outfitter client fee, all super‑permit lottery revenue, all resident $5 and non‑resident $50/125 bonus‑point revenue, and 5% of other float fees (excluding the nonrefundable permit application fee) must be spent on Smith River corridor protection and enhancement projects.
Reaffirms that the remaining corridor‑enhancement account funds may be used for general management, operation, and maintenance of the corridor.
Sets the effective date to the day the act is signed, making the changes immediate.
Adjusts the non‑resident bonus‑point fee from $50 to $125.
affected: Non‑resident recreational users of the Smith River
State Department of Natural Resources (or equivalent)

SB260.one_line: SB 260 sets procedures for changing hospital and school district boundaries and sharing tax revenue and student payments.
SB260.summary: SB 260 establishes a formal process for changing hospital‑ and school‑district boundaries when residents cannot reach public services or need better safety coverage. It sets petition, hearing, and election procedures, outlines how tax revenue is shared after a boundary change, and creates a reconciliation‑payment system for isolated students. The bill also amends the existing school‑district transfer law to clarify procedures and timelines.
changes: Allows qualified property owners to petition to move property into a different hospital district or to create a new hospital‑district division when access to public safety services is inadequate or improved safety is needed.

Requires a public hearing and, if approved, a county‑commissioner‑ordered election for the boundary change; if the election passes, the change takes effect on the first January 1 after July 1 following the election.

Mandates that when a hospital district is split, the new district levies the same millage for the first eight fiscal years and pays the original district a percentage of its tax collections (70%, 60%, 40%, 20% over years 1‑8).

Imposes a 3‑year split of taxable value for any territory transferred between school districts and requires each district to levy taxes to generate the agreed reconciliation payment for isolated pupils.
Creates a petition process for school districts to request a reconciliation payment from the resident district for isolated pupils, including a $100 processing fee and annual filing by June 1.
Amends § 20‑6‑105 to clarify the petition, hearing, and approval requirements for school‑district territory transfers, including a 4‑year waiting period for subsequent petitions.
Adds advisory‑council provisions for districts with significant isolated‑pupil enrollment and requires the county superintendent to notify the Department of Revenue of any approved transfers.
affected: Hospital‑district property owners in need of better access to services
County commissioners and board of county commissioners

SB261.one_line: Expands child‑welfare endangerment to include marijuana, drug production, and trafficking exposure.
SB261.summary: SB 261 expands Montana’s endanger‑the‑welfare‑of‑children law to cover marijuana exposure, drug‑related activities, and certain trafficking situations. It adds new felony‑level conduct, clarifies penalties, and allows parents to seek protection orders against unwanted contacts.
changes: Adds new conduct to the offense: exposing a child to marijuana, assisting a child in entering an adult‑use dispensary, or a place where human trafficking or dangerous‑drug production occurs;
Defines the offense for parents/guardians who knowingly contribute to a child’s delinquency by supplying intoxicants, encouraging marijuana use, or facilitating trafficking or drug‑production sites;
Creates a felony subsection for those who produce or possess meth‑production materials in a child’s presence, with up to 5‑year state prison and $10,000 fine (up to $25,000 if serious injury);
Provides a 6‑month county‑jail term and up to $500 fine for first‑time non‑felony endangerment, $1,000 fine for a second offense;
Allows parents/guardians to request an adult to stop contacting a child and, if contact continues, petition for a protection order under Title 40, chapter 15;
Expands admissible evidence in duty‑of‑care cases to include cruelty, neglect, and past bodily injury;
Permits courts to redirect fines or bonds to benefit the child’s welfare;
Clarifies that secondhand marijuana smoke incidental to lawful adult use is not covered.
affected: Parents and guardians of children under 18
Adults who assist or encourage minors in drug‑related or trafficking activities
Law‑enforcement and courts handling child‑welfare cases
Adults who contact children without legal supervision

SB262.one_line: SB 262 exempts certain small water‑and‑sewer plans from MEPA review and expands local and independent review authority.
SB262.summary: SB 262 removes the Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) review requirement for certain small water‑and‑sewer plans and subdivisions, allowing local governments and independent reviewers to handle those projects under new rules. The bill also updates delegation, certification, and fee‑sharing procedures for local agencies and independent reviewers.
changes: Exempts the Department from MEPA review of water or sewer system plans under Title 75, ch. 1, parts 1 and 2.  Grants the Department authority to delegate review of small public water and sewer systems and extensions to local government divisions that meet established standards, with a 90/10 fee split.  Amends 76‑4‑104 to allow local departments or boards of health to review subdivisions that connect to existing municipal or county water/sewer systems, provided they are certified and meet technical standards.  Creates a certification process for independent reviewers, including conflict‑of‑interest screening and fee reimbursement equal to that for certified local departments.  Adds exemptions for subdivisions 2 mi from high‑quality waters, ≤14 single‑family lots, and nonsignificant wastewater systems, with a rule‑making requirement to implement the exemption.  Updates fee, documentation, and appeal requirements for subdivision approvals.
affected: Local governments’ planning and health departments
Subdividers and developers of small residential subdivisions
numbers: 90% of review fee to local division
110 new files triggers independent reviewer assignment
December 31 2023 deadline for independent reviewer procedures

SB264.one_line: Eliminates the reasonable‑belief defense from Montana’s exhaust‑noise law.
SB264.summary: The bill removes the “reasonable grounds” defense from Montana’s exhaust‑noise law, meaning a driver can be convicted even if they believed the vehicle was compliant. It amends Section 61‑9‑435 to eliminate subsection (2).
changes: Amends Section 61‑9‑435 to delete subsection (2) that provides a defense for reasonable belief of compliance.
The new language makes a person charged with violating the 95‑dB exhaust limit subject to conviction regardless of any belief that the vehicle was not in violation.
The amendment does not alter the 95‑dB limit, the measurement standard, or the exclusion for motorcycles and quadricycles.
No new program, fund, or office is created.
The change applies only to enforcement of the existing noise‑limitation statute.
The amendment is a statutory revision, not a new law or penalty.
The bill does not specify an effective date; it takes effect when enacted.
numbers: Society of Automotive Engineers standard J1169 (May 1998)

SB265.one_line: Montana bans state use of federal digital currency, permits private crypto use, and sets up a token‑issuer certification process.
SB265.summary: SB 265 rewrites Montana’s cryptocurrency rules to ban state use of a federal digital dollar, allow private use of digital assets, set up a certification process for token issuers, and expand securities‑exemption rules for token sales. The bill creates a new “Financial Freedom and Innovation Act” that gives the securities commissioner broad rule‑making authority and requires periodic reporting from token issuers.
changes: Prohibits state agencies from accepting or requiring payment in a central‑bank digital currency (CBDC) and from participating in federal CBDC tests.
Allows individuals and businesses to accept digital assets as payment and to hold them in self‑hosted or hardware wallets.
Permits Montana residents and businesses to operate blockchain nodes, develop blockchain software, transfer digital assets, and stake tokens.

Creates a certification process for network‑token issuers: they must file detailed information with the commissioner, pay a filing fee, and update the commissioner every 6 months (or sooner if material facts change).
Provides a $250 million annual sales limit (adjusted for CPI) for token issuers seeking exemption under 30‑10‑105, with the commissioner able to revise the limit by rule.

Expands securities‑exemption categories in 30‑10‑105 to cover a wide range of token‑related transactions, including isolated transactions, certain broker‑dealer transactions, and intrastate offerings, while still allowing the commissioner to deny or revoke exemptions.
Adds definitions for key terms such as “central bank digital currency,” “network token,” “staking as a service,” and “decentralized network.”
Requires foreign token issuers to register with the Montana Secretary of State and meet all certification requirements before offering tokens in Montana.
affected: Montana businesses and individuals using digital assets
Potential investors in Montana token offerings
numbers: $1 million cap on intrastate offer sales
$10 000 cap per buyer for non‑accredited investors

SB271.one_line: Montana lifts its ban on paying student‑athletes for NIL use, with disclosure and conflict rules.
SB271.summary: The bill removes Montana’s prohibition on colleges and athletic organizations paying student‑athletes for the use of their name, image or likeness (NIL). It amends the state’s student‑athlete rights statute to allow NIL contracts, requires disclosure of such contracts, and clarifies that schools may still use an athlete’s NIL for school purposes. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑232, MCA to define and protect student‑athlete rights to earn NIL compensation and to retain an agent.
Allows postsecondary institutions, athletic associations, conferences or other intercollegiate sports authorities to provide NIL compensation to prospective or current student‑athletes.
Requires a student‑athlete entering a NIL contract to disclose the contract to a school official (or to the student’s agent if represented).

Permits schools to include provisions in scholarship agreements that allow the school to use the athlete’s NIL, prohibit its use on school property, or act as an agent for the athlete’s NIL contracts.
Maintains that NIL contracts may not conflict with team rules or existing school contracts, but such conflicts must be disclosed to the athlete or agent.
affected: Postsecondary institutions and athletic organizations in Montana
Student‑athletes at Montana colleges and universities
School officials responsible for NIL disclosures

SB275.one_line: Allows municipalities to revoke agricultural covenants on annexed land without subdivision review.
SB275.summary: SB 275 lets a municipal governing body revoke an agricultural covenant on annexed land and allow a land division to proceed without subdivision review. The bill amends the state code to add this exception and sets a public‑hearing requirement for other revocation cases.
changes: Amends §76‑3‑211, MCA, adding a new exception (c) that permits revocation when land is annexed into a municipality.
Allows the governing body to revoke a covenant and proceed with a land division without subdivision review under the annexation exception.
Requires a public hearing and written findings if the governing body seeks to revoke a covenant for public‑purpose use (subsection (2)).
Preserves existing sanitary restrictions under Title 76, Chapter 4.
Does not create new programs or criminal offenses.

SB276.one_line: SB 276 revises Montana voter‑ID rules, expands acceptable IDs, and tightens provisional‑ballot procedures.
SB276.summary: SB 276 amends Montana’s voter‑ID rules to broaden acceptable IDs, clarify provisional‑ballot procedures, and eliminate the “reasonable‑impediment” declaration for provisional ballots. The changes tighten ID verification while streamlining provisional‑ballot handling and enforcement.
changes: Expands the list of acceptable voter‑ID documents, adding Montana concealed‑carry permits and student photo IDs from Montana colleges and schools that are NAIA members

Rewrites the provisional‑ballot process so that voters who cannot present ID may still cast a provisional ballot, but the ballot is treated as provisional under 13‑15‑107 and must be verified by the next day or by the sixth day after election day
Eliminates the option for voters to file a declaration of a reasonable impediment to obtaining ID; the declaration is no longer required or permitted

Revises mail‑in voting rules to require that voters enclose either a driver’s‑license number, state‑ID number, last four SSN digits, or a copy of a photo ID and a current utility‑bill‑type document; otherwise the ballot is treated as provisional
Clarifies that provisional ballots must be signed by the voter or an authorized agent and that election officials must compare signatures to registration records before counting
Adds detailed procedures for handling provisional ballots that are challenged or that involve voters with unsound mind or felony sentences
Provides that election officials must notify voters whether their provisional ballot was counted and why
Includes a severability clause and states the act is effective immediately upon passage
numbers: 5 p.m. on the day after the election
3 p.m. on the sixth day after the election

SB278.one_line: SB 278 expands advanced‑opportunity funding, creates facilitators, and revises aid spending rules.
SB278.summary: SB 278 expands state funding for advanced‑opportunity programs, creates a new role called an advanced‑opportunity facilitator, and allows districts to use a portion of the aid to pay the facilitator while still receiving a quality‑educator payment. The bill also revises definitions, reporting requirements, and spending limits for the aid.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1503 to define “advanced opportunity,” “advanced opportunity aid,” “advanced opportunity facilitator,” and related terms, and sets aid percentages for elementary (4.5 %), high‑school (30 %), and K‑12 (18 %) districts.

Rewrites §20‑7‑1506 to establish eligibility, application, and reporting procedures for districts seeking advanced‑opportunity aid, including a strategic plan, measurable objectives, and annual progress reports.
Allows districts to spend up to 75 % of the aid on qualifying pupils’ out‑of‑pocket costs and the remainder on other K‑12 courses or to pay an advanced‑opportunity facilitator.
Permits districts to match up to 25 % of the aid from their adult‑education budget.
Amends §20‑9‑327 to include advanced‑opportunity facilitators as eligible recipients of the quality‑educator payment.
Adds coordination language with House Bill 252 and sets effective dates: the act takes effect on passage, while Sections 1 and 2 become effective July 1, 2025.
affected: School districts (elementary, high‑school, K‑12), advanced‑opportunity facilitators, qualifying pupils (grades 6‑12), state education agencies, and the Montana School for the Deaf and Blind, correctional facilities, and youth programs that receive quality‑educator payments.

SB279.one_line: Montana joins a multistate dietitian compact, adding background checks and a new commission to manage portable licensure.
SB279.summary: Montana would join a multistate dietitian licensure compact that lets qualified dietitians practice in other member states without a separate license, while keeping state‑level regulation and adding criminal‑background checks. The bill creates a compact commission, sets data‑sharing and rule‑making procedures, and allows states to withdraw after 180 days. The compact is effective when the seventh state enacts it.
changes: Montana becomes a member state of the dietitian licensure compact, creating a compact commission and an executive committee to oversee the compact.
Licensees must obtain a criminal‑history check (fingerprints) for initial licensure and renewal, and pay related fees.

Licensees may practice in other member states under a “compact privilege” that is valid until the expiration of their home‑state license and does not require additional continuing‑education credits in the remote state.
Member states must report adverse actions, investigative information, and other data to a shared data system and may impose adverse actions on compact privileges.
States can withdraw from the compact only after 180 days and must continue to recognize existing compact privileges for at least 180 days after withdrawal.
The compact includes dispute‑resolution, default, and termination procedures for member states, and allows the commission to levy assessments and fees on states and licensees.
affected: Licensed dietitians and dietitian applicants in Montana
Montana’s licensing board and Department of Justice
Montana’s Department of Labor and Industry
Other member states of the compact
numbers: 7 member states required for effective date
compact privilege valid until home‑state license expires
compact commission may levy assessments and fees
SB279.effective: when the seventh member state enacts the compact; Montana’s enactment triggers the compact’s effective date

SB280.one_line: Amends domestic‑violence grant rules to fund monitoring of offenders for specific assault offenses.
SB280.summary: The bill amends the domestic‑violence intervention statute to let the Montana Board of Crime Control fund local probation or compliance officers who monitor offenders who have been sentenced for partner or family‑member assault, strangulation, or a violation of an order of protection. It also allows the Board to grant money to courts that run offender‑intervention programs that meet Board standards.
changes: Amends §44‑7‑201 to authorize the Board to use the domestic‑violence intervention account to grant funds to communities for probation or compliance officers monitoring court‑ordered compliance for specific offenses.
Specifies the offenses: partner/family‑member assault (45‑5‑206), strangulation of a partner/family member (45‑5215), and violation of an order of protection (45‑5‑626).
Adds a grant option for courts to implement an offender‑intervention program that meets Board‑adopted standards.
Prescribes that the Board identify funding priorities, monitor expenditures, evaluate effectiveness, and adopt necessary rules for the program.
No new criminal offense or program beyond the existing domestic‑violence intervention account is created.
affected: Offenders sentenced for the specified domestic‑violence offenses

SB282.one_line: Limits Montana government access to electronic data to warrant‑based requests, with strict admissibility rules.
SB282.summary: SB 282 restricts Montana government from buying or accessing most electronic communications and data without a search warrant, limits admissibility of improperly obtained data, and clarifies disclosure rules for electronic communications.
changes: Prohibits government entities from purchasing electronic communications, their contents, paging or tracking device data, electronic funds transfer info, customer proprietary network data, precise geolocation, pseudonymous, or sensitive data unless a warrant or subpoena is issued.

Amends §46‑5‑112 to require a warrant for obtaining stored data on an electronic device, except in narrowly defined circumstances (consent, undercover officer, judicial exceptions, emergency, public disclosure, or correctional facilities).
Adds a prohibition that evidence obtained in violation of §46‑5‑112 or §1 is inadmissible in civil, criminal, or administrative proceedings and cannot be used to obtain a warrant.

Amends §46‑5‑602 to require a warrant or investigative subpoena for disclosure of electronic communications held by a service provider, with deletion of data after investigation or as required by law, except for incarcerated individuals.
Codifies §1 as part of Title 46, chapter 5, part 6, making it integral to the state’s privacy statutes.
affected: Individuals whose devices or communications may be accessed by government

SB286.one_line: Court decisions lose precedential value after new legislation.
SB286.summary: SB 286 states that a court’s interpretation of a statute is superseded by any later legislative action on that statute. It clarifies that case law has no binding effect once the legislature amends the relevant provisions. The bill merely codifies this principle and does not create new programs or impose new duties.
changes: 1. Declares that a court decision interpreting a statute yields to subsequent legislative action on the same statutory provisions.
2. Requires that this rule be codified as part of Title 1, Chapter 1, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
3. Imposes no new obligations, fees, or penalties.
4. Does not alter existing statutes or create new offices or funds.

SB288.one_line: Mandates seizure, testing, and rapid return of law‑enforcement weapons after officer‑involved shootings.
SB288.summary: The bill requires that any weapon used by a law‑enforcement officer in an officer‑involved shooting be seized, photographed, and tested by the state laboratory.  If no charges or appeals arise, the weapon must be returned to the agency within seven days.
changes: Seizes the officer’s weapon after an officer‑involved shooting for evidence collection and testing.
Mandates photographing the weapon and sending it to the state laboratory for test firing, cartridge‑case analysis, and documentation of unique characteristics.
Requires the weapon to be returned to the agency that seized it within seven days when the investigation ends and no charges or appeals are pending.
Applies these procedures to weapons collected under subsection (1) or during a coroner’s inquest.
Codifies the rule as part of Title 44, Chapter 3, Part 3 of the Montana Code.
affected: Law‑enforcement agencies that must redeploy returned weapons

SB289.one_line: County receives electronic notice when a property’s preliminary value drops over $1.5 million.
SB289.summary: SB 289 requires the Department of Revenue to electronically notify counties when a property’s preliminary market‑value decrease exceeds $1.5 million, and to share that information with municipalities. The notice must accompany the owner’s appraisal notice and can include multiple properties.
changes: County must receive an electronic notice if a property’s preliminary market value falls more than $1.5 million since the last reappraisal.
The notice must be sent no later than the owner’s original or revised classification and appraisal notice and must list both prior and preliminary values.
The Department must meet with the county upon request and provide any public data used to determine the preliminary value.
For centrally assessed properties, the notice is sent after apportionment is complete.
Class‑four residential property is excluded from the notification requirement.
The act is codified as part of Title 15, Chapter 7, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
The provisions take effect for property‑tax years beginning January 1, 2026.
affected: Property owners whose properties qualify for the notification

SB296.one_line: Mandates 1‑10 year prison for staff/volunteers who harm vulnerable persons in caregiving facilities.
SB296.summary: SB 296, known as Alan’s Law, adds a mandatory minimum prison term of 1‑10 years for anyone employed or volunteering in a caregiving facility who commits a misdemeanor or felony against a vulnerable person there. The sentence must run consecutively and cannot be deferred or suspended, except as allowed by existing statutes.
changes: Adds a mandatory minimum sentence of 1‑10 years for offenses against vulnerable persons committed by staff or volunteers in caregiving facilities.
Requires the additional sentence to run consecutively with the underlying offense’s sentence.
Prohibits deferral or suspension of the minimum term, except as provided in 46‑18‑222.
Defines “caregiving facility” to include a wide range of health‑care and child‑care settings.
Defines “vulnerable person” as a child, vulnerable adult, or incapacitated person.
Codifies the provisions into Title 46, Chapter 18, Part 2.
No new program or fund is created.
affected: Employees and volunteers of caregiving facilities
Offenders who commit crimes against vulnerable persons in those facilities

SB297.one_line: Montana expands privacy law with notice, opt‑out, and enforcement rules, plus new minor‑data protection requirements.
SB297.summary: SB 297 expands Montana’s privacy law to give consumers notice, opt‑out rights, and stronger controller duties, and adds new enforcement and data‑protection rules for minors. It amends existing privacy statutes, creates new obligations for controllers and processors, and establishes civil penalties for violations.
changes: Controllers must provide a privacy notice that lists data categories, purposes, and third‑party sharing, and must give consumers the right to confirm, correct, delete, obtain a copy of, and opt‑out of processing of their personal data within 45 days of a request.
Consumers can opt‑out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data, and profiling that produces legal or significant effects; opt‑out requests are handled via a secure, reliable mechanism.

Controllers must conduct a data‑protection assessment for any online service offered to minors that poses heightened risk, keep the assessment for 3 years or until service ends, and provide it to the Attorney General on request.

Controllers and processors must comply with a broad set of duties, including reasonable security, limited data collection, and the ability to cooperate with law‑enforcement inquiries; they may not impose discriminatory practices or use data for prohibited purposes.
The Attorney General gains exclusive enforcement authority, can issue civil investigative demands, and may bring civil actions with up to $7,500 per violation and recover attorney fees.
The bill repeals a 2023 law (Section 15, Chapter 681) and codifies the new provisions into Title 30, Chapter 14, Parts 1, 2, and 28.
affected: Controllers of personal data (businesses, app developers, schools)

SB300.one_line: Bill makes it a misdemeanor to harm or seize a service animal and requires full restitution.
SB300.summary: The bill makes it a misdemeanor to harass or harm a service animal or to take unauthorized control of one, and requires offenders to pay full restitution for damages. It also amends state law to clarify that a vicious dog may bite a service animal and that owners are liable, and expands the definition of a service animal in training.
changes: Creates two new misdemeanors: (1) harassment or harm of a service animal, punishable by up to $1,000 fine; (2) unauthorized control of a service animal, treated as misdemeanor theft under 45‑6‑301;
Mandates full restitution for damages (value of animal, training, veterinary care, handler’s medical and lost‑income expenses) for anyone convicted of either offense;
Amends 7‑23‑2109 to broaden the definition of a “vicious dog” to include service animals and to allow counties to regulate such dogs;
Amends 27‑1‑715 to hold owners liable for damages when their dog bites a service animal in public or private places;

Amends 49‑4‑214 to clarify that a service animal in training must wear visible identification, that handlers must keep the animal under control, and that places may ask for proof of disability and the animal’s work;
Adds codification instruction that Sections 1‑4 become part of Title 45, Chapter 8, Part 2.
affected: Owners of dogs that may be deemed vicious
Offenders who harass or take control of service animals
numbers: 20‑foot visibility requirement for training animal ID

SB301.one_line: Expands the commission’s power to approve new transmission projects and streamline cost approvals.
SB301.summary: SB 301 lets the Public Service Commission issue certificates of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) for new electric‑transmission projects and establishes a streamlined “advanced cost approval” process. It also defines advanced transmission technology and gives the commission rule‑making authority over the new procedures.
changes: 1. Grants the Commission authority to issue CPCNs for transmission facilities rated over 69 kV before construction begins.
2. Requires the Commission to decide on a CPCN within 270‑300 days of application and to consider reliability, cost‑benefit, and advanced technology use.
3. Creates an “advanced cost approval” pathway: utilities can apply for cost estimates before procurement; the Commission must review adequacy within 45 days and issue an order within 90 days.
4. Gives the Commission a presumption that approved costs are prudent if actual costs do not exceed the approved amount, and a duty to evaluate prudence if costs exceed the approval.
5. Provides the Commission with rule‑making authority to implement these procedures and codifies the provisions into Title 69, Chapter 4, Part 1.
6. The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Public utilities and other entities seeking to build transmission lines above 69 kV
The Department of Environmental Quality (limited role)

SB302.one_line: Revises MTAB procedures, adds informal review for residential property, expands evidentiary discretion.
SB302.summary: SB 302 revises the Montana tax‑appeal process to give the Montana Tax Appeal Board (MTAB) more flexibility, including an informal review option for class‑four residential property. It amends procedural rules, expands MTAB’s evidentiary discretion, and allows the board to adopt its own rules for informal hearings.
changes: Amends §15‑2‑301, MCA to give MTAB rule‑making authority over county‑board appeals
Provides MTAB the option to conduct informal reviews of class‑four residential property disputes
Allows MTAB to consider taxpayer‑submitted independent appraisals and to presume their correctness unless rebutted
Permits MTAB to conduct de novo reviews of industrial property and to use its own evidentiary rules
Authorizes MTAB to refer appeals to a member or hearings officer and to record testimony electronically at county seats
Supersedes the Montana Administrative Procedure Act for MTAB proceedings unless otherwise specified
Makes MTAB decisions final and binding, with judicial review limited to the provisions of §15‑2‑303
Allows MTAB to adopt rules for informal review procedures
affected: Property owners appealing county tax‑board decisions

SB303.one_line: Mandates annual reporting of state financial assistance to tribes and public posting of the summary.
SB303.summary: SB 303 requires Montana’s state agencies to report every year how much money they give—directly or via sub‑recipients—to tribal governments. The Office of Budget and Program Planning then compiles an annual summary and posts it online, while the Secretary of State sends a copy to each federally recognized tribe.
changes: 1. Designated state agencies must submit a detailed financial‑assistance report to the Office of Budget and Program Planning each fiscal year.
2. The report must list amounts, dates, recipients, federal assistance numbers, purposes, overhead costs, and program names for all direct and indirect transfers to tribes.

3. The Office of Budget and Program Planning must compile an annual summary of all agency reports and deliver it electronically to the State‑Tribal Relations Committee, the Legislative Finance Committee, the Office of the State Director of Indian Affairs, and each tribal government by specified deadlines.
4. The compiled summary must be posted on the Office of the State Director of Indian Affairs website.
5. The Secretary of State is required to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
affected: Designated state agencies (e.g., Departments of Agriculture, Commerce, Health, etc.)
Office of Budget and Program Planning
Office of the State Director of Indian Affairs
Federally recognized tribal governments in Montana

SB305.one_line: Mandates timely deposit and prudent‑investor compliance for funeral‑trust funds.
SB305.summary: SB 305 amends Montana’s funeral‑trust statute to require funeral providers to deposit or invest pre‑arranged‑funeral funds within 10 business days, keep them in a separate account, and apply the state’s prudent‑investor rule. The bill also clarifies that the deposits must be insured and that the trust is for the benefit of the contracting party.
changes: Amends §37‑19‑828 to mandate that money received under a pre‑arranged funeral contract be deposited or invested within 10 business days.

Requires the deposit or investment to be made in a banking institution, savings/​building‑and‑loan association, or credit union that maintains an office in Montana and is organized under state, another state, or federal law.
Specifies that the funds must be insured by a federal instrumentality and must comply with the prudent‑investor rule of Title 72, ch. 38, part 9, with no waiver allowed.

Establishes that the deposited or invested money constitutes a trust fund for the benefit of the person contracting for the funeral services and must be placed in a separate account in the name of the depositor as trustee.
Clarifies that the trust account must be in the name of the depositor acting as trustee for the contracting party.
affected: Consumers contracting for pre‑arranged funeral services

SB306.one_line: Prohibits sale of residential tax deeds to foreign entities and requires domestic status proof.
SB306.summary: The bill bars county treasurers from selling residential tax deeds to foreign entities and requires proof of domestic status for all bidders. It amends tax‑deed sale procedures to enforce this restriction and clarifies definitions of domestic and foreign entities.
changes: 1. Adds a prohibition that a county treasurer may not sell a residential property tax deed to a foreign entity. 2. Requires bidders at a tax‑deed auction to provide written proof of domestic entity status before any bid is accepted. 3. Amends the definition of “domestic entity” to include entities organized under U.S. federal or state law or under the law of a jurisdiction subject to U.S. jurisdiction with a principal place of business in the United States. 4. Amends the definition of “foreign entity” to cover foreign governments, political parties, entities outside the U.S. that are not U.S.‑jurisdictional, and entities organized under foreign law or with a principal place of business abroad. 5. Inserts the prohibition into the auction rules (Section 15‑18‑220) and adds a clause that the county treasurer may not accept an opening bid unless the bidder is a domestic entity.
who_is_affected':['County treasurers','Bidders at tax‑deed auctions','Foreign entities interested in Montana residential properties','Property owners facing tax‑deed sales'],
