numbers: half of most recent assessed value

SB309.one_line: Amends scenic‑historic byways rules to keep the advisory council and clarify local participation and signage.
SB309.summary: The bill amends Montana’s scenic‑historic byways program to keep the advisory council in place and expands the council’s role in setting criteria, reviewing nominations, and advising the commission. It also clarifies how localities may participate, exclude segments, and manage signage under the program. No new program or criminal offense is created, and the bill does not change funding levels or effective dates.
changes: Reinstates and expands the advisory council’s duties in the scenic‑historic byways program, including design, review, and recommendation of roads for inclusion or deletion.
Adds detailed criteria for road designation and exclusion, requiring input from the advisory council, commission, and department.
Specifies that localities may exclude road segments inconsistent with state criteria and may use certain signage types under federal and state law.
Clarifies that the department may expend any funds appropriated for the program upon commission direction.
Requires the department to adopt rules that include criteria for designation and address local participation, marketing, economic development, and property‑rights protections.
affected: Montana Scenic‑Historic Byways Advisory Council members
Montana Department of Transportation and related agencies
Local governments and municipalities that own or operate roads in the program
Private landowners adjacent to or visible from scenic‑historic byways
Tourism, historical, and economic development stakeholders

SB310.one_line: Creates a Trail Stewardship Grant Program with specific funding splits and advance payment rules.
SB310.summary: The bill creates a new Trail Stewardship Grant Program, sets how grant money is split among motorized, non‑motorized, and mixed‑use projects, expands eligible projects, allows advance payments, and specifies how unused funds are handled.
changes: Establishes the Trail Stewardship Grant Program within the existing Trails and Recreational Facilities Grant Program.
Allocates 40% of grant funds to motorized projects, 40% to non‑motorized projects, and 20% to projects serving both uses.
Expands eligible projects to include new trail construction, rehabilitation, trail‑side facilities, economic impact studies, data collection, and equipment purchases.
Permits applicants to request up to 75% of the grant in advance and a further 25% after the first advance is spent and reported.
Allows grant recipients to use up to 7% of the funds for administrative costs.
Requires any unspent grant money after three years to revert to the department and be deposited in the account established in 23‑1‑105.
Provides that the department may adopt rules to implement the program.
affected: Cities, counties, tribal governments, school districts, recreational clubs and organizations, state and federal agencies

SB311.one_line: Mandates annual training and reporting to improve state‑tribal legislative understanding.
SB311.summary: SB 311 requires the state director of Indian Affairs to supply legislators with regular training and resources on Indian law and tribal rights, amends a state agency training requirement, and sets new reporting deadlines for state‑tribal interactions.
changes: 1. Mandates the director of Indian Affairs, with the Legislative Services Division, to provide legislators with handbooks, training notifications, and links to Indian education resources on Indian law, federal Indian policy history, and tribal members’ legal rights.

2. Amends Section 2‑15‑143 to require the governor’s office to conduct annual training for state‑agency managers on tribal legal status and to convene an annual working meeting with tribal officials to discuss policy concerns and solutions.

3. Sets a new deadline (August 15 each year) for state agencies to submit reports to the governor on activities affecting tribes, and a September 15 deadline for the governor to provide tribal governments with an overview report.
4. Requires the Secretary of State to notify each federally recognized tribal government of the act’s passage.
5. Codifies the new training provision as part of Title 5, Chapter 11, Part 1 and declares the act effective July 1, 2025.
affected: state agency managers and key employees

SB315.one_line: Expands the tank‑release board’s powers and creates a preventive‑measure reimbursement program.
SB315.summary: SB 315 expands the Petroleum Tank Release Compensation Board’s authority, creates a new reimbursement program for preventive measures, and clarifies procedures for corrective‑action claims and board meetings.  The bill also codifies the petroleum‑tank‑cleanup fund and requires the board to report on its long‑term viability.  It takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: Establishes a $2,000‑per‑facility, 1,000‑day reimbursement cap for specified preventive measures (tank removal, gauge upgrades, piping and tank replacements, inspections).
Revises §75‑11‑309 to require immediate notification of releases, detailed investigations, and corrective‑action plans, with board‑led meetings for releases over $100,000.
Amends §75‑11‑313 to define the petroleum‑tank‑cleanup fund, its sources, uses, and loan‑repayment pledge.
Amends §75‑11‑318 to grant the board staff‑hiring power, quarterly meeting requirement, rule‑making authority, and a mandate to report fund viability to the department and auditor.
Adds a guarantee‑payment provision allowing the board to write guarantees for approved costs when the fund lacks liquid money.
Codifies the new preventive‑measure reimbursement program as part of Title 75, chapter 11, part 3.
Sets the effective date to January 1, 2026.
affected: State Petroleum Tank Release Compensation Board

SB316.one_line: Revises disability retirement rules for police and firefighters, tightening application and benefit calculations.
SB316.summary: SB 316 revises how disability retirement is applied and calculated for municipal police officers and firefighters, tightening application rules, clarifying benefit amounts, and extending retroactive coverage to those disabled by duty before Jan 1 2025.
changes: Amends §19‑2‑406 to require applications within 4 months of termination unless continuous disability, expands who may file, and adds board‑adopted rules on employer accommodations and medical review.
Rewrites §19‑9‑903 to set disability benefit percentages (½ of final average compensation or 2.5 % per year of service) and specifies line‑of‑duty benefits and survivor benefits.
Rewrites §19‑13‑803 to mirror §19‑9‑903 but uses highest average compensation and includes a minimum of ½ of that amount.
Provides that the act takes effect immediately upon passage and is retroactive to members disabled by duty on or before Jan 1 2025.
Clarifies that disability benefits convert to service benefits at normal retirement age but remain disability benefits for certain plans.
Adds board authority to order medical exams, hearings, subpoenas, and to retain medical personnel for assessments.
Ensures surviving spouses or dependent children receive benefits per the relevant survivor‑benefit sections.
affected: Municipal police officers’ retirement system members
numbers: ½ of final or highest average compensation

SB317.one_line: Exempts shortage psychiatric drugs from prior‑authorization and adds physician‑specialty review for adverse decisions.
SB317.summary: The bill amends Montana’s prior‑authorization rules to exempt psychiatric drugs that are in shortage (or discontinued) from prior‑authorization requirements. It also adds a physician‑specialty requirement for adverse determinations and prohibits manufacturers from predatory pricing during shortages.
changes: Amends §33‑32‑221 to add a new exemption (e) for psychiatric drugs listed as in shortage on the FDA’s quarterly shortage list.
Requires that any adverse prior‑authorization decision be made by a physician whose specialty matches the drug’s therapeutic area.
Establishes a quarterly static list of shortage psychiatric drugs, updated on April 1, July 1, October 1, and January 1.
Prohibits manufacturers of shortage drugs from engaging in predatory pricing or marketing related to the shortage, with enforcement under Title 30, Chapter 14.
Does not create a new program, fund, or criminal offense.
Does not alter funding or appropriations.

SB319.one_line: SB 319 creates a voluntary doula licensing program and allows Medicaid to cover certified doula services.
SB319.summary: SB 319 establishes a voluntary certification and licensing system for doulas, allows Medicaid to cover services from state‑certified doulas, and amends related statutes. The law takes effect Jan 1 2026 and ends Dec 31 2030.
changes: Creates a new voluntary certification and licensing program for doulas under Title 37, requiring application, fee payment, competency completion, and no disciplinary history; a limited license may be issued for supervised experience.
Allows the Department of Public Health and Human Services to include state‑certified doula services in the Montana Medicaid program as an optional benefit.
Amends §37‑1‑401 to incorporate doula licensure into the department’s licensing framework and to provide definitions and investigative procedures.
Amends §53‑6‑101 to add “services of doulas licensed under [sections 1‑4]” to the list of Medicaid‑covered services.
Provides a transition provision that permits unlicensed doulas who worked before Jan 1 2026 to obtain licensure if they can prove equivalent experience by Dec 31 2027.
Specifies that the act is effective Jan 1 2026 and terminates Dec 31 2030.
Requires the department to adopt rules to implement the new doula licensing and Medicaid coverage provisions.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB320.one_line: Creates a volunteer trade commission to study Montana‑Ireland trade and report annually.
SB320.summary: The bill creates a Montana‑Ireland Trade Commission to study and promote bilateral trade, investment, and cultural exchanges. It sets up a membership structure, fundraising authority, a special revenue account, and an annual reporting requirement to the governor and legislature. The commission will operate without paid staff, relying on volunteer members and funds raised through donations and events.
changes: Establishes a Montana‑Ireland Trade Commission with nine appointed members, including legislators, department directors, and two Montana residents.
Gives the commission authority to raise and accept funds, gifts, and donations, and requires those funds to be deposited in a special revenue account.
Mandates the commission to hold meetings, keep public records, and submit an annual report to the governor and legislature by September 1 each year.
Provides for the appointment of a chair from the legislative members and sets staggered two‑year terms for members.
Allows the commission to reimburse the Department of Commerce for administrative expenses from the special account.
Requires the commission to report on its activities, benefits to the state, and recommendations for legislative action.
affected: Montana legislators, the Governor, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Agriculture, the Commissioner of Higher Education, Irish‑American community leaders, Montana business and trade organizations, and the general public who may donate to the commission.

SB326.one_line: SB 326 expands Montana’s film‑tax‑credit program, adds new credit categories, creates a workforce‑training account, and allows credit resale for a fee.
SB326.summary: SB 326 expands Montana’s film‑tax‑credit program, extending it through 2045, raising the aggregate credit limit, adding new eligibility rules, and creating a workforce‑training account.  It also allows unused credits to be sold for a fee and gives the Department of Commerce rule‑making authority over the program.
changes: Extends the film‑tax‑credit program to December 31, 2045 and increases the aggregate credit limit to $12 million per calendar year.
Adds new credit categories for hiring veterans, enrolled tribal members, college students, and for using qualified Montana facilities or facilities in underserved areas.
Creates a dedicated film‑industry workforce‑training account in the state special revenue fund and requires the fee collected under 15‑31‑1010(2)(c) to be deposited there.
Allows unused allocated credits to be transferred to other entities for a fee and establishes a 2 % fee on unclaimed credits.
Replaces the 2021 Act (Chapter 509) with new definitions, eligibility criteria, and certification procedures for productions and post‑production companies.
Provides the Department of Commerce with rule‑making authority and a first‑come, first‑served allocation system for credit claims.
numbers: $5 million base investment threshold for credit eligibility
$7.5 million first‑tier compensation limit for actors, directors, etc.
$150,000 per‑person credit cap for many categories

SB328.one_line: Shortens appeal deadline to 30 days after county board mails decision and updates Montana board procedures.
SB328.summary: SB 328 shortens the period taxpayers have to appeal a county tax‑appeal board decision to the Montana Tax Appeal Board, changing the deadline from 45 days after the hearing to 30 days after the board mails its decision. The bill also updates procedural rules for the Montana board, including record‑keeping, appraisal handling, and hearing logistics. No new program or fund is created, and the act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Replaces the 45‑day post‑hearing deadline with a 30‑day deadline after the county board mails its decision.
Adds a requirement that the Montana board may request the county board to certify minutes and testimony.
Allows the Montana board to decide appeals on the record if all parties receive a transcript and may accept additional sworn statements.
Specifies that industrial property appeals must be reviewed de novo under the contested‑case provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act.
Permits the Montana board to refer appeals to a member or hearings officer who may conduct hearings and report back to the board.
Clarifies that the Montana board may consider a taxpayer’s independent appraisal under certain conditions and sets a presumption of correctness for residential property appraisals.
Authorizes electronic recording of testimony at county‑seat hearings and allows the cost to be paid from the board’s general appropriation.
Affirms that the Montana board’s decision is final and subject to judicial review only under the existing statutory framework.
States that the act applies to appeals from county board hearings occurring on or after the effective date.
affected: Montana Tax Appeal Board and its members/hearing officers
Department of Revenue’s Property Assessment Division
numbers: applicability: appeals from hearings on or after effective date

SB330.one_line: Creates a 27‑member task force to study blockchain and related tech, reporting by July 2026.
SB330.summary: The bill creates a temporary task force to study blockchain and related technologies, appoints 27 members from state officials, legislators, and industry, and requires a report by July 2026.
changes: Establishes a Montana Blockchain and Digital Innovation Task Force administered by the Department of Administration.

Appoints 27 members: 2 state officials (AG and State Auditor), 14 legislators (7 from the Senate, 7 from the House), and 11 industry experts (including trade, financial services, and technology specialists).
Designates a Senate president and House speaker to each select a co‑chair from the legislative members.
Sets member terms from appointment until Dec 31 2026, with a 30‑day appointment window after enactment.
Provides no salary or expense reimbursement for members, except legislative members may receive travel expenses per state law.
Defines a quorum as a majority of members and requires a majority of a quorum to act.
Mandates the task force to develop expertise and recommend policies on adoption, incentives, partnerships, and regulation of blockchain, fintech, and digital innovation.
Requires a written report to the Economic Affairs Interim Committee and Legislative Council by July 1 2026.
Terminates all provisions on Dec 31 2026.
affected: State officials (AG, State Auditor), legislators, appointed industry experts, and the Department of Administration

SB333.one_line: SB 333 ends the coal‑washing tax credit on July 1, 2027.
SB333.summary: SB 333 shortens the sunset date for the coal‑washing credit, ending the tax‑credit provisions on July 1, 2027. The bill simply terminates the credit; it does not create new programs or change other laws.
changes: Amends Section 7 of Chapter 433, Laws 2009 to state the coal‑washing credit expires July 1, 2027.
Amends Section 1 of Chapter 352, Laws 2015 to mirror the same termination language.
Notifies federally recognized tribal governments of the change via the Secretary of State.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
No new programs, funds, or offenses are created.
No fiscal allocations or new expenditures are added.
affected: Coal producers and miners who previously qualified for the coal‑washing credit
State tax authorities administering the credit

SB335.one_line: Mandates dental insurers to report loss ratios, publish data, and rebate excess revenue to protect consumers.
SB335.summary: The bill requires dental insurers to publicly report their medical‑loss ratios and other key data, sets thresholds for acceptable loss ratios, and mandates rebates or other remediation when insurers spend too little on patient care. It also gives the commissioner rule‑making authority to define the components of loss ratios and to enforce limits on rebates and quality‑improvement spending.
changes: 1. Requires annual filing of a dental‑loss‑ratio report by March 1 each year, including enrollee counts, cost‑sharing, deductibles, and coverage limits.
2. Makes the commissioner publish aggregate and insurer‑specific loss‑ratio data on a public website by January 1 of the following year.
3. Establishes a 3‑year average loss‑ratio benchmark and identifies insurers that are more than one standard deviation below the average as outliers.
4. Gives the commissioner authority to order rebates or other remediation for outlier insurers, requiring rebates by August 1 of the following fiscal year.
5. Allows the commissioner to set a minimum dental‑loss‑ratio percentage for insurers that remain outliers for two consecutive years.
6. Grants the commissioner rule‑making power to define clinical, quality‑improvement, and overhead expenditures and limits quality‑improvement spending to 5% of net premium revenue.
affected: Montana residents purchasing individual or group dental plans
numbers: 42 months (time before minimum loss‑ratio rule takes effect)

SB337.one_line: 5‑year tax exemption for developing residential subdivisions, funded by prepayment and fee.
SB337.summary: SB 337 creates a temporary 5‑year property‑tax exemption for all real property in a residential subdivision that is still under development.  Developers must prepay five times the prior year’s taxes and a 5 % fee; the exemption ends when a lot has a habitable dwelling or when 95 % of lots are completed, whichever comes first.
changes: 1. Grants a 5‑year tax exemption for any property in a residential subdivision that is undergoing development, regardless of conveyances or ownership changes.
2. Requires developers to submit a timely exemption application and, within 30 days after approval, prepay an amount equal to five times the prior year’s property taxes and assessments.
3. Adds a 5 % fee to the prepayment, payable before the tax year in which the exemption is sought.
4. Exemption expires on a lot once a habitable dwelling is constructed on that lot, or on December 31 of the year the subdivision is 95 % complete.
5. Amends §15‑10‑305 to clarify that exempt properties are excluded from mill‑levy calculations and that taxes on land splits are based on the prior year’s assessment.
6. Gives the Department authority to adopt rules to implement the exemption and related reporting.
7. Applies only to property‑tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

SB338.one_line: Allows judges to appoint administrators to receive workers’‑compensation payments for minors or incompetent persons.
SB338.summary: The bill amends Montana workers’‑compensation law to allow a judge‑appointed benefits administrator to receive payments on behalf of minors or incompetent persons. It also clarifies who may file petitions for such appointments and sets a two‑year filing deadline for disputes.
changes: Amends §39‑71‑742 to define a benefits administrator and allow payments to be made to that person for minors or incompetent claimants.
Adds a definition of “benefits administrator” as a person appointed by the workers’‑compensation judge.

Amends §39‑71‑2905 to permit a claimant, insurer, or uninsured employers’ fund to petition the judge for appointment of a benefits administrator without first satisfying dispute‑resolution requirements.
Specifies that a petition for a hearing before the judge must be filed within two years after benefits are denied.
Clarifies that the judge has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes after resolution requirements are met and can appoint or terminate a benefits administrator.
Provides that the act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Employers, insurers, and the uninsured employers’ fund

SB339.one_line: Reallocates oil‑gas tax revenue and refines damage‑mitigation account rules.
SB339.summary: SB 339 revises how Montana’s oil‑and‑gas production taxes are divided among counties, the state, and special accounts, and it changes the rules for depositing funds into the oil‑and‑gas production damage mitigation account. The bill also sets a new schedule for county allocations and modifies the minimum balance required before money can be added to the damage‑mitigation account.
changes: Amends §15‑36‑331 to specify that up to 0.08 % of the tax is deposited in the oil‑and‑gas natural‑resource distribution account and that any remaining funds go to the damage‑mitigation account unless the account balance is ≥ $10 million, in which case the money stays in the board’s expense account;

Replaces the existing county‑allocation percentages with a new schedule that lists a specific percentage for each county (e.g., Big Horn 45.05 %, Custer 69.53 %, etc.) and applies the same percentages to all other counties;

Revises §82‑11‑161 to require an annual allocation of up to $650,000 from the resource indemnity trust fund to the damage‑mitigation account unless the account balance is ≥ $1 million, and to deposit any unused allocation into the natural‑resources projects account;

Adds a provision that the board may authorize appropriation from the damage‑mitigation account to pay for plugging, reclaiming, or restoring abandoned wells when the responsible party cannot be identified or refuses to pay;
Specifies that interest earned on the damage‑mitigation account accrues to that account;
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1 , 2025.
affected: Montana Board of Oil and Gas
Local governments that fail to file reports or remit funds

SB341.one_line: SB 341 permits limited off‑premises displays and sales of recreational vehicles and expands the definition of motor vehicle.
SB341.summary: SB 341 amends Montana’s motor‑vehicle dealer rules to allow limited off‑premises displays and sales of recreational vehicles, boats, snowmobiles and off‑highway vehicles, and expands the definition of “motor vehicle” to include those types. It also revises the franchise and distributor definitions in the state’s motor‑vehicle statutes.
changes: Permits new dealers to conduct off‑premises displays and sales of recreational vehicles, boats, snowmobiles, and off‑highway vehicles for up to 10 consecutive days, with a cap of 10 such events per calendar year;
Allows a dealer to display a single vehicle at a non‑business location for up to 90 days if the display promotes a nonprofit event or a joint commercial endeavor;
Requires that any off‑premises display or sale be in the dealer’s licensed county unless the dealer’s franchise covers another county and no competing dealer is authorized there;
Adds a requirement that dealers affix the required Monroney or buyer’s‑guide label to any vehicle displayed or sold off‑premises;
Expands the statutory definition of “motor vehicle” to include recreational vehicles, motorboats, personal watercraft, snowmobiles and off‑highway vehicles;
Rewrites the definitions section (61‑4‑201) to clarify terms such as “community,” “distributor,” “franchise,” and “new motor vehicle dealer.”
numbers: 90 days for nonprofit or joint‑commercial displays

SB342.one_line: Chief justice appoints and directs the court administrator, amending personnel and duty provisions.
SB342.summary: SB 342 changes the appointment process for Montana’s court administrator so that the Supreme Court’s chief justice, not the court itself, selects and directs the administrator. It amends the personnel plan, appointment, and duties sections of the Montana Code to reflect this new authority and applies retroactively to administrators appointed before the act’s effective date. The bill has no new funding or program creation and is effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Chief justice now appoints the court administrator and directs the office’s duties.

Personnel plan for judicial branch employees (excluding justices, judges, the administrator, librarian, and clerk) is adopted by the Supreme Court and administered under the chief justice’s direction.
The office of court administrator is established with the chief justice holding the administrator at his/her pleasure.

Duties of the administrator are expanded to include budget requests, data reporting, IT coordination, improvement recommendations, indigent victim assistance, state funding administration, pretrial program oversight, treatment court support account, and personnel plan administration.
The act applies retroactively to any court administrator appointed on or before its effective date.
affected: Judicial branch employees (excluding justices, judges, librarian, clerk)

SB344.one_line: Revises veto delivery, adds Secretary of State notification and override vote process.
SB344.summary: The bill changes how a governor’s veto is delivered and received, allowing the governor to return a vetoed bill to the legislature even when it is not in session and requiring the Secretary of State to notify legislators and, if a two‑thirds override is possible, to conduct a vote. It also makes the changes effective immediately and retroactive to all vetoes from the start of the 69th session.
changes: Amends §5‑4‑306 to permit the governor to deliver a vetoed bill to the originating house when that house has adjourned for the day but not for the session, with the delivery being effective once the house is back in session or the bill is physically received by a clerk or secretary with a timestamped receipt.
If the legislature is not in session when a veto occurs, the governor must send the bill and veto message to the Secretary of State.

The Secretary of State must mail a copy of the bill and veto message to each legislator within five working days if the bill failed to reach two‑thirds approval; if the bill had two‑thirds approval, the Secretary must send a certified‑mail ballot and instructions for a possible override vote within five working days.
Legislators have 30 days to return a vote; the Secretary tallies votes within one working day and, if two‑thirds or more of each house vote to override, the bill becomes law.
The legislature may reconvene for a special session to reconsider any vetoed bill when it is not in session.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and applies retroactively to all vetoes from the start of the 69th session.

SB347.one_line: Revises residency rules, expands naturopathic scope, and tightens licensing exemptions for Montana medical practice.
SB347.summary: The bill amends Montana’s medical licensing statutes to tighten residency requirements, clarify definitions, and restrict unlicensed trainees from exempted practice. It also expands the scope of naturopathic physicians and revises several licensing exemptions.
changes: Replaces the definition of “approved residency” with a stricter ACGME‑based standard and allows the board to approve other programs after investigation.
Adds a requirement that residents must complete at least one PGY‑1 year of an approved residency before licensure, and allows the board to impose probation or other conditions.

Rewrites the exemptions for interns and resident physicians, limiting their practice to the hospital or clinic where they are training and requiring a license if they provide services outside that setting.
Expands the naturopathic physician’s scope of practice, allowing prescription of a limited formulary of therapeutic substances and permitting certain diagnostic and minor surgical procedures.
Creates a five‑member alternative health‑care formulary committee to set and annually review the naturopathic formulary.
Adds a requirement that physicians applying for expedited licensure in another state submit fingerprints for a background check.
Clarifies that unlicensed trainees cannot be exempt from licensing requirements.
Revises the definition of “practice of medicine” to include telemedicine and store‑forward technology.
Rewrites several licensing exemption clauses in §37‑3‑103 to clarify when a license is required for out‑of‑state physicians and other health‑care providers.
affected: The Montana Board of Medical Examiners
The Department of Labor and Industry

SB348.one_line: SB 348 tightens sexual‑assault penalties, mandates repeat‑offender registration, and expands victim categories.
SB348.summary: SB 348 revises Montana’s sexual‑assault statutes, tightening penalties, adding mandatory registration for repeat offenders, and expanding definitions of sexual‑offense victims and offenders.
changes: Amends §45‑5‑502 to increase fines and jail terms for first, second, and third‑or‑more convictions; adds life‑imprisonment or 4‑year minimum for certain victim‑age or injury circumstances; expands the definition of “sexual assault” to include attempts and flight.
Adds a mandatory sexual‑offender registration requirement for anyone convicted of a second sexual‑assault offense.
Rewrites §46‑23‑502 to broaden the definition of “sexual offense” and “sexual offender,” and to clarify who must register and where the registration agency is located.
Expands the list of protected victim categories (e.g., minors, people in care facilities, psychotherapy clients, school staff, youth‑care program participants).
Clarifies the scope of “sexual or violent offender” and “sexual‑violent predator” definitions.
Provides detailed exceptions for married couples and certain professional relationships.
Adjusts definitions of “municipality,” “resident,” and “transient” for registration purposes.
Reinforces the requirement that foreign convictions be considered only if the foreign jurisdiction is deemed to have a fair‑trial system.
affected: Sexual‑assault offenders (first, second, third convictions), potential repeat offenders, victims (minors, care‑facility residents, psychotherapy clients, school students), police departments, sheriff’s offices, correctional agencies, and the general public subject to registration requirements

SB350.one_line: Allows districts to bar non‑citizen or non‑resident homeschoolers from extracurriculars, with academic verification required.
SB350.summary: SB 350 amends the state’s extracurricular‑participation law to allow school districts and athletic organizations to bar non‑citizen or non‑resident homeschool students from participating in school activities, while still requiring academic eligibility to be verified. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §20‑5‑112 to permit districts/athletic bodies to restrict participation of homeschool students who are not U.S. citizens or Montana residents.
Allows such restrictions to be based on citizenship and residency status only.

Requires academic eligibility for non‑public or homeschool students to be attested by the non‑public school head administrator, or by the homeschool educator with principal verification, without student assessment.
Maintains that participating homeschool students must meet the same participation standards and rules as full‑time public‑school students.
The act is effective immediately upon passage.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Homeschool students who are not U.S. citizens or Montana residents
Athletic associations, conferences, and interscholastic sports organizations

SB355.one_line: SB 355 revises transmission‑line rules, adds bidding for $8 M+ projects, and sets sharing rules for incumbent utilities.
SB355.summary: SB 355 amends Montana’s electric‑utility statutes to define key terms, grant incumbent utilities a right‑of‑first‑refusal to build new transmission lines, and require a competitive bidding process for projects valued at $8 million or more. The bill also sets notice and sharing rules for lines that connect two incumbent utilities.
changes: Amends definitions in §69‑5‑201 (e.g., electric transmission line, federally registered planning authority, incumbent electric utility, transmission facilities).

Adds a right‑of‑first‑refusal for incumbent utilities to construct, own, and maintain new transmission lines that meet specified criteria (midwest reliability organization, federally approved, interconnectable).
Requires incumbent utilities to conduct a competitive bidding process for new transmission line projects valued at $8 million or more, with the utility allowed to participate as a bidder.
Mandates a 120‑day notice to the federally registered planning authority after approval of a project and allows the utility to waive its right to construct by notice.

Specifies that upon completion the incumbent utility owns the line and assumes maintenance responsibility, and that if a line connects two incumbent utilities it must be shared equally unless otherwise agreed.
Preserves the Public Service Commission’s authority to regulate utilities and make findings under §§69‑3‑109 and 69‑3‑201.
affected: Incumbent electric utilities (public utilities and electric cooperatives)
Potential bidders for new transmission line projects
Federally registered planning authorities (regional transmission organizations)

SB357.one_line: Extends water‑reservation deadlines and clarifies procedures for Missouri River basin reservations.
SB357.summary: The bill extends the deadline for perfecting state water reservations above Fort Peck Dam and gives the Department of Natural Resources the authority to adopt rules and review existing reservations. It amends the water‑reservation statutes to clarify application procedures, priority dates, and review requirements for reservations in the Missouri and Little Missouri River basins.
changes: Extends the perfection deadline for reservations above Fort Peck Dam to a new date (not specified in the text, but the act is effective immediately).
Amends §85‑2‑316 to clarify application requirements, cost responsibilities, and priority dating for all state water reservations.

Amends §85‑2‑331 to set new filing deadlines (July 1 1989 for above‑dam reservations, July 1 1991 for below‑dam and Little Missouri reservations) and to establish priority dates (July 1 1985 above‑dam, July 1 1989 Little Missouri).
Adds a review requirement: the department must review existing reservations at least once every 10 years and may extend, modify, or revoke them.
Provides that reservations may be transferred or reallocated under specified conditions and that they are not subject to the state water‑leasing program.
Requires the Secretary of State to notify federally recognized tribal governments of the act.
affected: State and local agencies applying for water reservations
Municipalities and conservation districts holding reservations above Fort Peck Dam
Applicants for reservations in the Missouri and Little Missouri River basins
numbers: July 1 1991 (filing deadline for below‑dam & Little Missouri reservations)
July 1 1989 (priority date for Little Missouri reservations)

SB360.one_line: SB 360 revises Montana election law, tightening officer conduct, ballot handling, and reporting deadlines.
SB360.summary: SB 360 amends Montana election statutes, adding new conduct rules for public officers, expanding definitions of election terms, tightening absentee‑ballot handling, and revising reporting deadlines for candidates and committees. The bill does not create a new program but clarifies existing law.
changes: Amends §2‑2‑121 to prohibit public officers/ employees from using state resources for private business, lobbying, or certain official acts unless disclosed or exempted; adds detailed conduct restrictions and disclosure requirements.

Rewrites §13‑1‑101 to expand and clarify definitions of election terms such as “candidate,” “ballot issue,” “contribution,” “election communication,” and many others, adding new definitions and removing old ones.
Revises §13‑13‑241 to set procedures for examining absentee‑ballot signature envelopes, handling provisional ballots, and timing of early ballot preparation and tabulation.
Amends §13‑37‑219 to limit contributions to a candidate whose office sought is unknown to the lowest applicable limit.
Rewrites §13‑37‑226 to specify new filing deadlines for candidate and committee reports, including quarterly, monthly, and special‑election schedules, and conditions for filing.
Amends §13‑37‑234 to broaden the interpretation of religious‑organization exemptions in campaign‑finance rules.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage and approval.
numbers: $500 total contribution/expenditure threshold for local elections

SB361.one_line: Mandates insurers to cooperate with DPHHS on Medicaid claims and prohibits procedural denials.
SB361.summary: The bill amends Montana’s health‑insurance law to require insurers and other pay‑entities to cooperate with the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) when the department submits Medicaid‑related claims. It obligates them to provide eligibility data, respond to inquiries, accept the department’s recovery rights, and not deny claims on procedural grounds within specified time limits.
changes: Adds a new subsection (d) to §33‑1‑111 requiring insurers, TPAs, HMOs, PBMs, etc. to accept DPHHS claims and not deny them on procedural grounds within 3‑year and 6‑year windows.
Specifies that insurers must provide eligibility data for Medicaid recipients and dependents upon request.
Mandates insurers to respond to DPHHS inquiries about claims within 3 years of service provision.
Requires insurers to accept DPHHS’s right of recovery and assignment of payment rights for Medicaid‑covered services.
Clarifies that the new requirements do not obligate insurers to pay for non‑covered services or pay from their own funds if they are not financially liable under the plan.
Provides that insurers may not be held liable for claims they do not otherwise bear and preserves indemnification rights for ultimate liability holders.

SB364.one_line: Limits remote kill‑switch use to warrant‑approved cases, with $10k damages for violations.
SB364.summary: SB 364 bars companies from remotely turning off or hard‑resetting a consumer device without a warrant, except for certain subscription, lease, or vehicle‑safety cases.  Violations trigger statutory damages of $10,000 per incident.  The law takes effect Oct. 1, 2025.
changes: Prohibits remote activation of a kill switch on personally owned electronic products without a court order or warrant.

Exempts kill‑switch use for (1) subscription/lease‑based services and motor‑vehicle collections, (2) safety‑related vehicle features (e.g., driver incapacitation, automated‑driving safeguards, idle‑engine shut‑off).
Defines key terms: electronic consumer product, entity, hard reset, kill switch.
Allows a kill switch to be activated on stolen property only with owner consent.
Creates a new part in Title 30, Chapter 14, and authorizes DOJ enforcement and civil action for violations.
affected: Manufacturers and distributors of consumer electronics

SB362.one_line: Allows fire chiefs to approve former felons as firefighters, with written physical exam filing.
SB362.summary: The bill amends Montana’s firefighter qualification rules to let a fire chief approve applicants who have been convicted of a misdemeanor or felony, provided they are not required to register as a sexual or violent offender. It also requires the physical exam to be written and filed with the city or town clerk. No new program or fund is created, and the changes apply only to municipal fire departments.
changes: Adds a discretionary exception that allows a fire chief to qualify an applicant with a misdemeanor or felony conviction, except when the conviction requires registration on the sexual or violent offender registry.
Replaces the physical examination requirement with a written determination that must be filed with the city or town clerk.
Keeps all other existing qualification criteria (citizenship, age, education, driver’s license, medical exam, fingerprinting, and no other disqualifying crime).
affected: Applicants with misdemeanor or felony convictions
numbers: physical examination by qualified medical professional
sexual or violent offender registry requirement

SB366.one_line: Revises county committee notification to allow e‑mail and clarifies timing and participation rules.
SB366.summary: SB 366 amends Montana’s central committee law to allow county convention calls to be emailed to precinct representatives and clarifies notification requirements. It also updates the language of §13‑38‑205, MCA, with no new programs or funds created.
changes: Amends §13‑38‑205, MCA, to permit e‑mail of the county convention call to precinct committee representatives.
Specifies that the call must be published in a newspaper at the county seat and mailed or e‑mailed at least 4 days before the convention.
Clarifies that the presiding officer of the county central committee must call the convention and that the call may not be less than 4 days prior.
Reiterates that only duly elected or appointed committee representatives or officers may participate in the convention.
Adds that if a committee representative is absent, the convention may appoint a qualified elector from the precinct to fill the vacancy.

SB365.one_line: Revises mine reclamation rules, adds siltation capacity standards, and includes a contingent‑voidness clause.
SB365.summary: SB 365 amends Montana’s mine‑reclamation rules to tighten requirements for siltation structures and gives the Department of Environmental Quality new rule‑making authority.  It also adds a contingent‑voidness clause that voids any provision if the U.S. Interior disapproves it under federal law.
changes: Amends §82‑4‑231 to expand reclamation‑plan detail and procedural steps for strip and underground mines.
Adds a new rule‑making authority for the Department to set design‑capacity requirements for siltation structures.

Requires siltation ponds to be built with a capacity equal to the anticipated precipitation event plus average mine inflow, and allows temporary capacity loss during multistorm events if the operator restores capacity promptly.
Imposes a contingent‑voidness provision: any part of the act that the U.S. Secretary of the Interior disapproves under 30 CFR 732 is automatically void.
Leaves all other existing reclamation and environmental‑quality provisions unchanged.
affected: Local governments and landowners affected by mine operations
U.S. Department of the Interior (for disapproval authority)

SB369.one_line: SB 369 mandates low‑cost suicide‑prevention training for Montana school staff and requires districts to include it in policies.
SB369.summary: SB 369 amends Montana’s youth suicide‑prevention law to require the Office of Public Instruction to provide low‑cost or free training for school staff and to mandate that all district employees receive at least two hours of such training every five years. Districts must also include these training requirements in their suicide‑prevention policies.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1310 to require the Office of Public Instruction to supply approved, low‑cost or no‑cost training materials and guidance.
Mandates that every employee who works directly with students receive annual youth suicide‑awareness training at no cost to the employee.
Requires each district to provide at least two hours of training every five years to all applicable staff.
Allows training to be delivered in-person, via videoconference, self‑study, online modules, or other methods approved by the local school board.
Adds a requirement that district suicide‑prevention policies describe the training requirements for employees.
Includes a liability disclaimer protecting the state and districts from lawsuits related to training implementation.
affected: School district employees who work directly with students
Students enrolled in Montana public schools

SB368.one_line: Allows DEQ to issue 14‑day notices for minor mine maintenance violations and imposes new penalties for willful non‑compliance.
SB368.summary: SB 368 lets the Montana Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) issue a 14‑day notice for minor maintenance violations at mines, with a 90‑day window for more serious non‑minor violations. It amends the state’s mining enforcement rules to clarify how and when notices, orders, and penalties are applied, and it adds new criminal penalties for willful violations.
changes: Amends 82‑4‑251 to create a new “minor maintenance correction letter” that gives a permittee 14 days to fix a violation that is not imminently dangerous or environmentally harmful.
Defines a minor maintenance item as a non‑imminent violation that can be corrected within 14 days and does not require a cessation order or public hearing.
Adds a 90‑day notice period for non‑minor violations that do not pose imminent danger, after which a cessation order may be issued if the violation persists.

Expands the penalty schedule in 82‑4‑254, allowing DEQ to waive penalties for minor violations and setting minimum/maximum administrative penalties ($100–$5,000 per violation, $750 per day of non‑abatement up to 30 days).
Introduces criminal penalties (misdemeanor, up to $10,000 fine or 1 year imprisonment) for willful violations, false statements, and interference with DEQ officials.
Provides a procedural framework for hearings, appeals, and judicial review of penalties and orders, including a 30‑day hearing request window and escrow of paid penalties pending review.

SB375.one_line: Prohibits sale of edible hemp products containing THC unless FDA‑approved.
SB375.summary: SB 375 bars the sale of any edible hemp product that contains THC unless the U.S. FDA has approved it as a food or drug. The bill defines hemp, hemp product, and consumer and immediately takes effect upon passage.
changes: Prohibits sale of edible hemp products containing THC to consumers unless FDA‑approved as food or drug.
Defines "hemp" as Cannabis sativa L. and all its parts, derivatives, and extracts, excluding synthetic cannabinoids.
Defines "consumer" as a member of the public who takes possession of the product and does not resell it.
Defines "hemp product" as any post‑harvest hemp intended for consumption, smoking, vaping, or other administration.
Codifies the prohibition as part of Title 50, Chapter 31, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.

SB373.one_line: Revises lien enforcement, removes summons, sets affidavit and notice rules, and clarifies sale procedures.
SB373.summary: SB 373 revises Montana’s lien‑enforcement rules, eliminating the need for a summons in most cases and clarifying where and how lien actions may be filed. It tightens the affidavit requirements for non‑possessory liens and sets specific notice and hearing timelines for owners.
changes: Summons no longer required for lien enforcement actions; an order to show cause replaces the summons.
Affidavit now required for non‑possessory special liens, detailing service, property, and unpaid charges.
Lien actions may be filed in the county where the contract was entered, the owner resided, or the property is located.
Notice to the owner must be served by certified mail at least 5 days before the hearing and by first‑class mail 21 days before.
The sheriff must advertise and sell the property to satisfy the lien, with proceeds applied in order of precedence.
Owners may request a hearing to contest the sale.

SB390.one_line: Expands smoking definition to include e‑devices and clarifies covered venues in Montana’s Clean Indoor Air Act.
SB390.summary: SB 390 amends Montana’s Clean Indoor Air Act to clarify what counts as smoking, adds a definition for electronic smoking devices, and expands the list of places covered by the law. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Redefines “smoking” to include use of marijuana or an electronic smoking device (e‑cigarette, dab rig, vape pen)
Adds a new definition for “electronic smoking device”
Expands the definition of “enclosed public place” to list specific venues such as bars, trains, health‑care facilities, and schools
Clarifies that a bar’s income must be at least 60 % from alcohol or gambling to qualify under the new definition
Revises Section 50‑40‑103 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new definitions
Effective date is the day the act is approved
No new program or fund is created
affected: Employees and patrons of bars, restaurants, stores, offices, schools, and other listed enclosed public places
Businesses that serve alcohol or gamble

SB392.one_line: Designates a 3‑mile stretch of MT 93 as a memorial highway and directs signage and map updates.
SB392.summary: SB 392 designates a 3‑mile stretch of MT 93 as the Laverne Parrish Memorial Highway, directs the Department of Transportation to install signage, and requires the highway to appear on the next state map. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Establishes the Laverne Parrish Memorial Highway on MT 93 between mile markers 48 and 51
Directs the Department of Transportation to design and install appropriate signs for the memorial highway
Mandates that the highway be included on the next publication of the state map
Codifies the provision as part of Title 60, Chapter 1, Part 2 of the Montana Statutes
Effective immediately upon passage and approval
affected: Montana Department of Transportation signage crews

SB380.one_line: SB 380 expands electronic vehicle processing, tightens licensing rules, and updates dealer and identification‑card procedures.
SB380.summary: SB 380 revises a wide range of Montana motor‑vehicle statutes, adding new definitions, expanding electronic processing, tightening licensing and registration rules, and clarifying dealer and identification‑card procedures. The bill also updates disability‑parking permits and the list of U.S. territories that issue Montana driver’s licenses.
changes: 1. Adds new definitions (e.g., "breach of the security of a data system", "authorized agent", "low‑speed electric vehicle") and expands the definition of a driver’s license to include temporary, learner, and non‑resident privileges.

2. Authorizes the Department of Justice and authorized agents to conduct electronic title, lien, and registration filings, and establishes a pilot program for electronic transactions with optional fees.
3. Revises disability‑parking permit application requirements, allowing licensed physicians, chiropractors, or advanced practice nurses to issue interim permits that expire five days after issuance.

4. Repeals and amends several sections of Title 61 (e.g., 61‑3‑413, 61‑3‑426, 61‑3‑473, 61‑5‑209) and updates dealer licensing rules, including new bond amounts, application requirements, and restrictions on wholesaler sales.
5. Expands the list of U.S. territories that may issue Montana driver’s licenses and identification cards, adding the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

6. Revises license‑plate rules, including new definitions for collector and general‑transportation collector’s items, and introduces new fees and validation procedures for special and personalized plates.
affected: Montana motor‑vehicle owners, dealers, wholesalers, auto‑auction operators, licensed physicians and nurses, non‑resident vehicle owners, and the Department of Justice’s licensing and registration staff
numbers: $1,000,000 penalty bond for non‑resident business title applicants

SB398.one_line: Increases municipal‑court civil action limits to $50,000 and expands jurisdiction over certain felony filings.
SB398.summary: SB 398 raises the monetary limits for certain civil actions that a municipal court can hear, effectively doubling the cap from $25,000 to $50,000 for collection, bond‑breach, contract‑breach, damage, forfeiture, and property‑recovery cases involving the city.
changes: Amends §3‑6‑103, MCA, to set the cap for municipal‑court jurisdiction on collection and related actions at $50,000 (up from $25,000).
Expands the list of proceedings the municipal court may hear, including bond‑breach, contract‑breach, damages, forfeiture, bond‑collection on appeal, and personal‑property recovery.
Adds a new subsection allowing applications for search warrants and felony complaints to be filed in municipal court, with the judge acting as a justice of the peace for preliminary hearings.
Clarifies that the city attorney may initiate felony charges within city limits, but the county attorney takes over if the case is filed in district court.
affected: Citizens and entities involved in civil actions against the city

SB393.one_line: Funds reimburse Flathead PL 280 enforcement costs, with specific distribution deadlines and withdrawal restrictions.
SB393.summary: The bill allocates $6 million from the general fund to reimburse Lake County and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes for costs of enforcing felony criminal jurisdiction on the Flathead Indian Reservation. It sets specific distribution deadlines and conditions tied to the county’s prior resolution and a joint agreement with the tribes.
changes: Appropriates $6 million for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to the Office of Budget and Program Planning.
Mandates $250,000 to each of Lake County and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes on or before July 31 2025 if the county rescinds its 2023 resolution to withdraw from PL 280.
Requires the remaining appropriation for FY 2025 to be split equally between the county and tribes within 30 days of a signed agreement on cost‑sharing for PL 280 implementation.
Requires the FY 2026 appropriation to be split equally by July 31 2026, contingent on confirmed compliance with the agreement.
Prevents the county from exercising its right to withdraw consent to enforce criminal jurisdiction until at least June 1 2027 (or June 30 2028 if the termination date is extended).
Makes the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Office of Budget and Program Planning

SB404.one_line: Local governments must forward new‑construction permits to the Department of Revenue within 90 days.
SB404.summary: SB 404 requires local governments and the Department of Labor and Industry to forward copies of new‑construction building and electrical permits to the Department of Revenue within 90 days, providing standardized location data. The bill simply creates a reporting requirement; it does not establish new programs or funds.
changes: Local governments (cities, towns, counties, consolidated city‑counties) must send a copy of any new‑construction building or electrical permit to the appropriate Revenue field office within 90 days of issuance.
The Department of Labor and Industry must also forward such permits to Revenue when it issues them.
The notification must include clear, consistent parcel location information (address, geocode, or legal description) in a format agreed with Revenue.
The requirement applies to permits issued in 2025 and onward, as codified in Title 15, Chapter 7, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
No new funding, offices, or penalties are created; the bill merely mandates data transmission.
The Department of Revenue may use the information to identify new construction for tax purposes.
affected: City, town, county, and consolidated city‑county governments
Montana Department of Labor and Industry

SB402.one_line: SB 402 clarifies child‑abuse definitions and mandates a written case determination after investigation.
SB402.summary: SB 402 amends the child‑abuse statute to clarify definitions and create a formal “case determination” process that classifies investigations as substantiated, unsubstantiated, or unfounded. The bill expands the scope of what counts as abuse, adds detailed definitions for abuse, neglect, and related terms, and requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to issue a written determination after each investigation.
changes: Amends Section 41‑3‑102 to add a new definition of “case determination” and to expand the definition of “child abuse or neglect.”
Requires the Department to issue a written determination—substantiated, unsubstantiated, or unfounded—after completing an investigation of a reported abuse or neglect case.
Adds detailed definitions for terms such as “abandonment,” “adequate health care,” “psychological abuse or neglect,” “protective services,” and several others that were not previously in the statute.
Expands the definition of abuse to include exposure to dangerous drugs, child sex trafficking, and certain criminal activities involving drugs.
Clarifies that religious beliefs alone do not constitute a finding of neglect for lack of medical care, but the state may still intervene if there is imminent substantial risk.
Introduces new terms such as “qualified expert witness,” “qualified individual,” and “safety and risk assessment” to guide investigations and court proceedings.
Maintains existing provisions for protective services, therapeutic needs assessment, and treatment plans, but places them within the new case‑determination framework.
No new funding or program is created; the bill only changes definitions and procedural requirements.
Effective July 1 2025.
effective_date":"July 1 2025"],
affected: department of public health and human services

SB410.one_line: Montana bans foreign‑adversary genetic tech, mandates U.S. data storage, and fines violations.
SB410.summary: The Montana Genomic Security Act bars medical and research facilities from using foreign‑adversary‑made genetic sequencers or software, requires domestic replacement, limits data storage to the U.S., mandates encryption and annual compliance certification, and imposes fines and whistleblower protections.
changes: Prohibits use of foreign‑adversary‑produced genetic sequencers or sequencing software in state medical and research facilities.
Mandates removal and replacement of any prohibited equipment with compliant devices or software.
Requires all genetic sequencing data to be stored within the United States and restricts remote access to non‑open data to written consent of the individual.
Imposes $10,000 fines for each violation of prohibited equipment use or off‑shore data storage, enforceable from the first full fiscal year after enactment.
Requires annual legal certification of compliance from each covered facility, with failure to certify treated as perjury.
Provides whistleblower protections and allows patients to recover at least $5,000 per unique use of their genomic data in a violation.
affected: Companies or entities storing genetic sequencing data
Patients and research subjects whose data is processed
numbers: $5,000 per unique use of genomic data
December 31 following effective date for certification
first full fiscal year after effective date for fines

SB409.one_line: Reallocates lodging tax revenue, expands a permanent emergency‑lodging grant program, and ends temporary statutes.
SB409.summary: SB 409 revises how the lodging‑facility‑use tax is collected and allocated, expands a temporary emergency‑lodging program for domestic‑violence and human‑trafficking victims into a permanent program, and amends several related statutes. The bill changes the distribution of tax proceeds, creates a new permanent grant program for short‑term lodging, and shortens the life of several temporary provisions.
changes: Amends 15‑65‑121 to require the Department of Commerce to distribute 4 % of lodging‑tax proceeds to a series of state accounts and to earmark specific percentages for the Montana Historical Society, university system, fish & wildlife, invasive‑species account, and a large share for the department itself; the remainder is split among regional nonprofit tourism corporations and other entities.

Rewrites 44‑4‑1505 to establish a permanent emergency‑lodging and recovery program, allowing licensed establishments to receive reimbursement grants (up to 5 nights per family per year) from the Department of Justice for sheltering victims of domestic violence or human trafficking.
Rewrites 44‑4‑1506 to create a dedicated state‑special‑revenue account for the emergency‑lodging program, administered by the Department of Justice.
Amends 12‑Ch. 563 (2021) and 10‑Ch. 758 (2023) to terminate certain temporary sections by June 30 2027 (or 2025 for some parts).
Repeals 90‑1‑122, removing the previous lodging‑tax allocation scheme.
Sets effective dates: most changes take effect July 1 2025; some temporary provisions expire June 30 2027.
The bill creates a new permanent grant program and a new special‑revenue account but does not create a new criminal offense.
affected: Montana heritage preservation and development commission
victims of domestic violence or human trafficking
SB409.effective: July 1 2025 (most provisions); temporary sections terminate June 30 2027

SB412.one_line: Fee waivers for former foster children under 21, funded by federal transition funds.
SB412.summary: The bill removes fees for a range of government documents that former foster children under 21 may need, while allowing the state to reimburse the waived amounts with federal transition‑funds. It also amends several statutes to codify the fee‑waiver rules and supersedes existing unfunded‑mandate provisions.
changes: Exempts former foster children under 21 from fees for certified birth‑certificate copies, replacement birth certificates, driver’s license applications/renewals, replacement licenses, ID cards, and university transcript releases (with a special rule for university fees).
Allows the Department of Public Health and Human Services to apply for and use federal transition‑funds to reimburse the waived fees, but only if such funds are received.
Adds rule‑making authority for the department to implement the fee‑waiver program and to set specific procedures for fee reimbursement.
Amends 7‑4‑2631, 20‑25‑515, 50‑15‑111, 61‑5‑111, 61‑5‑114, and 61‑12‑504 to incorporate the waiver language and to clarify that the waived fees may be collected from the department for reimbursement.
Supersedes existing unfunded‑mandate laws (1‑2‑112 through 1‑2‑116) that previously required agencies to collect these fees.
Codifies Sections 1 and 2 into Title 52, Chapter 2 of the Montana Code.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Department of Justice (driver’s license and ID card issuers)
State agencies that collect vital‑record fees
numbers: $8 for a certified copy of a birth certificate
30‑day period for fee payment to department

SB413.one_line: Montana criminalizes sharing pornographic deep‑fakes of non‑consenting people, with penalties up to $10,000 or 10 years in prison.
SB413.summary: Montana will make it a crime to share or threaten to share pornographic deep‑fakes of a non‑consenting person.  First‑time offenders face up to a $1,000 fine or a year in county jail; repeat or child‑targeted cases carry steeper penalties.  The law also sets clear exemptions for law‑enforcement, research, and court‑ordered use.
changes: Creates a new criminal offense: disclosing explicit synthetic media.
Defines key terms such as “explicit synthetic media,” “identifiable individual,” and “valuable consideration.”
Sets penalties: first offense up to $1,000 fine or 1‑year county jail; second offense up to $10,000 fine or 5‑year state prison; offenses involving minors up to $10,000 fine or 10‑year state prison.
Provides exemptions for disclosures made for reporting unlawful conduct, legitimate research or education, or in civil/criminal proceedings under court order.
Limits liability of internet service providers unless they actively aid disclosure.
affected: Individuals who create, share, or threaten to share pornographic deep‑fakes of non‑consenting people
Internet service providers (only if they aid disclosure)
Law‑enforcement, researchers, educators, and courts (exempted activities)

SB414.one_line: Rewrites garbage‑feeding rules, bans packaging, and sets misdemeanor penalties.
SB414.summary: The bill amends Montana’s garbage‑feeding statutes to clarify what counts as garbage, explicitly bans packaging materials from being fed to swine, and sets misdemeanor penalties for violations.
changes: Amends §81‑2‑501 to redefine “garbage” to include packaging materials and exclude non‑animal waste.
Adds a prohibition in §81‑2‑502 that makes it unlawful to feed any garbage—including packaging—to swine or other animals, except for a person’s own household garbage.
Rewrites §81‑2‑511 to impose a misdemeanor penalty of a $50‑$250 fine, up to 6 months’ imprisonment, or both, and allows daily violations to be counted separately and for courts to issue injunctions.
affected: Individuals or entities that feed garbage to swine or other animals
Farmers, feedlot operators, and anyone handling animal waste
Municipalities and private corporations that may dispose of packaging in animal feed

SB422.one_line: Expands cancer coverage, adds new benefits, and amends HMO and self‑funded plan rules.
SB422.summary: SB 422 expands insurance coverage for advanced or metastatic cancer and adds a wide range of new benefits to state‑run group plans. It bars insurers from conditioning drug coverage on prior drug failure, requires detailed cancer‑related benefits, and adds new mental‑health, telehealth, and well‑child provisions. The bill also amends several statutory sections to clarify health‑maintenance‑organization rules and self‑funded plan regulations.
changes: 1. Insurers cannot require a patient to have failed a different drug before covering a FDA‑approved cancer drug that follows best‑practice guidelines.

2. State‑run group plans must cover a list of new services, including in‑born‑error treatment, Down syndrome therapies, hearing‑loss treatment, fertility preservation, mental‑health care, telehealth, eye‑drop refills, and advanced‑cancer treatment.
3. Plans must provide well‑child care from birth to age 7 with no deductible and specific visit requirements.
4. Dependent coverage must continue until age 26, with premiums payable by the insured if the employer does not cover them.
5. State employee and university group plans must cover specific breast‑cancer surgery follow‑up and diabetes self‑management training and supplies.
6. Additional amendments clarify HMO regulatory exemptions and self‑funded plan applicability.
affected: Insured individuals with advanced or metastatic cancer

SB424.one_line: Expands property‑tax relief for 60‑90 % disabled veterans and updates income tables.
SB424.summary: SB 424 amends Montana’s disabled‑veteran property‑tax‑assistance program to broaden eligibility to veterans rated 60‑90 % disabled, revises income‑multiplier tables, and sets new annual inflation adjustments. The bill takes effect immediately and applies to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025.
changes: Expands eligibility to veterans rated 60‑90 % disabled, in addition to 100 % and 80 % ratings
Replaces the existing income‑multiplier tables with new tables that include separate brackets for 100 %, 80‑90 %, and 60‑90 % disabled veterans and their spouses
Adds a new definition of “Annual verification” and updates the PCE inflation‑factor calculation for annual income‑level adjustments
Requires that qualifying income thresholds be adjusted each year using the PCE inflation factor, rounded to the nearest dollar, and that they never fall below the prior year’s level

Maintains the requirement that the property be the primary residence, owned and occupied by the veteran (or surviving spouse) and that the veteran be a qualified veteran as defined in the amended statute
Sets the effective date to the passage of the act and limits applicability to property‑tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025

SB428.one_line: SB 428 expands local speed‑limit authority with specified limits, signage, and consultation rules.
SB428.summary: SB 428 amends Montana’s speed‑limit rules to give local authorities and county commissions broader, but still limited, authority to set or change limits on highways, arterial streets, school zones, and unpaved roads, with specified minimums, maximums, and signage requirements.
changes: Local authorities may set a reasonable and safe speed limit that (a) decreases limits at intersections in urban districts; (b) increases limits within urban districts up to 65 mph at night; (c) decreases limits outside urban districts but not below 35 mph on paved roads or 25 mph on paved/unpaved roads; (d) decreases limits in school zones, senior‑citizen‑center areas, or near designated crosswalks to no less than 15 mph.
County commissioners may set limits on county roads under subsections (1)(c) and (1)(d) without an engineering investigation.
Local authorities may set reasonable and safe limits on arterial streets that differ from the default urban‑district speed.
Variable speed limits may be adopted by local authorities if warranted by an engineering study, subject to 61‑8206.
Signage requirements: altered limits take effect when signs are posted; school‑zone limit changes require signs that show the new limit, penalty, and end of zone.
Special speed limits on state highways in municipalities or urban areas are exclusively set by the county commission per 61‑8‑309.

Consultation requirements: local authorities must consult the Department of Transportation and the commission when school zones include state highways or commission‑designated highways; they must also consult district officials for a school when establishing or altering a school‑zone area or setting a speed limit in that area.
Unpaved‑road limits set under subsection (1)(c) must be uniform for all motor‑vehicle types.
Violations of limits set under subsections (1)(a)–(c) are misdemeanors punishable under 61‑8‑711; violations under subsection (1)(d) are misdemeanors punishable under 61‑8‑726.
affected: Motorists on state highways, county roads, arterial streets, school zones, and unpaved roads

SB429.one_line: Rewrites fitness, contempt, and commitment rules, adding involuntary medication and cost‑sharing provisions.
SB429.summary: SB 429 revises Montana’s rules for determining and restoring a defendant’s fitness to stand trial, expands the definition of contempt, clarifies costs for psychiatric examinations and commitments, and authorizes involuntary medication. The bill takes effect immediately and preserves pre‑existing rights and proceedings.
changes: Redefines contempt to include a broader list of acts and clarifies civil vs. criminal contempt
Rewrites the state‑funded district court expense program to cover a wide range of trial‑related costs
Revises procedures for ordering psychiatric examinations, including who pays for examinations and associated expenses
Adds detailed rules for involuntary commitment, treatment plans, and involuntary medication, including required hearings and rights of the defendant
Prioritizes admissions to the Montana State Hospital for pre‑trial defendants and violent‑crime defendants
Provides rule‑making authority for the Department of Public Health and Human Services to adopt treatment‑review and medication‑board rules
Includes a saving clause that preserves rights and penalties incurred before the effective date
Effective immediately upon passage and approval
affected: court personnel (judges, clerks, reporters, probation officers)
Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: $0 (no charge to court admin for certain costs)

SB430.one_line: Rewrites civil‑commitment and emergency‑detention laws, tightening transport, contempt, and commitment limits.
SB430.summary: SB 430 revises Montana’s civil‑commitment and emergency‑detention statutes, tightening procedures for transporting patients, clarifying contempt, and replacing unfunded mandates. It expands the criteria for commitment, limits detention to 72 hrs, and requires professional‑person evaluation before transport.
changes: Amends 3‑1‑501, 3‑10‑402, and 3‑11‑303 to redefine contempt and its procedures for civil‑commitment cases
Rewrites 53‑21‑102 to specify emergency‑situation definitions and transport conditions to the state hospital

Revisions to 53‑21‑126 and 53‑21‑127 establish new trial, post‑trial, and disposition hearings, including limits on commitment length (≤3 mo in hospital, ≤6 mo in community) and involuntary medication review requirements
Amends 53‑21‑129 to set a 72‑hour maximum for emergency detention and require professional‑person assessment before transfer
Adds 53‑21‑181 allowing patients to be discharged on a professional’s written order during commitment
Amends 53‑21‑193 to prioritize community facilities over the state hospital and set bed‑availability rules
Supersedes unfunded mandate laws 1‑2‑112‑116 and includes a saving clause for pre‑existing rights and proceedings
Effective immediately upon passage
affected: Courts, judges, peace officers, professional persons, mental‑health facilities, patients and their families

SB426.one_line: Massive overhaul of Montana UCC to cover digital assets and ban central‑bank digital currency.
SB426.summary: The bill amends the Montana Uniform Commercial Code to modernize language for the digital age, add rules for transactions involving digital assets and cryptocurrency, prohibit the use of a central‑bank digital currency, and create a host of new definitions, procedures, and enforcement mechanisms for electronic records and digital securities.
changes: 1. Rewrites core UCC provisions (30‑1‑101, 30‑1‑107, 30‑1‑201, 30‑1‑212, 30‑1‑301, 30‑2‑102, 30‑2‑106, 30‑2‑201, 30‑2‑202, 30‑2‑205, 30‑2‑209, 30‑2A‑102, 30‑2A‑103, 30‑2A‑107, 30‑2A‑201, 30‑2A‑202, 30‑2A‑203, 30‑2A‑205, 30‑3‑102, 30‑3‑104, 30‑3‑125, 30‑3‑401, 30‑3‑605, 30‑4A‑103, 30‑4A‑105, 30‑4A‑201, 30‑4A‑202, 30‑4A‑207, 30‑4A‑208, 30‑4A‑210, 30‑4A‑211, 30‑4A‑305, 30‑5‑124, 30‑5‑136, 30‑7‑102, 30‑7‑107, 30‑8‑112, 30‑8‑113, 30‑8‑116, 30‑8‑120, 30‑8‑333, 30‑9A‑102, 30‑9A‑104, 30‑9A‑105, 30‑9A‑203, 30‑9A‑204, 30‑9A‑208, 30‑9A‑209, 30‑9A‑210, 30‑9A‑301, 30‑9A‑304, 30‑9A‑305, 30‑9A‑310, 30‑9A‑312, 30‑9A‑313, 30‑9A‑314, 30‑9A‑316, 30‑9A‑317, 30‑9A‑323, 30‑9A‑324, 30‑9A‑330, 30‑9A‑331, 30‑9A‑332, 30‑9A‑334, 30‑9A‑341, 30‑9A‑404, 30‑9A‑406, 30‑9A‑408, 30‑9A‑509, 30‑9A‑513, 30‑9A‑601, 30‑9A‑605, 30‑9A‑608, 30‑9A‑613, 30‑9A‑614, 30‑9A‑615, 30‑9A‑616, 30‑9A‑619, 30‑9A‑620, 30‑9A‑621, 30‑9A‑624, 30‑9A‑628, 71‑3‑125] to reflect new terminology and digital‑asset rules; 2. Adds new sections (e.g., 30‑8‑112, 30‑8‑116, 30‑8‑120, 30‑8‑333, 30‑9A‑102, 30‑9A‑104, 30‑9A‑105, 30‑9A‑203, 30‑9A‑204, 30‑9A‑208, 30‑9A‑209, 30‑9A‑210, 30‑9A‑301, 30‑9A‑304, 30‑9A‑305, 30‑9A‑310, 30‑9A‑312, 30‑9A‑313, 30‑9A‑314, 30‑9A‑316, 30‑9A‑317, 30‑9A‑323, 30‑9A‑324, 30‑9A‑330, 30‑9A‑331, 30‑9A‑332, 30‑9A‑334, 30‑9A‑341, 30‑9A‑404, 30‑9A‑406, 30‑9A‑408, 30‑9A‑509, 30‑9A‑513, 30‑9A‑601, 30‑9A‑605, 30‑9A‑608, 30‑9A‑613, 30‑9A‑614, 30‑9A‑615, 30‑9A‑616, 30‑9A‑619, 30‑9A‑620, 30‑9A‑621, 30‑9A‑624, 30‑9A‑628, 71‑3‑125] to create new rules for electronic documents, digital assets, and control of digital securities; 3. SB433.one_line: Revises roundabout right‑of‑way rules, especially for towing vehicles, and updates statutory language.
SB433.summary: The bill revises Montana’s right‑of‑way rules for roundabouts, clarifying how vehicles may enter, pass, and yield, especially when towing. It also updates the statutory language in Section 61‑8‑327 to reflect these rules.
changes: Defines a roundabout as a circular intersection and a towing vehicle as one that pulls another vehicle.
States that a vehicle passing a roundabout may only drive to the right of the island or center and has right‑of‑way over all approaching vehicles.
Requires vehicles approaching a roundabout to yield to all vehicles already circulating and prohibits entry that interferes with a towing vehicle entering simultaneously.
Allows a towing vehicle to deviate from its lane when multiple lanes exist, provided it signals and yields to other traffic; vehicles traveling in the same direction must yield and may not pass.
If two towing vehicles enter simultaneously, the left vehicle has right‑of‑way and the right vehicle must yield.
Amends Section 61‑8‑327 to incorporate these definitions and rules, and to specify that vehicles on a one‑way roadway may only travel in the designated direction.
Codifies the new Section 1 as part of Title 61, Chapter 8, Part 3 of the Montana Code.
affected: Drivers of vehicles approaching or circulating roundabouts
Local authorities and the Department of Transportation

SB435.one_line: SB 435 establishes 72‑hour holds, expands video hearings, and revises cost rules for mental‑health commitments.
SB435.summary: SB 435 creates a 72‑hour mental‑health hold, expands the use of electronic hearings, clarifies who may waive presence at hearings, and revises cost‑payment rules for involuntary commitment. It amends several existing statutes to streamline emergency detentions and to allow courts to conduct many mental‑health hearings via two‑way video.
changes: Adds a 72‑hour mental‑health hold that can be initiated by a mental‑health professional and requires notification of the county attorney and state public defender.
Requires a mental‑health professional to evaluate the detained person within 24 hours and to file a written report with the individual, county attorney, and public defender.
Allows the detained person to consent to medication but not to refuse lifesaving medication, and permits release at any time if the professional deems treatment no longer necessary.

Expands the right to waive physical presence at hearings to include the respondent, counsel, and a friend, with court approval and professional concurrence, and clarifies that the right to counsel and treatment cannot be waived.

Permits courts to conduct a wide range of mental‑health hearings (initial, detention, trial, post‑trial, extensions, rehospitalization, and release‑condition hearings) via two‑way electronic audio‑video communication.
Revises cost‑payment rules for pre‑commitment psychiatric services, prioritizing the respondent, private insurance, Medicaid, and then the county, and limits county liability after commitment.
