Amends emergency detention procedures to allow peace officers to detain individuals for a short period pending professional evaluation and to transport them to appropriate facilities if no local bed is available.

SB437.one_line: Redefines sex as biological only, amends 54 statutes, and repeals the old definition.
SB437.summary: SB 437 codifies Montana’s definition of sex, male, female, man, woman, father, and mother as strictly biological, excludes gender identity, and revises dozens of statutes to use that definition. The bill also amends many unrelated provisions—ranging from education enrollment rules to organ‑donation reporting—to reference the new definition of sex.
changes: 1. Creates a new statutory definition of sex, male, female, man, woman, father, and mother that limits sex to biological male or female and excludes gender identity or sexual intercourse.
2. Rewrites the definition of “gender” so that it is a synonym for sex only when used alone, and prohibits its use as a stand‑in for gender identity, expression, or role.

3. Amends 54 separate Montana Code sections (e.g., 2‑18‑208, 7‑15‑4207, 20‑7‑1306, 40‑1‑107, 50‑5‑105, 53‑20‑142, etc.) to replace any reference to sex or gender with the new definition and to ensure that discrimination provisions apply only to biological sex.
4. Repeals the old Section 1‑1‑201 (the previous definition of sex) and replaces it with the new definition.
5. Provides an immediate effective date upon passage and approval, with severability language for invalid portions.
affected: State agencies, public schools, charter schools, choice schools, health‑care facilities, employers, voters, parents, students, and any entity that uses the word “sex” or “gender” in Montana law.

SB440.one_line: SB 440 mandates county election result spreadsheets, statewide reconciliation, and legislative oversight.
SB440.summary: SB 440 requires each county to produce a detailed spreadsheet of its election results before canvassing, post it online, and submit it to the Secretary of State, who will compile a statewide reconciliation report and share it with the legislature and public. The bill also gives the Secretary of State authority to adopt rules and mandates legislative oversight if discrepancies arise.
changes: County election administrators must create a reconciliation spreadsheet with specified data fields before canvassing begins.
The spreadsheet must be posted on the county election website no later than the county canvass meeting.
A digital copy of the spreadsheet is retained permanently; a physical copy is kept per state record‑keeping rules.

The county must submit the spreadsheet to the Secretary of State before election certification, and the Secretary must prepare a statewide reconciliation report at least seven days prior to certification.
If discrepancies are found, the Secretary must refer the issue to legislative leadership and may convene the audit committee for investigation.

The Secretary must distribute the reconciliation report to the legislature, post it statewide, and present it to the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee after each primary or general election.
The Secretary may adopt rules to implement these requirements.
The bill codifies these provisions into Title 13, Chapter 15, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
numbers: no later than county canvass meeting

SB441.one_line: Creates a network to enforce hunting rules on block‑management lands with escalating bans for repeat offenders.
SB441.summary: SB 441 creates the Montana Block Management Enforcement Network (MBMEN) to help landowners enforce hunting rules on their enrolled lands. Landowners may opt‑in or opt‑out, and the network imposes escalating access bans for repeat offenders. The Department must provide education and the Commission may adopt implementing rules.
changes: Establishes the MMBEN as a framework for enforcing compliance with landowner rules and Montana law on block‑management lands.
Allows landowners enrolled in the block‑management program to choose to join or leave the network at any time.

Imposes a tiered ban on individuals who violate block‑management rules: first conviction—prohibited for the remainder of the current license year; second conviction—prohibited for up to three consecutive license years; third conviction—prohibited for life.
Requires the Department to provide educational information to visitors about the rules and consequences on MMBEN‑enrolled lands.
Gives the Commission rule‑making authority to implement the provisions.
affected: Landowners enrolled in the block‑management program
Hunters and other visitors accessing block‑management lands
Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks
numbers: first conviction—ban for remainder of current license year
second conviction—ban for up to 3 consecutive license years

SB442.one_line: Exempts lodging managers and adds new licensing exemptions, effective immediately.
SB442.summary: SB 442 removes the real‑property‑manager license requirement for managers of licensed lodging establishments and adds several new exemptions to the licensing law. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Exempts managers of lodging establishments licensed under Montana Title 50, Chapter 51 from the real‑property‑manager license requirement.
Adds a list of new exemptions, including owners of the property, family members, small‑unit landlords, attorneys, trustees, state officials, and others.
Clarifies that a broker or salesperson may act as a property manager, but a salesperson needs a supervising broker.
Defines “owner” for the exemption purposes as sole proprietor, LLC managing member, corporation shareholder, or partnership partner.
affected: Attorneys, trustees, state officials, and other listed exempt persons

SB444.one_line: Amends search‑warrant service to require showing the warrant to a lawful occupant and providing copies and receipts.
SB444.summary: The bill amends Montana’s search‑warrant procedure to require officers to show the warrant to a known lawful occupant of the property being searched and to provide a copy and receipt to that occupant or leave them at the premises. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §46‑5‑227 to add that a warrant must be exhibited to a known lawful occupant of the property being searched.
Requires the officer to give the occupant a copy of the warrant and a receipt for any property taken, or to leave those items at the premises.
Clarifies that failure to leave a copy and receipt does not make seized property inadmissible at trial.
The amendment applies to all search‑warrant service situations in Montana.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.

SB446.one_line: SB 446 mandates physician review for adverse determinations and grievances, amends prior‑authorization rules, and voids itself if HB 398 passes.
SB446.summary: SB 446 requires that only physicians licensed in Montana may make adverse determinations or review grievances for utilization‑review organizations, and it amends prior‑authorization rules to limit when insurers can deny coverage for certain drugs. The bill also provides automatic approval if an insurer or review organization fails to meet the new physician‑review requirements.
changes: 1. Only a Montana‑licensed physician may make an adverse determination for a utilization‑review organization, and that physician must have a specialty focused on the condition being reviewed and work under a medical director who is also a Montana physician.

2. Only a Montana‑licensed physician may review a grievance for a utilization‑review organization, must have the same specialty as the provider who manages the condition, and must not have been involved in the adverse determination or have a financial interest in the outcome.

3. Section 33‑32‑221 is amended to prohibit prior authorization denial for certain prescription drugs (e.g., long‑acting injectable antipsychotics, drugs for substance‑use disorder, drugs after 6 months of uninterrupted use, or therapeutic duplication when prior authorization was already granted).

4. Any adverse determination for a prescription drug during prior authorization must be made by a physician with the appropriate specialty; non‑physician prior‑authorization decisions that do not result in an adverse determination remain unchanged.
5. The bill codifies the new physician requirements as integral parts of Title 33, chapters 32 parts 2 and 3.
6. If House Bill 398 passes, the physician requirements in this bill are void.

SB447.one_line: Extends prior‑authorization validity, eliminates PA for many chronic treatments and prescriptions, and adds detailed definitions.
SB447.summary: The bill expands how long prior‑authorization (PA) approvals last, makes PA unnecessary for many chronic‑condition treatments, and bars PA for a wide range of prescription drugs. It also adds detailed definitions and coordination rules with other pending bills.
changes: PA certifications for services are valid for at least 3 years, or for the entire duration of a chronic condition, whichever is longer.
PA is no longer required for chronic‑condition treatments once a certification has been issued, and re‑certification may only be requested every 12 months if documentation is needed.

PA is prohibited for many prescription drugs, including: generic drugs used continuously for 6 months, drugs denied for therapeutic duplication, dosage changes within FDA limits, long‑acting injectable antipsychotics, non‑specialty Medicare Part D drugs, substance‑use‑disorder drugs within labeled doses, and at least one child‑ and one adult‑appropriate option in several therapeutic classes.
If an adverse determination is made for a drug, the insurer must provide a written notice with a list of reasonable therapeutic alternatives.
Adverse determinations for drugs must be made by a physician whose specialty matches the condition being treated.
The bill amends definitions in §33‑32‑102, §33‑32‑107, and §33‑32‑221 and includes coordination language that voids overlapping amendments in House Bills 398, 399, and 398/399 if both are enacted.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Health insurance issuers and their utilization review organizations
Prescription drug manufacturers and formulary managers

SB449.one_line: Streamlines prior‑auth rules, protects plan‑switchers, and bans retroactive denials in Montana.
SB449.summary: SB 449 revises Montana’s health‑utilization‑review rules to streamline coverage continuity, limit step‑therapy repeats, and remove retroactive denials. It also bars prior‑authorization on discharge prescriptions and mandates electronic submission of requests.
changes: Health‑insurance issuers must honor prior authorizations for at least 90 days when an enrollee switches plans, unless the new plan excludes the service
Enrollees cannot be forced to repeat a step‑therapy protocol if they have already tried the drug or a similar one and discontinued it for medical reasons
Prior authorizations for discharge prescriptions are automatically approved for a minimum of 3 days if the drug costs under $5 000/day and the physician notes the discharge
Retroactive denial of a prior authorization is prohibited except in cases of fraud, misrepresentation, non‑payment of premiums, or benefit exhaustion
Health‑insurance issuers and utilization‑review organizations must accept and respond to prior‑authorization requests electronically, using the SCRIPT standard when applicable
The bill codifies these provisions into Title 33, Chapter 32 and sets an effective date for new policies
Coordination clauses allow other pending bills to override specific sections if both are passed
The act applies only to policies issued or renewed on or after its effective date

SB456.one_line: Revises drug‑dispensing rules to let certain staff hand out medicines prepared by physicians.
SB456.summary: SB 456 amends the state’s drug‑dispensing rules to allow certain non‑practitioner health‑care staff to hand out medicines that a physician has prepared, and expands the types of practitioners who may dispense drugs. It also clarifies registration, record‑keeping, and controlled‑substance restrictions.
changes: Adds a new subsection permitting health‑care staff (other than the prescribing practitioner) to convey drugs that the practitioner has prepared and sealed, provided the staff member verifies patient identity and the package bears two forms of identification written by the provider.
Rewrites §37‑2‑104 to require physicians who dispense drugs to register with the board of pharmacy, pay a fee, and comply with board labeling, storage, inspection, and record‑keeping rules.

Specifies that physicians may dispense only drugs within their scope of practice unless they are engaged in pharmacy practice, and may not dispense controlled substances unless engaged in pharmacy practice.

Allows physicians to dispense drugs to patients who cannot obtain them from a community pharmacy, to provide emergency drugs, to give unit doses, to dispense occasionally, and to provide drug samples, even if not registered to dispense.

Expands the definition of “medical practitioner” to include naturopathic physicians and allows certain registered nurses and contract physicians at specific clinics to dispense non‑controlled drugs under written protocols.
Maintains that physicians may not dispense drugs to injured workers treated under Title 39, chapter 71, except in the limited circumstances listed in subsection (8).
affected: Physicians, naturopathic physicians, registered nurses, contract physicians, and other health‑care staff who may dispense drugs
Patients receiving drugs directly from a practitioner’s office
The board of pharmacy (for registration and fee collection)
numbers: $ fee set by board (no amount specified)
No caps on number of drugs

SB457.one_line: SB 457 creates a misdemeanor contempt offense and a formal legislative polling process for non‑compliance with subpoenas.
SB457.summary: SB 457 establishes a formal, two‑step process for holding witnesses or record‑holders in criminal contempt when they ignore a legislative subpoena.  It creates a new misdemeanor offense with a fine up to $1,000 or up to 12 months in county jail, and it amends the statutory subpoena framework to allow committees to pursue contempt through the legislature and the courts.
changes: Creates a new misdemeanor offense of criminal contempt of the legislature, punishable by up to $1,000 fine or 12 months in county jail.

Provides a detailed procedure for a house or senate (or committee) to certify contempt via a simple resolution or a proclamation, including a poll of legislators when the legislature is not in session.
Requires the secretary of state to conduct a legislative poll within 3 days, send ballots to legislators, and tally votes within 1 working day; a majority vote adopts the contempt finding.
Amends MCA §5‑5‑109 and §5‑11‑107 to allow committees to issue subpoenas, hold hearings, and pursue contempt through either legislative resolution or court action.
Codifies the new contempt procedures into Title 5, Chapter 5, Part 1 and Title 45, Chapter 7, Part 3 of the Montana Code.
Effective date is July 1, 2025.
affected: Witnesses or persons subpoenaed by the legislature or its committees
Legislators who must vote on contempt proclamations
The attorney general who prosecutes contempt cases
The secretary of state who administers the poll

SB458.one_line: Expands property‑assessed capital‑enhancement programs to fund public‑safety and resiliency projects with new contract and assessment rules.
SB458.summary: SB 458 expands Montana’s commercial property‑assessed capital‑enhancement programs to finance public‑safety and resiliency projects, in addition to energy‑conservation work. It amends the statutory framework to define new project types, set contract and program‑plan requirements, and clarify assessment rules. The bill takes effect October 1, 2025.
changes: Adds “public safety and resiliency improvement” projects to the types of work that can be financed under a commercial property‑assessed capital‑enhancement program.
Requires a detailed program plan that includes marketing, contractor standards, energy‑analysis requirements, and a model contract with full disclosure of costs and interest.
Mandates that contracts with property owners include a 3‑business‑day cancellation period, a property‑tax lien notice, and subordination agreements for mortgaged properties.
Specifies that assessments may not exceed the useful life of the financed project and must be billed with property taxes unless a special assessment ordinance applies.
Prescribes public‑hearing procedures and resolution requirements for establishing, changing, or terminating a program.
affected: Local governments (cities, counties, towns, consolidated city‑counties)
Commercial and industrial property owners (record owners)
Contractors and subcontractors performing eligible projects
Mortgage holders and loan servicers of financed properties

SB464.one_line: Mandates court‑appointed special advocates with defined qualifications, duties, and training for child‑abuse cases.
SB464.summary: SB 464 expands and clarifies the role of court‑appointed special advocates (guardians ad litem) in child‑abuse cases, setting qualifications, duties, training, and conflict‑of‑interest rules. It also amends definitions related to abuse, neglect, and special advocates, and updates the right‑to‑counsel provisions for parties in removal and placement proceedings.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑112 to require a court‑appointed special advocate for every child alleged abused or neglected, with specific age, commitment, background, and conflict‑of‑interest requirements; allows an attorney or other qualified person if no advocate is available; requires public expense if necessary.

Defines a special advocate as a trained volunteer officer of the court who advocates for a child’s best interests, and sets detailed duties including investigations, interviews, record access, confidentiality, reporting, court appearances, and monitoring of orders.
Mandates preservice and on‑the‑job training covering abuse recognition, child development, court process, and documentation; requires observation of court proceedings before appointment.
Adds that special advocates may not accept compensation, have conflicts, be related to parties, or use the position for gifts; requires confidentiality and no hearsay issues for reports.
Provides that any party may petition for removal of a special advocate who fails to perform duties; allows the advocate to raise conduct concerns to the court.
Amends §41‑3‑102 to expand definitions of abandonment, abuse, neglect, and related terms, and introduces a new definition of “special advocate.”

Amends §41‑3‑425 to clarify right‑to‑counsel for parties in removal/placement petitions, including indigent parents, children, and Indian child‑welfare cases, and allows court‑appointed counsel for special advocates.
No new program or criminal offense is created; the bill merely revises existing statutes.
affected: Attorneys and other qualified persons who may serve as special advocates
Parents, guardians, and other parties in child‑welfare proceedings
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: public expense for special advocate if necessary
June 30 2025 termination of certain bracketed language

SB466.one_line: Mandates courts to consider specified factors in child‑best‑interest decisions.
SB466.summary: SB 466 requires Montana courts to consider a set of factors when deciding a child’s best interests, but it does not assign any weight or create new programs. The bill merely codifies these factors into state law. It applies to all child‑custody or related court proceedings.
changes: Adds a statutory list of factors that must be considered in any best‑interest determination for a child.

SB468.one_line: Creates a registry for substantiated abuse cases, requires notice, hearing, and expungement procedures.
SB468.summary: SB 468 creates a statewide registry that lists people with substantiated child‑abuse or neglect findings.  Individuals must be notified and given a hearing before being entered, and they may petition for expungement after a 2‑year waiting period.  The bill also amends related child‑protection statutes and requires annual reporting to a committee.
changes: Establishes a central registry for individuals with substantiated child‑abuse or neglect determinations.
Requires written notice to the individual and a hearing before entry into the registry.
Creates a 2‑year waiting period before an individual can request expungement, with a 30‑day review by the department.
Provides a court‑based petition process for expungement if the department denies the request.
Mandates the department to destroy records upon expungement and to notify relevant parties.
Adds annual reporting requirements to the Children, Families, Health and Human Services Interim Committee.
affected: Individuals with substantiated child‑abuse or neglect determinations
Montana Department of Children, Families and Social Services
Employers, licensing agencies, and volunteer organizations that conduct background checks

SB471.one_line: SB 471 creates a misdemeanor for endangering pedestrians and sets tiered fines for crosswalk violations.
SB471.summary: SB 471 revises Montana’s pedestrian‑crossing traffic laws, creating a new misdemeanor offense called endangerment of pedestrians and setting tiered fines for violations. It also clarifies when drivers must yield to pedestrians and adds liability for damage to pedestrian‑actuated devices.
changes: Creates the misdemeanor offense of endangerment of pedestrians for violations of §61‑8‑502
Sets fines: $25‑$100 for first conviction, $50‑$200 for a second conviction within one year, $100‑$500 for third or subsequent convictions
Adds higher fines ($150‑$250) when the violation occurs at a pedestrian‑actuated device that is activated
Requires drivers who damage a pedestrian‑actuated device to pay replacement or repair costs
Provides civil contempt procedures for failure to pay fines, including court‑ordered enforcement or community service
Amends §61‑8‑502 to clarify yielding rules, right‑hand‑turn rules, and school‑crossing guard provisions
Defines “pedestrian‑actuated device” and reaffirms the definition of “vehicle”
Codifies the new penalties as part of Title 61, Chapter 8, Part 7

SB482.one_line: Mandates written contracts for college athletes’ NIL rights and limits schools’ control over them.
SB482.summary: The bill amends Montana’s student‑athlete statutes to require that any contract involving a college athlete’s name, image, or likeness be in writing and to clarify that schools cannot prohibit or penalize athletes for such contracts. It also expands the definition of a student‑athlete’s rights and limits schools’ ability to use an athlete’s likeness in certain ways.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑232 to define “student‑athlete rights” and prohibit schools from restricting or penalizing athletes for earning compensation from NIL contracts.
Adds a requirement that any contract related to a student‑athlete’s name, image, or likeness must be in writing and disclosed to the institution.
Allows schools to include provisions in scholarship agreements that permit the use of an athlete’s likeness, but prohibits schools from providing NIL compensation.
Preserves the ability of schools to enforce general conduct codes applicable to all students.
Amends §28‑2‑903 to make NIL contracts invalid unless written, extending the written‑contract rule to athlete contracts.

SB472.one_line: Revises streambed penalties, removes cap, adds forest practice exemption, and amends fine collection.
SB472.summary: The bill removes the cap on civil penalties for violations of the Natural Streambed and Land Preservation Act, adds an exemption for allowed forest practices, and amends how fines are collected and distributed. It also updates the penalty schedule for repeat offenders and clarifies restoration responsibilities. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Eliminates the statutory maximum for civil penalties under the Natural Streambed and Land Preservation Act.
Adds an exemption for persons engaging in forest practices permitted under Title 77, chapter 5, part 3.
Revises Section 75‑7‑123 to set new penalty limits: $500 fine or $5,000 per day, with caps of $100,000 for a first violation, $250,000 for a second, and no cap thereafter.
Updates Section 3‑10‑601 to clarify collection timing (10th day for fees, 5th day for fines) and distribution (50/50 to state and county funds).
Provides that restoration costs up to $15,000 can be collected in justice’s court; amounts above that must be pursued in district court.
Allows conservation districts to negotiate penalty amounts before court action.
affected: Property owners and developers in stream management zones

SB486.one_line: Allows districts to elect OPI to pay first‑year ESA remittance and sets accounting rules.
SB486.summary: SB 486 lets a school district elect to have the Office of Public Instruction (OPI) pay the first‑year remittance for a student in the Special Needs Equal Opportunity Education Savings Account (ESA) instead of the district. The bill amends the ESA funding rules to allow this option and specifies how the funds are to be accounted for and used.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑1709 to add subsection (2)(b) allowing a district to elect OPI payment of the first‑year remittance
Rewrites the remittance calculation and timing language to accommodate the new election
Adds accounting rules: 95 % of the remitted money must be deposited in the ESA trust for reimbursing parents, 5 % in an OPI ESA administration account
Specifies that the OPI must reduce the district’s BASE aid in the year the student leaves the program
Clarifies that the student is not counted for the district’s ANB calculation and that the ESA account closes on the student’s 24th birthday
Creates an OPI ESA administration account within the state special revenue fund and authorizes its use for program administration costs
affected: Parents of students in the ESA program
Students enrolled in the ESA program

SB487.one_line: SB 487 expands the End‑of‑Watch Trust, adds workers’ comp calculations, and mandates COBRA coverage for injured officers.
SB487.summary: SB 487 revises Montana’s End‑of‑Watch Trust to add workers’‑comp and retirement‑benefit calculations, allow children to receive payments after age 18, and give the Department of Justice rule‑making authority. It also expands the board, clarifies payment schedules, and requires COBRA coverage for injured or deceased officers. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Adds a requirement that applications for catastrophic‑injury payments include a workers’ compensation determination of permanent total disability and a state‑retirement benefit calculation.
Allows legal children of a law‑enforcement officer to receive trust payments after turning 18 if the officer is catastrophically injured and the child is still a dependent.
Empowers the Department of Justice to adopt rules governing application processing, appeals, information security, and reporting for the trust.
Revises definitions of “catastrophic injury,” “immediate family,” and “law‑enforcement officer” and clarifies the board’s composition and duties.
Sets a 60‑month payment schedule for injured or deceased officers, with monthly amounts starting at $7,000 and adjusted for workers’ comp and retirement benefits after month 12.
Requires annual attestation of continued eligibility and notification of marital status changes to maintain payments.
Mandates local governments to enroll injured or deceased officers and their families in COBRA continuation coverage for four months, then shift premium responsibility to the family.
Creates a volunteer board of five members appointed by the attorney general, including representatives from law‑enforcement associations.
Provides that all trust payments are exempt from execution under 25‑13‑608.

SB488.one_line: Expands consumer‑protection law to cover deceptive reviews, limits construction damages, and imposes age‑verification for harmful content.
SB488.summary: SB 488 expands Montana’s consumer‑protection law to cover deceptive online reviews, tightens the department’s ability to sue, limits damages in construction disputes, and creates a new age‑verification requirement for harmful‑to‑minors content. The bill amends four existing statutes and takes effect immediately.
changes: Adds false or misleading consumer reviews to the list of unlawful practices under §30‑14‑103.
Gives the Department of Justice a 5‑year statute of limitations to bring an action against unlawful practices.
Allows the department to seek temporary or permanent injunctions in district courts, with notice requirements and no bond needed.
Limits individual civil actions for construction‑related consumer losses to the greater of $500 or actual loss, bars punitive damages, and caps attorney fees at $250/hr.
Requires commercial entities that publish or distribute material harmful to minors to perform reasonable age‑verification; failure to do so makes the entity liable for damages and attorney fees.
Exempts news‑gathering organizations, ISPs, search engines, and cloud providers from liability for providing access to such content.
Requires the department to file an annual enforcement report and make it available online.
affected: Consumers who purchase goods or services
Commercial entities that post reviews or distribute online content
Internet service providers and cloud providers

SB490.one_line: Expands late registration to election day and authorizes statewide electronic voting rules.
SB490.summary: SB 490 expands the window for late voter registration and changes, allowing voters to register or update their information up to the day of a federal election, and requires county election officials to verify registrations before noon the day before. It also authorizes the Secretary of State to adopt statewide rules for electronic registration and voting, including provisional ballots and digital signatures, and allows the use of federal or private grants to fund implementation.
changes: Extends late registration eligibility to the day of a federal election, with verification required before noon the day before or on election day
Allows voters who register late to receive and return ballots at designated county or school locations, including on election day
Permits voters who have already received a ballot to change registration information only if the ballot is voided and not yet received by the election office

Authorizes the Secretary of State to adopt uniform statewide rules for electronic registration and voting, covering absentee ballot transmission, provisional ballots, digital signatures, and secrecy safeguards
Provides that the Secretary may seek and use grants from federal or other sources to implement the new rules
Declares the act non‑severable: if any part is invalid, the entire act is invalid
Amends §13‑21‑104 to require the Secretary to adopt rules under the Administrative Procedure Act
Amends §13‑2‑304 to specify new late‑registration deadlines and procedures for federal elections
affected: Secretary of State and election officials
numbers: grant funding from federal or private sources

SB492.one_line: Revises filing deadlines and disclosure details for Montana officials and candidates.
SB492.summary: SB 492 updates the timing, content, and filing procedures for business disclosure statements required of Montana’s statewide and district‑level elected officials, candidates, and appointed department directors. It tightens deadlines, expands the information that must be reported, and clarifies when filings are due and how they may be certified as unchanged.
changes: Extends the filing deadline for state officers, holdover senators, Supreme Court justices, and district court judges to December 15 of each even‑numbered year.
Requires candidates to file a disclosure within five days of filing for office.
Mandates that appointed officials file at the earlier of confirmation submission or assumption of office.

Adds detailed disclosure items: name, address, business type; current or past employers; >10% ownership in any business or >1% in a publicly traded company; officer/director roles in any entity; >10% ownership of non‑residential real property.
Allows a filing to be certified as unchanged from the most recent statement, with a commissioner‑provided certification form.
Makes all statements and certification forms available to the public upon request.
Clarifies that mutual‑fund holdings need not be disclosed.
affected: Candidates for statewide or district offices
Department directors and other appointed officials
numbers: 1% ownership threshold for publicly traded companies

SB493.one_line: SB 493 criminalizes unauthorized drone flights within 200 ft of private property, with a $500 fine and specific exemptions.
SB493.summary: SB 493 makes it a crime to fly a drone within 200 feet of someone’s property or home without permission, except for a list of authorized uses. Violators face a $500 fine.
changes: Creates a new criminal offense—criminal trespass by unmanned aerial vehicle.
Defines the offense as knowingly flying a UAV 200 ft or lower over another’s property without authorization.
Sets a $500 fine for conviction.

Exempts operations by federal, state, tribal, or local government units; peace officers; operations within an easement with owner permission; utility or broadband employees inspecting infrastructure; and operators with an active FAA license flying for legitimate business.
Codifies the new offense into Montana’s Title 45, Chapter 6, Part 2.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.

SB495.one_line: SB 495 eliminates the tobacco‑prevention advisory board and revises settlement fund use.
SB495.summary: SB 495 removes Montana’s Tobacco Prevention Advisory Board and revises how tobacco‑settlement money is allocated, keeping the 32 % and 17 % earmarks but eliminating the board’s funding and oversight role. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Repeals Section 17‑6‑610, eliminating the Tobacco Prevention Advisory Board and its authority to receive funds.
Amends Section 17‑6‑606 to preserve the 32 % and 17 % allocation of tobacco‑settlement proceeds to a state special revenue account, but removes the board’s funding provision from subsection (5).
Maintains the 2‑year rule that unappropriated funds must be transferred to the trust fund.
Keeps the Department of Public Health and Human Services as the manager of tobacco‑prevention programs and the authority to adopt implementation rules.
Allows private‑nature programs to be funded via contracted services.
The act is effective on passage and approval, with no transition period.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: 2 years for appropriation before transfer to trust fund

SB497.one_line: Creates civil‑immunity wellness programs for providers and limits reporting of participation.
SB497.summary: The bill creates a “professional program” to address burnout among health‑care providers, gives civil immunity to its staff, limits reporting of participant information to licensing boards, and amends reporting rules for incompetence or unprofessional conduct.
changes: Creates a new category of professional wellness programs for health‑care providers and exempts them from federal income tax.
Provides civil immunity for members or consultants of such programs from civil liability for actions taken while performing program duties.
Restricts reporting of a provider’s participation in a wellness program to licensing boards unless the provider is deemed incompetent or a danger to patients or the public.
Imposes evidentiary privilege on program proceedings, preventing their use as evidence in civil or licensing actions except under strict court‑ordered circumstances.
Amends Sections 37‑3‑401 and 37‑4‑312 to allow reporting of incompetence or unprofessional conduct while preserving the new privilege provisions.
Allows program personnel to report to boards only if the provider refuses or fails to comply with required evaluations or treatment.
Requires in‑camera review by courts or administrative hearings before disclosing privileged information.
affected: Members and consultants of professional wellness programs
Licensing boards (medical, dental, pharmacy, nursing, behavioral health)

SB498.one_line: Mandates party‑by‑party ballot handling in primary elections.
SB498.summary: SB 498 amends the state election code to require election judges in primary elections to separate ballots by party, count each party’s ballots separately, reconcile totals, list candidates separately, and bundle ballots by party. The changes apply immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑10‑311 to mandate that primary election judges separate ballots for each political party and count them separately.
Requires judges to reconcile the total number of party ballots with the number of electors voting, handling discrepancies per §13‑15‑201.
Orders judges to list each party’s candidates separately in tally books.
Mandates bundling of voted ballots by party for return to the election administrator, while unvoted ballots are bundled per §13‑12‑202.
Specifies that in counties counting solely by hand, judges must still separate ballots by party and count separately.

SB503.one_line: Allows expired opioid antagonists in schools and for eligible recipients with limited liability protection.
SB503.summary: The bill allows schools, eligible recipients, and health‑care professionals to use expired opioid antagonists (e.g., naloxone) in overdose emergencies and grants limited liability protection for those who do so. It amends state law to clarify protocols, expand access, and provide professional immunity, except in cases of gross negligence or intentional harm.
changes: Schools may stock and administer expired opioid antagonists under a written protocol and are shielded from liability unless gross negligence or intentional misconduct occurs.

Eligible recipients (e.g., individuals with a prescription) may possess, store, administer, or distribute expired antagonists without pharmacy‑practice restrictions and are protected from civil or criminal liability.

Medical practitioners and pharmacists prescribing or dispensing expired antagonists are given professional immunity from disciplinary action or liability, except for gross negligence or intentional tort.
The bill amends the definition of “opioid antagonist” to include expired drugs and clarifies that the immunity applies to both expired and non‑expired medications.
Schools must inform parents/guardians about the potential use of the antagonist and provide the protocol upon request.
Reporting requirements are added for eligible recipients who dispense the drug, as directed by the department.
The law does not create a new program or fund; it merely expands existing statutes.
No new criminal offense is created.
No significant fiscal impact is identified in the text.
who_is_affected

SB508.one_line: Bill lowers THC and alcohol DUI limits for under‑21 drivers and clarifies inference rules.
SB508.summary: The bill lowers the THC threshold for drivers under 21 to any detectable amount and keeps the 5 ng/mL limit for older drivers. It also adds a lower alcohol limit (0.02 g/dL) for under‑21 drivers and clarifies inference rules for alcohol tests.
changes: Any detectable THC (excluding inactive metabolites) in a driver under 21 constitutes DUI, regardless of level.
The alcohol DUI threshold for drivers under 21 is lowered to 0.02 g/dL.
The existing 5 ng/mL THC threshold for drivers 21 and older remains unchanged.
The bill retains the 0.08 g/dL alcohol threshold for noncommercial vehicles and 0.04 g/dL for commercial vehicles for all ages.
It adds inference rules for alcohol concentrations (0.04–0.08 and ≥0.08) and allows other evidence to be considered.
It authorizes municipalities to enact local ordinances mirroring the state provisions.
It imposes absolute liability for violations under this section.
It limits conviction to one offense per conduct.

SB511.one_line: Rewrites litigation‑financing rules, adds foreign‑investment restrictions, and tightens consumer protections.
SB511.summary: SB 511 revises Montana’s litigation‑financing laws, tightens consumer protections, and adds a new foreign‑investment regime that bars foreign adversaries from funding litigation in the state. The bill also requires disclosure of foreign‑person involvement and limits litigation‑financer conduct.
changes: Amends definitions in §31‑4‑102 to clarify who is a consumer, entity, litigation financer, and related terms.
Imposes new conduct limits on litigation financers in §31‑4‑104, such as prohibiting referral fees, excessive interest, and influence over legal strategy.
Mandates disclosure of litigation‑financing contracts to parties, courts, and insurers in §31‑4‑108 and requires timely delivery of contracts.

Creates a new “Foreign Investment in Litigation Financing Act” (Sections 6‑12) that bars foreign adversaries and persons of concern from financing litigation, requires registration with the Secretary of State, and mandates disclosure of foreign‑person details and contracts.
Adds joint and several liability for litigation financers for costs imposed on consumers or their counsel in §31‑4‑120.
Provides immediate effective date and applicability to contracts entered after that date.
affected: Foreign adversaries and persons of concern
numbers: applicability: contracts entered on or after effective date

SB514.one_line: Residents may hunt upland game birds 10 days before non‑residents, except mountain grouse.
SB514.summary: SB 514 amends the game‑bird season rules so that Montana residents may hunt upland game birds 10 days before non‑residents, except for mountain grouse. It also adds a definition for mountain grouse and makes a few other technical changes to the commission’s authority.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑304 to allow residents to begin hunting all upland game birds 10 days before non‑residents, except mountain grouse
Defines “mountain grouse” as blue, spruce (Franklin), and ruffed grouse
Preserves the commission’s existing authority to fix seasons, bag limits, and special seasons
Maintains provisions for special muzzleloader heritage season and wolf‑trapping season
Leaves all other hunting‑season rules unchanged
Sets the act’s effective date to March 1, 2026
affected: Montana residents who hunt upland game birds
Non‑resident hunters of upland game birds

SB516.one_line: SB 516 tightens licensing and oversight for Montana’s health‑care facilities, especially assisted‑living and community homes.
SB516.summary: SB 516 revises Montana’s health‑care licensing rules, updates definitions, and tightens standards for community homes and assisted‑living facilities. It adds new licensing requirements, clarifies what counts as a health‑care facility, and expands oversight of day‑care, abortion clinics, and substance‑use treatment centers.
changes: Amends the definition of a health‑care facility to include a broad list of hospitals, clinics, and treatment centers, and excludes certain outpatient and hospital types.
Adds a definition for “substance use disorder facility” and clarifies “abortion clinic” and “abortion‑inducing drug.”
Requires that facilities submit plans for preliminary inspection before construction and that licenses be renewed annually with a 45‑day inspection window.
Sets minimum standards for assisted‑living facilities, creating categories A–D with specific resident eligibility and care‑planning requirements.
Allows the Department to issue provisional or temporary licenses (up to 6 months or 1 year) when facilities are not fully compliant but are needed to serve the community.
Expands the Department’s authority to inspect, suspend, or revoke licenses for violations such as staff shortages, financial incapacity, or abuse.
Requires day‑care facilities to obtain written authorization before giving medicine to children, with limited emergency exceptions.
Updates community‑home licensing for persons with severe or developmental disabilities, including resident limits (8–12) and annual inspection requirements.
Adds new definitions and reporting requirements for Montana Medicaid services and trauma‑care data.
Modifies the Montana Medicaid program to clarify covered services, funding principles, and reporting obligations.
Adds a new section on “trauma register” and “trauma care committee” for quality improvement.
affected: Health‑care facilities (hospitals, clinics, treatment centers, day‑care centers, abortion clinics, substance‑use treatment facilities), assisted‑living and community‑home operators, licensed health‑care professionals, patients and residents, and the Department of Public Health and Human Services
numbers: $500 fine or 6‑month jail for unauthorized medicine in day‑care
$50,000 fine or 20‑year jail for serious injury or death

SB518.one_line: Transfers emergency‑care provider licensing to Labor and Industry and expands board membership.
SB518.summary: The bill moves the licensing of emergency‑care providers from the Board of Medical Examiners to the Department of Labor and Industry, expands the board’s membership, and creates new rules and reporting requirements for emergency‑care services.
changes: Transfers licensing authority for emergency‑care providers from the Board of Medical Examiners to the Department of Labor and Industry.

Reconfigures the Board of Medical Examiners to include a physician with emergency‑medicine experience, an osteopath, a podiatrist, a nutritionist, a physician assistant, an emergency‑care provider, and two public members.
Adds rule‑making authority for the Department of Labor and Industry to set training, licensure, and competency standards for emergency‑care providers and for community‑integrated health care.
Establishes a complaint‑screening and investigation process that involves the Department of Labor and Industry, the Department of Public Health and Human Services, and the Board of Medical Examiners.
Creates reporting requirements for complaints involving patient care by emergency‑care providers and for the use of marijuana for medical purposes.
Provides for a medical‑assistance program for licensees who are impaired and allows the board to require participation as a condition of licensure.
Includes provisions for mutual recognition agreements with other states for emergency‑care provider licensing.
Sets the effective date of the act to January 1, 2026.
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff
Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
Montana residents who may receive community‑integrated health care

SB520.one_line: SB 520 extends mining lease terms, allows modifications, and limits public access to proprietary geology.
SB520.summary: SB 520 revises Montana’s mining‑lease rules, extending minimum terms, allowing lease modifications, and tightening public‑inspection rights for proprietary geological data. The changes apply to both metalliferous‑and‑nonmetallic‑mineral leases on state lands and take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Leases for metalliferous minerals or gems must have a primary term of at least 10 years and may continue in production as long as minerals are produced in commercial quantities; nonmetallic‑mineral leases have similar 10‑year minimums with optional 5‑year non‑production extensions.
affected: Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
numbers: 5 years minimum withholding period for proprietary data

SB524.one_line: Rewrites rules for category D assisted‑living, limits residents, adds restraint approval, and creates diversion from state hospital.
SB524.summary: SB 524 revises Montana’s rules for category D assisted‑living facilities, allowing them to operate independently or with other licensed facilities, limiting residents to 15, and setting detailed admission, restraint, and diversion requirements. It also amends mental‑health commitment procedures to favor diversion to category D facilities and gives the Department of Public Health technical and reimbursement support.
changes: Allows category D assisted‑living facilities to be independent or colocated with other licensed facilities
Limits each category D facility to no more than 15 residents
Requires a monthly health‑care assessment and written care order for each resident
Mandates prior approval from the Department of Public Health for any use of restraints or seclusion
Creates a specialized reimbursement model for category D facilities, with enhanced payments for higher‑acuity residents
Amends mental‑health commitment statutes (53‑21‑127 and 53‑21‑199) to provide a diversion pathway to category D facilities
Establishes a court process for voluntary or involuntary diversion to a category D facility
Provides the Department with duties to supply technical assistance and standardized forms for facilities and practitioners
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB532.one_line: Allows one ADU per lot, limits size, restricts zoning, permits $250 fee, expires 2029.
SB532.summary: The bill requires counties to allow at least one accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on a lot with a single‑family home, sets limits on size and prohibits overly restrictive zoning rules, lets counties charge up to $250 for application review, and amends a subdivision‑deviation provision for ADUs. The rules expire on September 30 2029.
changes: Counties must permit a minimum of one ADU on any lot containing a single‑family dwelling, whether attached, detached, or internal.
ADUs may not exceed 75 % of the single‑family dwelling’s gross floor area or 1,000 sq ft, whichever is smaller.
Counties cannot require extra parking, matching exterior design, owner occupancy, familial relationships, impact fees, or more restrictive building standards for ADUs.
Counties may charge a one‑time application fee of up to $250 for ADU permits, in addition to normal building fees.
The bill amends § 76‑4‑130 to allow a 15‑day expedited review for ADU deviations when the parcel already has adequate public water and wastewater service.
Regulations adopted after the effective date that conflict with these provisions are void; until then, counties must follow the new rules.
The provisions do not override existing building, fire, or health codes.
The bill expires on September 30 2029.

SB534.one_line: Provides a 5‑year property‑tax exemption for new fiber and wireless infrastructure, requiring reinvestment of savings.
SB534.summary: The bill creates a 5‑year property‑tax exemption for new fiber‑optic, coaxial cable, and wireless infrastructure built after July 1 2021 (fiber) or the act’s effective date (wireless).  Owners must reinvest the tax savings in new infrastructure within two years, or the exemption is terminated and taxes may be recaptured.
changes: Exempts fiber‑optic or coaxial cable and wireless infrastructure placed in service after the specified dates from property tax for five years, with a 20 % annual phase‑out over ten years.
Requires owners to reinvest tax savings in new fiber or wireless infrastructure within two years to keep the exemption; failure triggers termination and possible recapture.
Adds record‑keeping and inspection requirements for owners claiming the exemption.
Allows local governments to post comments on proposed projects through a Department of Revenue website.
Provides for recapture of previously exempted taxes, interest, and penalties within ten years of the first claim.
Amends several property‑tax statutes (15‑6‑135, 15‑6‑156, 15‑6‑219, 15‑6‑243) to include the new exemption rules.

SB535.one_line: SB 535 creates licensing, profit‑sharing, and insurance‑support rules for experimental‑treatment centers.
SB535.summary: SB 535 establishes a licensing framework for experimental‑treatment centers, creates a health‑freedom requirement and an insurance‑premium support account, and amends several health‑care statutes to clarify patient consent, provider liability, and state immunity. The bill does not create a new program beyond the licensing and account structures, and it takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Creates a new license for experimental‑treatment centers, requiring a $10,000 application fee and a $5,000 annual renewal fee, with a 90‑day approval window

Mandates that licensed centers allocate 2 % of net annual profits to a health‑freedom and access requirement, either by providing free treatment or by contributing to an insurance‑premium support account
Establishes an insurance‑premium support account in the state special revenue fund to subsidize premiums for Montana residents earning 139–400 % of the federal poverty level
Amends the Right‑to‑Try Act provisions to clarify patient eligibility, informed‑consent requirements, and payment arrangements for experimental treatments
Adds disciplinary‑action and state‑action prohibitions that shield providers and facilities from punitive actions based solely on recommending or providing experimental treatments
Provides immunity from civil suits for manufacturers, pharmacists, providers, and facilities that comply in good faith with the act
Amends definitions in several Montana Code sections (33‑1‑102, 37‑3‑103, 50‑5‑101, 50‑12‑102‑110) to incorporate the new licensing, consent, and liability provisions
Requires the department to report annually on the use of the insurance‑premium support account
Sets the act in effect immediately upon passage
affected: State department of public health and human services

SB536.one_line: Revises contractor tax, adds ESOP credit, and creates exemption for good‑standing entities.
SB536.summary: SB 536 revises Montana’s contractor gross‑receipts tax, adds an exemption for qualified individuals and businesses, and creates a credit for employee‑stock‑ownership‑plan (ESOP) contractors that can offset income, corporate, and certain real‑property taxes. The bill also expands the credit carry‑forward period and gives the Department of Revenue rule‑making authority. The act takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: Adds an exemption from the contractor gross‑receipts tax for individuals and businesses that are in good standing and require an application to obtain the exemption.
Defines a new credit that ESOP corporations owned 100 % by employees may claim against their income or corporate taxes.
Extends the period over which ESOP contractors may carry forward unused credit to five succeeding tax years.
Allows the credit to offset certain real‑property and personal‑property taxes paid by the contractor, subject to proof of payment.
Authorizes the Department of Revenue to adopt rules to administer the credit and its carry‑forwards.
Amends sections 15‑50‑101 and 15‑50‑207 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new definitions, exemption, and credit provisions.
affected: Contractors performing public construction work in Montana
Employees who own 100 % of an ESOP corporation
Individuals and businesses in good standing seeking the tax exemption
Department of Revenue staff responsible for rule‑making and enforcement

SB537.one_line: Reallocates marijuana tax revenue to new wildlife, health, and law‑enforcement accounts and amends habitat‑management statutes.
SB537.summary: SB 537 reorganizes Montana’s marijuana‑tax revenue, creating several new special‑revenue accounts for wildlife, habitat, and law‑enforcement uses while directing funds to addiction‑prevention, behavioral‑health, and tribal programs. The bill also amends wildlife‑habitat statutes to establish a council, ranking rules, and funding mechanisms for weed‑control projects.
changes: Creates a dedicated marijuana state‑special‑revenue account and specifies how excess funds are transferred each fiscal year to new accounts (HEART, wildlife, park, trail, etc.)

Establishes a Habitat Legacy Account, a Big‑Game & Wildlife Highway Crossings Account, a Land & Wildlife Stewardship Account, and a Wildlife Habitat Improvement Project Account, each with defined transfer percentages and uses
Sets up a Wildlife Habitat Improvement Advisory Council with voting and non‑voting members and gives it authority to rank grant proposals
Amends wildlife‑habitat statutes (87‑5‑802‑808) to require project proposals to address noxious‑weed management, include cost‑sharing, measurable objectives, and grant‑matching commitments
Provides a 1.5% fee for certain law‑enforcement grant applications and earmarks funds for drug‑detection canine programs, sexual‑assault forensic kits, and other justice‑related uses
Allocates up to $7.5 million, $2 million, and $500,000 from the new accounts to the Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks for the 2025‑26 biennium
Requires annual reporting to the Children, Families & Health Committee on funded programs and grants
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025
affected: Montana state agencies (Revenue, Public Health & Human Services, Military Affairs, Fish, Wildlife & Parks, Justice), law‑enforcement agencies, tribal governments, homeless shelters, addiction‑prevention programs, wildlife‑habitat projects, and the general public who pays marijuana taxes
numbers: 4% each to park, trail, nongame wildlife
1.5% to DOJ for canine, investigation, testing
$7.5 million appropriation to Fish, Wildlife & Parks
$2 million appropriation to Fish, Wildlife & Parks

SB542.one_line: SB 542 freezes 2024 values, offers rebates, lowers rates, and creates new reduced‑tax programs for Montana property owners.
SB542.summary: SB 542 revises Montana’s property‑tax system, freezes 2024 property values for 2025‑26, creates a $400 or less rebate for principal residences, lowers rates for agricultural, residential, commercial, and long‑term rental properties, and establishes new homestead and rental‑property reduced‑tax programs with application, appeal, and refund provisions.
changes: Property values assessed in 2024 are used for 2025 and 2026 unless the Department of Revenue determines a value decline; the change is retroactive to the 2025 tax year.

A property‑tax rebate of $400 or the amount of taxes paid (whichever is less) is available to owners of a principal residence for the 2024 tax year; claims must be filed electronically or by mail between Aug 15–Oct 1 2025, with a deadline of Dec 1 2025.
Class III agricultural property rates are reduced; class IV residential and commercial rates are revised to a graduated scale (0.76%–2.2% for residential; 1.5%–1.89% for commercial/industrial).

New reduced‑tax rates are created: a homestead reduced tax rate for owner‑occupied residences and a rental‑property reduced tax rate for long‑term rentals; eligibility, application, and appeal procedures are set out in §§ 6–8.
The Department may refund a property owner who failed to claim the homestead reduced tax rate, based on the difference between paid taxes and what would have been due under the rate.
Statutory appropriations are provided for rebates, refunds, and reimbursements; rule‑making authority is granted to the Department of Revenue.
affected: property owners of single‑family homes, trailers, manufactured homes, and mobile homes; owners of long‑term rental units; owners of agricultural and commercial properties; county and local governments with fixed mill levies; taxpayers who may file appeals or refunds.
SB542.effective: Jan 1 2026 (most provisions); retroactive to 2025 tax year

SB545.one_line: Designates a highway segment, installs signs, updates maps, and adds a personalized‑plate fee.
SB545.summary: The bill designates a stretch of Highway 37 in Lincoln County as the Danny L. Radish Highway, requires the Department of Transportation to sign it and add it to state maps, and adds a $25 fee for new personalized license plates (with $10 for transfers/renewals) that goes to the general fund.
changes: Establishes the Danny L. Radish Highway on Highway 37, mile markers 63.6‑66.8 in Lincoln County.
Directs the Montana Department of Transportation to design and install signs for the new highway.
Mandates that state highway maps be updated to include the new highway when the department publishes them.
Amends § 61‑3‑406 to add a $25 fee for a new personalized license plate and a $10 fee for each transfer or renewal of such a plate.
Requires that revenue from the personalized‑plate fees be deposited in the state general fund.
Codifies the highway designation as part of Title 60, Chapter 1, Part 2 of the Montana Code.

SB544.one_line: Allows 2024 net‑operating‑loss carryover adjustments to align with federal amounts, deadline Oct 15 2025.
SB544.summary: SB 544 lets Montana taxpayers adjust their 2024 net‑operating‑loss carryovers to match federal amounts that were altered by the 2021 tax‑simplification law.  The election must be filed by Oct 15 2025 and applies retroactively to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2023.
changes: Allows a 2024 election to make a transition adjustment for a net‑operating‑loss carryover under IRC §172(a) to reconcile federal and Montana carryovers that differ as of Jan 1 2024.
The adjustment is the sum of all positive and negative differences between federal and Montana taxable income before Jan 1 2024.
If the Montana carryover is smaller than the federal carryover, the difference is a positive adjustment; if larger, it is a negative adjustment.
The election must be filed on a 2024 return (or an amended return) by Oct 15 2025 and must include a Department‑of‑Revenue‑published carryforward adjustment form.
The entire carryforward or carryback is applied to 2024 and, if needed, to subsequent years up to seven years, but it does not affect new carryovers or carrybacks after Dec 31 2023.
The Department may prescribe forms and adopt rules to administer the adjustment.
affected: Individual taxpayers with net‑operating‑loss carryovers affected by the 2021 tax‑simplification changes
numbers: Retroactive to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2023

SB550.one_line: Adds telecom assets to Class 5 property, creates new exemptions and recapture rules.
SB550.summary: SB 550 expands Montana’s Class 5 property definition to cover certain telecommunications assets and creates new tax‑exemption rules for fiber‑optic cable and pollution‑control equipment. The bill also sets a 3 % tax rate for most Class 5 property, specifies exemption criteria, and allows retroactive application to tax years after 12/31/2024.
changes: Adds telecommunications property to Class 5 property, including rural‑area telecom firms and firms owning property in ≤3 counties.
Defines and exempts air‑ and water‑pollution control and carbon‑capture equipment placed in service after 1/1/2014.
Exempts fiber‑optic or coaxial cable installed on/after 7/1/2021 for 5 years, then phases out at 20 %/yr, requiring reinvestment of tax savings into new cable within 2 years.
Sets a 3 % tax rate on all Class 5 property except the exempted categories.
Provides for recapture of improperly claimed exemptions, with interest and penalties, and allows cancellation if circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control.
Applies retroactively to property‑tax years beginning after 12/31/2024 and takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Telecom firms owning property in ≤3 counties
Owners of fiber‑optic or coaxial cable

SB552.one_line: Allows county attorneys to transfer suspended‑sentence cases to the new felony’s county and amends revocation and probation rules.
SB552.summary: SB 552 lets a county attorney file a petition to transfer a suspended‑or‑deferred‑sentence case to the county where a new felony is alleged, so both cases can be heard together. It amends the revocation process and probation‑supervision rules and adds a $120 filing fee.
changes: Allows county attorneys to petition to transfer a suspended or deferred sentence to the county where a new felony is alleged.
Amends §46‑18‑203 to permit the transfer and to set procedural requirements for revocation hearings.
Amends §46‑23‑1011 to clarify probation‑supervision procedures, including conditions, reporting, and conditional discharge.
Adds a $120 filing fee for petitions that request jurisdiction transfer.
Expands definitions of compliance and absconding violations and clarifies how time served is credited when a sentence is revoked.
Provides that a judge may modify or add probation conditions at any time and that the county attorney may file a petition to do so.
Sets out procedures for conditional discharge motions, victim notification, and the judge’s discretion in granting discharge.
Specifies that the revocation hearing must be held within 60 days of arrest and that the offender must be advised of rights at least 10 days before the hearing.
affected: Offenders with suspended or deferred sentences

SB555.one_line: SB 555 expands online gambling definitions, adds penalties, and redirects fines to the DOJ budget.
SB555.summary: SB 555 updates Montana’s gambling statutes, expanding the definition of internet gambling to cover online casinos and cryptocurrency, adding a carve‑out for casinos that accept no currency, and tightening penalties for illegal gambling. It also redirects all gambling‑related fines to the Department of Justice’s operating budget and clarifies misdemeanor and felony liability for violations.
changes: Redefines “internet gambling” to include online casinos and cryptocurrency‑based betting, except for casinos that accept no currency
Adds an exception allowing online casinos that do not accept any form of currency to operate legally
Revises the disposal of fines so all gambling‑related penalties go to the Department of Justice’s operating budget
Expands criminal penalties: adds misdemeanor liability for soliciting illegal gambling and felony penalties (up to $50,000 fine and 10‑year prison) for violations of the new gambling provisions
Amends definitions of antique gambling devices, associated gambling business, and other terms in §23‑5‑112
Clarifies that fines collected under parts 1‑8 or department rules are deposited in the state general fund operating budget of the Department of Justice
Adds a misdemeanor offense for advertising or soliciting participation in illegal gambling
Adds felony liability for operating an illegal internet gambling site, including offshore‑based sites that target Montana residents
affected: Individuals who advertise or solicit illegal gambling

SB553.one_line: SB 553 updates policy laws, creates new reporting and fee rules, and revises park‑dedication and travel‑credit provisions.
SB553.summary: SB 553 amends dozens of Montana statutes to update policy rules, create new reporting and fee‑collection mechanisms, and clarify definitions for travel credits, gift certificates, and park‑dedication requirements. The bill also establishes a temporary 9‑1‑1 GIS mapping fund, a high‑performance building program, and expands reporting obligations for many state agencies.
changes: Local governments may require residential developers to share costs of capital‑facility upgrades when future developments benefit from those upgrades, and the Department of Transportation may rule that developers pay a share of intersection or other improvements that reduce future costs.

Travel credits issued by airlines are now considered trust property of the possessor; they do not expire, may be redeemed for cash if the remaining value is under $5, and cannot be reduced by fees. A $1 fee is added to any ticket purchased for travel to or from Montana, with proceeds deposited in an enterprise‑fund account to combat human trafficking.

The bill revises park‑dedication rules for subdividers, setting cash or land donation percentages based on parcel size and allowing waivers for certain types of developments or for land set aside for parks, recreation, or conservation.
A temporary 9‑1‑1 GIS mapping fund is created for the state library to collect, maintain, and disseminate GIS data for public‑safety answering points; the fund is wound down in FY 2031.

A voluntary high‑performance building program is authorized for state agencies to improve energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality in existing buildings, with reporting required through June 30 2029.

The bill amends the universal‑system‑benefits program statutes to clarify utility and large‑customer credit rules, reporting requirements, and funding levels for renewable‑energy and low‑income‑energy assistance.
The energy‑and‑telecommunications interim committee is renamed the energy‑and‑technology interim committee; all references to the former are updated by the code commissioner.
The bill adds extensive reporting requirements for a wide array of state agencies and committees, many of which are new or expanded from existing statutes.
affected: state agencies (DOT, DOT, Dept. of Administration, Dept. of Justice, etc.)
Montana Department of Energy and Natural Resources
Montana Department of Health and Human Services
Montana Department of Labor and Industry
Montana Department of Agriculture and Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Montana Department of Labor and Industry
Montana Department of Health and Human Services
state agencies that must report to interim committees

SB560.one_line: Nonprofit hospitals must report community benefits, face a fee if shortfall, and fund critical‑access hospitals.
SB560.summary: SB 560 requires nonprofit hospitals to report community‑benefit spending and imposes a fee if that spending falls short of the hospital’s potential property‑tax liability.  The fee revenue is earmarked for critical‑access hospitals, and the bill also updates definitions and financial‑assistance rules for nonprofit hospitals.
changes: 1. Hospitals must file an annual community‑benefit report with the Department of Public Health and Human Services, detailing net community‑benefit expenses, net community‑building expenses, and bad‑debt/Medicare‑shortfall amounts from IRS Form 990 Schedule H.
2. Each hospital must provide a community‑benefit total that exceeds its prior‑year potential property‑tax liability; if it does not, the Department assesses a fee equal to the shortfall.
3. The assessed fee is deposited into a special revenue account in the State Special Revenue Fund to be disbursed to critical‑access hospitals on a per‑bed basis.

4. The Department of Revenue must prepare a “potential tax liability” statement for each nonprofit hospital, treating its property as class‑four commercial property and using prior‑year taxable value and mills.

5. Section 50‑5‑121 is amended to require nonprofit hospitals (including critical‑access and rural emergency hospitals) to have written financial‑assistance and community‑benefit policies that prohibit discrimination based on ability to pay, and to make those policies public.
6. The bill amends definitions in Section 50‑5‑101, adding a definition of “community benefit” that ties it to IRS Schedule H figures.
7. Rule‑making authority is granted to the Department of Public Health and Human Services (for reporting and fee rules) and to the Department of Revenue (for potential‑tax‑liability rules).
8. The act creates a new special revenue account and a funding program for critical‑access hospitals.
9. Effective dates: reporting and fee rules apply to critical‑access hospitals from Jan 1 2027; fee and other provisions apply from Jan 1 2031.
10. The bill does not create a new criminal offense.
who_is_affected:[
nonprofit hospitals (especially critical‑access and rural emergency hospitals)
state departments of Public Health and Human Services, Revenue, and Labor and Industry
numbers: June 30 (deadline for disbursement to critical‑access hospitals)

SB564.one_line: Creates a public procurement website and allows vendors to pay a bid fee.
SB564.summary: SB 564 requires the Department of Administration to build and run a public website that lists state procurement transactions and payments, and it amends procurement statutes to mandate the site and allow vendors to pay a bid‑fee to cover costs.
changes: Amends §18‑4‑126 to require a Department‑run website that posts each payment made by a purchasing agency, including contractor name, purpose, and amount.
Adds a new application‑fee requirement for vendors submitting bids or proposals to offset website costs.
Amends §18‑4‑302 to allow the Department to approve alternative procurement methods and to use publicly advertised catalog prices to reject lower bids.
Provides a 30‑day evaluation period for alternative‑method requests and requires written determinations of success.
Keeps existing procurement record‑retention requirements unchanged.
No new criminal offenses or state programs are created.

HB456.one_line: Expands child‑care scholarships to workers, sets new income limits, and appropriates $5.5 million.
HB456.summary: HB 456 expands Montana’s Best Beginnings child‑care scholarship program to include child‑care workers employed at licensed day‑care centers or registered family/group homes, sets new income eligibility rules, and appropriates $5.5 million for the first biennium.
changes: Amends §52‑2‑714 to add child‑care workers as scholarship recipients.
Amends §52‑2‑715 to set a 185 % FPL income threshold for families and a two‑times‑median‑income limit for workers, and requires workers to be employed for the minimum hours set by the department.
Appropriates $5.5 million from the general fund to the Department of Public Health and Human Services for each year of the 2025‑2026 biennium.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 , 2025.
affected: Low‑income families eligible for child‑care scholarships
Child‑care workers at licensed day‑care centers or registered family/group homes
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB462.one_line: HB 462 establishes a state‑wide HQIM selection and subsidy program with $5 million in appropriations.
HB462.summary: HB 462 creates a state‑wide process for selecting and subsidizing high‑quality instructional materials (HQIM) tied to revised content standards, and provides funding for professional development and implementation support.
changes: 1. Adds a new subsection to the content‑standard revision process that requires the superintendent to recommend 3‑5 sets of HQIM and cost estimates for each standard.

2. Amends §20‑7‑101 to require economic‑impact statements that include HQIM cost estimates and to delay implementation of new standards until the next legislative session unless the district can absorb the costs.

3. Amends §20‑7‑113 to allow the superintendent, with appropriated funds, to offer reduced‑cost access to up to three recommended HQIM and to require districts that receive subsidies to commit to professional‑development days for the first two years.

4. Amends §20‑7‑114 to give the superintendent, again with appropriated funds, the authority to provide in‑service training, consultation, and to monitor student achievement in districts adopting HQIM.

5. Provides a $5 million appropriation (split $3 million for K‑8 math HQIM and $2 million for high‑school math curriculum and PD) that must be spent on supporting districts in adopting revised math standards.
6. Sets the act’s effective date for July 1, 2025, and codifies the new material‑selection process as part of Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 1.
affected: Parents and taxpayers (through the negotiated rulemaking committee)
Montana Digital Academy and other curriculum‑support entities
numbers: July 1, 2026 implementation of revised math standards

HB477.one_line: Montana bans polystyrene foam containers in food businesses, allows limited exemptions, and collects fees for enforcement.
HB477.summary: Montana will ban the use of expanded polystyrene (styrofoam) containers in restaurants, hotels, and food‑packaging businesses, with phased dates from 2028‑2030.  Businesses may apply for an exemption if no acceptable alternative exists or if the ban causes undue hardship, and a fee will be charged for each exemption application.  The fee revenue will be deposited in the state’s environmental rehabilitation and response account and the Department of Environmental Quality will enforce the ban and set penalties.
changes: Prohibits restaurants and food establishments from serving or packaging food in polystyrene foam containers beginning Jan 1 2028, with broader bans extending to hotels and food packagers by 2030.

Creates an exemption process allowing applicants to use polystyrene foam if no acceptable alternative exists or if the ban causes undue hardship, or for specific purposes (transportation, construction, health, safety).
Authorizes the Department of Environmental Quality to adopt rules, issue fines, and enforce the ban.
Imposes a fee on each exemption application; the fee revenue and any related fines are deposited in the environmental rehabilitation and response account.
Amends the solid waste management account to include the new fee and related revenues.
Codifies the new rules as a part of Title 75, Chapter 10 of the Montana Code.
affected: Restaurants, food establishments, resorts, hotels, and food packagers
Businesses seeking exemptions from the ban
Taxpayers whose money is deposited in the environmental rehabilitation and response account

HB547.one_line: HB 547 preserves volunteer fire departments and requires a municipal fire chief in consolidated city‑county governments.
HB547.summary: HB 547 revises Montana’s fire‑protection statutes for consolidated city‑county governments. It requires a municipal fire chief, preserves existing volunteer fire departments after consolidation, and amends two statutory sections to clarify pension rights. The bill does not create new programs or funds.
changes: Mandates that a consolidated city‑county government must appoint a fire chief or director of fire service to manage the department per municipal ordinances.
Amends § 7‑33‑2110 to state that a city‑county consolidation does not affect the existence of volunteer fire districts, companies, or departments unless a charter explicitly changes that.
Amends § 7‑33‑2316 similarly to preserve volunteer fire entities and their pension/retirement benefits after consolidation.
Repeals the previous versions of §§ 7‑33‑2110 and 7‑33‑2316, replacing them with the amended language.
Codifies the new § 1 as part of Title 7, Chapter 3, Part 11, making it integral to the fire‑service statutes.
affected: Municipalities forming or already consolidated city‑county governments
Volunteer fire departments, companies, and districts within those governments
Fire personnel and pension/retirement plan participants

HB551.one_line: Funds districts to drop reduced‑price meal fees, with $600k each for 2025‑26.
HB551.summary: The bill creates a state program that gives school districts money to drop the small fee that families who qualify for reduced‑price meals must pay. The program is funded with $600,000 each for FY 2025 and FY 2026 and allows districts to request more money if needed. The superintendent of public instruction will set the rules and may accept private donations to cover shortfalls.
changes: Establishes a new state program to reimburse districts that eliminate reduced‑price copayments for lunch and breakfast.
Appropriates $600,000 from the state general fund for FY 2025 and FY 2026 to fund the program.
Empowers the superintendent of public instruction to adopt rules and administer the program.
Allows the superintendent to accept private or out‑of‑state donations if appropriated funds are insufficient.
