Requires the superintendent to request additional funding for the next biennium if needed.
If both this bill and House Bill 2 pass, the School Lunch Funding appropriations in HB 2 are void.
affected: School districts that choose to eliminate reduced‑price copayments.

HB605.one_line: Allows strip searches for >12‑hour detentions, requires same‑sex officers, and imposes a county fee.
HB605.summary: The bill amends Montana’s strip‑search law to allow a strip search of any person who will be held in jail or a correctional facility for more than 12 hours, requires the search to be conducted by an officer of the same sex and prohibits body‑cavity penetration, and mandates each county to pay a $250 fee to the Department of Justice for guideline development.
changes: Adds a new exception to §46‑5‑105: a person who will be housed for >12 hours may be strip‑searched (no cavity penetration) by a same‑sex peace officer or law‑enforcement employee.
Requires a $250 fee from each county to the Department of Justice for developing strip‑search guidelines.
Maintains the existing reasonable‑suspicion requirement for traffic or non‑felony arrests.
Clarifies that the search exception does not apply to felony arrests.
Keeps the prohibition on body‑cavity searches in the new exception.
No other substantive changes to the criminal‑law framework are made.
affected: Peace officers and law‑enforcement employees who conduct strip searches
Individuals detained for more than 12 hours in jail or correctional facilities

HB676.one_line: HB 676 revises state‑land and water‑right laws, ending Water Court adjudication and tightening improvement and ownership rules.
HB676.summary: HB 676 revises Montana’s state‑land and water‑right statutes, ending the Water Court’s adjudication duty, limiting the Board of Land Commissioners’ ability to acquire private water rights on state lands, and tightening rules on improvements and water‑right ownership. The bill also repeals a large block of water‑right adjudication provisions and amends several land‑lease sections.
changes: Eliminates the Water Court’s duty to adjudicate water rights effective July 1, 2030
Prohibits the Board of Land Commissioners from owning a private water right that is used on state lands
Requires that isolated parcels with water rights be sold to lessees of state lands
Amends §77‑6‑301 to allow lessees to install conservation‑related improvements and §77‑6‑302 to require registration and compensation for such improvements
Rewrites §77‑6‑302 to set procedures for valuation, compensation, and removal of improvements upon lease termination
Rewrites §77‑6‑301 and §77‑6‑302 to clarify ownership and compensation rules
Repeals numerous sections (85‑2‑212 through 85‑2‑282) that dealt with water‑right adjudication
Effective date is the passage and approval of the act
affected: Water‑right holders who use water on state lands
Potential buyers of isolated parcels with water rights

HB607.one_line: HB 607 expands hearing‑loss coverage to all ages and adds many new health‑benefit mandates for state plans.
HB607.summary: HB 607 expands hearing‑loss coverage from children to all ages and amends related insurance rules. It also adds a wide array of new health‑benefit requirements for state‑employee and university plans, and updates rules for retirees, judges, legislators, and public‑service employees.
changes: Rewrites §33‑22‑128 to require coverage for diagnosis and treatment of hearing loss for any covered person, not just children under 18; limits devices to one per ear every 3 years unless an audiologist orders more; removes special limits on deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for hearing‑loss services.
Amends §2‑18‑704 to extend group‑plan membership rights to retirees, surviving spouses, children, legislators, and judges, with specific notice and cost‑equivalence requirements.

Adds new mandatory coverages to state‑employee and Montana university group plans: inborn errors of metabolism, Down‑syndrome therapies, fertility preservation, mental‑illness treatment, telehealth, eye‑drop refills, well‑child care (birth‑7 yrs), hospital inpatient care for breast‑cancer surgery, diabetes self‑management training and supplies, and mental‑health coverage.
Requires state‑employee and university plans to provide COBRA continuation for law‑enforcement officers who die or are catastrophically injured in the line of duty, with a 4‑month paid premium.
Rewrites definitions and limits for hearing‑loss devices, medical‑necessity standards, and coverage applicability to a broad range of public‑service insurance programs.
Changes eligibility and renewal rules for dependents in state plans, including coverage until age 26 and special enrollment provisions.
Adds informational‑material requirements for cancer‑screening coverage.
Replaces or clarifies coverage limits for certain disease‑specific policies (disability income, hospital indemnity, etc.).
affected: Law‑enforcement officers, game wardens, firefighters, volunteer firefighters
Public‑service insurance plans (city, town, school district, etc.)
All insured persons under state‑employee or university group plans
Insured children and adults needing hearing‑loss services
numbers: $4 months COBRA premium paid by state

HB729.one_line: Mandates 10 % premium, full payment, receipt, and disclosure for surety appearance bonds.
HB729.summary: HB 729 amends Montana’s surety‑bond law to require bail‑bond producers to collect at least 10 % of the bond’s guaranteed amount as a premium, to collect that premium in full, and to provide a receipt. It also limits additional fees to those disclosed in a written schedule. The bill does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Amends §33‑26‑106, MCA, to mandate a minimum premium of 10 % of the guaranteed amount for surety appearance bonds.
Requires the premium be collected in full at the time of bond issuance.
Prohibits additional fees unless the producer discloses them and provides a fee schedule in the contract.
Mandates that a receipt be issued with the bond and power of attorney in accordance with §46‑9‑401.
Clarifies that the court or officer may allow a reasonable sum for the expense of procuring the surety in settlement of the account.
affected: Courts and officers who accept surety bonds

HB715.one_line: HB 715 updates Montana’s injunction law to a federal‑style standard and expands environmental‑review requirements.
HB715.summary: HB 715 revises Montana’s injunction statutes to adopt a federal‑style standard for mandatory preliminary injunctions, clarifies prohibitory injunctions, and reorganizes related language for clarity. The bill also amends environmental‑review provisions in § 75‑1‑201 and sets an effective date of October 1, 2025 for new causes of action.
changes: Replaces the current Montana standard for mandatory preliminary injunctions with a four‑factor test mirroring the federal standard (law/facts favor applicant; extreme damage; balance of equities; public interest).
Prohibits courts from using sliding‑scale or serious‑questions tests when evaluating preliminary injunctions.
Clarifies that an interpersonal injunction may be granted when a party threatens property removal or has applied for a protective order, and requires the applicant to prove the need.
Amends § 27‑19‑201 to adopt the new four‑factor test for prohibitory preliminary injunctions and to specify the same interpersonal‑injunction criteria.
Amends § 75‑1‑201 to expand environmental‑review requirements, including detailed alternative analysis, public‑interest considerations, and limits on challenges to agency decisions.
Sets the applicability of the act to causes of action filed on or after October 1, 2025.
Codifies the new provisions as part of Title 27, Chapter 19, Part 2.
affected: Montana courts and litigants seeking injunctions
Project sponsors and property owners subject to injunctions or environmental‑review decisions
numbers: no greenhouse‑gas review unless federal law requires

HB880.one_line: HB 880 creates a Medicaid reserve account and sets transfer rules to stabilize Medicaid funding.
HB880.summary: HB 880 creates a new Medicaid Stabilization Reserve Account, sets rules for transferring Medicaid funds into it, limits how the account can be used, and authorizes a one‑time $6 million transfer from the capital‑development account. The bill also appropriates $50,000 for Medicaid matching funds for the 2025‑26 biennium.
changes: Establishes a Medicaid Stabilization Reserve Account in the state special revenue fund and defines its purpose as mitigating Medicaid expenditure reductions.

Mandates that 50 % of any Medicaid appropriations that would otherwise revert to the general fund be transferred to the new account (and 50 % to the existing budget stabilization reserve) each fiscal year, unless the budget stabilization reserve is at its statutory limit, in which case 100 % goes to the Medicaid account.

Sets a ceiling: once the Medicaid account exceeds 1.5 % of general revenue appropriations in the second year of the biennium, further transfers are redirected to the capital‑development long‑range building program account.
Allows the governor to request use of the Medicaid account to offset proposed Medicaid reductions under 17‑7‑140, but only if the budget director certifies a projected general‑fund deficit.
Restricts appropriation of funds from the Medicaid account to state Medicaid matching funds and requires a budget‑director certification of deficit before appropriation.
Authorizes a one‑time $6 million transfer from the capital‑development long‑range building program account to the Medicaid account on or before June 30 2025.
Provides a $50,000 appropriation for the Department of Public Health and Human Services to supply state Medicaid matching funds for the 2025‑26 biennium.
Sets immediate effective date upon passage and specifies applicability to Medicaid appropriations for FY 2025 and onward.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB881.one_line: HB 881 expands Medicaid buy‑in to children with disabilities and funds the program.
HB881.summary: HB 881 expands Montana’s Medicaid buy‑in program so that children with disabilities can enroll, adds new rules and funding, and gives the department broad rule‑making authority.
changes: Amends §53‑6‑113 to allow the department to adopt rules for the Medicaid buy‑in program, including eligibility, rates, and provider qualifications
Rewrites §53‑6‑131 to clarify eligibility for Medicaid and the buy‑in program, including income limits, resource exclusions, and special rules for children in foster care or with disabilities
Rewrites §53‑6‑195 to define the purpose, eligibility, and cost‑sharing requirements for the buy‑in program for workers and children with disabilities
Provides specific appropriations for the biennium 2025‑2027 to fund the program (≈$1.9 M FY 2026, ≈$1.9 M FY 2027)
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1 2025
Extends the department’s rule‑making authority to cover eligibility, benefits, managed care, and cost‑sharing for the buy‑in program
affected: Montana residents with disabilities who are employed or under 19 with disabilities
Medicaid beneficiaries and the Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB7.one_line: SB 7 restores 20‑year service retirement eligibility for highway patrol and sheriff hires after July 1 2023.
SB7.summary: SB 7 restores the original retirement criteria for Highway Patrol Officers and Sheriffs, requiring 20 years of service regardless of age for those hired after July 1 2023. The changes apply retroactively to those hired on or after that date and take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §19‑6‑501 to require 20 years of service for all members hired on or after July 1 2023, eliminating the age‑50 requirement.
Amends §19‑7‑501 similarly, making 20 years of service the sole eligibility criterion for sheriffs hired on or after July 1 2023.
Provides that the new rules apply retroactively to members hired on or after July 1 2023.
Keeps the existing refund rights and IRS compliance language unchanged.
The act is effective immediately upon passage.
No new programs, funds, or offenses are created.
affected: Highway Patrol Officers hired on or after July 1 2023
Sheriffs hired on or after July 1 2023

HB952.one_line: Gov. can negotiate marijuana agreements with tribes, covering enforcement, commerce, research, and tax exemptions.
HB952.summary: HB 952 authorizes the governor to negotiate agreements with Montana tribal governments on all aspects of marijuana regulation, including enforcement, commerce, research, and taxation, and provides a $1,000 appropriation to support the process.
changes: Authorizes the governor to enter into agreements with federally recognized tribal governments on marijuana regulation;
Agreements may cover enforcement, commercial production, research, taxation, tribal immunities, and dispute resolution;
Agreements must apply to sales involving tribal enterprises or members and may allow tax exemptions for tribal‑owned or tribal‑member‑owned businesses;
Agreements must address public health, security, and cross‑border commerce;
The state appropriates $1,000 to the Office of Indian Affairs for the fiscal year beginning July 1 2025 to carry out these agreements;
The Secretary of State must notify all Montana tribes of the act;
The act is codified as part of Title 18, Chapter 11 and takes effect July 1 2025.
affected: State law enforcement and regulatory agencies

SB239.one_line: Bill expands amicus brief and intervention rights in subdivision and land‑use appeals.
SB239.summary: The bill amends Montana subdivision and land‑use law to require courts to invite governing bodies to file amicus briefs and to allow those bodies or related groups to intervene in related civil actions. It also expands the list of parties that may appeal subdivision decisions and clarifies the procedural steps for appeals and interventions.
changes: Amends §76‑3‑625 to require district courts to invite any governing body that administers a relevant statute to file an amicus curiae brief before issuing an interpretive order.
Permits a non‑party amicus to intervene after such an order and to seek a stay pending appeal.
Expands the list of parties eligible to appeal subdivision decisions to include subdividers, adjacent landowners, county commissioners, and municipalities within specified distances.
Amends §76‑25‑503 to mirror the amicus‑brief and intervention requirements for land‑use decisions, and to set out a detailed administrative appeal process before district‑court review.
Adds definitions and procedural clarifications (e.g., “aggrieved” and the timing of appeals).
Does not create new funding, programs, or criminal offenses.
affected: Governing bodies that administer subdivision statutes

SB258.one_line: Allows legislature to set school‑funding inflation adjustments beyond the automatic 3 % cap.
SB258.summary: SB 258 amends the state’s school‑funding formula to let the legislature set inflation adjustments that differ from the automatically calculated rate, while still allowing a 3 % cap unless the legislature chooses otherwise.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑326, MCA to specify how the superintendent calculates the inflation factor for basic and per‑ANB entitlements and related payments.
Defines the inflation factor as the cube‑root of the ratio of the July 1 CPI of the current year to the CPI three years earlier, applied separately for each year of the biennium.
Adds a 3 % maximum limit on the inflation adjustment unless the legislature authorizes a higher rate.
Explicitly allows the legislature, through appropriation or law‑making authority, to set inflationary adjustments that exceed the calculated rate and the 3 % cap.
Clarifies that “consumer price index” refers to the U.S. CPI‑U‑ALL‑CITY‑AVG with a 1982‑84 base of 100.
No new program or fund is created; the bill only revises calculation methodology and clarifies legislative authority.

SB394.one_line: Adds PTSD coverage for first responders under Montana workers’ compensation.
SB394.summary: SB 394 expands Montana’s workers’‑comp system to cover post‑traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) for first responders. It defines the injury, amends the statutory definition of injury to include PTSD, and sets the effective and applicability dates. The bill does not create a new program or fund.
changes: Defines a first responder as a firefighter, law‑enforcement officer, detention‑center/prison employee, or any other authorized emergency‑care provider;
Adds PTSD to the list of compensable injuries under Montana’s workers’‑comp and occupational‑disease statutes;
Amends the definition of “injury” in §39‑71‑119 to include PTSD and clarifies that it is caused by an accident;
Amends §39‑71‑105 to state that, except for PTSD, stress claims are not compensable;
Amends §39‑71‑116 to incorporate the new definition of injury and related procedural language;
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025 and limits its applicability to claims filed after that date for injuries caused by events occurring on or after the effective date.
affected: First‑responder workers (firefighters, police, detention‑center/prison staff, other emergency‑care providers)
Workers’‑comp insurers and the state workers’‑comp fund

HJ1.one_line: Resolution urges Congress to fully fund Montana reservation law‑enforcement and public‑safety programs.
HJ1.summary: HJ 1 is a joint resolution that urges the U.S. Congress to provide full funding for public‑safety and law‑enforcement programs on Montana’s Indian reservations. It also calls for DOJ‑Interior cooperation, tribal‑government resolutions, and a governor’s letter, all to be sent to Congress by June 30, 2025.
changes: Urges Congress to fully fund public‑safety and law‑enforcement agencies, programs, services, and activities on Montana reservations.
Urges the Department of Justice to develop a cooperative plan with the Department of the Interior for administering Indian‑Country public‑safety programs.

Urges DOJ to conduct government‑to‑government consultation with tribes to determine best ways to administer programs and allocate appropriated funds for tribal justice systems (law enforcement, courts, detention, indigent counsel, victim services, juvenile justice, rehabilitation, reentry, crime prevention).
Invites each federally recognized tribal government in Montana to adopt its own resolution urging Congress for full funding and to send that resolution to the Secretary of State by June 30, 2025.
Requests the Governor to write a supportive letter to Congress and to send that letter to the Secretary of State by June 30, 2025.

The Secretary of State is directed to collect all tribal resolutions and the governor’s letter by June 30, 2025, and to forward them with a copy of this resolution to the U.S. House Speaker, House and Senate leaders, and the Montana congressional delegation as soon as possible thereafter.
affected: Federally recognized tribal governments in Montana

HJ6.one_line: Resolution honors U.S. 250th anniversary and supports heritage organizations.
HJ6.summary: The Montana Legislature passed a joint resolution to honor the United States’ 250th anniversary in 2026, expressing support for the Sons and Daughters of the American Revolution and encouraging Montanans to celebrate the Declaration of Independence.

HJ4.one_line: Montana requests an AI study to review laws, ethics, rights, and impacts, due September 2026.
HJ4.summary: Montana’s legislature has requested an interim study on artificial intelligence. The study will examine existing laws, explore ethical codes and rights, and assess AI’s benefits and risks to state agencies and residents, with findings due before September 15, 2026.
changes: Designates the Legislative Council to appoint an interim or statutory committee (or staff) to conduct the AI study.
The study must review current state, other state, and federal AI regulations for applicability.
It must research an AI code of ethics for state agencies and an AI bill of rights for citizens.
It must examine transparency, disclosure, and civil/criminal liability for AI developers and deployers.
It must assess AI’s impact on employment, legal rights, privacy, and economic welfare in Montana.
Findings must be presented to a committee and reported to the 70th Legislature before the deadline.
affected: AI developers and deployers in Montana

HJ7.one_line: Montana legislature congratulates President Trump on his inauguration.
HJ7.summary: This joint resolution simply congratulates President Donald J. Trump on his 2025 inauguration and expresses Montana’s support for his policies. It contains no substantive policy changes or funding provisions.
changes: None – the resolution is purely ceremonial.
affected: Montana legislators, the Secretary of State, the President and Vice‑President of the United States, and the Montana Congressional delegation.

HJ9.one_line: Montana’s legislature condemns antisemitism, supports Israel, and orders the resolution sent to the President and Congress.
HJ9.summary: The resolution expresses Montana’s support for Israel, condemns antisemitism and terrorist attacks against Israel, and directs the Secretary of State to send a copy to the President and Montana’s congressional delegation.
changes: 1. Declares the Legislature’s condemnation of all antisemitism.
2. Condemns all terrorist attacks on Israel, naming Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran.
3. Reaffirms Israel’s right to exist and rejects calls for its destruction.
4. Orders the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to the U.S. President and Montana’s congressional delegation.

HJ10.one_line: Montana resolution urges federal action to bar boys from girls’ sports.
HJ10.summary: Montana’s House Joint Resolution HJ 10 declares that biological boys and men should not be allowed to compete in girls’ and women’s sports and urges the U.S. Congress to enact the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025. It is a symbolic statement with no enforceable provisions in Montana law.

HJ15.one_line: Resolution endorses expanding Montana’s electric transmission network and calls for regional cooperation.
HJ15.summary: The resolution expresses the Legislature’s support for expanding Montana’s electric transmission network and urges state and regional partners to pursue such projects. It does not create new laws or programs, merely endorses the need for increased capacity.
changes: Affirms that upgrading and expanding transmission infrastructure is essential for affordable, reliable electricity.
Encourages the use of Montana‑based skilled labor in transmission projects.
Highlights economic benefits and tax revenue potential from transmission upgrades.
Calls for collaboration with neighboring states and federal agencies.

Requests copies of the resolution be sent to the Governor, neighboring state governors, the Public Service Commission, rural electric cooperatives, the U.S. Department of Energy, BPA, Northwestern Energy, MDU, and Montana congressional delegation.
affected: Federal agencies involved in energy infrastructure

HJ17.one_line: Resolution urges federal reforms to speed energy projects and reduce regulatory delays.
HJ17.summary: The resolution is a formal request to the U.S. Congress and the President to streamline federal permitting and environmental review processes, repeal or modify recent EPA rules, and use national‑security powers to accelerate domestic energy projects. It does not create new law or programs, but urges action on existing regulations and executive authority. The resolution is a political statement rather than a binding legislative measure.
changes: Urges Congress to enact legislation that reforms federal permitting and environmental review under the NEPA, ESA, Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, and NRC regulations.

Calls for the EPA to immediately review, suspend, revise, or rescind two May 2024 power‑plant rules (the MATS RTR Rule and the GHG Rule) and to consider additional actions consistent with national‑security objectives.

Requests the President to expand emergency and national‑security authorities (National Emergencies Act, Defense Production Act, Energy Policy and Conservation Act, and national‑security exemptions in environmental laws) to expedite energy projects.
Encourages federal agencies to limit judicial delays, prevent misuse of environmental laws to block lawful infrastructure, and streamline permitting for rare‑earth and critical‑mineral mining.
Directs the Secretary of State to transmit the resolution to the President, congressional leaders, the EPA Administrator, and Montana’s congressional delegation.

HJ19.one_line: Montana declares the last full week of September as Frontotemporal Degeneration Awareness Week.
HJ19.summary: Montana’s legislature has declared the last full week of September as Frontotemporal Degeneration (FTD) Awareness Week and asked the governor to issue a proclamation. The resolution also directs the Secretary of State to forward the proclamation to the governor, the Department of Public Health and Human Services, and all county commissions. No new programs, funds, or laws are created.
changes: Declares the last full week of September as FTD Awareness Week in Montana.
Requests the governor to issue a proclamation for that week.
Directs the Secretary of State to send a copy of the resolution to the governor, the Department of Public Health and Human Services, and every county commission.
numbers: 60,000 people in the U.S. affected by FTD
3.6 years from symptom onset to diagnosis
7‑13 years life expectancy after symptoms begin

HJ20.one_line: Resolution requests longer border hours to boost Montana‑Canada trade and travel.
HJ20.summary: This joint resolution asks the federal government to extend operating hours at Montana‑Canada border ports to support trade and travel. It is a request, not a law, and carries no direct fiscal impact on Montana.
changes: Requests the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Agency to increase hours of service at Montana‑Canada customs ports of entry.
Requests the Secretary of State to forward copies of the resolution to the President of the United States and to Montana’s congressional delegation.
affected: U.S. Customs and Border Protection Agency

HJ23.one_line: Resolution creates a committee to simplify the Youth Court Act, report findings by Sept 2026.
HJ23.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to set up a committee to review and simplify the Montana Youth Court Act, requiring the committee’s findings be reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Designates an interim or statutory committee to study the Youth Court Act
Mandates committee input from county attorneys, court staff, and state agencies
Requires any proposed changes to stay consistent with the Act’s stated purposes and avoid punitive policy shifts
Limits the study to procedural simplification
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completion and reporting
Orders the final report to be submitted to the 70th Legislature
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HJ26.one_line: Resolution requests a study of guardianship issues to be completed by September 2026.
HJ26.summary: The resolution directs a study of Montana’s guardianship and conservatorship system, focusing on training, licensing, certification, and auditing. It requires the study to be finished by September 15, 2026 and its findings reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Designates an interim committee to study guardianship issues
The study will review current resources and compare other states’ programs
It will identify potential costs and funding sources for new programs
It will determine the appropriate administrative placement for any new program
Stakeholder input will be solicited from guardians, conservators, families, judges, and state agencies
The study must be completed before September 15, 2026 and reported to the Legislature
affected: State agencies (Public Health and Human Services, Department of Justice)

HJ27.one_line: Resolution authorizes a study to modernize Montana’s funeral‑service statutes and explore new disposition methods.
HJ27.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to conduct an interim study of Montana’s laws governing morticians and funeral services, with the goal of clarifying and modernizing statutes and exploring new final‑disposition methods such as natural organic reduction and alkaline hydrolysis. The study must be completed and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee or staff to examine existing statutes and department rules related to burial, cremation, mortician licensure, health‑and‑safety standards, and air‑quality permits for crematories.
Requires the study to review how other states incorporate new disposition technologies and to research available technologies not currently covered by Montana law.
Calls for proposals to update terminology, modernize language, and create a framework for adding new disposition methods to future statutes.

Mandates collaboration with industry professionals, tribal representatives, the board of funeral service, the Montana Funeral Directors Association, public health officials, and experts in alternative disposition methods.
Specifies that findings be presented to an appropriate committee and that the final report be delivered to the 70th Legislature.
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completion of the study and its presentation.
No new program, office, fund, or criminal offense is created; the resolution merely authorizes a study.
numbers: seven different titles of the Montana Code Annotated

HJ28.one_line: Resolution directs a study of federal grant opportunities for Montana governments, to be completed by Sept 15, 2026.
HJ28.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to set up an interim committee that will study federal grant opportunities available to Montana’s state, tribal, and local governments since 2020, assess current usage, identify gaps, and recommend ways to improve access, especially for small and rural entities. The study must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: 1. Requests the Legislative Council to appoint an interim committee to study federal grant opportunities for state, tribal, and local governments.
2. The committee must identify all grant opportunities available since 2020, determine which are currently used, and note any that are un‑ or under‑utilized.
3. It must analyze why some grants are consistently used while others are not, and investigate disparities faced by small, tribal, and rural entities compared to larger urban ones.
4. The committee must recommend strategies and resources to enhance grant acquisition and address any identified disparities.
5. The committee must work with stakeholders—including executive agencies, tribal and local governments, and federal representatives—to gather input and proposals.
6. The study must be completed and its findings presented to an appropriate committee before September 15, 2026, and the final results reported to the 70th Legislature.
affected: Local government entities (especially small, rural, and tribal)

HJ29.one_line: Resolution celebrates Montana‑Taiwan ties and urges deeper economic cooperation.
HJ29.summary: The resolution simply acknowledges and celebrates Montana’s long‑standing sister‑state relationship with Taiwan and urges the state to deepen economic, educational, and cultural ties. It contains no new laws or funding provisions.
changes: Reaffirms Montana’s commitment to strengthening ties with Taiwan
Commemorates the 40th anniversary of the sister‑state relationship
Advocates for Taiwan’s participation in international organizations
Endorses a closer economic and trade partnership, including a bilateral trade and tax agreement
Requests copies of the resolution be sent to the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Seattle and to relevant state and federal officials

HJ30.one_line: HJ 30 directs a study on housing density incentives to be completed by September 15, 2026.
HJ30.summary: HJ 30 is a joint resolution that directs the Legislative Council to commission an interim study on how to boost housing density and affordability in Montana. The study must examine incentives, state programs, tax impacts, infrastructure funding, and stakeholder input, and must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign an interim or statutory committee (or staff) to conduct a study on housing density incentives.

HJ31.one_line: Montana legislature honors support staff and sets April 3 as their day of recognition.
HJ31.summary: This joint resolution formally recognizes the contributions of educational support professionals in Montana’s public schools and designates April 3, 2025 as Educational Support Professionals Day. It is a symbolic act of appreciation and does not create new laws or programs.
changes: Declares that educational support professionals are recognized for their impact on student outcomes and learning environments.
Designates April 3, 2025 as Educational Support Professionals Day, coinciding with the national Paraprofessional Appreciation Day.
affected: Educational support professionals in Montana public schools

HJ32.one_line: Resolution requests a study of advanced investigator training and qualifications in Montana law enforcement.
HJ32.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study how many Montana law‑enforcement officers are trained to investigate serious crimes such as homicide and sexual assault, and whether more training or personnel are needed. The study must finish by September 15, 2026, and its findings must be reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee under MCA §5‑5‑217 to conduct the study.
The committee must review current training opportunities for serious‑crime investigations and survey agencies for qualified officers.
The committee must explore ways to increase the number of qualified investigators and recommend legislation if needed.
The study must be completed and reported before September 15, 2026.
The final report must be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
numbers: 16 departments with five or fewer officers
22 departments with five or fewer officers
HJ32.effective: not stated (study to be completed by September 15, 2026)

HJ33.one_line: Montana urges Congress to regulate unsolicited mortgage‑credit trigger leads.
HJ33.summary: The Legislature passes a joint resolution urging Congress to regulate or prohibit unsolicited mortgage‑credit offers (“trigger leads”) that target Montana homebuyers. It calls for federal action to remove preemption and protect consumers.
changes: None—this is a resolution that does not enact law but requests federal action.

HJ34.one_line: Resolution endorses Montana beef producers and opposes excessive regulation and lab‑grown meat.
HJ34.summary: HJ 34 is a joint resolution expressing the Montana Legislature’s support for the state’s beef industry and urging federal and state governments to protect ranchers from excessive regulation, taxes, and competition from lab‑grown meat. It also directs the Secretary of State to send copies of the resolution to various stakeholders.
changes: No new laws or programs are created; the resolution merely expresses support and opposition to certain policies.
affected: Montana beef producers, ranchers, farmers, and related rural communities

HJ40.one_line: Study whether fiscal notes should shift from executive to legislative production, due September 2026.
HJ40.summary: The resolution asks the Legislature to study whether fiscal notes—currently prepared by the executive branch—should instead be produced by the legislative branch. The study must be finished by September 15, 2026, and its findings reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Designates an interim or statutory committee to study the transfer of fiscal‑note responsibility.
Authorizes the Legislative Services Division to provide administrative, research, and legal support for the study.
Authorizes the Legislative Fiscal Division to provide additional research and fiscal analysis.
Requires the study’s conclusions, recommendations, and any findings to be reported to the 70th Legislature.
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completing the study.

HJ35.one_line: Montana urges federal agencies to change wildfire policies.
HJ35.summary: Montana’s legislature urges the federal government to change wildfire‑management policies, calling for more aggressive fire suppression, open forest roads, inclusion of wildfire smoke in EPA air‑quality standards, reversal of “let‑it‑burn” practices, and greater state‑local stakeholder involvement. The resolution is a formal request, not a law, and contains no new programs or funding.

HJ42.one_line: HJ 42 directs a study of state procurement to improve transparency and compliance.
HJ42.summary: HJ 42 is a joint resolution that orders an interim study of Montana state‑agency procurement practices, focusing on no‑bid contracts and transparency. The study must be finished by September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Designates a committee or staff to review procurement statutes and rules.
Examines how agencies decide when to use standard bidding versus other methods.
Samples contracts from the past four years to spot deviations from the Montana Procurement Act.
Tallies payments to vendors chosen outside the standard process.
Checks for waste, fraud, or abuse in those deviations.
Recommends changes to statutes, rules, and agency procedures to prevent future violations.
Includes stakeholder input and requires a final report to the Legislature.

HJ44.one_line: Resolution requests an interim study of EDCs and PFAS in Montana water, to be reported by Sept 15 2026.
HJ44.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of endocrine‑disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and PFAS in Montana’s water, reviewing current laws, sampling methods, health research, and prevalence, and to report findings to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Designates a Legislative Council‑appointed committee or staff to conduct the study
Requires review of existing state and federal water‑quality laws as they relate to EDCs
Mandates research on PFAS presence, sources, sampling, and exposure pathways
Calls for analysis of health‑effects research and prevalence of EDCs in Montana
Demands recommendations for future rulemaking or legal changes
Requires presentation of findings to a committee and reporting to the 70th Legislature before Sept 15 2026
affected: staff or committee assigned to the study

HJ47.one_line: HJ 47 directs a study of local government cooperation and consolidation to be completed by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ47.summary: HJ 47 is a joint resolution that asks the Legislative Council to commission an interim study of how Montana’s local governments cooperate and whether they should consolidate. The study must be finished by September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the next legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate a committee or staff to conduct the study
The study must identify opportunities for better inter‑governmental cooperation, review existing methods, and examine practices from other states
It must analyze potential consolidations and the fiscal impacts of cooperation or consolidation
Stakeholders such as local officials, county and city leagues, and the university’s local‑government center must be consulted
Findings must be presented to an appropriate committee and reported to the 70th Legislature
The study must be completed before September 15, 2026
affected: Local government entities (counties, municipalities, special districts)
Montana League of Cities and Towns
Montana State University Local Government Center

HJ45.one_line: Resolution requests a study on expungement barriers, to be reported as new legislation by the next session.
HJ45.summary: The resolution directs a legislative study of how expunged criminal records still affect people’s housing, employment, and other opportunities, and requires the study’s findings to be turned into new legislation by the next session. It does not create a new program or law itself.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to conduct a comprehensive interim study on expungement and collateral consequences.
The study must review current expungement laws, identify legal and discriminatory barriers, and examine interstate and commercial data‑sharing issues.
It should evaluate how landlords and employers interpret expunged records and explore incentive models for expungement‑friendly housing.
The committee must analyze recidivism, employment, wage growth, and housing stability before and after expungement.
It should compare Montana’s laws with other states and assess peer‑support models in reentry programs.
The committee is to recommend specific legal changes to address identified barriers and discrimination.
All work must be completed by September 15, 2026, and the final report must be presented as introduced legislation to the 70th Legislature.
affected: Individuals with criminal records seeking expungement
Employers, landlords, and other entities that conduct background checks
State agencies involved in corrections, public defense, and justice administration

HJ50.one_line: Resolution requests a study of owners’ association laws to be finished by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ50.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to commission a study of the Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act and related Montana laws, with the study to be completed by September 15, 2026, and its findings reported to the next Legislature. It does not create new law or programs.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate an interim or statutory committee or staff to conduct the study.
affected: Montana owners’ association stakeholders (bankers, title, realtors, etc.)
Montana residents who may be members of owners’ associations

HJ48.one_line: Resolution requests study on moving Montana’s primary election date and report findings by Sept 15, 2026.
HJ48.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to study whether Montana’s primary election should be moved to an earlier date in the presidential cycle.  The study must examine legal, administrative, and logistical impacts and report findings to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate a committee to study moving the primary election date
The committee must review all existing election dates, deadlines, and procedures that would need adjustment
It must assess conflicts with decennial redistricting timelines
It must evaluate impacts on election administrators and voters
It must examine effects on other elections and identify consolidation opportunities
It must weigh benefits, drawbacks, and trade‑offs for voters
It must develop draft legislation to change the primary date and related code amendments
The study must be completed and reported before September 15, 2026

HJ52.one_line: Resolution directs study of a state cattle assessment and reports results by September 2026.
HJ52.summary: The resolution asks the Legislature to form an interim committee to study whether Montana should adopt a state‑level cattle assessment to fund research, promotion, and education for the cattle industry, and to report findings by September 15, 2026. It does not create any new law or program, only a study mandate.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate an interim or statutory committee to examine the cattle industry’s profitability and marketability.

HJ53.one_line: HJ 53 directs a study on school safety to be completed by September 15, 2026.
HJ53.summary: HJ 53 is a joint resolution that asks the Legislative Council to set up a committee to study school safety in Montana. The committee will work with a broad range of stakeholders, review current laws and funding, and examine how the state can better implement the Ten Essential Actions for school safety. The study must finish and report its findings to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Creates an interim committee (or statutory committee) to conduct a study on school safety.
Mandates that the committee collaborate with 11 specified organizations and entities.
Requires the committee to review Montana’s implementation of the Ten Essential Actions for school safety, including best‑practice analysis and improvement recommendations.
Orders the committee to examine existing statutes and funding mechanisms for school safety and to suggest clarifications, coordination, and consolidation.
Calls for the committee to explore ways to promote cross‑agency coordination, possibly through a designated clearinghouse for model policies and training.
Specifies that the study, including presentation and review, must be completed before September 15, 2026, and that the final results be reported to the next Legislature.
affected: State agencies involved in school safety (Office of Public Instruction, Department of Justice, etc.)
numbers: Ten Essential Actions for school safety

HJ55.one_line: Resolution requests a study of property‑management licensing and practices, to be completed by Sept 15 2026.
HJ55.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to commission a study of Montana’s property‑management licensing, education, and fee structure, and to compare those rules with federal and out‑of‑state standards.  The study must gather stakeholder input, finish by September 15 2026, and report its findings to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests a committee or staff to review current licensing, education, and fee requirements for property managers in Montana.
Examines how those requirements align with the Montana Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, commercial rental laws, and foreign‑corporation rules.
Analyzes the costs charged to landowners and tenants that result from licensing and education mandates.
Identifies best‑practice education and practice models from other states.
Solicits feedback from property managers, landlords, tenants, tenant unions, attorneys, professional organizations, and housing policy experts.
Requires the study’s findings to be presented to an appropriate committee and reported to the Legislature by September 15 2026.

HJ61.one_line: Resolution creates a study committee to analyze Montana’s rising property‑insurance rates.
HJ61.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form an interim committee to study why Montana’s property‑insurance rates are rising, how that affects coverage and costs, and to recommend ways to make insurance more affordable. The committee must finish its work and report its findings to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Designates an interim committee to study the Montana property‑insurance market
The committee must evaluate causes, impacts, and policy options for stabilizing rates
The study must be completed and reported to the legislature by September 15, 2026
affected: Montana homeowners, landlords, tenants, businesses, and insurers

HJ56.one_line: Resolution directs study of Montana’s search‑and‑rescue funding and reimbursement rules.
HJ56.summary: The resolution asks the Legislative Council to create a study team to review Montana’s search‑and‑rescue (SAR) funding, reimbursement rules, and coordination, especially for tribal areas, and to report findings to the next legislature by Sept. 15, 2026.
changes: Creates an interim study committee (or staff) to examine SAR reimbursement, funding sources, and administrative processes.
The committee may propose legislation to adjust the $12,000 per‑operation cap, update inflation‑adjusted rates, and streamline reimbursement requests.
It will assess whether state funds adequately support tribal SAR operations and recommend changes if needed.
The study will review all SAR funding streams, including motor‑vehicle revenue and conservation‑license donations, and consider centralizing administration.
The committee must include representatives from county, municipal, tribal, fire, EMS, and state agencies, plus the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Task Force.
Results must be presented to a designated committee and reported to the 70th Legislature before Sept. 15, 2026.

HJ74.one_line: Montana requests a study on water reuse, to be finished by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ74.summary: Montana’s legislature asks an interim study to examine water‑reuse opportunities, barriers, and best practices, with findings due to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to study water‑reuse issues.
The committee must review statutes, infrastructure, and other states’ practices.
It must identify industries and regions that currently use or could benefit from reuse.
It must analyze legal, economic, and social barriers to implementation.
It must assess economic, environmental, and population drivers for reuse.
If needed, the committee may propose legislation to encourage reuse.
The study must be completed and its final report delivered to the 70th Legislature by Sept. 15, 2026.

HJ62.one_line: Resolution creates a study committee on wildfire resilience, due Sept 15, 2026.
HJ62.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to set up a committee to study wildfire impacts, current policies, and possible solutions in Montana, with a deadline of September 15, 2026. The committee must report its findings to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate a committee to conduct an interim study of wildfire prevention and resilience.
The study must examine wildfire impacts, economic/social/ ecological costs, pre‑ and post‑fire strategies, land‑use planning, building materials, defensible space, and legal/policy barriers.
It must explore incentives (tax credits, cost‑share, grants) and statewide regulation options for building codes, landscaping, and vegetation management.
The committee must develop hazard and risk maps and recommend how state agencies can support local governments.
All study work, including presentation and review, must be completed before September 15, 2026.
The final report, with findings and recommendations, must be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
affected: State agencies involved in land‑use and building regulation
numbers: more than 90% of population in high‑risk counties

HR2.one_line: Montana House resolution urges support for critical‑mineral development and study.
HR2.summary: The House of Representatives in Montana adopts a resolution urging state, federal, tribal, and local governments to support the exploration, development, processing, refining, recycling, and reuse of critical minerals within the state. It calls for further study and responsible development to benefit local communities and strengthen U.S. supply chains. No new laws, programs, or funding are created.
changes: Urges state, federal, tribal, and local jurisdictions to acknowledge and support critical‑mineral projects in Montana.
Calls for further study, identification, and responsible development of critical minerals.
Encourages collaboration with federal and tribal partners to advance Montana’s role in domestic supply chains.
Requests the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to the President, congressional leaders, and the Montana delegation.
No new statutes, programs, or funding mechanisms are established.
No regulatory or enforcement changes are introduced.

HR1.one_line: House adopts detailed rules governing officers, committees, decorum, and legislative procedure.
HR1.summary: The House adopted a comprehensive set of rules governing its internal operations, including officer duties, committee procedures, decorum, voting, and the handling of legislation. The resolution codifies how the House is organized, how business is conducted, and how members and staff are expected to behave.
changes: Adopts definitions and duties for House officers (Speaker, Speaker‑pro‑tempore, majority/minority leaders and whips).
Sets the Speaker’s authority over order, decorum, employee appointments, and the certification of bills and journals.
Establishes detailed procedures for committee appointments, meetings, hearings, and reporting of legislation.
Outlines decorum rules, including penalties for breaches and limits on speaking time.
Specifies the order of business, voting procedures, and the handling of motions, amendments, and the consent calendar.
Provides rules for the use of the House floor, lobbyists, and legislative interns.
Defines the process for introducing, reading, and passing legislation, including first, second, and third readings, and the role of the Committee of the Whole.
Sets procedures for the call of the House, quorum, and adjournments.
Establishes the House Rules Committee’s role in interpreting and appealing rule interpretations.
affected: Public and witnesses at committee hearings
numbers: 5‑minute speaking limits in Committee of the Whole
two‑thirds vote required to amend rules
two‑thirds vote to suspend a rule
two‑thirds vote to approve constitutional amendments

HR3.one_line: A House resolution urging federal action to safeguard Montanans’ personal data from DOGE.
HR3.summary: HR 3 is a House resolution urging Montana’s congressional delegation to press the President to protect Montanans’ personally identifiable information from the federal Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). It calls for immediate action to secure all databases containing such data and requests the Secretary of State send the resolution to Congress and the President.
changes: Requests the Montana congressional delegation to advocate to the President for protection of Montanans’ personal data held by DOGE.
affected: Montanans whose personal information may be stored in federal databases

HR5.one_line: Montana House designates April 14 week as “Two Lights for Tomorrow Week” to honor the 250th U.S. anniversary.
HR5.summary: The House designates the week of April 14, 2025 as “Two Lights for Tomorrow Week” to honor the U.S. 250th‑anniversary and encourages public displays of two lights and community reflection. It is a symbolic resolution with no new laws or programs.
changes: Designates a specific week in Montana as a commemorative observance.

HR6.one_line: Resolution urges retaining November mule‑deer hunt while tightening antlerless harvest by district.
HR6.summary: This House resolution urges the Fish and Wildlife Commission to keep the November mule‑deer season, including buck harvest during the rut, while tightening antlerless harvest in districts where populations are below target. It calls for district‑specific restrictions, a minimum start date of November 6, and a biological trigger based on a buck‑to‑doe ratio of 15:100.
changes: Encourages the Commission to retain the current November mule‑deer season and buck harvest during the rut.
Calls for aggressive restrictions on antlerless harvest in districts below population objectives.
Requests that antlerless harvest be limited in districts trending below objectives even if they are at target.
Proposes a minimum start date of November 6 for general districts to preserve hunting opportunity.
Supports rotating restrictions by district to allow rut harvests where possible.
Adds a biological trigger: if the buck‑to‑doe ratio falls below 15 bucks per 100 does, restrictions may be imposed.

SJ1.one_line: Adopts detailed joint rules for Montana’s legislature, covering remote participation, bill drafting, fiscal notes, and veto procedures.
SJ1.summary: The bill adopts a comprehensive set of joint legislative rules that govern how Montana’s Senate and House conduct business, including remote participation, bill drafting, voting, committee procedures, fiscal notes, and the Governor’s veto process. It establishes detailed protocols for remote voting, bill formatting, fiscal note requirements, and the timing of legislative actions. No new programs or criminal offenses are created; it merely codifies procedures.
changes: Allows members to participate remotely and vote by proxy only with caucus leader permission; remote members receive full privileges and compensation.
Requires electronic authentication for remote voting and Legislative Services Division to assist with technical issues.
Sets strict deadlines and procedures for drafting, introducing, and prioritizing bills, including limits on requests after December 5 and specific timelines for different bill types.
Mandates fiscal notes for any bill with potential revenue or expenditure impact, with detailed preparation and review procedures.
Establishes detailed rules for bill reading, engrossing, enrolling, and final action, including specific timelines for transmission between houses and Governor’s veto handling.
Provides procedures for suspending or amending joint rules, requiring concurrence of both houses and Rules Committee referral.
Requires public recording and availability of all votes, fiscal notes, and legislative documents.
Requires that all bills be posted online and that fiscal notes be made available to members and the public.
Requires that the Governor’s veto be overridden by a two‑thirds vote of each house present.
Sets the effective dates for statutes, appropriations, motor‑vehicle taxes, and joint resolutions.

SJ3.one_line: Montana urges Congress to relax CDL rules for pickup trucks and school buses.
SJ3.summary: Montana’s Senate and House passed a joint resolution urging Congress to relax federal commercial driver’s license (CDL) rules for pickup‑truck haulers and school bus drivers. The resolution simply requests changes; it does not create new laws or programs in Montana.
changes: Urges Congress to eliminate the CDL requirement for pickup trucks hauling non‑hazardous material on a single trailer.
Urges Congress to lower the licensing burden for school bus drivers to a level appropriate to their duties.
Requests the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to federal congressional members and committees, as well as to other state legislatures.

SJ5.one_line: Montana urges Congress to pass the SAFER Banking Act to aid marijuana businesses.
SJ5.summary: The resolution urges the U.S. Congress to enact the SAFER Banking Act of 2023, which would allow banks to serve marijuana‑related businesses without penalty. It also directs the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to federal leaders and Montana’s congressional delegation.
changes: Urges federal passage of the SAFER Banking Act of 2023.

SJ6.one_line: Legislature approves the Capitol development plan but rejects building a new Capitol.
SJ6.summary: The Legislature formally consents to and approves the Long‑Range Legislative Branch Capitol Development Plan, but explicitly rejects any future plan to build a new Capitol building. The resolution allows the Legislature to use the plan as a guide for future capital‑development decisions while keeping the existing Capitol as the primary location for legislative activity.
changes: Consents to and approves the Long‑Range Legislative Branch Capitol Development Plan as recommended by the Legislative Council
Rejects any future option in the plan that would construct a new Capitol building
Provides a planning and feasibility template for future capital‑development decisions
Leaves open the need for additional study and legislative input to determine implementation
Does not create any new program, office, or criminal offense
Does not allocate new funding or authorize new expenditures
Maintains that the existing Capitol building remains the primary site for legislative operations

SJ7.one_line: Resolution urges Montana universities to adopt shooting sports as collegiate athletics.
SJ7.summary: The resolution urges Montana’s public universities to recognize and support shooting sports as collegiate athletics, encouraging the creation of competitions, partnerships, endowments, and scholarships. It is a non‑binding request, not a law, and requires no new funding or programs to be established by the Legislature.
changes: Encourages the Board of Regents and university units to adopt shooting sports as collegiate sports.
Encourages universities to use campus resources and partner with non‑university entities to facilitate shooting competitions.
Encourages universities to develop endowments and offer scholarships for students competing in shooting sports.
Directs the Secretary of State to send a copy of the resolution to the Board of Regents and to leaders of all public colleges and universities in Montana.

SJ8.one_line: Resolution directs study of special districts, to finish by Sept. 15, 2026 and report findings.
SJ8.summary: The resolution asks the Legislative Council to study Montana’s special districts, categorizing them, examining their funding, data gaps, limits, and reporting. It requires the study to finish before September 15, 2026, with findings sent to the next legislature.
changes: Requests an interim study of special districts by the Legislative Council
Specifies five study topics: types, funding variation, data improvement, limits, and reporting adequacy
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for study completion
Mandates the final report be submitted to the 70th Legislature
numbers: 10% of statewide mill‑based property tax collections

SJ9.one_line: Resolution condemns federal debt, urges Congress to adopt disciplined fiscal rules.
SJ9.summary: SJ 9 is a joint resolution that condemns federal fiscal and monetary policy, warns of inflation and debt risks, and urges Congress to enact disciplined rules such as a balanced‑budget amendment and a gold‑linked dollar. It calls state legislatures to send similar resolutions to Congress.
changes: Declares that federal fiscal/monetary policy is harming Montanans and Americans.

SJ10.one_line: Montana honors NCSL’s 50th anniversary and sends a copy of the resolution to NCSL.
SJ10.summary: Montana’s Senate and House jointly honor the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) on its 50th anniversary, acknowledging its service to state legislators and staff. The resolution simply commends NCSL and directs the Legislative Services Division to send a copy of the resolution to NCSL. No policy changes or new programs are created.
changes: Recognizes and commends NCSL for its 50‑year service to state legislators, staff, and legislative institutions.
Directs the Legislative Services Division to forward a copy of the resolution to NCSL.

SJ11.one_line: Resolution creates a committee to study Montana farmer’s markets and report by Sept 15, 2026.
SJ11.summary: This resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study Montana’s farmer’s markets and local food systems, including economic impact, barriers, regulatory issues, and food‑security roles, and report findings to the next legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Creates an interim committee under section 5‑5‑217, MCA, to study farmer’s markets and food systems
Mandates the committee to consult a broad range of stakeholders (producers, market reps, health experts, etc.)
Requires the committee to examine economic impact, regulatory barriers, and the Montana Local Food Choice Act
Tasks the committee with assessing food‑security, nutrition, and national‑security implications
Calls for a review of consumer‑protection statutes and liability for producers
Requests analysis of collaborations with local governments, nonprofits, and private entities
Demands a final report to the 70th Legislature before September 15, 2026
affected: City and county public health officials
State departments (Public Health & Human Services, Agriculture)

SJ12.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s transmission capacity and economic impact, due September 2026.
SJ12.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to commission an interim study of Montana’s electric‑transmission capacity on paths 8, 18, 80, and 83, focusing on congestion, curtailments, and their economic effects.  The study must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign staff or a committee to conduct the study
Specifies five research tasks: assess available capacity, analyze economic impact, inventory interconnection queues, sample market depth and pricing, and recommend upgrades with cost‑benefit analysis
Mandates presentation of findings to an appropriate committee and final reporting to the Legislature
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completion of the study
Requires the study to be conducted before the 70th Legislature convenes
No new laws or programs are created—only a study is requested

SJ13.one_line: Resolution requests a 5‑year EMS study to be finished by Sept 15, 2026.
SJ13.summary: The Senate and House request an interim study of Montana’s emergency medical services (EMS) to assess planning, coordination, and funding gaps and to recommend solutions.  The study must be completed and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Designates the Legislative Council to appoint a committee or staff to conduct the study.
The study will examine EMS as a statewide essential service, current capabilities, future demand over five years, gaps, and funding mechanisms.
It requires coordination with counties and the Department of Public Health and Human Services to determine needed resources for the next five years.
Findings must be presented to an appropriate committee and reported to the 70th Legislature.
All study activities must conclude before September 15, 2026.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Montana residents, especially in rural areas

SJ16.one_line: Montana urges federal gov to set safety standards for automated vehicles.
SJ16.summary: Montana’s Senate and House passed a joint resolution urging Congress and the federal Department of Transportation to adopt safety rules for automated vehicles, especially for Montana’s harsh weather and wildlife‑heavy roads. The resolution simply requests federal action and does not create any state program or law.
changes: Urges U.S. Congress to enact laws ensuring automated vehicles can operate safely in all weather, including snow and ice.

SJ19.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s passenger transportation services, to be completed by 9/15/2026.
SJ19.summary: This resolution directs the Legislative Council to commission an interim study of Montana’s passenger transportation options, including rail, air, bus, and future autonomous vehicles, and to report findings to the next legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint an interim or statutory committee to study ways to improve passenger transportation and public transit services in Montana.
affected: Montana residents who rely on passenger transportation

SJ18.one_line: Resolution urges fair recreation consideration for Flathead Lake water‑level decisions.
SJ18.summary: The resolution urges federal and state decision‑makers to give Flathead Lake recreation a fair share of water‑level decisions and to include those needs in the next Columbia River Treaty and system‑operations plan.
changes: 1. Requests that all bodies influencing Flathead Lake pool levels consider recreation fairly versus hydropower, fish, and irrigation.
2. Calls for recreation needs to be explicitly reflected in the next Columbia River Treaty and Columbia River System Operations planning.

3. Directs the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the Technical Management Team, treaty negotiators (Bonneville Power Administration, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, British Columbia Hydro & Power Authority), and all federally recognized Montana tribes.
affected: Federal agencies (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Bonneville Power Administration, British Columbia Hydro & Power Authority)
State agencies involved in water‑level decisions
Recreational users of Flathead Lake (sailors, boaters, swimmers, anglers, campers)

SJ21.one_line: Resolution requests a study on interstate power‑grid compact, deadline September 15, 2026.
SJ21.summary: The resolution directs Montana’s Legislative Council to commission an interim study on the feasibility of an interstate power‑grid compact, setting a deadline of September 15, 2026, and requires the final report to be presented to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to establish a study team or staff to evaluate legal, regulatory, economic, and market‑based aspects of an interstate transmission compact.
affected: stakeholders such as consumer advocacy groups

SJ20.one_line: Resolution honors Montana’s WWII veterans and home‑front supporters.
SJ20.summary: The 69th Legislature passed a joint resolution to honor the 80th anniversary of World War II’s end and to recognize all Montanans who served or supported the war effort. It formally acknowledges the contributions of soldiers, women, and Native Americans from Montana. The resolution also directs the Secretary of State to circulate the document to various veterans’ organizations and state officials.
changes: Recognizes the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II.
Acknowledges all Montanans who served in the armed forces, at home and abroad.
Acknowledges all Montanans who aided the war effort on the home front.
affected: Montanans who served in World War II
Montanans who supported the war effort
numbers: 15 million U.S. men and women served

SJ26.one_line: Montana urges Congress to ban individual stock trades by its members and families.
SJ26.summary: Montana’s Senate and House passed a joint resolution urging the U.S. Congress to enact a law that bars members of Congress and their immediate families from trading individual stocks. The resolution is a formal request and does not create any new state program or law.
changes: Urges Congress to prohibit individual stock trading by members and their immediate families.
affected: Immediate families of members of Congress

SJ25.one_line: Montana urges Congress to mandate country‑of‑origin labeling for beef and pork.
SJ25.summary: Montana’s Senate and House jointly urge the U.S. Congress to require country‑of‑origin labeling for beef and pork products. The resolution simply requests federal action and sends copies to Montana’s congressional delegation and federal officials.

SJ27.one_line: Resolution urging Congress to expand brucellosis vaccine supply and state assistance.
SJ27.summary: SJ 27 is a joint resolution that urges the U.S. Congress to increase production and distribution of brucellosis vaccines for livestock and to provide rapid‑response assistance and grant funding to states. It does not create new state programs or laws, but requests federal action.
affected: federal agencies involved in vaccine production and distribution

SJ28.one_line: Resolution orders an ethics study, to finish by Sept 15 2026, and reports findings to the next Legislature.
SJ28.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to conduct an interim study of Montana’s ethics framework, focusing on procedural adjudication, jurisdictional overlaps, and potential revisions. The study must finish before September 15, 2026, and its findings will be forwarded to the 70th Legislature’s rules committees.
changes: 1. Requires the Legislative Council to study ethics issues and develop a legislative‑procedure‑based adjudication process.
2. Calls for an analysis of overlaps or gaps between the Legislature’s authority and the Commissioner of Political Practices’ jurisdiction.
3. Authorizes the Council to recommend revisions to the code of ethics and legislative rules if deemed necessary.
4. Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completing the study.
5. Mandates that the final report be submitted to the 70th Legislature’s rules committees and to the Legislature itself.
affected: State and local officers and employees subject to the ethics code

SJ29.one_line: Resolution requests a study on coordinating health and education services for children exposed to meth and fentanyl before birth.
SJ29.summary: The resolution asks the Legislature to set up an interim study that brings together the Department of Public Health and Human Services, the Office of Public Instruction, tribal and county partners, and early‑childhood providers to examine how best to help children who were exposed to methamphetamine and fentanyl before birth. The study must finish before September 15, 2026, and its findings must be reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint an interim committee to study coordination between DPHHS and OPI on prenatal‑exposure issues
The committee must work with tribal governments, county health departments, and early‑childhood providers
It must collect and review statistics on affected children
It must research how other states address similar problems
It must develop coordinated response proposals
The study must be completed by September 15, 2026 and its results reported to the 70th Legislature
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SJ35.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana voter list maintenance to be completed by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ35.summary: SJ 35 is a joint resolution that asks the Legislative Council to set up a committee to study how Montana keeps its voter rolls accurate and to recommend improvements. The study must finish before September 15, 2026, and its findings will be sent to the next legislature.
affected: Office of the Secretary of State

SJ33.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s prescription‑drug supply chain, to be completed by Sept 2026.
SJ33.summary: The resolution directs Montana’s Legislative Council to commission an interim study of the state’s prescription‑drug supply chain, focusing on pharmacy sustainability, affordability, and patient access.  The study must use only aggregated or voluntarily provided data, involve stakeholders, and produce recommendations for statutory or regulatory changes by September 15, 2026, with findings reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign an interim or statutory committee to conduct the study.
Mandates the study to examine the structure, roles, and decision‑making of all supply‑chain entities (pharmacies, PBMs, manufacturers, wholesalers, etc.).
Requires analysis of factors driving pharmacy openings, closures, and geographic access issues.
Calls for exploration of strategies to lower patient costs and support pharmacy sustainability, especially in rural areas.
Encourages comparison of best practices from other states’ health plans.
Prohibits use of proprietary or confidential business information; data must be aggregated or voluntarily provided.

Demands stakeholder engagement with documented input, and the development of statutory or regulatory recommendations that protect patient access, address cost impacts, and support independent pharmacies.
Specifies that findings be presented to a committee and finalized before September 15, 2026, with results reported to the Legislature.

SJ37.one_line: Resolution requests a behavioral‑health survey and future legislation to expand beds and reduce provider barriers.
SJ37.summary: The resolution directs a committee to survey Montana’s behavioral‑health capacity and to draft legislation to expand beds and reduce provider barriers. It requires the survey to finish by 15 Sept 2026 and the findings to be reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Designates a committee to conduct a survey of mental‑health beds and providers across the state
The survey must cover emergency detention, short‑term stabilization, long‑term voluntary treatment beds, crisis stabilizers, ongoing service providers, and licensed psychiatrists/psychologists
The committee is tasked with drafting laws to increase bed capacity for all three categories and to lower barriers for providers, especially in rural areas
The survey and any related reports must be completed before September 15, 2026
The final results, including recommendations, must be reported to the 70th Legislature
affected: State legislators and the Legislative Council

SJ36.one_line: Resolution requests a study on prosecutorial standards for dependent neglect cases.
SJ36.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee to study how Montana prosecutes dependent‑neglect cases and whether the Child Protection Unit should be expanded to handle all such cases statewide.  The study must be finished and its findings reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.  No new law or program is created—only a request for an interim study is made.
changes: Requests an interim committee to evaluate standardization of prosecution in dependent‑neglect cases.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services’ Child and Family Services Division
Families and children involved in dependent‑neglect cases

SJ42.one_line: Study noxious‑weed laws, powers, and methods; report findings as new legislation by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ42.summary: The Senate and House request an interim study of Montana’s noxious‑weed laws, powers of the District Weed Board and Coordinator, and possible new control methods. The study must finish by Sept. 15, 2026, and its findings must be turned into introduced legislation for the next session.
changes: 1. Directs the Legislative Council to form a committee to study and recommend changes to the state’s noxious‑weed statutes and regulations.
2. Requires the committee to review existing laws across nine Montana Code titles and to research current control strategies, including herbicides and equipment.
3. Calls for analysis of how other states structure noxious‑weed law, enforcement, responsibilities, and penalties.
4. Mandates proposals to update terminology, definitions, and modernize archaic statutory language.
5. Requires collaboration with a broad range of stakeholders, including district weed coordinators, the Weed Control Association, advisory councils, state agencies, and tribal representatives.
6. Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for the study’s completion and requires the final report to be presented as introduced legislation to the 70th Legislature.
affected: Montana state agencies involved in weed control

SJ48.one_line: Resolution directs an interim study of marijuana’s public‑health and safety impacts, to be reported by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ48.summary: SJ 48 is a joint resolution that directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of the public‑health and safety effects of Montana’s marijuana legalization. The study must cover emergency‑care trends, youth use, criminal‑justice impacts, treatment demand, mental‑health outcomes, and data gaps, and report findings to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to establish an interim or statutory committee to conduct a focused study on marijuana’s public‑health and safety impacts.

Mandates the committee to examine six specific areas: ER/urgent‑care trends, youth academic effects, criminal‑justice impacts, treatment‑service demand, mental‑health disorders, and data‑collection gaps.
