Requires stakeholder engagement from schools, health professionals, law enforcement, tribal and local leaders, and community coalitions.
Calls for objective, data‑driven analysis free from industry or political influence.
Compels the committee to produce a comprehensive report with data summaries, policy gaps, recommendations, and proposed legislative or regulatory strategies.
Sets a completion deadline of September 15, 2026, and requires the report to be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.

SR5.one_line: Adopts Senate rules covering leadership, committees, voting, decorum, and nominations.
SR5.summary: The Senate adopted a comprehensive set of rules governing its internal operations, including officer duties, committee procedures, voting and decorum, and the handling of nominations and confirmations. The resolution codifies the Senate’s organizational structure and procedural safeguards for legislative business.
changes: Adopts detailed officer roles and term limits for Senate leadership.
Establishes procedures for committee appointments, hearings, and reporting.
Defines voting rules, including limits on debate, motion precedence, and absentee voting.
Sets protocols for handling nominations, confirmations, and executive appointments.
Outlines rules for floor actions, including readings, amendments, and overrides of the governor’s veto.
Provides mechanisms for suspending rules and handling appeals of presiding officer decisions.
numbers: 14 legislative days for signing enrolled bills
one day for motion to change vote

SJ49.one_line: Resolution directs a study of Montana’s youth behavioral‑health prevention programs, to be finished by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ49.summary: SJ 49 is a joint resolution that asks the Legislative Council to set up an interim committee to study Montana’s youth‑and‑family behavioral‑health prevention programs. The committee will inventory programs, funding, workforce, and outcomes, compare other states’ models, and recommend a unified, data‑driven strategic plan. The study must finish by Sept. 15, 2026 and report its findings to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to create an interim or statutory committee under §5‑5‑217, MCA
The committee will conduct a comprehensive review of funding, services, workforce, and outcomes for youth‑focused prevention programs
It will inventory existing programs, funding streams, and workforce across state, local, tribal, and faith‑based settings
It will analyze data (e.g., YRBS, ACEs) to assess risk factors and trends
It will compare other jurisdictions’ coordinated prevention models and evaluate their applicability to Montana
It will produce recommendations for a unified, data‑driven strategic plan, including costs, timelines, and oversight mechanisms
The study must be completed and reported to the 70th Legislature by Sept. 15, 2026
affected: State agencies (DPHHS, Office of Public Instruction, Montana University System), tribal governments, local governments, nonprofit and faith‑based organizations, youth under 18 and their families

HB360.one_line: Montana pays child‑care facilities to boost wages and retention, starting July 2025.
HB360.summary: HB 360 establishes a $59.9 million program that pays licensed child‑care facilities to supplement wages, benefits, and bonuses for staff, and in family homes also to cover facility costs, equipment, training, and child mental‑health support. Funds are distributed monthly based on staff counts and must be spent only on the listed eligible uses. The program begins July 1, 2025, and is funded for FY 2025‑26 with a continuing base thereafter.
changes: Creates a state‑funded child‑care workforce recruitment and retention support payment program
Authorizes $59.9 million in FY 2025 and FY 2026 for the program
Distributes payments monthly to eligible facilities in proportion to staff numbers

Limits spending to specific personnel‑related uses (wage supplements, benefits, signing and longevity bonuses) and, for family homes, also facility costs, equipment, training and child mental‑health services
Requires facilities to be licensed day‑care centers, registered group or family day‑care homes
Codifies the program under Title 52, Chapter 2, Part 7 of the Montana Code
affected: Child‑care workers employed by those facilities

HB361.one_line: Creates state‑matching grants and teacher stipends for English‑language learners, funding through 2031.
HB361.summary: The bill creates a state‑matching grant program for school districts that serve English‑language learners and provides annual stipends for highly qualified teachers who work with those students. The grants are funded for two fiscal years and the stipends are paid for a limited period, ending in 2031.
changes: Establishes a state‑matching grant program for districts that receive federal subgrants to serve students with limited English proficiency; the state may match up to $10.20 for each dollar of the federal grant.

Creates two stipend levels for teachers with a culturally and linguistically diverse certificate or ESL endorsement: up to $500 (50% of the state quality‑teacher payment) and up to $1,000 (85% of the state quality‑teacher payment) for teachers in high‑poverty or impacted schools.
Defines the state’s share of each stipend and allows districts to contribute the remainder, with a cap on the state contribution.
Appropriates $5.1 million for the grant program and $25,000–$75,000 for stipends for FY 2026‑27, with the intent that the funds become part of the ongoing base.
Requires the Secretary of State to notify federally recognized tribal governments of the act.
Sets the act’s effective date July 1 2025 and terminates the grant and stipend provisions on June 30 2031.
affected: Public school districts receiving federal subgrants for English‑language learners
Teachers with culturally and linguistically diverse or ESL endorsements
School districts and education cooperatives that employ eligible teachers

HB362.one_line: Allows common‑element interest changes with 75 % owner consent and recorded amendment.
HB362.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Unit Ownership Act so that the undivided interest of each unit owner in common elements can be changed if at least 75 % of the owners who have an interest in that element agree and record the change. It does not create a new program or fund.
changes: Amends §70‑23‑403 to allow alteration of a unit owner’s undivided interest in common elements when 75 % of the owners with an interest in that element consent and record an amendment to the declaration.
Requires the amended declaration to specify the new percentages for each owner with an interest.
Maintains that the original percentage is based on the unit’s value relative to the combined value of all units with interest, not necessarily market value.
No other provisions are added or removed.
The amendment is purely procedural and does not affect other sections of the Act.
affected: Unit owners in condominiums, cooperatives, or other common‑element developments

HB364.one_line: Schools must file annual de‑identified immunization reports and enforce attendance for non‑vaccinated students.
HB364.summary: The bill requires every public school to keep de‑identified immunization records, file an annual aggregate report to the Department of Public Health and the local health department, and enforce attendance restrictions for students who are not fully vaccinated or who have conditional enrollment.
changes: Amends §20‑5‑406 to mandate that school governing authorities record each pupil’s immunization status and file an annual de‑identified report by December 1 each year.
Specifies the report must include total enrollment, number of exempted students, number fully vaccinated, and number with conditional enrollment.
Amends §20‑5‑408 to allow schools to prohibit attendance for conditionally enrolled students who fail to obtain required immunizations within the department‑established time period.
Adds a new section setting the effective date of the act to July 1, 2025.
Preserves FERPA privacy protections for individual health records.
affected: Department of Public Health and Local Health Departments
numbers: four data items in the report

HB363.one_line: Hybrid commission: 2 elected, 3 appointed, new districts, strict appointment rules.
HB363.summary: HB 363 revises the Montana Public Service Commission to make it a hybrid body of two elected and three appointed members, sets new district boundaries, term limits, and qualifications for appointees, and establishes a detailed appointment process.
changes: Commission now has five members: two elected from separate districts and three appointed by the governor and confirmed by the senate
Five public‑service districts are created, each electing one commissioner; districts are based on federal congressional districts and will be adjusted after each census

Elected commissioners serve four‑year terms (max 12 years in 24 years) and appointed commissioners serve six‑year terms (max 12 years in 24 years); vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment with party‑aligned requirements

Appointed commissioners must have at least two years’ separation from regulated entities, no financial ties to regulated entities, U.S. citizenship, 2‑year residency, industry experience from a distinct sector, and no recent political party activity
The governor may receive candidate suggestions from regulated entities but not from political parties; the senate must confirm qualifications and may not refuse appointments on unlisted grounds
Transition provisions shift the second and third district commissioners to new eastern and western congressional districts and set appointment deadlines for 2027‑2029
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.

HB366.one_line: Reimburses Lake County $5 million for felony jurisdiction transfer to Flathead Reservation.
HB366.summary: The bill appropriates $5 million from the general fund to reimburse Lake County for its role in transferring felony jurisdiction to the Flathead Indian Reservation. It sets the use of the funds, acknowledges the county’s withdrawal from PL 280, and establishes a June 30, 2027 deadline for completing the transition. The appropriation continues biennially until the state retrocedes from PL 280.
changes: Appropriates $2.5 million each fiscal year (FY 2025‑26) to the Department of Justice for Lake County and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes
Funds are to be divided equally between the tribes and Lake County for expenses related to enforcing felony jurisdiction on the Flathead Reservation
The appropriation is treated as part of the ongoing base for each biennium until the state retrocedes from Public Law 280
Lake County’s withdrawal from PL 280 remains effective if the transition is not completed by June 30, 2027, but the county may continue to assist at its discretion
The bill includes a severability clause and becomes effective July 1, 2025

HB370.one_line: Appropriates $65 million to Highway Patrol retirement fund, effective July 1, 2025.
HB370.summary: The bill appropriates $65 million from the general fund to the Montana Highway Patrol Officers’ Retirement System for FY 2025, providing a one‑time supplemental contribution. It takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Appropriates $65 million to the Highway Patrol Officers’ Retirement System pension fund for FY 2025.
The appropriation is a one‑time supplemental contribution.
The act becomes effective July 1, 2025.
affected: Montana Highway Patrol officers (active and retirees)

HB369.one_line: HB 369 creates a county road maintenance district funded by property‑tax assessments and requires its budget be included in the county’s general fund.
HB369.summary: HB 369 creates a county road maintenance district (CRMD) that can be formed when a majority of property owners petition for it.  The district would be funded by a property‑tax assessment and its budget must be included in the county’s general‑fund budget.  The bill also includes a $25,000 audit appropriation and a contingent‑voidness clause that voids the act if a county enters a long‑term maintenance agreement with a homeowners’ association.
changes: Authorizes a CRMD when the county board votes to discontinue county maintenance on county‑owned roads and a petition of ≥66 % of property owners is received.
Requires petitioners to submit a detailed maintenance plan (boundaries, roads, jurisdiction, maintenance type, assessment method).
Mandates a public hearing before the district is created.
The district’s annual budget must be prepared and submitted to the county board; the board cannot alter or exclude it.
Allows the district to assess the full maintenance cost against benefited property parcels using the method in 7‑12‑2151(1)(b).
Reduces the county’s general‑fund levy by the amount assessed by the district and requires that reduction to be reflected in the county’s road‑and‑bridge budgets.
Provides that the district may contract with public or private entities for maintenance services.
Adds a $25,000 appropriation for a biennial audit of Granite County’s 2024 finances.
Includes a contingent‑voidness provision that voids the act if the county signs a long‑term maintenance agreement with a homeowners’ association that covers future reconstruction and maintenance.
Amends §15‑10‑420 to clarify how the district’s assessment is applied to the county levy.
affected: Property owners in the proposed district

HB371.one_line: Bans mRNA vaccines for humans in Montana, fines $500 per violation.
HB371.summary: The bill bars any person from giving or administering mRNA‑based vaccines to humans in Montana, treating such a violation as a misdemeanor punishable by a $500 fine. It also requires the state labor board to review the licenses of violators. The bill does not create a new program or fund, merely imposes a prohibition and penalty.
changes: Prohibits the administration of any gene‑based vaccine for infectious diseases to a human in Montana.
Defines a gene‑based vaccine for infectious diseases as one made with mRNA, modified mRNA, self‑amplifying mRNA, or DNA technology.
Classifies a violation as a misdemeanor with a $500 fine per incident.
Mandates the Montana Department of Labor and Industry’s licensure board to review the license of any licensed person who violates the prohibition.
affected: Any person who administers a gene‑based vaccine

HB373.one_line: Creates a lottery‑education revenue account and mandates quarterly per‑educator distribution to all school districts.
HB373.summary: The bill creates a dedicated lottery‑education special revenue account and requires quarterly distribution of lottery proceeds to every school district on a per‑quality‑educator basis. It also expands the permissible uses of school flexibility funds and amends several statutes governing lottery revenue, appropriations, and school fund uses.
changes: Establishes a Lottery Education State Special Revenue Account within the State Special Revenue Fund, administered by the Office of Public Instruction.

Mandates that lottery revenues received under 23‑7‑402 be distributed quarterly (and annually by June 1) to all school districts on a per‑quality‑educator basis, calculated by dividing total funds by total quality educators in the preceding fiscal year.
Requires districts receiving funds to deposit them into their flexibility fund established under 20‑9‑543.
Amends 17‑7‑502 to clarify statutory appropriation requirements and lists applicable statutes.

Rewrites 20‑9‑543 to broaden permissible uses of school flexibility funds to include technology, facility upgrades, supplies, assessment, curriculum, staff training, teacher housing, recruitment incentives, and energy‑cost increases.
Rewrites 23‑7‑202 to give the lottery commission authority to maximize net revenue for schools and the STEM scholarship program and to adopt rules for lottery operations.

Rewrites 23‑7‑402 to set a 45% prize‑payment minimum, specify net‑revenue transfers (first $2.25 M to STEM scholarship, remainder to the Lottery Education Account), and allow spending‑authority increases upon review.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1, 2025 and applies it to all lottery net revenues from that quarter onward.
numbers: applies to fiscal quarters beginning July 1, 2025

HB374.one_line: Broadens nonprofit casino nights to include more live games and limits expanded nights to once per year.
HB374.summary: HB 374 revises Montana’s gambling statutes to broaden the types of games that nonprofit organizations may offer during casino nights and expanded casino nights. It expands the list of permitted live card games, adds bingo, keno, roulette, craps, and faro, and allows these events to occur once per year for nonprofits.
changes: Amends §23‑5‑112 to update definitions for antique gambling devices, applicants, and other terms used in the gambling code
Adds new definitions for nonprofit organization, casino night, expanded casino night, and related gaming terms
Expands the list of games allowed during a nonprofit’s casino night to include live card games, bingo, keno, and raffles
Expands the list of games allowed during an expanded casino night to include live blackjack, twenty‑one, jacks‑or‑better, baccarat, chemin de fer, roulette, craps, hazard, chuck‑a‑luck, and faro
Limits expanded casino nights to a maximum of one per year per nonprofit
Does not create new licensing or funding programs, only changes permissible activities
No new taxes or fees are imposed
No new enforcement authority is added beyond existing department powers
affected: Nonprofit organizations that host casino nights
Department of Justice (for rule‑making and enforcement)
Operators and dealers who provide the games
Participants in the expanded casino nights
numbers: live blackjack, twenty‑one, jacks‑or‑better, baccarat, chemin de fer

HB375.one_line: Mandates legislative polling and disclosure for statewide initiatives, with immediate effect.
HB375.summary: HB 375 requires the Secretary of State to mail a ballot to every legislator for each statewide initiative, tally the votes, and include those results in voter‑information pamphlets and certified ballot forms. It amends the MCA to add detailed disclosure requirements for statewide ballot issues and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: 1. Legislators receive a mailed ballot for each statewide initiative within 5 working days after the petition deadline; they may vote by mail, fax, or email and cannot change their vote once returned.
2. The Secretary of State must tally all returned votes within one working day and publish the results in pamphlets and certified ballot forms.
3. The pamphlet must contain the initiative’s title, fiscal statement, full text, ballot form, arguments for and against, rebuttals, and a summary of the legislative poll by party affiliation.

4. The certified ballot form must list each initiative’s number, placement method, title, explanatory statements, fiscal statement, yes/no wording, conflict statements, and the same legislative‑poll summary.
5. The act amends sections 13‑27‑401 and 13‑27‑501 of the Montana Code to incorporate these new disclosure and reporting requirements.
6. The act takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to initiatives submitted on or after that date.
affected: Secretary of State and county election officials

HB376.one_line: Mandates timely agency responses and allows budget cuts for non‑compliance.
HB376.summary: HB 376 requires state agencies to respond to legislators’ written requests within five legislative days. If an agency fails, the legislator can file a complaint, prompting a committee hearing and a possible 5 % budget cut for the agency.
changes: 1. Legislators may submit written requests limited to one bill or issue; agencies must reply within five legislative days.
2. A legislator may file a written complaint after the deadline, including details of the request, agency response, and proposed budget cut.
3. The appropriations committee must hold a hearing within three legislative days, with notice to the legislator and agency director.
4. The committee may vote to reduce the agency’s budget by up to 5 % for non‑compliance.
5. The hearing, discussion, and vote must be recorded and reported to the Senate President, House Speaker, and Governor within ten days.
6. The governor may add the committee’s vote to the director’s personnel file and impose disciplinary action, including termination.

HB377.one_line: HB 377 expands parental access to child health records while protecting abused children.
HB377.summary: HB 377 revises Montana’s child‑health‑care privacy law to give parents broader access to their child’s medical records, while still protecting children in cases of abuse or domestic violence. It amends the statutory language on consent, record‑access, and the role of health‑care representatives, and takes effect immediately.
changes: Amends §40‑6‑702 to require hospitals to obtain parental consent before performing any medical or mental‑health procedure on a child, except in emergencies or when a parent cannot be located.
Expands the definition of parental access to include all health‑care information, allowing parents to request and receive records within 10 days, except for abortion records.
Adds exclusions to parental access when a court order limits the parent’s rights, when the parent is a government entity, or when the parent is alleged to have abused or neglected the child.

Clarifies that a health‑care representative may act on a minor’s behalf only to the extent that the minor has consented to care, and that a minor who can consent without parental permission retains exclusive rights to that information.
Includes a severability clause and states the act is effective upon passage.

HB378.one_line: Repeals Montana’s ban on housing‑fee or property‑dedication requirements in local zoning and subdivision ordinances.
HB378.summary: HB 378 repeals Montana’s prohibition on local governments requiring housing‑related fees or property dedication for affordable‑housing purposes, and amends several zoning statutes to remove that restriction. The bill allows municipalities to impose such fees or dedications in zoning, subdivision, and development regulations.
changes: Amends §7‑2‑4203, §76‑2‑203, §76‑2‑302, §76‑25‑303, and §76‑25‑401 to state that local governments may not compel owners to pay a fee or dedicate real property for the purpose of providing housing for specified income levels or at specified sale prices.
Repeals §§76‑2‑114 and 76‑3‑514, which previously prohibited housing fees and property dedication.
The amendments preserve all other zoning and subdivision requirements, including provisions on manufactured housing, tiny dwellings, and historic preservation.
The bill does not create new programs, funds, or criminal offenses; it merely removes an existing restriction.
The changes apply to all Montana local governments (cities, towns, counties) that adopt zoning or subdivision ordinances.

HB379.one_line: Rewrites state land lease and sale rules, removes auctions, adds lessee rights and limits sales.
HB379.summary: HB 379 revises Montana’s rules for leasing and selling state land, eliminating auction requirements, allowing individual lease agreements, and tightening sale procedures and payment terms. It adds new definitions, limits cumulative land sales, and gives lessees preference and cancellation rights. The bill also repeals several old certificate‑of‑purchase provisions.
changes: Eliminates mandatory public auction sales, permitting direct individual agreements between lessees and the Department.
Adds new definitions for commercial lease, commercial purpose, land value, and termination.
Rewrites sale procedures: requires weekly newspaper notices, sets minimum 10 % down‑payment, 30‑day balance due, and bid‑bond rules.
Limits cumulative land sales to 250,000 acres, with 75 % isolated parcels and a 20,000‑acre one‑time cap.
Gives lessees the right to match the highest bid and to cancel sales with notice, paying preparation costs.
Repeals sections 77‑2‑327 through 77‑2‑335, removing old certificate‑of‑purchase rules.

HB382.one_line: Montana declares U.S. gold/silver coins legal tender, exempts exchanges from taxes, and protects owners from seizure.
HB382.summary: The bill declares U.S. gold and silver coins as legal tender in Montana, exempts exchanges of such specie from state income and sales taxes, and protects owners from state seizure or enforcement actions. It also amends tax code to treat gains or losses from specie transactions as taxable income or deductions and updates forfeiture provisions to include specie.
changes: 1. Defines “specie legal tender” as U.S. gold or silver coin and declares it legal tender in Montana.
2. Prohibits the state or its agencies from compelling acceptance of specie legal tender and from seizing it except as allowed by existing forfeiture law.
3. Exempts any exchange of one form of legal tender for another from individual income tax and from all sales taxes.
4. Adds to Montana’s tax code that gains or losses from the sale or exchange of specie legal tender are treated as taxable income (or deductions) under Sections 15‑30‑2101, 15‑30‑2120, and 45‑9‑206.
5. Amends Section 45‑9‑206 to list specie legal tender as property subject to criminal forfeiture in drug‑related cases.
6. Codifies the act as part of Title 30 and sets its effective date for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
affected: Montana residents and non‑residents who own or transact in U.S. gold or silver coins
Law enforcement and courts handling forfeiture cases
numbers: effective date: tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025
specie legal tender defined as U.S. gold or silver coin
exemption from individual income tax and all sales taxes

HB383.one_line: Adds unique URLs to every campaign‑finance file, report, and search result in Montana’s system.
HB383.summary: The bill amends Montana’s campaign‑finance rules to require the state’s electronic reporting system to give each file, report, and search result its own unique web address. The change takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Adds a requirement that every campaign‑finance file and report in the electronic system have a unique URL
Ensures each search result returned by the system also receives a distinct URL
Codifies the requirement as part of Title 13, Chapter 37, Part 2 of the Montana Code
Sets the effective date of the amendment to July 1, 2025
affected: Campaign committees and candidates filing reports
Montana Secretary of State’s Office (operator of the electronic system)
Voters and researchers accessing campaign‑finance information

HB385.one_line: Montana launches a two‑year school mental‑health grant pilot with reporting and evaluation requirements.
HB385.summary: Montana will create a two‑year pilot program that gives school districts grants to design student‑led mental‑health initiatives, with reporting and evaluation requirements. The program is funded with $250,000 per biennium and ends in 2029.
changes: Establishes a school mental‑health promotion pilot program administered by the Office of Public Instruction
Creates a grant application process that requires student, parent, staff, trustee, and community support
Provides grant amounts of at least $10,000, up to $25 per enrolled student or $50,000, capped at $50,000
Mandates a two‑year grant cycle with the possibility of a second cycle
Requires districts to deposit funds in a miscellaneous programs fund and use them only for mental‑health activities
Imposes biannual reporting on expenditures, activities, and effectiveness, and requires the Office to report to the Education Interim Committee
Allocates $250,000 from the general fund each biennium for grant distribution
Notifies federally recognized tribal governments of the act
Codifies the program under Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 13
Sets effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2029

HB386.one_line: Montana directs its health department to seek waivers for 12‑month continuous Medicaid eligibility for parents, caretakers, and expansion groups.
HB386.summary: The bill directs Montana’s Department of Public Health and Human Services to seek federal waivers that would allow parents, caretaker relatives, and Medicaid‑expansion beneficiaries to maintain continuous 12‑month Medicaid eligibility. It requires the department to submit the waiver applications by September 30 2025 and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Directs the department to apply for 1115 waivers to restore 12‑month continuous eligibility for specified groups.
Requires submission of waiver applications no later than September 30 2025.
Targets parents, caretaker relatives, and Medicaid‑expansion population as defined in federal statutes.
No new state program or funding is created.
No financial provisions are included.
The act is effective upon passage.
The bill does not alter existing Medicaid eligibility rules beyond the waiver request.
affected: Parents and caretaker relatives eligible for Medicaid
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB389.one_line: Sets 1,250‑ft, 3,000‑ft, and 7,920‑ft setbacks for new wind turbines.
HB389.summary: The bill establishes minimum setback distances for new wind turbine generators, requiring them to be at least 1,250 ft from any property line of a wind‑energy‑agreement holder, 3,000 ft from public roads, and 7,920 ft from non‑agreement property lines. The rules take effect on the act’s effective date and are codified in Title 75, Chapter 26.
changes: Sets a 1,250‑ft minimum distance from the tower base to any property line of a wind‑energy‑agreement holder.

HB390.one_line: Montana requires farm equipment makers to share parts, tools, and docs with independent repairers on fair terms.
HB390.summary: The bill creates a Montana “Agricultural Equipment Repair Bill of Rights Act” that requires manufacturers to provide owners and independent repair shops with fair‑and‑reasonable access to parts, tools, and documentation for diagnosing and fixing farm equipment.  It limits manufacturers’ use of software locks and other restrictions that would prevent independent repair, but does not impose new taxes or create a state program.
changes: 1.  Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools available to independent repair providers and owners on fair and reasonable terms, including updates.
2.  Manufacturers may not use parts‑pairing or other software mechanisms to block non‑manufacturer parts, reduce performance, or create deceptive alerts.
3.  For equipment with electronic locks, manufacturers must supply owners or independent repairers (with owner permission) the tools and documentation needed to reset the lock.
4.  The act excludes motor vehicles and industrial/construction equipment from its definition of “agricultural equipment.”
5.  The act does not require disclosure of trade secrets beyond what is necessary for repair, nor does it alter existing authorized‑repair‑provider agreements.
6.  The act becomes effective January 1 2026 and terminates automatically if Congress enacts a federal right‑to‑repair law for agricultural equipment.
affected: Owners or lessees of farm equipment

HB395.one_line: HB 395 amends voting‑law definitions and tightens mental‑health commitment and discharge procedures.
HB395.summary: HB 395 revises Montana’s voting‑law definitions and mental‑health‑commitment procedures, clarifying terms such as “unsound mind” and “penal institution” and tightening the process for involuntary commitment, discharge, and conditional release.
changes: Amends §13‑1‑101 to add new definitions for election‑related terms and to clarify the meaning of “unsound mind” and “penal institution.”

Rewrites §46‑14‑312 to allow courts to sentence defendants with a mental disease or developmental disability to a mental‑health or correctional facility instead of a mandatory minimum prison term, with a review process for release if the condition improves.

Revises §53‑21‑102 to expand the definition of “mental disorder” and to clarify the scope of mental‑health facilities, including behavioral‑health inpatient facilities and residential treatment centers.

Amends §53‑21‑127 to set specific timelines (within 5 days) for post‑trial disposition hearings, limit commitment periods to 3–6 months, and require courts to choose the least restrictive placement and to document findings on treatment alternatives.

Revises §53‑21‑181 to allow patients to be discharged by the professional person in charge during the commitment period, requires 5‑day notice of discharge, and guarantees referral to other mental‑health services upon discharge.

Rewrites §53‑21‑197 to give courts authority to revoke conditional release based on clear evidence of a mental‑disorder relapse or violation of release conditions, with mandatory updates to the treatment plan.
All changes are procedural and do not create new state programs or criminal offenses.

HB402.one_line: Designates Wolf Point as the Hall of Fame site and directs map and sign updates.
HB402.summary: The bill moves the Montana Cowboy Hall of Fame and Western Heritage Center to Wolf Point, directs state agencies to mark the new location on maps and road signs, and makes the change effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends Section 1‑1‑525, MCA, to designate Wolf Point as the site of the Hall of Fame and Western Heritage Center.
Requires the Department of Commerce and the Department of Transportation to identify Wolf Point on official state maps.
Mandates the Department of Transportation to replace or add road signs to recognize the new location.
Sets the effective date of the act to the day it is passed and approved.
affected: State agencies: Department of Commerce, Department of Transportation
Wolf Point city officials and residents
Visitors and tourists to the Hall of Fame

HB404.one_line: Bill bars Guard combat deployment without congressional war declaration or explicit call.
HB404.summary: The bill creates the “Defend the Guard Act,” which bars the Montana National Guard from being federalized for active‑combat duty unless Congress declares war or explicitly calls the Guard under the Constitution. It preserves the governor’s authority to activate the Guard for state‑controlled missions and allows federal missions under Title 10 if they do not conflict with the new restrictions.
changes: Requires an official U.S. congressional declaration of war or explicit call under Article I, §8, cl. 15 before the Guard can be released for active‑combat duty.
Prohibits state‑to‑federal transfer of Guard personnel for combat unless the above conditions are met.
Empowers the governor to enforce the restriction and to consent to Title 32 state‑controlled missions.
Allows Title 10 federal missions that do not violate the new restrictions.
Codifies the act as part of Title 10, Chapter 1 of the U.S. Code.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.

HB405.one_line: HB 405 hikes school‑bus mileage reimbursement rates to boost district transportation budgets.
HB405.summary: HB 405 raises the state’s mileage reimbursement rates for school‑bus and non‑bus travel, allowing districts to budget more for transportation. The new rates apply to all school fiscal years starting July 1 2025.
changes: Amends §20‑10‑141 to increase bus‑mile reimbursement rates from 85 ¢ to $1.58–$2.99 depending on bus capacity.
Adds a non‑bus mileage reimbursement rate of 85 ¢ per mile.
Clarifies that districts may budget beyond the maximum reimbursement but cannot claim reimbursement for those extra miles.
Requires that reimbursed vehicles be school buses driven by qualified drivers on approved routes.
Sets the effective date to July 1 2025 and limits applicability to fiscal years beginning on or after that date.
affected: Students and families using school transportation

HB407.one_line: Montana will regulate kratom with registration, quality standards, labeling, taxes, and penalties.
HB407.summary: The bill creates a comprehensive regulatory framework for kratom in Montana, requiring processors, distributors, and retailers to register, meet strict product‑quality standards, and label products with health warnings.  It imposes fines and criminal penalties for non‑compliance and establishes a dedicated revenue account for fees and taxes.
changes: Establishes a state‑wide registration system for kratom processors, distributors, and retailers, with annual fees ($500 for processors, $400 for distributors and retailers).
Sets strict product‑quality limits: no more than 2% 7‑hydroxy‑mitragynine, no synthetic materials, no dangerous non‑kratom substances, and requires ISO‑17025 lab certification for each batch.
Mandates labeling that includes age warnings, health‑care consultation advice, habit‑forming notice, FDA disclaimer, and detailed ingredient and serving‑size information.
Imposes a 5% excise tax on wholesale kratom sales, payable quarterly by distributors.
Creates civil penalties ($10k–$15k fines) and criminal penalties (misdemeanor for first violations, felony for controlled‑substance or synthetic kratom violations).
Provides a dedicated state special revenue account to hold all fees, taxes, and civil penalties, with excess funds transferred to the general fund.
affected: Food service establishments selling fresh kratom

HB408.one_line: Mandates device filters for minors, holds manufacturers and filter‑removers liable, and allows AG and parents to sue.
HB408.summary: The bill requires all new Montana‑activated tablets and smartphones to have a built‑in filter that blocks obscene content for minors, imposes civil liability on manufacturers that fail to provide such a filter, and creates liability for anyone who removes the filter from a minor’s device. It also allows the Attorney General to sue violators and lets parents sue manufacturers for damages.
changes: 1. Devices activated in Montana on or after Jan 1 2026 must contain a filter that blocks obscene content for minors and can be disabled only by a password.
2. Manufacturers are civilly liable if a device activated in Montana does not enable the required filter and a minor accesses obscene content.
3. A person who intentionally disables the filter on a minor’s device and the minor then accesses obscene content is liable in civil and criminal action (except parents/guardians).

4. The Attorney General may seek injunctions, recover civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation ($50,000 aggregate), attorney fees, and other relief, and may revoke a manufacturer’s license for repeated violations.

5. Parents or legal guardians may file private civil actions against manufacturers for actual damages or $50,000 per violation, and against non‑parent persons who disable the filter for $1,000 per violation.
6. The act is codified into Title 30, Chapter 14, Part 1 and takes effect Jan 1 2026.
affected: Parents and legal guardians of minors
Individuals who remove filters from minors’ devices
The Attorney General and state courts

HB412.one_line: Exempts certain home additions from tax hikes, limited by value, timing, and sale conditions.
HB412.summary: HB 412 exempts certain additions to class‑four residential homes from property‑tax increases, limited to the lesser of the added value or 15 % of last year’s value, and applies only once every six years. The exemption ends if the house is sold or if the addition is made within three years of a new build. The law takes effect for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2025.
changes: Provides a property‑tax exemption for adding living space to an existing class‑four residential structure.
The exemption equals the lesser of the increase in market value caused by the modification or 15 % of the prior year’s market value.
Exemptions cannot be granted for modifications made within three years of a new construction of a class‑four home.
Only one exemption may be granted to a property in any six‑year period.
The exemption terminates upon sale of the property.
The Department of Revenue will administer the exemption using existing resources and codify it under Title 15, Chapter 6, Part 2.
The act applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
affected: Property owners of class‑four residential homes adding living space
Department of Revenue staff administering exemptions

HB410.one_line: Majority approval of bonds and levies when turnout is 35 % or more, with revised thresholds and election procedures.
HB410.summary: HB 410 revises Montana’s bond‑ and mill‑levy election rules so that a majority of voters can approve many bonds and levies when turnout is at least 35 % (instead of the former 40 % or higher thresholds). It amends dozens of statutory sections to clarify how turnout is calculated, what majority is required, and when elections must be held. The bill also updates related procedures for county, municipal, school‑district, and special‑purpose bond elections, and adds a new section that allows a majority to approve certain bonds or levies held on a primary or general election in an even‑numbered year.
changes: Replaces the 40 % turnout requirement for bond and mill‑levy approvals with a 35 % turnout threshold when a majority of votes cast are in favor; retains a 60 % majority requirement when turnout is between 30 % and 35 % for bonds that previously required 60 % approval; keeps the 40 % threshold for turnout above 40 % but still requires a majority of votes cast.
Adds a new section (22) that sets the effective date as passage and approval and a new section (23) that limits the act’s applicability to elections held on or after that date.

Revises the language for how a county or municipality may covenant to levy a tax to cover bond deficits, and how school districts may issue bonds or obligations without a vote under certain conditions.
Rewrites the election‑notice and ballot‑statement requirements for mill‑levy elections (15‑10‑425) to include specific impact statements for homes of various values.
Clarifies the calculation of voter turnout for bond and levy elections, including how to handle elections held outside even‑numbered years.
affected: Voters in counties, cities, towns, and school districts
Taxpayers who may be subject to new or increased taxes
numbers: applicability: elections on or after effective date

HB418.one_line: Montana bans gene‑based vaccines in animals, restricts import, and fines veterinarians and pharmacists $500 per violation.
HB418.summary: The bill bans the use of any gene‑based vaccine in Montana animals, prohibits import of animals or semen that have been vaccinated, and creates penalties for veterinarians and pharmacists who dispense or sell such vaccines. It also amends existing veterinary‑practice statutes to clarify the ban and to require fines to be deposited in an animal‑health fund.
changes: Amends §37‑18‑102 to prohibit veterinarians from prescribing or dispensing any gene‑based vaccine (mRNA, modified‑mRNA, self‑amplifying mRNA, or DNA) and imposes a $500 misdemeanor fine per incident, with proceeds deposited in the animal health enterprise fund.
Amends §37‑18‑104 to clarify exemptions and to prohibit the sale of gene‑based vaccines by pharmacists, while preserving other veterinary‑practice provisions.
Amends §37‑18‑804 to forbid veterinary dispensing technicians from dispensing any gene‑based vaccine and restricts other dispensing activities.

Amends §81‑2‑703 to prohibit importation of livestock, poultry, fish, game, or semen that have been treated with or exposed to gene‑based vaccines, and requires health certificates or permits for all animal movements.
Adds a new penalty schedule and specifies that fines collected under §37‑18‑102(3)(b) be deposited in the animal health enterprise fund account established in §81‑2‑116.
Clarifies that the ban does not affect veterinary‑practice exemptions listed in §37‑18‑104 and does not alter other existing veterinary‑practice rules.

HB422.one_line: Allows covenants limiting sale or equity appreciation to specific income or occupation groups to run with land.
HB422.summary: HB 422 amends Montana’s covenant law to permit covenants that limit sale, lease, or equity appreciation of residential property to people with certain incomes or occupations, aiming to keep workforce housing affordable. The change adds this type of covenant to the list of those that run with the land. No new program or fund is created.
changes: Amends §70‑17‑203, MCA, adding subsection (2)(e) to list covenants that run with land.
Subsection (2)(e) specifically allows covenants restricting sale, lease, or owner’s share of equity appreciation to individuals with specified incomes or occupations.
The amendment does not alter other covenant categories or create new enforcement mechanisms.
No new state office, fund, or criminal offense is established.
affected: Potential buyers or tenants of workforce housing

HB420.one_line: HB 420 tightens tax‑deed rules, extends redemption, sets equity thresholds, and mandates online auctions.
HB420.summary: HB 420 revises Montana’s tax‑lien and tax‑deed rules to tighten notice requirements, extend redemption periods, set equity thresholds, and require online bidding at auctions. It also adds detailed fee schedules and a new surplus‑fund distribution scheme for unclaimed property.
changes: County treasurers must publish a notice within 10 days of receiving a tax record, detailing due dates, interest, penalties, and itemized levies, and send written notices to taxpayers and interested parties; notices may be posted online instead of mailed.

Redemption periods for tax liens are extended: 3 years (or 5 years) for most properties, 2 years for residential or commercial lots without a dwelling, and 5 years for certain special‑improvement‑district properties.
A tax deed may be issued only if the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest, and costs exceed the lesser of the property’s fair‑market value or $5,000, establishing an equity threshold.

Assignees must pay a $25 application fee and a $25 tax‑deed fee; the county treasurer may charge the assignee $25 for preparing the deed and related notices, with the fee deposited in the county general fund.

Public auctions must be held within 60 days of a tax‑deed application, with an opening bid equal to the sum of the redeemable amount, assignee payments, deed fees, and half the most recent assessed value (or an independent appraisal). Bids are required to be received electronically in real time.

Surplus funds from the auction (the portion equal to half the assessed value or any amount above the opening bid) are distributed to the legal titleholder of record within 30 days; unclaimed surplus is forwarded to the state as unclaimed property.

HB429.one_line: Creates a special revenue account to invest $50 million in precious metals, large‑cap digital assets, and stablecoins.
HB429.summary: The bill creates a new state special revenue account for investing in precious metals, large‑cap digital assets, and stablecoins, funded by a one‑time transfer of up to $50 million from the general fund. It authorizes the Board of Investments to hold those assets with a qualified custodian or through an exchange‑traded fund.
changes: Creates an Inflation Protection Act state special revenue account within the state special revenue fund.
Authorizes the Board of Investments to invest account funds in silver, gold, platinum, digital assets with >$750 B market cap, and stablecoins.
Requires all investment proceeds to remain in the account.
Mandates the state treasurer to transfer up to $50 million from the general fund to the account by July 15 2025.
Codifies the provisions as part of Title 17, chapter 1.
Effective July 1 2025.

HB433.one_line: Prevents gun‑rights deprivation pending trial except for forcible felonies or violent weapon crimes.
HB433.summary: HB 433 prohibits the state from depriving a person of the right to keep and bear arms while they are charged with a crime, except when charged with a forcible felony or a violent crime involving a weapon. The bill simply codifies this presumption of innocence into Montana’s gun‑rights law.
changes: Prevents any deprivation of gun‑rights pending trial for most crimes.
Excludes only charges of forcible felonies or violent crimes using a weapon.
Codifies the exception into Title 45, Chapter 8, Part 3 of the Montana Code.
No new programs, funds, or penalties are created.
No monetary or procedural changes beyond the prohibition.
The bill does not alter existing statutes beyond adding this exception.
affected: Individuals charged with crimes (except forcible felonies or violent weapon crimes).
Montana law‑enforcement agencies and courts handling gun‑rights issues.
numbers: 45-2-101 (definition of forcible felony and violent crime using a weapon)

HB437.one_line: Allows providers to dismiss criminal charges if state fails to prove intent and deviation from standards.
HB437.summary: HB 437 allows a health‑care provider to file a motion to dismiss a criminal complaint, information, or indictment that is based on the provider’s conduct in patient care.  The state must prove by a preponderance of evidence that the conduct was knowingly or purposely committed and fell outside accepted standards of care; otherwise the case is dismissed.
changes: Provides a statutory motion for dismissal of criminal charges against health‑care providers.  The provider may move to dismiss any criminal complaint, information, or indictment based on conduct in providing health care.  The court must hold a hearing promptly.  The state must prove, by preponderance of evidence, that the conduct was knowingly or purposely committed and outside accepted standards of care.  If the state fails to meet this burden, the charge is dismissed.  The provision is codified as part of Title 46, chapter 13, part 4.

HB436.one_line: Trappers must post a weather‑proof sign near trailheads where traps are set on public lands.
HB436.summary: Trappers on Montana public lands must post a sizable, weather‑proof notice sign within specified distances of trailheads or trails where traps or snares are located. The sign must display the department’s phone number, a title, and a statement about the legality of disturbing traps, with an exception for livestock owners between March 1 and October 1. Trappers are responsible for installing, maintaining, and replacing the sign if it becomes illegible or missing.
changes: Requires trappers to post a notice sign at trailheads or within 100 ft of a trail if traps/snares are within 1,000 ft of the trailhead or 100 ft of any trail point
The Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks must provide a printable or printed sign template
The sign must be at least 8½ × 11 in., weather‑resistant, display the department’s phone number, a title in ≥1‑inch letters, and a legal statement about disturbing traps
Trappers must replace an illegible or missing sign within 24 hrs of noticing or being informed
Trappers may only remove the sign after all traps/snares are removed
Defines “public trail” and “trailhead” for the purposes of the requirement
Codifies the requirement into Title 87, Chapter 2, Part 6
affected: Trappers on public lands administered by the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

HB439.one_line: Federal agents must notify Montana sheriffs before arrests, searches, or seizures, with limited exceptions.
HB439.summary: HB 439 requires federal employees and other agents who are not Montana peace officers to notify the county sheriff before making an arrest, search, or seizure in Montana, with limited exceptions. It also creates a requirement to notify the attorney general when the sheriff notification is exempted. The law takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Federal employees and other agents must give notice to the county sheriff (or a designee) before any arrest, search, or seizure in Montana, unless the subject is a sheriff employee or elected official, or the agent has probable cause that the subject has close connections to the sheriff.
If the sheriff‑notification exception applies, the agent must instead notify the Montana Attorney General.
The act codifies these provisions as part of Title 44 of the Montana Code, applying all Title 44 provisions to the new sections.
The law becomes effective on the day it is passed and approved.
affected: Federal employees and other agents acting on behalf of the federal government in Montana
Montana citizens who may be subject to federal arrests, searches, or seizures

HB440.one_line: Montana gives a 50 % tax credit on net income from selling Montana‑produced food, effective 2026 and ending 2031.
HB440.summary: The bill creates a tax credit that lets Montana taxpayers deduct 50 % of the net income a retailer earns from selling Montana‑produced food. It amends the state’s income‑tax rules to allow the subtraction and sets the credit to expire in 2031.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2120 to add a 50 % subtraction of net income from Montana‑produced food to federal taxable income for Montana tax purposes.
Adds a new subtraction to §15‑31‑113 that allows corporations to exclude 50 % of net income from the sale of Montana‑produced food from their gross income.
Defines “Montana‑produced food” as food or drink that is planted, cultivated, harvested, raised, collected, processed, or manufactured in Montana, excluding food prepared for onsite consumption.
Sets the credit to be available for tax years beginning after Dec. 31 2025 and to terminate Dec. 31 2031.
Requires the Department of Revenue to apply an inflation adjustment to the $5,500 subtraction for taxpayers 65 + and to calculate the 50 % subtraction on a per‑retailer basis.
Provides that the credit may only be claimed by residents who meet specific residency and military‑pension criteria and only for five consecutive years after becoming a resident.
Includes detailed rules for reporting and recapture for related savings and education accounts (though these are separate provisions).
affected: Montana residents who sell or purchase Montana‑produced food
Montana corporations that sell Montana‑produced food
Military retirees and pensioners who meet residency requirements

HB445.one_line: Adds a new goal requiring cursive instruction in Montana public schools.
HB445.summary: The bill amends the Montana Code to add a new legislative goal that requires schools to teach cursive handwriting. It takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑102, MCA, adding a new goal (item 10) that schools must provide instruction in reading and writing in cursive handwriting.
The amendment does not alter any other provisions of the code.
The effective date of the change is July 1, 2025.

HB451.one_line: Excludes certain school and debt‑service levies from tax‑increment calculations for new districts.
HB451.summary: HB 451 amends Montana’s tax‑increment‑financing rules to exclude certain school and debt‑service levies from the calculation of the tax increment for newly created districts. The changes apply immediately to districts created after the act’s effective date and to new voter‑approved levies adopted after that date.
changes: Amends §7‑15‑4286 to exclude university system mills, half of elementary/high‑school/state equalization mills, school‑district levies, and debt‑service levies from the tax‑increment calculation for newly created targeted economic‑development districts and urban renewal areas.
Specifies that new voter‑approved levies adopted after the act’s effective date are also excluded from the increment calculation.
Provides that any excess increment after permitted uses is remitted to the taxing jurisdictions in proportion to their share of the excluded mills.
Defines applicability to districts created on or after the effective date and to new levies adopted after that date.
Maintains the existing framework for remittance of excess increment to local governments.
Leaves the overall structure of special funds and bond‑related uses unchanged.
affected: Local governments creating targeted economic‑development districts or urban renewal areas
numbers: excluded mills: university system, half of elementary/high‑school/state equalization, school‑district, debt‑service

HB452.one_line: HB 452 makes assault on a public‑utility employee a felony with up to 20‑year prison terms and $50,000 fines.
HB452.summary: HB 452 makes assault on a public‑utility employee a felony, sets prison terms and fines, and codifies the offense in the state penal code.
changes: Defines assault on a public‑utility employee as a felony with four possible conduct elements (bodily injury, apprehension of injury with a weapon or appearance of one, bodily injury with a weapon, or serious bodily injury).

Imposes prison terms up to 20 years and fines up to $50,000, with specific limits for each conduct element (10 years for bodily injury or apprehension with a real weapon, 8 years for apprehension with an appearance of a weapon, 20 years for serious bodily injury).
Adds a codification instruction that the new offense becomes part of Title 45, Chapter 5, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
No new program, fund, or office is created.
affected: Persons who assault or threaten them

HB453.one_line: Montana permits crypto tax payments via third‑party processors, non‑taxable, effective 2026.
HB453.summary: Montana will let taxpayers pay state income taxes with cryptocurrency through approved third‑party processors, with all payments converted to U.S. dollars.  Crypto payments are not treated as taxable capital‑gain events.  The program begins after 12/31/2025.
changes: Establishes a state program for accepting cryptocurrency tax payments via third‑party processors
Requires the Department of Revenue to contract with such processors and convert all crypto to U.S. dollars
Declares that crypto tax payments are not taxable capital‑gain events
Provides the Department with rule‑making authority to administer the program
Codifies the provisions into Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code
Applies to income‑tax years beginning after December 31 2025

HB457.one_line: Revises income limits for Best Beginnings scholarships, appropriates $17 M, effective July 1 2025.
HB457.summary: The bill amends income eligibility for the Best Beginnings child‑care scholarship, sets new thresholds, appropriates $17 million for the program, and takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Amends §52‑2‑715 to set a qualifying income threshold at no less than 185 % of the federal poverty level or 85 % of state median income, whichever is higher; sets a maximum qualifying income no higher than the federal child‑care and development block grant limit.
Appropriates $17 million from the general fund to the Department of Public Health and Human Services for each year of the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to support the scholarship program.
Declares the appropriation part of the ongoing base for the next legislative session.
Effective date is July 1 2025.
affected: Families applying for Best Beginnings child‑care scholarships
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB460.one_line: Amend constitution to let voters petition for a grand jury that must be prosecuted by county attorneys.
HB460.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Constitution to let county voters petition for a grand jury. If enough signatures are gathered, the district judge must impanel a grand jury that can investigate, indict, and seek court orders, with county attorneys required to prosecute indictments within 90 days.
changes: Amends Article II, §20 to allow a grand jury to be summoned when 100 + 0.5 % of a county’s registered electors sign a petition;
The judge must impanel the grand jury once the petition is submitted to the county election administrator;
The grand jury may investigate any cause presented by petitioners and can issue indictments that must be prosecuted by the county attorney;
If the county attorney fails to prosecute within 90 days, the grand jury may be indicted for obstruction or may seek assistance from the attorney general or a private prosecutor;
The grand jury may also seek court orders and hire independent counsel;
The amendment requires a two‑thirds legislative vote and will be put to a public vote in the November 2026 election.

HB461.one_line: Exempts 67‑plus owners of primary residences from property tax increases for five years or more.
HB461.summary: HB 461 creates a property‑tax exemption for owner‑occupied residential property when the owner is 67 or older and has lived there for at least five years. The exemption equals the increase in market value from the base year, and it ends if the property is sold or substantially altered. Applicants must file by March 1 of the tax year and meet the primary‑residence criteria.
changes: Establishes a property‑tax exemption for class IV residential property owned and occupied by a taxpayer 67 or older for five or more years;
The exemption equals the difference between the current market value and the base‑year value;
The exemption terminates if the property is sold, or if new construction, remodeling (more than 100 sq ft) or reclassification occurs;
Owners must file an application by March 1 of the tax year, affirming ownership and primary‑residence status;
The department may verify residency and can request additional information;
If the exemption ends due to construction or reclassification, owners may reapply and the base year is adjusted;
The act applies to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Owners of class IV residential property 67 or older

HB465.one_line: Revises lien foreclosure limits, requires notice filing, discharges lien if notice omitted.
HB465.summary: The bill amends Montana’s lien‑foreclosure law to impose a two‑year limitation on filing a lien action and requires a notice of action to be filed within 90 days after that limitation expires. If the notice is not filed, the lien is automatically discharged. The changes clarify timing and documentation requirements for foreclosing on a lien.
changes: Adds a two‑year limitation period for initiating a lien action (Section 71‑3‑562(1)).
Requires a notice of action to be filed with the clerk and recorder no later than 90 days after the limitation period ends (Section 71‑3‑562(2)).
The notice must identify parties, court, property description, filing date, and attach a copy of the complaint (Section 71‑3‑562(2)).
If the notice is not filed within the 90‑day window, the lien is discharged (Section 71‑3‑562(3)).
affected: Lien holders filing actions against contracting owners
Contracting owners subject to lien actions
Clerks and recorders handling lien notices

HB469.one_line: HB 469 expands rule‑making for driver licenses and clarifies out‑of‑state license exemptions.
HB469.summary: HB 469 amends Montana’s driver‑licensing law to clarify which out‑of‑state licenses are exempt for non‑citizens who are unlawfully present, expands rule‑making authority for the Department of Justice, and adds a host of new licensing rules, including digital license options.
changes: Amends §61‑5‑104 to specify that non‑residents holding a valid out‑of‑state license may drive in Montana unless the license is issued exclusively to unlawfully present persons, and clarifies military‑related license provisions.

Amends §61‑14‑201 to grant the Department of Justice broad rule‑making authority over driver‑license standards, including grace periods, skill and vision tests, restricted and hardship licenses, and identification card rules.
Adds a new rule that any out‑of‑state license whose issuer cannot determine lawful presence is deemed invalid in Montana.
Requires the department to adopt rules for a digital driver‑license program by September 1 2025 and related implementation rules by July 1 2025.
Provides a severability clause to preserve valid portions of the act if any part is struck down.
No new criminal offense or state‑wide program is created; the act merely expands regulatory authority and clarifies exemptions.

HB470.one_line: Prohibits trigger leads in mortgage advertising and expands false‑advertising rules.
HB470.summary: HB 470 prohibits the use of trigger leads in mortgage advertising, expands the definition of false or deceptive advertising, and gives the Banking Commissioner authority to regulate trigger leads. It amends the mortgage‑loan‑originator rules to clarify what constitutes a trigger lead and to tighten advertising requirements for licensees.
changes: Adds trigger‑lead prohibition to the definition of false or deceptive advertising.
Amends §32‑9‑103 to define trigger lead and related terms (e.g., “administrative or clerical tasks,” “bona fide not‑for‑profit entity,” etc.).
Amends §32‑9‑149 to forbid advertising that relies on trigger leads and to require disclosure of material limitations and unique identifiers in all mortgage‑loan‑originator advertising.
Empowers the Banking Commissioner to adopt rules governing trigger leads and false or deceptive advertising.
Codifies the new trigger‑lead prohibition as part of Title 32, Chapter 9, Part 1.
Includes severability language.
No new program or criminal offense is created.
No fiscal impact language is provided.

HB472.one_line: Mandates settlement proceeds go to the general fund, with limited exceptions and a governor reporting requirement.
HB472.summary: The bill requires most state‑settlement proceeds to be deposited into the State General Fund, with a few specified exceptions, and allows the governor to deviate from that rule on a case‑by‑case basis. It also amends the statutes that govern how civil fines and settlement proceeds are handled and creates a small reporting requirement for the governor.
changes: 1. All settlement proceeds, after deducting litigation costs and attorney fees, must be deposited in the State General Fund unless an exception applies.

2. Exceptions include pre‑effective‑date settlements, Montana tobacco settlement trust fund money, recoveries under 30‑14‑143 and 30‑14‑226, restitution to victims, funds already authorized for other uses, and natural‑resource‑damage recoveries directed to special revenue accounts.

3. Sections 30‑14‑143 and 30‑14‑226 are amended to deposit civil fines, settlement proceeds, judgments, costs, and fees into state special revenue accounts, limit those balances to three times the department’s biennial appropriation, and transfer excess to the General Fund by the first business day in January of the following biennium.
4. The governor may authorize a different allocation of settlement proceeds under Section 4, and must report such use to the Legislative Finance Committee (Section 5).
5. A $10,000 appropriation is made to the Governor’s office for the July 1 – June 30, 2026 biennium to report on the use of that authority.
6. The act becomes effective July 1 , 2025.
numbers: three times the department’s biennial appropriation
first business day in January of the following biennium

HB478.one_line: Authorizes volunteer security teams with eligibility, training, and limited civil immunity for Montana organizations.
HB478.summary: The bill authorizes Montana organizations to form volunteer security teams, sets eligibility, training, and liability rules, and grants limited civil immunity to team members during declared emergencies. It requires background checks, a security policy, and ongoing training for armed volunteers. The bill does not create a new state program or fund, but it codifies these provisions into state law.
changes: Allows any qualifying organization to establish a volunteer security team under a written emergency action plan and security policy.

Imposes eligibility criteria: U.S. citizenship, 18+, concealed‑weapon permit or firearms certification, no serious criminal record, good moral character, high‑school diploma or equivalent, valid driver’s license, no disqualifying mental or physical conditions, and successful oral exam.
Mandates annual handgun proficiency and quarterly firearms training for armed volunteers, except for single‑person teams.
Creates an organizational structure with a director and team leader; the leader must coordinate training and keep records.
Provides civil immunity for volunteer members under Montana’s 27‑1‑722 during declared emergencies or sanctioned events, and allows justification of force under 45‑3‑102/103.
Exempts volunteer members from Title 37, chapter 60 requirements and limits immunity to declared emergencies or sanctioned events.
affected: Volunteer security teams, their members, and the organizations that host public events.
Event attendees and the public who may be protected by these teams.
numbers: civil immunity limited to declared emergencies

HB479.one_line: Candidates must disclose foreign citizenship and the Secretary of State must post it online.
HB479.summary: HB 479 requires every Montana candidate to disclose whether they hold citizenship in any foreign nation or federally‑recognized Indian tribe, and the Secretary of State must post that information online. The bill amends the nomination‑declaration statutes to add the citizenship question, makes the disclosure public, and adds a notification requirement to tribal governments. No new program or crime is created, and the act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑10‑201 to add a citizenship question to the declaration for nomination and requires the answer to be posted online by the Secretary of State.
Amends §13‑10‑211 to add the same citizenship question to write‑in declarations of intent and requires the information to be posted online.
Amends §13‑14‑112 to include the citizenship question in non‑partisan declarations and to post the answer online.
Adds a new section directing the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Preserves existing filing deadlines, fees, and other procedural requirements for nominations and write‑ins.
affected: Candidates for any public office (partisan, non‑partisan, write‑in)
Secretary of State and election administrators

HB481.one_line: HB 481 requires state agencies to publish and maintain EPA guidance documents on dedicated websites.
HB481.summary: HB 481 requires Montana’s Department of Environmental Quality, the Department of Agriculture, and the Board of Oil and Gas Conservation to post EPA guidance documents on state‑run websites and to maintain a record of rescinded documents. The bill also directs each agency to designate a dedicated website for these documents within 90 days of the act’s effective date.
changes: 1. Mandates each agency to publish any EPA guidance document received within 15 days on a designated website.
2. Requires each agency to designate a dedicated website for guidance documents within 90 days of the act’s effective date and to link to it from the agency’s main site.
3. Requires agencies to keep rescinded guidance documents on the website, marking them as rescinded and noting the rescission date.
4. Defines a “guidance document” broadly to include memoranda, notices, bulletins, directives, news releases, letters, blog posts, and no‑action letters, except rules issued under 5 U.S.C. § 553.
5. Codifies the provisions as part of the respective agency titles in the Montana Code (Title 75 for Environmental Quality, Title 80 for Agriculture, Title 82 for Oil & Gas Conservation).
affected: Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation

HB482.one_line: Mandates all Montana local elections be partisan, replacing nonpartisan elections.
HB482.summary: HB 482 mandates that all local government elections in Montana be conducted on a partisan basis, replacing any nonpartisan elections that currently exist. The bill amends several statutory sections to specify the partisan election requirement and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: Replaces nonpartisan election provisions with partisan election requirements in sections 7‑3‑219, 7‑3‑314, 7‑3‑413, 7‑3‑513, and 7‑3‑4262 of the Montana Code Annotated.
Amends the statutory basis sections for county‑manager, municipal council‑mayor, and municipal commission‑manager forms of government to include the new partisan election language.
Establishes that local elections shall be conducted on a partisan basis without reference to party affiliation in the case of appointments (section 7‑3‑4262).
Provides a saving clause that preserves rights, duties, penalties, and proceedings that existed before the effective date.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
numbers: No change to term lengths or commission size limits

HB484.one_line: Raises Montana’s minimum wage, removes $4 minimum for small businesses, and adjusts annually.
HB484.summary: The bill raises Montana’s minimum wage to the higher of the federal rate or a state‑set amount, with annual cost‑of‑living adjustments, and eliminates the $4 minimum for small businesses. It takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Amends §39‑3‑409 to set the state minimum wage at the greater of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act rate or a state‑determined amount, currently $12.06 per hour.
Provides an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment based on the CPI, effective January 1 of the following year.
A $4 per hour minimum wage for businesses with annual gross sales of $110,000 or less is removed.
The entire amendment becomes effective July 1 2025.
No new programs or funds are created.
affected: Small businesses with annual gross sales ≤$110,000

HB485.one_line: Bids become final prices unless parties agree otherwise in writing.
HB485.summary: The bill requires that a residential home construction bid be the final price unless the parties write a separate agreement.  Time‑and‑materials contracts are allowed only if the parties agree in writing.
changes: 1. A bid that has been accepted cannot be increased; it becomes the full contract price. 2. A residential home contract cannot be a time‑and‑materials arrangement unless the parties agree in writing. 3. The law does not apply if the parties, before bid acceptance, agree in writing that the bid is not the final amount, or if they agree to changes in scope, materials cost, or subcontractor bids.
who_is_affected":["homeowners","contractors","subcontractors"],

HB488.one_line: Allows disabled voters to return ballots electronically under a new encrypted system.
HB488.summary: The bill amends Montana election law to let disabled voters submit their ballots electronically, provided the transmission is encrypted and approved by the Secretary of State. It creates a $10,000 appropriation for developing the system, sets rules for security and transcription, and takes effect July 1 2025, applying to federal elections from November 2026 onward.
changes: Amends §13‑13‑246 to allow disabled voters to receive, complete, and return ballots electronically using an approved encrypted system.
Requires the Secretary of State to adopt rules that establish encryption and security standards for the electronic transmission system.
Creates a $10,000 appropriation from the general fund for the Secretary of State to design, program, and implement the system.
Specifies that electronically transmitted ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on election day to be counted.
Mandates a transcription process involving at least three election officials and a secure log for ballots returned electronically.

HB494.one_line: Reallocates tobacco settlement funds to prevention and children’s health programs, effective July 1 2025.
HB494.summary: HB 494 revises how tobacco‑settlement money is split and deposited, designating specific percentages for prevention programs and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, and sets a July 1 2025 effective date.
changes: Amends §17‑6‑606 to allocate 32 % of yearly settlement proceeds to a state special revenue account for tobacco‑disease‑prevention programs and 17 % to a separate account for matching federal funds for the Children’s Health Insurance Program; the remaining 51 % is not specified in this bill.
Specifies that funds in each account may only be used for the stated purposes and that the Department of Public Health and Human Services will manage the programs and adopt implementing rules.
Requires any unappropriated funds in either account to be transferred to the trust fund within two years of deposit.
Authorizes the legislature to appropriate money from the special revenue accounts for prevention programs, the advisory board, and private‑nature programs via contracts.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.
affected: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB489.one_line: Creates a 4 % local option sales tax for property‑tax relief, requiring voter approval and detailed reporting.
HB489.summary: HB 489 creates a 4 % local option sales tax that can be approved by voters in counties or consolidated city‑counties.  The revenue must be used for property‑tax relief for primary residences and long‑term rentals, with a portion passed to renters, and a small share goes to a state‑wide distribution account and retailer administrative costs.  The bill also amends tax‑collection rules and establishes reporting and audit requirements for local governments that levy the tax.
changes: 1. Allows counties and consolidated city‑counties to impose a local option sales tax of up to 4 % on certain retail goods and services (restaurants, bars, non‑SNAP food, airport landings, outfitting services).

2. Requires that 90 % of the tax revenue be used for property‑tax relief to primary residences and long‑term rentals, 9.75 % be deposited in a state distribution account for counties that do not levy the tax, and 0.25 % cover retailer administrative costs.
3. Sets a 10‑year maximum term for the tax and requires a 90‑day notice before it takes effect.

4. Mandates a voter approval process: a petition or governing‑body resolution must state rate, term, effective date, and purpose; the tax is approved only if at least 40 % of qualified electors vote and a majority vote for it.
5. Establishes administrative ordinances for collection, reporting, penalties, and an application process for property‑tax relief credits.
6. Adds detailed reporting and audit requirements for local governments that levy the tax, including disclosure of revenue, categories of retailers, and distribution of relief.
7. Amends existing tax statutes (15‑65‑112, 15‑68‑502, 15‑68‑820, etc.) to incorporate the new tax and its revenue‑distribution rules.
8. Creates a statutory appropriation for the local‑option‑tax distribution account in the state special revenue fund.
9. Provides that the tax will not be imposed on accommodations, rental cars, cleaning supplies, grooming/hygiene products, medical supplies, medicine, paper products, or pet food.
10. Sets an effective date of July 1 2026.
11. Includes codification instructions and a saving clause.
12. Requires that the tax be lowered to 2 % if a statewide general sales tax is adopted and the local option tax exceeds 2 %.
affected: County and consolidated city‑county governing bodies
Retailers and service providers subject to the tax
Property owners of primary residences and long‑term rentals

HB498.one_line: Prohibits fluoride addition to public water supplies and updates water‑system approval rules.
HB498.summary: The bill bars any person from adding fluoride to a public water supply system and amends the state’s water‑supply regulations to clarify that prohibition. It also revises rules governing the approval of water‑distribution and sewage‑system projects, including subdivision reviews, but the core change is the fluoride ban.
