changes: Amends §75‑6‑112 to prohibit the introduction of fluoride into any public water supply system.
Adds a new subsection to §75‑6‑112 that lists fluoride addition as a prohibited act.
Revises §76‑4‑104 to allow the department to adopt rules that enforce the fluoride prohibition and to clarify standards for water‑system approvals.
Maintains existing subdivision‑review requirements while adding specific language that fluoride addition is disallowed in any public water‑system project.
Does not create a new program or fund; it only modifies existing statutes.
No monetary amounts or funding provisions are included.
The bill does not alter any deadlines or effective‑date language for the new prohibition; it takes effect upon enactment.
affected: Residents who rely on public water supplies
State Department of Environmental Quality (or equivalent)

HB500.one_line: Allows chiropractors to prescribe limited drugs and adds their services to Medicaid.
HB500.summary: HB 500 expands chiropractic scope by allowing licensed chiropractors to obtain a prescriptive‑authority endorsement, authorizes them to prescribe a limited list of non‑controlled drugs, and adds chiropractic services to the Montana Medicaid benefit package. It also amends the chiropractic statutes to define the practice and the board’s rule‑making authority and to clarify Medicaid coverage. The bill creates a new prescriptive‑authority endorsement and a new Medicaid benefit for chiropractic care.
changes: Chiropractors may apply for a prescriptive‑authority endorsement from the Board of Chiropractors.

Endorsed chiropractors may prescribe, obtain, and administer specific non‑controlled drugs (muscle relaxants, COX‑2 inhibitors, NSAIDs, topical NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, topical anesthetics, trigger‑point injections).
The Board adopts rules on application procedures, educational qualifications, approved pharmacology programs, and drug procurement/storage/disposal protocols.
The Board may add or remove drugs from the authorized list within the scope of chiropractic practice.
Chiropractors without endorsement may not advertise or imply prescriptive authority.
The definition of chiropractic practice is expanded to include prescription of natural agents and excludes controlled drugs unless endorsed.
Chiropractic services are added to the list of services covered by Montana Medicaid (Section 53‑6‑101).
The bill amends sections 37‑12‑101, 37‑12‑104, 37‑12‑201, and 53‑6‑101 of the Montana Code to reflect these changes.
affected: Montana Medicaid program and its beneficiaries
Montana Department of Labor and Industry

HB501.one_line: HB 501 gives owners a quick, limited removal remedy and adds a new deceptive‑practice crime.
HB501.summary: HB 501 creates a limited, court‑free remedy that lets a residential owner or their agent ask local police to remove an unauthorized occupant, with specific conditions and notice requirements. It also adds a new criminal offense for deceptive property practices and outlines civil liability for wrongful removal. The bill is intended to streamline removal while protecting owners’ rights and providing remedies for wrongfully removed persons.
changes: Owners or authorized agents may file a written complaint with local law enforcement to have an unauthorized person immediately removed, provided a set of conditions (no tenancy, no family relation, no pending litigation, etc.) are met.
Law enforcement must verify the complaint, serve a 24‑hour notice to vacate, and may arrest the occupant for trespass or other crimes.
Local law enforcement may charge up to $50 for service and a reasonable hourly rate for stand‑by while the owner changes locks and removes property.
Unauthorized persons who are wrongfully removed may sue for actual damages, statutory damages equal to fair‑market rent, court costs, and attorney fees.
The bill creates a new criminal offense, “deceptive practices,” with penalties ranging from fines to imprisonment up to 10 years, depending on the value of the property or services involved.
Section 5 codifies the new provisions into Title 45, Chapter 6, Part 2.
No new state program or office is created; the bill merely expands existing law enforcement authority.
affected: Individuals engaged in deceptive property practices
numbers: up to 6 months jail (second offense, <$1,500 value)
up to 3 years jail (first offense, $1,500–$5,000 value)
up to 10 years jail (first offense, >$5,000 value)

HB506.one_line: Amends constitution to replace Supreme Court elections with governor appointments via a nomination committee.
HB506.summary: HB 506 amends the Montana Constitution to change how Supreme Court justices are selected, replacing direct election with a governor‑appointed process based on a nomination committee. The amendment requires a two‑thirds legislative vote and a public vote in November 2026, taking effect January 4, 2027, and applies only to vacancies occurring after that date.
changes: Supreme Court justices are no longer elected by the public; they are appointed by the governor from a list of nominees provided by a nomination committee.
The nomination committee consists of the Senate president, House speaker, minority leaders of each house, and two attorneys chosen by the committee members.

For term‑end vacancies the committee must submit 3–5 nominees 60 days before the term ends; the governor appoints within 60 days. If the committee fails, the governor selects from a lottery‑chosen list of 10 nominees.
For other vacancies the committee must submit 3–5 nominees within 60 days of notification; the governor appoints within 60 days, with the same fallback lottery process if the committee fails.
All appointments are subject to Senate confirmation as provided by law.

The amendment requires a two‑thirds vote in the legislature and a public vote in the November 2026 election; it becomes effective January 4, 2027, and applies only to vacancies occurring on or after that date.

HB508.one_line: Adds media‑literacy goals to Montana’s legislative‑goal statute for K‑12 schools.
HB508.summary: The bill amends the state’s legislative‑goal statute to add media‑literacy objectives for public elementary and secondary schools. It requires schools to help students access, evaluate, and create media while reducing susceptibility to false or manipulative information. No new program or funding is created; the change merely expands the list of goals the legislature deems important for schools.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑102, MCA, by inserting a new goal (7) that strengthens media literacy, with sub‑goals (a) and (b).
Adds a brief mention that financial‑literacy instruction is also supported (in the amended text).
No new funding, offices, or criminal offenses are established.

HB512.one_line: New school buses must have lap‑shoulder belts and districts must enforce belt‑use policies, with liability limits and fee adjustments.
HB512.summary: The bill requires any school bus purchased new on or after Jan 1 2026 to be equipped with lap‑shoulder belts and mandates districts to adopt enforceable belt‑use policies. It limits liability for non‑use, allows a budget‑based exemption, and adjusts registration fees, reimbursement rates, and definitions related to school buses.
changes: 1. New buses bought on/after Jan 1 2026 must have lap‑shoulder belts and meet Board of Public Education standards.
2. Districts must adopt a public, enforceable belt‑use policy, require all passengers to use belts, and maintain belts in good working order.
3. Liability for passenger injury is limited if the passenger failed to use or misused a belt and a policy exists; damages can be recovered only for broken or poorly maintained belts.
4. Exemption for buses purchased before Jan 1 2026 or for new buses if a board determines the district cannot afford belts based on market prices and a public vote approves the determination.

5. Several MCA sections are amended: definitions of “school bus,” “eligible transportee,” and “bus route”; bid‑letting rules for transportation contracts; mileage reimbursement rates; and registration fee schedules (including a 10 % fee reduction for belt‑equipped buses).
6. The act becomes effective July 1 2025 and applies to school years beginning July 1 2025.
7. A two‑thirds legislative vote is required because the bill limits governmental liability.

HB517.one_line: Amends Class D motor‑carrier rules to require regular garbage transport.
HB517.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Class D motor‑carrier rules to require that carriers transport garbage on a regular basis as part of their business. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §69‑12‑314 to add a new paragraph (2) requiring a Class D carrier to intend or actually engage in regular garbage transport.
Specifies that the carrier must file an application for a Class D certificate in accordance with the commission’s rules.
Sets the effective date to the passage of the act.

HB522.one_line: Mandates pesticide supply‑chain entities to warn consumers and the public about risks, creating liability for non‑compliance.
HB522.summary: HB 522 establishes that manufacturers, marketers, dealers, distributors, retailers, or sellers of pesticides must warn consumers, applicators, and the public about pesticide risks.  Failure to meet the warning duty creates liability under Montana law.
changes: Creates a statutory duty to warn for all pesticide supply‑chain entities.
Defines the duty as satisfied when the pesticide label is EPA‑approved and the product is registered with the EPA and Montana’s Department of Agriculture.
Makes failure to meet that duty a basis for a cause of action.
Codifies the duty as part of Title 27, Chapter 1, Part 7 of the Montana Code.
Includes severability and applicability provisions.
No new program or fund is created.

HB518.one_line: Revises motor‑carrier certificate hearing rules and protest limits, effective immediately.
HB518.summary: HB 518 amends Montana’s motor‑carrier certificate rules to clarify hearing procedures, protest limits, and denial conditions. It also sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §69‑12‑321 to specify that the commission must notify interested parties when a Class A, D, or E motor‑carrier application is filed or a transfer request is made.
Adds a requirement that any protest or hearing request must be scheduled within 60 days of receipt, or the commission may act without a hearing per its rules.
Limits protests to a carrier’s ability to meet §69‑12‑323(5) when the carrier is Class E or applies under §69‑12‑311(1)(a).

Clarifies that a Class D carrier applying for a public‑convenience‑and‑necessity certificate may be denied without a public hearing if the commission’s records show the route has been previously investigated and found unnecessary, unless the applicant shows material changes.
Establishes that a hearing is required if the applicant presents facts that materially change the conditions on the route or territory.
Declares the act effective immediately upon passage and approval.

HB524.one_line: HB 524 removes boardinghouses and roominghouses from hotel‑and‑motel health‑safety rules.
HB524.summary: HB 524 removes boardinghouses and roominghouses from the state’s hotel‑and‑motel public‑health and safety regulations, amending definitions and rule‑making authority for lodging facilities.
changes: Amends 50‑51‑102 to redefine bed‑and‑breakfast, day‑visitor, guest‑ranch, hotel/motel, outfitting/guide facility, roominghouse/boardinghouse, tourist home, and related terms; removes the requirement that boardinghouses/roominghouses be subject to the same health‑safety rules as hotels and motels.

Revises 50‑51‑103 to allow the Department of Public Health and Human Services to adopt rules for bed‑and‑breakfasts, hotels, motels, roominghouses, boardinghouses, and tourist homes, but limits rule‑making to those categories and allows voluntary guidelines for guest ranches and outfitting/guide facilities.

Revises 50‑51‑107 to prohibit hotels, motels, boardinghouses, and roominghouses from providing professional nursing or personal‑care services, while permitting third‑party providers to offer such services on the premises.
The bill does not create new funding or programs; it only changes regulatory definitions and scope of enforcement.
No new criminal offenses are created.
The bill does not alter any fiscal allocations or budgets.
affected: Guest ranch and outfitting/guide facility operators
Department of Public Health and Human Services staff

HB525.one_line: Montana mandates FDA certification, directory listing, and taxes for nicotine vapor products, with strict penalties for non‑compliance.
HB525.summary: HB 525 requires all nicotine‑containing vapor products sold in Montana to be certified as FDA‑compliant, creates a state‑maintained directory of approved products, imposes taxes, reporting, and enforcement requirements, and sets penalties for non‑compliance.
changes: Manufacturers must file an annual certification with the Attorney General proving FDA pre‑market approval or exemption, and pay a $2,500 filing fee (first time) and $1,000 for each subsequent annual filing.

A public directory of certified manufacturers and products will be posted on the Attorney General’s website starting Jan 1 2026, and only products listed may be sold after the directory’s publication.

Retailers, wholesalers, and importers must remove unlisted products from inventory within 60 days of directory publication; failure to do so can lead to seizure, forfeiture, and destruction of the products.
Non‑resident or foreign manufacturers must appoint a state agent for service of process and post a $25,000 surety bond to be listed in the directory.
Wholesalers must report quarterly units sold and provide invoices to the Attorney General; the state may conduct up to four unannounced inspections per year.
Violations trigger civil penalties ranging from $250 to $1,000 per product, license suspensions, and for manufacturers, a $10,000 penalty per product and possible misdemeanor for false statements.
affected: Wholesalers, importers, and retailers of vapor products
State Attorney General and Department of Revenue
numbers: $5 million minimum for special revenue fund
$68% of vapor tax to general fund

HB526.one_line: Montana adopts an interstate APRN compact, creating a commission and uniform licensure rules while allowing state enforcement.
HB526.summary: Montana will join an interstate compact that lets advanced‑practice registered nurses (APRNs) practice in any member state with a single multistate license, while still allowing each state to enforce its own rules and take disciplinary action. The bill creates a commission to administer the compact, sets uniform licensure requirements, and requires a coordinated information system for licensing and disciplinary data. It does not create a new fee‑based program or criminal offense.
changes: Establishes a multistate APRN compact that allows APRNs to practice in any member state with a single license, subject to each state’s own practice laws.
Creates the Interstate Commission of APRN Compact Administrators to set rules, manage a coordinated licensure information system, and enforce the compact.
Defines uniform licensure requirements (education, certification, criminal background, etc.) that all member states must meet for a multistate license.
Gives each state’s licensing board authority to take adverse action against an APRN’s multistate privilege and to share disciplinary information with other member states.
Requires a coordinated licensure information system that collects and shares data on APRN licensure, adverse actions, and alternative program participation.
Allows states to withdraw from the compact only after a 6‑month period and requires all states to enact the compact into law before it becomes effective.
Provides mechanisms for dispute resolution, default, and enforcement of the compact by the commission.
Does not impose new fees on APRNs; the commission may levy an annual assessment on member states to cover operating costs.
affected: Montana residents who receive care from APRNs
Other states that may become party to the compact

HB528.one_line: HB 528 revises property tax rates, limits revenue cuts, and adds a university levy with retroactive effect.
HB528.summary: HB 528 revises the tax rates for agricultural, residential, and commercial property, limits the reduction in school‑equalization and university revenue to $50 million for 2025, and amends the rules for calculating mill levies. The changes take effect immediately and apply retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
changes: Amends §15‑6‑133 to set new taxable percentages for class III agricultural land and non‑qualified agricultural parcels (2.16 % or 1.7 % of productive capacity, with a special 7× rate for certain parcels).

Amends §15‑6‑134 to set new taxable percentages for class IV residential and commercial property (1.35 % or 0.76 % of market value, with a 1.4× multiplier for values over $1.5 million and for commercial use).
Adds a temporary 6‑mill levy on all real and personal property to support the Montana university system, to be deposited in the state special revenue fund and terminating December 31 2028.

Revises §15‑10‑420 to clarify how governmental entities calculate the maximum number of mills they may impose, including limits tied to inflation and to a $50 million cap on reductions to school‑equalization and university revenue.
Provides that the act is effective upon passage and applies retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2024 and to the reappraisal cycle starting January 1 2025.
Limits the total reduction in school‑equalization and university revenue to no more than $50 million for 2025.

HB536.one_line: Prohibits hiring unauthorized aliens, imposes fines, license sanctions, civil damages, and funds enforcement.
HB536.summary: HB 536 makes it illegal for anyone to hire, recruit, refer, or employ an alien who is not legally authorized to work in Montana.  Violations trigger fines, license suspension or revocation, and civil damages.  The bill also authorizes enforcement and provides appropriations for investigation and prosecution.
changes: Amends §39‑2‑305 to prohibit hiring, recruiting, referring, or employing aliens without lawful work authorization; adds a $300 fine for violations; establishes license suspension/revocation periods of 1, 3, or 20 years for first, second, or subsequent violations; defines a single violation as hiring more than one unauthorized alien at once; allows prosecution of those who encourage or facilitate violations; creates civil cause‑action with statutory damages ($500 or $2,000 per day of unauthorized work, plus actual damages); allows affirmative defense via verified E‑Verify; authorizes peace officers to investigate; requires licensing authorities to enforce revocation/suspension orders without additional hearings; bars refund of license fees; prohibits re‑issuance of licenses during suspension; appropriates $5 million per year for FY 2026‑2027 to DOJ and county attorneys for enforcement; codifies new §2 as part of Title 39.

who_is_affected':['Employers, recruiters, referral agents, and anyone who hires or employs unauthorized aliens','Licensing authorities','County attorneys, attorney general, Department of Labor','Individuals harmed by unauthorized employment','Peace officers','Employees (authorized or unauthorized)'],
affected: Employers, recruiters, referral agents, and anyone who hires or employs unauthorized aliens
County attorneys, attorney general, Department of Labor

HB537.one_line: Montana will offer a refundable birth‑day tax credit up to $3,000, subject to income limits and review.
HB537.summary: Montana would give residents a refundable tax credit for the birth of a child, capped at $3,000 (or $1,500 in certain circumstances). The credit is calculated against state and federal taxes and employee contributions, and can be claimed on a Montana income‑tax return. The bill also adds the credit to a list of credits that the revenue interim committee must review every eight years.
changes: Creates a new refundable birth‑day tax credit for Montana residents.
Credit equals the lesser of $3,000 or the sum of Montana income tax, federal income tax, and employee contributions under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act.
Credit is reduced $150 for each $1,000 of federal adjusted gross income above $120,000 (married filing jointly) or $60,000 (other statuses).
Maximum credit is limited to $1,500 if parents are married filing separately or if unmarried parents do not share custody; the custodial parent may claim the full credit in that case.
The Department of Revenue may adopt rules to administer the credit.
Adds the birth‑day credit to the list of credits subject to biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
The credit becomes effective for tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Montana residents who have a child
Taxpayers filing Montana income tax returns
Taxpayers with federal adjusted gross income above the thresholds
Unmarried parents with or without shared custody

HB540.one_line: Expands corrections contracting powers, limits contract terms, and requires legislative oversight and risk‑assessment rules.
HB540.summary: The bill amends the Department of Corrections’ statutory authority to allow it to contract with private, nonprofit, or for‑profit Montana corporations for the establishment and maintenance of prerelease centers, residential methamphetamine treatment programs, sexual‑offender treatment programs, and day‑reporting programs. It also sets limits on contract terms, requires legislative oversight for long‑term contracts, and mandates rules for siting, community support, and risk assessment. The bill does not create a new program or crime, but expands the department’s contracting powers and oversight requirements.
changes: Amends §53‑1‑203 to add new subsections (c)–(n) authorizing contracts for prerelease, treatment, and sexual‑offender programs.
Allows contracts with private, nonprofit or for‑profit Montana corporations for residential methamphetamine and sexual‑offender treatment programs.
Limits contract terms to no more than 20 years and requires legislative audit committee review for any 20‑year contract.
Mandates the department to adopt rules for siting, establishment, and expansion of prerelease centers, including community‑support requirements and public hearings.
Requires the department to use risk‑assessment tools and integrate them into supervision and case‑management standards.
Adds provisions for day‑reporting programs and substitute care for delinquent youth, with rule‑making authority for program requirements.
affected: Private, nonprofit, and for‑profit Montana corporations

HB541.one_line: Adds drug‑based DUI, sets new penalties, and creates a felony for alcohol‑plus‑drug driving.
HB541.summary: The bill expands Montana’s DUI law to include driving while under the influence of any drug, sets new penalties for alcohol‑only, drug‑only, and combined‑substance offenses, and adds harsher penalties for repeat offenders and those with minors in the vehicle.
changes: Adds a new subsection (f) to §61‑8‑1002 making driving while under the influence of alcohol and a non‑prescribed controlled substance a felony.
Replaces the alcohol‑only DUI definition with a 0.08 BAC threshold for non‑commercial vehicles and a 0.04 BAC threshold for commercial vehicles, and adds a 5 ng/mL THC threshold for all vehicles.
Imposes a 5 ng/mL THC level as the legal limit for all drivers, regardless of vehicle type.
Sets a 0.02 BAC threshold for drivers under 21, with a 0.02 BAC or higher constituting a DUI.
Revises §61‑8‑1007 to provide specific imprisonment and fine ranges for first, second, and third offenses, with higher penalties when minors are present.
Adds mandatory chemical‑dependency treatment, license suspension, and possible sentence suspension for up to one year for all DUI convictions.
Creates a separate felony penalty schedule for the new combined‑substance offense, including a minimum 2‑day prison term and up to 25 years for repeat convictions.
affected: people who use non‑prescribed controlled substances

HB546.one_line: Limits legislation requests to study entities with a majority of legislators; amends criminal‑justice council composition.
HB546.summary: HB 546 limits which legislative‑branch study entities can request new laws to the state.  Only committees, task forces, working groups, commissions, or councils that have a majority of legislators may file legislation.  The bill also amends the criminal‑justice oversight council’s membership and powers, but that amendment is unrelated to the restriction.
changes: 1. Requires that any interim committee, task force, working group, commission, council, or other legislative‑branch‑attached entity that requests legislation must have a majority of its members be state legislators.

2. Amends § 53‑1‑216, MCA, to list the composition and duties of the Montana Criminal Justice Oversight Council (18 members, including legislators, judges, agency directors, and appointed representatives).
3. Adds a provision that the council may request legislation to enact changes to the criminal‑justice system.
4. Provides codification instructions for the new restriction section.
5. Leaves all other statutory language unchanged.
affected: Interim study entities attached to the legislative branch
Legislators who serve on committees, task forces, etc.
Members of the Montana Criminal Justice Oversight Council
numbers: majority of legislators required for request

HB542.one_line: Reclassifies third‑offense DUI as a felony, raises penalties, and expands treatment‑court options.
HB542.summary: HB 542 revises Montana’s DUI penalties, making a third‑offense a felony and tightening fines, imprisonment, and license‑suspension rules. It also expands treatment‑court options and clarifies how prior convictions affect sentencing.
changes: Third‑offense DUI is now a felony with mandatory minimum imprisonment of 30 days (up to 1 year) and fines of $2,500–$5,000, or $5,000–$10,000 if a passenger under 16 was present.

First‑ and second‑offense penalties are increased: first‑offense imprisonment 24–72 hrs (up to 6 mo) and fines $600–$1,000 (or $1,200–$2,000 with a minor passenger), second‑offense imprisonment 7–30 days (up to 1 yr) and fines $1,200–$2,000 (or $2,400–$4,000 with a minor passenger).
For aggravated DUI (61‑8‑1001) the third‑offense penalty is a felony with imprisonment 40–90 days (up to 1 yr) and fines $5,000–$10,000 (or $10,000 if a minor passenger).

The bill allows up to one year of sentence suspension if the offender completes a chemical‑dependency treatment program, but the mandatory minimum cannot be served under home arrest or suspended unless a judge finds medical‑care costs would be unreasonable.

License suspensions are extended: 90 days for first, 6 months for second, and 1 year for third or subsequent offenses, with no restricted license issued until reinstatement fees are paid and, if under 18, 30 days of suspension completed.

The bill amends 61‑8‑1008 to make fourth‑through‑subsequent offenses felonies with 13‑month to 2‑year prison terms (plus a 5‑year consecutive term) or a 5‑year treatment‑court program, and adds detailed probation conditions.
affected: Individuals convicted of DUI or aggravated DUI
Courts and judges handling DUI cases
numbers: 13‑month to 2‑year prison term for fourth‑through‑subsequent offenses
1‑year license suspension for third or later offenses

HB548.one_line: Revises expert‑testimony rules to require courts to assess four key factors before admission.
HB548.summary: The bill amends Montana’s evidence rules to require courts to evaluate four specific factors before allowing an expert witness to testify. It codifies these requirements into the state’s rules of evidence.
changes: Adds a new Section 1 that lists four factors courts must consider before admitting expert testimony under Rule 702.
Codifies Section 1 as part of Title 26, Chapter 1, Part 1 of the Montana Code, making it an integral part of the state’s evidence rules.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
The bill does not alter any existing procedural timelines or fees.
It does not impose new costs on litigants or the state.
It does not require additional training or certification for experts.
affected: Litigants in civil and criminal cases

HB550.one_line: Prohibits manufacturers from forcing Montana dealers to sell electric vehicles and expands dealer‑franchise protections.
HB550.summary: HB 550 prohibits automobile manufacturers and their affiliates from forcing new Montana dealers to sell electric or plug‑in hybrid vehicles. It also expands the state’s existing franchise‑dealer protections to cover a wide range of coercive practices, limits the ability of manufacturers to unilaterally change dealer agreements, and bars manufacturers from owning or operating dealerships in Montana.
changes: Manufacturers, distributors, importers, and their representatives may not require a new dealer to purchase or sell electric or plug‑in hybrid vehicles; such contractual provisions are void.

The bill amends §61‑4‑208 to prohibit a range of coercive actions by franchisors toward dealers, including forcing acceptance of vehicles, participation in advertising funds, location changes, exclusive facilities, and certain incentives.
It requires franchisors to allow dealers to obtain goods or services from alternative vendors that meet reasonable standards, and prohibits withholding incentives for minor clerical errors.
Franchisors may not delay or refuse delivery of vehicles or parts in a reasonable time, nor impose unreasonable sales‑quota requirements that ignore market conditions.

Any unilateral amendment or modification of a dealer’s franchise agreement that adversely affects the dealer’s rights or investment is void unless the dealer is given 60 days’ written notice and the department finds no good cause.
Manufacturers and their affiliates are prohibited from owning or operating a motor‑vehicle dealership in Montana, except for a temporary 1‑year transition period.
affected: Manufacturers, distributors, importers, and their representatives

HB552.one_line: Adds PTSD coverage for first responders in Montana’s workers’ compensation system.
HB552.summary: HB 552 expands Montana workers’ compensation to cover post‑traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) for first responders and other emergency‑response personnel.  The bill creates a new compensable injury category, defines who is a first responder, and amends the workers’‑compensation statutes to allow PTSD claims that are diagnosed under the DSM‑5 and caused by work‑related events.
changes: Adds a new compensable injury—post‑traumatic stress disorder—to the workers’ compensation system.

Defines “first responder” as professional or volunteer firefighters, law‑enforcement officers, dispatchers, county detention‑center or prison employees, and other authorized emergency‑response personnel.
Requires a DSM‑5 diagnosis of PTSD that is linked to a work‑related event, excluding personnel‑related actions such as disciplinary action.
Amends Sections 39‑71‑105, 39‑71‑116, and 39‑71‑119 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new injury category and its definitions.
Specifies that the new coverage applies to claims filed for events occurring on or after July 1 2025.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1 2025 and limits applicability to claims diagnosed after that date.
affected: First‑responder workers (firefighters, law‑enforcement officers, dispatchers, detention‑center/prison employees, other authorized emergency responders)
Workers’ compensation insurers and the state workers’ compensation fund
Claims examiners and medical providers handling PTSD claims

HB555.one_line: Revises chemical‑abortion rules, imposes felony penalties, and holds manufacturers liable for drug disposal.
HB555.summary: HB 555 revises Montana’s chemical‑abortion laws, imposing strict conditions on providers who supply or dispense abortion drugs that affect interstate commerce and holding drug manufacturers responsible for proper disposal of the drugs and their environmental impact. The bill creates new felony penalties for non‑compliance and codifies the provisions into state law.
changes: Health‑care providers must physically examine the patient, be present at the abortion, schedule a follow‑up within 7 days, and supply a catch kit and medical‑waste bag when providing or attempting a chemical abortion that affects interstate commerce.
Failure to meet any of those conditions makes the provider guilty of a felony, with a fine up to $10,000 and/or up to 3 years imprisonment per violation.
The law does not apply to abortions necessary to preserve a mother’s life or to treat ectopic pregnancies.

Manufacturers of abortion drugs are required to ensure proper disposal of discarded drugs and to remediate any endocrine‑disrupting by‑products that enter public wastewater systems; violations can be fined up to $20,000 per incident.
The act is codified into Title 50, Chapter 20 (provider provisions) and Title 75, Chapter 6, Part 1 (manufacturer provisions).
A severability clause allows valid portions of the act to remain effective if other parts are struck down.
affected: Licensed health‑care providers who prescribe or dispense abortion drugs

HB556.one_line: Limits AI use in health‑insurance utilization review and expands unfair‑practice rules.
HB556.summary: HB 556 limits how health‑insurance companies can use AI for utilization review, requiring that decisions be based on individual clinical data, not just group data, and that physicians still determine medical necessity. It also expands the definition of unfair claim settlement practices to include improper AI use. The bill imposes compliance, audit, and penalty provisions on insurers.
changes: Health‑insurance issuers must use AI only when it incorporates the enrollee’s medical history, the provider’s clinical circumstances, and other relevant clinical data.
AI tools cannot base decisions solely on group datasets or supplant provider judgment.
AI must not discriminate, must be fairly applied, and must be open to audit and periodic review.
AI cannot deny, delay, or modify care based on medical necessity; a licensed professional must make that determination.
Insurers must disclose AI use in written policies and procedures and ensure patient data is used only for its stated purpose.
The bill amends §33‑18‑201 to add a new unfair‑practice provision that prohibits insurers from using AI in a way that violates the new AI restrictions.
affected: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services
Montana Department of Health and Human Services

HB557.one_line: HB 557 limits pupil‑instruction days to instructional activities, excluding teacher‑organization meetings, and removes mandatory school closures.
HB557.summary: HB 557 limits pupil‑instruction‑related days to activities that improve instruction and align with BOP standards, explicitly excluding attendance at state teacher‑organization meetings. It also removes the requirement that trustees close schools for those meetings and clarifies teacher pay rules for attendance.
changes: Amends §20‑1‑304 to define a pupil‑instruction‑related day as teacher activities that improve instruction or align with BOP standards, and expressly prohibits using such days to attend state teacher‑organization meetings.

Sets a maximum of 7 pupil‑instruction‑related days per school year, with at least 3 for instructional or professional development activities, and states these days cannot count toward the required minimum aggregate hours of pupil instruction.

Rewrites §20‑4‑304 to allow trustees to close schools for annual instructional and professional development meetings only if those meetings meet the new §20‑1‑304 definition; otherwise schools need not close.
Clarifies that teachers may attend professional development meetings without loss of salary, but if they do not attend, they may not be paid for that day.
Establishes July 1 2025 as the effective date of the amendments.

HB558.one_line: Creates a nurse‑corps program for low‑cost home visits with liability limits and optional malpractice insurance.
HB558.summary: The bill creates a state‑run Nurse Corps program that lets licensed nurses provide low‑cost home visits to Medicare, Medicaid, and low‑income patients.  Nurses may charge $10 per visit, and the program limits their liability for ordinary negligence.  The board can require malpractice insurance and discipline nurses who violate the program’s rules.
changes: Establishes the Montana Nurse Corps Act and a statewide program for licensed nurses to give home health visits to eligible patients.
Defines eligible individuals as those enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, the Medical Assistance Program, or uninsured with income ≤400% of the federal poverty level.
Allows nurse‑corps members to charge $10 per patient contact and submit that charge to Medicare or Medicaid.
Limits nurse liability for ordinary negligence; only gross negligence or willful misconduct can result in civil damages.
Permits the Board of Nursing to procure a malpractice insurance policy for nurse‑corps members, subject to fee assessments on all licensed nurses.
Provides the Board with disciplinary authority to terminate a nurse’s participation in the program.
Codifies the new program as part of Title 37, Chapter 8, subject to existing nursing statutes.
numbers: fee assessed on all licensed nurses

HB564.one_line: Hunters must report elk/deer harvests; early reports earn points, late reports incur fees; department to build system.
HB564.summary: Hunters with deer or elk licenses must report each animal harvested to the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks. Early reports earn a bonus point; late reports trigger a $5‑$50 fee. The department will build a reporting system and can issue rules to enforce the law. The act takes effect March 1, 2026.
changes: Mandates reporting of every deer or elk harvested by licensed hunters each license year.
Allows hunters who report by February 15 to earn one bonus point for a deer or elk.
Imposes an administrative fee of $5‑$50 on hunters who fail to report by the end of the license year, payable before or with the next year’s license.
Requires the department to develop a system and provide physical forms for collecting reports.
Authorizes the department to issue rules to implement the reporting requirements.
Defines “hunting activity” to include harvest success, district, dates, and other relevant data.
affected: Deer and elk hunters holding Montana hunting licenses
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Department staff developing the reporting system

HB560.one_line: Creates a fund and grant program for small rural communities funded by extra wildlife‑license donations.
HB560.summary: The bill creates a Montana Hunters’ and Anglers’ Community Fund that collects extra money from wildlife‑conservation license purchases and uses it to award grants to small rural communities. A board of seven public members recommends grant recipients, and the Department of Commerce administers the program and can rule on its operation. The fund ends on June 30 2029.
changes: Establishes a special revenue account in the state special revenue fund for the hunters’ and anglers’ community fund
Allows donors to contribute any amount above the price of a wildlife‑conservation license or combination license
Transfers all such donations into the account by September 1 and March 1 each year
Creates a grant program with large grants up to $20,000 (multi‑year) and small grants up to $2,000
Defines eligible applicants as entities in communities with <7,500 people, including local/tribal governments, school districts, nonprofits, etc.
Prohibits grant use for marketing, advertising, advocacy, or political activities and for entities that file lawsuits after receiving funds

Creates a seven‑member board (speaker, house minority leader, senate president, senate minority leader, three governor appointees, plus a non‑voting director of Commerce) to recommend grant recipients
Authorizes the Department of Commerce to adopt rules and develop a plan to solicit contributions
Allows the department to use up to 10% of the account each year for administrative costs
Requires any unreserved money, interest, or earnings to remain in the account at year‑end
Amends Section 17‑7‑502 to clarify statutory appropriations
Sets effective date July 1 2025 and termination date June 30 2029
affected: Local and tribal governments, school districts, nonprofits, student clubs
Department of Commerce and its staff
Board members and applicants for grants

HB565.one_line: Mandates infertility coverage, including IVF, for all Montana health‑insurance plans effective Oct 1, 2025.
HB565.summary: HB 565 requires all Montana health‑insurance plans to cover infertility diagnosis and treatment, including in‑vitro fertilization, with a lifetime benefit of at least $40,000.  The bill also amends several state insurance statutes to clarify coverage for other health services and sets an effective date of October 1, 2025.
changes: All small‑group, large‑group, and individual plans issued in Montana must cover infertility diagnosis and treatment, including IVF, with a lifetime benefit of at least $40,000.
Coverage cannot be limited by exclusions, copayments, deductibles, coinsurance, benefit maximums, or waiting periods that are not applied to other prescription medications.
The bill amends sections 2‑18‑704 and 33‑35‑306 of the Montana Code to apply the new infertility coverage requirements to those statutes and to self‑funded multiple‑employer welfare arrangements.
The act applies to any policy, contract, or plan issued, delivered, amended, or renewed in Montana on or after October 1, 2025.
The bill does not create a new state program or criminal offense; it merely imposes coverage requirements on existing insurance plans.

The act includes additional provisions that broaden coverage for other health services (e.g., mental health, well‑child care, diabetes education) but the core change is the infertility coverage requirement.
affected: Health‑insurance companies doing business in Montana
Individuals, spouses, and non‑spouse dependents covered by those plans

HB569.one_line: Revises perjury laws, raises penalties, and mandates investigations of credible allegations.
HB569.summary: The bill amends Montana’s perjury and false‑swearing statutes, tightening definitions, raising penalties, adding mandatory minimums, and requiring investigative agencies to look into credible allegations. It also clarifies how inconsistent statements are prosecuted and limits convictions when a falsification is retracted early.
changes: Amends §45‑7‑201 to define perjury, set imprisonment of 6 months‑10 years, add a $50,000 fine, and establish a mandatory minimum of 1 year
Rewrites §45‑7‑202 to define false swearing, set imprisonment of 30‑90 days or up to 6 months, and a fine of $500‑$1,500
Adds a requirement that credible allegations of perjury or false swearing be investigated by an agency other than the judiciary or a court officer
Clarifies that a falsification is material if it could affect the proceeding, regardless of evidentiary admissibility
Allows a person to avoid conviction if they retract the falsification before it is exposed or substantially affects the proceeding
Permits prosecution on a single count of inconsistent statements without proving which was false
Replaces the old §45‑7‑202 with the new false‑swearing language and penalty schedule
affected: Individuals accused of perjury or false swearing

HB577.one_line: Replaces the Highway Patrol chief’s appointment with one made by the Attorney General, serving at the AG’s pleasure.
HB577.summary: The bill changes the law so that the Montana Highway Patrol chief is appointed by the Attorney General and serves at the AG’s pleasure, with tenure ending only for cause. It applies to any new appointment made after the act’s effective date.
changes: Amends §44‑1‑201, MCA to state that the Attorney General selects the Highway Patrol chief.
Requires the chief to hold the rank of colonel.
Adds that the chief serves at the Attorney General’s pleasure, terminating only for cause as defined elsewhere.
Specifies the act applies to appointments made on or after its effective date.
numbers: effective date: on or after the act’s effective date

HB579.one_line: Local governments must fund a reserve account before receiving renewable‑resource or coal‑endowment aid, with strict deposit and spending rules.
HB579.summary: The bill requires local governments to set up and fund a capital‑reserve account before they can receive renewable‑resource or coal‑endowment grants or loans. It sets deposit rules, spending limits, and a priority system for awarding assistance, and amends related statutes to incorporate the new requirements.
changes: Creates a mandatory capital‑reserve account for eligible local governments; account must be funded by Sept. 30 of the odd‑numbered year before the next legislative session.
Deposits must equal 10 % of water‑related revenues or $5 per acre‑foot for water‑storage dams; special districts cannot be used to fund the account.
Funds may only be spent on projects costing at least $50,000 and must be matched by the local government.
Amends §§ 85‑1‑605, 90‑6‑703, and 90‑6‑710 to incorporate the new reserve requirement, ranking methodology, and reporting obligations.
Adds a priority list for projects based on health‑safety urgency, cost‑effectiveness, local match ratio, and community support.
Requires the department to report emergency and planning grants to the governor and legislature each biennium.
affected: County, city, town, consolidated city‑county, irrigation district, drainage district, conservation district, water‑users’ association, ditch company, and other local governments (excluding tribal governments).
Applicants for renewable‑resource grants, loans, and Montana coal endowment funds.

HB581.one_line: Allows police chiefs to appoint special‑service officers as court officers and transport defendants.
HB581.summary: HB 581 lets a city police chief appoint a special‑service officer as a court officer, authorizes that officer to transport defendants to detention, and expands the definition of special‑service officer to include paid, full‑time officers.
changes: Amends 3‑6‑303 to allow the chief of police, with judge approval, to appoint one or more police officers, reserve officers, or full‑time/part‑time special‑service officers as court officers
Requires the appointed court officer to attend court sessions and perform duties the judge may assign
Grants a court officer the authority to transport a remanded defendant to the place of detention
Redefines “special‑service officer” in 7‑32‑201 to include unsworn, full‑time or part‑time, volunteer or paid members who may carry a firearm
Clarifies that reserve officers and special‑service officers have the same meanings as in 7‑32‑201
Leaves all other statutory language unchanged
affected: Police officers, reserve officers, and special‑service officers

HB583.one_line: Expands lottery commission powers over procurement, sales‑agent rules, and prize payments, effective immediately.
HB583.summary: HB 583 expands the State Lottery and Sports Wagering Commission’s authority, giving it oversight of all vendor contracts, detailed policy‑making powers, and reporting duties. It also amends sales‑agent rules, drawing procedures, and prize‑payment rules to increase transparency and protect the state’s revenue. The bill takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Adds a new subsection (3) to §23‑7‑202 giving the commission authority to approve all procurement decisions for vendor contracts used in the lottery operation.

Rewrites §23‑7‑301 to give the commission rule‑making power over sales‑agent licensing, location, bond requirements, and commission limits, and introduces a 10 % commission cap with optional incremental‑sales bonuses.
Rewrites §23‑7‑311 to require all drawings to be public, prohibit lottery employees or commission members from selecting winners, and allow prize payments by sales agents for small prizes.
Adds new rules for prize payment, including installment options for jackpots over $100,000, a 6‑month claim period, and forfeiture of unclaimed prizes.
Mandates quarterly and annual reports on lottery operations to the governor, Department of Administration, Legislative Auditor, and Legislature.
Provides the commission with the power to adopt rules on sports‑wagering sales‑agent commissions, licensing, and responsible‑gaming protections.
Establishes an immediate effective date upon passage.
affected: State Lottery and Sports Wagering Commission

HB593.one_line: Revises sexual‑abuse reporting to require detailed county attorney records and annual reporting to the attorney general.
HB593.summary: The bill amends Montana’s sexual‑abuse reporting statutes to require county attorneys to collect and retain investigative records, certify receipt of reports, and submit detailed annual reports to the attorney general. It also expands the Department of Public Health and Human Services’ reporting duties and sets up new reporting forms and confidentiality safeguards.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑210 to mandate that county attorneys gather all investigative materials on child‑sexual‑abuse reports, certify receipt to reporters, and retain records for 25 years.
Requires county attorneys to submit annual reports (January 1 and July 1) to the attorney general with case identifiers, dates, charges, convictions, sentences, and counts of unprosecuted reports.
Creates a standardized reporting form for county attorneys and declares the data confidential criminal‑justice information.
Expands §41‑3‑211 to obligate the Department to report the number of referrals to county attorneys each year and to advise the attorney general when it believes prosecution is warranted.
Adds §41‑3‑212 provisions requiring department employees to obtain specific facts, make audio recordings of phone reports, and protect reporter privacy.
Mandates the attorney general to report aggregated data to the Law & Justice Interim Committee and Interim Budget Committees by August 15 each year.
Specifies that county attorneys who fail to provide complete reports may be identified in the attorney general’s report.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services employees

HB597.one_line: Prohibits inactive voters from signing petitions, effective immediately.
HB597.summary: The bill amends Montana’s petition law to forbid inactive voters from signing petitions, while keeping other petition rules unchanged. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑27‑102 to add subsection (b) prohibiting inactive electors from signing petitions.
Leaves the prohibition on paying signature gatherers unchanged.
Adds a new Section 2 stating the act is effective on passage and approval.
affected: Inactive electors (voters who have not voted in the last election)
General public participating in petition drives

HB594.one_line: HB 594 bars local governments from adding licensing or permitting powers unless state law or delegation allows it.
HB594.summary: HB 594 amends Montana’s local‑government power statute (7‑1‑111) to clarify that local units cannot impose additional licensing or permitting requirements unless expressly authorized by state law or delegated by a state agency. The amendment lists specific prohibited powers and preserves existing local authority in certain areas such as public‑school assessments and employer‑employee relations.
changes: Amends Section 7‑1‑111 to add a new subsection (27) that bars local governments from requiring additional licensing, permitting, or authorization when the state is the original issuer, unless state law expressly allows it or delegates authority to the local unit.

Enumerates a broad set of powers that remain prohibited, including regulation of firearms, environmental permits, landlord‑tenant rules, fertilizer and seed regulation, amateur radio, vehicle movement fees, wildfire‑related ordinances, UAV use, carbon‑based fees, employer‑benefit mandates, nicotine product sales, and utility service connections.
Preserves existing local powers such as imposing assessments related to public‑school costs, exercising public‑employer powers over employees, and enforcing state‑mandated public‑school requirements.
Adds a new subsection (28) that explicitly bars local governments from prohibiting or impeding utility service connections, fuel use, or mandating solar equipment.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.

HB598.one_line: Limits ballot petition signatures to active voters and bars pay‑per‑signature schemes.
HB598.summary: The bill amends Montana’s petition law to require that only active registered voters may sign a ballot issue petition. It also confirms that signature gatherers cannot be paid based on the number of signatures collected. The law takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
changes: Amends §13‑27‑102 to restrict petition signatures to active registered voters only
Prohibits payment to signature gatherers based on the number of signatures collected
Sets the act’s effective date to the day it is passed and approved
No other provisions are added or removed
The amendment does not create a new program or office
The text does not alter any existing funding or fiscal allocations
affected: Individuals who would otherwise sign petitions as non‑voters
Election officials responsible for verifying signatures

HB604.one_line: Bans local guaranteed‑income programs and expands limits on local government powers.
HB604.summary: The bill bars any local government from creating or enforcing a guaranteed‑income program, declares such ordinances void, and gives the attorney general authority to issue cease‑and‑desist orders and sue for injunctive relief. It also amends a broad section of the Montana Code to prohibit local governments from exercising many powers that could affect private or civil relationships, including the administration of guaranteed‑income programs.
changes: Prohibits all political subdivisions from adopting, enforcing, or maintaining ordinances, orders, or rules that provide guaranteed income payments to individuals.
Declares any ordinance, order, or rule that does so null and void.
Empowers the attorney general to send cease‑and‑desist orders to violators and to sue for injunctive relief if non‑compliance occurs.
Defines “guaranteed income program” as unearned periodic cash payments not tied to work or training.

Amends Section 7‑1‑111, MCA, adding a new subsection that bars local governments from exercising a wide range of powers that could affect private or civil relationships, including the administration of guaranteed‑income programs.
affected: Local governments (counties, cities, school districts, special districts, etc.)
Individuals who might receive guaranteed‑income payments

HB609.one_line: Creates a felony for abortion trafficking with up to 5‑year prison and $1,000 fine.
HB609.summary: HB 609 creates a new felony called abortion trafficking, punishing anyone who transports or helps transport an unborn child to obtain an illegal abortion. It also amends the state’s homicide‑penalty code to apply the same $1,000 fine/5‑year prison maximum to this offense.
changes: Defines abortion trafficking as a crime when a person knowingly transports or aids transport of an unborn child to obtain an illegal abortion in Montana
Sets a maximum fine of $1,000 or up to 5 years’ imprisonment (or both) for conviction
Amends §50‑20‑112, MCA, to apply the same penalty limits to this new offense
Adds codification language making the new section part of Title 50, Chapter 20, Part 1
Specifies the act takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to acts committed thereafter

Includes a penalty‑exemption clause for the woman who receives the abortion and for failure to comply with a written‑certification requirement, but allows penalty against the mother of the unborn child
affected: Individuals who transport or assist transport of unborn children for illegal abortions

HB613.one_line: Libraries must match state grants dollar‑for‑dollar with local funds under new law effective July 2025.
HB613.summary: The bill amends the state aid formula for public libraries, requiring each recipient to match grant dollars dollar‑for‑dollar with local or tribal funds and to certify compliance. It also sets an effective date of July 1, 2025, and terminates the amended formula on July 1, 2029.
changes: Amends Section 22‑1‑327 to require a $1 matching contribution for every $1 grant, paid in cash by local or tribal governments, not by other state or federal money.
Adds a certification requirement that a responsible official confirm the match and compliance with the new matching rule.
Sets the amended formula to terminate on July 1, 2029, reverting to the prior law thereafter.
Specifies the act becomes effective July 1, 2025.

HB615.one_line: Reallocates coal‑severance‑tax interest to multiple state accounts and extends program dates.
HB615.summary: HB 615 revises how interest from the coal severance‑tax permanent fund is allocated, directing specific percentages to new and existing state accounts and extending several program termination dates. It also sets a July 1, 2025 effective date.
changes: Amends §15‑35‑108 to allocate 12 % of coal severance tax collections to the major‑repair long‑range building program, 0.90 % to basic library services, 3.77 % to conservation districts, 0.79 % to the Growth‑Through‑Agriculture account, 1.27 % to a parks permanent fund, 0.95 % to a renewable‑resource loan debt‑service fund, 0.63 % to a capitol‑arts trust fund, and 5.8 % to the coal natural‑resource account; $250,000 is credited to the coal‑and‑uranium mine permitting and reclamation program; all other revenue goes to the general fund.

The interest income of the permanent fund is split: $2 million annually to the Department of Justice for highway‑patrol salaries and the remainder to the Department of Transportation for the highway‑restricted account.
Extends termination dates for several appropriations and program provisions (e.g., June 30, 2027 and June 30, 2029).
Effective July 1, 2025.
affected: State departments (Justice, Agriculture, Commerce, Transportation), library federations, conservation districts, parks and recreation agencies, capitol art projects, and the general public via the general fund.

HB617.one_line: AG must notify public and lawmakers before state litigation, hold hearings, and maintain a public case register.
HB617.summary: HB 617 requires the Attorney General to notify the public and state lawmakers before initiating litigation that could affect the state, hold a public hearing, and post cost estimates and outcomes. It also creates a public register of all such cases and expands the AG’s supervisory role over county attorneys.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑501, MCA, adding a 10‑day notice requirement before the AG engages in litigation where the state may have an interest.
Mandates the AG produce a written statement of intent (including projected costs) to the governor, judiciary committees, and publish it online.
Requires a public hearing with at least 5 business days’ notice and a written response to public comments before proceeding.
Allows a 5‑day emergency exception with a post‑action statement of intent and justification.
Creates a permanent, publicly inspectable register of all AG‑initiated cases, updated within 30 days of conclusion with itemized costs.
Expands the AG’s supervisory powers over county attorneys, including ordering prosecutions and providing written opinions to state and local officials.

HB618.one_line: Bans state and local agencies from funding discriminatory or DEI‑promoting programs and gives the AG enforcement powers.
HB618.summary: The bill creates the Montana Individual Freedom Act, banning state and local agencies, including the Department of Military Affairs, from spending money on memberships, goods, or services from organizations that discriminate or that promote diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) or political/social activism. It gives the Attorney General investigatory and rule‑making authority to enforce the ban. The Act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Prohibits any state or local government agency from expending funds—regardless of source—to purchase memberships, goods, or services from any organization that discriminates on the basis of race, color, ethnicity, national origin, sex, disability, or religion.
Bans agencies from using state, local, or federal funds to support or maintain programs that advocate for DEI or engage in political or social activism.
Extends the same prohibitions to the Department of Military Affairs or militia.
Empowers the Attorney General to investigate alleged violations and adopt rules to enforce the Act.
Codifies the provisions as a new chapter in Title 49 of the Montana Code.
Effective July 1, 2025.
affected: Organizations that provide memberships, goods, or services to those agencies
Programs that promote DEI or political/social activism

HB619.one_line: Montana’s new Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act governs all condo, co‑op, and planned‑community developments.
HB619.summary: The Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act establishes a comprehensive framework for creating, governing, and terminating condominium, cooperative, and planned‑community developments in Montana. It defines key terms, sets out the rights and duties of unit owners and associations, prescribes procedures for amendments, assessments, and enforcement, and requires public offering statements and disclosure documents for sales. The act also creates new processes for eminent domain, leasehold communities, and master‑planned developments, and it provides detailed rules for insurance, financing, and dispute resolution.
changes: 1. Creates a new uniform act that applies to all common‑interest communities (condominiums, cooperatives, planned communities) and codifies existing Montana statutes on these entities.
2. Establishes detailed definitions for units, common elements, allocated interests, development rights, and special declarant rights.
3. Requires a declaration and, for condominiums and planned communities, a separate parcel for each unit that is separately taxed and assessed.
4. Sets procedures for creating, amending, and terminating common‑interest communities, including requirements for unit‑owner votes, executive‑board actions, and recording of amendments.
5. Provides a comprehensive system for assessments, liens, and foreclosure of units, including priority rules and procedures for recording and enforcing liens.
6. Mandates insurance coverage for common elements and specifies how insurance proceeds are handled.
7. Requires public offering statements and disclosure documents for any sale of a unit, and establishes purchaser rights to cancel contracts and to receive refunds if statements are not provided.
8. Creates new rules for leasehold common‑interest communities, master‑planned communities, and conversion buildings, including notice requirements and rights of tenants.
9. Establishes procedures for dispute resolution, including mandatory alternative dispute resolution and detailed rules for executive‑board meetings and voting.
10. Provides a transition schedule for pre‑existing communities, allowing them to adopt the act by amendment or election of unit owners.
11. Repeals a large block of existing Montana statutes (70‑23‑101 through 70‑23‑1105) that previously governed common‑interest communities.
12. Adds new sections on warranties, implied warranties, and limitation periods for purchasers.
13. Creates new processes for eminent domain takings of units and common elements, including reallocation of interests.
14. Provides new rules for the sale and disposition of units, including special assessments, foreclosure, and the handling of liens and security interests.
affected: Unit owners, developers (declarants), cooperative members, association boards and officers, lenders and security interest holders, purchasers of units, tenants in leasehold communities, and state agencies that enforce property and tax laws.
numbers: 10% (refund to purchaser if public offering statement omitted)

HB622.one_line: HB 622 establishes a new extreme‑risk protection order process to bar firearms for those deemed a danger.
HB622.summary: HB 622 creates a new court procedure for obtaining an extreme‑risk protection order that bars a person from possessing firearms.  The bill allows partners, family members, or law‑enforcement officers to petition for an ex‑parte or regular hearing, requires surrender of firearms, and establishes reporting, penalties, and instructional materials.  Orders last one year and may be renewed or terminated by the respondent.
changes: Establishes an extreme‑risk protection order (ERPO) process for partners, family members, or law‑enforcement officers to petition a district court.
Allows an ex‑parte ERPO to be issued before a hearing if the petitioner can show a significant risk of firearm‑related harm.
Mandates that any firearm in the respondent’s possession be surrendered to law‑enforcement or a federally licensed dealer, and that a concealed‑weapon permit be revoked.
Provides a 90‑day window for courts to supply standardized forms, instructions, and informational brochures to petitioners.
Sets a 1‑year term for ERPOs, with procedures for renewal, termination, and the respondent’s burden to prove no longer a risk.

Creates reporting requirements: orders must be entered in a statewide judicial information system, the national instant background‑check system, and other state computer systems, and the sheriff must revoke concealed‑weapon permits.
Imposes penalties: filing a false petition is a misdemeanor (up to $500 fine or 6 months jail); violating an ERPO is a felony (up to 10 years jail or $50,000 fine).
Requires the office of court administrator to develop and distribute instructional materials, translate them for significant non‑English‑speaking populations, and update them as needed.
Mandates annual reporting by clerks to the court administrator on ERPO statistics by county and court type.
affected: Firearm owners and concealed‑weapon permit holders
State court system and administrative offices
General public (through reporting and informational materials)
numbers: 90 days for court to provide forms
14 days to schedule hearing after petition
January 31 and April 1 for annual reports

HB630.one_line: Legislature must approve any new greenhouse‑gas or social‑cost rules before they take effect.
HB630.summary: HB 630 requires the Montana Legislature to approve any new rules or regulations issued by state departments, commissions, or boards that regulate greenhouse‑gas emissions or calculate the social cost of carbon for motor‑vehicle operation. Until the legislature approves such rules at the next session, they are not effective.
changes: Department, commission, or board rules on greenhouse‑gas regulation or social‑cost calculations cannot take effect without legislative approval at the next session.
The bill applies to all state agencies and local authorities that issue such rules.
It codifies the requirement into the relevant parts of the Montana Statutes (Title 61, 69, 75, 82).
affected: Local authorities that issue greenhouse‑gas rules
Motor‑vehicle operators subject to such rules

HB634.one_line: Repeals Montana’s Motion Picture Fair Trade Practices Act.
HB634.summary: The bill repeals Montana’s Motion Picture Fair Trade Practices Act, removing all statutory provisions that governed bidding and licensing for motion‑picture production and distribution.
changes: Repeals §30‑14‑301 (short title)
Repeals §30‑14‑302 (purpose)
Repeals §30‑14‑303 (definitions)
Repeals §30‑14‑304 (prohibition of blind bidding)
Repeals §30‑14‑305 (unlawful license‑agreement provisions)
Repeals §30‑14‑306 (bid requirements)
Repeals §30‑14‑307 (void acts)
Repeals §30‑14‑308 (violation as a misdemeanor)

HB635.one_line: Bill bans state/local DEI programs, gives AG enforcement powers, and allows private lawsuits with fines up to $10,000 per violation.
HB635.summary: The bill would prohibit state and local agencies from funding, creating, or supporting any program that influences hiring or other employment practices on the basis of race, sex, or religion, or that promotes what the bill defines as “divisive” concepts.  It gives the Attorney General broad investigative and enforcement powers, allows private lawsuits for damages, and imposes up to $10,000 fines for violations.
changes: 1. Defines “diversity, equity, and inclusion” programs and “divisive concepts” and prohibits state/local agencies from requiring, funding, or supporting such programs. 2. Prohibits agencies from establishing offices or staff whose duties include coordinating or promoting these programs. 3. Grants the Attorney General authority to investigate, subpoena, and prosecute alleged violations, and to seek injunctive relief. 4. Creates a private right of action for individuals harmed by a violation, allowing actual damages or $5,000 per violation. 5. Imposes civil fines of up to $10,000 per violation for non‑compliance with injunctions or for willful violations. 6. Requires codification of the new provisions as a chapter of Title 49 (the Montana Human Rights Act).
affected: Individuals who may be required to attend DEI‑related training
Private citizens who could sue for damages

HB637.one_line: Establishes a comprehensive legal framework for medical aid in dying in Montana.
HB637.summary: The bill establishes a legal framework for medical aid in dying (MAID) in Montana, setting detailed requirements for prescribing, waiting periods, documentation, and provider conscience‑based protections. It also creates reporting, insurance, and liability provisions while criminalizing coercion or tampering with MAID requests.
changes: Creates a statutory MAID program with eligibility, capacity, and terminal‑illness requirements; requires a 48‑hour waiting period before a prescription can be filled; mandates a detailed written request form and witness requirements; requires a consulting health‑care provider’s written confirmation of terminal status; provides conscience‑based immunity for providers and entities that refuse to participate; requires reporting to the Department of Public Health and Human Services and annual statistical reporting; establishes criminal penalties for forging or coercing MAID requests; allows government entities to claim costs from estates for public‑place self‑administration; clarifies insurance and will‑protection rules; and codifies the provisions as a new chapter of Title 50.

HB639.one_line: Broadens internet gambling definition, shifts fines to DOJ, and imposes harsher penalties for illegal gambling.
HB639.summary: HB 639 amends Montana’s gambling statutes to broaden the definition of internet gambling to include online casinos and cryptocurrency, shifts fines to the Department of Justice’s general fund, and tightens penalties for illegal gambling, including felony liability for operating illegal internet sites.
changes: Redefines "Internet gambling" to cover online casinos and any use of cryptocurrency for betting.
Adds online casinos that accept any currency to the list of prohibited gambling activities; non‑currency‑based online casinos remain allowed.
Directs all fines and penalties collected for gambling violations to be deposited in the Department of Justice’s operating budget of the state general fund.
Makes soliciting participation in illegal gambling a misdemeanor with specified penalties.
Raises the felony penalty for knowingly violating gambling provisions to a fine of up to $50,000, up to 10 years imprisonment, and automatic revocation of any gambling license or permit.
Adds a specific felony provision for operating an illegal internet gambling site within Montana, whether domestic or offshore.
affected: Individuals who solicit or participate in illegal gambling
Persons who operate or facilitate illegal internet gambling sites
numbers: fines deposited in DOJ operating budget
online casinos that accept any currency prohibited

HB640.one_line: HB 640 lets airport‑authority public‑safety officers join the firefighters’ retirement system effective July 1 2025.
HB640.summary: HB 640 expands the Firefighters’ Unified Retirement System to include public‑safety officers employed by airport authorities. It amends definitions and participation rules so that airport‑authority firefighters can elect to join the system and receive the same benefits as city and rural‑district firefighters.
changes: Amends §19‑13‑104 to define "public safety officer" as a full‑paid firefighter who also serves as a sworn peace officer for an airport authority.
Amends §19‑13‑210 to allow airport‑authority public‑safety officers to elect participation in the retirement system via ordinance or resolution.
Specifies that each firefighter hired before the election has 90 days to choose to remain in the Public Employees’ Retirement System or join the Firefighters’ Unified Retirement System.
Provides that firefighters hired after the election are automatically covered by the retirement system.
Adds an effective‑date clause: the changes take effect July 1 2025.
affected: City and rural fire departments that may elect to join the system

HB644.one_line: Allows counties to hire certified appraisers and sets notice rules for private‑property appraisals.
HB644.summary: The bill lets a county hire a certified property appraiser, subject to the Department of Revenue’s approval, and requires that county‑prepared appraisals be used for tax‑value certification. It also amends statutes to clarify the authority of county appraisers, the notice requirements for land‑owner consent, and the procedures for entering private property for appraisal or audit.
changes: Authorizes counties to employ a certified property appraiser with written permission from the Department of Revenue.
Requires county appraisers to submit annual appraisals by July 1 and mandates that those appraisals be used when certifying taxable values.
Amends §15‑7‑139 to exempt county and department appraisers from certain state rules and to establish notice and consent procedures for entering private land.
Amends §15‑7‑140 to require county treasurers to include a statement of land‑owner rights in tax‑notice publications.
Adds codification instructions tying the new provisions to Title 7, Chapter 1, Part 21.
affected: Landowners in counties that may be appraised

HB645.one_line: Mandates Montana residency and voter registration for petition signature gatherers.
HB645.summary: HB 645 requires that anyone who gathers signatures for a statewide ballot issue must be a Montana resident and a registered Montana voter. It amends the petition‑filing statutes to add this citizenship and registration requirement and requires a sworn affidavit from each gatherer confirming the requirement. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑27‑233 to state that a signature gatherer must be a Montana resident and a registered Montana voter.
Amends §13‑27‑302 to add an affidavit that the gatherer swears they meet the residency and voter‑registration requirement and that the signatures are genuine.
Adds a new section stating the act is effective upon passage and approval.
Replaces the generic language about signature gatherers with explicit Montana‑resident and registered‑voter language.
affected: Signature gatherers for statewide ballot issues
Montana voters who may sign petitions
numbers: Effective date: upon passage and approval

HB646.one_line: Replaces at‑large Supreme Court elections with district‑based elections across seven Montana districts.
HB646.summary: The bill requires Montana’s seven Supreme Court justices to be elected from seven newly defined geographic districts, replacing the current at‑large system. It establishes the districts, amends election statutes, and sets a transition plan for existing justices.
changes: Amends §3‑2‑101 to make each justice elected by the voters of a specific district rather than statewide; the chief justice is still elected statewide but selected by the court after 2032.
Creates §2 defining seven Supreme Court districts and mandates one justice per district; districts are to be reviewed after each decennial census.
Amends §13‑14‑211 to treat each district justice vacancy as a separate election office and assigns seat numbers to justices.
Provides a transition in §4: existing justices keep their seats until the effective date, then the chief justice assigns each to a district and the chief justice is assigned to the seventh district.
Specifies that justices running for reelection must do so in their assigned district unless they resign and file for another district.
Codifies §2 as part of Title 3, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
Includes severability and applicability provisions.
Effective date is not stated in the text.

HB647.one_line: HB 647 bars nonprofits from leasing state lands, preserving the board’s leasing authority for other uses.
HB647.summary: HB 647 prohibits state land leases to nonprofit organizations, except for the board’s own leasing authority. It amends many trust‑land leasing provisions to clarify that nonprofit entities may not lease state lands, while preserving the board’s broad leasing powers for commercial, mineral, and energy uses.
changes: 1. Adds a new restriction (77‑1‑113(2)) that any official, employee, or member of a nonprofit corporation may not lease state lands or timber on behalf of that nonprofit.

2. Repeals the exemption that allowed nonprofits to lease state lands by inserting the restriction into all leasing provisions (77‑1‑204, 77‑1‑904, 77‑3‑102, 77‑3‑201, 77‑3‑301, 77‑3‑401, 77‑3‑501, 77‑4‑101, 77‑4‑301, 77‑6‑102, 77‑6‑202, 77‑6‑503).
3. Leaves the board’s authority to lease state lands for commercial, mineral, and energy purposes unchanged, except that it must now comply with the new nonprofit restriction.
4. Maintains existing lease limits (e.g., 99‑year maximum for commercial leases) and bidding procedures.
5. Keeps all other procedural and fiduciary requirements for land banking, appraisal, and consultation with local governments.
6. Does not create any new program, fund, or criminal offense.
affected: State land trustees and board members
Nonprofit organizations that previously leased state lands

HB649.one_line: Creates a $3 million farm‑to‑food‑bank grant program with reporting and tribal notification requirements.
HB649.summary: The bill creates a $3 million farm‑to‑food‑bank grant program, administered by the Department of Agriculture, to support regional food hubs that buy and distribute Montana‑grown products to food pantries. Grants are awarded competitively with preferences for rural and tribal outreach, and the program is funded from a special revenue account and the general fund. Biennial reports on purchases and impact are required.
changes: Establishes a new farm‑to‑food‑bank grant program with a $3 million appropriation for the 2025‑2026 biennium.
Creates a special revenue account in the State Special Revenue Fund to hold program funds.
