Authorizes the Department of Agriculture to develop rules, award grants, and set preferences for applicants, including a 20 % cap on administrative costs.
Mandates that grant‑funded purchases be Montana‑grown and not replace existing food‑bank purchases funded elsewhere.
Requires the department to submit biennial evaluation reports to the Economic Affairs Interim Committee by September 1 of each preceding year.
Notifies federally recognized tribal governments of the act.
affected: Regional food hubs and food pantries
Low‑income consumers served by food banks

HB652.one_line: Eliminates state income tax on most military pensions and survivor benefits for Montana residents.
HB652.summary: HB 652 removes state income tax from most military pensions, retirements, and survivor benefits for Montana residents.  The bill amends tax‑definition sections, adds specific exemptions, and sets a delayed effective date of January 1 2026 for tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
changes: Amends Section 15‑30‑2101 to redefine terms and add a new definition for military pension/retirement income exempt from state tax
Amends Section 15‑30‑2120 to add the exemption to the list of items added to federal taxable income and to subtract the exemption from federal taxable income for Montana tax purposes
Repeals Section 4 of Chapter 650, Laws of 2023, which previously imposed a tax on military pensions
Provides that the exemption applies to tax years beginning after December 31 2025 and takes effect January 1 2026

Specifies that the exemption applies only to residents who were residents before receiving the benefit or who become residents after June 30 2023 and limits the benefit to five consecutive years for new residents
affected: Montana residents receiving military pensions, retirements, or survivor benefits

HB653.one_line: Parental right to child health records expanded, with 10‑day access and consent rules clarified.
HB653.summary: HB 653 expands parental access to a child’s health‑care records, requiring providers to give parents copies within 10 days and removing a child’s exclusive right to block disclosure. It also clarifies consent rules for surgical, mental‑health, and prescription care and limits access when a court order or abuse investigation is involved.
changes: Amends §40‑6‑702 to require providers to supply a child’s health‑care information to the parent at no charge, within 10 days of request, except for abortions and when a court order or abuse investigation limits access.

Adds a new subsection that allows a parent to give consent for surgical, physical, prescription, mental‑health evaluation, or treatment of a child, and requires telemedicine consent to verify parent identity.
Prohibits hospitals from performing surgery on a child without first obtaining parental consent unless an emergency exists or the parent cannot be located.
Clarifies that a minor who can consent to care without parental consent may exercise rights to information only for care they consented to.
Defines that a health‑care representative may act in good faith to represent the patient’s best interests.
Adds severability and immediate effective‑date provisions.
who_is_affected:[

HB654.one_line: HB 654 expands ANB counting for early‑literacy programs and funds a $1,000‑per‑student grant for district expansion.
HB654.summary: HB 654 expands how school districts can count students in early‑literacy classroom programs toward their average‑number‑belonging (ANB) and creates a $1,000‑per‑student grant to help districts grow those programs. The bill also establishes a temporary grant account and appropriates $2 million for the grants.
changes: Amends the ANB formula (20‑9‑311) to allow students in approved early‑literacy classroom‑based programs to be counted toward a district’s ANB.
Adds a new ANB‑increase provision (20‑9‑313 (1)(f)) that lets districts increase their ANB when they expand early‑literacy programs.
Creates a temporary early‑literacy targeted‑intervention boost grant program (Section 4) that pays $1,000 for every ANB increase a district receives under the new ANB rule.
Requires grant recipients to deposit the money in their miscellaneous programs fund and spend it by June 30 2027 on classroom modifications or curriculum related to the expansion.
Appropriates $2 million from the school facility and technology account for the grants and establishes a dedicated grant account (20‑9‑516).
Sets the act to take effect immediately, apply to fiscal years beginning July 1 2025, and terminate on June 30 2027.

HB657.one_line: Cities may review water/sewer projects if a licensed engineer is hired, meeting MEPA and takings rules.
HB657.summary: HB 657 allows cities and towns that hire a licensed professional engineer to review and approve the design and construction of public water and sewer systems and their extensions or alterations, provided they meet state environmental and property‑taking requirements.
changes: Authorizes municipal review of water and sewer system design and construction when a licensed engineer is employed or contracted.
Requires the review program to comply with the Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) and real‑property takings rules.
Mandates determinations of non‑degradation and nonsignificance under MEPA.
Codifies the new authority as part of Title 75, Chapter 6, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
No new funding or penalties are created.
The bill does not establish a new program beyond the review requirement.
affected: Cities and towns that employ or contract a licensed professional engineer
Licensed professional engineers hired by municipalities
Municipal departments responsible for water and sewer review

HB658.one_line: HB 658 limits local health board sanitation rules to state standards and protects existing onsite wastewater systems.
HB658.summary: HB 658 removes the ability of local boards of health to adopt sanitation rules that are stricter than state standards, exempts already‑installed onsite wastewater systems from new rules, and establishes a retroactive effective date. The bill amends the statutory language governing local health board powers and clarifies how and when local regulations may be more stringent than state law.
changes: Amends §50‑2‑116 to prohibit local boards from adopting sanitation rules that are more stringent than state standards, except where a written finding is made after a public hearing.
Exempts subsurface onsite wastewater treatment systems that are already installed and functioning from any amendment or update to local health board rules adopted after their approval.
Allows local boards to adopt rules that are more stringent than state standards only if a written finding is made based on evidence and peer‑reviewed studies.
Provides that local boards may charge a petition filing fee up to $250 for challenges to rules that are more stringent than state standards.
Adds a retroactive applicability clause so that the new rules apply to onsite wastewater systems installed on or before the effective date.
Clarifies that local boards may not impose additional requirements on landowners for new or updated onsite wastewater systems unless written directives with clear evidence are provided.
affected: Landowners with subsurface onsite wastewater treatment systems
Private businesses subject to sanitation rules
Residents and property owners in local jurisdictions

HB659.one_line: HB 659 revises local election rules for marijuana business approvals in counties opposed to Initiative 190.
HB659.summary: HB 659 amends the marijuana‑licensing law to clarify how local elections determine whether certain marijuana businesses may operate in counties that voted against Initiative 190, and it sets an immediate effective date. The bill establishes the categories that must be approved, the petition and voting procedures, and the conditions under which former medical licensees may continue operating.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑301, MCA, to specify that a marijuana business may not operate in a county that voted against Initiative 190 unless the business’s license category has been approved by the local jurisdiction and the business is licensed by the department.

Defines the seven marijuana‑business categories that require local approval in such counties (cultivator, manufacturer, medical dispensary, adult‑use dispensary, combined‑use licensee, testing laboratory, transporter).

Creates a petition‑and‑election process for qualified electors in a county or municipality to approve or prohibit each category, with voting thresholds (majority for counties, two‑thirds for municipalities).
Allows a county or municipality that previously approved a category to later prohibit it, with the prohibition taking effect 90 days after the election.

Exempts former medical‑marijuana licensees that do not apply for adult‑use dispensary licensure from local regulations for a grace period, and allows former medical licensees to apply for other categories if in good standing.
Specifies that local governments may not prohibit the transportation of marijuana on public roads.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.

HB660.one_line: DEQ must create and enforce rules to limit greenhouse‑gas emissions, with fee‑setting and study‑mandates.
HB660.summary: HB 660 requires the Montana Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) to develop and enforce rules that limit greenhouse‑gas emissions, expanding its regulatory authority beyond existing air‑pollution rules. The bill amends DEQ’s statutory powers, authorizes fee‑setting for certain permits, and mandates the department to conduct studies, provide technical assistance, and collaborate with local governments and other agencies.
changes: Amends § 75‑2‑112 to give DEQ explicit authority to adopt, amend, and repeal rules for limiting greenhouse‑gas emissions.
Requires DEQ to develop a comprehensive plan and enforce orders related to GHG limits.
Allows DEQ to issue fees for environmental‑impact analyses of redesignation applications (except on Indian reservations).
Mandates DEQ to conduct studies, provide technical assistance to local governments, and share costs (state share capped at 30 %).
Requires DEQ to collect and disseminate information and conduct educational programs on air contamination.
Authorizes DEQ to accept grants and other funds for the chapter’s purposes.
affected: Agricultural producers (subject to existing federal rules)

HB661.one_line: Amends game‑harassment law, broadening prohibited conduct and raising penalties for repeat offenders.
HB661.summary: This bill amends Montana’s game‑harassment law to broaden the definition of unlawful conduct against wildlife and to increase penalties for repeat offenders. It clarifies that landowners may protect their property and expands the range of vehicles and devices that may be used in harassment. The changes raise fines, extend imprisonment limits, and impose longer license forfeiture periods for second or subsequent violations.
changes: Amends §87‑6‑107 to prohibit concentrating, driving, rallying, stirring up, running, molesting, flushing, herding, chasing, harassing, or impeding game animals or birds with any self‑propelled, motor‑driven, or drawn vehicle or device, including aircraft and snowmobiles.
Adds an exception for landowners and their authorized agents who are immediately protecting their property.
Sets a first‑offense penalty of a fine of $50‑$1,000, up to 6 months in county jail, and possible forfeiture of hunting, fishing, or trapping licenses and recreational privileges.

Sets a second‑or‑subsequent‑offense penalty of a fine of $500‑$1,000, up to 6 months in county jail, and a 24‑month forfeiture of hunting, fishing, or trapping licenses and recreational privileges, unless the court imposes a longer period.
Clarifies that the penalties apply to violations within a 5‑year period.
affected: Individuals who use vehicles or devices to harass game animals or birds

HB662.one_line: Revises driver‑privacy law to require written consent, enable class actions, and mandate requester record‑keeping.
HB662.summary: HB 662 revises Montana’s Driver Privacy Protection Act to tighten consent requirements, create a class‑action remedy for misuse of disclosed data, and require the Department of Transportation to maintain a list of requesters. It adds detailed definitions, expands permissible uses, and imposes record‑keeping and fee rules for data requests.
changes: Adds a class‑action provision allowing harmed individuals to sue requesters for punitive damages, costs, and attorney fees.
Replaces the definition of “express consent” with a written or electronically signed authorization on a form prescribed by the Department.
Requires the Department to keep a public list of all requesters who submit a disclosure application, including scope and disposition of the request.
Expands the list of permissible uses of motor‑vehicle record information and clarifies when a social‑security number may be disclosed.
Imposes new fee‑collection rules, including cost‑recovery, convenience fees, and exemptions for certain government entities.
Mandates that any requester who sells or discloses personal information must keep 5‑year records of the transaction and the recipient.
Adds codification language to integrate the new section into Title 61, Chapter 11, Part 5.
affected: Individuals whose motor‑vehicle record information is disclosed
Requesters (private entities, government agencies, news media) who obtain motor‑vehicle record data
The Department of Transportation (DOT) and its staff
Courts and attorneys handling class‑action suits
numbers: Exemptions for governor’s office, tax appeal board, revenue, legislative agencies, criminal‑justice agencies

HB663.one_line: Prohibits race‑based decisions in Montana higher‑education and creates a private damages action.
HB663.summary: The bill bars Montana higher‑education institutions from considering race, color, ethnicity, or national origin in hiring, admissions, scholarships, or financial aid, and creates a private right of action with statutory and punitive damages. It also waives state sovereign immunity for such claims and sets an effective date of October 1, 2026.
changes: Prohibits use of race, color, ethnicity, or national origin in any admission, hiring, scholarship, or financial‑aid decision by a Montana higher‑education institution.
Disallows the use of aggregated data on those characteristics for such decisions.
Bans disclosure or acquisition of individual applicant data on those characteristics before final decisions.
Creates a private cause of action against institutions and, where appropriate, against officers, employees, or agents.
Provides for actual, compensatory, punitive, and statutory damages ($4,000) and injunctive relief.
Waives the state’s sovereign immunity for claims under the act.
Sets the act to take effect on October 1, 2026.
affected: Officers, employees, and agents of institutions

HB670.one_line: Utilities must roll over unused customer‑generated energy credits to a low‑income assistance fund quarterly.
HB670.summary: HB 670 requires utilities to transfer any unused customer‑generated kilowatt‑hour credits to a low‑income energy assistance fund. It amends the revenue code to create a dedicated fund for low‑income assistance and changes the net‑energy measurement rules so that unused credits are automatically rolled over to that fund.
changes: Amends §69‑8‑412 to establish a low‑income energy assistance fund administered by the Department of Public Health and Human Services.

Amends §69‑8‑603 to require that any unused customer‑generated kilowatt‑hour credits, accrued over a 12‑month period, be transferred to the low‑income assistance fund without compensation to the customer.
Specifies that the transfer occurs on the first day of each quarter (Jan 1, Apr 1, Jul 1, Oct 1).
Prescribes that the net‑energy measurement calculation includes crediting excess generation and billing for net consumption per existing metering rules.
Requires utilities to credit the low‑income assistance fund for unused credits in accordance with §69‑8‑402.
No new program beyond the fund is created; the fund already exists under the code but is now specifically tied to unused credits.
affected: Utility customers who generate excess electricity
State departments of revenue, environmental quality, public health and human services

HB673.one_line: Confidentiality for small 501(c)(4) contributions while tightening campaign‑finance reporting.
HB673.summary: HB 673 revises Montana’s campaign‑finance disclosure rules to keep the identities of 501(c)(4) donors who give less than $1,000 confidential, while tightening reporting requirements for candidates, committees, and incidental committees. The bill amends several statutes to add new definitions, adopt new rules, and clarify when donor information must be withheld or disclosed. It does not create a new program or fund, but it expands the scope of donor‑privacy protections and reporting obligations for political entities.
changes: Adds the definition of a “C4 donor” and clarifies the role of the commissioner of political practices.
Mandates that the commissioner adopt rules to implement the new donor‑privacy provisions and other reporting criteria.
Requires that contributions of less than $1,000 from a C4 donor remain confidential in all campaign‑finance reports.
Expands the definition of incidental committees and sets new reporting thresholds and timelines for them.
Specifies that certain contributions, loans, and expenditures must be itemized and disclosed, but exempts those below the $1,000 threshold for C4 donors.
Adjusts disclosure requirements for candidates, ballot‑issue committees, political parties, and joint fundraising committees to reflect the new confidentiality rule.

HB674.one_line: Revises the Code Commissioner’s duties to recommend repealing permanently enjoined unconstitutional laws.
HB674.summary: HB 674 revises the duties of the Montana Code Commissioner to add a requirement that the commissioner recommend legislation to eliminate laws that are permanently enjoined as unconstitutional. It also expands the commissioner’s reporting and codification responsibilities.
changes: Amends §1‑11‑204, MCA to require the commissioner to recommend repealing laws that a court has permanently enjoined for being facially unconstitutional.
Adds a new subsection (f) to the recommendation list, covering unenforced laws due to permanent enjoinments.
Expands the material the commissioner must prepare for publication, including constitutional documents, federal statutes, and procedural rules.
Mandates the commissioner to produce an annual “Official Report of the Montana Code Commissioner” detailing all substantive changes made during continuous recodification.
Requires the commissioner to recodify the Montana Code Annotated on a title‑by‑title basis as part of ongoing duties.
Allows the commissioner to confer with judiciary and bar members regarding recodification procedures.

HB675.one_line: HB 675 gives minors a civil remedy against drag‑performances and updates related definitions.
HB675.summary: HB 675 creates a private right of action for minors and their guardians against drag‑king or drag‑queen performances that violate state law, allowing damages and statutory penalties. It also amends the definition of drag‑related terms in the Montana Code. No new program or fund is established.
changes: Provides that a minor who attends a drag‑performance in violation of §20‑7‑135, or any adult or minor who attends such a performance, may sue the promoter, performer, or organizer.
Allows a minor’s parent or guardian to file suit on the minor’s behalf.
If the plaintiff prevails, the court may award actual damages, reasonable attorney fees, and a statutory damage of $5,000.
Limits the statute of limitations to 2½ years from the date the harm occurs.
Amends §45‑8‑117, MCA, to update the definitions of “drag king,” “drag queen,” “drag story hour,” “nude,” and related terms, and adds a definition of “sexually oriented performance.”
Codifies the new right of action as part of Title 27, Chapter 1, Part 5, and includes severability language.
affected: Parents or legal guardians of minors
Promoters, performers, and organizers of drag‑performances

HB677.one_line: Mandates license suspension for uninsured driving and tightens DUI suspension rules.
HB677.summary: The bill requires the Department of Motor Vehicles to suspend a driver’s license whenever a person is found to have knowingly driven without valid insurance, except when proof of insurance is provided. It also amends existing DUI‑related statutes to clarify how prior convictions are counted and to tighten the suspension and reinstatement rules for drivers with prior offenses. The changes affect all Montana drivers, insurance companies, and the DMV’s enforcement procedures.
changes: Amends §61‑5‑208 to mandate license suspension when a driver is determined to have driven without insurance, unless proof of coverage is supplied.
numbers: 1‑year suspension for second or subsequent DUI offenses
45‑day minimum for probationary license after first DUI
90‑day minimum for probationary license after second or subsequent DUI

HB678.one_line: Revises ballot‑issue language limits and impact lists, effective immediately.
HB678.summary: The bill amends Montana’s ballot‑issue rules to tighten the language of the statement of purpose and implication, limiting word counts and requiring an itemized impact list. It takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to all statewide ballot issues filed after that date.
changes: Amends §13‑27‑212 to set a 135‑word limit for the narrative portion of a statement of purpose and implication and a 150‑word limit for the bulleted impact list.
Requires the impact list to contain only facts, specific changes, and what stays the same—no opinions or assumptions.
Makes the statement of purpose and implication the petition title and ballot title for issues that reach the ballot.
Establishes the act’s effective date as the day it is passed and approved.
Applies the new rules to any statewide ballot issue submitted to the Secretary of State on or after the effective date.
Does not create new programs, funds, or offenses.
Does not alter any other statutory provisions.
affected: Secretary of State and election officials
numbers: effective date: day of passage and approval

HB688.one_line: HB 688 gives local governments election power to approve or ban marijuana business types and sets exemptions for existing medical licensees.
HB688.summary: HB 688 revises Montana’s marijuana laws to give local governments more control over where marijuana businesses can operate, requires local elections to approve or prohibit specific business types, and clarifies exemptions for existing medical‑marijuana licensees.
changes: Adds an opt‑in requirement for counties that voted against Initiative 190, allowing only those marijuana business categories that have been locally approved to operate there.
Requires local governments to hold elections (by petition) to approve or prohibit each marijuana business category in their jurisdiction, with ballots that specify the category and location.

Exempts former medical‑marijuana licensees that do not apply for adult‑use dispensary licensure from local regulation until their first renewal after Jan 1 2022, and exempts former licensees applying for other categories if they remain in good standing.

Allows counties with municipalities over 5,000 people to conduct separate votes for the municipality while still holding a county‑wide vote, and permits municipalities to overrule county approvals if they vote to prohibit a category.
Provides that a vote to prohibit a previously approved category takes effect 90 days after the election.
Clarifies that local governments cannot prohibit transportation of marijuana on public roads within their jurisdiction.
Adds language to Section 16‑12‑301, MCA, to codify these changes.
affected: Marijuana businesses (cultivators, manufacturers, dispensaries, testing labs, transport facilities)

HB689.one_line: Hospitals must publish full price lists, report fees, and face enforcement and debt‑collection limits.
HB689.summary: HB 689 requires Montana hospitals to publish detailed price lists for all services, report facility‑fee data, and provide clear notice of fees to patients. It creates enforcement mechanisms, a private right of action, and prohibits debt collection on non‑compliant charges.
changes: Hospitals must publish a machine‑readable, searchable list of all standard charges (gross, negotiated, cash, etc.) on their public website and provide hard copies on request.
Hospitals must also publish a consumer‑friendly list of at least 300 shoppable services with detailed pricing and ancillary‑service information.
Each hospital must submit the published lists and an annual facility‑fee report to the Department of Public Health and Human Services, including detailed fee‑type and revenue data.
The Department must publish all reports and lists on its website and accept electronic complaints about violations.
Non‑compliant hospitals may be sued for damages, must pay attorney fees, and may not pursue debt collection on items or services provided while non‑compliant.
The Department is authorized to adopt rules to implement the bill and report annually to the legislature.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB691.one_line: Amends criminal‑justice data‑warehouse law to expand data scope and formalize data‑sharing procedures.
HB691.summary: The bill amends the criminal‑justice data‑warehouse statute to clarify its purpose, data‑sharing procedures, and the board’s responsibilities. It expands the types of data to be tracked, authorizes various entities to contribute, and requires memoranda of understanding and confidentiality safeguards.
changes: Amends §44‑7‑126 to define the data‑warehouse purpose and specify the data it will store and analyze (e.g., full criminal histories, offense timing, sentencing details, custody status, program participation, drug‑involved offenses, pre‑trial release outcomes).

Requires the board of crime control to adopt memoranda of understanding with the Department of Administration and each contributing entity, outlining data content, schedule, confidentiality, and use restrictions.
Mandates the board to work with the Department of Administration to protect privacy and comply with state and federal privacy laws.
Authorizes the board to seek federal grant money for establishing and maintaining the warehouse and to prioritize distribution of those funds to contributors.
Allows the board to require contributors to deliver data in specified formats and schedules, and to collaborate with the council and entities on reporting policies.
Provides that the board may adopt a standard memorandum of understanding for state, local, and court data‑sharing agreements.
Allows the board to grant direct access to the Legislative Fiscal Analyst and Legislative Services Division Director under federal regulations.
affected: Tribal, federal, and nongovernmental entities that may contribute data
Legislative fiscal analyst and services division director

HB695.one_line: Pole owners with grant funds must allow attachments; attachers may sue for damages.
HB695.summary: HB 695 requires pole owners who receive broadband grant funds or offer broadband service to allow pole attachments, gives attachers the right to sue for damages, and mandates grant agreements to include this requirement. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Pole owners receiving broadband grant funding must permit attachers to access all poles in their in‑state service territory.
Grant agreements must include a clause requiring pole‑owner compliance with the attachment rule; prior agreements must be amended.
Attachers may file civil action in Lewis and Clark County district court for non‑compliance, with potential damages, equitable relief, and attorney fees.
Definitions clarify terms such as affiliate, attacher, broadband grant funding, department, and pole owner.
The rule is codified as a new chapter of Title 90 and applies under Title 90 provisions.
affected: Courts in Lewis and Clark County
numbers: District court: Lewis and Clark County

HB697.one_line: No privacy expectation for agency‑provided electronic communications by public employees.
HB697.summary: The bill declares that any email or electronic message sent or received on a public‑agency‑owned device or account is subject to public‑records laws, and that employees have no reasonable expectation of privacy in such communications. It also removes the need for agency counsel to review those messages when a public‑information request is made.
changes: Clarifies that public employees have no privacy expectation in agency‑provided electronic communications
Requires all such communications to be governed by public‑records laws and record‑retention schedules
Exempts agency legal counsel from reviewing these communications in response to public‑information requests
Defines “communications for work‑related purposes” to include employment terms and benefits
Codifies the rule as part of Title 2, Chapter 6, Part 10 of the Montana Statutes

HB698.one_line: Revises local approval and election rules for Montana marijuana businesses, limiting transport bans and requiring specific ballot wording.
HB698.summary: HB 698 revises Montana’s local‑government rules on marijuana businesses, clarifying when a county or city can approve or prohibit different license categories and how elections are conducted. It also limits local authority over transportation and requires a specific ballot wording for banning recreational dispensaries.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑301 to require local approval for most marijuana business categories in counties that voted against Initiative 190, except for counties that approved the measure
Provides a detailed election process for counties and municipalities to approve or prohibit specific business categories, including separate voting for municipalities over 5,000 residents
Allows former medical‑marijuana licensees to operate in their existing premises without local approval if they do not seek adult‑use licensure
Grants local governments the power to regulate marijuana businesses through ordinances, but exempts former medical licensees from new local regulations until their next renewal
Requires a specific ballot language for elections that would ban recreational marijuana dispensaries
Prohibits local governments from banning the transportation of marijuana on public roads
Clarifies that local approval is not needed in counties that approved Initiative 190
Sets a 90‑day effective period for votes that overturn prior approvals
affected: Department of Agriculture and Food Safety (state licensing agency)
numbers: July 1, 2021 and January 1, 2022 deadlines for former medical licensees

HB700.one_line: Shortens retirement plan amortization from 30 to 25 years for all statewide public employee systems.
HB700.summary: The bill shortens the required amortization period for all statewide defined‑benefit public employee retirement systems from 30 to 25 years, and updates the language in the policy statements for each system to reflect the new period. The change applies to all systems listed in the Montana Code and takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends Section 19‑2‑409 to limit the amortization period for unfunded liabilities to 25 years (instead of 30).

Rewrites Sections 19‑3‑109, 19‑5‑106, 19‑6‑107, 19‑7‑106, 19‑8‑106, 19‑9‑109, 19‑13‑111, 19‑17‑117, and 19‑20‑111 to state that additional benefits may only be added if the system amortizes in 25 years or less.
Adds a new Section 11 establishing the effective date of July 1, 2025.
Leaves special amortization periods for judges, highway patrol, sheriffs, and game wardens/peace officers unchanged (they remain governed by their specific statutes).
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No monetary amounts or funding allocations are specified.
affected: Statewide defined‑benefit public employee retirement systems
Judges, highway patrol officers, sheriffs, game wardens, peace officers, municipal police, firefighters, volunteer firefighters, teachers

HB701.one_line: Limits attorney fees to salary rate times hours for Montana government entities.
HB701.summary: The bill limits attorney fees that a Montana government entity must pay in litigation to the attorney’s hourly salary rate times the hours worked. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Attorney fees against state, political subdivisions, or state agencies cannot exceed the attorney’s hourly salary rate (per 2‑16‑405) multiplied by the hours actually spent on the case.
The calculation rule is codified as part of Title 25, Chapter 10, Part 7 of the Montana Code.
The law becomes effective upon passage and approval.
affected: Attorneys representing those entities in litigation

HB702.one_line: Adds a new UAV‑over‑prison felony and revises prison‑related assault and possession statutes.
HB702.summary: HB 702 adds a new felony for operating an unmanned aerial vehicle over a correctional institution, revises sentencing for assault with bodily fluid, expands the definition of illegal articles in prison‑related offenses, and amends the definition of a persistent felony offender. It also expands the list of definitions in the criminal‑procedure code.
changes: Creates a new offense: operating an unauthorized, unmanned aerial vehicle over a correctional institution, punishable by 1‑year minimum to >5‑year imprisonment.
Rewrites §45‑5‑214 to define assault with bodily fluid, set fines up to $1,000 and jail terms up to 3 years, and gives youth courts jurisdiction over minors.

Amends §45‑7‑307 to broaden the definition of “illegal article” to include cellphones, tobacco, weapons, dangerous drugs, and other prohibited items, and sets maximum sentences of 20 years for weapons, 10 years for dangerous drugs, and 13 months or $1,500 for other items transferred to a state‑prison inmate.
Adds a new section to §45‑7‑307 for “unauthorized communication” with a person in official detention, punishable by up to $100 fine or 10‑day county jail.
Rewrites §46‑1‑202 to add many new definitions (e.g., advanced‑practice registered nurse, persistent felony offender, etc.) that will be used in other criminal‑procedure statutes.
Codifies the new UAV‑over‑prison offense as part of Title 45, Chapter 7, Part 3.
affected: Prisoners and persons in official detention
Individuals who possess or transfer prohibited items in or to prisons
Courts and prosecutors dealing with persistent felony offenders

HB704.one_line: HB 704 limits groundwater use in key aquifers, expands permitting rules, and requires monitoring until 2032.
HB704.summary: HB 704 revises Montana’s groundwater laws, creating temporary controlled‑area designations, new permitting rules, and metering requirements. It limits groundwater appropriations in specified aquifers, expands the department’s rule‑making authority, and sets a 2032 termination date.
changes: Designates temporary legislative controlled groundwater closure areas in the Gallatin, Helena, Bitterroot, and Missoula Valley aquifers, limiting appropriations to permits or specific small‑use exceptions.
Creates temporary legislative controlled groundwater monitoring areas (Flathead Valley and Billings terrace level 3 aquifers) that require metering and biennial data reviews.

Amends permitting statutes (85‑2‑113, 85‑2‑306, 85‑2‑381, 85‑2‑506, 85‑2‑524) to give the Department broader rule‑making authority, fee‑setting powers, and new exception categories for small‑scale use.
Establishes new metering and reporting requirements for all new water rights and authorizations in controlled areas, including annual totalizing meter submissions.
Sets a termination date of January 1 2032 for the temporary controlled‑area provisions.
Provides that the act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Groundwater appropriators in the designated aquifers
Water right holders in the affected areas
Department of Natural Resources and its staff
Local governments and water‑right holders seeking permits

HB706.one_line: HB 706 mandates detailed fee documentation for state‑defending plaintiffs, except for low‑income parties.
HB706.summary: HB 706 requires a prevailing party in a lawsuit against the state to provide an engagement letter, detailed time‑keeping, and proof of payment when seeking attorney fees, unless the party’s net income and assets are $250,000 or less.
changes: Mandates an engagement letter with scope and hourly rates for any state‑defending lawsuit where the plaintiff seeks fees.
Requires daily time logs in <15‑minute increments, submitted within 60 days of work.
Demands proof of invoice payment within 30 days of receipt.
Exempts parties whose combined income and assets at the end of the most recent fiscal year do not exceed $250,000 from these requirements.
Allows redaction of attorney‑client privileged information in the required documents.
affected: Prevailing parties in state litigation seeking attorney fees

HB705.one_line: HB 705 lets county convention calls be sent electronically to precinct reps, updating §13‑38‑205.
HB705.summary: HB 705 amends Montana’s county‑central‑committee rules to allow the call of a county convention to be mailed electronically to precinct representatives, replacing the prior requirement for traditional mail. It also updates wording on officer selection and meeting procedures but does not create new programs or funds.
changes: Amends §13‑38‑205, MCA to permit electronic mail (or traditional mail) for sending the county convention call to precinct committee representatives.
Clarifies that the presiding officer must publish the call in a newspaper at the county seat and send copies at least four days before the convention.
Adds that the presiding officer and secretary of the county convention must issue and sign certificates of election of delegates and alternate delegates.
Maintains the requirement that the presiding officer and vice‑presiding officer must be of different genders and that officers need not be precinct committee representatives.
Leaves other procedural provisions (e.g., filling vacancies, proxy rules) unchanged.

HB709.one_line: New felony for human smuggling with heavy penalties, forfeiture, and tax‑exemption changes.
HB709.summary: The bill creates a new felony called human smuggling, sets stiff prison and fine penalties, and adds forfeiture and tax‑exemption rules for entities that facilitate smuggling. It also amends tax‑exemption statutes to remove exemptions for entities convicted of smuggling and to clarify tax treatment of unrelated‑business income for exempt entities.
changes: Defines human smuggling as a felony for knowingly transporting or harboring people who entered the U.S. illegally or violated immigration conditions.
Imposes a prison term of 2–20 years, a $400,000 fine, or both for individuals convicted of the offense.
Bars entities convicted of smuggling from receiving property tax exemptions under sections 15‑6‑201 and 15‑31‑102.
Creates a broad criminal forfeiture regime for property used or intended for smuggling, including money, equipment, conveyances, and proceeds of smuggling.
Establishes seizure procedures for peace officers and requires forfeiture proceedings to begin within 45 days of seizure.
Amends tax‑exemption statutes to remove exemptions for entities convicted of smuggling and to clarify how unrelated‑business income is taxed for exempt entities.
Specifies that proceeds from forfeited property go to holders of security interests and any remainder to the crime‑victims compensation account.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1 2025.
affected: Individuals who transport or harbor people who entered the U.S. illegally or violated immigration conditions
Entities that facilitate or profit from human smuggling
Property owners whose assets may be seized or forfeited
Tax‑exempt organizations that could lose exemptions if convicted
Peace officers and law‑enforcement agencies involved in seizure and forfeiture
Taxpayers whose property may be subject to forfeiture or new tax rules

HB722.one_line: HB 722 mandates one‑year retention of agency e‑mail records after employee exit and expands subcommittee authority over disposal.
HB722.summary: HB 722 requires that all electronic communications in a public employee’s agency‑provided e‑mail account be retained for at least one year after the employee’s last day of employment. The bill amends the state’s records‑management statutes to give the retention and disposition subcommittee and local government records committees authority to set and enforce this period and to approve or deny disposal of such records.
changes: 1. Amends §2‑6‑1012 to clarify that public agencies must manage electronic communications and retain them for at least one year after an employee’s last day of employment.

2. Adds a new subsection to §2‑6‑1109 giving the retention and disposition subcommittee the power to designate electronic communications as a record category that does not require a disposal request and to set a minimum one‑year retention period.
3. Extends the same authority to local governments through §2‑6‑1202, allowing local government records committees to designate the same retention period for employee e‑mail communications.
4. Creates a local government records destruction subcommittee (new §2‑6‑1202 (4)) to review disposal requests for records not on an approved schedule.

5. Amends several destruction‑of‑records provisions (7‑5‑2132, 7‑5‑4124, 20‑1‑212, 71‑3‑705, 71‑3‑810) to require written approval from the local government records destruction subcommittee before records can be destroyed.
6. Adds codification instructions to integrate the new local‑government subcommittee provisions into Title 2, Chapter 6, Part 12.
affected: Public employees whose e‑mail accounts are agency‑provided

HB724.one_line: Moves primary elections to May’s third Tuesday and notifies tribal governments.
HB724.summary: The bill changes Montana’s primary election date to the third Tuesday in May and adds a notice requirement to tribal governments. It also preserves the existing September primary rule for odd‑year elections and keeps the municipal election cost provision unchanged.
changes: Amends §13‑1‑107 to set the primary election date to the third Tuesday in May for even‑year general elections.
Leaves the September primary rule for odd‑year general elections intact.
Adds a new §2 requiring the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Maintains the existing municipal election cost provision in §13‑1‑107(3).
numbers: first Tuesday after the first Monday in June
Tuesday following the second Monday in September

HB727.one_line: Revises workers’‑compensation market‑concentration rules, adding a presumption of competition and corrective measures.
HB727.summary: HB 727 revises Montana’s workers’‑compensation market‑concentration rules, creating a presumption of competition that can be overturned only after a hearing and order.  The bill requires the commissioner to annually measure concentration with the Herfindahl‑Hirschman index, set a 1,800 threshold, and, if the market is deemed non‑competitive, mandate corrective actions such as encouraging new entrants and limiting mergers.
changes: Amends §33‑16‑1020 to establish a presumption of a competitive market unless the commissioner orders otherwise after a hearing; the order cannot expire more than one year after issuance.

The commissioner must annually calculate the Herfindahl‑Hirschman index for workers’‑compensation insurers (Plan 2 and Plan 3, the State Fund); if the index exceeds 1,800, the market is presumed non‑competitive and a public hearing is required.

If the hearing finds the market non‑competitive, the commissioner must order corrective measures, including promoting new insurers, limiting large mergers, educating consumers, and restricting producer‑agency premiums to the monopoly carrier by at least 50% until competition improves.
The list of corrective measures is not exhaustive; the commissioner may add other actions.
The commissioner must notify all customers, insurers, and producers after taking action.
The bill does not create a new program or criminal offense; it only amends existing market‑concentration provisions.
affected: Workers’ compensation insurers (Plan 2 and Plan 3, the State Fund)

HB728.one_line: HB 728 bars public entities from campaign contributions, exempting individual employees.
HB728.summary: HB 728 bars public entities from contributing to political campaigns and prohibits candidates from accepting such contributions, with civil penalties for violations. Individual public employees are exempt. The bill amends Montana’s campaign‑finance statutes to add these prohibitions.
changes: Adds a prohibition on any public entity, directly or via an intermediary, from making campaign contributions, expenditures, or promises to do so.
Makes it unlawful for a candidate to solicit, accept, or receive any contribution or expenditure from a public entity.
Creates a civil liability under M.S. 13‑37‑128 for individuals who violate the prohibition.
Exempts individual public employees from the prohibition.
Defines “public entity” to include any public association, union, hospital, nonprofit, school district, or municipality that receives state or federal funding.
Codifies the new prohibition as part of Title 13, Chapter 37, Part 2 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: public entities receiving state or federal funds
individuals who make or accept prohibited contributions

HB730.one_line: Amends custody law to treat a parent’s support of a child’s gender transition as not in the child’s best interests, while opposition may not be considered against the child’s best interests.
HB730.summary: HB 730 amends Montana’s child‑custody law to make a parent’s support of a child’s gender transition a factor that courts must view as not in the child’s best interests, while a parent’s opposition may not be considered against the child’s best interests. The amendment is immediate and applies to all parenting‑plan determinations.
changes: Replaces Section 40‑4‑212 to add new sub‑factors (l)(i) and (l)(ii) concerning a parent’s support or opposition to a child’s gender transition.  (l)(i) treats a parent who knowingly encourages transition as a factor equivalent to physical abuse; (l)(ii) states that a parent who opposes transition may not be deemed against the child’s best interests.  The amendment also adds a new subsection (l)(m) about frequent contact and a new subsection (m)(n) about vexatious amendment actions.  The rest of the section remains unchanged.  The act is effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Parents of children who are or may be transitioning genders
Courts handling custody and parenting‑plan cases

HB731.one_line: Publicly funded airports must provide free services to light aircraft under 9,000 lb.
HB731.summary: The bill requires any airport that receives public money to offer free parking, taxiing, and security access for light aircraft, defined as aircraft under 9,000 lb. It also prohibits charging fees unless they are clearly disclosed and agreed to in advance.
changes: Mandates free parking (up to 1 hr) and tie‑down parking (up to 3 days) for light aircraft at publicly funded airports.
Requires free taxiing and landing services for such aircraft.
Provides free access through security fencing in compliance with 49 CFR 1542 if applicable.
Prohibits any additional fees unless they are clearly noticed and specifically agreed to before each flight.
Defines “light aircraft” as any aircraft with a gross weight under 9,000 lb operating under 14 CFR part 91.
Codifies the new requirement as part of Title 67, chapter 1, part 1 of the Montana Code.
affected: Passengers and aircrew of light aircraft

HB733.one_line: Montana officials cannot enforce federal firearms laws that are more restrictive than state law, effective immediately and retroactive to 1889.
HB733.summary: HB 733 prohibits Montana peace officers and state employees from enforcing any federal firearms law that is more restrictive than state law, and it applies retroactively to all federal laws adopted after 1889.
changes: 1.  Montana officials cannot enforce any federal firearms law, rule, executive order, or regulation that is more restrictive than Montana law.
2.  The prohibition is codified as part of Title 45, chapter 8, part 3, and those existing provisions apply to the new section.
3.  The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
4.  The act applies retroactively to federal laws adopted or enacted on or after November 8, 1889, or to new, more restrictive interpretations of laws that existed on that date.

HB734.one_line: Prohibits menstrual‑product dispensers in male‑designated school restrooms, with enforcement and removal deadlines.
HB734.summary: HB 734 prohibits the placement of menstrual‑product dispensers in male‑designated restrooms at Montana public schools and higher‑education units. It requires removal of any existing dispensers within 60 days and allows enforcement by the superintendent or board of regents, with possible funding penalties for non‑compliance.
changes: 1. Bars the installation, provision, or maintenance of menstrual‑product dispensers in male‑designated restrooms.
2. Requires removal of any existing dispensers in those restrooms within 60 days of the act’s effective date.
3. Empowers the Superintendent of Public Instruction and the Board of Regents to oversee compliance for K‑12 and higher‑education institutions, respectively.
4. Gives the overseeing authority a 30‑day window to issue a written notice and require removal if a violation is found.
5. Allows the authority to withhold a portion of administrative funding until compliance is achieved.
6. Explicitly states that the ban does not apply to female‑designated restrooms or other appropriate locations such as nurse’s offices or health centers.
affected: Board of Regents of Higher Education

HB737.one_line: Voluntary waiver of firearm rights creates a do‑not‑sell list, removal procedures, and penalties.
HB737.summary: HB 737 creates a voluntary “do‑not‑sell” list that lets Montana residents voluntarily waive their firearm rights and have their names added to the federal instant‑background‑check system.  The bill sets out how people can add, remove, or expedite removal from the list, protects privacy and prohibits discrimination, and establishes penalties for false statements or for possessing a firearm after being added.  It also amends existing concealed‑carry statutes to allow temporary suspension of permits under the same procedures.
changes: Provides a voluntary waiver form that adds a person to the federal instant‑background‑check system within 24 hours of submission.
Allows a person to revoke the waiver within 21 calendar days, with removal and destruction of records, and to request expedited removal via a district‑court hearing.

Makes waiver documents confidential except to peace officers, the applicant, and attorneys, and bars entities from inquiring about or discriminating on the basis of a waiver except for jobs that require carrying a firearm.
Creates perjury and fine/penalty provisions for false statements on waiver forms and for possessing a firearm after being added to the list.
Amends §§ 45‑8‑312, 45‑8‑314, and 45‑8‑321 to allow temporary suspension of concealed‑carry permits under the same procedures as the new voluntary list.
Adds a contingent voidness clause that can nullify the new waiver forms if the Department of Public Health certifies they are insufficient.
Sets the act to take effect January 1 2026, unless the contingent voidness condition is met.
affected: Montana residents who own or possess a firearm permit
Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB738.one_line: Mandates mail notices, public hearings, and comment periods for county zoning changes.
HB738.summary: HB 738 revises Montana’s zoning‑boundary procedure, adding mandatory mail notices, public‑hearing requirements, and a 30‑day comment period before a county can adopt new zoning districts or regulations. The bill amends § 76‑2‑205 and codifies the new rules as part of Title 76, Chapter 2, Part 1, taking effect immediately upon passage.
changes: County commissioners must mail notice of proposed zoning‑boundary changes to all residents in the affected district 15–45 days before the public hearing, using one of four specified mailing methods.
Notices must also be posted in at least five public places and published weekly for two weeks in a county newspaper.
A public hearing must be held, giving residents an opportunity to speak on the proposal.
After the hearing, commissioners may adopt a resolution of intention to create the district and adopt regulations.
A 30‑day written‑comment period follows the publication of the resolution of intention, limited to property owners listed on the most recent assessment roll.
Within 30 days after the comment period, commissioners may adopt the resolution, creating the district or adopting regulations.
§ 76‑2‑205 of the Montana Code is amended to reflect these procedural steps.
The new provisions are codified as part of Title 76, Chapter 2, Part 1 and take effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Property owners listed on the assessment roll

HB746.one_line: Counties may adopt noise ordinances up to $200 fines, excluding incorporated cities.
HB746.summary: County governments may create and enforce noise ordinances, limited to $200 fines and no imprisonment. Ordinances cannot apply within incorporated city limits.
changes: Allows counties to adopt noise‑control ordinances that largely follow state statutes 7‑5‑103 through 7‑5‑107.
Ordinances may define covered areas, set exceptions, and specify time‑of‑day limits.
County ordinances may cover the entire county or any unincorporated area, but not incorporated cities or towns.
Violations may be fined up to $200; no jail time is permitted.
Section 1 is codified as part of Title 7, Chapter 5, Part 21 of the Montana Code.
affected: Residents and businesses in unincorporated county areas
numbers: Countywide or portion of county coverage

HB741.one_line: Revises procurement law definitions, exceptions, and mental‑health contracting rules, effective immediately.
HB741.summary: HB 741 revises Montana’s procurement statutes, broadening definitions, tightening exceptions, and adding new mental‑health contracting rules. It also repeals a rule‑making section and takes effect immediately.
changes: Amends §18‑4‑123 to clarify definitions of business, contractor, contract, procurement, etc.

Amends §18‑4‑132 to expand the scope of procurement law, add new procurement exceptions (e.g., Montana‑produced food, certain university contracts, and specific professional services), and clarify exclusions for grants, gifts, and certain contracts.
Amends §53‑21‑1007 to authorize the Department of Public Health and Human Services to contract for mental‑health services, encourage local‑government cost‑sharing, and promote provider choice.
Amends §90‑14‑110 to restrict community‑service contracts to those that meet specific criteria and do not involve prohibited activities.
Repeals §80‑11‑225, the rule‑making authority for committee procurement.
The act becomes effective on passage and approval.
affected: Contractors and vendors working with state agencies
University of Montana and Montana State University

HB747.one_line: Day‑care centers may set their own exemption policies for children under five, with required health‑hazard certification.
HB747.summary: Montana will let day‑care centers decide whether to accept children who have claimed an immunization exemption, but only for kids under five and only if the center has a policy that is communicated to parents. The change amends the state’s child‑care regulations to give centers that care for infants or at‑risk children the option to set their own exemption rules, while still requiring a health‑hazard certification from the department. The bill does not create new funding or criminal penalties.
changes: Amends §52‑2‑735 to add a subsection allowing day‑care centers that care for children under one year or who are at risk of severe illness to adopt a policy on accepting immunization exemptions.
Requires that such centers provide notice of their policy to parents or guardians.
Maintains that a health‑hazard certification (training or inspection) must be obtained before a license is issued.
affected: Parents and guardians of children under five
numbers: children under 1 year or at risk

HB748.one_line: Revises medical‑marijuana limits and expands civil protections for cardholders and physicians.
HB748.summary: HB 748 revises Montana’s medical‑marijuana limits, allowing registered cardholders to possess up to 1 ounce and purchase up to 5 ounces per month (1 ounce per day). It also expands civil‑protection provisions for cardholders and prescribing physicians and clarifies how exceptions and penalties work.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑515 to set possession limit to 1 ounce and monthly purchase limit to 5 ounces (1 ounce per day).
Adds a petition process for exceeding the monthly limit, requiring physician confirmation and department approval recorded in the seed‑to‑sale system.
Expands civil‑protection language: cardholders and physicians cannot be arrested, prosecuted, or disciplined solely for lawful possession or certification.
Allows civil penalties only if a cardholder’s use impairs job performance or a physician violates standards of care.
Clarifies that possession or card application alone does not create probable cause for search or inspection.
Requires cardholders to have a card before the protection applies; cards obtained after arrest do not shield from prosecution.
Presumes lawful use when a cardholder possesses a card and an amount within limits, but this presumption can be rebutted with evidence of excess or non‑medical use.

HB749.one_line: HB 749 gives contracting priority to local human‑service providers based on experience, tenure, partnerships, and job creation.
HB749.summary: HB 749 establishes a scoring system that gives contracting priority to local human‑service providers based on experience, tenure, partnerships, and job creation. It requires state departments to use these criteria when awarding contracts for public‑assistance and human‑services programs. The bill does not create new programs or funds, merely changes procurement practice.
changes: Mandates that state departments award contracts for human‑services, family‑services, housing assistance, and energy assistance using a four‑point scoring system.

The scoring system values (1) proven local program experience, (2) length of service in Montana, (3) ability to leverage local relationships, and (4) proposed in‑state job creation relative to the service region.
Codifies the new priority criteria as part of Title 18, Chapter 4, Part 3 of the Montana Code.
No new funding, offices, or criminal offenses are created.
affected: Montana state departments responsible for procurement of human‑services contracts
Local human‑service providers seeking state contracts
Program participants in housing and energy assistance

HB750.one_line: Mandates a 2% annual increase in Medicaid provider reimbursement rates.
HB750.summary: HB 750 mandates that the Montana Department of Health and Human Services raise Medicaid provider reimbursement rates each year by at least 2%, except where otherwise specified by existing law. The bill simply sets a minimum annual increase and codifies it into the state Medicaid statutes. No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
changes: The Department must raise reimbursement rates for covered services by a minimum of 2% each year.
The increase applies to all Medicaid‑covered services unless an exception is provided in § 53‑6‑125.
The provision is codified as part of Title 53, Chapter 6, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
No other changes to Medicaid policy or funding are included.
The bill does not establish new offices, funds, or criminal penalties.
The bill does not alter eligibility or benefit levels beyond the reimbursement rate.
affected: The Montana Department of Health and Human Services
Medicaid beneficiaries indirectly through potential service availability

HB753.one_line: Mandates D&E abortion imagery in Montana public‑school human‑sexuality instruction, with notification and parental‑withdrawal rules.
HB753.summary: HB 753 requires every Montana public‑school district that offers human sexuality instruction to include at least one visual image of a dilation‑and‑evacuation (D&E) abortion performed between 20 and 25 weeks’ gestation. It also adds notification and parental‑withdrawal provisions to the existing human‑sexuality‑instruction statute.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑120, MCA, to mandate a visual D&E abortion image in all human‑sexuality curricula.
Adds a 48‑hour prior‑notification requirement for any event or assembly that includes such instruction.
Requires annual parent/guardian notification of the curriculum content and availability of materials for public inspection.
Prohibits any person or entity that provides abortion services from offering or sponsoring related instructional materials to students or staff.
Preserves the existing right of parents or guardians to withdraw their child from human‑sexuality instruction.

HB751.one_line: Rewrites Supreme Court elections to be partisan, limits non‑partisan candidates, and standardizes ballot language.
HB751.summary: HB 751 revises Montana’s judicial‑election rules to make Supreme Court races partisan, allows parties to endorse and contribute to candidates, and limits non‑partisan candidates to a single “undisclosed” spot on the ballot. It also standardizes ballot language, retention questions, and clarifies how vacancies are numbered and certified.
changes: Supreme Court justices and the chief justice are now elected on partisan ballots; only one undisclosed candidate may appear if no party nominee exists.
Political parties may endorse and contribute to Supreme Court candidates, but may not contribute to non‑partisan judicial candidates.
Ballot language for retention questions is standardized to include the candidate’s party and a yes/no choice, with no write‑in space.
Each Supreme Court vacancy is treated as a separate office; the chief justice assigns a unique number to each seat and certifies it to the secretary of state.

Primary ballots for parties are prepared only when the party has candidates for more than half of the offices or more than one candidate for any office; otherwise the party is deemed to have no primary.

Non‑partisan offices and “undisclosed” Supreme Court candidates may appear on the same ballot as partisan offices only if clearly identified and voters are warned they may vote only once for that office.
affected: Supreme Court candidates, incumbents, and voters
Election administrators and the secretary of state

HB754.one_line: Revises child‑abuse law to bar using gender‑transition opposition as evidence and allows emergency removal of transitioning children.
HB754.summary: HB 754 revises child‑abuse statutes to prohibit using a child’s or parent’s opposition to gender transition as evidence, and it expands emergency removal to children who are transitioning with parental support. The bill also clarifies procedural requirements for removal, notification, and hearings.
changes: Adds vaccination status and opposition to a child’s gender transition as prohibited grounds for action in §41‑3‑135.
Defines a child who is transitioning gender with parental support as in immediate or apparent danger, allowing emergency removal under §41‑3‑301.
Requires detailed notification to parents/guardians within 24 hours of removal, including reasons, hearing dates, and rights to attend.
Mandates that an affidavit of removal be filed within 5 working days and submitted to the county attorney and state public defender.
Specifies that removed children may not be placed in jail and may be placed in kinship foster homes if requested.
affected: Parents or guardians of such children
Child protection specialists, peace officers, county attorneys

HB755.one_line: HB 755 bars non‑resident aliens and foreign entities from owning Montana real property, requiring sale within six months.
HB755.summary: HB 755 bars non‑resident aliens and foreign entities from owning Montana real property, requiring them to sell within six months and allowing county or state attorneys to enforce the rule. The law takes effect January 1, 2026 and applies to purchases made on or after that date.
changes: Prohibits ownership of real property by aliens who are not Montana residents and by foreign entities organized abroad or with a foreign principal place of business.
Mandates that any such prohibited ownership be divested within six months, after which the property may be sold at public auction by the county sheriff.
Empowers the Attorney General or the county attorney to file civil suits to enforce the prohibition.
Defines key terms: alien, foreign entity, real property, resident.
Codifies the prohibition as part of Title 70, chapter 1, part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
Sets the effective date to January 1, 2026 and limits applicability to property purchased on or after that date.
affected: Montana real‑property owners who acquire property from prohibited parties

HB758.one_line: HB 758 bars ambulance balance‑billing, sets new rates, and expands state‑plan coverage.
HB758.summary: HB 758 rewrites Montana’s ambulance‑billing rules to curb balance‑billing for out‑of‑network emergencies, sets new payment rates, and requires insurers to cover ambulance services at in‑network rates. It also adds a long list of new coverage mandates for state‑employee and university‑system plans, including diabetes education, mental‑health services, and well‑child care.
changes: Insurers cannot balance‑bill patients for ambulance ground transport; they must pay providers directly at the insurer’s in‑network rate or a local rate (or at least 400 % of Medicare if no local rate exists).
Out‑of‑network ambulance services may not charge patients more than $100 in out‑of‑pocket costs, and any cost‑sharing must be applied toward the plan’s deductible.
The Department of Insurance must create and publish a public database of local ambulance rates and require ambulance companies to submit annual rate catalogs.
Self‑funded group plans must opt‑in to these rules by notifying the Department; otherwise the rules do not apply.

The bill amends several sections of the Montana Code to add extensive coverage requirements for state‑employee and Montana‑university group plans (e.g., diabetes education, mental‑health, well‑child care, and specific cancer‑related inpatient coverage).
affected: State employees and retirees covered by state or university group plans
numbers: 400 % of Medicare rate if no local rate

HB761.one_line: Limits enforceability of residential covenants to pre‑acquisition restrictions, requiring written consent and recorded exceptions.
HB761.summary: HB 761 limits the enforceability of residential covenants so that a property owner cannot be bound by restrictions that are more onerous than those that existed when the owner first acquired the property, unless the owner expressly agrees in writing. It also amends the homeowners‑association statute to mirror this rule and requires written exceptions to be recorded.
changes: 1. A covenant, condition, or restriction cannot be enforced against a residential property owner if it imposes more restrictions than those that existed at the time of acquisition, unless the owner gives written consent at adoption or amendment.
2. Owners who claim an exception must record it with the county clerk and pay the recording fee, and must notify other owners of the exception and the date of conveyance.
3. Successors in interest cannot claim the exception if the covenant was adopted or amended before they purchased the property, except in cases of shared ownership, inheritance, or foreclosure.
4. The same limitations are applied to homeowners’ associations through an amendment to §70‑17‑901, MCA, requiring written consent for more onerous restrictions and recording of exceptions.

5. The changes do not invalidate existing covenants or create new private rights of action for events before the effective date (May 9 2019 for HOA covenants, and the act’s effective date for residential covenants).
affected: Owners of property subject to covenants, conditions, or restrictions
Other owners in the same community

HB766.one_line: Revises disqualification rules for Montana’s Medical Legal Panel, adding affidavit requirements and limits.
HB766.summary: HB 766 revises the rules for disqualifying members of Montana’s Medical Legal Panel, tightening conflict‑of‑interest standards and limiting how many members can be removed per case.
changes: Adds a new subsection (2) that lists specific circumstances—such as personal bias, family ties to a party, or economic interests—that trigger automatic disqualification of a panel member or proposed member.
Replaces the old disqualification language with a detailed affidavit‑based process, requiring parties to file written affidavits within 15 days of the director’s panel‑member list.
Limits each party to three disqualification requests for attorneys and three for health‑care providers per malpractice claim.
Empowers the director to assess affidavit sufficiency, remove disqualified members, and appoint replacements.
Allows a disqualified member (except for bias/prejudice cases) to disclose the basis for disqualification and seek a waiver agreement from the parties, which must be recorded.
Maintains the director’s authority to excuse a proposed panelist if appropriate.
numbers: three requests per party per claim

HB765.one_line: Reestablishes a guardianship stakeholder network and grant program, ending 2032.
HB765.summary: The bill creates a nine‑member interdisciplinary network to review and improve Montana’s adult guardianship laws, and it establishes a grant program to support indigent guardianship services. The network meets quarterly, and its recommendations guide the judicial branch’s grant awards, which must be geographically balanced and cannot go to network members. The act ends on September 30, 2032.
changes: Creates a nine‑member interdisciplinary network of guardianship stakeholders appointed by the chief justice with staggered four‑year terms (initial terms at least two years).
The network must meet at least four times a year and can be reimbursed for travel expenses.

The network’s duties include evaluating current guardianship laws, identifying less restrictive options, reviewing national standards, recommending outreach and training, and advising on grant awards.

Establishes a public guardianship grant program: the judicial branch may award grants to organizations that provide guardianship services to indigent individuals, with funds used for training family guardians, public defenders, judges, and volunteer guardians.
Grant decisions must consider the network’s recommendations and geographic balance; no grant may be given to any network member.
The Supreme Court Administrator must set procedures for grant applications, awards, distribution, and accountability.
The act is codified as part of Title 3, Chapter 1, Part 7, and terminates on September 30, 2032.
affected: Montana guardianship stakeholders (district courts, public health, advocacy groups, professional and unpaid guardians, volunteer councils, bar association, healthcare providers).
Organizations providing guardianship services to indigent adults.
Family members, public defenders, district court judges, and volunteer guardians who may receive training.
The judicial branch and Supreme Court Administrator (grant administration).

HB771.one_line: Allows Montana university students to live with family within a one‑hour drive, with quick approval and verification.
HB771.summary: HB 771 removes the requirement that Montana university students live on campus if they can live with an immediate family member within a one‑hour drive. The law allows off‑campus living, requires a brief verification form, and mandates prompt approval.
changes: Allows students to live off campus with an immediate family member within a one‑hour drive.
Universities may require a signed attestation form and can impose disciplinary action for false statements.
Requests must be approved or denied within two business days; denial is prohibited if criteria are met.
Defines “immediate family member” as a parent/guardian, grandparent, aunt/uncle, or 18‑year‑old sibling.
Codifies the provision into Title 20, Chapter 25, Part 5 of the Montana Code.
Effective July 1 2025.

HB772.one_line: Revises Montana’s writ of mandamus rules to tighten issuance criteria and clarify court appearance requirements.
HB772.summary: The bill amends Montana’s writ of mandamus statutes to tighten the criteria for issuance, clarify the required affidavit, and specify how the writ must be served and the parties’ appearance before the court. It does not create new programs or funds, only revises existing procedural rules.
changes: Amends §27‑26‑201 to require that a writ be issued only on an affidavit from a party with a beneficial interest and only when the criteria in §27‑19‑201 are met.
Rewrites §27‑26‑203 to define the form and content of both alternative and peremptory writs, including the requirement that parties appear before the court to address the merits of the writ.
Specifies that an alternative writ must command the party to act or to show cause, and that a peremptory writ must omit the show‑cause language and include a return day.
Clarifies that the writ may be either alternative or peremptory but must follow the new format.
affected: Litigants seeking a writ of mandamus

HB773.one_line: Streamlines transport planning by eliminating duplicate Commission reviews for MPO‑approved projects.
HB773.summary: HB 773, dubbed “Noah’s Act,” streamlines Montana’s transportation planning by removing duplicate reviews from the Transportation Commission for projects that align with approved metropolitan planning organization (MPO) plans. It also expands local authority for certain non‑operational safety projects and clarifies MPO definitions and contract‑letting procedures.
changes: Projects that match an MPO‑approved long‑range transportation plan no longer require a separate Transportation Commission review, provided the plan has been approved by the Department of Transportation (DOT).
Urban street or department roadway projects that implement an MPO‑approved plan and are approved by the local district administrator are exempt from Commission review.
Non‑operational safety improvements on urban streets and department roadways must be approved by the district administrator, not the Commission.
In areas without an MPO, district administrators may approve projects below a scale set by the DOT in rule‑making, again without Commission approval.

The bill amends sections 60‑2‑110 and 60‑2‑111 of the Montana Code to reference the new exemption (section 3) and to allow the Commission to delegate contract‑letting authority to the DOT or local governments.
The bill codifies these changes as part of Title 60, Chapter 2, Part 1, ensuring they are treated as statutory provisions rather than a temporary rule.
The definition of “metropolitan planning organization” is clarified to include any U.S. Code‑required MPO in an area with >50,000 residents that conducts transportation planning and programming.
affected: Municipalities and counties within metropolitan planning organization districts
Contractors and developers of transportation projects

HB776.one_line: HB 776 revises landlord‑tenant rules, extending notice periods and tightening landlord remedies for non‑compliance.
HB776.summary: HB 776 revises Montana’s residential landlord‑tenant statutes, adding new definitions, extending notice periods for rule changes, and tightening landlord remedies for non‑compliance. It also clarifies how month‑to‑month tenancies that began after a one‑year lease with a property‑management company are terminated or modified.
changes: Amends definitions in §70‑24‑103, adding detailed terms for abandonment, property‑management company, and tenant rules.
Revises §70‑24‑205 to make month‑to‑month tenancy automatic when no default extension is set and no 30‑day notice is given.

Rewrites §70‑24‑311 to require written, fair, and reasonably related rules; sets 7‑day, 30‑day, or 90‑day notice periods for rule changes depending on tenancy length and management company involvement.
Revises §70‑24‑422 to specify notice periods for various non‑compliance types (3‑day for pets or unauthorized persons, 14‑day for other issues) and allows treble damages for purposeful violations.

Amends §70‑24‑441 to require 90‑day notice for landlords terminating month‑to‑month tenancies that began after a one‑year lease with a property‑management company, while tenants still need only 30‑day notice.
Rewrites §70‑25‑201 to clarify security‑deposit deductions, including cleaning costs, and sets a 24‑hour window after written notice for tenant‑initiated cleaning.

Amends §70‑26‑109 to allow landlords to change month‑to‑month lease terms with 15‑day notice generally, but 90‑day notice when the tenancy began after a one‑year lease with a property‑management company.

HB777.one_line: Revises guardianship laws to add disclosure, certification, planning, and communication limits.
HB777.summary: The bill amends Montana’s guardianship and conservatorship laws to require disclosure of bankruptcy and certain criminal convictions, impose detailed certification and disclosure requirements on professional guardians, mandate a written plan for each ward, clarify guardian duties and limits on communication, and set transition deadlines for existing guardians. It also updates reporting and termination provisions for guardians and conservators.
changes: Pre‑appointment disclosure of bankruptcy or specified criminal convictions for all guardians and conservators, and prompt court disclosure if an agent has such history.

Professional guardians must submit a comprehensive certification packet—including national certification, conflict‑of‑interest, fee structure, staff credentials, and prior disciplinary history—along with any criminal convictions that arise after appointment.

Guardians of adults must file a 60‑day care plan detailing services, visitation, goals, and fees, and must provide notice to the ward and interested parties; the court reviews and may approve or require a new plan.

The bill clarifies guardian powers, especially regarding consent to medical treatment, life‑sustaining decisions, and financial management, and limits the ability to restrict a ward’s communication unless court‑ordered or justified by risk.
Existing guardians and conservators appointed before the effective date must comply with the new provisions by October 1 2028.
The bill amends sections 72‑5‑321 and 72‑5‑324 to update duties, reporting, and termination rules.
affected: Guardians and conservators (including professional and state‑appointed)
Agents and staff of professional guardians
