HB779.one_line: Adopts IHRA antisemitism definition, expands hate‑crime sentencing, and updates anti‑discrimination statutes.
HB779.summary: HB 779 revises Montana’s anti‑discrimination laws to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism. It requires state agencies to use that definition when reviewing complaints, expands sentence‑enhancement provisions for hate‑crime offenses, and explicitly adds antisemitism to the list of protected classes.
changes: 1. Adds the IHRA working definition of antisemitism to Sections 45‑5‑222 and 49‑1‑102, making it the standard for determining discriminatory intent.
2. Requires the Department of Labor and Industry to consider that definition when investigating or adjudicating discrimination complaints.

3. Expands the sentence‑enhancement clause in Section 45‑5‑222 to cover offenses committed because of the victim’s race, creed, religion, color, national origin, or involvement in civil‑rights activities, including damage to religious worship buildings.

4. Clarifies that antisemitism is treated as discrimination on the basis of race, religion, or national origin and is subject to the same evidentiary and First‑Amendment protections as other protected classes.
5. Codifies the new Section 1 as part of Title 49, Chapter 2, Part 3, and makes the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: State agencies that investigate discrimination complaints
Employers and public accommodations subject to anti‑discrimination laws

HB780.one_line: Adds public hearings and tighter review timelines for all statewide ballot‑issue proposals.
HB780.summary: HB 780 adds a required public hearing to every statewide ballot‑issue process and tightens the timing, review, and fiscal‑note requirements for statutory initiatives, statutory referenda, constitutional initiatives, and constitutional convention initiatives.
changes: Adds a mandatory public hearing during the legislative‑services‑division review period for all four types of ballot‑issue proposals.
Extends the 10‑day post‑adjournment sine die acceptance window to 130 days after the legislature first convenes, allowing earlier submissions.
Replaces the existing 14‑day review for statutory initiatives and 7‑day review for statutory referenda with new, explicit timelines and public‑hearing requirements.

Requires the budget director to determine and prepare a fiscal note (if needed) within 10 days and the attorney general to complete legal‑sufficiency and regulatory‑taking reviews within specified days.
Adds a new attorney‑general review for potential regulatory takings or significant material harm to business interests for all initiative types.
Provides that rejected proposals must be notified with the reason, and that approved proposals trigger a sample petition form.
Codifies the new public‑hearing requirement as part of Title 13, Chapter 27, Part 2.
affected: Secretary of State and Legislative Services Division

HB781.one_line: Requires buyers to notify dealers before suing for unfair vehicle‑sales practices.
HB781.summary: HB 781 requires a buyer of a vehicle to send a certified‑mail notice to the dealer describing a problem before filing a civil action for unfair or deceptive sales practices. The dealer has 28 days to respond; only after that may the buyer file a complaint.
changes: 1. Adds a pre‑filing notice requirement for buyers alleging violations of 30‑14‑133.
2. Notice must include buyer name, dealer name, VIN, make/model/year, and problem description.
3. Notice must be sent by certified mail to dealer’s last known address.
4. Dealer must respond within 28 days of mailing; only after that may the buyer file a complaint.
5. Section 30‑14‑133 is amended to incorporate this notice requirement and to apply to vehicle‑sale disputes.
6. Codifies the new notice requirement as part of Title 30, Chapter 14, Part 1.

HB782.one_line: Revises county planning board membership to include conservation district representation and city council appointments.
HB782.summary: HB 782 revises the composition of county planning boards, adding a requirement that at least one member be tied to a conservation or grazing district. It also clarifies that city or town representatives on the board must be appointed by their local councils. The changes apply to all county planning boards in Montana.
changes: Amends §76‑1‑211 to require that a county planning board have at least one member who is a member of a conservation district governing board, an associate member of a conservation district, or a member of a state cooperative grazing district, provided the individual resides in the county.
Maintains the minimum board size of five members appointed by county commissioners.
Specifies that any city or town added to the board under §76‑1‑111 must be appointed by the respective city council.
Does not alter any other board duties or powers.
Does not create new programs, funds, or offenses.

HB783.one_line: State‑employee plans must cover GLP‑1 drugs for obesity/PCOS and expand many other health services, with reporting and a $1.5 million implementation fund.
HB783.summary: The bill requires state‑employee group health plans to cover specific diabetes, obesity, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) treatments, expands coverage for a wide range of medical services, and mandates reporting and a one‑time $1.5 million appropriation for implementation. It amends several Montana statutes to clarify coverage rules and to exempt health‑maintenance organizations from certain insurance‑law requirements.
changes: Mandates coverage of glucagon‑like peptide‑1 receptor agonists for class 3 obesity, PCOS, and other FDA‑authorized conditions when medically necessary.

Requires coverage of PCOS when medically necessary and expands coverage of many other treatments (e.g., inborn errors of metabolism, Down syndrome therapies, mental‑health services, telehealth, well‑child care, diabetes self‑management training, insulin supplies, etc.) for state‑employee group plans.
Prohibits special cost‑containment limits (deductibles, coinsurance, copayments) on the specified GLP‑1 drugs and allows step‑therapy or prior‑authorization for other services.
Adds reporting requirements to several interim committees on utilization, cost, and savings by September 1 each year.
Amends § 2‑18‑704 to clarify continuation rights for retirees, survivors, and legislators/judges in state group plans, and requires full premium payment for continued coverage.
Amends § 33‑31‑111 and § 33‑35‑306 to exempt health‑maintenance organizations from certain insurance‑law provisions while retaining other regulatory requirements.
Provides a one‑time $1.5 million appropriation from the State General Fund for each fiscal year of the 2025‑2026 biennium to cover implementation costs.
affected: State employees and Montana University System employees and their families
Legislators and judges covered by state group plans
Department of Administration and relevant committees

HB784.one_line: Reallocates road‑construction funds, adds mileage‑based share, sets spending limits and bidding rules.
HB784.summary: HB 784 revises how the state distributes road‑construction and maintenance money to local governments, adding a new share based on daily vehicle miles traveled and redefining county, city, and town allocations. It also sets spending limits and bidding requirements for the funds.
changes: Amends §15‑70‑101 to split the $150,000 technical‑assistance block and distribute the rest among counties and cities/towns using new formulas that include rural mileage, rural population, daily vehicle miles, and land area for counties, and population, street/alley mileage, and daily vehicle miles for cities/towns.
Requires consolidated city‑county governments to treat city and county boundaries separately for allocation purposes, using census data to calculate separate population and mileage factors.

Imposes a 25 % cap on how much a town or third‑class city may spend on capital equipment and supplies for street/alley maintenance, with the option to place the remainder in a restricted asset account.

Mandates that all allocated funds be spent on rural roads or city/town streets and alleys, or used to match federal funds for primary/secondary highways, and that any construction contract above the thresholds in 7‑5‑2301 and 7‑5‑4302 be awarded to the lowest responsible bidder.

Specifies that population data for counties be updated annually and for cities biennially using the latest census or interim estimates, and that mileage and daily vehicle‑mile data be certified by local governments and calculated by the Department of Transportation.
Sets an effective date of July 1 2025 and requires that any unused balance in the former §15‑70‑127 bridge and road safety account be distributed on September 1 2023.

HB787.one_line: HB 787 limits route operators’ use of financial data, adds licensing fees, and tightens video‑gambling rules.
HB787.summary: HB 787 revises Montana’s gambling laws to curb unfair competition between route operators and alcohol‑licensing businesses, imposes new licensing fees and penalties, and tightens rules on video‑gambling machines.
changes: Route operators who also hold an alcohol‑retail license may not use confidential financial data to gain an advantage in acquiring or selling alcohol licenses or in operating gambling machines.
The state adds a $1,000 annual license fee for route operators (with possible waivers for manufacturers/distributors) and a one‑time application processing fee.
The department may revoke or refuse renewal of a route‑operator license if the operator violates the new financial‑data prohibition.

Video‑gambling machines are limited to approved types (bingo, poker, keno, video line, multigame) and the number of machines must match permits; replacement of a broken machine is allowed free of charge.
Operators cannot advertise or promote unapproved games, and must keep machines in areas controlled by the alcohol‑licensing operator to prevent under‑age access.
affected: Video‑gambling machine operators, distributors, and manufacturers
Consumers of gambling and alcohol services
numbers: $1,000 fee may be waived for manufacturers/distributors
$1,000 fee may be waived for manufacturers/distributors

HB788.one_line: Attorneys must disclose judge‑related contributions and face sanctions or lawsuits for non‑compliance.
HB788.summary: Attorneys of record in civil cases must disclose all campaign contributions or expenditures made in the past six years to the presiding judge’s campaign committee or to any independent/incidentals that supported the judge. Failure to do so creates a private right of action and allows the judge to sanction the attorney.
changes: Requires attorneys of record to file a disclosure statement listing all contributions or expenditures made in the past six years to the presiding judge’s campaign committee and to any independent, incidental, or third‑party organization that made an independent expenditure supporting that judge
If no such contributions exist, attorneys must file a statement indicating that fact
Disclosures must be filed with the attorney’s first appearance or any pleading, petition, motion, response, or other court‑addressed request
Attorneys must promptly file supplemental statements if any disclosed information changes, including a change in presiding judge or filing an appeal
Presiding judges may sanction attorneys for failure to file or serve the required disclosures
Opposing parties or attorneys have a private right of action against attorneys who fail to comply
Definitions for “contribution,” “expenditure,” “incidental committee,” “independent committee,” and “independent expenditure” are provided by Montana Code §13‑1‑101
The new disclosure requirement is codified as part of Title 25, Chapter 4, Part 1
affected: Attorneys of record in civil actions
Opposing parties and attorneys in civil actions

HB789.one_line: Allows up to $10,000 of surplus campaign funds to be contributed to a candidate’s own future campaign.
HB789.summary: The bill amends Montana’s surplus‑campaign‑funds law to allow a legislative candidate to transfer up to $10,000 of unused campaign money into their own future campaign, while still requiring the funds to be reported and prohibiting personal use or loans. The change does not create a new program or crime. The amendment applies to all candidates for state office. No fiscal impact is specified. The effective date is not stated. The bill is a modest procedural change.
changes: Amends §13‑37‑240 to permit a candidate to contribute up to $10,000 of surplus funds to their own future campaign within 120 days after filing the closing report.
Clarifies that such a contribution is from the candidate, not from past contributors, and cannot be treated as a loan.
Maintains the requirement that surplus funds be reported in a supplement to the closing campaign report.
Preserves the prohibition on using surplus funds for personal benefit or for another candidate’s campaign (except the future campaign provision).
Leaves other provisions of §13‑37‑240 unchanged.

HB790.one_line: Mandates fingerprint checks for DOR employees handling federal taxpayer data.
HB790.summary: The bill requires Department of Revenue (DOR) employees who handle federal taxpayer data to submit fingerprints for a criminal‑history check.  The DOR will obtain the results from the Department of Justice (DOJ) and pay the associated fees.  The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: DOR may request criminal‑history information from DOJ for its employees.
Employees with access to federal taxpayer data must submit fingerprints and sign a release.
DOJ will forward all criminal‑history records to DOR after the check.
DOR is responsible for paying all background‑check fees.
The provisions are codified as part of Title 15, chapter 1, part 1.
affected: Department of Revenue employees with federal taxpayer access

HB795.one_line: Expands expungement to nonviolent felonies with new eligibility and procedural rules.
HB795.summary: HB 795 expands Montana’s expungement law to allow certain nonviolent felonies to be erased, adds new eligibility rules, and clarifies the court’s discretion and procedural steps.
changes: Adds “nonviolent felony offense” to the list of offenses eligible for expungement.
Limits each person to one expungement petition in their lifetime.
Requires petitioners to be fingerprinted for identity verification.
Presumes expungement if the petitioner has no pending charges and has not re‑offended for 5 years (10 years for nonviolent felonies).
Excludes expungement for a list of violent or DUI‑related offenses and requires courts to consider age, time elapsed, rehabilitation, and risk of re‑offense.
Allows courts to expunge all, some, or none of multiple misdemeanors in a single order.
Specifies the parties that must receive the expungement order and the Department of Justice’s role in sealing records.
affected: Individuals convicted of misdemeanors or nonviolent felonies

HB798.one_line: Amend constitution to allow same‑sex marriage, requiring a two‑thirds vote and public approval.
HB798.summary: The bill proposes a constitutional amendment to repeal Montana’s ban on same‑sex marriage. It requires a two‑thirds legislative vote and, if passed, will be placed on the November 2026 ballot for a public vote, taking effect January 1 , 2027 if approved.
changes: Repeals Article XIII, §7 of the Montana Constitution, which prohibits same‑sex marriages.
Requires a two‑thirds affirmative roll‑call vote of the legislature to adopt the amendment.
If the amendment is approved by voters, it becomes effective January 1 , 2027.
The amendment will be printed on the November 2026 general election ballot with a simple YES/NO question.
affected: Montana residents, particularly same‑sex couples and the broader community

HB797.one_line: Creates provisional licensing for international physicians with strict eligibility and revocation provisions.
HB797.summary: HB 797 creates a new pathway for internationally‑licensed physicians to obtain provisional and then full practice licenses in Montana, provided they meet specific education, experience, exam, and immigration criteria. The act also allows revocation and appeal of provisional licenses and requires sponsoring health‑care providers to employ the physician during the provisional period.
changes: Establishes a provisional‑licensing process for international physicians who have a job offer from a Montana health‑care provider.
Requires the physician to be eligible for U.S. work authorization, have passed all three steps of the USMLE, and meet defined education, experience, and background‑check standards.
Allows the board to revoke a provisional license if the physician is not employed by the sponsoring provider or if the physician violates safety, competency, or conduct standards.
Provides a 120‑day appeal window to district court for revocation decisions, with reinstatement possible if the court finds the board’s action did not meet required standards.
Converts provisional licenses to full licenses automatically after three years of continuous active practice in the state.
Does not mandate licensing of any physician; the board may refuse to license if any required evidence or fees are missing.
Codifies the new provisions as a new part of Title 37, Chapter 3 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Internationally‑licensed physicians seeking to practice in Montana
Montana health‑care providers offering employment to such physicians
Montana physicians and patients who may be affected by the quality and safety standards for newly licensed physicians

HB800.one_line: HB 800 tightens landlord‑tenant rules, expands property disposal rights, and adds new trespass provisions.
HB800.summary: HB 800 revises Montana’s landlord‑tenant statutes to clarify when the residential and mobile‑home laws apply, tighten rules on invitees and trespassers, shorten court timelines for possession actions, and expand landlords’ rights to dispose of abandoned tenant property. The bill also adds procedural safeguards for storage and sale of such property and requires clear notice to tenants upon lease termination.
changes: Adds a new exclusion for ‘invitees’ who have not established a landlord‑tenant relationship; such invitees may be prosecuted for criminal trespass if they refuse to leave when asked.

HB799.one_line: Non‑resident property owners may vote once in mill‑levy elections, with ballots showing tax impacts on specific home values.
HB799.summary: HB 799 expands the definition of a qualified elector in mill‑levy elections to include non‑resident owners of property within the taxing jurisdiction. It requires that each such owner vote only once, even if they own multiple properties, and adds specific ballot disclosures about the impact on homes of certain values.
changes: Amends §15‑10‑425 to allow non‑resident property owners to vote in mill‑levy elections.
Defines a qualified elector as any elector under §13‑1‑101 plus owners of property in the jurisdiction.
Limits each owner to one vote per election regardless of how many properties they own.
Permits joint owners of the same property to each vote individually.
Adds required ballot statements: a warning that higher taxes may raise rental costs and a table showing the dollar impact on homes valued at $100,000, $300,000, and $600,000.
Requires the governing body to provide notice of the election as per §13‑1‑108.
Allows a governing body to reduce an approved levy in any fiscal year but not exceed the approved amount or extend its duration.
Defines “owner of property” as a title holder who presents proof of tax payment.
affected: County, consolidated government, city, town, school district, and other taxing entities; non‑resident property owners; residents who are electors; governing bodies that impose levies

HB802.one_line: Allows short‑term rentals of primary homes, ADUs, and neighboring lots, retroactively and immediately.
HB802.summary: HB 802 removes any local prohibition on renting a primary residence, an accessory dwelling unit, or a neighboring lot that shares a boundary with the owner’s home. The change applies retroactively to existing zoning rules and to all new rules adopted after the act’s effective date.
changes: 1. Local governments may not prohibit short‑term or any‑duration rentals of a primary residence, an ADU on the same parcel, or a neighboring lot sharing a boundary with the owner’s home.
2. The prohibition is codified as part of Title 76, Chapters 2‑1 through 2‑3.
3. The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
4. It applies retroactively to zoning regulations in force on the effective date that regulate rental use.
5. It applies to all zoning regulations adopted or amended after the effective date that regulate rental use.
affected: Property owners who rent out primary residences, ADUs, or neighboring lots
Local governments with zoning ordinances that previously banned such rentals

HB803.one_line: Revises asbestos litigation procedures, disclosure, and setoff rules.
HB803.summary: HB 803 revises Montana’s asbestos litigation rules to require earlier disclosure of trust claims, allow defendants to compel missing claims, and enable discovery of trust materials. It also establishes setoff rights for defendants and allows dismissal without prejudice when defendants are not properly identified or claimants fail to comply.
changes: Requires claimants to file a sworn statement and provide all trust‑claim materials within 30 days of filing an asbestos action.
Allows defendants to move the court to compel filing of any missing asbestos‑trust claims at least 60 days before trial, with trial delayed 90 days after compliance.
Permits defendants to discover trust‑claim materials and governance documents, which are deemed admissible and non‑privileged.
Provides defendants with setoff rights equal to the valuation in the trust’s governance documents for pending or awarded trust claims.
Enables dismissal without prejudice of an asbestos action if defendants are not identified in the required disclosures or if claimants fail to comply with disclosure requirements.
Codifies the new rules as a new part of Title 27 of the Montana Code.

HB805.one_line: Revises workers’‑compensation definitions, adds election rules, and allows insurers to deny claims for illegal aliens or those who leave the U.S.
HB805.summary: HB 805 revises Montana’s workers’‑compensation law to broaden coverage definitions, add new election rules for employers, and give insurers the authority to deny or close claims for illegal aliens or those who leave the U.S. while claiming benefits. It also amends the definition of a catastrophically injured worker and codifies the new provisions.
changes: Amends §39‑71‑118 to expand the definition of an employee/worker to include many categories of volunteers, students, and public‑service workers, with specific coverage limits for community‑service volunteers and other special groups.

Provides new election procedures that allow employers (including partnerships, LLCs, and corporations) to elect coverage for partners, owners, and exempt officers, specifying minimum and maximum wage levels for premium calculation.

Adds a new section (Section 2) giving insurers the right to deny or close workers’‑compensation claims if the claimant is an illegal alien or has left the U.S. or its territories while a claim is pending.
Amends §39‑71‑4003 to define “catastrophically injured” and to require inpatient care for at least 21 consecutive days in specified out‑of‑state or distant in‑state facilities.
Includes codification instructions (Section 4) to integrate the new provisions into Title 39, Chapter 71, Part 6.
No new state program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
The bill does not alter funding levels or create new costs; it mainly changes eligibility and administrative rules.
affected: Employers (including partnerships, LLCs, corporations, and public‑service entities)
Illegal aliens and workers who leave the U.S. while claiming benefits
numbers: $900 per month minimum wage for elected wages
$1½ times the state average weekly wage maximum
$200 per week minimum for certain elections
$1½ times the state average weekly wage maximum for officers

HB811.one_line: Expands definitions for customer‑generators and net‑metering, effective immediately.
HB811.summary: HB 811 expands the statutory definition of a customer‑generator and related net‑metering terms, clarifying the size limits and operational requirements for small renewable‑energy systems. The bill amends §69‑8‑103 to add these definitions and sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Adds the definition of "Customer‑generator" as a net‑metering user.
Defines "Net metering system" and limits its generating capacity to 50‑100 kW.
Clarifies operational requirements for such systems (on‑premises, parallel operation, primary offset of customer demand).
Amends §69‑8‑103 to include these new definitions.
Sets the effective date to the day the act is approved.
No new programs, funds, or charges are created.
No fiscal impact is specified in the text.
affected: Retail electricity customers who install small renewable‑energy systems
Public utilities and cooperative utilities that provide net‑metering
Customers who may be subject to nonbypassable rates or charges

HB812.one_line: Amends unemployment law to allow benefits for non‑professional school staff with specific denial rules.
HB812.summary: The bill amends Montana’s unemployment code to allow non‑professional employees of educational institutions to receive benefits when they are unemployed, while adding restrictions that prevent benefits during gaps between academic terms, vacation periods, or when a person is expected to return to work.
changes: Amends §39‑51‑2108 to permit benefits for non‑professional employees of public, charitable, or educational organizations under the same terms as other services.

Specifies that benefits may not be paid for any week that begins during a period between two successive academic years or terms, or during a paid sabbatical, if the employee performed services in the first period and is expected to perform services in the second.

Denies benefits for any week that begins during an established vacation or holiday recess if the employee performed services immediately before the recess and is expected to perform services immediately after.

Provides that if benefits are denied under these circumstances and the employee was not offered a position for the second period, the employee is entitled to retroactive payment for each week claimed.
Excludes non‑professional employees who are covered by 26 U.S.C. §3304(a)(6)(A)(ii)(I) from the definition of “individual” for these purposes.
Clarifies that benefits for employees who performed services while employed by an educational service agency are subject to the same denial rules.
Requires that the denial of benefits be based on the conditions outlined in the new subsections.
No new program, office, or criminal offense is created.
No fiscal impact is specified.
affected: Non‑professional employees of public, charitable, or educational institutions
numbers: two successive academic years or terms
established and customary vacation period or holiday recess

HB813.one_line: Bill establishes right‑to‑repair for agricultural emissions systems, requiring OEMs to supply parts and tools to independent repairers.
HB813.summary: The bill creates a right‑to‑repair regime for agricultural equipment emissions systems, requiring OEMs to provide parts, tools, and documentation to independent repair providers and owners on fair and reasonable terms. It prohibits OEMs from using software locks or other mechanisms to restrict repairs and imposes civil penalties for non‑compliance.
changes: Mandates OEMs to supply parts, tools, and documentation for emissions systems to independent repair providers and owners on fair and reasonable terms.
Prohibits OEMs from using parts‑pairing or software locks to prevent installation of non‑manufacturer parts or to reduce functionality.
Requires OEMs to provide special documentation, tools, and parts to override electronic locks only with owner permission.
Defines “fair and reasonable terms” to exclude unreasonable quantity restrictions, additional contracts, or fees for documentation and tools.
Imposes civil penalties under Montana’s unfair trade practice statutes for violations.
Applies retroactively to equipment manufactured on or after July 1 2015 and takes effect April 1 2026.

HB814.one_line: Mandates K‑12 district reorganization by 2029 with county superintendent reports due 2026.
HB814.summary: The bill requires every elementary school district in Montana to merge with the high‑school district that serves it by July 1, 2029, forming a single K‑12 district. County superintendents must submit a detailed reorganization plan to the Education Interim Committee by March 1, 2026, and the committee will review the plans and recommend any needed statutory changes. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Mandates reorganization of all elementary districts with their corresponding high‑school districts into single K‑12 districts by July 1, 2029 (unless exempted by §20‑6‑701(4)).

County superintendents must collaborate with district trustees and administrators to prepare a report by March 1, 2026, detailing current districts, enrollment data, noncontiguous territories, board composition, financial/educational concerns, and a reorganization timeline.
The report must also include any additional information the superintendent deems relevant.
The Education Interim Committee reviews the reports and may recommend statutory changes to the legislature.
The bill is codified as part of Title 20, Chapter 6, Part 4 of the Montana Statutes.
The act becomes effective immediately upon passage.

HB815.one_line: Transfers school election administration to county officials by 2029 with a 2026 reporting deadline.
HB815.summary: The bill requires that by July 1, 2029 all school elections be run by county election administrators, and it mandates a report by March 1, 2026 outlining the current system, financial and logistical issues, and a transition timeline. The report will be reviewed by a state committee that will recommend any needed statutory changes.
changes: Mandates a July 1, 2029 deadline for transferring all school election administration from school clerks to county election administrators.

Requires the Office of Public Instruction, county superintendents of schools, and county election administrators to submit a report by March 1, 2026 to the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee.
The report must describe current election structures, deadlines, responsibilities, financial/logistical concerns, and a transition timeline.
The State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee must review the report and recommend statutory changes to the 70th Legislature.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee

HB821.one_line: HB 821 raises initiative amendment thresholds to two‑thirds legislative approval and three‑fifths voter approval, effective July 1.
HB821.summary: HB 821 amends Montana’s constitution to raise the threshold for initiative‑proposed amendments to a two‑thirds legislative vote and a three‑fifths majority of voters, and sets a July 1 effective date. The bill also requires the amendment to appear on the 2026 ballot.
changes: Amends Article XIV, §9 to require a two‑thirds roll‑call vote of the legislature for any initiative amendment proposal
Sets the voter approval threshold to a majority of at least three‑fifths of those voting on the amendment
Requires the amendment to be printed on the 2026 general‑election ballot with a YES/NO option
Establishes that an approved amendment becomes effective on July 1 of the following year unless otherwise specified
Maintains the petition signature requirement of ten percent of qualified electors, including ten percent in each of two‑fifths of legislative districts
Requires the Secretary of State to publish the amendment twice a month for two months before the election
Keeps the existing publication and filing procedures for initiative petitions
numbers: 10% in each of two‑fifths of districts
HB821.effective: First day of July following approval

HB816.one_line: HB 816 raises DUI penalties, adds license‑suspension rules, and expands treatment‑based sentence suspensions.
HB816.summary: HB 816 revises Montana’s DUI laws, raising penalties, adding new fine and imprisonment ranges, and expanding license‑suspension rules. The bill amends the statutory definitions of misdemeanors and other terms and updates the penalty schedule for first‑through‑third‑offense DUI convictions, including special provisions for passengers under 16 and for aggravated DUI.
changes: Amends 45‑2‑101 to clarify definitions of misdemeanors, offenses, and related terms.
Rewrites 61‑8‑1007 to increase imprisonment and fine ranges for first, second, and third DUI violations, with higher penalties when passengers under 16 are present.
Adds new penalty ranges for violations of 61‑8‑1002(1)(b)‑(d) (e.g., higher fines and imprisonment for second and third violations).
Creates a new section (3) for 61‑8‑1002(1)(e) that imposes fines and short incarceration, plus mandatory license suspension and chemical‑dependency education.
Adds a section (4) for aggravated DUI (61‑8‑1001) with even higher imprisonment and fines, and license revocation/suspension requirements.

Allows suspension of the remainder of an imprisonment sentence for up to one year if the offender completes a chemical‑dependency treatment program, with conditions that the offender must meet during the suspended period.
affected: Courts and judges handling DUI cases

HB822.one_line: Raising the legislative vote threshold for constitutional amendments to two‑thirds and requiring voter approval in 2026.
HB822.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Constitution to raise the legislative vote threshold for a constitutional amendment from a simple majority to a two‑thirds majority. It also requires that any amendment approved by the legislature be placed on the November 2026 ballot and become effective July 1, 2027 if passed by a majority of voters.
changes: Replaces the current one‑third vote requirement with a two‑thirds affirmative roll‑call vote of all legislators.
Adds a new subsection specifying that the amendment must be submitted to voters at the next general election.
Mandates that the amendment be printed on the ballot with a clear YES/NO option.
States the amendment becomes part of the Constitution on July 1, 2027 after election certification.
Does not alter the voter approval threshold (remains a majority of electors).

HB824.one_line: Allows county number decals on personalized license plates in Montana.
HB824.summary: The bill amends Montana’s personalized‑plate rules to allow a county number decal on such plates. It adds a single sentence to the existing statute, making the decal optional and not otherwise restricted.
changes: Amends §61‑3‑403, MCA, to add a sentence permitting a county number decal on personalized plates.
No other changes to design, color, or character limits are made.
The amendment does not create new fees, programs, or enforcement provisions.
The change applies only to personalized license plates, not to standard or special plates.
The amendment does not alter the requirement that a registration decal be displayed.
The bill does not specify any new effective date; it takes effect when the act becomes law.
affected: Vehicle owners who have or wish to obtain personalized license plates.
Montana Department of Justice, Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) as the implementing agency.

HB826.one_line: Rises cigarette tax, adds new tobacco taxes, and details tribal exemption procedures.
HB826.summary: HB 826 raises the cigarette excise tax from $1.70 to $2.70 per 20‑pack, expands the tax to other tobacco products, and clarifies the tax‑exemption rules for tribal members and quota cigarettes.
changes: Increases the cigarette excise tax to $2.70 per 20‑pack (or $0.135 per cigarette).
Imposes a 50 % wholesale‑price tax on all non‑cigarette tobacco products, premium cigars (capped at $0.35 each), and moist snuff (85 ¢ per ounce).
Adds detailed procedures for pre‑collection, refund, and credit for cigarettes sold to tribal members under quota agreements.
Specifies that sales to tribal members are exempt only if the quota has not been met and that refunds/credits are limited to the tax due on the quota.
Requires wholesalers and retailers to pre‑collect and remit the new taxes, with penalties for non‑payment.
Clarifies that tobacco shipped out of state for retail sale is not subject to the new taxes.
affected: Montana wholesalers of cigarettes and other tobacco products
Feds‑recognized Indian tribes and their members on Montana reservations

HB827.one_line: Revises Montana tax adjustments for social‑security, military, and savings‑account income, adding new deductions and inflation‑adjusted age‑65 subtraction.
HB827.summary: HB 827 revises Montana’s rules for adding or subtracting amounts to federal taxable income when calculating Montana taxable income, including new treatment of social‑security benefits, military pensions, and various savings‑account withdrawals. The bill also creates new deductions for education‑savings contributions and adjusts the age‑65 subtraction for inflation. It takes effect Jan. 1 2026 for tax years beginning after Dec. 31 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2120 to add and subtract specific items to federal taxable income for Montana tax purposes, including new provisions for social‑security benefits, military pensions, and savings‑account withdrawals.
Creates a new deduction for contributions to Montana family‑education‑savings accounts and a similar deduction for the “achieving a better life experience” program, each limited to $3,000 per spouse.
Adjusts the age‑65 subtraction by applying an inflation factor each year, rounding to the nearest $10.
Adds new subtractions for certain military‑pension income and limits their use to residents who meet residency requirements and to a five‑year period.
Sets new base and adjusted base amounts for calculating taxable portions of social‑security and railroad retirement benefits, with different thresholds for single, joint, and surviving‑spouse filers.
Terminates several temporary subtractions (e.g., social‑security, railroad retirement, and certain savings‑account subtractions) on June 30 2025 or December 31 2033, as specified.
Specifies that the changes apply to tax years beginning after Dec. 31 2025 and become effective Jan. 1 2026.
affected: Montana residents with social‑security or railroad retirement income
Montana residents receiving military pensions or retirement income
Montana taxpayers who contribute to family‑education‑savings or “achieving a better life experience” accounts
Montana taxpayers with federal taxable income adjustments related to savings‑account withdrawals
numbers: age‑65 subtraction inflation factor applied annually
$3,000 per spouse deduction for education‑savings contributions

HB828.one_line: Mandates manufacturers to provide parts, tools, and documentation to repair powered wheelchairs under fair terms.
HB828.summary: The bill creates a “Powered Wheelchair Right‑to‑Repair Act” that requires manufacturers to give owners and independent repair shops access to parts, tools, and documentation needed to fix powered wheelchairs sold in Montana.  It sets fair‑price rules, limits liability, and makes violations unlawful under the state’s consumer‑protection law.
changes: Manufacturers must provide documentation, parts, and tools to owners or independent repair providers under fair and reasonable terms, including free electronic copies of documentation and no‑charge tools unless a physical copy is requested.
Parts must be sold to independent providers at the same cost and terms that the manufacturer offers to authorized repair providers, without unreasonable restrictions or obligations.
Manufacturers must supply tools and documentation for electronic security locks or other security functions so that repairs can be performed.
Violations of these requirements are deemed unlawful practices under the Montana Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act.

The act expressly does not require disclosure of trade secrets, does not alter existing authorized‑repair‑provider agreements, and limits manufacturer liability for damage caused by independent repairs.
affected: Owners or lessees of powered wheelchairs
numbers: no‑charge tools unless a physical copy is requested

HB829.one_line: HB 829 mandates AIS training, new pass fees, and tougher penalties for vessel operators.
HB829.summary: HB 829 requires all vessel operators to complete a short Montana aquatic‑invasive‑species (AIS) training course before they can obtain an AIS prevention pass. It amends the pass fee schedule, expands penalties for violations, and directs all related fees to a dedicated invasive‑species account.
changes: Imposes a 30‑minute video‑plus‑quiz AIS awareness course that must be completed before a pass can be issued.
Sets pass fees at $10 for non‑motorized vessels and $30 for motorized vessels, with annual renewal and non‑transferability.

Increases misdemeanor fines for negligent violations to $500 (first offense) and $750 (subsequent) and for purposeful violations to $975; adds a felony penalty of up to 2 years, $10,000 fine, and possible vessel forfeiture for knowingly introducing an AIS.
Expands civil penalties to up to $25,000 for violations not covered by the misdemeanor or felony provisions.
Mandates that all fees and civil penalties be deposited in the state’s invasive‑species account established in 80‑7‑1004.
Specifies that the act takes effect on January 1 2026.
affected: Department of Natural Resources and Conservation staff
Vessel owners who may face civil or criminal penalties
numbers: $10,000 fine and up to 2 years prison for felony

HB830.one_line: Creates a state‑funded emergency aid program for rural property owners with cost‑share requirements.
HB830.summary: The bill creates a state‑funded emergency quick‑response program that provides up to $10,000 in cost‑share grants to rural property owners for damage caused by catastrophic natural events.  Conservation districts administer the program, and the funds are deposited in a special revenue account and appropriated from the general fund.  The program is limited to five‑year cycles per owner and requires a cost‑share agreement before disbursement.
changes: Establishes a local emergency quick‑response account in the state special revenue fund.
Authorizes $1 million per quarter (total $8 million biennium) to be spent on immediate aid to rural property owners.
Creates a grant program administered by conservation districts, limited to $10,000 per owner per emergency and one award in any five‑year period.
Requires a cost‑share agreement where the district can pay up to 75% of total costs and the owner pays the remainder.
Allows the conservation district to retain up to 7% of the award for administration.
Mandates that unspent funds roll over to the next quarter and unspent biennium funds revert to the general fund.
affected: Rural property owners outside incorporated cities or towns
Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

HB835.one_line: Extends infant care program, authorizes $2 M funding, effective July 1 2025.
HB835.summary: HB 835 extends Montana’s at‑home infant care program to 3 years, authorizes a $2 million annual appropriation for 2025‑26, and sets July 1 2025 as the effective date.
changes: Amends §52‑2‑710 to define the at‑home infant care program and its eligibility and work‑requirement rules;
Adds a new subsection that allows parents under 18 to receive benefits outside the regular school year;
Authorizes a $2 million appropriation from the general fund for each year of the biennium beginning July 1 2025;
Specifies that the appropriation must be spent on the at‑home infant care program;
Declares the act effective July 1 2025;
Leaves the program’s funding tied to the ongoing base for the next legislative session.
affected: Low‑income families with infants under 2 years; parents (including stepparents, foster parents, guardians) who provide full‑time care; Department of Public Health and Human Services; state budget.

HB836.one_line: State creates a senior and military property‑tax‑deferral loan program funded by $50 million.
HB836.summary: HB 836 creates a state‑funded property‑tax‑deferral loan program for seniors and active‑duty military, allowing them to borrow money to pay higher property taxes and repay the loan with interest after death or sale of the home. The program is funded from the Housing Authority Enterprise Fund and requires the board to set rules and manage the account. The bill also amends several property‑tax‑notice and lien statutes to include information about the new loan program.
changes: Establishes a property‑tax‑deferral loan program for qualifying seniors (62+) and active‑duty military with 10–20% equity and 5‑year occupancy requirements.
Creates a dedicated loan account in the Housing Authority Enterprise Fund and requires the state treasurer to transfer $50 million to it by July 1, 2025.
Defines loan limits: initial loan up to the difference between 2022 taxes and current taxes; annual increases limited to the same difference.
Sets loan interest at the lesser of the prime mortgage rate or 5% and requires the loan to be a lien on the property.
Mandates repayment within 90 days after death, sale, or if the borrower provides false information.
Amends notice, lien, and appraisal statutes to include the loan program in all property‑tax‑assistance disclosures.
Requires the board to adopt rules implementing the program and to provide information to applicants.
The program is effective July 1, 2025.
affected: County treasurers and board of housing

HB837.one_line: Establishes a retired‑teacher induction program, paying up to 36 hours per retired teacher.
HB837.summary: HB 837 establishes a state‑wide retired‑teacher induction and mentoring program, allowing school districts to pair new teachers with retired teachers for up to 3 months and pay the retired teacher up to 36 hours at a district‑determined hourly rate. The bill appropriates $100,000 per biennium to fund the program and sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date.
changes: Creates a statewide retired‑teacher induction and mentoring program administered by the Office of Public Instruction.
Allows school‑district trustees to match a new teacher with a retired teacher for no more than 3 months (36 hours).
Districts may compensate the retired teacher at an hourly rate calculated from the district’s base pay divided by the collective‑bargaining‑agreement hours.
Districts must certify participation and hours to the superintendent on a prescribed form.
The state appropriates $100,000 per biennium (starting July 1 2025) to the Office of Public Instruction to pay districts for eligible hours.
The appropriation is intended to be part of the ongoing base for the next legislative session.

HB838.one_line: Allows Montana judicial candidates to list party affiliation on ballots and campaign materials.
HB838.summary: The bill lets Montana’s chief justice and supreme court justice candidates list a party affiliation on their nomination forms, ballots, and campaign materials, and it amends election‑law language to accommodate that change. It also appropriates $5,000 for website updates and sets a July 1, 2025 effective date, applying to elections held on or after Jan 1, 2026.
changes: Candidates for chief justice or supreme court justice may indicate a political party affiliation on their declaration for nomination.
Candidates may announce their party affiliation or endorsements publicly.
Ballot language is amended so that a candidate’s party name (up to three words) appears next to the candidate’s name for these offices; if no affiliation is indicated, the word "Nonpartisan" is used.

Election‑law provisions (sections 13‑10‑209, 13‑10‑602, 13‑12‑203, 13‑14‑112, 13‑14‑115, 13‑14‑212) are updated to allow party designations for these judicial races while preserving nonpartisan rules for other offices.
A $5,000 appropriation is added for the Secretary of State to update the website and perform computer programming related to judicial elections.
affected: Chief justice and supreme court justice candidates
Election administrators and the Secretary of State

HB839.one_line: Montana gives a $500 tax credit to long‑time residents earning under $100,000, effective 2026.
HB839.summary: Montana will give a $500 income‑tax credit to residents who have lived in the state for at least ten years and earned less than $100,000. The credit is non‑refundable, cannot be carried forward, and applies to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
changes: Creates a new $500 Montana 10‑year resident income‑tax credit for qualifying taxpayers.
Defines residency as at least seven months in a calendar year.
Limits the credit to taxpayers with income under $100,000.
Prevents refunding or carry‑over of the credit.
Adds the credit to the list of tax credits subject to biennial review by the Revenue Interim Committee.
Specifies that the credit will be reviewed in the biennium beginning July 1 2025 and thereafter every eight years.
Codifies the credit as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date to income‑tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Long‑time Montana residents with income under $100,000

HB840.one_line: Creates a nine‑member committee to investigate judicial independence, funded for 2025‑27.
HB840.summary: HB 840 creates a nine‑member legislative committee to investigate the independence and quality of district court judges and supreme court justices, with a mandate to report findings and disseminate information. The committee is funded for the 2025‑27 biennium and must finish its work by September 15, 2028, ending on December 31, 2028.
changes: Establishes a Judicial Branch Independence Investigation Committee of nine legislators (5 House, 4 Senate).
Mandates the committee to investigate judges’ independence, evaluate ruling quality, set standards, and report to the Law and Justice Interim Committee.
Authorizes the committee to contract out investigative work and to use its budget for dissemination of findings.
Provides staff support from the Legislative Services Division and allows committee members to receive salaries and expenses per 5‑2‑302.
Sets a completion deadline of September 15, 2028, with meetings prohibited during regular legislative sessions.
Allocates $400,000 (2025‑27 biennium) for investigative work and $73,000 for member reimbursements, with continued funding into the 2027‑28 biennium.
affected: Nine legislators appointed to the committee

HB841.one_line: Amend constitution to cap sales tax at 4% and earmark revenue to lower school/property taxes.
HB841.summary: The bill proposes a constitutional amendment that caps Montana’s statewide sales tax at 4% and mandates that any revenue from that tax, after administrative costs, be used only to lower property taxes that fund public schools and the university system, unless the legislature, by a three‑fourths vote, decides otherwise. The amendment would take effect July 1 after a 2026 referendum.
changes: Amends Article VIII, §16 of the Montana Constitution to limit the statewide sales/use tax rate to 4%.
Requires all sales/use‑tax revenue, net of administrative costs, to be applied solely to reduce property taxes supporting public schools and the university system.
Allows the legislature to reallocate the revenue for other purposes only if a three‑fourths majority in each house votes to do so.
Sets a two‑thirds legislative vote requirement for the constitutional amendment itself.
Establishes July 1, 2027, as the effective date if the amendment passes the 2026 general‑election vote.
Requires the amendment to be placed on the November 2026 ballot for a qualified electorate vote.

HB842.one_line: Allows a 4% sales tax to offset education property taxes, subject to a 2026 referendum.
HB842.summary: The bill would let Montana lawmakers impose a sales tax of up to 4% to offset property‑tax revenue for public schools and the university system, with several exemptions. It requires the measure to be put to a statewide referendum in the 2026 general election.
changes: Allows a sales tax not exceeding 4% to be enacted by the legislature.
The tax would be used only to reduce property taxes that fund public schools and the Montana University System.
The tax would primarily target final goods and services, exempting housing and utilities, groceries, fuel for transportation and agriculture, health care, and financial/insurance services.
The act would be codified as part of Title 15 of the Montana Code.
The measure becomes effective only after approval by the electorate.
The bill requires the full title and a yes/no referendum option to appear on the November 2026 ballot.
affected: Montana businesses selling taxable goods and services

HB843.one_line: HB 843 appropriates $2 million for state‑federal rapid‑rehousing funds, effective July 1 2025.
HB843.summary: HB 843 creates a state emergency solutions grant to supplement federal rapid‑rehousing funds for people at risk of homelessness. The bill appropriates $1 million each for FY 2025 and FY 2026, directs the Department of Public Health and Human Services to distribute the money in line with federal rules, and sets July 1 2025 as the effective date.
changes: Appropriates $1 million for FY 2025 and $1 million for FY 2026 to the Department of Public Health and Human Services.
Mandates that the funds be used only for rapid‑rehousing assistance under 24 CFR 576.104.
Requires distribution of the funds in the same manner as current federal emergency solutions grant funds.
Allows rental assistance up to 150 % of fair‑market rent and for participants earning below 80 % of AMI.
Says all appropriated funds must be distributed by the last day of each fiscal year.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.
affected: Individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness
Department of Public Health and Human Services
Federal emergency solutions grant program recipients

HB844.one_line: HB 844 expands class‑eight property tax exemptions and creates reimbursement for local governments.
HB844.summary: HB 844 revises Montana’s class‑eight property tax rules, expanding the exemption amount, adding a $250 cost exemption, and tying the exemption to inflation. It also creates a reimbursement program for local governments and the university system to offset revenue losses from the tax changes.
changes: Raises the class‑eight property exemption to $1.5 million and allows a $250 cost exemption for individual items.
Adjusts the exemption annually by an inflation factor based on the CPI for June of the prior year.
Adds a 5‑year partial exemption for manufacturing machinery placed in service after 12/31/2022, with a phased‑out schedule.
Creates a reimbursement mechanism for local governments, tax‑increment financing districts, and the 6‑mill university levy to compensate for reduced property‑tax revenue.
Requires local governments to approve abatement requests within 120 days and sets minimum abatement levels.
Applies only to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.

HB847.one_line: Funds two grizzly‑bear technicians in Region 3 with $210,000 annually, effective July 1 2025.
HB847.summary: HB 847 allocates $210,000 annually from the general license account to fund two full‑time grizzly‑bear technicians in Region 3, effective July 1 2025. The appropriation is intended to supplement existing agency funding and is to be considered part of the base budget thereafter.
changes: Appropriates $210,000 per fiscal year from the general license account for two full‑time bear‑technician positions in Region 3.
The funds supplement, not replace, existing Fish, Wildlife, and Parks funding for those positions.
The appropriation is earmarked for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 and is to be treated as part of the base budget in subsequent sessions, starting FY 2027.
The act becomes effective July 1 2025.
affected: Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks Department
Region 3 staff and grizzly‑bear management operations

HB848.one_line: Creates a rail account, deposits $2 million of taxes, and funds regional rail authorities for broad projects.
HB848.summary: The bill creates a “Big Sky Rail” account in the state’s special revenue fund, directs the first $2 million of certain taxes to that account, and requires the Department of Transportation to distribute the money to regional rail authorities that existed before Jan 1 2025.  The authorities may use the funds for administration, matching grants, and a broad range of rail‑related projects, including passenger‑station improvements and transit‑rental‑car facilities.
changes: Establishes a dedicated rail account in the special revenue fund (Section 1).
Deposits the first $2 million of all taxes, penalties, and interest collected by the Department of Revenue into that account (Section 3).
Statutorily appropriates the account’s money to the Department of Transportation (Section 1).
Requires the Department of Transportation to distribute the money by August 1 each year to regional rail authorities that were established before Jan 1 2025 (Section 1).
Amends the authority powers (Section 2) to allow use of the funds for administration, matching grants, cooperative relationships, and a wide range of rail‑related projects and services.
Amends tax‑deposit statute (Section 3) to specify the $2 million threshold.
Amends statutory‑appropriation statute (Section 4) to clarify the definition and validity of the appropriation.
Provides codification instructions (Section 5) and sets the effective date (July 1 2025) and termination date (June 30 2031).
affected: Taxpayers whose taxes contribute to the $2 million deposit

HB852.one_line: Bail‑bond law overhaul grants producers arrest powers, limits judge interference, and sets clear forfeiture timelines.
HB852.summary: HB 852 amends Montana’s bail‑bond statutes to give surety bail bond producers more authority and procedural rights, clarify timelines for forfeiture and bond discharge, and limit judicial interference with bond agreements.
changes: Adds a statute of limitations of two years for surety appearance bonds and requires courts to notify parties 30 days before expiration; bonds may be automatically exonerated if not renewed.
Gives surety bail bond producers the right to act as a party in all court actions involving their bonds, file motions, and receive timely notice of changes or forfeiture orders.

Allows producers to arrest and detain principals without a court‑issued warrant, provided they notify local law‑enforcement 6 hours before and again after the arrest, and permits pursuit across state lines if state law allows.
Authorizes producers to surrender defendants to courts or law‑enforcement and requires reporting of such surrenders to the commissioner of insurance.

Creates a new rule that judges may not interfere with a bond once it has been executed and the defendant released, except for fraud or procedural error, and prohibits judges from issuing secondary warrants for a released defendant.
Establishes a process for producers to obtain access to court records statewide, with application to the clerk of the Supreme Court and security requirements.

HB854.one_line: Montana offers a $50 credit for suppressor tax stamps, effective 2026‑2027, then ends.
HB854.summary: Montana will give taxpayers a credit on their state income tax equal to the cost of a firearm suppressor tax stamp, up to $50, for purchases made in 2026‑2027. The credit can only be claimed in the year the stamp is bought and is refunded if the taxpayer’s liability is lower than the credit. The law ends December 31, 2027.
changes: Creates a new state income‑tax credit for the cost of a federally required suppressor tax stamp, capped at $50 per taxpayer.
The credit must be claimed in the same tax year the stamp is purchased.
If a taxpayer’s tax liability is less than the credit, the excess credit is refunded to the taxpayer.
The credit applies only to income‑tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026.
The provision is codified as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
The law terminates on December 31, 2027, after which the credit no longer applies.
affected: Taxpayers who purchase a firearm suppressor tax stamp in 2026‑2027

HB856.one_line: Revises vacancy triggers, appropriates $100 for monitoring, effective July 1 2025, retroactive to Jan 1 2025.
HB856.summary: The bill amends Montana’s vacancy rules, expands the list of events that create a vacancy, appropriates a small monitoring fund, and makes the changes effective immediately with retroactive application to vacancies from January 1 2025.
changes: Amends §2‑16‑501 to list ten specific events that cause an office to become vacant, including death, mental‑disorder commitment, resignation, removal, loss of residency, prolonged absence, felony conviction, moral‑turpitude offense, failure to file oath or bond, and voided election/appointment
Adds a $100 appropriation to the Legislative Services Division for FY 2025 to monitor and report on the act’s status
Sets the act’s effective date as the day it passes and is approved
Provides retroactive applicability to vacancies beginning on or after January 1 2025

HB857.one_line: Adds a 10 % lease surcharge for conservation license holders to fund block‑management.
HB857.summary: HB 857 imposes a 10 % surcharge on the annual lease payment for hunting or fishing land that is paid to the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks when a conservation license is purchased. The surcharge revenue is earmarked for the block‑management program, and failure to pay it can lead to a five‑year revocation of hunting and fishing privileges.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑202 to require applicants for a conservation license to disclose whether they are leasing land and the lease amount;
Adds a 10 % surcharge on the applicant’s share of the annual lease payment;
Mandates that surcharge revenue be used to fund the block‑management program;
Provides that non‑payment may result in revocation of hunting and fishing privileges for at least five years;
Preserves existing license fee structure and optional search‑and‑rescue donation;
Keeps the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Hunters and anglers who lease land for hunting or fishing
The Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

HB858.one_line: Extends coal‑washing tax credit to 2027 and notifies Montana tribes.
HB858.summary: The bill extends the termination date of the coal‑washing severance‑tax credit to July 1 2027 and requires the secretary of state to notify all federally recognized Montana tribes. It has no other substantive changes and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Extends the credit’s termination date to July 1 2027 (instead of 2017)
Rewrites Section 7 of Chapter 433, Laws 2009, to reflect the new termination date
Rewrites Section 1 of Chapter 1, Laws 2015, to reflect the new termination date
Adds a new Section 3 that orders the secretary of state to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana
Adds a new Section 4 stating the act is effective on passage and approval
affected: Coal producers and operators in Montana
Federally recognized tribal governments in Montana

HB859.one_line: Creates a tax credit for cash donations to community‑improvement orgs, capped at 10 % of income or $3,000, with aggregate limits and carry‑forward.
HB859.summary: The bill creates a state income‑tax credit equal to a cash donation to a qualified community‑improvement organization, limited to 10 % of taxable income or $3,000, with aggregate limits of $2 million in 2026 and $5 million thereafter.  The credit may be carried forward three years, and the Department must pre‑approve contributions and issue receipts.  The bill also amends the tax‑credit review schedule to include this new credit.
changes: Provides a tax credit equal to the cash contribution to a community‑improvement organization, capped at 10 % of taxable income or $3,000, whichever is less.
Limits the total amount of credits that can be claimed each year to $2 million in 2026 and $5 million in 2027 and beyond, with a 20 % increase if 80 % of the limit is pre‑approved.
Allows unused credits to be carried forward for up to three tax years.
Requires the Department to pre‑approve contributions and issue receipts that taxpayers must attach to their returns.
Amends the review schedule for tax credits to include the new community‑improvement credit in the biennial review by the Revenue Interim Committee.
Defines “community‑improvement organization” and “local government unit” for the purposes of the credit.
affected: Individual taxpayers who donate cash to qualifying community‑improvement organizations
Small business corporations, pass‑through entities, and partnerships
Estates and trusts that make qualifying cash contributions
The Montana Department of Revenue (for pre‑approval and receipt issuance)

HB862.one_line: Transfers $100 to the fire‑suppression account by July 1, 2025.
HB862.summary: The bill directs the state treasurer to move $100 from the general fund to the fire‑suppression account by July 1, 2025, and declares the act effective on that date.
changes: Transfers $100 from the general fund to the fire suppression account (76‑13‑150).
Requires the transfer to occur by July 1, 2025.
Sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date of the act.

HB868.one_line: Replaces Montana’s flat capital‑gain tax with a new tiered schedule effective 2026.
HB868.summary: HB 868 revises Montana’s long‑term capital‑gain tax rates, creating a new tiered schedule that replaces the current flat 5.9% rate. The bill applies to tax years beginning after 2025 and adjusts brackets annually for inflation.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2103 to replace the current 5.9% flat rate with a multi‑tiered schedule for net long‑term capital gains, varying by filing status and income level.
Defines “net long‑term capital gains” and “nonqualified taxable income” for the new schedule.
Requires the Department to inflate the bracket amounts each year, rounding to the nearest $100, and use those adjusted brackets for the following tax year.
Specifies that the new rates apply only to income tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Montana taxpayers with net long‑term capital gains (individuals, estates, trusts)
Taxpayers filing jointly, head of household, single, married filing separately
Taxpayers with nonqualified taxable income that offsets capital‑gain brackets

HB851.one_line: Creates a new Department of Health Services and transfers all state‑owned health‑care facilities from Public Health and Human Services.
HB851.summary: HB 851 establishes a new Department of Health Services, transfers all state‑owned health‑care facilities and related human‑services functions from the Department of Public Health and Human Services, and authorizes an initial appropriation of $170 000 for the 2025‑2026 biennium.
changes: Creates the Department of Health Services and appoints a director by the governor

Transfers administration of state‑owned health‑care facilities (developmental disabilities, mental health, chemical dependency, veterans’ long‑term care) from the Department of Public Health and Human Services to the new department
Amends a long list of Montana Code sections (2‑15‑103 through 90‑7‑221) to reflect the new department’s authority, reporting, budgeting, and rule‑making powers
Provides an initial appropriation of $170 000 from the general fund for the new department
Mandates a transition of functions, personnel, and funds by July 1 , 2026, and requires the governor to issue executive orders assigning duties to the new department
Includes codification instructions for the new part of Title 2, Chapter 15
Specifies that the act does not affect pre‑existing rights or proceedings
Effective date is July 1 , 2025
affected: State‑owned health‑care facilities and their staff
Employees of the Department of Public Health and Human Services who will be transferred
The governor, the legislature, and the code commissioner for implementation
Patients served by the transferred facilities

HB870.one_line: One‑time $120,000 to DOJ for crime‑lab recruitment, effective July 1, 2025.
HB870.summary: HB 870 appropriates a one‑time $120,000 from the general fund for the Department of Justice to support recruitment and retention at the Montana State Crime Lab, with unspent funds returned to the general fund. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Appropriates $120,000 for the Montana State Crime Lab in FY 2025 and FY 2026.
Funds are earmarked only for recruitment and retention activities.
Unspent money must revert to the general fund.
The appropriation is a one‑time allocation, not recurring.

HB871.one_line: Bill removes zoning change requirement for water/sewer connections, appropriates $1,000, effective July 1, 2025.
HB871.summary: The bill removes a prohibition that required municipalities to change zoning before a parcel could connect to the municipal water or sewer system. It also appropriates $1,000 for updating related documents and takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §7‑13‑4312, MCA, to eliminate the requirement that a municipality change a parcel’s zoning to higher density before permitting connection to its water or sewer system.
Provides a $1,000 appropriation from the general fund to the Department of Environmental Quality for the biennium beginning July 1, 2025, to update municipal water and sewer system documents.
Sets the effective date of the amendment to July 1, 2025.
No other substantive changes are made to the statute or to funding.
The amendment does not create a new program, office, or criminal offense.
affected: Municipalities that operate water or sewer systems
Property owners and developers outside municipal limits

HB873.one_line: Creates a state‑funded relocation account for mobile‑home tenants and imposes a new assessment on owners who do not own the lot.
HB873.summary: The bill creates a state‑funded emergency relocation account for mobile‑home tenants who must move because of a park’s change of use.  It establishes a $1.50 per $100 assessment on mobile‑home owners who do not own the lot, directs license‑fee revenue into the account, and authorizes the Department of Commerce to administer the funds and issue payments.
changes: Creates a special revenue account in the state special revenue fund for mobile‑home relocation assistance.
Imposes a $1.50 per $100 taxable‑value assessment on mobile‑home owners who do not own the lot, collected by county treasurers and deposited into the account.
Reallocates portions of campground and trailer‑court license fees (85% to local rental, 21.25% to the relocation account, 11.25% to a board‑inspection fund).

Provides that tenants required to move may receive the lesser of actual moving costs within 100 mi or a maximum of $10,000 (single‑section) or $15,000 (multisection).  Tenants may also receive 50 % of the maximum moving‑expense amount if they abandon the home and meet title/ lien requirements.
Allows the Department of Commerce to contract with a nonprofit to administer the account and charge up to 10 % administrative fees.
Includes statutory appropriation of $500,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025, with the act effective July 1 2025 and terminating June 30 2029.
affected: Mobile‑home tenants who must relocate due to park change of use
Mobile‑home owners who do not own the lot
numbers: 85% of license fees to local rental

HB874.one_line: Entity owners of principal residences may claim a $500 rebate for 2022‑23 property taxes.
HB874.summary: HB 874 creates a $500 or lesser property‑tax rebate for owners of principal residences owned by an entity for the 2022 and 2023 tax years. It requires electronic or mailed claims by October 1 each year and limits eligibility to single‑family or mobile‑home units not exceeding one acre. The rebate is funded from the general fund and expires June 30, 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑1‑2302 to add a $500 (or less) rebate for 2022 and 2023 property taxes paid by entity owners of principal residences.
Mandates the Department of Revenue to mail notice of eligibility to potential claimants by June 30 of each year and to accept claims electronically or by mail by October 1.

Limits eligibility to single‑family, multi‑unit, trailer, manufactured or mobile homes and ≤1 acre of surrounding land owned by an entity, and prohibits a second rebate if one was already issued before the act’s effective date.
Provides that claims may be filed by the taxpayer, an estate representative, or a trust trustee under specified conditions.
Allows the Department to offset the rebate against any state debt owed by the claimant.
Funds the rebate and related administration costs from the general fund and terminates the appropriation on June 30 2025.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and approval.
affected: Entity owners of principal residences (single‑family, multi‑unit, trailer, manufactured or mobile homes)
Taxpayers who previously did not receive a rebate for 2022 or 2023
Department of Revenue staff processing claims
State debtors who may have rebates offset

HB877.one_line: Allows new large customers to get utility service and funds marketing and support for data‑center growth.
HB877.summary: The bill establishes a framework that allows new, large‑load customers—especially data‑center developers—to obtain service from public utilities without the Public Service Commission (PSC) blocking it, and it clarifies the PSC’s role in tariff setting. It also appropriates $50,000 for marketing and support activities and codifies the provisions into the utility regulation code.
changes: Amends §69‑8‑201 to permit any new customer (created after Oct. 1 2007) with ≥5,000 kW average monthly demand to request and receive supply service from a public utility, subject to PSC review.
Prevents the PSC from prohibiting a public utility from serving such large new customers.
Clarifies that the PSC may still set tariffs and regulatory processes for the service.
Adds a $25,000 appropriation to the Department of Commerce for marketing Montana as a data‑center location.
Adds a $25,000 appropriation to the State Energy Office to assist developers in acquiring generation resources.
Codifies the new policy language into Title 69, Chapter 8 of the Montana Code.
affected: New large electric customers (e.g., data‑center developers)

HB878.one_line: HB 878 expands coal‑tax‑trust‑fund housing loans, sets repayment rules, and caps loan size and interest.
HB878.summary: HB 878 authorizes additional coal‑tax‑trust‑fund money for low‑ and moderate‑income housing loans, revises investment rules, and sets repayment and interest requirements. It expands the fund’s use to housing, preserves capital in the trust, and imposes limits on loan size and interest rates.
changes: Authorizes $65‑115 million from the permanent coal tax trust fund for low‑ and moderate‑income housing loans (Section 2).
Amends Section 17‑6‑308 to allow the board to manage new loan portfolios, set repayment schedules, and deposit repayments back into the trust fund.
Limits individual loan amounts to no more than 10 % of the amount administered under the new housing subsection.
Requires loan repayments (principal) to be deposited into the coal tax trust fund until fully repaid; interest may be used for servicing costs.
Sets a minimum interest rate of 0.5 % below the current trust‑fund investment performance and requires loans to average that performance.
Imposes that loans be first‑lien, not exceed 95 % of development costs, and be for multifamily rental or mobile‑home‑park projects subject to property taxes.
affected: Low‑ and moderate‑income home buyers and developers
Municipalities and nonprofits applying for assistance

HB883.one_line: Cuts the Supreme Court’s budget to $18 million, voids other appropriations, and prohibits fund transfers.
HB883.summary: HB 883 cuts the Montana Supreme Court’s budget for the 2025‑2026 biennium to $18 million and prohibits any transfer of funds or authority to the court. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Sets the Supreme Court’s budget for the 2025‑2026 biennium at $18 million.
Voids any other appropriations or appropriation authority for the court enacted in the same or other acts.
Prohibits transferring district‑court funds or authority to the Supreme Court for that biennium.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
No new programs or offices are created.
No new criminal offenses are created.

HB879.one_line: Study federal directives’ economic impact, report by 2026, funded $215k.
HB879.summary: HB 879 directs the Legislative Finance Committee to conduct a comprehensive study of how federal directives issued since January 20 2025 have affected Montana’s economy, government, and communities. The study must be completed by September 1 2026 and the committee will report its findings to the governor, legislators, tribal governments, and the congressional delegation. The bill appropriates $215,000 for the study and is effective July 1 2025, terminating December 31 2026.
changes: Authorizes the Legislative Finance Committee to study federal directives issued since January 20 2025 and their economic impact on Montana citizens, local, tribal, and state governments, institutions, and businesses.
Allows the committee to create a bipartisan subcommittee (or additional subcommittees) to carry out the study and to request assistance from interim committees.

Requires the committee to issue a preliminary written report by January 1 2026 and a final report (or updated report) by September 1 2026, with copies sent to the governor, all state legislators, federally recognized tribal governments, and Montana’s congressional delegation.
Mandates the Legislative Fiscal Division to provide administrative staff support and fiscal analysis for the study.
Appropriates $215,000 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to pay for the study.
Includes a notification requirement that the Secretary of State send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government.
Specifies that the act is contingent upon the appropriation; if no appropriation is included the act is void.
Sets the effective date as July 1 2025 and the termination date as December 31 2026.

HB884.one_line: Creates a behavioral‑health trust fund, board, endowment, and grant program with quarterly interest transfers.
HB884.summary: The bill creates a Montana Behavioral Health Trust Fund, establishes a seven‑member board, and sets up an endowment that generates interest to support behavioral‑health programs.  It authorizes quarterly transfers of that interest into a state special‑revenue account and outlines how the board may grant funds to nonprofit and public community‑based organizations for mental‑health and substance‑use services.
