changes: Creates a Montana Behavioral Health Trust Fund and a seven‑member board with specified appointment sources and term limits
Establishes an endowment within the permanent fund that may receive appropriations, gifts, grants, and other transfers; only the interest earned is available for spending
Mandates quarterly transfers of the endowment’s interest into a state special‑revenue account and a statutory appropriation account

Defines eligible grant purposes (e.g., school mental‑health services, crisis care, housing for people leaving inpatient care, etc.) and requires the board to develop a state plan, set priorities, monitor expenditures, and adopt rules
Requires the board to keep program costs to a minimum and use existing DPHHS resources when possible
Imposes quarterly reporting to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee on grant projects, amounts, uses, duration, and recipients
Amends §17‑7‑502 to clarify statutory appropriation requirements
Transfers $65 million and $10 million from the capital‑development long‑range building program account into the trust fund and its special‑revenue account by June 30 2025
affected: Behavioral‑health service providers (nonprofits, public community‑based orgs), DPHHS staff, Montana residents receiving behavioral‑health services

HB885.one_line: HB 885 modernizes Medicaid service delivery, mandates mobile tech, and expands local assistance offices.
HB885.summary: HB 885 revises Montana Medicaid rules to make applications, renewals, and customer service more digital and responsive. It requires mobile‑first technology, plain‑language notices, a hotline with wait‑time and callback options, quarterly reporting, and the reopening of 10 public‑assistance offices.
changes: Accepts Medicaid applications, renewals, and required documents online, by phone, and via mobile upload;
Mandates text‑messaging and e‑mail communication with members who provide contact info;
Creates a hotline that offers an expected wait time and callback option for every caller;
Allows members whose coverage was terminated for procedural reasons to submit a renewal online or in print during a 90‑day reconsideration period;
Sets a target that at least 60 % of the Medicaid population be renewed ex‑parte by June 30 , 2026;
Requires all client‑facing technology to be mobile‑first and fully functional on phones, tablets, and computers by June 30 , 2026;
Orders written application notices and forms to be in plain language and translated into the state’s five most common languages;
Compels quarterly reports to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee on a detailed set of service‑delivery metrics;
Amends § 53‑2‑301 to mandate reopening 10 local offices of public assistance by June 30 , 2026 and sets criteria for their locations;
Appropriates $3 million plus $200,000 annually from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 , 2025 to implement the new office requirements (one‑time appropriation).
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services staff

HB887.one_line: Lodging tax funds property‑tax relief, tourism, and historic programs, tied to SB 90.
HB887.summary: HB 887 creates a lodging‑facility use tax and uses the proceeds to fund property‑tax relief for primary residences, tourism, historic preservation, and other state programs. The tax is collected on in‑state lodging, with a 4 % deduction for state‑agency lodging costs, and the remainder is split among several special‑revenue accounts and the state general fund. The bill also appropriates $50,000 for implementation and ties its validity to the passage of Senate Bill 90.
changes: Amends the lodging‑facility use tax (15‑65‑111) to require a 4 % deduction for state‑agency lodging and to deposit the rest in a special‑revenue account;

Distributes the remaining proceeds among the Montana historical society (1 %), university system (2.5 %), fish, wildlife & parks (6.5 %), invasive‑species account (1.4 %), the Department of Commerce (up to 63 % subject to limits), regional nonprofit tourism corporations (22.5 % or 50 % if a local entity exceeds $35 k), state‑tribal economic‑development commission (0.5 %), and the historical‑interpretation account (2.6 %);
Deposits 30 % of the 4 % deduction (less federal‑funded portion) into the state general fund and $400,000 annually into the heritage‑preservation account;
Creates a $50,000 appropriation to the Department of Revenue for implementing Senate Bill 90;
Makes the act void unless Senate Bill 90 is passed and approved;
Sets effective dates: the lodging‑tax allocation rules take effect July 1 , 2027, while the appropriation and coordination provisions take effect July 1 , 2025.
affected: Montana residents who own primary residences
numbers: 50 % to local convention & visitors bureau if >$35 k

HB889.one_line: HB 889 limits growth‑policy land‑use rules outside cities, tightens zoning, and funds local notification.
HB889.summary: HB 889 revises Montana’s growth‑policy and zoning rules, limiting how local governments can regulate land outside city limits and tightening minimum‑lot‑size and housing‑dedication provisions. It also adds an appropriation for the Commerce Dept. to notify localities of the changes and sets a July 1, 2025 effective date.
changes: Amends §76‑1‑601 to prohibit growth‑policy requirements that regulate land based on sensitivity, aesthetics, or non‑state‑standard soil‑water rules for land outside city limits, except for citizen‑initiated districts and commercial/industrial zones.
Rewrites §76‑2‑203 to clarify that zoning regulations must focus on material aspects, safety, public health, and public requirements, and must be compatible with nearby municipalities’ ordinances.
Rewrites §76‑2‑212 to restrict minimum‑lot‑size rules to land within 3 mi of a city or to areas where a county growth policy has set density projections.
Adds a $300 appropriation to the Department of Commerce for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to notify local governments of the changes.
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.

HB890.one_line: Bill mandates DOJ, Corrections, and Judicial Branch to share criminal‑history data with the state warehouse by Oct. 1 2025.
HB890.summary: HB 890 requires the Department of Justice, Department of Corrections, and the Judicial Branch to work together to share criminal‑history data with the state’s Criminal Justice Data Warehouse by Oct. 1 2025. If they can’t agree, the Corrections Department must provide the data. The bill also appropriates $6,000 for this effort.
changes: Amends § 44‑7‑126 to clarify the Criminal Justice Data Warehouse’s purpose, governance, and data‑sharing procedures.
Mandates a conference of the DOJ, Corrections, and Judicial Branch to decide how to deliver offenders’ criminal‑history records to the warehouse by Oct. 1 2025.
If consensus fails, the Corrections Department must supply the records.
Provides a $2,000 appropriation each to DOJ, Corrections, and the Judicial Branch for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to support the collaboration.
Requires the board to adopt MOUs, confidentiality safeguards, and grant‑seeking protocols for the warehouse.
affected: Local and non‑government entities that may contribute data
Offenders whose criminal histories are stored in the warehouse

HB892.one_line: Reallocates insurance‑premium tax revenue to fund property‑tax relief and amends license fee schedules.
HB892.summary: HB 892 reallocates a portion of insurance‑premium tax revenue to the State Property Tax Assistance Account, establishes a $10 million annual transfer, and creates a $50,000 appropriation to implement related Senate Bill 90. The bill amends fee schedules for insurance licenses and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: Amends §33‑2‑708 to set a $10 million annual transfer of insurance‑premium tax revenue to the State Property Tax Assistance Account.
Adds a $50,000 appropriation from the general fund for the Department of Revenue to implement Senate Bill 90.
Replaces existing fee schedule for insurance‑producer licenses with new amounts (e.g., $100 for non‑resident license application, $50 for biennial renewal, etc.).
Specifies that the commissioner may adopt rules for renewal fee dates and that the commissioner may charge $75 per course review, capped at $1,500 per biennium.
Mandates that 33 % of money collected under §33‑2‑705 be deposited in a special revenue account and that all fees be considered earned upon receipt.
Provides that overpayments in excess of $10 are refundable.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Insurance companies and producers applying for or renewing licenses
General fund recipients of the $50,000 appropriation

HB893.one_line: Creates a Montana Millions lottery to fund property‑tax relief, appropriates $50k, and is contingent on SB 90.
HB893.summary: HB 893 creates a Montana Millions lottery game to raise money for the state property‑tax assistance account, appropriates $50,000 to start the program, and ties its existence to Senate Bill 90. The lottery must run on July 4, offer four $1 million prizes, and sell 500,000 tickets at $20 each. The act takes effect immediately upon passage if SB 90 passes; otherwise it is void.
changes: Establishes a new annual lottery game (Montana Millions) with specified prize structure and ticket sales limits.
Mandates the Montana Lottery Commission to rule on the game’s design to maximize net revenue for the property‑tax assistance account.
Requires net proceeds (after costs and prizes) to be transferred to the state property‑tax assistance account.
Appropriates $50,000 from the general fund to the Department of Revenue for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to implement Senate Bill 90.
Codifies the lottery provisions as part of Title 23, Chapter 7, Part 3 of the Montana Statutes.
Makes the act void if Senate Bill 90 is not enacted; otherwise it becomes effective immediately upon passage.

HB894.one_line: HB 894 changes property appraisal to a 10‑year average market value and updates railroad assessment rules.
HB894.summary: HB 894 revises Montana’s property‑appraisal rules to use a 10‑year average market value (excluding the highest and lowest year) for most taxable property, clarifies valuation methods for residential, commercial, and special equipment, and updates the railroad‑property assessment formula. The bill also sets the effective date for the new rules to the 2027 reappraisal cycle.
changes: 1. All taxable property is now appraised at 100 % of the average market value for the assessment year plus the prior nine years, excluding the highest and lowest yearly data.
2. The market value is defined as the price a willing buyer and seller would agree upon, with depreciation considered under cost or income approaches.
3. Special mobile equipment, agricultural tools, and machinery are valued at the average wholesale value from national guides or a supplemental manual if no guide exists.

4. Residential, commercial, and condominium properties must be appraised using uniform professional standards; the department must use the same valuation method within a neighborhood unless a compelling reason exists.
5. Newly constructed, remodeled, or reclassified property is assessed at 100 % of its first‑year market value, then at an average of subsequent years up to the 10th year, again excluding extremes.

6. Railroad transportation property assessment is updated with a new formula that averages income, gross‑profit, and property change factors, and apportions value to Montana using a weighted average of five allocation ratios.
7. The bill establishes that the new rules take effect for the reappraisal cycle beginning January 1, 2027.
affected: property owners (residential, commercial, agricultural, and special equipment)
state Department of Revenue and Appraisal Board

HB895.one_line: Excludes 50 % of gain on sale of new homes below 85 % of county median value after 12/31/2025.
HB895.summary: HB 895 creates a Montana tax‑exclusion for a portion of the gain a taxpayer realizes when selling a newly constructed single‑family home or duplex that sells for less than 85 % of the county’s median residential value.  The exclusion is limited to sales made after December 31 2025 and is calculated using the county median value from the most recent periodic re‑appraisal.
changes: Adds a subtraction of 50 % of the gain from the sale of a newly constructed single‑family residence or duplex sold for < 85 % of county median value to Montana taxable income.
Defines the exclusion only for sales made after December 31 2025.
Requires the county median residential value to be recalculated every two years under the periodic re‑appraisal process.
Limits the exclusion to sales where the taxpayer did not receive additional compensation that would push the total above 85 % of the median value.
Does not alter any other tax provisions or create new programs.

HB902.one_line: Revises SNAP limits, adds transitional benefits, and requires annual reporting.
HB902.summary: HB 902 revises Montana’s SNAP rules, adds a transitional benefits program, and updates reporting and enforcement provisions. 5. Several sections of the Montana Code are amended to reflect the new rules, reporting, and enforcement provisions (e.g., Sections 39‑51‑403, 39‑51‑2208, 53‑2‑108, 53‑2‑201, 53‑2‑606, 53‑2‑901, 53‑2‑904, 53‑3‑115, 53‑4‑717).
6. An appropriation of $802,500 is authorized for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to implement the transitional benefits program.

HB905.summary: Property owners can receive a refund of the prior year’s property taxes if a local government fails to enforce anti‑nuisance laws or lets a nuisance persist, provided the owner can document reasonable mitigation expenses. The refund is capped at the amount of taxes paid the previous year and is processed through the Department of Revenue, with a 30‑day acceptance window and judicial review if rejected.
changes: Allows property owners to apply for a tax‑refund when a city, consolidated city‑county, or county either ignores enforcement of anti‑nuisance ordinances or permits a public nuisance that affects the owner’s property.

The refund can be applied for once per tax year; subsequent refunds are allowed if the nuisance persists and no settlement is reached.

Amends the definition of chiropractic practice to include prescription of natural agents and, with endorsement, certain drugs.
Revises the board’s organizational and rule‑making duties to include issuing the endorsement and setting educational standards.
Adds a codification instruction that the new endorsement provisions become part of Title 37, Chapter 12, Part 3.
affected: Chiropractic board and Department of Labor and Industry
numbers: Fee for endorsement application (amount not specified)
Formulary includes: OTC analgesics, prescription NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, topical analgesics/anti‑inflammatories, topical/oral corticosteroids
Board to adopt rules on educational hours and continuing education
No scheduled or controlled drugs allowed

HB928.one_line: Revises tax rates for nonprofit agricultural land, adds transmission‑line exemption, and updates tax‑deed fees.
HB928.summary: The bill revises Montana’s property‑tax rules for agricultural land owned by most nonprofit corporations, lowers the tax rate for such property, and adds new exemption and fee provisions for transmission‑line land and tax‑deed applications. It also amends several other tax‑assessment statutes, but the core change is a 2.16 % rate for nonprofit agricultural land (with special multipliers for certain land classes).
changes: Replaces the existing 2.16 % tax rate for class‑three agricultural property with a new rate that applies to nonprofit corporations owning agricultural land, except for churches, schools, hospitals, low‑income‑housing orgs, cemeteries, treatment centers, veteran housing, and rural utilities.
Adds a multiplier for nonqualified agricultural land (20‑160 acres) and for land acquired after the effective date, multiplying the base rate by 7 or 10 respectively.
Creates a new exemption for land within 660 ft of a transmission‑line right‑of‑way, with application deadlines and documentation requirements.
Adds a $25 application fee for county treasurers when an assignee files for a tax deed on residential property, and expands the fee schedule for other related tax‑deed procedures.
Amends sections on class‑four property, exempting certain commercial uses and adjusting rates for residential and commercial portions, and revises the tax‑deed application notice rules.
affected: Nonprofit corporations owning agricultural land (except the eight exempted types)
County treasurers and clerks handling tax‑deed applications
Landowners within 660 ft of a transmission line
Property owners subject to the new tax‑deed notice requirements
numbers: 2.16% tax rate for class‑three agricultural property
10× multiplier for land acquired after effective date
March 1 deadline for transmission‑line exemption applications
May 1‑May 30 notice window for tax‑deed auctions

HB930.one_line: Allows nighttime waterski towing with proper lighting and observer rules, funded by $1,000.
HB930.summary: HB 930 revises Montana’s waterskiing laws to allow nighttime towing when the vessel is properly illuminated, adds observer requirements, and authorizes a $1,000 appropriation for rule‑making and public outreach.
changes: Amends §23‑2‑529 to require an observer when towing waterskis or similar devices, with a second adult if the operator is 12 yrs or younger.
Adds a nighttime exception: towing is allowed from sunset to sunrise only if the vessel and towed person are properly illuminated per rules adopted by the Fish and Wildlife Commission.
Provides that all right‑of‑way rules for towing vessels also apply to the towed person.
Grants the Fish and Wildlife Commission authority to adopt rules on observation and safe towing based on water‑body usage density.
Authorizes a $1,000 appropriation from the general fund to the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks for rule development and information dissemination for FY 2025.
No new criminal offense or program is created beyond the rule‑making authority and small appropriation.
affected: Motorboat operators towing waterskis, surfboards, or similar devices
Observers and second adults required for towing
numbers: 12 years of age requirement for second observer

HB933.one_line: Utilities must file a 30‑day application, pay capped fees, and meet insurance and dispute‑resolution rules for railroad crossings.
HB933.summary: The Montana Railroad Crossing Clarity Act establishes a clear process for utilities to obtain right‑of‑way crossings over or adjacent to railroad property, sets specific fee limits, insurance requirements, and dispute‑resolution procedures, and prohibits mechanic’s liens. It applies to crossings in place before Oct. 1 2025 and those begun after Sept. 30 2025. The act does not create a new program but codifies rules and fee structures for existing and new crossings.
changes: Utilities must file a 30‑day notice and application, including a drawing, insurance certificate, and crossing fee, before construction.
Crossing fees are capped at the greater of $3,000 or $10 per linear foot, and are lifetime fees; annual fees are limited to 10% of the original fee or $300, whichever is lower.
Railroads may object to a crossing within 15 days; unresolved objections go to arbitration within 30 days.
Utilities must maintain insurance limits of at least $2 million per occurrence (or $5 million aggregate) and may be required to carry protective liability insurance during construction.
Utilities may assign crossing rights to related entities with railroad written permission, and must pay taxes or an equitable share of taxes on railroad property.
A reporting requirement is added: each crossing owner must file a completion report and a filing fee with the Department of Transportation within 60 days of completion.
affected: Public utilities, rural cooperatives, municipal utilities, and other service providers
Railroad property owners and adjacent landowners
Department of Transportation and state revenue funds

HB937.one_line: Montana will host a free, searchable list of admitted insurers and producers on the Insurance Commissioner’s website.
HB937.summary: The bill requires the Montana Insurance Commissioner to create and maintain a free, searchable online list of all admitted insurance carriers and producers. The list must be updated daily in a randomized order, organized by insurance type, and cannot be used for advertising. A $10,000 appropriation funds the effort for the 2025‑2026 biennium.
changes: Creates a public, searchable database of admitted insurers and producers on the Commissioner’s website.
The database must be randomized daily on the home page and organized by insurance classification with search fields.
No fee may be charged to insurers or producers for inclusion or for advertising on the site.
The site may not serve as advertising; the Commissioner cannot receive compensation for promoting any insurer or producer.
Commissioners must notify insurers and producers of the website and how to submit or update contact information.
Provides a $10,000 appropriation from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium to establish the list.
affected: Insurance producers licensed to sell Montana insurance

HB938.one_line: Lobbyists must disclose federal money use and pay a $10 fee before lobbying state or local agencies.
HB938.summary: HB 938 requires lobbyists who represent state or local agencies or nongovernmental organizations to file an oath‑based disclosure that shows whether the agency receives federal money and that the lobbyist’s pay is not funded by federal money. It adds a $10 filing fee, updates definitions, and adjusts the payment threshold for reporting. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Lobbyists must file an oath‑based disclosure before lobbying a state/local agency or NGO that receives federal money.
The disclosure must also verify that the lobbyist’s compensation is not derived from federal money.
A $10 filing fee is imposed and deposited into the general fund.
Non‑compliance triggers penalties under existing statutes (5‑7‑305, 5‑7‑306) and unsworn falsification for false statements.
Section 5‑7‑102 definitions are amended to clarify “appointed state official” and “business.”
Section 5‑7‑112 is amended to set a $2,150 payment threshold for 2004 and to require inflation‑adjusted updates each election year.
affected: Lobbyists representing state or local agencies
State and local agencies receiving federal money
The Montana Commissioner of Political Practices

HB941.one_line: Transfer ARPA interest to coal fund, allocate $100 for implementation, adjust related bills.
HB941.summary: The bill directs the state treasurer to move all interest earned on American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds into the coal severance tax permanent fund within 10 days of enactment, appropriates $100 from the general fund to the Department of Revenue for implementation, and contains coordination provisions that alter language in other pending bills depending on their passage.
changes: Transfers ARPA interest earnings to the coal severance tax permanent fund 10 days after the act takes effect.
Appropriates $100 from the general fund to the Department of Revenue for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to implement the transfer.
If both this act and House Bill 4 pass, removes a specific line of language from House Bill 4’s section 2.
If this act passes but Senate Bill 90 does not, amends its own section 1 to reference the coal severance tax permanent fund instead of the coal endowment regional water system fund.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.

HB942.one_line: Montana adds a $1,000 refundable child tax credit, phased out at higher incomes and adjusted for inflation.
HB942.summary: Montana will create a $1,000 refundable child tax credit for each qualifying child, adjusted for inflation and phased out at higher incomes. The credit is available to residents who file a state income tax return and meet earned‑income and SS‑number requirements. The bill also amends the state’s tax‑credit review schedule to include the new child credit.
changes: Establishes a refundable child tax credit of $1,000 per qualifying child.
Qualifying child: 5 years old or younger at the start of the tax year.
Credit is reduced by $100 for every $1,000 of federal AGI above $35,000 (single) or $65,000 (married filing jointly).
Credit and income thresholds are adjusted annually for inflation using the CPI for June of the previous year.
Adds the child credit to the list of credits reviewed by the revenue interim committee.
Codifies the credit as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
affected: Montana residents who file a state income tax return
Taxpayers with qualifying children under age 6
Taxpayers with earned income and a federal AGI above the thresholds
numbers: Inflation adjustment based on CPI June
Applicability: tax years beginning after December 31 2025

HB944.one_line: HB 944 requires extensive agency reporting and limits carry‑forward appropriations for fiscal discipline.
HB944.summary: HB 944 requires a wide range of state agencies to submit quarterly reports on budget, staffing, and program implementation, amends the law governing unexpended appropriations to limit carry‑forward amounts, and sets specific effective and termination dates.
changes: Mandates written reports from 12 state agencies on budget, staffing, and program status every 30 days after each budget‑committee meeting
Amends §17‑7‑304, MCA to restrict the carry‑forward of unexpended appropriations to 30 % and to specify re‑appropriation rules for the next two years
Rewrites §17‑7‑304 to clarify that most unexpended funds revert to original accounts, with specific exceptions for university system units and legislative entities
Adds a provision that the General Government Budget Committee may refer matters to the Legislative Auditor
Sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025 and termination dates for the reporting and appropriation provisions
affected: State agencies listed in the reporting schedule (e.g., Department of Revenue, Consumer Counsel, Office of the Commissioner, Department of Labor and Industry, Department of Administration, etc.)
The Office of Budget and Program Planning
The Board of Regents and university system units

HB945.one_line: Creates a $10 million grant program for rural child‑care infrastructure with matching‑fund and technical‑assistance requirements.
HB945.summary: HB 945 creates a $10 million grant program to fund new or expanded child‑care facilities, with priority for rural and underserved areas. Grants are one‑time, capped at $500,000 per project, and require matching funds and technical assistance. The program runs from July 1 2025 to June 30 2031.
changes: Establishes an early‑childhood‑education and child‑care infrastructure account in the state special revenue fund.
Authorizes the Department of Commerce to award up to $10 million in one‑time grants for capital projects at licensed or registered child‑care facilities and school districts.
Sets grant limits: $500,000 per project and $700,000 total per county (maximum two projects).
Requires applicants to provide matching funds equal to the grant amount and to submit detailed project plans, cost estimates, and quarterly progress reports.
Exempts grant projects from certain Title 75 environmental requirements.
Mandates technical assistance from the Department of Public Health and Human Services for all funded projects.
affected: County governments (maximum two projects per county)
Department of Commerce and Department of Public Health and Human Services

HB946.one_line: New lodging and rental‑car tax revenue funds a $400 property‑tax credit for principal residences.
HB946.summary: HB 946 revises Montana’s lodging‑ and rental‑car taxes to fund a new property‑tax‑credit program for principal residences.  The bill creates a temporary $400 credit for 2025 and a permanent credit beginning in 2026, funded from the lodging and rental‑car tax revenues.  It establishes a state property‑tax‑assistance account, sets up certification, appeal, and penalty procedures, and amends related tax‑code sections.
changes: Creates a temporary $400 property‑tax credit for 2024 payments (credited on 2025 bills) and a permanent credit starting in 2026, capped at the lesser of $400 or the amount of property taxes paid
Funds the credit from a new state property‑tax‑assistance account financed by lodging and rental‑car tax revenues
Establishes a certification process for principal residences, including electronic or mailed applications, with a $1.5 million annual cap on retained revenue and $100,000 for appeals
Provides a $300 % penalty and interest for false or fraudulent claims, and criminal penalties under 45‑7‑202
Adds appeal procedures: informal review, county tax‑appeal board, and Montana tax‑appeal board, with final decisions not appealable
Amends numerous Montana tax‑code sections (15‑15‑101, 15‑16‑101, 15‑17‑125, 15‑68‑102, 15‑68‑820, etc.) to incorporate the new credit and funding mechanisms
Codifies the new credit and account provisions into Title 15, chapter 6, and sets effective and termination dates (effective July 1 2025; sections 1‑4 terminate Dec 31 2025)
Includes coordination clauses that void the bill if Senate Bill 90 passes, and limits applicability to sales occurring on or after July 1 2025

HB947.one_line: Montana insurance plans must cover CGMs for diabetics when medically necessary, effective 2026.
HB947.summary: The bill requires every Montana disability, group, or individual health‑insurance plan to cover continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) and supplies for people with type I or type II diabetes when medically necessary. It also amends other diabetes‑related coverage provisions, codifies the changes, and provides a $25,000 appropriation for administration. The act takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: All disability and group insurance plans issued in Montana must cover CGMs and supplies when a provider prescribes them for a diabetic patient.
Coverage cannot be limited by disease stage or insulin need, and no special cost‑sharing limits may be imposed on CGM coverage.
The bill amends sections 2‑18‑704 and 33‑22‑129 to reinforce diabetes self‑management training, equipment limits, and insulin copayment caps.
It codifies the new CGM requirement as part of Title 33, Chapter 22, Part 3.
A $25,000 appropriation is provided for the Department of Administration to administer the plan changes.
The act applies to all policies, certificates, and contracts issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2026.
The effective date is January 1, 2026.

HB948.one_line: Revises insurance law to clarify department’s non‑criminal status and set referral procedures for criminal matters.
HB948.summary: HB 948 revises Montana’s insurance laws to clarify that the Insurance Department is not a criminal‑justice agency and requires that any criminal matters be referred to the Attorney General, county attorneys, or other criminal‑justice agencies. It amends examination, investigation, and confidentiality provisions and appropriates $250,000 for the Attorney General’s enforcement of criminal insurance laws.
changes: Amends §33‑1‑311 to state the Insurance Department is not a criminal‑justice agency and mandates referral of criminal matters to the Attorney General, county attorneys, or other criminal‑justice agencies.

Rewrites §33‑1‑409 to set procedures for examination reports, including filing deadlines, company rebuttal periods, and the commissioner’s authority to adopt, modify, reject, or order investigatory hearings.
Rewrites §33‑1‑1203 to give the commissioner authority to conduct independent fraud investigations, report findings to prosecuting authorities, and keep investigative records confidential.

Adds a new appropriation section providing $250,000 from the general fund to the Attorney General for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to enforce criminal insurance laws referred by the commissioner.
Sets the effective date of the act as July 1 2025.

HB950.one_line: Establishes a Montana trade office in Israel, funded $500,000 for 2025‑26, effective July 1 2025, terminating June 30 2033.
HB950.summary: The bill creates a Montana trade office in Israel, funded with $500,000 from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium and kept in the budget until June 30 2033. It authorizes the Department of Commerce to staff the office and promotes trade, tourism, and cultural ties in selected sectors. The office is purely promotional and does not regulate commerce.
changes: Establishes a Montana trade office in Israel staffed by at least one employee
Allocates $500,000 from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium to support the office
Keeps the appropriation in the state budget base through June 30 2033
Codifies the new office as part of Title 90, subject to its rules
Makes the act effective July 1 2025 and terminating June 30 2033
Limits the office’s purpose to promotion, not regulation of interstate or foreign commerce
Specifies target sectors: agriculture, culture, technology, security, defense research
Requires the Department of Commerce to maintain the office for the stated period
affected: Israeli businesses and tourists interested in Montana

HB951.one_line: Transfers $30 million to local road and bridge account, effective July 1, 2025.
HB951.summary: The bill directs the state treasurer to transfer $30 million from the general fund to the local road and bridge account by July 15, 2025, and sets the act’s effective date as July 1, 2025.
changes: Transfers $30 million from the general fund to the local road and bridge account in the state special revenue fund (15‑70‑132).
The transfer is a one‑time appropriation, not a recurring budget item.
The act becomes effective on July 1, 2025, and the transfer must be completed by July 15, 2025.
No other changes to the budget or program structure are made.
affected: Local governments receiving road and bridge funds
State treasurer and state budget office

HJ3.one_line: Legislature recommends the Transportation Commission prioritize safety improvements at Bowman's Corner intersection.
HJ3.summary: The Legislature passes a joint resolution urging the Transportation Commission to give priority to safety improvements at the intersection of U.S. Highway 287 and Montana Highway 200, known as Bowman's Corner. It is a recommendation, not a law, and does not create new programs or funding. The resolution simply directs the Commission’s attention to this specific project.
changes: Recommends the Transportation Commission prioritize safety improvements at Bowman's Corner (U.S. Highway 287 / Montana Highway 200).
Does not authorize new funds, mandates construction, or alter existing statutes.
Serves as a formal legislative recommendation to the Commission.
affected: Local residents and motorists near Bowman's Corner

HJ2.one_line: Sets official revenue estimates for Montana’s General Fund FY 2025‑2027.
HJ2.summary: The resolution sets official revenue estimates for Montana’s General Fund for FY 2025‑2027 and for selected nongeneral funds, accepting a preliminary 2024 balance and directing the Governor’s Office to use these figures for budgeting. It contains detailed tables of projected tax and fee receipts and the assumptions that underlie them. No new programs or laws are created—just a formal fiscal forecast for the Legislature and the Governor’s Office.
changes: Estimates the General Fund revenue at $3.266 billion (FY 2025), $3.532 billion (FY 2026), and $3.567 billion (FY 2027).
Accepts the preliminary unassigned 2024 General Fund balance of $1.028 billion for budget purposes.
Directs the Governor’s Office of Budget and Program Planning to treat these estimates as official for FY 2025‑2027.
Provides detailed tables of projected receipts from income taxes, property taxes, natural‑resource taxes, consumption taxes, and other sources for both general and selected nongeneral funds.
Lists the underlying assumptions (e.g., wage growth, oil prices, inflation) that drive the revenue projections.
No new statutes, programs, or penalties are created; it is purely an estimation resolution.
who_is_affected

HJ5.one_line: Montana applies for a federal convention to limit federal power and terms of office.
HJ5.summary: Montana’s legislature has applied to Congress for a federal convention of states under Article V, seeking amendments that would impose fiscal restraints on the federal government, limit its power and jurisdiction, and restrict terms of office for federal officials and members of Congress.
changes: Applies to Congress for a state‑convention under Article V.
Specifies that the convention’s purpose is to propose amendments limiting federal fiscal power, jurisdiction, and terms of office.
Directs the Secretary of State to send copies of the application to federal officials and to the presiding officers of all state legislatures.
States the application remains in effect until at least two‑thirds of the states have made similar applications on the same subject.
numbers: Article V of the U.S. Constitution

HJ8.one_line: Resolution directs study of Montana EV fees to design fair, nondiscriminatory road‑funding system.
HJ8.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study Montana’s electric‑vehicle (EV) registration fees and charging‑station taxes, compare them with other states’ practices, and propose a fair, nondiscriminatory system to help close the road‑funding gap. The study must be finished by September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Creates a study committee to examine EV fees and charging‑station taxes
Tasked with comparing current fees to those in other states
Must design a new, equitable taxation system for all high‑efficiency light vehicles
Subcommittee must include a DOT representative, economist, vehicle owners, and consumer advocate
Study must be completed by September 15, 2026
Results must be reported to the 70th Legislature

HJ12.one_line: Resolution urges Congress to drop electric‑vehicle mandates, affirming Montanans’ vehicle choice.
HJ12.summary: The resolution thanks President Trump for ending the federal electric‑vehicle mandate and urges Congress to remove all EV mandates, asserting that Montanans should choose their vehicle type. It is a symbolic request with no direct policy effect in Montana.
changes: Requests U.S. Congress to eliminate all electric‑vehicle mandates and obligations.

HJ11.one_line: Montana urges Congress to amend the Constitution to limit corporate campaign spending and require disclosure.
HJ11.summary: Montana’s House Joint Resolution urges Congress to amend the U.S. Constitution so that only human beings possess constitutional rights, and that federal, state, and local governments may regulate and limit campaign contributions and expenditures, including disclosure requirements. The resolution specifically calls for an amendment that would restrict corporate, union, and other artificial‑entity spending in elections and require public disclosure of all contributions and expenditures. It is a formal request to Congress, not a law that takes effect in Montana.
changes: Requests that Congress propose a constitutional amendment clarifying that constitutional rights belong only to human beings, not corporations or other artificial entities.
affected: Corporations, unions, political action committees, and other artificial entities involved in campaign finance

HJ13.one_line: Montana asks Congress to call a limited convention to set term limits for Congress.
HJ13.summary: Montana’s Legislature has adopted a joint resolution requesting that Congress convene a constitutional convention to propose term‑limits for members of Congress. The resolution simply applies the state’s request to the federal process; it does not create new programs or impose any state‑level action.
changes: 1. Applies to Congress the request for a limited convention to propose a term‑limit amendment for the House and Senate.
2. Directs the Montana Secretary of State to send copies of the resolution to federal leaders and state legislators.
3. Declares the application to be a continuing one until at least two‑thirds of states have applied on the same subject.
4. Specifies that the application is limited to the term‑limit subject and may not be aggregated with other subjects.
numbers: Article V of the U.S. Constitution

HJ14.one_line: Resolution asserts equal constitutional interpretive duties for all branches and circulates it to state and federal officials.
HJ14.summary: This resolution declares that the 1803 Marbury v. Madison decision does not grant the courts exclusive power to interpret the Constitution and that all three branches share equal responsibility. It also instructs the Secretary of State to circulate the resolution to various state and federal officials. No new law or program is created.
changes: Affirms that the legislature, executive, and judiciary have co‑equal constitutional interpretive duties.
Declares the court’s authority to determine constitutionality is not exclusive or final on other branches.
States that changes to the Constitution are the prerogative of the people, not any single branch.
Directs the Secretary of State to send copies of the resolution to the Montana Supreme Court, federal courts, the Governor, Attorney General, county attorneys, agency heads, and other officials.

HJ16.one_line: Resolution supports future renewable‑energy development and acknowledges its economic benefits.
HJ16.summary: The resolution acknowledges Montana’s high energy costs and the economic benefits of renewable‑energy projects, and it expresses support for future responsible development of wind, solar, and battery‑storage projects. It also directs copies to key state and federal stakeholders.
changes: None—this is a resolution, not a statutory change.
affected: Montana residents, businesses, local governments, and the renewable‑energy industry.
numbers: 39% net job growth in energy sector
second in wind potential, fourth in solar potential
20th for installed wind capacity, 42nd for installed solar capacity

HJ18.one_line: Montana backs D.C. statehood and calls on Congress to act.
HJ18.summary: Montana’s House Joint Resolution HJ 18‑1 declares the state supports admitting Washington, D.C. as a full state, opposes federal interference with D.C. self‑government, and urges Congress to grant statehood. It is a symbolic statement with no new laws or programs.
changes: Affirms Montana’s support for D.C. statehood.

HJ22.one_line: Montana acknowledges Jesus Christ as king and forwards the resolution to selected officials.
HJ22.summary: Montana’s legislature passed a joint resolution that formally acknowledges Jesus Christ as king over the state and the world. The resolution simply declares this belief and requests the Secretary of State to forward copies to select officials and tribal governments. No policy changes or spending are authorized.
changes: Declares that Montana acknowledges the kingship of Jesus Christ over all nations.
affected: Montana government officials, federally recognized tribal governments, the President of the United States, the Governor, and Montana’s congressional delegation.

HJ21.one_line: Montana urges Congress to keep Social Security fully funded for future generations.
HJ21.summary: Montana’s House Joint Resolution urges the U.S. Congress to keep Social Security fully funded for the next 75 years, citing the program’s importance to Montanans and the risks of future benefit cuts. It simply requests federal action and sends a copy to federal leaders and Montana’s congressional delegation.
changes: Requests Congress to increase Social Security funding with no cuts to preserve benefits for 75 years and beyond.
Directs the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to the President, House Speaker, Senate Majority Leader, and Montana’s congressional delegation.
affected: Montana residents who receive Social Security benefits
numbers: 66,000 seniors lifted out of poverty in 2022

HJ24.one_line: Montana supports Utah’s lawsuit claiming federal land retention is unconstitutional.
HJ24.summary: The resolution expresses Montana’s support for Utah’s lawsuit against the federal government over unappropriated public lands. It declares that Montana believes a similar federal land‑retention policy is unconstitutional and urges Utah to pursue a Supreme Court judgment. The resolution also lists recipients of a copy of the resolution.
changes: Declares that Montana believes the federal policy of retaining unappropriated lands is unconstitutional.
numbers: 8 million acres of unappropriated federal land

HJ36.one_line: Resolution encourages cursive instruction in Montana schools; no legal or fiscal changes.
HJ36.summary: The resolution urges Montana school districts to teach cursive handwriting, citing cognitive and historical benefits. It is a symbolic encouragement, not a binding law.
changes: Encourages districts to introduce cursive instruction at developmentally appropriate ages
Calls for ongoing exposure to cursive throughout students’ school careers
Requests the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to the Superintendent, Board of Public Education, and all public school boards
No new programs, funds, or regulations are created
No enforcement or penalties are specified

HJ25.one_line: Resolution urges Congress to repeal the 17th Amendment and restore state‑appointed senators.
HJ25.summary: The resolution urges the U.S. Congress to propose an amendment that would repeal the 17th Amendment and restore state legislature‑appointed senators. It outlines the proposed amendment’s provisions, including six‑year terms, state‑funded salaries, and state‑controlled removal.
changes: Requests Congress to propose a constitutional amendment repealing the 17th Amendment
Specifies that each state’s legislature would appoint two senators for six‑year terms
States that senators’ salaries and benefits would be paid by the state
Allows state legislatures to remove senators by majority vote
Requires each state to establish a liaison committee to communicate with its senators
Precludes Congress from legislating the senatorial selection process

HJ38.one_line: Resolution creates a committee to study public participation and report by September 2026.
HJ38.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to create a committee that will study how Montanans participate in the legislature, focusing on the new website, public comment tools, and accessibility for people with disabilities. The committee must finish its work and report findings to the next legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint an interim or statutory committee to study public participation in the legislative process.

HJ37.one_line: Resolution requests a PFAS study to be finished and reported by September 2026.
HJ37.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of PFAS (per‑fluoroalkyl and poly‑fluoroalkyl substances) in Montana, covering their presence, health risks, and possible solutions. The study must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign an interim or statutory committee, or provide staff, to conduct a PFAS study.
The study must examine sources, testing methods, exposure routes, health dangers, and potential remedies including public‑health actions, remediation, labeling, legal recovery, and product bans.
Findings must be presented to and reviewed by the designated committee.
All study activities must be completed before September 15, 2026.
The final report, with conclusions and recommendations, must be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created by this resolution.
affected: Montana state agencies (Environmental Quality, Justice, etc.)
Farmers and ranchers using sludge fertilizer

HJ39.one_line: Montana lawmakers affirm federal stewardship of national public lands and oppose any sale or transfer.
HJ39.summary: The resolution expresses Montana lawmakers’ support for keeping national public lands under federal stewardship and opposes any sale or transfer of those lands. It urges state officials to act against future attempts to dispose of public lands and requests the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to key federal officials.
changes: Affirms state support for federal management of national public lands.
affected: Montana public lands, federal land agencies, state officials, Montana Congressional Delegation

HJ41.one_line: Resolution requests a study of landlord‑tenant and mobile‑home‑lot laws, to be finished by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ41.summary: The resolution asks the Legislative Council to commission an interim study of Montana’s landlord‑tenant and mobile‑home‑lot rental laws, with a deadline of September 15, 2026, and to report findings to the next Legislature. It does not create new law or programs.
changes: Designates an interim or statutory committee to review the two statutes and identify outdated provisions.
affected: Landlords, tenants, mobile‑home park residents and owners, tenant unions, attorneys, housing policy experts.

HJ43.one_line: Resolution requests a study on coordinated homeless services to be completed by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ43.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to study how coordinated homeless services—especially wrap‑around and permanent supportive housing—benefit Montana. The study must include data review, stakeholder input, and cost‑savings analysis, and be finished before September 15, 2026, with results reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests a committee be formed to conduct a study on coordinated homeless services.
The committee must review wrap‑around services, services offered by housing developers, and permanent supportive housing opportunities.
It must examine efficacy, cost savings, and offsets related to health care and public safety.
It must analyze all available homelessness data, including county‑level information.
It must solicit input from shelters, service providers, former homeless residents, experts, local governments, and state staff.
The study must be completed and presented to a committee before September 15, 2026, and the final report sent to the next Legislature.
affected: State agencies involved in health care and public safety

HJ46.one_line: Study data‑center impacts on Montana’s economy and electric grid.
HJ46.summary: The resolution directs a study of how large data centers could affect Montana’s economy and electric grid, including potential rate impacts and regulatory needs.  It requires the final report to be presented to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee or staff to conduct an interim study on data‑center impacts.
Specifies study topics: grid adequacy, reliability, affordability, safety, economic effects on other customers, and potential regulatory sideboards.
Includes analysis of stranded‑asset mitigation (bonding, etc.) and classification of data centers as a distinct customer class.
Calls for examination of water demand, job market, tax revenue, and housing affordability impacts.
Mandates presentation of findings to an appropriate committee and reporting to the Legislature.
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completion of the study.
affected: Montana state agencies involved in energy regulation

HJ49.one_line: Resolution requests an interim study of U.S. Highway 212 east of Billings, to be completed by Sept. 15 2026.
HJ49.summary: The resolution asks the Legislature to commission an interim study of U.S. Highway 212 east of Billings, focusing on safety, road conditions, and services, and to report findings to the 70th Legislature by September 15 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee or staff to conduct the study
The study must investigate conditions, problems, and services for motorists on U.S. 212 east of Billings
It must use data from the Montana Department of Transportation and local stakeholders
It must examine solutions used on other rural roadways
Findings must be presented to a designated committee and reviewed
All work must be completed before September 15 2026
Final results must be reported to the 70th Legislature
affected: Motorists on U.S. 212 east of Billings
Local governments and communities along U.S. 212
Legislative Council and its appointed committee

HJ51.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s special‑education system to be reported by September 2026.
HJ51.summary: This resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study Montana’s special‑education system, its laws, funding, staffing, and student needs, and report findings to the next Legislature by mid‑2026. It does not create new programs or spend money, only requests a study.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate a committee under MCA §5‑5‑217 to study special education.

HJ54.one_line: Resolution requests a waste‑to‑energy study to be completed by September 15, 2026.
HJ54.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to conduct an interim study of waste‑to‑energy options, including technology, economics, and environmental impacts, with findings reported to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign an interim or statutory committee (or staff) to study waste‑to‑energy facilities
The study must assess whether such facilities could supplement Montana’s existing power mix
It must analyze the economic impact on citizens and industry if local governments or utilities pursue waste‑to‑energy
It must review the technologies used and historical implementation domestically and abroad
It must evaluate the social and environmental effects to determine if waste‑to‑energy is a safer alternative to current waste management
The study’s findings must be presented to a committee and reported to the 70th Legislature before September 15, 2026

HJ57.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s public‑safety communications system to be completed by 15 Sept 2026.
HJ57.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of Montana’s statewide public‑safety communications system, focusing on its performance during extreme‑weather events, governance, funding, and future technology needs. The study must be finished by 15 Sept 2026 and its findings reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to study the Statewide Public Safety Communications System Act and its implementation.
The study must examine governance, operational practices, coverage, funding, interoperability, and potential technology upgrades.
It requires consultation with a broad range of stakeholders, including DOJ, advisory council, local/tribal governments, 9‑1‑1 centers, and industry experts.
The committee must finish its work and submit a report to the 70th Legislature before 15 Sept 2026.
The resolution does not create any new program, fund, or crime; it merely mandates a study.
The resolution has no direct fiscal impact beyond the administrative cost of the study.
affected: Statewide Public Safety Communications System Advisory Council

HJ58.one_line: Resolution requests a study on leveraging school counselors, to be finished by Sept 15 2026.
HJ58.summary: This resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study how to better use school counselors to improve student outcomes, with a deadline of September 15, 2026. The committee must consult a range of stakeholders, assess counselor shortages and student‑counselor ratios, and report its findings to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate a committee to study school counseling effectiveness.
The committee must work with counselors, the Board of Public Education, the Office of Public Instruction, counseling programs, and advocacy groups.
It must examine counselor shortages, student‑counselor ratios, best practices, and successful models from other states.
The study must be completed and its results reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
The resolution does not create new funding, programs, or legislation—only a study mandate.

HJ59.one_line: Resolution creates a committee to study media‑literacy education and report findings by September 2026.
HJ59.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to set up a committee to study how Montana can improve media‑literacy education.  The committee must work with state and national partners, review existing standards and best practices, and report its findings to the Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint an interim or statutory committee under MCA §5‑5‑217 to examine media‑literacy enhancement through education
The committee must collaborate with the Office of Public Instruction, the Board of Public Education, educator‑preparation programs, and teachers of media literacy
It must develop a basic understanding of media literacy, its impacts, and current content standards
It must gather input from teachers, review best practices and challenges, and study successful efforts in other states
The study must be completed and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026

HJ60.one_line: Mandates a study of kratom’s effects and regulation, to be completed by September 2026.
HJ60.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study kratom’s uses, health effects, distribution, and existing regulations, and report findings to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to investigate kratom
The committee must examine forms, uses, health risks and benefits, prevalence, distribution, federal and state policies, and regulatory powers
It must consider stakeholder input and determine an appropriate state regulatory response
All study activities must finish before September 15, 2026
The committee must report its findings to the 70th Legislature
affected: Stakeholders in kratom industry and public health

HJ64.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s judicial selection and evaluation systems, to be reported by September 2026.
HJ64.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee that will study how Montana judges are selected and evaluated, compare other states’ methods, and recommend whether changes are needed. The study must be completed and reported to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Creates a study committee under section 5‑5‑217, MCA
The committee will review transparency options for judicial selection
It will compare other states’ election or appointment methods and evaluation systems
It will hold informational forums for judicial candidates
It will assess whether legislative or constitutional changes are warranted
The study must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026

HJ63.one_line: Resolution directs a study on early literacy and numeracy, to be finished by Sept 15, 2026 and reported to the Legislature.
HJ63.summary: The resolution asks the Legislative Council to set up a committee to study how to improve early‑literacy and numeracy in Montana, with a deadline of September 15, 2026, and requires the committee’s findings to be reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to designate a committee to conduct a study on early‑literacy and numeracy improvement.

The committee must collaborate with a wide range of stakeholders, including education boards, school staff, parents, early‑childhood providers, the state library, national experts, and other states’ policymakers.
It must develop an understanding of evidence‑based curriculum, ROI of programs, and the role of parental involvement and external initiatives.
It must examine and recommend improvements to assessment and data systems for teachers, district leaders, and state policymakers.
The study must be completed and its final report submitted to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
The resolution does not create any new program, fund, or law; it merely directs a study and reporting requirement.
affected: School district trustees, administrators, curriculum specialists, early‑grade teachers, instructional coaches, reading and math specialists, special‑education teachers, and ELL teachers

HJ66.one_line: Resolution directs study of federal funding impacts on DPHHS, report by Sept 15 2026.
HJ66.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Finance Committee to study how recent federal funding changes affect the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) and to report findings to the legislature before September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Finance Committee to review federal directives affecting DPHHS since Jan 20 2025
Analyzes impacts on agency operations, budgets, personnel, and program sustainment
Examines how revenue loss could reduce agency functionality and workforce
Requires presentation of findings to interim policy, modernization‑risk, and budget committees
Mandates completion of the study and report to the 70th Legislature by Sept 15 2026
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
State employees funded by federal dollars
Local, tribal, and state government programs linked to DPHHS
Montana citizens served by DPHHS programs

HJ65.one_line: Resolution requests a DUI study to be finished by Sept 15 2026 and reported to the Legislature.
HJ65.summary: The resolution requests an interim study of Montana’s DUI laws and related issues, to be completed by September 15 2026, with findings reported to the 70th Legislature. It does not create new programs or penalties, merely asks a committee to review and recommend changes.
changes: Designates an interim or statutory committee to study Montana’s DUI statutes and related matters
The committee must review current DUI laws, penalties, incarceration rates, treatment options, and cultural factors
The study must be finished before September 15 2026
Final findings must be reported to the 70th Legislature
No new laws, penalties, or programs are enacted by this resolution

HJ68.one_line: Resolution requests a study of the State Fund’s workers’ comp plan, to finish by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ68.summary: The resolution directs a study of the Montana State Fund’s Plan 3 workers’ compensation program, asking a committee to examine rates, tiers, discounts, dividends, and potential agent incentives. The study must finish before September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the next legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to study Plan 3 workers’ compensation insurance.
The committee must review class codes, rates, tiers, discounts, dividends, and agent incentive structures.
It must collaborate with stakeholders, including business owners and Fund representatives.
The study must be completed and reported by September 15, 2026.
Results will be presented to the 70th Legislature.

HJ67.one_line: Mandates a study of federal funding impacts on Montana’s education offices, to be reported by Sept 2026.
HJ67.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Finance Committee to study how recent federal funding changes affect Montana’s Office of Public Instruction and Office of the Commissioner of Higher Education, and to report findings to the legislature by September 15, 2026. It does not create new programs or spend money; it simply mandates a study and reporting requirement.
changes: Designates the Legislative Finance Committee to review federal directives issued since January 20, 2025 that impact the two education offices.
The committee must analyze impacts on agency operations, budgets, personnel, and program sustainment.
Findings must be presented to interim policy, modernization‑risk, and budget committees.
All study work must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
affected: Office of the Commissioner of Higher Education
Montana state employees funded by federal dollars
Local, tribal, and state government programs that rely on federal funding
HJ67.effective: not stated (study to be completed by Sept 15, 2026)

HJ69.one_line: Resolution requests a study of federal funding impacts on the Department of Military Affairs, to be finished by Sept 15 2026.
HJ69.summary: The resolution directs a study of how recent federal funding changes affect Montana’s Department of Military Affairs and requires the findings to be reported to the next legislature. It does not create new programs or laws, merely requests an analysis.
changes: 1. The Legislative Council must assign the Legislative Finance Committee to review federal directives issued since Jan 20 2025 that impact the Department of Military Affairs. 2. The committee must analyze impacts on agency operations, budgets, personnel, and program sustainment. 3. The study must also assess how revenue loss could lead to loss of agency operations and overall functionality. 4. Findings must be presented to interim policy, modernization‑risk, and budget committees. 5. The study must be completed before September 15 2026. 6. Final results must be reported to the 70th Legislature.

HJ70.one_line: Resolution orders a study of federal funding impacts on Montana’s Department of Transportation.
HJ70.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to commission an interim study of how recent federal funding changes affect Montana’s Department of Transportation.  The study must analyze impacts on operations, personnel, and programs, and report findings to the Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign the Legislative Finance Committee to conduct a study of federal directives affecting the Department of Transportation since January 20, 2025.
The study must examine effects on agency operations, budgets, personnel, and program sustainment, especially infrastructure projects.
Findings are to be presented to interim policy, modernization‑risk, and budget committees.
The study and its report must be completed before September 15, 2026.
The final report is to be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
affected: State, local, and tribal governments that rely on DOT programs
Montana citizens who use DOT services

HJ71.one_line: Resolution orders a study of federal funding impacts on DEQ, to be reported by September 2026.
HJ71.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Finance Committee to study how recent federal funding changes affect the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) and to report findings to the legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Finance Committee to review federal directives issued since January 20, 2025 that impact DEQ.
Analyzes the effects on agency operations, budgets, personnel, and program sustainment.
Examines potential loss of agency functionality and impacts on project operations.
Requires the committee to present findings to interim policy, modernization‑risk, and budget committees.
Mandates completion of the study and presentation of results to the 70th Legislature before September 15, 2026.
affected: Local, tribal, and state governments relying on DEQ services
Montana citizens affected by environmental services

HJ72.one_line: Resolution requests study of DOJ driver‑record data sharing, to be finished by Sept. 15, 2026.
HJ72.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of how the Montana Department of Justice shares personal data from driver records, covering why, what, where, how, and the impact of such sharing. The study must be completed and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign an interim or statutory committee (or staff) to examine the DOJ’s release of personal information from driver records.
affected: Federal, state, and local government agencies
Montana residents whose driver records may be shared

HJ75.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana State Hospital patient transition, to be completed by Sept 15, 2026.
HJ75.summary: The resolution asks the Legislature to commission a study of the Montana State Hospital’s patient‑transition services and to report findings to the next Legislature. It sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for the study’s completion and reporting. No new program or law is created—just an oversight study.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to assign a committee or staff to study the Montana State Hospital and patient‑transition issues.

Study must examine refurbishment of campus space, expansion of community supports, use of community programs, alternatives to court‑ordered fitness evaluations, and bed‑space projections versus community‑based costs.
Findings must be presented to a designated committee and reviewed before September 15, 2026.
Final results must be reported to the 70th Legislature.
affected: Montana State Hospital staff and patients

HJ73.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Block Management funding and expansion, to be reported by Sept 15, 2026.
HJ73.summary: The resolution directs a committee to study the long‑term funding, expansion, and stability of Montana’s Block Management hunting program and to report findings by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to examine current and future funding sources for the Block Management Program.
The committee must assess whether existing funding is sustainable and identify alternative funding options.
It must review landowner compensation caps and recommend adjustments if needed.
It must develop strategies to retain current landowners and attract new ones, thereby expanding acreage and participation.
The committee is required to propose any legislation necessary to sustain and grow the program.
The study’s findings must be reported to the 70th Legislature before September 15, 2026.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Landowners enrolled in the Block Management Program
Legislative Council and the appointed committee

HR7.one_line: Require new appropriations to be offset by specifying source programs in the same bill.
HR7.summary: The House resolution requires any new appropriation in a legislative bill to be offset by specifying the program(s) from which the funds will be reallocated. It is a procedural request, not a law that creates new programs or spending.
changes: Legislators must identify the source program(s) for any new appropriation within the same bill.
affected: state agencies whose funding may be reallocated

HR4.one_line: House censures two judges and urges their resignation.
HR4.summary: The House resolves to censure two Bozeman municipal judges for alleged misconduct and calls for their resignation. The resolution cites a series of actions taken by the judges that the House claims violated state law and abused their authority. No new law or program is created—this is purely a formal censure and recommendation.
changes: The House formally censures Judges J. Colleen Herrington and Karolina Tierney for official misconduct and malfeasance.
The resolution calls for the immediate resignation of both judges.
The Secretary of State is directed to send copies of the resolution to the judges and to the Chief Justice of the Montana Supreme Court.
The resolution declares that the judges have violated public trust and performed actions unbecoming of an elected official.

HR8.one_line: Resolution condemns Democratic Party racism, calls for apology, bans DEI/CRT/ESG in Montana.
HR8.summary: HR 8 is a House resolution that acknowledges the historical and ongoing racism associated with the Democratic Party and calls for reflection, apology, and the removal of certain diversity‑related frameworks in Montana. It does not create any new law or program.
changes: Recognizes the Democratic Party’s historical ties to slavery, segregation, and other racist policies.
Calls for a formal apology from the Montana Democratic Party and the Democratic National Committee.
Urges the party to consider reparations and restitution for past harms (though not funded by taxpayers).
Requests the Montana House to pursue legislation banning the use of diversity, equity, and inclusion frameworks, critical race theory, and ESG scoring in state institutions.
Invites members of the Montana Democratic Caucus to affirm the resolution as a step toward bipartisan healing.
Directs the Minority Leader to send copies of the resolution to various national and local organizations and leaders.
affected: Montana state institutions that currently use DEI, CRT, or ESG frameworks
National organizations listed in the resolution

HR9.one_line: Montana House urges Trump and Walz to pardon Chauvin and return a $27 million settlement.
HR9.summary: The House resolution urges President Trump and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz to pardon former officer Derek Chauvin, calls for the return of a $27 million settlement to Minneapolis, and demands an independent investigation into the case. It is a symbolic statement with no legal authority to alter any convictions or finances.
changes: Urges the President to grant a federal pardon to Chauvin for all federal charges.

SB2.one_line: Revises property‑tax levy rules to exclude TIF releases and updates school equalization account calculations.
SB2.summary: The bill amends how local governments calculate property‑tax levies so that the release of incremental taxable value from a tax‑increment financing (TIF) district is not treated as newly taxable property. It also revises the school equalization account rules and adds a coordination clause with SB 117.
changes: Amends §15‑10‑420 to exclude TIF‑released value from newly taxable property for levy calculations.
Rewrites §20‑9‑336 to set forecasting and multiplier rules for the school equalization and property‑tax‑reduction account.
Adds a coordination clause that voids the act if SB 117 also passes.
Specifies applicability to property‑tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025 for TIF districts created after the effective date.
affected: Local governmental entities that impose mill levies
numbers: 1/2 of average inflation rate over prior 3 years

SB4.one_line: Revises tax rules for 1‑acre homesites on agricultural land, granting market‑value assessment with a standard exemption.
SB4.summary: The bill revises Montana’s property‑tax rules so that a 1‑acre homesite on agricultural land is valued at market value but receives a tax exemption equal to the statewide average value of such homesites. It also amends several tax‑assessment statutes, clarifies exemption procedures for transmission‑line easements, and updates the intangible‑land‑value program. The changes take effect for tax years beginning after December 31 2026, with the act itself becoming effective January 1 2027.
changes: Classifies a 1‑acre parcel beneath a residential improvement on agricultural land as class IV property and requires it to be valued at market value, but allows a tax exemption equal to the statewide average value of a 1‑acre homesite on agricultural land.
Amends sections 15‑6‑134, 15‑6‑229, 15‑6‑240, 15‑7‑202, and 15‑7‑206 of the Montana Code to reflect the new valuation and exemption rules and to clarify existing exemption procedures.
Adds a new section establishing the effective date (January 1 2027) and an applicability date (tax years beginning after December 31 2026).
Maintains existing procedures for transmission‑line easement exemptions and the intangible‑land‑value assistance program, but updates language to align with the new homesite rules.
Does not create a new program or criminal offense; it only modifies tax‑assessment statutes.
The bill does not alter tax rates or create new taxes.
No new licensing or registration requirements are introduced.
affected: Property owners of 1‑acre homesites on agricultural land
Agricultural land owners with residential improvements
Applicants for the intangible‑land‑value assistance program

SB8.one_line: Montana will add an online voter‑registration system with verification and provisional‑registration rules.
SB8.summary: Montana will allow voters to register online, with the Secretary of State creating a secure website that verifies applicants against motor‑vehicle records.  The bill amends existing registration rules, adds new notification and provisional‑registration procedures, and requires the state to inform tribal governments.
changes: Creates an online voter‑registration portal on the Secretary of State’s website.
Applicants must affirm the truth of their information, consent to use their driver’s‑license or ID signature, and provide the required ID data (license/ID number or last four SSN digits).
The Secretary of State compares the application to motor‑vehicle records; mismatches result in automatic rejection with written notice.
Verified applications are added to the statewide voter‑registration system and forwarded to the county election administrator, who may challenge signatures and send confirmation notices to voters.
The portal will not accept applications 30 days before an election and will resume the day after an election.
The bill amends §13‑2‑110 to clarify required identification, provisional registration, and notification procedures.
The Secretary of State must send a copy of the act to all federally recognized tribal governments.
The act takes effect January 1 2026.

SB13.one_line: Shifts ballot‑statement review from the Supreme Court to district courts, preserving appeal rights.
SB13.summary: The bill removes the Montana Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction over ballot‑statement challenges, shifting all such cases to district courts. It amends the statute that governs ballot‑statement review, clarifies the procedures for filing, and repeals the existing Supreme Court‑only provision. The change is immediate and does not create new programs or funds.
changes: Amends §13‑27‑605 to allow only district courts to hear original proceedings on ballot‑statement challenges.
Replaces the Supreme Court’s exclusive jurisdiction with district‑court jurisdiction for all ballot‑statement disputes.
Preserves the right to appeal district‑court decisions to the Supreme Court.
Repeals §3‑2‑202, which previously granted the Supreme Court original jurisdiction over ballot‑statement review.
Maintains the existing timelines for filing and responding to complaints.
Keeps the Attorney General’s role in preparing and revising ballot statements after court orders.
affected: Proponents and opponents of statewide ballot measures

SB14.one_line: Mandates a one‑time audit of the Office of Disciplinary Counsel, funded by the Judicial Branch.
SB14.summary: The bill orders a one‑time performance audit of the Office of Disciplinary Counsel, to be conducted by the Legislative Auditor and fully funded by the Judicial Branch. The audit must cover funding sources, expenditures over the past decade, and budgetary functions, and be completed by December 15, 2026, with results reported to the Legislative Audit Committee and posted online.
