changes: Requires a single performance audit of the Office of Disciplinary Counsel.
Audit to be performed by the Legislative Auditor (or under its direction).
Audit must examine funding sources, dollar‑by‑dollar spending over the past 10 years, and budget/operational functions.
Audit scope to be risk‑based and follow industry standards (5‑13‑308).
Full cost of the audit to be paid by the Judicial Branch.
Audit report due to the Legislative Audit Committee by Dec. 15, 2026, then forwarded to the Law and Justice Interim Committee and posted on the Legislative Audit Division website.
Amends Section 5‑13‑102, MCA, to define “committee” as the Legislative Audit Committee and “state agency” broadly for entities that handle public money.

SB16.one_line: Allows legislative committees to commit witnesses to contempt for refusing subpoenas.
SB16.summary: The bill amends Montana’s contempt law to allow a legislative committee to commit a witness to contempt for refusing a subpoena or testimony. It clarifies that a majority‑vote resolution in the journal can impose misdemeanor contempt. The change applies immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §5‑5‑109, MCA, to give a legislative committee the power to commit a witness to contempt for refusing to obey a subpoena or to testify.
Requires the committee to enter a resolution in the journal and obtain a majority vote to commit the witness.
Defines the offense as a misdemeanor punishable under §46‑18‑212.
Adds a new subsection (3) that specifies the misdemeanor penalty.
Establishes that the act takes effect immediately upon approval.
affected: Witnesses subpoenaed by a legislative committee

SB15.one_line: Broadens impeachment grounds to include misdemeanors and misconduct for state officials.
SB15.summary: The bill amends Montana’s impeachment statute to broaden the list of offenses that can lead to impeachment. It adds misdemeanors and several categories of misconduct—malfeasance, incompetence, negligence, willful neglect, oppressive use of office, and general misconduct—to the grounds for impeaching the governor, other executive officers, department heads, and judicial officers. No new programs or funds are created, and the change takes effect immediately upon enactment.
changes: Amends Section 5‑5‑401, MCA, to include misdemeanors as a ground for impeachment
Adds malfeasance in corruption, incompetence, negligence, willful neglect of duty, oppressive use of office, and misconduct as additional grounds for impeachment
Expands liability to the governor, executive officers, heads of state departments, and judicial officers
No new offices, funds, or criminal offenses are created
The amendment takes effect immediately upon passage
No fiscal provisions are included
The text does not alter any existing penalties or procedures beyond the expanded grounds
The amendment does not establish a new impeachment process or body

SB21.one_line: Legislative leaders can jointly vacate a court’s mandamus writ against them, preventing enforcement and contempt.
SB21.summary: The bill amends Montana law to let the Senate president or House speaker, together with the governor or attorney general, jointly file a pleading that vacates a writ of mandamus issued against a legislator or the legislature. Once vacated, the writ cannot be enforced and the official cannot be held in contempt.
changes: Amends §27‑26‑102, MCA, adding a new subsection (3) that allows the Senate president or House speaker to file a joint pleading with the governor or attorney general to vacate a writ of mandamus issued against a legislator or the legislature.
Specifies the pleading must be signed by the legislative leader and either the governor or attorney general and filed within 10 business days of the writ’s issuance.
States that a vacated writ cannot be enforced and the official cannot be found in civil or criminal contempt of court.
Does not create any new program, fund, or criminal offense.
Does not impose new fiscal obligations.

SB20.one_line: Retired judges barred from constitutional‑challenge cases, but may still serve otherwise.
SB20.summary: The bill bars retired judges or justices from hearing any case that challenges a state statute’s constitutionality. It amends the qualifications for district‑court judges to include this restriction and clarifies that retired judges may still be called to duty for other matters, but not for constitutional challenges. The changes affect only retired judicial officers and the courts that might otherwise call them.
changes: Amends Section 3‑5‑202 to prohibit retired judges from hearing constitutional‑challenge cases.
Adds a new subsection to Section 19‑5‑103 that limits retired judges’ duties to non‑constitutional matters.
Preserves the ability of retired judges to be called to duty for other court or water‑court work.
Maintains existing compensation rules for retired judges when called to duty.
Leaves all other qualifications and duties for active judges unchanged.
affected: District courts that may call retired judges
Chief justice who may call retired judges
Parties challenging statutes in constitutional‑challenge cases
numbers: 8 years of service required for retirement call
180 days annual cap for daily salary compensation
Daily salary and monthly salary references

SB24.one_line: Raises fines for blocking railroad crossings to $25–$100, effective immediately.
SB24.summary: The bill amends Montana’s railroad‑crossing law to raise the minimum and maximum fines for blocking a crossing.  It makes it a misdemeanor to keep a train stopped for more than 15 minutes or to leave any object on the track at a highway crossing outside incorporated cities.
changes: Amends §69‑14‑626 to increase the fine range for blocking a railroad crossing to a minimum of $25 and a maximum of $100 (per the text’s wording).
Adds a new subsection that defines the offense as a misdemeanor and specifies the fine limits.
Sets the act’s effective date to the day it is passed and approved.
affected: Corporations, associations, or companies that obstruct railroad crossings outside incorporated cities and towns

SB28.one_line: Extends vehicle titling grace period to 60 days and adds a $10 late penalty.
SB28.summary: The bill extends the grace period for vehicle titling and temporary registration permits from 40 to 60 days, and adds a $10 late penalty for failing to complete title or registration within that period. It also updates related sections on title issuance, transfer, and special mobile equipment registration.
changes: Extends titling and registration grace period to 60 days (from 40).
Allows the department to mail a title to a secured party or lienholder within the 60‑day period.
Adds a $10 late penalty for transferees who do not complete title or registration within 60 days.
Maintains that a temporary registration permit must be displayed for operation during the grace period.
Updates special mobile equipment rules to keep the 60‑day expiration for temporary permits and decal renewal.
Requires a $5 decal fee and a $50 temporary permit fee, with $25 of the permit fee going to the state general fund and $25 to the Department of Transportation.

SB31.one_line: Makes Montana’s IOLTA program voluntary and gives lawyers three trust‑account options.
SB31.summary: The bill would make Montana’s mandatory IOLTA program voluntary and give lawyers three options for holding client funds: a non‑interest‑bearing account, an interest‑bearing account that pays interest to the client, or the existing IOLTA account that sends interest to a court‑chosen organization.
changes: Allows a lawyer to deposit client money in a non‑interest‑bearing trust account.
Allows a lawyer to deposit client money in an interest‑bearing account that pays the client the earned interest at reasonable intervals.
Allows a lawyer to deposit client money in the existing IOLTA account, where interest goes to a court‑chosen organization.
Requires written client consent for any of the above options.
Codifies these options into Title 37, chapter 61, part 4 of the Montana Code.
Does not create a new state program, office, or criminal offense.
Does not impose new taxes or appropriations.

SB42.one_line: SB 42 makes Montana’s judicial elections partisan, allowing party endorsements and contributions.
SB42.summary: SB 42 would make Montana’s judicial elections partisan, allowing candidates to run on party lines, accept endorsements, and receive party contributions. It also creates a new primary process for independent judicial candidates and changes how retention ballots are printed.
changes: Rewrites the election statutes for Supreme Court justices, district court judges, justices of the peace, and municipal court judges to require partisan nomination and election, except for incumbents who are the sole candidate; independent judicial candidates are exempt from signature and filing deadlines.
Introduces a separate primary election for independent judicial candidates that mirrors party primaries, with a 5 % vote threshold to advance to the general election.
Allows political parties to endorse judicial candidates and to contribute to their campaigns, while also permitting joint fundraising committees for statewide office candidates and parties.
Replaces the current non‑partisan ballot format for retention elections with a partisan format that includes the incumbent’s party designation.
Repeals several existing Montana Code sections that previously prohibited party contributions to judicial candidates and that defined the ballot format for retention elections.
Provides that independent judicial candidates are not subject to the usual signature requirements for petitioning to run.
Sets an effective date for the new rules and preserves pre‑existing rights and penalties that were in force before that date.
numbers: 1 year term for district court judges
1 year term for justices of the peace
1 year term for municipal court judges

SB43.one_line: Limits district‑court injunctions to their district; statewide enforcement requires Supreme Court appeal.
SB43.summary: The bill codifies that district‑court injunctions can only be enforced within the district where they were issued, and any attempt to extend them statewide must be appealed to the Montana Supreme Court. It also clarifies that injunctions cannot restrain the enforcement of a statute against a non‑party unless the Supreme Court is involved.
changes: Amends §27‑19‑101 to state that a district‑court injunction is enforceable only in the district where granted and that statewide enforcement requires Supreme Court appeal.
Amends §27‑19‑103 to list specific situations in which an injunction cannot be granted, including restraining a statute’s enforcement against a non‑party.
Adds a requirement that an injunction to restrain a statute for a constitutional violation must directly address the violation and be narrowly tailored.
Clarifies that injunctions cannot stay proceedings in federal courts, other states, or prevent execution of public statutes by law‑enforcement officers.
Specifies that injunctions cannot prevent the execution of a municipal legislative act or a labor dispute outside the parties’ labor status.
Leaves all other statutory language unchanged.

SB44.one_line: Codifies Montana’s separation‑of‑powers doctrine and clarifies branch powers and board duties.
SB44.summary: SB 44 codifies Montana’s separation‑of‑powers doctrine, defining the specific powers and limits of the legislative, executive, judicial, and educational boards, and amending related statutes. It does not create new programs or funds but reorganizes and clarifies existing authority.
changes: Codifies the separation‑of‑powers doctrine and enumerates the powers of each branch and of the Board of Regents and Board of Public Education.

Amends sections 2‑15‑1505 and 2‑15‑1507 to clarify that the Boards of Regents and Public Education are executive agencies and that their members are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Senate.

Defines the powers of the House and Senate (e.g., judging elections, adopting rules, impeaching), the governor and other executive officers (e.g., veto, budget, appointments), and the courts (e.g., jurisdiction, rules, disciplinary powers).
Adds definitions for terms such as “eminent domain,” “felony,” and “original jurisdiction.”
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Board of Regents of Higher Education

SB47.one_line: Adds a mandatory committee review step for legally‑sufficient statewide initiatives.
SB47.summary: The bill amends Montana’s ballot‑initiative statutes to add a mandatory legislative‑committee review step for any statewide initiative that a court or the attorney general finds legally sufficient. It also clarifies the formatting of yes‑and‑no statements, the timing of submissions, and the procedures for fiscal notes and legal‑sufficiency opinions.
changes: Adds a new review step (Section 13‑27‑228) requiring the appropriate interim committee or the legislative council to hold a public hearing and vote on whether to place a legally‑sufficient initiative on the ballot.
Requires the Secretary of State to forward the final text of a legally‑sufficient initiative to the legislative services division and then to the committee or council for review.
Allows the committee or council to request a fiscal note or a revised fiscal note if new information arises.
Requires the committee or council to vote within 14 days of receiving the initiative text, and the outcome must be reported to the Secretary of State.
Clarifies that the committee’s vote cannot alter the initiative’s title, statement of purpose, or yes‑and‑no statement on the ballot.
Adds a yes‑and‑no statement format (Section 13‑27‑213) that must appear beside the ballot diagram and may not contain additional material.
Extends the existing procedural timelines for statutory and constitutional initiatives, referenda, and convention initiatives, but does not change those timelines.
Sets the act’s effective date to the passage date and limits its applicability to initiatives filed on or after that date.
affected: Interim committees and the legislative council

SB49.one_line: Prevents judges from disciplining attorneys in office for actions taken while serving, except courtroom misconduct.
SB49.summary: The bill bars judges and other judicial officers from initiating or continuing professional discipline against attorneys who are serving as constitutional officers or legislators for actions taken while in office, except for courtroom misconduct. It also allows such attorneys to move to dismiss or quash any proceedings that do begin.
changes: 1. Judicial officers cannot start or conduct disciplinary actions against attorneys who are constitutional officers or legislators for actions performed during their term that could deter or retaliate against the attorney’s constitutional rights or impede office duties.
2. The prohibition applies even after the attorney leaves office if the alleged misconduct occurred while in office.
3. Judges or justices of the peace may still discipline an attorney for disruptive courtroom behavior.
4. Attorneys subject to a disciplinary proceeding can file a motion to dismiss or quash under this section.
5. The act is codified as part of Title 3, Chapter 1, Part 6 of the Montana Code.
6. The law takes effect immediately upon passage and is retroactive to January 1, 2024 for any proceedings that have already begun.
affected: Attorneys serving as constitutional officers (Governor, Lt. Gov., Attorney General, Secretary of State, Superintendent of Public Instruction)
Attorneys serving as members of the Montana Legislature
Judicial officers (judges, justices of the peace, Supreme Court justices, disciplinary counsel, commission on practice)
Courtroom participants subject to misconduct proceedings

SB50.one_line: Revises child‑abuse laws to require warrants, prompt petitions, and expanded prevention and reunification duties.
SB50.summary: SB 50 revises Montana’s child‑abuse and neglect laws to require a court warrant for most removals, mandate prompt petitions after emergency removals, and expand the department’s duties to prevent and reunify families. The bill also adds detailed procedural requirements for notifications, hearings, and preservation efforts.
changes: A child protection specialist, peace officer, or county attorney must apply for a warrant to remove a child; the warrant must be served within 10 days or is void.
Removal without a warrant is allowed only when probable cause exists that the child faces imminent and apparent sexual or physical abuse during the time needed to obtain a warrant.
An abuse‑and‑neglect petition must be filed within 72 hours (5 working days) of an emergency removal, and a show‑cause hearing must occur within 20 days of filing.
The department must notify parents and provide detailed information within 24 hours, and must maintain a voluntary registry of close relatives to be notified of a removal.
The bill expands the department’s duty to make reasonable efforts to prevent removal and to reunify families, outlining specific services, family‑team meetings, and community resource referrals.
Procedural changes to Sections 41‑3‑101, 41‑3‑102, 41‑3‑301, and 41‑3‑423 are codified and effective July 1 2026.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB52.one_line: Montana establishes a 3‑judge Court of Chancery for equitable relief, with 150‑day resolution and higher judge salaries.
SB52.summary: Montana will create a new three‑judge Court of Chancery to hear equitable and declaratory relief in constitutional, land‑use, and business matters, with a 150‑day case‑resolution goal and a 6‑year term for judges. The court will be supervised by the Supreme Court, funded by the governor, and its judges will earn 20 % more than associate Supreme Court justices. The court’s jurisdiction is limited to civil matters and it will not handle criminal cases or award punitive damages. The court is effective July 1 2025 and terminates June 30 2031.
changes: Creates a Montana Court of Chancery with three judges
Defines jurisdiction over constitutional, land‑use, and business equitable/declaratory relief and certain civil claims exceeding $80,000
Mandates removal of concurrent district‑court actions to the chancery court
Allows arbitration and mediation in pending matters
Sets a 150‑day resolution target, with optional extended calendar
Supplies administrative and staffing authority, including remote hearings
Establishes governor nomination and Senate confirmation of judges, 6‑year staggered terms, and chief judge designation
Provides 20 % higher salary than associate Supreme Court justices, with no reduction
Specifies funding from appropriations for judges’ salaries and staff expenses
Includes effective date July 1 2025 and termination June 30 2031
affected: Montana businesses, land‑use developers, citizens, and attorneys
Montana Supreme Court and its staff
Montana governor and state appropriations committee
Montana residents involved in constitutional or land‑use disputes

SB62.one_line: Phase‑out of Montana’s Medicaid expansion for able‑bodied adults, with waiver request for existing enrollees.
SB62.summary: The bill ends Montana’s Medicaid expansion for able‑bodied adults on September 1 2025, except for those already enrolled. The Department of Public Health and Human Services must apply for a federal waiver to keep existing enrollees funded and may add measures to protect program integrity.
changes: 1. No new enrollments in the expanded Medicaid program after 9/1/2025, except those already enrolled on 8/31/2025 and who remain continuously enrolled.
2. The Department must request a federal waiver to preserve current federal matching funds for those remaining enrollees.

3. The Department retains discretion to impose additional safeguards (e.g., community engagement, biannual redeterminations, lifetime benefit limits) if federal funds decline or responsibilities shift.
4. Amendments to Sections 53‑6‑1304, 28, 38, and 48 codify the termination and waiver procedures and require certification that no participants remain before final termination.
5. The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Able‑bodied adults eligible for Medicaid expansion
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB63.one_line: SB 63 bans electronic motion‑tracking devices for hunting and imposes fines, jail, and license forfeiture.
SB63.summary: SB 63 prohibits hunters from using electronic motion‑tracking devices or mechanisms to locate game, and expands the list of prohibited hunting aids. Violations carry fines, possible jail, and loss of hunting privileges.
changes: Amends §87‑6‑401 to add subsection (d) banning electronic motion‑tracking devices used to locate game or to relay location information to the hunter or another person on the same day.
Defines a dog used by a hunter as not a motion‑tracking device for purposes of the new subsection.
Adds penalties: $50‑$1,000 fine, up to 6 months in county jail, possible forfeiture of hunting licenses and hunting privileges, and restitution under §§87‑6‑905‑907.
Leaves other existing prohibitions (e.g., snare use, electronic calls, firearm silencing devices, prohibited archery equipment, shotgun/ rifle restrictions) unchanged.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Hunters who use electronic motion‑tracking devices or mechanisms
Hunters who communicate location data from such devices
Hunters who use other prohibited hunting aids listed in §87‑6‑401

SB66.one_line: Revises court terminology to clarify bias, conflict, and procedural definitions.
SB66.summary: SB 66 revises the Montana Code to clarify terminology used for judicial officers and their conduct. It defines terms such as bias, conflict of interest, impartiality, open‑mind­ness, and others, and amends Section 1‑1‑202 to incorporate these definitions.
changes: Amends Section 1‑1‑202, MCA, to include new definitions for terms related to judicial procedure and conduct.
Defines "bias" as prejudice arising for reasons other than facts or law, with examples of inference.
Defines "conflict of interest" as a financial, political, or other interest that could create bias.
Adds definitions for "deposition," "impartiality," "judicial officers," "judicial record," "open‑mind­ness," "oral examination," "registered mail," "testify," "writ," and "process."
affected: Legal practitioners and parties appearing before Montana courts
numbers: No monetary amounts or dates specified

SB68.one_line: SB 68 bars certain study committees from meeting during session, except specified committees.
SB68.summary: SB 68 eliminates the ability of study committees staffed by the Legislative Services Division to meet during a legislative session, except for a few specified committees. It amends the statutory language that currently prohibits such meetings while the legislature is in session.
changes: Amends §5‑5‑214, MCA, to clarify that study committees staffed by the Legislative Services Division may not meet while the legislature is in session.
The amendment explicitly excludes the Legislative Council, Legislative Finance Committee, Legislative Audit Committee, and any entity created by legislative rules from this restriction.
No new committees, funds, or offices are created.
The bill does not alter any fiscal provisions or create new expenses.
The change applies only to the meeting schedule of the affected committees.
The amendment does not affect the authority or duties of the committees, only their meeting timing.
affected: Study committees staffed by the Legislative Services Division
Other entities created by legislative rules

SB81.one_line: Amends gas‑storage leasing statutes, broadening definitions, capping bonds, and adding waste‑prevention rules.
SB81.summary: The bill amends Montana’s underground‑gas‑storage leasing statutes to broaden the definition of “gas or liquified gas,” clarify lease eligibility, set a $20,000 bond cap, and add a waste‑prevention requirement with forfeiture for violations. It gives the board rule‑making authority and expands the pool of state lands that can be leased for storage. No new program or criminal offense is created. The bill is a modest statutory amendment.
changes: Expands the definition of “gas or liquified gas” to include natural gases, CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases, other gaseous hydrocarbons, and their liquified forms.

Authorizes the board to lease state lands capable of storing gas or liquified gas, including lands where native gas deposits have been depleted, to qualified natural‑gas utilities and government agencies.
Limits lessee bonds to a maximum of $20,000 and requires a bond that indemnifies the state against loss or damage from lease violations.
Adds a waste‑prevention clause requiring lessees to take reasonable precautions to avoid waste of oil or gas and to prevent water intrusion into oil‑ or gas‑bearing strata.
Provides that violations of the waste‑prevention clause constitute grounds for lease forfeiture after a hearing before the board.
Gives the board rule‑making authority over leasing terms and the sale of gas remaining in depleted fields.
affected: State lands and their owners (the state)
Natural‑gas public utilities authorized to transport or distribute gas in Montana
Government agencies engaged in gas transportation or distribution
Lessee companies that would lease state lands for underground gas storage
Board of Natural Resources and Conservation (rule‑making authority)
numbers: State lands with capability to store gas or depleted native gas deposits
No specific dates or budgets mentioned

SB84.one_line: Revises present‑sentence investigation rules, expands mental‑health and victim‑loss reporting, and appropriates $2.4 M.
SB84.summary: SB 84 revises Montana’s present‑sentence investigation rules, expands when courts must order investigations, adds mental‑health and victim‑loss reporting, and authorizes a $2.4 million biennial appropriation for implementation.
changes: Amends §46‑12‑211 to allow two‑way audio‑video plea‑agreement disclosures and clarify court acceptance of plea agreements

SB89.one_line: Creates a new unit to conduct present‑sentence investigations for sexual and violent offenders and adds mandatory evaluations and fees.
SB89.summary: The bill creates a new Sexual and Violent Offender Presentence Investigation and Reporting Unit within the Department of Corrections, expands the types of offenses that trigger a present‑sentence investigation, and adds mandatory psychosexual and mental‑health evaluations for certain offenders. It also imposes a $50 fee for reports and clarifies who must pay evaluation costs.
changes: Establishes a dedicated unit of probation and parole officers to conduct present‑sentence investigations for sexual or violent offenses and certain misdemeanors.
Expands the statutory list of offenses that require a present‑sentence investigation, including all felonies, specific violent crimes, and misdemeanors originally charged as sexual or violent.

Mandates psychosexual evaluations for offenders convicted of specified sexual‑offender registration violations and other listed crimes, with costs paid by the defendant or, if indigent, by the court, county, or state.
Adds mental‑health evaluations for defendants convicted of certain violent offenses, with similar cost‑payment provisions.

Imposes a $50 fee on the defendant at the time the report is completed, unless the court finds the defendant unable to pay; the fee may be retained by the Department of Corrections to fund related contracts.
Requires that restitution information be included in the present‑sentence report when requested by the court or prosecutor.
affected: Defendants convicted of sexual or violent offenses
Defendants convicted of certain misdemeanors originally charged as sexual or violent

County attorneys, defense attorneys, and sentencing judges receiving reports

County or state when defendants are indigent

SB90.one_line: Creates a lodging‑tax funded property‑tax‑credit program for primary residences with certification, penalties, and a new special revenue account.
SB90.summary: SB 90 creates a state‑funded property‑tax‑credit program for owners of certified primary residences, funded by lodging‑tax and rental‑car‑tax revenue.  The bill authorizes a special revenue account, sets rules for certification, penalties for fraud, and an appeals process, and eliminates certain reporting requirements.  It also amends a wide range of tax‑and‑budget statutes to re‑allocate the proceeds of the lodging‑tax and related sales‑taxes to the new property‑tax‑assistance account and other state funds.
changes: Establishes a state property‑tax‑assistance account funded by lodging‑tax and rental‑car‑tax revenue and authorizes annual distribution to counties based on certified primary residences
Creates a certification process for primary residences, including application deadlines, required documentation, and a 7‑month residency test
Imposes a 2% administrative fee on the account and a $100,000 reserve for appeals

Sets up an appeals and review process through the Department of Revenue, county tax‑appeal boards, and the Montana tax‑appeal board

numbers: $400,000 annual deposit to heritage preservation account (in later sections)
65.5% of lodging‑tax proceeds to property‑tax‑assistance account

SB92.one_line: Montana attorneys may opt out of State Bar membership and dues, effective July 1, 2026.
SB92.summary: The bill makes membership and payment of dues to the State Bar of Montana voluntary for all licensed attorneys, removing the bar’s mandatory status. It does not create new programs or funds and will take effect July 1, 2026.
changes: Mandates that attorneys admitted by the Supreme Court may choose not to join the State Bar of Montana and may refuse to pay dues as a condition of licensure.
Reclassifies the State Bar’s membership requirement from mandatory to voluntary in the state’s statutes.
Leaves all other bar functions—disciplinary, educational, and administrative—unchanged.
Does not alter the Supreme Court’s authority to admit attorneys or discipline them.
Does not establish any new fees, funds, or offices.
Requires the statutory text to be codified as part of Title 37, Chapter 61, Part 2.
Sets the effective date for the change to July 1, 2026.

SB94.one_line: Limits public‑sector union use of state funds and sets rules for employee union activity.
SB94.summary: SB 94 limits public‑sector unions from using state money for organizing and sets rules for how public employees may engage in union activities. It amends labor‑law sections to clarify conduct, instructional‑day limits, and definitions.
changes: Prohibits public employers from contributing or expending public funds for labor‑organization activities and from paying employees for such work.
Allows employees to use unpaid or compensated leave for union work only under specific conditions and requires employers to report time spent and invoice the union for any compensation.
Amends 2‑2‑121 to expand prohibited private‑business conduct by public officers and employees.
Rewrites 20‑1‑304 and 20‑4‑304 to set limits on pupil‑instruction‑related days and require school‑district trustees to close schools for teacher professional‑development meetings without pay loss.
Rewrites 39‑31‑103 to define key terms (e.g., “appropriate unit,” “exclusive representative,” “representational activities”) and to clarify what counts as union activity.
Adds a provision allowing a board to waive the law for mass‑transit employers to meet federal requirements.
Includes codification, saving, severability, and applicability clauses.
No new state program or criminal offense is created.
affected: Public employers (state, local, school districts, etc.)
Labor organizations and their exclusive representatives

SB96.one_line: Prevents local bans on the use of working animals in commerce and service.
SB96.summary: The bill protects the use of working animals by preventing local governments from banning or otherwise restricting them. It defines working animals, limits local ordinances that would prohibit their use, and amends a broad state statute on local‑government powers to include this protection.
changes: Defines "working animal" as a nonhuman animal used for a specific duty in commerce or service, excluding livestock used for production

Prohibits any local‑government ordinance or resolution that terminates, bans, effectively bans, or creates undue hardship for the use of a working animal or animal enterprise in a wide range of activities (commerce, service, law enforcement, transportation, etc.)
Allows local governments to regulate animal care, public health, or public safety as long as those regulations do not conflict with the working‑animal protection
Supersedes any local ordinance that conflicts with the working‑animal protection but does not override zoning ordinances under Title 7, Chapter 1
Amends Section 7‑1‑111, MCA, to add a new subsection (31) that explicitly prohibits local‑government powers that would ban or restrict working animals

SB98.one_line: Lower cigarette tax for heated cigarettes to 85 ¢ per 20‑pack and add a 50 % wholesale tax on other tobacco products.
SB98.summary: The bill amends Montana’s cigarette tax to lower the rate on cigarettes that are heated but not burned to 85 ¢ per 20‑cigarette package (down from $1.70). It also clarifies pre‑collection, refund procedures for tribal sales, and adds a 50 % wholesale‑price tax on other tobacco products.
changes: Amends §16‑11‑111 to set the tax on heated‑but‑not‑burned cigarettes at 85 ¢ per 20‑cigarette package, instead of $1.70 for burned cigarettes.
Maintains the $1.70 tax for burned cigarettes and the existing 1/20‑per‑cigarette rule for non‑standard package sizes.
Preserves the exemption for sales to tribal members and the refund/credit process for wholesalers selling to tribes, with a one‑year claim window and quota limits.
Adds a 50 % wholesale‑price tax on all tobacco products other than cigarettes, premium cigars, and moist snuff (with a 35 ¢ cap on premium cigars and 85 ¢/oz on moist snuff).
Requires wholesalers to pre‑collect and remit these taxes to the department; non‑payment triggers penalties and interest.
Specifies that the new tax applies to wholesalers selling after June 30 2025 and takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Wholesalers of cigarettes and other tobacco products in Montana
Montana Indian tribes and tribal members

SB99.one_line: Expands UBI to include certain agricultural rental and accommodation income for tax‑exempt entities.
SB99.summary: The bill expands Montana’s definition of unrelated‑business income (UBI) to include certain rental income from agricultural property and income from providing accommodations. It amends the tax code to treat those incomes as taxable UBI and requires exempt organizations that earn such income to file a UBI return.
changes: Adds rental income from leasing agricultural property to the list of taxable UBI under §15‑31‑102(b)(b).
Adds income from providing accommodations (subject to §15‑65111 or §15‑68‑102) to taxable UBI under §15‑31‑102(b)(c).
Requires exempt organizations with UBI over $100 to file a UBI return and be taxed as other corporation income under §15‑31‑102(3)(a).
Applies the changes to tax‑year beginning after December 31 2025.
Amends §15‑30‑3404 and §15‑31‑102 to incorporate the new UBI definitions and reporting requirements.
No new programs or offices are created; it only expands existing tax rules.
No direct penalties or new rates are introduced beyond existing UBI rules.
affected: Exempt corporations and other tax‑exempt organizations that lease agricultural property or provide accommodations
Tax‑exempt organizations earning more than $100 in UBI
Montana Department of Revenue (for enforcement and reporting)

SB102.one_line: Limits education levy growth to 3 % above prior year’s assessed tax and removes carry‑forward for certain state mills.
SB102.summary: SB 102 limits how much state‑funded education levies can grow, capping the revenue from school‑equalization and vocational‑technical mills at no more than 3 % above the prior year’s assessed property tax. It also removes the carry‑forward authority for certain state mills and updates the calculation rules for all other mill levies.
changes: Replaces §15‑10‑420 to cap revenue from education levies at prior‑year assessed tax plus 3 % of that amount.
Disallows carry‑forward of mill authority for mills imposed under §§20‑9‑331, 20‑9‑333, 20‑9‑360, or 20‑25‑439.
Adjusts the calculation of the maximum number of mills to include a 3 % ceiling and requires rounding up to the nearest tenth of a mill.
Keeps the existing one‑half‑inflation‑adjustment rule for other levies but adds the 3 % cap for education levies.
Maintains exemptions for school‑district levies, newly created regional resource authorities, and certain airport‑authority levies.
Allows the department to adopt rules to implement the new limits.
affected: School districts and other entities that impose education levies
County and municipal governments that impose state‑mill levies

SB100.one_line: Revises assisted‑living payments, shifts funding, and mandates quarterly reporting.
SB100.summary: The bill revises how Medicaid‑covered assisted‑living costs are calculated, shifts funding from the Big Sky Waiver to the Community First Choice option, and requires quarterly reporting on both programs. It also sets an effective date of July 1, 2027 and includes a contingency that voids the transfer if CMS denies the plan amendment.
changes: Adjusts room‑and‑board payments for Medicaid beneficiaries: eligible persons pay either their SSI amount minus $100 or, if qualifying under 53‑6‑131(1)(e)(ii)(A), their countable gross income minus the Medicaid qualifying spend and $100.
Mandates the Department to apply for a CMS waiver and state‑plan amendment by Jan 1, 2028 to move assisted‑living services from the Big Sky Waiver to the Community First Choice option.
Transfers the actual cost of serving individuals from the Big Sky Waiver to the Community First Choice option as they move between programs.
Requires quarterly reports (average served, wait‑list size, provider changes, per‑capita expenditures, utilization rates) to the Health and Human Services Interim Budget Committee.
Provides that if CMS denies the plan amendment, the transfer provision is voided.

Health and Human Services Interim Budget Committee

SB112.one_line: Limits state purchases of opioid antagonists from settlement parties after June 30 2025.
SB112.summary: The bill bars Montana from using state or federal money to buy opioid‑antagonist drugs from companies that were parties to a settlement over opioid manufacturing or distribution, except for contracts already in place before July 1 2025. It also stops renewal of those contracts after June 30 2025 and allows settlement‑bound suppliers to continue until their settlement terms end.
changes: Prohibits new purchases of opioid antagonists from any entity that was a party to, or affiliated with, a settlement with the state over opioid manufacturing, sale, or distribution after June 30 2025.

Existing state contractors for opioid antagonists

SB108.one_line: Property‑tax levies or bonds over limits must be voter‑approved.
SB108.summary: SB 108 requires that any property‑tax levy or bond issued to pay a judgment, settlement, or tax protest that exceeds statutory limits must be approved by voters. The bill amends many tax‑levy and bond‑issue statutes to add this voter‑approval requirement and clarifies when bonds can be issued without an election.

SB114.one_line: Mandates Ten Commandments displays in all Montana public schools, allowing use of district or donated funds.
SB114.summary: The bill requires every public school building and classroom in Montana to display a poster or framed copy of the Ten Commandments, specifies size and font requirements, and allows districts to use their own or donated funds for the displays. It amends the state’s sectarian‑publication prohibition to explicitly permit the Ten Commandments display and clarifies that prayer may be offered but not compelled.

SB119.one_line: Repeals incumbent electric utility right‑of‑first‑refusal provisions, effective immediately.
SB119.summary: The bill removes Montana’s incumbent electric utility right‑of‑first‑refusal provision by repealing sections 69‑5‑201 and 69‑5‑202 of the Montana Code Annotated. The repeal takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.
changes: Repeals section 69‑5‑201, which previously defined the right‑of‑first‑refusal framework for incumbent utilities.

SB118.one_line: Montana expands student data privacy, creates a new data‑governing board, and sets a right to be forgotten.
SB118.summary: SB 118 expands student privacy in Montana’s K‑12 data system, giving students and parents a right to have their education records deleted and adding new safeguards against using social‑security numbers as identifiers. It also re‑organizes the state’s data‑governing board, task force, and reporting requirements to improve data quality and transparency.
changes: Creates a “right to be forgotten” that lets students or parents request deletion of their education data from the statewide K‑12 data system within 45 days, with a possible 45‑day extension; the request must be verifiable and can be submitted online, by mail, or email.

Prohibits any agency or school district from using a student’s social‑security number in whole or in part as a unique identifier in education or workforce data, though a matching key may be used for linkage.

Re‑authorizes and expands the Education and Workforce Data Governing Board, adding new duties such as developing privacy policies, a data inventory, and a model data‑sharing agreement, and requiring quarterly public meetings and video archiving.

Re‑establishes the K‑12 Data Task Force with a broader membership (senate and house committee officers, school administrators, board trustees, teachers, tech staff, parents, and clerks) and gives it advisory authority over data security, privacy, and system design.

Amends Sections 20‑7‑104, 20‑7‑105, 20‑7‑136‑138 to require a statewide K‑12 data system that eliminates redundant collections, links student data to higher‑education and workforce data, and protects records under FERPA and the new right to be forgotten.
Adds annual reporting requirements for school districts on staffing, finances, enrollment, and extracurricular activity data, and mandates public posting of district profiles and union agreements.
Provides rule‑making authority to the board and the superintendent to implement these provisions and to report annually on implementation.
Sets an effective date of July 1 2025.
affected: State agencies that collect education or workforce data
The Education and Workforce Data Governing Board

SB120.one_line: Establishes a structured process for selecting, overseeing, and removing Montana’s Article V convention commissioners.
SB120.summary: The bill establishes a formal process for selecting, overseeing, and removing Montana’s Article V convention commissioners, creates an advisory committee, and sets qualifications, duties, and limits for commissioners. It also provides rules for delegation conduct, compensation, and monitoring of authority. The bill does not create a new program beyond the convention delegation itself.
changes: Creates an Article V Commissioner Advisory Committee composed of one senator, one representative, and a third legislator approved by both chambers
Requires the legislature to appoint an odd‑numbered delegation of commissioners by joint resolution, with all appointments subject to a written commission and oath
Sets detailed qualifications for commissioners, including citizenship, residency, age, voter registration, and restrictions on recent federal employment, lobbying, or felony convictions
Provides that commissioners may be recalled or suspended by a joint resolution or, when the legislature is not in session, by the advisory committee pending a legislative vote
Defines a commissioning resolution that limits commissioners’ authority, prohibits voting on certain constitutional changes, and allows the legislature to issue additional instructions
Establishes that commissioners receive legislator‑level compensation and may not accept gifts over $200
Outlines delegation rules for choosing a chair, a floor‑voter, and a media spokesperson, and requires a majority quorum for decisions
Creates procedures for filling vacancies with interim commissioners selected by the advisory committee until the legislature appoints a permanent replacement
Empowers the advisory committee to monitor commissioners, notify state leaders of over‑reach, and remove commissioners or the delegation if authority is exceeded
Codifies the provisions as a new part of Title 5, Chapter 5 of the Montana Statutes
affected: Montana Article V Commissioner Advisory Committee members
Montana voters (indirectly through the convention process)

SB122.one_line: SB 122 revises employer‑contribution rates for three state retirement systems, caps annual changes, and permits county mill levies.
SB122.summary: SB 122 revises the employer‑contribution formulas for the Highway Patrol, Sheriff, and Game‑Warden/Peace Officer retirement systems, adding a statutory minimum rate, capping annual changes at ±0.5 %, and tying contributions to legacy, contemporary, and normal‑cost liabilities. It also allows counties to levy a mill tax to meet the required contributions and sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.
changes: Sets a minimum employer‑contribution rate of 38.33 % for Highway Patrol, 13.115 % for Sheriffs, and 10.56 % for Game‑Wardens/Peace Officers, effective July 1 2024.
Limits any annual increase or decrease in the actuarially determined contribution to 0.5 % of the prior year’s rate.

Defines the contribution as the sum of rates to pay legacy unfunded liability (amortized over 25 years), contemporary unfunded liability (amortized over 10 years), and normal cost of benefits, minus employee contributions.
Allows counties to levy a mill tax to meet the required employer contributions, subject to a public hearing and without election approval.
Requires the state to transfer $500,000 annually from the special revenue fund to the Highway Patrol pension trust fund until the funded ratio reaches 100 %.
Effective date of the amendments is July 1 2025.
affected: State‑run retirement systems for Highway Patrol, Sheriff, Game‑Warden, and Peace Officers
County governments responsible for employer contributions
Employees of those agencies (indirectly through contribution rates)

SB123.one_line: The bill lets the Division coordinate water‑permit activities during emergencies and amends related statutes for faster, coordinated action.
SB123.summary: SB 123 authorizes the Division of Disaster and Emergency Services to coordinate certain water‑related permits during a state of emergency or disaster, and amends several water‑quality statutes to streamline short‑term standards and emergency‑notice procedures.
changes: Division of Disaster and Emergency Services may coordinate local, state, and federal permitting activities for streams, wetlands, floodplains, and navigable waters during an emergency (Section 1).
The Division may not compel federal agencies to act, but it can track, share data, and develop benchmarks for permits listed in subsections (a)‑(i).
Section 2 and 3 require the Division to coordinate activities related to flood‑plain permits and river‑bed leases/leases during emergencies.
Section 4 amends 75‑5‑318 to allow narrative short‑term turbidity standards when numeric standards cannot be met, with conditions and monitoring.
Section 5 amends 75‑5‑402 to require the Division to submit its permit‑related activities for coordination during emergencies.
Section 6 amends 75‑7‑113 to streamline emergency‑notice and approval procedures for stream‑taking actions, including timelines for notification, onsite inspection, and arbitration.
Section 7 amends 87‑5‑502 to require notice of construction projects affecting streams and to subject such projects to Division coordination during emergencies.
affected: State agencies that issue or oversee water‑related permits
Federal agencies involved in stream and flood‑plain permitting
Local governments and private developers planning construction near streams
Applicants for stream‑bed leases or flood‑plain variances
The Division of Disaster and Emergency Services

SB125.one_line: Rewrites community‑home licensing to add written policies, public comment, and a formal complaint and hearing process.
SB125.summary: SB 125 revises Montana’s community‑home licensing law to require written policies, a public‑comment period, and a formal complaint process. It creates a new administrative procedure for investigating, conciliating, and hearing complaints, and gives the Department authority to order changes or revoke licenses.
changes: Amends §53‑20‑305 to mandate annual licensing and new standards for health, safety, and resident‑policy procedures.
Adds a 28‑day public‑comment period for proposed licenses and requires the Department to publish notice to nearby landowners.

Creates a formal complaint mechanism (Sections 2‑6) that allows residents or others to file complaints, triggers informal investigation, mediation, conciliation, and, if unresolved, a contested hearing.
Provides the Department with the power to issue orders requiring policy changes, conduct inspections, or suspend/revoke licenses.
Allows parties to seek civil remedies in district court after dismissal or non‑compliance with Department orders.
Codifies the new procedures as part of Title 53, Chapter 20, Part 3.
affected: Community homes for persons with developmental disabilities
Department of Public Health and Human Services
Landowners within one‑half mile of proposed homes

SB126.one_line: Revises tenant move‑out rules to limit cleaning deductions and tighten notice and lawsuit timelines.
SB126.summary: SB 126 revises Montana’s tenant‑move‑out rules, clarifying what counts as normal wear, limiting landlord cleaning‑charge deductions, tightening notice and inspection timelines, and tightening the timeframe for wrongful‑withholding lawsuits.
changes: Defines normal wear to include small nail holes, scuffs, and high‑traffic floor wear
Limits landlord cleaning‑charge deductions to the cost of a professional cleaner and excludes carpet or repainting after 2 years of tenancy
Requires landlords to give written notice of required cleaning and a 24‑hour window for tenant completion, unless the tenant has vacated without notice
Extends the period for a landlord to provide a written list of deductions and refund to 30 days after tenancy termination
Adds a 21‑day deadline for wrongful‑withholding lawsuits and clarifies that attorney fees may be awarded
Codifies the new definition of normal wear as part of Title 70, Chapter 25, Part 2

SB127.one_line: Reimburses defendants who successfully defend against forcible‑felony charges using a justifiable‑use‑of‑force defense.
SB127.summary: The bill requires that if a defendant successfully uses the justifiable‑use‑of‑force defense in a forcible‑felony case and is not convicted, the state must reimburse that defendant’s out‑of‑pocket costs and attorney fees. It also clarifies that such reimbursement comes from the prosecutor’s budget for the trial that ended in no conviction.
changes: 1. Establishes a statutory affirmative defense of justifiable use of force for a broad list of violent crimes.
2. Provides that a defendant who successfully raises this defense and is not convicted is entitled to reimbursement of out‑of‑pocket costs, attorney fees, and trial costs for that specific charge.
3. Requires that the reimbursement be paid from the prosecutor’s or prosecutor’s employer’s budget used to pay for the trial that did not result in a conviction.
4. States that if the defendant is convicted of other crimes for which the defense was not raised or was unsuccessful, the defendant bears the costs for those charges.
5. Codifies the new provision as part of Title 45, Chapter 3, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
affected: Defendants charged with forcible felonies who raise a justifiable use of force defense
numbers: No specific dollar amounts or caps

SB128.one_line: Prohibits removal of election duties from a county clerk while in office.
SB128.summary: The bill amends Montana’s election law to prohibit a county governing body from stripping the county clerk and recorder of election‑administration duties while that clerk is in office. It also clarifies the clerk’s responsibilities and allows the clerk to voluntarily relinquish those duties.
changes: Amends §13‑1‑301 to add a new subsection (b) that bars removal of election‑admin duties from the clerk during his or her current term; removal may only occur for future terms.
Adds a new subsection (c) permitting the clerk to voluntarily give up election‑admin duties during the current term.
Clarifies the clerk’s duties in §13‑1‑301(2) and (3).
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.

SB129.one_line: Allows voters to add a party preference to registration and lists it on voter rolls.
SB129.summary: The bill amends Montana’s voter‑registration statutes to let voters select a party affiliation on the standard registration and absentee‑ballot application. It also requires that party affiliation be listed on precinct and statewide voter lists, and it sets January 1 2026 as the effective date.
changes: Adds a party‑affiliation field to the standard voter‑registration and absentee‑ballot application form.
Allows any registered voter to add or change party affiliation at any time.
Requires election officials to print party affiliation on precinct and statewide voter lists when available.
Adds options for Democratic, Green, Libertarian, Republican, other party, and prefer‑not‑to‑answer to the affiliation list.
Preserves existing privacy provisions for law‑enforcement officers and victims of domestic violence.
Sets the act to take effect January 1 2026.

SB131.one_line: Repeals the constituent‑services account for prior contributions and charitable donations, effective immediately.
SB131.summary: The bill repeals Montana Code §13‑37‑403, which established a constituent‑services account for prior contributions and charitable donations. The repeal takes effect immediately upon passage. No new programs or funds are created.
changes: Repeals §13‑37‑403 of the Montana Code Annotated.
Eliminates the constituent‑services account for prior contributions and charitable donations.
No new statutes, offices, or funds are established.
The repeal is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
No additional provisions or amendments are added to the code.
The act contains no fiscal allocations or appropriations.
The repeal does not create any new criminal offense.
The act does not alter any existing procedures or requirements beyond removing the specified section.
affected: State agencies that maintained the constituent‑services account
Employees who managed or reported on the account
Donors who previously contributed to the account
Charitable organizations that received donations from the account

SB130.one_line: Revises recall law to drop required reasons, tighten petition form, and add penalties.
SB130.summary: The bill amends Montana’s recall law to remove the requirement that a recall petition include reasons, lets the electorate decide whether a statement of reasons is sufficient, and tightens the form and circulation rules for petitions. It also adds penalties for falsifying signatures, clarifies the officer’s right to respond, and expands the grounds for recall to include certain misconduct by school trustees and lobbyists. No new program or office is created.
changes: Replaces the grounds‑required language in §2‑16‑603 with a statement that no reasons are required for a recall petition, though a statement may be provided and its sufficiency is judged by voters, not courts.

Redrafts §2‑16‑616 to provide a detailed petition template, limits the reasons section to 200 words, and adds a warning that signing a false name or duplicate signatures is punishable by up to $500 fine or 10‑year imprisonment.

Rewrites §2‑16‑617 to set out the size, ruling, and numbering of circulation sheets, requires a sample sheet to be approved by the filing officer within one week, and requires a sworn statement of facts with the petition.

Amends §2‑16‑621 to require the filing officer to give written notice to the recalled officer, to include any statement of reasons if provided, and to give the officer a 10‑day window to submit a 200‑word justification for the ballot.
Rewrites §2‑16‑633 to specify the ballot wording for recall questions and to require the petition’s reasons and the officer’s justification to appear on the ballot.
Adds §5‑7‑305 penalties for violations of the recall chapter, including civil fines, license suspension, and the possibility of additional recall grounds for legislators.
Amends §20‑4‑114 to make a school trustee’s failure to report an official misconduct that triggers recall.
Includes a severability clause.
affected: County attorneys, attorneys general, and commissioners

SB135.one_line: Repeals termination of chemical‑dependency voucher program, restoring it immediately.
SB135.summary: The bill repeals a 2023 law that ended Montana’s chemical‑dependency treatment voucher program, restoring the program immediately. It has no new provisions beyond the repeal and takes effect as soon as it passes and is approved. The change simply reinstates the voucher program for eligible residents and providers.
changes: Repeals Section 7, Chapter 187 of the 2023 laws that terminated the chemical‑dependency voucher program.
Restores the voucher program to full operation immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Residents eligible for chemical‑dependency treatment vouchers

SB136.one_line: Prohibits patient consent as a defense to homicide for physician‑aid‑in‑dying.
SB136.summary: The bill removes physician‑assisted dying from Montana’s list of offenses that can be defended by patient consent. It amends the consent‑as‑defense statute to declare that a patient’s consent to physician‑aid‑in‑dying is not a defense to homicide.
changes: Amends §45‑2‑211 to add a new subsection (3)(a) stating that consent to physician‑aid‑in‑dying is ineffective as a defense to homicide.
Defines "physician aid in dying" as a physician’s purposeful, knowing prescription of a lethal dose that the patient may self‑administer.
Clarifies that this definition excludes withholding/withdrawing life‑sustaining treatment and comfort‑care medication.
Leaves all other consent‑as‑defense provisions unchanged.
Sets the effective date of the amendment to July 1 2025.
affected: Legal professionals handling homicide cases involving physician‑aid‑in‑dying

SB139.one_line: Eliminates clergy exemption from mandatory child‑abuse reporting in Montana.
SB139.summary: The bill removes the clergy exemption from Montana’s mandatory child‑abuse reporting law, requiring clergy to report suspected abuse unless a confession is made in a confidential religious context. It amends the reporting statute to include clergy as a required reporter and clarifies reporting requirements and confidentiality provisions.
changes: Adds clergy to the list of professionals required to report child abuse or neglect.
Defines exceptions for clergy when a confession is made in a confidential religious setting.
Specifies the content that must be included in a child‑abuse report.
Clarifies how the Department of Justice may share information with other professionals.
Maintains confidentiality obligations for those receiving report information.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage.

SB138.one_line: Teachers may temporarily exclude disruptive students for 24 hours with a return plan.
SB138.summary: The bill affirms teachers’ authority to maintain a positive classroom and allows them to temporarily exclude a pupil for up to 24 hours if the pupil’s behavior disrupts learning. School districts must adopt policies or employee‑agreement language that defines this authority and the exclusion process, and a return plan must be communicated before the pupil may return.
changes: Teachers in schools with at least a half‑time principal may temporarily exclude a pupil for up to 24 hours when the pupil’s behavior impedes teaching or learning.
Exclusion requires the teacher to direct the pupil to the principal, a principal’s designee, or another board‑designated individual.
The pupil cannot return until the principal or designee communicates a return plan to the teacher; the plan may include a behavioral contract, parent communication, and meetings with various parties.

Failure to comply with the return plan or repeated disruptive behavior can lead to further discipline, including permanent removal from the classroom, suspension, or expulsion, consistent with existing district policies and federal disability laws.

School districts must adopt a policy or include language in employee agreements that defines teachers’ authority and exclusion procedures, but the policy may not conflict with due‑process or federal disability protections.
The act is codified as part of Title 20, Chapter 4, Part 3, and takes effect July 1, 2025, applying to school years beginning on or after that date.

SB141.one_line: New legislators must join the PERS defined‑contribution plan; existing ones may keep or switch, with a 90‑day election.
SB141.summary: The bill changes Montana’s retirement rules so that any new legislator must join the Public Employees’ Retirement System’s defined‑contribution plan. Existing legislators may keep their current plan if they choose, but must file a written election within 90 days to continue participation.
changes: Amends §5‑2‑304, MCA, to require new legislators elected or appointed on or after July 1 2025 to become active members of the Public Employees’ Retirement System (PERS) defined‑contribution plan.
Allows legislators who are already active members of another public retirement system to retain that membership or switch to PERS, but not to be active in both simultaneously.
Requires a written, irrevocable election filed within 90 days of taking office to continue participation in a retirement system.
Mandates that the state contribute to the legislator’s PERS account at the same rate as the employer contribution, funded by legislative appropriations.
Sets the effective date of the changes to June 30 2025.
Provides that legislators who are inactive or retired members of a retirement system may return to active status in that system or join PERS, depending on the date of their election.
affected: Newly elected or appointed Montana legislators
Existing legislators who are members of other public retirement systems
numbers: state contribution equal to employer contribution

SB140.one_line: Montana adopts a multistate social work license, creates a commission, and sets data‑sharing and enforcement rules.
SB140.summary: Montana would join the Social Work Licensure Compact, creating a multistate license that lets social workers practice in any member state without separate state licenses, while preserving each state’s authority to regulate and discipline practitioners. The bill establishes a compact commission, data‑sharing rules, and procedures for adverse actions, fees, and dispute resolution. It also sets out how states can join, withdraw, or default from the compact.
changes: Montana adopts the Social Work Licensure Compact and becomes a member state.
A new Social Work Licensure Compact Commission is created to administer the compact, set rules, and manage a shared data system.

Licensed social workers may obtain a multistate license from their home state that authorizes practice in all member states, subject to passing a qualifying national exam and meeting state requirements.
States must report adverse actions and investigative information to the commission’s data system and can take adverse action against a multistate license in the remote state.
Member states can impose fees on multistate license applicants and on licensees for the cost of the commission’s operations.
The compact includes procedures for default, termination, and dispute resolution among member states, and allows states to withdraw after 180 days.
affected: Military families with active duty members
numbers: 7 member states required for effective date
SB140.effective: date the compact statute is enacted in the seventh member state

SB145.one_line: Mandates public access to meetings and records of education groups funded by public money.
SB145.summary: The bill requires that any education‑related membership organization or association that receives public or government funding—whether fully or partially—hold its meetings and keep its records open to the public, just as public bodies do. It simply extends existing open‑meeting laws to these groups. No new program or funding is created.
changes: All meetings of education membership organizations receiving public funds must be open to the public.
All records of such organizations must be available to the public.
The requirement applies to organizations composed of public or government entities or supported by public funds.
The rule is codified as part of Title 20, chapter 1, part 2, and follows those existing provisions.
affected: Associations receiving public or government funds
Public and government entities that are members of those organizations

SB142.one_line: Amends county officer salary law to add extra pay for election administrators and other officials, effective July 1 2025.
SB142.summary: The bill amends Montana’s county officer salary law to add specific extra pay for election administrators and other officials, sets new rules for calculating those additions, and requires a county compensation board to review and recommend salaries each year. It takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Adds up to $2,000–$4,000 extra salary for a clerk‑record‑election administrator when the roles are combined, and up to $2,000 for a separate election administrator position.
Provides $2,000 extra salary for county treasurer, clerk of district court, and justice of the peace, and allows a part‑time coroner salary to be set accordingly.
Requires the county sheriff to receive an additional $2,000 plus a 1 % longevity payment, and allows further discretionary salary from the county commissioners.
Adds specific salary increases for deputy county attorneys based on years of service.
Revises Section 7‑4‑2503 to require a county compensation board to review and recommend annual salary schedules, with a majority vote that includes at least two commissioners.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1 2025.

SB146.one_line: Limits government property restrictions to those narrowly tailored for compelling public‑health or safety interests.
SB146.summary: The bill creates a new “Private Property Protection Act” that limits government‑enforced restrictions on private property unless the restriction is the least‑restrictive means to achieve a compelling public‑health or safety interest. Property owners may sue to challenge such restrictions and obtain an injunction and attorney fees if the court finds the restriction unlawful.
changes: Creates a new statutory framework (Title 76 chapter) that defines and limits property‑use restrictions by state and local governments.
Requires any such restriction to be narrowly tailored, necessary, and the least restrictive means to serve a compelling public‑health or safety interest.

Exempts from the new limits: nuisance abatement, enforcement of license/permit terms (including federal requirements), final non‑appealable judicial determinations, tribal actions, and restrictive covenants unless imposed by a governmental entity.

Provides a cause of action for property owners: they may sue in competent court; the plaintiff wins unless the government proves the restriction meets the three‑prong test (necessary, narrowly tailored, least restrictive).
If successful, the court permanently enjoins the restriction and awards reasonable attorney fees and costs.
Imposes a five‑year statute of limitations from the date the owner becomes aware of the restriction.
affected: Private parties entering restrictive covenants (unless imposed by government)
numbers: Compelling governmental interest in public health or safety

SB150.one_line: Creates a cigar‑room endorsement permitting premium cigar smoking in a dedicated enclosed space with strict requirements.
SB150.summary: The bill creates a new “cigar bar room” endorsement for all‑beverages licensees that allows the smoking of premium cigars in a dedicated enclosed space, sets strict operational requirements, and exempts these rooms from the state’s indoor‑air smoking ban. It also mandates a gaming‑industry study and amends definitions of bars and cigar rooms in the alcohol‑licensing statutes.
changes: Allows all‑beverages licensees to apply for a cigar bar room endorsement that permits premium cigar smoking in a separate enclosed area.

Requires the endorsement holder to generate at least 10% of gross income from cigar sales, maintain a humidor, post a notice prohibiting other tobacco products, and keep the smoking area isolated from non‑smoking areas.
Exempts cigar bar rooms from the prohibition on smoking in enclosed public places under 50‑40‑104, but still requires a ventilation system and prohibits employees from entering while patrons smoke.
Imposes an annual $200 fee for the endorsement and requires annual reporting of cigar‑sale revenue to the department.
Adds a study mandate for the Department of Justice to analyze Montana’s gaming industry and report by Dec. 1 2026.
Amends 50‑40‑103 and 50‑40‑104 to define “cigar bar room” and to list it as an exception to the smoking‑in‑enclosed‑public‑place ban.
Provides a termination date for the study provision (Dec. 31 2026).
affected: Montana Department of Justice and Gaming Advisory Council

SB151.one_line: Creates family‑defense units, new staff, and standards for public defenders, effective July 1, 2025.
SB151.summary: The bill directs the state public defender’s director to create family‑defense and child‑representation units, establishes new standards for attorneys, and adds 21 new staff positions. It also limits contract‑attorney use and requires collaboration with public health to tap federal funds. The changes take effect July 1, 2025, with most new hires scheduled for FY 2025‑26.
changes: Creates up to two trial units for parents/guardians and one trial unit for children under 41‑3‑425.
Mandates the director to limit reliance on contract attorneys and to collaborate with the Department of Public Health for Title IV‑E funds.
Rewrites §47‑1‑105 to add duties for establishing qualifications, hiring, and evaluating division administrators and the new trial units.
Sets statewide qualification and training standards for public defenders, including specific child‑representation standards.
Authorizes 21 new staff positions (10 in FY 2025, 11 in FY 2026) for the public defender’s office.
Requires the director to approve strategic plans, budgets, and policies for caseload management and data reporting.
affected: Parents, guardians, and children in criminal cases
Judicial system and courts handling related cases

SB152.one_line: Amend constitution to allow limited private stock investment in coal trust and compensation funds.
SB152.summary: The bill amends Montana’s constitution to allow a portion of the coal severance tax trust fund, and the state compensation insurance fund, to be invested in private corporate stock. It also permits public retirement system assets to be invested in such stock, while keeping other public funds strictly in safe securities.
changes: Amends Article VIII, §13 to permit private corporate stock investments for the coal severance tax trust fund (up to 25 % of its assets) and the state compensation insurance fund (up to 25 % of its book value).
Allows public retirement system assets to be invested in private corporate stock under fiduciary rules.
Maintains that all other public funds must remain in safe securities (state, federal bonds, or other fixed‑rate instruments).
Requires a two‑thirds legislative vote to submit the amendment to voters.
The amendment becomes effective only after voter approval in the November 2026 election.
affected: Coal severance tax trust fund holders

SB153.one_line: Rises play and credit limits for video‑gambling machines, requires cash payouts, effective 2026.
SB153.summary: The bill raises the maximum amount a player may wager on a single video‑gambling machine game from $2 to $4 and increases the free‑game/credit limit from $800 to $1,199. It also requires licensees to pay all credits owed in cash and allows the department to set a voucher‑expiration period. The changes take effect on January 1, 2026 and apply only to machines put into operation on or after that date.
changes: Increases game‑play limit from $2 to $4 per game
Raises free‑game/credit limit from $800 to $1,199 per game
Mandates cash payment of all credits owed to a player
Empowers the department to rule on voucher expiration periods
Effective January 1, 2026
Applies only to machines operated on or after January 1, 2026

SB155.one_line: Creates a food‑safety panel that can limit foods with harmful additives and colors.
SB155.summary: The bill creates a three‑member, no‑pay panel on food safety that studies cumulative effects of additives and colors, and authorizes the Department of Agriculture to limit foods containing substances the panel deems harmful. It amends the state’s food‑additive regulations to give the department rule‑making authority and requires cooperation with the FDA.
changes: Creates a Food Safety Panel of three governor‑appointed members with specified scientific qualifications.
Panel meets quarterly, serves without compensation, and may be reimbursed under state reimbursement statutes.
Panel studies cumulative effects of food additives and colors and recommends limiting foods containing harmful substances.
Amends §50‑31‑108 to give the Department of Agriculture authority to adopt, amend, or repeal rules on additives, pesticides, and color additives, including zero tolerances and exemptions.
Allows the department to limit availability of foods identified by the panel as having negative toxic effects.
Amends §80‑1‑102 to require the department to enforce these rules in cooperation with the FDA.
Codifies the panel’s provisions as part of Title 80, Chapter 1, Part 1.
No new funding or program is created; the panel is staffed by existing state personnel.
affected: Retailers selling food with additives or colors

SB156.one_line: Revises evidentiary burdens and procedural safeguards in Montana child‑abuse and neglect cases.
SB156.summary: SB 156 revises the evidentiary standards in child‑abuse and neglect proceedings, tightening the burden of proof for various orders and adding procedural safeguards. It requires clear and convincing evidence for termination of parental rights, preponderance of the evidence for temporary legal custody, and proof beyond a reasonable doubt for termination. The bill also expands notice, service, and intervention rights for parents, foster parents, and other parties, and clarifies timelines for hearings and permanency determinations.
changes: Replaces the previous burden‑of‑proof thresholds with new standards: clear and convincing evidence for termination of parental rights, preponderance of the evidence for temporary legal custody, and proof beyond a reasonable doubt for termination of the parent‑child legal relationship.

Mandates that petitions for temporary legal custody, long‑term custody, and termination of parental rights be supported by the specified evidentiary standards and that the court must hold a hearing within the time limits set in the amended sections.

Adds detailed service and notice requirements for parents, putative fathers, foster parents, and other interested parties, including the right to counsel if indigent and the right to appear or intervene.

Requires the department to provide written notice to parents and foster parents explaining their rights and the permanency hearing schedule, and to submit reports to the court or review body at specified intervals.
Extends the maximum duration of temporary legal custody orders to six months and requires the court to state reasons for extensions and conditions for return to the parent.

Reinforces the requirement that a permanency hearing be held within 30 days of a determination that preservation or reunification services are unnecessary, and sets detailed reporting and decision‑making requirements for that hearing.
Clarifies that a standing master may not conduct a termination proceeding and that a qualified expert witness is required in Indian child cases.
Adds a new subsection allowing parents to petition for reinstatement of parental rights after two years, with specific procedural and evidentiary requirements.
affected: Foster parents, pre‑adoptive parents, and relatives caring for the child
County attorneys, attorneys general, and county‑hired attorneys
Courts and judges handling child‑abuse cases
Department of Children, Youth, and Families
Guardians ad litem and attorneys for children

SB157.one_line: Adds a 150 % charitable deduction for non‑itemizers and amends many Montana tax rules.
SB157.summary: SB 157 adds a Montana charitable‑deduction that can be up to 150 % of the amount that would be deductible on a federal return, but only if the taxpayer did not itemize federally. It also amends many other Montana income‑tax rules, including new deductions for certain savings‑account contributions and military‑related income, and changes how some federal adjustments are treated for Montana purposes.
changes: Adds a new charitable‑deduction: 150 % of the federal charitable deduction if the taxpayer did not itemize, or 50 % if the taxpayer did itemize.
Amends §15‑30‑2120 to change how federal adjustments are added or subtracted when computing Montana taxable income.
Introduces new deductions for contributions to Montana family‑education and other savings accounts (up to $3,000 per spouse).
Adds deductions for certain medical‑care and first‑time‑home‑buyer savings‑account withdrawals used for eligible purposes.
Provides special subtractions for military pensions, survivor benefits, and other military‑related income, with limits and residency requirements.
Extends a $5,500 subtraction for taxpayers age 65, adjusted for inflation each year.
Terminates several new provisions on June 30 2025 or December 31 2033.
Effective January 1 2026; applies to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Individual Montana taxpayers who itemize or do not itemize federal deductions
Taxpayers contributing to Montana family‑education or other savings accounts
Taxpayers with medical‑care or first‑time‑home‑buyer savings accounts
Taxpayers claiming Montana source wage income

SB158.one_line: Releases judicial investigation reports to the House, but limits public disclosure to impeachment use.
