SB158.summary: The bill amends the Judicial Standards Commission’s confidentiality rules and requires the commission to forward any investigation report and evidence on a judicial officer to the House of Representatives. It limits when the House may release that information to the public, allowing disclosure only if the report is used in impeachment proceedings.
changes: Amends §3‑1‑1105 to clarify that all papers filed with the commission or masters are confidential and that the commission may issue rules for enforcement and public disclosure when appropriate.
Amends §3‑1‑1106 to add a new subsection (3) requiring the commission to provide the House with a report and evidence from any investigation initiated under subsection (1)(a).
Adds a new subsection (5) restricting the House’s ability to release the report to the public; release is permitted only if the report is used in impeachment proceedings.
Clarifies notice requirements to the judicial officer and the Supreme Court under subsection (2).

SB159.one_line: Creates an educational opportunity fund, raises tax‑credit limits, and removes sunset dates on school‑and‑scholarship credits.
SB159.summary: SB 159 establishes a new educational opportunity fund inside Montana’s coal severance tax trust and uses earnings from that fund to raise the limits on state tax credits for donations to public schools and scholarship organizations.  The bill also removes sunset dates on the credit programs, sets aggregate limits and a 20 % increase rule tied to pre‑approval and fund earnings, and requires a $100 million transfer to the new fund by August 15 2025.
changes: Creates an educational opportunity fund within the coal severance tax trust and mandates a $100 million transfer to it by Aug. 15 2025

Raises the aggregate limit for school‑district tax credits to $2 million in 2023 and $5 million thereafter, with a 20 % increase if 80 % of the limit is pre‑approved and 50 % of the fund’s earnings are transferred to the general fund
Raises the aggregate limit for scholarship‑organization tax credits to the same amounts and increase rule
Allows tax credits equal to the donation (up to $200,000) for both school‑district and scholarship‑organization donations, with a 3‑year carry‑forward
Requires pre‑approval and receipt issuance by the department for each credit, and limits how much a district can retain (max $50,000 or 15 % of its general‑fund budget, whichever is greater)
Terminates sunset provisions in the existing credit statutes and several other temporary sections (e.g., Sections 8, 14, 9, 15, 10, 16, 25, 1‑6, 11‑18) by Dec. 31 2029

Amends the coal‑severance‑tax‑trust statute (17‑5‑703) to add the educational opportunity fund and to specify how earnings are transferred to the general fund (50 % annually) and to adjust other fund‑transfer rules
Repeals Section 33 of the 2015 law, Section 20 of the 2021 law, and Section 12 of the 2023 law
affected: Montana taxpayers who donate to public schools or scholarship organizations
School districts and scholarship organizations that receive donations
State Department of Revenue (for pre‑approval and receipt issuance)
General fund (receives 50 % of the educational opportunity fund’s earnings)
numbers: $100 million transfer to educational opportunity fund
50 % of fund earnings transferred to general fund
$50,000 or 15 % of district budget cap on retained donations

SB160.one_line: Requiring decommissioning bonds before construction of large wind and solar projects, with penalties for non‑submission.
SB160.summary: SB 160 revises Montana’s wind‑ and solar‑decommissioning laws to require a bond before construction and operation, sets detailed decommissioning timelines, and creates penalties for non‑submission. It also establishes a decommissioning account and clarifies when bonds may be released or increased.
changes: Owners of new wind (≥25 MW) or solar (≥2 MW) facilities must submit a decommissioning plan and bond before construction and within 12 months of commercial operation.
The bond amount is 125 % of the initial estimate and may be increased annually or if the facility expands; owners may appeal changes to the board.
Decommissioning must begin within 12 months of abandonment or end of useful life and be finished within 24 months unless the department approves a plan.
Owners who fail to submit a bond within the required period face a $1,500 administrative penalty plus $1,500 per day of delay.
A wind/solar decommissioning account is created in the state special revenue fund to hold penalties and interest; the department may use these funds only for decommissioning activities.
Certain small or repurposed facilities, or those on private land with a bond already posted, are exempt from bond requirements.
affected: Wind and solar facility owners (≥25 MW wind, ≥2 MW solar)
Bond‑paying entities (federal, tribal, county, local governments)
Owners of facilities on private land with existing bonds

SB164.one_line: Rewrites child‑endangerment law, adds meth and treatment prohibitions, and expands penalties.
SB164.summary: The bill amends Montana’s child‑endangerment law to broaden the definition of endangerment, prohibit certain medical treatments for children under 16, and increase penalties for meth‑related offenses involving children. It also adds new evidence rules and allows parents to seek protection orders against unwanted contact with a child. The law takes effect January 1, 2026.
changes: Amends §45‑5‑622 to define endangerment for children under 18 and add specific prohibited activities (e.g., meth exposure, certain medical treatments for children under 16).
Adds new misdemeanor and felony penalties for endangerment, including higher fines and jail terms for meth‑related conduct and for providing prohibited treatments.
Provides a mechanism for parents to request that an adult stop contacting a child and to petition for a protection order under Title 40, Chapter 15.
Expands admissible evidence in endangerment cases to include a list of cruelty, neglect, and medical neglect indicators.
Allows courts to order forfeiture of fines or bonds to benefit the child whose welfare was endangered.
affected: Parents, guardians, and other supervisors of children under 18
Adults who provide medical treatments to children under 16
Individuals who expose children to methamphetamine or its paraphernalia
Adults who contact children in ways that parents deem harmful
Courts and prosecutors handling child‑endangerment cases

SB169.one_line: Redefines intangible personal property for tax exemption, effective Jan 1 2026.
SB169.summary: The bill amends Montana’s definition of intangible personal property for tax purposes, clarifying that items such as stocks, bonds, licenses, copyrights, patents, trademarks, contracts, software, and franchises are exempt unless they are integral to a business or utility. It removes the value of such property from the unit value of centrally assessed property and takes effect on Jan 1 2026 for tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑6‑218 to define intangible personal property more explicitly.
Specifies that intangible property is exempt unless integral to a business or centrally assessed utility.
Requires removal of intangible property value from the unit value of centrally assessed property.
Sets effective date of Jan 1 2026 and applicability to tax years after Dec 31 2025.
No new programs or criminal offenses are created.
No monetary allocations are included.
affected: Property owners of intangible assets (stocks, bonds, licenses, copyrights, patents, trademarks, contracts, software, franchises)
Municipalities and utilities subject to centrally assessed property taxes

SB171.one_line: Transfers excess general‑fund money to reserve, then to coal fund per set percentages.
SB171.summary: SB 171 requires the state treasurer to move any excess general‑fund money that exceeds 0.5 % of that year’s appropriations into the budget stabilization reserve fund, and then, if the reserve grows beyond 16 % of general‑revenue appropriations, to transfer the surplus to the capital‑development account and, ultimately, to the Montana Coal Severance Tax Permanent Fund. The transfers are scheduled each fiscal year by August 1 and take effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §17‑7‑130 to mandate a biennial transfer of excess general‑fund revenue to the budget stabilization reserve fund.
Specifies that once the reserve exceeds 16 % of general‑revenue appropriations, the surplus is moved to the capital‑development long‑range building program account.

Further limits the reserve to 12 % of general‑revenue appropriations in the second year of the biennium, after which excess funds are split: 75 % to the capital‑development account, 10 % to the Montana Coal Severance Tax Permanent Fund, and 15 % remain in the general fund.
Requires the treasurer to certify the unaudited ending balance and revenue transfers each year and to calculate the operating reserve level before making transfers.
Sets the effective date of the changes to July 1, 2025.

SB173.one_line: New renter credit, amended elderly credit, and biennial review of tax credits take effect immediately.
SB173.summary: The bill creates a new “workforce renter’s tax credit” for renters under 62 with household income below $45,000, adds special treatment for teachers, and amends the existing elderly residential property tax credit to adjust phase‑out thresholds and inflation. It also revises the definition of the elderly credit, expands the list of credits subject to biennial review, and repeals several 2021 provisions. The changes apply retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2024 and take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Establishes a workforce renter’s credit up to $1,750 for qualifying renters under 62 with income < $45,000, with a teacher exemption for non‑teacher income.
Amends the elderly residential property tax credit to include new phase‑out percentages, a maximum credit cap of $1,700, and an inflation adjustment of gross household income.
Adds the workforce renter’s credit to the list of tax credits scheduled for biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
Revises definitions (e.g., deed‑restricted apartment, gross rent, rent‑equivalent tax) used in the credit calculations.
Repeals sections 4, 5, 9, and 10 of Chapter 476, Laws of 2021, and codifies the new credit under Title 15, Chapter 30.
Provides that the credit is refundable if it exceeds a taxpayer’s liability and can be claimed even with no taxable income.
affected: Montana taxpayers who claim the credit

SB176.one_line: Prohibits firearm‑related discrimination in insurance/finance, requires nondiscrimination certificates, and allows enforcement and private suits.
SB176.summary: SB 176 prohibits discrimination based on firearm possession in insurance, finance, and related contracts, requiring a nondiscrimination certificate for licensed entities. Violations can be fined up to $5,000 per day and are enforceable by the Attorney General and private parties.
changes: Requires insurance and financial license applicants to submit a certificate of nondiscrimination to the Secretary of State; applications lacking the certificate are incomplete.
Makes such certificates public records available for inspection during normal business hours.
Defines a violation of nondiscrimination as a separate offense each day it occurs, with a maximum fine of $5,000 per day.
Allows the Attorney General or county attorney to seek court orders to enforce the nondiscrimination provisions.
Permits private individuals to sue for injunctive relief, compensatory and punitive damages, and attorney fees if harmed by a violation.
Excludes employer‑employee contracts and workplace policies from the act’s scope.
affected: Individuals or entities harmed by discriminatory practices
County attorneys and the Attorney General
Members of the public inspecting certificates

SB179.one_line: Allows nonprofit living‑history groups to hold casino nights for fundraising under a new permit system.
SB179.summary: SB 179 allows nonprofit living‑history groups, volunteers, and reenacting organizations to hold “wild west casino nights” for fundraising and education.  The bill creates a permit process, limits the length and type of gambling, and sets rules for prizes, expenses, and tax treatment.
changes: Creates a new “Wild West Casino Nights Act” permitting nonprofit living‑history entities to conduct live gambling events for fundraising and education.
Establishes a $25 application fee and a permit that may be issued once per year to a nonprofit, volunteer, or reenacting organization.
Limits each event to 12 consecutive hours (or two 6‑hour sessions on different days in the same calendar year).
Prohibits compensation to staff who manage the event and limits prizes to merchandise or cash, with cash prizes capped by existing statutory limits.
Requires that 50 % or less of proceeds be spent on administrative expenses and that all proceeds be used for civic, charitable, or educational purposes.
Provides that the department may adopt rules for application, play, and record‑keeping, and that the permit fee is retained for administrative purposes.
Exempts these events from the usual bingo/keno tax, rake‑off, and other licensing fees that apply to commercial gambling.
Allows antique gambling devices to be used only in these events or for display, with a separate $50 license for selling more than three devices per year.
Sets misdemeanor and felony penalties for violations that do not apply to the exempted living‑history activities.
Defines “wild west casino night” and related terms and codifies the provisions as a new part of Title 23, Chapter 5.
Effective immediately upon passage and approval.
numbers: 1% bingo/keno tax exemption for exempted entities
$1,000 annual manufacturer license fee (not applicable to antique devices)

SB180.one_line: Revises child‑custody and adoption law to include cultural factors and new presumptions on vexatious parenting plans.
SB180.summary: The bill updates Montana’s child‑custody and adoption laws to broaden the list of factors courts must weigh, explicitly adding Indian heritage and other cultural considerations. It also clarifies presumptions about vexatious parenting plans and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments of the changes.
changes: Amends §40‑4‑212 to include Indian heritage, cultural, religious, and spiritual factors in best‑interest determinations.
Adds rebuttable presumptions that a parenting plan motion within 6 months of a child‑support action or a motion to amend a final plan without good‑faith effort is vexatious.
Rewrites §42‑5‑107 to require courts to consider cultural and heritage factors in contested adoptions and to add a new factor (f) for Indian heritage.
Extends the definition of “best interests” to include the child’s heritage in both custody and adoption contexts.
Mandates the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1 2025.
Clarifies that Indian child placements must meet federal and state Indian Child Welfare Act requirements.
Adds language that a parenting plan action brought within 6 months after a child‑support action is presumed vexatious unless contrary evidence is shown.
affected: Parents and children in custody or adoption proceedings

SB185.one_line: Amend constitution to restrict voting to U.S. citizens 18+ and submit to 2026 voters.
SB185.summary: The bill proposes a constitutional amendment that limits voting rights to U.S. citizens 18 or older who meet registration and residency requirements. It requires a two‑thirds legislative vote and will be submitted to voters in the November 2026 election, becoming effective upon approval by the electorate.
changes: Amends Article IV, §2 of the Montana Constitution to define a qualified elector as a U.S. citizen 18+ who meets registration and residency requirements, excluding felons in prison or those of unsound mind.
Requires a two‑thirds affirmative roll‑call vote of the legislature to adopt the amendment.
Sets the amendment’s effective date as the moment it is approved by the electorate.
Mandates that the amendment be placed on the November 2026 general election ballot with a YES/NO option.

SB186.one_line: Phase out the Water Court and transfer all final‑decree water‑rights work to district courts.
SB186.summary: The bill re‑establishes the Water Court’s authority only while final decrees are pending and then phases it out, transferring all water‑rights adjudication and enforcement to local district courts once a basin’s final decree is entered.  It amends several water‑rights statutes to give district courts jurisdiction over final‑decree matters, requires the Water Court to cease operation 180 days after all appeals are resolved, and provides a retroactive application to earlier final decrees.
changes: Amends 3‑7‑101, 3‑7‑212, 3‑7‑224, 3‑7‑501, 85‑2‑214, 85‑2‑234, 85‑2‑236, 85‑2‑309, and 85‑2‑406 to shift jurisdiction from the Water Court to district courts once a basin’s final decree is issued.
Mandates that the Water Court, water divisions, and water judges cease operation 180 days after all appeals and post‑decree motions are resolved.
Provides that district courts may enforce final‑decree matters, including abandonment, waste, and distribution actions, and may use pro‑temp, special, or standing masters for expedited review.
Requires the Water Court to send copies of final decrees and certificates of water right to the department and to judicial districts.
Adds a retroactive applicability clause that applies the new rules to final decrees issued before the act’s effective date.
Defines “water case” for purposes of expedited processing and emergency relief in district courts.
Sets procedural steps for district courts to determine venue, expedite review, and transmit judgments to the department.
affected: Water rights holders (individuals, tribes, federal agencies)
Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

SB187.one_line: Rewrites Medicaid to extend expansion, broaden services, and add reporting and tribal consultation requirements.
SB187.summary: SB 187 revises Montana’s Medicaid program, removing the expansion termination date, expanding coverage to include auxiliary personnel and traditional healing services, and adding new funding principles and reporting requirements. It amends core Medicaid statutes, repeals several prior laws, and sets effective‑date contingencies tied to CMS approvals.
changes: Eliminates the termination date for the Medicaid expansion program and allows it to continue indefinitely.
Expands covered services to include auxiliary personnel services, traditional healing services, fertility preservation, and planned home births, among others.
Amends Sections 53‑6‑101 and 53‑6‑155 to redefine authorized services, funding principles, and definitions related to abuse, fraud, and provider roles.
Repeals Sections 28 (2015), 38 (2019), 17 (2019), and Sections 3‑4 (2021) that previously limited or defined Medicaid provisions.
Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to apply to CMS for state‑plan amendments and to consult tribal health officials.
Imposes reporting to legislative committees on proposed rate changes, waivers, and budget impacts, and sets priority‑setting rules if funds are insufficient.
Establishes contingency effective dates that depend on CMS approval within 10 days of notification.
Notifies federally recognized tribal governments of the act’s passage.
Creates new definitions for abuse, fraud, and provider types within Medicaid statutes.
affected: Tribal governments and Indian health programs
Department of Public Health and Human Services
Legislative committees overseeing health and finance
SB187.effective: as stated (contingent on CMS approval within 10 days of notification)

SB189.one_line: Lower property‑tax rates for agriculture and residential/commercial property, retroactive to 2025.
SB189.summary: The bill lowers property‑tax rates for agricultural (class III) and residential/commercial (class IV) property, eliminates the high‑value‑residence surcharge, and applies the changes retroactively to tax years after 12/31/2024.
changes: Class III agricultural land is now taxed at 2.16% (1.85% for non‑qualified parcels) of productive‑capacity value, with a seven‑fold multiplier for certain non‑qualified parcels
Class IV residential and commercial property is taxed at 1.35% (0.76% for residential) of market value, with a 40 % surcharge on single‑family homes valued over $1.5 million
The special high‑value‑residence tax rate is removed
The act applies retroactively to tax years beginning after 12/31/2024 and to the 2025 reappraisal cycle
The effective date is the day the bill is passed and approved
The bill amends sections 15‑6‑133 and 15‑6‑134 of the Montana Code to reflect the new rates and definitions

SB192.one_line: Montana levies a 10 % tax on large digital‑advertising firms with state revenue, filing, payment, and audit rules.
SB192.summary: Montana will impose a 10 % tax on digital‑advertising firms that earn at least $25 million worldwide and generate at least $1 million in the state.  The tax is assessed on the firm’s share of state revenue, calculated by a U.S.‑wide apportionment fraction, and the revenue is deposited into the general fund.
changes: Imposes a 10 % tax on the assessable base (state‑derived digital‑ad revenue) for firms with ≥$25 M worldwide gross revenue from digital advertising services.
Requires firms to file an annual return by April 15 and, if expected state revenue >$1 M, a quarterly estimated‑tax declaration.
Establishes a 25 % minimum quarterly payment on estimated tax and full payment with the annual return.
Provides audit authority and record‑keeping requirements for the past five years.
Sets penalties, interest, and a 5‑year statute of limitations for tax adjustments.
Mandates that all revenue be deposited into the general fund.
Specifies the act becomes effective January 1 2026.
affected: Digital advertising firms with ≥$25 M worldwide gross revenue
Firms with >$1 M state‑derived digital‑ad revenue

SB195.one_line: Allows 18‑20‑year‑olds to drink beer or wine with a 21‑year‑old parent, guardian, or spouse, subject to local ordinance.
SB195.summary: The bill allows adults 18‑20 to possess and drink beer or table wine with a parent, guardian, or spouse who is 21 or older, but only on private property or licensed premises that permit it. Local governments may opt‑in to this rule by ordinance or resolution. The bill also amends several alcohol‑sale statutes to clarify age‑verification, training, and liability provisions.
changes: 1. Permits 18‑20‑year‑olds to possess/consume beer or table wine with a 21‑year‑old parent, guardian, or spouse on private property or licensed premises that allow it.
2. Requires counties or cities to adopt an ordinance or resolution to allow such consumption, giving local governments an opt‑in mechanism.
3. Amends 16‑3‑301 to clarify that licensed retailers may not sell to anyone under 21 except as provided in Section 1, and adds liability language for misrepresentation.
4. Amends 16‑3‑309 to allow counties/cities to enact ordinances permitting alcohol consumption by 18‑20‑year‑olds and to certify such ordinances to the department.
5. Amends 16‑4‑1002 and 16‑4‑1006 to reinforce responsible‑server training requirements and to include the new 18‑20 rule in training curricula.
6. Amends 16‑6‑305 to exempt 18‑20‑year‑olds from the usual prohibition on providing alcohol to minors, while preserving other liability and misdemeanor provisions.
affected: 18‑20‑year‑olds who wish to drink beer or table wine
parents, legal guardians, or spouses 21+ who may provide alcohol
local governments that choose to adopt the ordinance

SB196.one_line: Clarifies DUI control definitions and adds aggravated‑DUI criteria without creating new programs.
SB196.summary: The bill amends Montana’s DUI statutes to clarify when a person is in “actual physical control” of a vehicle and to define “aggravated driving under the influence.” It does not create new programs or criminal offenses.
changes: Amends §61‑8‑1001 to define “actual physical control” as operating or driving a motor vehicle on public roads, excluding certain non‑propelled or disabled‑vehicle situations.

Adds a definition of “aggravated driving under the influence” that includes violations of §61‑8‑1002(1)(a‑d) with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.16 or higher, court‑ordered ignition‑interlock installation, prior DUI‑related license suspension, or refusal to provide a breath sample under implied‑consent rules.

Reiterates existing definitions for terms such as alcoholic beverage, alcohol concentration, bus, commercial motor vehicle, drug, DUI court, highway, motor home, motor vehicle, open alcoholic beverage container, passenger area, and under‑the‑influence.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
No fiscal impact is specified.
affected: Drivers of motor vehicles on Montana public roads
numbers: 0.5% alcohol by volume for alcoholic beverage

SB197.one_line: Reinstates pre‑2023 surety‑bail licensing rules and clarifies bail‑bond procedures.
SB197.summary: The bill amends Montana’s surety‑bail and insurance licensing rules to largely restore pre‑2023 requirements, modifies examination and licensing procedures, clarifies bail‑bond forms, and repeals three outdated statutes. It does not create a new program or crime.
changes: Amends §33‑17‑212 to require written exams for new licenses, except for certain pre‑1961 or already‑licensed producers; allows the commissioner to contract exam services and recover costs from applicants.
Revises §33‑26‑108 to give the commissioner rule‑making authority over surety insurers dealing with commercial bail bonds, including collateral and forfeiture reporting.
Redrafts §46‑9‑401 to list acceptable bail forms (cash, securities, real‑estate, surety bonds, or driver’s license) and sets conditions for driver’s‑license bail.
Rewrites §46‑9‑510 to allow defendants or surety producers to surrender defendants to court or peace officers, requiring reporting to the commissioner.
Repeals §§33‑17‑1601, 33‑17‑1602, and 46‑6‑508, eliminating obsolete licensing and arrest provisions.
affected: Insurance producers and applicants for surety‑bail licenses
Surety insurers and bail bond producers
numbers: double the bail value for real‑estate collateral

SB199.one_line: Amends Medicaid expansion with new fees, engagement rules, and termination dates, effective immediately.
SB199.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Medicaid expansion (HELP) program by adding new taxpayer‑integrity fees, expanding community‑engagement requirements, and tightening termination rules for the program. It also creates a special revenue account for the new fees and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2660 to impose monthly fees on HELP participants who own excess equity in real property, vehicles, or agricultural land, with fee tiers of $100 plus $4 per $1,000 of excess equity or $4 per $100 of taxable value above $1,500.
Rewrites §53‑6‑1308 to require HELP participants aged 19‑55 to complete 80 hours of community‑engagement activities each month, with specific activities counted and a list of exemptions.

Revises several termination provisions (Sections 28, 38, 48, 17, 3, 4) to set June 30 2025 as a new termination date unless federal waivers are renewed, and adds a contingency clause that would terminate the act if a court finds the community‑engagement requirements invalid.
Creates a special revenue account (53‑6‑1315) for collecting and depositing the new taxpayer‑integrity fees.
Allows the state to collect unpaid fees through future income‑tax assessments or civil action.
Adds a non‑severability clause making all parts of the act dependent on one another.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Taxpayers owning excess equity in real property, vehicles, or agricultural land
State Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB202.one_line: Allows judges to appoint custodians to receive workers’ comp payments for minors or incompetent persons.
SB202.summary: The bill authorizes a workers’ compensation judge to appoint a benefits custodian who can receive payments on behalf of minors or incompetent persons. It amends the statutes to define the custodian, expands the judge’s appointment authority, and sets a two‑year filing window for petitions.
changes: Amends §39‑71‑742 to allow payments to be made to a benefits custodian for minors or incompetent persons.
Defines “benefits custodian” as a person appointed by the workers’ compensation judge.
Expands §39‑71‑2905 to give the judge exclusive jurisdiction over disputes and the power to appoint or terminate a benefits custodian.
Adds a new subsection that requires petitions for a hearing before the judge to be filed within two years after benefits are denied.
Provides that a claimant, insurer, or uninsured employers’ fund may petition for a custodian without first satisfying other dispute‑resolution steps.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.

SB203.one_line: Lower Montana income‑tax brackets, raise thresholds, and apply retroactively to post‑2024 years.
SB203.summary: The bill amends Montana’s income‑tax brackets to lower rates for all filing statuses, increases the threshold before the higher rate applies, and applies the changes retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31 2024. It also updates the inflation‑adjustment rule for the brackets and sets an immediate effective date.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2103 to lower the 4.7% and 5.9% brackets and raise the income thresholds for married joint, head of household, and single filers
Replaces the 4.7%/5.9% rates with new 4.7%/5.9% brackets and adds a 3.0%/4.1% rate for net long‑term capital gains with adjusted thresholds
Adds a new subsection that applies the modified inflation factor only from tax year 2026 onward
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval
Provides retroactive applicability to tax years beginning after December 31 2024
Requires the Department to recalculate bracket amounts each year using the modified inflation factor and round to the nearest $100
affected: Montana taxpayers of all filing statuses, including married joint, head of household, single, and estates/trusts

SB204.one_line: Limits most mill levies to 10 years, requires voter re‑approval, and amends tax‑increment and building‑reserve rules.
SB204.summary: SB 204 revises Montana’s mill‑levy election rules to limit the duration of most levies to 10 years, require voter re‑approval after that period, and carve out exceptions for certain school, community‑college, law‑enforcement, fire‑protection, and emergency‑medical levies. It also amends tax‑increment and building‑reserve provisions and sets a January 1, 2026 effective date.
changes: Limits most new or increased mill levies to a maximum 10‑year term unless re‑approved by voters; levies terminate on December 31 of the 10th year and every 10 years thereafter.
Provides specific exceptions so that levies for school, community‑college, law‑enforcement, fire‑protection, and emergency‑medical services are not subject to the 10‑year limit.
Amends the tax‑increment calculation rules in § 7‑15‑4286 to clarify which mill rates are included or excluded for targeted economic‑development districts.
Rewrites § 15‑10‑425 to require a resolution or charter amendment that states purpose, amount, mills, and duration (not exceeding 10 years except for the exempt levies).
Adds a new § 20‑9‑502 amendment that allows school districts to create building‑reserve sub‑funds for future construction or land acquisition, with limits on duration and amount.
Sets the act’s effective date to January 1, 2026 and applies the new durational limits to elections held on or after that date.
affected: County, city, town, school district, community‑college, and other local taxing entities that impose or increase mill levies
Local governments that rely on mill levies for funding
School districts that use building‑reserve levies

SB205.one_line: Revises Montana’s bond‑and‑tax election rules with new turnout thresholds and immediate effect.
SB205.summary: SB 205 revises Montana’s voter‑approval rules for county and municipal bond issues and mill‑levy taxes, tightening the thresholds and procedures for elections and clarifying how votes are counted. The bill also updates related tax‑levy and bond‑authorization provisions across several chapters of the Montana Code.
changes: Replaces the calculation of voter approval for county bond elections with a tiered percentage‑vote system (50%+ of voters, 60%+ of votes if turnout 30‑40%, rejection if turnout ≤30%).
Replaces the calculation for city/town bond elections with a similar tiered system (50%+ of voters, 60%+ of votes if turnout 40‑50%, rejection if turnout ≤40%).
Requires a separate election for county bond issues that pledge county tax revenue, with the same tiered approval thresholds as above.
Amends the mill‑levy election process to use the same tiered thresholds and requires a majority of votes cast when turnout is 50%+ or 60%+ when turnout is 40‑50%.
Adds a new section stating the act takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to elections held on or after that date.
Updates numerous related sections (e.g., health‑care facility levies, parks levies, technology fund levies) to reference the new election‑approval criteria.
Clarifies that a bond may be issued without an election only if the total debt service does not exceed revenue from the pledged source.
Requires that any covenant to levy a general tax for bond deficiencies be approved by voters.
Adds language that bond issuances are exempt from state property tax.
Adds a new section for applicability and effective date.

SB207.one_line: Prohibits banning or censoring users on free digital public squares, allowing civil damages.
SB207.summary: The bill bars private companies from banning, deplatforming, or censoring users on free digital public squares unless it violates law. It defines key terms and allows companies to terminate the platform. Users can sue for damages.
changes: Prohibits businesses from limiting or abridge users’ right to assemble or speak on a digital public square via digital prohibition, including banning or deplatforming.
Defines "digital public square" as a free online platform for some or all users.
Defines "digital prohibition" as banning, deplatforming, or censoring a user, and "deplatforming" as removing a user without their request.
Allows a business to terminate the digital public square but not to censor content or create standards that violate the prohibition.
Provides that violations expose the business to actual and punitive damages in a user‑initiated action.
Exempts a business from violation if it offers advertisements to users.
Requires the provisions to be codified under Title 30, Chapter 14 of the Montana Code.

SB209.one_line: Limits conservation easements to 40 years, protects recent agricultural use, and updates tax rules.
SB209.summary: The bill limits conservation easements to a maximum of 40 years, prohibits restrictions that would limit current or recent agricultural use, and bars easements that require land to be turned over to federal control. It also updates definitions and tax‑assessment rules for easements and requires the Secretary of State to notify tribal governments.
changes: Limits easement terms to 15–40 years (perpetuity still allowed)
Prohibits easements that prohibit or limit agricultural production on land used within the past 10 years
Prohibits easements that require conversion of land to federal administration and control
Amends definitions of “conservation easement” and related terms
Revises tax‑assessment rules so land subject to an easement cannot be re‑valued lower solely because of the easement
Adds a notification requirement to federally recognized tribal governments
Specifies the act applies to easements entered on or after Oct. 1 2025
affected: Public bodies and qualifying private organizations holding easements
Tax assessors and property owners subject to easements

SB210.one_line: SB 210 eliminates the statutory student‑regent seat on Montana’s Board of Regents.
SB210.summary: SB 210 removes the statutory requirement that the Montana Board of Regents include a student regent, amending the board‑membership statute and providing a transition appointment.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑1508 to delete the student‑regent seat and its associated qualifications.
The student‑regent provision (subsection 3(a)–(b)) is removed from the statute.
A new transition clause (Section 2) creates a temporary appointment to fill the vacancy left by the removal, effective July 1 2025, ending January 31 2030.
The governor is directed to appoint a replacement on February 1 2030 for a full seven‑year term.
The act takes effect July 1 2025.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.

SB215.one_line: Rewrites school‑funding definition, adds new formula, open enrollment, and decennial review.
SB215.summary: SB 215 revises Montana’s definition of the basic public‑school system and requires a new, more detailed funding formula that considers enrollment, special‑needs, geographic, and achievement factors, while adding open‑enrollment and transparency provisions. The bill also mandates a decennial review of the formula.
changes: Amends §20‑9‑309, MCA, to expand the definition of a basic system of free quality public elementary and secondary schools to include special‑needs programs, Indian‑heritage curricula, qualified staff, transportation, student‑achievement tracking, open enrollment, and transparency requirements.

Mandates that the legislature develop a funding formula that reflects the costs of the expanded basic system, incorporates the listed educationally relevant factors, and provides annual inflation adjustments.

Requires the formula to distribute funds equitably, use a statewide per‑student amount with weighted adjustments for student needs, and allow funds to follow students across district lines without extra local taxes.
Calls for consolidation of the budgetary fund structure to give districts flexibility while maintaining accountability.
Establishes a school‑funding interim commission that must review the formula at least every ten years.
affected: Students (including special‑needs, at‑risk, limited‑English, gifted, and American Indian students)
numbers: statewide per‑student amount with weighted adjustments
no additional local taxes for open enrollment

SB216.one_line: Creates a GME grant program and task force to boost Montana’s physician workforce.
SB216.summary: The bill creates a state‑run grant program to help start graduate medical education (GME) programs and establishes a 12‑member task force to administer it. The program can award up to $2 million per applicant and is funded with $6 million from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium. The task force reports annually to the governor and specified committees.
changes: Creates a 12‑member Montana Graduate Medical Education Task Force with staff from the Department of Labor and Industry
Establishes a grant program for health‑sector facilities to start or expand GME programs, with a maximum award of $2 million per recipient
Requires grant applicants to submit specialty, accreditation proof, 2‑year cost projection, and 5‑year sustainability plan
Mandates recipients to provide equal consideration to all qualified medical graduates and to report annual data to the task force
Allocates $6 million from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium to fund the grant program
Task force must file an annual report by September 1 each year detailing expenditures, grant recipients, program status, and accreditation
The Department of Labor and Industry must staff the task force
The act takes effect July 1, 2025
affected: Department of Labor and Industry staff

SB219.one_line: Mandates tribal and veteran representation on Montana’s Board of Housing.
SB219.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Board of Housing to mandate that at least one member be an enrolled tribal member and at least one be a veteran, while preserving the board’s existing composition and powers. It also requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally‑recognized Montana tribes of the change.
changes: Amends Section 2‑15‑1814 to require a tribal member and a veteran on the seven‑member Board of Housing
Specifies that members must have experience in housing, economics, or finance
Allows the board to elect its own presiding officer and other officers
Maintains the board’s quasi‑judicial status and administrative allocation to the Department of Commerce
Grants the department staff and services as determined by the board, with cost assessment
Clarifies that a board member is not automatically a conflict of interest for being a stockholder, officer, or employee of a lending institution
Adds a new Section 2 directing the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana

SB220.one_line: Mandates satellite offices on reservations, expands ID options, and revises polling‑place and provisional‑ballot rules.
SB220.summary: SB 220 establishes permanent satellite election offices on Indian reservations, expands voter‑registration and identification options, and revises polling‑place, absentee‑ballot, and provisional‑ballot procedures to better serve tribal members. It also requires counties to notify tribal governments and sets a January 1, 2026 effective date.
changes: County election officials must open at least one satellite office on each reservation in the county, unless the tribe decides otherwise, and the office must be operational within seven days of the start of voter registration.
Satellite offices must provide the same services as county main offices, including replacement ballots, in‑person absentee voting, and late registration.

Voter‑registration applications may use a non‑traditional address and a broader set of acceptable photo IDs, including tribal photo IDs, military IDs, and concealed‑carry permits; provisional registration is allowed if full ID is not provided.
Polling‑place designations for reservations must be communicated by tribal governing bodies, and polling places may be moved only within the reservation if necessary.
Absentee‑ballot rules now allow provisional voters to include a copy of their photo ID or a utility bill with the ballot envelope, and tribal photo IDs need not show an address or expiration date.
Provisional‑ballot handling is expanded to give voters up to 5 p.m. the day after the election to provide ID, and detailed procedures for verifying provisional ballots are added.
Election administrators must designate places of deposit on reservations, with at least one per town more than 13 mi from a satellite office, and poll watchers must be allowed at these sites.
The Secretary of State must send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government.
numbers: 30 days before primary to designate polling place
10 days before election to publish polling places
5 p.m. the day after election to provide ID for provisional ballots

SB222.one_line: Repeals Montana’s 2‑year lobbying ban for former public employees, effective immediately.
SB222.summary: The bill removes Montana’s 2‑year lobbying ban that applied to former public employees, allowing them to lobby immediately after leaving office. The repeal takes effect as soon as the bill is enacted.
changes: Repeals Section 5‑7‑310 of the Montana Code, which prohibited former public employees from lobbying for two years after leaving office.
affected: Former public employees who previously were subject to the 2‑year lobbying ban.

SB229.one_line: Limits temporary investigative authority and bans child removal without separate court order.
SB229.summary: The bill amends Montana’s child‑abuse law to forbid the Department of Public Health and Human Services from removing a child while it holds temporary investigative authority. It limits the authority’s duration to 90 days and requires a separate court petition for any removal or emergency protection. No new program or fund is created.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑433 to prohibit removal of a child under temporary investigative authority.
Limits temporary investigative authority to no more than 90 days.
Requires the department to petition the court for immediate protection and emergency services if removal is sought outside the immediate removal provisions.
Preserves the existing procedure for serving the petition as provided in §41‑3‑422.
Maintains the department’s ability to conduct investigations into allegations of abuse, neglect, or abandonment.
Clarifies that removal authority must be obtained separately from temporary investigative authority.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Children involved in abuse or neglect investigations

SB225.one_line: Montana renters earn a refundable tax credit up to $500, phased out at $35‑$45k income, ending 2028.
SB225.summary: The bill creates a renter’s income‑tax credit for households earning under $45,000, with the credit capped at $500 (or a percentage of that amount for incomes between $35,000 and $45,000). It amends related tax‑credit statutes, establishes a review schedule for various credits, and sets a 2028 termination date. The credit is refundable if it exceeds tax liability and cannot be claimed together with the elderly property‑tax credit.
changes: Establishes a renter’s income‑tax credit against Montana individual income tax for households with gross income < $45,000, limited to the lesser of $500 or rent‑equivalent tax exceeding 4% of income.
Provides a graduated reduction of the credit for households earning $35,000–$44,999, ranging from 40% to 10% depending on income bracket.
Amends §§ 15‑30‑2303, 15‑30‑2337, and 15‑30‑2340 to include the new credit and to set review schedules for several other tax credits.
Adds a codification instruction that the new credit becomes part of Title 15, Chapter 30.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage, retroactive to tax years beginning after Dec 31 2024, and terminates Dec 31 2028.
affected: Montana taxpayers claiming the elderly residential property tax credit
Montana Department of Revenue (for credit administration and review)

SB231.one_line: Department must attach up‑to‑date law‑enforcement and court reports to affidavits in child‑abuse petitions.
SB231.summary: SB 231 amends Montana child‑abuse law to require the Department of Public Health and Human Services to attach up‑to‑date law‑enforcement and court reports to its affidavit in every abuse or neglect petition, and to obtain reports on any adult named in the petition before filing. The bill also revises procedural rules for petitions and adjudications.
changes: Department must file an affidavit with the petition that includes verified, up‑to‑date information and, if available, attachments of law‑enforcement reports and court records on any criminal case involving the child.
Department must obtain and attach law‑enforcement reports concerning any adult named in the petition before the affidavit is filed.
Affidavit must also include any evidence that contradicts or does not support the alleged abuse or neglect.
The bill amends sections 41‑3‑422 and 41‑3‑437 to update procedural requirements for petitions and adjudications.
The amendments establish that petitions must be given highest preference for hearing dates and set specific time limits for adjudicatory hearings.
The bill does not create new programs or criminal offenses; it only modifies existing statutes.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
County attorneys, attorneys general, and county‑hired attorneys who file petitions
Children and families in child‑abuse proceedings

SB230.one_line: Revises child‑abuse reporting, removal, and record rules, adding protections for children in domestic‑violence households.
SB230.summary: The bill amends Montana’s child‑abuse statutes to clarify when the department must report sexual‑abuse allegations, expand the circumstances under which a child protection specialist can remove a child, and tighten notification and record‑keeping requirements. It also adds procedures for protecting children when a household member is a victim of partner or family‑member assault.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑202 to require immediate county‑attorney reporting for sexual‑abuse cases involving perpetrators 12 + years old, with specific exceptions for confidential services and county‑attorney employees.
Revises §41‑3‑301 to set detailed notification requirements for parents and the state public defender when a child is removed, including a 5‑day hearing window and a 24‑hour affidavit delivery.

Adds a new subsection to §41‑3‑301 that allows the department to protect children when a household member is a victim of partner or family‑member assault or strangulation, including removal of the alleged offender and referral of the victim to domestic‑violence programs.

Expands record‑keeping rules: safety and risk assessments must be retained for 25 years unless destroyed within 30 days after a 3‑year period, with special retention for cases involving abuse, repeat reports, or court orders.
Requires the department to verify receipt of reports and describe the level of response to reporters, and to provide a written safety and risk assessment within 60 days of investigation.
Clarifies that a child removed from a home cannot be placed in jail and allows the department to contact extended family for placement.
Adds procedural language for filing abuse‑and‑neglect petitions and show‑cause hearings within specified time frames.

SB234.one_line: Fingerprint checks for massage‑therapist licenses become mandatory as of July 1, 2025.
SB234.summary: SB 234 requires all new and renewing massage‑therapist license applicants to submit fingerprints for state and federal background checks, adding a fee for the check. The bill amends the licensure qualifications to include this requirement and sets July 1, 2025 as the effective and applicability date.
changes: Mandates fingerprint submission for all new and renewal applicants; the board must obtain state and federal criminal history checks.
Adds a fee for the background check to the applicant’s costs.
Allows the Montana Department of Justice to share fingerprint data with the FBI.
Amends Section 37‑33‑502 to list fingerprint submission as a licensure qualification.
Specifies that the new requirement applies to applications filed on or after July 1, 2025.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1, 2025.
numbers: High school diploma or equivalent (already existing)

SB240.one_line: Large banks must explain service denials and cannot discriminate based on protected speech or religion.
SB240.summary: The Equality in Financial Services Act requires large banks and payment processors to explain why they deny or terminate service and prohibits discrimination based on protected speech, religion, or business activity. It creates civil remedies and penalties for violations.
changes: Defines “discrimination” as using a social‑credit score to deny or restrict services.
Limits the definition of a financial institution to banks with >$100 B in assets or payment processors with >$100 B in annual transactions, plus affiliates.

Mandates that any refusal, restriction, or termination must be followed, within 90 days, by a written statement of specific reasons, delivered within 30 days, detailing the basis of the decision and citing the relevant terms of service.
Prohibits financial institutions from discriminating or coordinating with others to do so.
Provides for civil damages of $10 000 or actual damages (whichever is greater), with a multiplier for willful violations, and allows injunctive relief.
Codifies the act into Title 30, Chapter 14, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
Effective July 1 2025.
severability clause ensures remaining provisions survive invalidity.
affected: Large banks and payment processors (assets or transaction thresholds)
Individuals, partnerships, corporations, nonprofits, and other entities that may be denied or restricted services
Financial institutions that may face civil litigation and damages

SB250.one_line: Expands ombudsman staff, powers, and reporting, requiring timely responses and oversight of child‑protective services.
SB250.summary: SB 250 expands the child‑and‑family ombudsman’s staff, powers, and reporting duties, requiring timely responses to assistance requests, active help for complainants, and systematic oversight of child‑protective services. It also mandates annual public reports and gives the ombudsman authority to forward misconduct to the Department of Justice.
changes: Adds six new positions (2 intake/outreach specialists, 2 associate ombudsmen, 2 research/data analysts) that the ombudsman may hire.
Broadens the ombudsman’s duties to include timely responses, active assistance, investigation of reports, and oversight of the department’s child‑protective services.
Requires the ombudsman to forward reports of misconduct by child‑protection specialists to the Department of Justice and to the department for policy violations.
Mandates that the ombudsman submit systemic oversight reports twice a year, with the department required to respond within 60 days or provide a written extension.
If the department fails to respond, the ombudsman must send the report to the governor, department director, and the Children, Families, Health and Human Services Interim Committee.
Repeals Section 41‑3‑1213, which previously dealt with privilege of the ombudsman’s office.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Children and families who file assistance requests

SB254.one_line: Prohibits public funds for hiring lobbyists, allowing only per‑diem travel for officials’ own lobbying.
SB254.summary: The bill bars school districts, local governments, and judicial officers from spending public money to hire lobbyists or pay nonprofit lobbying groups that represent political subdivisions. It allows public officials to receive per‑diem travel and expense allowances for lobbying on behalf of their own subdivision or judiciary. The bill also amends conduct rules for public officers and expands limits on local‑government powers, but the core change is the prohibition on public‑funded lobbying.
changes: 1. Political subdivisions and judicial officers may not use public funds to hire or contract an individual for lobbying or to pay a nonprofit association that primarily represents political subdivisions and hires lobbyists.
2. Public officials may still receive per‑diem travel and expense allowances for lobbying on behalf of their own subdivision or judiciary.
3. Taxpayers or residents can seek injunctive relief and recover attorney fees if the prohibition is violated.
4. The bill amends 2‑2‑121 (rules of conduct for public officers) to clarify permissible lobbying activities and to prohibit certain private‑business lobbying.
5. Section 7‑1‑111 is amended to restrict local‑government powers that affect private or civil relationships, public schools, environmental decisions, and other areas.
6. The bill codifies the new restrictions as part of Title 5, Chapter 7.
affected: taxpayers and residents of affected subdivisions
numbers: no specific dollar amounts for new restrictions

SB259.one_line: Amends child‑protection law to clarify removal, notification, and domestic‑violence procedures.
SB259.summary: The bill amends child‑protection law to clarify when a child may be removed, expands notification and hearing requirements, and adds procedures for handling cases involving domestic‑violence victims. It also defines “imminent danger” and limits removal to jail.
changes: Amends §41‑3‑301 to allow immediate removal when a child is in imminent danger and to require notification of parents/guardians within 24 hours
Adds a requirement that law‑enforcement officers provide body‑camera footage to the judge and family at the initial hearing
Requires child‑protection specialists to file an affidavit and a petition within specified time‑frames after an emergency removal
Expands procedures for children whose parents are victims of partner or family‑member assault, including efforts to keep the child with the victim and to prevent removal
Defines “imminent danger” as certain, immediate, and impending danger with a high probability of death or serious injury
Provides that a child removed from a home may not be placed in jail and may be placed in a kinship foster home
Extends notification to include rights to attend hearings, receive copies of affidavits, and request kinship placement
Adds a requirement that the department may contact extended family for placement and case‑planning purposes

SB263.one_line: Amends water‑right rules to require board approval before the state claims lessee water rights.
SB263.summary: The bill amends the state’s water‑rights law to clarify that lessees may install and remove water‑related improvements on state land without departmental approval, and it creates a formal board‑review process before the state can claim ownership of a lessee’s water right. The new rules require notice, a hearing, and a 90‑day window for the department to seek court action. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §77‑6‑301 to allow lessees to install and remove water‑right improvements (e.g., wells, ditches, stock tanks) on state land without department authorization, provided the owner gives 90‑day notice of removal.
Creates §2 that bars the department from acquiring ownership of a lessee’s water right unless the Land Board authorizes it.
Requires the department to give a lessee 180‑day notice before seeking ownership and to submit a 90‑day notice to the board before filing a legal claim.
Provides a 60‑day window for the lessee or water‑right owner to request a board hearing to oppose the department’s claim.
If the board approves, the department may pursue legal proceedings to obtain ownership, with the court deciding the state’s interest.
Mandates the department to submit a list of all water rights it has acquired from lessees since July 1 1982 within 180 days of the act’s effective date.
Codifies the new section as part of Title 77, Chapter 1, Part 1, and makes the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Water‑right owners who lease state land
Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

SB255.one_line: Montana requires a $200 ID card for all adult recreational marijuana purchases, creating a new registry and revenue account.
SB255.summary: The bill creates a mandatory marijuana‑identification card system for adults 21+ who wish to buy recreational marijuana or products.  Cardholders must pay a $200 fee, provide proof of residency, and receive a laminated card that includes a photo, unique ID, and tracking data.  The state establishes a registry, sets up a seed‑to‑sale tracking system, and creates a special revenue account for marijuana taxes and penalties.  The bill also amends many existing marijuana statutes to incorporate the new card requirements, expand record‑keeping, and clarify enforcement and licensing procedures.
changes: Creates a new Montana Marijuana Identification Card (M‑ID) that must be held by anyone 21+ who purchases recreational marijuana or products; card costs $200 and is valid for one year.
Establishes a state registry of all cardholders and requires the Department of Revenue to issue, renew, and track cards, including photo and unique ID number.
Mandates that all adult‑use dispensaries and other licensed marijuana businesses verify a cardholder’s card and photo ID before sale and must track purchases in a seed‑to‑sale system.
Creates a dedicated marijuana state special revenue account in the state special revenue fund; excess funds are transferred to the HEART account and other specified accounts each fiscal year.
Requires the Department to adopt rules for card application, fee collection, renewal, and loss/expiration; cardholders must report name or address changes within 10 days.

Establishes penalties for non‑compliance with card rules (e.g., civil fines up to $250 for visible plants, $50 for public smoking, etc.) and for violations by licensees (up to $3,000 civil penalty or license revocation).
Sets effective dates: the card system becomes effective October 1 2025; the new provisions apply to sales on or after January 1 2026.
affected: Montana residents 21+ who wish to purchase recreational marijuana
Adult‑use dispensaries and other licensed marijuana businesses
The Department of Revenue and its staff
Law enforcement officers and the judiciary
numbers: $20 minimum annual fee for registered medical cardholders
$6 million cap for HEART account transfer
$20 minimum annual fee for registered cardholders
$250 civil fine for plants outside locked space
$6 million cap for HEART account transfer
$200,000 for veterans and surviving spouses account
$20 minimum annual fee for registered cardholders
$200 civil fine for plants outside locked space
$250 civil fine for plants visible from public
SB255.effective: October 1, 2025 (card system) and January 1, 2026 (applicability to sales)

SB267.one_line: Montana offers a 50 % tax credit, capped at $500,000, for charitable gifts to certified public‑infrastructure projects, effective 2026.
SB267.summary: Montana will allow taxpayers to claim a 50 % tax credit—up to $500,000—for charitable gifts to certified public‑infrastructure projects such as health clinics, senior centers, libraries, and museums. The credit can be carried forward for three years but cannot be refunded. The bill also adds the credit to the list of tax credits subject to biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
changes: Creates a new 50 % tax credit for charitable gifts to certified public‑infrastructure projects, capped at $500,000 per taxpayer per year.
Limits the credit to a maximum of $500,000 and allows it to be carried forward for three years but not refunded.
Requires state or local governments to submit eligibility information to the Department and for the Department to issue a receipt to the taxpayer.
Adds the new credit to the list of tax credits that the revenue interim committee must review biennially.
Codifies the credit under Title 15, chapters 30 and 31, and sets the effective date to income‑tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Amends § 15‑30‑2303 to include the new credit in the biennial review schedule.
No new program or criminal offense is created; it merely establishes a credit and reporting requirements.
affected: Individual taxpayers who donate to certified public‑infrastructure projects
State and local governments that certify and receive such projects
Montana Department of Revenue (for receipt issuance and record‑keeping)

SB266.one_line: Mandates multi‑unit housing in 5,000‑plus cities and requires adoption of specific housing‑promotion strategies.
SB266.summary: This bill amends Montana’s zoning statutes to require cities of 5,000+ residents to allow duplexes, triplexes, and fourplexes wherever single‑family homes are permitted, and to make those multi‑unit regulations no stricter than single‑family rules. It also adds a list of housing‑promotion strategies that local governments must adopt or be deemed to have adopted, and limits certain restrictive zoning practices.
changes: 1. Amends §76‑2‑304 to mandate that in municipalities with ≥5,000 residents, duplexes, triplexes, and fourplexes be permitted on any lot where a single‑family home is permitted, and that their regulations cannot be more restrictive than those for single‑family homes.

2. Adds §76‑25‑302 housing‑strategy requirements, obligating local governments to adopt at least five of a set of specified strategies (e.g., higher density near transit, reduced parking, removal of lot‑size limits, etc.) or be deemed to have adopted them if not already in place.

3. Inserts §76‑25‑303 limitations, prohibiting local governments from treating manufactured housing differently, imposing income‑level fees or property designations, restricting amateur radio antennas, and from imposing more restrictive rules on multi‑unit dwellings than on single‑family homes.
4. Provides definitions for duplex, triplex, fourplex, mixed‑use, multiple‑unit dwelling, and single‑family residence.
5. Sets a delayed effective date of October 1, 2026.
affected: Property owners and developers of multi‑unit housing
numbers: 25% reductions in parking, lot‑size, setbacks, etc.

SB268.one_line: Extends and expands the dependency‑court task force, setting new membership, study scope, and reporting deadlines.
SB268.summary: The bill extends the existing Task Force on Dependency and Neglect Court System through 2027, expands its membership, clarifies appointment and compensation rules, and sets a deadline for a final report and draft legislation. It does not create new programs or criminal offenses.
changes: Extends the task force’s term to June 30 2027 (previously 2025).
Adds a new member category: a tribal member with Indian Child Welfare Act experience, and clarifies the seven governor‑appointed members.
Requires all appointments to be made by July 1 2025 and allows the task force to fill vacancies after 60 days.
Expands the study scope to include both a separate court system and enhancements to the existing system, with detailed sub‑topics.
Limits task‑force meetings to no more than 12 days and requires a final report by September 15 2026.
Provides compensation rules for legislative and non‑legislative members, including travel and per diem.
Sets the effective date of the act to May 1 2025.
affected: Legislators, state agencies, county attorneys, law‑enforcement officers, child‑protection specialists, tribal members, public defenders, public‑health and corrections staff, and the general public involved in dependency and neglect cases.

SB269.one_line: SB 269 tightens day‑care health, safety, staffing, and background‑check rules in Montana.
SB269.summary: SB 269 amends Montana’s day‑care laws to tighten health, safety, staffing, and background‑check requirements for family and group day‑care homes. It adds detailed rules on insurance, contracts, space, discipline, sanitation, emergency plans, parental involvement, nutrition, supervision ratios, training, and qualifications, and limits the Department’s ability to impose stricter rules than the statute.
changes: Providers must keep proof of liability insurance and signed contracts with each family, including change‑notification clauses
Providers must submit annual fire, safety, and sanitation inspection reports and keep them available to the Department
Providers must maintain detailed vaccination records, notify of communicable illnesses, and follow strict medication and topical‑care protocols
Providers must adopt comprehensive fire‑safety and emergency‑response plans, conduct quarterly evacuation drills, and keep first‑aid supplies
Providers must limit children to 8 in a family home and 15 in a group home (with stricter ratios for infants), allow up to 3‑hour overlap care with written plans

Providers must complete a 3‑month‑old orientation training covering infection control, emergency response, and child‑maltreatment reporting, and staff working >500 hrs must do 16 hrs of ongoing professional development annually

Background checks (fingerprint, sex‑offender registry, child‑protective‑services, criminal record) are required every 5 years for all adults who work or reside in the home; the Department may suspend or revoke licenses for certain convictions
The Department may not adopt rules that are more stringent than the statutory requirements
The bill amends sections 52‑2‑704 and 52‑2‑714 to clarify the Department’s duties and scholarship program oversight
The act becomes effective the day after the 69th session adjourns
affected: support staff, volunteers, and residents of day‑care homes
parents and legal guardians of children in care
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services
SB269.effective: the day after the 69th regular legislative session adjourns

SB270.one_line: Amends elk‑licensing rules, adds replacement and special antlerless tags, sets fees, effective March 1 2026.
SB270.summary: The bill amends Montana’s elk‑licensing rules to allow the Department to issue replacement and special antlerless elk tags, set new fee structures, and give the commission authority to adjust fees and licensing limits. It also updates the resident deer‑and‑elk license fee schedule and establishes a March 1 , 2026 effective date.
changes: Amends §87‑2‑104 to permit replacement tags for lost, stolen, or destroyed licenses and for animals deemed unfit for consumption, with a $5 fee cap for replacements.
Adds rulemaking authority for the Department to issue multiple special licenses (antlerless elk, moose, bison, sheep) and to set hunting districts, numbers, and terms.
Specifies that Class B‑12 nonresident antlerless elk B tags cost $270 unless reduced by the commission.
Allows residents to obtain up to four antlerless elk B tags per license year and permits variable structures based on management goals.
Updates §87‑2‑501 to list the resident deer, elk, and bear license fees, including the new $20 fee for a resident antlerless elk B tag.
Adds a new section stating the act takes effect March 1 , 2026.
affected: Residents and non‑residents who hunt elk, deer, and other game
Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks (DFWPA) officials
numbers: $270 Class B‑12 antlerless elk B tag fee
$20 resident antlerless elk B tag fee
up to four antlerless elk B tags per resident per year

SB272.one_line: Establishes conduct rules for child‑protection specialists and complaint procedures.
SB272.summary: The bill creates a set of conduct rules for child‑protection specialists, allows parents or guardians to file complaints with the Child and Family Ombudsman, and authorizes the Commissioner of Political Practices to investigate those complaints using case information from the Department of Public Health and Human Services.  It also limits public access to certain hearing documents and amends related statutory sections.
changes: Defines prohibited conduct for specialists, including threatening criminal charges and preventing foster placement or guardianship based on advice or testimony.
Makes any violation a breach of public duty and allows filing of complaints with the Child and Family Ombudsman.
Empowers the Commissioner of Political Practices to investigate complaints and requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to disclose case information for that purpose.
Establishes that informal contested hearings are not open to the public and that certain documents are not public information.
Amends sections 2‑2‑136 and 41‑3‑205 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new rules.
Codifies the rules as part of Title 41, Chapter 3, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
affected: Applicants for certification as child protection specialists
Parents, guardians, and other persons with custody of a child
The Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB273.one_line: Broadens assault definition, sets penalties, and gives victims sole filing authority.
SB273.summary: The bill amends Montana’s assault statute to broaden the definition, sets a $500 fine or up to six months in county jail, and gives victims the sole authority to decide whether to file a charge—except when the victim is disabled.
changes: Amends §45‑5‑201 to include five new assault elements (bodily injury, negligent weapon use, insulting contact, reasonable apprehension, and drug‑related assault).
Adds a penalty of up to $500 fine, up to six months in county jail, or both for a conviction.
States that the victim alone decides if a charge is filed, except when the victim is developmentally disabled, physically disabled, or mentally ill.

SB277.one_line: Prohibits public employers from deducting or collecting union dues or political contributions from employees’ pay.
SB277.summary: SB 277 bars public employers from deducting or helping collect union dues, political committee fees, or other political contributions from public employees’ pay. It amends several Montana Code sections to define the practice as an unfair labor practice and sets July 1 2025 as the effective date for new collective‑bargaining agreements.
changes: Amends §2‑2‑121 and §2‑2‑122 to prohibit public employers from using public resources to collect or facilitate union or political contributions.
Rewrites §17‑8‑212 to allow state‑sponsored deductions for union dues and political contributions only with written employee authorization.
Rewrites §39‑31‑203 to make deduction or assistance in collecting dues, fees, or contributions from public employees unlawful and treat violations as ethics violations.
Rewrites §39‑31‑401 to add deduction/collection of dues or contributions as an unfair labor practice for public employers.
Rewrites §39‑31‑402 to add the same prohibition for labor organizations and to forbid using agency‑shop fees for political contributions.
Adds a severability clause, effective‑date clause (July 1 2025), and applicability clause limiting the act to agreements executed or modified on or after that date.
affected: Public employers (state agencies, school districts, etc.)
Union dues and political contribution collectors

SB274.one_line: Extends property‑tax relief to 60‑90 % disabled veterans and updates income‑based multipliers.
SB274.summary: SB 274 revises Montana’s disabled‑veteran property‑tax‑assistance program to extend benefits to veterans rated 60 %–90 % disabled, updates income‑based multipliers, and sets an immediate effective date with applicability from 2026.
changes: Amends §15‑6‑301 to define terms such as “annual verification,” “PCE inflation factor,” and “qualified veteran.”

Amends §15‑6‑311 to expand eligibility to veterans with 60 %–90 % disability ratings and to adjust the income‑multiplier tables for single, married, head‑of‑household, and surviving‑spouse categories.
Adds a new section that makes the act effective immediately upon passage and sets the first applicable property‑tax year to begin after December 31 2025.
Requires qualifying‑income thresholds to be adjusted annually using the PCE inflation factor, rounded to the nearest dollar, with a rule that prevents a decrease in thresholds.
Keeps the property‑tax‑exemption in effect only while income and residency requirements are met and the veteran or spouse is the owner and occupant.
Defines the “primary residence” and “qualified property” for the purpose of the program.
Clarifies that the exemption applies only to the veteran’s or spouse’s primary residence and not to additional dwellings.
Ensures that the exemption is tied to the veteran’s or spouse’s disability rating as verified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

SB281.one_line: Prohibits electioneering within 100 feet of polling places and outside lines of voters, with immediate effect.
SB281.summary: The bill amends Montana’s election‑electioning statute to prohibit campaigning within 100 feet of a polling place or a line of voters outside the location. It also bars candidates and their staff from giving food, drink, or other items to voters in those areas and prohibits the display of campaign insignia at the polls. The act requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally recognized tribal governments and takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §13‑35‑211 to add a 100‑foot restriction around polling places and outside lines of voters;
Prohibits candidates, family members, and campaign workers from distributing alcohol, tobacco, food, drink, or other items to voters within those 100‑foot zones;
Bans the sale, display, or wearing of campaign badges, buttons, or insignia at or near the polls;
Prevents soliciting voting intentions from electors before or after they cast a ballot;
Mandates the Secretary of State to send a copy of the new law to every federally recognized tribal government;
The law becomes effective immediately upon passage and approval.

SB283.one_line: Limits turbine height to 350 ft and requires FAA lighting on towers over 200 ft, effective 2026.
SB283.summary: The bill limits wind turbine towers to 350 ft and requires FAA‑approved aircraft‑detection lighting on towers over 200 ft, applying to facilities ≥25 MW. It takes effect Jan 1 2026, with a delayed start for new installations. Existing towers are exempt.
changes: Sets a maximum tower height of 350 ft for new or installed turbines (from ground to rotor hub).
Exempts towers built before Jan 1 2026 from the height limit.
Mandates FAA‑approved aircraft‑detection lighting on all turbines over 200 ft in height.
Prohibits excessive lighting on turbines, except for FAA minimums.
Defines key terms such as turbine rotor hub, wind generation facility, and aircraft‑detecting lighting system.
Codifies the provisions into Title 75, Chapter 26 of the Montana Code.
Effective date of all provisions is Jan 1 2026.
affected: Wind turbine owners/operators with facilities ≥25 MW
State regulatory agencies overseeing wind energy

SB284.one_line: Merges 10th/14th districts, adds a ninth judge to the 13th, revises judge counts, and sets transition and effective dates.
SB284.summary: The bill merges the 10th and 14th judicial districts, adds a ninth judge to the 13th district, and revises the statutory list of districts and judge counts. It sets transition rules for vacancies and specifies effective dates.
changes: Redefines the 22 judicial districts and their county compositions (Section 1).
Sets the number of judges per district, adding a ninth judge to the 13th district and adjusting counts for several others (Section 2).

Merges the 10th and 14th districts into a single district; prohibits gubernatorial appointments to vacancies in those districts and requires senate confirmation for the new 13th‑district judge (Section 3).
Requires a 6‑year election for the ninth judge in the 13th district at the November 2030 election (Section 3).
Establishes effective dates: the act takes effect on passage, with Sections 1‑2 effective Jan 6 2031 or earlier if a vacancy occurs (Section 4).
affected: Judges and judicial staff in the 10th, 14th, and 13th districts
County residents served by those districts

SB285.one_line: Amends child‑care licensing rules, updates terminology, safety, staffing, and immunization requirements.
SB285.summary: The bill amends the child‑care licensing rules to align terminology with state statutes, clarify definitions, and update requirements for day‑care centers, family and group homes, and other care settings. It removes references to school‑age care from the day‑care rules, revises licensing and registration thresholds, and adds detailed standards for staffing, safety, hygiene, nutrition, and immunization. The changes also expand background‑check requirements and establish new training and certification obligations for staff and directors.
changes: Renames all child‑care terms to match statutory language (e.g., “child care center” → “day‑care center”).
Replaces references to school‑age care in day‑care rules and limits the scope of the rules to day‑care facilities only.
