Rewrites definitions for applicants, capacity, child, child‑care, center, facility, and related terms, and adds new definitions for RCE, FFN, and others.

Revises licensing and registration thresholds: day‑care centers must be licensed; group and family homes must register; school‑age and drop‑in facilities may opt for licensing or registration; providers serving seven or more children must be licensed or registered.
Adds detailed child‑to‑staff ratios, group‑size limits, and special rules for nap time, night care, and overlap care.
Introduces comprehensive safety, hygiene, and environmental rules for indoor/outdoor space, fire safety, water supply, and sanitation.
Sets strict requirements for director, teacher, substitute, trainee, and support staff qualifications, including background checks, CPR/first‑aid certification, and annual training.
Expands immunization requirements for children in all licensed/registered day‑care facilities and clarifies exemptions for medical, religious, foster‑care, and homeless children.
Repeals several obsolete administrative rules (e.g., ARM 37.96.806, 901, 903, 904, 908, 910).
affected: Directors, teachers, substitutes, trainees, support staff
Parents and guardians of children in care
numbers: 30‑day conditional attendance grace period for homeless/foster children
SB285.effective: first day following final adjournment of the 69th regular legislative session

SB287.one_line: Creates a multi‑account trust, expands tax‑assistance, and redefines pension and debt‑free fund rules.
SB287.summary: The bill creates a Montana Growth and Opportunity Trust that receives volatile revenues and distributes interest to several special‑revenue accounts, establishes new state‑special‑revenue accounts for water development, better local bridges, early childhood, and property‑tax assistance, and sets rules for transferring and investing those funds. It also amends many property‑tax, pension, and debt‑management statutes, expands the state property‑tax‑assistance program, and creates new boards and trust funds for early childhood and housing. The act requires the treasurer to transfer specific amounts from the general fund to the new accounts and to set transfer limits and reporting requirements.
changes: Creates the Montana Growth and Opportunity Trust and defines its funding, investment, and distribution rules.
Establishes four new state‑special‑revenue accounts (water development, better local bridge, early childhood, property‑tax assistance) and sets how interest from the Trust is allocated to them.
Amends property‑tax notice, appraisal, and appeal procedures (15‑7‑102, 15‑15‑101‑103) to provide more information and streamline informal reviews.

Revises pension and debt‑free account rules (17‑6‑214, 17‑7‑130, 17‑7‑134) to change how interest income is split between the general fund and debt‑free account and how transfers to pension funds are made.
Extends the state property‑tax‑assistance program to primary residences, adds certification, penalty, and appeal provisions (sections 30‑33).
Provides detailed transfer schedules from the general fund to the new accounts and sets limits on volatile‑revenue transfers (section 18).
Adds new boards (early childhood, housing trust) and outlines their membership, duties, and funding limits.
Rewrites several finance and budget‑stabilization provisions (17‑7‑130, 17‑7‑134, 17‑6‑214) to change how surplus funds are moved to the Trust, pension fund, and debt‑free account.
Imposes new reporting and audit requirements for the Trust and the special‑revenue accounts.
Sets effective date as passage and approval.

SB290.one_line: Mandates higher liability limits for TNC drivers and adds under‑insured coverage to all motor‑vehicle policies.
SB290.summary: The bill expands mandatory liability coverage for motor vehicles in Montana to include under‑insured motorists and requires drivers of transportation‑network‑carrier (TNC) vehicles to carry higher limits and proof of coverage. It amends existing statutes to add coverage options and enforcement provisions for TNC drivers.
changes: Adds under‑insured motorist coverage to the list of required coverages for all motor‑vehicle liability policies.
Allows the named insured to reject under‑insured motorist coverage, but only if the insurer is not required to provide it at renewal.

Amends the TNC driver insurance requirements to require $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident / $25,000 property damage while logged on but not in a ride, and $1,000,000 per incident while in a ride.
Mandates that TNC drivers carry proof of coverage and disclose coverage status and ride status to police and insurers in an accident.
Requires that if a driver’s personal policy lapses or is insufficient, the TNC’s policy must cover the claim from the first dollar and defend the claim.
Allows TNC insurance to be held by the driver, the carrier, or a combination, and permits placement with any insurer authorized under Title 33, including surplus lines.
affected: Motor vehicle owners and drivers in Montana
Police and insurers involved in accident investigations

SB291.one_line: Revises wage definition for workers’ comp, adds lodging, and requires annual rule updates.
SB291.summary: The bill amends Montana’s workers’‑compensation wage definition to add lodging and other non‑cash benefits, requires the Department of Labor to update the lodging‑value rule each year, and clarifies how wages are calculated for benefit purposes.
changes: Amends §39‑71‑123 to include lodging, rent, and housing as wages when based on actual value set by administrative rule
Adds a requirement that the Department of Labor annually revise the rule that sets the value of lodging used in wage calculations
Expands the list of items that are considered wages (e.g., board, piecework, incentive plans, profit‑sharing, etc.)
Specifies that wages do not include certain reimbursements, retirement, disability, medical, death, vacation, or public‑assistance payments
Clarifies wage calculation methods for injury claims, including use of the last four pay periods or an extended period up to one year
Defines how wages are calculated for concurrent employment and volunteers for compensation benefit purposes
numbers: Montana Informational Wage Rates by Occupation

SB292.one_line: Expands seller liability for economic harm and adds defenses and presumptions to Montana product‑liability law.
SB292.summary: SB 292 expands Montana’s product‑liability law to hold sellers liable for economic harm caused by unreasonably dangerous products and adds a host of affirmative defenses and presumptions. The bill amends §27‑1‑719 to make sellers responsible for both physical and economic injury, even if they exercised all care, and sets strict time limits and conditions for bringing claims.
changes: Amends §27‑1‑719 to make sellers liable for economic harm from defective, unreasonably dangerous products; requires seller to be in the business of selling and product to reach consumer unchanged.
Adds a rebuttably presumed non‑defect and non‑negligence of seller unless evidence shows otherwise.
Provides a list of affirmative defenses for sellers, including misuse, contributory negligence, and lack of control over manufacturing.
Imposes a 10‑year statute of limitations for most claims, with exceptions for concealed defects, recalls, real‑property products, and long‑latency diseases.
Requires plaintiffs to prove by preponderance that a seller had substantial control over manufacturing or that the seller was not also the manufacturer unless specific conditions are met.
Defines key terms such as "seller," "manufacturer," and "product liability action."
affected: Plaintiffs seeking economic or physical injury damages
numbers: 2‑year limitation for products with >10‑year useful life
January 1 2031 termination of certain seller definition

SB294.one_line: Utilities must file 100% renewable plans by mid‑2026 for committee review.
SB294.summary: Montana utilities must submit a 100% renewable‑energy plan by mid‑2026, and the Energy & Telecommunications Interim Committee will review, solicit public comment, and recommend actions to the Legislature.
changes: 1. Requires every public utility to develop a plan for 100 % renewable retail sales by May 30, 2026.
2. The plan must also address greenhouse‑gas‑emission reductions.
3. Utilities must file the plan with the Energy & Telecommunications Interim Committee by June 1, 2026.
4. The committee must review the plans, invite public comment, and submit any recommendations to the Legislature.
5. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.

SB293.one_line: Claimants may request insurer coverage limits before suing, with insurers required to respond within 45 days or face sanctions.
SB293.summary: Claimants may now request a potential tortfeasor’s insurance limits before filing suit.  Insurers must respond within 45 days, or face court‑ordered sanctions.  The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Allows a claimant to serve a written request for insurance coverage and limits on the insurer of a potentially liable party before filing a personal‑injury or wrongful‑death action.
The request must be signed by the claimant’s attorney or the claimant if unrepresented and must state that the claim is well‑grounded and not intended to harass.
Insurers must reply with a statement of existence and limits of coverage within 45 days of service.
If an insurer fails to respond, the claimant may petition the court in the subsequent action to impose sanctions for non‑compliance.
The requested insurance information is not admissible as evidence at trial, and disclosure must comply with the Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act.
The new provision is codified as part of Title 27, chapter 1, part 2, and takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Claimants seeking personal‑injury or wrongful‑death damages

SB298.one_line: Expands the Secretary of State’s duties and gives it supervisory power over county election administrators.
SB298.summary: The bill amends the Montana Constitution and statutes to expand the Secretary of State’s duties, give the office supervisory authority over county election administrators, and impose new filing rules for entities using the term “cooperative.” It also adds reporting and record‑keeping requirements for the Secretary of State.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑401 to add 15 new duties for the Secretary of State, including fee‑book maintenance, electronic filing system development, and reporting on watercourse name changes.
Adds a supervisory power clause (§5) that allows the Secretary of State to direct county election administrators and require reports on voter registration and election management.
Amends §13‑1‑301 to clarify that the county clerk/recorder is the election administrator unless otherwise designated, and gives the Secretary of State supervisory authority over them.

Adds a new subsection (3) to §2‑15‑401 that prohibits the Secretary of State from accepting filings from entities that use “cooperative” in their name unless they are a cooperative under specific statutes, with a fine of $50‑$1,000 for violations.
Provides that the prohibition does not apply to entities formed before October 1 2023.
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1 2025.
affected: Business entities using “cooperative” in their name
Secretary of State and its staff

SB295.one_line: Restores injured workers’ right to choose a treating physician and clarifies insurer designation and reimbursement rules.
SB295.summary: The bill restores an injured worker’s right to pick a treating physician and clarifies how insurers may designate or approve doctors, including managed‑care and preferred‑provider arrangements. It amends the workers’‑compensation statutes to require written notice, set reimbursement rates, and limits insurer liability for non‑preferred care. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Workers may choose an initial treating physician from the list in §39‑71‑116(42) and can later change the doctor with insurer consent.
Insurers may designate or approve a treating physician after liability is accepted, but the worker’s choice takes precedence if the chosen doctor agrees to the insurer’s requirements.
Reimbursement rates are set: 110 % of the department’s fee schedule for the designated treating physician, 90 % for referred providers, and 100 % for any provider used before designation.
Insurers must give workers individual written notice of referral to a managed‑care or preferred‑provider organization; workplace postings do not satisfy this requirement.
Insurers are not liable for charges from non‑preferred providers unless the worker needs emergency care, which is paid at 100 % of the fee schedule.

The department is directed to certify managed‑care organizations and may adopt rules for certification; insurers may contract with certified entities and workers may choose a local managed‑care organization that contracts with the insurer.
affected: Treating physicians and other health‑care providers
The Montana Department of Labor and Industry

SB304.one_line: Amends lakeshore law to tighten permits, enforce stop‑work orders, and raise penalties.
SB304.summary: The bill amends Montana’s lakeshore protection law to clarify definitions, streamline permit processing, require stop‑work orders and surety bonds for unauthorized work, and increase penalties for violations. It also encourages cooperation among multiple governing bodies and directs fines to local county funds.
changes: Amends the definition of a lake and lakeshore to include specific size, usage, and elevation criteria.
Requires local governing bodies to issue stop‑work orders for unauthorized lakeshore work and to enforce them until compliance.
Sets a 90‑day deadline for permit decisions and allows governing bodies to require surety bonds before issuing permits.
Encourages multiple governing bodies to coordinate and establish compatible permit criteria.
Raises misdemeanor penalties: first violation up to $3,000 fine or 30‑day jail, second violation up to $10,000 fine or 30‑day jail, and imposes a 180‑day work pause after two violations in a year.
Allows governing bodies to file liens against violators for all related costs and directs collected fines to the county general fund.
affected: Landowners and contractors working on or near lakeshore

SB299.one_line: SB 299 expands parental rights, requires school‑board policies, and authorizes state suits for violations.
SB299.summary: SB 299 expands parental rights in Montana schools, requiring school boards to adopt policies that give parents full access to records, advance notice and consent for certain instruction, and procedures to object or withdraw their children. It also authorizes state officials to sue districts for violations and provides parents with legal remedies and attorney‑fee recovery.
changes: Amends §40‑6‑701 to codify a broad, narrowly‑tailored interference standard for any government action affecting parental rights.

Rewrites §40‑6‑703 to mandate school‑board policies that give parents notice, consent, and withdrawal rights for instruction, presentations, clubs, and pronoun use, and establishes complaint and appeal procedures.
Rewrites §40‑6‑707 to affirm that parents’ rights are broader than the statutory list and cannot be burdened by government action.
Repeals §40‑6‑708, eliminating a prior construction provision.
Authorizes the attorney general, superintendent of public instruction, or county attorney to file suits against districts for violations of the new parental‑rights provisions.
Provides parents the right to recover reasonable attorney fees and costs when they prevail in such actions.
affected: Parents of students in Montana public schools

SB308.one_line: SB 308 caps workers’‑compensation benefits at $2,885 per week, replacing the average‑wage limit.
SB308.summary: SB 308 removes the cap that limits workers’‑compensation benefits to the state’s average weekly wage and replaces it with a $2,885‑per‑week ceiling. It also amends the definitions of who is covered, the calculation of temporary and permanent disability benefits, and the death‑benefit rules to apply the new ceiling.
changes: Limits weekly benefits to a maximum of $2,885 instead of the state’s average weekly wage.
Redefines employee/worker categories and election procedures for coverage.
Adjusts temporary total disability, permanent total disability, permanent partial disability, and death‑benefit formulas to use the new $2,885 cap.
Adds provisions for cost‑of‑living adjustments and interaction with Social Security benefits.
Specifies election and reporting rules for partners, sole proprietors, and volunteers.
affected: Workers and volunteers covered by workers’ compensation
numbers: 1½ times the state’s average weekly wage

SB307.one_line: Reallocates marijuana tax revenue to prevention, enforcement, and treatment programs, creating new accounts and an accountability council.
SB307.summary: The bill reallocates marijuana‑tax revenue to fund prevention, law‑enforcement, and treatment programs, creates a new accountability council, and sets up detailed distribution rules for the money. It also amends several existing revenue‑account statutes to route excess funds to specific state accounts.
changes: Creates a marijuana prevention account in the state special revenue fund and directs its money to the Marijuana Tax Revenue Accountability Council and to grants for substance‑misuse and youth‑suicide prevention.
Establishes a Marijuana Tax Revenue Accountability Council, defines its membership, terms, duties, and reporting obligations.
Creates a marijuana law‑enforcement operations account and allocates 99 % of its money to a new Marijuana Law Enforcement Office and 1 % to local grants for counties that approved Initiative 190.

Amends the existing marijuana revenue account (16‑12‑111) to require that excess funds be transferred to the Healing and Ending Addiction Through Recovery and Treatment (HEART) account and then distributed to several other state accounts (fish & wildlife, parks, trails, nongame wildlife, veterans, and general fund).
Amends the HEART account (16‑12‑122) to specify its use for statewide prevention, treatment, and recovery services, including tribal grants.
Amends several other special‑revenue accounts (10‑2‑108, 23‑1‑105, 23‑2‑108, 53‑21‑1111, 87‑5‑121) to allow marijuana‑tax money to be deposited and used in those accounts.
Adds a requirement that the council submit an annual marijuana‑impact report to several interim committees.
Sets the effective date for all changes to July 1 , 2025.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Local governments in counties that approved Initiative 190
Montana residents who pay marijuana taxes

SB312.one_line: Eliminates limitations on childhood sexual‑abuse torts and adds revival provisions for barred claims.
SB312.summary: The bill amends Montana’s tort statute to eliminate the statute of limitations for childhood sexual‑abuse claims and adds special revival provisions for claims that would otherwise be barred. It also expands liability for entities that failed to prevent known abuse.
changes: Amends §27‑2‑216 to allow any childhood sexual‑abuse tort to be filed at any time, removing the usual limitation period.
Adds a 1‑year revival window (until May 7 2020) for claims where the perpetrator is alive and has admitted or been convicted of the abuse.
Extends the revival window to claims against entities that knew or should have known of abuse and failed to act.
Defines “childhood sexual abuse” to include a broad list of statutory offenses.
Preserves the 27‑year age limit and 3‑year discovery rule for claims against individuals, but those limits are overridden by the revival provisions.
affected: Organizations that may have had knowledge of abuse

SB314.one_line: Prohibits parties from replacing a candidate found ineligible after the filing deadline or by constitutional disqualification.
SB314.summary: The bill amends Montana election law to bar a political party from appointing a replacement candidate when the original candidate is found ineligible. It clarifies that parties may only replace a candidate who dies or withdraws before the filing deadline, and prohibits replacement if the candidate is disqualified after the deadline or by constitutional grounds.
changes: Amends §13‑10‑326 to add a new subsection (3) that prohibits a party from appointing a replacement when the candidate is disqualified by the Montana Constitution, has no prior filing, or the ballot‑certification deadline has passed.
Keeps the existing rule that a party may appoint a replacement if a candidate dies or withdraws before the filing deadline.
Keeps the rule that a party may appoint a replacement after the primary if no candidate was nominated and the original candidate died after the filing deadline.
Does not create any new program, fund, or office.
Does not impose new fees or penalties.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
numbers: Article IV, §8 of the Montana Constitution

SB313.one_line: Montana bans sex‑based wage discrimination, mandates pay disclosure, and creates enforcement and record‑keeping rules.
SB313.summary: The bill creates a Wage Opportunity and Transparency Act that prohibits wage discrimination by sex, requires employers to disclose pay ranges in job postings, mandates record‑keeping, and establishes a commissioner‑run complaint and enforcement system.  Employees can sue for back‑pay and damages, and employers face fines for non‑compliance with disclosure and record‑keeping rules.
changes: Prohibits employers from paying different wages to employees of different sexes for substantially similar work, except when justified by specific, reasonably applied factors such as seniority, merit, production, location, education, or travel.
Bans employers from asking for, requiring, or using an applicant’s wage or salary history unless the applicant voluntarily discloses it or the employer has made a job offer.
Mandates that every job posting for a position with 15 or more employees include the hourly or salary rate (or a range) and a description of all benefits and other compensation.
Requires employers with 15 or more employees to post promotion opportunities to all current employees on the same calendar day and to provide wage scales for internal transfers upon request.
Obliges employers to keep job‑description and wage‑rate history records for each employee for the duration of employment plus two years thereafter.
Creates a commissioner‑run complaint, mediation, and enforcement process, with civil‑action rights and potential fines of $500‑$10,000 per violation.
Provides for liquidated damages and back‑pay remedies in civil suits, and allows courts to award reasonable attorney fees.
Codifies the new provisions as a new part of Title 39, Chapter 3 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: All Montana employees and job applicants
Commissioner of Labor and related administrative staff
numbers: 2‑year statute of limitations for civil action

SB318.one_line: Revises custody law, adds mandatory abuse‑focused training for judges and guardians, expands evidence and best‑interest factors.
SB318.summary: SB 318 revises Montana’s child‑custody law to give courts greater authority to consider domestic‑violence and abuse evidence, requires judges and standing masters to complete trauma‑informed training, and tightens guardian‑ad‑litem qualifications and fees. It also updates best‑interest factors and amends parenting‑plan amendment rules.
changes: Mandates annual, evidence‑based training for all judges and standing masters on domestic violence, child abuse, and related trauma before they preside over custody cases.
Requires judges and standing masters to file a certificate of completion of the prescribed training before assuming office.

Limits guardian‑ad‑litem appointments to attorneys (excluding county attorneys, deputy county attorneys, or public‑health staff) and requires them to complete 20 hrs initial and 15 hrs biennial training on abuse and violence.
Expands the court’s admissible evidence in custody cases to include past restraining orders, arrests, and convictions for domestic violence or child abuse when a parent is a predominant aggressor.
Adds new best‑interest factors that explicitly consider physical or psychological abuse, chemical dependency, and the impact of abuse on the child’s safety.
Revises parenting‑plan amendment procedures to allow court‑discretionary changes based on new circumstances, with added safeguards against vexatious amendments.
Supersedes certain unfunded mandate statutes (1‑2‑112‑116) and repeals a previous training section (3‑10‑203).
numbers: effective on passage for other sections

SB321.one_line: Montana adds child, child‑care worker, and employer tax credits, with inflation adjustments and a review mandate.
SB321.summary: Montana will give residents a child tax credit of up to $1,200 per qualifying child, a credit for child‑care workers, and a new employer credit for dependent‑care assistance. The credits are adjusted annually for inflation and are available to taxpayers who meet income and eligibility requirements. The bill also requires a biennial review of all new and existing tax credits by a revenue interim committee.
changes: Creates a child tax credit of $1,200 per qualifying child (or $600 for certain cases) subject to income limits and inflation adjustments.
Adds a credit for child‑care workers of $1,600 (or $1,000) for those employed ≥6 months and ≥20 hours/week, with annual inflation adjustment.
Establishes a business‑supported dependent‑care credit for employers, limited to $5,000 ($2,500) per employee and subject to use‑based and location restrictions.
Amends §15‑30‑2303 to list the new credits for biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
Requires the department to adopt rules and annually adjust credit amounts for inflation.
Sets applicability to income‑tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
affected: Taxpayers filing Montana income tax returns
numbers: Inflation adjustment factor based on CPI June 2025

SB322.one_line: Expands business equipment tax exemption, adds inflation adjustment, and reimburses local governments for lost revenue.
SB322.summary: The bill expands the tax‑exempt amount for business equipment (class 8 property) to $1.5 million, adjusts the exemption annually for inflation, and adds a $500‑cost exemption for individual items. It also creates a reimbursement program for local governments and tax‑increment districts to offset the revenue loss from the increased exemption.
changes: Increases the class 8 property exemption to $1.5 million (from $1 million) and applies a 1.5% tax on the first $6 million above that exemption, 3% on amounts above $6 million.
Adjusts the exemption amount each year by an inflation factor based on the CPI for June of the prior year versus the current year, rounded to the nearest $1,000.
Exempts any single piece of personal property costing $500 or less from property tax.
Provides a 5‑year partial exemption for manufacturing machinery, fixtures, and equipment placed in service after 12/31/2022, with a 20% annual phase‑out thereafter.

Creates a reimbursement program that pays local governments, tax‑increment financing districts, and the 6‑mill university levy the difference between the tax revenue that would have been collected under the old exemption and the revenue collected under the new exemption, with growth rates of ½ the average inflation for the first part and 0% for the second part.
Distributes the reimbursement amounts to local governments under the entitlement share payments and to the university levy under the state special revenue fund.
Applies only to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.

SB323.one_line: Low‑rate tax cut and higher earned‑income credit for Montana residents, ending 2026.
SB323.summary: The bill lowers Montana’s top individual income‑tax rate to 4.9% and increases the earned‑income tax credit to 15% of the federal credit. It also adjusts capital‑gain brackets and sets inflation‑adjusted thresholds. The changes apply to the 2026 tax year and expire December 31 2026.
changes: Reduces the top marginal individual income‑tax rate from 5.9% to 4.9% for all filing statuses.
Increases the state earned‑income tax credit to 15% of the federal credit (up from 10%).
Adjusts net long‑term capital‑gain brackets and applies a 3.0%/4.1% rate structure tied to non‑qualified income.
Inflates bracket amounts each year by the inflation factor, rounded to the nearest $100.
Effective for tax years beginning after Dec 31 2025 (income tax) and Dec 31 2026 (credit), terminating Dec 31 2026.
Applies to all Montana residents filing individual income taxes.
Does not create new programs or criminal offenses.
affected: Montana residents filing individual income taxes
Taxpayers with net long‑term capital gains
Individuals eligible for the earned‑income tax credit

SB325.one_line: Montana creates a state‑run family‑leave insurance program with employer/employee contributions and extensive enforcement rules.
SB325.summary: Montana will create a state‑run family and medical leave insurance program that employers and employees (and self‑employed people) must contribute to.  Benefits are paid from an enterprise fund, are subject to solvency rules, and are coordinated with existing federal leave laws.  The bill also sets job‑protection, privacy, and enforcement provisions and amends state statutes to reflect the new program.
changes: Establishes a separate family and medical leave insurance fund financed by employer and employee contributions; self‑employed people may elect coverage.
Sets contribution rates (up to 1 % of an employee’s monthly wages, split 50/50) and outlines how employers with different sizes pay the employer share.
Defines eligibility, benefit calculation (up to $1,000 per week or 50 % of average annual wage plus 0.96 % of excess), maximum 480 hours per benefit year, and coordination with FMLA and other leave.
Provides job‑protection and health‑benefit continuation for employees on leave, and allows employers to offer higher benefits but not lower.
Creates enforcement mechanisms: penalties for non‑payment, false statements, and wrongful denial; allows civil action and arbitration; establishes lien and levy authority for unpaid contributions.
Amends state statutes (2‑18‑606 and 45‑6‑301) to incorporate the new leave policy and to redefine theft offenses.
Sets effective dates: program operations begin July 1 2026; self‑employed coverage elections effective Jan 1 2027.
affected: Covered employers (private and tribal), employees of those employers, self‑employed individuals, state employees, tribal governments
numbers: $500 fine for first‑time theft under new statute
$5,000 and $10,000 thresholds for higher theft penalties

SB324.one_line: Rewrites vehicle‑registration fees, creates special revenue accounts for patrol, crime victims, and bridge grants, and reallocates fee proceeds.
SB324.summary: SB 324 revises Montana vehicle‑registration fees, creates special revenue accounts for highway‑patrol salaries, crime‑victim services, and local‑bridge grants, and sets new rules for how fee proceeds are split and deposited.  The bill also adjusts fee schedules for high‑MSRP vehicles, adds inflation‑adjusted MSRP increases, and requires a $50 million transfer to the bridge fund.
changes: Amends registration‑fee schedule to add a 1 % MSRP‑based fee for vehicles priced above $150,000 (light vehicles) or $300,000 (motor homes) and a $825 annual surcharge for 10‑year‑old or newer vehicles; the surcharge becomes 1 % of MSRP for the first year and $825 thereafter, effective Jan 1 2026.

Creates a “victims‑of‑crime” special revenue account (Section 4) and a “better‑local‑bridge” account (Section 5) in the state special revenue fund; all registration‑fee revenue is deposited into these accounts.
Allocates the bridge‑account money for grants to local governments for off‑system bridge construction (minimum 20 % local match) and up to 5 % for DOT administrative costs.
Releases $50 million from the general fund into the bridge account by June 30 2025 (Section 7).
Repeals the old motor‑vehicle‑division administrative‑fee section (61‑3‑111).
Imposes a 2 % annual inflation adjustment on the MSRP thresholds for high‑MSRP vehicles beginning Jan 1 2027.
Sets effective dates: most provisions take effect Jan 1 2026; Sections 5 and 7 take effect on passage; Sections 2 and 6 take effect June 30 2027.
Adds detailed deposit‑allocation rules for fee proceeds (e.g., 38 % to the highway‑patrol account, 62 % to the motor‑vehicle‑division account, etc.).
affected: Vehicle owners (light vehicles, motor homes, trailers, etc.)

SB329.one_line: Employers must e‑Verify new hires, face fines, and may be barred from state contracts for a year.
SB329.summary: Employers with more than 50 workers must use e‑Verify for every new hire, keep records for the longer of the employment term or three years, and face fines if they fail to verify or employ unauthorized workers. The attorney general gains broad investigative and enforcement powers, including fines, license suspension, and a public list that bars state‑contract bidding for one year.
changes: Requires employers with >50 employees to register for e‑Verify and submit new‑hire data within 3 business days of hire.
Prohibits hiring, continuing, or re‑hiring an employee whose work authorization is not verified; provisional status until verification.
Mandates record‑keeping of verified work authorization for the longer of employment or 3 years.
Empowers the attorney general to investigate complaints, issue warnings, impose fines ($2,500 or $5,000 per violation), and suspend or revoke business licenses.
Creates a public list of fined employers that bars them from state contracts for up to one year.
Allows employers to appeal fines to district court with an appeal bond equal to the fine amount.
Provides safe‑harbor presumption of compliance for good‑faith verifications and limits local governments from enacting ordinances that conflict with the act.
affected: Employees who may be terminated for non‑verification

SB327.one_line: Rewrites vehicle registration fees, adjusts local entitlement shares, and reallocates motor‑vehicle revenue to new state accounts.
SB327.summary: SB 327 revises Montana’s motor‑vehicle registration fee schedule, adjusts entitlement‑share payments to local governments, and reallocates motor‑vehicle revenue to several state accounts. The bill changes fee amounts for many vehicle types, adds new fee categories, and modifies how local‑government entitlement shares are calculated and distributed.
changes: Replaces the existing fee schedule in 61‑3‑321 with new amounts for light vehicles, heavy trucks, motor homes, motorcycles, trailers, boats, and other vehicles; adds several new one‑time and annual fees (e.g., $9 “state‑park” fee, $10 fee for certain vehicles, $5 optional fee).

Revises entitlement‑share calculations in 15‑1‑121: defines a base component, growth rate, and allocation formulas for counties, consolidated local governments, and cities/towns; sets minimum growth rates and caps for specific years.
Adds a new transfer of $59,209 from the general fund to the adoption services account, increasing 10 % each year.

Creates new fixed transfers from the general fund to motor‑vehicle‑related special revenue accounts (e.g., 1.48 % to the motor‑vehicle recycling program, 1.50 % to the noxious‑weed account, various percentages to fish & wildlife, veterans, and search & rescue).
Specifies that revenue collected under the new fee schedule is deposited in the general fund unless otherwise directed.
Provides procedures for local‑government payment, withholding, and appeal of entitlement‑share amounts.
affected: Local governments (counties, consolidated local governments, cities, towns), motor‑vehicle owners, dealers, and the state general fund
numbers: 1.48 % of motor‑vehicle revenue to recycling program

SB331.one_line: Mandates sprinklers for all state buildings, preserves small‑dwelling exemptions, and adds medical gas and worship‑site rules.
SB331.summary: The bill amends Montana’s state building code to require automatic fire sprinklers or suppression systems in all state‑owned buildings, while preserving existing exemptions for small residential structures and adding detailed rules for medical gas piping and religious worship sites.
changes: Amends §50‑60‑203, MCA to add a new rule that all state‑owned buildings must have automatic fire sprinklers or fire suppression systems.
Keeps the existing exemption that single‑family dwellings or buildings with ≤2 units need not have sprinklers.
Adds provisions for medical gas piping compliance and inspection reporting.
Specifies that places of worship may provide temporary overnight accommodations only if they have a sprinkler system or a hard‑wired alarm and an exit to a public way.
Does not alter energy‑efficiency or solar‑panel requirements.
Does not create new funding or criminal penalties.
affected: Places of worship offering overnight stays

SB332.one_line: Replaces election of Montana Supreme Court clerk with appointment by justices, removes deputy appointment power.
SB332.summary: The bill changes how Montana’s Supreme Court clerk is chosen, making the clerk appointed by a majority vote of the justices and removing the clerk’s power to appoint a deputy. It also updates several statutes that list the clerk among state officers and adjusts ballot‑order rules for statewide offices.
changes: Replaces the election of the clerk of the Supreme Court with appointment by a majority vote of the justices; the clerk serves at the court’s pleasure.
Eliminates the clerk’s authority to appoint a deputy clerk.
Amends the residence requirement (Section 2‑16‑111) to include the clerk of the Supreme Court.
Amends salary determination (Section 2‑16‑405) to include the clerk of the Supreme Court in the list of officials whose salaries are set by comparative surveys.
Amends vacancy filling (Section 2‑16‑505) to state that a vacancy in the clerk’s office is filled by the governor’s appointment until the next general election.
Amends ballot‑order rules (Section 13‑12‑207) to list the clerk of the Supreme Court among statewide offices in a specific order.
Amends tie‑vote procedure (Section 13‑16‑504) to include the clerk of the Supreme Court as an office subject to legislative election in the event of a tie.
Repeals Section 3‑2‑406, which previously allowed the clerk to appoint a deputy clerk.
Sets effective dates: the act becomes effective January 1, 2031, with certain sections effective January 6, 2031, and applies only to vacancies after the current clerk’s term ends on that date.
numbers: June 30 of each even‑numbered year (salary survey deadline)

SB334.one_line: Expands Medicaid to able‑bodied adults who meet community‑engagement and premium requirements, contingent on federal waiver approval.
SB334.summary: The bill expands Medicaid to able‑bodied adults who complete a set of community‑engagement activities and meet federal waiver requirements. It amends several Medicaid statutes, creates a temporary workforce‑development program, and establishes reporting, premium, and exemption rules for the new coverage. The expansion is contingent on a federal waiver and will terminate in 2029 unless conditions change.
changes: Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services to apply for a federal waiver and, if approved, expand Medicaid to able‑bodied adults who meet income, age, and community‑engagement criteria.
Amends sections 39‑12‑103, 53‑6‑1304, 53‑6‑1307, 53‑6‑1308, and 53‑6‑1313 to define eligibility, premiums, reporting, and exemptions for the new program.
Creates a temporary workforce‑development program under the Montana HELP Act that contracts with private entities to provide training and supportive services to Medicaid participants.
Imposes a 2% annual premium that rises to 4% and requires collection through the state revenue system, with special provisions for low‑income participants.
Establishes a 80‑hour monthly community‑engagement requirement with a detailed list of activities that count toward it and a comprehensive exemption process.
Provides contingent voidness provisions that can terminate the expansion if the federal waiver is not obtained or if conditions are not met after May 1 2026.
affected: Able‑bodied adults 19‑65 with income up to 138% FPL
Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB336.one_line: Redefines short‑term rentals as residential, limits bans, protects existing rentals, and requires analysis for new restrictions.
SB336.summary: The bill redefines short‑term rentals as a residential use, limits how municipalities and counties can prohibit them, and requires a detailed analysis when a zoning rule restricts or bans them. Existing rentals are protected from new restrictions, and the changes take effect immediately with retroactive application to covenants that do not explicitly address short‑term rentals.
changes: Short‑term rentals are defined as a residential use, not a commercial one, unless a covenant or HOA bylaw explicitly says otherwise.

Municipalities and counties may only prohibit short‑term rentals if the entire jurisdiction or zoning district is expressly prohibited; otherwise, they are permitted in any area zoned for residential use.
An express prohibition cannot block the rental of a primary residence or a unit adjacent to the owner’s primary residence.
If a jurisdiction restricts or prohibits short‑term rentals, any existing rentals that comply with state licensing and tax rules are considered legal non‑conforming uses.
Existing short‑term rentals that existed before the effective date cannot be newly prohibited or further restricted by new regulations.
Zoning regulations that restrict or prohibit short‑term rentals must provide a public hearing and a specific analysis showing that the restriction meets safety, health, and public‑service criteria.
The bill amends definitions in 15‑68‑101 and several zoning statutes (76‑2‑104, 76‑2‑203, 76‑2‑303, 76‑25‑303) to incorporate the new residential definition and analysis requirements.
The act applies retroactively to covenants and HOA bylaws that do not clearly and expressly address short‑term rentals.

SB340.one_line: SB 340 adds a $240 fee for MEPA challenges, speeds remand actions, limits new challenges, and routes fees into special funds.
SB340.summary: SB 340 revises Montana’s environmental‑review and challenge procedures, adds a $240 filing fee for agency‑action challenges, requires agencies to expedite remanded actions, limits subsequent challenges to new issues, and makes plaintiffs pay record‑preparation costs. It also amends fee‑collection rules to deposit certain fees into environmental, domestic‑violence, and other special accounts.
changes: Adds a $240 filing fee for civil actions challenging a final agency action under the Montana Environmental Protection Act (MEPA).

Requires agencies to complete required environmental reviews or corrective actions within 90 days of a court remand, with possible 60‑day extensions only by court approval or written agreement of all parties.
Limits subsequent challenges after a remand to issues that are materially different from those raised previously and could not have been raised earlier.
Makes plaintiffs responsible for paying the agency’s costs to compile and submit a certified record of the decision in a challenge.
Prohibits the award of attorney fees or costs to the prevailing party in MEPA‑related actions.
Amends fee‑collection statutes (25‑1‑201, 75‑1‑110, 75‑1‑201) to route specific fees into special funds (environmental rehabilitation, domestic‑violence, etc.).
Establishes an environmental rehabilitation and response account in the state special revenue fund and specifies its use for reclamation, remediation, and emergency response.
Rewrites the environmental‑impact‑statement requirements in 75‑1‑201 to clarify agency duties, alternative analysis, and consultation procedures.
Sets an immediate effective date (passage and approval) and an applicability date for actions filed thereafter.
Includes severability and applicability provisions.
affected: District court clerks collecting filing fees

SB345.one_line: Revises evidentiary standards and insurer‑ordered medical exams in workers’ compensation.
SB345.summary: The bill revises Montana’s workers’‑compensation rules to tighten the evidentiary standards for medical‑provider testimony, expand the insurer’s right to require independent examinations, and clarify expense reimbursements for claimants who submit to such exams. It amends §39‑71‑605 to detail the procedures, costs, and consequences of refusing or failing to comply with insurer‑ordered examinations. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Treating‑physician opinions must be weighed by the examiner’s education, training, experience, extent of interaction with the employee, and credibility.

SB343.one_line: Reallocates coal‑severance tax revenue to boost the permanent trust fund and other state accounts.
SB343.summary: SB 343 amends how coal‑severance‑tax revenue is split, boosting the permanent trust fund and redirecting remaining amounts from the general fund to that trust. It also sets specific percentages for other state accounts and establishes a $250,000 annual transfer to a permitting and reclamation program.
changes: Reallocates 50 % of all coal severance tax revenue to the permanent trust fund, including any excess; all other revenue is moved from the general fund to the trust after July 1 2027.
Shifts 12 % of revenue to the major repair long‑range building program account.

Allocates 0.90 % (2020) and 0.93 % (2021) and thereafter to basic library services; 3.77 % (2020) and 3.71 % (2021) to conservation districts; 0.79 % (2020) and 0.82 % (2021) to the Growth‑Through‑Agriculture account; 1.27 % to a parks permanent fund; 0.95 % to a renewable‑resource‑loan debt‑service fund; 0.63 % to a capitol‑art trust; 5.8 % to the coal natural‑resource account; and a $250,000 annual credit to the permitting and reclamation program.

moderate (reallocation of existing tax revenue; no new spending authorized)
