SB346.one_line: Revises workers’‑compensation rules to allow interim payments, clarify liability‑free medical claims, and tighten non‑compliance penalties.
SB346.summary: The bill amends Montana’s workers’‑compensation statutes to give the Department more power to order interim payments, clarify when insurers may pay medical claims without admitting liability, and tighten rules on benefit termination for non‑compliance with medical treatment.
changes: Allows the Department to order insurers to pay disputed biweekly benefits for up to 49 days before a hearing or mediation, with a right to appeal and potential reimbursement if the insurer is found not liable
Requires insurers to notify workers within 10 days when they pay a medical claim without admitting liability, and allows workers to request an investigation into liability
Gives insurers the right to terminate benefits for 14 days if a worker unreasonably refuses treatment or cooperation, with specific exclusions for invasive procedures and certain types of cooperation

Limits the application of the new interim‑payment authority to disputes over physician selection, refusal to cooperate with medical care, unaccepted body parts, nurse‑case‑manager cooperation, or independent medical examinations
Stays compensation benefits on appeal under the new interim‑payment provision
Clarifies that insurers are not required to pay compensation benefits under the medical‑claim‑without‑liability section

SB349.one_line: DEQ gains sole authority over fossil‑fuel power plants, voiding if EPA repeals two rules.
SB349.summary: The bill gives Montana’s Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) sole authority to regulate air‑, water‑, and emission standards for existing fossil‑fuel electric plants, while declaring federal agencies lack authority to impede their operation. It also creates a contingency that voids the act if the EPA repeals two specific federal rules. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: DEQ becomes the sole permitting and oversight authority for all existing coal, natural‑gas, and oil‑fired power plants in Montana.
Federal agencies are declared unable to adopt rules or deny permits that would stop these plants without significant economic investment.
The act includes a contingent voidness clause: if the EPA repeals 89 Fed. Reg. 38508 or 89 Fed. Reg. 39798, the bill is automatically void.
DEQ must notify the code commissioner if the contingency is triggered.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
No new funding, program, or criminal offense is created.

SB351.one_line: Limits carry‑forward mill authority for certain statewide mills, effective immediately and retroactive to 2025 tax years.
SB351.summary: SB 351 limits the state’s ability to carry forward mill authority for certain statewide mills, revamping the calculation of allowable mills and setting an immediate effective date with retroactive application to tax years after 12/31/2024.
changes: Amends §15‑10‑420 to exclude mills imposed under §§20‑9‑331, 20‑9‑333, 20‑9‑360, and 20‑25‑439 from the carry‑forward rule.
Rewrites the calculation of maximum mills to use prior‑year assessed taxes plus half the 3‑year inflation average, with a new rounding rule to the nearest tenth of a mill.
Adds a new Section 2 that bars carry‑forward mills calculated for the excluded statutes from use after 12/31/2024.
Provides an immediate effective date (upon passage) and retroactive applicability to tax years beginning after 12/31/2024.
Allows the department to adopt rules for implementation, including valuation‑change methods.
Specifies that certain levies (judgment, emergency, airport, etc.) are not affected by the carry‑forward restriction.
Clarifies that newly taxable property and certain tax‑increment financing district rules remain unchanged.
Sets the act to apply retroactively within the meaning of §1‑2‑109.
affected: Statewide governmental entities that impose mill levies
School districts and regional resource authorities
Property owners subject to mill levies
numbers: half of the average rate of inflation for the prior 3 years
tenth of a mill rounding rule

SB352.one_line: Extends legislative speech‑and‑debate privilege to staff, preventing compelled testimony or disclosure.
SB352.summary: The bill extends Montana’s legislative speech‑and‑debate privilege to staff, preventing them from being compelled to testify or disclose privileged information. It amends the state’s liability statute to define “legislative staff” and codifies the new privilege in the existing liability chapter. The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: 1. Adds a new section that grants legislative staff the same evidentiary privilege as legislators, barring them from testifying or disclosing privileged legislative information in court or other proceedings.

2. Amends §2‑9‑101 to define “legislative staff” (employees or contractors of the legislative branch, personal staff of leadership, and certain attorneys or consultants funded by the state) and clarifies the scope of the privilege.
3. Amends §2‑9‑901 to include the new definitions and to codify the privilege within Title 2, Chapter 9, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
4. Declares the act effective immediately upon passage and approval.
5. Provides that the privilege applies to any information that would be privileged if held by a legislator.
6. Requires that privileged information remain confidential and that the introduction or discussion of a bill does not waive the privilege.
affected: Legislative staff (employees, contractors, personal staff, attorneys, consultants)
State liability claims involving legislative staff

SB353.one_line: Limits minors’ right‑to‑try to only those with a terminal illness confirmed by a treating provider.
SB353.summary: The bill amends Montana’s right‑to‑try law to prohibit minors from receiving investigational drugs, biological products, or devices unless they have a terminal illness confirmed by their treating physician.
changes: Amends §50‑12‑104, MCA, to add a new subsection that bars minors from right‑to‑try treatments unless they have a terminal illness attested by a treating health‑care provider.
Requires that a minor’s treating provider document the terminal‑illness status before any investigational product may be administered.
Maintains the existing requirement that the patient (or parent/guardian) provide written informed consent.
No new program or fund is created; the bill only restricts eligibility within the existing right‑to‑try framework.
The amendment does not alter any financial provisions or create new criminal offenses.

SB354.one_line: Mandates a federal waiver to ban SNAP purchases of soft drinks and candy, with reporting and enforcement provisions.
SB354.summary: The bill directs Montana’s Department of Public Health and Human Services to request a federal waiver that would prohibit the use of SNAP benefits to buy soft drinks and candy.  If granted, the restriction would take effect within six months; if denied, the department must report annually on the request and spending patterns.
changes: Mandates the department to submit a waiver request to USDA for a SNAP purchase restriction on soft drinks and candy
Requires the waiver request to include justification, implementation plan, outreach strategy, and reporting mechanism
If the waiver is approved, the restriction must be enforced within six months of federal authorization
If denied, the department must resubmit annually and file an annual report to the governor and a state committee
The bill codifies these provisions under Montana’s Title 53, Chapter 2, Part 9
The act becomes effective immediately upon passage and federal approval
affected: Montana retailers that accept SNAP benefits
Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
SB354.effective: immediate upon passage and federal approval

SB356.one_line: Prohibits insurers from forcing claimants to use specific repair shops and mandates a list of qualified shops.
SB356.summary: The bill amends Montana’s insurance law to prohibit insurers from forcing claimants to use specific body‑repair shops, from ignoring OEM repair instructions, and from limiting the number of repair shops in a direct‑repair program. It also requires insurers to provide claimants with a list of qualified shops and sets standards for shop quality and pricing. The law takes effect immediately upon passage and applies to all new motor‑vehicle insurance claims.
changes: Amends §33‑18‑224 to forbid insurers from requiring or encouraging a claimant to use a particular repair shop, from ignoring agreed repair costs, or from disregarding OEM repair instructions or safety inspections.
Limits insurers’ ability to cap the number of shops in a direct‑repair program unless the shops meet specified quality and equipment criteria.
Mandates insurers to furnish claimants with a non‑biased list of nearby, qualified repair shops and to inform claimants that they may choose any shop they wish.
Defines that insurers must pay reasonable and necessary repair costs at market price, but are not liable for work done at a shop not on the insurer’s list.
Prohibits repair shops from charging claimants more than an uninsured customer for the same service.
Specifies that the law applies to all motor‑vehicle insurance claims made on or after the effective date.
affected: Insurance companies, producers, adjusters, and independent adjusters
Automobile body repair businesses and locations
numbers: applicability: claims made on or after effective date

SB358.one_line: SB 358 expands permitting rules, creates controlled‑ground‑water areas, and mandates statewide non‑compliance outreach.
SB358.summary: SB 358 amends Montana’s ground‑water laws to tighten permitting, expand monitoring, and create new controlled‑ground‑water areas while adding enforcement and educational outreach. The bill revises exemption rules, requires metering and reporting, and establishes new monitoring and control areas for aquifers, water‑quantity and water‑quality concerns.
changes: Amends §85‑2‑113 to allow the Department to set fees for public services and to adopt rules for interim permits, measuring devices, and emergency appropriations.
Rewrites §85‑2‑306 to clarify when ground‑water appropriations are exempt from permits, add notice requirements, and set limits for stream‑depletion zones and other special cases.
Creates new legislative aquifer closures and monitoring areas (Gallatin, Helena, Bitterroot, Missoula, Flathead, Billings, and others) with rules for metering, reporting, and fines.
Adds a new §7 requiring the Department to identify suspected non‑compliant water use by December 31 2026 and to mail notices to landowners, with a grace period for compliance.
Establishes procedures for petitions, rulemaking, and removal of controlled‑ground‑water areas, including criteria for public‑health, water‑quantity, and water‑quality designations.
Provides that the Secretary of State must send copies of the act to all federally recognized tribal governments and codifies the new sections into Title 85.
affected: ground‑water users (farmers, ranchers, municipalities, private wells)
Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
numbers: 0.5 acre‑ft per year (permit‑exempt limit in some areas)

SB359.one_line: Montana bans handheld device use while driving, imposes fines, and adds distracted‑driving points to habitual‑offender rules.
SB359.summary: The bill creates a statewide prohibition on using portable wireless or stand‑alone electronic devices while driving, except for hands‑free voice communication and navigation. Violations carry civil fines and are exempt for certain emergency or work‑related uses. It also amends the habitual‑traffic‑offender point schedule to include distracted‑driving points.
changes: 1. Prohibits holding, texting, watching videos, or recording with a portable wireless or stand‑alone device while driving, except for hands‑free voice calls or navigation.
2. Exempts voice‑based communication, navigation, GPS use, emergency reporting, and certain work‑related uses.
3. Sets civil penalties: $75‑$149 for a first offense, $150‑$250 for subsequent offenses.
4. Adds a new definition of “portable wireless communication device” and “stand‑alone electronic device.”
5. Amends Section 61‑11‑203 to add a 5‑point “distracted driving” entry to the habitual‑traffic‑offender point schedule.
6. Requires the Department of Transportation to assign points and determine habitual offenders per the new schedule.

SB363.one_line: Amends tourist home definition and adds new lodging categories with guest limits and operating day thresholds.
SB363.summary: The bill amends Montana’s definition of a tourist home and related lodging terms, adding new categories such as bed‑and‑breakfast, day visitor, guest ranch, outfitting and guide facility, and clarifying limits on guests and operating days. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §50‑51‑102 to redefine "tourist home" as an entire private home or condominium never occupied by an owner/manager and rented to transient guests.

Introduces new definitions for "bed and breakfast," "day visitor," "guest ranch," "outfitting and guide facility," "hotel/motel," "roominghouse/boardinghouse," "seasonal establishment," and "small establishment," with specific criteria for guest limits and operating days.
Clarifies that a "tourist home" cannot be occupied by an owner or manager and is rented in its entirety to transient guests.
Adds that a "day visitor" is a guest who participates in recreational activities but does not stay overnight and may be served incidental food.
Defines "guest ranch" and "outfitting and guide facility" as small or seasonal establishments with specified amenities and guest‑accommodation limits.
Sets the act’s effective date to the day it is passed and approved.
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created.
affected: Owners of private homes or condominiums that rent out entire units
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (for licensing)

SB367.one_line: Revises child‑welfare law to strengthen citizen review boards, expand oversight, and streamline hearings.
SB367.summary: SB 367 revises Montana’s child‑welfare law to strengthen citizen review boards, expand their authority and oversight, and tighten procedural requirements for petitions, hearings, and permanency decisions. It mandates new board membership rules, training, record access, and reporting, while clarifying timelines for show‑cause and permanency hearings and expanding the role of the court administrator and the legislature in overseeing the system. The bill also repeals the foster‑care review committee and requires the state to develop a high‑risk‑child care system.
changes: Creates a minimum number of citizen review boards and requires the court administrator to appoint them; boards must have 3‑5 members, be recruited from foster‑care experts, tribal representatives, and residents, and serve without compensation.
Boards must meet at least quarterly, receive training (16 hrs orientation, 8 hrs continuing education), and have access to all relevant case records within 10 working days of request.

Petitions for child abuse/neglect must be filed by a county attorney, attorney general, or county‑hired attorney with an affidavit and notice; the court must schedule a show‑cause hearing within 20 days and a permanency hearing within 30 days of a determination that reunification is not needed.
Show‑cause and permanency hearings now allow the board to review cases and make written findings; the court may adopt the board’s recommendations or schedule a hearing if it objects.
The bill repeals the foster‑care review committee (41‑3‑115) and expands the role of the court administrator in overseeing board operations and reporting to the governor and legislature.
It requires the state to develop a high‑risk‑child care system through a committee (52‑2‑304) that coordinates funding, data, and services across agencies.
affected: County attorneys, attorney general, and county‑hired attorneys; district court judges; court administrators; citizen review board members; child‑welfare department staff; foster parents, pre‑adoptive parents, and relatives; parents and guardians of children in foster care; the Montana Legislature; the Governor; and the public (through reporting).
numbers: minimum number of boards equal to department’s regional divisions

SB370.one_line: Jury summonsers get $60/day, $25 extra if selected, with county reimbursement.
SB370.summary: The bill amends the jury‑pay statute to set a daily per diem of $60 for all jurors and an additional $25 for those actually selected to serve. It also creates a reimbursement mechanism for counties to recover those costs from the Department of Justice’s Office of Court Administrator.
changes: Amends §3‑15‑201, MCA, to specify a $60 per‑day fee for all jurors and an extra $25 per day for those selected to serve.
Replaces the old $12 per‑day amount with the new $60 figure.
Adds a new section authorizing the Department of Justice’s Office of Court Administrator to reimburse counties for the per‑day and mileage costs in criminal cases.
Requires counties to submit an invoice within 30 days of the final day of a criminal trial or settlement to receive reimbursement.
Clarifies that jurors excused on the first day or special jurors not sworn in forfeit per‑diem and mileage.
No new criminal offense or program is created.
No explicit budget appropriation is listed.
affected: Department of Justice Office of Court Administrator

SB371.one_line: Tax credit for Montana‑produced goods: 50 % net‑income subtraction from federal taxable income.
SB371.summary: The bill creates a tax credit for Montana‑produced goods, allowing taxpayers to subtract 50 % of the net income from such sales from their federal taxable income. It amends the state’s income‑tax rules to define Montana‑produced goods and adjusts how federal adjustments are applied to Montana income. The changes take effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑30‑2120 to allow a 50 % subtraction from federal taxable income for net income from Montana‑produced goods
Amends §15‑31‑113 to define “Montana‑produced goods” and exclude 50 % of net income from such goods from corporate gross income
Adds a new subsection that applies the subtraction only to income‑tax years beginning after 12/31/2025
Provides detailed definitions of Montana‑produced goods (food, drink, devices, crafts, etc.)
Adjusts other federal‑state income‑tax adjustments (interest, deductions, etc.) as listed in the bill
Sets the effective date for the new rules to the 2026 tax year
affected: Montana residents who sell Montana‑produced goods
Individual and corporate taxpayers who claim the subtraction
Businesses that produce or sell goods identified as Montana‑produced

SB372.one_line: Montana hospitals must set and report nurse‑to‑patient ratios and staffing plans.
SB372.summary: The bill requires every Montana hospital to create a staffing committee that develops an annual nurse‑staffing plan and posts it publicly. It sets minimum nurse‑to‑patient ratios for each unit and mandates record‑keeping and reporting to the Department of Public Health and Human Services.
changes: Creates a mandatory nurse‑staffing committee in every licensed hospital; at least 50% of its members must be non‑supervisory registered nurses.
Requires the committee to develop, approve, and update annually a nurse‑staffing plan that specifies skill mix, patient‑to‑RN ratios, staffing gaps, and use of temporary staff.
Mandates posting the staffing plan in each care unit and maintaining shift‑by‑shift records of patient counts, RN counts, and supporting personnel.

Imposes specific minimum nurse‑to‑patient ratios for 12 unit types (ER, ICU, labor & delivery, postpartum, OR, oncology, PACU, intermediate care, medical‑surgical, cardiac telemetry, psychiatric, pediatric).
Requires hospitals to submit the plan and a written certification of adequacy to the Department each year.
Defines “nurse” as a licensed registered professional nurse who provides direct patient care.
Codifies the provisions into Title 50, Chapter 5 of the Montana Statutes.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB376.one_line: Montana enacts a right‑to‑work law banning mandatory union dues and requiring written consent.
SB376.summary: The bill creates a state‑wide right‑to‑work law that prohibits employers from requiring employees to join or financially support a labor organization, mandates written authorization for any deductions, and requires employers to post a notice of the right to choose. Violations are criminal misdemeanors with up to $1,000 fines and civil remedies are available. The act amends existing public‑employee labor‑law provisions to reflect the same freedom‑of‑choice language.
changes: Prohibits employers from conditioning employment on union membership or dues payment.

SB374.one_line: Revises contempt law to protect free speech, limit fines, and safeguard non‑lawyers and officers.
SB374.summary: The bill amends Montana’s contempt‑of‑court statutes to limit when a gag order or criticism can be deemed contempt, expand the right of non‑lawyers to provide legal information, set lower maximum fines, require a jury for certain incarcerations, and allow affidavits of bias or misconduct to halt sanctions. It also clarifies the distinction between civil and criminal contempt and adds procedural safeguards for law‑enforcement officers and non‑lawyers.
changes: Violating a gag order is no longer automatically contempt if the violator asserts First‑Amendment rights and has not intentionally infringed another’s privacy; criticism that alleges a court violated law is also exempt.
Non‑lawyers may appear with a plaintiff or defendant and give legal information without being guilty of practicing law, provided they do not deceive the court.
Maximum fines for civil or criminal contempt are capped at $50 per day or $500 total, and incarceration may not exceed 30 days without a jury trial.
A contemnor who shows by affidavit prejudice, bias, or misconduct by the court must have fines or imprisonment stopped until a hearing; another judge must conduct that hearing.

Law‑enforcement officers who disobey unlawful orders are not guilty of contempt; officers who disobey lawful orders may be fined but not imprisoned, and any contempt order against an officer is subject to independent review.
affected: Plaintiffs, defendants, and their non‑lawyer advisors
numbers: $500 fine or 6 months imprisonment for criminal contempt

SB378.one_line: Creates a Tribal Relations Management Team in DPHHS with defined roles and tribal notification.
SB378.summary: The bill creates a Tribal Relations Management Team in the Department of Public Health and Human Services, consisting of a Tribal Relations Manager and a Director of American Indian Health, each with defined duties. It also requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally‑recognized Montana tribes of the act and codifies the new team within existing state law.
changes: Establishes a Tribal Relations Management Team in DPHHS with two distinct positions: Tribal Relations Manager and Director of American Indian Health.

Defines specific duties for each position, including communication, consultation facilitation, policy guidance, and annual reporting for the manager; and disparity identification, strategy development, and forum facilitation for the director.
Prohibits the same individual from holding both positions simultaneously.
Mandates the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
Codifies the new team as part of Title 2, Chapter 15, Part 22 of the Montana Code.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services staff
Federal government agencies involved in tribal health

SB379.one_line: Mandates written tribal‑consultation policies, liaison roles, training, and annual reporting for Montana state agencies.
SB379.summary: SB 379 requires Montana state agencies to create written tribal‑consultation policies, appoint a tribal liaison, and report annually to the governor and tribes. It also mandates training, record‑keeping, and reporting to legislative committees.
changes: Amends §§ 2‑15‑141 and 2‑15‑143 to define “consultation” and expand agency duties
Mandates each state agency to develop a written consultation policy by July 1 2026 and update it at least biannually
Requires agencies to designate an employee as a tribal liaison (subject to appropriations) who reports to the agency head
Obligates agencies to provide regular training on government‑to‑government relations and cultural competency
Establishes annual reporting requirements to the governor, tribal governments, and legislative committees
Creates a notification requirement for the secretary of state to send a copy of the act to all federally recognized tribes in Montana

SB377.one_line: Reassigns banking oversight to the State Auditor and expands enforcement powers for banks and credit unions.
SB377.summary: The bill reorganizes Montana’s banking and financial‑institution regulatory framework, placing the Division of Banking and Financial Institutions under the State Auditor’s supervision and redefining the Commissioner of Securities, Insurance, and Banking and Financial Institutions. It amends numerous statutory sections to clarify definitions, expand the auditor’s appointment powers, and strengthen oversight of banks, credit unions, and other financial entities. The bill also revises the structure of several interim committees, updates consumer‑credit definitions, and introduces new enforcement procedures for unsafe or unsound practices, including cease‑and‑desist orders and suspension of board members. No new program or criminal offense is created; the changes mainly shift authority and clarify existing rules.
changes: Replaces the Division of Banking and Financial Institutions with the State Auditor’s office as the primary regulator of banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions.

Redefines the Commissioner of Securities, Insurance, and Banking and Financial Institutions as a deputy of the State Auditor who performs the auditor’s duties when the auditor is absent or the office is vacant.
Amends 2‑15‑601 and 2‑15‑602 to give the State Auditor the authority to regulate and oversee securities, insurance, and banking/financial institutions and to appoint a deputy commissioner.
Revises the economic‑affairs and administration‑and‑veterans’ interim committees to include the Division of Banking and Financial Institutions and related agencies in their oversight panels.
Updates definitions in sections 31‑1‑202, 31‑1‑703, 31‑3‑125, and 31‑3‑152 to clarify consumer‑credit terminology and the role of the Department of Administration.

Introduces new enforcement mechanisms (e.g., notice of charges, cease‑and‑desist orders, temporary orders, and suspension of board members) under the Division of Banking and Financial Institutions for unsafe or unsound practices.
Amends sections 32‑1‑109 through 32‑1‑921 and 32‑2‑603 to strengthen supervisory powers, examination procedures, and penalties for violations by banks, credit unions, and service providers.
Adds a codification and effective‑date section, making the changes operative on January 1 2026.
affected: Commissioner of Securities, Insurance, and Banking and Financial Institutions
Banks, credit unions, trust companies, and other financial institutions
Board members, officers, and employees of financial institutions
Interim committee members and state agencies linked to banking oversight
numbers: $5,000 (maximum fine for false statements in credit union books)
$10,000 (maximum fine for fraud by credit union staff)
$20,000 (maximum fine for theft of credit union funds)
$1,000 (maximum fine for false statements to obtain a loan)
$1,000 (maximum fine for violation of notice or final order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$6,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$6,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)
$1,000 (maximum fine for misdemeanor of board member violating order)

SB381.one_line: Creates a homesteading program for state lands under 100 acres, requiring 10‑year residency and a 5‑year home‑building deadline.
SB381.summary: The bill creates a new homesteading program for state‑owned lands under 100 acres, allowing Montana residents who have lived in the state for ten years to purchase parcels at full market value and build a primary residence within five years. If the requirements are not met, the land reverts to the state and the purchase price is refunded. The Department of Natural Resources and Conservation will identify eligible lands, set rules, and manage sales.
changes: Department must identify all state lands <100 contiguous acres that meet specified suitability criteria within one year of the act’s effective date
Eligible lands are sold only to “qualified homesteaders” (continuous Montana residents for 10 years) in parcels no larger than 5 acres
Homestead deeds are sold at full market value determined by appraisal of comparable sales
Qualified homesteaders must construct a permanent‑foundation home on the property and make it their primary residence within five years
If the home is not built within five years, title reverts to the state and the purchase price is refunded
The department is exempt from subdivision laws for these sales, but new water or sewage systems must be approved under existing Title 76 rules
The department must adopt rules to implement the program
Section 1 is codified as part of Title 77, chapter 1, part 1
The program is limited to lands not designated as state parks, fishing access sites, or otherwise restricted
The act does not create a new crime or tax
The act does not provide funding; it relies on market‑value sales for revenue
affected: Montana residents who have lived in the state for 10 years
Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
Potential homesteaders who may build homes
State government (revenue from sales, potential refunds)

SB382.one_line: Bill requires state entities to accept religious or informed‑consent immunization exemptions and prohibits discrimination based on vaccination status.
SB382.summary: The bill requires state agencies, local governments, licensed day‑care providers, health‑care providers, and other state‑licensed entities to accept religious or informed‑consent immunization exemptions without question.  It amends the immunization‑exemption statutes to clarify the procedures for religious, medical, and informed‑consent exemptions and adds a new anti‑discrimination provision that protects people from being denied services or employment based on vaccination status or an immunity passport.
changes: 1. Mandates that state agencies, political subdivisions, licensed day‑care providers, licensed health‑care providers, and other state‑licensed entities must accept religious or informed‑consent immunization exemptions without question or malice.
2. Adds a penalty: entities that fail to comply may lose state funding.
3. Provides aggrieved parties the right to file complaints under Title 49, chapter 2, part 5 and seek compensatory damages, costs, and attorney fees.

4. Amends Section 20‑5‑405 to specify the procedures and documentation required for religious, medical, and informed‑consent exemptions, and limits the department’s ability to impose additional requirements.

5. Amends Section 49‑2‑312 to prohibit discrimination based on vaccination status or possession of an immunity passport, except for school and day‑care vaccine requirements, and clarifies that recommending vaccination or voluntary disclosure of status is not unlawful.
6. Codifies the new anti‑discrimination provision as part of Title 49, chapter 2, part 3, and makes the act effective immediately upon passage.
affected: Individuals seeking religious or informed‑consent immunization exemptions
Employers and public accommodations that might discriminate on vaccination status

SB383.one_line: Revises partner‑family assault law to clarify definitions, expand penalties, mandate counseling, and bar victim charges.
SB383.summary: The bill revises Montana’s partner‑or‑family‑member assault statutes to clarify definitions, expand penalties, require counseling and restitution, and prohibit victims from being charged. It also limits the number of parties that can be charged in a single incident.
changes: Amends §45‑5‑206 to define ‘family member,’ ‘partner,’ and ‘victim’ and to add self‑defense provisions
Adds detailed sentencing ranges, fines, and imprisonment terms for first, second, and subsequent offenses
Mandates offender counseling, chemical‑dependency assessment, and minimum 40‑hour treatment, with court‑approved providers
Requires offenders to pay restitution for medical, housing, wage loss, counseling, and probation costs
Allows courts to prohibit firearm possession if a firearm was used in the assault
Provides victims with written copies of sentences and limits charging to one party per incident
Amends §45‑5‑215 to set penalties for strangulation, require counseling, and prohibit victim charging
affected: Offenders of partner or family member assault
Victims of partner or family member assault

SB384.one_line: Adds a 15‑day temporary‑hardship removal authority for children, with new notification and hearing rules.
SB384.summary: The bill creates a new, temporary‑hardship removal authority for the Department of Public Health and Human Services, allowing a child to be removed for up to 15 days when parents cannot provide safe care. It amends existing child‑protection statutes to add this removal option, clarify notification and hearing timelines, and expand definitions of abandonment and temporary hardship.
changes: Adds a new removal authority for temporary hardship, limiting removal to 15 days unless parents cannot resume care, in which case an emergency petition may be filed
Amends sections 41‑3‑102, 41‑3‑202, 41‑3‑301, and 41‑3‑306 to incorporate the temporary‑hardship removal and its procedural requirements
Defines “temporary hardship” as a temporary physical, medical, or legal circumstance preventing safe supervision
Requires the Department to notify parents within 24 hours of removal, provide reasons, hearing dates, and contact info, and to return the child within 15 days
Establishes that a hearing is not required if the child is released before the 5‑day emergency hearing, but a show‑cause hearing must be held within 20 days if the child remains out of home
Adds provisions for kinship placement and extended family involvement during placement
Codifies the new removal authority as part of Title 41, Chapter 3, Part 3
affected: Parents or legal guardians of children
Department of Public Health and Human Services staff

SB385.one_line: Montana establishes a three‑judge Government Claims Court to hear civil actions against the state, with staggered terms and higher salaries.
SB385.summary: Montana will create a new three‑judge Government Claims Court that hears civil actions against the state, including constitutional and administrative challenges, and asbestos‑related claims. Judges are appointed by the governor, confirmed by the senate, serve staggered six‑year terms, and receive a salary 20 % above an associate justice. The court will operate in Helena, use district‑court rules, and its decisions are appealable to the Supreme Court. The bill also amends several existing statutes to recognize the new court as a court of record and to allow asbestos‑claims cases to be removed to it.
changes: Creates a three‑judge Government Claims Court with jurisdiction over civil claims against the state, including constitutional and administrative challenges, and asbestos‑related claims; excludes local zoning challenges.
Appoints judges by the governor and confirms them by the senate; judges serve staggered six‑year terms.
Sets judge salary at 20 % above an associate justice’s salary and prohibits salary reductions during a term.
Establishes court staff (clerk, reporter, law clerks) and requires the court to use district‑court rules, with the option to empanel advisory or trial juries.
Provides for removal of civil actions from district courts to the Government Claims Court within 30 days of service of the first summons.

Amends several Montana statutes (2‑4‑702, 3‑1‑101, 3‑1‑102, 3‑1‑201, 3‑5‑115, 3‑5‑302, 3‑20‑102, 19‑5‑301) to recognize the new court as a court of record, to allow asbestos‑claims cases to be removed, and to include the court in the retirement system.
affected: Citizens filing civil claims against the state

SB386.one_line: Exempts local meat processors from state inspection and licensing for in‑state direct sales to consumers.
SB386.summary: The Montana Local Meat Act exempts processors who raise, slaughter, and sell local meat directly to consumers from most state food‑inspection, licensing, and labeling requirements, provided the sale is in‑state, direct, and the consumer is informed that the product is uninspected. The bill amends numerous food‑law sections to carve out these processors from enforcement and rule‑making, while preserving other health and safety rules for all other food businesses. The act is contingent on a federal decision that allows direct‑to‑consumer sales of uninspected meat.
changes: Exempts processors who raise, slaughter, and sell local meat on their own premises or custom‑slaughtered livestock from state licensure, permitting, certification, packaging, labeling, and inspection requirements; only the processor’s own sales to informed end consumers are covered.
Requires processors to provide a written warning that the meat is uninspected, not to be resold, and to disclose their own health and processing standards.
Carves out these processors from the department’s authority to adopt rules, conduct inspections, or take samples under the food‑law sections that normally apply to meat products.
Preserves all other food‑law rules for homemade food, cottage food, and other food businesses; those entities remain subject to licensing and inspection.
Adds a contingent effective‑date provision that delays enforcement until a federal law or court decision permits direct‑to‑consumer sales of uninspected meat.
Allows the department to adopt rules for other food categories but explicitly excludes local meat and local meat products from such rules.
Provides that the governor must certify within 90 days that federal law permits the sales for the act to take effect.
Maintains existing penalties for violations of the broader food‑law provisions, but exempts local meat processors from those penalties.
affected: Local meat processors who raise, slaughter, and sell on their own premises or custom‑slaughtered livestock
Informed end consumers of local meat
State food‑inspection agencies and local health officers
Other food businesses (cottage food, homemade food, etc.) that remain regulated

SB387.one_line: Revises electric‑bike laws, adds low‑speed electric vehicle licensing and registration, and updates related definitions.
SB387.summary: The bill amends Montana’s electric‑bicycle statutes to clarify definitions, expand the categories of electric‑assisted bicycles, and establish new licensing and registration requirements for low‑speed electric vehicles and other motorized devices.
changes: Amends §61‑8‑102 to define electric‑assisted bicycles as Class 1, 2, or 3 vehicles and sets speed limits (≤20 mph for Class 1/2, ≤28 mph for Class 3).
Adds a new definition of “low‑speed electric vehicle” (4‑wheel, 20–40 mph, electric‑powered, with specific safety and identification requirements).
Creates a new “low‑speed restricted driver’s license” that permits operation of low‑speed electric vehicles or golf carts without a full driver’s license.
Requires registration and titling of low‑speed electric vehicles and establishes a temporary registration permit for up to 90 days.
Expands the definition of “electric personal assistive mobility device” to include two‑wheel, self‑balancing, 12.5 mph‑limited devices.
Revises the definition of “electric‑assisted bicycle” to include a 750‑W motor and clarifies pedal‑assistance rules.
Adds new definitions for “authorized agent,” “authorized agent agreement,” and related motor‑vehicle record‑keeping provisions.
Adjusts other vehicle classifications (e.g., “autocycle,” “moped”) to align with the new electric‑vehicle categories.

SB388.one_line: Carves out a broad recording exception for public officials while performing official duties.
SB388.summary: The bill amends Montana’s privacy‑in‑communications law to carve out a broad exception for recording conversations with public officials or employees while they are performing official duties. It also clarifies when the exception applies to public meetings, warned parties, and health‑care emergency calls, and it limits liability for certain disclosures of intimate images. The rest of the statute, including penalties, remains unchanged.
changes: Amends §45‑8‑213 to add an exception for recording a conversation with an elected or appointed public official or public employee when the official or employee is performing official duty.

Defines that the exception applies to recordings made in the performance of official duty, to conversations with officials/employees while they are performing official duty, to persons speaking at public meetings, to persons given a warning of the recording, and to health‑care emergency calls.

Adds a separate exception for the publication of intimate images that are voluntarily exposed in public or commercial settings, made in the public interest, or disclosed in law‑enforcement, legal, or medical contexts.
Leaves the rest of §45‑8‑213 (definitions, penalties, and general privacy‑in‑communications offenses) unchanged.
Clarifies that the exception does not apply to the interception of electronic communications unless the official or employee is performing official duty or the parties have been warned.
affected: Individuals who record conversations with officials/employees

SB389.one_line: Self‑storage operators must mitigate damages when tenants vacate early.
SB389.summary: The bill requires self‑storage operators to take reasonable steps to mitigate damages when a renter vacates a unit before the lease ends.
changes: Adds a duty of mitigation for operators when a renter leaves early.

SB395.one_line: Statutory codification of Montana’s standing requirements for lawsuits.
SB395.summary: The bill codifies Montana’s standing rules, requiring a claimant to show a concrete, individualized injury caused by the defendant and that the court can grant relief. It makes these rules statutory, effective July 1 2025, and applies only to cases filed after that date.
changes: Creates a statutory definition of legal standing for Montana courts
Requires claimants to prove a specific injury, causation, and redressability
Declares generalized or speculative injuries insufficient for standing
Precludes standing based solely on public importance or policy disagreement
Codifies these rules as a new part of Title 1 of the Montana Code
Sets July 1 2025 as the effective date
Limits applicability to lawsuits filed on or after the effective date
affected: Defendants who might otherwise face lawsuits
Legislature and executive branches (by clarifying limits)

SB391.one_line: Revises opencut‑mining notice, participation, and bond requirements to strengthen public review.
SB391.summary: SB 391 revises Montana’s opencut‑mining notice and participation rules, tightening public‑comment timelines, expanding required documentation, and clarifying when a public meeting is required. It also adds new definitions, expands the list of required bonds and reclamation steps, and gives the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) more authority to review and reject applications.
changes: DEQ must review a complete opencut‑permit application within 5 working days and may declare it abandoned if the applicant fails to respond to a written request within 1 year (or 30 days after notice of abandonment).

Public notice of a complete application must be published twice in a local newspaper, mailed to county commissioners and surface owners within ½ mile, and posted at the site; the applicant must provide a map or directions to a map on the DEQ website.
A public meeting is required if 51 % of owners of occupied dwelling units within ½ mile or 10 owners are notified; otherwise the applicant may waive the meeting if the Department agrees.
Amendments that increase permitted acreage by 50 % or more trigger the same notice and meeting requirements; smaller amendments are exempt.
The bill adds a $500 fee to the opencut fund and requires a reclamation bond, soil‑test pits, historic‑preservation consultation, and a detailed plan of operation.
The Department may prohibit an operation if the applicant has a pattern of violations or is in current violation of this part.
affected: local property owners within ½ mile

SB396.one_line: Libraries must keep sexual or graphic sexual material in adult or young‑adult sections and allow community objections.
SB396.summary: The bill requires public libraries to keep any material that contains sexual or graphic sexual content in the young‑adult or adult sections, and it gives the chief librarian the authority to move items if a community member objects. It also amends several library statutes to incorporate these placement rules and clarifies the duties of library boards and staff.
changes: 1. Mandates that all resources with sexual content be placed only in the young‑adult or adult sections, regardless of intended age. 2. Requires graphic sexual content to be placed only in the adult section. 3. Gives a community member the right to object to placement; the chief librarian must relocate the item accordingly. 4. Requires digital content to have age‑based protections matching the same placement rules. 5. Amends sections 22‑1‑301, 22‑1‑309, 22‑1‑310, 22‑1‑326, and 22‑1‑712 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new placement requirements and clarify board and chief librarian duties. 6. Adds a codification instruction that the new section becomes part of Title 22, Chapter 1, Part 3.

SB397.one_line: Revises central assessment to require independent appraisals when department and owner disagree on appraiser.
SB397.summary: The bill amends Montana’s property‑assessment law to give property owners a right to have a qualified independent appraiser hired when the Department of Revenue and the owner cannot agree on a specific appraiser.  If no agreement is reached, the department selects and pays for the appraisal and may modify the results, with the owner receiving a copy of the appraisal before any changes.  The changes take effect January 1 2026 and apply to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑23‑102 to allow a qualified independent appraiser to be hired when the department and owner agree on a particular appraiser, share costs, and accept the results;

If no written agreement is reached, the department selects an appraiser, pays for the appraisal, considers the results, may accept or modify them, and must provide the owner with a copy before modification;
Adds mediation and appeal provisions under §15‑1‑212 and the Montana Tax Appeal Board;
Sets effective date of January 1 2026;
Limits applicability to property tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Property owners subject to central assessment
Department of Revenue (and its appraiser selection process)

SB399.one_line: Re‑dates primary elections and mandates separate ballots and counting when held with school elections.
SB399.summary: The bill moves Montana’s primary elections to the first Tuesday after the first Monday in May (for even‑year general elections) and to the first Tuesday after the second Monday in September (for odd‑year general elections). It requires separate ballots and separate counting when a primary and a school election occur on the same day, with primary ballots counted first. The bill also mandates that the Secretary of State notify all federally recognized tribal governments of the changes.
changes: Shifts primary election dates to May for even‑year general elections and to September for odd‑year general elections
Requires separate ballots for primary and school elections held on the same day
Requires primary ballots to be counted before school ballots
Maintains that municipal election costs are paid by the municipality
Requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to each federally recognized tribal government in Montana
numbers: first Tuesday after the first Monday
first Tuesday after the second Monday
municipal election cost paid by municipality

SB400.one_line: Owners of residential property must vote on easement changes; majority needed unless all consent in writing.
SB400.summary: SB 400 lets every owner of a residential property subject to a recorded easement, covenant, condition, or restriction vote on its adoption, removal, or amendment.  A majority vote is required unless all owners consent in writing, in which case a vote can be waived.  The bill also preserves owners’ rights to vote on HOA matters and sets a 30‑day notice and voting period.
changes: Requires all owners of a property subject to a recorded easement, covenant, condition, or restriction to be given notice and an opportunity to vote on any adoption, removal, or amendment of that instrument.  A majority vote of lot owners is needed unless all owners consent in writing, in which case a vote may be waived.  Owners retain the right to vote on HOA elections, dues increases, and litigation decisions, with a 30‑day notice period that may be shortened in emergencies.  The bill allows owners to demand longer notice or higher thresholds if they wish.  The changes are codified as part of Title 70, Chapter 17, Part 2, and take effect immediately upon passage.
