SB401.one_line: Limits agencies from adding new definitions to rules unless legislated.
SB401.summary: The bill amends the Montana Administrative Procedure Act to prevent state agencies from adding or changing definitions in their rules when those definitions already exist in state law. Agencies must cite the statutory definition or, if a new definition is needed for clarification, propose a legislative bill before the next session. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends MCA §2‑4‑301 to prohibit agencies from adopting or amending definitions that are already codified in the Montana Code.
Allows agencies to incorporate existing statutory definitions by citation but not to create new ones.
If an agency wants a clarification definition not in statute, it must propose a bill for introduction to the appropriate interim committee by 5‑5‑202 (the specified date).

When amending an existing rule, agencies must delete any definitions in the rule and replace them with statutory citations unless the definition is a clarification, in which case a bill must be proposed.
The act explicitly states that no authority is conferred or augmented for agencies to adopt, administer, or enforce any rule beyond what is already authorized.
The effective date of the amendments is July 1, 2025.

SB403.one_line: Creates a 9‑day muzzleloader heritage season for deer and elk, giving the Commission control over its dates and rules.
SB403.summary: The bill amends the state’s game‑law code to give the Fish and Wildlife Commission authority to set dates, lengths, and rules for a new muzzleloader heritage hunting season, while preserving its existing powers to regulate seasons, bag limits, and special licenses. It creates a 9‑day season for deer and elk that can only be hunted with a muzzleloading rifle meeting specified technical criteria.
changes: Amends §87‑1‑304 to grant the Commission authority to fix seasons, bag limits, possession limits, and season limits for all game, fish, and fur‑bearing animals.
Adds the ability to open or close seasons, declare special seasons, and issue special licenses for game birds, fish, or fur‑bearing animals.
Creates a new special muzzleloader heritage hunting season that begins the second Saturday after the regular season and lasts nine days.
Allows the Commission to set the dates and length of that muzzleloader season and to adopt rules governing its use.

Specifies that during the muzzleloader season, deer or elk may be taken only with a muzzleloading rifle of at least 45 caliber, no more than two barrels, and using loose black powder or equivalent, ignited by a flintlock, wheel lock, matchlock, or percussion mechanism.
Preserves existing Commission powers such as district creation, closed seasons, and special license issuance for other species.
No new criminal offenses or state programs are created beyond the new season designation.
affected: Hunters of deer and elk who wish to use muzzleloading rifles
Property owners in districts subject to closed seasons

SB405.one_line: Transfers $50 million to Housing Montana Fund and updates related rules.
SB405.summary: The bill transfers $50 million from the general fund to the Housing Montana Fund, requires the Department of Commerce to update related rules, and takes effect July 1 2025.
changes: Transfers $50 million from the general fund to the Housing Montana Fund within 15 days of the effective date.
Mandates the Department of Commerce to review and update rules under 90‑6‑136 starting the effective date.
Requires any rule amendments to be adopted before the 70th legislative session.
The act becomes effective July 1 2025.

SB406.one_line: Utilities must meet 1 % kWh savings targets, submit assessments, and share benefits with customers under new commission rules.
SB406.summary: Montana will require investor‑owned electric utilities to pursue cost‑effective energy‑conservation programs that meet a minimum savings target, and the commission will set rules, approve plans, and share benefits with customers.  Utilities must submit assessments, plans, and verification reports, and may earn performance‑based incentives for exceeding targets.
changes: Utilities must implement energy‑conservation programs that achieve at least the greater of 1 % of the prior 5‑year average kWh sales or the target in the utility’s most recent assessment by Dec. 31 2026.

Utilities must submit an independent energy‑conservation assessment within 2 years of the act’s effective date, update it every 2 years, and develop a plan to acquire all cost‑effective conservation up to Dec. 31 2027.
The commission will adopt rules covering evaluation, verification, stakeholder input, cost allocation, and public communication of conservation programs.
Utilities must submit comprehensive verification reports every 4 years (or less frequently if the commission allows) to the commission, prepared by an independent evaluator.

The commission will recover actual costs of conservation activities through annual cost adjustments and may provide performance‑based incentives that split net economic benefits 70/30 or 60/40 between customers and utilities for savings above the annual target.
The act authorizes the commission to promulgate necessary rules and to integrate them with existing utility‑conservation rules.

SB407.one_line: SB 407 bars non‑official flags, mandates “In God We Trust” displays, and amends sectarian‑publication rules.
SB407.summary: SB 407 bars non‑official flags and banners from public school property, mandates every classroom display the national motto “In God We Trust,” and amends the sectarian‑publication prohibition to allow that motto and other religious materials. The bill also authorizes districts to use their own or donated funds for the displays.
changes: Prohibits any flag, banner, or symbol that promotes a social cause, political activism, or social activism from being displayed on public school property, except for official U.S., Montana, or U.S. armed‑forces flags and seals.
Requires each public school building and each classroom to display the national motto “In God We Trust” on a poster, framed document, or plaque at least 8 in × 10 in in a prominent, readable font.
Authorizes school districts to spend their own or donated funds to purchase or accept donated displays of the motto.

Amends § 20‑7‑112, MCA, to clarify that sectarian or denominational publications may not be distributed, but that the Bible, other religious materials, the motto, and religious discussion are permitted.
Adds a codification instruction that Sections 1 and 2 become part of Title 20, Chapter 7, Part 1.
Includes a severability clause and sets the effective date for July 1 2025.

SB408.one_line: Bill makes all legislative drafting files public records, available immediately upon request.
SB408.summary: SB 408 declares that all legislative bill‑drafting files are public records and must be made available upon request under Montana’s public‑records laws, effective immediately upon passage.
changes: 1. Classifies every legislative bill‑drafting file as a public record under §2‑6‑1002.
2. Requires the state to provide those files to any requester in accordance with Title 2, Chapter 6, Part 10 of the Montana Code.

3. Defines a bill‑drafting file to include draft versions, model legislation, research, legal analysis, and all e‑mail or other communications involving the drafter, the legislator, or any third party.
4. Provides a severability clause so that if any part of the act is invalid, the remaining valid parts continue to apply.
5. States the act will be codified as part of Title 2, Chapter 6, Part 10 and will take effect immediately upon passage.

SB411.one_line: Allows video recordings to be treated as wills if clear intent is proven, requiring formal court review.
SB411.summary: The bill lets an audio‑visual recording—such as a video of a person speaking—be treated as a valid will, revocation, or amendment if the court finds clear evidence that the decedent intended it to be a will. It also updates related probate rules and requires formal court proceedings to admit such recordings. The changes affect how wills are executed, probated, and recorded, and they add new evidence standards for audiovisual wills.
changes: Allows an audio‑visual recording to be treated as a will, revocation, amendment, or revival if clear evidence of intent is shown.
Requires a formal court proceeding with findings that the decedent was of sound mind, free and voluntary, not under undue influence, and that the recording is a true copy.
Adds a written transcript of the recording to the court order and treats the order as a written will for ancillary probate.
Requires that a deposited will may not be an audiovisual recording and that courts cannot take custody of such recordings.
Sets July 1 2027 as the effective date.
The bill does not create a new program or crime.

SB415.one_line: Milk must display a best‑by date; non‑compliant milk can be seized; no new rules allowed.
SB415.summary: The bill requires pasteurized grade‑A milk to carry a “best by” (or use‑by) date and a pasteurization date on the container, sets labeling standards, allows seizure of non‑compliant milk, and prohibits the Department of Livestock from making new rules. It also amends an existing rule to drop the definition of a sell‑by date and repeals four related statutes. The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Processors must establish a best‑by date for each unit of grade‑A milk
Packagers must affix both best‑by and pasteurization dates on every container
Labels must meet size, contrast, and placement requirements (≥1/8″ height, Arabic numerals, top seal or upper half of jug)
Milk sold without required labeling can be seized and destroyed by department agents
The Department of Livestock may not adopt new rules to implement this section
The department must amend ARM 32.8.101 to remove the definition of a sell‑by date
ARM 32.8.202‑206 are repealed
The new labeling rules are codified as part of Title 81, Chapter 21
The act becomes effective on passage

SB416.one_line: Mandates sell‑by and best‑by dates on pasteurized milk, allows extensions with proof, and repeals old rules.
SB416.summary: The bill requires pasteurized milk sold in Montana to carry a “sell‑by” date (17 days after pasteurization) and a “best‑by” date, sets labeling standards, allows processors to request extensions with scientific proof, and gives the Department of Livestock the authority to rule on the process. It repeals older milk‑labeling statutes and amends the existing rule to remove the old definition of a sell‑by date.
changes: Mandates a 17‑day sell‑by date and a best‑by date on all grade A pasteurized milk containers
Requires the dates to be printed in Arabic numerals or standard day/month abbreviations and meet size/contrast requirements
Allows processors to apply for a longer sell‑by date if they submit a form with scientific sampling and testing evidence
The Department of Livestock must approve such extensions and maintain them only while ongoing sampling meets bacterial limits
Labels must be at least 1/8 in. high and placed on the top seal or upper half of the container
Exempts processors not selling to the public or selling out of state from the labeling rule
Violations may be seized and destroyed by Department agents
The Department must adopt rules to implement the new requirements
Amends ARM 32.8.101 to drop the old sell‑by definition and repeals ARM 32.8.202‑206
affected: Processors of grade A pasteurized milk
Retailers selling milk to the public

SB417.one_line: Mandates insurance coverage for glucose‑ and weight‑loss injectables and expands health‑service benefits for Montana residents.
SB417.summary: SB 417 requires Montana health‑insurance plans to cover injectable medicines that improve glucose control or promote weight loss for adults with prediabetes, gestational diabetes, or obesity. It also amends several insurance‑law sections to expand coverage for a wide range of health services, including well‑child care, diabetes self‑management, mental‑health services, and certain benefits for state employees and university staff.
changes: All individual and group insurance plans sold in Montana must cover medically‑necessary injectable medicines prescribed on‑ or off‑label to improve glucose or weight loss for adults with prediabetes, gestational diabetes, or obesity, unless the member is on a Medicare‑advantage prescription‑drug plan.
Covered members must receive advance written notice and participate in a lifestyle‑management plan to keep coverage.

The bill amends 2‑18‑704, 33‑31‑111, and 33‑35‑306 to broaden coverage requirements for state employee and university group plans, adding mandates for well‑child care, diabetes self‑management training, mental‑health coverage, and other specific services.

It requires state employee and university group plans to cover injectable medicines for glucose and weight loss, and to provide coverage for a list of therapies (e.g., inborn errors of metabolism, Down syndrome therapies, fertility preservation, etc.).
The amendments clarify that health‑maintenance organizations are exempt from certain practice‑of‑medicine rules but remain subject to other insurance regulations.
The bill includes provisions for COBRA continuation coverage for law‑enforcement officers who are catastrophically injured or die in the line of duty.
affected: group plan members (state employees, university staff, and their families)

SB418.one_line: SB 418 modernizes Montana’s home‑based‑business rules, limiting local‑government power while allowing narrowly regulated operations.
SB418.summary: SB 418 rewrites Montana’s home‑based‑business rules, allowing such businesses to operate in residential dwellings while limiting local‑government power to regulate them. It defines “home‑based” and “no‑impact” businesses, sets narrow conditions for municipal regulation, and preserves existing zoning and environmental statutes.
changes: Amends §7‑1‑111 to prohibit local governments from exercising many powers that affect private or civil relationships, including prohibitions on home‑based businesses, except where expressly authorized by state law.

Rewrites §7‑21‑4204 to declare that a municipality may not prohibit a no‑impact home‑based business and may only impose narrowly tailored regulations for health, safety, compatibility, or illegal activity.

Amends §76‑2‑304 to make use of a residential dwelling for a home‑based business a permitted zoning use, except where deed restrictions or other documents apply, and limits requirements such as rezoning or fire‑sprinkler installation.
Amends §76‑2‑309 to give priority to regulations made under §76‑2‑304 when they conflict with other statutes or ordinances.

Defines “home‑based business” and “no‑impact home‑based business” and sets criteria for the latter (≤ municipal occupancy, lawful goods, no street traffic, indoor or yard‑only, not visible from street).
Preserves the ability of municipalities to regulate certain hazardous or high‑impact businesses (e.g., slaughterhouses, breweries, etc.) under §7‑21‑4204.
Does not create a new state program or criminal offense; it merely revises existing statutes.
affected: Residents of neighborhoods where home‑based businesses operate
numbers: no more than two dwelling units
no‑impact business must not be visible from street

SB419.one_line: Revises pension service credit rules for Montana legislators, effective July 1, 2025.
SB419.summary: The bill amends Montana’s pension law to clarify how legislative members earn service credit and how their retirement benefits are calculated. It sets the effective date for the changes to July 1, 2025.
changes: Amends §19‑3‑521 to state that a legislator’s service credit begins when they assume office and applies only to the portion of each year they pay contributions.

Specifies that benefit calculations use the plan provisions applicable to the earliest period of required contributions or purchased credit, but not earlier than the member’s start date, unless the member had prior covered non‑legislative employment.
Adds a new section establishing the act’s effective date of July 1, 2025.
affected: Legislative members of the Montana Legislature
Pension plan administrators for legislative members

SB420.one_line: Limits local park fees for children to $25/month or $10 for three days.
SB420.summary: The bill caps fees that local governments can charge children for park and recreation use at $25 per month or $10 for a three‑day period, with the same limits applying to sports‑team fees. It also updates a broad prohibition on local‑government fee powers and sets an effective date of July 1, 2025.
changes: Limits child park fees to $25/month or $10 for any consecutive three‑day period
Limits sports‑team fees to the same amounts per child
Defines “child,” “children’s sports team,” and “local government”
Exempts contracts in place before July 1, 2025 from the new limits
Amends §7‑1‑111, MCA to prohibit local‑government powers that would allow fees above these limits
Codifies the fee limits as part of Title 7, Chapter 1, Part 1
Effective July 1, 2025
affected: Local governments (counties, cities, towns, special districts)
Children under 18 using parks and recreation facilities

SB421.one_line: Landlords must refund unused application fees within 20 days and limit deductible costs to $25, with clear notice and credit‑check rules.
SB421.summary: Landlords who charge application fees must refund any unused portion within 20 days and can only keep up to $25 for specific services.  Credit or criminal background checks must be provided within 7 days, remain valid for 6 months, and cannot exceed the landlord’s actual cost.  Applicants can sue for wrongful withholding and attorneys’ fees may be awarded.
changes: Mandates a 20‑day refund of any application fee not tied to a signed lease or a lease that has the same effect as a signed lease.
Allows landlords to deduct only out‑of‑pocket costs (not exceeding $25) for specific services, with written notice of the allocation at the time of fee collection.
Requires credit or criminal background checks to be delivered within 7 days, valid for 6 months, and the fee for such checks may not exceed the landlord’s actual cost.
Permits landlords to waive the application fee entirely if a valid credit or criminal check is provided within the prior 6 months.
Creates a civil action for wrongful withholding of an application fee, with damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld and possible attorney‑fee awards.

SB423.one_line: Amends the Lewis and Clark Highway route and requires local consultation for an alternate Missoula segment.
SB423.summary: The bill amends the statutory definition of the Lewis and Clark Highway to specify a new route that follows U.S. 93 from Lolo to Missoula, then U.S. 12/10 east to Garrison, and finally U.S. 12 east to the North Dakota line. It also requires the Department and Board to consult local governments to find an alternate Missoula segment that avoids certain residential streets.
changes: Amends Section 60‑1‑202, MCA, to redefine the Lewis and Clark Highway’s path.
Specifies the highway must use U.S. 93 from Lolo to Missoula, U.S. 12/10 from Missoula to Garrison, and U.S. 12 from Garrison to the North Dakota line.
Excludes the segment between south Higgins Avenue and Arthur Avenue north of, or along, 6th South Street in Missoula.
Mandates that the Department and Board consult Missoula County and the city of Missoula to determine an alternate route that minimizes travel through primarily residential neighborhoods.
affected: Motorists traveling the Lewis and Clark Highway

SB425.one_line: Prohibits out‑of‑state confinement for inmates with Montana children under 13, except in limited cases.
SB425.summary: The bill amends the Montana Corrections Act to forbid the Department of Corrections from sending inmates to out‑of‑state facilities if the inmate has a child under 13 who lives in Montana. It also clarifies that the department may still place inmates elsewhere only when the inmate’s parental rights are terminated or the inmate is convicted of a sexual offense.
changes: Amends §53‑30‑106, MCA, adding a new subsection (4) that prohibits out‑of‑state confinement for inmates with Montana residents under 13, except when parental rights are terminated or the inmate is convicted of a sexual offense.
Keeps existing provisions allowing temporary stops to admissions when capacity is exceeded and permits placement in other jurisdictions or contracts with other states, counties, or private entities.
Clarifies that the department may not select an inmate for out‑of‑state confinement under the stated circumstances.
affected: Inmates of the Department of Corrections
Parents of inmates with children under 13 in Montana
Out‑of‑state detention facilities that might otherwise house Montana inmates

SB427.one_line: Sets specific setback distances for traps on public lands and expands wildlife commission rule‑making authority.
SB427.summary: The bill establishes specific setback distances for ground sets and snares on public lands, expands the commission’s rule‑making authority, and amends the wildlife commission’s powers and trapping‑offense penalties. It requires traps to be set a set distance from roads, trails, campgrounds, and high‑use trails, and gives the commission authority to adjust those distances and create additional rules.
changes: Creates mandatory setback distances of 50 ft for furbearers, predators, and nongame wildlife from roads/trails, 1,000 ft from campgrounds/recreation sites, 300 ft from trailheads (1,000 ft for lethal sets), 150 ft for wolves, and 500 ft from high‑use trails/roads.
Allows the commission to expand or establish additional setback distances for high‑use areas, campgrounds, recreation sites, and trailheads.
Amends Section 87‑1‑301 to clarify the commission’s policy, rule‑making, and approval powers, including wildlife population management, budget review, and construction projects.

Amends Section 87‑6‑601 to require traps to be tagged, set in accordance with the new setbacks, and not endanger livestock; adds penalties of $50‑$1,000, up to 6 months imprisonment, and possible forfeiture of licenses.
affected: Trappers and hunters on public lands

SB431.one_line: Limits new use restrictions on residential property unless owners consent in writing.
SB431.summary: The bill limits how homeowners’ associations and other parties can enforce covenants that impose new or stricter use restrictions on a property after the owner acquires it.  Owners must give written consent for any new restriction, and exceptions must be recorded and notified to other owners.  The law applies to residential real‑property covenants and to HOA‑enforced covenants, with a few carve‑outs for legal‑required restrictions and pre‑existing covenants that were enforceable at acquisition.
changes: Owners of residential real property may not be bound by a covenant, condition, or restriction that imposes more onerous use limits than those that existed when they acquired the property, unless they expressly agree in writing at the time of adoption or amendment.
If an owner claims an exception, they must record it with the county clerk, pay the recording fee, and notify other affected owners of the exception and the date of conveyance.
Successors‑in‑interest cannot claim the exception unless they are the previous owner, a family member inheriting the property, or a lender who foreclosed.
The prohibition does not apply to covenants required to comply with federal, state, or local laws, ordinances, or regulations.
The amendment to §70‑17‑901 (HOA restrictions) mirrors the same rules for HOA‑enforced covenants, with the effective date set to May 9 2019 for pre‑existing covenants.
The act is effective immediately upon passage and approval.
numbers: May 9 2019 (effective date for pre‑existing HOA covenants)

SB432.one_line: Amends utility relocation definitions, excluding engineering costs, for all utilities.
SB432.summary: The bill amends the definition of “cost of relocation” in Montana’s utility relocation law, clarifying that engineering costs are excluded and that the definition applies to all utilities, including water, sewer, cable, and broadband providers. No new programs or fees are created.
changes: Redefines “cost of relocation” to exclude engineering costs for design, locating, staking, inspecting, or other incidental engineering expenses.

Clarifies that the definition applies to all utilities, including publicly, privately, cooperatively owned utilities, water and sewer facilities, cable service providers, and broadband service providers.
Leaves all other provisions of §60‑4‑401, MCA unchanged.
affected: All utility companies operating in Montana (public, private, cooperative, water, sewer, cable, broadband).

SB434.one_line: Montana offers a $400 property‑tax rebate for 2024 principal‑residence owners, with strict filing rules and penalties for fraud.
SB434.summary: The bill creates a one‑time $400 rebate (or the lesser of $400 and the amount actually paid) for Montana residents who owned and lived in a principal residence during 2024.  Claimants must file electronically or by mail by October 1 2025, and the rebate is not subject to state income tax.  The act also amends income‑tax rules to include the rebate as a deduction and imposes penalties for false claims.
changes: Provides a $400 property‑tax rebate for 2024 principal‑residence owners, limited to the lesser of $400 or taxes paid;
Rebate is not counted as taxable income for Montana income tax;
Claims must be filed electronically (Aug 15–Oct 1 2025) or by mail (postmarked by Oct 1 2025);
Only one rebate per taxpayer per year;
Rebate may be offset against state debts;
False or fraudulent claims subject to criminal prosecution, 300% penalty, interest, and potential distraint;
Amends §15‑30‑2120 to allow the rebate as a deduction from federal taxable income;
Rebate program ends June 30 2026.
affected: Montana residents who own and occupy a principal residence during 2024
Taxpayers who may owe state debts

SB436.one_line: Revises groundwater‑right rules, expands permit exceptions, and adds tribal notification.
SB436.summary: SB 436 revises Montana’s groundwater‑right rules, clarifying definitions, expanding permit exceptions, and adding a notification requirement for tribal governments. It streamlines how wells and springs may be used without a permit, sets limits on flow and volume, and tightens the filing and certification process for new water rights.
changes: Amends Section 85‑2‑102 to clarify the definition of an “appropriation” and related terms such as aquifer recharge, storage‑and‑recovery projects, and combined appropriations.
Adds a new definition of “combined appropriation” that allows multiple wells or springs in the same aquifer to be treated as a single right if the department deems it appropriate.

Expands the list of circumstances in which a groundwater well or developed spring may be used without a permit, including small‑scale non‑consumptive geothermal use, low‑flow fire‑suppression wells, and low‑volume private use wells that stay outside a stream‑depletion zone.

Sets quantitative limits for wells that can be used without a permit (e.g., 350 gpm for geothermal, 35 gpm and 10 acre‑feet/year for other uses, 20 gpm and 2 acre‑feet/year within a stream‑depletion zone).

Requires a written notice of completion to be filed within 60 days of building a well or spring; the notice must be corrected within 30 days of any defect or within a period the department may allow (up to 6 months).
Makes a certificate of water right unavailable until a correct and complete notice is filed and the department has verified land‑owner notification or federal special‑use authorization.
Adds a new section that requires the Secretary of State to send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
The bill does not create a new program or criminal offense; it amends existing water‑right statutes and clarifies permitting and filing procedures.
The changes are largely procedural and regulatory, with no new funding or budget provisions.
affected: Groundwater developers (well and spring owners), local governments, fire agencies, geothermal operators, private water users, the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation, and federally recognized tribal governments

SB438.one_line: Allows out‑of‑state telehealth providers to register, sets fees and notification rules, and exempts certain low‑volume or emergency services.
SB438.summary: SB 438 revises Montana’s telehealth laws to allow out‑of‑state providers to register, sets registration fees, requires notification of disciplinary actions, and gives the Department of Labor and Industry disciplinary authority. It also exempts certain low‑volume or emergency services from registration and eliminates in‑person photo requirements.
changes: Out‑of‑state providers may register with a board, oversight entity, or the Department of Labor and Industry to provide telehealth services to Montana patients.
A registration fee may be charged, but it cannot exceed the fee for in‑state licensure of the same provider type.

Providers must notify the board/department of any disciplinary action or restriction on their out‑of‑state license within five business days; failure to do so can result in suspension or revocation of the Montana registration.

Certain services—emergency care, after‑care for in‑state procedures, consultation with an in‑state provider, civil or criminal testimony, or fewer than ten encounters per year—are exempt from the registration requirement.
The bill removes the requirement for an in‑person photo or signature for registration; all required information may be submitted electronically.
The Department of Labor and Industry is granted rule‑making authority to implement these provisions.
affected: Out‑of‑state health care providers who wish to offer telehealth services in Montana
Montana boards, oversight entities, and the Department of Labor and Industry
Montana courts and administrative bodies handling disputes over telehealth services
numbers: registration fee not to exceed in‑state licensure fee

SB439.one_line: Mandates address‑change sharing for voter‑list updates and eliminates unfunded mandates.
SB439.summary: The bill amends Montana’s voter‑registration statutes to require the clerk of court and the Department of Motor Vehicles to forward all address‑change notices to the county election administrator, who will then update the voter list. It also replaces a series of unfunded mandate provisions with a single, broad superseding clause. No new program or crime is created, and the bill contains no explicit funding or cost estimates.
changes: Amends §3‑15‑405 to mandate that the clerk of court send any returned‑as‑undeliverable or new‑address notice to the county election administrator for voter‑list updating.
Amends §13‑2‑220 to add detailed procedures for annual voter‑list maintenance, including mailing confirmation notices, door‑to‑door canvassing, and use of utility‑company change‑of‑address data.
Amends §61‑5‑115 to require the DMV to forward all driver‑license address changes to the county election administrator for voter‑list updates.
Supersedes the unfunded mandate statutes 1‑2‑112 through 1‑2‑116 with a single new section that eliminates those requirements.
Adds a new section (Section 4) that declares the superseding of the unfunded mandate laws.
No new funding, program, or criminal offense is created.
The bill does not alter any election‑date or ballot‑processing rules beyond the updated maintenance procedures.
numbers: 90 days (must complete procedures before primary/general election)

SB443.one_line: Limits THC, sets license fees, and restricts high‑potency sales to medical cardholders.
SB443.summary: The bill amends Montana’s marijuana laws to cap THC concentrations and package limits, sets a $5,000 initial license fee for dispensaries, and allows higher‑potency products only for registered medical cardholders.
changes: Amends §16‑12‑224 to impose a $5,000 initial license fee and a $5,000 incremental fee for each additional location;
Adds a rule that dispensaries may set THC limits and adopt inspection and financial‑interest rules;
Limits all marijuana products sold at dispensaries to a maximum of 15% total THC;

Sets specific package limits: 1 oz flower ≤35% THC, capsules ≤100 mg THC per capsule (≤800 mg per package), tinctures ≤800 mg THC, edibles ≤100 mg THC (≤10 mg per serving), topicals ≤6% THC (≤800 mg per package), suppositories/patches ≤100 mg THC (≤800 mg per package);
Allows a ±10% deviation for other products up to 800 mg THC;
Permits dispensaries to sell higher‑potency products only to registered medical cardholders;
Prohibits transactions that would let consumers exceed possession limits set in §16‑12‑106 and §16‑12‑515.

SB445.one_line: Utilities must provide real‑time dashboards and quarterly power‑source reports by June 1, 2026.
SB445.summary: SB 445 requires investor‑owned utilities to launch a real‑time energy dashboard and public utilities to issue quarterly power‑source disclosures, both by June 1, 2026, to give consumers clearer insight into the costs and sources of their electricity. The bill defines key terms and sets reporting requirements but does not create new funding or penalties.
changes: Investor‑owned utilities must design, build, and host a web‑based energy dashboard that displays real‑time or best‑approximated data on each in‑state rate‑based resource’s contribution to the grid and its unit cost.

The dashboard must show year‑to‑date contribution, operating capacity, production cost, and average cost per megawatt‑hour for each resource, and calculate the cost per kilowatt‑hour for an average residential customer.
Utilities must disclose any surge in production cost or unavailability of a resource on the dashboard.

Public utilities must provide a quarterly power‑source disclosure that lists the kilowatt‑hour consumption and average unit cost by source and technology (coal, natural gas, hydroelectric, wind, solar, and any other resource).
The disclosure must also include power purchased from non‑contracted, same‑day markets during the quarter.
All reporting must be completed on or before June 1, 2026, and the act becomes effective on that date.
affected: Residential and small commercial energy consumers

SB448.one_line: Mandates prompt payment, sets penalties, and gives carriers and the DOJ enforcement powers for health claims.
SB448.summary: SB 448 establishes strict prompt‑payment rules for Montana health carriers, defines clean claims, sets deficiency‑notification deadlines, imposes interest and penalties for late payment, and gives carriers and the Department of Justice enforcement authority and a private right of action. The law applies to all claims filed on or after Jan. 1 2026.
changes: Health carriers must pay clean claims within 14 days for electronic claims and 30 days for paper claims, or face interest and penalties.

SB450.one_line: Allows legislative leaders to file amicus briefs and use legislative funds for legal costs.
SB450.summary: The bill authorizes Montana’s Speaker of the House and President of the Senate to file amicus‑curiae briefs in state or federal cases that involve interpreting state statutes or referendums. It allows them to use legislative funds for legal costs, subject to appropriation, and preserves existing attorney‑general and legislative immunities.
changes: Legislative officers (Speaker and Senate President) may act as amicus curiae in relevant litigation.
They may file briefs individually or jointly.
The bill permits use of legislative appropriations, approved by the Legislative Council, to pay attorney fees and costs for such briefs.
Participation does not waive legislative immunity or privilege.
The Attorney General’s authority to represent the state remains unchanged.
numbers: applicability: proceedings initiated on or after effective date
funding: subject to available appropriation authority

SB451.one_line: Amends library law to define purpose, core functions, and restrict unrelated services.
SB451.summary: The bill amends Montana’s public‑library statute to define the library’s purpose and core functions, and bars libraries from offering services that fall outside those functions.
changes: Amends §22‑1‑302 to state that a free public library’s purpose is to encourage establishment, financing, and administration of libraries that give residents the opportunity to enrich themselves through reading.

Lists eight core functions that a library must provide: (a) access to information (print & digital, including inter‑library lending); (b) educational support for students (research materials, tutoring, homework help); (c) access to technology (computers, internet, online learning platforms); (d) promotion of literacy and reading (programming for all ages); (e) access to meeting spaces for outside groups; (f) access to reading areas; (g) facilitation of information transmission and sharing (copying, materials); and (h) any other core function consistent with the purpose of free public libraries;
Prohibits a free public library from offering any services that are unrelated to the stated purpose or core functions.

SB452.one_line: Montana mandates AI disclosure and opt‑out for online media makers, excluding government entities.
SB452.summary: Montana will require online media makers to disclose when AI is used and give users an opt‑out. AI‑generated content must carry visible or audio markers that survive deletion. The law excludes government entities.
changes: Manufacturers of publicly distributed online media that use AI to direct, control, or focus information must disclose that AI is used and provide an opt‑out option to users.
Any online media created wholly or partly by AI must contain identifiable markers (visual or audio) that alert users to AI use, and embedded markers that remain if the original markers are removed.
The requirement does not apply to governmental entities as defined in Montana Code §2‑17‑551.

Definitions clarify that “artificial intelligence” means computer systems or algorithms that imitate human behavior and control information flow, and “markers” include visual or audio disclosures such as watermarks, bylines, or warnings.
The section is to be codified as part of Title 30 of the Montana Code.
No new program, office, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Online media manufacturers that distribute content publicly in Montana

SB453.one_line: Montana residents’ electronic data is protected from sale or federal transfer without consent.
SB453.summary: The bill declares that electronic data created for a Montana resident is the resident’s property and may not be sold or given to the federal government without the resident’s express consent. It requires actual payment and notice for any sale, limits adhesion contracts, and gives individuals and entities a private right of action for violations.
changes: Recognizes electronic data as personal property held in trust by anyone who possesses it.
Makes ownership of such data non‑descentible in intestate succession and requires permanent deletion after death unless a successor is elected.
Prohibits the sale of electronic data to any third party, including the federal government, without the owner’s express consent and requires actual consideration for any sale.
Mandates notice to the owner when data is provided to the federal government, except when a warrant or subpoena is issued with a court order not to notify.
Bars the use of adhesion contracts that force forfeiture or nominal consideration for electronic data.
Creates a private cause of action and allows the attorney general or county attorney to seek injunctions and damages for violations.
affected: Montana residents who own electronic data
Entities that possess or manage such data (e.g., telecoms, financial institutions, software providers)
Federal government agencies that might seek data
Courts and attorneys handling related civil actions
numbers: reasonable time after death for deletion
notice required prior to or at time of provision
no specific dollar amounts or budgets mentioned

SB454.one_line: Rewrites Montana tow‑truck law, adds insurance, inspection, training, and a state rotation system.
SB454.summary: The bill amends Montana’s commercial tow‑truck statutes to tighten definitions, classification, insurance, inspection, and storage requirements and to create a formal state law‑enforcement rotation system. It adds new training, equipment, and record‑keeping standards for operators who wish to participate in the rotation and imposes stricter insurance limits and storage rules for all commercial tow‑truck operators.
changes: Redefines key terms (boom, operator, qualified operator, rotation area) and adds new certification and experience requirements for operators and their employees.

Reclassifies tow‑truck equipment into five classes (A‑E) with specific manufacturer‑rated weight and capacity thresholds and preserves legacy classifications for trucks that meet inspection standards as of Jan. 1 2026.
Sets minimum liability insurance limits ($300k for Class A, $500k for Class B, $750k for Class C) plus cargo and garage‑keeper coverage and requires proof of insurance to the Department.
Mandates annual safety inspections, decal issuance, and inspection/decal fees that must be deposited in a highway non‑restricted account.

Creates a state law‑enforcement rotation system that assigns qualified operators to rotation lists based on equipment class, requires a letter of appointment, and establishes training, traffic‑control, and equipment standards for rotation participation.
Imposes detailed storage, staffing, and record‑keeping requirements for operators who hold a letter of appointment, including separate business locations, impound areas, and financial records.
Provides a waiver process for operators who meet public‑service needs but cannot meet all requirements.
Adds provisions for local law‑enforcement rotation systems that must comply with the state system.
Requires operators to display required federal and state markings on all tow trucks.
Allows operators to be removed from the rotation for 30 days if they fail to meet rotational requirements.
affected: Commercial tow‑truck operators, tow‑truck companies, tow‑truck employees, local law‑enforcement agencies, and the Montana Highway Patrol

SB455.one_line: SB 455 bars roadside solicitation, mandates written proof, and adds penalties and rotation‑system updates.
SB455.summary: SB 455 prohibits towing and roadside companies from soliciting services at accident or disabled‑vehicle scenes, requires written proof of requests, and imposes misdemeanor penalties and license suspensions for violations. It also amends the state towing‑rotation system and expands good‑faith immunity for emergency responders.
changes: Bans towing/roadside operators from stopping to solicit services at accident or disabled‑vehicle scenes
Requires operators to provide written documentation of each roadside assistance request (owner, motor‑club, or law‑enforcement request) and keep records for 3 years
Imposes misdemeanor fines and up to permanent suspension from the state towing‑rotation system for first‑, second‑, and third‑offense violations by operators and companies
Adds misdemeanor penalties for first responders who direct motorists to a particular tow company
Amends §61‑8‑908 to clarify the rotation system, required operator information, and display requirements
Amends §61‑8‑909 to broaden good‑faith immunity for emergency responders
Codifies the new section as part of Title 61, Chapter 8, Part 9

SB459.one_line: Limits Board investments to jurisdictions with inspected public‑accounting firms, mandates divestment and SEC consultation.
SB459.summary: The bill amends Montana’s investment rules to restrict the Board of Investments from buying securities in jurisdictions lacking adequate public‑accounting oversight and requires divestment when such oversight is absent. It also mandates biennial consultation with the SEC and sets a July 1, 2025 effective date.
changes: Limits Board investments to securities listed only in jurisdictions where a registered public‑accounting firm has been inspected per federal law.
Prohibits investment in securities from jurisdictions where inspection is impossible due to local law or policy.
Requires the Board to consult with the SEC every two years to confirm compliance.
Mandates divestment from prohibited securities when it can be done without loss or when deemed prudent.
Defines key terms such as "Board" and "registered public accounting firm" for the purposes of the act.
Codifies the new rules as part of Title 17, Chapter 6, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date of the amendments to July 1, 2025.

SB460.one_line: Expands DEQ’s authority over open‑cut gravel pits to protect water resources and enforce permits.
SB460.summary: The bill amends Montana’s gravel‑pit law (MCA § 82‑4‑422) to give the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) broader authority to issue, amend, and enforce permits for open‑cut mining, adopt rules, and protect surface and groundwater. It also requires DEQ to adopt uniform filing procedures and to conduct hearings with subpoena power. The changes strengthen regulatory oversight of gravel‑pit operations.
changes: Amends § 82‑4‑422 to expand DEQ’s powers to issue, amend, and enforce permits for open‑cut mining.
Adds a duty for DEQ to adopt rules that establish uniform procedures for filing records, issuing permits, and filing annual reports.
Requires DEQ to adopt rules that protect surface and groundwater from water‑quality and quantity deterioration caused by open‑cut operations.
Empowers the DEQ board to conduct hearings, administer oaths, subpoena witnesses, compel attendance, and require production of relevant records.
affected: Witnesses and parties in DEQ hearings

SB461.one_line: Limits kratom sales, exempts fresh non‑synthesized products, effective June 1 2025.
SB461.summary: The bill creates a “Kratom Consumer Protection Act” that prohibits the sale or distribution of kratom products to the public unless expressly authorized, bars sales to anyone under 21, and sets strict limits on the composition of kratom products.  It exempts entities that sell fresh, non‑synthesized kratom that meets the stated limits from state or local prohibition.  The act takes effect June 1 2025.
changes: Prohibits selling, giving, or distributing kratom products to the public unless authorized by law
Bans sales of kratom to persons under 21 years old
Defines key terms (kratom, kratom extract, processor, product, synthesized material)
Sets product limits: no more than 2% 7‑hydroxymitragynine, no synthesized material, no dangerous non‑kratom substances, no combustible/vaporizable/injectable forms
Exempts entities that sell fresh, non‑synthesized kratom meeting those limits from state or local prohibition
Codifies the provisions into Title 30, Chapter 14 of the Montana Code
Effective June 1 2025

SB462.one_line: Revises driver‑licensing ages, county exam scheduling, and disqualifying conditions, effective July 1 2025.
SB462.summary: The bill amends Montana’s driver‑licensing statutes to allow counties to schedule a motor‑vehicle exam once a month and to clarify age and eligibility limits, including a new 13‑year‑old hardship exception. It also updates the list of disqualifying conditions and requires proof of lawful presence for non‑citizens. The changes take effect July 1 2025.
changes: County motor‑vehicle exam scheduling may occur at least once a month if requested by the county.
The minimum age for a driver’s license is set at 16, with a 15½‑year‑old exception for those who complete an approved driver‑education course.
A 13‑year‑old may obtain a restricted license if hardship is demonstrated.
The list of disqualifying conditions is expanded to include drug addiction, mental disability, and lack of financial responsibility.
Non‑citizen applicants must be verified as lawfully present using federal alien‑verification procedures.
The act becomes effective July 1 2025.
affected: Applicants with disabilities or financial responsibility issues

SB463.one_line: Revises child‑abuse reporting, expands mandatory reporters, and creates new certification for public‑safety communications officers.
SB463.summary: The bill amends Montana’s child‑abuse reporting laws to expand who must report, tighten certification for public‑safety communications officers, and give the department new record‑keeping and reporting duties. It also replaces a series of unfunded mandates and sets new effective and termination dates.
changes: Redefines and expands the list of mandatory reporters for child‑abuse and neglect, adding health‑care professionals, religious healers, school staff, and others; requires infant‑drug‑risk reporting by certain health professionals.
Creates a new certification requirement for public‑safety communications officers, including a basic course and child‑abuse training, and establishes penalties for non‑compliance.
Adds a new “public safety communications officer” reporting channel for child‑abuse reports and requires immediate audio recording and transmission of 9‑1‑1 calls to the department.
Imposes new record‑keeping and disclosure rules for child‑abuse investigations, safety‑risk assessments, and related reports, including retention periods and confidentiality exceptions.
Supersedes a set of unfunded mandate statutes (1‑2‑112 through 1‑2‑116) and provides new effective and termination dates for the amended provisions.
Revises reporting requirements for the legislature, including biennial reports on various state programs and financial matters.
Adds rule‑making authority for the Department of Public Health and Human Services to adopt procedures for reporting, recording, and transmitting child‑abuse information.
Mandates the department to report annually to the attorney general and the law‑and‑justice interim committee on referrals to county attorneys.
Requires the department to adopt rules governing the retention and disclosure of safety‑risk assessments and related case records.
Sets a new effective date of October 1 2025 for most provisions, with some sections effective October 1 2030 and others terminating September 30 2030.
affected: Mandatory reporters (health professionals, school staff, religious healers, etc.)
Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB465.one_line: Revises special‑advocate law, expands reporting, confidentiality, and review procedures in Montana child‑welfare system.
SB465.summary: The bill amends Montana’s child‑welfare statutes to clarify the definition and funding of court‑appointed special advocates, tighten reporting and confidentiality rules, and expand the role of foster‑care review committees and boards. It limits the use of the special‑advocate account to volunteer advocates, requires new procedures for appointing and training special advocates, and expands mandatory reporting duties for a wide range of professionals.
changes: Creates a dedicated court‑appointed special advocate account in the state special revenue fund and bars its use for paid advocates; establishes procedures for funding and distribution of that account.

Redefines “special advocate” as a trained volunteer officer of the court and sets training, duties, and appointment requirements for special advocates, including the possibility of paid advocates only if the special‑advocate account is not used.
Expands mandatory reporting obligations to a broad list of professionals (healthcare, educators, clergy, law‑enforcement, etc.) and clarifies the content and timing of reports.
Rewrites confidentiality provisions (41‑3‑205) to specify who may receive case records, how records may be shared, and the circumstances under which disclosure is permitted.

Amends the foster‑care review process (41‑3‑115, 41‑3‑1010) to require board reviews within the Adoption and Safe Families Act time limits, expand board membership, and require presence of key personnel at reviews.
Adds or expands rights to counsel for parties in child‑welfare petitions (41‑3‑425) and clarifies procedures for appointing special advocates in termination hearings (41‑3‑607).
affected: paid attorneys who may serve as special advocates
healthcare providers, educators, clergy, law‑enforcement officers, and other mandatory reporters
parents, guardians, and children in foster care
numbers: Adoption and Safe Families Act time limits (42 U.S.C. 675(5))

SB467.one_line: Revisions tighten licensing, protect child data, and shift inspection duties from local health authorities to the department.
SB467.summary: SB 467 revises Montana’s child‑care statutes, clarifying definitions, tightening licensing and registration requirements, and protecting confidential child data. It removes certain local‑public‑health‑authority inspection duties, adds new record‑keeping and reporting obligations, and sets limits on group‑day‑care‑home staffing.
changes: Amends 52‑2‑702 to restate purpose and legislative intent for child‑care services
Rewrites 52‑2‑703 to update definitions of child, day‑care, and various provider types
Revises 52‑2‑722 to require applications be filed in the applicant’s county or through a tribal governing body and mandates a 30‑day decision period
Updates 52‑2‑723 to list specific licensing requirements for day‑care centers (staffing, background checks, insurance, intake records, etc.)
Amends 52‑2‑725 to require renewal requests be written 30 days before expiration
Revises 52‑2‑731 to broaden the department’s standard‑setting authority and clarify record‑keeping
Rewrites 52‑2‑732 to require licensees/registrants to keep confidential child data and allow department inspections
Amends 52‑2‑735 to adopt health‑protection rules, require immunization for under‑5s, and set local‑public‑health‑authority training/inspection fees
Adds 52‑2‑737 to mandate at least two caregivers when more than eight children are present in a group‑day‑care home
Removes the requirement for local public‑health authorities to perform certain inspections and provide training, shifting those duties to the department

SB469.one_line: Rewrites mental‑health service‑area authority law, expands DPHHS duties, and mandates new reporting and funding structures.
SB469.summary: The bill amends Montana’s mental‑health service‑area authority statutes to give the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) new planning, reporting, and funding duties, requires the creation of at least three service‑area authorities, and adds detailed board‑and‑committee rules. It also supersedes earlier unfunded‑mandate laws and mandates notification to tribal governments.
changes: Amends §53‑21‑1002 to expand DPHHS duties in mental‑health planning, contracting, quality management, and reporting.

Amends §53‑21‑1006 to require public meetings, establish leadership committees and boards, set board composition (majority consumers/family), and grant boards authority to contract, manage funds, and report to the governor, department, and legislature.
Mandates the department to provide an annual contract to each service‑area authority covering administrative, informational, and programmatic support.
Requires the department to support the creation of at least three service‑area authorities, including staffing and technical assistance.
Supersedes existing unfunded‑mandate statutes (1‑2‑112‑116) and requires the Secretary of State to notify all federally recognized tribal governments.
Adds reporting requirements for boards (annual reports, budgets, recommendations, surveys).

SB470.one_line: Revises election judge selection, notification, training, and complaint procedures.
SB470.summary: SB 470 revises how election judges are chosen, notified, and trained, adds a complaint process for county central committees, and requires notification when a judge is removed. The bill also sets deadlines for submitting nominee lists and for training completion.
changes: County central committees must submit lists of qualified electors at least 45 days before the primary; the election administrator must notify committees 90 days before the deadline to submit lists.
Election judges are selected from these lists, with requirements that each board include representatives of at least two parties and that no more than a simple majority come from a single party.
If a judge is permanently removed for violation or disruption, the election administrator must notify the county central committee.
A county central committee may file a complaint with the governing body if it does not receive required notification or if the list is not used in selecting judges.
Training is required before each election; all judges must receive instruction on current procedures, and a certificate of completion is required to serve (except in emergencies).
The act becomes effective January 1 2026.

SB473.one_line: Montana bans geo‑engineering weather modification, except for approved cloud‑seeding, effective immediately.
SB473.summary: Montana’s SB 473 bars all geo‑engineering weather modification within state borders, except for approved cloud‑seeding activities. It defines key terms and makes the prohibition effective immediately upon passage.
changes: Prohibits intentional injection, release, or dispersal of chemicals or apparatuses for geo‑engineering, temperature alteration, or sunlight intensity control.
Excludes cloud‑seeding activities already authorized under Title 85, Chapter 3.
Defines "geo‑engineering" to include stratospheric aerosol injection, solar radiation management, marine cloud brightening, and other large‑scale climate interventions.
Codifies the prohibition as part of Title 75, Chapter 2, so existing regulatory framework applies.
Makes the act effective immediately upon passage and approval.
No new program or office is created; it merely adds a prohibition.
No monetary allocations or appropriations are included.
affected: Individuals, companies, or organizations that would conduct geo‑engineering within Montana
State agencies responsible for enforcing the prohibition

SB474.one_line: Bill allows religious, medical, and informed‑consent immunization exemptions and bans vaccination‑status discrimination.
SB474.summary: The bill requires that schools accept religious, medical, and personal‑medical informed‑consent exemptions to required immunizations, limits liability for those who grant exemptions, and prohibits discrimination based on vaccination status except for school requirements. It amends existing statutes to clarify exemption procedures and protects individuals from civil liability when they are exempted.
changes: Amends §20‑5‑405 to allow religious, medical, and personal‑medical informed‑consent exemptions for school enrollment; specifies required written statements, notarized affidavits, and conditions for each exemption type.
Adds a new subsection that bars civil liability for anyone who accepts an exemption, except for government entities.
Amends §49‑2‑312 to prohibit discrimination based on vaccination status or immunity passports, with specific carve‑outs for school vaccination requirements and health‑care facilities.
Defines “immunity passport” and “vaccination status” for the purposes of the anti‑discrimination provision.
Provides that the department cannot review or deny medical exemption statements and that exemption forms may not impose additional burdens.
Establishes that exemption records must be kept with the student’s immunization record and may not be copied without consent.
Sets the act to take effect immediately upon passage and approval.
affected: Students and parents seeking immunization exemptions
Health‑care providers who issue medical exemption statements
Employers and public accommodations that may discriminate based on vaccination status
Government entities that may accept exemptions

SB475.one_line: Bans aluminum‑containing vaccines in Montana, requiring manufacturers to supply aluminum‑free alternatives.
SB475.summary: The bill bans any vaccine that contains aluminum from being sold or administered in Montana and requires manufacturers to provide an aluminum‑free alternative within a set timeline. It also creates enforcement mechanisms for the Department of Public Health and Human Services and the Department of Labor and Industry. The act becomes effective only after the state confirms that aluminum‑free vaccines are available.
changes: Prohibits sale or use of any vaccine containing aluminum within Montana.
Health‑care providers may not administer aluminum‑containing vaccines.
The Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) is authorized to enforce the ban and to require manufacturers/distributors to submit a compliance plan.
DPHHS must notify all manufacturers, distributors, and providers within 30 days of the act’s effective date.

Manufacturers/distributors must submit an implementation plan within one year, including a 90‑day compliance timeline, removal of aluminum‑containing vaccines, and distribution of aluminum‑free vaccines.
DPHHS must certify to the code commissioner when aluminum‑free vaccines become available, triggering the implementation plan.
The act is codified as a new part of Title 50, Chapter 17, and is effective upon passage unless the contingency in §4 is met.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
SB475.effective: Effective upon passage, contingent on certification of aluminum‑free vaccine availability

SB476.one_line: Codifies separation of powers and defines education board powers.
SB476.summary: The bill codifies Montana’s separation‑of‑powers doctrine, explicitly defines the powers of each branch and the two education boards, and amends the statutes that create those boards to clarify that they are executive agencies. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Codifies the doctrine that executive and judicial powers are limited to those enumerated in the Constitution and law.
affected: Montana governor and other executive officers
Montana Supreme Court and other courts
Board of Regents of Higher Education

SB477.one_line: Family‑transfer land divisions exempt from full review but require hearing, affidavit, tax certification, and penalties for evasion.
SB477.summary: SB 477 revises Montana’s subdivision law to allow certain family‑transfer land divisions to bypass full subdivision review, but requires a public hearing, an affidavit, and tax certification. The bill sets limits on lot size, tax payment, and a two‑year transfer restriction, and imposes penalties for evasion.
changes: Exempts specific family‑transfer divisions from full subdivision review while still requiring survey and zoning compliance
Mandates a public hearing and notice to adjacent owners and water users before a division is approved
Requires the county treasurer to certify that all taxes on the land to be divided are paid, with prorated assessment for centrally assessed property
Limits family‑transfer divisions to parcels of at least 5 acres unless the zoning district allows smaller lots
Imposes a two‑year restriction on transfer or conveyance of a division received by an immediate family member or spouse
Provides a $5,000 civil penalty for each division that is proven to have been used to evade subdivision regulations
Allows governing bodies to waive the two‑year restriction in hardship cases and to set a shorter period if they choose
affected: Landowners seeking to divide land for family transfer
Adjacent property owners and water users

SB478.one_line: Higher‑education institutions must reimburse students for certain vaccine‑related medical costs.
SB478.summary: Higher‑education institutions must reimburse students for specific medical costs incurred after a COVID‑19 vaccine. Students must prove vaccination, a vaccine‑related diagnosis, and provide cost records. The law applies immediately upon passage.
changes: Institutions must pay medical costs for myocarditis, pericarditis, thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome, Guillain‑Barré syndrome, or other vaccine‑associated diseases diagnosed after vaccination.
Students must submit vaccination records, medical certification of the diagnosis, and cost documentation to receive reimbursement.
Reimbursement includes treatment costs and lost wages due to the disease.
The requirement applies to all public postsecondary institutions governed or coordinated by the Board of Regents.
The act is codified as part of Title 20, Chapter 25, Part 3 of the Montana Statutes.
The law takes effect on passage and approval.
affected: Students who received a COVID‑19 vaccine and developed a listed disease

SB479.one_line: Re‑criminalizes out‑of‑office chemical abortions and fines manufacturers for improper drug disposal.
SB479.summary: The bill tightens rules on at‑home chemical abortions, making it a felony for providers to give or attempt to give an abortion drug without an in‑person exam, follow‑up, and proper disposal kit. It also imposes fines on drug manufacturers for improper disposal of abortion medication and its endocrine‑disrupting by‑products.
changes: Providers must physically examine the patient, be present at the abortion, schedule a follow‑up within 7 days, and supply a catch kit and medical waste bag for disposal; otherwise the act is a felony with up to $10,000 fine and 3‑year prison.
The felony exception applies only when the abortion is necessary to preserve the life of the mother.

Manufacturers of abortion drugs are held responsible for proper disposal of discarded medication and for cleaning up endocrine‑disrupting by‑products that enter wastewater; violations can be fined up to $20,000 per incident.
The act codifies its provisions into existing Montana statutes (Title 50, Chapter 20 for provider rules; Title 75, Chapter 6, Part 1 for manufacturer rules).
The bill includes severability language to preserve valid portions if any part is struck down.
affected: Health‑care providers prescribing or dispensing abortion drugs

SB480.one_line: Prohibits firing guns within 500 yards of inhabited dwellings on class II waters and expands restrictions on recreational use.
SB480.summary: SB 480 restricts the use of class II waters by adding a new prohibition on firing a gun within 500 yards of an inhabited dwelling. It also expands the list of activities that are not allowed on class II waters and gives the Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Commission authority to adopt rules governing recreational use of class I and class II waters.
changes: Amends § 23‑2‑302, MCA, to prohibit the discharge of a firearm within 500 yards of an inhabited dwelling or outbuilding on class II waters; temporary absences of inhabitants do not change the prohibition.

Adds several new activities that are excluded from recreational use of class II waters, including big‑game hunting, overnight camping, placement of permanent or seasonal objects, and other non‑water‑related activities.

Requires the commission to adopt rules under § 87‑1‑303 to govern recreational use of class I and class II waters, including procedures for requesting orders, issuing findings, and identifying streams that are not or only limitedly recreationally usable.
Clarifies that the public’s right to use class II waters does not give an easement to cross private property, and that state‑owned school‑trust lands remain unaffected.
affected: Recreational users of class II waters (e.g., anglers, boaters, hunters)
Landowners whose property borders class II waters

SB481.one_line: Prohibits motorboats on class II waters and requires new commission rules for recreational use.
SB481.summary: The bill amends Montana’s recreational‑water statute to ban motorboats and personal watercraft on class II waters, while allowing other non‑motorized uses. It requires the Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Commission to adopt rules governing all recreational use of class I and class II waters, including procedures for public requests and limits on capacity.
changes: Amends §23‑2‑302 to prohibit motorboats or personal watercraft on class II waters; other recreational uses remain allowed.
Adds a prohibition on using motorboats or personal watercraft on class II waters.
Mandates the commission to adopt rules under §87‑1‑303 governing recreational use of class I and class II waters.
Requires the rules to include procedures for public requests for orders, for limiting or prohibiting use, and for identifying streams that cannot be used recreationally.
Preserves existing public rights on state‑owned lands such as school trust lands and lessee rights.
Does not create a new state program or criminal offense.
affected: Recreational users of class II waters
The Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Commission
Landowners whose private waters are class II
Public who may request use restrictions

SB483.one_line: Rewrites step‑therapy rules to require evidence‑based protocols, public access, and rapid exception decisions.
SB483.summary: SB 483 revises Montana’s health‑care statutes to tighten step‑therapy rules, require transparent criteria, and mandate timely exception decisions. It also expands definitions and reporting requirements for insurers and utilization‑review organizations.
changes: Amends §33‑32‑102 to add detailed definitions of terms such as “step‑therapy protocol,” “clinical review criteria,” and “step‑therapy exception determination.”
Mandates that step‑therapy protocols be based on clinical practice guidelines developed by multidisciplinary panels that disclose conflicts of interest and are publicly available.
numbers: annual reporting to the state auditor

SB484.one_line: Limits ticket resale prices, authorizes venue‑approved higher prices, and criminalizes violations.
SB484.summary: The bill prohibits reselling event tickets above the printed price plus a modest service fee, creates a misdemeanor for violations, and allows venue owners to authorize higher‑priced sales with written permission.
changes: Limits resale price to the printed ticket price plus tax and a service charge no greater than $3 or 10% of the printed price, whichever is higher.
Allows venue owners/operators to authorize higher resale prices in writing, specifying the exact price.
Makes violating the price limit a misdemeanor punishable by up to a $1,000 fine per offense.
Codifies the new rule as part of Title 30, Chapter 14, Part 2 of the Montana Code.
No other provisions are added or removed.

SB485.one_line: Mandates free hygiene items for inmates, expands correctional program authority, and removes unfunded mandates.
SB485.summary: SB 485 revises Montana’s incarceration laws to require state and local correctional facilities to provide inmates with free hygiene and stationery items, establish policies for their distribution, and expand the Department of Corrections’ authority to create and contract for prerelease, treatment, and residential programs. The bill also supersedes existing unfunded‑mandate statutes and amends the department’s powers and duties, including data collection and contract oversight.
changes: Amends §7‑32‑2222, MCA, to mandate that each detention center provide soap, toilet paper, toothbrush, toothpaste, comb, feminine hygiene products, letter envelopes, writing paper, and postage stamps to inmates at no cost upon admission or by request.

Requires each detention center to develop, publish, and distribute a written policy and procedure for making those hygiene products available, including special procedures for inmates who cannot access general‑population areas.

Amends §53‑1‑203, MCA, to broaden the Department of Corrections’ authority to adopt rules for siting and expanding prerelease centers, contracting for residential methamphetamine treatment programs, and contracting with private or nonprofit entities for various correctional services.
Adds a new §3 that expressly supersedes and modifies the requirements of 1‑2‑112 through 1‑2‑116, thereby eliminating those unfunded‑mandate statutes.
Imposes a 20‑year maximum on contracts for prerelease and treatment programs, requiring legislative audit committee review before any contract exceeds that term.
Mandates the department to maintain data on discharged individuals, delinquent youth placements, and to provide funding and oversight for youth correctional facilities.
affected: Inmates and persons under state or local correctional supervision
State and local correctional facilities and their staff
Department of Corrections and its contractors
