SB489.one_line: Prohibits Montana credit unions from acquiring banks or bank assets or liabilities.
SB489.summary: The bill amends Montana’s credit‑union statutes to explicitly forbid a credit union from acquiring a bank, a bank’s assets, or liabilities. It clarifies that the general powers listed in §32‑3‑401 do not include any bank‑related acquisitions.
changes: Amends §32‑3‑401, MCA, adding a new paragraph that states a credit union may not acquire a bank, a bank’s assets, a bank’s liabilities, or any other aspect of a bank’s business.
Re‑states the existing general powers of a credit union but inserts the prohibition as a separate clause.
No new programs, funds, or licensing requirements are created.
The amendment does not alter any other sections of the statute.
The text does not impose new fees, taxes, or reporting obligations.
The amendment is purely a prohibition and does not affect existing credit‑union operations beyond preventing bank acquisitions.

SB494.one_line: Bill mandates testing of new voting systems and longer retention of audit logs for public record.
SB494.summary: The bill requires election administrators to test new or upgraded voting systems, retain audit logs for 22 months, and amend retention rules for ballots and audit records. It also revises the counting‑board procedures for manual and machine counts.
changes:
1. Mandates a test of the election‑management system whenever a new voting system is acquired or after upgrades, patches, or hardware removal.
2. Extends the retention period for audit logs and cast‑vote records to 22 months and requires them to be kept as public records.
3. Amends §13‑1‑303 to specify 12‑month retention for non‑federal elections and 22‑month retention for federal elections, with opening only for recounts or audits.
4. Adds a 22‑month retention requirement for audit logs/records under §13‑15‑206 and requires perpetual public record retention for counties using vote‑counting machines that produce audit logs.
5. Revises §13‑15‑206 to require election administrators to print, examine, and retain audit logs before and after vote counts and to follow procedures if a system is suspected of malfunctioning.
6. Codifies the new testing requirement as part of Title 13, Chapter 17, Part 1.

SB491.one_line: Creates a state fund to pay for sexual‑assault forensic exams and evidence kits, removing local agency cost responsibility.
SB491.summary: The bill creates a state special revenue fund to pay for sexual‑assault medical forensic examinations and evidence kits, eliminates the obligation of local law‑enforcement agencies to cover those costs, and establishes an annual appropriation of $800,000 for the fund. It also amends related statutes to define the fund’s use, transfer excess marijuana‑revenue funds, and create a restorative‑justice fund.
changes: Establishes a sexual assault medical forensic examination fund within the state special revenue fund.
Mandates the Department of Justice to purchase evidence kits, reimburse medical providers up to $800 per exam, and maintain a secure electronic reimbursement system.
Transfers excess marijuana‑state special revenue funds to the fund and other specified accounts, including a $375,000–$800,000 allocation to the new fund.

Rewrites Section 46‑15‑411 to make the local law‑enforcement agency responsible for paying for the examination only if the department cannot cover it, and clarifies that treatment costs are not covered.
Amends Section 46‑15‑412 to require submission of kits to the Division of Forensic Science within 30 days.
Provides an annual appropriation of $800,000 for the fund and designates it as part of the ongoing base budget.
Adds notification to federally recognized tribal governments and codification instructions.
affected: Montana state budget and special revenue accounts
numbers: $375,000–$800,000 transfer to fund from marijuana revenue
4% to trails and recreational facilities account

SB496.one_line: Allows legislature to rent governor’s residence when not occupied, effective 2026.
SB496.summary: The bill creates a policy for using the governor’s official residence when the governor chooses not to live there. It allows the legislature to rent the house to temporary staff, especially those with disabilities, and gives the Department of Administration authority to set rules and fees. The policy takes effect on January 1, 2026.
changes: If the governor notifies the Department of Administration that he/she will not occupy the executive residence, the residence is declared available for use.
The residence may be rented to temporary employees of the legislature during interim and session periods, with preference for employees with disabilities.
The Department of Administration, together with the Legislative Services Division, may adopt rules establishing occupancy limits, rental fees, and other implementation details.
The term “executive residence” is defined as the state‑owned house at 2 Carson Street, Helena.
The provisions are codified as part of Title 2, Chapter 17, Part 8 of the Montana Code.
The act becomes effective January 1, 2026.

SB499.one_line: Revises voter‑list maintenance to focus on permanent address changes and expands absentee‑ballot procedures.
SB499.summary: SB 499 amends Montana voter‑registration rules so that only permanent address changes trigger the state’s annual address‑verification process, and it expands the absentee‑ballot application procedures to include more ways to confirm a voter’s address and to remove voters from the absentee list.
changes: Amends §13‑2‑220 to require election administrators to confirm permanent‑address changes via national change‑of‑address files and mailed notices, and to move unresponsive voters to the inactive list after 30 days.
Adds a 90‑day pre‑election deadline for completing address‑verification procedures.
Revises §13‑13‑212 to broaden absentee‑ballot requests: written requests, phone/fax, and online confirmation of address changes are allowed.
Requires biennial mailed address‑confirmation forms to voters listed in the national change‑of‑address system, with optional online response.
Allows voters to remove themselves from the absentee list and to re‑apply for future absentee ballots.
Maintains that inactive voters must reactivate their registration before receiving ballots.
affected: Election administrators and county election officials
Voters on the absentee ballot list
Voters who are inactive or removed from the absentee list

SB501.one_line: Tenants can buy a rental unit before a landlord sells it, with a 45‑day decision window.
SB501.summary: The Keep Montanans Housed Act gives tenants the right of first refusal to buy a rental unit or the property it sits on before the landlord can sell or vacate it.  Tenants have 45 days to accept the offer and may challenge the price by hiring an appraiser at their own expense.
changes: Landlords must offer tenants the opportunity to purchase the dwelling unit or its underlying property before selling or vacating it for demolition, repurposing, or sale.
The offer must be a bona‑fide sale offer, not a partial ownership arrangement.
The sale price cannot exceed the market value or the appraised value of the unit or property.
Tenants have 45 days to accept the offer; if they reject or do not respond, the landlord may sell to a third party at the same price and terms.
Tenants may request an appraiser’s determination of value at their own cost if they believe the offer is not bona‑fide.

SB500.one_line: Amends land‑sale rules for cabin/home‑site parcels, adjusting bonds, cancellation rights, and cost duties.
SB500.summary: The bill amends Montana’s land‑banking rules to give cabin and home‑site lessees the right to cancel a sale, lowers the required bid bond for such parcels, and clarifies who pays for sale‑preparation costs.  It also sets notice periods and limits the amount of land that can be sold at one time.  The changes take effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Lessee of a cabin or home‑site may cancel a sale up to 10 days before auction, provided no bid bond has been posted; if a bid bond is posted the sale cannot be canceled.
Bid bonds for cabin/home‑site sales are reduced to 5 % of the minimum sale price (vs. 20 % for other parcels).
The board may not sell more than 250,000 acres in total, and no more than 20,000 acres in a single transaction unless revenue is used to purchase land under § 77‑2‑364.

Lessee must pay the department for preparation costs (appraisals, surveys, etc.) within 10 days after preliminary approval; if the lessee buys the parcel those funds are applied to actual costs, otherwise they are refunded and the purchaser pays the costs.
The department retains the successful bidder’s bid bond and forfeits it to the trust if the bidder fails to complete the sale.
Lessee receives 60 days’ notice of a proposed sale and may propose an exchange; the lessee also has rights to match the highest bid under § 77‑2‑324.
The sale of a cabin or home‑site is exempt from certain Title 75 environmental review requirements.
affected: Lessee of cabin or home‑site land
Potential buyers of cabin or home‑site parcels
Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

SB502.one_line: Limits investment firms from buying single‑family homes within 45 days of listing.
SB502.summary: SB 502 limits investment firms from buying a single‑family home within 45 days of its listing, and makes such contracts voidable by the seller. The bill codifies the restriction under Montana’s real‑estate statutes and preserves pre‑existing rights and penalties. It does not create a new program or offense.
changes: Investment firms cannot enter an executory contract to purchase a single‑family dwelling listed for sale until 45 days after the listing date.
If a contract is entered in violation, the seller may void it at any time before full execution.
The restriction is codified as part of Title 70, Chapter 1, Part 5 of the Montana Statutes.
The act does not alter any rights, duties, penalties, or proceedings that existed before its effective date.
affected: Investment firms that buy single‑family homes
Real‑estate agents and attorneys handling such contracts

SB504.one_line: Creates a $75 million grant program for nonprofit permanent supportive housing, funded by $75 million transfers.
SB504.summary: The bill creates a state grant program to fund permanent supportive housing for low‑income, homeless or at‑risk individuals. It authorizes up to $75 million in grants, establishes a dedicated account, and sets eligibility, application, and disbursement rules. The program is funded with $75 million transferred into the account on July 1, 2025.
changes: Establishes a permanent supportive housing development account within the state special revenue fund.
Authorizes the Department of Commerce to award up to $75 million in grants to nonprofit corporations for acquisition, construction, rehabilitation, or equipment of permanent supportive housing.
Creates eligibility and application procedures, including a deadline, priority, and guidelines adopted by the Department.
Sets grant conditions: recipients must sign a grant agreement with a project management plan, meet design standards, and may receive reduced funds if actual costs are lower than projections.
Allocates $50 million from the general fund and $25 million from the behavioral health system for future generations fund to the account within 15 days of the effective date.
Defines permanent supportive housing and homeless per federal standards.
affected: Nonprofit corporations developing permanent supportive housing
Persons earning ≤60% of area median income who are homeless or at risk
Department of Commerce and State Treasurer

SB505.one_line: Prohibits local zoning of wind‑generation facilities and empowers counties to block them with a majority‑owner petition.
SB505.summary: The bill amends Montana’s zoning statutes to prohibit local governments from allowing wind‑generation facilities and gives county commissioners the power to create zoning districts that can ban such facilities when a majority of affected property owners petition for it.
changes: Amends §7‑1‑111 to prohibit local governments from exercising any power that would allow the construction of wind‑generation facilities (defined in §75‑26‑301).

Adds a new subsection to §76‑2‑101 that allows county commissioners to create a planning and zoning district to prohibit wind‑generation facilities when 60 % of affected owners petition (55 % if the purpose is to prohibit wind facilities).

Requires that such a district be at least 40 acres and that the board of county commissioners must provide draft development patterns, resolutions, and zoning regulations to the public before deciding on the petition.
Limits the creation of a district to areas not already zoned by an incorporated city.
Gives a 6‑month window for challenges to the district‑creation process.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.

SB506.one_line: Legislators may use a personal e‑mail for public contact, subject to public‑records rules.
SB506.summary: Legislators may now choose a personal e‑mail address as their primary contact for public communications, but must manage those messages under state public‑records rules. The law takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Allows a legislator to select a non‑legislative e‑mail as their primary contact address.
Requires the chosen address to be listed on the legislator’s public profile.
Makes the legislator responsible for managing communications at that address under Montana’s public‑records and records‑management plans.
Codifies the provision as part of Title 5, Chapter 11, Part 4 of the Montana Code.
The act becomes effective on passage.
affected: Members of the public contacting legislators

SB507.one_line: Prohibits book bans in Montana schools and libraries and mandates objection‑review policies.
SB507.summary: The bill amends Montana law to prohibit school and public libraries from excluding or banning books solely because of the author’s background or the book’s viewpoint. It requires school‑district trustees and public‑library boards to adopt policies and procedures for reviewing objections, keeping challenged materials available during review, and reporting outcomes to state officials. The changes also protect library staff from retaliation for following the new policies.
changes: Amends §20‑7‑204 to forbid exclusion of a book or resource based on the creator’s background or the material’s viewpoint, and to require trustee approval for selection.

SB510.one_line: Revises district governance, election rules, and property‑addition/removal procedures.
SB510.summary: SB 510 revises Montana’s urban transportation district statutes to clarify board composition, election procedures, and property‑addition/removal rules. It limits exactions, allows removal of recently added or long‑unserved areas without debt, and requires districts to document added areas.
changes: Amends §7‑14‑202 to define “Board,” “Commissioners,” and “Direct transportation service.”

Rewrites §7‑14‑212 to require districts to be governed by a transportation board and to let county, city, or town governing bodies decide whether the board is elected or appointed, set terms, and establish procedures for vacancies and elections.
affected: Property owners within or adjacent to transportation districts
Voters in areas added to or removed from districts

SB509.one_line: Mandates free, fair access to embedded software, parts, and tools for Montana farm equipment owners and repairers.
SB509.summary: The bill requires that any software embedded in Montana’s farm equipment be treated as a sold product, not a license, and that owners and independent repair shops have free, fair access to all software, parts, tools, and documentation needed to keep the equipment fully functional.  It prohibits manufacturers from restricting use, imposing hidden fees, or using software‑based lock‑out mechanisms that prevent repair or resale.
changes: Treats embedded software as a sold product, not a license, for all farm equipment.
Prohibits manufacturers from requiring owners to enter agreements that limit software use for the equipment’s useful life.
Mandates that all rights, parts, tools, and documentation transfer automatically to new owners upon sale.
Requires manufacturers to provide free, fair‑priced parts, tools, and documentation to owners and independent repair providers.
Bans the use of parts‑pairing or other software tricks that block replacement parts, reduce performance, or create deceptive alerts.
Ensures that any electronic lock needed for diagnosis or repair can be deactivated and re‑activated with documentation, tools, and parts made available on fair and reasonable terms.
Makes violations an unfair or deceptive trade practice under Montana’s consumer‑protection law, subject to existing penalties.
Effective January 1 2026.
codifies the provisions into Title 30, Chapter 11, Part 8.

SB512.one_line: Mandates public disclosure of property‑tax settlement agreements and formalizes mediation for valuation disputes.
SB512.summary: The bill requires the Department of Revenue to post on its website every settlement agreement it reaches with a taxpayer over the assessed value of centrally‑assessed or industrial property, including the original and agreed‑upon valuations. It also amends the dispute‑resolution rules to create a formal dispute‑resolution office and mandates mediation for valuation disputes, with a $100 fee and a 60‑day pre‑hearing requirement.
changes: 1. Amends §15‑1‑211 to establish a dispute‑resolution office and formalize notice, mediation, and final‑decision timelines for property‑tax disputes.
2. Amends §15‑1‑212 to require that any settlement agreement on centrally‑assessed or industrial property be publicly disclosed on the Department’s website and to set a $100 mediation fee.
3. Adds a new section that applies the changes to property‑tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2025.
4. Requires the Department to disclose the pre‑settlement valuation and the agreed valuation for each settlement.
5. Mandates that mediation be conducted privately, confidentially, and within 60 days of a contested case hearing, with parties sharing mediator costs.
affected: Property owners of centrally‑assessed and industrial property

SB513.one_line: Expand family education services, report annually, effective July 1 2025, ending June 30 2027.
SB513.summary: The bill directs the Department of Public Health and Human Services to expand the Family Education and Support Services program to accommodate all qualified families by July 1 2026, requires annual reporting to a legislative committee, and sets an effective date of July 1 2025 with termination on June 30 2027.
changes: 1. Requires the department to increase program capacity to serve all qualified families by July 1 2026.

2. Mandates annual reports to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee on family benefits, program readiness for future health care use, and comparative outcomes versus non‑participants.
3. Establishes an effective date of July 1 2025 and a termination date of June 30 2027 for the act’s provisions.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services
Qualified families applying to the Family Education and Support Services program

SB517.one_line: Revises irrigation‑district commissioner elections to require residency and restrict voting to the candidate’s land division.
SB517.summary: The bill amends the law governing irrigation‑district commissioner elections to require candidates to live in the district they seek to represent and limits the voting electorate to residents of the specific land division in which the candidate is running. It takes effect immediately upon passage.
changes: Amends §85‑7‑1702 to add a residency requirement for candidates.
Limits each candidate’s electorate to voters who reside in the land division where the candidate is running.
Specifies that the term of office is three years and that commissioners organize within 40 days of election.
Keeps the election timing and filing procedures unchanged.
Provides an immediate effective date upon passage.

SB515.one_line: Montana will adopt a multistate cosmetology license, require background checks, and create a commission to administer the compact.
SB515.summary: Montana will join a multistate cosmetology licensure compact that creates a single multistate license, requires criminal‑history checks for applicants and renewals, and establishes a commission to administer the compact and share data among member states.
changes: Creates a cosmetology licensure compact and a commission to administer it.
Establishes a multistate license that authorizes practice in all member states for licensed cosmetologists.
Requires applicants for a multistate license (and renewals) to submit fingerprints for state and federal criminal‑history checks and to pay related fees.
Mandates that each member state report adverse actions, investigative information, and other required data to a shared data system.
Allows member states to impose adverse actions on multistate licensees and to suspend or revoke the license in all member states if the home state takes action.
Provides procedures for re‑issuance of a multistate license when a licensee changes home state and for withdrawal or termination of a member state.
Includes rules for dispute resolution, enforcement, and default procedures for member states.
Codifies the compact into Montana’s statutes (Title 37, Chapter 31).
affected: Licensed cosmetologists in Montana and other compact states
State licensing authorities in Montana and other compact states
Active military members and spouses who are cosmetologists
SB515.effective: on the date the compact statute is enacted in the seventh member state

SB519.one_line: Requiring written permission for property‑valuation staff to enter private land for appraisals.
SB519.summary: The bill requires Montana Department of Revenue property‑valuation staff to obtain written permission before entering private land to appraise or audit property. It sets notice, response, and appointment procedures and limits the use of denied‑entry estimates for tax‑appeal decisions. The law takes effect January 1, 2026, applying to appraisals after December 31, 2025.
changes: Amends §15‑7‑139 to mandate written permission from landowners or their agents before property‑valuation staff may enter private land for appraisal or audit.

Requires the department to publish an annual notice in each county’s general‑circulation newspaper, detailing the right of landowners to request presence and to submit written permission within 30 days of publication.
Establishes procedures for landowners to notify the department of their requirement for presence and to schedule an entry date; if denied or unresponsive, the department may estimate value.
Limits county and Montana tax‑appeal boards from adjusting estimated values unless the landowner gives permission or submits a certified appraisal within one year.
Specifies that staff must carry identification and that entry is limited to established roads and trails unless otherwise approved.
Mandates the department to adopt rules to implement these changes, including extensions for landowner responses.
Sets the effective date to January 1, 2026, applying to appraisals after December 31, 2025.
affected: Property owners and their agents in Montana
Landowners who may be denied entry or must provide certified appraisals

SB521.one_line: Mandates a statewide mental‑health curriculum plan with reporting and tribal notification.
SB521.summary: The bill directs Montana’s Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) and the Office of Public Instruction (OPI) to create a statewide mental‑health curriculum plan that expands the existing suicide‑prevention grant program to all public schools. It requires interim and final reports to two legislative committees and mandates notification of federally recognized tribes.
changes: 1. DPHHS and OPI must develop a comprehensive plan to implement a universal mental‑health education program in all public schools, building on the PAX Good Behavior Game curriculum.

2. The plan must include curriculum details, financial/technical support mechanisms, data collection, success metrics, focus areas (bullying, suicide, substance use), teacher integration, cost estimates, implementation strategy, and requested legislative support.

3. Interim reports are required by September 1 2025 and January 1 2026, and a final plan must be submitted by May 1 2026 to the Education Interim Committee and the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee.
4. The Secretary of State must send a copy of the act to every federally recognized tribal government in Montana.
5. The act takes effect immediately upon passage and approval.

SB522.one_line: Mandates Medicaid waiting‑list reductions, prioritizes services, and requires annual reporting.
SB522.summary: The bill directs the Montana Department of Health and Human Services to cut or eliminate Medicaid waiting lists, prioritizing certain services and requiring annual reporting. It does not create a new program or fund, but mandates actions and reporting. The bill is a legislative act, not a study request.
changes: 1. The department must implement administrative, programmatic, and funding initiatives to reduce or eliminate waiting lists for all Medicaid‑covered services.
2. Initiatives may include applying for waivers, adjusting reimbursement rates, adding add‑on rates, or other federal‑policy‑compliant measures.

3. Priority focus is on senior and long‑term care, behavioral health, dental services, family education and support services, and home‑based/community‑based services under the developmental disabilities waiver.
4. The department must submit an annual report to the legislature detailing each waiting list, current reduction efforts, and projected elimination dates.
5. The bill defines a “waiting list” as a list of enrolled Medicaid beneficiaries who cannot receive a service within 90 days due to funding, provider, enrollment slot, or supply constraints.
6. Section 1 is codified as part of Title 53, Chapter 6 of the Montana Code.
7. No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
affected: Montana Department of Health and Human Services

SB523.one_line: Revises Medicaid reimbursement to add annual CPI‑based adjustments for non‑physician contracts.
SB523.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Medicaid reimbursement rules to require that contracts with non‑physician providers include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment. It also updates the inflation‑adjustment formula for physicians’ conversion factors.
changes: Amends §53‑6‑125 to add a new subsection (2) that applies only to contracts with non‑physician providers.
Requires those contracts to include a provision that raises the fee for covered services each year by at least the consumer‑price‑index (CPI) for medical care, applied every 12 months.
Keeps the existing inflation‑adjustment rule for physicians’ conversion factors, but clarifies that the same CPI rule applies to non‑physician contracts.
Sets the effective date of the changes to July 1 2025.
affected: Non‑physician Medicaid providers (e.g., nurse practitioners, physician assistants, therapists)
Physicians (indirectly, through the unchanged conversion‑factor rule)
numbers: consumer price index for medical care

SB525.one_line: Allows school chaplains, sets policy, consent, and publication requirements, effective July 1, 2025.
SB525.summary: The bill allows school districts and public charter schools to hire paid or volunteer chaplains, sets minimum policy requirements, requires parental consent and background checks, and lets a chaplain replace a counselor. It also mandates publishing chaplains’ names and affiliations on the school website. The act takes effect July 1, 2025.
changes: School districts and charter schools may adopt a policy authorizing chaplains to provide supports, services, and programs to students.

SB526.one_line: Establishes a $1.5 million grant program for tribal colleges to develop community‑health‑aide education.
SB526.summary: SB 526 establishes a grant program to fund tribal colleges that develop or expand community‑health‑aide and dental‑health‑aide education programs. Grants can total up to $3 million per recipient and require annual reporting on graduates, certifications, service settings, and health‑outcome data. The program is funded with $1.5 million from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium and is effective July 1 , 2025.
changes: Creates a new grant program administered by the commissioner of higher education for tribal colleges that develop or expand community‑health‑aide or dental‑health‑aide education programs.
Allows a one‑time startup grant of up to $1 million and annual recurring grants of up to $500,000 for up to four years, with a total cap of $3 million per recipient.
Requires grantees to report annually on graduate numbers, certifications, practice settings, cost‑effectiveness, and a comprehensive set of population‑health metrics.
Allocates $1.5 million from the general fund for the 2025‑2026 biennium to support the program and designates it as part of the ongoing base for the next session.
Mandates the secretary of state to notify all federally recognized Montana tribes of the act.
Specifies that the act becomes effective July 1 , 2025.
affected: Community health aide and dental health aide providers
Tribal health clinics and their patients
Montana state government (commissioner of higher education, secretary of state)

SB528.one_line: Montana permits up to 3% credit‑card fees with pre‑transaction disclosure, excluding debt collectors.
SB528.summary: Montana will allow landlords, merchants, and other parties to charge a credit‑card fee up to 3% of the transaction, provided they disclose the fee beforehand. The rule does not apply to debt‑collection entities.
changes: Allows certain parties to charge a credit‑card transaction fee up to 3% of the total amount or as otherwise agreed in contract.
Requires the fee to be clearly disclosed before the transaction is completed.
Excludes debt‑collection entities from the fee limitation and disclosure requirement.
Codifies the fee limitation as part of Title 31, Chapter 2, Part 1 of the Montana Statutes.
Does not create a new program, fund, or criminal offense.
Does not impose new taxes or appropriations.
Does not alter any existing fee‑setting mechanisms beyond the 3% cap.
affected: Other parties who accept credit cards
Consumers who use credit cards for these transactions

SB527.one_line: Mandates infertility coverage and expands health benefits for Montana residents and public‑service workers.
SB527.summary: The Building Families Act requires Montana health‑insurance plans to cover infertility diagnosis and treatment, including IVF, with a lifetime benefit of at least $25,000.  It also amends state insurance statutes to expand coverage for a wide range of health services and clarifies eligibility and benefits for state employees, retirees, and certain public‑service workers.  The bill takes effect for policies issued on or after October 1 , 2025.
changes: All small‑group, large‑group, and individual health‑insurance plans issued in Montana must cover infertility diagnosis and treatment, including IVF, with a lifetime benefit of at least $25,000.

Insurers may not impose exclusions, limitations, or cost‑sharing (deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, benefit maximums, waiting periods) on infertility services that differ from those applied to other prescription drugs or medical services.

The bill amends sections 2‑18‑704 and 33‑35‑306 of the Montana Code to require continued group‑plan membership for retirees, survivors, and certain public‑service employees, and to clarify COBRA and other continuation benefits.

It expands mandatory coverage for a broad list of health services (e.g., inborn errors of metabolism, Down syndrome therapies, mental‑health services, telehealth, well‑child care, diabetes self‑management, and hospital inpatient care for breast‑cancer surgery).
The act applies to all insurance policies, contracts, or benefit plans issued, delivered, amended, or renewed in Montana on or after October 1 , 2025.
The bill does not create a new state program or criminal offense; it modifies existing insurance regulations.
affected: State employees, retirees, and certain public‑service workers (judges, legislators, law‑enforcement officers, firefighters, etc.)
numbers: 4 months COBRA coverage for law‑enforcement families

SB529.one_line: Limits 501(c)(4) contributions to $2,500 and bars foreign‑money‑influenced donations.
SB529.summary: SB 529 limits 501(c)(4) organizations to $2,500 per political or joint‑fundraising committee, bars them from donating directly to candidates, and forbids them from contributing if they received foreign money in the past four years. Violations trigger civil penalties.
changes: Limits 501(c)(4) contributions to political/joint‑fundraising committees to $2,500 each
Prohibits 501(c)(4) entities from making direct or indirect contributions to candidates
Prohibits 501(c)(4) entities from contributing to political/joint‑fundraising committees if they received foreign national contributions in the prior four years
Creates civil penalties for violations under Montana election law
Codifies the new rules as a new part of Title 13, Chapter 37
Preserves pre‑existing rights, penalties, and proceedings

SB530.one_line: SB 530 strengthens notice, reason disclosure, and cure rights for Montana insurance nonrenewals and cancellations.
SB530.summary: SB 530 revises Montana’s insurance statutes to strengthen consumer protections on nonrenewals and cancellations. It requires insurers to give advance notice, disclose reasons, and allow insureds to cure deficiencies. The bill also limits the use of inquiries and clarifies notice timelines for various property‑and‑casualty policies.
changes: Insurers must provide at least 45‑90 days’ written notice of nonrenewal or cancellation, including reasons, and mail or deliver a copy to the insured’s producer.
A written request from an insured within 60 business days of a notice triggers the insurer to furnish the grounds used for the decision within 21 days.
Insurers may not refuse renewal based on a single loss unless that loss was previously disclosed as a nonrenewal criterion.
Inquiries about coverage cannot be used to deny or increase coverage, and insurers cannot report such inquiries to consumer‑reporting agencies.

For motor‑vehicle liability policies, the insurer must give 45‑90 days’ notice of nonrenewal and, if requested, provide reasons within 15 days; failure to comply allows the commissioner to issue a certificate of facts.
Home‑insurance policies cannot be cancelled or not renewed without 45‑90 days’ notice and a stated reason, except for nonpayment where 20‑day notice is sufficient.
affected: Insureds holding property‑and‑casualty policies (including motor‑vehicle liability and home insurance)
numbers: 15 days to furnish reasons to commissioner
20‑day notice for nonpayment of home insurance

SB531.one_line: Montana offers a refundable $300 credit for qualifying firearm safes, subject to strict standards and review.
SB531.summary: Montana will give taxpayers a refundable credit equal to the purchase price of a qualifying firearm safe, up to $300, for tax years beginning 2026. The safe must meet strict security and testing standards. The credit is added to the list of tax credits for review by the revenue interim committee.
changes: Creates a refundable individual income‑tax credit for buying a firearm safe, limited to $300 per taxpayer per year.
The credit must be claimed in the year the safe is purchased and is equal to the safe’s purchase price.
The safe must meet detailed construction, lock‑mechanism, and testing requirements (e.g., 10,000‑combination lock, 12‑gauge steel walls, UL rating).
Adds the safe‑purchase credit to the list of credits that the revenue interim committee must review biennially.
The credit applies to tax years beginning January 1 2026 and onward.
The credit is codified as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
affected: Individual taxpayers who buy qualifying firearm safes
Montana Department of Revenue (for credit administration)
Safe manufacturers and testing labs (for compliance)
numbers: December 31 2028 termination of some review provisions

SB533.one_line: Creates a $5 pass for non‑ambulatory motorized trail users, sets penalties, and opens a special revenue account.
SB533.summary: SB 533 establishes a non‑ambulatory motorized recreation pass for people who cannot walk, sets fees and penalties, requires the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks to open and classify trails, and creates a dedicated revenue account.
changes: Creates a $5 non‑ambulatory motorized recreation pass that must be affixed to motorized equipment used on state recreational trails or roads.
Imposes misdemeanor penalties ($60 fine for missing the pass, $250 fine for using equipment without a pass, and up to $1,000 fine or 6‑month imprisonment for false statements).
Mandates the Department to reopen trails for pass holders, maintain them, and post restrictions at trailheads and online.
Requires the Department to classify all public trails as Class I, II, or III and post the classification.
Establishes a special revenue fund account to receive pass fees and two‑thirds of fines, with one‑third of fines going to the account.
Provides rule‑making authority for the Department to implement the pass, trail classification, and restrictions.
affected: Non‑ambulatory individuals who use motorized equipment
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

SB538.one_line: Adds Montana deduction for federal QBI and education‑savings contributions, with other tax adjustments and retroactive application.
SB538.summary: The bill amends Montana’s income‑tax rules to add a deduction for the federal qualified‑business‑income (QBI) deduction and to allow Montana taxpayers to deduct certain education‑savings contributions. It also makes a number of other adjustments to how federal items are added or subtracted when computing Montana taxable income, and it sets an immediate effective date with retroactive application to tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
changes: Adds a Montana deduction equal to the amount of a taxpayer’s federal QBI deduction under IRC §199A.
Allows individuals to deduct up to $3,000 (or $3,000 per spouse) of contributions to Montana family‑education‑savings accounts or qualified tuition programs, with a recapture tax for withdrawals.

Adjusts the Montana adjustment list so that several federal items—such as certain interest, medical‑care‑savings‑account withdrawals, and military‑pension subtractions—are added or subtracted when determining Montana taxable income.
Provides that the deduction for QBI is added to federal taxable income when computing Montana taxable income.
Sets the act to be effective immediately upon passage and retroactive to tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
Includes a limited set of other adjustments (e.g., military‑pension subtractions, scholarship subtractions, and a $5,500 subtraction for taxpayers age 65) that are scheduled to expire by 2033.
Does not create a new state program or criminal offense.
affected: Montana residents who claim the federal QBI deduction
Individuals who contribute to Montana family‑education‑savings or qualified tuition accounts
Taxpayers whose federal taxable income includes the listed items (interest, medical‑care‑savings withdrawals, military pensions, etc.)

SB539.one_line: Reclassifies local property assessments, limits rural district charges, and creates a direct appeal path to the Tax Appeal Board.
SB539.summary: SB 539 revises how Montana local governments classify and assess property‑related charges, clarifies when an assessment is a tax versus a fee, limits certain rural special‑district assessments, and creates a direct appeal path to the Montana Tax Appeal Board for specific department decisions. It amends statutory language on district assessments and tax‑exemption appeals, and sets effective and retroactive dates for the changes.
changes: Defines a special assessment as a charge that compensates a local government for services directly benefiting the assessed property, with the benefit commensurate and realized in a reasonable future time; otherwise the charge is a tax.
Presumes any assessment by a special district, special improvement district, or rural improvement district is a special assessment unless a property owner proves otherwise.

Amends 7‑12‑2108 to clarify when a county board may charge for improvements that provide more than local benefit, including exclusions for class‑three properties lacking residential structures and not contiguous to the district.

Amends 15‑2‑302 to allow direct appeals from the Department of Revenue to the Montana Tax Appeal Board for certain property‑tax and exemption decisions, with a 30‑day filing window and a final, binding board decision.
Codifies the new definition of assessment in Title 7, Chapter 6, Part 40, and specifies that the new rules apply to assessments after December 31 2026.
Provides retroactive applicability of the district‑assessment amendment to board determinations made before the act’s effective date for assessments imposed after December 31 2025.
Sets the act’s effective date as October 1 2025, with the district‑assessment amendment taking effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Local governments (cities, counties, special districts, rural improvement districts)
Property owners subject to local assessments
Taxpayers appealing Department of Revenue decisions
numbers: one‑half of total assessed value (district assessment threshold)

SB540.one_line: SB 540 revises tax rules for energy and telecom assets, adding exemptions, recapture, and new assessment standards.
SB540.summary: SB 540 revises Montana’s property‑tax rules for certain energy‑generation and telecommunications assets, creating new tax‑exemption and assessment rules for qualified data centers and fiber‑optic infrastructure while tightening recapture procedures. The bill amends existing statutes, sets new taxable rates, and establishes a 15‑year exemption period for qualifying assets.
changes: Amends §§ 15‑6‑156, 15‑6‑162, and 15‑23‑101 to redefine Class 13 and Class 17 property categories and their taxable percentages.
Creates a 5‑year tax exemption (with a 20 % annual phase‑out) for fiber‑optic or coaxial cable installed after July 1 2021, subject to reinvestment and record‑keeping requirements.
Defines “qualified data center” and establishes a 0.9 % tax rate for such centers and their local dedicated communications infrastructure, with a 15‑year exemption period for the infrastructure.

Imposes recapture rules: if a property owner fails to reinvest tax savings or otherwise violates the exemption, the department may terminate the exemption and local governments may recapture unpaid taxes, interest, and penalties within 10 years.
Requires local assessment of qualified data centers and their dedicated communications infrastructure, and mandates annual reporting of installed costs to the department.
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and approval and makes it retroactive to property‑tax years beginning after December 31 2024.
Specifies coordination provisions that void overlapping amendments from House Bill 424 if both bills pass.
Provides definitions for electrical generation facilities, fiber‑optic cable, and other technical terms.
Adjusts central assessment rules for certain railroad, pipeline, and airline property under § 15‑23‑101.

SB541.one_line: Creates a pollinator task force, funds it, and requires a strategy report.
SB541.summary: The bill creates a 14‑member Pollinator Health Task Force, funds it with $50,000, requires a strategy report to the legislature, and sets a two‑year term ending Dec. 31 2026.
changes: Establishes a Pollinator Health Task Force with 14 appointed members from state agencies, industry, academia, tribes, and youth;
Provides compensation rules: state employees may only be reimbursed for travel, non‑employees receive $50 per day plus travel reimbursement;
Task force must develop a state pollinator health strategy covering research, education, habitat, pest management, partnerships, and communication;
Task force must submit a report of findings and recommendations to the 70th Legislature;
Appropriates $50,000 from the general fund for the biennium July 1 2025–June 30 2026 to cover task force costs;
Secretary of State must notify all federally recognized Montana tribes of the act;
Act takes effect upon passage and is in force July 1 2025, terminating Dec. 31 2026.
affected: State agencies (Agriculture, Natural Resources, Fish & Wildlife), industry groups (fruit, seed, berry, other pollinator‑dependent), pesticide distributors, conservation orgs, beekeepers, Montana Indian tribes, youth agricultural groups, and the general public

SB543.one_line: Allows judicial candidates to list party affiliation and adjusts ballot and fee rules accordingly.
SB543.summary: The bill allows Montana’s chief‑justice and supreme‑court justice candidates to list a political party on their nomination paperwork and on the ballot, and it amends filing‑fee, ballot‑preparation, and nonpartisan‑office rules to accommodate that change. It also clarifies how nonpartisan offices and retention elections are handled.
changes: Candidates for chief justice or supreme‑court justice may indicate a party affiliation on their declaration for nomination and on the primary and general ballots.
The filing fee for these judicial offices is set at $1,750 (per the amended fee schedule).

Primary ballots must be prepared separately for each party that has more than half of the offices or more than one candidate, with nonpartisan offices either on separate or shared ballots as specified.
Nonpartisan offices may be excluded from a primary if candidate numbers fall below thresholds; election administrators can decide and must notify the governing body.
Retention ballots for incumbent judicial officers may omit party or nonpartisan designations and simply ask voters to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’.
The act applies to elections held on or after January 1, 2026.
The bill does not create a new state program or criminal offense.
affected: Voters in primary and general elections for those offices
numbers: nonpartisan primary thresholds (three times the number to be elected, fewer than three candidates)

SB546.one_line: Creates a phased‑out 4.7 % income‑based tax credit for Montana individual taxpayers.
SB546.summary: The bill creates a new, income‑based tax credit for Montana individual taxpayers, giving a 4.7 % credit on the first portion of taxable income that phases out as income rises. It also amends the tax‑credit review schedule to include this new credit. The credit is available only for tax years beginning after December 31 2025 and takes effect January 1 2026.
changes: Establishes a one‑time income‑based tax credit equal to 4.7 % of the first $2,000 (joint), $1,500 (head of household), or $1,000 (single or married filing separately) of Montana taxable income.
Phases the credit out by reducing it 0.094 % for every additional $2,000 (joint), $1,500 (head of household), or $1,000 (single or married filing separately) of taxable income.
Limits the credit to the taxpayer’s income‑tax liability; no carry‑forward or carry‑back is allowed.
Adds the new credit to the biennial review list for the revenue interim committee, requiring periodic evaluation of its effectiveness.
Codifies the credit as part of Title 15, Chapter 30 of the Montana Code.
Sets the effective date to January 1 2026 and applicability to tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
affected: Individual Montana taxpayers filing state income tax returns
Taxpayers who are claimed as dependents (excluded)
Taxpayers with taxable income above the phase‑out thresholds
Taxpayers seeking to claim the credit in future tax years
numbers: $1,000 single or married filing separately limit

SB547.one_line: Expands disability parking eligibility, adds fee for pregnant women, and clarifies temporary/permanent permits.
SB547.summary: The bill expands who can receive a disability parking permit, adds a temporary permit for pregnant women, and requires a $10 fee that goes to the State General Fund. It amends the eligibility criteria and clarifies temporary and permanent permit rules.
changes: Adds a new category for pregnant women, allowing a temporary permit for up to one year with a $10 fee
Expands the list of medical conditions that qualify for a temporary or permanent permit
Allows agencies or businesses that transport people with disabilities to obtain permits for loading/unloading only
Limits applicants to one permit unless they are a transportation agency

Specifies that temporary permits for conditions expected to improve within 6 months may be issued for up to 6 months, and if the condition persists, a new temporary permit may be issued for up to 24 months

Requires that all temporary permits be issued by the Department of Justice based on certification from a licensed physician, chiropractor, or advanced practice registered nurse (or certified midwife for pregnant women)
Mandates that the $10 fee for a pregnant woman’s temporary permit be deposited in the State General Fund
Amends Section 49‑4‑301, MCA, to reflect the new eligibility and fee provisions
Sets the effective date of the act to July 1 2025
affected: Transportation agencies or businesses that serve people with disabilities
Department of Justice (for processing and fee collection)

SB548.one_line: Montana requires foreign agents to register, report, and face fines, and bars certain foreign corporations from incentives.
SB548.summary: The bill requires anyone in Montana who represents a foreign government, corporation, or educational institution to register with the Secretary of State, pay a $150 fee, and file monthly reports. It imposes hefty fines for non‑registration, late or false reporting, and creates a whistleblower hotline. It also disqualifies foreign‑adversary corporations from state economic‑development incentives.
changes: 1. Adds a foreign‑agent registration requirement for individuals acting on behalf of foreign governments, corporations, or educational institutions when interacting with state officials or public institutions.
2. Establishes a $150 filing fee, to be deposited in the state general fund.
3. Mandates monthly reports detailing meetings, policy matters, contributions, and compensation, and requires the Secretary of State to publish these reports online.
4. Sets civil penalties: $25,000 for failure to register, $15,000 for each late or missing monthly report, and $100,000 for falsifying or incomplete reports.
5. Grants the Attorney General and county prosecutors authority to prosecute violations and creates a whistleblower hotline that can lead to a 50% share of fines for successful convictions.
6. Disqualifies foreign corporations from state economic‑development incentives if they are from a foreign‑adversary country or have a 5%+ stake held by such entities.
affected: Individuals interacting with Montana state officials

SB549.one_line: Montana offers a $1,250 tax credit for qualifying K‑12 education expenses starting 2026.
SB549.summary: Montana will allow taxpayers to claim a credit of up to $1,250 for qualifying K‑12 education expenses paid by parents, guardians, or teachers. The credit applies to a wide range of costs—including tuition, supplies, tutoring, and transportation—and is available even for taxpayers with no taxable income, though it cannot be refunded if the tax liability is lower than the credit.
changes: Creates a new income‑tax credit for primary and secondary education expenses, capped at $1,250 per taxpayer per year.
Defines “education expenses” broadly to include tuition, instructional materials, tutoring, therapies, assessments, school services, supplies, transportation, and cooperative program fees.

Allows the credit to be claimed by parents, guardians, or teachers who pay the expenses, even if they have no taxable income, but the credit is not refundable if the tax liability is less than the credit amount.
Amends §15‑30‑2303 to list the new credit among those subject to biennial review by the revenue interim committee.
Specifies that the credit is effective for income‑tax years beginning January 1, 2026.
Requires codification of the credit as part of Title 15, Chapter 30.
No new program or fund is created; it is a tax‑credit provision.
No direct fiscal impact is specified beyond the credit amount.
affected: Taxpayers who pay K‑12 education expenses (parents, guardians, teachers).
Public schools and accredited or non‑accredited education providers that bill these expenses.

SB551.one_line: Creates a regulated, taxed framework for internet fantasy sports contests in Montana.
SB551.summary: SB 551 creates a legal framework for internet fantasy‑sports contests in Montana, establishing licensing, regulatory, tax, and record‑keeping requirements for service providers.
changes: 1. Defines key terms (applicant, licensee, fantasy sports contest, internet fantasy sports contest, etc.) and sets the legal definition of a fantasy sports contest.
2. Makes it legal for licensed providers to run internet fantasy sports contests and requires a $5,000 initial license fee (renewal $1,000 or $5,000 if adjusted revenues ≥$150,000).
3. Imposes a 6.75 % tax on adjusted revenues and a regulatory fee set by the Department of Justice, with all fees deposited into the general fund.

4. Grants the Department of Justice broad powers to license, investigate, audit, and enforce compliance, including the ability to suspend or revoke licenses and impose civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation.

5. Requires providers to keep detailed records, conduct annual audits, report criminal or suspicious activity, and provide responsible‑gaming information. Violations can result in fines and criminal charges for false statements.
6. Adds age restrictions (players must be ≥18) and prohibits credit‑card payments for contests.
