SB554.one_line: Limits nonprofit hospital charges to 300 % of Medicare, imposes tax and reporting if exceeded.
SB554.summary: SB 554 limits nonprofit hospitals from charging more than 300 % of Medicare reimbursement for any service.  If they do, the state imposes a progressive excess‑charge tax, revokes nonprofit status, and requires detailed reporting and financial‑assistance policies.
changes: Limits non‑critical‑access nonprofit hospitals to 300 % of Medicare rates for any service or item; charges above that trigger a tax.
Imposes an excess‑charge tax (25 % in 2027, 35 % in 2028, 45 % in 2029, 50 % thereafter) on the amount over 300 % for qualifying patients.
Creates a dedicated tax account and specifies how the revenue may be used (65 % Medicaid, 25 % rural workforce, 10 % administration).
Requires hospitals to adopt written financial‑assistance and community‑benefit policies and to make them public.
Mandates annual reporting to the Department of Public Health and Human Services and the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee.
Provides extensive audit, collection, penalty, and confidentiality procedures for the tax.
Revokes nonprofit status for any hospital that repeatedly charges over 300 % of Medicare rates.
affected: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

SB556.one_line: Creates a state board to regulate ski lifts, requiring registration, fees, inspections, and enforcement.
SB556.summary: The bill creates a new state board to regulate passenger ropeways (ski lifts, chair‑lifts, etc.), requiring operators to register, pay fees, and submit to inspections and rule‑making. The board can issue certificates, impose corrective orders, suspend registrations, and enforce compliance through court action.
changes: Establishes a seven‑member Board of Passenger Ropeway Safety appointed by the governor with staggered four‑year terms.
Mandates annual registration of all passenger ropeways, with initial and supplemental applications and annual certificates.
Imposes annual fees ($100 rope tow, $200 chair lift, $300 aerial tramway) and a 0.25 % assessment on gross receipts to fund the board.
Authorizes the board to adopt safety rules, conduct inspections, issue corrective orders, suspend registrations, and bring injunctive proceedings.
Provides governmental immunity for board members and contractors for official actions.
Amends existing Montana Code sections 23‑2‑702 and 23‑2‑734 and repeals 23‑2‑731 to incorporate the new requirements.

SB557.one_line: Creates an opt‑out website for political mailings, funded by committee fees.
SB557.summary: The bill creates a state‑run opt‑out website for political mailings, requires committees and parties to pay a maintenance fee, and deposits those fees into a special revenue account for website upkeep. It also mandates that the opt‑out list be shared with political groups.
changes: Establishes a public website for individuals to opt out of political campaign mailings.
Mandates that the opt‑out list be made available to all political committees and party organizations.
Authorizes the Commissioner of Political Practices to set a fee for website maintenance.
Requires all political committees and party organizations to pay that fee equally.
Creates a dedicated account in the State Special Revenue Fund to receive and use the collected fees for website maintenance.
Codifies the new provisions into Title 13, Chapter 37, Part 1 of the Montana Code.
numbers: fee collected from all political committees and party organizations
funded account in the State Special Revenue Fund

SB559.one_line: SB 559 creates a $100 appeal process for DEQ permits, with board or court hearings and priority for >$1 million projects.
SB559.summary: SB 559 establishes a formal appeals process for Montana DEQ permit decisions, requiring a $100 filing fee and a 30‑day deadline.  Appeals can be heard by the DEQ board or a district court, with priority given to projects costing over $1 million.  The bill amends several DEQ statutes to codify the new procedures and sets July 1, 2025 as the effective date.
changes: Creates a new appeals procedure for DEQ permit approvals or denials, including a $100 fee and 30‑day filing deadline.
Allows appeals to be heard by either the DEQ board or a district court, with the board hearing subject to contested‑case rules.
Requires that appeals be filed in the county where the proposed activity occurs (or any county if multi‑county).
Gives projects costing >$1 million priority over other civil actions pending in the same court.
Amends sections 75‑2‑211, 75‑2‑213, and 75‑5‑107 of the Montana Code to incorporate the new appeal rules and codify venue requirements.
Codifies the new sections into Title 75, Chapter 2, Part 1 and Title 82 chapters 4‑1, 4‑2, and 4‑3.
Sets the act’s effective date as July 1, 2025.

SB558.one_line: Montana replaces property tax with a 4% statewide sales tax, creating a new school‑reduction account.
SB558.summary: Montana will replace the statewide property‑mill levy with a 4% general sales and use tax, channeling all revenue into a school equalization and property‑tax‑reduction account. The law creates a new statewide sales‑tax program, new tax‑collection rules, and a new tax‑proceeds account while eliminating the existing property‑mill levies.
changes: 1. Establishes a 4% statewide sales and use tax on tangible personal property, electronically transferred products, and services, replacing the former property‑mill levy.
2. Requires the Department of Revenue to collect, remit, and deposit all sales‑tax revenue into a dedicated school equalization and property‑tax‑reduction account.
3. Grants the Department authority to enter into a streamlined sales‑use‑tax agreement with other states, adopting uniform rules for exemption certificates, collection, and reporting.

4. Sets exemption thresholds: sales to non‑collecting retailers with < $100,000 annual sales or <200 transactions are exempt from collection duties; minors under 18 with <$1,000 annual sales are exempt.
5. Provides a 30‑day relief period for retailers who fail to collect a new rate within 30 days of enactment.
6. Creates new licensing, reporting, and enforcement procedures for retailers, including permits, returns, and penalties for non‑compliance.
affected: Retailers (in‑state and out‑of‑state), non‑collecting retailers, consumers, state and local governments, school districts, and the Department of Revenue
numbers: $100,000 annual sales threshold for non‑collecting retailers

SB561.one_line: Reforms Montana’s Public Service Commission: five members, new districts, stricter appointment rules, and term limits.
SB561.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Public Service Commission (PSC) structure, election and appointment rules, term limits, qualifications, and district boundaries, and sets an immediate effective date. It expands the PSC to five members, changes how districts are drawn, tightens appointment qualifications, and clarifies vacancy procedures.
changes: Replaces the PSC with five members—two elected, three appointed; each elected member must come from a distinct district and be elected on a partisan basis.
Redraws PSC districts to match federal congressional districts and provides a process for adjusting them after census changes.
Sets term limits: elected commissioners may serve up to 12 years in a 24‑year period; appointed commissioners may serve up to 12 years in a 24‑year period, with a 6‑year term for each appointment.

Imposes new qualifications for appointed commissioners, including a 4‑year separation from regulated entities, no financial interests in regulated entities, U.S. citizenship, 2‑year residency, and relevant experience in finance, law, or energy.
Requires a $100 filing fee and documentation of qualifications for appointed commissioners before gubernatorial nomination.
Revises vacancy procedures: governor must appoint a replacement from a list provided by the relevant political party, with a 45‑day deadline and confirmation by a two‑thirds Senate vote.
Adds transition provisions for current commissioners and sets specific appointment deadlines for 2027‑2029.
Codifies the new sections as part of Title 69, Chapter 1, Part 1.
Includes severability and immediate effective‑date clauses.
affected: Public Service Commission members (elected and appointed)
Political parties involved in PSC appointments

SB563.one_line: Creates provisional resident licenses for new graduates, requiring supervision and collaborative agreements.
SB563.summary: The bill establishes a new provisional resident license for recent medical graduates in Montana, sets qualifications, fees, and supervisory requirements, and amends existing licensing statutes to allow supervised practice under a collaborative agreement. It also creates rules for provisional licenses and coordinates with a related House bill.
changes: Amends §37‑3‑301 to add a provisional resident license and clarify licensing rules.
Amends §37‑3‑307 to define qualifications for resident and provisional resident licenses, including supervision by a licensed physician, fee payment, and renewal limits.
Creates a provisional resident license valid for up to two years, requiring a collaborative practice agreement and a 1‑year renewal.
Sets a 1‑year maximum for a resident license, with possible 1‑year renewals if the applicant remains in good standing in an approved residency.
Adds rule‑making authority for the board to establish limitations on provisional licenses and collaborative agreements.
Includes coordination language with House Bill 414 to allow provisional licenses pending certain conditions (exam, work experience, etc.).
affected: Montana Department of Medicine and Board of Medicine
numbers: 21‑day practice period for out‑of‑state licensed physicians

SB565.one_line: Creates an endowment, board, and account to fund early‑childhood programs and imposes a renewal fee for lapsed licenses.
SB565.summary: The bill creates a Montana Endowment for Early Childhood, a board, and an early‑childhood account that will receive quarterly interest from the endowment and a $25 renewal fee for lapsed child‑care licenses.  Grants are authorized for workforce development, quality improvement, affordability, innovation, and emergency assistance for child‑care providers, with annual reporting to legislative committees.
changes: Establishes a seven‑member board appointed by the governor to oversee an early‑childhood account and endowment.
Creates a permanent endowment that can receive appropriations, gifts, and a renewal fee, but only its interest may be spent.
Creates a special revenue account that can be used only for early‑childhood programs and grants described in the bill.
Authorizes the board to award grants for workforce development, quality improvement, affordability, innovation, and emergency assistance to nonprofit or public organizations.
Adds a $25 fee for renewing a lapsed day‑care license or registration certificate, payable to the special revenue account.
Requires the board to report annually to the Education Interim Committee and the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee.
Transfers $150 million from the general fund to the endowment by August 1 2025.
The act takes effect immediately upon passage.
affected: Montana child‑care providers (day‑care centers, family day‑care homes, group day‑care homes)
Nonprofit and public early‑childhood service organizations
Montana taxpayers (via the endowment and fee revenue)
State agencies: Department of Public Health and Human Services, Department of Labor and Industry, Office of Public Instruction, Department of Commerce
Legislative committees: Education Interim Committee, Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee

SB566.one_line: Regulates private child‑transport companies with registration, notification, and restraint bans.
SB566.summary: The bill creates a regulatory framework for private companies that transport children, requiring annual registration, fee payment, and quarterly public listings. It mandates advance electronic notification of each child transport, records retention for ten years, and grants access to those records for the child, the Department of Justice, and the Department of Public Health and Human Services. It also bans the use of restraints or visual impairment and limits pickups to 6 a.m.–9 p.m.
changes: Requires secure youth transportation companies to register annually with the Department of Public Health and Human Services and pay a prescribed fee.
Mandates quarterly publication of a publicly accessible list of registered providers.
Imposes a 48‑hour advance electronic notification requirement for every child transport, including detailed child, parent, company, employee, and pickup/leave information.
Establishes a ten‑year retention period for notification records and allows the Department of Justice and the child to access those records.
Prohibits companies from using chemical or physical restraints or visually impairing a child and restricts pickups to between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m.
Codifies the provisions as part of Title 52, Chapter 2 of the Montana Code.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SJ2.one_line: Legislature disapproves nine Montana Supreme Court rules and requests explanatory testimony.
SJ2.summary: The Senate and House disapprove a list of rules adopted by the Montana Supreme Court and request explanatory testimony. No new programs or funds are created. The resolution simply rejects the specified rules.
changes: Disapproves revisions to AF 07‑0157 (Civil Procedure) adopted Oct 12 2021 and Jun 28 2022
Disapproves revisions to AF 07‑0110 (Uniform District Court Rules) adopted Aug 30 2023
Disapproves revisions to AF 11‑0360 (Uniform Caseload Filing Standards)
Disapproves revisions to AF 07‑0016 (Rules of Appellate Procedure) adopted Dec 14 2021
Disapproves revisions to AF 14‑0745 (Temporary Electronic Filing Rules) adopted Feb 22 2022, Mar 26 2024, Apr 24 2024
Disapproves AF 06‑0377 (Public Access to Trial Court Public Record Portal) adopted Apr 7 2022
Disapproves revisions to AF 06‑0163 (Continuing Legal Education) adopted Mar 15 2022, Mar 1 2023, and proposed Jun 25 2024
Disapproves revisions to AF 06‑0628 (Lawyer Disciplinary Enforcement) adopted Oct 12 2021
Disapproves revisions to AF 14‑0356 (Judicial Standards Commission Rules) proposed Aug 26 2024

SJ4.one_line: Montana asks Congress to call a convention for a balanced‑budget constitutional amendment.
SJ4.summary: Montana’s Senate Joint Resolution 4 requests that Congress convene a national convention to propose a constitutional amendment that would require the federal government to maintain a balanced budget each fiscal year. The resolution simply asks for the application; it does not create any new state program or law.
changes: Applies to Congress under Article V for a convention limited to a balanced‑budget amendment.

SJ14.one_line: Resolution petitions Congress to release Montana wilderness‑study and roadless lands for multiple use.
SJ14.summary: The resolution urges Congress to release all Montana wilderness‑study and inventoried‑roadless lands for multiple‑use management, arguing that the lands have been in legal limbo for decades and that their release would benefit state citizens and the economy. It is a formal petition, not a law, and does not create new programs or funds.
changes: Petitions Congress to remove all lands listed in the Montana Wilderness Study Act of 1977 and the National Landscape Conservation System from consideration for wilderness designation.
Petitions Congress to release all inventoried roadless areas identified by the Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
Calls for the Secretary of Agriculture and Secretary of the Interior to evaluate watershed impacts of any land‑management alternatives.
Requests the Secretary of State to forward copies of the resolution to federal officials and the Governor.
affected: Federal land management agencies (Bureau of Land Management, Forest Service)

SJ15.one_line: Montana Legislature calls for reversal of Obergefell, restoring marriage to state control.
SJ15.summary: The resolution declares that Montana rejects the Supreme Court’s Obergefell v. Hodges decision and urges the Court to reverse it, restoring marriage to a state‑level, one‑man‑one‑woman definition. It does not enact any new law or policy, merely expresses the Legislature’s position.

SJ17.one_line: Resolution requests a study of resident hunter satisfaction and requires resulting bills.
SJ17.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to study resident hunter satisfaction with non‑resident hunting pressure and to produce bills that address any problems found. It requires a committee to gather data, consult stakeholders, and report its findings by September 15, 2026. The study’s results must be turned into legislative proposals for the next session.
changes: Requests an interim study of resident hunter satisfaction with non‑resident hunting pressure.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks

SJ22.one_line: Resolution urges Congress to repeal the 17th Amendment and restore state‑appointed U.S. Senators.
SJ22.summary: The resolution urges the U.S. Congress to repeal the 17th Amendment and replace it with a state‑legislature‑appointed Senate. It proposes a model amendment that would restore state control over Senate selection and establish liaison committees. The resolution itself does not create any new state program or law.
changes: Calls for a U.S. constitutional amendment that repeals the 17th Amendment and restores state legislature appointment of U.S. Senators
Specifies that each state would appoint two six‑year senators, subject to removal by the state legislature
Requires each state legislature to create a liaison committee to liaise with its senators and review federal legislation
States that senators’ salaries and benefits would be paid by the state
Precludes Congress from changing the senatorial selection process
Preserves the terms of any senators already elected before the amendment becomes effective
Requests the Secretary of State to forward copies of the resolution to federal leaders and Montana’s congressional delegation.

SB562.one_line: Revises Montana election law to use top‑two primaries for many offices.
SB562.summary: The bill amends Montana’s election statutes to require a top‑two primary for a wide range of offices—statewide, legislative, and county positions—so that the two candidates with the most votes, regardless of party, advance to the general election. It also revises numerous related provisions, including filing deadlines, party‑affiliation rules, vacancy‑appointment procedures, ballot‑design requirements, and recount thresholds, while tightening campaign‑finance limits and clarifying election‑evidence standards.
changes: Replaces the current partisan‑primary system with a top‑two primary for specified offices, allowing the two highest‑vote candidates to advance regardless of party affiliation.
Adjusts filing‑deadline rules (e.g., 145‑day minimum, 85‑day maximum, 10‑day withdrawal deadline) and party‑preference declarations in candidacy filings.
Rewrites vacancy‑appointment procedures for legislative and county offices, including new formulas for selecting appointees and timelines for notifications and appointments.
Revises ballot‑design and candidate‑name placement rules, including rotation, party‑preference labeling, and prohibition of party endorsements on ballots.
Updates recount rules, setting a 0.25%–0.5% margin threshold for a candidate to request a recount and requiring a bond to cover recount costs.
Reinforces campaign‑finance limits (e.g., $1,000 for statewide candidates, $400 for other offices) and clarifies the definition of contributions and independent expenditures.
affected: Candidates for state, legislative, and county offices
Political parties and their central committees

SJ23.one_line: Mandates an interim study of market‑sensitive crops and ag tech impacts on Montana exports.
SJ23.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of how market‑sensitive crops and agricultural technologies affect Montana’s export markets, shipping practices, and regulatory environment. The study must be finished by September 15, 2026, and its findings reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: 1. Requires the Legislative Council to appoint an interim committee to study market‑sensitive crops and technologies.
2. The committee must review export markets, shipping practices, and regulatory impacts on Montana products.
3. The study must assess financial effects of import restrictions, chemical residues, and production costs for producers.
4. Findings, conclusions, and recommendations must be presented to the committee and reported to the Legislature.
5. The study must be completed before September 15, 2026.

SJ30.one_line: Study the child‑abuse registry and recommend reforms by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ30.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to form an interim committee to study Montana’s child‑abuse and neglect registry, evaluate its procedures, and recommend reforms, with a deadline of September 15, 2026. The committee will also monitor the expungement process and report findings to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Creates an interim committee to study the child‑abuse and neglect registry.
affected: Department of Public Health and Human Services

SJ24.one_line: Montana legislature recommends joining the National Popular Vote Compact.
SJ24.summary: Montana’s legislature recommends that the state join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, a pact that would award presidential electoral votes based on the national popular vote rather than state-by‑state results. The resolution also directs the Secretary of State to inform federal congressional members and tribal governments of the recommendation. No new laws or programs are enacted, and the resolution contains no fiscal provisions.
changes: Recommends Montana join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact for future presidential elections.
Directs the Secretary of State to send copies of the resolution to Montana’s congressional delegation and federally recognized tribal governments.
affected: federally recognized tribal governments in Montana
numbers: 5 presidents who won without the popular vote
17 states plus D.C. have passed the law
270 electoral votes needed for compact to take effect

SJ31.one_line: Study mandatory child‑abuse reporting, training, and alternatives before Sept 15 2026.
SJ31.summary: Montana’s Senate and House request an interim study of mandatory child‑abuse reporting, asking a committee to examine training, alternative responses, and reporting procedures, with findings due before September 15, 2026.
changes: Creates a study committee to review mandatory reporting practices
Examines uniform training for mandatory reporters
Identifies steps for gathering information before reporting
Explores alternatives to reporting and referrals to services
Recommends changes to reporting procedures
Proposes legislation based on study findings

SJ32.one_line: Resolution requests a study of citizen review boards for child protection, to finish by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ32.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission a study of Montana’s Citizen Review Board Program for child‑protective services, asking for funding options, administrative needs, coordination among governments, and statewide standards. The study must finish by September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests an interim study of the Citizen Review Board Program for child and family services.

Specifies study topics: funding (including nongovernment revenue), administrative needs, intergovernmental coordination, statewide standards, cost savings from reduced court involvement, and ways to improve the child‑protection system.
Mandates that the study be completed and presented before September 15, 2026.
Requires the final report to be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
affected: City, county, tribal, and state governments involved in child protection

SJ34.one_line: Resolution requests an interim study of Montana’s child‑care system to be completed by September 2026.
SJ34.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of Montana’s child‑care system, focusing on availability, affordability, quality, and regulatory barriers.  The study must be completed by September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint an interim or statutory committee to investigate day‑care barriers.

SJ39.one_line: Resolution requests a study of a specialty court for constitutional and government claims, report due September 2026.
SJ39.summary: The resolution directs the Legislature to study the feasibility of creating a specialty court for constitutional and government claims, with a report due before September 15, 2026. It does not create a court or impose any new law, only requests an interim study and a final report to the next Legislature.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to conduct a study of Montana’s judicial structure and the potential creation of a specialty court for constitutional and government claims.
affected: Montana litigants in constitutional and government claims

SJ38.one_line: Resolution directs a study of Montana’s property‑tax system, to be finished by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ38.summary: This resolution directs the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to study Montana’s property‑tax system, covering classes, rates, valuations, exemptions, settlements, and potential consolidation. The study must finish before September 15, 2026, and its findings will be reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Creates a study mandate for the Legislative Council to appoint a committee under §5‑5‑217, MCA.
The committee must examine property‑tax classes, rates, valuation methods, exemptions, settlement procedures, and consolidation options.
The study must be completed and its final report delivered to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
The resolution does not alter any tax law or create new programs; it only requires a study and reporting.
No fiscal allocations or budget changes are specified.
No new criminal offenses or licenses are created.
affected: Local governments (cities, counties, school districts, special districts)

SJ40.one_line: Legislative Council must study legislative procurement and leadership funds, finish by Sept 15 2026, report to next legislature.
SJ40.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to conduct an interim study of how the Montana Legislature procures goods and services and spends leadership funds, with a deadline of September 15, 2026, and to report findings to the next legislature.
changes: 1. Requires the Legislative Council to study the legislative procurement process and leadership‑fund expenditures.
2. Study must examine internal controls, procedures, procurement development, training needs, and transparency for public and legislators.
3. Study must consider possible revisions to the Montana Procurement Act as it applies to the Legislature.
4. All study activities must be finished by September 15, 2026.
5. Final report, including findings and recommendations, must be submitted to the 70th Legislature.

SJ41.one_line: Resolution directs a study to expand and streamline home‑based child‑care in Montana.
SJ41.summary: The resolution directs a committee to study how to expand and streamline home‑based and family child‑care in Montana, especially in rural areas, and to draft legislation that would codify licensure and regulation. The study must be finished by September 15, 2026, and its findings reported to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Creates an interim committee (Children, Families, Health, and Human Services) to study home‑based/family child‑care.
Task the committee to explore ways to develop sustainable, long‑term home‑based child‑care, especially in rural communities.
Task the committee to streamline licensure and regulation of home‑based and family day‑care providers.
Task the committee to investigate other barriers to providing and accessing home‑based day‑care.
Require the committee to draft legislation that would codify licensure and regulation of these providers.
Mandate the study’s completion and reporting to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.

SJ43.one_line: Resolution requests a study of Montana’s criminal‑justice data warehouse by September 2026.
SJ43.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to task the Criminal Justice Oversight Council with studying how Montana’s new criminal‑justice data warehouse has been implemented and what outcomes it has produced. The study must be finished and reported to the next Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council assign the study to the Criminal Justice Oversight Council.
Mandates the council to review the warehouse’s history, stakeholder views, funding distribution, current status, and future goals.
Requires the council to collect input from courts, tribal governments, law‑enforcement agencies, corrections facilities, and health agencies.
Sets a deadline of September 15, 2026 for completing the study and reporting results to the 70th Legislature.
Does not create new programs, funds, or criminal offenses; it only authorizes a study.
affected: Office of the State Public Defender
Department of Public Health and Human Services

SJ44.one_line: Resolution requests a study of affordable‑housing programs to be completed by Sept. 15, 2026.
SJ44.summary: This resolution directs the Legislature to commission a study of Montana’s affordable‑housing programs, asking a committee or staff to analyze costs, benefits, and effectiveness of local, state, and federal incentives. The study must be finished and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026.
changes: Requests the Legislative Council to set up an interim or statutory committee (or staff) to conduct the study
The study must evaluate cost‑additions of subsidized versus non‑subsidized housing projects
It must prepare a cost‑benefit analysis of state‑level affordable‑housing incentives, including HB 819 and the Coal Trust Multifamily Homes loan program
It must review housing‑choice voucher programs and compare them to other subsidy programs
It must identify the most successful programs in Montana and analyze why they work
Stakeholders such as the Department of Commerce, Board of Housing, Board of Investments, Governor’s Office of Economic Development, developers, contractors, and nonprofits must be engaged
If staff conduct the study, findings must be presented to a committee for review
The study must be completed and reported to the 70th Legislature by September 15, 2026

SJ45.one_line: Resolution orders a study on the executive residence’s use and renovation, due by 15 Sept 2026.
SJ45.summary: The Senate Joint Resolution requests an interim study to decide how to use the state‑owned executive residence when the governor has another home. The study must be finished by 15 Sept 2026 and its findings reported as introduced legislation to the next Legislature.
changes: Creates a study mandate for the Legislative Council to appoint a committee to review the executive residence’s condition and renovation plans.
The committee must compile lists of necessary (needs) and non‑essential (wants) renovations.
It must explore options for funding, demolition, new construction, alternative uses, or sale of the property.
The study’s conclusions must be reported to the 70th Legislature as introduced legislation.
The study must be completed before 15 Sept 2026.

SJ46.one_line: Resolution creates a study committee to examine Montana’s food security and agriculture by Sept 2026.
SJ46.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to form a committee to study Montana’s food security and agricultural prosperity, covering availability, production, access, value‑adding, existing programs, and challenges, with a deadline of September 15, 2026. The committee must report its findings to the 70th Legislature.
changes: Establishes an interim study committee under Section 5‑5‑217, MCA

The committee will examine food availability, production, access, value‑adding opportunities, existing programs (e.g., Farmers to Families Food Box Program, Made in Montana, Grown in Montana), distributed food, and challenges such as soil health and pollinator decline
The study must be completed and reported by September 15, 2026
The committee is to collaborate with the public, state agencies, and stakeholders in agriculture, food banks, nutrition science, and local food retail
Results, including findings and recommendations, must be reported to the 70th Legislature
No new programs, funds, or criminal offenses are created
affected: Montana farmers, ranchers, food producers, food banks, local food retailers, state agencies involved in agriculture and food security

SJ47.one_line: Resolution requests study of local government creation processes, to be reported by Sept 15, 2026.
SJ47.summary: The resolution directs the Legislative Council to conduct an interim study of Montana’s statutes governing the creation, alteration, and abandonment of local governments, with a deadline of September 15, 2026, and to report findings to the 70th Legislature. It calls for stakeholder input and a review of potential redundancies or modern‑age needs in the incorporation process. The study itself is not a law but a request for analysis and reporting.
changes: Designates a committee or staff to review existing statutory processes for creating, altering, or abandoning local governments.
Examines the history of successful city or town incorporations to identify duplicative or contradictory requirements.
Assesses whether current requirements are appropriate or need modernization.
Engages stakeholders such as the Montana League of Cities and Towns, Montana Association of Counties, Montana State University Local Government Center, county commissioners, and community members.
Requires findings to be presented to an appropriate committee if staff conduct the study.
Mandates completion of the study and reporting to the Legislature by September 15, 2026.
affected: Committee or staff assigned to the study
Montana League of Cities and Towns
Montana State University Local Government Center
Community members in areas interested in new municipalities or counties

SJ50.one_line: Resolution requests an interim study of COVID‑19 treatments and reports results by 2026.
SJ50.summary: This resolution directs the Legislature to commission an interim study of the medical response to COVID‑19, including vaccines, treatments, and experimental therapies, and to report findings to the next session. The study must be completed by September 15, 2026.
changes: Designates a Legislative Council‑appointed committee or staff to conduct the study.
Specifies the study must examine vaccines, remdesivir, dexamethasone, ivermectin, and other treatments, plus the Right‑to‑Try Act outcomes.
Requires the committee to present findings to a designated committee and to the Legislature.
Mandates completion of the study by September 15, 2026.
Requests that the final report be submitted to the 70th Legislature.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created.
No monetary allocations are included.
affected: Montana legislators, Legislative Council, appointed committee members, state health‑care providers, patients affected by COVID‑19 treatments

SR4.one_line: Senate resolution urges constitutional amendment to ban corporate campaign contributions and limit spending.
SR4.summary: The Senate resolution urges Congress to amend the U.S. Constitution to prohibit corporate campaign contributions and limit political spending, and requests that the amendment be sent to the states for ratification. It also directs the Secretary of State to forward the resolution to all federal legislators.
changes: Urges Congress to propose a constitutional amendment banning corporate campaign contributions and expenditures.

SR1.one_line: Adopts Senate rules governing officers, staff, committees, decorum, and legislative procedures.
SR1.summary: The Senate adopted a comprehensive set of rules governing its officers, staff, committees, decorum, voting, and procedures for nominations, confirmations, and legislative business. The rules establish the duties of the President, leaders, and staff, outline committee operations, set limits on debate, and detail the process for handling nominations and confirmations. No new programs or funds are created; the rules simply codify how the Senate will conduct itself.
changes: Adopts a full set of Senate rules covering officers, staff, committees, decorum, and voting procedures.
Defines the President’s authority over calendar, assignments, and certification of bills.
Establishes committee appointment, classification, and hearing notice requirements.
Sets limits on debate, motion precedence, and procedures for the Committee of the Whole.
Provides detailed rules for nominations, confirmations, and handling of Governor and House amendments.
Outlines absentee voting, call of the Senate, and override of veto procedures.
affected: Senate officers (President, President pro tempore, leaders, whips)
numbers: 3 legislative days notice for committee hearings
1 day for motion to change vote

SR18.one_line: Senate confirms Governor’s appointment of Amanda Knuteson to the Board of Environmental Review.
SR18.summary: The Senate approves and confirms the Governor’s appointment of Amanda Knuteson to the Board of Environmental Review. The resolution simply records the appointment and directs the Secretary of the Senate to forward the confirmation to the Secretary of State and the Governor. No new policy or funding is created.
changes: Confirms the Governor’s appointment of Amanda Knuteson to the Board of Environmental Review.

SR68.one_line: Montana Senate confirms governor’s appointment to the Massage Therapy Board.
SR68.summary: The Senate confirms the governor’s appointment of Chell Little to the Board of Massage Therapy, approving the appointment and directing the Secretary of the Senate to forward the resolution to the Secretary of State and the governor. The resolution has no other substantive effect.
changes: Confirms the governor’s appointment of Chell Little to the Board of Massage Therapy.
affected: Board of Massage Therapy member Chell Little

HB417.one_line: Mandates a non‑resident hunting impact study and hunter reporting before next‑year license purchase.
HB417.summary: HB 417 establishes the Montana Hunters First Act, requiring the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks to conduct a study of non‑resident hunting impacts and to publish a report by Dec 1 2026. It also mandates that every licensed hunter report all game taken before buying a new license for the next year.
changes: Creates the Montana Hunters First Act and codifies it in state law

Requires the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks to conduct a non‑resident hunting impact study covering deer and elk, using data such as hunter days, harvest, land use, population trends, and licensing
The study must be completed and a public report published by Dec 1 2026, including methods, findings, and issues for legislature and commission
Mandates that every person issued a hunting license must report all game taken to the Department before purchasing a new license for the following year
Gives the Department authority to rule on reporting systems, deadlines, and penalties
The study provision (Section 2) expires Dec 31 2026; the reporting requirement (Section 3) takes effect Mar 1 2026
Effective dates: all sections effective upon passage, except Section 3 which starts Mar 1 2026
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks staff

HB425.one_line: Peace officers liable for damages when illegally entering wrong property during suspect pursuit.
HB425.summary: The bill makes peace officers liable for property damage and injuries to occupants when they illegally enter the wrong dwelling or building while pursuing a suspect, or when a suspect takes occupants hostage during apprehension. It expands existing liability rules to cover these situations. The changes apply to all peace officers and law‑enforcement agencies in Montana.
changes: Peace officers become liable for all property damage and injuries to occupants when they enter a dwelling or building that is not the correct location during a suspect pursuit.
Liability also applies when a suspect takes occupants hostage during the apprehension or attempted apprehension.
The bill codifies these liability provisions as part of Title 27, Chapter 1, Part 7 of the Montana Code.
No new program, fund, or criminal offense is created; it simply expands existing liability rules.
affected: Occupants of residential or other buildings
Insurance carriers for officers and agencies

HB459.one_line: Adds two physician assistants to Montana’s 12‑member Board of Medical Examiners.
HB459.summary: HB 459 amends the Montana Board of Medical Examiners to add two physician assistants to its 12‑member roster, expanding the board’s professional diversity. The change does not alter duties, compensation, or other board functions.
changes: Amends §2‑15‑1731, MCA to list 12 board members instead of the previous composition.
Adds two physician assistants as separate board seats.
Retains existing seats for five MDs, one DO, one podiatrist, one nutritionist, one emergency‑care provider, and two public members.
Maintains the requirement that the five MDs cannot all be from the same county.
Preserves the board’s allocation to the department as prescribed in §2‑15‑121.
affected: Montana Department of Health and Human Services

HB507.one_line: Constitutional amendment to allow a 4 % sales tax for K‑12 education funding, requiring legislative and voter approval.
HB507.summary: HB 507 proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Montana to impose a 4 % statewide sales and use tax, with the net revenue earmarked for reducing property taxes that fund K‑12 education. The amendment requires a two‑thirds legislative vote to pass the proposal and a majority vote of the electorate in the November 2026 election to become effective on July 1, 2027.
changes: Amends Article VIII, § 16 of the Montana Constitution to permit a 4 % statewide sales/use tax whose net revenue may be used to lower property taxes for K‑12 schools, unless the legislature votes ¾‑majority to allocate it elsewhere.
Adds a new section requiring a two‑thirds affirmative roll‑call vote of the legislature to adopt the amendment.
Specifies that the amendment becomes effective July 1, 2027 if approved by voters.
Mandates that the amendment be placed on the November 2026 ballot with a simple yes/no vote.
No other procedural or fiscal provisions are added.

HB510.one_line: HB 510 modernizes Medicaid application, reporting, and local assistance offices in Montana.
HB510.summary: HB 510 revises Montana Medicaid to streamline applications, improve customer service, and expand local assistance offices. It mandates online and mobile‑first application tools, plain‑language notices, quarterly reporting, and a $3 million appropriation to reopen 10 public‑assistance offices by June 30 2026.
changes: 1. Requires the Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) to accept Medicaid applications, renewals, recertifications, and periodic reports online, by phone, and via mobile‑device uploads.
2. Authorizes text‑messaging and e‑mail communication with members who provide contact information, and requires the department to give an expected wait time and a callback option on its hotline.
3. Allows members whose coverage was terminated for procedural reasons to submit a renewal online or in print during a 90‑day reconsideration period.
4. Sets a target of at least 60 % ex‑parte renewal rate of the total Medicaid population by June 30 2026 and requires mobile‑first technology for all client‑facing systems by that date.
5. Mandates that all written application notices and forms be written in plain language and translated into the state’s five most common languages.
6. Requires quarterly reports to the Children, Families, Health, and Human Services Interim Committee on a detailed set of service‑delivery metrics.

7. Amends § 53‑2‑301, MCA, to require DPHHS to establish one or more local offices of public assistance in each county (or combine counties as needed) and to reopen 10 offices by June 30 2026, with reopening decisions based on call volume, distance, disenrollment rates, and reenrollment patterns.
8. Provides a $3 million biennial appropriation from the general fund for implementing the new public‑assistance office requirements.
affected: Montana residents who use the Medicaid hotline

HB519.one_line: HB 519 ends the preference‑point system for nonresident big‑game licenses and repeals land‑owner preference law.
HB519.summary: HB 519 eliminates the nonresident preference point system for Class B‑10 and B‑11 big‑game combination licenses, restoring the standard lottery drawing. It also repeals the existing land‑owner preference statute (87‑2‑714).
changes: Replaces the preference‑point lottery with a standard lottery for nonresident B‑10 and B‑11 licenses.
A nonresident may no longer purchase preference points to gain priority in the drawing.
The 75/25 split between preference‑point holders and non‑point holders is removed.
Section 87‑2‑714, which allowed landowners to give preference to certain nonresident hunters, is repealed.
The act contains no new fees or programs beyond the existing lottery framework.
The act takes effect on March 1 2026.
affected: Nonresident hunters seeking B‑10 or B‑11 licenses
Landowners who previously could give preference to nonresident hunters

HB529.one_line: Revisions streamline Montana’s lien‑enforcement process, eliminating summons and tightening filing and hearing timelines.
HB529.summary: HB 529 revises Montana’s lien‑enforcement law to streamline the process for filing a lien action, eliminate the need for a summons, and clarify filing locations and hearing timelines. It also updates the order‑to‑show‑cause rules and the sheriff’s sale procedure for lien‑covered property.
changes: Amends §71‑3‑1203 to allow a lienor to file a lien enforcement action in the county where the contract was entered, the owner lived, or the property is located.
Removes the requirement to issue or serve a summons; the order to show cause serves as the notice of action.
Specifies that an affidavit (or for non‑possessory special liens, a supporting document and statement of charges) must be filed with the court.
Sets a 20‑working‑day maximum between issuance of the order to show cause and the hearing date.
Requires the sheriff to serve the owner by certified mail and first‑class mail at least 5 days before the hearing and to sell the property at public auction to satisfy the lien.
Outlines the distribution of sale proceeds: first to the lien, then to other lienholders in order of precedence, with any remainder to the owner.

HB559.one_line: HB 559 designates summer river stretches as commercial‑fishing‑free for two days per week with public input and rulemaking deadlines.
HB559.summary: HB 559 establishes a rule‑making process to designate specific stretches of Montana’s rivers as commercial fishing, guiding, and outfitting‑free for two days each week during the summer. The bill requires the Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks to identify these stretches, solicit public input, and submit recommendations to the commission by 2027, with rules to be adopted by 2026.
changes: 1. Requires the department to identify river stretches that will be closed to commercial fishing, guiding, and outfitting for two days per week between the third Saturday in May and Labor Day.
2. The closed days must include at least one Saturday and are limited to the specified rivers listed in the bill.
3. The department must publish public notices and hold hearings or collaborative processes before finalizing the stretches.
4. Recommendations must be submitted to the commission no later than October 1 2027; the commission has six months to adopt, modify, or reject each recommendation.
5. Rules implementing the closed‑day designations must be adopted by May 15 2026.
6. The provisions are codified as part of Title 87, chapter 3, part 1 of the Montana Code.
affected: Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks
numbers: third Saturday of May to Labor Day

HB570.one_line: State‑funded airports must provide free services to light aircraft under defined limits.
HB570.summary: The bill requires any airport that receives state money to give light aircraft free landing, taxiing, parking (up to 7 days), and passenger/crew access through existing security fencing. No fees may be charged unless explicitly agreed to in advance. It defines light aircraft as ≤12,500 lb gross weight under 14‑part 91.
changes: State‑funded airports must allow free landings, taxiing, and up to 7‑day tie‑down parking for light aircraft.
Airports must provide passenger/crew access through existing security fencing with vehicle parking for at least four vehicles.
No landing, taxiing, parking, or security fees may be charged unless the owner/operator/passenger agrees in advance and the fee is clearly noticed.
The definition of “light aircraft” is set to aircraft ≤12,500 lb gross weight under 14‑part 91.
The provision is codified as part of Title 67, chapter 1, part 1.
affected: Passengers and aircrew of light aircraft

HB596.one_line: Amends Class D motor‑carrier rules to exempt irregular garbage services from certificate requirements.
HB596.summary: The bill amends Montana’s Class D motor‑carrier rules to clarify that only carriers that regularly haul garbage need a Class D certificate.  One‑time, irregular garbage‑cleanup services may operate without the certificate, provided they use non‑commercial‑driver‑license vehicles.  No new program or funding is created.
changes: Amends §69‑12‑314 to state that a Class D carrier must actually transport garbage on a regular basis to qualify for a certificate.
Adds a new subsection allowing a person or entity that provides garbage‑cleanup and transportation on an irregular, one‑time basis to operate without a Class D certificate.
Specifies that such irregular services may not use vehicles that require a commercial driver’s license or other special driver’s license.
Leaves all other requirements of §69‑12‑314 unchanged.
No new fees, funds, or enforcement mechanisms are introduced.
affected: Vehicle owners used for irregular garbage transport

HB608.one_line: Expands cannabis regulatory authority to all THC products with new definitions and rule‑making powers.
HB608.summary: The bill expands the Cannabis Control Division’s authority to regulate all THC‑containing products, adding detailed definitions, rule‑making powers, and licensing requirements. It amends existing statutes to clarify what constitutes a THC product, a medical cardholder, and a marijuana business, and it gives the department broad regulatory and fee‑setting authority.
changes: Expands the Cannabis Control Division’s regulatory scope to all THC products, including testing, licensing, distribution, sale, and taxation
Amends §16‑12‑102 to define terms such as “adult‑use dispensary,” “consumer,” “affiliate,” and “beneficial owner”
Amends §16‑12‑112 to grant the department rule‑making authority over licensing procedures, security, labeling, testing, advertising, and fee setting
Provides codification instructions to incorporate the new section into Title 16, Chapter 12, Part 1
Sets the act’s effective date to passage and approval
affected: Cannabis licensees (cultivators, manufacturers, dispensaries, transporters, testing labs)
Department of Revenue staff and regulators

HB774.one_line: Ensures parity for non‑opioid pain drugs in Medicaid and commercial plans, with new transparency and regulatory clarifications.
HB774.summary: HB 774 requires Medicaid and commercial insurers in Montana to give non‑opioid pain drugs the same coverage and cost‑sharing treatment as opioids, preventing formulary or utilization‑management practices that disadvantage non‑opioids. It also amends several insurance‑law sections to clarify how health‑maintenance organizations and self‑funded plans are regulated and to improve transparency of drug‑benefit information.
changes: Mandates that Medicaid’s formulary and preferred‑drug list cannot place non‑opioid pain drugs at a disadvantage relative to opioids or narcotics.
Requires the same parity for commercial insurance plans issued or renewed in Montana, including self‑funded employee plans, unless preempted by federal law.
Provides an exception process for prescribers to override restrictive coverage of a non‑opioid if the provider deems it appropriate.
Amends insurance‑law sections (33‑31‑111, 33‑32‑106, 33‑35‑306, 53‑6‑1010) to clarify HMO regulation, disclosure of utilization‑review plans, and drug‑benefit transparency.
Adds codification instructions to integrate the new parity provisions into existing statutes.
Extends consumer representation and objective‑data requirements to formulary committees under the new Medicaid specifications.

HB820.one_line: Free parking for veteran and National Guard faculty, staff, and students at Montana universities.
HB820.summary: The bill requires Montana university campuses to waive parking fees for veterans and Montana National Guard members who are faculty, staff, or students, and gives each campus president authority to give them priority when issuing permits. Proof of service is required, and the rule is codified in the state’s higher‑education statutes.
changes: Regents cannot charge parking fees to veteran or National Guard faculty, staff, or students at any Montana University System unit.
Campus presidents must give priority to these individuals when issuing on‑campus parking permits.
Eligible individuals must present proof of service to the parking office.
Presidents may establish additional rules governing the free permits.
affected: Montana National Guard faculty, staff, and students

HB875.one_line: Amends contract law to give resident bidders preference, with performance exceptions, and appropriates $500 for educational materials.
HB875.summary: The bill amends Montana’s public‑contract law to allow resident bidders a preference equal to that of any reciprocal state, but only if the lowest bidder meets performance standards. It also creates a $500 appropriation for educational outreach. The changes apply to construction, repair, and public‑works contracts.
changes: Amends §18‑1‑102 to require a resident bidder to receive a preference equal to that of any reciprocal state or country when the lowest bidder is non‑resident.
Adds a performance‑based exception: the preference is denied if the lowest bidder has no prior performance, has requested more than two extensions, or failed warranty work.
Allows a contract awarded to the lowest bidder to be canceled and reassigned to the second‑lowest bidder if any of the above exceptions apply.
Appropriates $500 from the general fund for the biennium beginning July 1 2025 to update educational materials about the new requirements.
The bill does not create a new program or offense; it merely amends existing contract law and provides a small appropriation.

HB865.one_line: HB 865 expands mill‑levy limits, creates a reserve account, and tightens new‑property calculations.
HB865.summary: HB 865 revises Montana’s property‑tax rules, adding a new “large‑taxpayer reserve account” for cities and counties, expanding the ability to exceed mill‑levy limits with voter approval, and tightening how new taxable property is counted and how inflation is factored into levy calculations.
changes: Cities, counties, and consolidated city‑counties may create a large‑taxpayer reserve account and deposit 10 % of revenue from newly taxable property (excluding class 4) each year
Deposits can be used to pay capital‑bond debt, reduce levies for up to 10 years, attract industry, provide employment incentives, or fund new‑development infrastructure
Funds in the account must remain until a large taxpayer permanently ceases operations or its taxable value drops 25 % or more
The state’s statutory maximum mill levy is increased to the amount needed to cover last year’s assessed taxes plus ½ the average inflation rate of the prior three years, capped at 4 %
Municipalities may exceed the statutory mill‑levy limit only if a resolution is passed and a majority of voters approve the additional levy in an election

The calculation of newly taxable property now includes specific percentages for certain classes and abatement categories, and the reserve‑account deposit requirement gives a 50 % or 40 % weighting depending on whether the account is used
The bill amends sections 7‑6‑4431 and 15‑10‑420 to implement these changes and clarifies exclusions and carry‑forward rules
affected: City, county, and consolidated city‑county governing bodies
Voters in municipalities that may be asked to approve additional levies
Property owners subject to new taxable‑property calculations
numbers: ½ average inflation of prior 3 years

HB934.one_line: HB 934 shifts assisted‑living services to a lower‑cost Medicaid option and sets new payment rules and reporting.
HB934.summary: HB 934 creates a new Medicaid‑covered assisted‑living payment formula, shifts services from the Big Sky Waiver to the Community First Choice Option program, and requires quarterly reporting and a $56,000 appropriation to implement the changes. The act also establishes a contingency clause that voids the transfer if the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services deny the necessary waiver.
changes: Introduces a new room‑and‑board payment formula for assisted‑living services under Medicaid, tied to SSI or gross income minus a $200 personal‑needs allowance.

Directs the Department of Public Health and Human Services to apply for a waiver and state‑plan amendment by Jan 1 2026 to move assisted‑living services from the Big Sky Waiver to the Community First Choice Option program.
Mandates that any savings from the transfer be retained in the Big Sky Waiver program to serve waiting‑list individuals.
Requires quarterly reports (starting 2027 biennium) to the Health and Human Services Budget Committee on service numbers, waiting lists, per‑capita costs, and assisted‑living enrollment.
Appropriates $56,000 for FY ending June 30 2026 to hire a staff person to draft the waiver, update rules, and review policies.
Includes a contingent‑voidness provision: if CMS denies the waiver, the transfer provisions are voided.
affected: Montana Medicaid beneficiaries in assisted‑living facilities
Department of Public Health and Human Services
Health and Human Services Budget Committee
Individuals on the Big Sky Waiver waiting list
numbers: 50% state general fund, 50% federal special revenue fund

HB909.one_line: Creates a Technology Interim Committee and funds it for IT oversight.
HB909.summary: HB 909 creates a new Technology Interim Committee, amends several statutes to give it oversight over state IT projects, and provides funding for the committee and a research analyst. It also redefines the list of interim committees and adds procedural rules for the Legislative Council.
changes: Establishes a Technology Interim Committee with rule‑review, draft‑legislation review, program‑evaluation, and monitoring duties for the Division of the Department of Administration that implements the Montana Information Technology Act.
The committee must review long‑range IT appropriations, legislation, and best‑practice standards, and coordinate with the Legislative Finance Committee.
Section 2 amends § 2‑17‑526 to require the Office of Budget and Program Planning to prepare a statewide IT project budget summary, including major purchases, cost estimates, and funding sources.
Section 3 amends § 5‑5‑202 to list the Technology Committee among the legislature’s interim committees and sets jurisdiction‑referral procedures.
Section 4 amends § 5‑5‑228 to clarify the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee’s duties (not directly affecting the new committee).
Section 5 amends § 5‑11‑105 to give the Legislative Council additional procedural powers over interim committees, including setting schedules and deadlines.
Section 6 appropriates $84,300 for committee member compensation and $243,290 to hire a research analyst for the Technology Committee.
Section 8 sets the act’s effective date to July 1 2025.

SB32.one_line: Rewrites Montana property‑tax classes, rates, and local levy limits, adding new exemptions for renewable‑energy and data‑center projects.
SB32.summary: SB 32 revises Montana’s property‑tax framework, redefining many property classes, adjusting tax rates, and expanding local mill‑levy authority. The bill also adds new tax‑exemption rules for renewable‑energy and data‑center projects and clarifies how newly taxable property is counted for levy calculations.
changes: Rewrites Sections 15‑6‑132 through 15‑6‑163 to redefine property classes (e.g., metal‑mine income, agricultural land, residential, commercial, renewable‑energy, data‑center, green‑hydrogen, etc.) and their taxable percentages, including new exemptions and phased‑in rates for certain classes.
Adds detailed rules for local governments to levy mills equal to the 2025 mill levy plus an inflation adjustment, with carry‑over authority for unused mill capacity.

Introduces new tax‑exemption and abatement provisions for fiber‑optic cable, renewable‑energy facilities, data centers, and green‑hydrogen projects, including certification requirements and recapture procedures.

Revises the calculation of “newly taxable property” for levy purposes, expanding the definition to include annexation, construction, transfer, subdivision, and changes in tax‑increment financing districts.
Specifies that the act applies to property‑tax years beginning after December 31 2025.
No new criminal offenses or state‑funds are created; the bill amends existing statutes.
affected: property owners in classes 2‑18 (e.g., metal‑mine operators, farmers, residential and commercial real‑estate owners, renewable‑energy developers, data‑center operators, green‑hydrogen producers), local governments, and the Montana Department of Revenue and Environmental Quality
numbers: inflation adjustment (½ average rate of inflation for prior 3 years)
new tax‑exempt periods (5 years for fiber‑optic, 10 years for certain renewable‑energy projects)
$25 million investment threshold for green‑hydrogen tax rate
$1.5 million threshold for residential property rate increase

session.headline: Montana’s Twenty‑Twenty‑Five Legislative Session Focuses on Regulation and Funding
session.overview: The 69th Montana Legislature numbered 1759 bills. 802 became law, 173 resolutions were adopted, 741 failed, 19 were vetoed and 23 were withdrawn. Counting bills only (not resolutions), Republican-sponsored bills were enacted at 683 of 1179 (57%) and Democratic-sponsored bills at 119 of 337 (35%). The largest groups of new laws were in Business, Labor & Professions (149), Criminal Justice & Courts (112), Health Care & Human Services (100), Natural Resources, Energy & Environment (93). 203 new laws create a program, fund, office, licence or crime. The session produced a mix of regulatory rollbacks, new licensing frameworks, and expanded public‑service funding that reflects a balance between business interests and community protections.  A significant portion of the enacted bills addressed consumer protection, criminal justice accountability, and education investment while also expanding natural‑resource financing and public‑safety capabilities.  The legislature’s priorities appear to center on tightening oversight in high‑profile industries, strengthening enforcement in the criminal‑justice system, and investing in long‑term infrastructure and workforce development.  At the same time, the session saw a number of vetoed proposals that would have broadened state‑wide programs or altered existing funding formulas, indicating a cautious approach to large‑scale policy shifts.

themes.theme: Regulatory rollbacks and expansions in business and communications
themes.narrative: The legislature rolled back rate regulation for public utilities with HB45, removing the universal service fund and exempting internet‑enabled services from oversight.  It expanded licensing in the alcohol industry through HB86, creating a new distributor license and revising beer‑and‑wine wholesaling rules, while HB211 added a third‑party delivery license to the regulatory framework.  Business licensing was further tightened with HB239, which replaced registration with a licensing program for construction contractors and home inspectors.  The state also consolidated health‑care licensing boards in HB438, creating a single board effective next year.  These measures collectively shift regulatory authority toward market mechanisms while establishing new oversight structures for emerging industries.

themes.theme: Strengthening consumer protection and licensing across multiple sectors
themes.narrative: Consumer protection was expanded with HB114, adding disclosure and anti‑deceptive advertising requirements for insurance and financial planning.  HB137 standardized salesperson and adviser fees statewide, while HB123 revised self‑pour rules to allow controlled self‑pouring and electronic dispensing of beer and wine.  The alcohol licensing framework was broadened by HB211, creating a third‑party delivery license that sets strict rules for retailers and drivers.  HB86 also introduced new distributor licensing requirements for the beer‑and‑wine industry, ensuring consistent oversight across the supply chain.  Together these bills reinforce consumer safeguards while modernizing licensing for evolving market practices.

themes.theme: Expanding criminal justice accountability and penalties
themes.narrative: The session saw a series of reforms that tightened penalties for violent and sexual offenses, such as HB44, which added harsher penalties for tampering that hinders homicide death‑determination.  HB66 adopted federal military laws for the National Guard, while HB82 created a new grooming offense and expanded child‑porn statutes.  The legislature also reorganized the public defender system with HB102, adding a conflict division and expanding training duties.  HB267 introduced a new DUI homicide crime, tightening license‑suspension rules, and HB344 added a drug‑based DUI offense to broaden criminal liability.  These measures collectively increase accountability within the criminal‑justice system and expand the range of offenses subject to prosecution.

themes.theme: Investing in education funding and early literacy
themes.narrative: Education funding was increased with HB15, which raised school‑funding formulas for inflation and took effect July 1, 2025.  HB24 tightened kindergarten hour rules and expanded ANB counting, while HB28 set a 90‑day approval window for charter schools.  HB251 tightened charter‑school rules, limited costs, and expanded funding options to prioritize personalized learning.  Early‑literacy interventions were expanded through HB338 and HB628, and HB567 rewarded county‑wide collaboration with a 50 % educator‑payment boost.  HB606 modernized reorganization rules, added superintendent duties, and granted building‑reserve levy authority for school districts, creating a more robust framework for educational governance.

themes.theme: Enhancing natural resource management and renewable financing
themes.narrative: The legislature expanded renewable‑resource financing with HB6 and HB7, creating grant and loan programs for water, irrigation, reclamation, and storage projects that allocate millions in appropriations.  HB8 increased the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation’s borrowing authority through coal‑severance bonds, requiring supermajority approval for state debt.  HB31 imposed bond rules and a decommissioning lien on wind and solar plants, while HB47 rewrote the building‑energy program, cutting bond authority and setting a 3 % interest cap.  HB368 created a Colstrip water‑infrastructure account and reallocated coal severance‑tax revenue to support water projects.  These measures collectively strengthen financial tools for renewable energy and natural‑resource stewardship.

themes.theme: Broadening public safety and emergency response capabilities
themes.narrative: Public‑safety measures were expanded with HB72, which removed the 15‑day cap on double pay for enlisted militia on state duty.  HB75 revised officer training timelines and clarified basic‑course requirements, while HB128 barred wrongful termination of volunteer emergency‑service employees after probation.  HB257 added broadband to the list of critical infrastructure and increased penalties for trespassing or damage.  HB745 mandated fingerprint‑based background checks for anyone with unsupervised student contact and added criminal‑history checks to teacher licensure.  SB362 allowed fire chiefs to approve former felons as firefighters under written physical exam requirements, broadening workforce options for emergency services.

biggest_fiscal_moves.why: The bill creates trust contributions and deletion rights for monetized family videos, generating a new revenue stream that supports child‑care programs.
By eliminating public‑service‑commission rate regulation and the universal service fund, the bill reduces regulatory costs for utilities while freeing up funds for other priorities.
The bill consolidates school‑facility funding and boosts aid, replacing an old natural‑resource payment with a more efficient allocation of resources to education.
The bill bars Montana content providers from distributing child sexual abuse material and creates civil remedies for victims, generating revenue through enforcement fees.
The bill establishes a petition‑based reconciliation payment system and new rules for territory transfers, creating a new revenue source for state programs.
The bill creates a new distributor license and overhauls beer‑and‑wine wholesaling rules, generating licensing fees that support state revenue.
The bill revises motor‑vehicle statutes for clarity, consolidates definitions, and updates fees and penalties, creating a more predictable revenue stream from vehicle licensing.
The bill expands the film‑tax‑credit program, adds new credit categories, creates a workforce‑training account, and allows credit resale for a fee, generating additional tax‑credit revenue.
The bill reallocates marijuana tax revenue to wildlife, health, and law‑enforcement accounts, creating a new source of funding for public services.
The bill appropriates coal‑endowment funds for water, bridge, emergency, and planning grants, ensuring targeted investment in critical infrastructure.

notable_new_programs_or_crimes.what: Reorganizes the public defender system, adds a conflict division, and expands reporting and training duties.
Adopts the Physician Assistant Compact, creates a commission, and mandates criminal background checks for PA licensure.
Expands funding incentives, adds housing‑cost authority, and restores full advanced‑opportunity aid.
Creates a new DUI homicide crime, tightens penalties, and expands license‑suspension rules.
Adds a drug‑based DUI offense, tightens penalties, and expands rehabilitation and license‑suspension rules for all drivers.
Mandates trust contributions and deletion rights for monetized family videos, creating a new revenue stream for child‑care programs.

session.what_failed_or_was_vetoed: The session ended with nineteen bills that were vetoed, covering a range of proposals from expanding teacher‑training programs to broadening child‑care scholarship eligibility.  These vetoed measures would have introduced new statewide programs or altered existing funding formulas, such as a state‑wide mentor program for teachers, an expanded child‑care scholarship for workers, and a new high‑quality instructional materials subsidy.  Other vetoed bills aimed to modify natural‑resource regulations, adjust retirement eligibility for law enforcement, and change the structure of public‑service licensing.  The legislature also rejected proposals that would have broadened state‑wide data collection on school funding, adjusted the school‑funding inflation formula, and expanded PTSD coverage for first responders.  The vetoes reflect a cautious approach to large‑scale policy changes, leaving many proposed programs and reforms pending further debate.
session.caveats: Automated summaries can miss contextual nuances and may not fully capture the legislative intent behind each bill.  They rely on available data and may overlook informal debates or procedural details that influence final outcomes.  Readers should consult official legislative documents for complete information.
